_childDocuments_.review: Truly exceptional game. The lack of attention Lamplighters League gets is criminal. This is one of those rare games which has multiple systems which all reinforce each other and result in a game vastly greater than the sum of its parts. You know how most games are better played in Iron Man mode, but most people can't bring themselves to do it? Lamplighter's doesn't have that problem. When I goof up while taking the stealthy approach, the resulting combat doesn't feel like a punishment, instead it's an exciting challenge. When you successfully stealth a mission, you feel like a master spy, outwitting overwhelming odds. When you fail the stealth and get caught, the result is typically a combat against apparently-overwhelming odds, but where you actually have all the tools you need to succeed, but just barely. When you win, you feel like a tactical genius. Either way, it feels great!The combat system does a good job rewarding stealthy approaches, and the stealth system does a good job keeping the combat fresh. The strategic-level progression is well-tuned - I have not yet encountered the problem most games like this have where once you get past the early game your party has essentially infinite resources and steamrolls the opposition. Thus far, it's stayed challenging throughout. I think folks complain about the strategic-level progression because they are so used to the alternative a game that doesn't get easy can feel really punishing.Characters are well-thought-out and unique, and don't feel like cookie-cutter units or slight reflavorings of different classes. Changing up your team radically changes how you play. The variety of characters and the dual level up systems provide a decent variety of options for customizing your party without compromising the uniqueness of the individual characters. The combo-potential is extraordinary, and a clever player can find all sorts of fun interactions between the different character abilities. Combat is challenging enough that applying them makes you feel clever, not like a cheater.I haven't had much in the way of technical issues, just some minor bugs. The horror stories seem to mostly come from X-Box.I've been playing computer games for 30 years, I don't get excited about a new game very often, but this one is truly excellent. Do yourself a favor and check it out!
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I adore the setting and the cinematic aesthetic quality that this game has. Unfortunately, it falls short in many areas that are very important for Turn-Based Tactics games. Too many in fact that it's impossible to ignore. I've never played XCOM so I can't make that kind of apples-to-apples comparison, but I can at least make some observations based on the few tactics games that I've played.First off, panning to the edges of your screen to scout out the map feels clunky. Even on recon mode, you hit these walls that are meant to tell you that an area is non-traversable, but it feels like the game wants you to blindly feel your way around the invisible walls of the map when all you really want is to get a lay of the land. Imagine trying to get a bird's eye view of a labyrinth but only being able to observe 1 hallway at a time and hitting a wall when you try to scan surrounding areas. It makes me wonder why panning/free cam is even a thing if it doesn't feel free at all. I would have thought the fog of war was enough to bring balance to that feature but they really added a layer of annoyance on top of what was already appropriate.Speaking of Recon Mode, it's a pain in the ass to observe certain objects. As far as I can tell, investigation points aren't easy to spot unless you hover very close to them. Lore books and enemies are okay, but I don't want to scan every inch of a map just for a small bit of context that may or may not contribute anything to the overall lore. A better indicator similar to the way lore books shine would have been a good way to point those in recon mode to fun flavor text. As far as I'm concerned, if something is inconsequential (lore-wise) and too annoying to find, then it's not worth looking for it.The Motion Blur is horrible. I typically play through my games with Motion Blur and DOF, but those games also have more precise setting controls for camera movement. I could not find a way to just have a birds-eye view of the enemy units performing their attacks without the camera shaking violently and blurring like there's no tomorrow moving from 1 unit that's on one end of the screen to the other. This is even worse with Action Cam turned on (even only some of the time) so I had to disable that feature completely. As previously mentioned, a static bird's-eye view to observe all pieces as they move would have fixed this. Some games have fixed this issue by allowing moves to auto-complete.To a lesser extent, there are some small bugs/issues here and there that I encountered. Sometimes the enemy's action would not complete. Incapacitated enemies also seem to get thrown around like a ragdoll when hitting a completely unrelated unit. The achievement for defeating Lady Nicastro in the tutorial mission is also not working completely as intended (there's a Reddit thread on it).Lastly, I don't know how they picked out which character to turn into DLC. I totally think that Nocturne belongs to the Base Agent cast just as much as anyone not named Eddie, Ingrid, and Lateef. It seems like such a roll-the-dice decision that it wouldn't have mattered which one of them became DLC. As far as I'm concerned, she contributes just as much to the lore as every other expedition recruit. I don't believe any of these characters should be locked behind DLC and that was an unsavory move that seems to only subtract from the base game.I really wanted to love this game. I completed everything it had to offer after putting roughly 55 hours in. Unfortunately, it did not live up to the hype and the price tag. I hope another game with this aesthetic comes along because the proof of concept is definitely there. It's just that the game did not have enough polish that you'd expect from a game backed by this publisher.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: This could have been a good game, but it really is not. The developer has a good history with similar types of games in the shadow run universe, and one would have assumed that this would also have worked in a pulp action novel setting. But it does not.The primary gameplay loop is parts repetitive, parts clunky and parts plain tedious. You run your team of agents through the same set pieces repeatedly to gather worthless resources or to reduce the difficulty of the three main missions you must run until you get to the final.The agents are not balanced against one another. You quickly establish your A team and maybe one backup, and you will be using them over and over again. Which is a shame, because on paper these could be interesting characters. You lack the resources to properly develop multiple, and with some being clearly superior to others, why would you bother.The characters sadly do not add much to the story. The story does not add much to the story. The game would like you to be invested in the struggle against unsurmountable odds, but what it boils down to is, that you all sit in a mansion on an island and you go out on a number of fetch-quests to unlock the entrance to the big shiny tower and stop the bad guys from completing their respective apocalypse scenario.Which also happens to be one of the bigger plot holes for me. The three antagonists have mutually exclusive goals. They cannot achieve their goal without actively denying it their allies theirs. Why would they be willing to work together? They have no competition, save the rag tag band of mercenaries and it is established early on, that they are not the sort of people to let anyone stand in their way. Maybe that’s a staple of such stories, but I found it off putting. The gameplay is separated into real time sneaking and scouting parts and the turn-based combat sections.I found the latter to be entertaining, up to a certain point. There is little enemy variety. Apart from a few monsters that show up over the course of the game, you are fighting the gas mask mook brigade, all the way to the end.The enemies increase in numbers, but you usually quickly take care of that. What makes it a grind are the frequent reinforcement points, that needlessly stretch these fights out. First, they spawn the same enemies, that you just put into the ground, and second they do so on a timer. You know exactly when they arrive, from which point. Which makes it super easy to dispatch them, but really you are taking four to five extra turns to wait for these poor saps to show up, so you can mow them down in one turn. The real time sneaking parts are necessary I suppose. You do need to explore the area, but it's done in such a clunky fashion, that I stopped lining up everything perfectly after the third or fourth encounter. You hide your guys behind one of the many, many chest-high obstacles littered around. Which you must do, one by one. First you ungroup the character. Then you move them into position. And then you can do so for the next. Which does not sound so bad, but it cannot be done in parallel. One at a time. And after a while this loses its charm, because after you fire your first shot enemies’ scramble. And if that happens all your careful positioning may have lost its edge. A bit frustrating.Overall, this could have been an interesting game. The set pieces do look interesting. But they are used in the same configuration repeatedly. Even in the special main missions. The character artwork has its charm, but the characters are cardboard cutouts. The story is nonexistent. The gameplay gets stale very quickly. For those that are wondering. I did manage to complete the game on standard difficulty. I wanted to see if there was more to it, than the poor first impression I got in the first two hours. Did not improve. Cannot recommend. Spend your money and time on something else.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:Art DesignMusicGreat Voice ActingGeneral aesthetic polishUnique blend of XCOM + stealth that works surprisingly well and doesn't fall apart as quickly as it should on paperCONS:Lategame difficulty scaling is terrible and breaks the flow of the gamePerformance is atrociousAn obvious dominant strategy emerges and is essentially forced onto you by mission designThe difference in power levels between characters is enormousAn entire character is behind a paywallOVERALL: 6/10This is very much a "mixed" review for a lot of reasons, I wish there was more nuance on the recommended scale. The major issues with the game are with the performance and how difficulty is scaled into the lategame, and both of these things hold back the game enormously and are very difficult to solve for different reasons.First, performance is simply not good. This game is remarkably hard to run at playable framerates on anything but the finest graphics cards; with my 1070ti my frames peak at 50 and generally hover in the mid-30s on basically minimum settings. I don't know how much can be done on this front at this point. It's annoying, and if you have the "standard" setup with a 1060 and a decent processor this game will be basically unplayable on minimum settings, which is always a shame.The difficulty scaling is an issue that kinda cuts down to the core of the game, on the other hand. In the lategame, missions are made harder by simultaneously clumping more enemies together and making a higher proportion of enemies immune to stealth takedowns. There was a mission I played recently where a group of 8 and another group of 4 enemies, all immune to stealth kills, were clumped up in one area. Fighting them in combat without taking at least one stress break (an instant reset condition due to an absurdly harsh post-mission punishment) would be near-impossible, yet none of the enemies can be taken down out of combat either. This leads to the style of gameplay that will define the late stage of every campaign, and the biggest single problem with the game: luring enemies across the map until they're separated from their group, then ganging up on them. This is simultaneously extremely tedious due to a total lack of useful tools for luring enemies (meaning you run into their detection circle and stay around the edge of their vision to repeatedly cause them to chase you), extremely punishing since getting fully detected by this enemy will trigger combat with the entire area, and totally unrewarding once you do kill them. But if you've played the game you'll know this is the only viable way to clear many later missions, and this is a really serious problem. It shouldn't be possible to do, yet it's the also only way to approach a lot of late encounters. Until this issue is addressed entirely this game can never break the 6/10 mark for me.This is a stealth game with combat as a failure condition, but it forces you to do more and more combat the further you get if you don't want to cheese everything using luring tactics. This loop just doesn't work for me, and I don't think it'll work for you either. Just to clarify, I love turn-based tactical combat; I'm a fire emblem and XCOM nerd and love Shadowrun as well, but this game doesn't have any of the things that make those games' combat systems so great, and long battles are an absolute slog due to the lack of depth.To get deeper into the combat, there are two characters who can essentially infinitely gain action points if certain conditions are met, and these characters are extremely strong in comparison to the rest of the cast. One of them can also exploit this to near-infinitely chain their signature/ultimate ability, and successfully doing this is by far the best way to deal with combat against large groups, to the point where this character, Celestine, is essentially indispensable for every lategame mission.Character progression is designed in such a way that greatly rewards simply sticking to 3 main agents and 1 supplementary (since some mission types allow 4 characters and most allow 3). The experience cost of powerful abilities ramps up pretty drastically and those lategame abilities are still a much better use than taking a bunch of low-level stuff on a peripheral character. There's critically no way to assess a mission and its goals beforehand to tell which agents you should ideally bring, since this more depends on the spread of enemy types and the nominal objective means very little on this front. So the strategy that makes the most sense is to pump up 3-4 characters to max as soon as possible and never deploying any characters outside your main team. The fact that the game basically screams that this is the intended way to play, however, doesn't prevent them from having one of the most bizarrely punishing mechanics with no workaround.When an agent or enemy is missed by an attack and hit by certain abilities, they will gain Stress points. When this bar is filled, for the next 2 turns the character will be reduced to 1 Action Point instead of 2, and will be vulnerable to an execution, and instant kill. As far as I know the enemies are not capable of using execution moves, but even if they were and that was the only punishment for being stress broken, it would be many times less punishing than the current setup. A character being downed in combat can be stabilized, returning them to half health, and this can be done up to 3 times in a mission. The post-mission cost is that if the agent enters another mission the next week they can only be revived twice when downed, but this can be totally circumvented by spending an abundant medicine currency that has no other uses. Early on it can matter, but lategame there's never a reason to worry about agents going down. After being stress broken a single time, however, there is a 3-week crippling debuff applied to the character and these are so harsh that the character must sit out for that entire time. There is no mechanic for healing this or making the debuffs less severe, meaning a stress break is esentially infinitely worse than allowing that agent to be downed, and you should instantly reset to your last save if it happens. A unique character is locked behind a paywall at launch, which is just silly and totally predatory in my opinion, but I'm a person who thinks that about any paid DLC so take that with a grain of salt. My playthrough did not include this character so they may significantly affect the balance of the cast as discussed previously.There are some baffling design decisions that hold this game extremely far back from its potential, and I hope that these will be addressed because the core game here really is great. But until some massive balance changes come out, don't pick this game up unless there's a large sale, because the lategame is a total disaster currently. Some of the problems mentioned suddenly appear out of nowhere as the game progresses and some mechanics randomly disappear due to bizarre balancing, when these things would be on more of a sliding scale if they were implemented better.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a blast. X-Com-style tactical combat and light base/upgrade management by way of Shadowrun: Hong Kong, 30s adventure serials, Indiana Jones, Call of C'thulu, and with a dash of Overwatch character design. Music is jazzy, smooth, bouncing, and dramatic in all the right places. Combat is fun.That said, it has quite a few shortcomings that seem mostly addressable in future patches. Semi-frequent graphical glitches and stuttering are annoying, but mostly fine on my mid-range machine. Game difficulty seems inconsistent, and while I'm not a personal fan of "Doomsday Clock"-style mechanics, this game's version of it would benefit from clearer tooltips and UI clues to make it more graspable. There's a card mechanic, which seems compulsory in a 2020s video game but something that I continue to find somewhat inexplicable. Skill points are shared by the entire party so agents don't get left behind, but since skill points are directly tied to health/damage upgrades, you in practice end up mostly putting your points in your 3 or 4 favorite characters since the difficulty steadily rises and you don't want someone sitting out missions for taking an injury.Characters are charming and their personality shines through...voice acting is mostly good, but the direction is a little iffy; there are lots of lines where the voices have clearly put the emphasis on the wrong word or they've just misinterpreted the line and said it differently than the text of the conversation implies. (e.g., a non-game related example would be if a character asked, 'Your place or mine?' and the character responded 'Let's do your PLACE', instead of 'Let's do YOUR place.' It's a nitpicky detail but it happens often enough that it stands out).The lack of RPG elements is somewhat disappointing, given how wonderfully they were executed in the Shadowrun trilogy.  Things like character creation, dialogue trees/checks, and interacting with the environment outside of the game's core loop (tactical stealth--> tactical combat--> repeat) are conspicuously absent. It would have been really cool to see more of this 30s adventure serial / supernatural film noir world outside of enemy compounds and a few cutscenes, but no points deducted for that since the game never really promised these elements in the first place. I think I was mentally stuck in the Shadowrun: Hong Kong expectation zone.All in all, a fun, slightly messy labor of clear love. If you like tactical combat, it's deep enough to warrant a look.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I don't understand why this game sold so poorly. The mix of real-time exploration, timing-based real-time and turn-based mode is brilliant.The fresh setting, good AI of the opponents, nice story, motivating development of the likeable group, The Lamplighters League offers so much good gameplay, is nice to look at, very nice fitting music and a lot more.But above all, the developers' desire and passion is evident. It is very well thought out, has great balancing and lots of lovely details. I really like this game and it makes me think a little that it was definitely not a financial success. I know a lot of games that actually offer much less, were developed without passion according to a formula, but that sold much better. It's puzzling how this market works.If I were to criticize something, it would be the fixed camera perspective and the lack of a quick save. I really can't think of anything else.A clear recommendation for anyone looking for a compact, turn-based adventure!

_childDocuments_.review: - Very lush presentation, especially for HBS, who used to make Kickstarter games on a tight budget. A jazz soundtrack that seems like it was recorded live, a nice animated intro menu that sets the tone, and animated story cinematics. Lots of voice acting. The UI and fonts have a period-flavored vibe but are mostly crisp and minimalist.- The gameplay is a straight shot of Shadowrun with a little chaser of Commandos or Shadow Tactics. You've got a team of specialized agents, each with their own skills; you move them around a 3-D gameworld in real time, where they cut wires or unlock doors or lay traps for patrolling guards. When you get caught and combat starts, it switches to turn-based tactics on a square grid with characters who have unique powers and 2AP each turn with which to use them. You know the drill.- I really can't emphasize enough how much this game feels like a 2023 update and improvement of the Shadowrun games, gameplay-wise. If you just picture Dragonfall but the world is fully 3-D so you can rotate the camera, the view is more zoomed-in to better see the character models, the models themselves are more stylish, the UI is de-janked, etc, you're like 85% of the way there. It seems like using this engine to remake the Shadowruns would be a really easy layup.- One place where the game is unfortunately similar to Shadowrun (and a step back from BATTLETECH) is the combat animations. They're about as impactful as a sponge. Punches look kinda weightless, gunshots feel anemic. It's not a dealbreaker but it's kind of a bummer and feels like a notable miss after 2022-2023 where we had Chaos Gate: Daemonhunters and Midnight Suns.- The tone and story so far are very charming. The vibe is very...all-ages, semi-lighthearted adventure. Do you remember the Disney movie Atlantis: The Lost Empire? It's like that. Absolute kryptonite for level 9 edgelords but I recommend it to everyone else who enjoys wholesome adventure and beating up Nazis.- The only technical issue I've experienced is a bit of stuttering, mostly when using the recon view (a higher-up overhead view of the map). It'd be a problem in an FPS but in a turn-based tactics game it's barely even worth mentioning.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- Nice art design- Cool setting and time period- Fun combat- Good voice acting- Controls are good- Music is very good- Works good on the Steam Deck with no tinkering neededNegatives:- Not a fan of the Camera, needs some work- I don't like that a character was tied behind a preorder & now cost $10 Canadian to buy. Make preorders some weapon or some item, NOT a full on character. _childDocuments_.review: HBS has done it again, everything I loved about the Shadowrun games and then some. Impeccable music, fun characters, satisfying gameplay (both the real-time stuff and the combat proper, turned Lateef into a dodge-tank to give the enemies some of the funniest turns, and really in general, I love that all the characters play very differently). I'm not done yet, but I'm not too far from the end. There were a lot of nights this past week I couldn't put the game down cuz the gameplay loop is my exact jam.If I had to complain: there were moments where I ended up fighting the camera to get it into the right position and it could use more map variety, plus more incentive to pick up new party members and try them out (cuz the characters carry this game's story and it feels like a luxury I can't afford to grab everyone in one playthrough, which I love doing normally), I wanna know more about literally all of them. Solid 8/10 game, could become a 9/10 with the right DLC

_childDocuments_.review: The Lamplighters League is a turn based tactics game similar to XCOM, where a group of thieves and adventurers must stop the Banished Court from using occult magic to enter an ancient tower and conquer the world.The game was developed by Harebrained Schemes, who are experienced in the turn based genre, having previously worked on Battletech and the Shadowrun trilogy. I enjoyed all of those games.•	Depending on the mission type, you’ll control a squad of three or four characters. On your turn each character has two action points to move, attack, activate a special ability, or use a consumable such as a grenade or medkit. Attacks have hit percentages so there’s a chance you’ll miss, and environmental objects provide full or half cover.•	Before entering combat you can move around in real time and use stealth abilities to eliminate enemies, reducing the number you’ll have to fight.•	The Banished Court’s army includes Human soldiers, mummies, skeletons, shades, and other monsters. Enemies have a mixture of melee and ranged attacks, and other magical abilities such as summoning minions, slowing your characters, or setting large areas on fire.•	There are also three powerful bosses, the leaders of separate factions within the Banished Court. They have unique abilities, and you’ll definitely have to fight them during important story missions, but they can also appear in regular missions.•	There are ten characters to recruit who have their own unique skills, which could provide interesting tactical combinations, although I only got six of them because of the campaign’s time limits. My favourites were Ingrid, a melee specialist who can gain extra ability points for each kill, Eddie, whose guns can hit multiple enemies per attack, Lateef, who specialises in distracting enemies and evading their attacks, and Ana who is the healer.•	I played on the “adventurer” (medium) difficulty, which was quite challenging, mainly because of the high number of enemies. I regularly saw 10-14 enemies per encounter, plus 1-2 teleporters which would each spawn 3 reinforcements after a few turns, plus some enemies can summon minions. And of course the more powerful enemies have lots of health, so you have to hit them multiple times. Meanwhile, with so many enemies on the map, it can sometimes be hard to find opportunities for stealth kills because they’re all standing in each other’s vision cones. Plus most non-Human enemies are immune to takedowns anyway.•	Thankfully, as your characters level up they can acquire several abilities which give them extra attacks or free movement. Ingrid in particular is pretty much essential for crowd control, if you use other characters to wound enemies so that Ingrid can get the kills. You also don’t have to kill every enemy on the map. After completing the mission objectives you could just try to run to the exit. And you can save during missions, so I got into the habit of saving after each encounter just in case something went wrong.•	Characters who participate in missions can also equip magical playing cards which give them passive or active abilities, including powerful attacks, extra ability points, increased health, an area of effect heal, or regaining health from each kill. However, if they take too much damage, they’ll gain a temporary debuff card.•	On the world map, you’ll see three separate Doomsday clocks relating to each of the Banished Court’s factions. As they complete activities each week, their progress meters will advance. When they reach specific “break points”, the enemies you fight in missions will become more powerful. And if either Doomsday clock reaches the maximum level, you’ll lose the campaign.•	Every completed mission will set back one of the faction’s clocks, but as you can only perform one mission each week (even after you’ve recruited enough characters to field two teams), the other two factions will usually advance. And you can never reduce them below a break point. This means you can’t stop the clocks fully, you can only try to slow them down long enough to complete your own objectives. When I reached the final mission, each Doomsday clock was around two thirds full, so I wasn’t in immediate danger of losing, but you can’t afford to waste much time.•	In addition to story missions where you’ll steal various items needed to enter the tower and sever the Banished Court’s connection to magic, there are optional missions to recruit more characters or reset a Doomsday clock back to the last break point. You can perform missions in any order.•	Characters who aren’t in your active squad for the next mission can be sent to gather information to reveal new missions, or to collect supplies needed to craft consumables, improved armour, and special upgrades.•	You’ll also see a random event each week, which gives you a choice of reward. This can include various supplies, but for obvious reasons I always chose to reduce a faction’s doomsday clock when that was an option.•	Story is basic, but its at least good enough to provide motivation to complete the campaign. You’ll get more details from post mission debriefs as well as lore documents which can be found during missions.•	Between missions, characters will talk to each other which lets you learn about their personalities and backstory.•	Voice acting is quite good.•	It took me 36 hours to finish the campaign.•	I didn’t have any problems with crashes or framerate.•	Unless I set all the graphics to low, this game pushes my graphics card temperature higher than AAA games like Horizon Forbidden West and Last of Us. While I would describe Lamplighters League’s graphics as “fine”, they’re certainly not AAA quality.•	There are a limited number of maps, so I regularly saw repeats of maps I’d visited previously. One time I even saw the same map for two consecutive missions.The Lamplighters League is a good game which has challenging combat, and while it has some flaws, fans of the turn based tactics genre will probably find something to enjoy. Its worth picking up on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Gem for me.It has the right amount of Indiana Jones vibes mixed with X-Com style combat with a bit of stealth and stealth takedowns.And after a short intro phase of introduction missions and some recruitment missions you are thrown into the world map where you need to decide on which missions you want to do.Sabotage the enemy?Sent out one agent for some research/supply mission?Go on a recruitment mission?Get the story going?Also you can equip and skill your agents.Armor slot, magic item slot, tool slot and up to four unlockable one use items each agent (starting with one slot on low level) plus a tarot card system giving agents unique abilities gives plenty of builds.The characters of your team are unique and to my liking.Very much so.They are a bunch of merry thieves.Well, not all are merry. Some are quite grumpy.But I like all in a way. It clicks well for me.Does it have a AAA Budget like other games?Hell, no.Is it perfect?No, there are some squabbles.Sometimes the controls are a bit clunky.But the game has a SOUL.Plus the setting is definitely well used and just...does it job well.The speakers of the characters as well as the soundtrack are two things helping along quite well.Especially the soundtrack.it is a piece of art and I enjoy it very much.Bought the deluxe edition and certainly am enjoying the soundtrack even without the game.The game is scratching all the right itches for me.:-)Update:Game opens up quite a bit mid-game and later.The decisions to do are a nice strategic quagmire:Shall I thwart one of the three enemy factions?Shall I instead recruit a new character?Shall I pick up some supplies or ally to gear up or open up some more crafting possibilities?Your agents can be captured (you can free them in a rescue mission) or killed on missions.When getting downed they get injured and need some healing taking out the agent depending on the damage received.Tarot cards give a nice twist mixing up abilities.Your melees can get some ranged tarot weapon or ability.Your ranged ones vice versa.You can later even craft these tarot cards.That mixes up the skill trees quite a bit and adds further variability.For those dreading Deathclocks:The game lets you plenty time to skill up, craft and plunder locations.The Deathclock can be set back like in X-Com by doing missions to sabotage and assassinate faction henchman.On the easiest level the setback from these missions can make you go on nearly forever.On medium it gives a nice "What should I choose for missions feel" and still can set back the Deathclock Counter substantially.Some may argue "Ah - gods! Deathclock..."But in this game - as it is a chase of a group of misfit heroes after some sinister organization - it fits.The game revolves around thwarting, being faster on pick-up of relics and recruitment which ever has a look at the deathclock.And with being able to set back the Death Clock substantially even on Mid-Difficulty you can still go without much pressure.There are several "thresholds" on the enemy factions where they get more "abilities" or unlock more foe variants.But as your agents grow in skill with their skill-tree and tarot cards (which are upgradable or can be crafted) it only is a natural way of adjusting the enemies to heroes leveling up.The mix between stealth takedowns and real combat is good in my opinions.As the takedown skills have a limit you cannot clear a whole map by stealth.But you can reduce the enemies to such a small number you can just steamroll them with your team.Also going into a fight does not alert the whole map.Unless you really crash into things like a bull or just want it.Usable items are found on the map so you can replenish and plunder all you want.You can even plunder things after the level is cleared and there are hidden stashes throughout the maps.And your takedown skills can even be refreshed by items in the level.Any usable items picked up on the map you can carry with you and place in your stash.So you can save on supply buys with things you plundered doing missions.The only thing missing so far for me is that you may sell these things.But then this is a minor squabble as I do not feel to harshly restricted by it.Plundering levels saves you "money" (supplies) for buying hero items in the shop.All in all I like how the game opens up more and more on the way.Thumbs up!Good playing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up! I like the game!I rarely buy games on release but wait for bug fixes and patches - and the next sale is sure to come. After the initial bad reviews, I've now bought the game 3 months later and can't complain.Graphics/bugsI have a solid gaming laptop and play LL at maximum performance. Only when starting a new mission does it take a little longer to load. After that it runs smoothly and without lags.Many people report bugs and glitchs. So far I've had only one enemy get stuck between a wall and a lamppost at the start of a round match, so I had to reload. I also haven't noticed any problems with walls often obscuring the view or anything similar. Maybe these bugs have been fixed.ComfortOf course the navigation or some things (like quick save) could be better, but for me this does not reduce the fun of the game.AII play on medium difficulty and you can handle it. If you use the Recon mode and proceed strategically (secure/cover/higher positions) it works with real time and tactical combat. The enemies also behave quite well, if there are a lot of them, they come, if there are only a few, they sometimes entrench themselves and also use dynamite boxes and barrels standing around against the agents.I like the 1920s setting, archeology theme and Indiana Jones feeling. You shouldn't expect the greatest story, but I think it fits. The main characters are simple but I love the cool scandinavian girl, the cunning arab thief and the loudmouthed, slightly naive, shooting cowboy. I like LL's combination of real time and round strategy, so I will play the game to the end. I would probably buy a second part too.Update after successful end of the campaignBugApart from the issue described above, there were no other bugs.In a special mission in a pyramid there were frequent problems with the view, which could be solved by slightly rotating the viewpoint. It is generally noted that when four agents are moving in a group, the last agent in the line gets stuck on steps and has to be moved up manually.ComfortAfter 90 hours of playing, there are a few ideas on how to improve the comfort of the game, but it worked fine as it was.AIWow, in more difficult missions from the middle of the game you are sometimes glad of a savegame. On a miserable working day for the agents, it can quickly become 3 vs 34 opponents...ConclusionIt took me 43 missions to play through the campaign, in which I may have carried out several missions 2-3 times at each location. Since I also recruited the maximum of 10 agents, there was enough variety. As a result, the game didn't feel repetitive to me.Maybe I will try the game again in the next difficulty level...

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is solid and the setting interesting there will be no further updates, patches or content released. A lot of lingering bugs, needed QOL adjustments, and potential content will never happen. Had it remained supported I feel like the game could have been truly great and the IP has room to grow for sure, but it was dropped pretty quickly post release.

_childDocuments_.review: Xcom, but with fleshed out characters, cool  1930s setting and nice cartoony design. The real time stealth mode was clunky, and by the end of it, I had no use for all the resources I've gathered, but it was actually fun to just stay in the hideout and listen to the character banter. The turn based combat was good as well. Endgame combos were insane.Also, I actually read most of the lore entries. They were interesting!

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like some decent play testing would have made this game have much better reviews. First- F any game that tries to stuff a superfluous game launcher down your throat. Second- On hard mode, in my experience, you cannot win if you bother recruiting the side characters that the game encourages you to recruit. I recruited 7 out of 10 side characters. That means I "wasted" a few turns on the strategy map. There are three clocks you have to race to avoid losing the game. If one of the villains pushes hard while the other two do nothing, one of the clocks sky rockets to the end and defeats you. This is exactly what happened while I recruited additional champs. My, apparently incorrect, assumption was that I could use all my champs at the same time and therefore make up the lost time with additional people. As it turns out, that is not how it works- recruiting additional champs really only hurts you. I easily won every single battle and still lost the game and I lost because I chose to explore additional content. Just. Terrible. Balance. How is it that no one noticed this in development? The game undermines itself and player enjoyment. You make a pretty good game and then beat yourself by making it unfun for no good reason?

_childDocuments_.review: Summary Review: A guarded yes. This is a turn based tactical game with some character management, base management and stealth elements thrown in. Essentially, this is an XCOM2 Lite with a sprinkling of some Desperados Lite. Should you pay top coin for this game? Well, for 50 Euros I had more expectations, primarilly with regards to base building (non-existent), base management (pretty basic), character customization (adequate, but could use more features). If you want a somewhat easier ride than XCOM2 without having to worry too much about base/character optimization then this is for you. Due to the fact that post XCOM2, there are other games out there that do a much better job at turn based tactics (See the suberb "Expeditions: Rome" by THQ Nordic) whilst asking for less money, I can only recommend this as a "purchase when in sale". Although I like the combat and the characters combine their abilities really well together, this game isn't worth 50 Euros as it is.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: GreatFinally a well made game, after many years of a lot of superficial games that lacked that feeling of a job well done.However, if you don't like turn-based games, this game may not be for you. But if you do like turn-based RPGs, The Lamplighters League, is a simple game, but well made with great love and care. A classic gem, like they only made in the old days. A classic, but well told story from an alternate reality of 1932. A game with many heroes, each with their unique abilities, heroes of which some you'll fall in love with and others probably not.The cartoon-like graphics are not annoying, not even for me who am a fan of realistic graphics, but in my opinion, the most precious thing is the voice acting. Not only is it done by professional actors but it has something magical about it that makes you fall in love with the characters in a unique way. Sometimes I had the feeling that I was watching (or rather, listening to) a triple A movie, like Indiana Jones. Glorious!PRO: Simplicity, without feeling like something is missing. Voice acting. Repeatability.CON: Small bugsFriendly advice. Save all the time. Sometimes you fall into traps, other times, very rarely, the game hangs on enemy turn and you can't get out unless you stop the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoying my time with the game so far, looking forward to sinking more time into it. High Points:-Great voice acting and snappy dialogue that nails the game's pulpy tone-Wonderful big band soundtrack-Well-executed alt 1930s setting -Solid real-time/turn based tacticsLow Points:-A few odd bugs, here and there (i,.e. camera clipping into a wall one time during a close-up combat animation), but nothing majorMaking each member of the squad a fully fleshed out character and giving them each a unique moveset really helps set this game apart from other turn-based squad tactics games (such as XCOM). If you're into XCOM or Mutant Year Zero, I highly recommend you check it out.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fantastic game. The setting is appropriately moody, the characters are fun, the stealth is clever and doesn't make me grumpy (A thing I normally detest being snuck into non-stealth genres), and the combat is quite engaging. _childDocuments_.review: The Lamplighters League takes place in the 1930s where a man who was part of a former heroic team, now all dead, attempts to recruit thieves, murderers, renegades, and adventurers for hire to fight against his old group's enemies. Your opponents are three different groups that are attempting to access a mystical tower that will allow their leader to reshape the world in the way that they want. Each week you send three or four agents on a main mission and some of your other agents on side missions where they gain items from safehouses or spend intel to unlock new special missions. Based on your actions, you can lower faction progress level but will typically see two factions coming closer to reaching their goal while slowing the third. As each faction's circular meter fills up they gain new benefits when you fight against them. Completing missions gives you skill points to improve your agents as well as giving you random Undrawn Hand cards, of which each agent can eventually equip three of that give access to new active or passive abilities. These cards can be upgraded over time either by spending Ink that you gain from discarded or replaced cards or by drawing the same ability again and equipping it onto the same skill. The goal is to complete the heist missions needed to steal an object from each faction as well as the missions that give you the keys to accessing the tower before you go onto the game's finale.Each mission takes place on a fairly small map where you move your agents by themselves or in a group trying to avoid, stealth kill, or engage groups of enemies while trying to complete a main or side objective while also gathering items and supplies. The actual manipulation of your characters in real time here is both pretty basic and somehow never feels good to control, even the way enemy visual cones are handled is odd compared to similar games. A lot of the equipment you find will never be remotely useful and the kind of equipment you can buy is very limited in scope.The combat can be pretty good as you gain varied characters with their own styles of play that can work together well and be further enhanced by different Undrawn Hand cards. Even the characters that seem to be thought of as much worse than others can work well in certain teams and with certain upgrades and consumables that fit with their unique passive abilities. Problems come from the game doing a horrible job at explaining anything. You have no effective way to look up what status effects do, how long those buffs or debuffs last, what will trigger and who has reaction attacks, some abilities only partially tell you what they do, and many improvements have the usual lazy descriptions with text like greatly improved crit chance/increases accuracy/increases damage/increases ammo capacity/etc without giving you the numbers you want to have in anything but especially in a turn based strategy game. It is constantly trying to mess with the target you are aiming at. I've had it randomly perform actions where it used consumable items that I was at no point even close to selecting. Certain abilities like ones that can knock enemies down are so much more useful than anything else and can lead to the majority of fights being extremely easy.The randomness preventing you from using the characters you want in a playthrough by limiting who or when you can recruit or making it difficult to get the randomly generated cards at the end of the mission that you actually want to use with a particular character who had to have gone on that mission. The terrible, and far to common in the genre, decision to limit party size to three characters (though 4 can be available in recruitment missions when you find the new character and in some of the main missions) is made even worse in this particular game due to the three types of classes each character can be. You typically want to have one of each of in a party to be able to do the interactions with the environment to find alternate paths and items which even further limits how you are likely to make use of the game's agents. While skill points earned in a mission can be spent on any character you have, the random Undrawn Hand cards have to be equipped, turned into upgrades for copies, or discarded right away and can only be assigned to the characters who participated in a mission. This can make it hard to get what you want, or what is even useful on certain characters, making it worse is that there are a few cards that are pretty much made specifically to fit one or two characters and would be of poor use on the other 10 or 11 (and some that just look to be a poor choice on anyone).Map are frequently reused with no changes other than potential faction or enemy variety based on their current threat level. After 15 random missions two map repeated twice and one repeated three times (this became four times a few missions later). Even if a mission objective is different this does little to change how the maps play out as a main objective can be as simple as picking something up, killing a certain enemy, or destroying a device before having to move to a small area for extraction (that is, for some reason, located in a place that usually requires you getting through one more large camp of enemies).Random text events that were added to the game after launch are an improvement to the game. Giving you a text scenario with three options to choose that can benefit you in different ways. They did do a strange thing at times where an option might have a specific agent doing something (possibly something that keeps them busy for the weak possibly just them as flavor text) but the option with an agent can sometimes have the exact same reward as one of the other two options, usually having a specific person could give better results but here it seems like that might have been the case while it was in development but then that was ignored. While the results aren't always that interesting, these events add more flavor to the setting, enemies, and agents while also allowing you to potentially gain items you need or to have another way to manage the threat of one or all three enemy factions giving you a bit more freedom to play the missions you want to play. The additional setting information is also nice because the character conversations between missions and there varied personalities is one of the better parts of the game, as is some of the back and forth that can happen between them during missions.When you aren't dealing with too much randomness and get into a fight with the characters and abilities you want it can feel like a decent game is there but it falls far short of the developer's previous narrative and exploration elements found in their Shadowrun games and the gameplay mechanics of Battletech while completely failing at the overworld system and a desire for multiple runs that the game seems to be going for. Even the 1930's pulp style adventurers dealing with mystical cult like enemies was better handled in the game Pathway that also handles multiple quick rougelite style runs with a small team of characters that some elements of this game feel like it might have been aiming for at some point in its development. It has what could have been an interesting setting as well as fun varied characters whose abilities can synergize well if used in certain pairs but handles nearly every system poorly.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: Two major issues I've run into are the enemy softlocking the game on the "enemy phase". Basically they just freeze and never take any action. The second is a spreading black fog that covers everything you can see at random. The AI is awful and the designers countered this by giving enemies ever increasing HP pools/damage (while fighting up to x2 the number of units you field). The entire game is basically alpha strike everything or go for disables. The strategy layer is just 3 doomsday clock scenarios that you have to balance while also doing side missions which for the most part do not reset the clock. Doing important story missions should at least lower the overall threat level considerably but dont. Recruiting units also moves the clock forward. Awful design.Edit: Just randomly had all of my units equipped cards/equipment stop working mid-game. I just keep finding stuff that doesn't work. If this game wasnt part of a bundle I'd be mad as hell. Many cool ideas but everything is so poorly executed.The game also runs terribly, the skill UI hitches when hovering over any skill. It has all the same issues that Battletech did. Hairbrained Schemes just doesnt polish their games and this one has been abandoned.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Man, both this game and HareBrained Schemes deserved better. It is really cool. Features both XCom-like tactical battles and Commandos-like stealth sections. Characters are great, they talk a lot during base conversations like Fire Emblem's support system. There is an ABSURD amount of lore to be found in missions such as posters, notebooks, letters, newspapers etc. You can clearly see how much passion and effort went into this game. You fight against 3 factions with different aesthethics and motives. There is a time limit system, but it is not unforgiving. I've recruited every single agent and completed the game with some time to spare. Downsides is mostly technichal. Performance is a bit iffy. It has stutters and slowdowns a bit frequently. I have encountered only a single but through my playthrough, so my experience was pretty much bug free. Sad to see this game flop despite its quality, but I'm still looking forward to HBS's next games.

_childDocuments_.review: The decline continues for the studio that brought us the excellent Shadowrun games. Don't know why I bought this game after reading this in their news update celebrating the game's release: "There was a moment during development where we were, in fact, facing down the fact that infiltration just wasn’t fun and there was a big deadline coming up fast. We needed to rethink things, and we needed to do it quickly. Under that pressure the team prototyped and implemented the real time takedowns in just a few weeks."Well you guys tried but infiltration still isn't fun and neither is the half baked turn based combat layer. Both are too shallow and repetitive and bring nothing new to the table. Seriously, adding real time takedowns to stealth was the genius idea moment for you guys???? Is this 1994??????

_childDocuments_.review: Played this for the first time nearly a year after it's release and a lot of patches later. Not sure how buggy the game was on release but by the time I got my handS on it was a pretty smooth experience.  Still a little wonky, but no more then most games. What I liked: Loved the story/pulp fiction setting. They play to the motif and own it, making the entire ride quite enjoyable. The characters are solidly written and even got a few snickers out of me in the dialogue, it all fits the aesthetic their going for excellently. Combat is fun and decent challenge, between 10+ agents (depending on DLC), skill trees, equipment, and the undrawn hand buffs there is a good amount of variety and strategic builds to experiment with.  It did feel a little easy in the end once you figure our your ideal builds, learn a few tricks, and the enemy AI runs out of ways to surprise you.  I plugged about 50 hours into my first play through, but I was trying to do as MUCH as possible in a single run (got all but 5 achievements).  I bet it could be done in a much quicker fashion though especially on second play through. What could have been better: I got this game for the combat not stealth, but it's a part of the game play loop all the same. I am disappointed the stealth stuff never evolves after the tutorial. There is no upgrades or ways to make stealth more viable and more and more enemies are immune to stealth take-downs, so it just becomes more irrelevant as the game goes on. Some sort of upgrade tree like more take-down charges or environmental options to maybe eliminate harder enemies would have gone a long way in keeping this aspect of the game relevant for the entire play through.  Also would have a liked at least a handful of missions where you use 5 or more agents, being limited to 3-4 the entire game I think is a missed opportunity especially feels at odds when it comes to things like the final mission, where story would suggest all hands on deck, not 40% hands on deck (if you max out all 10 agents).  I'm a fan when strategy games like X-com let you grow your squad size via upgrades or plot moments, would have liked to see that here at least a little.  Also a lack of specialty missions, there are a few in here and each one is pretty solid, but for the most part it's the same 15 or so (don't know the actual number) maps over and over, I found myself replaying maps in the back-half or listening to same dialogue through the missions. A few more story missions like maybe an attack of the island or something would have been fun. Ending also feels a bit anti-climatic. Overall: I got nitpicks, but picked this game up on sale and am happy with my experience. Shame this company went under cause I would have kept on the lookout for a sequel.  It's a damn solid game and if you're looking for a turn based strategy game that has something a bit more unique to say, you will find that here.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:- A simple, but interesting story with a great cast of characters to recruit. - Really unique and different characters for you to use, so your play style will change drastically depending on which characters you unlock and invest skill points into. Some RNG is involved, but you always get a good mix in the early campaign and can form a great trio and quartet.- The enemy types are varied and challenging.- On "The Survivor" (Hard) level, the meta game (map) challenge is intense and fun and the enemy encounters can be fatal if you don't weigh your options properly.- The visuals and music are greatThe Bad:- The ending narrative is a bit light- Maps are reused with slight variations, but if you drag on the campaign for very long, you will notice the repetition.- Ally AI behavior can, sometimes, be disappointing (e.g. when you charm and enemy into a temporary ally). They sometimes waste the turn just running from cover to cover instead of attacking, which is annoying when you have them charmed for only two turns.The Conclusion:This is a really great game and gave me a lot of hours of enjoyment and I would recommend picking it up for anyone that loves T-RPGs like the XCOM series. The asking price is a bit high for what we get imo, but when it's on sale for <= $35, then I'd recommend the buy.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I am delighted with this game, and look forward to my session with it every evening.The setting is colorful and charming, the graphics simultaneously lush and frugal (16G storage requirement is unheard of in 2023 and very welcome at my rural download speeds), the soundtrack cinematic and period-immersive.  The entire game is a pleasure for the ears and eyes, right down to villain logos and the foley of menu items opening.I could never get into HBS's Shadowrun or Battletech because I don't care for the IP of either.  Strange Brigade was a game whose original IP excited me but that didn't hold my interest as a game at all.  LL has a setting that sparks my imagination AND works as a enjoyable game.  The characters have real, albeit pulpy, personalities and real playstyle differences that emerge from their different skillsets, and they interact, both in scripted inter-character dialogue (that you can skip for replays) and organically in gameplay.The gameplay is very kind to arthritic adult gamers.  (There are dozens of us!)  Basically you alternate periods of real-time but low-twitch Infiltration with turn-based zero-twitch Combat.  Infiltration sneaks around, reconnoiters, steals things, knocks out guards, sets up ambushes if necessary.  Combat finishes the job once you've established your tactical advantage, or gets your dinner out of the fire if you fumbled at some point in Infiltration.  You've moving on a square grid, there are turns taken: this is not an immersive sim, though the setting is plenty immersive.  Infiltration is real-time but not kinetically punishing: it does require active attention, so it doesn't mix well with a crying infant or a toddler needing attention or a cookpot on the stove, but it's not going to leave you in pain. When Infiltration ends there will be a bout of turn-based combat, and that's not hard on the joints at all.  You cannot save a game in live fire combat, but you can do so at any point in Infiltration, and individual firefights don't last too long.  If I'm called away from a game mid firefight I'll just close the game and accept that it'll roll back to the last time that I saved in Infiltration, or at an autosave point otherwise.Addressing common complaints:The game has more missions than discrete maps, so it reuses maps between different missions.  The maps themselves are carefully crafted, and reward the player who studies their layouts and learns their cache points, but if you get bored or merely immersion-broken (that's a word, now) with seeing the same warehouse in the same place every sixth mission you will not like this.There exists day zero DLC.  I didn't buy the DLC because I don't purchase DLC for any new game.  It looks like the game is structured at its core for future buy-in updates of additional characters to increase replayability and maintain a revenue stream.  I have no problem with this in the abstract, but it would be a more compelling case for LL if there were more than one, the bump from ten characters to eleven not being especially compelling.There exist the inevitable bugs of any release day game purchase.  None of them have been game-breaking for me.  My experience is of course not universal: if it were, I would be the world's greatest QA asset, my services in demand across the globe.  Bugs stink.  I used to be in the business, I get it.  But I don't regret my completely out-of-character opening day purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: What a fun little game! with an unreasonable price tag :/ It was really enjoyable when I first got into it, but the joy didnt last very long; here's my thoughts. First the 😁Good😁:The game is thoroughly voice acted; there are plenty of conversations and interactions between all (most?) party members, which adds a lot of depth. The lines are not always particularly "good" or "substantial", but some characters have nice chemistry between them and it's nice to explore it through the plentiful dialogue. I was *very*pleasantly surprised by that.The soundtrack is also really nice. Even though it kinda lacks in variety, it's dynamic and nicely hypes you up to power through the missions. The 😐Alright😐:The style is nice. It's going for that interwar aesthetic that is so prevalent among media that explore archaeology and the unknown (see 1st Indiana Jones, The Mummy, the entire Lovecraft anthology, etc) and i'm all for it. It even has a bit of lovecraft mythos into it, which I absolutely love. However it is not as consistent and satisfying when it comes to the characters. They mostly look like they would fit right in on Fortnite; they have this budget, glowy sparkle that Epic Games characters have, and it really subtracts from the whole. The customization (in terms of gear) is there but it's fairly simplistic, boosting only 1 (or maybe two) stats at a time; not a lot of nuance to it. The 😕Weh😕:The gameplay itself is...  well, pretty unsatisfying. I like that the abilities are relatively simple, but there's so many elements that clutter the experience. The "stealth takedowns" mechanic that you are introduced to as the very first combat mechanic soon becomes obsolete, as many enemies are immune to it. Because of that you are not able to actually skip any of the fights (except for some very niche cases), which become progressively more bothersome as the game progresses. The enemies constantly increase in number, and they have large-ish health bars and stalling abilities that dont really let you power through the fights, when at the SAME time they dont drop anything (gear, money, or even xp) so there's no real incentive to actually fight other than finishing the mission. Even though the game gives you the "liberty" of choosing your next mission, it actually forces your hand because if you dont it ramps up the difficulty way too soon, and might even bring the game to a swift end. On top of that, the areas are often reused with certain paths/areas blocked, a mechanic that those who have played Dragon Age 2 are oh-too familiar with. TLDR: And that is what my overall feeling was when I decided to call it quits; the game feels a lot like a Dragon Age installment, except slightly worse in every way (which is hard to do). The writing is too basic for a "Store Rich" game, the stakes too unremarkable for an "Adventure", the customization not present for an "RPG", and the fights too tedious to actually apply "Tactics". It would be an outstanding! entry at the 10-15 euro price range, and having a smaller idea of itself. However, while I dont regret trying it, I cannot recommend it as is

_childDocuments_.review: So no lie, the friction points actually kept me up last night, I couldn't sleep so y'all get this review.  On a very surface level the game is cool.  In fact the story and characters, world building and antagonists are all well-execututed.  And the basic pieces of stealth-explore-take down and go loud turn based combat are fine but here the execution is much less successful.  0) you move way too slowly when exploring.  Way too much needed to double tap to "run"  just doing basic traversal.  And also the controls are pretty creaky, which leads to....1) the optimal way to play the game is maximizing the stealth takedowns.  Done perfectly you can almost completely bypass combat or trivialize it so much that triggering a regular combat feels like you "messed up"  which can happen pretty easily due to the janky controls.  2) this is slow though.  And makes the relatively small mission maps take forever.  3) If you ignore the take down system combat can be pretty overwhelming.  Even early in the game.  4) The takedowns don't change or evolve during the game.  No upgrades, no new ones from new characters etc.  However the maps gradually introduce immune enemies.  I am guessing the design curve is supposed to be that as you level up your characters you are better able to handle combat and can thus rely less on the takedowns.  But I have no idea how you are supposed to know what this curve actually is.  Especially since absent scouting, you don't know how many enemies you are activating when you "go loud".  4.5) the take over by takedown immune enemies also sort of invalidates the how you play the first 1/2 of the campaign.  Which is pretty clumsy.  5) There is an equipment/consumable system that seems largely superfluous.  The numbers on consumables don't seem meaningful and the resources you use to buy them (as well as equipment) are so scarce that it hardly matters anyway.  6) the doom clocks are completely unmanagable.  7) there's little point in recruiting additional agents (you start with 3, and are required to do recruit one more in the tutorial, one more after that and you are basically good).  If you could allocate agents to slowing/reversing doom clocks when not on a mission *and* there was some incentive to rotate your team, these last 2 bowls are filled with one spoon.  I really wanted to love this game, and would very much appreciate a chat with a dev to see how much of the finished game lined up with the vision and how much was compromised.  Overall style and story are like an 8.5/10.  Gameplay is more like 3.5.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first reviewed this game I gave it a downvote, I’m going to keep the text of my original review below because the complaints still are valid, but I want to write a modification given I’ve put several more hours into the game. The tactical difficulty does rise slightly around late and mid game, and the constant threat of defeat on the strategy layer is excellent. But most of all, I just love the genre way too much to not have a blast with this game. It still isn’t difficult enough, so I very much suggest the hard difficulty, but the setting, maps, most of the characters, and the music all are just rife with the beauty of the treasure hunting genre, which is one of my favorite. Plus the worldbuilding is pretty interesting, a lot of work was put into this making the factions and characters feel unique and interesting while still harkening back to tropes of the genre, My original review:This game is too easy. And at the same time too hard. Let me explain.There is no way to 'lose' the game. There is no iron man mode. The game expects you to basically save scum your way to victory, because the game is 'balanced' around you either winning every mission, and the only strategy involved is which missions to pick to avoid the doom clocks (which do seem well implemented and WILL make you lose the game) or you fail one mission, losing all your agents (the most common non victory situation) and then you save scum until you win. This is not like other XCOM likes where you have to recover from defeat via desperate and careful management of your remaining resources. In this game how you recover from a large or small defeat is via save scumming. If you are unwise enough to try to keep playing after a squad wile you'll lose quickly as the game isn't balanced around losing several characters. Theoretically you could recruit multiple characters but there's very little reason to do this beyond a roster of 5 or so. Because you only send 3 on a mission (sometimes 4) and there are at most 2 other one person assignments that you can send agents on. It is far better to have a few characters you put a lot of upgrade points into, making them these few unkillable experts who you keep using. Which I suppose is fun but its clear the design intended you to recruit several agents and try to level up the whole roster. But this feels like a trap. Because new agents are not really worth getting, the amount of agent death is absurdly low, except for the aforementioned squad wipes that the game isn't balanced around and thus you are forced to save scum out of. This is because characters have huge pools of HP. this is not like XCOM where a character can get one shot if left out of cover. No no, in this magical world of the 1930s, unarmored heros and minions can take a half dozen 45. caliber bullets to the chest and be just fine. This wouldn't be so bad if the game let you actually lose. But it doesn't. it just says 'hey maybe save scum your way to victory.' it doesn't even do you the service of showing some sort of cinematic of your defeat when you run out of agents. Which seems like a sort of insult of 'this game wasn't designed for you to have refused to save scum. What you want consequences for your mistakes? Not in this game you don't!"And that's my biggest complaint: Lack of consequences. Even having a character downed is easily fixed by a healing resource that you have what feels like an infinite supply of. the consequences for a stress break are interesting, and one of the few things encouraging a larger party size, to give heroes the chance to rest. But overall mistakes are just too easy to account for to the point that it doesn't even feel like I'm playing a game. Which is especially bad as the supposed theme of the game is "play the hand you are dealt." But that's not true. the actual theme is "if you don't like your hand, shuffle and draw again until you win." That's not gameplay. It's tedium.

_childDocuments_.review: Strong characterization. Charming. Solid voice acting. A fun story, with pulpy stakes. Leans heavily on classic story tropes; executes them well and demonstrates why they became classics. So far, haven't met a single character I don't either love, or love to hate.Doesn't play as tightly with tactics and advancement as some of my other favorite turn-based tactical games; I feel it more than makes up for it with the infiltration-mode interaction and (generally) grab-and-scoot mission objectives. It's not a game where "if the guns come out,  you've already lost", but it IS a game where "go in guns blazing" might be a second or even third priority depending on the job. And when you do go in, it feels good. I will never get tired of starting a fight by having Ingrid just hurtle across the map, clothesline three unsuspecting goons and take them out of the action before the fight begins, and then be in position to punch 4 more before they can act. It feels great.This is a good game. There's room for improvement; I've hit some instabilities and crashes, I wish there were larger skill trees and a few more customization/tactical options, it does feel like it's designed for repeated shorter plays than for one sprawling playthrough. There's also room for expansion: it's a self-contained story, but there's room for more characters, room for more stories, room for followup games in this setting with or without the same crew.I know the reasons we're unlikely to get those. I'm happy we got this game as it is. I hope there's a future where we get more.

_childDocuments_.review: A game replete with charm and engaging gameplay reminiscent of X-COM. However, it occasionally falls short, particularly in the realm of sound design. I've also encountered stuttering during gameplay, which I suspect is due to shaders not being pre-cached. As for the gameplay, it is quite enjoyable. The mechanics allow for a style of combat that evokes memories of Commandos, though without the intricate nuances that make such a playstyle obligatory. Personally, I find going into battles more to my liking. Thankfully, the game doesn't punish you if you decide to do so, at least in a way that feels unfair. While I hope for a successful future for Harebrained with this title, perhaps even a sequel, I must not get ahead of myself; there is still much of the game left to explore. There are some potential improvements I'd like to see though. I question the decision to have shared skill points. I understand it is there so you can level up agents left out of the fight, but it might just be better to also allow them to level up and have skill points of their own. Another minor issue is the dialogue system in the hideout. The need to click to advance the conversation feels outdated. While I understand its value for accessibility, an auto-progression option for dialogue would be a welcome addition. Anyway, I do recommend this game if you enjoy X-COM-like games and if you are not a sound effect snob like me (though even if you are, you might be able to push through the presentation lack)

_childDocuments_.review: The pulpy adventure theme caught my eye, and I wanted to scratch my X-Com itch but I think part of the way through the game I started to feel that it was enough fun to appreciate it on its own right and not as a temporary fix for the nostalgia of another beloved title. The characters feel very unique both in and out of combat, and I came to appreciate the little interactions between them between missions as my team grew.   However, once I had my set three that I really liked (Ingrid, Purnima, and Ana Sofia), I found exactly zero incentive to use anyone else and quickly delegated the others to doing other missions as I continuously wooped the ♥♥♥♥ out of/barely survived.  Grateful that I also invested in The Alexandrite for those occasional 4 Agent missions, or when I really just had to sit someone out from a brutal affect on the stress break cards.But one of the things I appreciated most was that you absolutely have the option to just sneak your way through stuff and bypass fights and act like thieves in the night.  Setting up fights on your own terms, or just booking it when you get caught, made for some of my favourite little moments in this game, and the voice acting and music were well directed for the aesthetic of the time period the game takes place in.  And even with what I'd consider a pretty limited array of enemy-types to face off against, fighting them rarely felt repetitive and I really do credit the well laid out map designs for that.  Nice work!
