_childDocuments_.review: The Lamplighters League is a title that piqued my interest thanks to its aesthetics and setting, reminding me of Indiana Jones and the like. Unfortunately, it has many details that in my opinion detract from the experience, such as slightly clunky controls and a stealth mode that feels half-baked. Despite its flaws, it managed to capture my attention from start to finish, thanks to diverse characters, and an interesting story.The story is about a tower that hides within an unimaginable power, and the Lamplighters League, who have been trying to stop it from falling into the wrong hands. Faced with the growing threat of the Banished Court, Locke, the last surviving member of the league, decides to take on the fight from another angle, hiring spies, thieves and misfits; every kind of criminal motivated by money, or personal reasons. With subterfuge experts on his side, he seeks to hinder the advance of the Court and put a stop to the coming catastrophe. We'll command these criminals, or agents, as they are called in-game, and we’ll send them on missions of rescue, assassination, sabotage, etc. Initially we’ll have three characters, each with their own infiltration class and skills. The classes are divided between Bruisers, bullies who prefer brute force; Saboteurs, experts in the art of opening doors and placing explosives; and Sneaks, who, living up to their name, prefer to attack from the shadows.While the class and infiltration skills are the same for everyone, each agent has their own personal repertoire for combat; like Ingrid, who can perform a spinning attack and take down enemies, or Eddie, who can fire a volley of bullets over an area. Some abilities are the aces up each agent's sleeve, and can usually only be used once per combat, so you have to think carefully when to use them; fortunately, they can sometimes be recharged with certain actions. By the way, these moves can be learned and improved witg a skill tree, using points obtained in the quests.I really liked this about The Lamplighters League, that the points are obtained as a mission reward, no need to complete extra objectives or anything, and are shared with all agents, even inactive ones; and, since the game allows us to send a maximum of three agents per mission, sometimes four, I found it a good mechanic that let me to build benched characters easily.The missions are divided into some categories, nothing fancy but that generates a slight variety, such as going to rescue an agent to join us or fight against a Scion (powerful leaders of the Banished Court) to slow their advance towards the tower. They also have two phases, which are infiltration (real time, where we’ll have the class skills such as sneak attacks or explosives), and turn-based combat, where we can move and act by using action points.In addition to going for the objectives, if we explore a little we can find cards from "the undrawn hand" that provide bonuses to our agents, both in the form of parameters and new skills. This system is related to another one, which is the stress system. The stress points are a counter that reflects the agent's sanity, and when it fills up it can harm them in various ways, like hindering the effects of their cards, so you have to keep that under control with objects or skills. It should be noted that the enemies are also affected by this mechanic, and inducing stress on strong enemies is a very viable strategy.Apart from this, falling in combat has its own downsides, from being wounded to losing the agent completely. Luckily, falling once or twice is solved by healing the agents at the base, or letting them rest for a bit; and, as an added bonus, I read that the normal mode allows agents to survive death, although they will be kidnapped and we’ll have to go rescue them, which sounds neat (although I didn't get to try it).But that's not all that's involved in doing missions, as in addition to heading to the tower itself, we'll have to prevent the "doomsday clock" from advancing; and its name says it all, eh? This mechanic is a visual representation of how close the Court's goons are to the tower, and we'll have deploy agents on missions that hinder them, or suffer the consequences. This implies negative modifiers in missions, and parameter increases for enemies.I must say that I found it a bit tedious, since balancing the three factions and the quests you want to do can be tricky. After all we can only do one quest per week, while the rest vanish (although some come back from time to time). I understand it's to promote replayability, but it left me a bit sad to miss out on new agents because I had to stop the Court from advancing. But that's the game, and needless to say, if any of the Scions completes their clock, it's game over.Before moving on from missions, I wanted to delve a bit into the clunky controls and half-baked stealth I mentioned. To me it felt a bit weird to handle the characters with the keyboard, and a bit imprecise with mouse; according to a friend it's easier with a joystick, but I didn't try it. The stealth thing is because sometimes it creates some strange situations, like the AI running directly to the agents (even when hidden) when something happens, and those moments felt a bit artificial. Leaving aside the missions, we also have a base of operations for both our agents and our allies, people that we can recruit to provide services, such as a blacksmith. This is where we’ll also make use of the skill tree, and witness interactions between the characters, which is one of the aspects that entertained me the most; especially, I liked that they are very cliché, like the "femme fatale" or the master thief, and I think they fit very well in their roles.I said it before, but what I liked most about the game was its theme and setting, a mix of Indiana Jones, secret wars and espionage, and a mythical aspect in the form of creatures and impure gods of the deep. Another detail that I loved were the text fragments that can be found in the maps, whispers or stories that let the imagination run wild, like witnessing a pair of eyes watching us from the shadows or a silhouette that invites us to approach them under the waves. These are things that don't affect the game at all, but I found myself actively looking for them, and they added a little more flavor to the experience.I'll make a brief mention of the audiovisual section, which is quite nice. Gloomy streets, mysterious jungles, it's all very well presented (although performance was weird). The soundtrack is particularly cool, and I really liked the voice acting; I feel it's one of the strongest aspects of the game. Other gripe I had was the action camera, which moves cinematically over a character's shoulder when attacking. Sometimes there are obstacles like walls or clouds of smoke (or even the screen going completely black) that don't let you see the attack at all, and it breaks the immersion a bit when it happens. At least it can be disabled.In conclusion, The Lamplighters League is a game that I think could become a real gem with some fixes, but that for now remains in my mind as a game that I enjoyed dryly. While the characters and setting were what resonated with me the most, the combat isn't bad and adds some variety thanks to the abilities of each one. I didn't find the infiltration mode and stealth particularly exciting, and not being able to access the menu on enemy turns is something I almost forgot to mention... So frustrating to have to wait an entire round to be able to load or save to exit, especially in missions with dozens of enemies.It's a title that despite everything I seem to have complained about, I liked it, and its ending really moved me a little bit, since it conveys a nice message, although cliché; but, I like clichés, at least well handled. I recommend it to those who are looking for something similar to XCOM but not so much, with a mystical air and a certain charm!
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Like the X-Com series, this game is played in two parts.  A tactical, turn-based combat map portion and then a base management portion.  Each week you pick a different mission to go on, against one of 3 boss enemies called "Scions".  While your efforts impede the Scion your team engages, the other two gain influence.  Let any Scion's influence (called doomsday clock) fill up, and you lose.One interesting element of Lamplighters League is that in the tactical map, you have a real-time mode where you move around and explore.  Alert the guards to your presence, and you enter turn-based battles.  Each agent on your squad has special real-time "take-downs" which can help you in real-time mode to thin out the enemies before the turn-based battles commence.A great game, with lots of recruit-able agents, and an Indiana Jones 1930's theme.  Nice banter dialogue between your agents, level-up progressions, and strategy choices to make!
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. The first trailer I saw, I was hooked and excited to play this.Unfortunately, it fell below my expectations and struggled to reach my lowest standards.It lacks a lot of polish in many areas.The camera is janky, the action selection feels stiff and the frame rate drops a lot in random places.I can understand the direction they want to capture but it gets overthrown by the lack of attention to detail.My hope is that this game gets a serious second look at but considering their dlc is purchasing an entire character, I don't hold much hope.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, 1.5 campaigns down in like a week, and I think I'm prepared to give this a positive review.It's at the mid-point between beloved classic Xcom 2, and a bit of indie gem Renowned Explorers International Society. It has you start off with 3 folks that can feel a bit underpowered, but by the end game, no matter which combo I brought, they were able to pull off some absolutely broken combos, which I adore. There's a huge amount of ways that the bonus abilities from cards, trinkets, and your agents special abilities can combo. The mechanics are deep enough that mastery is rewarded, but simple enough that they can combine in fresh ways without you having to go "Why doesn't that work" from missing some odd sub-clause.The characters are fun, the story is pretty solid, though it faded into the back a bit. By the end I saw some maps reused a decent amount, but the enemy variety and agent abilities meant it flowed a bit differently each time.On the subject of the real-time stealth; this was the point I thought I wouldn't like before I bought it. And after playing through a full campaign, it's... fine? There are games that do it better, but it's not bad. Setting up your bruiser to take down a group of 3 enemies at a go is fun, picking off lone snipers with a sneak is tactically useful and all that. But it isn't required. More than a few missions I threw that all in the bin, went in guns blazing, and it still worked out, stealth is just a tool. I'll be playing through this a few times at least to see all the different agent combinations.Overall, very happy with it. HBS hasn't made a game I dislike yet, and here's hoping they land on their feet after all this paradox headache. Very excited for whatever they make next!
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: This could have been the greatest stealth/turn based game ever released. Instead it's a mess of bugs, unfair gameplay (eg opponents move around at will during your turn, even attacking you) and impossible tasks that just get more and more frustrating as you are 3 against 16-20 much stronger enemies that on some levels spawn more, even on the lowest difficulty setting. Then the developers dropped it after 2 patches (that didn't fix everything) and left us with a wildly disappointing game.  Such a shame and I am tired of paying for 1/2 finished games!
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY want to love this game but the controls are ♥♥♥♥♥♥. You'll be in the world map and suddenly its impossible to enter a mission. Characters will lose the ability to jog. You tell someone to move behind cover, they'll vault over it. You tell a character during battle to move to a specific point, only for the game to not let you because there's a dropped item there and your character has a full inventory so they cant pick it up and that somehow makes the square impossible to walk to?Seriously, HBS, fix the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls in your game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: The previous games made by this developer have been successful because of their writing, not their mechanics; The project leads on this one did not get the memo.Instead of focusing on the character interactions and lore, the main pull for this game are the mechanics introduced in Shadowrun: Hong Kong's Matrix sections: stealth action with turn based combat.  If you have played that game, you will know that the matrix sections are easily the worst part of the game, being tedious at best, but often just frustrating and exhausting.This game is fundamentally flawed in that the core gameplay loop is the worst part of another successful game.Apparently Harebrained suffered a series of layoffs during the development of this title, but Paradox pushed them onto the same release schedule, which would account for the low quality.  Gotta love modern game development!The only thing this game has going for it is it's art design, which while being cohesive, for no reason at all completely chugs on my mid-end PC on even the medium-low settings, struggling to put out a smooth 30fps while seemingly nothing is happening.Just a massive disappointment.Also the game crashed on me 3 times in the first two missions! Great first impression!Edit: Harebrained were released from contract right after completing the game, and due to this, the game is no longer being maintained despite it still being a mess, and I am unable to get a refund.  Don't buy this, go play Shadowrun
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: This game is mediocre. The developers took a large number of elements from XCOM 2 and put their own spin on them, with the result being an unfortunate product that is much worse than XCOM 2 in every way. It never crashed, but the game itself felt like a beta. Everything lacks polish and nothing holds together well:- The controls are quite bad. You'll be running around the world then encounter a small step and all of a sudden have to click in just the right spot to keep moving. But the rest of your team might not follow. Occasional other pathing issues. You move around with your team grouped with a "leader", but often if you move the leader up against cover the others will just stand right next to the cover and not duck.- The camera is questionable. Found myself wishing I could zoom out more or pan away from my characters. Sometimes your view gets blocked by obstacles.- The lack of tooltips is awful and really shows how little effort went into ensuring quality. When you see an item in the world (and most items just look like generic nondescript boxes or bottles), you have to move right next to it to see what it is. Very tedious. Even then you don't get told what the function is, you have to pick it up then mouse to some other tooltip (I forget where they appear and where they don't, very inconsistent) to see the function.- There are a couple "special" resources that feel very tacked on and are not explained at all. "KA" in particular is very hard to find but is required for the lower half of all "Ally" research trees. Just weird, I completed the game having gotten I think exactly 1 KA but a surplus of the other special resource.- Most items are not very useful.This is more subjective, but I found the art style, story, and characters bland and kind of irritating. It's comic book-like and really lacks any sense of darkness or dread. Also, it's just lame that they make the main "bruiser" character a slender blonde chick. She has the ability to punch through brick walls. It's PC silliness that doesn't even fit with the rest of the game's aesthetic.The turn-based combat is the heart of the game. Like everything else, it is mediocre. I'm a fan of the genre, so I played it through (max difficulty) and there were a few decent large battles towards the end. But mostly it's poorly balanced and just not that fun, totally lacks the intensity of XCOM. In general it's way too easy if you're an XCOM vet, it was only in the last third of the game that I had any difficulty at all and even then, not much.The real-time stealth element also kinda sucks, I found it just not very fun. Also it is very hard to predict how many enemies will be "activated" when you engage, sometimes you engage an enemy and only that enemy is activated, at other times (with other enemies a similar distance away) like 12 enemies will be activated. Annoying and needs better UX.All in all this just seems unfinished, unpolished, rushed to market. In theory it could be a good game, but the craft and execution just isn't there. I played it to completion but wouldn't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Long-time Xcom fan. Picked this up expecting something similar and wasn't disappointed. Characters each play unique right out of the gate and get some pretty wild skill synergies towards the endgame, personalities are very entertaining. The Realtime stealth takes some getting used to, but once you learn the nuance you can occasionally skip whole missions, so I liked it. Honestly glad the stealth isn't turn-based, cause I feel like it'd slow down the pace a lot. Biggest complaint I have is the strategic side of the game pushes you to rush to the end (even on normal) so you're likely to finish a run without even seeing half the non-starting characters (and the characters are the game's major strength). My first play through on normal took about 30 hours, but I could see replays being about 20. I unlocked 3 additional units (for a total of 6) early on and didn't have any more show up until I hit the final mission. Really enjoying my time with it though, enough to do another run on easy just to see all the characters.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: What more can I say about a game that I got 100% Achievement for? I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love this game! Can't say enough good things about it. Damn shame we wont see any new content about but this one is for the history books. If you're on the fence about getting it, hop off that fence onto the side of those who have bought and played this game. 100% Achievement is possible in one playthrough. it'll take you 60+ hours to do it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I have just completed my first run through of this game and have thoroughly enjoyed it. Admittedly it is somewhat 'unpolished' with some minor bugs,  slightly clunky interface and some balance issues (all of which would have been fixed, I'm sure, if this game hadn't been strangled shortly after birth.) However, the basic game play is quite sound and provides a fun and challenging experience. Whilst clearly influenced strongly by XCOM2 War of the Chosen, with an Indiana Jones theme (a description given by many other reviewers) there are sufficient additions and innovations to make it a good game in its own right. Such a shame it won't be developed any further.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I tried so very hard to like the game but its just so... mediocre. They did nothing with the setting, its just some brown boring theme. And the premade characters are just one/two trick ponies that quip every now and then, I cared much more about randomized characters i watched grow in XCOM than these talking pieces of cartboard.As for the gameplay, the Stealth system they lifted right out of Mutant Year Zero completely ruins the pace of the game and the encounter balance (you either have too many enemies or you thinned out the crowd too much, its  never just right)... the mechanic sucks just like it did in Mutant, why even copy it ?. The combat is pretty repetitive because enemies are not very interesting and the starvation of shared skill points means you are very encouraged to just use the early characters you leveled up not having any other choice rather than try any of the untrained guys you get later and need dozens of mission rewards to get back into a similar power levelI thought about playing more before making this review but to be honest i cant make myself to start up the game again and i just cant recommend a game that causes that kind of thing on me, there are much better games on this style out there like Showgunners or the Last Spell, go play those.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: This is actually my first review on Steam, but other reviews for this game made me hesitant to try it, so I wanted to put something out there for anyone who was like me.  There are so many reviews saying it's buggy or laggy or problematic.  I didn't experience ANY of those things.What I got was an interesting story in a supernatural world; a story of scoundrels and heroes who do what must be done to save the world.  The game is interesting, enjoyable, and on more than one occasion, I found myself up far too late to play just one more round.Was it a perfect game? No - I wish there were more events that slowed or stopped the doomsday clocks so I could have taken the time to recruit everyone, develop the entire tech tree, explore combinations of team compositions without feeling like I always had to take my BEST team just to stay ahead of the advancing enemies.  And, while the cards are a nice twist, again, there's not a full chance to explore the best combinations (partly because they are completely random), and it would have been nice if some of the late game inventory had a greater upside or upgrades that allowed you to really take advantage of builds.Still, all that being said, if you liked the tactical turned-based approach of XCOM, if you like the 30's noir style that mixes supernatural themes with retro-futurism technology, if you like lining up your enemies and knocking them down, this game is worth it if you grab it on any sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the cartoonish characters, it is a competent addition to the growing range of XCOM type games. You know the ones where you send your squad on turn-based combat missions to various places, which become very similar over time. I like the game, but with these types, I get bored after a while, returning occasionally over time, or not. 65/100
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: The game is in many ways similar to other turn based squad strategy games **cough*XCOM*cough**, where it really shines is the characters have unique personalities  and abiliities. Allows for some interesting decision making. I found the scenario to be also enticing. It is 20's occult noir with some twists and turns.Xcom with some noir occult scenario thrown in? Count me in.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: A solid 5/10. There's really no reason to dislike this game. It has a nice setting, some memorable characters and a nice, player friendly interface. Otherwise though it's completely mediocre. The meat and sauce of the genre - stealth and combat are just dull and unengaging. Maps are tiny and straightforward, with only one route towards the goal, no room for experiments. And finally the collectibles and resources are just scattered at random, for example it doesn't matter if you fight in a jungle, in the city's back alleys or in a museum hall... you just find toolboxes laying here and there. After all, not a bad game, still after a dozen hours I just lack an appetite for it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Earlier frustrated review below for reference. Assuming you can survive with only one manual save game at a time, it seems reasonably stable, with that one save (and auto saves) surviving the ongoing and occasional full system crash.I've finished the damn thing (Steam refused a refund)and, well, like most of the professional reviews.... it's ok, but not great and not what it should have been. I think my  annoyance is the promise of the aesthetic and the writing that is just let down by the overall shallowness of story and gameplay.The real time pre turn based bits are awkward and fussy, the enemies and maps repeat and become a grind and the motivations of Locke are insufficiently explained. Scraps of "Lore" are initially compelling but they don't LEAD anywhere. The final mission is underwhelming with no real emotional punch and no real closure. Characters are cartoons on screen and 2D in personality and background - you keep thinking more will emerge but it never does. All in all, it feels like the abridged, kid sized version of the game the developers wanted to make. And, sadly, because of Paradox splitting from Harebrained, it looks like there won't be the resources or investment to improve things or make a worthier sequel. _______The game crashed with a video error (full BSOD) and then deleted ALL the save games in my active campaign.I love the aesthetic and the lore, but hate that you put out something so half arsed in control mechanics and above all STABILITY. I'd love to know what happens, but I'm not starting over. Refund requested.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: To paraphrase someone else's review: a decent offering if you like the genre, but it wont sell you on the genre if you have no experience with it.EDIT: One thing I forgot with my original review. I do have a soft spot for the setting, 1930's fiction is an underused setting in my opinion and I wish it was used more often.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: It's extremely charming, I can't deny that, but that's the nicest thing I have to say about it.The Noir, early-20th-century adventure style is  and really interesting, and I just wish that the actual game I had to play to make it work wasn't really unpolished and hard to enjoy.But as it is, this is the sort of game where you boot up the tutorial, one of the  is that the camera controls are way to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fast, like, obviously "did they even play their own game?" too fast, and that's the level of polish for . I'll be honest with you, I didn't even get out of the tutorial. Even worse, I  the tutorial mission in an encounter that absolutely did not feel fair for my first time touching the game, and just kinda looked at it and said "This game isn't worth giving more chances."The setting and some of the writing are literally the only reasons I'm even considering giving this game more chances, and frankly, I'd rather ask for a Steam Refund and get my $30 back.Damned shame too, because I really like the previous games by this studio. But they  play better than this hot mess.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: This is a surprisingly good game, and I commend Harebrained Games for coming up with a fun, original title.The combat is well balanced and the story pretty engaging, although it is always hard to land entirely new lore in a compelling way in a brand new game.My favorite character is definitely Ingrid who turns into a real bad-ass by the end of the game, and I like the progression of skills and story throughout the game.This is a solid game that will give you around 60 hours of solid gameplay, although it probably doesn't have much repeat playability.The highlights are the excellent soundtrack, great voice acting and clever backstory.The lowlights are patchy performance when scrolling (even on a high-end PC), occasional bugs and a lack of variety with the enemies.Overall, I give his a 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this game. The style and theme is fun. But I believe it came out too early for release. There's clear bugs, bad stealth logic, and missing design/tooltips that could aid understanding of game elements. Maybe I'll give it a go again in the future after several more rounds of patches.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: A rough gem is the best way to describe this game. Many of the systems and designs are fun but not polished or taken as far as they could. I did enjoy my journey through it and fans of X-com can probably find lots to like. But I don't feel I need to return to it. There are more polished games with better replay value out there.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: 3 hours in and I think I have a pretty shaped opinion of this now. If you want a perfect XCOM clone, this isnt really it. XCOM meets indiana Jones in theme and style but under the hood there are some issues. I'm trying really hard to love this game by the way. the good.Its got a great style, sound track, voice acting, skill tree and ability deck. The game feels fair. The missions are adequate length and its nice how there are things hidden about the place. Theres a great hint of the occult throughout and magic is seen in places. Interacting with terrain is always a massive bonus! Love throwing electro mines in the water! The XCOM cover system works nicely, is clear and concise.The UI is nice. I have no issues with it IN COMBATTheres a lot to love.The Not so good....The stealth aspect of this game is awful. In Real time, theres a sort of hint that you should be able to setup an ambush and roll with an amazing wipeout. This game does this aspect terribly. Most of the time you will get caught beforehand from someone wandering round and you have no time to reflect on this and reloads happen. This is a big deal as it is a massive part to the game. How combats are initiated. For comparrison, Valkeria Chronicles is a real time and turn based and tackles it but better. Shadow tactics too (or the cowboy one) have the stealth and turn based aspect too. Its a real shame, because most of the game is really solid. And this isnt an easy fix, it would mean changing the fundamentals of how the game sets itself up.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I've been having a lot of fun with this. Production value is high, Art style is slick and the tactics side is not overly punishing when you make a mistake. It's kinda of a niche title and while it's not flawless, if we want to continue seeing games in this genre being made, we need to support them. While not flawless, it's easy to appreciate for all the things it does well. If you liked X-COM 2, you're probably like this too.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: A genuinely really good tactical shooter that was unfortunately screwed over by its publisher.Overall there are a lot of interesting mechanics and opportunities for strategy. It's kinda short and has lots of random elements so it has a lot of replay value. It also has some really extensive and interesting lore, along with compelling characters. I particularly enjoy the conversations your agents can have between missions. It can be sort of janky, but its not really anything that will impact your experience too much.Also, it has really good voice acting. Like, absurdly good. Look up the voice cast: one of them was the voice of Lady Dimitrescu!anyway, 10/10, would recommend, but maybe on sale cuz $50 is way overpriced
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Perfectly satisfied my urge for X-COM like combat. The story was fun, though not overly complex. The standout elements are the characters. I never thought I'd get strong characterization in a turn-based tactical game, but the voice acting and writing for the character interactions was top notch. I don't know if this game will ever get a sequel, but the world and characters are quality IP.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Overall it's pretty good, if you like the turn-based tactics genre. But it does have a lot of issues, both minor and more annoying.My biggest gripe has to do with the performance. The game seems pretty badly optimized, with lots of stuttering and freezes whenever there's a lot of movement going on in real time mode (especially with pathing, I think). Saving and reloading takes a surprisingly long time (and I couldn't find a quick save or quick load operation, if it exists). Lot of frame rate drops whenever too much stuff is getting rendered in the distance.The gameplay is pretty good, though the lack of options makes it repetitive pretty quickly. The card concept to tailor the bonus abilities on units is a pretty nice idea, though some are far more useful than others. Still, it's a pretty nice idea. That said, it's hard to justify running more than 4 agents at once; at least on Survivor difficulty, though, there isn't really time to take a breather due to how fast the clock builds up, especially near the end of the game, and recruiting an extra agent (who mostly is only useful for a little bit of additional resources per turn) simply isn't worth spending one of your 25-ish weeks on. The game starts far too easy, but the difficulty does ramp up fairly aggressively by the end, as you run into groups of over a dozen enemies at a time. The story missions are also much longer than the random ones (the latter of which are essentially 3 fights). I like the idea of the stealth focus in the game, where fighting isn't always the best options, but I feel like there really should have been better ways to allow the player to be sneaky. Having a whole swath of enemies be immune to stealth takedowns feels like it defeats the purpose of those abilities, and just encourages splitting groups to take them out one or two at a time (which again renders the stealth abilities pointless). I basically stopped using the stealth abilities about half the way through as they stopped being useful compared to simply luring enemies out of their zone to kill them individually.Despite some serious problems, it's still a pretty fun game. The characters are fairly diverse in their abilities, and I do like that melee is actually viable (arguably preferable) due to how much CC they provide. Hopefully they'll address the technical issues that hurt the gameplay experience, in which case it'll be quite a solid turn-based tactics game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: It could have use a little bit more development time to smooth out some QoL issues but I thought this was a great XCOM-like tactics game. A cool, fun setting. Interesting characters. Good music. I really like the way the different characters' abilities play out and the way you can equip them to create really powerful combos where you generate a whole lot of Action Points and wipe out the enemy team before they can even damage you.I wish there was more of a reason to recruit agents outside of the ones the game requires of you. The writing of the characters is interesting but recruiting agents aside from the starting three, a choice between two that progresses the story, and a then an optional extra kinda feels like a waste of time. Especially since the starting three characters are SO good.I'd have liked a Free Mode after you beat the game to start over with 3 Agents of your choosing. Otherwise, I don't really see myself replaying the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: 45 minutes in and completed the first two tutorial missions... then the game soft locked. Based on what I saw, the game is trying to be a consol/controller friendly introduction to Turn Based Strategy games... but presents all of the systems and information in confusing ways. _childDocuments_.review: Great game!Awesome setting. Cool and memorable characters. Charming art style. Thematically rich levels that feel like real places, instead of just like walled off battle arenas. Each hero really brings a different slate of tactics to the table, giving each encounter (and playthrough) the opportunity to feel different, depending on who you recruit and bring on missions. _childDocuments_.review: The Lamplighters League  This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements in games (minor spoilers ahead).The Lamplighters League is a tactical RPG set in a fictional world where three different factions, each with its own leader/hero, of the same Illuminati-type organization are trying to take over the work, and a benefactor and his group of lamplighter’s are the only ones standing in their way. The villains are a mix of nazi-like soldiers, cultists, ghosts, monsters and undead mixing science fiction and fantasy, science and magic, that is also present in the combat stage and the character’s abilities and attacks. The game has both real time infiltration where you collect resources and thin the herd with outside combat abilities and turn based combat, like X-COM: War of the Chosen that greatly inspired this game. The 3D engine graphics and cutscenes are good, especially in 4K with ultra graphics if you can run them. In the last level due to the number of particles and lighting effects the game crashed and I had to scale down the graphics. The characters have a slight cartoonish look and animations that took me some time to get used to, but overall, the maps, the headquarters and the environment and lighting effects look great. Unfortunately the maps aren’t randomly generated and will start to repeat themselves, although with new enemies, objectives and item locations.The voice acting is also excellent, both the lines which are consistent with the personality and profession the characters have but also the accents where you can easily spot where the characters come from even without checking the name and their appearance.The gameplay, as I’ve mentioned is healy inspired by XCOM and other similar games, but something sets it apart is the off combat abilities and the act that instead of classes of soldier and some abilities that is also a skill line for each of the heroes and also a system of extra abilities you collect during and after the missions that provide extra abilities and complement the existing ones, offering new tactical options.Given this abundance of abilities and bonuses, I advise any veteran of this kind of game to play in the highest difficulty, and even if you pick it, with the right heroes and bonus cards you can wipe even the enemy heroes in one turn and almost one shot them. SPOILER: The important thing when playing in hard mode, is thinning the herd to avoid getting overwhelmed either by using abilities or luring some enemies outside the main group. Enemy heroes in particular are very aggressive and easy to lure. Another important thing is always doing the hardest mission to get more resources and reload if needed. Mistakes can snowball and it is better to avoid them not to compromise the rest of the game, the counters will keep increasing so choosing the right missions is very important. Picking missions with enemy heroes will grant an extra bonus, but it’s better if they are in a level 2 or 3 difficulty mission or a recruitment mission.The achievements aren’t very hard but getting them in hard mode and completing the campaign might be hard to accomplish, reloading a few times before the end of the mission to get recruitment missions in the hideout. I only discovered near the end of the game that these missions appear randomly after reloads and one achievement requires getting 10 agents and picking Isaac (free DLC) prevented me from getting Fedir so I also had to start 2 or 3 campaigns to get him. I also found out that in custom games reloading won’t change the first 3 heroes the game offers you in the beginning. So even if you’re not using a particular agent, make a save, get him, and reload afterwards if needed.The achievements that require specific pairs of agents can easily be done in custom games. The guide claims the “defeat Nicastro in the tutorial” achievement is bugged but can easily be completed on easy, you just need to defeat her in two turns.          Regarding bugs there are a few ragdoll related ones once in a while, corpses flying when you shoot another target, but all minor inconveniences IMO. After saving during a mission on hard mode, the game will show “custom game” on that slot but you can ignore it as you’ll still complete the campaign and get the achievement.   41 Achievements. Around 40 to 50 hours, spent in one run + 3 or 4 to get the last agent. Not picking Issac will save some time. In hindsight I think I could have also completed the last mission a few weeks earlier. Medium, some missions will be easy others will require some trial and error.  Medium, the hardest achievement will be completing the game on hard, but it will only require a few reloads and some grinding if you build an efficient team and get the important upgrades and best cards.  The Lamplighters League is a great tactics game with excellent graphics, presentation and visual effects, and the story and characters are written and interesting. The amount of abilities and tactical options sets it apart but it’s a shame the maps aren’t randomly generated. Still, a great experience for fans of the genre IMO. .

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately there is quite an allure to this game that comes to an end at empty promises. Game play by hour 10 is stagnant which with the current systems is insurmountable. The biggest takeaway is that it would have benefited from a streamlined story. The same mission repeats over and over until you hit a major story point, at which you are confronted with a similar mission that is just longer. The warnings from the press prior to release were valid and it is such a shame to see the shell of a great game be wasted away. I would not buy at anything more than half price and only if you are ready for a 20-30 hour slog that has you asking "are we done yet". 3/10

_childDocuments_.review: The turn-based community has most definitely been sleeping on The Lamplighter's League. It is a phenomenal experience that combines a charming setting with surprisingly in-depth gameplay mechanics. Having just given up on XCOM 2 for it's overly punishing and unbalanced design, I stumbled onto The Lamplighters League and it was the perfect rebound to scratch the itch. What it does right: unique setting, established characters, and of course addictive turn-based gameplay. Each character that you unlock will feel meaningful and kitting them out with various gear and skills adds a nice progression to the mix. The gameplay really blew me away in terms of variety as I was expecting something a lot more watered down. Conventional melee and ranged weapons are combined with a number of unique powers to keep gameplay fresh and challenging. While it did feel a little too easy for the first several hours, the "Normal" difficulty ultimately offered a tough but rewarding experience.As for the negatives, there aren't many. The doomsday clock which this genre has come to embrace quite heavily was a bit unique in it's implementation but despite normally providing a sense of expediency to the world/time management, this one did the opposite. Managing each of the 3 independent clocks slowed down the main story progression in a way that felt a little grindy - with the most impactful missions not offering much in the way of tangible reward, and vice-versa. On that same topic, the number of playable heroes is relatively small and the dedicated missions to unlock said heroes barely slowed the clocks at all, making them feel not worth pursuing.Small gripes aside, this was a truly awesome experience and it deserves way more attention than it has received. Technically speaking I had almost no issues and content-wise, it's well worth the base price of $50.

Sad that Paradox parted ways with Harebrained Schemes after this came out, would of loved to see some DLC and a sequel for this.  Hopefully this game continues to find an audience and Paradox and Harebrained can work something out for more content.

_childDocuments_.review: The Lamplighters League’s stimulating turn-based battles encourage you to carefully consider your actions each turn. Use your agents unique abilities in just the right order and you can go well beyond the default number of action points, while taking down entire groups of opponents.Pairing different agents allows you to unlock ability combinations that, aside from being outright satisfying to pull off, also help even the odds, given how you’re always outnumbered.While its ambitions as a global adventure aren’t quite fulfilled, its – admittedly good – writing feels pushed to the side, and the procedural generation it employs doesn’t always keep things fresh, taking control of this group of unlikely allies and helping them save the world is well worth it..

_childDocuments_.review: Here is what I don't like:- The game's controls are clunky, you can easily miss-click and waste a "once per mission" ability. And inadvertently switch between agents by clicking on one (the guys huddle). The multishot abilities are horrible to use. The double shots usually work, but the Light them Up ability usually fires at only one target instead of six (it says to use Space for additional targets, and as soon as I hit Space, it fires at one target). Sometimes I am not allowed to pick a target by mouse and must use the keys, which leave sometimes out what I want to shoot (like an oilbarrel). - That we get no map is another highlight. - That we have to wander right next to an item to see what it is, is horribly tedious. - Not being able to switch cards between agents is the next problem. I can hand the cards only to the team that just finished a mission, but not to the agent that would profit from it.- When checking an item, you have to guess what it does, there is no description. A mouseover shouldn't have been all that hard to program I think.- There are many unexplained things. The research trees require something named K.A. in the resource bar. I have no idea what that is or how to get it. It looks as if I would get only three pieces of the metal required for the final agent upgrade - I am guessing, though, it isn't made clear either way.- The cards are a neat idea, but it is nigh impossible to get a fully upgraded team. Leaving out that I cannot upgrade to level 5 cards and am limited to level 4, it is still statistically unlikely. Upgrading a card with ink costs 512 ink between level 3 and 4. Since you get only 4 or 6 ink per card destroyed, that isn't viable. Finding another copy of the same card is possible, but not not common. And you have to either use or destroy the cards right after the mission and can use them only on the team that done it. So you may find the copy that gets you level 3 or 4, but the agent who needs it isn't on the team. - I am not a big fan of timers. And the three doom clocks are not my thing. It reads on the world screen that defeating a scion grants a large amount of threat reduction. That has amounted to exactly one point twice. The same I get without fighting the scion. It is basically like XCOM which you play with a squad of three or four agents instead of soldiers, but with uglier graphics. I think it is an actual curse that all games with a vibe of Cthulhu in it are not great.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is a tactical game similar to games like X-Com or Jagged Alliance but does not contain the same level of micro management. Playing missions is clearly the main task for the player. Tactically it offers a lot of options and if one does not work out you can always try from a different angle. That is really beneficial for any players with a low frustration level.Even though different classes exist they are very individual. So far the game has not forced me to play a certain set of characters to finish a mission. I chose whomever I liked best. The dialogues are witty and the audio in general is astonishing. I am not sure when I have encountered such a devoted atmosphere in a game lately. The visuals complement this impression.On the negative side I find the controls sometimes a bit counterintuitive, but not on a level that you cannot get used to it. The doomsday clock is unnecessary and simply reduces fun. Also saving and loading could be a bit quicker, but since the game is much more tolerant against characters getting a hit here and there, it does not matter so much.Overall I can recommend this game without restrictions.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never left a Steam review before, but I am legally obligated to for this game. I work in narrative design and Lamplighters' writing and characterization are some of the best I have seen in ANY game, including big-name RPG series. I spent the entire time wishing that I had been a part of its creation, because the devs should be INCREDIBLY proud of what they made.Personally I don't care as much about mechanics/optimized gameplay if the writing has me hooked, but even so I found very little to complain about here. There were only a couple of things that I noted, and they were incredibly minor.tl;dr - if you like turn-based strategy gameplay that's accompanied by evocative writing and distinct and consistent characterization—and ESPECIALLY if you are a fan of Indiana Jones/Atlantis/The Mummy/etc—you would be sorely missing out if you skipped this game.(and now for a less professionally-framed opinion: aaaaaaaaaaAAAAAAAAAAAA IT'S SO SO SO AAAAA)

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little strategy game where you can whittle enemies away in real time before fully engaging. Story is...fine...and the characters are okay though some are clearly overpowered. Art style is amusingly cartoony.The 'threat' concept is interesting though I always hate having a ticking clock over my head when I play the game and you'll have to play some missions just to keep it in check, not because you want to actually do that mission.Game is, unfortunately, still buggy. _childDocuments_.review: 1. The game is not bad, scoring 7/10, but the optimization is indeed lacking. With an I7-13700K + RTX4080, the FPS sometimes drops below 60 at 4K resolution.2. Bugs appear in the later stages of the game, for example: being unable to perform detection or attack actions in front of enemies.3. Characters heavily rely on cards, and the biggest issue with the cards is that they cannot be saved. This means that if a character does not engage in battles, they cannot acquire cards, and some characters are very dependent on cards for assistance, resulting in an imbalance in the strength of different characters.4. Ally NPCs have advanced to level 3 equipment slots, but not a single piece of level 3 equipment has appeared. All level 3 equipment requires participation in different battles to obtain, but due to the setting of the doomsday clock, the game progresses rapidly in the mid to late stages, causing me to not have time to rescue the two teammates that appeared, and I was unable to try out new characters, which is quite unfortunate.

_childDocuments_.review: I really am not a great reviewer here on steam, but after playing what I think is about half of the game and seeing how little attention and love it's getting, I – as an xcom and Phoenix Point veteran – just had to step up, because I immensely enjoy Lamplighters League (LL)!I will do some in depth game analyses in a second, but before that a quick pro and con:Pro:-	Story setting is just engaging, I like the 1930/40s adventure atmosphere-	The soundtrack that accompanies it, is just epic-	The English voice actors are doing a good job in setting the characters apart and I enjoy the flavor conversations-	There game has small video sequences when something important happens / the story progresses. Not in game graphic, but animated slides and video. Always a huge plus in my book, if the player gets rewarded for progressing with more than just a text box.-	The three enemy factions each have their own doom timer clock. According to their individual advancements with their plan, their unique faction will get new units and bonuses. That makes the strategy map really fun in my eyes-	Also, the three enemy factions are circled around different lore and will thus field different units. Even though they share the grunt units each faction has its own special forces that introduce new unit types the further their faction progresses. On top each faction has a unique “champion” (scion) which further sets them apart.-	There seem to be quite a few maps with different settings: reaching from the jungle to inside an archeological museum – that’s just great. Even though I have already played maps twice in those cases I had different starting points and different mission objectives, so it didn’t feel like a repeat-	Talking about different mission objectives: I have so far enjoyed the variety. Oftentimes you are recovering or sabotaging something which results in a tactical battle – but that’s what I am there for. But I just had a battle where I had to defend against enemy waves and hold a certain area – nothing spectacularly new in the genre, but so far it has been an entertaining mix-	The tactical battles have been fun so far and on the highest difficulty I had two really demanding so far.-	The character leveling and customizing works for me (But more on that in detail at the end)-	It is just a different take on the genre that is a real interesting mix between elements from the turn-based tactics genre (xcom, jagged alliance 3, etc).Con:-	The graphics is of course average at best and the cartoonish style is as always an attempt to hide that. It is no AAA production after all. -	There are certain interface decisions that are a turn off. Much like in xcom 1 you cannot see character debuffs on your characters but have to open another window for that. I hope this gets a do over, because that isn’t very 2023.-	All in all I enjoyed a good release, there are some bug and polish issues.-	Day 1 DLC release cash grabRecommendation:-	From what I could gather from the media, the publisher already dropped the developing studio because the launch did not meet expectations. So even though the game will receive some more bug fix support, it is reasonable to assume that no big tweaks or future content is coming. So the game pretty much is what it is, however if you are into the genre at all I would still highly recommend dipping your toe into the water in the first sale or so.Still not satisfied? Still wondering how it compares to xcom? Let me try to outline that for you:This game isn't the new xcom, but nothing ever really is and imho there is good reason to doubt that even the next xcom, will be the next xcom (in regards of living up to expectations) - but that is another discussion. LL handles classes and skills different from xcom, but as I will elaborate that is a huge upside in my opinion, because I don’t need a bad xcom clone. And even though I have played a lot of Xcom, I gotta say: Xcom offers you a lot of choices concerning gear etc, but a good chunk of that you will never use, because it doesn't compliment your play style. So even though it offers a lot of customization options, you probably never used half of them. From where I am standing LL has streamlined these more unrealistic options, so I am not missing too much. The big difference is, that LL introduces characters instead of random soldiers and this design choice cascades into a lot of game mechanics:- It allows the game to be a bit more story driven and have a bit more character flavor (good thing obviously!). - Each character has a unique weapon and a unique skill tree. So even though you still have classes (bruiser, sneak and saboteur) each of the 2-3 available characters per class are still unique. For example even though Lateef and Purnima are both sneak-class characters, they play totally different in a tactical mission: While lateef is a midrange shooter relying on evasion to dodge enemy attacks, Purnima does not have as many defensive abilities, but she doesn't need to, because she and her sniper rilfe can just hang back from the rest of the squad. -The characters are further set apart because each one has a unique special ability: While Lateef can deploy a decoy which forces enemies to attack it, Purnima has a mighty ricochet shot that can hit multiple enemies. Since your squad is limited to three characters you will always have to weigh which characters (special) abilities you value most. - The characters different play styles are further engrained by their unique skill trees, that cater to their abilities. Ultimately you will level through the whole skill tree of a character, so there is no real lock out along the lines of “if I take this ability, I cannot have that one.” This may seem like a huge restriction, but for me it feels totally fine, because this sets a game apart. Purnima has a background story that ties her to her sniper rifle, why would she part with it to become a gunslinger? If you want one, just use Lateef or Eddie which are characters that center around that playstyle. All in all the whole squad building with characters that have fixed skills and strengths reminds me more of Jagged Alliance 3 than xcom. But like I said, that feels totally fine because it sets the game apart.-But the characters class isn’t obsolete since each class has a unique function on the tactical map (the Bruiser can break down walls, the sneak characters can climb and the Saboteurs unlock doors) the characters skills are not the only things to consider: If you don’t have a saboteur in your squad valuable resources you could have gathered will remain unavailable to you. So squad building forces you to make decisions.-And if that isn't enough for you: There still is a way to individualize your characters. Each character has slot for bonus abilities (which is implemented via cards you find on missions) so you can further develop each character by giving them up to three different skills that are not in their standard arsenal. There is a variety of options (have at least seen a dozen or so) that come in three different levels, so each skill can be leveled up for stronger effects. Also your characters have slots for trinket, armor and a weapon. All of that might not reach the customization levels of xcom or Phoenix point, but there is still plenty of room to tinker around. TL;DRThe character centered gameplay sets it apart from the genre defining title xcom and as I said, that is not necessarily a bad thing. There is less squad and weapon customization then in other titles, but you do not need it, because each character already plays vastly different anyway. It is a different take on a beloved genre and one that I really enjoy – and you might as well!

_childDocuments_.review: I've really enjoyed the game so far. It marries a setting and tone that I love with a gameplay that I really enjoy, and I've had a great time revealing more of the story and seeing new dynamics form in gameplay with ability unlocks and map features.There certainly are some downsides: I think that tooltips could be more clear, and I am never a fan of the Paradox-standard Day 1 DLC. But, the game shines for me regardless, and I foresee myself spending a lot of time in this world, with these characters.I recommend fans of either genre (be it X-Com-style play or Adventure Pulp Setting) to snag this. Not only is the game a lot of fun to dive into, but the art style is endearing and solid, and Everist's score really shines. Go save the world, and get paid!
