_childDocuments_.review: i will get to the point straight away, here are the key takeaways from this game- The camera FIGHTS you. When you select an ability, you are forced to cycle through targets unless they are in frame for you to click on, but the camera decides the beast angle for you. - There is a weird ghosting that I have seen in some maps that was not present on the one in the gameplay, but it is severe occasionally. - The concept and the setting is very enticing. Everything is also fully voice acted which I very much appreciate. - Although they play very differently, there are 3 classes. The brawler, the saboteur and the sneak.- Speaking of sneak, the stealth in this game is not very intuitive and not very inspiring either. - Most of the time you can only bring 3 agents with you in each mission. - You must balance doing missions to reduce the threat level for each of the 3 factions you are fighting, and doing other missions to secure a bigger roster by recruiting people. - The game retails for 50$ which in my opinion is not justified. Here is why:If there were not a plethora of other options in this genre that are nearly excellent at what they do, then this would be a no brainer. If you LOVE the turn based genre and you are in dire need of new games to play, this can be a very viable choice. But there are other options out there that come to mind first when thinking of turn based games, and they are both better at their execution as well as their price tag.Steam Curator: Once more, a perfectly fine game to grab on a steep discount, but by no means something you should consider over the competition, unless you have completed the competition and you have that scratch to itch.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: A good little squad tactical with heart and a twist.  Important to understand, the crew before you (the ones that are dead) tried the straight up fight and this is the aftermath.  Facetanking this game is not the way, this isn't a place for a fair fight.  Great setting, and music.  Limited map selection and sometimes the setup is a bit on the nose for... everything going on in today's world.  If it hadn't been rushed out the door we'd have seen another classic.  Given the release and support, there are some pacing, game-play, and tutorial pieces that don't fit quite right (e.g. stress breaks and action economy needed an introduction)
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Top tier voice acting, world building, music, character writing and animations.But the gameplay just doesn't quite work. In the early game its intriguing. The combat/stealth hybrid creates variety within each mission. But by the late game, the opportunities for stealth become non-existent. There are too many enemies watching every nook and cranny.The character upgrade system is also pretty barebones. Characters have 3-4 powers that can be upgraded overtime and a few buff abilites. That's it. Enemy variety is there but combat often feels the same because you don't have any new powers to try.Maybe more variety in characters would help, but good luck trying to recruit everyone. Your enemies have a timetable that increases their power and if the timetable reaches its zenith, you lose. So you have to pick and choose who to join your cause. Which is cool, until the repetitiveness kicks in.Mission variety is not there either. Only 3-4 missions exist in the game and while enemy placement can change, it isn't enough to change your strategy. Missions can and do repeat on the same levels too. So that too can add to the repetitiveness.Its really disappointing, because the setting and presentation are so unique and engaging. You will hear compelling stories from the characters for hours between missions and it never gets old. The music is perfection, lifting you up when you win, ramping up the tension in key moments while a subdued melody swells at the base. It kept me playing as long as I did.But the gameplay grows stale. And after awhile I wanted a movie of these characters rather then this video game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I'm a fan of Harebrained's Shadowrun games, which this borrows the combat from.There are a lot of weird technical problems I ran into, such as clicking on one model only for the game to register another model. This often spells death for a tactics game and having to reload an old save.I'm not a big fan of stealth, but just when I started to get the hang of it the game overloads the board with enemies immune to the mechanic. Why are there even stealth sections, then?Much like other folks on here, I had some glitches and corrupted save files. The game also received its last patch before I bought it, which makes the future of it look pretty grim.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like it's heavily inspired on XCOM 2 War of the Chosen, including 3 'boss' enemies that you encounter on missions and the need to stop timers by doing missions. I loved XCOM, and this game provides a fresh story, setting and a few new ideas. So that's a positive for me.The thing that I'm missing so far though is difficulty. Your characters are very strong and flexible. Enemies are really easy to control and overall pretty dumb. So far it hasn't felt like I'm in anywhere near the same kind of danger as in XCOM. You don't really have to worry about engagement setup as much and can pretty much fight yourself out of any situation. Without that threat the missions don't feel as satisfying. Hopefully it will get harder as the story progresses.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Game is buggy. After playing 18 hours and I'm supposed to be in the "endgame", I'm unable to proceed as it won't show the "last mission". From some research, it seems like the game doesn't know I've collected the prerequisites to begin the last mission, despite giving me the dialog that I've collected all 4 parts as well as the other 3 parts required.So if you want a game that you can't complete due to a game breaking bug, along with save file corruption, this is that game. Otherwise don't bother buying or playing this game. It had so much potential but its just too broken.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Great expectationsFirst of all, it's a good game. If you like XCOM and tactical genre. i finished game on my steam deck from the second try.In my opinion game have several problems: 1) most of the time you don't have a chance knock out some enemies before start the battle through unique characters powers. 2) Problem with the difficult. After 1/3 of the game difficult rise above the sky, BUT if you do not have a good team.3)Overpowered characters. When you realized that some characters way to overpowered than other, you are going to beat the game. My team (Ana sofia+Eddi+Engrid) beat enemies without a sweat, like dr. Manhattan against smartest termites.4)Story line. Its very interesting at the beginning, but becoming less and less exiting. Ending is disappointing. I like graphic style, music, entourage and the characters. I do not regret completing the game, but wish it was a little better. To bad its failed in sells.7.5/10 On the steam deck: low graphic settings and 20 fps limit.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I love tactical games and Harebrained Schemes makes some of the best in the industry. This game has been wonderful so far. The mechanics are rock solid, but not cliche. The Undrawn Hand, a suite of interesting items, and the range of character abilities mean that every squad and mission loadout present you with unique and impactful tactical choices. The characters are lively, fully voice acted, and have deep backstories that you get to explore the more you play. The theme of the game is on-point with a beautiful pulp-y 1930s exploration motif - a la Indiana Jones or Eldritch Horror. I am a little over half way through the game and I have even enjoyed the variety of mission types from supply pilfering, assassinations, monument destruction, heists, rescue missions, and operation disruptions. If you are the kind of person who really loved XCOM but wish it had more character development and sass - this is the game for you. If you are the kind of person who loved Shadowrun but wish there was more gameplay flexibility (real-time infiltration) - this is the game for you. If you are the kind of person who just really needs a little escapism from the harsh realities of this world - I can wholeheartedly endorse this game. I really hope more people play Lamplighters League to experience the fun I have. I have had 0 performance issues. The game is beautiful. The story is deep. The studio made a great quality game and it deserves that recognition. :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Lamplighters League is an excellent addition to the turn-based combat genre, and it has a mixture of real-time strategy thrown in. You'll find yourself sneaking around the map, trying to kill an extra enemy or two before the tactical fight kicks in. The maps are manageable, with 2 to 3 fights on each one. So if you fail one, you'll only lose about a half hour if you don't save during the middle of it, which is allowed. You can save anywhere in the game. Between missions, you'll be able to upgrade your agents and listen to the banter between them. The humor throughout the game is awesome. I can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: They really nailed the Jules Verne / Indiana Jones Atmosphere. Especially with the great soundtrack.Combined with a tactical gameplay, that - despite not being as complex as in XCOM2 - gives lots of cool choices to the player, makes this my personal game of the year.Having played more than 30 hours, i have yet to encounter a single crash... so i guess I got a bit lucky there.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. It is very more-ish and you constantly catch yourself wanting to play just one more mission. I hope this does well for the team. I can only recommend it, as the characters are interesting and have really nice build in area of synergy. I still have to master the card mechanic and I bet there is still lots more to see. Really great game, go play it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome! The difficulty might be somewhat lower than XCOM 2, but the story does intrigue you in such a manner that you want to keep playing. The game is not perfect, maybe a tad imbalanced at points and the controls a tad awkward at times. However the game deserves much more credit than in currently gets, it is much more polished than the negative critiques want to imply, and is overall very much fun!
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this one, I was hesitant from the mixed review, but the mythos is very cool, the combat is good, there are a lot of tactical possibilities and different mixes of people.  What I find especially cool is, as a player of Cultist Simulator and Library of Hours this one feels like it fits perfectly into that universe.  I like thinking that I'm playing out these battles while the Exile is Exiling and the Librarian is Librarianing.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: It's good. I don't need to explain in details the premise, you know what you're getting into, it's delightful. The gameplay is X-Com (or shadowrun: hongkong) style cover-based turn-based class-based combat, combined with real-time stealth stuff where you can eliminate the enemies one-by-one first or prepare your agents' location first before you initiate combat. But even if you don't do the real time part, if you're used to x-com style turn-based strategy you can eliminate all the enemies no problem. There's a lot of environmental interaction you can take advantage of, water you can electrify, oil you can burn, barrels you can shoot. You probably need to grind side missions so you can get money for your agent's consumables or upgrading their equipments, there's nothing too wild there. Problem is that the interface is really clunky and finicky, not a good combination with real-time gameplay. I keep getting ambushed by the enemies because I was wrestling with the interface in real time, which is a shame because that means I didn't get to use a lot of the set up provided by the map.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: "3.6 roentgen, not great, not terrible."This one isn't bad. But not good either.The setting is maybe the only part that's completely positive. Everything else is just mediocre or worse. The story isn't interesting. The two halves of the core gameplay don't make a whole. And it's incredibly repetitive.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: This should be a success but PDX is already writing it off as a $22.7m lossThis takes MANY MANY ideas from XCOM War of the Chosen and throws it into a unique setting and adds in a couple new mechanics to make it a bit more original. The Game is fun, The VA do really well, and the story is interesting. A pity some short sighted bean counters are going to neuter any chances for it to really shine with DLC and QoL patches because the core foundation here is really solid.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: 64 hours of play at the time of this review.If you are a hardcore XCOM/XCOM-2 player with a solid understanding of the genre, than this game is perfect for you. A 1920's style strategic masterpiece in my opinion.As a veteran of the genre, I picked up on the game's rules and mechanics very quickly and finished the campaign on survivor (legend) difficulty on my very 1st run (ending on week 33).I gotta tell ya, this game puts your wits to the test as you are sometimes placed under impossible odds with enemies numbering anywhere between 5 and 20 facing your 3 or 4 agent squad.That is, if you managed to botch your infiltration in order to minimize the enemy troops or went loud too early.The sneaky aspect of the game takes getting used to, but IS KEY to high level victory. It is even possible to finish entire missions without going loud (engaging combat) at all (not all missions - some have built in scenes that force combat). I would add that the strategic management of the world map is very key to a successful 'survivor' difficulty run. You do not have enough time to dilly dally and the villains threaten to reach victory as early as weeks 25-30 if you are not careful. Unfortunately, there is no 'iron-man' mode here (although there should be in my opinion for those in need of serious challenge) so it is possible to save scum your way out of super sticky situations.As for combat, with crazy combo capabilities between the agents squad, the tech trees, and most importantly the undrawn hand cards, you can pull off amazing heists and triumph in the face of impossible odds.I highly recommended the base game. As for the Nocturne DLC, I would not recommend buying it as agent Nocturne is one of the weakest if not the weakest member of the bunch I managed to recruit and I did not manage to find a strong enough synergy between her and other team members in survivor.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I was so hopeful. The price drop encouraged me to buy this game, and you can feel that it was a great idea that was never completed. For example, someone surely understood after a while that fights in which the agents get no xp and no benefits would become something players would wish to avoid. Alas, the stealth system of this game doesn't really allow for this to happen. Fights are useless, best-avoided, if at all possible. I'm luring enemies away from their teams and trying to kill them in isolation, but this is just a waste of time. The best thing about it is the combination of agents and special abilities they gain through Cards. This creates great replayability. However, again, the main loop of fight/gain isn't there. You gain something from finishing the map, whether you killed 1 enemy, 20, or 50. You just work harder.Really sad this will never be properly "patched" to a sort of 2.0 version where core loops are improved.Play it for the promise of what it could be, not for what it is. Use WeMod whenever it gets tediously boring to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: For a game priced as a AAA game, expectations are set very high, but overall The Lamplighter's League is enjoyable and addictive. I particularly appreciate the Indiana Jones-like setting, which is a fun and underutilized backdrop for world-building. However, it does have its shortcomings:Cons:- I wish there were more playable characters, strategies, and abilities. The game lacks depth and diversity in its strategic elements.- I encountered occasional bugs in gameplay. Notably, my characters would become unable to use the 'move' ability unless I hard-reset the game.- Battles can be quite demanding even on normal settings. Simple mistakes are difficult to recover from, often leading to relying on frequent save scumming for thorough gameplay.Pros:- The game offers a significant amount of potential playtime, with hours and hours of missions to keep players engaged.- The world-building is charming, featuring fun characters and boasting quality voice acting.- The battles strike a good balance between complexity, skill, and playability.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I personally like this game, its setting and the atmosphere being shaped by an eldritch background. The graphics style representing the 1920's-1930's (if I'm right) adds to the atmosphere as well as the very good voice acting. There is mystery all around which is enough to let me want to know more and to find out what is behind everything. The characters have their own skill trees, tarot cards add to the mystery and the character abilities - don't want to spoil anything so I stop going into details here...My system:Processor: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X 8-CoreGraphics-Card: Nvidia Geforce RTX 3070, Driver Version 537.42OS: Windows 10Considering other reviews:Some negative reviews have been posted after play times of less than 2 hours - some even after 0.5 hours. Those cannot represent a well balanced impression. Other reviews are negative because of reasons I did not encounter or cannot share, e.g.:- stuttering and fps drops ( I had no such problems - maybe they should update their system and graphics driver)- bugs (played several missions and didn't encounter any bug so far)- path finding problems (sometimes characters follow a non-optimized path - no big deal though)- someone complained and gave a negative review because of a missing 'quick save' button - really?- some complain because of the 'Day One DLC' - well, then don't buy the DLC... (there are a lot of characters in the game and I think it is not a cut out of content if one single character is provided by a DLC - you can play the whole game without it)- some reviews complain about the key-controls and their default settings (you can easily change every key to your liking in the options)- some reviews complain about overwhelming enemy numbers, a bad stealth system and a useless recon system (to better use the recon system: un-group, let one character advance, recon and then you'll see the enemies positions and useful environment without risking the whole team, use the strike from behind and other abilities and you will not find anything overwhelming)Concerning turn based combat rules and combat flow this game obviously took a lot of good ideas from other games like Xcom, Marvel-Midnightsuns, Battle Tech (The gathering of characters and their conversations remind me of the briefings on the bridge) and more. They also were inspired by those games concerning movement and combat controls, game play, dialog(-system) and a few other things.There are some drawbacks, e.g. the reduced number of items the characters may carry and therefore have to leave behind equipment they've found during a mission and maybe later have to buy the same things by investing supplies.All in all I encountered few drawbacks but instead had a lot of fun with this game.I recommend this game to players who like Xcom related turn based combat, mystery, eldritch, good voice acting, 1920's to 1930's mission environment represented in some kind of comic graphic style (which is surprisingly fitting to this setting). Maybe the full day one price of 49$ is a bit high, though.EDIT: I've encountered an annoying bug with Ingrid - sometimes after she'd attacked an enemy and thereby was spending the first AP she suddenly can only target her team mates with the attack on the 2nd AP. If you let her do something different at that point, a healing for example, everything is working fine afterwards, but you had to spend the AP on something you didn't want her to do...
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: The Mummy meets XCom. If you like Pulp-era adventure and tactical turn-based combat, you'll love this. Like either one, you'll still almost certainly enjoy it. Great atmosphere, flawless period soundtrack, good voice work, unique characters, solid combat system, and a fairly straightforward, but well-executed narrative. With a bit more polish from a few rounds of patches, this will be a real gem.Cons: Recon Mode stutters. The "Hero Cam" still needs work. Occasionally taking a position that leaves you unable to see what actually happened. The last of these can be turned off. But it shouldn't have to be. I've heard of more serious bugs, but haven't experienced them. And I'd put both of these in the "minor annoyance" level. The Day 1 DLC is disappointing. I wasn't a fan of Midnight Sun or Mass Effect cutting off characters and dropping them behind a paywall. Not a fan here either. The price might be a tad high. But then again, Jagged Alliance 3 dropped at the same price. And they're comparable in style and production quality. So if it's high, it's high across the board. Overall, I give it a soft buy at present. If you're sure the premise and gameplay would hook you, get it. If you're not, wait for a sale and take a chance on it then.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: There's a good game in there but it still needs some work. Currently the balancing is off in regards to the doomsday clock and the stealth isn't quite there yet, with enemies alerted to any action far to quickly requiring the player to trick the AI with exploits rather than skill. That said the characters plus art style are great and the faults could be fixed with a couple of update. Recommend holding off on purchase for now until fixed so not to spoil the experience
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game. Good story so far.Exploration feels like Phantom DoctrineCombat plays like Jagged Alliance 3Mission Prep is very similar to XCOM Chimera SquadThe one takeaway I had was not being able to use the instant kill knock out abilities when outside of combat and in turn-based mode. Even though, some enemies are immune to these abilities, the devs could've still allowed them to be used while not revealed. Still, I do enjoy games like JA3 that try to mix real time and turn based modes when in and out of combat.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game, I really do. I am a complete sucker for The Pulp Fiction 1900s setting the this game had it all with scifi ghosts, lovecraftian death cults, and even a Not Nazi in the mix. Unfortunately the for some very stupid reason the game is not built to let you enjoy it. The difficulty is not a problem, if you played tactical rpgs before you can take on any tactical challenge with not too much problem. No, the worst thing about this game is how to rush you at every single point. There will be no time at all to learn it. No time to get new agents. No time but to rush the main mission or suffer a slow 20+ hour death spiral before you realize that even if you played perfectly, you will lose because 2+ Scions will reach the tower in one week. Do yourself a favor and listen to the publisher, This game is a 22 million dollar loss.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Woah - this is not very good. I played it for 39 minutes only but I knew I wasn't going to enjoy it. The game makes odd choices. The idea is basically that each character has a role in the group. The thief picks locks, the brute can punch down walls. Yet there was one scene where the thief had to open a door, yet he got to the door by effectively climbing over the side via a climbing net. Which begs the question why the other character could not do the same. I then sat there wondering why the thief just didn't pick the lock but had to open it from the other side. Very strange choice.When you move through the game environment and not in combat, you move in real time. The designers decided to ration character abilities in this section to two uses. All this does is limit stuff you can do. (You can only knock out 2 guards if you are the thief for example. Or use a brawl ability twice if you are the bruiser) Actual turn based combat was also very unsatisfying. You can't use those cool abilities that we just spoke of for a start. Your characters are stuck (at this level I suspect) with basic abilities like move and attack. The first battle was not a good intro to the game. It pits the heroes against 4 gun-toting goons and incredibly one of your characters has brought fists to a gun fight. Meaning one character is relegated to being the closer and the other has to soften them up. Which is fine until you remember that you are up against 4 and the action economy here is very much against you. What was also against me was the curse of xcom. A dice roller that keeps missing. All in all it led to a very unsatisfying intro. The game didn't do much to draw you in to the story either. That was enough for me to check out the rest of the game. Not enough to hold my interest. Odd game design choices. Poorly thought out combat. Shame. I really wanted a 1930s style pulp adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Cool concept, poorly executed. Too many reasons to list on why it was close but falls short. Harebrained Schemes makes some amazing games. I have a feeling this was all Paradox that ruined it. If only Harebrained could acquire the rights to Shadowrun again and make more of those games. Those were where they truly shined.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Profoundly disappointing.   The bar was set pretty high for Harebrained Studios, based on their superb BATTLETECH and Shadowrun adaptations.   I still play BATTLETECH weekly, all these years after its release, for example.That said, this game is merely mediocre.   The obvious point of comparison would be XCOM, if you took away the base management, research, compelling narrative, and squad management elements.    XCOM and XCOM2 would both be fairly mediocre with those redactions, as well.The presentation was fairly polished, but it didn't amaze.   The music was good enough to be unobtrusive.   I think that this title was a miscalculation by HBS:  Their real strengths have been adapting others IP.   Lamplighter's League demonstrates that creating a compelling universe, whole cloth, is beyond them at present.  It was pointed out to me that HBS skipped Battletech 2 to do this game.   A decision that was driven largely by the cost of licensing the BATTLETECH IP.   They should have kept the license. Disappointing, I'm sure, for the investors.No way is this worth $50.   At a $15 price point, it would be a good value.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: A very atmospheric adventure in the 1930s in the style of Indiana Jones. The game is very addictive, excellent story. Unfortunately, there are only 3 agent classes. And in general there are a lot of simplifications. But despite this it is interesting to play. I had great fun. I recommend.GOOD:✔️Engaging Story: The narrative is rich and captivating, drawing players into an enchanting world filled with mysteries and secrets.✔️Atmospheric✔️Turn-Based Combat✔️Skill TreeBAD:❌Too Simplified❌Grouping - Ungrouping
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: After playing a few hours in this game I feel like I need to warn other people. I'm not the most diligent on GPU driver updates, but after the game crashed 3-4x I went ahead and made sure nothing was an issue on my end, and the game continues to crash on even the first couple of missions. It's fun at the beginning, but it got boring very fast as character develpment is boring and not really add much in the later game. I "only" played it for 14 hours but i already got bored after 5 and it did not became better. _childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Having just finished my first playthrough of The Lamplighters League, I can confidently say it's a highly enjoyable adventure that seamlessly blends real-time strategy with turn-based combat. The mix of Indiana Jones-esque exploration and XCOM-style tactical elements kept me hooked from the start to the final chapter. While there were some performance hiccups and balancing issues (difficulty ramps up quickly and then towards the end, it sporadically gets easier and harder), they didn't overshadow the game's captivating lore and memorable characters. It's a shame it didn't receive adequate post-release support, but even as it stands, it's a gem of a game that's definitely worth diving into.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Theres a lot of 'good' here. The art style is well done, the characters are unique, interesting, and have depth. Voice acting is solid. The 'Indiana Jones' style to how the story is played out and presented is fun and vibrant. Overall this was pretty solid. If I had to cherry pick some 'cons' I would say that it felt a little too easy for me. By mid game Ingrid and Sawyer could basically solo a full map without any stealth clears (and, in fact, did once). Celestine can basically give herself infinite AP as well. Combat in general lacked some kind of...pull. It was mainly kick this, punch that, shoot this. Rinse repeat. Tactically it is very straight forward and if you can get stress breaks, they're free kills. XCom this is not (though Celestine does somehow miss a surprisingly large amount of 90% throws that others do not...).Would definitely give this a go if you're a turn-based/tactical guy. I know it got a bad rap at launch but this played well, was bug free, and a good solid 30-40 hours of playtime. Check it out.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I will give this a positive rating.  It is a good game, yet I feel that it is less than the sum of its parts.  The obvious comparison is that of XCOM and XCOM2.  I find the game to be less enjoyable, but I struggle to define why.  I think a major part of it is the story.  I am so over the "end of the world" story lines.  It doesn't feel believable to me.  Saving a princess is a realistic achievement, as is trying to defend earth from aliens.  Neither of those are end of world scenarios, although they have large personal stakes.  They try to make the individual agents personable, but I guess it is a little lacking as nothing truly ever bad happens to the agents.  For example, if an agent could lose a loved one, depending on player actions, it might make them more real.  Instead, they give a lot of decent backstory, but after you understand the end game goals of the game, the game just follows a pattern until the end.  Rinse and Repeat.  The game has pacing issues too - the missions take over an hour to complete - I wish that they were a bit faster.  Certain parts of the game could use some changes.  You can buy supplies in the game, but in the end the items you find are better, and I find myself taking lots of items out of the mission instead of buying supplies to send agents in with.  So at the end, I have a ton of money and nothing to spend it on.  There is also the stress mechanic.  You have 2 ways of defeating an enemy.  Taking hit points to 0 through regular attacks, or doing enough stress attacks that they have a stress break, and a coup de grace attack instantly kills them.  Decent idea, however, there is no advantage of one approach to another.  It would be better if some mobs were high hp, low stress, and others were low hp and high stress, so that you can strategize with one type of attack or another.  But instead, as mobs scale in hit points, they also scale in stress resistance, so there really isn't an advantage of focusing on one over the other.There are other parts of the game that are great and make replayability a good option (I have played through the game twice).  Agents are very different, and when combined together can result in radically different play styles.  The undrawn hand cards also give powerful abilities to your agents, and there are a ton of them, so you are unlikely to have the same setup on your agents between campaigns.
_childDocuments_.name: The Lamplighters League

_childDocuments_.review: First things first: I played tactics games since the 1990s, I beat the newest XCOM/XCOM2 and JA3 on the highest difficulty settings on ironman. That's not boast, but give you a little background on my experience as a player and how to judge my very positive review:So let me first say, back when the game was released, everybody was playing BGIII. As was I and I totally overlooked this beautiful (yet unfortunately a little unpolished) gem of a game. I thought BGIII was my game of the year 2023, but this game is a very, very strong contender. If you buy this and expect a run-of-the-mill XCOM-clone you WILL be bitterly disappointed. Yes, there is a world strategy layer, but compared to XCOM there's no base building. Yes, it's mainly a turn-based tactics game, but it additionally has a little bit of real-time stealth gameplay, which in itself is fine and workable, but could be fleshed out more. Don't expect to be able totally stealth missions, you are not supposed to. But thinning out the herd before smashing it in TBT-G is satisfying enough. It is a turn-based tactics game first and foremost. But it somehow plays totally different to XCOM to me. You don't have your standard JOE/JANE DOE characters which get assigned a class with generic powers or abilities. Instead, you get fleshed out unique agents, each with its own unique set of skills and powers. Where as in XCOM you often MIN/MAX different classes for best outcome, here the biggest question is, which agent suits your preferences and compliments your team of 3/4 agents, with which you battle your enemies in the field. So, once you start the turn-based combat every encounter produces a new puzzle for you to solve: How to kill/beat the most enemies each round given the abilities of your agents most effectively (there basically is no hunkering down, you have to take the initiative). In XCOM I found myself playing very defensively, whereas here you almost have to play aggressively.  For me it's a very welcome change of pace.As I said, strategically your only choices, since there is no base building, are what missions to take, so you can hold out and do the critical missions to progress the story.  Yes, there is not only ONE doom clock but THREE, one for each opposing faction. What I don't get, is the complains about the clocks being unfair. If your strategy game is lacking, or it is too stressful for you, play the game on a custom difficulty level with lower difficulty settings for the strategy layer and higher for the combat? The game is supposed to be hard und you are supposed to feel like the time is running out. Would you rather prefer an Indiana Jones/Super-Hero crossover movie, where the heroes have all the time in the world, or rather one where the stakes are high?It will be close, and sometimes you will be facing the question, whether to do two prepare missions before the actual critical heist mission or take your time, but for me that's part of the fun. Let me assure you, that unless you totally ♥♥♥♥ up in the strategy layer, the game is (easily?) beatable at the highest difficulty level. And there is my next point: I also don't understand the griping about the difficulty level in general. Yes, at the highest level, the game throws tons of enemies at you, but if you are careful and recon the levels/set pieces and try to thin the herd first, you should rarely run into total wipes, especially if you are familiar with other turn-based games. (Tip: Save between the set pieces during the missions).I believe the most difficult thing is, to choose the right team to do the job. And here comes the next awesome thing, that makes this game stick out of the crowd of XCOM-Clones. It has a mechanic called undrawn hand. The undrawn hand are Cards with certain passive or active abilities that you get for finishing missions and can permanently assign to you agents. You can build massively overpowered synergies in-agent and team-wise. (At the end of the game, Ingrid was running around the field batting every enemy death like the hammer of Thor!) At the beginning you start with 3 agents; you can recruit more during your play. Each agent skills can be upgraded, so choose your team wisely! This makes the game exciting and fresh every time. You can also recruit 3 allies, which I highly recommend doing, who upgrade your stats for you whole team or give you very strong items. Only if you combine all three: team-synergies, agent upgrades and the right allies upgrades you will be able to beat the game. The learning/difficulty curve for me was very steep at the beginning of the game, but once you field 3/4 fully upgraded agents with good and high-level undrawn hand cards and good items, you will be nearly unbeatable. Just remember that you are supposed to use everything in your arsenal during the missions (especially in the beginning)!What I really love about this game, is the 1930s setting, the world-building (through Notes), the phenomenal soundtrack and Incredibles-like art style of the game. I just love it; it goes together so well and is fresh a new for a XCOM veteran like me. It actually draws me in and makes the stakes so much higher for me personally.At the end let me clarify what I meant with unpolished in the first paragraph: I actually did not run into any bugs (game breaking or otherwise). Please consider that I just recently bought the game in the Steam Summer Sale, so it was all patched up and I keep my system up-to-date with newest HW & SW. With unpolished I meant, that you can feel, that some corners where cut to either budget restrains or the pressure to release. The LL interactions could be animated more, the stealth could be fleshed out more, the levels could be more varied. Better animated cutscenes (like the intro) would have made the game feel more special than it already is. I believe if Paradox would have given Harebrained more resources or alternatively more time to finish the game, it would have benefitted the reception greatly (less bugs at release, more polish, better release window). It's a real shame Harebrained and Paradox hat a falling out and there won't be any successor to Lamplighters League. I need more of the good stuff.All in all, I have to say, that I really love this game and prefer it to the newer XCOMs and JAIII. Reading the reviews, I started the game expecting a challenge. a bug fest and mediocre gameplay, but was totally surprised by how good this game can be. I was totally sucked in by the world building and intriguing and at times very difficult gameplay. I had to face difficult decisions and there were many close calls, especially at the beginning, but when finishing this game in week 40 with 4 totally upgraded agents I was wiping the floor with the Banished court. My campaign lasted around 35 hours and I was grinning the whole time! I can wholly recommend this game to any tactic aficionado out there!TLDR; game good, much buy! PS: For beginners I can recommend the "Beginners Guide" in steam works, it helped me in the beginning to understand the gameplay mechanics, since the game itself is a little bit stingy on information.PPS: English isn't my mother tongue, so if you find weird grammar, syntax, typos, or otherwise, good for you! ;)Regars, WW

_childDocuments_.review: Lamplighter's League is basically if XCOM and Indiana Jones had a baby and if said baby had a cartoony artstyle; and that's a good thing. The stealthy takedown stuff is straight from Mutant Year Zero: Road to Eden (another great game for XCOM fans) and is a nice way to spice up the XCOM formula.The story is nothing to write home about but the characters more than make up for it, with each one having some entertaining dialogue with other characters. The playable characters have fun and varied personalities and the "Scions" aka the bad guys are a bit campy but not in a bad way. The artstyle is very stylish, looks unique, and combos very well with the story, vibe, and gameplay of Lamplighter's League.Gameplay is where This game REALLY shines, with about a dozen unique characters with their own personalities, abilities, and passives. There are also a good amount of equipment, consumables, and Undrawn Hand cards (the best part of the customization by far) to make each playthrough/team composition unique. The enemy designs and their abilities are also very nicely varied; giving a good amount of fodder to shred with your broken as heck endgame team. The Undrawn Hand is somewhat RNG-dependant when it comes to what cards you draw at the end of a mission, which can understandably frustrate some players; but that just adds more replay value in my book.I think that the Lamplighter's League is overall a great game for XCOM addicts such as myself!

_childDocuments_.review: Initial thoughts:  Very fun.  Many missions allow for you to either lean into stealth for fighting, as you prefer.After playing more and coming back to change my review:What started out fun quickly became NOT FUN.  By mid-game, the stealth element is no longer a viable strategy for achieving objectives, and is instead a highly necessary way to shave the gaggle of 15-20 enemies in the cluster ahead down to 12-15 instead before starting your impossible fight against 5-1 odds against opponents with more hit points than you.  Early on: play through missions and finish them.  Mid-game:  save-reload for 4 or 5 attempts at first fight, achieve main objective, but then have to save-reload second fight on way to exit for 3 or 4 tries, and then save-reload some more for 12-15 tries at the 20 + dual re-inforcements gaggle with zero chance of stealthing past because apparently Locke likes to plan your exits from DEEP INSIDE ENEMY ENCAMPMENTS rather than say, where you were dropped off in the first place.  (Game design, anyone?)I've wasted most of my day on a single mission, and then realized the best thing to do was UNINSTALL.Also, the farther into the game you get, the buggier it becomes.I really WANTED to enjoy this game, and for the first 10 or 15 hours I did.  But the next 10 were horrid.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to say it, because I want to love this game.  I frankly find the real time part a little too finicky.  The enemies will be on top of you and sounding the alarm before you can sort out using one of your very limited takedowns.  Honestly, with as many enemies as you might find in a mission, the takedowns may as well not exist.  Also, the game tells you that only the lead character in your squad counts towards hiding from enemies, but I have not found this to be the case.  Controlling the thief, if you have your squad grouped, you will not get the half visibility circle you should.  Plus, characters have to be close to regroup, so you can separate them and go through the trouble of regrouping after, or you can hobble yourself.Additionally, I do NOT like the Stress mechanic.  There is no way that I can see of reducing it during a fight.  If one of your characters breaks, they will get a penalty card that may as well take them entirely out of commission for several missions.  Hard pass.Finally, they are clearly going for an Xcom style here, and the turn based combat is fine.  It definitely is in the vein of Xcom with the missing of a high percentage shot for better or worse.  What I dislike is how they handle time.  Even Firaxis relented and included an option to double the length of the enemy "timer" to defeat, and there were ways to reduce this timer further.  I obviously haven't beaten the game, but I hear this is not the case.  There are 10 agents I believe, but you will not have time to recruit them all before running out of time and losing.  Frankly, that is a deal breaker right there.  I want to enjoy all the content I paid for without gimmicks limiting me.  If I want to play on easy and grind away at missions for fun, let me.  If I want to play on hard and risk failure without the right strategic moves, that's good, too.  I want options, and this game I feel is not giving them to the player.

_childDocuments_.review: There is absolutely zero reason to purchase this game, especially if you can play it with game pass. The mechanics are horrible, the movement is atrocious, stealth is virtually non-existent and generally during battle one is overwhelmingly out-gunned and out-manned. Usually at a 4 to 1 ratio, which makes it very difficult to engage. There is virtually no stealth option to speak of, leaving no options to not engage, One is left to attempt a guess as to when to attack, not knowing how large the forces one is attacking actually are. This makes no tactical sense, and makes the game unfun!Unfortunately, there are several other issues as well. First, the screen or the game, seems to just freeze at times. Especially when moving through certain sections, which makes judging an attack move almost impossible. The RECON screen is the next best thing to worthless, as it does not show enemy troops or other loot items. What is the point of a RECON screen command if it shows nothing of value??? It is completely incomprehensible how these big name factories keep putting out garbage that is not worth a tinkers damn I have spent another 53 hours trying to find redemption in the Lamplighters League video game. First and foremost, the story is absolutely top notch and the primary reason I was drawn to the game in the first place, I saw the pre-purchase releases and was immediately intrigued. I know a hit when I see one. Unfortunately, the problem was not the story, nor was it turn based combat sequences that so many people turned away from. It was the real-time mechanics that clashed so profusely with the turn based battle mechanics. It left the heroes severely over-matched, out gunned and out maneuvered, especially in the early game.  That made the game unrewarding and un-fun. I have since played many more hours and have come to appreciate a few things regarding this game. However, my main point is to point out that most people playing these games are not professional video game players and do not make gobs of money sitting in front of a console or PC 40 to 60 hours a week playing newly introduced video games for a living, which seems to be the standard that these developers go by. Some tech wiz with a 170 IQ is going to present a very different dynamic to a video game than the general public.  That is why they produced billions with Mario Bros. Hello, McFly???? Not everybody can grasp the complexity of every game. This one seems extreme and should be tempered down. Easy should mean, easy. It should not be too difficult to play at all. Besides, you'd get more sales if it was fun, not necessarily difficult.   Nevertheless, I was forced to play with third party adaptive mods just to get through most of the game. it is just far too difficult and complex, As I stated, not everyone is a tech genius or video game virtuoso.  If the game had been just a bit less difficult, my comments would have been very different, I waited for 3 months for this game to be released, anticipating the awesomeness of what I thought to be a fantastic adventure, unfortunately, my hopes were dashed into the gutter with a game that just left it on the floor, with no one willing to pick it up. The movement should be redesigned as there far too many buttons to recognize and commit to memory. One accidental wrong button push could doom the entire mission and essentially jeopardize the whole game. It is what it is, Unfortunately, the dev's made it far too difficult for us mere humans. I have no idea why they made this game so extremely difficult. I was essentially forced to get third party mods in order to get through the game. There was no chance otherwise. The movement of characters is just flat out atrocious. Some characters would simply go wandering off when the rest of the group was hiding. Apparently, that problem was hot fixed, yet, there are still issues with movement. Often times the battles finish but the characters remain in turn-based movement after combat has concluded. I was not able to complete the game despite having third party mods that gave me big time powers.  What does that tell you?  The game is way too hard! Which makes it NOT FUN!!!!!! Most of the greatest games are not super difficult. For example: Mario Cart, a great game that is pretty simple.  Why is it that these dev's think that something has to be unfathomably difficult to be good? Just keep it simple stupid! If it's good, we'll let you know.Furthermore, this game crashes every time I try to play. I have had to replay almost every level at least twice if not more. That, too, makes it UNFUN!!! This game is so stupidly dysfunctional, it makes uncle crackhead look normal.    Why make a game so awesome story-wise, that sucks so horrifically game-wise. The game is effing horrible, yet the story is absolutely incredible.  How do you get such a massive dichotomy from one developer? I would not recommend this title unless you love game crashes during important sequences. Every other episode crashes and it is infuriating and stupid.  Not a game I would recommend to anyone. Too much BS.                                                                                                                 I really don't understand how characters can die in mid-mission without being targeted or hit by an enemy combatant?!? I mean, WTF?  This game is so horrendously dysfunctional that the characters die by sheer heart attack during combat play!?! Really? Are you effing kidding me?              This title had an opportunity to be the game of the year, maybe the game of the decade, but effed it up so badly that is absolutely the worst game of the decade. How can eff something up that bad??????

_childDocuments_.review: Lamplighters League is a game that follows the XCom 2 blueprint closely. There are your core team made up in this game of a band of outsiders, each with there own unique skills from ranged combat to melee fighters, how you use them is up to you. Each of these beyond the core starting trio can be hired/Saved from the Banished court the games villains. Some are supply based heroes that work at base to upgrade your gear/cards and health. There's a world map where missions and sorties appear, you can send two agents on single missions and a group of agents on one main mission each week. at the end of the week the damage you've done to the Court and their gains are added up. Here the game diverts from XCom by adding it's own twist. There is not one but 3 doomsday clocks, one for each faction of the court and you must balance missions across the board to stop these clocks filling up.After a mission if you've gathered all the collectables you can from each mission, the game gives you a set of cards called the unseen hand. These cards act as passive buffs or extra skills that can be used in missions. You start off being able to equip one but can upgrade to 3 cards by the end. These cards can also be upgraded either by combining duplicates or using ink that you get from abandons cards. Some cards on the right hero can be game changing.Each faction also has a Scion or boss who act a bit like war of the chosens big trio of villains. These guys aren't that tough but can be a real pain. take one down and you can cut a chunk of which ever factions doomsday clock they came from.Missions are real time sneak then turn based combat where positioning is everything. So don't get caught out in the open.All of this is wrapped up in an Indiana Jones slightly cartoon animation vibe that actually works really well.Where the game falls down for me is in the shear amount of enemies each mission sends at you with reinforcements and enemy spawning commandants or Egyptian Jackals. You need to find ways for your 3 heroes to deal with this onslaught. my best tactic was to create choke points. Also the shear number of different upgrade materials you need to advance the merchant heroes upgrade trees is annoying. through a run you probably only get enough to upgrade one tree fully. Skill points are also split across all heroes so if you get a good hero late on in the game the chances of getting them to fully upgrade are slim. I only managed 3 complete heroes. I got missions for two heroes just before the final mission really annoying though might prompt some to reply the game.I did get a huge amount of fun from the game but it's steep price might put some off. I would recommend it to those looking for a solid tactical turn based game along the lines of XCom 2

_childDocuments_.review: People often throw terms like "unplayable" around when negatively reviewing a game. It has been a long time since I purchased a game that was in fact truly unplayable. I think around 1997 or 1998 maybe. Something with WW2 tanks that just wouldn't run on the family PC or recognize any controllers or even KB+M with any amount of tinkering. But the Lamplighters League has brought back all that old nostalgia with a game that does not in fact load or play, or even give a discernible error message with which to identify and fix any problems or incompatibility. Even after pulling log files from the launcher its something of a mystery, after realizing my launcher wasn't the latest (or able to update apparently except using Beta versions) there persists an unfortunate inability of the game to validate my key which even relinking accounts will not solve. It remains a mystery how I could buy a product from Paradox on Steam and then attempt to play that product on Steam with my Steam account linked to my Paradox account and still have no record of ownership.However, at least I am not alone in my ignorance; Paradox will never know what is wrong either since the Telemetry service can't find anything to report.I bought the title based on both the snazzy dieselpunk setting and my glowing past experiences with Harebrained Schemes, but sadly The Lamplighters League is thus far sinking somewhere below Empire of Sin and Salem in the ghetto of Paradox's misfit toys.

_childDocuments_.review: The Lamplighters League:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ The Lamplighters League is about to take on its most powerful enemies, an organisation of three dominant individuals and their minions known as the Banished Court. But these days, The Lamplighters League is only one person, Mr. L, instead of many of the crème de la crème of scholars and fighters. To combat this new and fearless organisation, he can only hire the best misfits and lead them into dangerous missions in an alternative world set in the 1930s.The Lamplighters League is a strategy game that combines real-time and turn-based, and a storyline with plenty of depth developed by Harebrained Schemes and published by Paradox Interactive on the 4th of October, 2023, on the Steam platform. The game is also available on Xbox Series X|S.I must say that I enjoyed this title, but it has some flaws that frustrated me the more I played the game. I liked the combination of real-time and turn-based in this game at first; I remember saying to myself, “This looks super cool, I'm going to enjoy this one.”  But after the great introduction and the first few missions, it became tedious. You basically have more and more enemies and more powerful enemies within each mission; that is how the difficulty increases. On the one hand, it is good for the challenge, and on the other hand, it becomes pretty much impossible to beat the level if you are not saving constantly after each time you kill an enemy. And it takes more time than other games to save, and the loading is not the greatest either.  But let’s look at the game setting and gameplay in general first.After finishing your first few missions, your three main characters will arrive at Mr. L's (Mr Locke’s) hideout. There, you can go to the world map, upgrade your character skills, research new goodies through the allies you rescued through your playthrough and purchase goodies for your next mission. The game is laid out on a weekly cycle, and you’ll have different types of missions on the world map. It will also show you the three different individual groups (Nicastro, Marteau and Strum). You’ll have a fair few missions to choose from weekly. The ones with Nicastro, Marteau and Strum will have heat gauges, and if you are successful, it will also demonstrate how the heat will decrease against that particular group. You’ll need to have three and sometimes four agents on these main missions. For Rescue missions for with new agents and allies, you also need three agents. For gathering information and collecting items in safehouses, one agent is what you need as long as you have enough intel points at the hideout, and these missions will be done automatically for you.Regarding the main missions, it will start in real-time. One of the three or four characters will take the lead, but you can swap them anytime. You can also ungroup them, which is useful for searching the area for enemies and goodies. Goodies include intel folders that you need to activate one agent's mission, supplies to buy items and equipment at the hideout, aether for your allies' research, booklets of information, motes of fate cards and things like grenades, medical kits, etc. There is a reconnaissance option that you can use if you want to scroll through the level layout, but it doesn’t show you where the goodies or the enemies are. You need to have your agents close by to see goodies and enemies. As I mentioned above, as you progress through the weeks, so does the difficulty (more enemies on the map) and what you’ll start doing is to lure one enemy far enough away from the others before they are alerted of your presence so can fight (turn-based combat) that single foe instead of the entire group. Sure, you can use your character takedowns to eliminate one to three enemies at once with the Ingrid takedown, but you only have a set of two to three takedowns per character. Yes, you can recharge takedowns for one character by collecting the second wind icon on the map, but there is usually only one of those per map. Sometimes, you cannot use takedowns, as some enemies are immune to them. Enemies have an awareness diameter when you step into or on the edge of that diameter, which is light beige. The enemy will detect your presence and start to grow red outward toward its boundary. As long as you move toward where you want to be and you are still in the beige boundary, you are right, but as soon as it becomes red and one of your characters is in there, the alert will ring loud. If you haven’t been able to lure him away from the others, all the enemies will be alerted, and if there is a reinforcement tower nearby, it will become a struggle. The other thing you need to worry about is the stress factor, although it goes both ways as it is also applied to your enemies. Each time a character gets hit, his or her stress gauge will go up, and when it’s full, your character will be penalised by an action point and will be in greater danger of being killed.  Regarding enemies, when they are fully stressed, you can utilise the execution perk to farewell them. The other point to mention is that if your characters have an impacted card with stress, their stress level will rise by one point in every turn-based combat session, further increasing the difficulty. The layout of the levels is good, and you can use elements/items (such as water and shock mines or firebombs and petrol) in your favour to inflict damage on enemies. And if you find the cards, you can add new perks to one or two of your agents at the end of the mission. That also depends on whether you have unlocked all card spaces (maximum three) on your characters. The other point is you can upgrade a card by stacking them up if it is the same perk, of course, or by upgrading them with ink points.  There is a good variety of enemies, and I like the mummies; as you shoot them, they ignite and explode, spreading fire around them and damaging nearby enemies.The graphics are stunning, and the soundtrack is just brilliant. I haven’t encountered many bugs, but I don’t like to wait too long to load saved games. And I think they need to revisit the difficulty as it is now; it is very unbalanced. I enjoy the story, the depth of the characters and the dialogue between them at the hideout.Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Great graphics and soundtrack+	Thoroughly enjoyed the real-time and turn-based combination in missions+	Great characters and story+	Good variety of enemies+	AchievementsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	Difficulty progression week by week is unbalanced-	Too long to load saved games-	A few bugs here and there-	No Trading cards as yet.Even though the unbalanced difficulty progression affected my experience, I thoroughly enjoyed the real-time and turn-based setup in The Lamplighters League missions.7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Harebrained Schemes' The Lamplighters League is an uncanny case of what, I, in my brainstorming as a Tumblr-certified Hysterical Pseudointellectual™, have called a "Metaparallel"; a piece of fiction or part of a piece which serves a similar role within its own fictional universe, as it does when a real person looks at the story from an analytical perspective. (e.g. a character who spreads chaos to entertain themselves, but who is also very entertaining for the reader)The Lamplighters League is a Metaparallel in the sense that it is a story about ruthless, dangerous, self-serving and violent individuals who end up using their willingness to get their hands dirty without hesitation in order to fight for a greater good, because it must be done for various reasons.The game itself, in its quality and general execution, reflects that, as it is a rough and badly balanced turn-based tactical hero shooter, which fumbles many of its ideas and promises, and ends up rather messy as a result.Yet, I couldn't help but fall in love with it, and see it through while completely addicted to the gameplay, perhaps because of this charm, the Wabi Sabi (Beauty of Imperfection), so to say.Truth be told, I was biased in favor óf this game when it was first announced via an animated trailer in early 2023.The game immediately presented itself as featuring multiple of my favorite tropes and genres; pulp-style action-thrillers, slightly altered and fictionalized historical 1930s setting, a colorful and international cast of main characters with eccentric personalities and an aesthetic that combines 30s art-deco with comic books of the age, as well as an art style reminiscent of modern cinematic 3D animation, but subtly adapted to mesh with the aforementioned comic books.Similar to the timeless masterpiece Team Fortress 2’s inspiration from the Cold War’s 1960s, The Lamplighters League takes inspiration in equal parts from the decade it is set in and from western pop culture and media of said decade, to create an aromatic pulp (ha) for the audience to get immersed in.It being to me personally so much of what the cool kids call “a vibe” sadly makes it impossible for me to be totally unbiased.That being said, I did have my fair share of frustrations with the game in and for itself, so who knows?The game, while fantastical and adventurous as a whole, is not shy about its inspiration. The turn of the 20th century proved to be the modern world’s baptism by fire, and its results continue to shape the world till this day.While the plot revolves around a fantastical “Shadow War” between two conspiracies, the titular Lamplighters League and the power-hungry Banished Court, especially the latter has some serious subtext going on.The three softly competing noble houses of the court each represent a plague and existential threat to worldwide peace and freedom in real life. While their leaders, the court’s scions, may be as flat of personalities as the wood pulp that the game’s inspirations were printed on, they, similar to what I said about General Di Ravello in my review for Just Cause 3, serve as excellent baseline examples of the evil individuals that inspired them, precisely by being comical exaggerations of their core aspects.House Nicastro, ran by Lady Zorana Nicastro, who, as a character design, is essentially the medieval torture device called ‘The Iron Maiden’ (a metallic sarcophagus with spikes all over the inside of its door-like cover which are arranged and designed in precisely such a way that they, when slammed shut, cause the most possible pain over the longest amount of time to whatever poor soul is bleeding out inside), personified.She represents religious zealotry and those who give up their own humanity and will go to lengths that are arguably less imaginable than the supposedly horrific Gods they themselves pray to.House Marteau, ran by Business Tycoon Trace Marteau, who is just all aspects of the ‘Evil Narcissist Corporate Boss’ trope ran through a blender, represents ruthless industrialism and in some ways, libertarianism as a whole.A man who’s abandoned all morals for the sake of not what is actually progressive, but what he (and only he) deems as being progressive, and who has no problem with making everyone else work just like the slaves his parents probably commanded, before he inherited their fortune.House Strum, ran by Lord Wolfram Strum (whose voice actor, and take that assessment from a German, does the most hilarious impression of a caricature of a german Nazi that I’ve ever heard) is one of my favorite comic book villain tropes. An immovable wall of a man with a pea-sized brain, who seems almost unkillable, and who’s achieved this power by strong-manning his way to the top of the aristocracy he was born into, and then proceeding to loot all mystics and magics he could get his dinner plate-sized hands on while claiming the archaic “Right of Conquest” as a means of justification.These three are the closest thing this game features to boss battles, and that takes me to my own little conspiracy theory on why I think this game has so many issues.I believe that Harebrained Schemes had a much more bold vision for The Lamplighters League than what the game ended up being, but as a relatively small studio, just couldn’t secure the funding needed to make it happen, unlike what they managed with their previous work on Battletech, as that was based on a licensed property and had essentially unlimited budget.This is an issue that absolutely plagues indie games these days. The AAA industry keeps blasting the budgets for their games higher and higher, and Indie developers would need to deliver similarly polished spectacles in order to have a chance at competition. This is why so many indies these days are rogue-likes, so that no money needs to be spent on actual level design and replay value. It seems Harebrained Schemes knew this and, despite the limitations, wanted to compromise on their vision as little as possible, or at least make compromises which they hoped wouldn’t be as noticeable.This is why the game has none of the animated cutscenes, 100% unique levels, proper character introductions, or any meaningful gameplay in between missions which it totally deserves.In turn, arising from this, we get massive issues in terms of balancing and repetition, how missions can degrade to an hour-long mess of status effects upon status effects stacked on top of each other, all while bathed in all manners of frame rate-killing particle effects.Yet, the character designs, aesthetic, dialogues, addictively thrilling base gameplay loop and FANTASTIC orchestral soundtrack by Jon Everist allow me to accept these flaws as flaws that really only serve to give the game character and make it feel more grounded and relatable, just like its own protagonists.People who aren’t heroes like the old Lamplighters League, but people who do what they’ve got to do, for personal reasons.It’s almost as if the developers at Harebrained Schemes are Lamplighters themselves.

_childDocuments_.review: One shot the final boss for 421 damage. Take that, Marteau!The game is good, but not great. I don't have a beefy computer, so playing it on laptop is a bit of a laggy experience sometimes (especially in the final level). For the stealth/turn based strategy games I've played, I had an enjoyable experience overall, from experiencing the different archetypes to really combing through the large heist maps. Although some resources (like Kings Aether and Seric Steel) are harder to pick up, it never feels incredibly necessary to get too many of them in order to progress.This game's gimmick comes from the undrawn hand, which means character kits can go wildly in any direction on any playthrough. Although the randomness was a bit annoying sometimes (drawing a card I desperately wanted on another lamplighter that wasn't on the mission), the ability to get ink to later upgrade was a fine addition. I'm not sure if most of the rare cards are worth it though; I think I only found one of them to work well on a run so far. Still, if you've got some cool synergies in your cards, you can really get some absurd damage outputs, which I find cool to experience compared to X-COM's more set damage/health values.One negative I'd give is the camera and choice of targeting. When choosing targets for attack, I have no idea how the game chooses which enemy/interactable to choose first. The camera can sometimes be nauseating if the choices are all around the character in a circle, or if there's large distances between possible targets. Multi-target attacks also are really annoying to deal with when you want the multi-target to go to one character. Finally, I very often have my bruiser try to target the auto-hit knocked down enemy, but the first choice always ends up being a merc standing next to the downed person for some reason. Puzzling choice, but more of a personal gripe since it takes forever to change targets (due to the aforementioned lag).Overall, very fun. Game doesn't overstay its welcome if you play your cards right (no pun intended). Campaign also paces itself very well in terms of the story. Finale is always fun to fight depending on how far the doomsday clock is on each scion.

_childDocuments_.review: (Play time is +20 hours from Game Pass)Bit of a difficult one to wholeheartedly recommend. The turnbased combat is well done and offers some nicely unique characters, working within 3 broad archetypes, who come together for some fun synergies. The score is lush - I absolutely adore what it's doing. The setting is alright - it's aiming for a PG friendly occult vibe which can begin to feel a bit too safe and one note as you get further into the campaign.The real time portion is really where I feel this game suffers a lot. It's clunky and has little weird glitches where characters will group and ungroup without any input from you or not show as being safely behind cover for unknown reasons, and you feel you're fighting the controls and procedurally generated terrain as much as anything else. It's not really working for me at all as a stealth portion - more a run in and try to get off a skill and hope the small group isn't going to trigger a larger one you've not been able to scout/spot. Or that the skill goes off before you're spotted cos the game decides to lag out.Can fully understand those negging this for non-cosmetic content DLC on launch. Yes, there are plenty of other characters but Nocturne is a fully voiced character with some interesting abilities and should not be behind a day one paywall to make for a £50 game on here. So a very, very cautious recommend from me. Performance for me has been sluggish in the real time portions, which contributes to my dislike of those. With it being on Game Pass, trying before buying would be my recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: I probably have over 100 games in my Steam library, and have played every game you can mention, and this game is, quite simply, one of my favorite games of all time. It is such a tragedy that the studio got shut down and the game didn't get a chance to attract the audience it deserves.  What's so great about Lamplighters' League?  Most importantly, it's fun.  The challenges (particularly on the hard setting, which is where it should be played) are all like chess games: no matter how many times you play, you wind up getting into new, interesting circumstances.  Combat is great.  There are aspects by which you modify the game as it goes -- the 'undrawn hand' mechanic, as well as the 'allies' features, not to mention the fact that there are more interesting player characters than you really need to play the game in any one run -- make it so that you really feel like you're making the game uniquely your own.But even better, the production value is much higher than it has any reason to be.  The animations of the characters are smooth and unique to each one.  The somewhat programmatic, somewhat designed levels are visually beautiful and well put together -- they never get boring or repetitive in any run.  The story is interesting and engaging.  The writing is great, the music is great, and the voice acting is absolutely fantastic.  I played this game for hours and hours and hours, and kept discovering new audio snippets with every mission.I had so much anticipation for this game, and based on the lousy early news about it, I didn't play it.  I then discovered it on Xbox Game Pass (I bought it again on Steam to see if it would run well on the Steam Deck -- it looks terrible there, so not worth it).  I have gotten so much enjoyment out of this game, which reminds me so much of the Doc Savage and other pulp novels my dad introduced me to as a kid, and was such a fun game to boot -- I think it's a crime that it got killed way too early.  Someone, somewhere at Paradox is a corporate jerk, and does not understand how to let a great piece of fiction build an audience.Does anyone out there feel as I do?  This is certainly a far superior game to Marvel's Midnight Suns, or Classified '44 (although that's a perfectly decent game, it's not in the same league), or any of the other turn based games since XCom 2 and its expansions.  HBS, if you ever want to launch a Indiegogo campaign for a sequel, I'm all in.
