_childDocuments_.review: I played through the OG game as well as NG+ and spent around 5.5 hours on the game. Next, I'll try to 100% the game which will probably take me another five hours. The gameplay is really enjoyable though I wish there were a few more abilities to play with as well as more distinct enemy design gameplaywise. The art style is currently my favorite art style out of any game I ever played, it's that well designed. The game runs great but I had some issues with Gsync so I had to turn vsync on, but it didn't seem to impact latency that much. The hud looks really clean but the ability notifications are too intrusive for my liking. Some effects also look unfinished, for example the electric eels when they collide and cause a shockwave or the white trail of the boomerang when it hits a wall and comes back.The music composed by the CEO of Devolver Digital Ben Caulkins really fits the game and has some crazy time signatures. While the soundtrack is good in game, I wouldn't really listen to it in any other context, I wish it took a bit more inspiration from tunes like Piano Black (composed by Yoko Kanno) or The Real Man (composed by the Seatbelts). The music also doesn't always fit the level, well the music fits the entire game but if I presented you with a random song there’s a high likelihood you wouldn't know which level it was from. Some stages like Poisonous well and Vashkatar have very fitting music but the music from most other stages kind of 'blends together'.What really holds this game back is a lack of content, there are a lot of reused assets throughout the levels especially in new game plus. There are twelve 'real' stages which are all mostly unique in design and setting. There are four bosses that frequently get reused in the game. While they are well designed, I would've liked a few more bosses. I personally don't like the 'ultimate ability' at all, I would've much preferred another basic ability to add to my kit. I also have a few gripes with the recall system. There are some enemies that always face you and that you can only hit on the back, so using recall is encouraged. This doesn't really work smoothly though even after a lot of practice it's not reliable enough to use in speedruns. I would like to see it tweaked to follow your crosshair more or a command (lclick and rclick combined) to let the boomerang stay in place after being thrown so that you can control the trajectory of the recall more. The healing system is very frustrating at the moment. You have to stand still on a platform and have to wait a couple seconds to heal. Most of the time I lose more health from standing still on the platform than actually healing. This can be remedied by reducing the healing time (devs I hope you are reading this).The double/triple kill ability system is really interesting, there are no cooldowns it’s up to you to get a double kill to gain access to scattershot which you can then use to get a triple kill in order to get needle. This works well most of the time but in large stages like Resonance engine it’s a bit too tedious to get a double kill at times, so having more control over recall would be greatly appreciated. The blaze ability is great for crowd control and it’s great that it’s usable grounded as well as mid-air when you make contact with an enemy. Scattershot only charges by using the boomerang while needle charges from pretty much any triple kill. Since scattershot is essential for some speedrun strats giving more control over recall would be hugely appreciated. More abilities to play with would be great but I don’t think that’ll ever happen. A teleport & assassination ability would be great for getting rid of those shield enemies and gaining easy access to the enemies they’re protecting and would fit the game decently well since the ultimate ability is just that but multiple times.I did encounter some minor bugs: the game stutters only when entering the last wave of a stage, I don’t know if this is just me but here is some insight on my settings & setup (gsync on, low latency mode on in Nvidia control panel and vsync on in game. I’m using vsync in game because gsync doesn’t seem to work. I’m playing the game on a 144hz monitor at 123 fps locked. I do this with other games as well and gsync works just fine but with this game it doesn’t.) In the Atsil’s quarry stage I got stuck in the wall once while slingshotting myself to the wall near a platform.Finally, I just have to give the devs some props for the great gyro controls and flick-stick system as well as the really convenient accessibility and gameplay options. I hope the game gets more content down the line, this game really deserves it.

_childDocuments_.review: What an epic gamer game.Got this not really knowing what to expect, it looked cool and new. Turns out this was one of the biggest surprises of 2021, and not a regrettable one at that. Now I do have my very few critiques, the biggest one not even really being about the game itself, but I am seriously happy I got Boomerang X.First and foremost, the gameplay. It was probably the most intriguing thing that pulled me into it. It looked new, truly original and unique to anything I have seen or played. At first I was worried going into it that the whole gameplay would just be throwing a boomerang at guys and catching it, but as you go on you get much more abilities and strategies to how you want to play. Boomerang X influences you to really use your boomerang and fly around with it, which is super freaking fun. If you kill multiple guys with one throw, you can get combo powers and continue down the chain of combos and powers. It’s extremely addicting and fun. After most every level you get sent to the “Tuning Room” where you unlock a new ability. This is where one of my critiques is, while I do enjoy more gameplay material, I don’t feel that you ever get to use your current abilities to the fullest extent, considering you get more to memorize quickly and the game being how short it is (more on that later). With that said, all the new abilities are good editions that you will need to use frequently. I really love the one shot type gameplay, but kind of like what they did in Ghostrunner, it has layers to the one shot. Sometimes you need to deactivate a barrier by killing something specific or by hitting a certain spot (being the red crystals). It's just enjoyable gameplay all around.Next, the graphics. Not too much to talk about here. It looks pretty astounding in terms of its art style and it goes along with this trend of being unique. The only game I can think of that looks somewhat similar would be Aragami, but even then, this game sticks to a certain color palette that I've never seen. It consists of yellow black, white and red (mostly).Next, I want to talk about the audio. I really love it. The music is intense when it needs to be but maintains the consistent strum of the string. Whenever you recall your boomerang it makes a drum beat. Things like that. It’s again- unique. That's a great word to describe Boomerang X. Unique. Some audio queues can get a bit repetitive but it's all fun and games in the end.Okay, now for the big topic. Game length and price. It took me about 2.5 hrs to beat the basic campaign, for $20 at full price, that is almost unacceptable. I got it for $15, which is still quite a stretch. So why am I recommending this game? Replayability. That's a common theme with short games like this. You can replay them with ease. I beat this game in like one sitting and I'd gladly do it again. But that's not even considering… . In the reviews I heard horror stories of this supposed challenge, to think I had thought the game was already ballbusting, here comes the big one. I started it, and to be honest, it aint that bad. It kind of continuates the difficulty it left off at the end of the basic campaign, and that completely makes sense. I can see myself beating it within 2-3 sittings. So, where am I going with this?If you consider yourself a fellow god gamer and decide that you really want your money's worth, and want to replay the game or play new game +, then it is worth it. However, if you're a casual gamer and are just here to do it once and check out, I don't think you should. I’d say it trends towards hardcore gamers or even speedrunners. It's a quick game, in and out within a giffy, but if you're down for some more action after you beat it, it IS worth the money. I’m down for some more and I will definitely be finishing NG+ and probably filling the other two save slots as well. So my final rating, combining all of these factors together, is....8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game, but a bit overpriced for its length. I beat it in about 3 hours, although it does seem like I'll get a bit more time out of New Game+. I'm not normally the kind of person who whines about the amount of hours a game has, but when compared to games of similar quality like Dusk or Ultrakill that will cost you the same amount despite being much longer, I really don't think Boomerang X justifies its price. That said, if you pick it up on sale or happen to have cash to burn, Boomerang X is still very much worth the time. It is a very unique game, taking the frantic gameplay of other movement shooters and cranking it up to a ridiculous degree, with finely tuned mechanics that perfectly compliment that gameplay with their use of speed and momentum. The contrast of the simple combat in the early game to the sometimes incomprehensibly fast and intricate arenas of the late game is astounding, and yet the progression between the two is so smooth that I almost didn't notice how quickly I went from a basic dodge-jump-shoot loop to perfectly slingshotting around and in between enemies, slowing down time, and hitting them from behind with a boomerang-railgun blast, without even needing to consider touching the ground while doing so. and that's not even getting into how good the writing is. Despite all my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this really is a fantastic game, and I really hope to see more from the developers.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, this is a game about throwing a boomerang and killing things, but it is first and foremost a game about movement, disecting the space and planning ahead looking for the angles to chain kills and be ready for the next target - when time freezes, it's almost like a puzzle. The movement uses the 3Dimensions of the space completely, which means you need to process a lot of information - it is INTENSE and you better take advantage of that precious bullet time because you are going to need it. Gravity could be your best friend or your worst foe and learning when to call the boomerang or when to move towards it is an art that, once mastered, will make you dance with your mouse.You can beat the normal game in under 3 hours but you will keep playing either at New Game + or replaying its arenas because this game is truly amazing and there is nothing really like it out there. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is freaking amazing. It has a very fine-tuned difficulty curve and pacing that doesn't overwhelm you with all the introductions of new abilities and enemy types. No mechanic in this game feels out of place or bad to play around with, it was honestly one of my best 2 hours spent on a video game. I really hope the dev will keep making new content for this game and adding more levels because it is quite short to complete. It's a no-brainer must-play if you are into games with full action and pure adrenaline rush.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: boomerang x is a perfect game for what it is. i can't think of a single flaw. the art is great, but you don't have to stare at it for a long time to appreciate it. the mechanics are great and the attacks complement the enemies better than doom. the movement is very fun and keeps me wanting come back. it does everything a movement shooter does and more. the major problem of this game is not what it is however, but what it isn't. boomerang x may be one of the top movement shooters of the previous decade, but it's terribly short. 20 dollars for a 3 hour campaign is awful, especially if you can get doom eternal for 20 dollars on sale now. it's not like this game couldn't have been longer either. there are certain mechanics that definitely could have used levels built around them. boomerang x may be the perfect game, but if you want bang for your buck, it leaves much to be desired.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: Fun. Fast Paced. But like others have said, pretty short. My game time says 1.8 hrs at the time of this review, but if I wasn't taking my time, it would be closer to 1.5hrs or less. I got the game on sale, so I'm pretty satisfied with my purchase for the time I had and knowing I'll for sure be coming back for New Game+ and maybe some of the challenging achievements. I do hope they eventually expand with some DLC because atm, the content is pretty thin.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: One of the fastest-paced, ball-to-the-walls in-the-air combat, extremely tight controls, crazy amazingly fun abilities, and a new-game plus that makes the game harder while still retaining the same amount of fun, games I have ever played. A short but extremely joyful boomerang adventure that will make you crave to play once more. I recommend this game to anyone and everyone, as it is worth your time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: Okay okay, now that I have completed the game here are my thoughts. This has to be one of my favorite arena shooters of all time, personally. The gameplay is rather simple, but they've expanded enough to where it feels just right. To me, there isn't a combat dance and more of a combat race, how fast are you going to kill the enemies before they mess up your day. Similar to other arena shooters, you gotta keep moving, but the game literally encourages you to move by left clicks on your mouse. Fantastic.The style of the game, is PERFECTION. The inspiration of Eastern Asian culture, the inspiration from the Samurai Jack, and them cool ass insects. The game just oozes with creativity, the colors brimming around the cell shaded backgrounds. Just take a moment to look at the background, buy the OST. You'll be amazed at how much passion went into the style, feel, and look of the game. I still have issues, two of them actually. Maybe three?  The game is super short, and ofc they're giving more life to the game with New game+ and the future update with Endless mode, but the game is still short.Another small picky picky gripe is that some of the enemies don't feel like they have much of a presence compared to others in the game. The eels? Leech? Whichever they are, they don't feel like they have much in terms of danger zones/ force you to change directions of where you're heading. Maybe endless mode will change that, but that's just something that I remember while playing. This is not so much an issue and more so a wish, I really would like to see a sequel to this game at some point, I see a lot of things the dev team can bring to the table with such a simple concept of how the combat works. Good job Dang!, I am now a fan of the indie team. <3
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those short games that is actually worth it, not only does the basegame have a ton of replayability, but NG+ really adds to what could have been too short of an experience. On top of that, even once you've experienced everything you still come back because there are so many challenges to try, one that I'm looking forward too is a no-flux run.This game's artstyle is beautiful and so well put together, I love looking at each stage before I start it, because the amount of detail they cram into these levels you go through at mach 10 is way more than is needed, and it shows just how much the devs put into it. Shoutout to Devolver for introducing me to all my favorite games.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: For as short as this game is, it's really fun.Like the only few issues I have with the game would be as I mentioned the shortness of this game.Like 1.5 Hours or so and it's done, and that's with deaths, and without me just speedrunning.I wouldn't be surprised if you could speedrun this game in under 10 minutes or something like that, specially with the slingshot and time stop abilities combined.One other issue would be the price, I feel as if $20 is a bit much for a game which doesn't offer much in terms of content.However, in my opinion, if players were given the ability to design and publish their own levels to the workshop and whatnot, it'd make the game a lot more replayable and enjoyable, and with that added, I'd forgive the $20 price as I could just design make own levels and whatnot and make up for it myself.Personally I'd say the game is a 7/10, not bad, but could be improved slightly.the pros of the game are the art style, gameplay, and the given variety of enemies present, which prevents the game from getting boring, or from being too easy.the cons of the game would be the price, and how short the game is.Most of this is my own opinion, if you want the game, and the price isn't a issue to you, then that's perfectly fine.I hope you enjoy playing it in that case.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: Boomerang X is a great a game. It has an WONDERFUL style, unique levels that offer new abilities and enemies every time, amazing mechanics and a movement system that feels smoother than cutting warm butter.However, there are 2 main problems i have with this game:1. I completed this game in less than 2 hours2. This game does not have much challenge until the later levels, which admittedly don't take too long to get to. This is also ignoring the absolute waterboardingwhilstgettingyournutssawedoff difficulty that is the new game+.So in a lot of ways this game is VERY SIMILAR to Titanfall 2, with it's short and concentrated campaign, varied levels and mobility that would make Spider-Man shed a tear. And just like Titanfall, I would recommend you get it at slight discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: From the moment that Boomerang X's demo hit Steam, it was possible that DANG! and Devlover had a hit brewing, and the full experience delivers on that promise. No occasional difficulty spikes can get in the way of this exciting mixture of retro FPS movement and stylish action, and Boomerang X will likely remain a contender for one of 2021's best indie titles throughout the rest of the calendar year.Want to know more? My full review is available now over on .
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely amazing! Super intense fast paced combat even if you're using slow mo all the time. The difficulty helps acclimate you to the mechanics and get good as the game progresses. You easily identify and learn from your mistakes and get better and better with every reset of a level you failed. the environments look gorgeous and the verticality and possible movement is insane! All of that with very simple mechanics to understand and few keybinds which just pleases my old school shooter fan side a lot! even if it's somewhat short it's well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: Godly arena shooter. The game makes you extremely powerful but the excellent enemy encounter design keeps the game intense and fun at all times. It's short, but the length felt perfect to me. And if you were left wanting more (like me) the game has a new game + mode with modified enemy encounters for higher difficulty. Highly recommended if you enjoy DOOM, Devil Daggers, any other PVE arena FPS, or watching gameplay excites you in any way.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is incredibly frantic and fast-paced, but the difficulty increase means that you're never left completely in the dust by what the game expects of you.  Has a lot of options for accessibility and even options to let you beat levels easier if you need them, though no real "easy/normal/hard" difficulty sliders exist.  Also while a single first-time playthrough is only about 2 hours, it feels like the real game starts with NG+ once you beat the game once.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, the art style. So unique and pleasant to the eye, very calming to look at,yet still manages to be intriguing with the bit of mystery in the world design, which hints at lore.Level design varies nicely, and there is a big variant of enemies that helps keep the game from feeling like a shooting gallery.The versatile movement system with the sling mechanism, combined with the bunny hop like jumps, makes a lot of this game, and allows for various ways to approach.Additional abilities add nicely to the loop,And the well lit rooms designed give the game a mixed look of both cheerful yet horrid, with the enemies made of what seems like a sort of darkness.Loving this game so far, will update upon completion.Recommend this dearly for all bullet hell lovers and beginners as this is a very approachable level of difficulty.May the centipede be with you.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review: Stylish, fast-paced, high-skill "shooter". A few simple mechanics work together beautifully to have you throwing yourself around the arena, smashing weak spots in slow motion. It's great!It's also got the best gyro controls in any game outside of using certain input remappers (only with a DualShock 4, for now), and it's the first ever game to natively offer "flick stick" controls.So maybe that last part biases me a bit. But I can't help but recommend this super slick game.
_childDocuments_.name: Boomerang X

_childDocuments_.review:
Harness the power of a mystical boomerang to fling yourself through the air. Slice, fly, and blast through arenas swarming with evil creatures. Stay agile or meet your doom. 

Fight otherworldly forces and look cool doing it. Impress the boomerang with stylish tricks and it'll grant you stranger powers - powers that'll let you defeat the forces of the depths with greater ease. Kaspidae smiles upon you and your killer moves...

name: Foretales
detailed_description: A terrible curse is ravaging the realm and the only one who can stop it is a small-time thief named Volepain. The Weaver entrusted the instruments of creation to her children, the Nymphants. The Weaver put in the hands of her children the fate of the world’s creation and stability. The instruments of creation have the power to create and destroy the many worlds of Foretales. Discover the true goals of the Nymphants and the Cult or embrace the Maelstorm for eternity! Foretales tells the story of a world doomed by a dark prophecy. With the clock ticking on the apocalypse, it’s up to you to decide how to use what little time is left. If you want to find the path to salvation, you’ll need to decide what’s best for you and your companions! Featuring: EXPANSIVE BRANCHING STORYLINES WITH MULTIPLE ENDINGS CARD-BASED GAMEPLAY DECKSPLORATION GAMEPLAY UNIQUE “BOARD GAME” FEEL SUPERB ARTISTIC DIRECTION ORIGINAL SCORE BY CHRISTOPHE HÉRAL ( RAYMAN , BEYOND GOOD & EVIL ) TURN-BASED CARD COMBAT GREAT REPLAY VALUE ORIGINAL STORY AND WORLD HUGE CAST OF CHARACTERS NARRATION BY TRAVIS WILLINGHAM ( CRITICAL ROLE , The Legend of Vox Machina )

short_description: Decide the fate of the world in this ingenious story-driven card game. Foretales offers a unique take on the adventure genre, with a multitude of playstyles and story paths through which you can save the world… or bring about its end.

_childDocuments_.review: Foretales is a genre mashup that is hard to explain. Here is the rundown:1) You choose your mission from those available trying to prevent "dooms" from popping. In general depending on your path you have 1-2 options to choose from and each option you pick "locks" you out of other options.2) The mission itself works by cards flipping on the table and based on your cards you "combine" them with the cards on the table to earn resources, fight enemies, and/or advance the story. For example if the card on the table is "wealthy noble" you can use your "pickpocket" card to earn gold, or your "eavesdrop" card to learn secrets, or you "aimed shot" to straight up kill them for lots of gold and items but also it adds enemies to the "search" deck.3) As locations are revealed if there are enemies in your search deck they might sppawn there. Otherwise many locations also straight up spawn enemies. Guards will protect warehouses, bandits will ambush you etc. When there are enemies on a card it "locks" it so you can't interact with it until you clear the enemies. You can often move around them but sometimes the location you need or the entire board is locked down going into comat.4) Generally combat starts with a "negotiation" phase where you can use resources you've earned like money, food, fame or infamy to bribe or charm or scare away enemies. Enemy parties have a "morale" counter so if you can eliminate 1-2 of their higher ranking members the rest of the party will flee. 5) Otherwise you can go straight into combat which is usually a bad thing. Not only does leaving a string of bodies potentially lock you out of missions but it can also add more enemies to the searrch deck making further advancement harder. You have the ability to play cards (i.e. throw a bomb or snipe a target) but actual combat is pretty straight forward and brutal. Your people can very quickly be overwhelemed so it is important to thin the herd. You also never really "level up" per se so as you start facing harder and harder enemies it relies on you being smarter about combat as opposed to letting your stats ride you to victory.6) Some missions the goal is to just get through the location deck to the end point. Some missions require you to get a macguffin first like the key to a jail sell or the map to the treasure. Some missions are straight up puzzles that involve carefully reading card descriptions and studying card artwork to figure out what needs to be on the board and what cards you need to interact with in order to get to the end condition.7) You are told what will happen (generally) when you put a card from your hand on the table but until you've played through it you don't always know what will happen "next" so some of the puzzles can be quite difficult.8) Your cards are used as you use them. Resources are spent, and cards from your hand are discarded. You can Rest, generally about 5 times or so but most times it comes with a price like paying gold or eating food to avoid bad stuff. Resting restores 3 cards to your characters decks. Characters start with about 12 cards give or take and depending on the mission they can get kind of long, especially when you're first playing a mission and don't know what to do so you spend a lot of cards just going in circles trying this and that before you figure out the exit..9) You play through to the end and then discover the New Game+ that unlocks NEW options based on your previous decisions. Basically you can unlock new cards for old missions that can lead you on new routes or lets you quickly bypass previous obstacles.. The game has 3 endings and I imagine it requires you to play through at least once before you can unlock the "good" ending although I'm just on my second playthrough so who knows. 10) There is 1 character that you have to have and a selection of (so far) 4 others you can use. Each mission is limited to 3 characters and your hand size is fixed so if you have 1 character you draw 6 cards from their deck but if you have 3 characters you draw 2 from each. Each chracter's deck does different things so depending on the mission it might make sense to not do a full party just so you aren't burning cards looking for  the one card you actually need. For example sneaking into a prison and avoiding fights means maybe you don't need the big bruiser who isn't going to be very helpful. Overall the story and setting are good, the game mechanics are interesting as a mashup if not individually spectacular. Definitely a unique experience and very replayable, at least until you unlock all the endings and side stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a "slay the spire" combat card game, this is not that game. This game is a resource management / choose your own adventure / choices matter  story driven card game. You will be choosing different story scenarios and trying to make the best out of a bad situation. PROSGreat art, writing, musicCharming charactersVery polished game (no bugs, good ui. etc)Choices matter A LOT (scenarios you choose, objectives you complete, who you save, who you kill, etc)Many characters with different functions, abilities, and strengthsCONSSome puzzles could be better explained but this is solved by pressing the "light bulb" multiple times for different hintsCombat is basic and almost non-existent as it's almost always better to mercy / intimidate / resource the enemy awayFor the price, this game is well worth the play through.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I tried my hardest to like this game. It started off so fantastically: Exploring the world and seeing what I can and cannot do was so fun, but by GOD does it get tedious later on. The whole point of the game is trial and error, but sometimes there's just no hint what-so-ever as to what you're supposed to be doing. And having to repeat the entire series of events the exact same way every time, changing a single thing each time and seeing what happens becomes so boring. It helps that there's a rewind option, but please: Let me skip cutscenes at least. I can't count how many times I've seen cinematics that make no contextual sense based on what your character should know.For that reason I cannot recommend the game in it's current state. Fix the repeating dialog and give us the option to skip cutscenes. Also please let the Guide Character guide us more in the later areas. We already know what we're meant to do: Just tell me how to do it for god's sakes because I can't fumble around forever and see what happens later once it's too late to rewind.I do want to add that the game looks fantasic. Visually it's incredible and there's so much soul in this thing. The dialog is also pretty solid and the core gameplay works really well. I'm just being forced to see the same thing over and over and over again and there's only so much nice art I can look at before I get tired.On a much smaller side note it is kind of upsetting how many named characters are mostly meaningless. (Spoilers Ahead).Venin is just a short bossfight. Why is it SO hard to win through morale if there's no reward for it? Other aspects of the game reward you for performing complicated actions. (It also doesn't help that I thought I'd get the "Ultimate Weapon" by combining the Crocodile Blade with something so getting it from Venin felt kinda lame).The Cat Thief also does nothing? It's a tough fight that there's no reason to take??The Adeile does nothing either, though that's less upsetting. It just felt wierd that there's an entire mission dedicated to her and we see her the one time. We don't even go back to her afterwards like the mission asked us to.Volepain's Dad is another named character that doesn't do anything. The only purpose I guess he serves is to lead players astray.I guess overall this game needs a bit more of that "Actions have Consequences" vibe that it claims to have. The only thing that has a consequence is killing people, I really wanted to see characters I'd helped earlier show up later in the story to help me.Even so, I don't regret buying the game. It was good fun for most of the time I had it and I loved exploring the early and mid game. I just don't think the late game is worth playing in it's current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This one is unfortunately a mixed bag, but the effort and creativity behind it absolutely deserve a recommendation.The art direction, music, UI, story, are all excellent. The core gameplay is very good too, and the "decisions matter" aspect is well made.After 8 hours I have completed the first playthrough, which is actually only the beginning if one wants to understand everything and get to the true ending.Sounds like a great time, except there are two things which make it... not so.- Too many parts of it feel repetitive, because instead of genuine strategy, you're forced to keep trying coupling your cards with the correct board cards. It's sometimes interesting because you can guess what you need to do; sometimes it's just banging your head against the wall until it works. Another point connected to repetitiveness is that you're going to see the same cards and linked events/minions in many missions.- Connected to that point, many parts of the game are just way, way too obscure. Like, objects or allies that are incredibly important to the story (especially if you want to get to the true end), but require a multi-step planning that you just have no way of even guessing you need to do. That might just be my own perception, but I unfortunately did not feel like going for another playthrough after the end. Still, if perusing narrative games is your thing, then absolutely go for it because this game still has more qualities than flaws.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: ✔ unique combination of a puzzle with a card game (not a deck-builder!)✔ story-driven✔ seamless integration of choices made through card-related mechanics (as opposed to additional dialogue options etc)✘ sometimes, especially in later levels the gameplay degenerates into eternal cycling over possible cards trying to find the exact setup you need✘ staying in previous levels of a mission is encouraged (to grind for resources)✘ game finishes sooner than you would expect and requires multiple runs to get to a proper ending. What's worse this new run requires partially going through the same missions without an option of a skip (I decided to not go through this)Overall a neutral review, but it ended on in an unsatisfying way, so I lean negative.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Judging from my playtime, yes I genuinely like this game. The narrative is so immersive that I kept coming back to see what will happen next. The mechanics is quite simple to grasp, yet it's good enough to deliver a satisfying gameplay experience. Personally, my favourite part about this game is you can tackle certain objectives in a number of ways, and you'd be amazed by how subtle some of them are.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Don't make the mistake of assuming this is something like a Slay the Spire or other card battler. It's a narrative exploration game with resource management and puzzle-like battles, more in common with a gamebook adventure like Sorcery! than a roguelite. If you're the kind of person who enjoys going back through old areas and finding new things to do, playing with 'what ifs' and being surprised at what the developers thought you might do, this game's worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I have only played through the first two missions, but already the care and polish that went into this game are a delight. The art is stunning - each new card is a joy to behold, the portraits all exude charisma. And the writing got a few good chuckles out of me. I was a bit worried about how complex the gameplay might be, but it gets very intuitive once you make it past the tutorial phase. It plays very smoothly - the kind of game that makes you want to cancel your week-end plans :)
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This one goes straight in my top favorite card games. The narrative aspect is perfect, like the dialogues and the narrator, not too much, just the perfect amount. The clever way of combinning the skills and item cards with map cards and/or event cards. There are some REALLY fun combination to be made! The fact that you can literally try to be a hero or a "villain" so to speak, by killing everyone in your path or stealing everything, it's just so much fun. The music and ambiences are great and fit perfectly. I really dig the visuals, not only the cards but the different types of background for each part of a mission and the change of mood... Man, it's just... Perfect!Clearly you guys put a lot of effort into this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This game really annoyed me. It’s a shame, I enjoyed the voice acting, the art style and the characters and some of the ideas in the gameplay, but in execution, it just made me feel like I was trapped on a Mobius strip.The player is given multiple ‘location piles’ for each mission/quest, where each pile represents a place you can go or a person you can interact with. The final card you need to complete the quest is hidden somewhere within the deck, with multiple ways of reaching it (violence, persuasion, threats, bribes), but there’s no way of knowing how far away the ‘victory card’ is. So often I found myself spending valuable action cards to gather loot or explore each deck, only to find that I had gone round in a circle. There’s no sense of direction or depth to any of the location piles. Sometimes the same location or NPC will show up in a completely different pile. This wouldn’t be too much of an issue if you could experiment, but your action cards are finite. To replenish them, you have to rest; and you only have a certain amount of rest periods before an automatic game over. I get that this was done to add some replayability to the game, but in execution it just feels like I’m being punished for experimenting with card combinations.On the other hand - I got an achievement, first try, for freeing Leo from prison without raising the alarm. Didn’t plan to do that, I just stumbled blindly into the circumstances which allowed me to do so. It didn’t really feel like I earned or accomplished something cool because I couldn’t see the end goal before I’d already tripped over it.Sometimes you’ll get into combat. I like that you can bargain your way out of fights with the use of food, fame, bribes, infamy, NPCs etc. That’s a really cool mechanic. But I’ve tried doing multiple versions of each game where I play violently versus pacifism and there doesn’t seem to be any difference to the outcome. The game told me that there’s a moral high-ground element, but it doesn’t really reward you for choosing either path.Oddly enough, I feel like this adventure game has the same problem that plagued a lot of early adventure games. Where the player is hopelessly going around in circles, rubbing things in their inventory against things in the game world in the vague hope that something will react appropriately and turn into progress. It’s just happening with cards instead of a DOS cursor.If I was going to offer constructive critique, I would suggest giving a sense of ‘depth’ to each location pile, so the player at least had some vague idea of how deep a loop they are about to dive into. That could give a better sense of economy to the action cards and it may give a bigger sense of risk versus reward? Also, maybe treat each location pile as a cardinal direction on a compass, rather than having the same cards and locations and people showing up in different piles. Might help give the player a better sense of where they reside spatially, within the abstraction of the card-generated world.TDLR ; fun story-driven game with some neat art, characters and concepts. I didn't find the Gameplay very intuitive.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: A very well made game, does a good job of actually having a story/campaign integrated into a card game.  Plenty of encounters with various puzzles and challenges rather than just killing hoards of enemies.  There are also quite a few branching paths through the story for replayability.  One thing I want to point out is that in order to get the "Final" ending, you'll need to play through the game at least 3 times, as the game is meant to be played multiple times where you unlock certain things that let you get the final ending in a later playthrough.  This can make certain missions rather tedious when you have to do them multiple times.  But overall, the game is very well done and I enjoyed it.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to give this a positive review at first, but after much consideration I won't.Foretales is a beautiful game with a neat little story, some interesting gameplay and on the surface gives you many options how you want to approach things ... but once you've "beaten" it (or come close to it) you'll realize that there is - in fact - no player agency at all, but a very specific set of choices you have to make to actually get to the ending. Everything else ends in failure and a ... restart. Yes, a restart of a 6+ hours long campaign that will needlessly frustrate you with lots of RNG.Gameplay consists of several cards on the table you have to explore with your own cards. That can be your characters, items, or supplies like food, gold, etc. Each one will have a different effect, and some can't be used. Finishing a mission usually requires you to reach a certain card, then interact with it in a particular way, repeating this process ad nauseum. This was fine for the first chapter or so, but then it got rather cryptic and tedious. And this is by intent. The developers want you to "learn" and use that knowledge in subsequent playthroughs, but honestly, the moment to moment gameplay drags on too much and the campaign is way too long for that to be enjoyable, especially since you can, of course, still make "mistakes" in later playthroughs. The narrator did tell me something very important, I guess, after I failed, but I'm 100% certain that going down that route will have different negative consequences that require at least 1 or even 2 more playthroughs, and I hate having my time wasted, trying to get the right cards with the right combinations to move forward. A 2nd playthrough could in theory be warranted, by simply doing something very different, but even then it's still the same stale gameplay that just doesn't hold up for this long.Like I said, I thought this was about player choice and I begrudgingly accepted the loss of a character, despite seemingly having no way to actually save that person. After a time the game tells you that this particular character is going to be assassinated after the next mission. It gave me two missions to choose from and told me that one should know who wanted to assassinate my party member, so naturally I chose that mission, and lo and behold I actually DID learn who was the culprit, yet there was nothing I could do with that knowledge. Apparently, I was supposed to bring the party member in question on this mission... there are conflicting infos online, but the assassin never appeared for me, so my character just died. This was especially annoying since the rest of the group should have immediately known who the murderer was, since only a mission prior we uncovered the truth about another murder involving this shady character, yet my party was like "who could it be? Never heard about something like this". And I'm here shouting at the screen "Yes, you have! 5 minutes ago!"This happens repeatedly throughout the game. The triggers are somewhat broken. Characters forget vital information and repeat things, because, again, there is no real choice here. You're supposed to go down one route, and then this might not happen, I reckon. For instance, I was supposed to bring a certain object to another character. When I met him the first time I told him I no longer possessed said object, because I returned it to another character. Then I told him about my visions, etc. Next time I meet that character the same interaction plays out again. No, I don't have that object anymore, but I do have visions. Ah, that changes everything. Does it? It's already changed everything last time we talked. And like I said, this happens quite a bit.In any case, Foretales IS enjoyable. For a time. Like half the play time to be honest, until you realize how meaningless your own choices have been and that it's not an interactive story, but rather a puzzle game, in which you're trying to find out the correct order of things. Like, letting your friends get carried off to execution, because you can save them later, thus gaining more time to actually prevent the doomsday ending.It's also 20 bucks. Not a bargain price. Not terribly expensive, either, but ultimately, that's for you to decide. What would have made this game better for me:- The story actually takes your actions into account and develops without a "oh, you failed" state. Actual actions and consequences. My character's father dying did nothing to further the story. It had no real impact.- If you're going for the "you will only get the true ending after multiple playthroughs", then you need to spice up the gameplay somehow. Maybe even have some more character development. Like, my main character got an attack buff, as well as some HP buffs during the first run, and some new cards. Let that carry over. Then introduce new mechanics, new enemies, perhaps. You could tailor the story around that, e.g. you could teach characters once you rescue them, or you could skip the entire rescue process to begin with and tell an actually slightly new story now with all characters remembering what happened, as long as they were in Volepain's party.- And for the love of god, let me skip dialogue lines completely.If you treat the game more like a rogue-light (very light) it might have more legs to stand on for 20 bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR in case you don't want to watch the video:1. If you're looking for gameplay as seen in Slay The Spire - this isn't it. This also isn't a clone of StS; in fact the gameplay here is very different!2. The concept is simple; drag and drop cards of different types of resources like money, food, fame (good reputation), grim (ie. evil reputation) to other cards like locations, enemies, merchants, quest NPCs etc. Sounds simple, but there are usually more than 2-3 different ways to solve a problem, which means you can play in a multitude of ways.3. The way you play, will inadvertently influence the story, and the story lines you pick will also influence the way you play!4. I won't spoil too much but you'll grow attached to your party members, and depending on the story, you'll have to make some tough choices!5. The only downside, I would say, is that it can get overwhelming at first, especially with so many possibilities and things to do; its easy to get lost!I highly recommend this to fans of story driven deckbuilding games!
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Playing Foretales is like playing a story driven tabletop game with some rough features. You play through a number of connected missions where you have different decks of cards and resources: you got all basic decks like enemy deck, exploration deck and player cards deck, as well as resources like food, gold, fame and others. Each mission contains non-story encounters, as well as a story related encounters where you are able to make some story related decisions.The major factor of the gameplay is the order of missions and story decisions you make through the game. Some missions may become unavailable after you complete some other mission. So you have to decide which missions you want to complete and which you can sacrifice to achieve a specific game ending. I believe it was made for the replayability. Those achievements show that you will need to complete the game multiple times. So be aware of this requirement if you eager to hunt for achievements.Overall I liked the game, so here iswhat I found GOOD in Foretales:+ Nice art style that reminds me of an old Disney creations, just what I like.+ The story is quite good and slightly intriguing.+ Easy-to-learn gameplay mechanicswhat I found BAD or "Not-So-Good" in Foretales:- Sometimes the items hand can get overloaded with cards which will make it difficult to browse using a mouse pointer. The game literally screams for a controller support.- No Skip option for story videos between missions and text pop-ups during the mission.- There is neither a difficulty setting nor a story mode, so keep this in mind before you start playing Foretales.~ Only some of the main story lines and story teller banters are voiced and you will have to read a lot, keep this in mind as well. It's not really that bad since most of the times the story lines contains only a few sentences.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly well made. Has the feel of a single-player board-game combined with a point-and-click adventure (in terms of puzzle construction not mechanics). Largely about resource management and has a big focus on narrative.The biggest problem this game has is that the branching/divergent narrative aspect really makes you want to replay it, but having no way to skip through dialogue you're familiar with makes that extremely frustrating. Even more of an issue: the tutorial is presented to you in the form of in-world dialogue. If you lean towards the impatient side (like me) this is chafing to the point that you probably won't get more than one or two play-throughs of the game. Still, so well done that it's worth picking up to play through even if you only do it once or twice. On the off chance a dev reads this, I am on my knees: either add dialogue fast-forward/tutorial skipping in as a feature or please please please put it in the next game you make in this style and advertise the hell out of that feature.

_childDocuments_.review: There are some clever and fun mechanics here, and I think many of the ideas presented could form the basis of an excellent deckbuilding rpg/roguelite. Unfortunately, too much of the game is obfuscated behind specific card combinations that you have no real way to know without a significant amount of RNG and experimentation. While experimentation can be fun and rewarding, this failed to hit its mark.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a hidden gem among thousand of others digital card games. Create your own adventure mixed with card manipulation and card-driven scenarios.Its design is quite simple, yet it's so refreshing in the genre. The simple idea that you can play cards on other cards and get different results from doing this, is what keeps you invested and drives replayability. Forget about keywords and card effects written in boring manner. You get just an idea of what the card represents and then you discover all different scenarios, when it can be used to achieve various effects.Besides gameplay, there is beautiful music and good writing with jokes that actually makes you laugh. If you are into card games and adventure games this will blow your mind away.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for September 2023, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before October 3rd, 2023, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A narrative card game based on exploration and abilities. Foretales is a different type of card game.  This is a combination of resource management and a discovery or exploration game. Players have to navigate through a sea of cards.  Each mission has a specific story associated with it, usually with a couple of ways to complete the task.  Players will use character abilities, as well as items they find to achieve various goals, such as freeing their friend from a jail cell or trading for a necklace.  There’s also a combat system where players can negotiate around enemy encounters, rather than be forced to fight their way through the enemies every time. Foretales is a hard game to explain but for the right people, this will be great.  But at its heart, it’s a card game.  Also, the first two missions were well designed but the third mission I reached had a bit of a “Where do I go” vibe to it.  I’m sure certain cards had to be combined to get to the right location but it wasn’t clear how to.  There’s a hint system but it was vague enough that I could imagine the game may become a bit frustrating at times. Pick this up if you like Hand of Fate.  This is trying to be in that same vein, but it lacks a bit of that level of polish, but with the combat system being purely card-based, this also might win over some people who didn’t enjoy Hand of Fate battles.  The narrative design is solid here, and the entire game is an overarching story, with what feels like a few decisions based on time management as well, but also allows players to fail without a penaltyIf you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: I need a 'meh' option.If you are a fan of strategic card games, this game is not for you. However, if you like story games with some puzzling, you may enjoy this game.The card playing strategy is not at all deep. The primary objective is to build and manage the resources (gold, food, fame, grim, etc) to use when in combat or for various other tasks. The character-specific cards are what you use on locations to gather these resources. There are some variances, obviously, but at it's core, this is what the game entails. It becomes very repetitive very quickly. There isn't so much thinking or puzzling out what to do since it is usually pretty obvious how to complete your objective. The only thing that slows you down is your approach - do you use resources to barter your way through combat, or do you fight, which increases the search party which means more people to fight. It can get a bit annoying, but since this is the only feature that actually slows down the gameplay, I can see why it was put in.As someone who doesn't particularly like strategy games and prefers story games, I do enjoy this one. I just find it dull at times. I can only play for a short period of time before I need to take a break, since the gameplay loop is so repetitive that I find my attention drifting. The game is very pretty and the characters are somewhat interesting, but that is about it.Luckily, I got it on Humble Bundle. I would not pay full price for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A story-heavy card adventure with irksome mechanics.This game is clearly crafted with a lot of care. The method of story advancement and the way you can choose how to resolve world events are both clever. The story itself is pretty fun as are the characters.Unfortunately I did not enjoy the actual gameplay at all. Having to drag every card over every event to see the outcomes was tedious. _childDocuments_.review: Foretales is a narrative card game, a little bit like Fantasy Flight's Arkham Horror or similar games. It's got a good framing device of anthropomorphic animals and animals that you wouldn't usually see - like a Shoebill.The story begins with you stealing a Lyre that creates visions and you're trying to stop those visions coming to pass. The game gives you a few paths to follow to try and do that in the form of a huge dealt out deck of cards that slowly flip over as you progress. You click on it then get a few levels where you do whatever the goal of that card was.Helping some miners strike, recruiting a druid, doing a trial, various different things.Each character - and you can have a maximum of 3 at once - has a deck of around 9-11 cards and you draw enough to fill a hand of six. These cards are almost conceptual rather than having defined effects. Volepain, your main character, has some pickpocket cards and they do exactly what you'd expect. The others have things that just give a rough description like "Leo can sniff out help".You play the cards onto exploration cards that it deals out. They'll be locations - an alleyway, a tavern, a boat. And it tells you what effect it'll have before you play. You also have some resources you raise during the levels that you can use. These are Gold, Food, Fame and Grim. Usually you're spending them to go through fights or to get favours from characters you draw from the exploration deck.The "challenge" here comes from trying to solve the puzzle of the level while not running out of your draw deck. You can rest to restore 3 cards of your 9 but the rests are limited and usually punish you in a minor way as well so it does try and prevent you from doing this. The punishment/rest mechanic doesn't add tonnes of difficulty or anything but that's how the challenge of each level is set up. Do the puzzle before you run out of cards.It's a fine framework, the artwork is cute and the concept is fine. However because of the branching nature of the story and the way the game presents the levels you're doing as you progress it starts to come apart for me.Firstly the story has to take into account that you've got quite a few different choices to go through. So characters beyond Volepain can't have much to say since you straight up might not have them. And things you did in the past you may not have done, so they just don't get mentioned. I rescued Volepain's dad Peter and it felt like it might as well not have happened, he just vanished after I'd done it. Especially bad since there was a disaster after that rescue and I feel like I don't know what happened to him after that.For me this makes the story feel a lot less meaningful. I totally understand WHY it is like it is but the previous steps of the story barely feel like they matter and that makes the current story feel pointless, ephemeral. The actual meat of the game is more like a puzzle than a card game. You kinda have to guess what combo of cards (or what SINGLE SPECIFIC card) has to be used on different cards to get to the point you want to get. This isn't super difficult but at times you can go down the wrong path and one bit I was struggling with for a solid hour until I restarted and did it almost immediately. I think I'd skipped some cards and wasn't able to easily get them back.It feels a bit like an escape room at times. There's a lightbulb that gives you vague clues but sometimes you just go the wrong way and have to start over.I'd honestly be fine with this but there's a lot of unskippable dialogue. For example I'm searching for a prophet and every time the refugee card gets drawn I have a 10 bubble conversation with them that I have to click through and it isn't fast. If I feed them they also tell me a joke about weevils that I've heard about 30 times now and it's getting very tiring. It ties into the fact that in a later quest that same card might suddenly be relevant, even though it feels like it's still the same people and it shouldn't be relevant.There's no character advancement at all. And no character development because as I say - it doesn't know if you'll have those people. So Leo who you're with from the start has barely had a line since the first quest of the game. You get very occasional new cards for the characters in their starting quests but that's it. It feels stale. So the story doesn't adapt to what I've done, the characters don't change and don't really interact.The art is lovely, the concept is lovely but it just isn't clicking for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Foretales is a charming narrative based card game with a fun cryptic gameplay loop set in a quirky world with some irreverent humor and personalities. The turn-by-turn card play is fun and alluring, and the music and atmosphere is captivating. Any session of Foretales is an enjoyable experience.So why do I not recommend this game? Well, despite the gameplay loop being solid, the overarching structure of the game is so grating and irritating that pushing myself to sit down and play this is like pulling teeth. The overarching story progression is full of restarts, replays, and dead-end narrative branches that really make it overstay its welcome.If the idea of sinking multiple hours into a story branch to see if it even leads anywhere is not appealing to you, I would not buy this gaming expecting to ever truly complete it. Foretales incorporates a refreshing blend between card play and narrative story telling that really engages your investigative intuition. Each mission plays out on a table with a field of location cards that elicit different narrative results based on the card you place over them from your hand.  The main entertainment comes from figuring out what narrative consequence will happen if you play cards from your hand on each location card. (There are various visual icons and clues that help you understand what will happen). For example, playing a gold card on a location with refugees might earn you favor or even a one-use ally, but playing a steal card might net you some cash along with grim points and more guards in the patrol deck to worry about. Interacting with the world through cards is actually really fun! Each character in your party has a deck of cards with unique abilities. If you run out of cards of any character, you lose, so you have to manage the distribution and replenishing of character cards you play. You also have a second hand of resource and item cards. Battles take a second to get used to. There is a pre-battle phase where you can try to bribe or scare enemy cards away, or buff up your own cards. Each turn of the actual battle has your characters attacking enemies opposite them in the same column. After you get used to how it plays out, it’s easy to understand. Typically, avoiding actually having to deal damage is usually ideal. In general, there is a lot of reading in this game; not lengthy paragraphs or anything. But every part of the game takes place with at least a line of dialogue text that carries the story forward (outside of the narration, there is no voice acting for the characters). Often, critical information for your mission is explained in these dialogues. To help, a collection of dialogue you’ve seen is available in the upper left corner, and hints to your current objective are in the upper right. Sometimes what you need to do is so cryptic that the hints can almost feel necessary. So far all of this is good fun, and I found the gameplay very intriguing. It’s definitely at its best when you are moving the story forward and things are working out smoothly. But my grief began once I started to experience the repetitive “death-then-replay” meta-narrative design that this game resides within. Dying in this game, only to realize you need to replay the story from the beginning, feels really bad. I don’t mean dying in a mission where you just have to replay that mission. I mean dying where you fail to save the world in the narrative branch you chose, and you now enter a new universe timeline where you start from the beginning again. I didn’t understand this is how the game was structured. I couldn’t understand why I had to keep restarting the story. Was I doing something wrong? Was I just bad at this game? Was I  to die and restart again? It wasn’t clear. I later learned in forums that you are indeed supposed to go down certain narrative branches, which lead to you failing, in order to unlock knowledge and therefore narrative branches for future timelines where you can reach actual endings. I was very disappointed to find this out… I’ve played many roguelike games where you play a run, die, and try again. Often these have been roguelites where there’s some meta-progression where you unlock or something. Or you at least better learn how to beat the levels, like in a true roguelike. And this could feel rewarding, enticing you to try one more run. But those runs were always short enough to justify the repetitive gameplay loops. Maybe they ask an hour of your time per run.  But Foretales asks that you play multiple missions on a timeline before telling you “sorry, the decision you made a few missions ago actually doomed this timeline” without telling you what you did wrong or why this timeline was doomed, so there’s no way to really learn from your mistakes. It’s too cryptic. I don’t know if going through a timeline I was in and failing actually unlocked some knowledge or progressed the meta-story in some way, or if I just played through a wasted timeline because I went down a dead-end branch. It’s extremely frustrating not knowing if what I’m doing is actually moving me closer to finishing the story, or if I’m just going around in circles. Foretales is a fun game mechanically. But its overall meta-structure is so cryptic and unclear that it ends up staying way past its welcome. I feel it is poor design to have narrative paths (that you’ve invested substantial time in) lead into what feels like total failures, only to put you back at the first mission after a quick throwaway cutscene. It feels so bad to find yourself at the beginning yet again, staring at the first mission after all that time you put into the narrative, realizing you have to go through it all yet again. With there being no clear way to understand if what you did progressed the meta-game at all, it leaves you feeling lost and frustrated. So, unlike a well-made roguelike, this game does not feel good to replay. It feels like pulling teeth. Just like the basic gameplay mechanics, the atmosphere is inviting and refreshing. The presentation of each location in the narrative is basically done with different lighting, card art, sound effects, and music. And it all comes together so well that you forget your looking down at a table. You really become engrossed in the world and feel like you’re at a new location. It’s visually a well-polished game and it works really well. Foretales is a game with great gameplay mechanics and atmospheric presentation, but is seriously disappointing by its implementation within a repetitive and frustrating meta-story progression system. If this were a game I felt was satisfying enough to play through a single timeline and experience an ending, I would say it’s worth at least checking out. But because your timeline run, and many after that, are guaranteed to end in failure and essentially a restart, I don’t think I can even recommend you check this game out. Which is a shame, because there is a good game in here. My advice is pass on this one.(P.S. I always strive to at least complete the story of my games. Ideally, I like to try for 100% completion, if I feel the achievements are reasonable for me….I think Foretales might need to be a game I leave incomplete. For my own sanity.)

_childDocuments_.review: Before you read: Just remember that I didn't actual finish the game to the final ending, instead I just finish the first run.Since there is a lot of positive review already, I'd put down some point I found so you can think about it before purchasing it.-Overall, I think this game would feels great if we can have a ending in one try.It's not a "bad game", but there do have some issue with it. Since you can't really go to best end in one try (instead, you'll need to retry multiple time for true ending),  the second try of the story feel a bit lame (because there are barely new mechanic, only partial new story, but like 50% you're gonna play something you've just played).So it makes overall experience a bit repetitive after your first round.Also, combat lack some synergy so you might found it start to felt boring after about 3~4hrs (in new runs, there are no difference).During replay, the narrator and animation can't be speed up, also levels you've played before need to be replayed.For me, this game is more like a old school Japanese visual novel (the one you might need to reply same stuff again and again to get to the best ending) but package in a fancy way.I personal think, if you're interest on buying in this game, ask your self can you play same story with small different again and again, if your answer is yes, than maybe this game is for you.For one who want interesting card puzzle/combat, or a trpg-like story that is interesting enough, I think you might be a bit disappointed for this game's approach after you first round.So for personal taste, I'd say I won't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly charming, beautiful to look at, and consistently surprising.  If you are at all a fan of interesting narrative experiences with a good dash of supporting gameplay, pick this one up.  While you should go in expecting to do multiple playthroughs to get to certain endings, there's some smart design here that accelerates later playthroughs a good bit.  One of the more unique games I've played this year!

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of winding storylines with meaningful decisions that have a genuine impact on the story that unfolds, gameplay that grants you the flexibility to play however you like, or the deckbuilding genre (loosely) then you should absolutely give Foretales a go.It's by no means perfect - some mechanics feel a bit redundant, or like they can be ignored entirely - but it's clear that a lot of love has been poured into this game, and that's reflected in the warm, fuzzy feeling I found myself getting as I explored the game's narrative and discovered the wealth of hidden interactions the developers have sprinkled liberally throughout the game. As a generic example, an early story beat has you trying to get past a bunch of guards, currently fending off a rowdy crowd, to get into a building. The game gives you the tools to achieve your goal in at least four (that I discovered, there could well be more) different ways. Not many games, let alone card games, can profess to allow the same.This is a game I really want to love, and it is absolutely worth your time and price of entry... but it does fall a step or two short of greatness. I've found myself playing one or two full chains of scenarios and then setting the game down because I started to find the gameplay loop repetitive, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. I'd rather mete out my time playing a good game that gets repetitive than burn myself out on a great game that takes too long to get anywhere.Don't go into this game expecting an experience like Inscryption or Slay The Spire because that would do both of those games, and Foretales, a disservice. It's a simpler experience than either of the above, but it's not trying to compete with them in complexity. It instead aims to tell a sometimes-intense, sometimes-silly tale of a rogue and his band of friends trying to survive and save the world, and in that aspect, it succeeds entirely.The best analogy I can give is that the game feels like a "choose your own adventure" book with plenty of extras - an enjoyable narrator, beautiful artwork, more agency over the decisions you make, and more mechanics than a book could ever provide - or a digital, whimsical equivalent to Arkham Horror: The Card Game. If that sounds like something you're interested in, this is a game you should play.
