_childDocuments_.review: 6.5/10.  An episodic card battler deckbuilder in which you strategically select your next battle based on various resources and needs.  Very good storylines and narrations and a good amount of interesting content.  It plays similarly to Banners of Ruin with more of a puzzle element in the path choices.  I rated it slightly lower because combat feels a little too punishing.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I normally do not like completly card-based games, but actually enjoyed this. It is funny and different, although it can be a bit repetitive. There are different ways to progress in the story and it gives you a feeling of freedom, but you still have to do some steps exactly right, which takes a way from the feeling of you being in control of the game. But it is still a good game, and if you want an interesting story and a chill way to play a game, this one is for you
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite special and not what I expected (in a good way)! It sets itself apart from other card games.I want to give some info to set the right expectations.Unlike other card games this one is less focused on deck building, multipliers, RNG and game breaking synergies. It's a time loop puzzle game.Much more like an adventure game where each card is an action that you apply onto a location/character. There are no clear texts and numbers that tell you what each do. Context and critical thinking is everything.Even the time loop approach is unconventional. You don't play short loops but instead the progression is reminiscent of Nier.The first run get's you accustomed to everything and can take you 12 hours. The game then changes the writing and other mechanics to reduce repetition. Each consecutive run can will be shorter. 6 hours. Then 4.There are many endings and optional encounters. The writing is fantastic although the story and overall mystery a bit bland.The art, music and atmosphere of each location makes it a joy to play.I have some other small gripes but the overall experience is great.Go check it out if you want to play something that feels new!
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: It's a card game, but not like Magic: The Gathering or Slay The Spire. It's more like a puzzle game, with each level being a puzzle. It's not particularly challenging; more of an emphasis on story. Even the combat isn't really combat. There are branching paths. Multiple playthroughs are required in order to get the true endings, and there is no way of circumventing that. It took me 3 playthroughs.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: A game with a very unique story telling presentation. They did a really good job of joining a choose-your-own-adventure style story with card game mechanics and constraints. The cards, music and table merge together to make a satisfying audiovisual experience, with minimal dialogue and narration needed. Even though the demo is no longer up, your first 20 minutes of gameplay is what was in the demo, so two hours is more than enough to determine if you like the mechanics, as the game does not hold anything from you the moment you start playing. Worth paying full price in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest, the gameplay doesn't really appeal to me. Cycling through looped encounters to get resources just feels really dull, but that's the game.That said, a lot of effort seems to have gone into the non-gameplay elements. I didn't encounter any bugs or glitches and the art's super. While I'm unlikely to continue with it, if you do like this style of adventure game, then I'd certainly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I went in wanting to enjoy this game, and if you really like the story and don't mind feeling frustrated, needing to repeat the game to find the best solution as well as being OK with making sacrifices, then you might like it. Overall, the card game aspect was incredibly shallow and felt really just like a visual novel with pretty minor puzzles and frustrating mechanics. Was not at all motivated to repeat after running out of time on the first run (and therefore failing)
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Not a game for everyone, but a game with one of the most unique experiences I have ever played. I would highly recommend to patient fans of puzzle games. It's less a card game in the traditional sense (deck building does not exist) and more a game where you have to use your characters' social abilities (each represented by a card) to progress through situations in changing circumstances. Every character ability can be played in any situation, though they do not all have unique effects, giving the game a feel similar to a choose-your-own adventure story with more complex mechanics. I've seen every ending the game has to offer. I really and truly fell in love with the various characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements in games.Some story and gameplay spoilers ahead. Foretales a card deck based puzzle game that, unlike Cultist Simulator, it’s very easy to play and accessible. The results of the card combinations are shown before you do your move, and the illustrations and descriptions of the cards are clear enough for you to understand them and easily guess what works and what doesn’t.The story is very complex and can branch out in a few different ways, depending on the choices you make and the missions you choose to play. Soon you’ll realize you can’t play them all and you’ll need to do several runs to get all the bits of information you need to reach the good and true ending of the game. The writing is solid, for both the events of the story and for the dialogues between the characters, and the events of the story will keep you engaged.The illustrations of the cards and art style work very well with anthropomorphized animals (think of Zootopia) that populate this fantasy world and you can see the connections between the type of animals and their attributes and personality. Overall the graphics, visual effects and animations look great.The narration and sound are also excellent, especially the narrator who is voiced by Travis Willingham who recently gave voice to Grog (Legend of Vox Machina) but has a vast career in voice acting. References to popular culture are common and the jokes are hilarious.As mentioned, the gameplay is simple, but finding the ideal combination of skills/items and locations/characters requires a bit of trial and error. The best way to deal with some bosses sometimes isn’t very clear at first, but there’s always a better non-violent way of completing the levels. Gathering resources might seem hard at first but with a bit of practice you’ll be finishing levels with tons of extra resources, as they are almost always quite abundant if you know where and how to get them.  41 Achievements. Around 30 hours, following some guides for the achievements. Easy, you just have to pick all the different dialogue options. Easy, but takes a lot of time and several runs to complete everything. The game doesn’t have a save/load system and forces you to complete a run, but later allows you to replay one mission or pick another occurring at the same time. My runs weren’t always ideal and I lost some hours here and there as the guides available weren’t very clear on some of the tasks.   Foretales is a great card puzzle game with very well written characters and a complex story, with 3 different endings and several side missions. It’s easy and fun to play but takes some time to learn the best card combinations to play efficiently. Not having a save/load system makes some of the achievements very time consuming.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: A polished and engaging deck-building choose-your-own-adventure RPG. Not much like Slay The Spire, more similar in spirit to Griftlands (i.e. a much heavier focus on story).Story choices are limited, so it rewards investment in playing the characters. Doing so is encouraged by recurring dialogue and an emphasis on narrative. Great art as well!
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: 9.7 / 10if you know me, you know i love me some timeline games. foretales is a BANGER timeline game that utilizes a card system - but instead of focusing on deckbuilding, it focuses on puzzles and figuring out how cards interact with one another. five playthroughs in, and there's absolutely more i've missed. timothy my beloved. the only detractor is that i wish some instances of your protagonist being surprised about something was replaced with different dialogue on a loop. notable is the "gah... where are they taking him?!" at the start of every run... after we've already figured out where he's going. still, though, it's an insanely good game and i cannot recommend it enough.damn worth the full price of $20. no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cut content "DLC", just the art book and soundtrack if you're about those.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare that you get to play a new kind of game but this is one of them and it's great. While it uses card mechanics I would say it's closer to a point and click than a card game but I do find this system a lot more enjoyable than a point and click. The game requires you to play it a few times to get to the real ending but this works well with the way the story is written, it's not so much about the main plot as it is about fun situations and character interactions, I like to compare it to the Asterix and Obelix comics in that regard so just playing a mission with different characters keeps it fun on repeated playthroughs. I do have to mention that I probably got to the ending in the right amount of runs as there are stretches of the game that I didn't find anything new during my final journey and those did feel a bit like a slog, I imagine if I had to do it again, with even less new encounters, it would have been very annoying. I would however say it's not really a game you need to beat to get the full enjoyment out of, I don't feel like I've gotten that much more on the perfect run compared to the previous one where I failed to save the world.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I can't in good faith recommend this game, as it's just too flawed. Given a bit more effort it could be great, but as is it's got too many issues.To set the expectations: this is a narrative-driven game with pretty light cardgame mechanics. You could easily strip the cards away and keep the same game. It's more about resource management than what 'cardgame' might make you expect on steam.It's mostly well executed, with pretty graphics and works smoothly most of the time. There's multiple bugs, but a reset tends to fix most of them and just loses you some progress or an extra reward you don't really need. It has a lot of charm, and the first few hours are fun.The bad mainly comes from the way the story works: the MC has visions of the future, including past runs. For the 'perfect' ending, you need to have done at least 2 runs. Unfortunately, one off those will be almost identical to your final run, and the replay value is atrocious. You do the exact same thing, solve the same puzzles, and the game's not fun enough to make that enjoyable. Worse, besides some added dialogue and small events, all dialogue repeats and is unskippable, including a narrator who frequently spends 20 seconds talking before you can do anything again. Or a bard you visit frequently, who gives the same 5 textbox explanation each time, and says a little repeating poem after each possible action. It's cute the first time, but after that it gets frustrating.There's 'branching paths', or rather events you can pick between or do in a different order. This would be neat, except that there's no acknowledgement for any order except the 'perfect' one. Do them in the opposite order, and the lines make no sense. The devs decided to make non-linearity and repeats a core part of the game, but then didn't put in the effort from a narrative or gameplay perspective to make that enjoyable.At the start of a 4th run, the game literally gives you a character that lets you skip large chunks, showing the devs know that it isn't fun, but the 3rd run is already going to be near-identical to at least 1 before it (there's only 2 real 'routes'). And that still leaves the endlessly repeating slow dialogue, unskippable cutscenes, identical missions and all the missing material. To make the easiest comparison: in the Stanley Parable, the devs have thought of everything you can do. In this game, despite giving the idea of freedom, the devs put no effort into accounting for what a player might do. It's got a great linear experience, but deviating makes the dialogue incoherent and the game forces you to repeat said linear experience anyway. There's just not enough effort put in, and from what the devs said it'll never get patched in either.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very unique turn on narrative games. I just finished my first playthrough (I lost) and I can't wait to start a new one with different choices.There is a lot of small interactions to try out, and the gameplay is very fluid.Obviously the game is also stunningly beautiful !A huge congrats to the developers
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Fortales started as an excellent narrative driven game with cards but its reliance on repeating missions with unskippable dialogue took away from the positive experience.To explain how the game plays: Over the course of the game you pick missions which unlock ones but lock others.Inside the mission, each character you control has a deck of cards with skills. Using skill on a location card will have an effect that is dependent on both the skill and location type. For example, there is a skill that Calls for attention. This can either summon curious townsfolk or enemy monsters depending on if you are using the skill on the city streets or on an infested mine.Selecting which cards to apply to which location is the core of the game and has a resource management and puzzle aspect to it which is well implemented. Most outcomes are reasonable given the interactions. Plus the game even tells you what the outcomes are so you don't need to guess or memorize them.I had a lot of fun with this aspect of the game, and even the game in general as it provided an interesting, well written story. Unfortunately, despite it not being a roguelike, to reach the "True ending" (or normal one) you need to replay the game, completing missions in a certain order a few times. While there are hints on what the order should be (even better if you took notes) it can still require a bit of experimentation to get it right. This would be fine if the missions weren't as long or there was a good way to skip all dialogue which there is plenty of.On top of that, replaying missions isn't as fun because there is usually one or two ways to solve the puzzle so the entire concept of having to go through the missions again is flawed and felt like a chore. + Good story+ Interesting puzzle/resource management hybrid with cards+ Love the artwork. * Most puzzles are well designed but there are some questionable ones. On one mission you can recruit an ally that a says it's great at avoiding traps but applying that ally to a trap location kills them. What? - Necessity of replaying missions to get to a good ending without having the skip dialogue option. This is a slog to get through even when you know what you need to do. Foretales is an excellent narrative driven puzzle game with cards, but requires repeating missions without the ability to skip any of the many dialogues which quickly becomes frustrating. Careful recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Among several things, this game features nice art, witty narration, and a unique mechanism that gives players many choices and paths through each level. In addition, the story of the game allows players to experiment with different approaches, and discover new and interesting interactions on each run. Other than an ending that leaves a lot to be desired, this game is well worth a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very unique and interesting. You use cards to interact with the world around you so it is kinda like a table top campaign you'd play at a friend's house. I am a sucker for card games so the aesthetic really got me! I also really love the art style and sound design, there is a lot of attention to detail to keep you immersed in the world. Great game, get it if you are looking for something fresh or really like tabletop games like DnD.One thing I would really like to see in an update by the way would be a "fast" mode for the animations. The game has great replayability so it really makes sense to make it go faster with a setting at least for missions you've completed in the past.

_childDocuments_.review: Just played for an hour before going to work and felt compelled to drop by to say how much I love this game. _childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Tentative recommendation.I was totally drawn in for a couple of hours. The artwork is beautiful, the design is great, and the gameplay feels dynamic - you never really feel like you are just looking at a couple of digital cards on a table. Things fall apart a bit as you go on though. This is essentially a puzzle game that you solve using cards. This is a problem. Reason being? Cards are random. random and limited. What this means is that you may have figured out how to complete a puzzle, but then you're still stuck with an awkward grind trying to find the cards you need to make this work. When you are relying on random cards from multiple decks, and have only limited room on the board, this can become more tedious than fun.In short, I like the idea, but the idea just doesn't translate all that well into a fun game. Maybe if you could tweak your decks to improve the odds of getting what you need? I don't know.Soft recommendation for the good visuals and enjoyable setting.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Foretales is a sly fox among card battlers, cunningly cloaked in the guise of a narrative escapade. It dances to its own tune, more akin to a fine gamebook adventure, where wit and guile are your trusty companions.So, here's the scoop: you're on a mission, gallivanting about to stave off impending doom. But beware, each decision you make locks away other tantalizing paths, so choose wisely, my friend.Now, onto the heart of the matter - the missions themselves, a delightful dance of cards upon the table. You'll weave your hand with those laid out before you, earning coin, confronting foes, and spinning tales as you go.But tread lightly, for every corner turned may reveal a fresh challenge, with enemies lurking like mischievous sprites. Combat, when it comes, is no dalliance; it's a gritty affair where strategy reigns supreme.And then the missions! From straightforward jaunts to brain-teasing conundrums, there's no shortage of adventure to be had. But fear not the unknown, for therein lies the charm.Resource management, my dear Watson, is key. Spend your cards wisely, for rest comes at a cost, and every decision weighs upon your fate.And let's not forget about the characters - each one's got their own bag of tricks, like a magician at a kid's party. So mix and match, find the right combo, and you'll be laughing all the way to victory.With multiple endings and secrets aplenty, this game is, like a dodgy kebab after a night out. Seriously, it's got that replay value that'll have you hooked until you've uncovered every last secret and seen all the endings. Trust me, you won't be putting this one down anytime soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: An innovative game in its own right, Foretales is a mesh of interesting ideas and gameplay mechanics that makes it such a joy to play. The game itself is a card-based adventure where you play as Volepain, a hornbill (as he will oh-so-politely remind you) who was blessed/cursed (he seems to think it's the latter) with visions of the future after stealing a magical lyre from the local noble's home. In this game, the cards you have are the actions and tools you need to navigate the many locations or to interact with the people during an adventure. Combat here is also entirely optional, especially since Volepain and his friends (most of them anyway) are more "thieves" than "fighters". The game gives you plenty of ways to bribe, scare, or essentially demoralize the enemy to the point where they will flee the fight. Of course, some enemies - the ones affected by the beast-ilence - aren't as easily routed (you can only use Food) so you might actually need to fight them at the end. Unlike most story-driven card games, Foretales also has plenty of replayability, namely because you've only can go on a handful of adventures during the time limit before those adventures will be closed to you. This encourages the player to replay the game just to try out other adventure paths and uncover new story endings. Plus, there are actually many secrets in each of the adventures (like side quests or hidden options that will only be unlocked if you've got the specific card - want to burn down the inn and cause total mayhem? Well, you'll need the firebomb first!) so if you're determined to find them all, it might add a few more fun hours to your total playtime.Foretales is truly one of the more unique adventure-driven card games that I've played over the years, and it's definitely a game that I'll be comparing other similar titles to for the time to come!
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: An unique and very well made game!I started getting flustered later on because of how difficult it is identifying which cards to use to advance, but upon reading various walk-throughs, it became apparent just how complex the storytelling is in this game and that's a good thing on top of an already good thing.  So I'd recommend considering having a walkthrough handy for when you get stuck.  Between that and the annoying narrator, everything else is super nice and fresh, well worth anyone's time.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my new favorite Story-based RPGs, and I think it needs more attention than it's getting! ForeTales could be seen as a very standard RPG, if not for a couple twists that make the game feel fresh and fun. Firstly is the card system. Your adventurers all have moves they can do, represented by a deck of cards that you as the player draw a hand of. these cards can interact with another deck of cards on the board, The locations. These are places like watchtowers, shops, or jail cells. You can use character cards on the locations, like using a thievery card on a shop to take some food, or using an archery card to shoot a merchant and get some money (for a large bit of infamy, of course.) The resources you get from those cards can be used on locations in kind, like giving some street urchins food in exchange for information, or paying off guards so you don't have to tussle with them. I only have two gripes about this system, and they're not a big deal. The first is that animations can be a bit lengthy for things like drawing new locations and stuff, and if you have a big combo planned or know what you want to do, it can really take a while. the second is that voice lines for particular actions aren't very numerous. For example, using a steal action will get you repeated lines often enough for it to be noticeable. Both are  very minor and could be patched easily! Neither of these should prevent you from buying this game.The second aspect that separates the game is that the protagonist can see the future, sort of. It happens after the first mission, where you see a series of horrible events that seem destined to happen. The mission selector is a series of cards that represent tasks to complete. some cards don't represent tasks and instead signify of the horrible events that might happen. the game doesn't tell you which tasks will affect which events. each event has a countdown, and if you take no action (or take the wrong action), it'll play out as foretold. Your actions within missions can change things, as well. A murderous maniac will have a harder time with diplomacy, for example. I hope that I can convince at least a few people to try this one out. It has great art and presentation, a fun story, and good gameplay!
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: A really inventive narrative game that almost calls to mind playing a Powered By the Apocalypse-style tabletop game. Very clever mechanical interactions between your party's skills and the situations you come up against, and a plethora of hidden events and secrets to find. My only gripe is that the 'good ending' route is a bit counterintuitive in how it's achieved, and if there were any in-game hints on how to get it, I didn't see them. Making a poor choice on your path can mean not realizing something's gone wrong until hours later, and that's definitely not ideal. Still, it's an experience I don't regret having.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recomend anyone get this game as it's a really excellent narrative puzzle cardgame where you use differnt character cards to manipulate and progress the story. it's really brilliant, together with very well written characters, outstanding art and a main plot that keeps unweaving and evolving, you have a winner! Highly reccomended
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This is a must play for fans of narrative games or RPGs. It's a choices-matter RPG presented as a card game, and it manages to blend DnD-style open-ended choices with a really intricate branching narrative.But it's not *just* a branching narrative in way most branching story games are. It's done in a nuanced and meaningful way that feels like an extension of the moment-to-moment choices you make with your cards. Without revealing too much, this game has a StarFox-esque branching mission structure, and it takes that idea and evolves it into something very special.I've never played a game like this before, and it keeps surprising me as I play more.The art, music, and presentation is also top-tier. There is a pretty crazy volume of card art in this game, all extremely high quality and well beyond what you'd expect from a small budget game.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sold on the idea at first but this is a very compelling puzzle adventure game with beautiful art direction. It can get a little hard to remember certain details on repeated runs though and things can get repetitive, though the game takes care of some of that.But all in all this game is a big net positive that I'm really enjoying. Just maybe be prepared to take a few notes on things you can't quite work out in case they become relevant again next time you play.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: The art is beautiful, the story is rich the music is amazing and the gameplay is uniqueif you're looking for a game that's as much puzzle as card game with a lot of branching choices whose consequences at sometimes not felt for a long long time then this is for you. Don't worry if you choose wrong, its a time loop! you will be making those decisions again.If there's one problem with the game the nature of the time loop is one where you will be facing certain dialogue exchange and missions again and again and the only meta progression is your growing knowledge but there is a fun to that. At times in your loops it may seem that the solution is impossible but I assure you, there is a way to save the world and have everyone walk away alive. Well everyone in the party at least.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write reviews for games often, but this game caught me absolutely off-hand. While looking for a simple, indie game to maybe spend a few hours on a weekend I stumbled upon Foretales and oh boy, am I glad I did. You can clearly see the love developers put into this game just by looking how polished everything is. The artwork is outstanding, the music feels like it belongs there and in turn, you as a player, belong in the world. And the amount of Easter eggs and pop-culture references makes it a fun experience of constantly going "Aha, I know that one!"This is a masterfully crafted, story based card game. Wouldn't really call it hard, but the puzzle aspects do make you plan for the future. You are free to role-play a pacifist, mastermind bird who always finds ways to overcome every issue with wit (mostly gold) or a mass murdering, deranged, friend to a gorilla, that breaks necks, blows up buildings and shakes down snakes. The narrator (who is a fantastic piece of the game that you should experience yourself) will often suggest being nice, but don't get close to colour purple, he gets a bit spicy ;)Of course, the game has a few issues. It can be overwhelming for a new, vision-bearing avian player, but it will get more clear in time, I swear. Some parts of the game will naturally need to be replayed a few times if you wish to see all that the game has to offer and that can become a little tedious, but on the bright side, past experiences make it way quicker.All in all, I'm being cheesy, but wishing to not spoil anything, my advice is to play this masterpiece of a game. It's definitely worth its price and on a sale... Well, it's going to be a steal. Make sure to have your nimble hands ready.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun little game. Offers some challenges while also allowing for a good narrative storyline. Also, if you need your hand held there is a hint button. I've only needed it on one level involving a library was a bit annoying with little clues, but beyond that no complaints. Definitely worth the price tag.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Warning! The second half of this review contains some story spoilers, but they will be kept vague.  I adore this game. Plain and simple. It's one of those games that you go scrolling through steam trying to find, but no game quite scratches the itch. A race against the clock, trying to navigate through the world, before something terrible happens. Your character has a deck of cards, normally with a somewhat broad title like, "Nimble hands". Each card is context sensitive, so Nimble hands can be used to pickpocket, collect, or in other ways be thief-like. As such a large part of the game is trying to figure out what to use where. However, the process is logical. Need a key off a warden? Nimble hands to steal it, kill them in combat, or just lockpick the door. The general gameplay loop is really fun the first time through. Speaking of:  SPOILERS PAST THIS POINT!!!!  Eventually you will die. Normally, you'll run out of time on a doom card (the game's "timer"). When this happens, you lose. Game over. And you Start over from the beginning. This is where a lot of games that have you replay the same section can lose me, because you'll have one of two things happen:  1. The game stays the same. Nothing changes other than you, as the player. Your knowledge and skill improves, but the game stays the same. These tend to lose me, as it can get boring replaying the same thing repeatedly, but if pulled off well, can still be good.  2. The game changes. This is what Foretails does. You and volepain act as one, both learning and improving together. Certain knowledge from previous attempts carry over, allowing you to skip a lot of the trial and error, because even if the player doesn't remember the solution, Volepain does. The dialogue changes, and the game becomes much quicker. It doesn't stop there, either, as every new attempt, the game gives you something to make the gameplay loop shorter, while keeping the writing fresh.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I'm making this review well before I've finished the game. However, Foretales is a wonderfully done card based RPG. Gives all the vibes of a homebrew D&D campaign as far as story and humor is concerned.  It's somewhat similar to Hand of Fate, minus the 3D action/combat portions. It's well worth the $20 asking price. If anything give the demo a shot for what the game is like.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This game is captivating! I find myself playing it four hours on end not realizing how much time is passing. It's incredibly immersive with the art and the writing being amazing! The "decksploration" appears off putting but ends up making perfect sense and helps you feel immersed once you master it. I cannot recommend this game enough, and there's so much to do! I just "failed" my first run and am now realizing just how much there is to this game and it's replayability.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Initially, the game was pretty sweet. It was different from regular card games or card builders. The visual, sounds... story even. It all seems good. So I enjoyed playing. But for some reason, the game didn't really get me invested in what was going on. I wasn't curious about what would happen if I do X or Y. I think that may be because the game lacked a bit of a challenge. There were no missions that I'd fail. I'd just do stuff and somehow succeed. Also because while there is some story at the beginning and end, along with some encounters, as a whole the story was on the background. So instead, I just picked whatever mission was available and did it. And then another. And my initial joy of it feeling different got replaced by a gradual feeling of boredom, as it didn't really keep things fresh. You did the same old. Sure, with new characters, new enemies, new encounter cards and such it never was the same, but enemies are not often fought anyway, so that wasn't really interesting. The encounter cards where different than the ones before, but at the same time the same, and the new characters just made you a bit stronger. So as I played on, I figured I'd least play til the last mission (as I had no interest of playing again, trying a different route), but even that grew boring and eventually I found myself playing without enjoying it. So this isn't a clear case of no. More like... a meh. Nothing bad, but it couldn't keep up the initial positive impression.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I can only give Foretales a weak recommendation, as there's no 'neutral' option. The art is really nice, and initially the gameplay is pretty fun! However, there is a large amount of repetition, as you have to finish the game a minimum of three times to get the 'good' ending. This is a bit of a weird choice in what is essentially a point and click adventure game in disguise, as you play through the same scenarios repeatedly and they always have the same methods of solving the various challenges you face.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I would highly recommend this game!! I got it in the Humble Bundle, and boy am I glad I did. This game is a little outside of my comfort zone as far as most things go, but I don't regret playing it in the slightest. The gameplay is very unique, you participate in a series of strategy-based interactions, all through the medium of playing cards in various environments. The story is enthralling, and multilinear, with different endings and different paths you can take through the game. The characters are comedic at times, but still manage to carry weight enough that you want to make the best choices for them.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Story-based deck-builder, with story-based rng . Think "King's Quest" meets "Banner of Ruin" and this is what you get. The game is genuinely fun, and there is a lot to explore. I enjoy trying to figure out alternate or even secret solutions on my own. Def recommend you don't look up spoilers. The game isn't exceptionally difficult. I "beat" it in 7 hours, but got the bad ending. Worth another playthrough
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: I quite enjoyed my time with it, it's a neat little puzzle/adventure kind of game, not quite sure how to describe it. The story is interesting, I'm not certain i would say it's "good" or well told as it would vary wildly depending on the route chosen.As i said, i quite enjoyed the game overall, hence the recommendation, but:I never actually finished it, not completely anyway. I won't spoil it, just know that you probably won't reach the true ending on your first playthrough. Which isn't an issue per se, no the issue for me was that a single playthrough can take a LONG time. My 15 hours were spent on just two playthroughs, two paths through the story and i have no idea how many paths i would need to properly finish the game.Using the cards, figuring things out and trying new routes through the story is all quite well and good, but the luster wore off before i could finish the game. After my second playthrough, i just couldn't be bothered to spend HOURS on a third run, hoping to learn a bit more about the world and story or maybe, just maybe, finish the game this time.In conclusion:it's a good game, that I do recommend, but i would caution against repetitive gameplay if you want the true ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: It's an innovative and well made game, but personally I can't recommend it due to the illusion of choices, which greatly diminishes the feeling of Emergent gameplay, let me explain.  In some games you are given choices over what to do and how to do them, and there are no obvious "best" approach, just what you ended up doing and you try to make the best out of the situation. This game, however, does have that one "best" solution. The problem is - you won't know that. You won't know what the ideal solution is until it's past that point.  Here are two examples:  1. In the first region of first real mission, if you try to save your friend, the very first rest option requires you to spend money to get some item you don't know if you'd need. Or you could just get a free rest. But you may not want to pay or even save up that much money because the game told you to free your friend by paying money... and the other way is to have enough crime point. You don't know which is the better option to spend your money, but you don't get crime points easily either. Now, turns out, if you don't pick the spend money to rest option, in the second region you'd miss a new card, which is kinda important. But you wouldn't know that, because that's literally in the different stage...2. Once you have freed your friend and moved into the third region - there's a bandit camp - full of bandits. Well normally you can't solo an entire bandit camp, right? The game tells you to rendezvous with your friend, and naturally, you want to team up with your friend first, then go tackle the camp, right? And the game has always allowed you to explore/linger on the map longer, so you'd think the game is designed for you to tackle the camp later, right? WRONG! WRONG! WRONG! The moment you meet your friend, that mission ends right away. You've been taught that you could be free to stay and explore in the past stages, but no, the mission arbitrarily just ends. And oh BTW, did you know that if you bring a mercenary from the prison with you, you could get to a weapon hideout in the bandit camp? Well now you do, and I hope you'd know the best strategy to do mission 1 now!  And the biggest vice of all - the game told you could retry the missions if you failed - but it didn't say you could redo a mission if you passed! And it's right - if you win even if you missed a bunch of useful things, you CANNOT GO BACK! And this is just the first mission, I can only image the number of things I'd miss starts to snowball due to the difficulty getting higher as I keep missing more things. This is what I mean by the illusion of choice. The game clearly awards you for playing it a certain way, but you won't know that after you've played the stage. And I guess you could intentionally lose the game so you'd retry the mission, but that just seems awful as the missions can get long. And honestly, it's not that charming for me to click through the game again. The charm of the story lies in the first playthrough, once you know what's going to happen, then you're just going through the motions to game the system. But that's what this game tries to do - it needs you to game the system. Try and retry until you have discovered all the secrets, and then go in for the ultimate setup. This is a utter failure on the "emergent gameplay/storytelling".  I like the story and the UI/voice acting is charming, but the actual game itself is not fun to play as it shoehorns us into playing it in ways that we can't know what to do but it presumes we do. This is just not fun to play, as a game. If you like the charm of the game, maybe go watch a Let's Play or something.

_childDocuments_.review: Foretales is a Nintendo Switch game that's somehow ended up on Steam as well.  This furry friendly visual novel has a twist... instead of just clicking next/skip to plod through the badly written E-book dialogue, you have to play Old Maid or something with a bunch of cards.  Like, combining inventory objects and using trial and error to see which cards will work together.  I suppose you could see this as a Monkey Island adventure game with the adventure game component ripped out, leaving you just to do inventory actions to progress through the story. The shallow premise made me a little confused as to why this wasn't on mobile phones, which is what it seemed designed for.  Likewise it's not a browser game (but it sure could be), and as we all know, if Firefox or Chrome can do the whole thing, why does it need to be a paid product on Steam?  And paid product this is, with an eye watering near-AAA $20 USD price tag (for a Nintendo Switch E-book!!!!)There's an overwhelming amount of mediocre Visual Novel/E-book style cutscenes in this game.  So you'll spend a huge amount of time not playing the game, but clicking through endless lines of poorly written VN text cutscenes because the developers couldn't work out how to relate their narrative through the game mechanics, and decided instead it would be better to compete with reading a book for your time.  We're here to play games, not watch hours of garbage intersituals.  I know that's the point of this "game", but it's also a serious problem.  My gaming rig is not a Kindle. Because this is designed for handheld/portable gaming appliances, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the low power handheld gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the mobile game developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for low power handhelds forces upon a game.  While this might run well on a Steam Deck, we must remember the vast majority of gamers here are gaming on PC.So, should you buy this e-book?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?Foretales has the far too high price of $20 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  For comparison, the $20 asking price for this game could get you games like "Europa Universalis IV", "Rust" or "Lethal Company".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

_childDocuments_.review: Foretales is a really wonderful narrative adventure! Witty and fun writing, lots of excellent art of animal folk, and an intriguing story with a couple of twists that caught me off guard made it a fast favorite!Now, before we get more in depth about Foretales, we need to address the elephant in the room.Her name is Lady Isabeau.She is very good.After that, there are two things you need to know to enjoy this game: 1) "card-based" is not the same as "deck builder" and 2) you need to be able to persevere through defeat.First point, Foretales uses decks of cards to represent the environment, the inhabitants, the inventory, and the actions - You don't make a deck of cards for the characters so much as the characters have a predetermined deck of cards that represent their traits, skills, and abilities. Your job as the player to navigate that deck and find the right ability to use on the right set-piece for the results you need to advance. It all plays out like a shifting puzzle of asking what each character can do that can solve your current predicament... or get you into new and exciting trouble!The second point - trying my best to explain this without spoiling the game, but you should play a run through to the very end, even if defeat looks certain. Overall, Foretales is an easy recommend to anyone who wants a fun and interactive story. The writing is fun and interesting enough to have you seeing what every combination makes, the puzzles feels rewarding to solve, the art is delightful and there are some very cute easter eggs and references among the cards. The only caveat is that if you go into Foretales hoping for an arcade-y deck-building experience, you will be disappointed - this game fills a very different niche from the waves of deck builders, and it fills that different niche exquisitely.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't really recommend this game. It's alright, but it's wildly repetitive. You get four characters max at a time (but can only take 3 on a quest), each has a deck, and each character has about 12 cards, and each character draws 2 at a time. They shuffle endlessly and repeat. You're on a board where location cards are also infinitely shuffled and loop, until you draw a key card you need for a quest, then go to the next area. You get no new cards over time, you don't unlock anything, the dialogue repeats a lot... and then, at the end of the game, if you don't get a perfect playthrough, it starts you over back at the beginning, so you can just go do it alllll over again. Yay. This game feels like it's a barebones single idea someone had and then they didn't expand on it at all. I wouldn't even buy it on sale unless it was like literally two dollars.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a story game, and a childish one at that. There is no challenge to it whatsoever. It's too easy to gain an abundance of resources, which trivializes combat encounters. The storyteller voice makes me feel like my hand is being held and that I'm ca. 5 years old. It's far from a tight, balanced experience. It's unbalanced in the favor of the player, so defeating bosses and missions does not feel at all rewarding. The resting mechanic, which is supposed to limit how much time you can spend in each region before you fail or can move on, is way too lenient, and the optimal way to play (to stay in a region farming as much resources as possible before moving on) just punishes the player by needlessly stretching out the time required to complete a quest. Since you don't need that many resources to succeed on missions, playing less optimally and wasting opportunities to gain resources, is oddly the better way to play the game, which feels odd and unrewarding on a tactical level. Strange for a card-based game, there's no deckbuilding, and strange for a scenario-based game, there's no meta progression aside from story. The art is well done, but animals that talk and dress like humans is far from an original idea. The cards are interesting in that they are based on the context of the location you want to use them on, and each card has different uses for exploration and combat, but this also makes your cards feel less corporeal and less powerful and lacking descriptions of their uses beyond an intuitive understanding. I appreciate the fact that it's mainly a narrative story experience, but why then include all these poorly balanced systems that bloat and needlessly complicate the game? At first glance it seems to have tactical depth, with its lengthy tutorial, but it never seems to deliver on that front. The game seems confused as to what kind of player it's made for. To some people I would recommend it, but generally, no. A good concept, but an unoriginal world, and with the unbalanced, bloated tactical aspect... I wanted to like it, but the air quickly went out of this bubble.

_childDocuments_.review: A card-based narrative letting you choose your own path through its story.Foretales puts you in the boots of Volepain, a small-time thief who stumbles into an adventure that sees him try to recover a number of magical artefacts in an effort to avert a world-ending disaster. This leads to you having to make your way through various locations, all the while having to track down acquaintances, make new allies and help out strangers.This journey is presented as a collection of playing cards, each depicting a possible event, with you having to choose which to deal with one after the other, creating a branching path through the game's story. Events come with a time limit, forcing you to choose only a limited amount of them to complete while missing out on certain other ones. Each event completed provides you with certain advantages, which influence the availability of future events as well as the options you have in them, further diversifying the ways things will play out.Starting an event presents you with a location, represented by a number of cards depicting characters or objects. You're also given a number of different resources and a hand of cards drawn from your deck, which you can play to interact with the available location cards, i.e. by using a steal action on an onlooker to gain gold. A location card you interact with is discarded and replaced either with a specific one brought on by the action performed or one drawn randomly from the location's deck.Using this basic system, you're essentially meant to discover certain location cards to end the event, either by depleting the location's deck or by triggering certain interactions, all while managing your various resources. You're given a limited number of cards from your deck to achieve this before the event fails, meaning you have to play your cards strategically. To make this harder, Foretales also feature fights, which see you using your hand cards to damage or otherwise affect enemies, further decreasing the amount of cards you have available as well as the limited health points of your characters, though I rarely found them to be too challenging.Just like the fights, these puzzles rarely felt too challenging, mostly requiring some trial and error to figure out the required interactions. I found exploring the interactions available to you to be probably the most interesting aspect of the game, but also more than once found myself growing quite frustrated as certain interactions just aren't very intuitive and can require quite a bit of luck in regards to card draw. This aspect of exploration sadly also tends to get lost on subsequent playthroughs.The characters mentioned before add different abilities to your deck, thus influencing the options you have available during events. You can enter an event with up to two characters in addition to Volepain, forcing you to make a decision on who's abilities are most likely to benefit you during it. Events may unlock new characters as well as cards for them to use, further expanding your options as you go through them.As for the narrative, Foretales at its core tells a rather benign save the world story, set in a similarly bland medieval world. However, the game also presents some neat mysteries and adds some decent twists and turns throughout its runtime, which did a good job at keeping me interested. This is aided by the way things are written, with banter between characters and even the general narration feeling quite charming.Due to the non-linear nature of the game, you'll need multiple playthroughs to see most of what it has to offer story-wise and to find the game's proper ending. This is explained in-universe in a rather interesting way, with you retaining certain things from previous runs. This helps keep the game fresh, though I still found myself somewhat bored when repeating events I'd already seen and knew the solution to.Foretales also does a great job of presenting all of this through great visual and audio design. While most of the game is visualized just through cards, these are placed in a 3D environment matching the atmosphere of the places you're exploring, which does a great job of immersing you in the game's world. Similarly, every action is accompanied by playful visual effects and meaty audio cues, giving even simple actions a nice weighty feeling.Beyond its sound effects, Foretales also features a fitting if basic soundtrack and a narrator voicing out most of the actions you take as well as story transitions. While I very much enjoyed the charming narration, certain lines became rather annoying when repeatedly using certain actions or on subsequent playthroughs.Overall, I had a good time with Foretales, largely due to its charm, interesting narrative premise and the initial experiences of experimenting with the card gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty good, especially if you get it on sale. Its not a deck builder or rouge-like, though, if that is what you were expecting of it. It uses card based characters and narration to tell the story, and to beat the game you have to play it through multiple times making certain choices along the way.  It took me three runs through, the last run being the quickest, before beating it. If you enjoy a time loop style of story with self referential humor and some nerdy cultural references, then you might like this game. Oh yeah also if you're a furry you might enjoy the artwork Once you have a feel for how the interactions and combat are meant to play out then the game goes pretty quickly as you have a good idea of what to expect when certain cards come up for interactions. I loved the art for the cards and the character interactions, although there were times when a character might mention something that you haven't yet encountered in the run (it was clearly a mistake or oversight and not an intentional reference by the characters), but luckily that was pretty rare. One thing I didn't enjoy was the narrator commenting on absolutely every interaction I had, and sometimes it was annoyingly condescending like when giving poor kids money or something lol, it just bugged me. I had the narrator volume down to just 10% (because on 0% I couldn't tell when he was finished talking) for nearly the entire game except for the last run through. Without any spoilers lets just say there is a reason why the narrator is there and after you discover that reason it makes it more interesting to hear the commentary and for some reason it becomes slightly less snarky as well.Overall, it was an enjoyable experience. I would really recommend for folks who like story driven games.

_childDocuments_.review: A positive narrative puzzle experience that I loved the demo for, but the full game does not build up on it as much as I would like - so while I recommend it, it is not a must play in any way. The characters are fun, the interactions are enjoyable, some card game novelty exists and the polish is there. However, it lacks a certain depth in both the card game mechanics and the story progression. I generally enjoy this type of games, but to properly enjoy this one I still had to give it the benefit of the doubt for quite a while.In more detail, and with some spoilers:There are many enjoyable sides to the game, perhaps too many to list. For example, I love the choices of animals for almost all characters, even the extremely minor ones. So I will go with the bad stuff, with the intention of it being constructive criticism.The game requires quite a bit of repetition: repeating card cycles to get resources you will need in the next, likely more challenging region, repeating similar regions, similar missions, and finally - the run itself. At around the time when you reach the true ending, you can finally make these runs more quickly because you learned how much preparation you need for a specific mission, and what order you need to do them in. This creates a series of smaller issues, some of which may actually be fixable for a much smoother experience, while others are likely not as simple:That's all I wanted to say. If you've read this far, thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Foretales, a game that looks like a tabletop game, feels like a tabletop game but is a single player story experience. Gameplay revolves around managing resources and completing missions, those feel like puzzles, with multiple ways to complete them. Some alter the story and lead to multiple endings/situations. This game changes, the more you play it, for reasons you shouldn't know without playing it. Gameplay, feeling, plot and drive feels totally different in 2 hours compared to 15  this review, I'll talk about 3 time frames of playtime: "Early" - 0-8 Hours playtime "Mid" 9-19 Hours Playtime "Late" 19-25 Hours playtimeSadly, Foretales is one of those games that you can't talk what it is about, if you know before playing, part of the experience is lost. In a sad combo, is ALSO one of those games that you have no clue what it REALLY is about until you hit the "Mid" game. Like I previously said, plot and drive completely change over time. In my opinion, it feels pretty good. the story is pretty good overall. I'll ♥♥♥♥ on it during this review but I really like the story, game kept me hooked and invested, specially the in "Late" game. If you want to spoil yourself WHICH I DON'T RECOMMEND, here's what the game is truly about, I'd say you discover this about 8 hours into the game: The game has the tabletop style, VERY stylish. The way the game is presented with cards and a table is an S+. The narrator tops it off with an amazing performance that complements it all in a perfect way. Art is S+, it's furry, but it ain't weird or sexual in any way. Everything in this game is well drawn and art-wise nothing feels rushed or cheap. Dialogue is well written. characters feel good, consistent and express themselves sufficiently. They aren't the focus tho. Humor is subtle, quick and doesn't feel at all out of place or tone. Music is good, no beautiful pieces but works. Every aspect in the game complements each other, making this game quite unique and stylish, in a good way.Although presentation is S+, in the grand scheme of things looks like they are presenting bread slices with a golden plate. this game had A LOT of time to explain every detail, expand the universe, yet they chose not to do it. That's a weird choice, as the universe feels complex and a lot of things could've been expanded on. In the end, it works, but a lot of potential has been wasted.I feel plot-wise, "Mid" is the weakest part of the game. Sadly, that's the longest part. didn't ruin the game but Mid sometimes felt like a chore.True ending was quite a let-down. A lot of build-up and hype that resolved into a "Eh" ending. No climax. I felt I wasn't properly rewarded for grinding the true ending. Resource based gameplay isn't for everyone. The game plays like a puzzle, but never got old to me, might get old really fast for you, though. I'd say gameplay changes a bit during "Mid" and "Late":  but you can mostly get the feeling for the game in the first two hours.This game has tons of love and effort into it, but it's clear it wasn't play tested that well. There's some oversights. Once, I spent over 30m running in circles in a mission looking for a river, almost hitting a game-over. It was the only place I used the tips system and It didn't help. They kept talking about a river and it there was no river....Imagine my face when I noticed the river was behind one of the stacked regions that had been substituted in the table by a card effect.There's no "Fast Mode", like other card games that makes some parts of the game feel like a chore. Some dialogue are....unnecessary. (It's hard to talk about this without spoiling some parts of the game. This doesn't mean it's bad dialogue, only that some parts take your immersion out for reasons).Some missions are convoluted and could be shorter without sacrificing anything meaningful TL;DR This game is presented in a beautiful way, the narrator does a fantastic job. Story isn't god of war Ragnarok but it's intriguing and interesting. Art is very good and gameplay is simple fun and puzzle-like. Characters are consistent, fun and although not that deep, they're still fun companions. Game suffers from a long playtime and a wasted opportunity on it's universe. This game gets very cheap during sales, If it looks interesting to you, pick it up! you'll definitely not regret giving it a shot even if you don't like it!
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting take on an adventure game with card elements.I've enjoyed the writing of the missions that I've done so far. The characters are charming and the pacing keeps you interested in the story. The story is separated into missions. Participating in different missions might lock out others, so choices matter as far as experiencing the journey- encouraging multiple playthroughs. Missions themselves usually have optional side objectives to power up your brigands. The game itself is simple and doesn't require too much strategy. It's simple resource management. This could be a good thing or a bad thing, depending on who you are. It's a fun little romp that's text heavy and will require some trial and error to get a perfected run. All in all, I'd say you could complete the story in a couple days. If you want a more long-term card game, this isn't it. However, what it does offer is quaint, relaxing, and enjoyable. I think this game blends the adventure genre and card genre well. There's something to be had here for future releases or for inspiring other projects. Might be worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: is a little rough around the edges, but the great dialogue, art and card/currency management will help you slog through the occasional obscure puzzle or mission repetition. I should emphasise that these rough patches are the exception, and there were definitely times when I felt smart for solving a puzzle or playing efficiently .Fair warning that the game is predominantly character driven and isn't particularly deep mechanics-wise. The word "casual" is a better descriptor than "shallow" here but, then again, I'm no board game junkie. You're mostly using whatever cards you draw to prioritise and maximise resource gains while deducing then saving the right cards to fulfil a goal or solve a puzzle. Bad luck protection presents itself with the ability to discard one card to draw a different one of your choice (which isn't  in most game scenarios but is a lot better than just relying solely on luck). There are a few interesting alternate routes to take or achievements to gain if you're clever (or sometimes deliberately stupid) with your actions, as well as their associated dialogue. Speaking of, dialogue is absolutely what makes this game for me. Character development goes hand in hand with all sorts of neat little details. For instance; you can get rum in some missions by buying it, stealing or whatever, and have a party member drink it to gain "Grim" (a resource). However, it also prompts a reaction from said character. It was through rum that I learned that one character accidentally got her parents divorced when practising her diplomacy skills on them, and that the main character isn't even old enough to drink, thus taking damage whenever he uses rum on himself. Aside from player choices and story plot points, these interesting details and similar interactions you're rewarded with for exploring and experimenting help to characterise your party well.The game obviously isn't perfect, but it definitely held me for as long as it wanted to and was enjoyable throughout. The interesting ideas the game plays with (most that I can't describe without spoiling them) make it worth the ride, and the characters are sympathetic and well developed in order to make it all work out in the end. Don't worry about having to replay the game too much  unless you can't stand not getting the true ending. After all, it should be easier when you've already been here before. Right?A brief epilogue would have been nice, like just a few still images of what happens to our characters after the ending over the credits would have been all you needed.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hooked on this game the moment I first started it,  it oozes polish and has all the elements of a well structured story game. _childDocuments_.review: Foretales is probably not for everyone, but it was definitely for me.This is a puzzle game that uses cards to display locations and characters as well as using them to represent character abilities and resources. The overall story focuses on trying to save the world from destruction, but there are very few ways to do this on the time limit that the game gives. Despite the narrative adventure vaneer, make no mistake, the heart of this game is puzzle solving. Part of the puzzle is learning what resources are skills are necessary to move forward, and the other part is decoding the narrative to learn what has to be done to move forward in the first place. Anyone who does not enjoy reading long strings of text, possibly several times on the hunt for clues, should probably stay away.Literally anyone else should give this game a try.Every single card in this game has impact and purpose, even if it's not readily apparent, and learning exactly what you can do with them is one of the most fun parts of the game, and it lets you improve through knowledge of the game's landscape. If you gain new power it's almost always because you explored new possibilities which can either lead to whole new options or just speed up what was a tedious process before. For example: you could spend a lot of hard earned fame to reduce a certain trader's outrageous price for a boat, but why bother? You have a diplomat with you who can achieve the same result with just one card. Still don't have the gold? Cut out the middle-step: use your big strong friend to just rob the guy. I'm sure it won't have unintended consequences.Parts of this game are frustratingly obtuse when it comes to what you have to do, but these are far and away eclipsed by the extremely clever moments that either demand you think outside the box, invite you to improvise, or both at once. The ending, once you finally reach it, is very abrupt, and outside of achievements I wouldn't say there's a ton of replay value unless you intend to try and speed run the game. Even so, this is definitely worth your time for the gorgeous and expertly crafted narrative puzzle it puts together. It feels like a natural evolution of a "choose your own adventure" book that also embraces everything that can be done as a video game. I loved this, and I hope you do to.

_childDocuments_.review: An innovative, immersive, and ingenious narrative card game. Fans of games such as Steve Jackson's Sorcery! and Inscryption will find a lot to love about this game, from its breadth of narrative choices to its diagetic tabletop presentation. Be warned, however, that it takes some commitment to reach the game's "good" ending. Without spoiling what happens, I will divulge that it will take several playthroughs of the game's campaign before you can even figure out how to get the good ending, and each playthrough can take anywhere from 10 to just a couple of hours to complete. The game does provide many ways to speed up subsequent runs, but it might not be enough for people averse to replaying old missions many times. I personally thought the game kept each run fresh with its branching paths and various companions whose unique skills change how each mission is completed, and the ultimate satisfaction of getting the last perfect run left me extremely pleased. I can only hope other developers follow Alkemi's example of creating unique experiences with the digital card game framework that go beyond simple copies of Slay the Spire.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: This game is stylish, the exploration of interacting cards is fun, and the narrative is great.I've been having a lot of fun playing this one.I do really wish it was possible to enjoy a "good" ending without playing the whole thing 4 times in the "correct" order, but honestly, the game is fun enough that I will probably get around to all 4 playthroughs (eventually).If you think you might like this game, you'll probably love it.

_childDocuments_.review: A card game that is easy to pick up, but hard to master. It challenges you to use your imagination, logic, and ability to read context clues. It's incredibly fun to play, figuring out what cards would result what effect when played on what other card. There is always a solution available to complete each mission, but depending on who you bring along into your party, side missions or easier solutions open up to you. Accompanied by beautiful music in the background, be prepared to play this game several times as you rack your brain to defeat your foes, avert disaster, and even spy several shout-outs and references that made me (and hopefully you too) smile and laugh a little.

_childDocuments_.review: Good job developers!This game has the vibes of Spearhead Games studio: "Stories: the path of Destinies" and "Omensight"-Antropomoph animal charachters - check-Time loop - check-Requirement to fail few first walkthroughs in order to gain knowledge for the true ending - check-Narrator behind the scenes - checkWhile gameplay reminds most of The Cultist Simulator, only divided on missions and directed on storytelling.You have resourses, skills, items and followers/minions as cards that could be used in different situation for multiple purposes and wide range of outcomes. You can bribe, scare, use your fame, stealth, diplomasy, or good old ultraviolence to acheeve your goals. Yoe are free to choose and have plenty of options. Each misssion has many ways of finishing it with any charachters on your plate, so it's up to you and your playstyle how do  want to walk through this adventure.It's the way of trials and errors, but if you enjoy this kind of games - you shouldn't miss this one!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a lot of fun! It's more of a resource management/exploration game than a traditional deck builder and honestly I find that more enjoyable and engaging. You balance your food/gold/fame and other resources to help you solve/discover new solutions. Your character actions also act as a resource pool to draw from. Each character has a certain number of things they can do to create new outcomes and gain different resources/find new locations, before they have to rest (which consumes OTHER resources.) That's where the exploration comes in. You kind of just start mixing "solution A" with "solution B" and see what result you get in terms of either story/battle/new resources. Most scenarios will require you to restart as you often come to dead ends or realize that there was an easier, better way that will help you in the long run, but I rarely ever got irritated by it. That's the nature of a game that asks you to explore its possibilities. And I really like that aspect of it. Need some apples to feed a hungry guard? Trade gold for it OR pick pocket the wealthy merchant. Need booze to get the pirates on your side? Run a hustle on the local sailors, or search for the smugglers secret stash.The thing that probably is the most appealing and is what will draw most people in is the art style. I loved it and finding new character cards be they cultists or less than morally grey bandits, then looking at their art and reading the flavor text associated with each new person/object/place brings this world to life. Which leads me to talk about the writing.This is probably my main flaw with the game. The writing is charming and made me laugh, though I do really wish there was more depth in each of the characters. They are all pretty one-note and given that this is a game about exploring different narrative threads, I would have liked to see more from them after they join your party. Maybe if they each had their own wants and needs to be met besides just helping you save the world. BUT! The big choices you make in the game offer quite a variety of playthroughs, and none of them are "Good choice, Bad choice". They come down options things like, do you want to join sides with the hulking gorilla and help his protesting miners (join the struggle comrade), or appeal to the order of mothers and gain the negotiator? Both of which open entirely different routes and areas. Neither are bad or good, just different avenues to be explored that make me want to do a second play through (and I rarely do second playthroughs)Oh and I love the music. It reminds me a lot of Crystal Chronicles which is my favorite Fantasy OST.8/10. This game is def worth your time, even though its not perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: Foretales

_childDocuments_.review: Uff, this game needs way more content for such an 3rd chapter time kill :SI really like the artstyle and alot of the interactions+all the cool animals they brought up into the game as soldiers, mercs, etc. .But getting time stomped in the 3rd chapter, one mission before the end really makes me sad :/.I mean the game gets really repetitive after some hours, ( the same biome cards, same follower cards, same enemies ) and in the first playthrough i hold on just to see all the cool new interactions, biomes, lvl my chars, etcs. which the 3 chapters have to offer.... but now i shall do the same thing all over again just faster to reach an ending?Don´t get me wrong, i like the game and the stuff that i played through was solid, but it´s not nearly enough content to make me wanna go another whole campaign run, just because i don´t reached an "ending" yet.Stuff that bothers me the most: You don´t have a backpack to transport stuff from one main mission to another. You really have to grind through all the ressources again every main mission. You don´t keep any ressources, followers or cool items you hardly earned in the main mission beforehand. In my opinion that was unnecessary grindy, for a storytelling game.Like really, this game is all about ressource management, just inflicted with cool cards. To do the same stuff always over and over again, so you have your pool of ressources to complete the mission was so lame after 5 hours.The secound thing was the cool linking in points of interesting within each other to reach cooler loot or cooler followers. In fact i really loved it in the beginning but in the midgame i find out, that the amount of stuff you get from those end chains is totally unworth the amount of spended ability cards for it. The only thing which was somewhat satisfying was the steal 7 Gold from the rich persons "path" with upgraded volpain "steal" or find the mercenarys "path" ( but in the end you just get one merc.....so still meh, but not so worse then the others :/ )The third thing is the combat. There are so many cool ideas and stuff you cold do with this lovely mechanics, cards and enemy types. Hell, i would play through a whole "build up your army" mode of the game, where you have to recruit new soldiers, find new consumables, do some side quest stuff, gear up or buy/ find new soldiers, patch up wounded soldiers or bury your expected losses you have to take. ( A little bit like nowhere prophet ).Sadly tho, you rarely use this combat stuff at all, because killing enemys ( even the dirtiest dirt of the cultists ) in the mindset of the game is a bad thing, which leads to bad karma stuff happening.So i ended up just using the bribe mechanic to click me through almost every encounter, which made the encounters pretty unnecessary at all. So many cool enemys and effects, which i, beside the artwork, completed ignored my whole playthrough.Just throwing coins into the club and move through the crowd with my big daddy mantle of reputation was totally enough for the whole game. ( Which in fact wasn´t as much fun as you might think it was ).

Each mission ends up being quite freeform, and then you realize that completing missions in different ways or in a different order changes other missions down the road, or even which missions become available. _childDocuments_.review: Yeah it is good.As a seasoned boardgamer, i can see more in this game than non-boardgamers, and i can say it is really fleshed out and well designed.Everything fits, art, story, music, accessibility, rules, control.As for the game loop, you must manipulate cards, manage resources, find strategic ways of doing things which is very rewarding.I only wonder what happens when i finish my first playthrough towards the end, and what about replaybility, apart from making different choices, in the same story. _childDocuments_.review: I bought this due to the review on RockPaperShotgun.I'm really, really liking Foretales. A terrible curse is ravaging the realm and the only one who can stop it is a small-time thief named Volepain.

The Weaver put in the hands of her children the fate of the world's creation and stability. The instruments of creation have the power to create and destroy the many worlds of Foretales.

Discover the true goals of the Nymphants and the Cult or embrace the Maelstorm for eternity!
