_childDocuments_.review: is a wonderfully charming puzzle game with a whimsically punny but still heartwarming story and a delightful cast of characters. The game also uses a special pathfinding mechanic that involves manipulation of pieces of the map, quite unlike anything I have seen before. The artwork also shines in its hand-drawn style, creating a puzzle game that is visually pleasing to all ages.The very specific nature of the puzzles in this game involves spatial manipulation of the puzzle pieces, and arranging them just right so that you can progress. These puzzle pieces are the very land that you are walking around on, and The clues come from people that you can interact with or from specific on-screen hints. The one thing to keep in mind is that aside from what is available, there's also empty space to consider for possibilities. There are a lot of hidden pieces that show up only when you put the other associating pieces correctly with respect to each other.As of writing, I am only about halfway through the game and I am taking my time with the puzzles. I have been stuck on a couple of them but eventually running around enough and putting the small bits of clues together, I have been able to progress without too much difficulty. I am looking forward to slowly tackling the rest of the game. The times when I am stuck in this game, I am not too frustrated, I just take a step back, go think about something else or play a different game, then come back with a fresh mind and try to think through from a different perspective.The puzzles are not difficult at all. In fact, a lot of them are fairly easy. The clues are right under your nose, and you just have to piece the small bits of information together. There have been quite a few smiles of amusement as my brain became attuned to the specific clues, and a lot of times they are not too subtle either.My experience so far has been nothing but pleasant and relaxing, and I look forward to finishing the game and savoring the process along the way.I am using a controller, which I think works well. Keyboard also works fine.Lovely hand-drawn artwork with nice colors and drawing style. Very pleasing to look at. Here's an example:Subtle background music that is calming and pretty well-suited for this game. The sound effects are fine for the most part.Anyone who enjoys puzzle games will probably enjoy this game and its neat mechanics.The base price is $19.99 and some people will be able to rush through the game in 6-8 hours, but the quality of the game is there and I think this game is worth it. I am guessing it will take me close to the 10-hour mark to finish the game. is just a delightful puzzle game with nice art and an original mechanic that's original and fun. Quite enjoyable and absolutely worth your time and attention. If you think the price is a bit high for what you might want to spend, I think it's fair to wait for a better sale price. But definitely add it to your wishlist and keep a close eye on it!Overall score: 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a wholesome and great game. Nice music, magnificent artstyle and a great story. The game is puzzle based, mostly easy to play but can sometimes be a bit difficult. I was bored so I randomly downloaded this game and I'm sad I didn't do it sooner. I really reccomend it, it's not long, around 4 hours to complete it.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this in the Humble Bundle. I honestly don't understand what others like about this game.The game is quite short. I am currently nearing the end of the story at less than 4 hours in. The art is decent if the style sits well with you, but for me it's not particularly appealing, and the music is forgettable. I found the characters shallow and uninteresting. It's a puzzle game in a way, but the puzzles are not interesting. Often, the solution is found by pulling up your map, moving something, and seeing what changes. The solutions are often either too obvious or too vague; there's very little middle ground. Above all, I find the speed of the game to be very slow. Since I don't really enjoy the world, I'm now at a point where I just want to finish it, and even with the speed boots the character moves at a pace that makes the process tedious. I finally had to close the game because I just could not stand all the back and forth and needed a break.I guess if you're looking for a very low-key experience, this would be a good game, but it's not one I enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: In summary, a great game.I was looking for something nice and cozy, and this game delivered just that. The music and the artstyle brings this small picturebook-like world to life, and it is beautiful. Some of the puzzles did have me confused at first, but with enough determination they aren't that hard to figure out. Very early on, when I was unaware of a game mechanic.2. Toward the end, when I solved part of one of the hardest puzzles by accident, but quickly undid my solution, leading to more confusion. Other than those two instances, the game did a solid job of pushing me to experiment and rarely felt tedious or frustrating. Really nice, wholesome little game.

_childDocuments_.review: From the vegetation moving gently as you pass to the novel puzzle-solving mechanic, this is a well though-out and visually appealing game.There's no punishment for a mistake you would not have made if you hadn't had a tough day at work, and the narrative is rewarding in these uncertain times. _childDocuments_.review: This is a very cute and fun puzzle game. For the most part, puzzles are intuitive - if you get stuck, take a moment to consider any clues the environment gives you (people, signs, etc.) as for the most part, these will be enough to figure it out. There are a few tricky patches, but overall it's a nice difficulty level where solutions are not always obvious, but can usually be deduced. My five year old and I are playing this together, and she loves collecting the map pieces. (For her, the directional puzzles and connection puzzles that reward her with new map pieces are far more fun than revealing "hidden" tiles. I like both types!) The storyline is clever, taking you from one area to the next, and sometimes back again, while never over-staying in a region long enough to get bored. My daughter thought the hook of "little girl looking for her grandma" was great, and she's decided this is now her favorite game.

_childDocuments_.review: Adorable and incredibly cute. The music is great. But the narrative lets it down. It's an adult trying to pretend to be a kid, and it's painfully obvious. The mechanic of moving the map around is great. But that's the main mechanic, other than pressing A to interact.Also, if you miss a line of text telling you what to do, you're in bad luck. It'll give a cryptic clue as to what it said.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally played this on gamepass, but after my sub ended I wound up buying this game.If you ever played the game Carcasonne, it reminds me of that with the tile placement, but theres these puzzle mechanics like 'i live west of this other person' so you pick up the tile he's on, and put it west of that other house, and suddenly the house appears. Its a really cool and innovative puzzle game. Each area Carto visits has a new self-contained story, with an overarching story of her trying to find her grandmother after she fell out of the airship (and somehow survived without a scratch). Its just really fun and unique if you like puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Played the demo, glad I got the game.Carto is a cute, stylized puzzle game with an interesting and consistent main conceit - move and rotate map squares to solve problems. It has some very clever ideas and solutions and it's pretty much a joy to play.Pros:Visuals are cute, polished, and in a consistent style that works for the gameThe story is easy to follow without feeling flatThe characters are fun and each has a pretty distinct personalityThe gameplay is generally fun and interestingThe music and sfx are goodMiddles:A pretty short game. I got through 8 chapters in three hours. If you want to play a shorter puzzle game it's a good option!Child-safe and child-oriented by all appearances - whether that appeals to you or not is up to you.Cons:Some solutions are unintuitive to the point of requiring guides (the last puzzle in the desert in particular)Found a piece of a secret out of the way I didn't know existed so now I get to worry that I missed moreGameplay is occasionally a little clunkyReturning to the , although it is neat, quickly becomes tedious and annoyingOverall, it's a pretty good game providing you go in with an exploratory mindset! The game encourages you to try new things - pay attention to what characters are saying, but go out and explore!Some solutions feel a little weird (), but overall it's pretty satisfying.

The mechanics are great, changing the map according to the descriptions from the people you talk to etc. In the first chapters that worked really well and was fun. But around the middle of the game (according to walkthroughs), I started missing hints. Not sure if they are just very obscure or I'm too bad at getting them, but I had to guess or consult a walkthrough more and more often, the further I got. Eventually I decided not to finish the game, because it got so annoying.I decided for a cautious recommendation, for the idea and the first part that I really enjoyed. Maybe it's just me, that I got stuck so often later on. I would wait for a sale though.

_childDocuments_.review: Delightfully adorable, a wonderful palate cleanser, and absolutely recommended no matter your age. I would say its a game about Culture, Curiosity, Unity, Communication, History as well as the preservation of history. _childDocuments_.review: Puzzles are satisfying but not overly difficult.  Plenty of changes to the formulae that keep the game fresh.  Art is cute and simple, but beautifully done.  Music is relaxing and suitable.  Dialogue is interesting without being over the top, if a little sparse.   My main complaint would be that the story is a bit laser-focused and maps rather small, with very few opportunities to choose what to do next.  As such, the pacing is a bit brisk if you don’t have trouble with the figuring out the solutions.   That said, it also means no fat or empty filler - no grinding or aimless wandering to pad the hours.  It also means there's no compelling reason to replay (apart from achievement hunters) .
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: «Carto» is one of those games that make you feel all warm and fuzzy inside. It's easy to enjoy in small portions or finish in one take. The art style is beautiful and the story is very cute – what I personally enjoyed the most is that one gets to meet most of the characters multiple times, which makes for better storytelling, in my opinion.The puzzles are okay, a little too easy most times for my liking, but the technique is new (to me at least) and it was fun to try and build the most efficient or most coherent maps. Also, in each chapter there are new ways to work with parts of the map, which makes the flow of the game much more interesting. I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes relaxing puzzle games with a nice, thoughtful story, and on top of that one gets some wonderful scenery throughout.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: What a gem this game is!A heartwarming story with beautiful art and cheerful characters. I really enjoyed how unique each tribe/area was: in fact, I wish I could have stayed in each place longer and learned more about them. They were all so friendly and welcoming to Carto that it really cheered me up, and despite the limited interactions with each area I still came away with a sense of depth and history for each place.The map-movement feature was such an innovative take on the puzzle-game genre, and figuring out all the clues was rewarding without being too frustrating.If I have a criticism, it's that the game was too short. This is mainly because I was so wrapped up in the story that I wanted it to go on further and further, but also because I feel £15 is slightly expensive for 5 hours of gameplay. That being said, I had a wonderful time in Carto's world, and would definitely recommend the game to others.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game in the most recent Humble Choice, and I was very pleasantly surprised by this cute and clever game! The puzzles can get a little opaque and frustrating at times, so don't feel guilty if you feel the need to consult a walkthrough at times like I did lolIf you're a fan of any kind of puzzle or exploration game, definitely think about checking this title out.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful indie game, a fun art style and unique puzzle style. It truly is an inventive way of creating a puzzle game and I enjoyed it thoroughly. It's like those wooden sliding puzzles, but better! A cute story and many different area's to go through make it a pretty engaging game. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys puzzle games, and those who like unique game dynamics seen in Carto with the map puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A cute, fun little puzzle game about adventuring, making friends & drawing maps. The character writing is excellent, the world is gorgeous & it's impossible not to feel cheerful while playing this game. A strong recommendation from me, though it is a little on the short side, even for trying to get all of achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: It's a short game, but it's fun! I finished it in about 6 hours but I did have to get hints from a video because if you miss a message a character says, sometimes you don't know where you're going next. It happened only a couple of times, but I would have been stuck on those parts for hours instead of minutes. All in all, would recommend,
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is cute, quirky, and even quite funny at times, but somehow I just didn't enjoy it. I can appreciate how some people might find it relaxing, but I just found myself getting impatient with the slow pace of the game. Some of the puzzles are quite clever, but it gets pretty samey after a while - listen to the characters, interpret the dialogue to find a new map configuration, rinse and repeat.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Charming, if short, puzzle game. Few puzzles are hard, though the 'secret' ones are harder (of them, there's only two out of six where I'm not happy about the clues, now that I know what they're hinting at. One's too subtle for my tastes, the other's obvious enough but the game interrupts you with a cutscene at the point where you'd be most likely to experiment, and then gives you the chance to leave the chapter shortly after.)Buy it if you're up for 4-5 hours (plus, for me at least, maybe an hour of replaying to unlock the secrets) of a cute, if at times shallow, story with light and, in my opinion, unusual puzzle mechanics involving maps.Not very replayable, other than for the secrets and if you want to re-experience the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: fun way to use map pieces for puzzles! were sometimes difficult to know when to 'spawn' a tile vs find it in the wilderness but an online guide can set you straight.  i am disappointed that collecting secret tiles MUST be done in a single run instead of collected later by replaying certain chapters, so i'm not going back to finish the achievements but it was still a fun playthrough
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: I loved playing Carto, the design is so cute, the characters are great, the story line is great and the concept is amazing. I loved controlling the land/map with the different map pieces I found along the way. I think it is a very cleverly set up game, I was very impressed. The puzzles were fun too however I found myself looking for answers online a few times as some of the puzzles are not very obvious and were hard to understand. All in all I enjoyed Carto a lot and would recommend to anyone looking for a sweet, cozy game with a little bit of a puzzle challenge.MY RATING - 9/10 -  ☆ ☆ ☆ ☆ ☆ ☆ ☆ ☆ ☆
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a bad game but it is simply too short and the gameplay too simple to honestly recommend. That's a shame, because the premise of the game is very interesting. You are a 'cartographer', which means you have the ability to manipulate the very ground you walk on. The game world is broken into map segments, which you can pick up, rotate, and place down in any order you'd like (respecting matching up map boundary patterns.)The problem is it feels like this idea is never really expanded on or taken as far as its potential. It rarely goes beyond simply finding the right fit for 2-4 map pieces so you can get to a specific spot. There are a few glimmers of gameplay going beyond that, with things on the map reacting to the specific rotation of a map piece, but it still feels vastly underutilised as the core gameplay mechanic.Since the gameplay is weak, it would be good if the story made up for it, but that is also fairly barebones. The overarching plot is that you are lost and trying to find your granny, but how you get there feels completely disconnected from what you do. Your motivation is simply the game telling you "go here, do this, OK now go here, now do this..." etc. Despite this, it can be confusing to know what to do next at times - the game relies on giving the player hints as to what to do, but without the tasks being interconnected, they feel more like an unrelated series of tasks strung together than following a connected storyline.You meet characters along the way but most come and go with very few lines of dialogue, so it never feels like you're really building up to anything. You're just doing a series of vaguely connected tasks until you reach the end.The presentation is nice at least and the watercolour-style art is pleasing to look at, if nothing groundbreaking. Carto is certainly not a bad game but it does not live up to the potential of the idea behind it.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game with a unique premise. Makes you think outside the box and come up with ways to find things using the pieces of the map you have. The full story took me about 7 hours to finish, I did not get 100 percent completion. This is a great game to get for a weekend activity. Short enough that I didn't get bored halfway through. The story is very cute with lots of fun characters to meet. And the art style is fun with soft colors. Loved it!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Unpopular option. Cute as hell but started frustrating in chapter 5. Interesting premise, but you need to solve everything in the right order. First, in the forrest chapter, I put together the rune but you can't do that only after you put together the stone that tells you what the rune looks like. Rune was obvious, put together 4 small stones, not. After that the sand chapter. It tells you the person is in the middle of the ruins. You only put together 1 way to work. Then you need to go to the well, but no rope, so you have to go back to the camel AGAIN so you spit out the scarf. Why? I already speak that camel, I could pick up the coconut. Why can't I pick up the scarf? Why I can't solve it the way that is obvious to me? Sign... It is a pretty game, but not for everyone. If it was frustrating to me, it would frustrate a kid so much more.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Such a gem! The gameplay mechanic is simple, smart and tons of fun! Puzzles are never too hard and still feel like a challenge. The art is super cute and the texts are kept short yet they are filled with creative details. The qirky characters are just lovely. The length of the game is perfect for a few cozy evenings.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a short puzzle game with a delightful art, music and story. The puzzles use all the same mechanic of playing with map pieces, which is original and fun, and the story is kind and warming. The game's length is perfect in my opinion, not very short but not long either, just the ideal for the gameplay not to become repetitive.I recommend Carto if you are looking for a fun and not very hard puzzle game with a cheerful art and music design.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: This game is super cute, graphics are great and it’s really well made: I encountered no bugs and it runs well even on my 9-year old Mac with Intel HD 4000 built-in graphics. So I hate to give it a negative, but it just really lacks on gameplay and story.Gameplay is basically what you see in the trailer: rearranging map pieces rearranges corresponding parts of the world, there are a few cool related puzzles, but that’s about it. The game is to a large extent a walking simulator.Story is very superficial: gotta find a grandma and help everyone along the way. Some parts also make no sense. For example: (not a spoiler, because it’s at the start of the game) the “tradition” to kick children out of tribe at 15 years old (historically, if you were kicked out of tribe, it used to mean almost certain death). It makes even less sense that this “tradition” can be preserved with “their people” through generations, because if everyone leaves separately, who is even “their people” at that point to preserve it?If you’d like a simple relaxing walk-like experience - I recommend it,but if you are looking for gameplay - no.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly adorable! It's lighthearted, playful, inquisitive, and fulfilling!The story is somewhat straightforward, but it's also pretty clear that there has been a lot of thought put into the world-building! Almost every time I decided to look into a new corner or interact with a book, I felt rewarded with a little bit of information or progression.The primary mechanic of moving the tiles that make up the map is honestly really interesting! I especially love how that system was given unique modifiers or special additions in each area. It really helped make the world feel more diverse!I did find the controls to be a little difficult, but that's my only complaint! Using a controller is HIGHLY recommended, though I NEEDED it to prevent cramping my hands.9/10 everything is so cute!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10!!The cutest (and most challenging) puzzle game ever! I love the uniqueness of the game mechanics and kudos to the developers for making so many fun and mind-boggling puzzles with it. Don't let the cute game design fool you into thinking this is child's play; I had to look at several guides several time to figure out how to solve some of the puzzles!! For the good parts: - THE ART STYLE! IS! SO LOVABLE!! From the characters to the environment design; it's so lovely and pleasing to look at (and I can tell they're made with so much love),- Both the BGM and SFX are very nice and fitting for every terrain,- The controls are okay; I can play it perfectly fine on my keyboard with the default settings, and- I didn't encounter any glitches throughout my gameplay. Kudos!!I don't have much critic to make, other than to add more visual cues for the puzzles or maybe add a hint system because, my God, have I mentioned how hard the puzzles are? I also would appreciate it if the game has a quick-access quest bar to show what we should do next and the clues we've figured out so far. Every time I continue the game, I had to go back and talk to several NPCs several times when I load in my checkpoint so I know what to do, which took a long time. Anyways, Carto is such a precious lil baby and ALSO I LOVE  The game is now one of my favorites (despite how hard the puzzles are) and I await more games from this developer!! :-D
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels well polished. It's got a unique puzzle mechanic that doesn't feel repetitive as they keep iterating on that mechanic throughout the game. It's got nice visuals and a cute short story. It's very short (just under 5 hours for 100%) but in my opinion, that's a good thing. The one big negative thing about this game is that the puzzles never feel very satisfying to solve. Overall, it's an interesting little experience worth checking out if you get it for cheap.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a great game! It's adorable, it's wholesome, it's challenging, it's funny, but most of all, it's fun! This is such a unique twist on a puzzle game. You go on such great adventures, meeting really interesting people along the way. There's plenty of things to interact with, people to talk to, problems to solve, puns to giggle at, and some cute surprises along the way. The puzzles aren't too easy, but aren't too hard either.My only problem is that it wasn't long enough. As with most indie games, this is something you finish in a few hours, not a few months. I really hope they release more chapters so I can take Carto on some new adventures!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a very sweet, cleverly designed matching & shape based puzzle game. There is a strong focus on exploration featuring plenty of adorable hand-drawn characters and locations. Puzzles mainly play by manipulating your map to gain access to areas previously not accessible, usually netting you a new map piece and/or progress in the story. There are other types of puzzles in the mix to keep the game fresh and challenging.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: While not everyone would have been interested in drawing up maps or fascinated with the idea of being able to map out a whole town in the most efficient way, we all have been in a situation where you just despise the travel time. Of how far away the places you want or need to go to that at the least will need a dedicated day and at the most days to get there and back. Not to mention the money needed and the stress that increases in relation to how far you need to travel. Or perhaps traffic is going too slow and you just wish you could just skip past to your destination. If only there was a way to just teleport to your destination.Well, Carto must have spawned from these types of situations in some way. In Carto, you play a young girl named Carto who lives with her Grandmother in an airship. Her Grandmother happens to be a cartographer, but not any cartographer as she makes maps by connecting map pieces, which in tern alters the world so it matches the map. It looks like our little Carto may take over the mantle as we see her watching her Grandmother. However, Carto’s curiosity and wonder at the power of the map pieces gets her to connect a piece with a storm to the piece that they’re currently on. Leading Carto the fall out of the airship along with her Grandmother’s map, which the pieces all scatter. Once she wakes up, she finds herself on a mysterious island and a journey that will bring her to many other locations and people that need her help and in turn will try to help her. Maybe you’ll even meet a new friend.From here, you’ll be using the map pieces to your advantage to both be able to travel around and solve puzzles. You start with a good handful in each new location and you’ll need to pick up any stray pieces to add to your map. At any time you can bring out your map and rearrange or add new pieces, though there are some rules. The pieces can only be connected if it has the same border. You can’t connect a water border with a forest border, but you can if both borders were forests. Properly connecting the pieces gives you more room to walk around, give you access to talk to the people that happen to be living where you are, be able to travel faster as you’ll be able to switch the piece you’re on with another that’s closer (or just put you closer) and even solve puzzles.The puzzles are a mix of some being vague, obvious to figure out due to the visual clues and what you already know, and ones that doesn’t make sense at the moment until you suddenly get an Eureka moment once you need to solve it to continue. It can be easy as a map piece needing to be turned or put somewhere else in relation to the other pieces. Though, it can be vague where the context clues doesn’t make sense or the clue you got doesn’t really shed some light on the situation. The vague puzzles were the ones that I got stuck on and will most likely be the ones you will as well. For me, it was mostly the rule where a map piece can suddenly appear if you arrange the needed pieces in the required way. While another one had me confused with “following footsteps in the yellow desert” when if anything both desert types looked yellow. Though, Carto does also bring out some inventive solutions as well. Like puzzles where you’re supposed to be lost don’t give you a mess of map pieces to deal with, but a couple so it’s more manageable. Make use of the fact that turning a map piece affects how everything is placed or facing. There was even one where you have to open a safe and, if you didn’t figure it out by the combination numbers you’re given, you’re clued in more by it being the only map piece that makes a weird sound when you turn it.Each new location will throw in a new curveball for you to figure out as well. Making the puzzles slightly harder as the new feature will cause you to put some more thought in placement or figure out how to properly connect the pieces. The last new location Carto will visit is the hardest of the bunch.There are some secrets or optional stuff to find if you’re up for it. There are six puzzle pieces hidden in different chapters. You’ll have to be pretty keen and be really curious take over to find them all yourself. Though, you can finish the whole game and not realize that they’re there to be found. Other than two, which you’re not really pointed to and rely on you happening to do the required step, you’re given a vague hint on what you need to do to obtain that puzzle piece, though it is easily be written off as nothing. Once you get all six by either figuring it out yourself or checking out a guide, you’re given access to the airship so you can look at some concept art. There is also a library called the Story Chalet that Carto will be at that will give you some more lore on the world so you can understand the people and why the different tribes do what they do. And even a book that is creepily telling the same exact events you’re going through. If you read everything, it will come up as an achievement. Luckily, once you finish the game, you can select a chapter to start at so you don’t have to replay the whole game if you happen to miss anything, just that chapter. It doesn’t work like a chapter select usually does, which certainly confused me, as the option to select a chapter to start at only appears when selecting a new save file rather than being an option in the save you just finished.I really enjoyed my journey with Carto through the seven hours I spent with it. There may have been some vague puzzles and some will get tired of the map mechanic despite some wild pieces being thrown in, but it has a cute story, the art style is so cute as it looks like it can easily be in a children’s book, and features a unique map mechanic that’s used pretty well. I’m glad I decided to try out the demo or else I wouldn’t have picked up this gem as soon as I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovable story, places and characters. Has a unique take as a puzzle game. Has just enough exploration feature to keep one's curiousity appeased.Simple, not difficult. Relaxing. Satisfying. Honestly the price may be a little more than i would pay for as the game is pretty short so if you can get it on sale, definitely pick this one up.Would definitely recommend to friends who likes cute things, puzzles, and animals.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Very original game where you have can alter the game world by moving and rotating pieces of the map. This feature is used to solve puzzles and to reach new parts of the game world, where you meet a bunch of funny people who give you new quests.The puzzles are a mixed bag: some of them are very clever, while others are rather easy or trial&error boring. But the charming characters and lovely art made me enjoy the game until the end. Definitely recommended if you want to play something new.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A relatively short game that none the less makes an impression. By discovering and rearranging map "tiles", you create and change the landscape around you while helping people you meet along the way.  The graphics, soundtrack, and characters are perfectly fit the cartoonish child-friendly vibe.  Some "puzzles" are harder than others, but most can be solved with a little persistance.  There are some hidden achievements along the way that may add some replay value.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: I've got nothing bad to say about this game after completing it, other than some puzzles being difficult or just not that easy to understand the objective of like the forest fog mission or the mapping out the icicle but that's natural for all puzzle games. Honestly, why am I even talking about the negative, let's go to the good stuff. Carto is a wonderful hand-drawn world-discovering game where we are playing as little girls collecting missing maps to unrevealing the world and creating a path to get back to her grandma.In this game, expect to experience different cultures with their unique quirks, as well as a lot of charming, likeable characters who are more than NPC asking you to do some fetch quest; instead caring and helpful to get Carto back to her grandma, (after we help them of course). There are a lot of imaginative puzzles where we are using the maps we collected to map out the world, from like organising them in the correct order to unveiling some new lands and secrets you'll be thinking ''that's clever''. It does take some time to be an expert in using the mapping mechanics and some of the puzzles are no joke though, requiring you to think outside of the box or unlock more than 5% of your brain power. Make sure you're at least sober whilst playing little gem, but I promise you once you get the hang of it you're in for a heartwarming adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a lovely short breeze adventure,  everything here is full of charm and charisma, as a puzzle games it is one of a kind, from time to time there will be that puzzle game that has a neat unique ideia, and executes upon it beautifully, and thats Carto.The idea of moving not the player but the map is really interesting, and here it works like a charm, as a little cartographer you'll navigate your way  using the maps itself, the original idea is expanded upon greatly and  it doesn't overstay its welcome,  it's so well thought.That alongside with a charming cast of characters, a lot of animal friends! and a heartwarming finale adds up to a must play puzzle game, maybe they could use some hint system at some point, but other than that, it's a delight.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Landscape-altering map puzzle game, that is the first time I ever played the game like this, and I believe it is also the first game that has this concept. If I had to choose phrases that would represent Carto, those would be charming, cute, wholesome, beautiful, comfy, and heartwarming. Oh, and also mind-boggling and "oh god i think i need a big brain".They have 10 Chapters, and 6 type of biomes: island, grasslands, forest, desert, volcano, iceberg. Each has different type of puzzles that all of them involving you altering the landscape through your map, they may have one of these or combinations of them:- Matching - Move map tiles based on exactly the clue you have- Extrapolating - Move map tiles to reveal the hidden tile based on its surrounding criteria- Sub-maps - Sometimes you can use your map indoors or even on a cave- Pathfinder - You have to go to different places, using only the limited number of eligible tiles repeatedly.- Multilevel tiles - Sometimes surface level tiles' position and direction is linked to its underground counterpart.- Tetris tiles - Tetris tilesThe story is very heartwarming and a bit slow-paced, good for you if you are looking for the comfyness of this game and wanted to enjoy it to the fullest. You will remember most of the characters you met, that's just how good the storytelling was. I'm just a little bit disappointed that they are not voiced uwu, but that is okay.Song 10/10. Art 10/10. Story 10/10. Gameplay 10/10. Replayability rating 7/10. Overall 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A cute, fairly easy puzzle game with the spirit of a childlike wonder that wouldn't seem out of place in a book of fairy tales. It's greater than the sum of its parts, with the soft art style, clever use of its one puzzle mechanism, and simple story of family-friendly adventure coming together to create a memorable, pleasant experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a decent game that I can't help but feel didn't fully live up to its potential. There is some creative use of the map mechanics in the game, but they're all very simple and limited in scope. Some are outright frustrating like the ice slider puzzle towards the end which is a rather harsh and sudden shift in difficulty that forces the game into a really weird position. On the one hand most of the game up until that point is pretty simple and appears to be made for kids, but then it ramps up to the point that any kid trying to solve the puzzles is going to get very frustrated very quickly. Another case of a game that couldn't pick a lane and stick with it.Now all those complaints aside, as so many other people have commented, the game makes up for it's issues with a very endearing set of characters and interactions that honestly reminds me of A Hat in Time. Very cute, very sweet, and very little over arching conflict and drama in the story and world. Overall I'd say a 7/10, good for a night of mostly chill puzzle solving.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Such a creative and unique puzzle game fitting of the title Carto.Carto is such a cutie and the story of how she searches for her Granny as a "Carto"-grapher is very heartwarming and touching.The story unfolds very nicely and plays well with the cartography mechanic of moving the map pieces.The puzzles can be challenging but it really gets the brain running.Its a short but wonderful experience.Really recommend it if you are in for a short touching and fun experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is probably the most heartwarming game I've ever played. The progression is slow and steady, the game relies entirely on a single puzzle mechanic, but that didn't stop me from playing through all 3 hours of the story with the warmest smile on my face. Everything about this game - the writing, the art style, the story, the music - just nails the perfect balance of charm without going overboard.I wouldn't consider Carto a puzzle game per se. The puzzles are far from the primary purpose of this game, and certainly aren't what makes it great. The puzzle mechanic is a smart idea, and it works well throughout the game - but if that is the reason you're buying Carto, you'll probably be disappointed. Rather, you should consider it a visual novel of sorts. The story is what drives the game, and does so amazingly well.If spending an afternoon playing through the cutest story you've ever seen sounds like a good time to you, then Carto can be warmly recommended. If you're the kind of person who needs great and evolving gameplay to stay captive then I'd probably give it a pass; but even I, who's usually a relatively hardcore gamer, would happily spend the $20 for this game again.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a really lovely game, with a wholesome story, likable characters and puzzles designed around one cool core mechanic.Carto not only manages to be cute, but it also features a unique puzzle design, where you manipulate and reshape the terrain around you. The devs explored this idea to a surprising degree and created a cohesive, well designed and animated world that fits this gameplay. I do have to mention that unfortunately some of the puzzles are very obscure and require a guide to complete. It's not always clear what the game wants from you.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Charming game about little Carto who gets separated in a storm from her granny and has to navigate through a vast world to find her way back. On her journey she will visit different lands and meet the people living there. From them she will learn about their culture, traditions and wishes. And even though Carto herself needs help, she is always ready to help others in need and with them she will experience one big adventure!Gameplay wise it's a puzzle game where you have to rotate map pieces to create new paths for yourself, but as you can't stand on the piece you wish to rotate, it can take some shuffling for you to find the right way. Sometimes you can even uncover some secrets! The puzzles are mostly straightforward, but some are pretty hard (especially the icebergs), so younger audience might require some help with it. I have really enjoyed the puzzles, it felt nice to see the world uncovering before you. The game has really cute colorful graphics and charming music. Overall experience is very relaxing and once you reach the end you will be filled with heartwarming feeling. <3 I can totally recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A very short game with a fun mechanic. The game was not very complex, but I think some parts of it could be explained better. There were a few of the puzzles that actually required you to think, which was nice. The story was kind of generic, but all of the characters had their own personalities and it was clear that a lot of care went into this game since it seems very polished.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: I did enjoy this game overall, but I can't decide if I was pleasantly surprised by the amount of content, or if I felt like it outstayed its welcome. I played it in short bursts because, although it's cute, it didn't always hold my interest for long periods of time. There were a few occasions when I wasn't sure what I was supposed to be doing, but on the whole the puzzles were a nice mix of "easy" vs "fun to figure out". The game mechanic of manipulating and moving map pieces to get around, or to make things happen, is simple enough - but it gets used in some more challenging and creative ways in later chapters. The ending was quite heartwarming and I think that left me feeling more positive about the game as a whole than I sometimes did while playing it, but overall I would still recommend it.YAYS:- Cute and relaxing, nice art style and non-intrusive music- Based around a simple concept but with some interesting uses- Interesting characters and cultures, developed enough to have their own customs and lore- PuppiesNAYS:- Didn't hold my interest for long periods of time so it took me a while to finish it- I felt like they could have done even more with the concept/mechanic (but on the other hand it did feel long enough)
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a short, innovative, story focused game. You take on the role of Carto, a young girl who has been separated from her Grandmother, and must travel to many exotic locations, meeting many different cultures, to reunite. The central gameplay gimmick is that the world you explore can be changed by rearranging your map. You basically place tiles Carcassone style (i.e. you can place map tiles so long as the edges of the tile match the edge of the tile you place it next to) and then explore what you just connected. This game is adorable, fun, and charming in every way. The art style has this bright, childish quality to it, but is actually quite beautiful at times. The soundtrack is simple but fits the mood of whatever place you are in. The character writing is strong, with each of the people you meet having fun personalities. And everything also has this touch of the fantastical and whimsical that ties it all together.The main story is unfortunately pretty lackluster. You try to find your Granny, thats it. You get a clue as to where she is, and when you get there, she is somewhere else. Repeat a few times. What the story chooses to focus on instead is the culture of the people you meet. You start of on an island of people who send their children away at 15 for them to sail and explore the ocean, never to return. That is their tradition. This sounds a little messed up, or at least a bit sad, but they treat it with warmth and humor, and you can see the importance of this tradition to the people. I love this stuff, because it has this undercurrent of a sad, very adult, reality, but its presented in a vibrant and charming way. Its adult but kid friendly, and the game walks that tightrope well.As the game progresses the gameplay also evolves with every chapter, adding new challenges and elements to keep things fresh.  It gets more difficult as you get along as well. In general the gameplay keeps you engaged with its puzzles, with whatever particular new mechanic you are working with being integrated with the story of the people of the island you are on. The gameplay serves the story elements well.Carto is definitely quality over quantity, as the game is fairly short. I beat it in just over 4 hours, though I clearly missed some secrets. That said, I had a great time playing it and its one of those experiences you look on fondly after completing it.Overall, if you like charm, fun, and creativity, you will like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I love, love, LOVED this game!!! It had such a unique and sweet story-line. I loved the storytelling so much!It took me ~7.5 hours to complete on my first run. Starts off easy for learning the controls, but then becomes sufficiently challenging :). I liked that the challenges were not absolutely insane or ridiculous to crack. Some puzzle games I've played have me checking every possible answer 1000 times until I either find it by mistake or give up and check a play-through guide, only to find out it is the stupidest, most unintuitive solution or it was something I already tried but did only slightly off the mark, even with puzzle experience. I am glad this was not the case for Carto! This game was relaxing but captivating, easy to follow, and I had to think to solve the puzzles but I never really got frustrated. The animation is in such a cute style, and the background music/sounds add to the vibe of it perfectly. I felt like they effectively used colour and a simple yet beautiful art style to express the story and character relationships (both to each other and their respective landscapes/roles) well. My only gripe was the controls really threw me off at the start. That could just have been a me-thing as well, as I have muscle memory from other games which sometimes had me clicking the wrong buttons by accident. I personally would have preferred WASD instead of arrow keys to move, but you can change the controls/key-binds if you'd like, and as I got further I understood more why they were laid out the way that they were. I would recommend tuning your left hand controls to suit how you feel most comfortable, but default is not too bad. They also have a legend that shows which key does what in the actual game screen which definitely came in handy for me at the start! Other than that, I had no qualms :).All in all, it made me super happy and every aspect got me excited. If you are looking for a puzzle game to do over a weekend or so, I would say this game is a perfect match. I was able to connect with the characters and genuinely felt sad when I had to say good bye to some (lol). A lot of little details connect between the islands that make it feel cohesive. I also think people from all age groups could find joy with it as well, if you'd like to play with a young one :).

_childDocuments_.review: If I were to describe this game in one word, it would be "delightful". I played it on steam deck, and ran into no performance issues whatsoever; I imagine you could run this game on a smartwatch if you were so inclined. The aesthetics are simply wonderful. The art style is beautiful, the soundtrack is relaxing, and the characters and story are ... Odd, but wonderfully charming. The gameplay took a full chapter to fully click with me, but once it did, it became really enjoyable. It's a very interesting mix of genres, combining exploration and puzzle elements in one near package. It starts off quite tame, and frankly a tad boring, but quickly shows its true colors as an easy to understand but intricate mechanic with more depth than I thought possible. Every chapter brings something new to the simple premise of "move the map to move the world", and I am here for every bit of it. The only thing I can really complain about is the length. 4 and a half hours in, and I've beaten the main game. If I'm wrong, I'll come back and correct this review. Overall, I fully recommend this game. I personally would wait for a sale, but that has more to do with me being a frugal f@@k than the game. _childDocuments_.review: Carto is a delightful little feelgood puzzle adventure. You play a little cartographer traversing the world trying to get back to your grandmother. You get to explore a big bright world full of friendly people. The game also features a unique puzzle mechanic for changing the world and story progression. The main draw for this game is the puzzle mechanism it uses for building and traversing the various areas you come across in your journey. While the general idea is that you'll rotate pieces on a map to get to various points there are some deeper elements to it as the story progresses. The puzzles themselves never stray far from this encompassing idea of map rotation but with each biome you encounter there's some nuances to the way pieces fit together. I felt that this kept things feeling fresh and made you change your approach to different challenges you encounter on your journey. With each area you encountered you not only looked at the overall larger map but also found clues in your environment on how to manipulate your map to progress. As for the puzzles themselves they weren't terribly difficult and sometimes the inhabitants would give you hints for them but the hints were pretty vague so I had to at times think outside the box... or make a box. But this also kind of lends itself to Carto's charm. While everyone's rooting for you to find your grandma they're also very grateful to have your help with whatever task they're burdened with. As Carto's world grows the problems she has to solve gets more complex. This is the type of game you can play and appreciate at any age. All sorts of family friendliness going on. Or fun with family. Even though this is a single player experience I could see myself letting my less game inclined older parental units giving it a go, if only to see how they approach the brain teaser like puzzles.Overall the cute artwork, music and story makes Carto one of those underrated overlooked gems that's a delight to play in a single sitting or two, depending on how quickly you can figure out the puzzles. It's got a lighthearted story with charm that's fun for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: The world of Carto is made up of tiles, which you can move and rotate to reshape the world around you. Primarily you’re going to be moving tiles around to solve puzzles, but there is also a very satisfying reward to be had from simply moving tiles around to try and make the world a more pleasing shape, to make sure all your roads link up, or that the villagers’ houses are all clustered into a village of your own design.Puzzles are generally not too taxing, nothing is likely to stump you for long. The concept of moving tiles has been explored thoroughly, with one or two later puzzles feeling like reskinned versions of earlier ones, and some that barely qualify as puzzles at all. But this is not a game you play for a challenge, play it because it’s lovely, because it’s soothing, because it’s just plain charming to experience.Fittingly for a game built around maps, the exploring is the real draw, rather than the puzzling. You’re playing to get more of the frequently amusing dialogue, the calming music, the lighthearted verging on silly story. If you’re not in the mood for a little whimsy, this is probably going to miss completely, but if you want a lovely little world to decompress in for 5 hours or so, this is a winner.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute and wholesome puzzle adventure game with adorable characters.(Unless, y'know, if you find the concept of a child god fiddling with your very land making your house appear and disappear terrifying.)I like the concept of moving map pieces and connecting them to forge my own path and unlock new places.You sort of have a freedom to place the map pieces anywhere you want as long as they don't conflict with the adjacent piece, but the game mechanic requires you to connect key pieces in a specific pattern to progress the story.The story is very linear and you can't return to the previous map until the story sends you back, but you can revisit chapters when you start a new game after completing the story the first time in case you've missed finding secret puzzle pieces.The one downside is that it's relatively short with little replayability, but revisiting all the places and seeing the characters again during the ending sequence made my heart all warm and fuzzy, and that was satisfying enough for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a sweet little girl, who comes from a cartographer’s family. During a storm, while she and her grandma are flying with an airship, she gets lost. After that, she wakes up on a strange and unknown island. That is when her journey begins. By helping all the extraordinary, and kind of quirky, people she meets, she manages to get reunited with her grandmother. Her cartography skill  is basically the game itself. You will be arranging and rearranging the pieces of the map, which is a huge puzzle in itself, to overcome mini challenges to get to the end. All those challenges are based on logic, environmental cues, and data from dialogues. The biggest constraint and difficulty is that not all of the puzzle pieces can be matched with each other but need to be placed according to the morphology of the map (forest, fields, sea, river etc). Furthermore, some puzzle pieces require some process to appear (ex. the "object / person" you are looking for is surrounded by bushes). So, it is up to you how you will place or rotate the pieces to form what you are asked to. To finish the game (and complete all the achievements) you need to pay attention to the environment in which you move, as it hides various clues you need to do (ex. Maybe you will hear a strange noise, or there might be some footsteps leading you in a specific direction etc). Each of the game's chapters takes place in a different location, which has its own distinct culture and characters, which I found out to be very interesting. The music and the graphic style are relaxing, and I think they both match the “sweet” style of the game, which is like a story you can narrate to a kid.

The characters are endearing, and the dialogues are full of humor and warmth, making every interaction in Carto's world a delight.It's the perfect game for those looking for a creative and unconventional experience, combined with a stunning visual style and an emotional story.

_childDocuments_.review: Pleasant, cheerful puzzle-adventure. Carto is lost in a lightning storm and has to find back to her airship-adventurer granny. And sort of teams up with a companion who has to leave her island to find her future in the big world. It is actually better than it sounds ;-)   Game mechanics based on moving map pieces ("puzzle squares") around so that things connect, sometimes paths, sometimes types of landscape, sometimes other things...Sounds simple, can be surprisingly challenging.  Quests to find stuff, fetch stuff, solve clues to move forwards, and so on in familiar style. Well made and enjoyable. Nothing tense or stress, platforming or timed, or scary. So that's thumbs up from me :-)Varied character gallery, some I liked better than others, some quite funny, some not-my-humour, none are all that deep. A bit annoying that in most dialogues the NPCs have more to say if you click on them a second time, but you have to then wait through the first set of comments, again. Tedious.  Visually : cheerful and crisp. But leaning towards the japanese-childrens-cartoon-style which I personally am not keen on and found a bit too cute. Along with the dialogues, which tend heavily towards breathlessly naive cutey-pie.  So a bit too cute for my personal taste, but hey, other people may think differently. And no biggie in a game that overall was fun to play.  Saving worked well.  Ran smooth on my simple gear, KB+M. And the bonus scenes while the credits rolled were really quite... delightful, and gave me a happy smile right at the end.( I must add, though, that I found the travelling companion quite an annoying, selfish me-first kind of person. Maybe the type just rubbed against the grain for me, or cultural cues read differently, or something.... )

_childDocuments_.review: Good difficulty ramp with a few extremely clever puzzles. Some of the later puzzles will make you work for the solution. Sweet and somewhat surreal story about traveling the world to reunite with your grandmother, with loose themes about the (positive and negative) value of upholding traditions. Kept me smiling all the way through.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice little relaxing game. Puzzles are well balanced - not too hard, but also not too easy. The game makes clever use of its mechanics. While it doesn't push the applications of each mechanic to their limits, it's probably for the best - the puzzles are fairly rarely reused and the game feels pretty fresh throughout the whole run. It never strays off course, never asks the player to complete a time or dexteriety challenge - by which it lends itself to being a really relaxing and welcoming experience. There were a couple of times where I felt the game didn't communicate well what was expected of me, forcing me to run around the map and try to interact with everybody and everything, but in general the instructions are pretty clear and the pacing is fun.The game looks and sounds very nice, I found the visual aesthetic especially pleasing. Though I must admit, I was surprised that the game constantly jumped between locking the framerate at 60 and 30 fps - which resulted in some visual incoherency. The music is pretty simplistic, but doesn't get annoying and conveys well the nature of each biom. While the story itself isn't all that riveting, the funny, likeable characters inhabiting the lands make up for that, making your adventure more about the journey and less about the destination.This is a very nice, relaxing, coherent puzzle game with a bit of a story and some fun characters added as the background. It's not a "must play", but if you enjoy this type of games, you will enjoy Carto.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Such a great and cutesie puzzle game. The pacing and difficulty in this game is incredibly well done. _childDocuments_.review: Grade:  52.1%  FA very simple game, it neither fails hard nor takes full advantage of its simplicity to do anything really compelling. It's funny, with a lovely art style, and these two are really the highlights of the game!But the rest is all mediocre at best. _childDocuments_.review: Carto's biggest virtue is its wholesome atmosphere, meaning the illustration and animation, the sounds and music, as well as the positive and calm energy it creates. In my opinion the biggest disadvantage of the game is that one can consume much time in order to be able to move on to the game as in most cases it is unclear what one should do in order to continue. It is normal to consult a guide in order to get a trophy or to bypass a difficult part of a game, but it can be very annoying if one needs it for almost half the game.I understand that the whole point and purpose of the game is to create a book-like experience but we still talk about a game, so if there was some kind of help option in order to use it when one is stuck the game would be a lot more entertaining and a lot less frustrating. _childDocuments_.review: Carto | 🌕🌕🌗🌑🌑 2.5/5 |I picked up Carto, loving its delightful art and animation style while being intrigued by its unique construction and puzzle mechanics. So I was surprised to find the game's story somewhat dull and its mechanics kind of tedious by the halfway point. At its heart, it plays like any other top-down adventure game, where you'll see yourself running around the game map, conversing with the many charming characters that inhabit it, and assisting with their problems. The unique difference here is that the map is split into pieces, so you'll solve these problems by manipulating each of these pieces to evolve the map, attempting to find the solution.To accomplish this, you'll find yourself swapping between the main game and the puzzle view constantly, which does tend to break up the immersion as you're unable to see the result of your changes until you go back to the main game. This is far more apparent towards the tail end of the game, where the pieces and puzzles become more complicated, resulting in more trail and error and unfortunately, frustration. Overall, while the mechanic is "fine", it does feel a little unrefined or not quite fleshed out enough.There's no denying that the game is cute and cosy. This is evident in its numerous chapters, where each has its own goal and a new set of characters. However, the conversations generally all feel like fluff, and you soon lose interest in what they have to say once you realise none of it matters once you move onto the next chapter.All that said, Carto is far from a bad game. There's plenty to enjoy here, so I was on the fence on which way to fall. However for myself I feel for its asking price and its flaws, I felt a little underwhelmed by both the story and by its unique mechanic by the end. I'd recommend waiting for a sale or trying the demo before jumping in.

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a cozy and cute puzzle game with a wholesome story, great graphical design and relaxing soundtrack! It's very enjoyable, split up in chapters allowing you to take your time playing through the game.You play as Carto, a young girl getting lost from her grandmother. The main goal is to find her, but along the way you explore various areas and meet new friends. Each chapter is a new area and it gives you new challenges, making the puzzle system not getting too repetetive. Speaking of the puzzle system; the main one is related to maps - you move around map pieces to move around and to solve various puzzles. It's quite refreshing and I haven't personally seen anything like it before - at least not in this type of game.If you are to play this game on PC I do recommend using a gamepad for the best experience.I recommend this game if you love wholesomeness, interesting puzzles and just a great indie-title! I hope we'll see more games from this studio :D

_childDocuments_.review: An adorably puzzling adventure about the coming of age and exploring a world of kindness.Entirely wholesome from start to end, Carto is a pleasant experience and manages it expertly without being too saccharine. The writing's endearing with its lovely cast of characters, meeting each of them and their respective group or tribe is a wholly welcoming experience that is made even more loving as you get to know them personally in each chapter. The puzzles are also wonderfully designed, even with the same base mechanics of moving the geography of the region by moving the corresponding pieces on a map, the set in each chapter all feel clever from one another and continue to ramp up in difficulty and ingenuity. It actually got quite difficult near the end! All in all it's a great game.

Carto is a puzzle exploration game where you play as a little girl that moves on a map that is made of different pages/parts (more are also found in the map) that can be moved and rotated by you, to solve puzzles and progress in the game.  20 Achievements, around half are story related. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love Carto. It has such a gorgeous art style and the story is charming and wholesome. I loved the first half, and would have had nothing but glowing words for it if it has continued to the same standard. Overall, it's a very enjoyable game, but it feels dashed off towards the end. The quality of both the puzzles and writing declines as you go through the game. In contrast to the first half - which really shines with making the way forward intuitive and nicely flowing - the latter half has a few times where the ability to progress is gated behind a conversation that the game doesn't give the player any indication is the likely next step. The return to the island, especially, has one where you have to go to leave the island before you're allowed to complete the cartography puzzle, very strange.The big negative for me though is the hidden achievements, some of which require you to play through a significant chunk of the game again just to trigger a tiny interaction. That kind of this is really annoying, especially with a story based game like this that has almost no replayability; not that it should, just realise that your players will not want to sit through the same unskippable conversations again. It really soured an otherwise excellent game for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so complex, but really fun when you really get into it and solving all of the advanced world/map-shifting puzzles! You are this character named Carto who is in search of her grandma, and you meet many lovely villagers/people along the way. Anyway, back to my main point, I've *really* gotta thank Lee-Kuo Chen (design), Kuan Hung Chen (art), Eddie Yu (sound) and Chia-Yu Chen (programming) for creating this absolute masterpiece of a game - I can tell so much careful work and thought has been put into it. I was able to do most of the puzzles, however, I do admit that I had to use a walkthrough for certain puzzles . I love playing these kind of games because they really exercise your brain. The hand-drawn graphics are adorable, and the music pieces for each stage can get a bit repetitive, but when you're so focused on the puzzle/s, you just kind of forget they're on a loop. The controls are easy to do, and if you don't like it, you can assign your own control keys in the settings, which is very handy. Overall, I think if you enjoy difficult/mind-bending/world-shifting puzzles, this is the game for you! I believe it took me 5-6 days to complete, with needed breaks in between because my brain was just so *mind-blown* at times, and I needed a break from struggling with a puzzle for a while so that I could get back to it later on with fresh brain cells, haha.

_childDocuments_.review: (#515 out of 1000+) First impressions?  is an absolutely gorgeous, delightfully comfy game and I love it death. is one of those games that doesn't sound too interesting when you describe it, but when its in your hands, you can't help but smile at how charmingly everything fits together. One of those special, rare games that manages to mine greatness out of deceptively simple systems and mechanics. Put simply,  is built around a very simple puzzle gimmick. For fans of classic RPGs, it's a gimmick not dissimilar to  city building mechanic: the world is in disarray, and it is up to you restore the land (and perhaps make a few improvement) but arranging landscape tiles on a map grid. Each tile possess different terrain that can potentially affect adjacent tiles, and how you shape the landscape -- and how you place landmarks in relation to each other -- has a drastic and immediate affect on the world and the people who live in it. Sometimes you'll be rearranging the world simply to find your way through it, other times -- well, most of the time -- you'll be modifying the world to suit the interests of NPCs. In thanks they will often reward you with additional map tiles, which you will then use to further manipulate the landscape, creating increasingly complex continental layouts as you juggle the desires of more and more people making more and more demands of your cartographic contortions.Story-wise,  is fundamentally a puzzle game first and foremost, and an adventure game only a distant second. The premise is fairly loose, and though there are characters and dialog and plot, they mostly serve only as vehicles to direct you from one problem to solve to the next. You play as some kind of deity -- or at least the mischievous child of one -- on an adventure to restore the world to its correct form in the wake of an accidental almost-apocalypse. The people you meet typically have little to say that lamenting whatever problem they have with the world when you meet, and later celebrating the serendipity of your solution. Occasionally you'll get a bit more characterization or world-building -- especially from the more prominent NPCs that shuttle you from one region (or chapter) of the world to the next -- but, while flavorful, the story is only really an excuse. It works just as well as it could, maintaining a laid-back atmosphere that meshes well with the lighthearted, casual nature of the puzzles that will occupy most of your time and focus.And -- though I speak now as someone who was once a very strange child who spent an inordinate amount of time playing with globes and drawing countless maps (based both on reality and imagination) on incalculable sheets of paper -- I find this whole experience -- from concept to execution -- utterly delightful. The only complaint I can think to offer is simply that I want more! And, I must admit, I'm not sure this is an appetite that could ever fully be satiated. But, if nothing else, I would greatly appreciate something like a sandbox mode w/ randomized quests and/or something like a "free build" mode.  core campaign is certainly engaging and surprisingly charming, but it's dreadfully brief and over far too soon. And, tragically, far too linear. A second playthrough, sadly, will resemble the first far too closely.Last but also least: there's the issue of the bugs. Which were... well, not as  as I would've hoped. Most annoying are the recurring issues with input devices -- my gamepad would randomly stop working,  suddenly, and when the gamepad disconnects there's nothing to be done as the game refuses to recognize a mouse. The only solution is to use the keyboard to manually exit and do a forced shut-down via the Windows Task Manager. That this occurred on more than just one or two occasions proved an unfortunate blight on an otherwise thoroughly delightful game.But, insofar as these things go, these issues are, I think, very easy to forgive.The ultimate appeal of  down to a single question: do you love maps and cartography? If not,  will very likely bore you to tears. But if not, if you're at all like myself and have spent far more time than you'd ever care to admit scribbling out your own maps by pen or pencil for as long as you can remember -- well, then, in that case I can all but promise that you will discover in  a new (if brief) obsession.

_childDocuments_.review: Carto, the cute little puzzler, developed by Sunhead Games, published by Humble Games, scores overwhelmingly positive reviews on Steam.By means of an isometric view, the player controls Carto, a young girl in search of her grandmother. Through exploring a map, new map tiles can be found, and placed to expand the existing world. These map tiles can be rearranged, the player has to rotate and move them around, in such a way new options become available. This tile system, the bread and butter in Carto, is a puzzle / riddle in its own unique way.On your journey to find grandma, several npc’s are encountered, who gives you quests that have to be completed to progress the storyline. Some of the puzzles, especially in the beginning of the game when the mechanics are new, are quite difficult to figure out. The brain really needs to work sufficiently to solve some of the issues encountered. Puzzles are original in design, with a lot of variation. Some of them are rather hard, but one can manage when focusing enough.Graphics are colorful, cute and cartoony, very suited for a game like this. Attention to detail there is as well, on a few occasions you can see symbols placed on the map tiles, which also are used in real life topographic maps.Overall, the game is divided into ten chapters, each one with its own distinct world location and scenery.Catchy music enhance the experience, and suits well with the cute, relaxing nature of the game. Invigorating sound effects are implemented whenever you solve a puzzle, which gives a rewarding enjoyment.Twenty achievements have to be unlocked to achieve the perfect game. Ten of them which are storyline linked and can not be missed upon finishing the game. The other ten achievements are rather tricky to figure out be oneself, some are elaborate, some are easy to overlook. Nonetheless, with the help of the Steam communities guides, Carto is an excellent addition to an achievements hunters’ library. Perfection can be achieved in one playthrough. There also is an option to restart any chapter, via the main menu, when one has finished the game once. A very handy way to pick up those missing achievements afterwards. Carto can be perfected in about ten to twelve hours easily.Myself, I enjoyed Carto a lot, played every time when my free time was rather limited. Since the game is considered short, it was an refreshing experience during coffee breaks.From unique visual style to gripping, innovative gameplay, Carto delivers on all fronts.Recommended for: puzzle game lovers, achievement hunters & casual gamersCheers,SultanK
