_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a puzzle game where you have to manipulate an overworld map that's divided into square tiles in order to make new paths to explore new areas and complete tasks. Sometimes you will be run out of tiles to build a desired overworld map and have to find new ones. To gain a new tile you can either: 1) collect a paper-shape object on the ground when you are in an explore mode, 2) manipulate an overworld map to have a required shape and make a (hidden) tile pop up. The first method is pretty straightforward with (maybe too many) tutorial on it already. But the second one is not, the game didn't teach you that this method exists AT ALL.The first time that the player have to find a new piece in the second method, is that the game ask the player to find a hidden spot in a center of "4 flower tiles". At this point it is naturally for players to arrange those flower tiles into 2x2 square in the overworld map and then walk into the center to check for the hidden spot. Nothing happen. After that players might spend lots of time trying to rotate/rearrange tiles in this fashion, hopefully to find a correct solution. Just to find that the 2x2 square is totally wrong, but the correct solution is to arrange them into a plus sign (+) with a hole in the middle, just then the hidden tile pop up!So my question is, why the game doesn't introduce this method before? It doesn't have to be a full tutorial, just a smart little puzzle design that make players feel like they solve the puzzle themselves (like using just 2 tiles to make another one), not by throwing an impossible puzzle (according to player's point of view) and left them to look up at a walkthrough if they can't solve it. (And don't forget that the arrangement of 2x2 will solve some quests without finding new tiles too.)This is not a Eureka moment for a puzzle game, but a frustration with curses and willing to give up. And I think this is a critically poor designed puzzle that rendering the game unplayable. Hence a thumb down.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: What an unique game! Child-like without being childish, features lovely watercolor artwork and is a brainteaser! I don't believe I've played something similar: it feels very boardgame-like in the sense it's very tactile, the way you manipulate the tiles to advance the game. The writing is very sparse, but full of character; the story is simple, but enjoyable.Being a game about cartography, about maps and how they relate to the real world, there can be a little bit of frustration when things don't match up. Navigating usually involves being a little lost and the map the game offers you sometimes doesn't have very clear indications, but like in real life a few informed guesses can get you to the next marker. There was only one occasion where I honestly don't know how you were supposed to get to the answer. It soured me a little, but the next chapter was so charming I didn't care. In the final chapters I kinda lost my patience trying to figure out what to do, partly because I just didn't know if there was something I was missing or not. That's when the sometimes opaque nature of the game works against it. My suggestion is not to rush to the end. If you get stuck and start getting frustrated, go do something else. A cool head and some patience will get you through eventually.Carto is a map and a map is different from GPS: it requires not simply following a line, but actually reading the world.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: I love Carto.Let me accentuate how much; I bought it 4 times (Xbox, PC via Microsoft, Nintendo Switch and now Steam) and have finished it even more often since I first discovered it via Game Pass, never boring of the beautifully crafted world that makes this game special.The characters are both lovable, as well as wonderfully weird at times, making for a unique and charming experience.Carto’s art style is incredibly delightful, like a warm blanket, reminding me of the picture books from my childhood.The puzzles aren’t what I’d call ‘challenging’ but the gameplay involving the maps is a lot of fun and solving them still feels rewarding. There need to be more games with this gameplay mechanic.If you’re into puzzle games with a lot of heart, a cute story and characters, and a kind of ‘boardgame-y’ spin on puzzlers, this game is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A great game! The concept of the map pieces makes for original puzzles, that sets the game apart from other games of the same genre. The cute story, lore and characters also make the game more enjoyable: you don't feel like you just have to solve puzzle after puzzle, and I thought it was actually well put together.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a really cute puzzle adventure game where you play as Carto who is trying to reunite with her grandmother. Some of the puzzles were more complex than others, but I never got that stuck throughout the game and always found the solutions really clever. Ever chapter felt unique and the areas were so fun to explore! There's a wide variety of characters you come across that were all enjoyable and memorable, and the soundtrack is really good. Overall, this game was very enjoyable, and you should definitely check it out!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A short and sweet puzzle adventure. The cutesy sprite art will be polarising you will love or hate it.Music is calm and relaxing, no voice acting allowing the player character the communicated via :-)  expressions!game-play centres around exploration and light puzzle solving primarily by alerting the map.I will call this game better for the younger gamer then the salty old school gamers (then again many older gamers LIKE games like this). I will recommend this game to all who read this as it made for a relaxing couple of afternoons.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A charming game with an innovative mechanic to puzzle, highly recommended for people looking for a relaxing experience. I bought this game as part of the Humble Choice of August, and this game alone makes the whole bundle worth it, in my opinion.Carto is a puzzle game in which you have to rearrange the different tiles of many scenarios during the events that take place after falling from an airship where you were traveling with your granny. I have to admit that, before starting the game, I just expected a simple game, whose main attractive would be its cute graphics, but I never imagined that this game would give me a hugely innovative puzzle experience. After 5 hours I spent to complete the game, I'm not tired of this mechanic. It feels great to see how rearranging tiles is translated in shifts from the "micro" to "macro" world. Puzzles are not complicated, maybe the latter ones required more time, but they were kind of straight-forward to resolve. To comment on a small aspect I would change, I think the difficulty scale is a low, maybe this is intentional to avoid frustrations and make this game a better overall experience, but personally I am missing a bit of that "scalable difficulty"Another of the points that surprised me in a good way is the world building. Your adventure will occur in many different places where you will meet many interesting character, who will make all the stages full of life and give you a lot of information about the world. In this aspect, this title reminds me to games such as Wandersong or even Dust: An Elysian Tail, wwhere, although throughout the game your final purpose is clear and all the actions in which you participate bring you closer to your final goal, that won't deny you for knowing interesting side characters along your adventures.Overall, this game is 100% recoomendable if you enjoy the aspects that I listed before, and if you have certain doubts about this game, you can await to the next sale (the last one was 40%, and it is definitely worth it for that price
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: I thought it's gonna be a puzzle focus game, and it turned out to be more of a rpg adventure game, not disappointed though, it still has some fun puzzles. The game itself is just so cute and light-hearted in every way, the wholesome story and characters, the adorable Carto, and the simple but refined visuals. A great game to play if you just wanna chill and relax!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: this game has such unique gameplay mechanics and an original narrative that will be hard to soon forget. having lost my own adventurous and daring Granny to cancer mid 2021, Carto was the breath of fresh air I didn't know I needed. the puzzles are intuitive and clever, increasing in difficulty but still serving as a smooth introduction to new players of the genre. the exploration was rewarding and the in depth personalities of each adorable, hand drawn character carried an aura of warmth that lasted through the whole story.if you like puzzles and adorable narratives, this gem and the heartwarming feeling you get as the credits roll is well worth the price tag. I loved every second of it :)
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A fun puzzle game with a significant emphasis on child-friendly exploration and whimsical narrative. You constantly manipulate the map to aid the many happily amusing characters you meet across a variety of environments in your quest to get back home. The paper-like visuals are very pleasant and the humour or at least the genuine attempt thereof is instrumental in creating a consistently joyous atmosphere.As much as I hate to admit, I personally found the game to be a little challenging at times, but remaining in that world trying to find the solution was always fun. If you explore each square and interact with the world enough you honestly get enough clues to know how to progress.The individuality of each character works so well to breathe life into the game. I found myself caring for these characters even after the happy ending.An appreciative palate-cleanser between more elaborate games.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Heartwarming and delightful. A little girl is separated from her gran, and the very deepest depths of human depravity she encounters along the way are people too preoccupied to help her search but who wish her the very best. (This describes most of the characters, admittedly.) A light game for a dark time.Gameplay, you say? Manipulating the map is a cool concept, but from the elevator pitch it felt too weak to support a whole game. I was afraid that it would either become monotonous, or end up with a confusing mess of layered gameplay mechanics. Not so - the game does a great job of trying out a new novel mechanic with each level, then mostly retiring it to explore something else with the next.Not too short, doesn't overstay its welcome, and good for a replay if your heart needs warming anew.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely and original relaxed puzzle/exploration/adventure game which has you, in a story-driven manner, explore a charming hand-drawn world consisting of several biomes. The game uses an innovative map mechanic that has you arrange and rearrange square tiles to get around, trigger events, etc.  This interesting puzzle mechanic is applied creatively to other aspects as well.  The beautiful hand-drawn graphics look nice even at higher resolutions and are complemented by a nice soundscape.I haven't finished the game yet but already know I'd buy a sequel in a heartbeat. How about basing that on hexagonal (or octagonal) tiles? 😃
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the entire storyline of Carto, and fell in love with the gameplay, story, and characters. Carto is a cute 2d styled puzzle game. You explore the world as a little cartographer using your map to solve puzzles, 'riddles' and challenges. The puzzles may appear simple, but you can sometimes spend ages trying to figure out what each means, and how to solve them. If you like challenging puzzles, with cute characters, and a unique storyline, this game i recommend for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: The arto got me to buy it, but the carto is why i stayed.The puzzles do get harder from time to time, but still good. Those AHA moments are always the best part, especially after turning around a bunch of map sections just to see what trick they're gonna give me next. It's also good game to play when you have a few hours of time to spare before getting back to whatever it was you were doing.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A fun bit of puzzle play.To be honest, some of the puzzles are real brain twisters, there is even one that seems to only be solved by luck and repetition, but for the most part it's fun.The core mechanism of the game is your ability to rearrange the map, which is made up of little squares. Sometimes it is arranging them so you can go places, sometimes it is arranging them in such a way that a new piece pops up in the middle. But they do get kind of complicated.Odd, because on first glance it seems like a game aimed at children, but it rapidly becomes frustrating, so I wouldn't think to buy it for a small child. Still, the story draws me in, and most of the puzzles, while they do get difficult, have my getting there in the end.An easy two thumbs up. NOTE: I did get this game for free, but from a friend, not the developer.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a wonderful game about friendship, family and discovery. You'll meet a colorful cast of characters along your way in this beautifully vibrant world, solve mysteries and learn about what it means to be the ultimate cartographer. The gameplay is like nothing I've ever seen and to my knowledge, hasn't been replicated since (which is a shame). The game can take anywhere from 5-7 hours to finish, and it doesn't overstay its welcome at all. I'd say this is worth playing just for the gameplay alone, but there's so much more to see and many friends to meet in this cute little adventure game. Definitely recommending this one!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game thinking that the map construction mechanic was interesting. Sadly, after just 20 minutes I was already bored of it. There are twists, of course; this is a puzzle game at heart. So there are certain rules to how to build the map to unlock new pieces, kind of like in Dorfromantik. But the gameplay loop... it's just build the map to get more world to explore to find another piece of the map to build the map... and so on.And that by itself would've been fine, if the characters were interesting and the music wouldn't loop after 12 seconds. The writing is simple; it's something you'd see in a child's cartoon. In fact, I'd describe this game as a perfect game for children. Simple and cute.And while I personally enjoy simple and cute games, this was perhaps a little too simple. It is what it is - and nothing more, so don't expect some kind of revolutionary design. That's all I'm saying here - it's not bad, just simple. Do you enjoy simplicity? You might like this. I didn't. Hope this helps!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a very cozy, and wholesome. I LOVE the artwork. The art is what drew me to the game to begin with, and I loved every moment of it while playing. All the characters are adorable with fun personalities. I love the whole concept of the game. Some of the puzzles were extremely hard, and I don't know how I would have figured theme out on my own. I know I'm not good at puzzles, so I can only speak for myself. I would love a Carto 2! :)
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: -  It's really hard not to gush over the gorgeous storybook visuals. Given the prominence of books and paper in many central story and gameplay elements, it makes a lot of sense to adopt the style of another printed medium. It admittedly would have been interesting to see what it would look like if everything had a cartographic style, but that would have robbed the visuals of their color and cuteness-  I'm a little split on how I feel about every edge being kinda squiggly, but it wasn't bothersome enough to really matter. It enhances the "softness" of the character and environment designs, at least-  While not universally true, I almost always expect a fairly chill and relaxed soundtrack in a puzzle game. Carto's music offers no surprises in terms of mood in that regard. It's still an interesting set of songs, though. What really struck me, if you'll pardon the pun, was the impressive diversity in percussion. Drums, chimes, maracas, triangles, tamborine, either a xylophone or marimba (both?), and perhaps even a glockenspiel get layered into some really complex rhythms. Sure, there's a healthy dose of woodwinds, strings, and synth, but the tracks that got me tapping my feet were the ones where the percussion section was going wild- The plot follows Carto, a little girl who travels the skies making maps with her grandmother in their airship. But they're no ordinary maps; these are collected in a magical atlas. They have the power to combine, divide, and shuffle the world itself by reorganizing map pieces- Being that Carto is a curious little girl, she wants to try it out for herself. For reasons unknown, she combines a thundercloud piece with a piece containing their airship, resulting in Carto falling from the sky with the atlas. Unfortunately, scraps of paper are torn from the atlas and carried all over the world by the storm's winds- The narrative takes form as Carto tries to make the atlas whole again, meets a wide range of colorful characters in need of help, and attempts to track down her grandmother- It's a very cute story, and it's pretty much devoid of bad vibes outside of the conflict that's set up in the initial cutscene. That's not necessarily a bad thing for a puzzle game, but it does make the plot less engrossing. Instead, most beats are fairly chill and positive, centering around helping people. The absence of intrigue takes a lot of "spice" out of the game- If you read the plot description, you may have already correctly inferred that Carto's primary puzzle dynamic involves arranging map pieces on the grid to reshape the world. Sometimes, you'll need to listen to characters who point out specific landmarks in cardinal directions relative to each other in order to make a location or person appear. Other times, you'll have to arrange pieces in a certain way to reveal new sections of the map (e.g., lining up two broken bridge pieces to make a bridge piece appear between them)- As the map pieces are almost always 1x1 squares, the main restriction on placement is the geography of each side. Mountains must touch mountains, water must touch water, plains must touch plains, etc. Any side is allowed to be unconnected to anything- This changes in the game's final section, where pièces become, for a lack of a better term, "Tetris-y". This ramps up the difficulty a touch and makes the puzzles more interesting- That last bullet belies my primary complaint about Carto: it's really easy. There are, of course, a few clever puzzles (the Library section was by far my favorite), but I was able to autopilot large portions of this game. I like the feeling of "eureka" moments after I've been stumped by a devious puzzle for a while, and Carto simply couldn't muster the difficulty necessary to provide those- Carto is a game of soft edges, literally and figuratively. In the context of the audiovisual design, this works fairly well, but the plot and gameplay suffer from an overly gentle approach. These qualities certainly make Carto a more relaxing experience, but also a less enticing one- It ran well and looked nice on the Steam Deck- . While Carto promises an extremely cute and eminently chill playthrough, don't go in expecting much challenge or excitement. It's probably a better game for those who go in with a better mindset than I did, but I was left wanting a bit more at almost every turn
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A really casual and cute puzzle game. Usually puzzle games rely too heavily on the same gimmick that it can become boring but this seamlessly combines both puzzle, story and exploration without leaning too heavily on either aspect. The story element in this isn't an after thought but a part of the puzzle. It's also easy to follow and isn't too dialogue heavy.7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A simple, relaxing game, with tricky puzzles, comical characters and cute creatures. The side characters not only matter, but they even granting the life and the memories of the journey, what you wanna (and will) remember. The main storyline is simple, but this is the same reason it is interesting to me. This, and the base game mechanics are, what makes the magic ;)(P.S.: I'm sorry in advance for grammar mistakes, English is not my first language)
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: No veg options.I like the cute style. There's some awkwardly slow, unskippable dialogue here and there, but most of it I found to be entertaining. I was, however, completely thrown off by having to kill a bird and having to actively "interact" with the game to eat it. I know it's "just a game", but man, this made me lose all my appetite for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: A very cute, charming and happy game. I adore the art style and the characters, all brought together in a fantastical, beautiful world. The puzzles themselves range from really easy to very confusing, there were several times I looked up a guide and thought 'oh I could've figured that out myself if I played with it long enough' but just as many times I read the solution and found myself thinking 'how on earth was I meant to figure that out?'. Overall a great game to pick up if you don't mind having to look up a guide, especially for hidden achievements, but it might get a bit frustrating without one. Honestly, just know what you're getting into, the cutesy graphics doesn't mean its easy, but its worth the time :)
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a story driven puzzle game.  I play all sorts of puzzle games and this one is different from any that I have played before.  It keeps you guessing just enough to not get frustrated.  Just when you think you wont figure it out...Bam. It comes to you.  Plus the story cute.  The tiny clues given in the small friends you meet along the way are just enough to keep you going in the right direction.  Most importantly...the music, art and overall visual of the game is pleasing and relaxing.  I have only really just begun....but I already know I will finish this game and enjoy the whole journey.  Cheers to a great game!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game! I like everything about it: the art style, a recurring music theme and most of all a heart warming story. It made me feel like I'm a child again! I played Carto in 10-15 min coffee breaks but if I'd had time I would have finished it in one go. Puzzles are cleverly designed and there was never a time I felt completely stuck. A few nitpicks which don't take away anything from this 10/10 masterpiece:1. There's a scene where a whole village is singing, playing music and dancing together. Why did it have to end so quickly? I wanted to stay in that moment for 10 minutes, not 10 seconds :)2. The game wouldn't be any worse if that single reference to demonic goats was removed.3. I didn't enjoy stopping a bird from migrating and ending his journey on a plate.Highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Charming and satisfactorily clever. Outside of a few specific puzzles, the game isn’t particularly a head-scratcher which, depending on your approach, could be a preferable feature. After a point early on, the map mechanics don't change in any spectacular ways and they begin to take a backseat to the growing story. Generally, playing Carto makes for a very comfortable time. Still, I do wish that a little more had been done to further explore the potential within the landscape moving/flipping gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesomeeee. You are navigating by moving and turning pieces of the map around, finding the way to go, or how to solve a quest. The art style is great, so is the plot. It's not a very long game, but it's a beautiful journey. You got separated from your grandma and you're looking for a way to find her, and on the way, you meet many characters that need your help. I really enjoyed this game and I am definitely gonna replay it at some point.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun little game. Simple mechanics with somewhat non-linear options. It is not challenging in the head-banging way, but it is intriguing and fairly relaxing at the same time. You can modify a map by moving and rotating available map tiles until it has the characteristics you need, in order to achieve goals such as finding items, meeting people, creating a specific kind of terrain layout.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Cool puzzle mechanics and nice watercolor graphics were things that caught my eye for this game.It's not a traditional puzzle game, it's more like a puzzle game mixed with an adventure game. While most puzzles are simple, there are times when you are not solving the puzzle, but instead trying to understand what the puzzle actually even is. I gave up 3 times (Chapter 5, Chapter 6, Chapter 9) and looked for help on Youtube. The first time, I had the "duh" moment for not getting what I had to do, but Chapter 9 is something else, even after watching the walkthrough, it seemed like people brute-forced the solution with trial and error, not with logic.There were some amusing moments in the dialogs, but most of the dialogs feel like content filler. Occasionally there are hints about what you need to do next, but luckily, plot-advancing characters repeat the hints when talking with them again. I get that it's made by indie-studio, but I think fully voiced dialogs would have been much better - something that you wouldn't want to skip past fast. Probably difficult to find voice actors for child characters, but it would make sense when the game/story is aimed at kids.Cute graphics are probably the best part of this game, some people seem to like the sound and music too, but for me, it got very annoying very quickly.I didn't encounter any bugs, so the game is well-polished, but I feel like it could have used more user testing to iron out the confusing parts.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Much like watching a good-spirited studio ghibli movie, this game leaves a warm fuzzy feeling in your heart. It is one of the few games that are recommended for a kid audience on this platform, as well as grown-ups wanting a break from everyday serious topics. Carto and all other characters are cute and well meaning, mostly with minor troubles such as having lost sight of their loving wive for an entire 20 minutes. The gameplay is as advertised playing around with the world-building map mechanic and walking about with a few head-scratching puzzles. The ideas of maps and reshuffling thereof are clever and played with in a satisfying way. At times the solutions to the puzzles are merely hinted at, sometimes in a way that the player may not recognize them as such. To be noted is that getting stuck in this game is not a cause for shame, as my university degree certainly didn't save me from missing the path every once in a while.The story is simplistic, but heart-warming. Carto has been separated from her nice grandma and departs on her adventure of finding her way home, meeting nice people along the way. There's not much in terms of demanding story elements or themes, but a wholesome atmosphere of careless fun makes up for it.All in all, I recommend this title as a nice wholesome break from the real world or a good introduction into what our world should be like for children finding their way home.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

_childDocuments_.review: Carto is a chill adventure game wrapped around a unique, world-shifting puzzle mechanic. Use this power to explore mysterious lands, help a quirky cast of new friends, and guide Carto on her journey home.
_childDocuments_.name: Carto

name: INDUSTRIA
detailed_description: NORA'S JOURNEY CONTINUES WITH INDUSTRIA 2! About the Game On the evening of the fall of the Berlin wall, a young woman plunges headlong into a parallel dimension to find her missing work colleague who has disappeared under mysterious circumstances. While the checkpoints in East Berlin are still being overrun by crowds of people, Nora escapes from this world, into unknown layers of time and into an unknown fate. Profound story: Experience a classic story-driven first-person shooter with about 4 hours of gameplay Tight atmosphere: Dive into a lovingly designed world full of mystery and lynchesque surreality Deadly danger: Enemies lurk around every corner - defend yourself with 5 different weapons Unique setting: Berlin at the time of the fall of the wall meets a surreal industrialized city Experimental soundtrack: Synthesizer, acoustic instruments and melancholic vocals Berlin, 9th November 1989: The streets are full of people. After four decades of division, thousands of cars are rolling across the inner-German border. The Wall is finally open! At the same time a man disappears in a secret research facility near East Berlin. His goodbye message reaches you too late. You drive back to the office, where the State Security has already destroyed all records of the research project. The complex is deserted and empty. The search for Walter takes you deep into the center of the facility - right into the heart of the universe, where time seems to stand still. The dark secret lurks - well hidden - behind the curtain. In the end, it is horrible insights and the questions of responsibility that make you dive deeper and deeper into a strange, surreal yet familiar world.

name: Bleak Faith: Forsaken
detailed_description: Explore the last remnants of civilization in this vast, unforgiving, and interconnected world. Learn what is left of its history. Discover pockets of civilization in the perpetually expanding Omnistructure. Lose yourself in a journey unlike any other. Open World and Exploration Explore the Omnistructure for the first time ever. Rich in atmosphere and rife with danger, be prepared to be immersed in a new world unlike any you've experienced before. Not every path is paved and catered to you, so be prepared to run, climb, leap, to ascend in Bleak Faith. Hardcore Combat Experience Combat is dangerous and will push you to your limits. Positioning, timing, and resource-management are all things you must keep in mind at all times. Expect to be challenged. Epic Boss Fights Be prepared for memorable boss fights with unique soundtracks. Bosses ramp the danger levels even higher and ensure a thrilling ride through the manifold sectors of the Omnistructure. RPG Progression and Playstyle Versatility Choose a class and progress into your perfect playstyle. But remember, not every choice is reversible, so decide wisely what direction you take your character in.

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY hope the developers read my review. I love the souls genre and the aesthetic of abstract/atmospheric horror games. I also really respect the time and effort that it takes to create a video game.On to the review: I sadly think this game is very bad. Normally if an indie game is unpolished or lacking in certain features, I would give some credit, but this game is just bad. From simple issues that annoy the crap out of you to design choices that are SERIOUSLY questionable, this game just falls completely flat. Even at 25$, it feels overpriced. An analogy I would use is Dark Souls is a ferrari and this game is a beat up 2005 Toyota Camry. The beat up 2005 Camry will get the job done if you need it, but why the hell would I pay 50% the price of a ferrari for it? To anyone wanting to buy this to save money, just spend the extra on an actually good game.Controls: The controls are horrific. I think I remember the starting scene saying that it was optimized for mouse and keyboard maybe? I certainly hope so because the experience on a controller is terrible. The default button to interact is right trigger? Or you select items in menus with B, instead of A? I accidentally fast traveled immediately because I pressed B to get out of the menu, but it turns out that B selects things. It should be EXTREMELY easy to make controller mappings user-friendly. It feels like the developers have never played a video game before and just bound actions to random buttons.Gameplay/Combat: One review I read said that the game utilizes a combo system, and the combat feels clunky if you dont use it. I would argue the combat feels clunky regardless. Your character moves extremely fast regardless of what you want to do, but the enemies typically move slow (similarly to DS1 or DS2 enemies). This creates a terrible experience while fighting. Your character also swings super slowly despite moving very fast? It feels like bloodborne movement with DS1 greatsword swinging. Also the movement feels...off. Its hard to describe, but its similar to mortal shell movement. The rate at which you move and the animations of your character are clearly not in sync. It creates a very bizarre and unpolished feeling. Visuals: The design of the visuals are appealing. I like the environment that they are going for. This is the main reason that I even bought the game. The graphics arent amazing, but I am okay with this due to the small design team. My main reason that I cant even give the visuals a complete pass is because the animations are particle effects are TERRIBLE. Weirdly enough, many of these effects would actually be better if they were just removed from the game. For example, when you stab a giant enemy in the back, rays of bright white light erupt from their back, covering your ENTIRE screen. How does this even make sense? Just remove that all together, its terrible. Level design: The level design feels terrible. Half of the areas are just bridges and pathways with single enemies. It doesnt feel very interactive or real. It almost feel like this floating arrangement of pieces that you traverse alone with the occasional enemy. In some cases, it feels appropriate due to the abstract nature of the game, but in most areas, it just feels like poor level design.Conclusion: The main things I look for in good indie games is gameplay. Gameplay is King. If a game looks mediocre, but the movement and combat is a crisp and refreshing expansion to the Souls genre, I would still LOVE the game. Sadly this game just falls flat in general.

_childDocuments_.review: The aesthetics of Bleak Faith were a huge draw for me to try this game and I really want to like it, but there are several things are preventing me from being able to recommend the game. Combat is very rough. Enemy and character animations are choppy and often fall out of sync with the sound effects which makes it difficult to time attacks and dodges. Camera movement is a bit laggy. Boss mechanics feel very inconsistent as well which makes it challenging to learn. This game is frustrating to play for all the wrong reasons. I found myself enjoying the game a bit more around the 7 hour mark, but less so beyond that. Playing with the graphics settings did help reduce screen stutter and make the movement much more smooth. Combat is still really janky but I’ve gotten the hang of how to work with it. Exploring the world was fun for a while but with such numerous areas that lead to nothing it feels like a big waste of time as time goes on. Object collision is very poor so it’s easy to end up in unintended areas. Around the 20+ hour mark each play session made me feel more and more annoyed by how unpolished the game is. Game play feels more like a chore than a fun experience given the myriad of issues. I might still try to finish the game at some point, but there are plenty of better things to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Normally for Steam reviews I just make my lil jokes leave a thumbs up and keep it pushing but I'm gonna try to detail my opinions on the gameLIKED:- The latest patches made it A LOT more stable it's still a little jank but I'm not clipping through the environment every 2 seconds- Overall the recent changes have substantially improved the game (I feel pretty qualified in saying this bc I initialy sailed the high seas before going legit so I saw the game fundamentally change in the middle of a playthrough lmao) by including controller options that aren't designed by an insane person and getting rid of the equipment as level/build in favor of a more conventional leveling system that works better imo- Level design is fantastic and reminds me a lot of how From approached level design in DS1 but with an added scale that truly makes you feel like one small organism that exists inside an enormous structure- Atmosphere is king here I know everyone and their mom compares it to Blame! but that's genuinely the only other piece of media that comes close tonally- The score for this game is S tier like the main composer really hit a slam dunk with this OST it's probably in my top 5 atp- New level system is fairly simple when compared to other soulslikes/bornes but I think it really works for this game (ex: STR is the catch-all scaling stat for melee weapons and dictates your equip load so you can easily switch between unga/bunga and a lighter quick build and have both be viable)DISLIKED:- Probs honestly just a skill issue on my end but I wish the Handler Echoes were all more directly in the critical path my first playthrough I wasn't able to find the 5th Echo which led me to be pretty underpowered through the endgame- SPOILER ON THIS POINT: - The  boss fight has one of my all time least favorite mechanics in games (the player can't deal noticeable damage to the boss for extended periods of time regardless of player proficiency or risk taking) like yeah it looks cool desert power etc etc but probably one of the lamest fights this side of Bed of Chaos- Some of the textures in the game still need some refinement there was more than a few instances where I genuinely couldn't tell if I'd gone out of bounds or not- That swinging platform section: like I get that it's 100% optional (though for a pretty decent accessory) but cmon guys who told yall this was a good idea lmaoREALLY ♥♥♥♥♥♥ HATED:OVERALL:Despite the flaws I'd still rec this game if you really appreciate atmosphere and/or don't mind games being a little rough around the edges

_childDocuments_.review: I waited two years for this game to release. I checked the website monthly, subscribed to their YT channel, and followed BFF twitter. I was so hyped when it first launched back in March, only to be met with bugs and glitches, and a largely broken game. It was playable, but not enjoyable. So I put the game down for over a month to let the devs get to work. I joined their discord server and watched the daily laundry lists of patch notes roll out, fixing bugs, polishing features, replacing animation where needed. I waited. In late April the updates slowed so I planned to go back and try again.So I went back and played another six or so hours before I came to the conclusion that I don't like BFF.To clarify, this is simply because of game play reasons. The art is gorgeous. Lore is deep and enthralling. But the game play is simply so mediocre. It feels like youre sliding on the ground as you attack, causing you to lunge yourself off ledges, of which there are many. The parry system is unreliable, though every single enemy from a plate-clad soldier to some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in rags can perfectly parry your attacks. And those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ invisible floating enemies in the hub area? ♥♥♥♥ those guys. Why are they there? They don't add to the experience, they just piss me off! Oh and those walkers that can just teleport you to a height that will kill you from fall damage, why!? Going back to attacks, unless you are using a spear or a glaive you have to the ass to ass with enemies in order to land your attacks. Oh and you better not have that torch equipped when you press the attack button, because you'll be locked in on torch mode for 30 seconds while some secret sadistic timer ticks down, keeping you from your actual weapons.I REALLY wanted to like this game, but its just not it. Even after a month plus of polishing, its just not it. On the discord bug reports still occur daily and the poor devs are still chugging along doing their damnest to fix them. I think this game should be in the running for "Labor of Love" at the end of the year because of all the effort the devs are putting in. And yes, I know three-four duded made it, thats why I wanted to play it as well. But I just don't like it.TL;DR- gorgeous game held back by mediocre game play, never ending list of bugs, and horrendous enemy design.Edit: Several months later the game just isn't fun. Now that I've beaten three bosses and done a syncing event the red knights have spawned and its impossible to move around the map without the knights with axes and a red sash to chasing you to the ends of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ earth and two tap you through your shield and heavy armor. I don't see the point in continuing to play if my build (heavy armor and shield perks) cannot perform well or even have the ability to soak up damage like its suppose to. Not to mention that if you die enough times to the red knights your save gets deleted. So whats the point then?

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-IMMERSIVE atmosphere and environment. If you love the manga "BLAME!", you'll love this. It's honestly hard to find a game that quite matches this type of genre as a game. The closest is maybe bloodborne or Nier Automata?-Cool and unique bosses (although there isnt any special ai like elden ring, enemy moves are generally predictable)-Vertical level ascent instead of traveling horizontally (like scaling a tower)-Lots of hidden areas and secrets-Lots of different mobs, some mobs may be beaten easier by using a different type of weapon-no stupid leveling system, instead its all about the gear you find!-plenty of healing potions-good amount of playing style: dual wield, bow, mage, heavy-duelist style combat (everyone complains about the combat but honestly its all about the stamina, once you get used to it, the combat is actually a lot easier than you think. when you do a move it will queue it up! sort of like a rhythm game. Ive played elden ring and i think the combat is much simpler and easier than elden ring.)Cons:-Dont use a controller. Use mouse and keyboard and gameplay should be a lot less buggy!-blurry view of faraway environments-environment looks like it was made in 2010-advertisements and trailers over hype this game (combat is a lot slower than in the videos)-LOTS of bugs: getting stuck in places, dying randomly, environment glitches (cap your fps and please adjust your settings, like  sensitivity)-Not a lot of NPCs? Not much items that give lore either. (game seems half baked, not much story substance despite the cool environment-dungeon dark cavelike music, but not much dynamic epic soundtracks. (gets boring after a while)-forget dodging if you are near the enemy, it just doesnt seem to work (it will definitely not work if you have no stamina)In summary: Yeah it is impressive that only 3 developers made this game, however it doesn't mean that this game cant be improved. In fact, if the combat and movement werent so floaty and if the game ran on unreal engine 5, I believe that this would make this one of the best games of this genre out there.

The combo system is OK but you can time it the same every time and get different results.Where to start?  Well it feels kind of unfinished.  The hitboxes are a pretty big issue.  The combat feels pretty underwhelming.  It feels a lot like Steel Rising and Dark Souls 1 had a illegitimate baby and then dropped it on its head. _childDocuments_.review: What particularly stands out, as many others have mentioned in their reviews, is the very dark atmosphere of the game. It's a mixture of megastructures and a decaying landscape in a futuristic style, with some medieval elements like knight armor and weapons.Honestly, I can only recommend this game to those who enjoy extensive exploration, as it is essential to progress. However, I believe, and statistics on game completion support this, that this is the game's biggest weakness. It’s not uncommon to have no idea where to go next. This is due to the numerous shortcuts, which can almost be described as labyrinthine.The game excels with a variety of weapons and items that allow for an individualized playstyle. The landscape is incredibly well-designed, and the soundtrack complements it perfectly. The story is very interesting, but, typical of a Soulslike game, it is somewhat hidden and found in item descriptions. The game isn't particularly difficult. With the leveling system, bosses and enemies can be easily defeated after some grinding.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, like many other Souls likes, has lots of amazing concepts, and infinite potential, but with terrible implementation. Level design is mazelike, with muddy textures, and reused washed out assets cobbled together, making it difficult to discern where you've been and where to go next, with no in game direction to lead you. The combat is clunky, slow, and punishing, without any of the forgiving pieces of Souls to balance out the difficulty, such as I-frames, upgradable Estus flasks, and level grinding and farming. The movement is slippery, with the simplest movement sending you careening off cliffs and ledges. The jumping is floaty, with shallow jumps that don't allow much adjustment. Add all of this in a setting that takes place exclusively over massive pits, girders, catwalks, and cliffs, with some areas actually forcing you to do platforming, and you get a recipe for trial-and-error disaster. The incredible number of commands is unusual, with the mapping being unreasonably unique, meaning there are too many inputs and too few buttons on a controller, and you will have to remap things if you are used to playing other games on M&K. The graphics are not the best visually, with muddy textures, Vsync issues, framerate issues, camera lock on issues, clipping issues, physics issues, and a host of visual bugs, but the visuals have their moments, such as in brightly lit areas with water and vivid colors... but the game takes place in a grey and brown hellscape covered over mostly in darkness sapped of color. The architecture and art style are the best things about the game, giving the game a fresh setting and feel while also remaining similar to the rest of the Souls-likes of recent memory. The amount of loot pickups for crafting is very rewarding, and it's fun to realize that you will never run out of materials to craft healing, potions and ammo, until you realize you can only carry 2 heals, and 5 arrows at a time before having to restock. Hit-boxes are all over the place, with you and your enemies' blades often going right through each other with no effect. Attack spamming is punished by a combo system which takes something that should be simple, striking more than once, a punishing mini game, that if you do not master quickly, you will be left why you are standing there unable to attack when you have full stamina. All of the systems are left unexplained, and there is no tutorial section per se, it's up to you to figure it out. The game would be more fun and less frustrating without this "combo system." You can jump, but you cannot do a jumping attack. The game also froze on me twice in 6 hours, and could not get consistent frames above 40 fps, with all settings on Medium. The game still has frame hitches too, even with dynamic resolution on. Traversing between large areas means a long multiple second screen freeze while the new one loads in. The armor sets, weapons, enemies and level designs, are all fascinating however, and make me want to keep playing the game, but without performance improvements, and massive changes to game systems to make it less of a chore, I would recommend no one play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I am updating my review after having beaten the game now. I would give it a NEUTRAL rating if I could but since that's not an option I will recommend it and say it's worth trying out at least if the game's art style and world appeals to you. However if you aren't in a rush and don't mind waiting I would say wait a year since the devs seem committed to keep working on and updating the game.It's very janky and buggy, hitboxes on attacks will sometimes just not work, the movement is very floaty and will never quite feel right. You aren't punished for dying in this game which is good because you will often die through no fault of your own.The combat system does actually have some interesting mechanics and ideas but the aforementioned jankiness and questionable balance drags it down. There are no i-frames on dodges or dashes so you have to physically move out of the way of attacks to avoid them. The hitboxes - when they actually work - are usually quite good so having no i-frames isn't a huge problem. Blocking/deflecting takes too much stamina and parrying isn't very rewarding most of the time so you will end up just using positioning/dashing to avoid and punish enemy attacks. Basically on paper you have a good amount of defensive mechanics but 2 out of 3 are just not really worth using.When I look at preview footage of this game that the developers put out before it's release I am just left with utter confusion because that looks like the 1.0 build and the build I'm playing feels like an Alpha compared to that. It makes me wonder just how many things they scrapped and redid or if the previews were even footage of a real game.Every weapon has unique skills (some only passive) but the active abilities (similar to weapon arts in Dark Souls 3/Elden Ring) are useless if you aren't running an intelligence build since ability damage only scales with your intelligence stat.The story is pretty much nonexistent, it feels purposefully vague and nonsensical, there are no item descriptions or even really much of an intro to introduce the world to you. It made zero sense. The few cutscenes that are in the game don't tell you anything and some of them are straight up bugged, they don't load properly or have audio issues.So I have ragged on this game quite a bit already but despite that I am still giving it a positive (well, neutral really) review and that's just because there are moments of brilliance underneath it all. The world is surreal and fascinating, the soundtrack and sound design in general really sets the tone and the art style is great. In this regard it's unlike any other game I've played and that's it's strongest point.Everything in the world is interconnected, sometimes in absurd or nonsensical ways but it ends up playing into the surreal nature of it all. When it all just comes together and works it sometimes can remind you of the best of Dark Souls 1.This game still can use a lot of work and I wish the developers the best of luck. I'm definitely willing to play through it again in the future when it has improved.

_childDocuments_.review: Barely played, but that's all it took to refund it. I really wanted to dig into Bleak Faith; it looks absolutely rad. But it didn't take long to decide it absolutely wasn't likely to be worth the pain I felt in the first hour. This is actually my first ever refunded game.Summary: Controller was a waste. KB/M was weak but doable. Blocking blocked no damage. Dodging was grossly delayed. Enemies behaved strangely, including super slow-mo actions. Somehow, parrying worked every time. Nothing of real value to make me want playing.Controller didn't work for me. I fiddled with the sensitivity to absolutely no effect, until I realized mouse sensitivity was the only thing that affected controller sensitivity. Why, you may ask? Because it seems they shoehorned kbm controls into the controller mapping. My first clue was in the starting sequence when I had to name my save file and happened to tap my controller thumbstick...only to see it typing "wwwaaaassaawd." Yeah, the thumbstick is, quite literally, wasd.So I switched to kbm just to help things work smoothly, which didn't excite me for a game that plays akin to a soulslike. I got it to work well enough (despite alt being the default jump button). It didn't take me long to try to block an attack only to have full damage go right through my shield. I tried to dodge only to see the dodge activate nearly a second later. Then, that same enemy somehow super slow-rolled for like five full seconds. Another enemy had the same kind of super slow-mo when attacking.Maybe it was all just a fluke and I'm the only one with those types of experiences. But this was what defined my brief time in the game, with absolutely nothing there that gave me the motivation to push forward. And, thus, we have my first ever refunded game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start off by saying this game definitely has some jank, now it's not A terrible amount and they are mostly minor problems like being able to platform to places you aren't supposed to and having to respawn since there was no way back. That tends to be where most the issue are at, the platforming side of the game doesn't feel great to do and the fact that your character has to do A full u-turn to turn around is definitely annoying and can cause issues on ledges. that being said it is manageable just takes some trial and error. Otherwise the only other issues I've encountered are the occasional enemy that gets flung out of existence, some clipping in the environment and some random stuttering that happened twice in odd locations.Now for the pros and why I recommend the game. First and foremost is the setting, the world is absolutely incredible you really feel the inspiration from Nihei, from the environment, enemies, atmosphere and color palate it all looks incredible.Then you also have the equipment, there is A large variety to find and they all look unique and can help create A variety of builds. I was apprehensive when I hear there was no leveling, but my fears were unfounded, there's plenty of ways to play this game and the equipment determines your build.Combat takes A while to get used to because it takes A while to get used to the combo system, but overall once you get the hang of it the combat feels plenty satisfying.While this game may have been designed around k+m, the controller is plenty usable and that's how i'm playing, though you'll definitely want to tinker around with the settings A bit.Finally this game has to be one of the best optimized games Iv'e played in A long time and considering all the horribly optimized game we've been getting it's A breath of fresh air since Wo long was massively disappointing in that regard.Overall the positives outway the negatives for me and i'm sure the game will only get better since they seem determined to stick with the game and continue patching out the problems, adding to that the price of the game is perfectly reasonable given how much content is in the game and the fact that only 3 people developed this is pretty incredible.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: The use of assets seen in other titles is potentially innocent? The review will not take this into account anymore.I've put a few more hours in and it feels like a slog. Combat is easily the worst part of the game for a variety of reasons:-Firstly, swinging weapons just does not feel good. There is a timing aspect to the game (press attack at the correct time for faster combos) but it feels arbitrary and frustrating to just do a normal attack string.-The camera seems to be set very low, so it's difficult to see over your character and properly gauge range and distance in combat; I frequently just missed attacks from attacking out of range.-Sometimes the first move in your attack string will be a later move from the combo, for no reason that I can tell. When this happens, the game will sometimes ignore that this has happened and move on to the second move in the combo, and sometimes it will instead continue on from where it started (for example, if a normal string is 1 2 3 4, sometimes doing four attacks gives you 3 2 3 4 and sometimes you get 3 4 1 2). This makes it kinda frustrating to plan your attacks, especially with some of the moves that lunge forward or have a windup before attacking.-There's a huge delay in getting a shield up, so sword+board is mostly just sword.-In addition to the above, one-handed weapons feel like they have inconsistent stagger (in addition to the non-flowing combos) so you're probably going to take hits often from an enemy that just powers through.-Targeting in multi-enemy fights is awful - when you lock on to a target it stays on them and the only way to flick between targets is with the D-Pad (which was inconsistent when I tried it). This gives the second enemy freedom to just move into spots you can't see well and makes managing fights very hard.-Enemy aggro range is enormous, and frequently you'll find yourself joined by more enemies if you're taking too long killing the first (which really helps highlight the targeting problems). In addition, there was one area where an enemy had aggro'd me from spawn and moved to the top of the ladder-shortcut I had unlocked, preventing me from climbing the ladder.-Giant fights just *suck* - you have to break a health bar on their legs to make them fall over so you can go into a climbing sequence to stab them in vital areas, however you can't target their legs so there's a lot of wild flailing, the leg health bar resets once you go into the climbing sequence and you have to do it multiple times per kill. Giants also move around a bunch and will happily clip into walls, which makes sticking by their legs and reacting to attacks difficult (you have to do a lot of camera work for it)-Archer enemies have no visible indications of when they're going to attack - there's an arrow pull-back noise but they can just release at any given time. This is usually fine because they do minimal damage, but one progression area was blocked by a double archer encounter who would hit me for ~60% of my HP per arrow, or the same amount of stamina if shielding.--Moving on from combat, the world design is generally great and nails the atmosphere of a ruined dystopia.There are some places this falls down though and it's mostly in the attempts to make thing interconnected. I came across more than a few time where I'd pick one of a few branching paths that just led me around to where I started, with no real reason for the whole loop to exist. There are also the ladders - oh god the ladders - which are often excessively long, and I feel like there could be more engaging ways of getting people from A to B.Progression is tied to player equipment and not a farmable resource, which means you don't have to go find your bloodstain / grave / death spot to recover things! This removes the need to carefully go back to where you died, which is great, but it also (with the branching paths) led me to exploring a few different places very shallowly.However, I'm getting thrown a whole load of equipment leveling consumables that the Handler NPC cannot do anything with; she can only level stuff so high (which increases with items you find during exploration), but all of my gear has dropped already above the level I can increase to which leaves me in something of a rut progression-wise.Overall, I cannot recommend this game as it stands because it just feels like a chore to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, I get it. You heard the controls were awful. You heard the game was riddled with bugs. You trust no-life internet addicts with more critiques and bandwagon campaigns than actual, original opinions. Thats fine and if that is the case, this game is not for you.However, if you're willing to appreciate what the game is instead of what it's not, then I think you'll find a gem in this game.Bleak Faith isn't pushing boundaries in combat, visuals, crafting, or any other various cogs in the total game. One thing it does push though is atmosphere. Now, I'm not sure how much this matters to most gamers but, to me, it's everything. It sets the overall tone of everything that follows the main menu. It's lonely, oppressive and existentially eldritch in nature. This is what sold me on the game within the first 30 minutes. The world seems to be heavily influenced by the manga "Blame"- if you know you know, and if you don't I highly recommend reading that as well. I'm still not very far from the beginning in the game and that's partly because the world gives you multiple paths for exploration, semi-steep learning/adjustment curve to the combat (i dont think it's bad at all though like many have said, just different), along with no clear direction or explanation of literally anything (i'm a fan of this though).I totally understand why this game would not appeal to some but I think it'll also be an incredible experience for those who click with it. Just wanted to give my take on it so that maybe someone who was gonna pass it up, decides to give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the game at launch and while I loved the aesthetic and vibe of the game, performance and general jank turned me off after a few hours. After a year of changes, upgrades, and additions, I think this game is a hidden masterpiece. While there is still definitely some jank, as you might expect from a three person dev team making game of this magnitude, it only added to the charm. The world design and exploration were absolutely top notch. Truly inspired vision for a game that has come to life despite the budget limitations. It reminds me a lot of the BLAME! manga. All of the bosses are fantastic (minus worm god), with some cool moves and visuals. The game is not overly challenging, but rewards exploration, has a variety of build options that feel fun to play, and offers a very unique perspective on the souls-like genre that I genuinely believe is worth experiencing. I hope this studio keeps improving the game or even perhaps moves onto a new project,, because it is clear to me they have passion for this art.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR    Simply put, this game is awesome. Although there are some annoying bugs, it is to be expected with a new game, and it certainly doesn't mean it'll be like this forever. The game play and exploration is really fun. Art style is really inspiring and I dig the music a lot. Learning the mechanics of the game and spending some time getting used to them helps a ton. I'm excited to see what'll come next as I continue playing./----------------------------------------------------/    I want to start off by saying that this game is simply beautiful. It's clear to me that the devs put their hearts and souls into making this game. It truly is an inspiration to me. The story, game play, music, stetting, mood, enemy types, and art styles are truly unique.     Now, are there some bugs? Absolutely. Are they game breaking? Not entirely. I'll be straight up, the first hour of this game was pretty rough. Getting a feel of the mechanics took a minute, and experiencing the bugs right out of the gate while learning how to play was difficult. , this it is to be expected with a new game and I don't doubt that there will be improvements in the future.    I would like to make it very clear that the rest of my time playing this game was a blast. After defeating the first boss and progressing to the next area, the rest of my experience was a lot smoother. When I  how to use the mechanics of the game, such as perfect parrying, stamina management, and player positioning, it became extremely enjoyable. One of my favorite mechanics by far is the combo system. The idea of finding the rhythm of your weapon is very intriguing. Getting to the central area and exploring the different regions of the Omnistructure was nothing short of awe. Also, the synergy between the gear stats, perks, skills, and weapons look promising. I'm very excited to try out some sick builds.    As I said before, I did run into some bugs that were rather unpleasant. This includes enemies doing more damage than their supposed to, levers pushing me through walls, and the parrying system causing attacks to sometimes phase through my character.     I will admit that it's taken a bit of readjusting for the controls. I typically use a controller for this genre of games, but I had to switch to M+KB since I had some difficulties playing with my PS5 controller at first. Thankfully, the M+KB controls aren't hard to get down. It just takes some time to get used to.    This game was designed to be difficult, which I appreciate, and I feel that this difficulty tells another story on its own. It has been a fun challenge so far, and I can't wait to see what else is in store through out the rest of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, so I just wrapped up my recent second playthrough and I wanted to lay out my thoughts as this game keeps lingering with me. All in all, this game is such a mixed bag - but that bag has a lot of potential that I keep coming back to despite my other games in my recent backlog.The art direction and soundtrack are easily some of the most inspired and attention grabbing that I've seen in a Soulslike, the sense of scale is massive and makes the game feel larger than it actually is - combined with moody and atmospheric music and helps sell the idea of an incomprehensible silkpunk world. The armor and weaponry is both a mix of post apocalyptic sci-fi and gothic medieval, though I wish there were more futuristic weapons.The gameplay is also serviceable enough for the genre, plenty of weapons and builds to choose - due to how upgrades and gear sockets are handled, you can essentially change your build at any time if you discover something new, which has always been an issue with me in the genre since I tend to be indecisive and due a jack of all trades build in most games. Progression is kind of wonky though, as killing bosses won't make you much more powerful besides perk points - the real progression is upgrading gear, which requires you to explore areas fully and find randomly littered upgrades for your only vendor in the game.Enemies aren't as varied as they could be, and some are so tanky near the end that just aren't worth the effort to fight and dying to them repeatedly feels like a chore instead of a learning experience. Many enemies have jank movement and physics that still need to be addressed - bosses especially. Since rolling/dodging has no i-frames, bosses should have some better defined attacks. Some of the later game bosses just throw bullet hells at you and aren't fun to fight in the slightest.The story is probably the most cryptic and underdeveloped aspect of the game. After two full playthroughs, I still have no idea what my character is or what our involvement is with the various NPC's. While they did add new characters and lore notes, this is something the developers will have to keep working on in new patches - this game has so much potential for a rich universe and it would be a shame to underwrite it.Performance is definitely not the best, though this game is totally still playable on steam deck and my system. You'll see about 30 fps mostly on there with settings tweaked, but I feel like they could be further optimized to look better. Game did crash a few times, but wasn't repeatable and load screens are quick enough besides the initial boot into menu.All in all, for everything that I enjoyed there was something that kept holding the game back. I'm really disappointed that the beta footage seen a year ago is nothing like the current product, anc that gameplay looked much better than what we have currently - the HUD was better in my opinion, climbing was an apparent mechanic before it seemed to be cut entirely, and some weapons and armor seen in old footage is nowhere in the newer content.I'm still recommending the game since I think fans of soulslikes will find something of value here, but I think most would be better off waiting until newer updates. Here's hoping a few months from now the reception will be improved.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my basically favorite kind of game: small teams doing something weird, unique, and incredibly ambitious. The kind of game that might be a little tarnished on the surface, but absolutely has the soul underneath. So, as of writing this I'm a little over 3 hours in, just beat the first boss and left the starting area. Now just to get this out of the way, yes, there is some jank here. But it's extremely important to remember that jank does not mean 'bad', it just means managing your expectations a little. First things first, it's being recommended right now to keep the fps locked at or under 90 to smooth some potential issues with physics and movement. While this isn't necessarily ideal it's a *very* easy fix and still quite a solid performance ceiling (It is still better than Bloodborne's 30 cap, after all).Movement can be a bit twitchy at first but I found myself acclimating fairly quickly, even on mouse/keyboard. Controller support is present but still being finalized as of launch. While I would generally prefer to play a game like this on a controller I was surprised by how well the M+K controls work once I moved a couple buttons around. For comparison, it at least felt better than how I remember DS1 playing on M+K. I will probably switch once support is fully up and running but for now it works well. I've had a few minor bugs that add a little spice to the experience but were easily resolvable. The inventory screen froze once, and a mini-boss didn't reset progress after I died, that sort of thing. Truth be told I'm not even 100% sure that last one *was* a bug in and of itself. Either way it actually made it easier to kill since damage carried over from attempt to attempt, but I figure it's worth pointing out.Ok, with the rough spots out of the way lets get to the real meat. The environment work is frankly incredible, both in terms of aesthetics and mechanical level design. The sense of exploration and slowly piecing together info about the world tend to be huge draws for me, both in Soulslikes and games in general. And while it's understandable why so many other entries in the genre tend to focus more primarily on combat, it does leave me occasionally a little disappointed that the setting and lore doesn't always get the same care. But the Omnistructure's atmosphere is immediate and *thick*. The strange blend of decaying fantasy, sci-fi horror, and brutalist megastructure is exactly my kind of jam and seeing it so well realized is thrilling. Draping that over the clever layout of side-passages, secrets, and shortcuts make the world a joy to peel apart. It's possibly as close as anyone has come to the Blame! rpg I've always wanted, while still very much establishing it's own identity.The mechanics might not be the main highlight for me but make no mistake, I do love how it plays so far. There's some strong enemy variety and a simple timing-based combo system akin to the first Witcher adds a neat little wrinkle to the usual stamina-based combat. Character progression is gear based over a 'souls'/XP system, both in new loot and eventually upgrades as well as perk unlocks. This means nothing is lost on death other than resetting to a checkpoint, which definitely softens the blow from any misjudged jumps or combat encounters gone wrong. While it's a little early for me to say how this affects the overall balance or build variation, even in just the starting area it does a good job rewarding exploration and my character has already made solid progress from where they started.The comparison I kept coming back to as I played was that it almost feels like Bleak Faith is to Soulslikes as what something like STALKER is to open-world shooters. To be clear, Bleak Faith hasn't been nearly as outright *unstable* as STALKER can be. But for all their comparative roughness and eccentricities there's a real magic to the worlds they depict and the way you interact with them. Nowhere else I've been in a game *feels* quite like this, and I want to go back the moment I hit exit.Some people are going to bounce off it, which is fair. If you prioritize combat above all else in games like this you may want to wait and see what it looks like post patches. But if you can get on the same wavelength of atmospheric exploration there's really something truly special here. And once a bit of inbound polish lands it'll shine all the brighter.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like souls-likes such as Mortal Shell, you'll love this game!The art direction, world design, and sound track are all easily the strongest points of this game. The developers certainly had a vision, and they really delivered on it. This game has some very impressive and good-looking vistas, and they manage to impress even through this game's predominantly brown and gray color palette.The gameplay is alright. Not the best I've ever experienced in the souls-like genre, but I'd say it feels fairly fun and engaging, with a few exceptions.The loot/itemization, and gameplay systems are all decent, and present perhaps the biggest twist to souls-like games.The game's weakest quality: it lacks polish. This game is an indie, and it shows. Decent amount of jankiness, and a handful of bugs. The devs are hard at work as I type this fixing the bugs with frequent patches, which is nice to see, but the buggy experience and lack of polish certainly stop this from being anywhere close to a 10/10 in my book.I'm enjoying the game greatly though, and think the bugs can be overlooked. Would recommend you pick this up if you're tapped out on Elden Ring, and Wo Long Fallen Dynasty, and looking for a good 3D-action RPG. It's easily worth its price tag in total game time.

_childDocuments_.review: Is the game buggy? Yes.Is it playable? Yes.Let's be honest, I've only played 1.5h at the time of publishing this review, and the game was released today. AAA has bugs in D1, so what did you expect?The developers said the game was optimized for M+KB, and that they were working on the controller. Is the game worth it? For me, it is. The atmosphere is incredible, and knowing that the team is only three people makes the game even more impressive. So, yes, I recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: As the game is right now, I cannot in good conscience recommend it until it has gotten some serious bugfixes and tweaks. As an avid soulslike enthusiast, I embraced this game with open arms, but after having played it more, I have stumbled upon more and more issues in regards to enemy AI, pacing, controls and overall feel of the entire game leaves a lot to be desired.There is a lack of polish in almost every facet of this game, be it UI, animations, collision detection and graphical glitches (spawning in without the floor not having rendered, and falling to your death or memory leak type of stutter that can happen randomly and don't go away until the game is restarted).I applaud the dev team for their passion project, there is certainly a charm to this title with its vast open interconnected (albeit pretty empty) world, but I question the legitimacy of the price tag attached to the product they have released.Furthermore, it seems that there are animations copied directly from other popular games in the genre, which doesn’t instill confidence in me.I may have wasted my money on this, and I am to blame for it, as I pushed onwards in hopes of finding the good parts of the game, but for now it seems bleak (pun intended).I will try to push on for a bit more, but as it stands this is not a finished product that can compete in this price range, not even close! Mortal Shell and Hellpoint are examples of good entries in the genre, Bleak faith – Forsaken hasn’t convinced me yet.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really sad that I can't like this game. Halfway through writing this, something occured to me. This game would be fantastic if it was not aiming to be a souls-likeI've had my eye on Bleak Faith for a while now for the same reason as others; the art style and world design.Whilst at first glance these aspects are fantastic. Even after the numerous patches so far, I'm not sure this game will ever feel finished. The lack of controller support makes the game almost unplayable for any souls-like veteran. Yes the basic funtion is there but for the souls like genre, you need responsiveness and reliability, which are not present.Little things ruin the experience for me, like how your block button does nothing unless you have your weapon drawn, and how you can't switch targets with the right stick.As per recommendation by the developers, I tried MnK. Sadly, as anyone who has experienced or researched the souls like style in any detail, this input method just doesn't work with all of the things you have to worry about.I think it's great that the asset thing is being sorted out but to be honest I could've looked past that if I had got to experience the world. If this was simply an adventure game without the strong emphasis on difficulty and combat, this would have been a great experience on MnK.I really hope the devs keep working on this for the sake of all those who are sticking with the game. I really hope in a years time I can change this review to a recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: So far its like a sci-fi/medieval souls-like. I have had my eye on this since they announced it years ago. Ive been waiting for the game to be stable, functional and drop in price a bit. Since the last patch alot of people were saying that it was THE patch. So I bought it. So far I am very impressed. The world is dark and interesting and I like to read the little notes about the lore and i feel compelled to keep pushing forward to see the environments and maybe learn some answers. The mechanics are a mix of dark souls and dragons dogma/shadow of the colossus which is a cool combo. There is a bit of a learning curve but now i feel im getting the hang of it. Some enemies are very grotesque and disturbing, which i really like. There are a bit more robo enemies than i thought but they are still pretty creepy which is cool. There are alot of weapons and armor combos and i love the "weight" in combat. it feels good to hit enemies and when you kill them there is force applied to their corpses. Also you can chop their limbs off and i think more souls games should look into that. The world is pretty massive. You can climb some skyscrapers to the top, or swim deep below the water. Theres not much in those areas but its still cool and it adds to the magnitude of the world. Im only 2 main bosses in so I may add more when I finish the game.
