_childDocuments_.review: For starters, I returned the game for now. I was hooked when I watched the trailer. For a newer game I know there are always prone to be glitches or bugs found. I really wanted to give it a chance though since it just launched. I love soul based games - even though this one isn't soul based (from what I saw starting out). The graphics are killer though. I can't wait to see this game improve itself and become a success. I know it will release later this year on the other consoles. I hope at that point I'll be able to enjoy it again. I do like the "concept" of the game. I would say give it a chance once the bugs are patched. I didn't enjoy the "dodge" in the game play. It was tricky and/or buggy. When pressed the character didn't move or dodge out of the way... like most games would. Sometimes my weapon wouldn't switch to the other and I had issues with it registering my attack button. For now its a no. Like I said...can't wait to see where it goes and maybe be able to play it again.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Faith: Forsaken

_childDocuments_.review: At first I was about to leave this game a positive review to balance out the negative ones, because I thought the game wasn't THAT bad. The graphics are very good, the game is very atmospheric, and the combat has a nice rhythm to it when you figure it out...But then I walked for a good 20 minutes without seeing any enemies, only to realize I found myself out of bounds. I didn't clip through any walls, I didn't make fancy jumps, I just walked. And soon enough I had somehow traveled below the map, ultimately falling infinitely after accidentally walking off  the edge of the world. I just wanted to find a second boss to fight for crying out loud.I have no clue where to go, and I have to CONSTANTLY think if I'm currently out of bounds, or on a path to new content. Everything looks the same, above and below the map. The level design is convoluted too, it's constantly looping back on itself, and I have spent the 2 hours of playing just looping the same areas over and over again.

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's really hard to do a review for the game.  But I try.  Positive:- The atmosphere is unique and well implemented.  - The soundtrack is incredibly great.  I've rarely heard anything so appropriate to the mood.  - The designs of the worlds, enemies and locations are very creative and integrate well into the world.  Negatives: - The combat system is very spongy and clunky.  - I have the feeling that some sounds are missing.  For example, the character doesn't feel like it makes any noise when running.  Conclusion: I think if the developers improve and patch a few things, it could be a great Souls-like.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Faith: Forsaken

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to give this game a chance. Reading other reviews I was certain I would still be able to enjoy the game. Unfortunately, there is an underwater world where you have to follow lights all the way down to a cool looking alternate dimension, but I could not get there for a second time. I say second time because I played this game on my friends account at his house and was able to solve the puzzle within a few tries. I bought the game enthusiastic about how different it felt and wanted to beat the game. But when I got to this puzzle, the game kept making me die at the red lamps as if I was losing oxygen even though I was right next to them. I'm sure there are many other bugs like this that just dont let you continue with the game. That's unfortunate because I really gave this game an chance with an optimistic mindset but it is just bugged beyond repair. Maybe I will reinstall 6 months down the line when the game is polished enough to play.

_childDocuments_.review: One hell of an Indie game.  There are issues with controls on a controller and a few bugs here or there such as falling through the floor of an elevator or hits not registering with certain weapons and the movement does feel a bit icy.  But with that said, it's an indie game and that is taken into account for me.  Hoping that with continued patches the game will continue to blossom.The universe in the game is phenomenal and beautifully dark.  I enjoy games in the dark souls genre that don't hold your hand and combat can be both aggravating and celebratory which is exactly what this game delivers.  In my first moments of the game I was struggling with the enemies.  However, once I acquired more gear and learned more of the game mechanics I got a sense of accomplishment as the enemies seemed easier, for now.  And as with any dark souls type game gravity is the most formidable foe!For me, I will continue to play this game and look forward to whatever updates/patches come out as I work my way through to completion.  Normally I don't leave reviews but with the hype of this game due to the outstanding trailers, the overwhelming number of negative reviews about poor controller mechanics on a PC game and the few bugs here or there on an Indie game I wanted to give a different perspective, my perspective.  Is it a top notch $60 game made by a company with a huge budget and a large staff? No, so to judge it or expect as such I feel is unfair.  This game is an Indie game (which normally I don't play Indie games due to most of them lack captivating story, game play, decent graphics, etc. to me) and for that I applaud the developer team and look forward to the patches as more people play and give their feedback of things that need to be fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 1 is a big part of my childhood and I honestly can’t objectively review the game. This is only a review of this remaster, and I am somewhat lukewarm about it. It is a great way to experience Final Fantasy for the first time, it takes some of the QoL improvements from later versions like being able to buy items in bulk, adding more items like high potion, price adjustments for items, and faster leveling with a higher level cap. The remaster also has the original magic system where you can cast so many spells for different spell levels instead of a single MP pool. This is a defining aspect of FF1 and one I am happy to see restored although the inclusion of ethers is a bit of a disappointment considering how cheap they are. The big omission is the bonus dungeons from the GBA/PSP remake which I am torn on. On one hand, they gave players items that unbalanced gameplay and made the final dungeon and boss trivial, but it would have been nice to see some sort of extra post-game content, maybe something other than randomized dungeons with bosses from other Final Fantasy games. Still, this is a $10 budget title so I get why they didn’t spend the time and money rewriting the DoS dungeons that weren’t that great anyway.Graphics: whether or not you prefer the new pixel art is up to you. Personally I like the way characters look, especially after the class change occurs. I always thought the advanced versions of characters had tiny heads. What I don’t like is the way certain effects are pixelated. This remaster should have had all new hand made pixel redesigns for everything but with many spell effects or status ailment markers it looks like they use 3D acceleration that they display at a low resolution to simulate pixel art. It gets pretty distracting at times. Why not just have two frames of green bubbles floating over the characters’ heads to denote poison?Music: There are some good remixes in this remaster. The main battle theme, Final Fantasy (the song that plays when you cross the bridge north of Cornelia), and Mayota’s theme are standouts. But others don’t have the energy they should. The last dungeon’s music doesn’t feel epic. The boss fight music sounds like the orchestra is bored. Maybe I’m used to the original chip tunes where you couldn’t play a note softly if you wanted to but some of these tunes ruin the moment. The music in the original volcano was so wild and intense and this version just doesn’t have the same oomph.I don’t think this is a bad version of the game at all, in fact I will recommend it to new players. But if you adore the extra DoS dungeons I don’t think I can recommend it over the PSP version, and their exclusion shouldn’t be too surprising since this is a budget title made to require less maintenance on the ever changing mobile market than the ports that already existed there. I will probably play through this a few more times and  a couple of years when I want to revisit it for the hundredth time, I’ll fire up the PSX version on hard mode as that’s still my favorite. But if you’re a new player or you love the art style and the music, this version is perfectly fine.

_childDocuments_.review: Of all the Pixel Remasters, this is probably the safest and easiest recommendation to make. It's not without its changes or version differences, but the simplicity means it is practically as good as other versions but now it's on PC instead of dead consoles.For the record, I still prefer the GBA  release. However, the only thing the Pixel Remaster is truly lacking are the bonus dungeons which, in all honesty, aren't as worth it as some might think. Now, if this was a Final Fantasy  review, I couldn't say that, but it's not.The sprites are clean, the backgrounds look amazing, and the music sounds terrific. Like the original NES version it uses the Spell Charges based on Dungeons & Dragons, which is what the game was heavily inspired by, but it actually uses a different base for the enemy and boss stats. I'm not sure  one they're based on, but it's certainly not the original game because the bosses had more health. It's not the old mobile edition, either, because in that one bosses took hardly any damage from magic yet that's not a problem here!This means the game plays smoothly, and you have a good selection of play styles to go with since there's six classes but only 4 party slots. The old joke "Four White Mages" that the players guide suggested may  be viable in this version, but you're more than welcome to try! If you look around you might find some interesting challenge guides like the "Solo Red Mage". It's worth noting that the Red Mage is the  job that does not change stat growth when transitioning to the Red Wizard later on. Personally, I found this far more doable on the GBA version which had an MP pool and really miss that.That is one of the issues I have with Final Fantasy 1, whether you use Spell Charges or MP pools will change the feel of the game, and I certainly think the former is more difficult to balance out and requires more planning. The latter would have been a nice option to include just for people who wanted to use it instead. Final Fantasy classic has been released a number of times and some options would have been nice. Besides the magic system, my other gripe is that the bestiary is only accessible on the title screen. There's really no reason for this, and other versions have had it in the menu. You also cannot  the menu. The RGB sliders for the windows are gone, which is a loss.Still, it's a splendid, if dated, game. There's barely any story so you're just there for the sake of the gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent remaster of FF1! The game and UI feel good to play even when playing on PC while using a controller. Everything looks clean and the pixel-style graphics don't look out of place even at 1080p. You can tell that the Pixel Remaster team focused on removing all the clunkiness that previously released FF tiles on Steam have experienced (FF13/FF3 3D Remake).In terms of completion, this is the shortest game in the entire franchise. Makes a lot of sense considering it's the first in both name and spirit. The story is also very simple but allows players a glimpse of the recurring "maintaining world balance" theme in the early numbered titles (the theme of crystals and etc).FF PR is nearly the perfect game for any JRPG enjoyer who is craving a classic and wants to dive deeper into the franchise and the genre. The one downside is that for someone who may come from a modern gaming background, the lack of a sort item feature in a remastered version may seem odd. Regardless, the game is short and simple, the type of game you can finish over the weekend, but does not cut corners when it comes to important elements like the UI and a good OST. The price is absolutely fair for what you get and I urge first-time players to possibly give this one a go before you progressively consume/enjoy FF1-4.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played every version of Final Fantasy 1 and this is definitely one of if not the best version of it.Easily accessible, fair price, the sprites look great, and the game play is very close to the NES with modern day convinces.If you have never played FF1 I highly recommend trying out this version of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Game Time: 8HRs - 100% achievement completion.Final Fantasy 1 brings me back to my childhood with a Game Boy Advance when I was around 7 yrs old. There's nothing wrong with this game, and even when searching for the Tyrannosaur (for the bestiary achievement) for 65 minutes (finding the Warmech actually only took me about 5 minutes!), I didn't mind. The minimap is a great addition, I love the way they've kept the game looking pixelated (unlike the ios and android releases), and I like the old magic system (no MP, but spell slots instead).The only bad thing about this release is the lack of the four optional dungeons that were added from Dawn of Souls onward. _childDocuments_.review: December 18th, 1987 – that’s the day  was released on the Famicom. And now, 35 years later, the name “Final Fantasy” is synonymous with one of the biggest videogame franchises worldwide, spanning more than fifteen numbered mainline entries and an overwhelming number of spin-offs. It’s safe to say that everyone somewhat familiar with videogames has heard of Final Fantasy – hell, the protagonist of , Lightning, was even  back in 2016!Anyhow, it’s safe to say that  was pretty successful considering what it caused afterwards – but does the game itself still hold up today? As part of the 35th anniversary of the franchise, publisher Square Enix re-released  as part of a “Pixel Remaster” collection – giving the old games a fresh coat of paint with updated pixel graphics and a newly arranged soundtrack while still staying faithful to the originals.In the case of this particular “Pixel Remaster” of , a few gameplay changes are also included. I’ll refer to the  for a detailed summary of the version differences but the most important additions include the ability to (quick-)save anywhere, statistics for found/missed treasure chests, (mini)maps for the overworld & dungeons as well as an Auto-Battle option. All these changes are greatly welcome additions in my opinion, as they remove some possible frustrations such as repeatedly entering the same battle orders. And even purists should be pleased, as all these additions are entirely optional and can be ignored/turned off if you don’t want to use them.However, with all these welcome additions, it’s a shame that the “Pixel Remaster” of  omits content that was added in previous re-releases of the original game, such as the four bonus dungeons added in the GBA release. On the one hand, I can understand these omissions as the “Pixel Remasters” are supposed to stay as faithful to the original games as possible. On the other hand, if the missing bonus content could be turned on and off via toggle, it would allow players to choose between staying faithful and getting more content. The font used in this new version of  has also been quite divisive, though this can be changed With these additions and omissions detailed now, let’s move on to talk about how the “Pixel Remaster” of  actually plays. And to be honest, I was quite surprised how well it still holds up – as long as you keep your expectations in check.Even with the fresh coat of paint, the Pixel Remaster of  is – at its core – still 35 years old. There’s no huge, suspenseful plot – a few dialogue boxes and a few “cutscenes” (lifted from the PS1 re-release of the original) is all you get. Save the kingdom/world, you chosen heroes, you know how it is. If you want to play  for the story, you might as well just read a short Wikipedia plot summary and you’ll see how little there is – but again, this is a game from 1987. As for the gameplay, it also offers what you’re probably expecting.  is a turn based JRPG with a party of four custom heroes of different jobs, ranging from mages to thieves to warriors. As part of the main story, you’ll travel to different dungeons via an overworld, fight monsters in random encounters, level up, obtain loot or open treasure chests, restock and gear up in different towns by visiting shops. It’s the basic concept that’s still the backbone of many JRPGs, just more … “simple”. There are no side quests, there’s no fast travel, no gear upgrading, no character moments, no inventory management, no crafting and so on.That said, even when  obviously can’t offer what todays JRPGs are able to, there’s no denying that a more basic JRPG experience like one still has a certain charm to it. You might’ve already forgotten most of it just days after playing through  but the game in its straightforwardness also offers an extremely smooth experience. Once you’ve accepted the limitations of a game from its time,  just works without a hitch – for the most part. It offers a really nice flow, allowing you to easily clear dungeon after dungeon with no unnecessary intermissions and detours. Especially as modern JRPGs that can be overloaded with different systems & mechanics, overly complicated plotlines and 30-minute cutscenes, it’s just nice to “take a break” with a straightforward 14h affair like .That said, there are still two things I want to mention.For one, I wouldn’t recommend  as an entry-point to the genre for people unfamiliar with (J)RPGs. That might seem odd at first, considering how a more “basic” game like  should usually makes for a great introductory experience. But while  might offer fewer systems/mechanics than (more) modern experiences with their complexity, it’s important to note that  offers no tutorial whatsoever. That’s completely ordinary for a game of its time but newcomers to the genre might feel lost or overwhelmed as a consequence. If you’ve got no previous experience with (J)RPGs, I’d recommend choosing a modern (J)RPG with a decent, thorough tutorial instead.Another reason for this would be the difficulty curve of . For the most part, experienced players will find  to be quite an easy game. If you know how to gear up properly, open up a few treasure chests and invest in the right spells, you’ll just breeze through the game. That is, unless you encounter one of two exceptions, which are part of the reason why I wouldn’t recommend  to everyone.First,  uses a random encounter system. And especially in the beginning of the game, with your party just starting out, some bad encounter luck can immediately lead to the party’s demise. Just minutes after starting the game, just walking to the first dungeon after setting up my party, a particularly unfavorable group of enemies completely obliterated my heroes with little to do against it. A quick reload and the rest of the beginning went off without a hitch but for people with less experience, the beginning hours of   might prove quite frustrating.The second difficulty spike would be the final boss of the game, who is quite more difficult than previous bosses you encountered. Not only does he hit hard without some defensive spells in place, in this Pixel Remaster he’s also got a 2% chance each turn to replenish half of his total health. That’s why unprepared parties hoping to encounter the credits soon might be in for a bad surprise, I personally thought I was doing well in the final dungeon until the final boss taught me otherwise – requiring me to reload and engage in even more final preparations.To conclude, I’d say that the “Pixel Remaster” of  is a great version of a game that’s not for everyone. I appreciate the modern gameplay additions as well as the updated graphics & music - but can only recommend this game to those, who are fine with leaving a lot of modern JRPG developments behind - if just for a few hours.

_childDocuments_.review: It's important to remember that this game was a hail-mary project in 1987.  There's not a lot here, even for Final Fantasy fans.  At this point, the only elements that carried over to future installments are a handful of monsters, the plot device of Crystals, Warriors of Light, and uh... CHAOS?  Most of the game is a fairly linear journey from one locked door to the next.  These locked doors are dressed up in various ways; sometimes it's a bridge that needs repairing, other times it's a boulder in front of a cave, but either way, the point is the same.  There's a dungeon somewhere that has the key, so you'll need to fight through the dungeon and get the key to progress.  Unlike Zelda dungeons, there are rarely if ever puzzles here, only winding pathways meant to confuse you and wear you down through random encounters.  Fortunately, this version of the game scales fairly well, so as long as you fight every fight, and gear yourself as well as you can, you shouldn't have any trouble fighting through everything this game throws at you.It bears mentioning that this game has been modernized from it's original design.  Unlike the original, mages do not have D&D-inspired "spell slots" but classic FF MP.  The presentation and music likewise has been vastly improved over the originals.  Diehard fans unwilling to compromise on these elements might be disappointed, but more open-minded fans or players new to the series will most likely be grateful that the play experience has been smoothed out.  Overall, it's not hard to get through this game, so I recommend it for those interested in the series' origins.  It's an interested baseline to compare future installments against, but it should surprise no one that it has been bested countless times in the decades since its original release.

_childDocuments_.review: 3/5What on earth?I have to wonder if those bragging on the 'graphics' of this remaster actually played the original NES version of Final Fantasy?I read a bunch of reviews and decided to take the $12 plunge, even though I have free emulators which I still tinker around with.Pixel takes their name seriously, because the very first thing I was greeted with in-game was pixels.  Very . . . large pixels?!This game looks like it was drawn in MS Paint by a 10 year old.  At least in emulators, you can adjust the pixelation and have a smooth appearance, and on the original NES the image looks fine blown up on a large modern screen.I just can't get past the pixels.  Everything is blocky.  The only optimization I could find was toggling between 'Classic View' and 'New View,' but the only difference is the Classic view added lines around the screen which made the appearance blurry instead of blocky--neither of which is comfortable to look at.  The visual quality is terrible.If you can get past the extremely pixelated and headache inducing screenplay, at least the other improvements are nice.I strongly support the jumping avatars when reviewing weapons, armor and spells in shops as in later versions of Final Fantasy, and that has been implemented.I am happy with the stacking of items and reduced prices.  The dashing and diagonal walking features are good improvements.I also enjoy that stronger mobs were appearing in the beginner areas.The resolution options are great--if only they fixed the issues I have with the extremely pronounced pixelations.The sound is really nice, although not being able to skip through some cut scenes is annoying.Keyboard binding options are limited because you cannot bind directionals to your arrow keys (I ended up using the number pad instead).Auto combat is OK to have in some cases.It is nice to have multiple save slots and longer character names.I just cannot see myself hurting my eyes to watch the screen for hours staring at either awful blocks or a blurry game screen.  I own and have played and conquered every original Final Fantasy console game on each system in the series--even the original Gameboy.  So you can imagine my disappointment here.At this point, I will probably stick to my free emulators of the original NES Final Fantasy rather than this remaster due to the visual inferiority.What a bummer.  :(

_childDocuments_.review: How do you recommend Final Fantasy 1 in the modern day? I mean, you don't. If you don't like old JRPGs, this isn't for you. Some old JRPGs force you to grind because they're difficult; FF1 does by being a long, pretty repetitive game about managing resources. The grind is the game. If you don't like JRPGs, and want to play a Pixel Remaster (but why though?), honestly wait for FFVI.If you've never played Final Fantasy 1 and like old JRPGs, though, this is in my mind the definitive version. Dawn of Souls for GBA and PSP is *probably* a strictly better videogame, but this game does a better job of capturing the feeling of playing Final Fantasy 1. Rather than trying to take an old, crusty game and make it a good, modern (for the mid 2000's) game, this remaster tries to capture the feeling of playing Final Fantasy 1 for the first time in the early 90's. In that respect, it succeeds totally and utterly. The remixed soundtrack sounds like we imagined it back then. The new graphics look like what we thought things looked like back then. It rules. This is the version you want. Don't try to play a "good" version of Final Fantasy. Play a faithful one, to appreciate where the series went.If you've played Final Fantasy before, this is a bit of a harder sell. The remixes are all excellent. Probably worth it for that alone (I bought the bundle because I know FF6 is going to have remix of Kids Run Through the City that'll make me cry). Unless you're a weirdo, you probably don't need to play FF1 again. Go play Dragon Quest 3, which is this game but good. This is the crustiest Final Fantasy, the one that predated the most of DQ3/4 and FF2/3's innovations. It has little personality and little strategy. The rebalances here are nice, and make the game more playable than ever, and the remixes might be worth it on their own, but buddy, you don't need to replay FF1. Skip to FF2, which you've not beaten in the first place, and appreciate Akitoshi Kawazu's *systems*.If you don't fit any of those groups, sure, play FF1. Why not? Maybe you'll feel happier.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: I'm old enough to have played the original as a teen, but I didn't have an NES, and despite my enjoyment of Bard's Tale on my old C-64, I sort of lost my taste for turn-based combat after Zelda came out on the SNES.  But now I'm 50 and getting 'cultured', and I can't think of a better way to learn my gaming history than through these Pixel Remasters.The good:The remastered music is really the biggest draw here. Nobuo Uemitsu's themes are iconic at this point, and the orchestral versions here are simply rousing.Great quality of life improvements like maps.The combat is a simple turn-based affair, but it's fun and if you're used to playing RPGMaker games, you'll certainly feel right at home.Colorful graphics. Just the right amount of remaster, imho, while still retaining a lot of the original charm.Not frustratingly difficult.The meh:FF is all about those random encounters that constantly interrupt your progress. Yes, you know what you're getting into with a FF game, but this is still an acquired taste.I finished this in about 23 hours, and I think it could've been a tad shorter. But your mileage may vary.The bad:Knowing where to go for the next step in your quest is unnecessarily cryptic. Many, many times I never would've figured out where to go next if it hadn't been for an online walkthrough. I'd recommend: The story is just barely there, and your characters are not given any personality or back story. NPCs are there just there to provide one line of cryptic dialog.The twist ending is barely comprehensible and muddied my enjoyment of what little story there was.Verdict: So should you play this in 2022? Well, I enjoyed my 20 or so hours, and I'm looking forward to tackling all the early games in the series now. But do not be afraid of getting help from the Internet.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a big Final Fantasy fan, having started with 7 on the PS1 in the late 90s. I own several versions of Final Fantasy 1, but I never got around to finishing it. Being able to play on the Steam Deck, with quality of life additions such as quick saves and auto battles, made the game feel much more accessible, and its dungeons much less stressful. The game takes place on the world map from the very beginning, with progression tied to obtaining items and transport types to venture further afield. The updated graphics look fantastic. Nobuo Uematsu's music is second to none and brings the world to life. Combat is fairly undefined in comparison to later additions in the series. The majority of the well known magic and status effects are there, but, for the most part, you can get through the game with standard physical attacks. There are no missable achievements. Collectibles (chests and bestiary entries) are easy to track. A couple of the rng based monster spawns may prove a little time-consuming. All in all, it's a fun and easy 100%. I would recommend this version of the game to anyone who is new to the Final Fantasy series, hasn't played this entry, or simply wants to go back to relive it.

_childDocuments_.review: Square Enix has succeeded in presenting the "definitive edition" of the original Final Fantasy. The 16-bit-style graphics look great while remaining very faithful to the 8-bit original. The orchestral audio is a treat. The quality-of-life adjustments such as auto-battle and maps are wonderful. Unlike the old mobile remake (PSP, Android, and iOS), which was way too easy, this "remaster" finds the happy medium between it and the intense, antiquated grinding of the NES. It also maintains the original "Vancian" spell slot system of the original (but with the option to purchase Ethers that restore one spell slot per level). This combined with the higher difficulty level shows that this version takes much more inspiration from the NES original than the old mobile remake. I would unequivocally recommend this version to any newcomer, and I would no longer recommend the old remake at all. Truly this is a masterclass in how to deliver a remake.

_childDocuments_.review: For a classic RPG, I think this version holds up well. The mixture of elements from the original NES version, with the bug fixes, stat tweaks to the classes, and  QoL changes that came with the ports afterwards make this one of the best versions of Final Fantasy I. It might not be what people would consider the "definitive" version (I believe that title goes to the GBA version), but the extra content that isn't featured isn't really a deal breaker here. Things I did like:* Auto battle is a freakin' godsend. It doubles the speed and repeats the last action used. This makes grinding more tolerable.* Quick save is basically a single "save anywhere" slot. Unlike other versions where they make you quit the game and erase it when you load it. This can be very helpful when you're deep in a dungeon* The game also saves a check point every time you change scenes on the map, which is nice when you get a game over* A lot of the strategies you might find on the internet still work.Though for a list of things that did annoy me a little:* Random encounters are frequent. You barely get 5 seconds in before the next one. * While auto battle is nice, the fact that it performs the last action done can make it a double edged sword* That one dungeon is still that one dungeon.

_childDocuments_.review: A classic from old ages remastered for a new era. For the first time on PC, it's the original Final Fantasy. Even if it doesn't include the extra content from the GBA and PSP ports, the idea of these ports is to recreate an experience for the modern age. I have played the GBA version, and I can say that I like some QoL features introduced in this port:- Forced encounters are now represented as NPCs or monster-in-a-box chests (this one is from the FF games from 2 onwards).- Experience levels are adjusted so the leveling process goes faster, therefore, the game is on the easy side for the most part.- The spell system goes back to the spell charge system from the original and PS1 version. You would think that maybe this would make spell usage impractical, but I see this as a welcoming change, as you have to think on when to use the spells sparingly. Of course there's items that can cast spells, which can alleviate this problem, allowing you to save the MP for the bosses.- New to this version is also the auto battle system, which makes battles faster, you can even set actions to do with auto battle in order to clear battles even quicker.The graphics are nice-looking. It's not 3D or anything, but I like how it looks. The music, dear gosh, the music... it has been rearranged for this version, and it sounds really great. Only one song I kind of say "meh" is the airship one, but if that's the only song that was the black spot on an otherwise great soundtrack, that says something.Overall, I'm quite pleased with this version of Final Fantasy. I recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like no review is perfect without coming at this from three perspectives:1. Played the OG and all the remakes: This is the bucket I fall into, and I can say that there's never going to be a time when I don't want the Final Fantasy games updated to later platforms. Now that this game (along with the rest of the collection) is on Steam, it's really nice to know that I might not have to buy yet another copy of this game. I've been through iteration after iteration of this game, and honestly, I'd say this one is the second best (falling short to the PSP remake simply for portability if you are without a Steamdeck, like me). Where this game shines is not only its beautiful pixel art, but the fact that you can mod this to play it how YOU want to play it. Whatever makes you the happiest with your experience, the modding community has you covered and more. If this is your fifth or sixth time picking this up, I can tell you that you aren't missing much from other iterations save for a new look and a new score. At this point, it's more just about the support of games being done in this fashion (looking at you, Breath of Fire/Capcom), instead of being lost on the older consoles.2. Played only the remakes: You've probably got the least to gain from this game, because most of what's been added has been in the previous games, and in some instances, you're not getting all of the extras that were put into other games (like the extra dungeons in Dawn of Souls). Unless you are an avid fan, a collector, or simply want this in a Steam format, you can probably skip this iteration.3. Brand new to this game/the franchise/JRPGs: First of all, welcome! Coming into old Final Fantasy (or old JRPGs in general) can be challenging sometimes, even when they are updated a bit for the later consoles. That being said, I do think there's value in trying out the game that really started it all, and this is a really good iteration of the first game without having to pay a fortune for second hand versions of the other iterations. You have access to mods, potential portability if you are playing on the Steamdeck, and a copy on Steam which would mean not having to chase down a new copy due to an outdated console. There are a lot of benefits for you in this category, so I would encourage you to scoop this up when you can.And that, as they say, is that.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 1987 is an incredibly important game to me, as is Final Fantasy I & II: Dawn of Souls. This is not those games. In bringing FF1 to a modern audience, Square Enix has neutered any and all of the grit you could find in earlier versions of this game. Now I know that many of these options can be turned off, but as they are presented as "opt out", they feel like part of the core experience of this release. I'm talking about always-on maps, battle speed-up, and the ability to turn encounters off. I never touched the XP scaling or full heal options. I know that Final Fantasy usually isn't about difficulty, but I prefer it when it comes with some tension. I felt that in FF'87 and in Dawn of Souls.Difficulty aside, the presentation here (the main selling point of the Pixel Remasters) is an incohesive mess. Different pisel sizes between map assets and player sprites, HD textured spell effects, strangely low-detailed characters sprites, I could go on. They're clearly going for that "NES+" look while totally forgetting what both the NES and SNES looked like. This is an improvement over the mobile port of VI, but what was so wrong with the Dawn of Souls sprites? those are beautiful 16-bit renderings of the NES games that inject more character into the world, yet still feel like the original game. The look of the PIxel Remasters is excusable for the NES games, but I can't believe how bad the SNES games look. We'll see if I get that far in my playthrough of the classic games. It's still an enjoyable game, but this is pretty far from what I'd call a faithful remaster. 3/5

_childDocuments_.review: The game that started the series, now with a fresh coat of paint and some quality of life changes.Take control of a party of 4 and select the roles for them. Choose between:- The Fighter. A tanky warrior who can take a hit and dish them out.- The Black Belt. Hits harder than a Fighter, all with fists that are rated E for Everyone.- The Thief. Stab them with daggars and small swords with faster speeds.- The White Mage. The healer. Casts Holy magics to protect the party and harm the undead.- The Black Mage. Can't take a hit, but can definitely hurt large groups of enemies with Fire, Lightning and Ice spells.- The Red Mage. The Jack-of-all-trades. Can wield both Black and White magics, and slice your enemies as well.And go rescue a princess, and find your team on a quest to save the world from certain doom.This is the first in the series that can be a little archaic at times. Thankfully, the remastered version of this game has addressed alot of the issues that would make the game more enjoyable, including the ability to save your game whenever you want.The ability to pick and choose how your team is composed of can help add in its replayability. Go for a traditional run and then switch it up to see if you can make it through with 4 white mages or go for an all Black Mage run and see how fast you can just murder the enemy before they murder you.This game was enjoyable to me as a kid back when I first played it on the GameBoy Advanced. And it still is just as good today. Give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't bad considering what it is and where it came from. While there were times that i did enjoy the game, the lack of any major plot, the complete guessing game for the latter half of the game of where to go and what to do (I had to use a guide), made it frustrating. There isn't anyone telling you where to go, what to do next, how to go about it, etc. Most of that you get a vague idea from the NPCs around the towns, but a lot of it is trial and error. Trial and error would not be an issue, if the game did not throw you into a random encounter every 10-15 steps. I had to have spent half my game time in random encounters. It got absolutely ridiculous how many there are. Yes, FF is known for grinding/random encounters, but good lord. Cutting the encounters in half could easily reduce your in-game time by half as well, just to give you an idea. There are achievements for killing 100, 300, 500, etc monsters, and I got the 500 monster achievement in the first few hours.On the issue of grinding/random encounters - the game has terrible balancing issues. I easily defeated 95% of random encounters and never fled(which is almost useless), got to the final boss around level 46(apparently average was 30 on some forums??), and he was still incredibly difficult. Some bosses of the game you can step on like its a joke, and then struggle on others. You may run across 5 random enemies that all cast Thunder on you, and completely wipe your team, and then go 100 encounters barely taking 10 damage, just to kill a major boss before you even buff your entire team.Status effects do not end after battles, you need max healing items/status effect potions to constantly heal after battle, they have not introduced the MP system yet so you only get so many uses with magic and then have to spam ether potions to get mana back.The entire story line can be summarized in a few sentences, the characters are no named, do not continue into later entries, and completely forgettable(literally)Recently, FF origins was released and is essentially a retelling/re imagine of this entry since the main character of that game is a major character in this game. It also reuses the same locations, etc.If you're bored and want a throwback, then go ahead. The game is only $12 so you'll definitely get your money's worth. However, you won't miss anything if you do not play this game, and the series only improved in later entries.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, hearkened on the first adventure once more after some time taken to truly experience the game as if it's brand new again. It amazes me, and stuns me to say "No wonder this saved the series." Truly for a story written in the time it was you really do take in every dialogue as best as you can. Don't get me wrong of course for a game that is aged also comes with how short it was, but to still be able to envelope almost 15 and a half hours of playtime just tells you how easily this game captures and ensnares you. All it takes is getting past the one major flaw which wasn't even a flaw back in the day, the grind. Unfortunately, unlike the console port releases of these Pixel Remasters it did not come with the Boost Menu. I will say that is good and a bad thing. The reason it's good is that it forces you to play the game quite legit without any XP boost or Gil boost. It's a bad thing because for those out there who want to experience the game and story but at a faster pace then without the presence of mods you just have to bear and grin it.If I could make a recommendation, if a developer reads this review please look into maybe adding that menu into these ports as I'm sure people would love to have it present other than that to those thinking about buying this and playing the classics I highly recommend it and rate Final Fantasy a 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I won't lie, a part of me wants to use the word 'generic' when it comes to a good portion of this game, but then it clicks with me that this game is quite literally where a lot of the aspects we consider to be 'generic' were popularized. The story is straight forward, big evil Chaos, warriors of light, get the crystals, save the world. It's nothing we haven't seen dozens of times over at this point, yet despite all of this, I found an obscene amount of charm playing through this game. I once tried playing through the original back on the NES but gave up due to how cryptic everything felt. The Pixel Remaster does take a few strides in remedying this, making the whole experience feel a lot more streamlined and straight forward.I really appreciate this entry into the series, though clearly there are a number of balancing issues and what not, it's truly worth a play through in my opinion. The music is so iconic that, even though I never really put time into the franchise before, I get a whiff of nostalgia the moment I hear the victory theme or the menu music. I currently have a goal of completing the entire Final Fantasy franchise on Steam while obtaining every achievement possible and this entry took me just over 22 hours while taking it nice and slow. Final Fantasy 1 gets two thumbs up from me!

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:-Incredible remastered soundtrack-Gorgeous new sprite work-Some welcome QoL improvements to smooth things out a bitCONS:-Default font is too small (There's an easy fix for this online), and doesn't fit the visual style-Dualsense controller support requires third-party apps like DS4WindowsOTHER:-This is a full remaster of the original NES/Famicom version, so don't expect the bonus content added in the GBA release. This didn't bother me at all personally, but for some people it may be a dealbreaker.-Some well-known grinding spots (Peninsula of Power for example) have been removed. This is another one that may or may not be an issue depending on who you are.The original Final Fantasy has been re-released many times over the years, but in my personal opinion this is the definitive experience. This is a beautiful remaster of the NES/Famicom original release, with great new spritework that looks akin to the SNES releases (with some extra effects here and there) and an absolutely incredible reworked soundtrack. Since it's the first entry in the series, it's pretty simple overall. However, I feel that in the modern day this kind of adds to its charm. Everything is very basic and straightforward, nothing too complicated or hard to figure out. This IS based on the original release of the game, so there is NO additional content that was added in the GBA release. For me this wasn't a problem, but I know a lot of people swear by that version of the game so if that's an issue for you, be aware of it before you buy. I'd say if you're just looking for some retro JRPG comfort food though, this is a pretty good choice. One thing I will note though is that the default font is really bad. It's far too small for any resolution and its style doesn't match the rest of the game around it. There's a way to fix it, which can be easily found online, but it shouldn't have to be that way. If you like to use your Dualsense controller for PC gaming, you'll need to use DS4Windows to get it working with this game as it only supports Dualshock 4 and Xbox controllers for now. Hopefully Square Enix addresses these minor issues and puts out official fixes, but if not you'll just have to do a tiny bit of legwork yourself. Either way, this is a perfectly fine game and should be in the collection of any JRPG lover.

_childDocuments_.review: This is really all there is to it. A prophecy of four warriors setting out to vanquish the source of darkness by reclaiming the four elemental crystals from the Fiends corrupting them. Unlike later entries, which may also be similarly lightweight in their story, regrettably FFI also does not spare a lot of time in its worldbuilding, for example, by introducing flavor dialogue to the NPCs inhabitating the various towns around the world.Instead, virtually all dialogue in the game is meant to nudge players towards the various dungeons and tasks they have to accomplish to proceed. From a gameplay perspective, this is a very interesting design choice, as the game can be fairly confusing due to this structure but therefore also rewards actually exploring and talking and, frankly, interacting with the world, as barren as it may be. Regrettably, none of this plays into the hands of its storytelling, and ultimately FFI is a nice glimpse into the very framework that will shape many of its later entries but can’t well be recommended for it on its own.As the first entry in the Final Fantasy franchise, it is to no surprise that it also features the most rudimentary combat system. No ATB gauge, no job system—or at least not in any sense that the series would define later on. Instead, it is a very strictly turn-based RPG in which the player chooses from six basic classes to create a party of their own four Warriors of Light.This is also where the first issues arise as the different classes are very unbalanced between one another, with a more deciding factor of which is better than the next being how much you are willing to grind for money to keep them all up-to-par. Any martial job (Thief and Monk), for example, ends up almost strictly inferior to the Warrior. Magic classes, on the other hand, are more situational altogether and also are not limited by Mana, like in later games. Instead, FFI features limited spell slots akin to its Dungeons & Dragons inspiration.Amplifying these issues is that the game is utterly trivial with arguably only one or two exceptions if you remain noticeably underleveled—which is likewise difficult to accomplish given the fairly high encounter rate. Often you don’t get to take more than a handful of steps before getting tossed into combat with up to nine enemies, which can be a pretty grueling slog in and of itself.Lastly, the dungeon design is also unimpressive. Of course, there aren’t many gimmicks or puzzles; this isn’t expected, but there also isn’t a lot of structure to the game either. Each dungeon is just a little larger than it needs to be, all to make it labyrinthine rather than interesting to navigate. This becomes even more obvious at the abundance of simply totally empty rooms and dead ends, and if you are lucky and run into a chest, it will most likely contain both enemies and total garbage. For example, even the very penultimate dungeon has a chest that contains nothing but the very clothes you start the game with, or a potion that heals maybe a tenth of your total HP by that point.It’s useless, unrewarding, and sadly, a relic of a time when dungeons were designed to be played as a marathon to endure rather than to be necessarily fun. And I’m sure it added to the sense of adventure back when the game was released—at the detriment of FFI,'modern’ JRPGs, or frankly even starting as early as FFIII, have the luxury of providing both.I will not stop praising the Pixel Remasters for the amazing job they do in improving the presentation of these games. FFI is almost four decades old by now, and while a remake like this can only do so much while staying faithful to the original experience, it is thoroughly impressive as to how decent FFI can look all things considered.As per usual, enemy sprites, spell effects, and the overworld design have improved the most. Iconic bosses like the Marilith look distinct, and even more so if you played peripheral Final Fantasy I content such as the amazing .As with the other Pixel Remasters, FFI also offers an immediately accessible Gallery of Concept Art, although this one is noticeably more anemic than other titles and only features a handful of art pieces for you to browse. The soundtrack, while overall good, is also a little lackluster. Again, not in its quality, but rather in its quantity and in the range of tones it covers. There really is only one flavor of song, rather than a broad range—which speaks volumes about how the game doesn’t very much feature even a story that would warrant a more varied soundtrack.None. FFI ran perfectly well, and unlike the other Pixel Remaster I played, it also never locked up after combat. I also did not encounter any other miscellaneous issues, bugs, glitches, or otherwise.Final Fantasy I isn’t bad by any means; if the goal is to archive the original experience and to make it more accessible to hop-in, experience, and tourist a little, and then to move on—then I think this remake is impeccable. However, that also doesn’t make it fun to play and neither worth recommending it for the average person. It is simply not enjoyable anymore due to the total lack of storytelling of any kind nor any engaging mechanics to sink your teeth into barring, maybe, the idea of challenge runs, which seem to indeed be fairly popular with Final Fantasy I in particular. I had an okay time with it, going into it with just that aforementioned expectation of a bit of an archaic game—just to see where it all originated from. Anyone that thoroughly wants to have a video game alongside a timecapsule is likely better off looking to games such as the aforementioned  which, while it isn’t exactly a remake of FFI, reinterprets the story and at the very least makes an attempt of recontextualizing a narrative experience out of the skeleton of the original FFI.

_childDocuments_.review: This was the third version of this game I have played. It's not the best version but still a good game. I had issues with the screen going white and freezing. I had the game completely restart my PC as well. I lost a lot of progress from this. Save every where all the time. Save yourself the headache. Visually the game looks great! The attack spells really pop. The hardest part of this game is figuring out where to go next. I confess I had to look up where to go. I never had a single death until lvl 35. Around 50 I had 2 more. Before 60 I had a fourth death. Most deaths can be attributed Instant kills. That you simply cannot survive. The fienďs are largely overrated. While they look great, they are simple no challenge to defeat. Harder to find them, than fight them. This led me to believe I was ready to fight Chaos and beat the game. I fought Chaos at lvl 62. This was a mistake. I would normally lvl all characters to lvl 99 before finishing the game. I was led to believe that Chaos wouldn't be a challenge so I fought him early. I was recked. While I did win the fight it was crazy hard. Harder than everything else in the game! Chaos was killing a character every three rounds. I spent so much time rezzing people. He could kill any character with a single punch. Not to mention he was just soaking all the flares I hit him with. Lol I had 28 hours in the game at completion. Would I recommend this title for other people? Yes! I couldn't beat this game as a kid but as an adult I get to remember my love for the series and actually finish the game. I tried out an XBox 360 controller around the final push for the Chaos shrine. It was fantastic! I wish I had used it for the whole game. Worth the money. Lots of nostalgia. A Good Buy!

_childDocuments_.review: Having never played FF1 I was not sure what to expect. The game is fairly basic compared to modern RPGs - I still enjoyed it though.It was interesting to see the beginning of the Final Fantasy series. Seeing enemies from the 3D games in their first iterations; item names and such are pretty much exactly the same as in the 'modern' games - which was cool to see first hand.I think the game being relatively short actually works well for it. I had originally planned to play it through without looking at any guides. However as the game goes on, it gets increasingly difficult to know where to go and what to do next. I suppose most RPGs of the time were like this. There's usually one NPC in a random town that will give you a hint about what you need to do to progress. I think looking briefly at a guide when this happens is better than going to back to talk to every single NPC in the game. At least it was for me, as it kept my frustrations in check.The battles themselves weren't too tough - I only wiped once. You can have unlimited save slots when on the world map, but you also get one "quick save slot" to use whenever you're not in battle. Which I thought had a good balance to it. You can speed up battles also, which helps clear trash mobs quickly. The story was pretty basic, and character development wasn't a thing. The fun I think was in exploring and trying to build a team of 4 heroes who can kick monster butt. I'm looking forward to playing FF2!

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun dungeons-and-dragons adventure game from the 80s.  I've heard about this series before and was excited to try it out, and the first game did not disappoint.  The story was well-written, you grow slowly but surely along your journey, and it is all around just fun to adventure through the caves and see what treasure awaits you in each area.  It occurred to me early on that gameplay reminded me of the Pokemon games, but the first games of that series didn't come out until almost a decade later, meaning that those games likely took multiple gameplay elements from this game when creating it.  I didn't enjoy looking for one of the insanely elusive beasts for full completion, but when I got it, it felt like an accomplishment, so I can't be mad.  All in all, a fantastic game, and I really look forward to checking out the rest of the series.  9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: 100% in sub 12 hours if you turn off encounters occasionally.I would keep your expectations in check and go in with the mindset of just experiencing how the series started. _childDocuments_.review: This review was written entirely by AI !Ah, Final Fantasy I, the OG of the fantasy gaming world! It's like stepping into a time machine back to the pixelated era when knights were just blocks with swords, and magic was just a colorful explosion of squares. If you ever wondered what your parents played in their childhood, well, here's your answer!First things first, character creation. You've got four brave heroes to choose from – a Fighter, a Thief, a Black Belt, and a White Mage. It's like assembling a D-list Avengers team. "Fear not, evil-doers! We have a guy in pajamas who can punch you to submission, and a sneaky guy who can probably pickpocket your lunch money."But don't worry, each character comes with their unique set of skills. The Fighter swings his sword like a boss, the Thief... well, steals stuff (what a surprise!), and the Black Belt is a master of martial arts. Then there's the White Mage – the magical healer of the group. But honestly, they must've gotten their medical degree from the "School of Band-Aids and Cure Potions" because it takes forever for them to patch up the squad!The combat system is a classic turn-based affair. Picture this: a bunch of enemies on one side, your ragtag team of adventurers on the other. It's like a playground brawl, but instead of using fists, you throw spells and weapons at each other. "I cast FIRE!" cue a tiny puff of smoke – Wow, that was intimidating!Oh, and let's not forget the infamous targeting system. Your heroes must have gone to the "Oblivious Archery Academy" because they love targeting thin air. You point at an enemy, and they're like, "Nah, I feel like hitting that empty space over there. More challenging, you know?" Perhaps they got inspired by a blindfolded dart-throwing contest.And how can we not talk about the fantastic plot? Cue dramatic music – "The world is shrouded in darkness, evil forces are rising, and you, four nameless adventurers, are destined to save the day!" Yes, because nothing says epic quest like having absolutely no backstory or motivation. It's like being handed a butter knife and being told to slay a dragon.But you know what? Despite the outdated graphics, the clunky mechanics, and the story that feels like a product of a mad lib, Final Fantasy I has a charm that's hard to resist. It's like watching a black-and-white movie – sure, it's old-fashioned, but it's a piece of gaming history!So, gather your quirky team of not-so-superheroes, brace yourself for nonsensical combat, and dive headfirst into the fantasy realm of yesteryears. Final Fantasy I: Where it all began, and where you'll realize that sometimes, the journey is more about laughter and nostalgia than saving the world. Happy adventuring, pixelated warriors!

_childDocuments_.review: Well what can I say about this game that hasn't been said before.Basically it is exactly what the description says. It's a 16 bit remaster redo of the original Final Fantasy. It is a bit easier than I remember the NES version being, but not by much. They kept the original magic system, which is good as I remember playing the GBA version of this and they took it away which made it so much easier too. The magic system was part of the strategy of the original and despite what some people might say, I never thought it was unbalanced.I picked it up early to get the discount, wallpapers, and soundtrack items. You only really get 2 different wallpapers but you get 4 versions of each for different resolutions which can be nice. The soundtrack was a bit disappointing as it only contains 3 tracks and I was hoping that it would be the full soundtrack. It is nice to have those three though, and for less than $10 for all of these items I can't complain too much. To find the wallpaper and music right click on the game in your library, and navigate and click "view local files". They'll be in the folder under extras. I expect that the extras for Final Fantasy 2 are similar to this one, but I"m not sure yet. I do plan on getting it as well before the sale ends as I want the extra stuff and discount.All in all this is a decent port and I recommend it for both veterans and newbies a like.

_childDocuments_.review: A fine remaster of a timeless classic. Final Fantasy is a "best of" kind of remake. It most closely resembles the NES classic, but it's taken a lot from modern design to make it more approachable. For instance, saving anywhere, auto-saves, ect. The leveling system is more similar to newer versions, but it retains the "charge" based magic system, where you have finite MP for each spell rank. The jobs retain a similar balance to the newer revisions. It winds up being relatively easy, however. The leveling system made the progression a little wonky. In FF1's original version, the max level is 50. This version changes it to 100, and as a result seems to suffer from early parts of the game being far easier than they were in the original, especially the first few dungeons. Visually, it's gorgeous. The original artwork from the NES version is redrawn, all based on Yoshitaka Amano's beautiful artwork. The spell effects are nice and appropriately flashy for the time, and status effects and the like are all clearly presented. The only issue that you might have with the visuals is the font that is used in the English version. This is easily fixed via a minor adjustment to the files of the game, but personally I didn't mind the font all that much. The audio work is very good as well. Excellent arrangements of the entire OST, and decent sound effects. Overall, I recommend this game. It's a simple and short JRPG. After all, it was the very first in a series that continues to this day, so it should be taken in a similar manner to how people approach going back to Super Mario Bros, a timeless classic. I completed it with every achievement in around 12 hours, 2 of those were hunting for WarMECH. Happy hunting, and may you walk in the light of the crystal.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Will always love the series and nostalgia. While the Pixel Remasters aren’t perfect, they’re certainly the best and most convenient ways to play these classic games. Especially on the SteamDeck. The soundtracks are lovingly orchestrated and the pixel art is gorgeous, though the latter does lose some detail in the translation.Now…onto the next one. FF II. 😁

_childDocuments_.review: FF 1/16I am going through all the FF games. As the first game in the series, it holds up very well in terms of its gameplay - this is a result of its dungeon-crawling mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: Great remaster of the original. Music is great, QoL enhancements are excellent, and i liked the new sprites just fine. People complain about the fonts but I honestly had no issues with it, I had to look up comparisons to the stock font and the workaround japanese font to see the difference they were talking about, but it wasn't anything too noticeable to gripe about to me.Things that could be better are display issues like no vsync and having lines through the game when exploring. Also had issues where it always started the game in windowed mode even though it was set to fullscreen, which meant i had to swap to windowed mode and then back to fullscreen everytime i started up the game, which also reset the game whenever you swapped the display option. _childDocuments_.review: First things first, I never played these classic final fantasy games back in the day, so my perspective is one free of nostalgia and I'm simply judging these as they are with some consideration for when they originally came out.Final Fantasy feels, by modern day standards at least, sort of like a demo or prototype for an indie RPG that wants more funding. It's incredibly shallow, in basically every way. This game is kinda interesting because it feels like the pure distilled essence of what a JRPG is, which makes sense. That distillation does mean this game feels like the bare minimum in every category. The story is laughably simple, the 4 elements of nature have crystals, and these crystals have bad guys next to them that make bad things happen. Go to the 4 crystals and kill the bad guys next to them. Something something chaos, The End. Something kinda neat is the fact that you can pick the classes of your party, so you have some choice there, but once you decide the game is pretty braindead up until the final boss, who is a MASSIVE difficulty spike. I had a Warrior/Ninja/RedMage/BlackMage party and reached the final boss at level 41 with no difficulty up to that point. I had to grind up to level 60 to have a chance at beating the final boss. Not interesting, his damage and HP was just too high. The gameplay is pretty barebones, just spells and attacks, but most classes should only do one or the other. Black magic feels horribly weak in this game, I basically had only 3 party members for all intents and purposes since magic never did more damage than my warrior hitting them with his sword. Oh yeah, and this game feels like it shares a lot of DNA with DnD for some reason, lot's of monsters just lifted from DnD and some weapons too. The game even uses spell slots like DnD does, not a fan, yet another reason magic sucks in this game.As far as the remaster thing goes, the music is great, and the sprite-work is fine (I think it's better in the other games). This game is pretty important as it lays the foundation for what a JRPG is, and just the fact that these games are playable in a convenient state on PC and not rotting on an NES cart is good. Overall, if your curious like I was, or just want to replay a game from your childhood, this is pretty much exactly how you would want to experience it. So even though I think the actual game is pretty lame in all honesty, it's getting a thumbs up from me considering the quality of the remaster and its significance in video game history.

_childDocuments_.review: The definitive version of the first Final Fantasy.Not just 'definitive version on PC.' Not just 'definitive re-release.'If you are going to play Final Fantasy 1 once in your entire life... this is the version it should be.All the bugs of the NES version? Fixed. Int works and powers up your magic now. All the spells function as intended. Weapons with attack bonuses against certain monsters? Working.The visuals? Great renditions of many of the sprites we've seen since the WonderSwan, but plenty of brand-new work and solid updates as well, with some of the best looking 2D water I've seen in a game. Castles stand out on the world map when you're flying in the airship. The Master looks like Johnny Bravo wearing a leotard. Top notch.The gameplay? It's your classic turn-based Final Fantasy, but there are plenty of tweaks under the hood to make this version stand out. White and black mages have a good amount more physical oomph to their melee attacks than they used to, the re-vamped magic system makes lower-level magic still worth using even late game, the ready availability of status-removing items is welcome given that enemies seem to be more prone to dealing such effects in combat, and the soft extension of the level cap means that there's no more reason to worry about short-changing yourself if you get around to the class change late. Combine that with the ability to track treasure locations on the world map, the MUCH improved bestiary, maps *in dungeons,* and even full access to the soundtrack and concept art galleries?If you're a fan of Final Fantasy, you're doing yourself a disservice NOT playing this version. If you're a first-timer, it's still the best current experience of the title.

It's not a big deal to me because no one is forcing you to use them if you want the extra challenge. _childDocuments_.review: Amazing rendition of the NES version of the game. A lot of quirky mathematical bugs present in the original version have been fixed and now all the spells and abilities work as intended. It's not exactly a 1:1 version of the NES edition because it has all the quality of life additions from the GBA version of the game added except none of the bonus dungeons from GBA or PSP.This is a bare bones NES version of the game, characters auto-target the next enemy in line instead of missing, Red Wizards can now learn Exit and Teleport (previously couldn't on the NES version). Chaos boasts 20,000 HP instead of 2000 and can no longer flee the fight if you're too over leveled. The level cap has been raised from 50 to 99 as well so you'll need to compensate from the NES version by doubling your levels for any specific area... You needed to be on level 27 - 30 to easily take out Chaos in the original version, you need to be somewhere around 60 now.Magic can now be replenished with newly added Ethers as well, which makes the game a lot more casual. The ship puzzle game is also included still, as well as all the original cryptic secrets such as pressing select and B to bring up the map screen (except this is now integrated in to the hot keys on your controller)The sprite art in this version takes a while to get used to as it's the original NES sprite art with a face lift. It seems weird at first but it grew on me over time. I've accepted it now but the PSP version is still the superior remake of the game.Great game, fun to play and with all the numerous resources available, quite easily mastered at this stage in it's life. It's an amazing nostalgia trip down memory lane!

_childDocuments_.review: Ethical considerations of recharging people for the same game repeatedly aside, since I really don't mind given the clear amount of love poured into these remasters, speaking generally. This is the granddaddy of them all, and as such I recommend it whole-heartedly for nostalgic and preservationist value alone. The Uematsu-overseen new music arrangements are downright astonishing and rich, making the game truly enjoyable to play and savor. Somewhat tedious dungeons are entirely saved by a soundtrack that frequently slaps.The other extras are worth their weight in gold. It's too bad the included soundtrack DLC is only select tracks, but they are nonetheless of superb quality. The game does have an in-game music player with every track unlocked from the start, so if you purchased on Android or iOs you could theoretically have the soundtracks to go. And the bestiary provides a helpful guide for tracking down where your missing monsters may be. The design documents might be my favorite extra though. Much like the original Mega Man documents from Capcom's lovely remasters, it's a delight to take a walk through the original artwork and being able to recognize the creative work done to translate the evocative and impressive character designs into their pixelized incarnation.These games are surely some solid jewels in the crown for Square-Enix and there's never been a better time to kill Chaos. Go see what all the fuss is about.

_childDocuments_.review: FF1 on NES is amazing for the following reasons:1) The first 2 chapters are hardcore. Once you get pass the bridge, if you don't grind a little before fighting the pirates, you're gonna Game Over. If you don't stock up on Antidotes before entering your first dungeon filled with poisonous enemies, you're gonna Game Over.  If you don't actually buy Potions and Phoenix Downs cause you can't rely entirely on White Magic spells due to their limited use, YOU'RE GONNA GAME OVER!  I mean, if you find FF4 and FF6 too easy, then FF1 is gonna be a challenge.2) Once you get passed Chapter 2, grinded, learned lots of good spells, the game actually becomes easier! Much easier! _childDocuments_.review: I never grew up with Final Fantasy, JRPG's, or really any various Japanese media in general in the way a lot of people from my generation did. I was influenced primarily by Western RPGs and CRPGs. As an adult, I've become obsessed with Tabletop RPGs (something which directly influenced Final Fantasy and RPGs in general).All of that changed when I played Final Fantasy XIV and dove in so thoroughly in that world that it's since become my favorite game of all time and the game I have the most playtime in by far. So since then, I've always wanted to explore more of the genre and games that are part of the legacy that game shares in.I will play through each game in order of release and endeavor to complete them so far as my patience and earnest attempts will allow, and as I do so I will document my thoughts through these reviews.This is my Journey.Being a game originally from 1987, the story and dialogue of this game is incredibly bare bones and mostly serves to provide the minimum amount of context and clues to motivate the player to explore the world, delve dungeons, and fight monsters. It is very classic fantasy through and through, which is both very endearing and a little boring by modern standards. But what it does very well is give you the feeling of going on a true, classic fantasy adventure of your own, like a minimalist D&D campaign. Compared to the lofty precedents the series is known for, this is a stark difference, but I'm certain that it was game changing at the time.This is where the differences between the original game as it was designed to be played and how the game plays now due to the changes and conveniences offered by the Pixel Remaster make the two experiences almost like playing entirely different games. From my understanding, the original game was very much an old school dungeon crawler where managing resources and time was incredibly important. Saving was restricted to resting in town or outside of dungeons, and there were no convenient maps to track exploration so dungeons felt much more labyrinthine and dangerous. With the ability to save wherever, scout the map for directions, and now even turn encounters on or off entirely at will, the game is largely undemanding to play in a way that I think probably takes a lot of the identity of the game away.That said, I'm honestly not really sure I would have bothered to complete the game without those conveniences. The gameplay is simple and dated, and there's very little narrative to be motivated by or interesting mechanics or challenges to invest into. The difficulty of the original game seems more trying on your patience than actually fun beyond the first hour or two, so I see why they changed it.Still, I wish there were more options to customize the convenience features of this game, or a classic mode you can start a new game in that gives you an experience closer to the original in more ways than statistics like I know some mods do.As the game is now with these conveniences, barring the last boss of the game, it's largely a game you just go through the motions with. That said, it's strangely satisfying to go into the trance the game puts you in of constant little adventures that don't ask too much of you. There's always something new to see or do, even if that stuff is largely surface level or aesthetic.It wasn't until I went and played an emulated version of the original game, as well as various similar updated ports of classic JPRGs such as Dragon Quest that I realized just how much of a true upgrade this is both visually and in terms of usability. The presentation is colorful, smooth, and very appealing. It has a particular aesthetic that it mostly sticks to and overall I'm very happy with it and excited that all of the classic 2D games have gotten this treatment.Also it goes without saying, but the music and sound is delightful and even though you hear a lot of the same few tracks over and over the entire time, it strangely never really gets old.This game is definitely simple and dated, but surprisingly less so than you might expect due to its age. It's a bit overly safe with conveniences that really muddy the identity of the design of the original game, but those conveniences are arguably necessary to make the experience more palatable to play all these years later. Overall, I'm very glad I completed the game and am very much looking forward to taking this momentum into the rest of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: See where a genre-defining series began!While the story & overall gameplay feels outdated compared to where Final Fantasy is at now, FF1 is a nice, simple, fun game where you can switch off your brain a bit and just enjoy the sprite work, grind away as you work towards stopping Garland, the game has some nice Quality of Life changes, such as Quick saving, which the O.G didn't, which helps to remove some of the annoyance.If your a fan of Final Fantasy and don't mind the downgrade in systems, this is totally worth playing, IMO, best done as a "buffer" RPG between some longer games.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic little trip down nostalgia lane. This is where the Final Fantasy series started. Albeit a bit spruced up and lots of bug fixes. The original NES release had many statuses and spells that flat out didn't work or do anything.If you're looking for a simple turn-based pixel sprite jrpg to play or have an itch for a little nostalgia trip, this is most certainly an excellent way to play the game.With a few fan mods such as swapping out the font, colored icons, darker ui, etc... this game really shines and looks fabulous.Give it a whirl, and don't let those claiming this is FF1-easymode fool you. They're just wearing rose-tinted nostalgia goggles and misremembering the original to be tougher than it actually was. The only thing that made it seem tougher was the grind required, bugs for many spells that didn't work, and a small inventory that required better item management.
