_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: The original Final Fantasy for the NES was a success for good reason, and this aesthetically pleasing update is a great way to experience it.As with the original, you can have the fun of choosing and naming your own four-character adventuring party, and arming them with weapons and spells. The geographic scope of the explore-able world expands at a nicely measured pace, and large dungeons call for careful management of resources.The Pixel Remaster fixes the original's bugs, so formerly useless enhancement spells become highly useful. The Remaster also accelerates leveling up and makes items easier to afford, so this version is light on grind. If anything, it overcompensates: by halfway into the game you may already have more money than you have use for it. The party will reach milestones at a higher EXP level in the Remaster than in the original, and can go beyond Level 50. This leads regular battles to skew a little too easy; the game's quick pace and auto-battle feature reduce the tedium of the easier battles. Fights against the Four Fiends and the final boss remain challenging. My first playthrough took about 17 hours.The Pixel Remaster faithfully updates the original game's characters and monsters to a Final-Fantasy-V-like visual standard. The world looks great, too; the sea has a bit of extra shine, and the graphical upgrades enhance each town's and dungeon's unique style.The original Final Fantasy was never big on characterization and didn't need to be. The Remaster doesn't overhaul the story; it adds only a few brief cut scenes. Most of its writing changes are in NPCs' regular lines. The Remaster lends them a more conversational style and a bit of personality. A few NPCs give additional hints to help heroes in case they've lost track of what to do next.My biggest complaints about the Remaster: the font, and the mini-map. Many have complained about the wimpy, narrow, non-pixel font. I got used to it and it ceased to bother me, but if you want to mod the font, I hear that isn't too hard to do.The mini-map itself is nice to have when you want it. If you don't want it, you can dismiss it with a single button, but the problem is it always comes back, any time you go to a different area or come out of battle. I found no in-game control for making the mini-map  away. (If anyone knows a way to disable the mini-map permanently, I'd welcome a comment!)The Pixel Remaster's sound effects resemble those of the SNES Final Fantasy titles, and so are a good match for the game's visuals. The background music goes beyond this with top-tier production; it's a joy to listen to and (in my opinion) the biggest reason to buy this Pixel Remaster even if you already have another playable version of Final Fantasy. Though there are a couple tracks where I don't agree with the arrangement direction, the soundtrack as a whole is beautifully arranged, especially where it counts most: the overworld theme and the regular battle theme. 11/10, would buy this game just for the music.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: I'm surprised how much I loved this game. The pixel-art and updated music is fantastic. The auto-battle copies your last inputs and helps with the grind. Late in the game I found that using the healing helm as an item meant I could just plow through mobs like they were nothing.  I have two criticism, It's embarrassing for any lo-fi pc game to not have is no easy fix for the screen tearing you get if you run this thing higher than 1920 x 1020, and I wished they'd do is add the extra dungeons from the PS1 remake.  I recommend this game if you've ever been curios about the original game and want something chill to play as you watch Netflix or YouTube.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game was an absolute blast. The gameplay was enjoyable and felt classic. Everything I love about other Final Fantasy games in its original form. The story felt a bit lacking, you can choose the name of the characters in your party and there isn't an option to have the original names (likely because there aren't any or I missed something) and as you travel around you do find some cool stories and details but nothing really amazing. It was still one of the most fun experiences I have had playing a game, makes me wish I had the opportunity to be part of the NES community that got to play it originally. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game growing up, but this FAITHFUL remaster of the original is not worth the money to me. Emulating the GBA or PSP version will provide you with a LOT of bonus content, some even far harder than the endgame. While I appreciate faithful remasters, an option to play the updated version would've been not only ideal, but logical. This remaster, is a lazy cash-grab. "Restarting the game with different class configurations" is not ideal endgame content, nor is it ENDGAME content AT ALL, furthermore we're lacking at least a dozen bosses we could've otherwise challenged. Shinryu? Omega? Legendary challenges, absent. An absence of more compelling artwork, content & challenges, is not how you do a "faithful" remaster. Not worth my money."Final Fantasy I-II Dawn of Souls," IS THE SUPERIOR REMAKE.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I am going to be honest about this. These "remasters" are just lazy attempts at a remaster... they are not truly remasters.. these pixel remasters are just attempts at a quick cash grab. SquareEnix is just preying on people's nostalgia chords and heart strings to get a quick buck. The only thing really different about these "remasters" are they made the sprites a little brighter looking... they added in some cheap magic effects that look like they came right out of RPGMaker... added in 8 directional movement, which is not even needed really.. added in a mini map which helps, but again, not needed... The biggest thing is the fact that they didn't even include ANY of the end game or bonus content (ie, bonus dungeons/bosses/weapons and equipment/new classes) which would have made all the difference. I am not trying to bash and smear these games. I grew up playing these games and loved them, as did most people who enjoy jrpgs. But from what I have gathered, most who bought this game agree with me. And for the prices they are charging for these "remasters".. cmon really SE? Like I said, I'm not trying to persuade others not to buy the game, they are good games, but for a so called "remaster" just no... these are not even what most people consider a remaster. Maybe they could add in the bonus content and people would be happier, but I just feel like this is just a very lazy effort for a quick cash grab. I wont be purchasing anymore of these pixel remasters. I would say, the older versions (SNES, PSP, GBA, or heck even a emulated version) are the far superior versions, especially FF1 Dawn of Souls version, THAT is the best one. I would say wait until these go on sale for maybe 8 bucks or so.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr It's a fine way to experience FF1, but has a few key flaws. Recommended, especially if you want a faithful remake.Well, speaking as someone that's just completed their 8th playthrough of Final Fantasy I over the years, I figured it worth writing a small review from a superfan of the game. Yes, I'm one of those weirdos that adores FF1.This is purely an analysis of the port and what it offers compares to previous outings. For the actual game itself, look elsewhere.The Good•Stellar, brand new remixes of all the music. Fantastic stuff, and arguably the best FF1 has ever sounded.•Probably the most faithful remake of Final Fantasy I ever produced ever since the Wanderswan port.•Technically and mechanically sound- no 30 FPS cap or mobile UI garbage here. The occasional hiccup on more edge cases, but they're patching those.•WarMECH is still a force to be reckoned with, and rare as ever (I got three spawns in two hours)•The Gallery and Music Player features are nice additions for FF1 superfans.•The special effects add new depth- and I'm not speaking about the sprites. They've gone in and added things such as blowing debris in the earth cavern, fog in the marsh dungeon, etc that look REALLY nice and don't clash with the 16-bit art style.•Auto-Battle is a lovely addition, and a smart one too. If you set your casters to continually cast healing spells/items, they will always target the lowest health party member. It also speeds up slightly while auto-battle is active, though not enough in my opinion.The Neutral•It uses the Vancian Magic System from the original. What this means is that magic is on one of eight tiers, and each tier has its own MP pool. This is how FF1 is meant to be played if you ask me- magic is wildly overpowered otherwise. However, if you preferred the MP system of the Dawn of Souls and PSP versions, you may find this a turn off.•It seems to share the re-balancing of the Dawn of Souls ports. Not surprising, but if you were expecting things to be closer to the NES in terms of balance, you won't find that here. Not a negative in my opinion, though not a positive either- bosses are still absurdly squishy barring Chaos himself.•No speed-up option, despite other FF remasters having it- I recommend hooking Cheat Engine to the game and using it to hyperspeed like on an emulator- it's what I did. I've already beat FF1 on a real NES with Four White Mages (it'll never work), I've done my time. Bonus points in that this only speeds up the game itself, not the audio like an emulator would.•Brand new artwork. Many don't like the new sprites, however the included CRT filter isn't a half-step like most- it actually seems to blur the pixels together to simulate a CRT and is very nice. Give it a shot. I will say however that the Job Advancement sprites (Knight, Ninja, Master, Red/Black/White Wizard) look VERY wonky as they're styled after the NES sprites, which already looked bizarre without being SNES-ified.•This is technically a graphical downgrade from the PSP version- from 32-bit, gorgeous sprites to 16-bit. Up to you how you feel about that, but it's worth mentioning that there is a more visually impressive version of the game with more content out there, if less faithful.The Bad•Missing the Dawn of Souls content. No superbosses from FF2-6 and new equipment here. This is very disappointing, as that content was sorely needed in my opinion due to how bare bones FF1 is compared to later entries.•You can't press L+R to run from battles. This makes running away incredibly tedious- you must press right, then down, then confirm for Flee on every single party member, every time you want to run. Square clearly doesn't mind adding quality of life to the Pixel Remasters, as they added Auto-Battle, so this omission is puzzling.•The font is atrocious, but easily fixable by replacing the font files. No downloads required, check the Guides section on Steam to learn how.So this port has a lot of good, and a few key flaws. The missing content really bites- it may have been relatively minor, but in a game like FF1 more bosses were highly appreciated. This isn't a bad way to experience Final Fantasy I, be it your first time or as a return player. However, if you want a faithful take on the original FF1 without the ugliness of the half-functioning NES version, this is probably the best experience out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest, because of the font, I had a very negative impression of Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster (and the others). However, by downloading and replacing the font with "snes-ff6-font", I immediately enjoyed the look and feel of the game a lot more.First off, the gameplay is still fun and holds up for the most part. There were a few times where the game doesn't tell you where you should go next, or they will mention a character's name that you should talk to but they don't tell you what town he is. I wish the Pixel Remaster introduced some waypoints for these situations so the player didn't have to look it up in a walkthrough.It took me about ~12 hours to beat the game. I didn't have to grind that much, but there were instances where I had to retreat from a dungeon to heal in the first half of the game. After my characters were promoted and I got several of the spell items from the Trial Dungeon, the game got significantly easier.The sound and music in the Pixel Remaster is amazing. It's worth the purchase price alone. These are full orchestrated remasters of the original songs, and they are the best versions out of any of the remakes, even the PSP version.I sort of like the PSP sprites better in some cases, however I will say the animation and lighting is at its best in the Pixel Remaster. Water in particular is very standout. The flow of the water animates with much more detail and purpose than it did in the PSP version, and light across the ocean is gorgeous.This version also introduces a lot of new features and bug fixes over the NES version of the game, which makes the Thief/Ninja a lot more viable, among other things. White and Black Mages feel a little weak at first, but luckily there is ethers to replenish spell points without having to go back to town. The auto-battle became really useful later on in the game when you wanted to take advantage of the various spell items, like the Healer Staff (which is very OP item lol).Honestly, other than lack of waypoints, I think this is the perfect version of Final Fantasy to play assuming you are willing to spend a few minutes to replace the font. Square Enix, please just replace the font in the base package so people don't have to... thanks.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh god, this game has not aged well, yet I simply can't not recommend it.Look. It's an NES classic, I get that. But it's also a 1987 RPG. This isn't like games past the mid-90s where grinding was kept to a minimum if not completely unnecessary, and you could do everything your first try. FF1 is a game that expects you to leave a dungeon halfway once it gets too tough and come back to fight another day, because back then, that was how they squeezed playtime out of you to justify the pricetag. Expect to grind, a lot. Also expect to always be short on Gil. For the love of god, USE BOOSTS. Crank Gil and EXP to 2x and turn off random encounters once they get annoying. Maybe you think it's too easy this way, but it makes this the definitive version.On the plus side, the soundtrack is great, the graphics are appealing, and I find many of FF1's quirks fascinating. The limited spellcasting is interesting since it makes you think a bit more, and the fact that you're stuck with a party chosen at the start ends up giving the game a lot of replay value. You can also sequence break, adding even more replay value, and it can actually be to your benefit.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: If you have never played the very first Final Fantasy before, and you are okay with a fresh coat of SNES looking paint, then give this one a try!The music, the pixely heroes, everything has a SNESish feel to it but smoothed out, which I know some people went NUTS about online when the game first came out. Me personally, not to toot my own horn, I played the early Final Fantasies back in the day (I in the 90s, "II" in the late 90s (later called IV as it was meant to be), III in the early 2000s, II in the mid 2000s, V and VI in the mid 2000s), and this is a pretty good port! Reimagining? Whatever you want to call it!I LOVE THAT THEY "FIXED" THE OLD BATTLE SYSTEM!! Let me explain. In the original FF, you would have a group of enemies (up to 9 sometimes), and each party member would target one. If the enemy everyone targeted is slain, the party members who were also poised to attack would have their attacks "miss", It forced you to calculate how many hit points an enemy had, how much damage which character will do blah blah blah, I hated it!! This just warps any attack from a defeated enemy onto the next one in line, making all that calculation a thing of the past! LIKE THIS GAME! HAHAHA! ...sorry, I got carried away.

_childDocuments_.review: Square, now known as Square Enix, has made another remaster of the game that made be a fan of the series, the original NES version of Final Fantasy. Known as the “Pixel Remaster” and released on Android as well as Steam, this was made as an attempt to recapture the feeling of the original game. I’m here to do a deep dive on this remaster and ask one single question: Was this even necessary? It’s great to see the original Final Fantasy released on Steam, but I question if this release was the best method of doing so.Let’s go back to what I said about this being an attempt to recapture the feeling of the original game. This new remaster has taken the core gameplay of the original, without any of the new additions and changes introduced in previous remasters, and gives it a 16 bit era coat of paint. The issue is that those previous additions were all meaningful changes that did nothing but add and improve the original NES game. Let’s start with that new 16 bit look. I will admit, it’s the best feature of this new remaster. That being said, the game had a new look way back on the PS1 remaster, and kept that new look throughout the concurrent remasters on the Wonderswan, Game Boy Advance, Android, and PSP releases. The new look is a bit of a sidestep in my opinion. If you prefer the look of the 16 bit Final Fantasy titles, this new look is a lot closer to that era than the previous look which was more in line with a 32 bit title. However, it’s all aesthetic compared to the other changes.The first change is removing content. Starting with the Game Boy Advance release, we got new dungeons that unlocked as each of the four fiends were defeated. These dungeons were all optional, and gave the player the chance to fight some baddies from later installments in the Final Fantasy franchise to get some unique, and perhaps overpowered, loot. The PSP release got a fifth extra dungeon with more new loot, a wild puzzles, and a superboss at the end. These were all removed in the Pixel remaster. I have to ask myself why these were removed. They were completely optional, the game was totally beatable without traversing these dungeons, but made for a great way to expand the game after beating the main quest or as a new place to grind for new levels and gain new equipment instead of the same old locations. The entrances were all off the beaten path of the main storyline locations and could be ignored by players who weren’t interested or didn’t enjoy the new dungeons. At the least, there could have been an option just to turn the entrances on or off depending on what the player preferred.The second change is the magic system. The original game used a “magic charge” system, similar to the Dungeons and Dragons tabletop game. In this magic charge system, there are 8 levels of spells, and each level has a certain number of casts, maxxing out at nine casts per level. Later games changed this to the “magic point” system, where each character has a number of magic points that go up when they level up, and each spell has a magic point cost to cast, going up as the spell increases in power. The magic charge system is great for tabletop RPGs, as there are normally only a few battles and the math is very easy to keep track of. However, there are MANY more battles in Final Fantasy, and you find yourself hoarding your magic charges for fear of running out when you need them. This makes your mages useless in normal battles as they don’t deal a lot of physical damage, but you are wanting to save your magic charges for powerful bosses or those moments where you face hoards of monsters. You don’t have the problem of keeping track of spell magic points needed and your current magic points, as the game does it for you, unlike in a table top setting.These two changes make the game feel more like a regression than a step forward. I completely understand wanting to bring back the original experience, but there was another, much easier way of doing that. The NES game still exists. Square still owns the rights to it. For those wanting the original experience Square could have easily taken the original game, added controller support for Steam and touch support for mobile players and released it. That would be an even better way for players to get the original experience, as it would be identical. Still…..there is an even better way.Years back, Square did a remaster of this game for the Sony PSP. It was simply an amazing experience. It took the graphical style they used on the PS1 and made all the sprites sharp and crisp, with plenty of details for backgrounds and absolutely stunning magic spell effects when a spell was cast. It included all the bonus dungeons in the GBA release, and than added another as well. The soundtrack was also absolutely stunning, although I will say the Pixel Remaster soundtrack is very well made as well. It was the best way to play the original Final Fantasy. In this case, if Square would have taken the lazy way out and just ported that version of the game to mobile and Steam, we would have a very strong release. Package in the NES original version as a selectable game, and you have the best of both worlds. Square could have even done what 343 studios did with Halo Anniversay Edition, where you could push a button to switch between the original X-Box version and the Anniversay version instantly. It would have been a cool feel to play the remaster, than at the push of a button swap over to the NES version (some coding would need done to swap your current magic points to charges, or to not allow a switch if you were in a bonus dungeon, but this could have been done). For some reason, instead Square decided to rebuild the game entirely, but what they have built just doesn’t compare to previous remasters. It’s a lesser experience, and there’s no reason for it to be a lesser experience, as they quite literally have the best version already made.For players looking to play the original Final Fantasy, if they want to just drop some money and immediately play, the Pixel Remaster works, but the player is losing out on so much more content. I would recommend to instead recommend them to purchase the PSP version of the game, which can be found for around $20. If they need a PSP itself, it can be found for around $40. All PSPs can be hacked with custom firmware, than allowing the game to be ripped and played where ever you wish. There is a great PSP emulator called PPSSPP that runs great on Android, giving you a portable version of this game better than can be found in the Google Play store. This same emulator is on Windows and Linux through Retroarch, allowing you to play there too. This gives you the added benefit of being able to copy your game save from your PC to your phone to continue progress where ever you wish to play. This is a feature that is also not included in the Pixel Remaster, as even if you buy the game on both Steam and Android, there is no way for your game saves to go across between the two games.I love the Final Fantasy franchise, and the original game is great. And the Pixel Remaster is not a bad game by any means. However, there are better ways to play this classic game, better ways released by Square-Enix themselves, and the player is robbing themselves of an amazing experience in the sake of an “original feel” that’s actually not original because of the bumped up graphics. If someone wants to play the game with the original feel, the NES version is available for dirt cheap at around 20 to 30 dollars, and an original NES or a clone NES can be had for as cheap as 20 dollars to around 200 for a Retro AVS system if one wants to play with the best clarity they can get with HDMI output and minimal latency. If they want to play it with all the upgrades, there is the PSP version. This Pixel Remaster stands in a strange middle area that makes it’s version of the game feel unnecessary.

_childDocuments_.review: I did two different playthroughs in the 20 hours I have here. This version of the game is super easy, and very quick. I got 100% in less than 10 hours, most other versions were at least 20 hours. Everything did feel a lot faster, spells, attacks and just battles were less than 30 seconds sometimes. The GBA and PSP games made FF1 easier but the extra content and revamp of the final boss made the balance better. But this game isn't really that well balanced. The early game use to be the hardest part. And I'm happy that there is no grinding required but I didn't feel like I really played the game all that much. Maybe I've played FF1 too many times (We're talking at least 20+) but I didn't really care for this version's difficulty. Other things that are well done is the music, graphics and presentation. The music of the game has carried me through the years and everything here was re-done to perfection. The 16-bit graphics are very gorgeous and I like that they kept everything to the original just with an added coat of paint as it were.I do recommend this version for new players. And for fans of FF1 stay to your favorite version because this probably won't be it, mine is the PS1 version, plays the same as the NES but with a nice coat of paint and actual boss music!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: I've attempted the original version of this game numerous times with no success, but with this remaster and the modern concessions it makes (fast-forwarding combat, an actual map, etc.), you can steamroll your way through in a matter of hours! The graphics are gorgeous, with an upgrade to timeless 16-bit sprites paying off in spades. Kudos to the music department as well for the absolutely beautiful new versions of the classic FF songs! I've seen a few people complain that the final boss is too hard, and he's definitely a massive difficulty spike, but with a lot of patience and cunning, you can sweat it out no problem! Took him down on my first attempt at only Level 55 (Granted, it was a 25-minute fight and things got pretty hairy at times). If you have yet to beat this classic, this remaster is definitely the way to go!

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's never played the original Final Fantasy, this remaster really sparked my interest. This is gaming history right here! The project that started it all. Honestly, I wish there was a "middle of the road" rating, because honestly, I think it's pretty decent, despite the age. However, there's a few things that really drag it down for me.First, the random encounters. There's too many of them. It's particularly irritating when you're traveling by sea or river, and just want to find your next destination. Second, there's the complete lack of any meaningful characters and story. Luckily, Final Fantasy II and III made some good leaps ahead in that department. But here? Things are very dry. The game is driven primarily by fetch quests and backtracking from beginning to end. Now, to give the game some merit, the boss fights are very well done! Nice and challenging, but not too frustrating. And the music is a delight to listen to, particularly the dungeon themes. I know some people aren't a fan of the sprite designs, but I think they look adorable.I wanted to like this game more. Truly, I did. And while I appreciate how it established a solid base, it's just a bit too archaic for me. I'm looking forward to the fourth, fifth, and sixth installments being made available though! I have more experience with them.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful, simple pixel adventure where you get to choose  the type of characters you send into the world. A gem of a RPG that holds up really well for today's standards, if not a little basic. I wouldn't say this is my favorite, but I would say it entertained me enough to seek out and snag all the little achievements. Don't be stingy with the helpful guides, use them! This is coming from someone who would rather go in blind in a modern game than ever risk spoilers. But, older games such as these, while not story heavy, can really get you turned around with the lack of guidance. However, even though this is a remastered title of a game produced in the 80s, I'd say it was well done. The NPC's typically would give some helpful information and unlike The Legend of Zelda, you didn't have to blow up some random rock with zero reasoning to do so other than you felt like it. Speaking of The Legend of Zelda, the first Final Fantasy really gave off those vibes. You start with your group right off the bat and go right into saving a Princess, a Prince, and a whole kingdom, of course. Each "dungeon" was based on an element and you had to defeat the bosses to get what you needed to move forward. I liked the simplicity of it. But, do be warned, it doesn't hold a candle to modern day RPGs with good stories, fleshed out characters and other fun extras. This is strictly "going back to the basics" and there is nothing wrong with that either. I appreciated just being able to name my character, because these days you rarely get to do that anymore. The game ran really well and I must confess, this is one of my first Final Fantasy games (if you don't count FF14). I wanted to start from where it all began and I really enjoyed it. Some of the things I really didn't enjoy: the empty rooms. Like, come on, who puts a bunch of empty rooms in a dungeon to just open up and stare into then walk away? The amount of dead ends were appalling and made me grateful for using a guide. Again, do not be afraid to use that for this game. Back then, you needed a guide book to get through most games without pulling out your hair. There was a bit of a story, but I wouldn't say it was much of anything. If you want to play this game then I suggest you understand it's Turn Based Strategy first and everything else second. Don't go in expecting anything other than a fun JRPG with mindless characters trying to save a kingdom. I do recommend this to most players. Those who want to see the beginning of FF who never played them back in the day. It's fun to see the roots of a series, where it all started. I also recommend this for anyone who is looking for a simple turn based combat that doesn't have a lot of complex systems, and is relatively easy to beat. The soundtrack wasn't bad to listen to either.

_childDocuments_.review: This is where it all began and where it might have just ended. The word "Final" in "Final Fantasy" really meant a Final stretch for Square at the time. This title was either going to be a success or the nearly bankrupt company would be no more. Well we all know how that ended. Final Fantasy is a flagship for Square Enix for decades and this title started it all.To be clear, you're not really getting the original experience with this release. The old pixel art Final Fantasy games have been re-released and re-made so many times by now on various platforms, each making some changes to how the game works, a lot of people have different favorite and are ultimately going to be disappointed when another release does something differently. The original FFI came out on NES and GBA and if you want a real authentic experience, you'd turn to those. The game on NES was significantly harder and it's what any purist really wants to play. My very first experience with FF I was actually on a Java phone back in 2007 or 2008 if you can believe that exists. The pixel remaster series we have here are far from the original feel. So what do we have on our hands anyway?There were no drastic changes to systems, the game feels pretty authetic, you will have an easier time leveling and overall, the game is much easier than its original release, which, to be honest, if you are going into this with the intent to re-live some memories or experience a piece of history in a more laid-back and casual way, is just perfect. It's missing something the PSP version had, which was the ability to save everywhere, here, just like in the original release, you can only save in the overworld, so you best make sure you're prepared before stepping into a dungeon. Pixel art is beautiful and draws from the original sprites found on NES & the soundtrack deserves a praise, original scores rendered beautifully in an orchestral version. Fun fact, when Nobuo Uematsu was originally composing music for these early titles, despite being limited by the hardware, having to make a chiptune/midi music, he always thought of it as orchestral music, which now makes it possible to render the OST that way without having to alter it greatly. No enemies are missing nor been added. Previously mentioned PSP version had a bonus dungeon you could do, featuring bosses from future games for example. That's not here, what was in the original is here and nothing more. Game also features an auto-battle option where your characters will simply repeat the last taken actions, this also speeds up the encounter, this makes traversing the overworld map much less of a 'chore' as you can run into quite a bit of random encounters going from point A to point B, filled up with pretty uneventful battles.The story of the game is told in a simple way, there are no long dialogues or cutscenes, everything is to the point, short and sweet. Given the limitations of the early hardware, it's a miracle they've been able to squeeze a game like this on that tiny storage medium which could go anywhere from 8 kilobytes to just about a megabyte and you have to store everything there... Code, music, sprites. So naturally, you can't expect an overarching story, but it's still a satisfying one.For the completionists, there are some steam achievements and not all of them can be achieved by simply beating the game. If you intend on not using any guides and maps, the most notable ones would be having to fill up your bestiary as the bestiary doesn't really tell you where to look for what you're missing, which will have you spending more times in areas, scouting if there aren't some rare spwans in there. As well as having to open every treasure chest in the game and while there are not any secret rooms or walls to walk through, missing that odd chest in a corner of a dungeon room is pretty easy. Now saying that, this version of the game does feature a map and a minimap, when you open a map in a dungeon, you're presented with a layout of the room you're in and it shows you everything there is, including chests and by the sprite you can tell if it's open or not. If you go the the world map, there's a list of locations that you can scroll through and it sows you how many chests are in each area and how many are open. So that makes it a lot easier to complete. Or you can completely turn off the mini map and just ignore it exists if you chose to do so.Overall, I think this is a satisfying release, not something the hardcore crowd will appreciate due to the game being significantly easier than its original form for many reasons, but something you can casually launch and enjoy to relive a piece of history. Final Fantasy I Pixel Remaster gets my seal of approval.

_childDocuments_.review: Almost all RPG fans have heard of the name “Final Fantasy” and many RPG fans are fans of the Final Fantasy series, but many from the modern gaming community do not know the significance and importance of Final Fantasy’s release. We would, most likely, not have the RPGs we have today without this game. Taking inspiration from Dragon Quest, Wizardry, Ultima, and Dungeons and Dragons; Final Fantasy would be the game to popularize RPG video games on a console and in the west in a time where RPGs were mainly in the PC market globally. Final Fantasy would innovate, and set the standard, for future RPGs to come. It would also continue to do this with its subsequent entries. It was this game that put RPGs in the mainstream and would inspire game developers to make more RPGs. No true RPG fan can dispute the significance of this RPG in the greater RPG landscape we have now.It would be one of the first of console RPGs to be narratively driven, take advantage of all the space of the Famicom and NES cartridges and the hardware of those systems, see a full cast of party members, be strategic in nature, and take advantage of a class system that gave a lot of replayability. It was very ambitious for its time and was a major risk for Square, as they didn’t see the appeal of a game based on RPG elements in a time where Square was in financial trouble and the console video game industry did not deem it profitable until Dragon Quest, or Dragon Warrior in the west, released.This game is a remaster of the Famicom version, not the NES version, with QOL improvements, many bug fixes, updated visuals, and updated music from some of the original development team. This is the definitive way to play the original game with its intended vision, but it is highly suggested to people getting into the series to not start with this game. Surprisingly, this game has stood the test of time and still holds up today. Many in this review section would have you believe that the new fixes and QOL features should not have been included, as it takes away from the original experience. I would disagree because some of these criticisms are based on the NES version rather than the Famicom version, which both have a lot of differences of their own including a lot of censorship. I would also say that this new version gives new players to the game, and the series, greater accessibility. Bugs such as the Peninsula of Power were not intended to be in the game. The progression structure of the game was very deliberate in that the game was supposed to be hard in the very beginning. This would teach the player how to manage their resources, be strategic, and encourage turning back from a dungeon to restock, heal up, and return to the dungeon to continue exploring until they got the key item, or reach the boss, they needed. This in itself would make grinding unnecessary, as grinding in an RPG is considered an indication that the player is not deploying, or lacks, any type of strategy to encounters, commonly known as a “skill issue,” or running away from encounters, which is encouraged in the original game and is a viable strategy. This is quite evident when watching speedrunners play the game or any RPG for that matter. For context, the original Final Fantasy version was considered to be the hardest in the franchise because trying to attack an enemy that was already killed would waste a party member’s turn. This makes realistic sense when we think of two people attacking an enemy at the same time, but a major problem that made the game hard was that some of the spells didn’t work. Final Fantasy is a charming and simple RPG in today’s standards and it is a good remaster to see where the series all started. The updated visuals bring the character models, monster sprites, backgrounds, and locations new life and gives the rest of the games in the pixel remasters an artistic cohesion while still capturing the charm of the original game.The game remains true to its original by going back to the spell slot magic system and staying true to the classic turn-based combat system where strategy and party composition matter for your playstyle. Exploration, as it ever was, remains expansive for players that like to have an adventure with rich and diverse environments in a nonlinear nature. This encourages the player to explore everything, take on new challenges, expand your arsenal, and increase your party's power. No way points that break the immersion, just figuring out where to go next and giving you a true RPG experience that rewards your progression.While the narrative is primitive by modern standards due to the time of its release and compared to later entries, it establishes the foundation for the series’s mastercrafted stories. The soundtrack is as memorable as any other Final Fantasy. The music is something you will never forget and all incredibly redone and modernized while still staying true to the originals.Finally this title comes to Steam and it isn't a bad mobile port. Thank you Square Enix.When the original first released, it was easily a . However, in this modern landscape with the context of its creation in mind, this game is a .Please Square Enix, give us a full Dragon Quest series release on Steam. This will be a series of reviews for each mainline Final Fantasy game. If you are interested in what I have to say about each mainline entry feel free to follow me. I will be replaying each game to completion and then completing and reviewing other critically acclaimed and classic RPGs. This is by no means a retrospective. There are already great Youtube channels that have done that for each mainline title and the series as a whole

_childDocuments_.review: First off, i would like to say that I have been into Final Fantasy since the first day it released on NES.I can't.I can't because I wasn't into Final Fantasy until about 6 months after the first day it released on NES. For those first six months i watched my buddy play it every weekend, while I was more into the Ultimas on NES. So I've been familiar with the game since the first day it released on NES. Yes...I am an old gamer.Since that day until now, I have played many different versions of the first game. Apart from the many years and playthroughs on NES, I've played it on PSX, GBA, PSP, and even on Wonderswan (what a miss that one was...<insert sarcasm here>).  I've gone through all of them at least once except the PSP version...for some reason I couldn't digest that version properly. But I am most familiar with the NES version.This is probably the 2nd best version I have played. It isn't without some weird differences, but most of these differences will not even be noticed or missed. So if you have never played Final Fantasy, this is a good enough place to start.Yes the Peninsula of Power is gone. But it really isn't an issue...because you level up so super fast in this version, you won't even need it. Seriously, my White Mage had the ability to cast level 8 spells by the time I exited the Earth Cave. Obviously I couldn't use level 8 spells at that time, but I had 3 stocked. And because you level up so fast, there isn't much of a challenge compared to the NES version.The silver sword has been removed from Elfland. Not a big deal since the challenge has been lowered.The invisible woman is gone, but I think she has been gone for a while. I think that may have been fixed on the PSX version.The growth is a little wonky. I had a party consisting of a Fighter, Black Belt, White Mage, and Red Mage. Why for most the first half of the game was my Fighter doing less damage than my Red Mage with the same weapon?  Why does my White mage have the 2nd most hp in the group? I have never seen armor drop the absorb on a Black Belt before. And Knights can no longer use white magic (And I assume the same for Ninjas with black magic).Leveling up goes beyond 50 now. I assume to level 99. I only got to 60, because I didn't feel like spending the extra...maybe...30 mins of grinding to get to 99. (Ok it doesn't go that fast, but you are bound to go up about 2 - 3 levels just getting from the first to last level of the final dungeon.)Edit (because I forgot to add this): There are no longer any more monster tiles in front of chests or doors. Instead the monster encounters are in the chests...which is a lot better, and makes more sense. I have forgotten enough times in my life to open the chest before stepping away. (End edit)And I still hate the ice cave and marsh cave. (Note: those aren't different...I just wanted to mention I never liked them.)Even after saying all this, I really like this version, even though the challenge drops. But the challenge felt like it left when the party's attacks could be redirected if their target was killed by another before they attacked. It still feels like a more solid version than the previous remakes (definitely over the wonderswan with its miss rate of like 75%). I actually miss weapon and armor management to give extra spells to characters from the NES version.  And of course thankfully no "ineffective".The first Final Fantasy isn't the strongest in the series...but it is one of the most addictive of the series, due to the many different ways your can set up your party at the beginning. So it is worth the price tag? Yes. i think so. And I can even see myself playing this more than the NES version now. The NES version will always have a lot of memories for me....but it is time to make new memories.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to recommend this game, but I can't.  I've played almost every version of FF1, from the original NES to the PSP version, and this game is just...a complete game with missing parts.   Spoiler warnings ahead!They removed some of the charm of what made Final Fantasy 1 what it is. They removed the Peninsula of Power, something that survived 34+ years of games and has become a staple in FF1.  They removed the Path of Giants, and replaced it with 2 NPCs that trigger a battle if you talk to them. They removed spiked monster tiles and replaced them with either monster-in-a-box or just got rid of them altogether. The pixel graphics are a great throwback. The music is spectacular. Everything is here, except...everything they took away for some reason. They released a game that is worse than every other version before it in terms of gameplay. The original NES FF1 had spell slots, which FF1PR brought back. And the only way to replenish the spell slots was using House/Cottages in the open world map, or sleeping in an inn.  In FF1PR, as stated before, they brought back the spell slots (instead of MP), but they introduced ethers. So the whole point of bringing back spell slots is pointless because now it is just MP with extra steps. The Dawn of Souls version of FF1 introduced new bonus dungeons that offered fun puzzles, better equipment, and fun bosses from other Final Fantasy games. In FF1PR, they removed these bonus dungeons. So there is nothing extra in this game besides a bestiary.  And these seem like minor points of contention, but FF1 doesn't have much content in the first place. The game is pretty simple: Go from A to B to C to D until the end. You can do some things out of order, but that really doesn't offer any gameplay difference. So, if this is your first FF1, this is a great game because it is a classic Final Fantasy experience. If you experienced the other FF1 releases, you will find yourself disappointed every time you come across a change or something removed because there really was no point in removing these things. There is no reason to remove the Power Peninsula or the Hallway of Giants. FF1 removed and changed too many things and didn't replace them with anything substantial. Because of that, I cannot recommend it for veteran Final Fantasy fans who played other versions.

The new soundtrack is the best part, and having fast forward in the battles is always appreciated. _childDocuments_.review: This was a decent enough update to the first Final Fantasy. There are some really nice quality of life changes, some of which make some of the few grind sessions (mostly early game, as you catch up and then some later on) quicker if you want them to be. This one keeps the system where each level of magic has its own number of uses, which was in the original but not in a lot of the remakes.It should be noted that this doesn't have anything like the bonus dungeons or bosses from the GBA version. _childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster is an excellent modern port of a classic. _childDocuments_.review: Feels pretty good for a remaster, but it isn't quite a 1 to 1 remaster as it comes with a lot of QOL changes that were not in the NES version but lacks the extra content from the later versions. I have played the game multiple times on both GBA and PSP so the hours I have for going through the game was just from me already knowing where to go already. You play as the four warriors of light who seek to restore the light to the crystals they hold, that is the plot, it is a very basic RPG plot.Game looks, feels, sounds, and plays really smooth IMO, a lot of people had complaints at the launch for this about the text font and stuff but I never really had an issue with any of it personally. I never really found the game was straight forward on where to go, you can usually figure it out based on where you have been and what the NPCs in towns tell you. Combat gets repetitive sometimes in certain spots that are big jogs to get through.The game in my country is $15.99 Canadian, which means I got less than an hour per dollar and I completed the game and achievements, I kinda figured this was going to be case but I enjoy these games and to me it was worth it, someone who has never played this one before will more than likely spend more time on it. Take that as you will.I had watched my late grandfather play this on the original NES when I was very young, I had even attempted to play it after he had gone and I thought the game was very difficult. The pixel remaster felt much easier than the NES version but I think being a young kid vs an adult makes a big difference along with some of the QOL changes (if you target the same enemy and party member 1 kills them party member 2 still tries to attack the empty space while in the pixel remaster they just target the next enemy in line) and the better translation. Overall I would recommend the game, it is the first Final Fantasy game so it has some value with that. If you have already played the game on other platforms it has nothing more to add since it is only the original game and does not have any bonus content from the Dawn of Souls or Anniversary versions, so you may not feel like you got all that you paid for with it. Anyone who has not played the game before you will more than likely not have this issue as there is lots to read and explore in the game, while the review may sound like I do not recommend the game I do think it is worth at least one playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: The classic JRPG that started them all...For beginner RPG players and people who would want to experience the Final Fantasy franchise for the first time, I recommend playing the pixel remaster of this Original Classic. Or maybe if you are more of a challenge-hungry gamer/into old-school classic stuff, play the original NES/Famicom version.This is also great for avid gamers and RPG fans alike.

_childDocuments_.review: A good remaster. If you play through with a standard party and grind a lot, it will not be hard. The original game has different values for a number of things, so that old monster chart you might still have won't help. (Warmech has 2x the HP!) It has none of the additions that accrued to the game over the years like so much cruft, and is pretty close to the raw experience I had as a kid. Note that unlike some FF's, because you can pick any combination of characters in your party, and because of the more traditional pen-and-paper style inspired game design, you might puzzled why the game gave you a second katana, or why there are churches to resurrect your characters when phoenix downs exist. It does have major QOL improvements, the most notable are essentially those that most modern players of JRPG's would recognize. In particular the game is less grindy -- this does not make the game easier(!) -- but if you grind the same amount you did when you originally played, it WILL be easy (grinding is a difficulty slider, folks!) It also removes the old mechanic where a character would whiff if the monster they were attacking died before they attacked. There are numerous other things - some simply offset that this game did not come with charts showing you the layouts of dungeons - very important in this game.This game has always had an amazing amount of replayability, and there are a number of challenges we used to do that are possible thanks to being faithful to the original design. Some of these include making a party of all one class (say, Monk or White Mage), speedrunning the game, or attempting to get the class change at the lowest possible level (two zombie dragons is a challenge for that party!)Thanks to the guys for putting this together, seems like it was a big effort.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy I Pixel Remaster is a high quality polished and upgraded version of the original Final Fantasy that came out for the NES. The game has been ported over to PC with new graphics, sound, and quality of life enhancements. You can pick it up on Steam for the semi-reasonable price of $10.I picked this game up for two reasons:    I had never owned a Final Fantasy game before    I have a soft spot for retro gamesI figured it looks good, and is selling for a decent price, so I would give the original Final Fantasy a try.Being the first game in what would come to be a long and ongoing series, the plot is fairly simple and heavily inspired by Western fantasy. You play as four "Warriors of Light", who have arrived to fulfill a prophecy that you would come to save a land shrouded in darkness. You go from town to town, and are given fairly simple quests to either fetch and item, or kill an enemy. Now I will talk about a couple different aspects of the game.Gameplay: The game is a turn-based RPG. The way it works is pretty intuitive. One quality of life enhancement that was added was the ability to auto-run through battles, which really helps to get you through some of the grind of random encounters. The way it works is the animations are sped up, and your characters continually repeat their last action. Another part I liked about the game is that for a turn-based RPG, there was little to no grind. As long as I went out of my way to get the extra treasure in dungeons, I just about never found myself having to grind random encounters. The encounters from getting the treasure was enough that I could pretty continually progress.There is also a new addition of a map of whatever area you're in. You can choose not to use this if you wish. It shows you the locations of treasure and generally where to go. This can get rid of some of the challenge as some of the dungeons are built like mazes, so this would have been a bit more difficult in the original NES version.I did have to look up a guide. The game didn't always give me the most clear direction, and there were a few times where I found myself wandering around the map because I didn't spot a location. I won't really fault the game for this, however. I mean, the game came out in the 80's.Other than that, fairly simple, enjoyable, and intuitive turn-based gameplay.Sound: Sound was good. The original OST was completely redone, so rather than the retro sound that the NES would have, you get beautiful orchestral renditions of the OST. Good stuff.Graphics: The graphics have been completely redone. Some people complained and said things like "The PSP graphics were better!". But the PSP graphics had a completely different art style. The style here was supposed to capture the true intent of the graphics of the NES. So what you see, is supposed to be like things SHOULD'VE looked back then, but the capability just wasn't there.However, people did have one good complaint. The font in the vanilla game doesn't fit the aesthetic, and just generally sucks. However, there are simple mods that replace the font with something better.Overall: I'll give the game a 8/10. I'd recommend it if you're in to the type of game that it is. The price is decent and you're getting a high quality remaster. Maybe I'll pick up the FFVI remaster sometime.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy looks and plays better than ever, in a way that Square never managed to pull off with many of its Dragon Quest remakes. These remasters are gorgeous visually and audibly, and the ability to speed up movement or turn off battles with the click of a button means you won't; be wading through hours of random battles while you're stuck searching for the next dungeon.They honestly made the game better than ever. I can't wait to play Final Fantasy 2 for the first time!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: It's important to remember that despite the fresh coat of paint, this is still a game from 1987. However, don't let this detract you. I was pleasantly surprised by how well the game has aged. It certainly isn't the deepest rpg in the world. We really are talking about the bare bones here. This is excusable though considering it's age. I think that has long has you are aware of what you are playing and temper your expectations accordingly, I think you will be pleasantly surprised as too how well this title holds up. Just again, expect the very bare bones.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing that stood out to me was the music.  I was completely shocked.  It's an extremely high quality but faithful version of the soundtrack.I appreciate the graphics for what they are.  I like the PS1 and what I saw of the PSP graphics, but they were going with a more pixel style here and I think they accomplished what they were going for.There are some minor annoyances.  It's necessary to alt+enter to go into full screen every time the game is started.  Hopefully they patch that.  As of this review, it''s also necessary to use the graphics driver to force v-sync since it's not an option in game.  They chose a really narrow font that quite a few people dislike.  I'm sure most would be fine with it, but it's a minor annoyance that (for me) the Japanese font is superior to the one they use for English, but a simple file copy and rename allows the use of the wider font.  I noticed no issues with the font substitution.For the game itself, I loved it.  I do think it's very easy to level, and people who meticulously explore will very likely end up steamrolling the game past a certain point, depending on the chosen party composition.  They fixed all the numerous bugs from the original making what used to be useless spells extremely powerful this time around.I think they did a great job with this remaster.  It definitely does not cost too much, especially accounting for inflation.  Take a look at the credits list to understand how the price is not expensive for what they put into this.  It's a real shame they didn't incorporate the bonus content prior re-releases had, but for what they went for I think they did an amazing job.  Especially that soundtrack.  It's so good it deserves mentioning twice.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: The biggest problem I have with this release is the typeface used for the in-game text. It's extremely small and looks so out of place in a game that is otherwise crafted with pixel-perfect spritework. What's even more baffling is that the battle text looks great. I wish they had just used that for the dialogue and menus instead. Another complaint I have is a somewhat minor inconvenience, but even after setting the game to use Full Screen mode, the game always starts in Windowed. Every time I launch the game, I have to go back into the config menu to change it back to full screen mode. Hopefully this will be fixed in a future patch.These gripes aside, I have nothing but praise for everything else. The sprite work in this version strikes a good balance between updated visuals and staying faithful to the NES original. I am one of those who was not a fan of the "clean" graphics of the PSP version or how vastly the art style differed from basically every other 2D Final Fantasy game. Visually, this game is an improvement in every way in my opinion.By far, the most impressive feature here is the audio. The remastered music is nothing short of outstanding, and from the very beginning I found myself looking forward to pushing forward into new areas just to hear what it SOUNDS like in this version of the game. Overall, I personally consider this to be the definitive version of FF1 now. It doesn't have the optional dungeons that were added to some previous remakes, but to be honest, I found those to be unnecessary fluff in the first place. The core game is fully intact and better than ever.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: I have never played the original Final Fantasy 1 or any re-released version of it so I can't tell you how this compares to anything previous. However, I can tell you that this pixel remaster was a great experience and it was enjoyable to see how such a long running and influential franchise had its beginnings. There are a plethora of bonus options in the game that help modernize it a bit such as an auto-battler/xp multiplier if you're interested in that, however the game can be played completely vanilla. I recommend it to newcomers for sure, and I think if you've played this in the past and enjoyed it, you'll likely have fun with it again.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:  It's Final Fantasy 1, with better graphics, ad no chance your NES won't read the cart wrong and you have to spit all over the contacts by blowing into the cartridge.  Some nice quality of life improvements makes it easier to pick up for a more modern audience.  This is worth a shot if you're a fan of the franchise, to see where it all came from.  A nice chill out type of game that is a good deal more open-ended than some FF entries.CONS:  No GrImp or GrOgre.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from a long time player of Final Fantasy games, I feel ashamed to admit that I never really played the original six. I grew up on the PS1 titles, and went from there. Over the years I have tried to play the originals, but found myself dropping them within the first half hour. Finally completing Final Fantasy I feels like an accomplishment in itself. As a long time player of the series, I was shocked to see some of the Final Fantasy staples completely missing from this game. It makes sense in retrospect, it was the first game in the series and also 1987. Games and RPGs were still in their infancy.Was Final Fantasy a good game? Yes, for what it was. My biggest gripe with the game it's rudimentary magic system that feels very outdated and terrible to use. Otherwise, Final Fantasy is a good time, with it's bare-bones story and even more bare-bones combat.All-in-all, I am glad to have finally played and finished the first in the series, and am looking forward to seeing how the mechanics in the series evolves as I continue throughout the first six.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: FF1 is an excellent JRPG. It's also a very simple one, so don't expect too big of a challenge or too complex of systems. The remaster sadly doesn't include any of the extra content from previous remasters like the 20th anniversary PSP one, but it plays well and without the original bugs. Still, probably worth getting on sale for the collection or achievements over just emulating as it runs quite well and the pixel art is solid.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Doesn't come with the bonus dungeons that were added in the GBA/PSP versions. I really liked the Soul of Chaos bonus dungeon. _childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: An all time classic. One of the first games next to Dragon Quest to pioneer and solidify the basics of JRPGS for the next few decades. The Dna of all modern jrpgs are seen here from the basic ui and leveling design. This was my first Final Fantasy game and I was surprised by how much I enjoyed it. This is, however, a remake, so I can't really give a verdict on whether it is better than the original or other ports that have come out over the years. From a newcomers perspective, if you are also new to the franchise, this was a pretty good start. I will be checking out the sequel next.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy is a classic, and the steam version makes the pixels a bit better scaled. For a game so old, I actually felt like the game aged reasonably well. Sprites/pixels age way better than early polygon art. There really isn't too much to the story - fight bosses, rescue world, etc. However, there is a nostalgia touch to the game that really makes it fun (though tbh it would just be another rpgmaker game otherwise).Overall, fun nostalgia game that aged reasonably well. Though if you want something more modern, you may want to skip the game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: For fans of the classic series or newcomers looking for a quality introduction into the older games, Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster is a great way to experience the series. The Pixel Remaster does an excellent job of keeping the surprisingly well-aged gameplay that started the series intact while updating it with more modern pixel art and a beautiful soundtrack. Outside of a few confusing moments and poorly balanced bosses, Final Fantasy is a game I would readily recommend to modern RPG fans, and it’s a great introduction to the genre’s classics.Pros-------- Beautiful updated Pixel Art- Beautiful Soundtrack- Rewarding Exploration- Modern presentation of a classic RPGCons-------- Missing content from other Final Fantasy releases- Sometimes hard to tell where to goFinal Fantasy Pixel Remaster is a great way to experience the first entry in one of gaming’s biggest franchises. Compared to more recent Final Fantasy games this one is simple; the story is interesting but it’s not the dramatic saga seen in subsequent games. But as much as the epic storytelling has made more recent Final Fantasy games great, the simplistic approach to this is part of what makes it so timeless, even though none of that was intentional.Also F*** Warmech
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Have played this game countless times. Have done speed runs for this title on different platforms. I enjoy the redone music with real instruments. This is one of the quintessential titles for a JRPG enthusiast. Would consider installing the mod for the text but it really didn't bother me at all. _childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I did not come into the series expecting to love it but I definitely did coming out of this game! The story and gameplay are simplistic and wholesome, as you travel the world discovering hidden civilizations, slay foul beasts of legends, and grow stronger with every struggle. The ending drives home the series title "Final Fantasy" with its lesson to the player that even though the stories we play are nothing but a fantasy, they live on in each and every one of our hearts. Very much worth the purchase and made a fan out of me!

_childDocuments_.review: Update: So, I've since completed this game 100%, which feels surprising to do, even if it only took about 17 hours total. In all honesty, this was a great trip back down memory lane from when I first played it on the GBA at least 2 decades ago. I have a better appreciation for it now, tbh, and I do like that they opted to make things more affordable in the game and thus less grindy. I will gladly get this on PS4 for the Platinum Trophy, and I'm kinda kicking myself for getting the Deck to play this portably now that there's a Switch version, but then again, that CE looks great. Too bad they wouldn't make one for PC exclusive players, though.Eh, I can see how it looks on an OLED screen this time, at least.Original review: So, I've spent some more time with the game, and adjusted the review with an edit. Here's the original, starting with some gripes. Then the edit comes. If you read it through to the end, I thank you.|||Firstly, the pricing. 12 bucks for 1, 12 bucks for 2, EIGHTEEN for 3, and the same for 4, 5, and 6, respectively. Regardless of whether or not this would come to home consoles, you're telling me that almost 100 dollars is a reasonable price for all 6 games?!On top of that, likely no extra stuff like in the GBA and PSP ports and 3 is clearly only priced the same as 4-6 cause they're taking advantage of the fact that this is the first time the NES version has hit Western Shores. It's honestly appalling.So, I highly suggest you get these on a sale, even knowing how good 5 of these 6 games are. As for my gripe with 1 itself, it's the magic system.I didn't like the lack of MP in 3's remake, and I don't like it now.Aside from corporate crap and the MP issue, this is so far enjoyable. I think one interesting detail is you can actually move around diagonally. I don't remember if that was ever a thing in the GBA or PSP version, so I imagine they adjusted it for this pixel remaster.Anyway, I close this off with this question: Square, why are you acting like nobody wanted this on consoles and act as if there was zero feedback about it when literally the moment the trailer said "Coming to Steam and Mobile only" everyone watching collectively said "Wait, what about the Switch?!"Come on, now. And make it an ACTUAL compilation title fairly priced, please. Even Konami was fair with the Castlevania collection priced at 20 bucks for 8 old games.Freaking. Konami.Edit: Okay, so, it may be likely that the magic system might not be as bad as it was for me in FFIII 3D, as while grinding in this game, the numbers for how many times you can use magic were rising faster than I thought they would. So, I guess we'll see further how much better it'll be later on. Plus, it's clear that this is staying that much more true to the NES version as I noticed that you don't get a Broad/Longsword from the first boss and the Thief class doesn't steal like, you know, a Thief does.In addition, it seems there are some clarifications I have failed to state. Simply put, I've played the first 6 FF games before. I beat 1 on GBA, don't like the level up mechanics of 2(wow what a take), came close to beating 3 in 3D but never got around to it, 4 is my fave entry of them all(still mad that there's no Interlude or After Years inclusion like with, say, the PSP compilation title), beat 5 once and don't remember much at all about it, and, I'm very sorry to say, I never got around to finishing 6 in any form. I don't hate any of these titles sans 2, I want them to be fairly priced due to how long ago they were released, and preferably as a compilation for each of access and room for stuff like concept art to showcase like with most older games these days.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

I plan to continue on with the remainder of the pixel remasters (1-6). :) The game is simple, but fun, and the scope of it is a bit easier to manage for me these days than some of the really epic CRPGs. _childDocuments_.review: Very interesting trip down memory lane. It is an easy way to see where the series started, and what elements were there from the beginning. The presentation is obviously a lot more manageable than the old NES cart. This does not have the bells and whistles of other versions. Its mostly a straight port. The game itself is very bare bones, but that is to be expected being the progenitor of the series. There is not much difficulty to be found in the battles or bosses after the first couple hours. The challenge is mostly figuring out where to go next based on the often subtle direction given in game. Which is a far cry from modern games railroad'ing you along. I enjoyed it, but I'm a big fan of the series.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: The-- and I do mean "the"-- classic CRPG, next to DragonQuest.  And even if you're all about the graphics and speaking and whatever new wrinkle has been added lately, there's something-- actually, a lot of somethings-- to be said for the simple classic gameplay.There are games that have to be played.  Super Mario.  Sonic.  And Final Fantasy.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: They finally gave us what we needed. The original game with all the cruft removed. A solid inventory system, a detailed map system, an auto-combat system that actually makes the grinding quick and enjoyable. Yeah, I had the NES version and believe me, the original took 60+ hours to do what this accomplishes in a perfectly enjoyable 14.  If you're about Final Fantasy's rather Dungeons & Dragon's like origins, this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: A great remaster of a classic game. The remastered graphics and music are very nice. Some quality of life improvements take care of some of the really annoying stuff from the originals, run and auto-battle are life savers.Achievements compared to previous steam releases are a breeze and they decided to not let someone put in psychopathic achievements (looking at you 'all jobs to 99 for all characters' FF3 remake!).Unless you're a die hard FF fan wait for a sale. This game isn't very long literally one third of my play time was dedicated to hunting a single spawn for an achievement. I ran into  it after an hour and it fled. I kept looking for it for another 3 hours for bestiary completion, but no, just encountering it counted so I wasted my time.Plan for <10 hours and remember that just encountering a monster counts towards bestiary completion.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: I recently started playing this series starting of course with where it all started. One thing that I will probably say on every review I do of each of these games is that Square Enix should've included the instruction manual as a PDF DLC that these old games came with. They're specific to each game so you don't spoil changes in future games by looking at the wikia and there's really no information in the game itself that details what does what. Like how Blindness causes your melee attacks to miss more.If you're used to playing new games only then one thing you need to keep in mind at all times is that there is no quest log, if you skip through those dialogue points like you do in modern games you can and will be lost. Talk to every NPC you see to get hints and information. I myself have a .txt file and kept a log of who I interacted with in what city and what they said if it sounded important and I got through the game without trouble.In my journey, I went with a Warrior, Thief, Black Mage and White Mage. Throughout most of it I personally considered the Black Mage to be a burden since he has ♥♥♥♥ defense and dies easily combined with very limited MP for spells. But that was probably my fault, I was being careful with using spells and his Physical damage is also ♥♥♥♥ but in hindsight, I probably should've just bought the max stock for Ether to regain MP. Regardless, after getting the titles or upgrades to each role, the Black Wizard became much more useful and he was even instrumental in defeating the final boss due to his damage output.I did not like the status spells you can cast, they were very inaccurate and I don't think I even bothered using them most of the time. The enemies that it did manage to hit didn't have the same clear indication that they were affected by it so for all I know, it only affected them for one turn which makes the spells themselves completely and utterly a waste of time.Some specialized weapons were also kind of lame. Like the Werebuster, it has a buff against beasts but how can you tell what's classified as a beast and what isn't? Then all of a sudden you have a stronger sword so should you even bother? I kept these weapons but I think I just always switched to the strongest damage dealing weapon I received.The game and story overall though was enjoyable. Back then these games forced you to pay attention and in my opinion that helped you be more engaged with the story. I only played offline that's why I only have like 0 hrs but I believe the in-game time is how long you played which means I played for 18 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent port of the Dawn of Souls version (no, really, it flat out uses all of the assets from Dawn of Souls, except for slightly modified character sprites), with a few features added and many more removed, I'm just glad FF 1 and 2 are finally available on Steam after all these years, even if it is the worst remake.There's no more extra content, so you can casually complete the game within a day, and they even made it easier by making shops cheaper, adding automaps that show you where everything is and where to go, adding an auto-battle feature that makes the game go by even faster, allowing you to save anywhere, rebalancing the classes and enemies, and they fixed all the bugs from the other versions (including the Peninsula of Power, which is just blasphemy).  It also adds diagonal movement, as well as quite possibly the best orchestral rearrangements yetBut... the issue is, Square said the reason they omitted the extra content was because they wanted veterans of the serie to enjoy a nostalgic trip that was as close to the original experience as possible.  Well, considering the Dawn of Souls graphics, the orchestral rearrangements, and the countless QoL updates, bugfixes and rebalances, plus the complete lack of toggles to disable all of these new features (even the vastly superior PSP version with its extra content allowed you to at least choose tween soundtracks), I'd say Square was flat out full of ♥♥♥♥, and this was just a shameless cashgrab once againAnd yet, I'm just glad we finally have FF1 and 2 on Steam
