_childDocuments_.review: As someone who’s spent a large amount of time in Eorzea (FF XIV), as well as some vacations to neighboring Final Fantasy lands, I’d always had an interest in discovering its roots. Once the Pixel Remasters of the first six games released, I finally had my excuse to hop in and experience the series from the very beginning. Is Final Fantasy the best game I’ve ever played in my entire life? Nope, of course not. That said, I still had a lot of fun with it and loved seeing the origin of a series I’ve come to love.Starting with how I played the game, I opted for the modernized text and soundtrack. The text was simply for readability, but I debated quite a bit on whether to listen to the original soundtrack over the orchestral mixes. Ultimately, I decided if I wanted to revisit the original games, there would still be merit in that and the original soundtrack would be present, plus Square typically knocks it out of the park with their music, so I was excited to see what the modernized version had to offer. I’m glad I did, as I enjoyed several tracks and Chaos Shrine specifically is a very beautiful piece that I will continue to listen to. I compared several of the tracks to their NES counterparts, and while they were also great, I’m glad I chose this path.I was pretty impressed with the party system; as soon as you boot up, the game asks you which four classes you’d like for your Warriors of Light, and I didn’t expect many options from a game made in 1987, but you’re given 6 classes to choose from and can even double-dip if you’re particularly keen on a given class. I went with Fighter, Thief, Red Mage, and Black Mage and each character filled a pivotal role up until the endgame, where unfortunately my Thief, (at this time a Ninja), was essentially useless and delegated to potion throwing. From what I’ve read, this is just an unfortunate class to choose in FF I, but aside from that, every other character is viable in some capacity.The combat was the most traditional turn-based combat you can possibly imagine. This doesn’t mean unfun, and there was some depth in what options I had available to me among my casters and physical fighters, but it was very predictable and there was rarely a surprise in any encounter. By the end of the game, I’d found a formula that was more or less able to handle any fight, though the final boss did take several tries to finally bring down. Even with this being the case, I still found myself fighting each random encounter, (only turning them off when I had to run to safety), simply because it was good, old-fashioned fun.The weakest part of the game is the story. “Warriors of Light, go light four crystals which will allow you to fight the big, bad guy!” It’s just a super generic plotline, but at the same time, I’m looking at this from a modern point of view, and it very well could have been far less cliche upon its original release. Even if that were the case however, the story doesn’t have much to offer someone who’s played games with much better stories. On top of that, exploration is very open-ended in the sense that your next objective may be clear across the map and, without a guide, it is very tough to actually pin down where anything is beyond a vague direction, which can definitely bog down the pacing.Ultimately, I had fun with my playthrough, and I’d absolutely recommend the game to anyone who has enjoyed a Final Fantasy title. It’s fun to see where it all began, and it’s more than just a historical piece; it has life of its own and is a genuinely enjoyable game in its own right. At the very least, it’s given me the determination to play the entirety of the series, and I can’t wait to see what else it’s got in store for me.Cinematic playthrough here:

_childDocuments_.review: Know what? I enjoyed this so much I'm going to give it an actual review. The Final Fantasy pixel remaster is a great way to play the first game, whether you're a veteran fan of the series or a newcomer that's played another one and just wants to see its origins and follow its progression. This version (I've played the NES game, PS1 version, and PSP version.) has the best graphics and music out of all of them. I believe the music is the same as what was used for the PSP version, but I can't back this up with certainty because I haven't touched it in years. Either way, the graphics are great, the music is great, and I have very little room to find complaints. But if I  to find some...Chaos is so hard as to seem bugged. Full heals and one-hit kills are common. Luckily, it lets you load from the beginning of the last room instead of requiring you to load from outside of the Chaos Shrine. Prepare to grind for a couple of hours right at the end before you fight him, and to try multiple times. This was annoying. No New Game+ - This would really add to the replay-ability. As good as it is, I've played through it a few other times and don't see a reason to play through it again without something like this. I would encourage anyone to play around with their parties, though.The red mage seems a little bit nerfed, as well, even more so than in the past.  A note about my game time: I just left it open a lot. It's not very taxing so I would walk away and let it run while I did other stuff. Seriously recommended, even at full price. 8.0 / 10 - and it's a strong 8.0/10 - I expect all of the pixel remasters to hit around this score.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 1 holds a special place in my heart. It's not just a game; it's an adventure that ignited my love for the RPG genre. Released in 1987, it set the standard for what an epic fantasy journey should be.The game's simplicity is its charm. You start with a group of four heroes, each with their own unique abilities and classes. From there, you embark on a quest to save the world from darkness, battling monsters, exploring dungeons, and uncovering ancient secrets.What I love most about Final Fantasy 1 is its sense of exploration and discovery. There's a thrill in venturing into uncharted territories, never knowing what dangers or treasures await. The world feels vast and mysterious, filled with hidden passages and powerful foes.The turn-based combat system is both strategic and satisfying. You must carefully plan your actions, choosing the right spells and tactics to overcome tough adversaries. And the boss battles? They're intense and memorable, requiring quick thinking and a bit of luck to emerge victorious.Of course, let's not forget the music. Nobuo Uematsu's iconic score elevates the game to another level, immersing you in its fantastical world with each melody.Final Fantasy 1 may be old-school by today's standards, but its timeless gameplay and endearing charm continue to captivate players even after all these years. If you're a fan of classic RPGs or just looking for a nostalgic trip down memory lane, do yourself a favor and give Final Fantasy 1 a try. You won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me just say that I love this game, probably my second favorite NES-game of all time after SMB3. Everything about it is so addictive, and this remaster really does promote the great aesthetics this game has even more. From the music to the pixel art, everything is very well-presented.That being said - this version of the game vows to be as true to the original NES-game as possible, so I understand why they removed all the bonus dungeons and stuff in the GBA-versions and other versions of the game. I don't agree with the decision. I can't say for sure what features would've been nice to keep and what are better off gone, but removing content like extra dungeons etc really sucks imo- especially considering all the earlier FF-games on Steam they replaced the remasters with have them, but I can't buy those versions instead because they've all been delisted. It's even weirder considering they choose to keep the stats of *certain* enemies the same as the changed ones in versions of the game with bonus dungeons instead of the original stats in the NES-game, leaving you potentially weak as hell as the game expects you to have leveled in the bonus dungeons that are not there. Not a massive problem or anything - but a bit of an ick.I've heard these pixel remasters are easily moddible, however from my quick search I couldn't really find any mod that implements the bonus dungeons missing from the game, but maybe I'm just not looking hard enough.Aside from that- it's a good remaster of a classic game, get it if you like old-school RPGs!

_childDocuments_.review: Wow... just wow.  I really can't say that I'm the type of person who will buy an RPG and then literally play it all day and night from start to finish in one sitting.. but here I am at nearly 6AM and instead of finally going to sleep, I decided to post a review.   To keep this brief, this game was nothing short of greatness.  They really cared about this remake and it really shows in every aspect of the game.  They stayed true to the original and added several quality of life features.The visuals, the sound design and especially the music were just amazing to re-experience.  The menus worked beautifully and were extremely responsive... if you are the type of player who is able to VERY quickly navigate a menu (talking about several key presses per second) this menu can keep up.I honestly came into this game expecting that something would rub me the wrong way as many of the more recent 2D remake/ports have.  Whether its the graphics, or the bugs, the music or just the design choices, 2D ports/releases always seem to let me down in some way or another.. but not this one.Never have I experienced FF1 like this.  They truly crafted this game with care and it shows.This is a gem upon a pedestal.I am so excited to start FF2.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the earliest memories I had as a child when I owned the NES. I think I was 5 or 6 when I played it.  I believe it was my brother and his friend Seth who ended up actually beating the game. I found it very difficult to play, but that didn't stop my love for it and my fascination as I watched my brother lay it all the way through. Then, 35 years later, I decided to look up on the game on Steam and found a Pixel remastering.  It retained all the music and everything about the original that made it truly special whilst fixing a few things that it greatly needed (e.g., party members attacking the next enemy instead of attacking the dead space where a former enemy was at, etc.).When the menu started with the iconic music playing, I was elated with wonderful waves of nostalgia. Yes, the game's story line is linear, but there is beauty in the simplicity of this game....I really wish I could put into words how this remastering has brought me real joy and happiness in my heart.  Now it's time for me to buy Final Fantasy 4 Pixel Remaster and relieve my most favorite RPG of all time!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, 1987. A time when video games didn't hold your hand. You were expected to explore and experiment and forge your own path of discoveries. But Final Fantasy saw that and thought: "But what if we made it just a little bit more accessible?" And gave birth to everybody's favorite citizen of Cornelia, the Exotic Dancer! Now, they didn't call her that in the game, but you look at that sprite, and you indulge her in conversation, and after she calls you "handsome" and winks at you, she flirtatiously offers to give you a "funny dance," and even my dense as diamond dumb ass autistic brain matter can put two and two together. Our sexy dancer friend's proclivities to flirt with anyone who makes eye contact with her aside, she sure seems to know some things she really shouldn't sometimes. Perhaps she is the secret fifth Warrior of Light all along! But even if she isn't, I enjoyed our banter nonetheless. She always knew just what to say to get me going (places). But I didn't like relying on her. She exists purely to be an accessibility feature, and I am not the kid I was when I first played this game (and never finished it). I'm a seasoned game connoisseur. I don't need a dedicated hint system. I'm a proud explorer! The majority of Final Fantasy is pretty easy to follow, provided you do the usual RPG thing and talk to everyone as you pass by the various locales of the world. There's plenty of bread crumbs to follow. There will always be at least a couple nudges in NPC dialogue here and there to guide you to your next quest, or an item you get naturally reminds you of something you came across earlier that could obviously use said item. Right up until there isn't. Indeed, when I reached a certain point in this game, I have a key item I obtained from my last quest, and absolutely no clue where to go, who to give it to, what to use it on, and believe you me, I tried everything I could think of. I went all over the world that was open to me, every single locale, and spoke to every NPC in the game up 'till that point, as surely I had missed something? There was even a guy who was searching for that very item -- usually an obvious "talk to this person" flag if ever there was one! -- but no, he simply said the exact same thing he said before I had the item. There wasn't the slightest crumb to be found. So I finally decided, okay, fine, I'll swallow my Gamer Pride™, and actually engage with the Hint System of the game. I will travel all the way back to the very beginning area of the game and confess my woes to my exotic dancer friend. And on that one fateful day, the one day when I was at my wit's end, the day I needed her most, do you know what she said to me? "I don't know what else to tell ya! How 'bout we have that dance? Whaddaya say?" ...10/10 would get danced on again.

The language options are extensive.  Two things: Options Menu doesn't have Sound Settings.  I can't find the way to turn off the in game sound in the settings menu.  It is annoying to have to do it from my volume mixer.  Also, getting rid of the annoying "beep" sound but keeping the other music would be nice.   While there is a run function for in the cities, some parts of the game move slowly.  Being able to speed things up would be nice. _childDocuments_.review: After spending over 6000 Hours in Final Fantasy XIV, I figured that it would be a good idea to see where everything started, and thanks to these lovely Pixel Remasters of the first few Final Fantasy games, it is easier than ever to do.    FF1 has a classic RPG Plot. You control a party of the chosen Warriors, foretold by a prophecy to save the world. Nonetheless the story the game weaves from it, is fun to follow and has some unexpected twists.  If you, like me, only played FF14 before, you will meet some characters you know from there, and it put a smile on my face each time.    If you think of a classic turned based RPG you pretty much think of Final Fantasy 1. Before you start, you build your 4 Players party, that you can freely configurate and start into your adventure, fight enemies, equip your party with the Gil you earned, and discover the world. In opposite to modern RPG’s, you won’t find pointers on the map, but need to figure out where to go next via NPC conversations. Lovely pixel look, with charming music that will become stuck in your head for a while.       Stable 60fps, never encountered a bug, or crash or any other problem.    Playing Final Fantasy 1 feels like a small, very enjoyable, time travel journey to the origins of RPG’s, that I can wholeheartedly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this, but something felt off the whole time.  Not just that the graphics and spell names had changed, but it just felt way too easy.  It wasn't until I hit level50 on Tiamat's bridge trying to find "WarMech" now named "Death Machine" I guess that I realized they had changed the leveling and the XP.  50 was no longer the max level, and hitting level50 took 30+ hours in the original.  I hit 50 in 10 hours on this version of the game.When reading guides online, that's when I realized this is some weird frankenstein version of Dawn of Souls.  They took the tech, like the graphics updates and the balancing changes with leveling from Dawn of Souls, but then removed stuff from Dawn of Souls like the extra dungeons and end game content present in Dawn of Souls!  But they the leveling in place!  So the game is way way way too easy with no end-game content like Dawn of Souls.So besides the disappointing partial updates from Dawn of Souls with no extra dungeons, and the bad balancing feel making the game unrewarding and challengeless, they made it so you can supposedly change your spells but you can't.  You can forget a spell, but it won't let you learn any other spell than the one that was previous in the slot.  Again, a feature from Dawn of Souls which looks like is broken on this implementation.I'm down voting.  They should have included full Dawn of Souls content or none of it at all, because they broke the balance of the game with what they did.

_childDocuments_.review: I got to Chaos, the last boss, in 13 hours and it felt like the most tedious grind to fight them. Up until that point there is some sort of strategy and counter play, but Chaos is resistant to everything and one shots your guys often. Not compelling. Up until that point I was really looking forward to doing another playthrough with a new lineup. The game felt so similar to my experiences with the original nes version so many years ago. The pacing definitely felt a lot faster, but I was starting to see that as an advantage, faster play meant it would be easier to get into a new playthrough. After that battle with Chaos though I felt like any sense of fun had been sucked from the game for me. I don't see any reason to every do that fight again, so there is no point in playing this ever again. Giving a boss 5x the hit points of any previous bosses is just lazy and boring and disrespects the players in my opinion. That isn't real challenge.I really wanted to do another run or two, but yeah, no.oh well

_childDocuments_.review: Two central observations: Final Fantasy 1 aches with age and this remake rather than improving the gameplay, instead strips it of everything that actually did work in the original version.While it is true, the original version could be extremely tedious, this version nerfs every aspect of the game.  For reference, I'm the type of JRPG player who NEVER grinds for EXP/Gold if I can avoid it but will attempt to get every treasure in a dungeon.  Playing this way I was flooded with Gil to the extent that whenever I visited a new town (including the first) I could afford every single purchase my team could use.  I don't think I fought a boss that lasted more than 4 turns until the final dungeon. I got one game over to random mob, zero game overs to bosses.One of the major aspects of playing the original version is that dungeons were battles of atrophy: without ethers you had to judicially choose when to use your magic saving enough for the dungeon boss.  The dungeons were designed to take multiple trips to explore them completely.  So this was a combination of exploration and strategy. While slow, it was somewhat compelling. Being able to afford dozens of ethers means your black mage can just single handily nuke every random encounter.  I've played dozens of old-school JRPGs and the random battles in this version of FF1 feel like speed-bumps more than nearly all of them.  Extremely low risk, extremely low reward, and extremely high encounter rate. The final dungeon in the original was grueling to get through because of its huge size and sparse treasures, this version feels almost like trolling (here's another hour of 8 second random battles to blow through!).I love the aesthetics of this remaster.  The graphics, music, mini-maps, art galleries are very welcome.  But the nerfed beyond belief gameplay makes me worry about how Square might bungle FF4 through FF6, the ones I was looking forward to the most...

_childDocuments_.review: First review I've ever written and I'm happy it is about this game. I love this game. Absolutely. Just finished getting the 100% achievement for it. That being said, I'm familiar with the story and the directions to go. Where it took a casual stroll for me to be 13 hours it may take someone else new to the series longer as they stumble and talk to people along the way. That is 100% okay. The old games are definitely a take at your own pace kind of deal. I feel like they did it justice and they added some neat QoL changes like maps and such which they knew 95% of people would google as they have in past iterations of FFI. I've played the NES/GBA versions as well and have to say that they have really knocked it out of the park with the musical score and the pacing of the game. I understand that every remaster/remake game will have a segment of the OG diehards that are clamoring for the slower walk speed, the very slow exp gain and other such things that really made the game more long and drawn out for a game that was a max of 1 MB on an NES cart. However, you gotta remember... --- This is a way for them to both bring back the games we know and love and also introduce them to a new audience. ---- Some people desire the 3 hours of grind in one area of the game and I respect that. I really do. Maybe they could add in a difficulty modifier for it. Maybe someone could create a mod for it.But this definitely feels like something they brought back for all those people where even FFX was their first game! As someone that is here for the story and the music and even the beautiful battle effects... I'm in love all over with this game. I would definitely recommend it to players old and new.

_childDocuments_.review: Without a doubt, this is the most accessible version of the original Final Fantasy you can play. With updated pixel art, re-balanced stats for classes, enemies, weapons, and spells, and a soundtrack that I believe is worth the price of admission alone, this feels like everything the original Final Fantasy wanted to be all the way back in 1987. However, you must curb your expectations when playing, as the game is as formulaic as one might expect when jumping into a game made over 30+ years ago. Simplistic turn-based combat alongside a story that only serves as a reason for why you're fighting in the first place (although the ending can be seen as a precursor to some of the more complex ♥♥♥♥ the series will delve into later on). "Quests" only amount to you getting one thing from somewhere to do another thing that MIGHT lead to you doing something important, and the party you control does not react with ANY OF IT. You're here to get ♥♥♥♥ done, and that's it.Then there are some of the more archaic game design choices that was preserved for this release. Some of these include:       - Ambushing stun-locking zombies.        - Enemies that can one-shot any character with just their attacks       - Quest locations that are difficult, almost cryptic to find that lead to trial and errorIt needs to be said that yes, this was the beginning of the franchise, and laid the groundwork for many JRPGs that were soon to follow. But as the years go on, this becomes more of a hard sell to anyone who is not a fan of the series, as you're now competing with other RPGs that have more engaging gameplay and/or stories to tell. I feel this game functions best when accompanied by the other games in the pixel remaster series, which was probably the intention. As a stand-alone release, that's where it becomes difficult to recommend. I love this game, but that's because I love the simplistic style this game was released in. But if you're able to put aside everything I mentioned above, then I do think there is a lot to like here. If anything, you'll have a newfound appreciation not only for the rest of the series moving forward but for JRPGs in general!

Not to mention the main vechicle that drives you through the story and progression is grinding for cash and man things like spells and new armor get so insanely expensive by the end GOD.and this remaster does not include the new extra bosses and enemies from the GBA/20th anniversary releases so again not a lot of contnet.But really if you can look past that its a great run through a historically important JRPG with amazing musicsolid 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best release of FF1 to date. It is very true to the original, including the spell level mp system, which I've only seen in the PS1 Final Fantasy Origins release. The new music remixes are fantastic updates to the original music.It may not be worth the price if you already own a modern release, such as the "old version" android/ios releases, but if this is your first trip into FF1 it's a great choice. It's also great for those of us who want a PC version, because FF1 never got a PC release (not counting emulators). This new release is also on android/ios, though there does not appear to be any cross-platform saving.The controller support has one issue: If you have more than one controller plugged in, the game gets confused. I had my steam controller and my flight stick plugged in at the same time, and it was completely unplayable with the controller. I unplugged the flight stick, and then it worked flawlessly with the steam controller.

_childDocuments_.review: In terms of being a life-long FF fan, why not? This is where it all began and if nothing else you'll get a bit more context for the references made in Stranger of Paradise, Dissidia and FFXIV.If you want to play an FF game that is simple, straightforward and easy over a weekend or so and don't care too much about the story so much as getting a few lines of goofy dialogue and a turn based RPG system you can tinker with, go for it. This is an old game that has been made to look pretty without compromising the original sprite style, has had the soundtrack touched up very nicely and several bugs fixed.The trade off is the extra content from PSX, GBA and PSP versions are gone meaning no bonus dungeons or FMVs. This is as close as you can get to a pure FFI NES experience in the modern day without having to sift through the issues of expensive out-of-production consoles and cartridges, buying an NES classic or emulation/piracy and with the convenience of text being easier to read and understand than the shorthand used in the original release.In terms of how it relates to Stranger of Paradise and Dissidia, If you do want more of a challenge within this game I highly recommend an all Monk or all White Mage run.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately for me there are some changes that fundamentally change the first 1/3 ramp into the game that I don't enjoy.Perhaps it is the eternal war between the expectations of nostalgia and the objective truth of reality. Perhaps the game better matches the original intent; certainly I can appreciate in the era of the cartridge you could never provide an update and buggy games that shipped remained buggy in all their quirky charm.For me the removal of the silver sword and the giant peninsula are sad losses. The sword provided a great functional choice, intended or not, between grinding or progressing story. You could choose if you wanted to grind now and ease combat for a considerable period of time, or take on more challenging battles now but progress the story faster.The peninsula served a similar functional purpose, with grinding in the moment easing the coming progression.As it stands now, the game is a monotonously linear power curve for the first half of the game until you get the airship. There is no way to 'get ahead' of an area, and so I find it boring.I appreciate that my opinion isn't for everyone, but this game is special to me. I passed it with a lvl-27 party of three fighters and a white mage back in the 80s before most readers of this were born. Back then there was literally no internet, no guide, no access to the Nintendo help line (parents really didn't see the value of paying for that), and no friends who played RPGs to bounce ideas off. Seriously, most people back then had no idea what an RPG was and D&D was the devil's work making kids commit horrible crimes, burning people alive, forcing kids into cults, and many more weird paranoid delusions. I honestly don't know if anyone in my school actually played PnP games; it was that rare.The box art for FF spurred my imagination and that's why I bought it. I had to explore every nook and cranny of this game to get through it and that familiarity is near impossible to come by anymore; it's just too easy to check youtube for "The Way(Tm)". TLDR: I'd rather play a rom. And the screen tearing is terrible.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for Square to release all six of their early games in a pixel perfect format for over 20 years, and I can safely say that this is yet another cash grab that does nothing to stay true to the original. I was really looking forward to playing these remasters, but felt like a kid waking up on Christmas morning only to find a giant steaming turd in my stocking.I played the game for less than ten minutes and I noticed the following issues. #1. There's a massive amount of screen tearing when you're moving on the map, or in a town. #2. The font they chose is horrendous, and does not match the pixel graphics whatsoever.#3. The 'Classic' mode graphics option is an absolute joke. All it does is try to mimic scanlines, but fails miserably and you're just left with a blurry mess. #4. The 'pixel perfect' graphics lack depth and give an extremely muddy appearance.#5. The music is good, but it really doesn't suit the style of graphics. They should have included the option to switch between the modern and 8 bit soundtracks.I'm sure there are more flaws that I'm missing, but this was enough to make me stop playing and jump straight to review. I can't tell you how pissed off I am that Square-Enix ruined yet another port of these classic games. Seriously people, stop supporting this horrible company and let them go bankrupt so that another company can take control of these games.* Square has since released two patches for the game in an attempt to fix some of the issues, but absolutely nothing has changed in regards to the problems that I listed in my review.** Square has since release a console version of this game, and nearly every complaint I made in my review was finally addressed. Unfortunately Square has still not addressed these problems on the PC version, so don't buy this game on Steam, buy it on console!

_childDocuments_.review: So after completing this game 100% of all it has to offer, here are my thoughts on the game as is. I'll start with the TL;DR review...PROs:- Visuals and effects are excellent and nicely crafted- Remastered soundtrack is wonderful to listen to. (Especially with certain boss fights)- The auto-battle feature is a godsend for grinding while progressing- The minimap feature saved me so much time while going thru dungeons/locations looking for treasure- The overworld map with key locations telling you how many chests/items you've collected/have left is perfect for the completionists out thereCONs:- Screen tearing is a constant issue- God-awful font choice that I had to fix (thank you internet)- Config settings don't properly save/carry over when you boot up the game again.- Bestiary can only be accessed from the title screen and not in-game (For completionists, this is annoying)- No bonus content from previous remakes (though it wasn't an issue for me I feel like you have to be aware of this)TL;DR: 8/10. Some issues could be fixed on the technical side. But on the gameplay side, if you want an experience closer to the original game but updated graphically, it's fun and honestly a nicely made remaster.----More of my thoughts----This game felt shorter than I remember it being. I think it could be because I already played it and I knew where I was going, or the game had enough enemy encounters to make it easier to go thru the game without having to stop and grind out levels.One major gripe I had going thru the game tho... WHY WERE THERE SO MANY CHESTS THAT HAD MONSTERS IN THEM!?On another note, I know that there are people, and I can respect their opinions, who wished that this remaster had the bonus content that appeared in the GBA version and the anniversary version, but for me personally I don't really mind that this remaster chose to stay closer to the original instead of updating the remakes in terms of content.Other than that, if you're a sucker for pixel style that's closer to GBA style than the anniversary style like I am, I recommend this remaster wholeheartedly if you're planning on going back thru the FF series or if you're just starting out.

_childDocuments_.review: As a longtime (read early '80's) RPG player, I recently decided to play through and review all of the FF pixel remasters.  This is my first review of that set.Games were very, very different 30 years ago, and if you aren't prepared for that fact, you are not prepared to enjoy this remaster.  Allow me to elucidate.Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster has a great many modern "quality of life" improvements over the original version.  Most noticeable is that menus do not immediately suck your soul out of your ass.  Eventually they do, but not, ya know... immediately.  There is a map, which is a technology not invented in games until many years later.  Just being able to see where you are going is a blessing you young whippersnappers will never fully appreciate.  Also, there are online walkthroughs, so ya know... you don't have to level up 12x trying to figure out where you're supposed to go, let alone how to get there.Nevertheless, it's still a classic RPG, so... you're totally going to be told to "rescue the princess, and here is your stick, good luck my guy,"  If you don't use a guide, you're going to spend 3-4x as long just wandering around like "WTF where is the.. I don't even know!?"  So there's your warning about classic RPGs.There are a ton of Final Fantasy tropes you're going to see making their very first appearance, and that's a lot of fun.  As an FFXI player, it was a lot of fun having Bahamut be like "here's a free level up" rather than... ya know... the plot of Chains of Promathia.  There is enough loot hunting and such to keep things from being a straight grind-through though, so in the end, if you want a bit of nostalgia, or a connection to your gaming roots, I think you'll enjoy this.  If you're looking for a game reminiscent of anything made in the last 25 years... you're going to be disappointed....you total noob.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's how I'll put this: If you're going to play the original Final Fantasy, this version is probably the way to do it. If you're on the fence about playing some of these earlier FF games, here's what you need to know about this game: This is like one of the first JRPGs ever made. Things that it does that were novel at the time are old hat now. There are some balance issues. The game doesn't always do a good job of leading you down the right path. There are some things about it that are undeniably good, like the music. And I'll say this game has a certain "je ne sais quoi" that your average RPG Maker game might not have. But the fact is mechanically this game is not very complex or interesting if you've played a lot of JRPGs and are coming back to this one. And there's not REALLY a story to be spoken of, just a situation that needs fixing and a band of travelers here to fix it. Aside from that it's solid but not really exceptional - a cool look at the origins of one the biggest video game franchises/an entire genre - but make no mistake, the franchise and the genre have gotten better since this game's original release.I ultimately recommend the game, with the caveat that you understand what it is before going into it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game offers a refreshed version of the original. Notably, the game re-instates the vancian magic system, rather than the MP-based one featured in the previous GBA and PSP remakes. Other differences include slightly lowered prices in stores, removel of the level 50 level cap and an easier exp curve. (Also, I vaguely suspect the difficulty on the final boss fight has been massively increased?)Most of the changes are welcome ones, to allow for a considerably less grindy experience. To that end, the new auto-battle/fast-forward feature is a godsend when battling lower-level mooks that require little strategy. There's an argument to be made that including an all-seeing map makes the dungeons a little too easy, though.Overall, I recommend the Pixel Remaster if you haven't played the original yet, based on the fast-forward feature alone.

_childDocuments_.review: PLEASE READ TO THE END OR ELSE YOU'LL BE CONFUSEDHonestly, I don't recommend this game on its own. Final Fantasy as a franchise has spanned so many console generations we're farther away from the release of the GameCube than how old FF1 was when the GameCube released. The age shows. This was a different time in gaming, back when the length of the game was what determined the worth as a product, not the entertainment value. Games that lasted longer (artificially or no) were always considered the most bang for your buck, whether you're buying it for your kid or putting it up for rent in every Blockbuster in America. This game is a slot, random encounters every 4 seconds that range from overly punishing in the first few hours to downright insultingly easy halfway through. Enemies don't scale to progress, which is most evident when you reach the final stretch of the Shrine of Chaos where you can one shot every non Black Flan enemy in a single turn with a standard attack from a WHITE MAGE. Honestly 4 steps for an encounter you insta win with the Auto-Battle feature sounds more like a mobile Idle game than a JRPG, and it plays the same way. The only time I was truly challenged was on the final boss, but only because it has a FULL HEAL MOVE. If you aren't fast enough, all your progress and all the hi-ethers you've been hording (not out of necessity but because they're generally useless outside of boss encounters) have gone to waste. All of this isn't even mentioning how much of a methane-spewing crawl through a tar pit that achieving 100% feels like. Ever wanted to shiny hunt a pokemon without the satisfaction of having a different colored jpeg and one shooting the enemy with your over leveled Knight? Try completing the bestiary! There's two less than 5% encounters that take place in and next to the final rooms of their dungeons respectively. Seriously, why is the Iron Golem a 1.4% encounter rate?You might be thinking "Why are you recommending this game if you don't recommend it in the text?" For it's historical value of course. Final Fantasy as a franchise is old enough to where their kids (sequels and spinoffs) could feasibly be in High School, college, hell maybe even vote or have kids of their own! Final Fantasy 7 has its own spinoff game, movie, remake (that's not a remake it's a sequel but whatever) spinoff that GOT a remake, mobile game, etc. It's such a transcendent experience to play through the beginnings of the franchise that defined mine and the two generations before my childhoods. Seeing enemies like the Sagahin knowing they'll blossom into their own beast tribe in 14, seeing the Gnomes knowing that they'll influence the Tarutarus and Lalafells in both the MMOs, seeing the origins of my favorite class Red Mage (that ended up being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in this game specifically), having an NPC throw out the name Cid and being like "I know that guy! All of the Cids from 2-15!" It's fun to retroactively piece together the beginning of so many references and tropes in the series, and fighting chaos, though a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fight, legitimately felt like an accomplishment when I got that final toe curling ass clenching hit that triggered the oh so satisfying cross hatch fadeout. I cannot stress this enough, FF1 IS NOT FUN! However, if you're a FF fan and you want to see the beginning of it all, please play FF1. Just don't finish the bestiary ;)

_childDocuments_.review: I love the music and I love the general layout of the graphics.  Although the music in this version is OUTSTANDING, I do wish there were options to change between the new orchestrated music, the ps1 soundtrack, and the original 8 bit chiptunes.  I also love the included beastiary.  On the surface it seems pretty outstanding.  The visuals are top notch and the way the background animations like flowing water and stuff was done looks magical.However...The scrolling both on the overworld and while in dungeons or towns seems to be missing frames and is EXTREMELY noticeable, especially when playing on larger screens.I don't like how this version seems to be stuck on easy mode with no way to change the difficulty.  In about 5 or 10 battles I was already like level 4 with well over 100 hp.  Lame.  In the original I would still be getting my ass handed to me at this point.  Also there is also no need to grind money apparently because at the beginning of the game I had enough money already - without even fighting - to buy everyone's starter gear - weapons, armor and magic and still had plenty left over if I wanted some other stuff.I was afraid to walk a few steps away from the first castle in the original, but in this version, at around level 4, I can waltz straight up to Chaos Temple without hardly an enemy encounter and go right in an start winning battles against skeletons.  You definitely wouldn't have done that in either the original Nintendo or PlayStation versions so early on into the game.The overworld map is stuck onscreen at all times, you can only resize it which I found to be a bummer.  Also the option to disable the ----- annoying onscreen control reminders ----- is absent from the config menu.  I wish this version had included ALL the extra content such as extra dungeons and whatnot that has been released for this game on other platforms.This version of this game holds your hand and for anyone looking for a grind or for a more difficult overall experience, I suggest you look to one of the other versions, at least at the time I am writing this review.I hope future patches fix some or all of this stuff because I really want to love this game, but it feels rushed and not very well thought out from a hardcore ff series fan's perspective.  I would appreciate an option for tougher battles and leveling up for real if nothing else.TLDR:This game looks and sound fantastic except for the scrolling, which isnt smooth at all and really needs to be addressed imho.  The pixel art is very well done and the orchestrated music is the best so far.  However, the gameplay itself seems dumbed down and far, far too simplified.  I still recommended this game, but there's still plenty of room for improvement in the form of future updates or patches.

_childDocuments_.review: Ahh, nostalgia made well. Finally.The pixel remasters are great. They listened, they went back, they fixed. Mostly. Maybe even more. It's less detailed, or more pixely let's say, and the characters look way more like their original counterparts. It fits really well.The new arranged soundtrack is a real banger. They nailed it. The original core soundtrack itself is absolutely incredible, and in my opinion slightly forgotten compared to the later entries in the series. There are some real quality tunes here.The game itself is a gem. Everything classic about Final Fantasy is here, and started here. It still is a very solid JRPG (although very basic nowadays). It plays super well, especially this version with all of its quality of life improvements and snappy combat. It's a game from the 80s in its core so nothing will blow your mind in writing or world building, but that's expected. _childDocuments_.review: This first entry is the simplest form of the Final Fantasy formula. It is, however surprising, still completely recognizable.  The first Final Fantasy already had the white and black mages that will become series staples, as well as an airship, crystals, and ancient technological marvels. The story, as direct and bare-bones as it is, even makes as little sense as the rest of the franchise it would go on to inspire. The updated graphics manage to hold onto the determinedly dated look of a game old enough to run for president while still bringing a brightness and much needed clarity to the original's designs. What doesn't seem to survive the modern refresh, perhaps rightfully so, is the game's intentional obtuseness. Progression can get a little 'How would anyone have figured that out on their own?!' from time to time. But the nonsensical dead-ends in dungeons, which only appear to be there to trap players and compound the already steep cost of constant random battles, are completely thwarted by this version's detailed maps. Quick saves in dungeons and free saves anywhere else likewise prevent a misstep or disastrous encounter from being any more punishing than you'd want it to be. Then there's the bestiary and the chest collection markers stopping the obscure rare spawn or hidden treasure from eluding you undetected...This is certainly a changed, friendlier version of the NES original. After gaining a few levels, even attrition won't trouble you anymore. The game becomes quite easy.  Combat, however, with all its satisfying flash and sense of discovery, stays engaging. And if a particular match up fails to grab you after its 100th appearance, auto-battle will take care of that for you right away. If this remodeled version of Final Fantasy 1 was three times as long, as some later series installments are, it may have worn out its welcome. But as it is, a collection of modern creature comforts with an updated but still nostalgic coat of paint, it's a solidly enjoyable time.

_childDocuments_.review: ✅Music✅D&D-like MP system➖Weak story➖debilitating status effects➖Random battle overloadGame World: Final Fantasy 1 (FF1) takes place on a relatively large map for a game first released in the late 1980s. You have numerous areas to visit on the overmap - towns, caves, and castles, each with their own type of residents - humans, elves, and dwarves. I think by today’s standards the overworld actually still even holds up and is comparable to other modern RPGs like Cat’s Quest in its size. I was thoroughly impressed by how large the world is despite its age. I still managed to find unique areas, some secrets, and various paths to my destination. This is a good world despite its age. Narrative: Surprisingly, the weakest point in FF1’s game is probably the basic and shallow narrative. It plays like a Saturday morning cartoon in its depth and complexity. This is truly a story of good versus evil and not much else at all. Your characters don’t speak and everyone that speaks to you does so in a way as if it was written by a high schooler - they just walk up to you and blurt out their problems and/or information with zero respect for immersion. Another thing too, which is probably more a feature with the games of this era is FF1 definitely does not hold your hand and finding the right NPC to tell you where to go is crazy. There was no real direction so after learning that I needed some random rock in some cave I’ve never been to before really solidified my decision on using a guide. There is no way I’d ever figure this out without a guide lol. I would recommend this guide for anyone starting playing FF1 for the first time: Length: I beat the game in 36 hours, but that was taking my time, doing side stuff, and AFK a couple times. I would say the true length is about 20-25 hrs. Controls: Pretty simple for a NES-based RPG. I played the entire game on my controller and you have the normal 2D overhead controls. No complaints here. Mechanics: Some neat aspects, even by today's standards. So you start off with choosing a class for your characters. A party of 4 and you choose between warrior, monk, thief, red mage, white mage, and black mage. Right away, I love that you have different classes to choose from. The next thing you’ll notice is MP. In other FF games your mana is usually a set number and spells cost a set number. In FF1, it's more like D&D in that you have 8 tiers of spells and can cast a spell a certain amount of times per tier. The last thing I found pretty neat that I want to highlight is how some equippable items have reusable abilities. Later in the game you’ll find things like a staff that casts Fira, or gloves that raise attack. These are reusable and add a type of “Ability” feature to classes that are otherwise one-dimensional. There are definitely some negatives, like how melee classes like warrior and monk have absolutely nothing to do ever but attack, which is nice that they can make use of on-use items, but still, I wish they had some sort of unique active ability. Moving on from characters, the encounter rate seems very excessive. Thankfully you can turn off encounters or enable auto-battling as you will need a ton of fights to grind, but wow, every 10 steps is a new fight, and this wears you down over the course of a dungeon. Difficulty: The enemy AI is absolutely braindead retarded except for the final boss, who is on the opposite end of the spectrum and will wipe the floor with you with his crazy OP spells and high attacks. Enemies that do debilitations like poison are annoying since it doesn’t seem like poison ever wears off and ticks between battles. I found the game generally very easy except for the final boss. Quality: Let's be real, it's based on a 30+ something year old game. You’re not buying FF1 for the graphics and it's not going to deliver anything above SNES quality to you. UI: Basic and dated. The UI has obviously had some quality of life revisions, but this is still 1990’s era boxy UI. Performance: No issues on my PC. i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSDSound Effects: Subpar. The sound effects are also fairly basic and sound like NES sounds. Music: Now we’re talking. The music here is stellar. This has clearly been redone for the newer versions of FF1. Nearly all zones have a great soundtrack. Props to the master, Nobou Uematsu. Aside from achievements, there isn’t much worth replaying. You can grind to kill a monster harder than the final boss. You can also start up a new game as different class combinations. But that’s really it. Ok, so a game from 1989 in 2024? I mean it’s obviously showing its age, but on top all the cracks Square Enix paints a lush coating of varnish. I’m thankful to experience the first game of the series that I enjoy so much on a modern platform. The simplicity is part of the charm here. The feeling that this very path you’re walking in this game is the same path that thousands have walked before you. I don’t mean to get nostalgic here, but to me, that’s the big selling point of playing FF1: like a time capsule game. To experience the beginning of a series that defined a company and a genre. Even not on sale, $12 is respectable. You can find my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: FINAL FANTASY feels like a nostalgic journey from a simpler time with a fresh coat of paint for modern audiences. The game is short and sweet, which is what you'd expect from something originally released so many years ago.The core gameplay is enjoyable, especially with the addition of the auto-battle system which automates some tedious encounters if you know you're going to be using the same commands throughout. The art style and music are perfect for this game without being over-the-top or distracting.I also very much enjoyed that every achievement can be done in one run of the game, which means the game isn't forcing you to go back and replay it once you've completed the adventure for the first time. The replayability comes from wanting to try out different party compositions, especially since there are more than four jobs available for only four party members. Personally, I like being able to 100% a game in a reasonable amount of time and enjoy myself the whole way through, which this game accomplishes.One small gripe I have with this game is that it's a little confusing to know what to do at certain points, which can be frustrating if you haven't picked up the game in a few days and forgot what you were doing during the last play session. I found myself having to seek out a guide every now and then so I didn't keep running around aimlessly.I also found that the game itself is pretty easy, honestly. I was never under-leveled at any point (perhaps from getting lost in the overworld trying to figure out what to do), and was able to purchase anything I wanted for the most part because of how much money you get from battles and chests. There weren't many points where I had to go run around and grind out some cash via random encounters, which was nice but I also would have appreciated if the monsters were turned up just a notch on the difficulty scale to get me sweating a little bit.Overall, I highly recommend this game if you're looking for something simple, nostalgic, and not terribly long. As a fan of the series, it's a cool glimpse into the origins of all the jobs, monsters, and other themes that FINAL FANTASY is known for.

_childDocuments_.review: Great updated sound and graphics. Unfortunately, this is not an exact copy of the original version of the game. There were minor differences that affected strategic key elements of how the original was played. For example, specific treasure chests don't contain certain major key items  (ie. swords, armor) have been changed and have been replaced with healing potions and gold. Another example is places where certain enemies found in certain locations have been changed. These locations were strategic in the original for leveling up characters before a big encounter or moving on to harder areas.  Although minor, it does affect the game play to a degree that hardcore FF fans will notice. This version also seems to be way less challenging, as if the level of difficulty has been reduced to reach, almost effortlessly, key points in the game. All in all, It is a good introduction to the original FF , but not an exact remake.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game exclusively if you have never played the original, and simply love Final Fantasy and want to experience it. That being said, this remaster bears very little resemblance to the original game: new graphics, new audio. That and there have been key changes in gameplay over the years that dictate how the play plays the game: the original is about managing very limited resources, the remasters and remakes over the year have stripped this out, removed all the difficulty from the game, made the rewards larger, the loot tables no longer make sense (you'll be looting clothes from guarded chests 10+ hours into the game at Ice Caverns and the Zeus Gauntlets were replaced by a potion like 2/3's through the game lol). The original game didn't have hard combat, it was about exploring dangerous dungeons, figuring out what you needed, then buying it and hoping you had enough to last the dungeon. You needed to know which enemies to fight and which ones to run away from. A bad ambush at any time could wipe your entire party or drain your resources to the point you couldn't get out of the dungeon, or you couldn't reach the end. That's all gone. You've got a mini map. Enemies are not very threatening. Frequency of combat is still very high so you will end up extremely overlevelled and with tons of cash so item management stops being a problem within the first few hours.With these changes in mind, what Final Fantasy is: is a game that kinda looks like FF1 and sounds kinda like FF1, but doesn't play like FF1. It's an auto-battler where you walk from point A to B. The autobattle will set the only commands you ever need to loop infinitely: attack, as you are slowed down by a battle every 2 seconds by mobs that will never threaten you.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: FF1 is a good game, but it's very simple, so just know that before you play it. The story is super light, characters are minimal, and the combat doesn't get very advanced. That said, it's fun to play, and you never feel like you have to grind. Also, the music is fantastic, as you'd expect from a Final Fantasy game. It's hard to know what to do at times, but that is to be expected from such an old game. I recommend using a guide if you get stuck. Sometimes, what you to do can be a bit strange. Other than that, I really like all the modern touching up they've done. It looks good, sounds good, you can speed up combat, auto battle, use a CRT filter if you want and so on. It's a fun little adventure where you can see how the series started. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good remaster of the NES original, however if you are specifically looking to just play FF1 and you aren't looking to get the Pixel Remaster bundle I would advise against it. The PSP and GBA versions of this game have additional content and I think are the better versions if you just want to play FF1. This is still a very good remaster, the new music is excellent and the new over world textures (for the most part) are spectacular. Very useful auto battle feature to mow through the hordes of endless random encounters. If you're looking for a challenge though, I would steer clear. FF1 isn't typically a crazy hard game outside of the original NES version but I have had the least amount of trouble on this version. There aren't any game breaking glitches as far as I'm aware that make you overpowered like in other versions but the game itself just seems to be much easier than it was before.6.5/10. It's a classic. If you like old school RPGs or want to see how Final Fantasy got it's start then give it a shot. There's not much story here but the game play loop is satisfying enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a new player to the saga, I had never played the Final Fantasy series but being so well known and seeing so many people who liked it, I decided to start with the first game in my adult age.In general I liked the game, the style it has is already known to me from other 2D pixel type games and the gameplay is similar to Dragon Quest, the only game I've played from the genre.In the graphic section, the maps are quite basic but varied, especially I liked that the backgrounds vary in each battle scene, which are quite well designed and combine very well with the scenarios to create a good atmosphere. The rest of the graphics have nothing remarkable, but they do their job.The soundtrack is undoubtedly the best part, at least for me, very well achieved and they made a good decision when it came to making it orchestrated and not 8bit style, since a game as famous as this one deserves this effort. It has as an extra, a player where you can play all the music. Definitely epic and good themes.The story is very basic, everything develops from talking to the characters, although that gives little depth to it, so you have to talk a lot so it doesn't have much more, although of course, since it's a game so old it is normal for this aspect to be like this. The end is somewhat far-fetched for such little explanation to the rest of the adventure and if you want to understand it well, it requires too much personal research.The characters are selectable and this is an aspect that I really liked, since it gives the game replayability, however they don't have any depth or feelings, so it doesn't allow you to identify with any of them or understand them.The gameplay is normal, without standing out in any way. A basic turn-based combat that has the possibility of automatic combat, which is appreciated since there are many battles. In fact, so many battles get a bit tiring, since when it comes to exploring it's fine but if you want to advance in the story you have to talk to different people and in different cities and you can't go from one to another directly (at least at the beginning), so you have to do meaningless battles of which there are many. In that aspect the game becomes heavy and boring, although I suppose that is the concept of these games and if I want to play more of these I will have to get used to it. In the dungeons there is a lot to explore but also pointless since there is a map that tells you where the treasures are and the path to follow, so it doesn't make sense to explore much (I suppose there was no map in the original game).Lastly, on the issue of difficulty, the game was not difficult for me, the battles were easy even in automatic mode (except for some bosses) and I had no problems, although for some people it may be a problem since there is no challenge in the game . However the last boss was too hard, he kept healing himself and I beat him at the end by chance. I don't see the point in having the rest of the game so easy and the last boss so hard, the normal thing would have been a normal level progression forcing the player to level up as more difficult bosses are encountered.In conclusion, a small and simple game, I have enjoyed it except for some monotonous, unfair or boring parts, with a good balance and a good introduction to the genre. It took me about 12 hours to do the main story, there are also no side quests other than the achievements or the bestiary. Now I will play Final Fantasy II in its version also of Pixel Remaster, apparently the most up-to-date.For everything, I give it a score of 6.5 / 10.

Some gripes that I had were that the game felt much too easy after a certain point, with some notable exceptions being the Tiamat, War Mech, and Chaos boss battles in particular. _childDocuments_.review: I've played this game quite a few times. Last year I've tried out the GBA version, and now I've gotten to the Pixel Remaster - the latest attempt of Square Enix to rerelease the original anthology of 2D games, after some ok and some not-so-good attempts.I think FF1 is still a good game. The NES version is perhaps a little too dated to be enjoyed, but I don't think this remake is completely perfect. While the style is suitable and cute, I find that it lacks some stranger visions of the original game, and with, strangely, no option to turn on the original style, it's a little bit of a bummer that the original game's atmosphere has been just kind of forgotten through the years.While the game barely has story, it was always funny to me that Final Fantasy has been wild from the beginning, with mechs and inexplicable plot twists sending games off the rails in the final act. Hell, you basically complete the entirety of Dragon Quest's story in the first 20 minutes.You play as a party of four unnamed characters who you can name anything you want, and you can give them any job you want. I usually go with simple Warrior-Thief-Two Mages, but this time I tried out a Monk instead of a Thief. He kinda sucked, wouldn't recommend. In general, I feel like Warrior received the most care from any melee fighters due to sheer amount of equipment. The Mages only don't seem as underdeveloped due to a fairly unique magic system where for each level of spell you can choose what spells to learn (or, well, just buy). There are 4 spells available for each level but only three slots, which provides some further freedom.Battles in the remake remove the penalty for constantly attacking one enemy where, if they were to die, other party members would keep attacking them on their turn. Along with that a number of boosts (read cheat codes) and a fast forward/auto battle mode have been added. While I think an option for original battle mode could've been made, fast forward is a nice addition since the bestiary of this game is lacking. Most diverse enemies are all in dungeons, so while you're adventuring out on the overworld you'll be constantly harassed by packs of dogs of each color of the rainbow, and it's a blessing to be able to kill them faster. It's not a hard game, but due to the fact that you can encounter up to 9 enemies in each fight means fights that are easy can be LONG.I don't think the pacing of the game is the best, asking you to go back to some places and oftentimes not being clear about what to do in the backhalf, but the exploration is neat thanks to all dungeons feeling different. Only one of them is a fairly featureless cave! Another new feature that helps here is the map. You always have a mini-map, and can also open a large map of a room at any given point, which kind of defeats the purpose of exploring the dungeon and remembering stuff, since everything including chests is marked.I've played with the original BGM but have listened to new arrangements, which are nice! I think FF1 still has some boppin' tunes like the town and the battle theme. As I've mentioned, it's a shame you can't play with original visuals. Some of the enemy sprites were charming and the battle void was weird. FF1 was a strange game and I don't particularly like that instead of keeping some strange elements, it was remade to be just like every other game.Still, it's a cool remake, and if you want to play the game, well worth playing. New options can help to aliviate some grinding and tons of enemy encounters, since you can not only boost EXP/Gil but turn them off for a while completely. I've played around with them around the Tiamat fight and wouldn't really recommend the boosts in particular since the game just gets boring if made easier. I've still had a fun time 100%ing it, but it left me wanting something a bit closer to the original experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get this straight; this game is NOT mind bendingly hard like the NES version was (or so they say; I missed out on that one). I wish it was a little harder because battles are trivial but I'm glad it's not as hard as the original; grinding all day is not fun!The graphics are nice, reminiscent of the SNES - not too fancy, but a definite step up from the original game. Music is awesome. There's now an actual boss fight theme, separate from the main battle theme!The story of the game is pretty simple but it does have some wibbly wobbly timey wimey stuff at the end that must have been mind blowing back in the 80s.The credits I swear are stuck in the same timey wimey stuff because they go on forever!Pro tip: if there is a castle with a town next to it, you can go into both separately. _childDocuments_.review: After beating the very last boss of the game with; a Warrior/Knight, a Thief/Ninja, a White-Mage/White-Wizard, and a Black-Mage/Black-Wizard. (Yes, there are 6 classes to choose from for a party of 4 in this game. Monk/Master and Red-Mage/Red-Wizard are the other 2.) ((You get to name your characters and go with any combination/battle-order you desire. So you could go 2 Warriors/Knights with 2 Red-Mages/Red-Wizards, for example.)) The game took me about 26 hours to beat, because I think it records your hours while the game's paused. It's a turn taking game but easily as fun as any of the first Pokemon titles for Nintendo's Game-Boy/Game-Boy-Colour portable gaming consoles. I beat the last boss of the game with great difficulty. I actually walked away thinking it was practically unbeatable until I figured out the use of the 'Temper' spell being used on my fighters over and over, increasing the magical damage every time; and the Warrior/Knight and the Thief/Ninja needed to be under the haste spell, but only casted once for each of them. It might sound like bull s*** but I swear to you that I killed the last boss in the game. You want your whole party to be around level 50, by the way. Flying the airship is a trip, I love how fast and productive that thing is, you never bump into enemies.. There's a lot of secrets in this game, just to proceed, it's quite a memory-based puzzle game. It's also an extremely great game for improving your arithmetic skills. A lot of people think that turn taking games are bogus but I love them for the fact that it's more fun and relaxing than doing absolutely nothing or staring at walls; most of the time. You feel rewarded by this game through your amount of work that you've put in. You don't find reward in being super fast or attentive; this game completely lets you play at any pace. You can be just learning what video games are and this would be a great game. This is also a great game for someone who's learning to read. You don't need to play fast to win, you just need to have done a lot of thinking. And you have to read to progress in the game; plus, often you may get lost and do a lot of circles trying to figure out where to go next. Anyway, I give this game a 10/10 rating. I recommend it to any retro gaming fans. Thank you very much for reading this, take care, have a great time, and good bye for now.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-  Many of us have fond memories of playing early pixel RPGs, and indeed nostalgia may or may not be a large reason behind why you're here in the first place! The remastered art in this edition captures the simple but appealing attraction of the original games, with all of the colour and detail available to technology today. Note: I've seen a few reviews complain about the frame rate of this edition. I didn't find this an issue, bar a second before random encounters when the game would stutter briefly. It didn't change the handling of the overall experience, but it did feel like a warning that a battle was coming!-  Though at times repetitive (I'll get to that more shortly), the  soundtrack is immersive and catchy. Seriously, it'll be stuck as your very own internal BGM for the rest of the day. Like the pixel graphics, the remastered arrangement takes the original 8-bit music and gives it a lick of fully-orchestrated paint. The BGM arrangements walking around dungeons later in the game are increasingly tense (and stunning), -  As with many RPGs,  can be played with either brute force (read: grinding too many levels) or careful strategy. It's extremely satisfying figuring out plans for your team of heroes, choosing which spells to learn, and which armour enchants to cast. Many enemies have specific resistances and weaknesses, so it feels like an adventure (either in-game or on wiki!) to learn. -  While the story isn't groundbreaking or packed full of intricate layers, it  set up so that multiple playthroughs feel lore friendly, so it's not as jarring reappearing back at the start if you choose. Plus, you can have plenty of fun doing challenges like the White Mage Party challenge. (Speaking of which, choosing your own party at the beginning leaves a lot of room to experiment with different builds and job dynamics!) Cons:-  While I said the game is replayable — that's only if you can endure random encounters every few steps of the world map () and in dungeons. Thankfully, the remastered edition adds the 'auto battle' function, so you can easily fast forward overworld battles (though you'll want to watch you don't do this anywhere that difficult monsters can appear). So, if you're not a fan of random encounter games, this mightn't be the one for you. -  Though the music in towns, boss battles, and dungeons is stellar, every random encounter plays the same battle music. After a 10 - 20 hour long play through, this becomes tedious. Why does the same battle music that plays near the first town also play for encounters in the final dungeon? It feels jarring. Similarly, the pause menu interrupts whatever the BGM is in your current location to play something else.-  To me, this is equal parts pro and con. If you're getting tired of open world games with never ending 700 hour stories that you can't possibly hope to complete within the next year, then this will be a great change of pace. However, don't go searching for a ground breaking story here because you'll likely be disappointed. For one, the team you start and play through with have no lines or connection to the world bar being the 'warriors of light', so it might be hard to feel attached to them based on story alone. That said, personally, I found (what we now recognise as) the classic FF 'warriors and crystals of light' story charming — particularly given that the lack of any questing system forces the player to search for the story threads through organic[ish] conversation in towns. But if you're looking for onion like layers of story, this likely won't be for you either. Conclusion:

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Autocombat, fast forward, and best music so farMultiplayer: NoCompletion: 9 hrs (with previous experience)Cards: Yes | Cloud: YesFinal Fantasy Pixel Remaster is yet another remake of the first game released in 1987. The world is going to ruin, and a prophecy foretells of four warriors each bearing a crystal who will save the land. While it's a JRPG in every sense, I prefer to think of the game as an overhead dungeon crawler, as you delve into various dungeons, making multiple trips to get further each time using a party of your own design. The plot is really just an excuse to rob all dungeons blind, as the game is from an era where it was rather difficult to tell a meaningful story.This particular remake is close to the Playstation version with a few tweaks from other games as well. The difficulty is akin to the easy mode of the Playstation version. Leveling is several times faster, while items are much cheaper. Dead enemies are untargetable the moment they die, item shops have a greatly expanded inventory including inexpensive ethers that let you cast to your heart's content. Characters don't have limited inventory space, and you can use items such as phoenix down in combat. I believe this version uses a buffed thief, as this one kept pace on damage, though their mitigation is still terrible until later on.A number of changes are in place as well. For one, you can walk diagonally! There are no monster tiles any more, which always guaranteed an encounter when stepped on. Instead they have been replaced with monsters in chests and an occasional monster guard that you can see on the main screen. There are also some new monster configurations such as being able to combat 6 ogres at once. While the 15 puzzle minigame makes its return, there appears to be no reward whatsoever for completing it. The intelligence stat now influences spell damage in a significant way, making black mage into a powerhouse nuker, and this also affects the output of spells cast from items. Unfortunately red mage seems to have suffered, as I now have trouble one-shotting, sometimes even needing three castings to kill a mob with spells.One very welcome feature is the autobattle. Once activated, your characters will "mimic" the last command inputted for them, and the game will go into fast forward mode. This allows for some cool tricks like spamming heal staff or gauntlet every round without any further input from you. Another very useful feature is the in-game map. While in a dungeon, you can scroll around the map to see the layout of the entire floor, so it is much harder to get lost now. Furthermore, as long as you are inside a room, the map will reveal all chests on the floor, making item collection much easier.The graphics are okay. I actually prefer the PSX or PSP artwork, and the sprites need higher contrast shading in my opinion. The font choice could be better as it looks squished. The randomized name selection is severely limited, I'd actually prefer a completely random name like Jaquhi or something. As cool as the cutscenes and end credits are, a skip function is desperately needed. The game could also use an encounter rate slider, as it got tedious having to mow down stuff after a while, especially when sailing. Finally, there's no RL+Sel+Start shortcut to reset the game. The closest thing is to access the configuration menu to reset to title, but I'd rather be able to reset in the middle of combat as well.The music is another beast altogether. It's an amazing soundtrack that has no right to be as good as it is. It borrows heavily from the already excellent PSX music, but manages to improve upon it even further which I didn't think possible. The game also comes with a free "DLC: OST & Wallpaper". Don't be fooled by "OST" descriptor, all it is is three modified mp3s stored in the game's installed directory. I have not experienced crashes, but I have seen a bug, such as how using quick save will default your normal save selection to the first slot. This may cause the player to accidently overwrite the first slot unintentionally. For the life of me I do not know why filling the bestiary is a requirement for 100% completion. This means having to seek out Warmech, with its abysmal encounter rate. I counted, and it took me around 80 battles to finally run into it, having started at level 50 and ending at level 62.I rate Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster a B+. Despite the flaws I always have fun speeding through the game. I grew up on Final Fantasy, and played a bunch of the remakes over the years, so there's definitely some bias here. If you are new to Final Fantasy this is an okay place to start, but be prepared for a lack of hand holding or proper guidance. I am a little baffled at the lack of a randomizer function. It would have been the perfect opportunity to cash in on the randomizer crowd, as that is arguably the most popular way to play the game these days.Edit: Nominating for best soundtrack 2021
