_childDocuments_.review: I was not expecting this game to be as good as it was. A truly open world RPG originating on the NES!!! Amazing story, classic gameplay, and a proper remaster done with care.I got my start in Final Fantasy with FF7 on the PS1, and I played through FFX. Prior to now FF7 was the only one I had beat. I must say it was a joy from start to finish, and am looking forward to playing through the rest of the franchise (all the non-MMO ones anyway).The story is classic fantasy where you play as a party of heroes (that you get to pick classes for btw), who are tasked with saving the world by restoring the light to the 4 elemental crystals throughout. These have been drained by Fiends that you must defeat. The map is decently sized with a fair amount of locations to travel to and explore. You find your way to the various towns, villages, and dungeons defeating foes in classic turn based combat. Levelling felt really good to me. I didn't really have to XP farm as I ended the game at level 47, and I just played through the story. I spent some time collecting treasure, and filling out the bestiary but I did not go out of my way too much. There are a lot of items to find in the world and if you take time in the last few dungeons you'll get the most powerful weapons and armor for the final dungeon and boss. Probably not necessary, but felt worthwhile to me. I played as the warrior, black mage, white mage, and thief, and the party felt very well balanced. The only drawback for me personally was it was not always clear where you were supposed to go next or what you were missing. It seemed like the devs wanted you to explore and talk to EVERY NPC to find all the clues for where to go, but it was tedious. I did have to look up what to do a couple times between major locations.I played this entirely on Steam Deck and it ran flawlessly. 60hz/60fps and didn't break a sweat (not surprising, but still nice). I had 0 crashes or frame dips. The deck is tailored for this kind of experience. It took me about 15.5 hours to complete.Overall, I was VERY pleasantly surprised by how solid this game was. The story, gameplay, progression, combat, and exploration felt unbelievably balanced and fun. My only real complaint was the lack of direction at times, but as long as you talk to everyone and take note of certain conversations you won't need any guide to complete this one.

_childDocuments_.review: A great way to experience one of the foundational RPGs in a modern context. _childDocuments_.review: Despite the fact that this version of Final Fantasy does not include the bonus content from the Dawn of Souls and 20th Anniversary edition releases, this is, in my opinion, the definitive version of Final Fantasy I. This remaster is a delightful blend of preserving so much of what was in the original NES/Famicom release, such as the designs of the character and monster sprites and the spell charge system, while also introducing convenience features and quality of life enhancements that were either in few or none of the previous versions, such as Ethers and Phoenix Downs, the Quick Save, which grants you 1 universal save slot that can be made even inside of dungeons, or the lovely item collection tracker that shows you how many items and chests you've acquired in each town and dungeon.This version isn't without its downsides, of course. The bestiary, while helpful, cannot be accessed while you're actually playing the game, and instead may only be accessed from the title screen, and the difficulty still spikes in places like the Marsh Cave, but between an absolutely beautiful new arrangement of the soundtrack, pleasantly revised, yet faithful graphics, snappy pacing to combat, and a number of helpful features like auto-battle and Quick Save, this is the most accessible the original Final Fantasy has ever been, and after all these years, it's still a charming game that offers an adventure in a world totally unlike that of any entry in the series since.

_childDocuments_.review: Initial thoughts after playing for 30 minutes and reaching Elf Town. Edit after 100% Achievements: Still holds up. 10/10 would buy again. So max level looks to be 100, The level up screen is lovely and does a great job showing what you gained.Uses the "old" spell system, no MP.(WOOT)More items in the item shop. Remedy , Hi Potions, and more are available from the start.Weapons and armor stats more easily displayed.8 direction movement.Sounds great, and font/text is easy to read on a 42 inch screen.Auto-battle can be set to continue through and remembers the commands you issued. So once you get items that can be used in combat, this will be great. Early on, if you use spells, it targets the caster/random enemy. Maps everywhere. There is a world mini map, a larger world map, and dungeon maps. All are beautiful. "Dancing Girl" in the first town will give you reminders of where to go next. Nice if you take a long break. CONSFeels easier(I think this is due to the level revamp)Most "cut scenes" are unskippable. So you have to watch the bridge being build, the opening scroll when you make it to the bridge, etc.Silver sword is not available in elf town(matches the GBA versions).No option to auto run in town, you have to hold the button. Churches are not marked on the mini map(other shops are).Peninsula of Power appears to have been fixed.(Removed)"Fixed" battles(like the wizards guarding the crown) now trigger when you open the chest and cant be repeated. EDIT: It looks like this is half true. There are purple robed NPC in the areas of "fixed" battles that you can talk to and get a battle with the mobs(wizards in the marsh cave for example). They respawn when you leave the screen, so its still POSSIBLE to redo some battles, but not as easy. The Giant hallway works the same way with 2 robed figures for battles then you have to zone out. Still a CON but not as bad. Auto equip for the monk STILL thinks weapons are best, after about level 5 they NEVER are. Overall it feels like a great way to play this classic. The game is challenging and a bit grindy until the first crystal is saved. Afterward, things became smoother, gil was plentiful, and my party members rarely, if ever, died. _childDocuments_.review: I have played every version of FFI that's been officially released in English, and I have to say that this doesn't feel like a "remaster". Perhaps it's the fact that I've bought every version of this game you've tried to sell me, or maybe it's the fact that this version of the game is even easier than the Dawn of Souls version on GBA. At first, I didn't think much of the difficulty, but it wasn't until I arrived in Melmond that I noticed the ability to purchase Ethers. Considering later on you'll be doing so much grinding that you'll have mountains of money, and the fact that in this game, Ethers cost the same amount as a Hi-Potion... that breaks the difficulty so much. What's the point of giving us 9 casts per level if it's cheap and easy to refill the MP? Phoenix Downs are cheap, too. What made the original game so difficult was the limited items and magic, so the player had to be very strategic and try to make it through a whole challenging dungeon. I wholeheartedly thought that this version was going to be on the level of the NES in difficulty, or maybe even the PSX version on normal, but I didn't get that from the Pixel Remaster. I still had fun playing it even with the difficulty being so off, though, so make of that what you will.I also feel as if the stat balancing between the six playable character classes has been... pretty weird. I don't remember White Mage EVER having more HP than a BlackBelt/Monk in any version before. As in, her HP growth almost kept up with the Fighter's! Was not expecting that! Wasn't complaining, either...The music is fantastic and well worth the price of admission, though. The OST for the NES version is classic stuff, and this version's take is... *chef's kiss* The pixel art looks great, and I love the spell effects and battle transitions. I just really appreciate the total aesthetic for Final Fantasy. This is my favorite presentation of the game thus far, even if I miss the revamped character designs featured in Dawn of Souls. The way it looks, feels, and sounds are certainly worthy of the monkier of 'Remaster'!

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy for the NES was the second game I ever owned or played, so it's fair to say it holds a special place in my heart.  I've played this game many, many, many times: Dawn of Souls on GBA, the Wonderswan remake, the Anniversary Edition and yes, even the mobile abortion.  This port is a weird amalgamation: it lacks the bonus content from Dawn of Souls and 30th Anniversary but retains the cut scenes, it uses the original magic charge system but retains the easy mode difficulty and inventory system, it also seems to have pixel art done in at least three different styles.  It's a right pick and mix of improvements is what I'm getting at, and not only has Square done better, fans have done better.That, of course, is the turbo nerd talking.  Does Final Fantasy hold up in the modern age?  More specifically, is this an RPG you want to spend $10 on?  Well, I can at least attest that the changes make it a bit more accessible overall and it is a pretty simple game.  That's kind of why I like it.  I can speed run the GBA version in under three hours, and it's fair to say it isn't wasting your time.  This version has several QoL features like diagonal movement, quick leveling and fast battles which makes me excited to see what real speedruns will do.  That said, whatever this game did back then has been done better later on.  If you aren't nostalgic for this game specifically I can't see it appealing to anything other than hardcore RPG nerds looking to plow through another one.I'm not going to pretend this version is bad, it's playable and it's Final Fantasy.  However, it's not faithful enough to the original for me to recommend it for nostalgia seekers or people who want to see where it started, and it's missing a bunch of bonus content from later ports to justify it for fans who want another reason to run through it.  As a replacement for the god awful mobile ports these *are* quite a bit better, and it's nice to have Final Fantasy officially on PC, but if you want to play the original game with a modern flare I'd recommend an emulator and either the FF Randomizer or Dawn of Souls.  Otherwise this seems like a game for speed runners and turbo nerds only.

_childDocuments_.review: It's the first Final Fantasy game, that should be the main explanation and should summarize the game analysis by default.So, let's dive into details. If you came here after playing ANY other Final Fantasy game, or any J-RPG launched after this game, you need to adapt your expectations before playing this game. Many of the mechanics you'll see in other Final Fantasy games, or even in Lufia, Terranigma, Chrono Trigger and Dragon Quest titles aren't exactly here. So, to get down on business:- Please let me remind you that the original game is .  old. This means that the graphics you'll see here are mainly based on the Game Boy Advance remake, with a tweak here and there. And even this GBA remake had to redraw much of the original game, giving you the feeling that you're playing an RPG Maker title, instead of an commercial released game. If you cannot understand this, or if you have problems with the (outdated) graphics, then this game is not for you;- The main characters are <Insert Your Name Here> times four. The names you place ain't relevant, won't be mentioned by any NPC and they are the "silent protagonist" type of character. Since there's no character development at all, some people might also dislike this;- There are no status effects that progress after the battle. Items that counter status effects are to be used within the battle;- The experience grind is there if you wish, but after the latest patch, you can easily improve your EXP rate and play it without much grinding at all. Money can be also irrelevant should you wish to raise the money drop rate;- The story progresses in a manner that  or else you'll be stuck very early in the game. NPC's have bits of information that you'll need. Don't let anyone go without squeezing their intel;- This game offers some sidequests, but you must pay attention to find them. As said earlier,  to find them;- You can achieve everything in this game in a single run, without concerns about places that you can't go. For the overachievers, there's very little that requires RNG to be your guide.In the end, my gaming thoughts about this one. I've played the NES version back in the day, and the GBA version years later. There are a few things that there are in the GBA version that weren't placed in this version, nor are the FMV's of the original Playstation version. Maybe they'll add those in an later update? But even without those extra stuff, the gameplay is solid and a must if you're a fan of the series.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Beat the game in about 7 hours.  at just under 10 hours, I'm 2 monsters short of completing the bestiary and unlocking all achievements. Ive played every FF1 that has been release, except the mobile ports.Pros - Pretty much the original game with a few QoL changes like Hi-Potions and Ethers.  Uses the OG magic system, so no MP.  Leveling and gil seems... streamlined.  The game is faster overall, and not because the content has been cut - its all there.  Significantly less time buying mass amounts of items like potions, since you can buy more than 1 at a time - a feature that did not exist in the OG.  I distinctly remember being 5 or 6 years old, spending what felt like an hour buying 99 antidotes one at a time.  Cons - Not really a con, more of a odd feeling based off nostalgia glasses. The game FEELS easier.  It isn't...  Just that leveling up feels faster because of the auto battle system.  Less time grinding means that its easier to be over leveled by the time you get to the next dungeon.  Did notice that windowed borderless would be remembered in settings between game launches, but would not launch in windowed borderless and had to be reset in settings every time.Overall - fantastic recreation of the game.  I personally did not have any major issues and had no issue with the fonts.  Game is faster due to modern QoL features/changes, but otherwise is as I recall the old NES cart version.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: And so it begins. The origins of one of the most popular Japanese RPG franchises. Overall very impressed with this instalment. It’s not the longest and most complex of the Final Fantasy games by a long shot. But it’s a short, fun romp with some nice bosses and artwork. The music is fantastic, I was really impressed with what they have done with the soundtrack here. The graphics were fine, had the odd issues with a bit of stutter here and there while scrolling about, but this didn’t really affect my enjoyment of the game. The font wasn’t great, but I played a little bit on steamlink to my phone and can see why they maybe went with that option. In comparison to the original game or the version on the PlayStation it did feel quite a bit easier overall, but most of this was probably for quality of life reasons. I’m looking forward to continuing my playthrough with Final Fantasy II.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a lot of FF14 and at some point just got curious about the other games. Had a quick look and started with the first game in the series. While the game is a bit simple and grindy from time to time it was really fun. I discovered about 2/3 through the game that some items have on use effects which spiced things up a lot and made me approach situations differently. Suddenly my monk was the parties healer while going from point A to B. I really enjoyed it. I found the game to be not really difficult and the story was also not really present.. I think. But I had a lot of fun playing be it as my main game or as a side game on my second monitor. Cannot wait to tackle FF2!Ps. A walkthrough guide is recommended if you don't feel like exploring a lot and keeping track of npc tips!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: It's a strange mix of the original FF1 with some modern elements - you can enter shops/buildings and walk around, each party member starts with some basic eq, bugs seem to be fixed, each area has a nice map, which shows you where the shops are located. You can also enable a CRT Scanline mode in the options (which is meh, install Reshade if you want to customise something better).Magic users use the old vancian magic system, instead of Magic Points, like in later FF games.An intro explaining the backstory, which was not present in the original, was added.Some quality of life changes have also been added. For example, a guard blocks the gate of Corneria, if you try to leave it for the first time and he takes you to the castle. This way new players won't be confused and won't miss talking with the king, who explains that you need to find Sarah and kill Garland.Battles are faster and smoother. The various jobs also seem to be rebalanced (I think the Thief got a slight buff for example). You can also enable an auto-battle mode, to quickly deal with grinding or low-level mobs.The new music is fantastic. Probably the best part of the remaster.Beware of the last battle with Chaos - his Curaja spell has been fixed, and it now heals him 9999 HP instead of 999. He can be now really tough, if you don't have a high dmg party. The Caravan where you buy the fairy in the bottle was changed to the GBA version, and if you talk to the trader again, he will sell you some useful tonics, if you have problems.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: I always wanted to play all the FF games in order and I can confidently say Im glad I choose this version to start off the series with. I truly belive this is the best way to experience the original final fantasy game without some of the tedious things the origonal game brought. The small quality of life changes that they put into this game with simple things such as a map really makes this game 10 million times more fun then if they just updated the graphics and music and called it a day. You still have to deal with constant random encounters and the aggravation of trying to figure out what to do next sometiems,  But to me thats just the charm of the first game of this huge series. I truly recommend this game to everyone who is curious on how this awsome franchise gained it start. There's a reason this game was a national hit when it first came out
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: After 3-4 years of being out on Steam, they finally brought the console features to PC, so you don't have to deal with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ font anymore. Barring the extra content from previous remasters/remakes, this is probably the definitive version to play indeed. The characters look sharp and the music rearrangement is great.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: This game was absolute blast to play with hours of content. Fans seem to be divisive with the art style, but I'm personally a fan. The pixel art is very clearly retro in terms of the pixel count, but a bit more modern with the color palettes since softer gradients are used. Specifically, this isn't a more paint brushed style like the PSP version, but it also doesn't have the more restricted contrasting color palette like the GBA. I would recommend this game to...There are some criticisms that I have of this title though.Some nice have feature requests...
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: The remaster does a good job of re-experiencing the game. The difficulty is toned down such that you can just focus on the story and mechanics if you're new to the genre. As a long time fan, i still enjoyed it because i never found the original to be particularly hard anyways. All the QoL boosts like having a map showing the rough location of missed monsters or chests, are fantastic. You don't need to necessarily follow a 100% guide to point yourself in the right direction. Also the music is wonderful, of course!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: There is something about playing a game like this that makes you realize how special games were back then. Open world RPG, create your own character, and enjoy a story where you can literally change the names of the characters to yourself and your friends. You were the heroes or heroines. You could make the game as challenging or as easy as you wanted. Oh,  what's that? Elden RIng does that too? Know your place boy, and understand the shoulders on which Elden Ring and all RPGs stand on. 10 out of 10.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: As a long-time FF fan it was really nice to see where some of the franchise's recurring elements begun and the influence of D&D on early FF. The fast-forward feature for the fights is an excellent quality of life upgrade, especially considering the fights here are a bit less interesting compared to the other FF titles (less unique abilities, mostly Attacking and Magic Casting). Overall great game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: for first impressions from someone who's played the original NES game and the GBA remake, this is competent and worth the price, especially as an entry point for newcomers who want to get into the classics.the only thing i have mixed feelings on is the rebalance; not counting that the game moves at an incredibly faster speed than both the NES and GBA versions, regular stat values have been adjusted to reduce the difficulty and cut down on grind, which was the appeal for the original games for me. i remember it taking me up to 2-3 hours to reach the elven town during all my playthroughs, and in this remaster i arrived there in under 45 minutes. while i think the difficulty cut was necessary to appeal to more audiences i also think when you take away the grind there's not much to experience other than a rapid-fire journey, gunning it from town to town and obliterating mobs with little strategy. this can definitely benefit the longer, story-driven later titles like 3-6 but for 1 and 2 where the questin' is pretty much the whole game it very much trivializes it. i can, at the very least, hope for a mod along the way that implements the original values and gives the game its original difficulty. i am a complete classic final fantasy sucker so despite this issue i still find the gameplay satisfying, as it is still the original game at heart, and while the pacing may be broken a bit, it still has the sense of adventure that always has me coming back. also please add sound options and v-sync
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first time playing through Final Fantasy 1, and I have to say that I am quite pleased with it-...Although the level up pacing felt a little slow, the story wasn't that great, but I could feel the strong sense of adventure that someone who was playing this for the first time at the time of its release could feel. It felt nice to play an original classic remastered for my own eyes, and it seems to be relatively faithful to the original.  ultimately though, the game pacing was alright, I spent a lot of hours in the game, and with this remake, it allows you to save after beating the final boss unlike many games like it. So it was a fun play- I did get confused as to where to go, even after reading the story, but I had a fun play through of this game.I am hoping to play all of the games in order and beat them, and I will rank them here.So far1st Place - Final Fantasy 1
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Playing through Final Fantasy I again was so nostalgic for me so many great memories.This version of Final Fantasy I is great if you like the NES version, I do, so I really enjoyed it, there are no bonus dungeons or any extra content from the PSP version, you are just going to get the original NES version. It's not a bad thing but it would have been nice to see the bonus stuff here. But besides that I had a lot of fun with the pixel remaster it's a good package the graphics are great and the gameplay is good like always.So do I recommend it? Yes if you like the original Final Fantasy, you'll have trip down memory lane like I did.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty much what it says on the tin. This is a remaster of the original Final Fantasy with pixel graphics. The graphics themselves haven't even changed all that much, and seem to be based on the original pixel art, which is an aesthetic I can appreciate far better than the PSP version's graphics which always seemed a bit off to my eyes. The only complaint I really have is that the default font for English is weird and narrow for no good reason. Luckily there's a fix for it where you can swap some font files around in the game directory and it works like a charm. If you're one of the people who prefers the PSP/GBA remakes, you'll likely be disappointed here. The extra dungeons are not present, and the magic system uses spell slots instead of an MP pool. The cute little cutscenes from the PSP/GBA/PSX versions made it in, though. Overall, this shouldn't be considered the 'definitive' edition, more of a nice and simple update to the old school original.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best version because you can MOD it.  It's that simple.  Prefer the old graphics and music - easily modded in with a few mods.  Want the NES or PSX difficulty - there is a mod for it.  Want it harder than any of the previous versions - there is a "challenging" option in that same mod.  Want the missing additional content from the GBA/PSX versions - there is a mod doing just that. I played the original with my buddy on his couch when we were in Primary school.  I've also tried the GBA and PSP versions.  I tried the 8-bit mods and they are well done, but honestly prefer the updated music and the Magicite sprites (GBA/PSP versions).  I can cater my current play-through to look and sound exactly the way I want on PC with this version. Nostalgia tells me that I had more fun with my friend when we were kids, but the reality is the QoL changes in this version are way better than nostalgia-colored glasses.  But you can have it your way no matter what with this version.

_childDocuments_.review: In FINAL FANTASY, the tale begins when four young warriors, each possessing a Crystal, are summoned to bring the world back to a harmonious elemental balance. During their voyage, they discover a nefarious entity has created turmoil in the structure of time in order to take control of the world, causing the heroes to travel to places they never imagined possible. This all-new anniversary edition contain the best treatment of the classic RPG and features all-new character art, updated graphics, new dungeons, full 16:9 widescreen presentation and an updated camera view that gives players a new vantage point. [Square Enix]

name: FINAL FANTASY II
detailed_description: FINAL FANTASY I-VI Bundle Purchase the bundle now to receive all soundtracks and wallpapers from FF1-6! Soundtracks and Wallpapers will unlock in line with each title’s launch. See individual store pages for details. The games that inspired a generation come to life once more, in the ultimate 2D pixel remaster! Purchase the bundle and receive FINAL FANTASY FINAL FANTASY II FINAL FANTASY III FINAL FANTASY IV FINAL FANTASY V FINAL FANTASY VI This bundle lets you purchase all six games from FINAL FANTASY 1 to FINAL FANTASY 6 at a discount price. It also contains a sound track, featuring total of 20 tracks and total of 14 unique wallpapers. Enjoy universally updated 2D pixel graphics and the beautifully rearranged soundtrack. Gameplay is improved with modernised UI, and extras such as a beastiary, illustration gallery and music player allow further immersion into the world of the game. ＊These games are newly developed remaster editions based on the original titles. Some of the changes and additional elements found in other remakes of these games are not included. About the Game A remodeled 2D take on the second game in the world-renowned FINAL FANTASY series! Enjoy the timeless story told through charming retro graphics. All the magic of the original, with improved ease of play. Our epic tale begins with four young souls orphaned during the struggle between the Palamecian Empire and the rebel army. On their journey, the youths join forces with the white wizard Minwu, Prince Gordon of Kashuan, Leila the pirate, and many others. Behold the beautiful and sometimes tragic twists of fate that await you on your adventure. FFII introduced a unique skill level system that strengthens different attributes of the characters depending on their fighting style instead of leveling up. Use the key terms you learn in conversation to unlock new information and progress in the story. This innovative game series takes an ambitious turn in this second installment in the FINAL FANTASY series! ----------------------------------------------------------------------- ■ Beautifully revived with new graphics and sound! Universally updated 2D pixel graphics, including the iconic FINAL FANTASY character pixel designs created by Kazuko Shibuya, the original artist and current collaborator. Beautifully rearranged soundtrack in a faithful FINAL FANTASY style, overseen by original composer Nobuo Uematsu. ■Improved gameplay! Including modernized UI, auto-battle options, and more. Switch the soundtrack between the rearranged version, created for the pixel remaster, or the original version, capturing the sound of the original game. Now possible to switch between different fonts, including the default font and a pixel-based font based on the atmosphere of the original game. Additional boost features to expand gameplay options, including switching off random encounters, compensatory HP, and adjusting weapon skill level gained multipliers between 0 and 4. Dive into the world of the game with supplemental extras like the bestiary, illustration gallery, and music player. (This remaster is based on the original 'FINAL FANTASY II' game released in 1988. Features and/or content may differ from previously rereleased versions of the game.)

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this one, it has a different leveling system than all the other FF titles.  It is a use-based approach.  However, at times I really wondered if it was worth it.  Some of graphics upgrades were not as impressive as other FF Pixel remasters, but there was a few nice extras in there.One thing that bugged me is the auto-equip feature doesn't take into account your skills, so it will equip any weapon if it has higher attack.Also, I didn't like that the hidden stat magic penalty is not displayed anywhere in game.Magic users are hard to level and I really wondered if it was worth it at all, seeing as how most magic doesn't compete with bashing your way with weapons - even magic resistant ones.Apparently many bosses were nerfed in this version according to some websites.  Most of them are a joke, just auto attack everything.All in all, pretty fun little game, not to long or difficult.

_childDocuments_.review: Now, let's dive deep into this game's review. It's an NES game with a very nice polishing on it. The original game was already a great improvement on the first game, and they took their time to attempt improvements and upgrades here.- This is the first Final Fantasy name with the concept of Magic Points (or mana). In the first game, they used an D&D-styled system using magic points per skill level. You could use Cure or Fire until your MP reserve run dry, in comparison with the first game where you could cast only nine times in the maximum;- The traditional levelling system was abolished. In it's place they developed an advanced and complex "expertise" system that goes up to sixteen levels, where you would level your stats individually, depending on the weapon (or lack of) and gear equipped. This would somewhat be adapted in other future games with different mix-and-match systems, like the Espers in Final Fantasy 6. For an NES game, that was incredible - and it still is. Games like the original World of Warcraft and even newer ones, like New World, developed something that could be clearly based on this levelling system;- There's also an specific magic expertise system, that also goes up to sixteen and empowers the magic as the level increases. The animation of the magic also improves as you level, where the Ultima level 1 spell looks like a figment of light and its tenth level looks like the traditional spell of other games;- This is also the first game where there's a story going on with your characters - you have 3 males and a female, all with their pre-determined names and every one of them have their own thoughts about the story and what's going on. Alongside the 4 main characters, there are also a reasonable number of "guest characters" that will join you for the duration of the story. This gives more depth to the story and the characters, a new thing that the original Final Fantasy 1 game lacked;- This game also have some missable content. There are eventual dungeons and places where you can enter once only, so you can easily miss out a chest or an bestiary entry if you rush through the game fast enough. If you're going for the platinum achievement, you should pay greater attention to your surroundings;- The only thing that this game misses out, in my opinion, is that it ain't long enough. The story itself is short, but even still... we can't demand too much for a NES game. _childDocuments_.review: I have no idea if I would recommend this game or not. The beginning of the game is so good. The challenge is apparent, the skill up system is really cool and the rpg element they added was an awesome touch at first.Eventually, those very things begin to annoy you. There are so many weapons to skill up so exploring what weapons you like isn't really optimal. There are a ton of spells and leveling them up is a pain in the neck. I just picked a few spells I liked and spread them across 3 party members. Damaging spells were terrible to level but healing and buffs seemed optimal in this environment.I said 3 party members because you have a constantly rotating 4th party member and that may just be the worst thing this game does. The skills don't transfer, the spells don't transfer, the 'level ups' don't transfer so there's no point in keeping them alive since they steal potential stamina stats by getting hit instead of you.The encounter rate on this game is also ridiculously high, which is fine for me since I like grinding, but even I started getting annoyed by the amount of useless rooms where the encounter rate seems higher and you're placed in the center of these fake rooms. Eventually I pulled up a guide to go directly where I needed to go because the game actively made me hate exploring.I still liked the game though. The story bits and 'cut scenes' were cool and although it wasn't anything mind blowing, I imagine it being a big deal for the time it was originally released. I also think the things that were tried in this game were first attempts at things that were perfected in future games. So for that I appreciate that this game exists. FF2 walked so others could run.

_childDocuments_.review: Final fantasy 1 was a pretty chill game with a little bit of a challenge during dungeons, almost an idle game to play while you watch something else. The only problem is that every single one of these aspects suck massive ♥♥♥♥.Spells are nearly useless, if you use swords, you keep changing swords throughout the game and improving your sword skill. If you use spells, each spell you take starts from level 1 dealing minimal damage, so did you just get Ultima spell? Buckle up to farm enemies for 2 hours in a 15 hour game so it can start dealing damage.Weapons are limiting. If you're level 20 in axes, you don't want to make use of the cool sword you just dropped. And if you didn't train unarmed or swords? Well you just got ♥♥♥♥♥♥ baby, because there won't be any meaningful drops for those weapon types throughout the game.Storytelling is frustating. There is a dialogue system where you learn words from npcs and can tell these words to other npcs to further the quests. The problem is that which words you have to use with which npcs is completely nonsensical like one of those old point and click games. It's trial and error completely if you don't use a walkthrough. Also the plot itself is not any better than on FF1. It's just as simple, just with more dialogue.Dungeons feel like having your nipples pinched by a pirana. If a dungeon has a difficult to reach chest, it's probably an empty chest with a potion inside and monsters to fight before you get it. If there are 9 doors in a dungeon, 8 of them lead to empty rooms full of mobs. The entire dungeon design feels like a beeves & butthead joke.Regarding the returning aspects of the series, here is the first time you meet cid in person (he's mentioned in FF1 but not featured), the first time you see dragons and dragoons and i think that's it. Also the last boss literally goes to hell, ♥♥♥♥♥ everyone up and comes back for your ass, which was pretty funny. But all in all this is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game you're better avoiding, FF1 is a much better experience if you're looking for old school idle jrpgs.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first review of a game on steam, but I feel as though this needs to be said. I love Final Fantasy. I always have, especially the pre-3D games that have been released and re-released over the years. I started with origins on the PS1 back in the day playing those versions of 1 and 2 for many many hours. As time went on I bought the GBA versions and eventually the special PSP versions which I still play to this day. I was excited to hear about these pixel remasters because I could go through and enjoy these games on my pc for the first (sans-emulator). With that out of the way however, I simply cannot reccomend this game based upon how they have handled the port of it, and I will explain below.First off: The movement. This is more of a personal nitpick more than anything else, because of years and years of being used to simple four directional movement of the characters on the screen, having a diagonal movement added in on inbetween directional presses actually screws with how I normally move about in those games and it's a bit jarring. That is not the reason I'm giving this a negative review, more of a sidenote for anyone who's used to the original ports of the game.Secondly: Combat tweaksThis is the first big one that struck me as I started playing the game. There's a handful of differences which completely change how the game is played and how combat is done. In the original ports, (Up to the PSP release), combat was decided on the first two rows of enemies being able to hit you, and you being able to hit them physically. Magic could reach to the back, but only the first two rows were accessible. This extended to the player's side as well, with fighters who were placed in the back row not able to take damage from the normal physical sources of damage (outside of bows). With their new system that they have implemented, instead, we can now access all of the rows of enemies, and cool, yeah, I kinda like it, but we have damage fall off for every row past the first that we can attack. This is troublesome because some builds for teams on the old ports required that immunity to the rows behind the first two to be able to adequately funciton, and the immunity for back row fighters is now removed as well, they just take half damage from melee sources (either 33.3% or 25% depending on if guard is used as well). And that leads into another point, the shields.Shields in the original ports were usually a key item for not only speedrunners, but also general players who understood the complexity of the mechanics. Shields, if used on both hands nullified the attack completely and simply increased evasion, magic evasion, and the "shield" skill level, which was usually a fairly improtant skill for later on to evade or signifigantly reduce incoming damage, both melee and magic. They now instead only provide a minor bonus to defense and evade chances, while giving full access to the bare handed attack instead (at 50% power from pure unarmed). This messes with a lot of grinding strategies that were developed due to the lack of attack shields gave the player. (Also small sidenote, not being able to use curative items on enemies sucks for dealing with the undead and a relatively fresh party.)third point: the game's performance.Everyhting else up to this point could be forgiven, brushed aside as just a new system that they were implementing, if not for how certain means of grinding impact performance. Allow me to elaborate.In my hundreds, if not thousands, of hours playing this specific game, I have learned many means to easily grind spells and tactics to ensure that your party can become broken and absolutely godlike as soon as you recieve Minwu and the canoe. It allows access to Mysidia and the gear therein along with powerful creatures that you can utilize to grind up the skills and levels of your fighters. In the old ports, this was just a series of incremental increases towards mastery. To break it down further, with magic, and with weapons, you have levels that you can increase for the variety of weapon types, and the two schools of magic therein; white and black magic. The more you cast a specific spell, or the more you swing a specific weapon, the more that particular thing levels up and becomes more powerful/useful to you throughout the game. In the older ports of this game, up to and including the PSP versions, you could stack any number of spells and whatnot on your party in the fight, allowing you to essentially spam the spells you want to level. For instance, on my copy of the PSP port, I recently got Firion's white magic spell list to completely level 16, or the max allowed in the game, along with max weapon skills for all party members. This was more of a personal challenge than any intended goal, but still it felt good achieving it. In contrast, I make it to Mysidia on this port and begin my normal spell spam to level up things and make a powerful starting party, and lo and behold, after about 6-7 casts of blink and protect a piece, things begin to slow down. First off I noticed a fairly severe pause after the animation was finished, and then it got even worse after moving to the spell selection menu. I was suffering from severe frame lag, dropping from my normal 60+ to under 10 fps while in that menu or any other sub menu from within combat. That, unfortunately mixed with the other tweaks that they have made to the combat system as a whole have made the game pretty much unplayable to me, and I do not reccomend any true veterens of Final Fantasy 2 purchase this port of the game now or into the future unless they make a "classic" mode or something like that for the combat, along with fixing the severe lag and stuttering caused by multiple buff stacking. It wasnt an issue on the PSP, so it shouldn't be an issue on the pc port. Apologies for typos, and whatnot.

_childDocuments_.review: Gem with Engaging Progression and Intense StorytellingRating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐Review:Final Fantasy 2 holds a special place in my heart as a timeless classic that introduced some groundbreaking features to the franchise. While it may not be the most widely celebrated installment in the series, it deserves recognition for its unique progression system and captivating storytelling.One of the standout aspects of Final Fantasy 2 is its innovative character development system. Unlike traditional RPGs of its time, this game did away with the conventional leveling system and instead implemented a skill-based progression. Characters grow stronger in specific areas by actively using those skills. This dynamic approach added depth and a sense of personalization to each character's growth, allowing for strategic customization that felt satisfying and rewarding.The narrative of Final Fantasy 2 is another commendable aspect. It takes players on an emotionally charged journey, delving deep into the personal struggles and growth of the main characters. The game tackles themes of friendship, sacrifice, and redemption, which resonated strongly with me. The storytelling is well-crafted, featuring memorable moments that kept me engrossed throughout my playthrough.Additionally, the world-building in Final Fantasy 2 is impressive. The game presents a vast and diverse world, with each location feeling distinct and alive. Exploring different regions and interacting with various NPCs added an immersive layer to the gameplay experience. The attention to detail in the graphics and sound design further enhanced the atmosphere, making it easy to get lost in the game's enchanting universe.While Final Fantasy 2 does have some flaws, such as occasional balancing issues and a steep learning curve, these minor setbacks should not deter fans of the series or RPG enthusiasts from experiencing this gem. The game's strengths far outweigh its weaknesses, and it ultimately offers a memorable and enjoyable adventure.In conclusion, Final Fantasy 2 is a must-play for fans of the series and a noteworthy entry in the RPG genre. Its unique character progression, engaging storytelling, and immersive world make it a standout title that deserves recognition. If you're looking for a classic RPG experience with a touch of innovation and a captivating narrative, Final Fantasy 2 is well worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing through Final Fantasy 2 is similar to reading an outdated scientific book that has already been disproven: the flaws become apparent pretty fast and they hit hard, but the boldness of its attempted innovations and a certain kind of masochistic curiosity keep you coming back for more. I definitely only recommend this game if you have either played and enjoyed another one of the old-school Final Fantasy games, or are curious about the steady evolution of this massive franchise. If you aren't in either of those groups, all it offers you is a frustrating experience marred by repetitive gameplay, abysmal level design and interesting ideas trampled by poorly-thought out executions. If you're willing to set those aside, though, it's not hard to appreciate the ingenuity of said ideas and have some fun with the unique way this game handles character building and progression.That being said, do play while following a guide if you don't want to be masively frustrated. Final Fantasy 2 is riddled with permanently-missable content and cheap level designs specially engineered to make you backtrack through its tiresome dungeons, so spare yourself the grief and pull up your walkthrough of choice. You'll thank yourself later on. All things considered, I wouldn't say FF2 is a bad game, but it's far from being a good one, either. The Pixel Remaster gives shining luster to a dated and flawed product with flawless presentation in the graphics and music departments, and adds a key quality-of-life feature in the form of autosaves. This game is full of tricky encounter mappings and difficulty spikes, so you'll really enjoy having these. After dumping 20 hours of my life into this game, I can say I'll never, ever replay it, but I can't say I regret the experience, either.

_childDocuments_.review: Another classic 80s RPG is playable on Steam, this time Final Fantasy II.Final Fantasy II introduces several iconic things to the series including Chocobos, Dragoons, Cid, and Genji gear. It's also the first to feature named playable characters and a substantial narrative.This game stands out for its leveling system. Instead of characters having levels and getting stat gains with each one, there are instead conditions by which stats have a likelihood of increasing after battle. For instance, the more damage a character takes in battle, the greater the chance that their Stamina and max HP increase. Characters also lack a class or job. Instead, they have skill levels with weapons and spells that will increase as you use them. These systems can be quite exploitable if you know how they work, but you will not need to do this to beat the game. Most bosses don't have enough health or do enough damage to be threatening, and are quite easy without doing any dedicated leveling. The only times I was defeated in this game was due to being unlucky with status effects around the midgame, which means I was never truly challenged, unfortunately.Compared to other versions, this one restores some of the style of the original Famicom release. This also means the game lacks the expanded story seen in the PSP version, which is a real shame. Generally, the story of this game is quite weak. Many of the plot points seem forced, and you are given full access to the world very early despite the story being linear, which was a bit overwhelming. The addition of the minimap in this version is convenient, but I would argue too much so. You also can't turn it off. The game probably won't be your favourite in the series, but it is still relatively short compared to modern RPGs, so give this one a go!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Having spent some time playing Final Fantasy II Pixel remaster (after completing the first game) I can see Square-Enix put quite the effort remastering the first six entries in the Final Fantasy series.Final Fantasy II shows off a story aspect that would later be used in future installments such as a rag tag group of rebels taking down an evil empire (This one being ruled by an Emperor who looks like David Bowie as Jareth the Goblin King from Labrynth, that alone makes this game worth playing through.) Graphic wise, the sprites look similar to the original NES sprites but scaled up to 16-bit (Which means some monsters are looking at the player, which is amusing.) Sound: The music and in game sounds sound good, Nobuo Uematsu's music sounds amazing.Gameplay: Final Fantasy II has a mixed reputation here, unlike most other JRPGs Final Fantasy II's method of powering up involves using physical attacks to increase Strength or using Magic to increase your magic related stats. Unlike the original NES and PSX origins versions there's no stat decrease (Which was carried over from the Gameboy Advanced and PSP version) so that's another plus. This system of stat gaining would later be implimented in the SaGa games.Unfortunately there's no Soul of Rebirth post game content like the Gameboy Advance and PSP versions but that doens't take away to much from this port's experience.All in all I recommend Final Fantasy II pixel remaster.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend with a caveat of understanding that this game is, in my opinion, pretty average. It has odd systems for how it works and it doesn't fully explain a lot of them. However, my caveat to recommending it depends on why you're playing the game. If it is because you're a big fan of Final Fantasy, the Saga games, Turn-Based JRPGs, or want to see the legacy of video games, I think it is worth trying. However, if you are not any of those things, I'd say the game is very dated compared to most experiences out there. Hope this helps!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing remaster of FF2. I love all the quality of life benefits, as well as freely configuring how you want to enjoy the game.The character leveling is ahead of its time. Although it has some flaws in story, the world is amazingly open, and filled with a comprehensive bestiary that is upgraded from FF1. The music, absolute classic, even with the rearranges.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this is an excellent remaster, with great new artwork and amazing new (I mean, remasters of old songs I guess) music, anything inconvenient or un-fun about this game is a result of the gameplay of the original game itself, and not the fault of the remaster; however, the original gameplay: what makes final fantasy 2 what it is, is the most grindy and inconvenient in the series. Unlike FFVI for example, where you merely need to complete a battle in order for spells to level, in FF2 you have to *use* them, even for spells you would almost never use like esuna, you have to cast them on healthy party members hundreds of times in order to have an effective hit percentage. Thankfully, the remaster has an autobattle system, where the game repeats the actions you used in the last turn, so grinding is a bit more tolerable, but still, spells level at the end of battle, and if you have gained more xp for that spell than needed to level it up, the xp you gained counts towards nothing, so it's not like you can leave the game on autobattle forever and get spells to max level, you have to keep an eye on it (though the game continues to play even when alt-tabbed, so you can watch a vid while doing this). To give you an idea of the grind, I spent the majority of the game using three party members to repeat spells which don't harm the enemy, and one party member for attacking so the grind didn't take too long, I did this with most battles, at the end getting my spells to about level 6 or 7 (out of 16), this adds a lot of time to the game. That being said, if you are willing to undergo the grind, this game has a really good story, and pretty fascinating lore for what was originally a NES game, I kinda wished for more stories in this world after playing  (as each FF game is set in a different world except for like, 10-2 and Dissidia). And its gameplay can be rewarding, even if it's not everyone's cup of tea. If you decide to play this game, remember: NOT ALL OF YOUR SPELLS NEED TO REACH LEVEL 16. I finished the game with spells around level 6-9: keep in mind, while the game is grindy, it really isn't necessary to grind as much as possible.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I can see why there's not a lot of love for this game. I did about 5 - 6 hours of grinding throughout the game and ended up finishing the final boss in 4 turns, so that was probably overkill. The choices and conversations some of the characters have are too short and left me puzzled why they would come to that conclusion. Idk if I could recommend this game to other players honestly. Its definitely a niche game and I feel like I didn't gain much insight into much of the franchise. Give it a try if its on sale, or play it on an emulator so you can at least play the mini game on the snow mobile to get some cool early rewards, because its not in this version.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Much improvement to the first game in terms of story. I enjoyed the plot, and the environment was tons of fun to explore, and the fact that you had a constantly rotating 4th party member was really interesting. My only real complaint is the lack of a proper level up system, which made achievement hunting much harder. Still very fun.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Most people I know hate this game because it's objectively one of the worst FF games but I love it because I'm a nerd that loves to grind in the beginning of the game, become OP and then mow down everyone obstacle in my path until I beat the game. You can literally play through the entire game as just Firion equipped with nothing but 2 shields and the Teleport spell and you can take out 90% of the enemies in this game and punch the remaining 10% to death.Also, taking a moment to appreciate how much the plot has advanced since FF1, we see a myriad of guest party members and side-characters with fleshed out personalities and storylines. This is also when the series would start introducing DRAMA into the plot. The story of FF2 takes some twists and turns and deals with heavier subject matter than FF1. IMO this game is worth a shot if you're a fan of Final Fantasy, at the very least so you can appreciate the franchise's roots.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Playing through all the classic PR Final Fantasy games and wow this was a huge step up from the first. Crazy how much they changed with only a year between releases.The skill system is divisive but I found it to be almost great just wish the latter levels for weapons and spells weren't so annoying to level up but I can see what they were going for and it's actually pretty ahead of it's time.The story was a huge upgrade telling a pretty compelling tale of a group of rebels fighting against the empire. Pretty simple compared to modern game stories but compared to the first game it's a huge improvement. I enjoyed the drama and not being afraid to show the cost of the war in terms of death and destruction.Good stuff looking forward to where the series goes from here!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy I stands the test of time. Final Fantasy II does not. Though it was the first game to introduce some awesome staples to the series (chocobos!!! dragoons!!), it suffers from some 'interesting' design choices.  If you are playing this game to see where Final Fantasy has come from, then be prepared for:- boring, long dungeons with empty rooms designed to waste your time- grindy combat that will boil down to you auto attacking the same 3-4 creatures every 6 tiles- a magic system and level up system that doesn't feel intuitive or rewarding to invest in (aside from Cure)If you plan to play this game, do yourself a major favor and look up maps of the dungeons. I would say I was impressed with the final story beats, but it's hard to recommend the long grind before hand.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: The re-orchestrated soundtrack is great. The story is pretty good, a few good twists and great moments throughout the game.Gameplay is pretty good, though can be a bit tedious if you're grinding out your magic and weapon levels. Also if you grind out too hard the game does end up too easy which is a shame compared to the other games in the series that sorta balance for that.There is a lot of backtracking and revisiting a lot of areas throughout the game which does hamper the pacing a bit but all in all a good experience in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: FF2 is an amazing game if you enjoy the ability to mold your team as you see fit. You'll gain stats based on weapon hits, current stats (evade for agility), spell casts, hits on target, mp use, ect... The game however isn't that challenging but does have more story elements than the prior release.Some faults of course are the stun loops, but this can even happen in FF1. Lots of empty rooms with no real purpose (not sure but I don't think there are increased encounter rates in those rooms). Another issue is that encounters are generally very high in this game.My 1st play through was done with a full party less the side kick. We had around 6k each and I finished the game without the use of the blood sword. My 2nd run as I missed time sensitive chests I did completely solo with my other party members ko'd. I finished with around 8K hp, and killed the final boss with two hits (blood sword). It was actually easier to play solo than with a party due to the way stats acquire in this game. I don't think I'll do a 3rd run anytime soon, but if I did it would be all casters.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: There's nothing wrong with the port, in fact this is a pretty good version of FF2. But, FF2 just isn't a good game. The lack of a job system, the lack of levels, the really basic flow of the plot, the one note characters, there's really not much here. The good thing is that your hit points go up naturally as you fight battles, you don't have to just get hit. None of your stats ever go down either. It makes it much easier to just equip your characters however you want and play the game. If the actual plot or dungeons were more interesting that'd be great. But, I don't like playing the game. The dungeons are just mazes and the encounter rate is sky high. With the fact that the only thing you're guaranteed to get out of a fight is gil, that high encounter rate just becomes frustrating. The soundtrack is fantastic as are all the remastered soundtracks, but you won't hear it outside of towns, with the high encounter rate what you'll be hearing over and over again is the first 20 seconds of the battle music over and over again.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: So... Final Fantasy 2 is... weird but not bad, let me explain. Final Fantasy 2 is VERY different than final fantasy 1 or really any other final fantasy for that matter, and the reason for that is the leveling system, or rather weapon progression system. In order to level up spells, weapons, and stats you need to use them which is fine, your obviously going to use your spells and weapons, but that's not the problem, the problem is how it's done. Every monster in the game has a rank stemming from 1-7 when you reach certain thresholds with your weapon levels you'll stop gaining weapon experience, the solution? Go fight higher ranked monsters, simple enough right? And to be totally honest yeah it is pretty much that simple, unless you want to get your weapons and spells to level 16, then it becomes a hassle, but most people aren't going to do that. which leads me to my final conclusion about the leveling system, it's not bad it's just different. Final Fantasy 2 is a good game, and while it might have moments that make you a bit angry or confused it's really not that bad, plus look at all the things it did for the series, chocobo's were first introduced here and so was Cid, Final Fantasy 2 is greatly important to the series, and that's why I think it's worth playing and checking out
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I really didn't enjoy playing Final Fantasy II. My biggest complaint is with the dungeons. Due to the trap rooms and floors that are dead-ends, it makes going through them a complete drag. I'm also not a big fan of the leveling system, I never found it satisfying because you're either too weak or  totally overpowered. It makes the fighting boring. Also, there's a ton of backtracking on the overworld. I'm not gonna say much about story but for an NES game, it's kind of cool. There are some memorable plot moments, and some characters are alright. The music is good, much better than other versions of Final Fantasy II. If you're looking to try Final Fantasy, play any other game in the series.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I was told multiple times this Final Fantasy was the worst. I wanted to give it a fair chance so I went in with an open mind. I am glad I did since I had a pleasant experience. The leveling system is different from most other RPGs, but the story is actually good. The only part I really had to grind for was getting the achievement of leveling a weapon skill and magic to max. I highly suggest giving it a chance. The music in the final dungeon is well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Ok to start if you want traditional leveling system this game is not for you. However there are Weapon and Spell ranks along with a natural stat progression system the more you attack the more your Strength goes up, the more you use magic the higher your intellect and MP will goes along with Spell Ranks. The story does have some issues with telling you where to go for progression however the world isn't huge so its not to much of an issue and if all else fails go back to the first town odds are that's the solution

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting changes on the mechanics founded in Final Fantasy I. Although levelling spells to a high level is not required to beat the game, it was a bit annoying having to grind spell levels by repeatedly casting them, particularly the status effect spells which are pretty much useless until you've levelled them up. Plot is still the dated, basic high fantasy fare like the first game, but has enough cool parts combined with the updated graphics to offset this somewhat.
