_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable but ultimately broken and badly designed.  Without the generous auto-save system this game would be a hard no.  Right now its just a stay away until the below is patched.With the fact that enemies inflict statuses on 100% of hits, even those that do 0 damage and that enemies such as Couerls exist, and cause death on attack (Even with a Ribbon or Protect ring equipped) this game is just poorly thought out.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: The second entry into the Final Fantasy series honestly has a lot of ups and downs in my opinion, so much so that it's hard to say whether or not I would recommend it. One of my favorite aspects of the previous game was just the fact that I could shut my brain off and grind up a level here and there and I found some enjoyment out of that - an enjoyment that Final Fantasy 2 took away by removing both levels and classes from the game. That being said, I think that what we got to replace it is system far greater to the extent that I genuinely think that most RPGs even to this day could benefit from adapting. Instead of choosing to be a Warrior, throwing on a Longsword, and just blitzing levels, instead you only have proficiency.Any character can be a master of any and/or all things, they just need to use that weapon/skill enough to actually get good with it. It's the idea of practice makes perfect only with this system, you're not restricted in any way on what you can do. The game balances itself out not by telling you that you can't do something, but by telling you that if you want to master two separate things, you have to put in twice the work and effort. It really hearkens back to my days playing Morrowind, jumping around just to improve my jump skill while spamming Conjuration spells while traversing the world - perfecting and leveling skills like a mad woman.I'm not too well versed in the Final Fantasy world, I'm still early on in my playthrough of the franchise, but this entry does introduce a lot of iconic monsters that I recognize from other games in the franchise such as Bomb, Coeurl, Malboro, Behemoth, and the fricking Adamantoise. During the part of the game where Adamantoise first shows up, I feel like I was a bit under-leveled so each encounter with it ended up being a full-on boss fight where 90% of my attacks wouldn't pass its DPS check. That's definitely on me for not preparing enough but that frustration during that part has cemented Adamantoise as the opposition hence forth.As someone who's attempting to obtained every achievement for this franchise, Final Fantasy 2 pushed me to some mental limits when it came to its map design. It truly felt at times that whoever designed these maps, especially Pandemonium, truly hated me. I was heck bent on obtaining every chest in the game so when I entered a maze-like room that basically asked me to spend the better half of 15 minute traversing this one maze 3 times to get each and every chest, I truly felt like I was just trying to push to the end of the game. Map design aside, I genuinely loved the new proficiency mechanic despite its flaws and adored the new mainstay entries into the franchise. Despite the shortcomings of Final Fantasy 2, I did have a lot of fun playing through it even though the story didn't really grab me. In the end, I do think Final Fantasy 2 is a good entry into the series and worth a try for sure. Final Fantasy 2 gets a thumbs up from me!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Good for it's time, not really worth the effort for today's gamers.Was it great at it's time? Definitely. Did it pave the way for many of the great JRPGs to come? Almost certainly. However, this review is whether or not I recommend this game to a modern audience that could be devoting their time and money into a game available today.The answer to this question is undoubtedly no for me. Unless you are playing for nostalgic purposes or to play through the whole series (which, admittedly, is how I found myself playing), I don't see any reason to pick this up over modern games. The story is bland (only a few steps up over the first game), the main characters have almost no character to speak of, and the gameplay itself is rather tedious. There are plenty of classic games that hold their own against modern RPGs, but this simply isn't one of them.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute mess following up immediately after the first title of the series, the game kicks all familiarity with the character customization out the window. No specified classes/Jobs, the level system is helplessly confusing due to the simple character level ups getting completely removed and replaced by frequent power ups to specific stats related to the playstyle of the given character I assume. Any character can equip anything, which sounds cool but hugely breaks down the simplicity of the first game. The game is enjoyable but a large downgrade from Final Fantasy 1 as it rapidly shoots up in complexity in comparison, leading to massive confusion on my part as I started my playthrough. Another addition to the second entry are limited time encounters and treasures, for which I just went ahead and used a guide to avoid missing the 100% achievement completion. It´s still a cool and pretty game nonetheless, just extremely messy.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Coeurls in this game are busted. While they're supposed to have a chance of causing death upon normal attacks, in the pixel remaster, it's guaranteed, leaving the only way to actually get through the final dungeons of the game to be save-scumming every encounter that wipes your team. A 6-coeurl ambush all but guarantees your death before even a chance to move.These pixel remasters need to be better.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I never had the opportunity to finish this game when I originally played it on PSOne all those years ago. It was slow, kinda boring and repetitive with a lot of grinding. This Pixel Remaster is still all of those things, but I'm a huge fan of the art style and even enjoy using the tube filter from time to time.I'm about halfway done with the story and it's very basic, very slow and the dungeons are way too large to be enjoyable with random battles every 3-5 seconds, but they're snappy and pretty. It's definitely still an NES era JRPG with some minor QoL improvements, but I would have loved a fast forward feature or the ability to turn off random battles like in other remasters of previous FF games. Still, all in all, this will be a great game to revisit when the steam deck launches. If you liked the original FF games on NES or even Final Fantasy 4 (2 on SNES), you'll probably enjoy this version. Sidenote: before release people panned the font choice. After playing for 8 hours I honestly don't know. I understand they chose a modern, smooth font because it would scale for various display resolutions nicely, but it's really not that bad.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Having gone through and completed this again with this newest release, I can honestly say that I'm in love with the Pixel Remaster's. I love the rearranged music, the updated graphics, bug fixes, etc. I still think the PSP version of 1 and 2 are still the best editions, but for a game going back to it's original roots, they have done an amazing job with this game. I'm looking forward to working through 3-6 now that I've beaten 1 and 2. I highly recommend for fans of the original as well as new fans wanting to experience the start of this franchise at it's most basic roots. I'm so happy that these are on modern platforms now. Plus for this one, I love getting to cheese the system for stats and whatnot.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Despite some differences between this game and the previous one, I could almost copy and paste  of Final Fantasy I here because my recommendations would be essentially the same.In short, if you're a Final Fantasy fan or a jRPG fan with plenty of time, give it a try, it's not a bad game. If not, just skip it. If you have limited time to play then there are simply better games out there.To give my own experience, I found the story to be much better then Final Fantasy I, but it still feels weak compared to the later games. Character personalities are also a little better but still very minimal. That said, I did enjoy the nostalgic feeling of playing it again, and it’s nice to see some of the things introduced here that would later regularly appear in the series.However there is one major annoyance I have with this game and that is the leveling system.  Rather than using traditional levels and experience points, it uses a skill-based leveling system. This approach isn't necessarily bad, but here it feels very clunky in my opinion. I had the same issue with the original version for the NES and If I remember correctly it was even worse.I’ll give it a thumbs up because as I said, it’s not a bad game despite the awful leveling system. However, I have to admit that it is mostly because of the nostalgic experience.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: The original version of this game is honestly...pretty bad. The difficulty curve is through the roof, and the inherent game's systems are...not the best the series has to offer. I never finished an NES version of this game, nor any remake before this one.Which sucks, because the story is great here! The main character system is still here, which sucks, but the game is so much easier that you can mostly not care about it and just experience the story, which again, is great!The Pixel Remaster stuff in general is all great, and if you like the FF series you should just get them for your platform of choice.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: ✅Music✅Autosave and Quicksave are lifesavers➖Shallow combat…quantity over quality➖Ask/Learn chat system➖Extreme quest ambiguity➖Tons of backtracking➖No downscaling magic (?)➖Restrictive leveling system➖1 turn, full party KO/CC spells are cheap➖Absurd magic leveling grind➖Lack of turn order in combat hinders strategyGame World: Much like FF1, Final Fantasy II (FF2) takes place on a 2D map of a fantasy world. The game consists of the movement world and the combat screen. In the movement world you move on a 2D plane to various shops in the local map, and cities or destinations on the world map. In the combat screen, you control your characters as you use attacks and spells against enemies. I felt that the game world is fairly typical for old fantasy games, and as the Final Fantasy series basically invented it all, it's no wonder the fantasy tropes start here. Narrative: Since I just played FF1, I am able to start the comparisons here. I’m happy to say that FF2’s story has vastly improved since FF1. Yes, the dialog is still stupidly simple, and yes the new learn/ask system is frustrating at best, but there's actually a plot now instead of “You are foretold heroes who must kill bad guy who will destroy planet!”. In FF2, you start the game off playing as a group of four young adults (brothers/sisters?) who are ambushed and left for dead by soldiers. You are rescued by a group of rebels and decide to help their cause while searching for your final party member who is missing. You end up on a grand adventure filled with dragons, (the first!) chocobo, airships, and other Final Fantasy story staples as you work to overthrow the evil empire. The plot actually has some small twists and turns. I also like how there is more gravitas with party members. Yes I said members, as in plural, Square(soft) has learned the ability to have multiple party members, but they come and go, you cannot pick from a pool. Overall, the plot is much more refined and better made than FF1, while the dialog still leaves much to be desired. Length: I beat the game in about 28.5 hours.Controls: Same as FF1, I used a controller and the input was basic RPG game-like. I had no issues with any controls. Mechanics: whooo boy, here we go. For me FF2’s mechanics were a complete clusterf__k compared to FF1. I understand that Final Fantasy as a series always changes things up with each iteration to try new things, but I felt like many of the design choices here were steps back. I’m just going to go in order of my negative con’s above. The combat is pretty darn shallow. To be fair, FF1 was just as shallow, but I would even say that FF2’s is somehow worse. There’s still a random battle every 5-7 steps, so immediately you are overwhelmed by constant fighting. This wouldn’t be a problem if the fights were anything but auto attacks, which they are in 99% of every fight in the game. To expand slightly on the combat system, there are no more classes in FF2, you gain boosts to your stats at the end of each fight depending on if you “used” the stat enough. If you got hit then your HP may go up. Cast spells and your MP and int/spirit will increase. I actually found this interesting at the start until I realized the ridiculous grind potential here. Also the pigeonholing into a specific build is rough. Weapons use the same leveling system, so if you use an axe or sword constantly, those will be higher level. But then if you find an awesome spear, you can’t really use it well because your spear level will be lower. Next is the quest ambiguity. I am shocked by how little information is given to the player, good luck playing this without a guide. The part that really cemented this for me was when I had to find a town that I had no idea where it was on the map, then get to the town, and talk to a bookshelf to say a very specific thing. This would have taken me ages to figure out. Not worth the trouble, use a guide. To add into the quest ambiguity is the constant backtracking. You end up going between two ports something like 10x back and forth as you progress the first half of the game. The magic system is similar to weapons in that you can only level up spells if you use them. A spell starts at level 1 and costs 1 MP. Near the end I was casting Ultima and Flare multiple times in every fight and it took forever for them to level. Leveling magic is a GRIND. Furthermore, if I level up my Cure from using it and its level 10, maybe I only want to cast it at level 5 to save some MP…nope, downcasting doesn’t appear to be a thing. Lastly is the lack of an ATB gauge or turn order. Sometimes my characters would go in whatever order they wanted, which sucks when I’m trying to revive someone and cure them and cast Berserk/Haste/Blink on them, but this isn’t possible because you will very likely go out of order from your revives and spells, making any sort of tactics impossible when its based on RNG. Difficulty: I was shocked by how insanely hard this game must have been on release with no QoL upgrades like quick save and auto save. Some of the dungeons here are just BRUTAL. It's not uncommon to constantly die to normal enemies who have ridiculous AUTO ATTACK status effects, like Stone, which is an instant KO, and sleep, which is either nothing or a huge issue. Most of the bosses are jokes, most of the fights themselves are jokes, but there are like 10 enemies in the game who are just bats__t insane. Quality: Graphical quality is not something you should care about if you’re playing a 30 year old game. It looks and feels like a NES game. UI: About the same as FF1, I can’t say I noticed much difference. Performance: No issues on desktop PC. i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSDSound Effects: Nothing really stands out here, basic sound effects. Music: The music is quite good. I didn’t feel like it was as good as FF1, but still obviously redone with the pixel remaster, and done quite well. I would venture to say even less so than FF1. There are achievements that are relatively easy to get as you naturally go through the game. The part where it's worse than FF1 is the leveling system. You can’t really try new or different things other than weapons, or maybe making a different character a mage-type.You shouldn’t be persuaded by my review if you are after the full Final Fantasy experience, from start to end, you’ll end up playing the best and the worst anyways. I’m not sure if I would consider FF2 the worst, but it's quite close to my top bad FF’s right alongside FF15. Can’t wait to get to FF13. My rankings for FF is currently: FF1 FF2You can find my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty much the "Chain of Memories" of Final Fantasy's mainline franchise, but actually flawed.Story is in fact better than the first game, but the progression mechanics just...doesn't work well. Wanna raise HP? Hit yourself. It's a cheesy way to do it. Wanna kill the final boss in 10 seconds? Just keep hitting him with the blood sword w/ a broken % damage n such over and over till he dies. Seriously, this is so unbalanced and broken. I would only recommend this for people who only cares about the story. Trying to get the Master of II achievement would be a frustrating grind.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I never got a chance to play the real Final Fantasy 2 here in the US, so I have been looking forward to this for a while. It's a pretty decent RPG, with the graphics and some quest elements very similar to FF1, but with a really neat twist with how they removed the class system and put in (what we'd now call) an Elder Scrolls progression system. As long as you don't abuse the system by attacking your teammates, it works really well - skills will progress up to a point and then get capped based on enemy difficulty, so you can't just grind your way to infinite power off goblins. If you want to get good at spellcasting, you have to cast spells over and over.The fast-forward mode really helps with this - you can have your teammates repeatedly and quickly cast the same spells over and over to help level them up.The story is sort of whatever and running through combat after combat on fast forward mode can be a little bit tedious, but it is overall an enjoyable game with an awesome world map theme by Nobuo Uematsu.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: This game is SO Freaking annoying! Now I see why there are so many people hating on it on forums. The random encounter rate is ANNOYING AF!!! I can't go 10 seconds w/o a random fight in a dungeon! The fights aren't even challenging at all - they're just annoying and make me level up too fast. I'm literally in the 2nd dungeon of the game and my characters have over 200 HP. The enemies are doing like 4-10 dmg to me IF they hit. I've only gotten my weapon skills at level 4 and I'm already fed up with this game. This is the first time I give up any FF series game this quickly. I loved FF1 but FF2 is the worst FF I've ever played. DO NOT buy this one. Skip it and go straight to FF3.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I would only recommend this game to fan of Final Fantasy already. This is not the best or the funnest of all the FF games. If this will be your first FF Game I would recommend starting with a different one. It is an older game so it is expected that some things are not to the quality of of current game, but if you like and want to experience the history of gaming pick this up.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite everything, I unironically love Final Fantasy 2. I've played it through Origins on the PSX, and completed it (and its bonus post-game) in Dawn of Souls for the GBA. The Pixel Remaster is arguably my favorite version, even if it excludes added content for "purist" play. Even then, it's still FF2. Make of that what you will.The rough edges of the original game are smoothed out well. The encounter rates for "trap rooms" are seriously toned down; instead of an ensured fight or two, you'll rarely have one there. Weapon and spell levels increase as quick as the GBA and PSP ports, and I'd argue that grinding is only necessary to get new spells up to speed with trained ones. Characters also get HP increases periodically when you win fights. If you dual-wield and drop a foe with the first weapon, your character also redirects the second weapon to a new target. When a "guest" member leaves your party, you also get all their equipment this time around; nothing they've used gets lost if you don't strip them down. And like every Pixel Remaster, the musicians went above and beyond for new covers of classic tunes.That said? I don't know if I can recommend this remaster to everyone. They added back the spell penalties from equipment from the older versions. That's normally not an issue -- stick to cuirasses, daggers / staves and no other armor, and you'll be fine. However, you start to realize that direct damage spells are pretty mediocre. Sure, you can clear most of a group if they're weak to an elemental blast. Good luck doing much if they're not, even if it still whittles them down. And if they're not vulnerable to an element, single-target blasts can be underwhelming compared to swinging a sword at their face.There's still plenty of spells that all do the same thing (Fog and Silence stop spells; Hold, Sleep and Stop all shut down foes; Death, Toad, Mini, Warp and Teleport all instantly defeat foes). I found dropping a dece-level Blink and Berserk on my rebel heroes trivializes a lot of fights; enemies rarely hit (especially with shields used) and weapons tear through them like tissue paper. The last dungeon I've played in my current file was a total slog that didn't challenge me. I got impatient enough to just have everyone dual-wield to speed things along. I cannot say the same of the PSX version or, gods help you, the original Famicom release.And then there's other stuff that's still a pain for many players. Stray too far off the course on the world map, and you'll still get mauled by high-level enemies. Trap rooms and meandering dungeon design still wastes your time, even if you don't get ambushed nine times out of ten in the former anymore. Enemies feel like they always apply status effects with their attacks if you get hit once (though weapons with ailments do too, even if there's no indication of it after hitting foes).As such? If you know the game's flaws and still wanna give it a chance, you may just like FF2 PR. If you're a crazy loon like me who loves the game despite its flaws, give it a go. If you've always hated the originals, I can't say this version will change your mind. If you're brave enough either way, old or new? Bear this in mind, fellow rebel curs: the password is Wild Rose. Remember it well!

_childDocuments_.review: This entry in the Final Fantasy series is beloved by many but strongly hated by others. Regarded as an oddity that broke the rules of the series upon release, time has somewhat mitigated the outraged reaction. While it tried a number of new systems and ideas (some ambitious failures, some that took off and became mainstays of the series, and a few that showed promise but were never used again) ultimately it remained true to itself and the classic feel of the series.Just like every other Final Fantasy.ANYWAY, Final Fantasy 2 is one of my favorites for really weird reasons, namely it was the harbinger of a few things that stuck around and got iterated upon -- but not in Final Fantasy! This was kind of the first prototype SaGa game. With magic, weapons and stats all having numbers that only go up through constant use in battle, rather than passively according to a leveling chart, this is the Odd Duck of Final Fantasy.It also gave rise to the meme of "three orphans punching each other to raise their stats". Don't worry, you don't need to do that here. Numbers go up reasonable fast and your HP stat seems to always passively increase as long as you show up, which is a nice change for the Pixel Remaster version. Another worthwhile change is dual-wielding. Previously it was a lot less useful than it is here, you can really carve up the monster population with two swords and some ambition to swing 'em.Between those improvements and the boost to music power you get when an all-star staff remixes already classic tunes, Final Fantasy II Pixel Remaster is probably the best version of the game available. It's certainly the best legally-available-on-PC version out there. It's still a Final Fantasy: Melodramatic plot, lotsa monsters, high adventure, great music. It's just always been one of the weirder games in the series, and FFIIPR does nothing to change that.I'm cool with that. I liked it anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're here reading reviews for this game, you've probably already heard the lamentations about it's progression system and it's overall place in the series. And your biggest question right now, whether you're new to Final Fantasy or played later entries, is why should I play this one?FFII's story is lackluster, worse even than FFI's in my opinion, and its overdramatization of character deaths, implementation of keyword-based dialogue, and the occasional cinematic does nothing to save that. It is short, this version has no endgame, and theres no incentive to do much other than grind pointlessly or push to the end. Unless you’re playing all the FF games and this is next on your list, in which case you can expect at the least beautiful pixel art and spectacular music, the only saving grace for this game is its unusual progression system. But boy is it a good saving grace.Besides a completionist's fancy or a historian hoping to go back and witness how such a huge series evolved, the best experience about this game to me is it's unique but controversial skill progression system. Play the game to experiment with that alone, if nothing else.Unlike others who have spent hours critisizing it, I find system incredibly ahead of it's time, though poorly executed. This system is not unlike what we see in the Call of Cthulhu tabletop, The Elder Scrolls, and Cyberpunk 2077, where your skills increase as you use them rather than putting points into skills you didnt even touch every time you gain a level (looking at you, Fallout: NV character with 1 Charisma and Speech 100 who hasn't engaged in dialogue since leaving Doc Mitchell's house). It is, in my opinion, the superior form of RPG progression, and even though FFII's rendition is flawed in its grindy nature and exploitable targeting options, it is mind-blowing to me that such systems were in place this far back in gaming history. The system builds off of just how much you choose to put into it and thus allows any character, with enough time, to learn any weapon and any spell. Does this sacrifice the uniqueness of RPG specializing? Only if you let it -- its not any different than Skyrim in that respect. Does it make for the creation of immensely overpowered Ultima-spamming party members? Yeah, but so does choosing 4 Black Wizards in FFI. Can the system be exploited by attacking your own party members? Yeah, but don't act like training with your comrades in swordfights and spell duels is anything immersion-breaking.I believe in use-based RPG progression superiority.

_childDocuments_.review: Having now finished this game I can say that while FF2 is a pretty weak entry in the series, it's not as bad as people say. The good parts of this remaster are the graphics and the phenomenal orchestrated soundtrack. Autobattle, quick saves and autosaves are also lifesaver features without which I might not have finished the game.The leveling system isn't bad in concept and for the most part it works fine. The part where it falls flat is how slow it is to level spells, especially situational spells which you don't need to use often. The game also has poor descriptions of game systems and several hidden mechanics which are critically important but not explained or mentioned anywhere in-game. Without knowing about these mechanics you will not be able to make good decisions with your characters which makes the game experience worse. If you plan to play this game, I suggest looking up the "magic penalty" system of FF2.I would recommend this game to big fans of Final Fantasy who are just looking to experience more of the series, for that it is worth a playthrough. But to a general consumer there are far better JRPGs available and FF2 doesn't hold up that well. If you want to play this specific part of FF history though, the pixel remaster is a good choice.Edit: A recent patch has added the "Magic Inteference" stat which lets you see the magic penalty of equipment and the cumulative effect on the character, which is a big improvement, although the game still doesn't explain what the stat does.

_childDocuments_.review: ❤️❤️🤍🤍🤍⚠️ Brutal difficulty, harder than the original Famicom version.  Note: My own enjoyment in this game is probably much higher than for most people as I enjoy going out of my way to break these games, something which is basically necessary to beat this one. Basically, find out which spells and items are overpowered, and exploit the hell out of them to beat the game. So, I was extremely impressed by the story. For an NES game it’s very intricate and involved, and if I could have played this as a kid and understood what was happening, it would have probably been one of my favorite games of all time… if I could have gotten past the awful game mechanics. That said, this game, and this version of the game is hard to recommend. While I think they struck a nice balance with the pixel remaster of the first game where it could be played by both those curious about the game because of its historical significance, and where veterans could still make it more challenging by just not using the things that made the game easier… this game has none of that. Where they made the first game more approachable, here they decided to make the second game harder than the already difficult original. If you want to play this, expect to be active in the Steam forum and read up on guides before you even start playing. So, what makes the game so broken?First you must understand the leveling system. Final Fantasy 2 uses the training system (Dungeon Master, Elder Scrolls) where the more you use something (like a sword, spell, shield) the better you become with it. That sounds great, but the system is so poorly implemented that it’s a hassle to deal with. You want to use your magic spells because they get stronger… but that makes them cost more, so you don’t actually want to use them  much because you’ll run out of mana and ethers are super expensive. If you don’t use the spells juuust the right amount, they won’t deal any significant damage to be worth using to begin with. You don’t know what the enemies you’ll be facing will be strong against, what elements they’ll drain (=you heal them with the spell) or what they’re weak against, so you obviously need to use all elemental spells in equal amount. But they only level up when you use them. In battle. And you can’t even avoid this system because it doesn’t take long at all until you start to encounter enemies that are, basically, immune to physical attacks. Speaking of… You want to get better at using swords? Sure, but you can’t train against monsters that are too weak and you need to use a weapon that deals low damage because XP is based on the  you do. That’s not how this system is supposed to work. Skills are supposed to naturally grow through use over the course of the game.In the original game people used to attack their own party members or themselves in order to level up skills. I haven’t done this while playing the pixel remaster since I think it’s a stupid, unimmersive system, but hey, they kept that “feature”, so that’s one way to deal with the poor levelling curve, I guess. Another massive problem in the game is that it will now randomly give stats after combat. While that’s nice for the most part, they’ve decided to include health in this. The problem with health is that while you want enough to get by and not get one-shotted in the beginning, the game has anti-grinding measures in place where mid to late game enemies, and bosses, do a percentage of your health per hit as damage, or drain a percentage of your HP to heal themselves with. The more health you have, the more health the boss will heal. The more health you get, the harder the game (and final battle) will become. And there’s no way to avoid it. For some inexplicable reason the price for Ether and Phoenix Downs have skyrocketed between FF1 and FF2 making them luxury items, which makes no sense. In FF1 they weren’t even needed, but were very cheap. In this version you absolutely  them for regular and casual gameplay, but they’re so expensive that you can’t get them. And remember, you really shouldn’t grind for gold because your HP will get too high, which could potentially mean that you can’t beat the game. Another broken thing is that enemies have a 100% hit chance when it comes to causing additional effects such as poison, confuse, petrify, instant death and so on when they hit you with a physical attack. This was not the case in the original version.The encounter rate is insanely high in this game and if you are unlucky and get ambushed, a group of even the weakest enemies can stunlock and wipe your entire party. Even at 99 agility and 99% evasion, I was still getting ambushed by enemies. This game is not playable casually. If, however, you’re one of those players who likes to pick these games apart and break them in spectacular ways, then you’ll have fun with this one. There are a few overpowered weapons, items and spells in the game that make the game substantially easier to get through. For casual play, even a simple task like exploring a dungeon is just not enjoyable without a map, and the in-game map is not good enough since most doors in dungeons lead to “trap rooms” that are designed with high encounter rates that lead nowhere and only serve to whittle away your resources and kill you.  One fantastic change from the original however, is that they made it so that your characters can no longer lose skill points, so that’s pretty nice. All in all, I personally enjoyed the story and the game a lot and since I have no qualms about using overpowered gear/items/in-depth knowledge of game mechanics the difficulty curve was manageable to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing Final Fantasy 2 for the first time was experience I was not expecting.  I would say that the pixel remaster has more than likely brought this title a long way with new music, graphics and game play refinement.  I really enjoyed the customization of characters through leveling stats based on the way you use the characters in battle.  You can see an early development of the job system in this game play mechanic.  Having characters that can be molded in any direction you choose feels rewarding.  The ever rotating fourth character was interesting and kept the game fresh.One major point that grabbed me and created investment in the world was how you return to locations several times through out the story.  This felt a bit unique in a Final Fantasy game where you often are always moving forward onto the next location.  In Final Fantasy 2 the world is given a touch of reality as you set off to visit a location to accomplish a task and then return to share your accomplishments and move the story forward.  Revising locals and witnessing the world change as the story drives forward was very rewarding.I would not shy away from this title due to others perceptions of older versions of this title.  Final Fantasy 2 was very enjoyable and unique in way worthy of being played.

_childDocuments_.review: This game kinda sucks but it is very much worth playing.  It's similar to FF8 where a lot of wild ideas were attempted, leading to something that is grueling to play but is an interesting piece of JRPG history.  Below the dotted line I'm going to ramble about the systems and why they do and don't work.  For the TLDR bottom line, skip below it.----------------------------------------FF2 tried its hardest to evolve beyond its prequel while also trying to match the advancements brought by Dragon Quest 2.  Any character can equip any piece of equipment.  Differences in equipment are somewhat small, and without the restrictions the characters loadouts become mostly homogenized until the occasional piece of unique equipment pops up. This could also be said for FF1, but the equipment restrictions along with the player's choice in party composition created more decision points as to how to distribute gear based on what the game has given you.  This game also abandoned the EXP/Level system for a system where utilizing a stat, swinging a weapon, or casting a spell would naturally make you more proficient in it.  It's a very simple concept that's easy to understand, but doesn't mesh perfectly with the rest of the game as those three types of stat increases all function in different ways.  You don't need to deck your characters out with shields and ram them together while goblins watch despite what you may have heard.  Stats don't need to be watched or managed and will gradually rise as long as you have a role in mind for that character.  Weapon proficiency will only rise if you are fighting enemies at an equal or higher strength than you, and it feels less like leveling up a skill and more like trying not to fall behind. You're encouraged to pick a weapon type for each character and stick with it; hopefully that type has good endgame equipment.  Due to the games ludicrously high encounter rate, you'll often hit caps in weapon skills quickly which makes it not too much of a chore to swap around. Magic is the most powerful form of customization you have for a character, but actually does require you to intentionally try to grind out each spell's level to make it useful.  Magic choices can greatly specialize a character, but require great amounts of money or getting them randomly from enemy drops. These three types of stats all have little bits of stress related to each that spoil the goal of having a simple system where you just do stuff and grow. A cool new feature is a rudimentary dialog system where you can learn key terms and use those with different people to move the story forward. It's a fun concept and ties into the role play of a young rebel who whispers his organization's keyword to guys in a dark alley to identify his allegiance.  Unfortunately it is only used to move the main story forward and only in a linear fashion as only certain NPCs use the system.  It's a 3 piece menu to advance a dialog box where a simple button press could continue the conversation and only is used otherwise in the endgame to get a powerful weapon.  This exemplifies the FF2 experience now that I think about it.  The honest intention to have fun new ways to play an RPG result in you just being a cog that keeps the RPG machine going.The story is good for it's era.  You can see the roots for FF4's more complex plot here.  The flow of the story requires a lot of backtracking to your home base which works narratively but lacks the efficient simplicity of FF1's system of adventuring while following the bread crumb trail given by NPCs.  Your fourth party member rotates out for a whole gang of people who are interesting enough story-wise, but never spend enough time with you to feel like true members of the group or even grow to be the same power level mechanically.  ----------------------------------------FF2 has a lot of clever ideas that differ from the usual FF formula that wouldn't come to true fruition until the birth of the Squaresofts's SaGa games.  These ideas are weakened by scaling those up to a full JRPG experience. The clash of good ideas that proliferated through the series with the poor or misguided decisions in game design make it something worth playing for historical purposes or for Final Fantasy completionists. This port has adjustments and features that improve the experience but unfortunately ignored the high encounter rate that pads out the game.  It's a recommend for a Final Fantasy fan, but not someone who is an aspiring fan.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance , it seems like a simple pixel remastered edition wouldn't worth the $20 asking price. But boy , I couldn't be more wrong . The remastered Soundtracks alone , is worth the price and is fantastic to listen to .There is an insane amount of effort poured into Optimization , Modernization to each and every sprite of characters and every corner of the game , just so they can catch up to the recent version of the re-re-released FF2 . Firion (who is the game protagonist) for example , has receive a far more vibrant pixel rework , which makes his outfit more in line with the original Yoshitaka Amano artwork .On top of that , there is an improved mini map , more user-friendly ui and player interaction with chest and items .  Each Unique NPC in the town has also receive an exquisite update in charming sprites . Even the char animation is completely redone , with transparency effects . One example would be when you are healing within the sanctuary , or your character has gotten poisoned , there is a green transparent outline surrounding your characters . You will have to be a big fan of the original to appreciate these . All of these , on top of having to stay extremely faithful to the original NES version of FF2 , discarding all of the changes made from past re-re-release edition , including the overworld FF2 music which received an extension back from the PSP version , that is no easy task .Overall it is  a job well done , SquareEnix .  As a huge fan of original NES FF2 , I would gladly recommend this to the fans of the original game .P/S : The support for wide-screen is another sweet bonus for people who owned a wide-screen monitor .

_childDocuments_.review: Final fantasy II is a game that's incredibly hard to recommend... but completely impossible not to.Hot take: anyone who tells you this is their favorite Final Fantasy game is either lying or has never played any of the other mainstream titles (except maybe 8, but that's another kettle of fish entirely.) Final Fantasy II is a mess, with a broken 'leveling' system, frustrating dungeon design, and writing that at times is laughable, both intentionally and unintentionally so.Having said all that, it's also important to remember the context of its original release though, and for a game that came out in the late 80s, on an 8 bit console that couldn't even manage an arcade-perfect version of Pac Man... it's got a lot going for it, and despite its flaws it shows a drive for innovation that the series would continue to demonstrate over the next decade plus of releases. And this? This is the best version of the game released to date.Don't come into FFII expecting the down and dirty basics of FFI, or to see the fleshing out of the classes that would define the series in FFIII. FFII is its own beast, with its own quirks, and while it DOES introduce a great many things that would go on to be series staples, from the recurring Cid character to chocobos to even dragoons, it ALSO manages to veer wildly from the path Square would take the main series in in terms of actual gameplay.First things first: yes, this is basically the prototype for the SaGa/Final Fantasy Legends games that would garner popularity on the Game Boy and later even the PS1. As such, FFII DOES have a strong legacy in Square's annals of video games. That said, prototype is absolutely the key word here, and it shows in the way the game's freeform leveling works. No classes, no character levels as a whole per se: instead, imagine a system more akin to something like the Elder Scrolls titles, where using a skill allows you to improve it. Except, there's a catch: whereas the Elder Scrolls games will let you do some customization up front most of the time, or grant you shortcuts to gaining skills by hiring trainers and the like, FFII offers no such luxuries. Your characters are blank slates in almost the truest sense of the word: you are given basic starting weapons, sure, but no skill in using them, and no spells. Weapon types and individual spells all have their own levels, and while their growth can be somewhat planned, many of your other attributes are much harder to plan or predict, being granted through some arcane mix of use and random luck.Case in point: as with most players, I set out from the start of my playthrough of the Steam version with the plan to make Maria my black mage, with my other characters dabbling in black and white as necessary. I am currently outside one of the late game caves... and of my 3 main characters, Maria has the lowest MP and Magic stats in my party, despite being the single character I most consistently cast magic with. On the other hand, despite keeping her in the back row for about half the game, she has managed to accumulate more HP than Firion, my go-to swords person who somehow has managed to gain less Strength than she has despite her using bows almost the whole game and him having the highest weapon stats in my team.This is but one of the games myriad problems, from sometimes frustrating dungeon design (made much less so by the inclusion of maps and item tracking in this new version,) to travel annoyances (the game fails to offer any meaningful fast travel until over half-way through its run time,) to an uninteresting overworld and more.Having said all of that... it still manages to offer a very unique experience. For one thing, FFII has always (in my opinion at least) had one of the most interesting soundtracks in the entire FF series, many of its tunes carrying a melancholy timber unique to this game. That hasn't been lost in this version: if anything, the much improved instrumentation and often doubled (or more) length of the tracks allows for an audio landscape that is more engrossing than any other version of the game before it. This includes the new take on the Chocobo theme, presented for the first time in a version of FFII in its complete (later) form rather than the maybe 4-second loop of the original. This is but one of the improvements the game has made, including adjustments to leveling rates, enemy AI, removal of bugs, and the aforementioned maps, which are, to my mind, the single biggest selling point of the entire Pixel Remaster series so far. Honestly, of all its flaws and boons, II's biggest issue is in its pacing. What seems at first like an impressively sized world is sadly lacking in terms of notable features or areas to explore, and instead asks the player to do a lot -- a LOT -- of backtracking to progress the story. This wouldn't be such a big deal if, like with FFI or even FFIII, you received early access to reliable (player controlled) quick travel options... but sadly, II requires you to spend much of that backtracking time winding your way between hills and oceans on foot. There are attempts to mitigate this with paid quicker travel options by ocean and airship early-game, but the expense of those options -- in a game where inn rates go up the more you need to heal (and you can't pay to partially heal,) and with as many money issues as you'll be having early game unless you do copious amounts of extraneous grinding -- makes them impractical. Chocobos are found in precisely one location, flee when you dismount, and are in a location that is generally inconvenient to get to, to the point they serve as little more than a novelty rather than an aid. Many key locations are intentionally surrounded by semicircles or ridges of mountains and other barriers, so that even late game -- when you have a ship but haven't yet acquired the airship for the last hour or so of play -- you are left with docking on one side only to spend several minutes weaving through random encounter-infested mazes to reach your destination, only to have to re-do that same maze on your way back out, in many cases more than once.And yet... at its heart, it's still Final Fantasy. There's the glimmerings here of the stories and characters that later games would be defined by, the familiar battle themes and the series' iconic visual stylings are all present, and despite how radically different its leveling is from absolutely every other main-series title... in the end, it still winds up feeling distinctly Final Fantasy. Final Fantasy II's flaws, unlike those of I or III, aren't really found in bugs or limitations of the time, but are instead inherent in the actual design choices made for the game, making them basically impossible to fix in the Pixel Remaster without not only re-making but re-imagining the entire experience... and yet, the end result is still a game worth playing, at least once.Flawed? Absolutely. But it's a game that even within the varied world of Final Fantasy titles stands out for its unique traits, both good and bad, and deserves recognition for its place in the series' history.If you're not a fan of the Final Fantasy franchise then this game is not going to be the one that changes that. If you've never played a game in the series before then this is the absolute *worst* entry point i can imagine for it: play the pixel remasters of I or III first, or any of the other later games. Yes, even VIII or the oft-maligned XIII.If you ARE a Final Fantasy fan, even a relatively casual one... consider giving II a shot. Again, anyone who tells you II is their favorite Final Fantasy is lying through their teeth (or thinking about II on SNES which was a bastardized IV, and problematic in and of itself.) But at the end of the day... II is still a Final Fantasy game.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get the first thing out of the way. If you own and have beaten a prior version like PSP or old Android port, I can't recommend Pixel Remaster. it doesn't add enough new to justify purchasing it again, and regular contentwise it's based on NES and PS1 versions and has none of the Dawn of Souls extra content.With that said, this is a competent port of a flawed yet interesting game. Every port since NES tweaks mechanics in some way to attempt to balance the game or make it easier. Pixel Remaster in that regard is based on PSP version most closely, with growth rates for weapons and spell being fast early on and then getting slower. At the same time it reintroduced a semi-hidden mechanic that was absent since PS1 days. Magic Penalties on weapons and shields. Meaning if you want your build to be more magic oriented, for maximum efficiency you must use either Knife, Staff or go Barehanded. On the plus side MP growth is faster than it has ever been, even without exploiting the game mechanics, which allows one to use magic more freely than ever.If you haven't played played FF2 before and are interested in trying it out, this is a good option for that, if you don't have access to PSP version.

_childDocuments_.review: If you thought FF1 was super easy to beat, get ready for an actual challenge with this game.Not only is the levelling system much more complex in FF2, but it has twice as many different mobs as its predecessor -- and many of them are extremely cheap. You'll often get sleep/stun locked to death, or have Stone/Instant KO forced down your throat a bunch, and until you get the best gear in the game, you likely won't be able to do a thing about it. The mobs in this game are not a joke, especially in the final dungeon where you can get Game Over'd at ANY TIME, even if you have 5000+ HP on everybody. Thus it's a really good idea to use Quick Save a bunch in this game.On top of that, there are a LOT of missables all throughout this game. Fortunately you're gonna get help finding them (thanks to the Community tab), but whatever you do, DO NOT RUSH THE STORY. Otherwise it's gonna be a real pain when you miss something important and you're forced to start over from scratch in order to get 100% game completion.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna start with: THIS IS A LONG ONE AS I REALLY DO LOVE THIS GAME. If you don't like reading blocks of text, then scroll ahead. Anyway, the current definitive version of this game is not the Pixel Remaster but the PSP version. (Although the music in this is far superior).Is it a flawed game? It is. I recognize that. Do I consider it the best Final Fantasy mainline game? No. In fact, it's far from the best. Then why is it my favorite? Simple. Because underneath the flawed mechanics and system, I believe that there is something beautiful that people often overlook."How could you like this one? This game is basically Star Wars blah blah rebel versus empire?"Final Fantasy 2's story is somewhat simple. I agree. It's about four orphans that joined a rebel group to fight the evil empire and the evil emperor. But does that automatically make the story bad? Is a simple story bad just because it is simple -- and it resembles the story of another series? See, I think the criticisms this game receives over its story is kind of... unfair. Simple doesn't equate to bad. "But what about the fact that it is basically Star Wars?" Well, if you simplify the way you describe it, then yeah, it is basically Star Wars but if you play it, you'll see for yourself that it is actually different. That it is its own. Also, even if the story is simple, I'd argue that it does simplicity rather masterfully -- still flawed, but worth looking into."Heh, whatever. The main party is too bland anyway. They rarely talk."See, this is what we call silent protagonists. As you play the game, you'll notice how much you are attached to the game's world. You feel immersed in the game's atmosphere. The characters that join in your party feel like actual people. You know why? It's because your characters do not talk -- mostly. Silent protagonists are empty vessels for the player to put themselves into. This way, they could experience the world of the game with their own eyes, not with the eyes of somebody else. It wouldn't be as immersive if they are playing as someone with their own personality. But as what was mentioned, they still have dialogue. Just not in a way that breaks the illusion of you playing as you.But that is not to say that Final Fantasy 2 has protagonists that doesn't have personality. No. In fact, the art (Not in this version -- Pixel Remaster) actually does its job on conveying the characters' personalities.Firion is the de facto leader of the group. His art shows decisiveness, and bravery.Maria is the heart of the group. This is shown both in her PSP portrait and in her dialogues. For spoiler reasons, I wouldn't go in too deep at the dialogue part.Guy is the soft but clearly strong dude in the group."Meh. Whatever. The encounter rate is dumb."Agreed. But this is why I feel that if you really want to experience Final Fantasy 2 at its best, then play the PSP version. Pixel Remaster and the other versions retain one of the most annoying aspects of the game -- the stupidly high encounter rate."The music is great though."True."♥♥♥♥♥♥ leveling system as well."Different strokes for different people. A lot of people actually enjoyed that system of it. Did I enjoy? No. I found it very lacking, but still passable. But hey, you might like it.Anyway, Final Fantasy 2 is a flawed game with a simple story that isn't perfect, but I still consider to be great. It has a mediocre villain, mediocre leveling system and sometimes, unfair enemy encounters. But if you ask me, underneath all of those negative things about it. It is still a Final Fantasy game that is worth it to experience. Would I recommend the Pixel Remaster version, sure. But please do remember that it is not FF2 at its best. If you want the game at its best, find the PSP version.Rebel Army Theme one of the best Final Fantasy music. Peace.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II Pixel Remaster is a lovely remake of a game that people tend to either love or hate. Its strongest element is arguably its story, and that’s why I feel it’s hurt so much by cutting the excellent extra content added in the Game Boy Advance version. With that in mind, I think it’s best to stick with the old version of the game if you already own it and it still works. This new version is more modern in its presentation and UI, and ultimately it will be the one that survives. It’s also the only one you can buy now, so if you want to play Final Fantasy II it’s this or nothing. I enjoy the game, but you will need to be willing to put up with its eccentricities if you seek to do the same.

_childDocuments_.review: After  with the first Final Fantasy in its Pixel Remaster version, I had high hopes for . I knew that it was the least liked mainline  title as shown in a  – but there’s always a chance that one might feel different than the majority, right? Well, as it turns out, I’m indeed with the majority on this one:  is a game you really don’t “need” to play unless you really want to beat them all.Let’s start with the (few) good things here: Thanks to the Pixel Remaster,  looks reasonably good (especially compared to the original Famicom version) and the soundtrack is once again really well done. As I  for , the Pixel Remaster also introduces a few gameplay changes, all of which are greatly appreciated. These include maps for all areas, an auto-battle option & more. Once again missing is bonus content introduced with previous re-releases of . In this case, this would be the  bonus questline and the  dungeons from the PSP version of the game. For a detailed history of each  version, I’ll also once again refer .Anyway, as mentioned, the Pixel Remaster of  looks and sounds great. I also appreciate the improvements to the plot compared to its predecessor, even featuring protagonist dialogue! Still, let’s keep in mind that  was originally released in 1988 – which means the story itself is still pretty basic, with characters only getting a few lines of dialogues at best throughout the entire (!) game. If you want to play  because you want to know the plot, I’d recommend just checking the  instead. Its premise (group of rebels vs big empire) might sound interesting but again, just a few textboxes every now and then can’t really provide anything more than what ends up as a really barebones/basic storyline.However, the reasons as to why I wouldn’t recommend to anyone but hardcore  fans are all found in the gameplay provided here. The biggest offender here is certainly the levelling system, which could best be described as an experiment that doesn’t/didn’t work out. Let me explain why.First of,  departed from the experience-based combat system used in its predecessor (gathering experience points results in level ups, which in turn increase character stats). Instead, characters level up abilities/stats by using them: If you want to increase the level of a cure spell for example (resulting in more health restored), you’ll have to use that cure spell over and over until it gains a level. The same goes for weapon types (keep fighting with swords in order to increase your sword level) and abilities (take damage in order to increase your max health).Now, on paper, this might not sound too bad. In fact, it might even sound like  offers a bigger degree of character customization compared to its predecessor, allowing you to only level the spells/weapons/attributes you really need! But in practice, it’s more of a hindrance than anything.Here's an example: As a turn-based RPG,  features numerous positive and negative status effects. Negative status effects that otherwise last after battle can be cured using the white magic spell . After a character learns the spell Esuna using a tome, the spell is only at level 1 and can only remove the status effects “Poison” and “Darkness”. Only once Esuna is at spell level 5, all possible lasting status effects like “Stone” can be removed – which is course means that you’ll definitely want Esuna at level 5, unless you’re planning to invest in all possible status removal items (which is definitely valid but let’s ignore that possibility for now). But how does one get Esuna to level 5? The answer is easy: Keep casting Esuna in battle, even if your party members are perfectly healthy. There’s no other way, really – if you only use Esuna once you actually acquire negative status effects, levelling will take forever. And as you can’t cast Esuna on healthy party members outside of battle, you’ll have to waste your MP on casting a then useless spell in a lot of battles. Sounds great, right?Consider this: If you want to change up your party in any way throughout later parts in the game, you’ll need to level new spells/weapons types/attributes from scratch again. Want to replace your spell from the first dungeon with a new one you found later on? Get ready for a lot of casting until the power of your old spell is matched! Want to switch weapon types? Here’s to a lot of lower damage until you reach the numbers of your previous weapon types! And so on. The levelling system present punishes late-game experimentation.But even if you make up your party composition and strategies early on,  will make sure that these won’t last – thanks to temporary party members. While you got three permanent party members from the beginning, your fourth party member will change – a lot. And not only do these new characters come with different strength and weaknesses, each time, they’ll also need be as strong as the rest of the party. Especially the last party member, added right before the final dungeons of the game, will most likely never be as strong as your starting members.In addition to this convoluted levelling systems (play with shields in both hands for a few hours in order to level up your evasion rates for later in the game – trust me),  also features way too many random encounters. This is especially annoying when you get to the end of a long dungeon - only to find out that you were supposed to do something on the first floor before heading to the last (still angry about that one, ). As you can’t even move for 10 seconds before triggering another encounter, I really wish there was a way to (temporarily) turn them off.Lastly,  occasionally does a terrible job of telling you where to go next – something the original  was definitely better at. I recommend consulting a walkthrough  in order to prevent frustration – and if you’re an achievement hunter, I’ll even urge you to do so, as certain treasure chests and bestiary entries are entirely missable.Concluding, thanks to its many gameplay problems and only few upsides, I see no reason why anyone should bother with  – unless you’re a hardcore fan of the franchise, of course. It can easily be skipped without missing a thing and even in the same franchise, there a way better titles to check out instead. Even the well-appreciated updates of the Pixel Remaster can't change that, unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II features an ensemble cast; while there are still four main characters, they are no Warriors of Light, they aren’t blessed by Crystals, and many of the temporary party members throughout the game leave as swiftly as they joined. Instead, FFII is the quintessential story about an evil empire conquering the remainder of the world—nothing more, nothing less—with the player party consisting of the resistance fighters aiming to take down the Emperor.While FFI barely featured any story, FFII attempts to weave a bit more of a narrative. Dialogue in general is a lot more prevalent and is further supported by one of FFII’s two most striking features: A sort of primitive dialogue system consisting of ‘Keywords’. Whenever an NPC brings up a phrase that is of interest to the player, it is highlighted and can be added to things players can ask about. Often this results in empty or pointless dialogue, but it is a bit of a proof of concept to nudge FF into a design that is decidedly more story focused, even if it barely impacts gameplay. A byproduct of this sort of keyphrase system is that a lot of dialogue leans into further worldbuilding, offering more exposition about the world at large rather than just pointing the player to wherever the next dungeon may be. This is appreciated, even though FFII remains generally lackluster in its writing.Neither the player party nor the Emperor are well characterized. Since keyphrases replace properly written inter-party dialogue, there are only a few situations in which your own characters even get a chance to express themselves. Firion’s strongest moment is barely a few moments long, when he is seduced by a monster, which is afterwards referred to as Firion being a womanizer. Maria and Guy, who are your other two permanent party members, hardly have any more development either. That being the case, the fourth-party member slot is broadly flexible, and various characters join and leave according to current events in the story. Naturally, this also means that they have a bit more writing and context to them, but by no means comes this close to, for example, FFIV’s party dynamics.Overall, FFII is only a marginal step forward in terms of story. I do find the keyphrase system interesting but underdeveloped. Characters, party members or not, broadly just are not developed properly throughout a story whose setting is already as barebones as it could possibly get. The final nail in the coffin being the Emperor having next to no presence in the story until the very final hours of the game.FFII innovates a bit upon FFI’s combat in interesting ways. Sadly, just like the keyphrase system, these are ideas that ultimately are just too poorly implemented to make the game enjoyable. FFII still does not feature the series’ later ATB gauge, which means that it is indeed a strict turn-based combat system. Instead of the spell slots of FFI, it also introduces Mana as a resource for the player, making magic a lot more of a flexible option. It does not feature jobs; instead, any character can equip any weapons and magic, and levels such independently.Theoretically, this means that a player equipping a sword will continuously grow better in using this weapon class as they use it, with their stats increasing accordingly—making each character technically a hybrid between the tools the player chooses to focus them on. Nevertheless, each character also has personal stat growths, which may nudge them more strongly towards magic over martial combat or vice versa.I really wish Square tried to experiment with this system of character progression more, but as it stands in FFII as the only game that uses it, it’s a total mess. Stat growth balloons out very early, meaning most of the game is a total joke until the very last dungeon, if at all. It is also very opaque as to how your actions in combat increase your stats—for example, for the longest time, my skills with Swords on Firion were capped at 12/16. How come, I thought, since I was almost using them exclusively over any magic? However, the game assigns enemies both a rank, which determines whether they allow for you to gain skill experience on them at all, as well as that experience being dependent on your number of hits during combat. Effectively, this means that the most efficient way to level any weapon extremely quickly is to equip the weakest weapon available and then wail on the most spongy enemy available to you, resulting in a rank per combat and skyrocketing your effectiveness within minutes.All of this is to say that I do kind of like the concept of skills increasing in effectiveness as you use them as a way to progress your character, but that the implementation is hopelessly unbalanced and unfun. Equally unfun is the exploration of dungeons—which is by far the biggest part of FFII. Frankly, the vast majority of your time is spent in the various caverns and castles, all of which are unbearable to play thanks to a ludicrous encounter rate. You can barely take a few steps before any region in this game will force you into an encounter. It is a constant, horrible annoyance and is further stretched out by the same design of FFI, at times forcing you against a ridiculous number of enemies as well. Thankfully, this is where my incessant complaints stop. As with all Pixel Remasters, FFII looks very good all things considered. Sprites and effects are fantastic, as is the featured gallery from the main menu. The soundtrack was actually very surprising to me and is leagues better than both FFI and FFIII. The Rebel Army theme is about as iconic as the series’ , however the most standout track for me is it’s Battle Theme B, used for most bosses and is one of the most unique themes I’ve heard in the series altogether.As with the other Pixel Remasters, FFII broadly runs very well. I have not experienced any crashes, bugs, or otherwise; however, there are minor graphical issues that can crop up occasionally. Moving around the town of Mysidia, for example, slightly distorts the buildings in an effect that is similar to screen tearing.Final Fantasy II isn’t a very liked game already, and it having been the last of the classic Final Fantasy titles I had yet to play, I can absolutely see why. It’s a rushed successor to a title that was more popular than SquareSoft expected, which resulted in a bunch of concepts that seem like they may be good on paper but ultimately hamstrung the game and were then discarded for future titles with no further attempts to reconcile them as part of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: FF1 pixel remake is solid for what it is, but I have no idea why FF2 is so bad. There are so many bugs present that make casual playthrough horrible. A bug that made me seriously hate this game is the fact that pretty much none of the status prev. items (ribbion, protection ring, genji armor, etc.) do not work. This led to a frustrating end dungeon where Coreuls are a common enemy to be found in packs of 4-6 (unless paired with an easily killable Lamia). This is all well and good if their basic attack weren't a 1 shot with no way to prevent it. The only way to avoid a party-wide wipe is to insta kill them (each has 1000 hp, so even dual wielding weapons can be a tall order to kill them all if there is 6; unless you overgrind beyond belief) before they can attack you first as there is no way to prevent them from one shotting you if their attack lands. Another exceedingly annoying result of this isn't confined to just one enemy, but many. I found that not all prevention items (such as resisting sleep) work, only a handful do. As a result there can be many times when I equip my party with the appropriate equipment to avoid the stun locks that can happen, and yet they still happen; in addition, if you outlevel the content (like I like to do) you can be sitting there for quite a while as you hope that *maybe* you will break free from the endless CC chain just to one shot the super easy to kill enemy(enemies). Those simple bugs made the mid-end game (ESPECIALLY the end dungeon) dreadful to play through. The end dungeon single handily ruined the game for me simply because of how infuriating it is to have to quick save after every encounter because half of the encounters in the end dungeon can end in your defeat simply because of bugs that should have been fixed.FF1 did not have this issue (or it could also be that since the end game of FF1 didn't have the infuriating mobs that you face in the end game of FF2 making it a nonissue), and while I have yet to play FF3 I have heard it is far and away the best of the 3 remakes so I would assume this pretty obvious bug does not exist.I have heard of mistranslations existing on this remake, but things like the ribbon is known to prevent things such as sleep. That is the point of the ribbon in FF games- they prevent effects like that, and when it doesn't do that it exceeds a mistranslation and is just a bug.The weird (arguably bad) level up system, magic system, etc. can be attributed to prodcuts of their time. I am happy they didn't rework these like they did when it came to FF1 remakes on other devices and how they completely reworked the combat because I wanted to experience them as they were no matter how bad they are; however, these bugs that make the end game one of the worst gaming experiences I have ever had, to the point that it pissed me off enough to write this novel about how bad they are, makes me not recommend this game. Once the bugs are fixed then sure, it isn't a bad game if you can get past the products of their time game mechanics. But until the bugs are fixed, avoid this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is evidence that Steam really needs a Mixed option for Reviews. There's things I loved, things I felt needed to be better explained and glitches that should have been dealt with.This game really captures the feel of a devastating war, the loss of life extending to party members. Not only that, but the atmosphere of damaged towns added to the Pixel Perfect remaster helps captures this feel. And while the main party members does not have the same strength of characterisation you'd see in later entries, the journeys of the side characters along with the sheer ruthlessness of the emperor makes up for it. As for the battle system, it felt good you could build the party the way you suited them through picking the weapons and magic they used, although not as refined as SaGa series inspired by FF2 even in the remaster feel gives a distinct feel of customisation. And the refinements such as showing the current party's weapon levels at the end of battle to give a feel of progression along with auto-battle for encounters that can be trivially dealt with, not only auto-repeating commands but speeding up the battle as well.However, I feel there are areas of the gameplay that should have been better explained. Namely not only how some weapons, shields and heavy armour hinders magic, but this is never said up front in game, merely something the player has to discover. The descriptions could benefit by making it clear what penalties equipment bring to magic. I will say, while this bothered me at first, I eventually adapted and appreciated how it made use of light armour and how dual wielding could be used as a way to make up for the lack of shields for characters built as mages, giving them an evasion bonus along with an extra attack. That being said, I feel that while the penalties were good to apply to heavy armour, maybe they shouldn't have been applied to weapons and shields. And then there was the weapon levelling that is linked to HOW MUCH you use the weapon in a battle, which meant I spent days trying to get weapons to level 16 until I switched to a weaker weapon, which while extending the battle ensured weapon levels increased.And then there's things of this game that made me feel it was a remaster that was rushed. First, the life spell when used on a group of enemies can freeze the game if it kills more than one. This is a pity as it is a good way to level the spell along with kill undead with out the risk of killing living enemies. However, this is minor change compared to the fact that certain status effects are not protected by equipment that should protect from these ailments, namely instant death attacks which means if you get in an ambush against the wrong group of enemies, you could risk getting a game over before you even have time to flee. Good thing this game has auto-save whenever you enter a new room. More minor issues I noticed is that facing one boss turned random encounter turns off auto-battle and the credits music featuring FF2 music suddenly gets interrupted at the first quarter by louder FF1 music.Until the two major glitches are fixed, I can't give this a true positive review that should be given a mixed review label instead. However, if Square Enix returns to finally remove terrible glitches from the game, the heavily mixed feelings would disappear. In any case, I do not regret playing through Final Fantasy 2, though I feel due to the issues it is not as definitive a version of the game as it tries to write itself off as compared to the Final Fantasy 1 Pixel Perfect Remaster.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is a strange case in some ways. The original Final Fantasy had the barest semblance of a plot and was obviously going for a D&D-but-on-TV type thing to the point of using a vancian spellcasting system and literally using many monsters from the D&D Monster Manual, and it still managed to revolutionize the genre and laid the basis for what would later be common tropes and elements in the series and of the genre itself, such as a medieval fantasy world with a technologically advanced ancient past, the use of ships and airships, and a plot that involved saving the world by defeating some dude attempting to bring an evil-deity-related apocalypse.This sequel improves upon the formula by having a more complex plot revolving around an evil empire on a campaign of conquest and a band of rebels trying to fight back, and by having more detailed main characters and NPC's with actual names and backstories and motivations, as well as by adding a keyword system that allows you to investigate plot points by talking to important NPC's and learning said words from them and being able to specifically ask about each word. But most importantly, by ditching the previous magic system for the more familiar MP-based spellcasting mechanic. So far, so good. Problem is, they also decided to improve upon the leveling system, and they did it by making it skill-based and dependent on what you actually do instead of on earning XP to gain levels, so you gain the illusion that you're completely free to do whatever you want, when what actually happens is that unless you deliberately pick a role for each character and specialize in it emulating classic FF classes/jobs, you risk having characters that know how to do a lot of things badly instead of a few things well, which will make things harder for you in the long run. In addition it's no longer clear whether you're overpowered or underpowered for a specific area because character levels are not a thing. What you have is stats and HP and MP as well as skill levels for each spell and weapon. It's interesting but needlessly vague and convoluted.I've often heard this is the worst old-school Final Fantasy game by far, and maybe that caused me to go into it with very low expectations, because I actually enjoyed it a lot and it's objectively better than the first one in almost every way.
