_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 2 has always been something of an odd duck due to some of its more infamous design choices, many of which have been retained over its many remakes. But the Pixel Remaster version left me pleasantly surprised.One of the most significant changes in this version is that you now gain HP naturally as you fight battles, meaning you no longer have to hit yourself to gain HP, which was one of the most infamous frustrations it was known for. Stat and weapon/spell leveling comes much more naturally and there is now very little need to grind, so you can enjoy playing through the story normally and not have to worry about playing it "right." I think MP was the only stat that I had to go out of my way to grind for, and even then it was doable in a very reasonable amount of time.Some of the more sadistic exploration choices of the game have also been improved: there are no longer midgame monsters waiting to slaughter you ten steps south of the first town, and you can go reasonably further from Fynn castle without meeting the same fate. The game still does punish going too far off the beaten path, but is much more fair about it. Even the dungeons' notorious "monster closets" have had their encounter rates reduced and I was able to leave them much more easily.I guess I'm in a weird position because I'll never really think of FF2 as a "good" Final Fantasy game but this is by far the best and most enjoyable version of the game to play, save for the 100% Status Effect issue mentioned in other reviews which is hopefully not intentional and will be patched out in due time, but presents a serious balance issue as it is now. And of course the other issues present in the other FF Pixel Remasters such as not remembering Fullscreen settings, the font, etc.Other than that... They really did it. They finally made FF2 a reasonably fun game. And while I know many people who are diving into the Pixel Remaster series will likely skip this one, I really do commend the effort into getting its system to work good and feel good. And I no longer have to feel like a meticulous minmaxer to get the most out of it. For that alone, I really recommend giving this a try,

_childDocuments_.review: So, just beat FF2 Pixel Remaster.Final review? Absolute crap. Total rush job. Preemptively addressing the "we're trying to be faithful to the original" point? Sometimes the original just didn't age well. Admitting weakness is the first step towards improvement in general, but for some reason Squeenix couldn't care less. Maybe it was that they figured that because the 2nd one had the least amount of fans, or that it had a reputation of being crap, that perhaps they figured "ah hell, fans are just gonna buy the bundle anyway, we might as well just consider it extra content, not spend too much time balancing it". Enemies have enemy types, but it never matters because I just cheese it anyway. Magic is OP in the early-to-midgame and then becomes underpowered and its damage grows at an impossibly slow pace, especially with the hidden intelligence penalty for wearing armor- a mechanic they never even tell the players. Ultima is a pathetic joke with overly complex (and unnecessary) damage calculations, which asks you to level up both weapons levels of all types AND magic, and given that you have to use magic religiously to even have it come close to the convenience and accessibility of the "no SP required" physical attacks, good luck leveling up magic, too. Especially Life. Or Esuna. Or Basuna, whose utility isn't integrated with Esuna for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason. No explanation of which ailments Esuna can heal. Esuna can heal Stone when it reaches level 6. The game will not tell you that. Punishes players for experimenting with weapons/magic for the sake of falling behind in other weapon levels. It's as if the developers for Pixel Remaster never considered what magic/weapon levels their party would be at, at any given time. The world map is empty and lifeless. There are trees here, a marsh there, a lake here, but nothing about the geography matters. Vast stretches of haphazardly placed grass and woods, with zero cohesion or interest. It's just... barren. A lot of the games DO this to some extent, but amid how few locations on the world map there are it's abysmally apparent here.Sorry Nobuo Uematsu, but the GBA/PSX/PSP version of the world map theme is superior to yours, conveys the hopelessness of the story. In fact, ♥♥♥♥ it, the entire Pixel Remaster OST is inferior to its GBA/PSX/PSP iteration. The fanmade Super Nintendo version of this OST sounds better (and given the visual presentation, would be more cohesive to the overall presentation anyway). If you don't believe me? Listen for yourself. (      ).Oh, and no Soul of Rebirth. ♥♥♥♥ the players for wanting to have the game be held to the same standard of content as previous versions, right? The encounter rate. You level your stats up too fast and the encounter rate never slows down proportional to your fighting strength against enemies. It's lazy design and it makes dungeon navigation even more of a slog. Which is a shame especially given the dungeons are poorly designed, anyway; long hallways that form a circumference around the room to maximize walk length doesn't test navigational skill, it only tests my patience. The game doesn't seem to have any kind of considered difficulty curve, opting for the quantity of encounters over quality. Which means that if you manage to take down the captains in Fynn by neutering them with the Ancient Sword and get sweet, sweet revenge for say, 10-30 minutes, the rest of the game bends to your will. In fact, the Ancient Sword essentially breaks the whole game. Get it, swing it at an enemy that would normally kill you in 1-2 hits, and watch them flounder. The game mechanically says "you win" hours upon hours on end after that, and the only tactical consideration you need at that point is deciding which weapon level you want to grind. There was no doubt, or thrill, or any kind of mental indication that told me that I might lose. And the game doesn't have icons to even indicate which status effects you've inflicted on the enemy. The only indication that I know I've cursed an enemy with my Ancient Sword is when another party member attacks it and it drops like a fly. I guess the developers though "meh, what the hell, the battles don't really engage the player anyway." It's enough to deal with people IRL that don't try, but when it's a video game that I (theoretically) play in the pursuit of having fun, that doesn't try?At what point does it test my skills at playing the game making 90% of the rooms trap rooms that trigger a random encounter? And don't tell me it's "preparedness for long dungeons", or, "heal after every battle". That's common sense, by the time I've reached Jade Passage, let alone the literal dozens of other doors leading to a surprise encounter. But occasionally it leads to a room full of chests! "Hi Potion". This is just player contempt, at this point.I went into FF2PR thinking "there is no way this game is as bad as people say". And the first few hours were legitimately fun, quickly leveling up my weapon levels and going from disadvantage to advantage. But that feeling of advantage never really went away, the learning curve didn't go vertical enough for me to care about what I equipped or what I used other than my defaults. Eventually it disengaged me and felt more like a chore, a slog, playing it only to spite the developers for daring me to give up and quit. Maybe it's because I'm getting old and jaded to think back on the GBA version with rose-tinted glasses, but even with that filter it in retrospect only went to the level of "this wasn't as bad as everyone says". Well, this version really is as bad as everyone say-*trap room encounter* this version really is as *enemy encounter* this version really is as *enemy encounter* this ver*enemy encounter*

_childDocuments_.review: While I spent a few hours on the Famicom version of Final Fantasy II, this was my first time making significant progress and completing it. While I can’t compare it in depth to previous versions, here are a few thoughts. The story is pretty enjoyable with a lot more moving pieces and characters than the first game. The story of youths helping a rebellion defeat an evil Empire is hardly original, but you feel like you’re completing a series of smaller goals on a path toward larger gains, instead of just wandering around the world lighting the four crystals as in the original. There are a considerable number of NPC’s this time around, with actual personalities, and this includes additional party members who join you temporarily. As it’s still a Famicom game at its core, you won’t find nearly as much dialogue and interaction as on FF4-FF6.Combat is generally enjoyable, if very easy. FF2 is infamous for its stat growth system based on actions rather than experience points and levels. Taking damage increases max HP, using magic makes it more powerful, weapon skill increases as you play. While this required more consideration and planning on the Famicom, here you will generally be fine if you fight most random battles as you play. It’s really hard to set yourself back too badly but I feel the flow is best if you pick one weapon type for each character, and a small number of spells and stick to them.There are a ton of major historical series firsts here, including the introduction of the Chocobo, monsters like the Behemoth and Malboro, and many others that I don’t want to spoil. But if you saw something in FF4 and thought it was cool, there’s a decent chance that it first appeared in this game in some form. Even if the game isn’t your cup of tea in terms of game design, it might be worth visiting just to fill in these gaps. I consider myself knowledgeable about even the games I haven’t played much, but there were a few that surprised me as well. Graphics are quite nice, visually similar to the FF1 Pixel Remaster but with a little more visual flare shown during major story events. Enemy design continues to be very faithful to the source material. I’m pleased that unlike the Famicom version, there are no major art assets that feel ripped from the first game. As in FF1, you’ll need to manually replace the default font for the best experience, and screen tearing continues to be an issue, but there are workarounds. In what will most likely become a clear trend with all the Pixel remasters, it seems that play-testing was limited. Using physical attacks, some enemies can inflict status effects on you, including instant death with 100% success. It appears to be a bug specific to this version, but is mitigated somewhat by the fact that there’s an autosave made with each screen transition. There is one monster-in-a-box that took me 20 attempts due to this issue.  The opposite issue also exists- weapons like the Sleep Blade will affect enemies 100% of the time, including all bosses, so you have a built in cheat mode thanks to sloppy design. There are once again quality of life improvements such as detailed maps in-game, autosave, quicksave, Steam Achievements and Bestiary. Additional content from other remakes are not present here. While I’m not nostalgic for the Famicom version, many are, and it’s unfortunately that Square Enix once again did not provide any difficulty options, toggles for music, or anything that might cater to those who prefer the original experience.

_childDocuments_.review: From my Youtube Review:Man, I am a sucker for Final Fantasy games. I believe there are more of those on this channel than any other series out there. Regardless of that, this is the first time Final Fantasy II has shown up here. My wife loves this game, but I've always had a hard time getting over the levelling system.  She started this one while I played FFI and as she went, would tell me about how streamline the leveling is in this one. Since I had planned to play all six games in the pixel remaster edition, it came that time to finally get over my awkward feelings about the leveling in this.  I hate running from a battle. I would make my last stand on some desperate hill of Marlboro breath and dead allies before retreat. I hated how the older versions required running as a pre-requisite for increasing, I think, evasion? Also the older version, increasing one stat would lower another and I wasn't having that. With this version of FFII, you increase a stat, you keep it...and no more running. I was finally down to play this game. It felt odd at first, Seeing a strength point here, some HP there, maybe a weapon every now and then, but after a few hours of story and grinding, the whole system clicked into place for me and I was really enjoying it. Magic and weapons can be used by anyone, so you could go all out with everyone, but it was better to specialize a bit. Firion was my white mage learning all white magic, Maria was my black mage, and guy was my beater who ended up learning the spells I liked the most from white and black.I'm a completionism at heart, but since there was no end lvl goal, I didn't feel the need to max out my characters. Doing so would have been herculean. Towards the end it takes nearly a thousand cast of Ultima to level it up from say twelve to thirteen, and even more to get it maxed to 16. Leveling all the weapons would have been crazy too since the higher they go, only stronger monsters give points to them, I imagine by lvl 14 or so, I would have to grind nothing but Iron Giants to get them maxed. There may be an easier way I am overlooking, but I got all the steam achievements, that's what really matters nowadays. Like the first Final Fantasy, the pixel graphics are beautiful, crisp and HD. Also like the first, the music is an awesome mix of Uematsu re-masters, renditions, re-makes and clearly some Black Mages influence in there. The soundtrack is awesome and the I love many of the pieces from this game. One of my favorites is the boss music with the stilted electric guitar and the ghostly choral singing...too bad I didn't hear it long enough as most boss battles in this version are a joke. literally one to three rounds of auto attack and the majority are done. That is really my only complaint about this game, you can easily overpower since nearly every battle awards some kind of stat increase. Honestly, the complaint is small since it's still an enjoyable experience. My only regret is that I waited so long to finally go through Final Fantasy II, but it took this version of the game to get me around to playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 2 is commonly listed as one of the, if not the single worst game in the series. This version of the game is an improvement on the original in my opinion, even if it was my first time playing, I can tell the Pixel Remaster alleviates many of the issues that earned FFII's rank at the bottom. Older games suffered from artificial difficulty, punishing consequences & grindy leveling. Sometimes you feel overpowered in this game, but that's OK.The QOL additions (fast-battle, menus, etc) help a ton to make the older systems flow as you'd expect. The Skyrim-style skill progression feels OK in this game, not great, but I can appreciate what Square was going for. The obvious balancing done to make the game easier is what makes this old game flow nicely - older games were very grindy, and while some people will be annoyed that the game is less challenging; it makes it that much more digestible for someone looking to experience the first real Final Fantasy game. (By which I mean it introduces many of the games' iconic features - Chocobos, Cid, larger storyline, etc...) If you haven't played the original games (like I hadn't) this is a great way (if not THE way) to dive in. If you're a fan of the old-school difficulties this and other early JRPG's can throw at you, this will probably be too easy. I think it's still worth supporting releases of legacy games in either case. Overall, great to experience one of the most influential games in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II ought to be a game about choice, but in this version of the game, it is not. Why? The magic penalty is back.FFII easily has the most complex EXP progression system compared to any RPG before it, and is still more complex than every subsequent Final Fantasy game. This is the game that inspired The Elder Scrolls' progression system -- every physical attack gets you a chance at gaining Strength, every magic attack can get you boosts to Intelligence, every dodged hit can get you Agility boosts, and every hit taken can boost HP or vitality. Every weapon and spell has its own skill to level up, to a maximum of 16. In theory, this "gain what you use" approach means the player could have ultimate freedom to build their party however they choose. Want a battlemage who's really good at wielding swords and axes? How about a rogue who also specializes in debuff spells? This progression system could accommodate those unique builds, in theory. This *seems* to have been the developers' intention when making the game, and it would have been a great departure from other games on the market: Dragon Quest, Final Fantasy, Wizardry, Ultima, and of course, Dungeons & Dragons all placed party members in rigid, inflexible roles. But it is not a departure at all, because there's one massive, game-ruining problem: The INT/SOUL penalty. This was a "feature" in the Famicom version that had been removed in the GBA and PSP ports of the game, but now it's back in the Pixel remaster. It operated like the magic check penalty in Dungeons & Dragons. If you have a weapon or armor equipped, expect to see a *severe* penalty to magic, to the point where it becomes useless. If you tried being, for example, a paladin healer who physically attacks sometimes, heals other times, or use the "Life" spell to turn undead, you would have to go into the item menu during battle and unequip everything sometimes every. other. turn. It's a tedious, slow, painful process made only slightly better with improved UI compared to the Famicom version. Even though the system seems to encourage freedom, the game actively punishes you for making your party anything but your average, boring Fighter, White Mage, and Black Mage. This was a horrible misstep. If the idea was to branch out and multiclass, the INT/SOUL penalty made it impossible. This is literally the standard job system in disguise. What was even the point of having a "gain what you use" progression system if you're forced into narrow classes just like every other RPG on the market? With the INT/SOUL penalty, Final Fantasy II is worse off, and has zero replay value.Some argue that this is a balancing mechanism. If the INT/SOUL penalty didn't exist, you could just have every party member max out every weapon and spell and be a master of all without any drawbacks. However, this is a 15 hour game where grinding isn't required if you plan ahead and form effective strategies. Maxing everything out is a tedious, unnecessary process that will easily quadruple the game length, at least. If you want to powerlevel and make the game boring, go crazy, but it's at a cost of time and sanity. What this means is the game was already balanced without the INT/SOUL penalty for any normal playthrough. The penalty was an overcorrection that breaks any freedom the novel progression system may have otherwise introduced.This worst part of all this is that none of this is told to the player. There's no message when equipping armor, no tutorial, or no dialogue from NPCs. Users who datamined the Famicom version found that the weapons and armors all had different penalties, and again, there's no way to know this in-game, or whether the Pixel remaster has the same penalties as the Famicom version. The only people who would possibly know this system exists are the small handful of people who bothered to emulate the Famicom version and actively read the guides. This will undoubtedly alienate new players, who will more likely than not give their party members both magic and armor, then wonder why their spells are so terrible. Not knowing to unequip the armor, they'll be more likely to stop using magic altogether, then get stuck at the Sargeant and/or Adamantoise fights where physical attacks only do single digits of damage. If Square insists on bringing this awful mechanic back, players need some indication that it exists, or new players *will* rage quit and get a refund.The INT/SOUL penalty ruins the Pixel remaster for me. I hate to say this, because I love all the other Pixel remasters so far. To date, these are the best graphics and music we've seen in the classic final fantasy games. I wish there were difficulty settings or some way to turn off the INT/SOUL penalty. Now I'll have to choose between strong presentation in the Pixel remaster or engaging gameplay on the PSP.There is no definitive version of FFII.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a long time since I played any other version of FF2, however I really liked the presentation of this one, it looks and sounds great.  It's a good game for the most part but there are a couple of things that can make it a bit annoying to play.I'm not one to shy away from a fight in RPGs and often grind way too much just for the fun of watching my stats grow, and this game has a ton of that.  You could if you wanted max out all your stats HP/MP/STR/INT, etc right outside the first town if you wanted to.  The real problem with random encounters however, is how often you run into them.  If you don't want to grind endlessly then running into a fight every 10 or so steps is going to get really old, really fast.You could run away from battle (especially if you are already way over leveled for the area) and while that speeds things up tremendously, it still gets really tedious.This gets really bad when you are running across the entire world back and forth trying to figure out where you are suppose to go, or who you are suppose to talk to.  I haven't played this game in a long time so a lot of it felt new again as it was mostly forgotten, and due to this my characters were much stronger than they should have been for the entire game, with it only getting worse the further I got.This version seems to have made some alterations to the way enemy's status effects hit you.  If their physical attack can apply a status effect, then it does 100% of the time, unless you manage to outright evade the attack.  Even getting hit for 0 damage still applies the effect.  This can feel pretty broken when you are completely stomping everything in the game in 1 or 2 hits, then you encounter a group of 6 enemies that can paralyze you and then stun lock you for the entire fight.  Even though you could just breath on the enemy and it would normally die, instead you are stuck there suffering for what could be several minutes of them giving you the equivalent of paper cuts, or mosquito bites until you are finally dead.  These enemies can be so weak at times that they even try to run away from the fight, which has actually saved me on more than one occasion.  Eventually once you get high enough evasion this also becomes a none-issue but to rely on getting lucky, or having broken stats really seems like a design flaw.If this is your first time playing FF2 I recommend reading up on how the leveling system works, as it does not have a traditional EXP and level up mechanism in place.If this isn't your first time playing the game its likely you already understand how this works and won't have much problems  with the game in the long term.Aside from the above complaint the game looks great and the music was very well recomposed.  People have also started to mod the game, so perhaps in the future things like 100% status effect cheesing from enemies as well as party members (status effect inflicting weapons) will be fixed/modified to be more fun / less broken to play.Looking forward to starting FF3.

_childDocuments_.review: The story this time takes major leaps ahead from the first entry, with the edition of actual dramatic elements. I even like the keyword dialogue mechanic, as it gives a fun illusion of dialogue options and encourages you to pay attention to lore, although I don't think it ever makes a reappearance in the series. Still, the rest of the game mechanics take major steps back from the first, with a completely overambitious leveling system that's ultimately broken, dungeons that are a chore, with far too many trap doors and unmarked secret pathways, and many encounters that that are to easily set up to wipe your party with stun-locking and insta-kills, if you get bad RNG. Overall, while the story focus is improvement, it's still not actually that good of one, falling to far to many cliche's, and is not at all fun to play. Another I'd recommend skipping unless you're a hardcore fan.

_childDocuments_.review: What a weird change for leveling up mechanics in comparison to the original Final Fantasy. You don't level up your character, but you have to level up any particular battle proficiency: right or left arm and weapon or shield, and any single spell in the game. You have a limit of spells you can learn, which kind of sucks, if you ask me. I can understand why this game was so much left behind by people when it came first came out originally in Japan (and not officially in the Western hemisphere via roms and fan translations years later). It's an easy game to beat though, you can brute force your way to the final boss based almost only on physical attacks. For instance, I only used the very important (apparently) Ultima spell once, and then totally forgot about it. Some enemies can only be beaten via spell, simple spells like Fire, Thunder or Blizzard will do though.At the end of the day, it's a good satisfactory game and a nice way to play the game if you can't or don't feel like buying an old Famicom (8 bit), getting the cartridge from eBay and learn how to patch it with an unofficial translation. Even if you would do so, you won't be getting the amazing soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought this game was really interesting but ultimately not worth a full playthrough. The skill based leveling, the maze like dungeon design and the choice to try and deliver a story with some player interaction and puzzle solving were ahead of their time. However, most of them fell pretty flat: The skill based leveling is quite random and makes the process a bit of a chore with little variety available to change weapons and/or playstyles later without a massive grind. _childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting hybrid.  Magic penalties are back in full force on all equipment, which means you have to watch what your mage oriented characters equip, unlike previous ports where some or all of those penalties were removed.  It seems as if stat decreases have been removed, so you don't have to worry about having your black mage attack every so often so they can contribute without using MP.  No chance of gaining STR and losing INT.  Stat gains are more frequent overall.  So the leveling system still has some micromanagement, but with quality of life improvements.  Otherwise the updated music, graphics, and elements such as the maps, modern item use, etc. make it a far easier entry point to the game for those who aren't old school hardcore.  Still prefer the ports such as Dawn of Souls with the bonus dungeons myself, but this is a nice, balanced update that's worth a play for some of the feel of the original leveling system.

_childDocuments_.review: FFII gets a bad wrap because of how the leveling system works but I didn’t think it was all that bad, until the end game at least. Basically, everything in the game is leveled through combat and usage. You don’t gain experience points in the sense that you’re accustomed to. If you wanna use swords, then you level up your sword lvl through combat.  You can switch weapons at anytime but you gotta level them up as well. Same thing with magic. The more you use Fire for example, it’ll level up. Same goes with your attributes. Your defense goes up by getting hit, and your MP will go up the more you use magic. It’s not a terrible system, it’s just flawed as hell because it’s based off enemy level (weapon and magic levels are at least). This in itself isn’t bad, but the game seemingly hits a brick wall mid-late game because it determines everything is “too easy”, even in the final few dungeons. It doesn't make the game harder or challenging, just somewhat frustrating. I should add I was using the 2x boosts until after mid-game, at which point I went ahead and bumped it up to 4x because I was ready for it to end.Other than that, it felt similar to FF1 as far as exploring the world and dungeon crawling goes. _childDocuments_.review: This is more of a "maybe" recommend. It's the weakest of the 3 Pixel Remasters released so far, by a lot. I like Saga games, and this game is a fantastic intro to the Saga series because it's so easy, but teaches you some of the same ways to get stronger that carry over to the Saga franchise. The big difference here is, in FF2 you have weapon skills but only plain attacks (no techniques like in Romancing Saga/Saga Frontier/etc.). You have a ton of spells, probably more than most Saga games have, but they're mostly your typical FF spells from the other games.So you get a pretty easy FF framework, and a hint of the potential that the Saga franchise really maximizes. If you want something like that, this isn't a terrible game. Less engaging than FF1 and FF3? I'd say yeah.The music is good, but I also feel like it got the least attention out of the Pixel Remaster games so far.

_childDocuments_.review: What an interesting followup to the first game. It builds upon not just the mechanics of its predecessor, but also on its story. From the very beginning you can customize your heroes into a personalized gang of nobodies who will save the world. You can multi-skill into a mage/warrior or go purely unarmed, and new weapons like the bow allow for more strategic combat. The new dialogue system, while not perfect, allow you to feel like you have a little more impact on the destiny of the world. The story reverses the dynamic of the original, instead of stopping evil from creeping its way into the world, you must nurture good into an evil world just as how you must nurture your heroes into becoming strong in what they specialize in. The ending leaves the player off with one interesting question "Can people ever truly forgive someone for their sins? Can that person forgive even themselves?". I like to believe that when Leon left in his isolation, he nurtured himself, traveling the world, finding his strengths and perfecting them, and died forgiving himself because as the first game had shown, even thousand's of years worth a evil can be eradicated as long as good people keep on living.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to review this mostly based of the quality of the port. I will assume that people buying this are aware of the quality of Final Fantasy II. As a short review of the game itself, Final Fantasy II is an incredibly flawed yet experimental entry. The entry has its fans, but generally accepted as a bad entry. The main reason for this is the experimental progression system. FFII features a usage-based progression system. The problem is how this progression happens. For one, progression has RNG added making it tedious to level. The means for leveling stats is also backwards such as unequiping all armor to level agility or equipping weak weapons to be able to hit multiple times to level weapon levels. All in all, the progression system is broken. Other issues include bad dungeon design and poor balancing. The positive as that this game has great music and a pretty good story for the time. Though, the story might seem lacking to modern players. Also, the game does well to establish its own identity after FF1, which will set the tone for the entire series. Lastly, many series staples were introduced in this game: Cid, Chocobos, Behemoth, etc... So, it is a very historical entry worth playing for any fan.  Now, onto the review of the port itself. There have been quite a few ports for Final Fantasy II throughout the years, usually packaged with the first Final Fantasy. When they were packaged together, it made buying FFII a more worthwhile endeavor admittedly. The original Famicom version was a lot less polished than the version here or any future version of the game. This version keeps the improvements from future ports in tact. Ultima isn't broken like in the original. The stats of the enemies are from the GBA release and this version is much easier than the original. Items that were added later were also kept in this release. The game still manages a challenge though despite these additions. If you have played FFII on GBA or PSP you will be familiar with the difficulty. The sprites and animation are superb in this game, resembling the SNES-era FF titles. There was a lot of effort put into this game. This also shows with the music. Nobuo Uematsu supervised the music himself and this shows. The music is much more complex without compromising the original tracks. More instruments were used to create the music. You will hear vocals now in Pandemonium. The combination of sprite work and music makes these ports standout from previous ports. The biggest flaw in this port is the lack of additional content added with the GBA release. This game is very vanilla. The additional campaign featuring Minwu is missing here. Extra dungeons and superbosses are also missing in this version. Thus, this is not a definitive port in that it is missing extra content. Though obvious, the FMV added with the PS1 release is also missing. The extra campaign is the biggest disappointment and loss here. Also, not a total loss, but I prefer character art used for the portraits rather than pixels. All in all, while not definitive, this is the easiest and most inexpensive way to buy and play this game. Featuring nice pixel art and great music, I recommend this port highly.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished this game - ignore the 40 hours played, left the game open in the background. More like 25-30 total. You can probably do it in a lot less, too. - Some of my favorite graphics in any Pixel Remaster FF, and the music is, as usual, wonderful.- An attempt at least at an emotionally affecting story, less paper-thin than the first game, and you start to see how some of the series themes developed. It's pretty standard 'save the world' stuff all the same, but it's quite nice. It's an FF game.- The game systems merit some attention. The developers should be commended for trying out a complex and innovative progression and reward system. The fact that every weaponskill, every spell, is leveled up individually and no character is beholden to a specific job means that you can play the game your way, and customize your team heavily. Similarly, there are a lot of special effect weapons that do certain things to certain enemy classes. This was probably a really advanced game when it first came out in 1988.- Aforementioned game systems may have been innovative, and good job for trying something new, but in practice they are a pain in the behind. Leveling up individual spells in particular is more annoying than fun, and grinding pack after pack just hoping to get your Flare up one more level doesn't feel great. You also don't really feel much stronger later in the game. Gameplay is probably less fun than original FF, and definitely less fun than the next few games.- Level design isn't great. Again, props to the original devs trying to make dungeons with some depth, but they feel convoluted and confusing. This is at least alleviated by the fact that in these remasters, the infamous 'trap rooms' have been toned down and are now mostly empty. FF1 dungeons, though simpler, are probably better. - Encounter design is flat out awful. What on earth were they thinking? Just a few examples, a pack of antlions can stun your entire group before you can react, and then you just watch while you slowly die. Malboros the same but worse, Coeurls oneshot you, and going into mid/late game literally  applies status debuff, half your time is spent applying gold needle and antidote out of combat. I could go on, but you get the picture. It is bad.- Story pacing. You don't discover much as the start of the game has you going to most cities and talking to most everyone important. Sure, you discover things later on, but there's not much in the way of exploration here. The story also feels a bit disjointed with all the walking back and forth to talk to people. Sure, if you're a big FF fan who wants to see the origin of chocobos and CId and stuff like that. Otherwise I wouldn't recommend it. And unless you're seriously into having a bad time, play through it with a walkthrough and a map. dungeon maps will save you so much time that the game tries to waste for you. As a historical document and a look at how the series developed it's cool. It does not stand up as a good game today, even remastered. For completionists only. If you're curious about old FF, go and play FFIV and have a great time with a great game instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a handful of FF games (ie. VII and up) but I recently realized I've never beaten one. So I made it my mission for the foreseeable future to play them all in Chronological order. As of this writing I have beaten FFI, and Stranger of Paradise.Disclaimer* I know as soon as I hit post I'm gonna have a sea of unwashed purist neckbeards telling me I didn't get the proper experience because I played the Pixel Remaster instead of refinancing my house to get an NES of DKOldies and play the original famicom release. I don't care. Now first and foremost, this game gets a bad wrap. Most will say it's because of the lack of structure in team building. No character has a specific class like in the previous (and others moving forward) installments, and this lack of structure can lead to a bit of paralysis via decision, which is typically something I have an issue with in my own right. That being said I didn't have a problem. Looking at stats, the characters have a pretty cut and dry bias towards their strengths, so it wasn't difficult to figure out who my fighter/paladin, black mage, and tank were (hint* I just said them in order). Outside of that I was able to just play the game normally and I did fine. I enjoyed the revolving door of 4th characters, which made the world feel more alive and kept tactics a bit more interesting compared to the "hit everything" vibe of FFI. That't not to say I didn't spend the majority of my time doing exactly that, but it was better. My biggest gripe with this installment of the beloved series is that this game should have been called "Empty Room Simulator 1988". Dungeon design was dull as hell. Granted they were textured and colored beautifully, but each floor has a handful of doors in it, and typically one of them leads to the next floor but the other ones are just square and empty. 95% of the doors in the dungeons of this game were completely empty. Now I acknowledge the fact that this was done by developers to make the possibility of a random encounter go up, therefore making the dungeon, and therefore the game, longer to complete. I get that. That does not stop me from hating it every single time. It's boring, it's lame, and it only furthered my tedium while playing. The amount of back and forth you have to do in this game borders on tedious as well. You get a mission at Altair to go to A, B, and C, and then it's back to Altair to do it again. As such the amount of locations on the map left me wanting. This world is so much smaller and empty compared to FFI, which was teeming with life and secrets in comparison. When I finally got the airship near the end of the game I flew around and explored as I am wont to do, hoping to find a place I hadn't seen yet where I could unlock hidden riches or equipment to aid the last leg of my journey and was left disappointed by the realization that I had already seen all there was to see. I won't say this is a bad game, but I will say that this game feels unfulfilling. The first game was great, it laid the groundwork for what would become one of the most well loved series in Gaming, but instead of capitalizing on that great first go, this game was the sophomore slump. I played this game to be able to say I had, and now that I have I don't believe I'll be playing it again.

_childDocuments_.review: While my attempts to play the original Final Fantasy usually failed because of how hard and outdated it was, while also having a really simple story, Final Fantasy II in addition to the difficulty and chunkiness was also really weird. All of my attempts quickly hit a wall and every time I’ve tried to check on some guides to help me start, I’d read about some bizarre but seemingly necessary tricks where you’d grind for a few hours by hitting your own party members. With the Pixel Remaster version I was finally able to give the game a proper look and appreciate what it tried to be. Even though it still has some questionable decisions.What’s possibly most important to note about Final Fantasy II is that unlike the first game in the series, this one is focusing very heavily on the story. It’s not a very complicated story, of course, but it’s considerably deeper than I’ve expected it to be, with very distinct characters and quite a few well delivered moments and twists in the tale. The playable characters are all named (though, as was the case with Final Fantasy titles before voice acting, you can rename them) and each of them has distinct personality and look. For the first time in the series your party often changes, as only 3 of the 4 characters you name at the start are available through the entire game. Thus the fourth slot is often taken by an NPC with their own goals and unique characteristics, something that FFIV would later expand upon greatly. And you even get a unique take on a dialogue system, with “key words” that you can “learn” and “ask” NPCs about. It’s not exactly Morrowind, of course, and it’s not much deeper than if the dialogues were simply linear, as they tend to be in the series. But it was an interesting experiment nonetheless.But that’s not the biggest experiment of the game. What FFII is best known for (or more like infamous) is how the stats and abilities of characters develop in the game. There’s no conventional experience and leveling up system here and instead each separate stat and ability has a chance to improve as you use it. Losing HP or MP in the battle means you get a chance to increase the maximum values for them after the battle is won. Using spells and certain weapon types means having a chance to slowly improve them, making their use more powerful. And stats are tied to actions, like attacking, using white or black magic and etc. It’s a really neat idea and something that has been experimented with in other games and series. But the success of this approach always hangs on the implementation.In the original game, I feel, the implementation was way too challenging which lead to that infamous grinding, where your go into battles to hit yourself and abuse bugs. Not helped by the fact that while conventional levels don’t exist, the difficulty of areas seems to be tied to invisible thresholds, where if you try to go into a harder area early, you simply do 0 damage to enemies, while they just one shot kill you, until you upgrade your stats, abilities and equipment enough to go beyond the threshold and be able to fight them normally. But in the Pixel Remaster version, a lot of the huge annoyances have been fixed. Just like with the PR version of FF, most of the limitations of the NES original are gone, with no “ineffective” hits and now even using two weapons automatically re-aims the second weapon attack in the same turn if the first target is down. HP is increased from time to time even if you don’t take damage and seemingly at a higher rate. Same goes for MP and stat improvement in general. Most of the time, there’s no need to even consider grinding to just go through the game – as long as you don’t flee all battles or try to avoid them, you’re slowly but surely improving and getting to the stat levels expected by the game.Yet it’s not entirely without grind. First quarter of the game, for example, can very easily be done without using magic at all and by just attacking everything. But then the game introduces enemies and bosses that have extremely high physical resistance and must be fought with magic. If you haven’t leveled that up at all, your characters have level 1 spells, that barely do damage, and almost no MP to use at that point. And so the grind starts. It’s worth noting that while spells used outside the battle (the ones that can be used) still improve with each use, the stats and MP doesn’t. So you must get into fights to get over that hurdle. And later on, from time to time, the game will throw unexpected and annoying difficulty spikes at you that, unless you’re using very specific equipment or leveling up specific abilities, you might have a hard time getting around without grinding for a bit. Which is, frankly, annoying in the game even at fast forward auto-battle speeds.The biggest issue the game has, though, is that several enemy types have a status effect that disables your party members tied to their basic attack. And in what seems to be the balance change made specifically for Pixel Remaster, that status effect now has either the 100% or almost 100% chance of hitting your party member, even if they have high stats and specific equipment that protects them from said status effect. The attack may do 0 damage, but the effect will work, as long as it’s not a miss. And what that means, is that if you ever get ambushed by 4 or more enemies that have basic attacks with such status effects (like stone, instant death, paralysis), you’re basically dead before you can even take a turn. No matter how good your party members are and what equipment they have, they will all be out of the battle in the first turn.If not for the really strange design choices like this, I would’ve loved Final Fantasy II in the Pixel Remaster form. It really feels like a huge step up from the simplicity of the original Final Fantasy in terms of story and even dungeon design. The music is as wonderful as ever in the series. The art is great. And most of the gameplay in PR is fun, with the way your characters improve actually being fun, as every single battle is a chance for a stat or ability improvement. But those strange instant death ambush encounters and difficulty spikes do get annoying after a while, which sours the experience a bit. Still, it is a great remaster of a game that is far more fun and interesting than I expected it to be and I’m glad that I’ve played it.

_childDocuments_.review: If I can sum up the game in one word, it would be "deceptive"  I realize this game has always been a bit of a slog since it was created 30 years ago, but it really needed to be changed, and while this remaster has gotten a nice new paint job, it still was a pain to get through.This is my first full playthrough with the game, and i never played any other RPG the way I played this.  Every battle took 5-10 minutes at a time because I was trying to grind out spells and weapons to make them somewhat competent, because when I do ZERO damage to monsters, I am under the impression that I'm not strong enough to beat them.  The scaling is all over the place.  Some places it's too easy and them randomly you fight Cockatrices that turn you to stone in one hit.   Ailments hit 100% every time, so you better level up your evasion and blink spells or you will have a bad time.  It is also possible to be stun locked with the sleep spell, and sit there helpless as a golem slowly beats your life away.Did you know you can beat the emperor with just a Poison Axe?  The weapon causes poison EVERY time and in the battle it did 1000hp of damage every turn so you can theoretically win with a low level party and let poison defeat him in 10 turns or so. I overgrinded for this game because I was worried i wouldn't be able to handle the end game, but by then it was a joke. Speaking of which, any game where you can casually watch a show or read a book while you're playing at the same time, is a bad game, and I'm always enjoying my level grinding, except for this game. Also what other game has you purposely hitting your team or using life or healing spells haphazardly to level up?The trap rooms are the worst.  So many doors link to empty rooms with high encounter rates and very little treasure worth your time and when there was a treasure, it was usually booby trapped with an enemy encounter that would almost kill you every time if you're not prepared.  Most treasure was not worth getting at all. In fact in a lot of the late dungeons, they still give out potions. POTIONS near the end of the game!  What good is a potion with characters at 3000 hp? These dungeon are purely busy work of the most transparent sort.The spell system I feel is also problematic.  How come when you cast on two targets, it's just as low as casting on 6 targets?  I should not be doing the same 20 damage on 2 zombies as I do 6 zombies.  Unless you're targeting one monster, your magic doesn't matter. There's also something that most new gamers aren't aware of, the MAGIC PENALTY.  That is when you equip armor or heavy weapons and as a result your magic spells are severely handicapped.  The problem is the player is NEVER told this in this game.  The menus don't tell you the weapons have a magic penalty nether do any of the NPCs tell you.  So most of you unaware of this would be confused to why their magic isn't working at all, even as high as level 16.  For a remaster trying to bring in a new generation of players, this is a grave oversight to not mention this at all.  If you are playing this, I would recommend checking a wiki on all the armor and weapons from the previous versions to look up the penalties yourself.Honestly though, this game has always had problems, so I don't blame the remaster entirely, in fact some of what they did was better the the original.  Still I feel this game needs to be reworked.  The Romancing Saga titles took this type of leveling and made it work.  I shouldn't have to waste spells or hit my party purposely to level up.  As for this game, it has suffered from a lot of shortcomings that I feel the remaster isn't enough to enjoy as is.  I cannot recommend this game to people who are either new to RPGS or are used to a certain way they play.  This game doesn't respect your time.  I've played many Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest games, and this was by far the worst experience I've had with one.

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first time completing this game. 42 1/2 hours at time of completion. I mean I knew about it when I was a kid but I was always playing Final Fantasy 4 and Final Fantasy 6 as a kid. I never completed one of these titles until Part 4. This was a really weird game to get into. This title seems like completely backwards from other titles in the franchise. Leveling skills makes it harder to gauge how you are standing against enemies. I know other people would recommend choosing a class for each character and having said characters play specific roles. Why? I made every character melee /white mage/ black mage. All purpose characters. There were a number of spells I never used or bothered with. The enemies had a weapon quality standard. Often times when melee attacking you would simply do zero damage because your weapon wasn't strong enough to injure them. Took me awhile to figure that out. I had the same White screen Issues as the First game. I had the game crash and reboot my Pc more often than the First game. This was the first title that I actually had Data corruption loss. I would think with modern Pcs that would be a thing of the past. Its not. I would have completely lost everything during the data loss if it wasn't for the auto save that I didn't even know about. So after that I started saving my game in two slots. Lol The story was weird. Hard to get into. The First boss to beat the heck out of me was the Lamia. Every boss before that one was a piece of cake. I have to admit I like chasing achievements. Steam titles or at least the Final Fantasy titles do not seem to do this very well. I am hoping this improves in future titles. I was disappointed how the game handled the main characters. I kept 3 main all the time and kept swapping out the fourth slot over and over. I hated this. I would get a new character and have to level them plus they would have no magic progress almost every time. I would get attached to a new character just to have them permanently leave the party shorty there after. I couldn't stand it. I can't believe I had to keep getting under powered characters hopping in and out of the group. It sucked! By the time I got to the last character to join my party. All of my main characters Had over 6k in hit points and had spells leveled up over level 10. My last party member barely had 1k and no spells. It was ridiculous. I never really caught him up with my main three. I didn't like how they handled the airship in this game. You don't really get the airship until the end of the game when you don't really need it much by than. There was an event that happened before you get to play that people in game would talk about. I think. It would have been much better if you had got to witness it. Way more meaningful. would have helped the story along. Most of the bad guys in this title were throw away. Not challenging, not meaningful except the final boss. You could literally walk any where in the game except two islands. I loved how the ship was set up in this game. You could park the ship any where and go ashore and you didn't have to park at a dock. Awesome! I wish all the titles would have done this. I can't think of another title that did this so well or at all. Some of the monster designs were great others not so much. I wonder if this title was the beginning stage for Final Fantasy 6 which is similar in a couple ways but did it much better. If you want to jump into a Final Fantasy title you could play this game but there are much better titles in the Franchise. I wouldn't recommend this game unless you are hardcore into theses games. I really have no idea what the developers were going for with this title. Perhaps it was a test run for stat leveling. I don't know. Go play a better game.

_childDocuments_.review: I immediately jumped into Final Fantasy II after playing through the first one. I had a rather good time and still had the itch for more. I found that FF2 is not quite more of the same and has a different groove to it.Both games look the same. The Pixel Remaster controls, graphics and music are as good as they were for the first game. In this regard, there's no real difference. The big change is in the game play itself and how you develop your characters. You kind of start with a blank slate and build up your characters based on their actions, rather than just aimlessly levelling up like the first game. It's quite similar to Oblivion or Skyrim in that regard. If you want this spell or weapon to get good, you've got to use it... a lot. It takes a fair bit of time to get the ball rolling. It changes things up from the previous game but can be a little tedious by the end. I don't really have any complaints about the game other than the enemies that use stun attacks. I found myself getting stun locked with nothing I could do and even by the end game, this was a quick game over. These enemies are quite annoying. Thankfully, they're few and far between with the quick save system really keeps it from being a serious problem.Final Fantasy 2 is a good game. I personally preferred the first, but I had a good time with it. I'm sure fans of JRPG's will find more than enough in the game to warrant a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really great port, overall. The only three gripes I have are:1) There are a couple of serious glitches in this particular game that can cause it to freeze or nearly freeze. Since casting lots of buff spells in one battle is the only way to level them and casting Life on undead enemies is a major intended use of the spell, these are serious problems.2) It's too easy if you do any grinding or optimization whatsoever, and then the later random encounters feel really pointless and time-wasting. I don't really like hardcore difficulty in games, but this just felt a bit monotonous and disappointing toward the end. (The plot was fun, though.)3) All of the Pixel Remaster games seem to have a problem where gamepad inputs get screwed up if the game detects any mouse movement at all.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: They dropped the ball on what this remaster could have been, but it was still fun to play. What I like:This game pioneered some interesting mechanics, it feels very open - there isn't much to do outside the linear story, but you can at least explore and start building your characters very early if you'd like to. I enjoy that you can travel 80% of the world map right away and run into really powerful monsters you have no business fighting. I like that the characters are completely flexible for you to make them into whatever you feel suits them best, with perhaps some natural affinities. I have mixed feelings on the rotating 4th characters, it always felt like you were starting over and it wasn't worth investing effort into building them. I wish , at the end they were all available and you could choose which companion you had in your party.The enemies are pretty fun and unique looking.I really like when the player is forced to diversify in order to succeed instead of using a single tactic for the entire play-through. It feels really good that your characters seem to naturally grow in whatever stats and skills they're using.Unarmed is hilariously strong even against some of the tougher enemies. What I don't like:After some time you seem to hit a bit of a cap on how the skills and spells are leveled and it feels bad to have hit a "cap" without understanding why. I feel that it should have been touched up in this remaster as this is a primary cause of dissatisfaction for players. As it stands you'll have to spend some time reading a guide to get a handle on what's happening. This was a pretty good one:  . Some of the achievements MUST be gotten in the middle of the game - I like to play however I want and then do the achievements at the end when I am satisfied. Some chests and key terms can't be gotten if you don't get them at the right time and you'll have to play the entire game over again. Random encounters are too common, I feel like it's 5-10 steps and then another fight; it's so jarring I can barely remember where I was heading before the battle. Heavy equipment lowers your character's magic damage which makes sense, but is not obvious at all when equipping them. Most of the treasures in chests are useless and it feels bad to explore 100 empty rooms to finally find one that has actual treasure in it and then get rewarded with early game loot you don't need. Half of the status effects are extremely powerful and can wipe your party if you're not careful, but feel very underwhelming when using them yourself unless you dedicate a significant amount of work into building them - when it is probably more efficient to just spam damage skills instead.It's not clear what status and other effects enemies are susceptible to unless you read a wiki or guide.Engagements don't seem to last long enough to justify using anything other than attacks / specific elemental weakness spells. The story is a bit of a downer, feels like you didn't save much There's a lot of unexplained plot holes , try not to think about it I guess. There's blatant bugs that could have easily been fixed for this remaster, the most annoying I've encountered is casting Life on a group of undead can hang the game forcing you to revert to your last save. There's little warning when your 4th character swaps out, so you may lose valuable gear they had equipped.

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I start with the sequel to Final Fantasy I? Let's start with the obvious changes to it's predecessor; the game mechanics:In contrast to FFI, FFII does not have archetypical characters that are specialised in one certain fighting style. Each character can spellcast or melee/range fight. Leveling system is changed as well, now instead of leveling your character, you individually level up your actions and stats. Meaning that if you cast a certain spell, only that specific spell gain the experience to level up. Each individual spell can level up to cap level of level 16.  Same with your melee or range weapon, but you level up each weapon type instead of individual weapon. Same as with spell casting the cap level is at level 16 with weapon types. Lastly you individually level up your character stats such as your max health, max MP, evasion, strength, dexterity, etc.FFII plays with a party set-up of 4 characters, but only 3 party members are the core that you play from start to finish. The 4th member changes during the progression of the story/game. There are a total of 4 different characters that will be your 4th party member. Each time you play one of these different characters their stats, weapons and spells all start at beginner level.Which annoyed me slightly, I mean, there is even a character swap near the end-game. Imagine you have 3 out of 4 partymembers at end-game stats and weapon levels and you have your last party member at beginner level. I can understand that story wise the swapping of the characters is necessary, but I would make the stats go from one over to the other. I wouldn't mind if the weapons and spells are at beginning level, but atleast the stats as the stats also influence your damage output of your weapons.The narrative of FFII is very significant, as it is the start of the archetypical storyline that is later being reused in later additions of the Final Fantasy franchise. It is the first time we see the narrative of the large evil Empire on expansion drift versus the small good kingdom that defend themselves. In FFII they cut out the races of Elves and Dwarves in their worldbuilding, which were inside the world of FFI. On a personal note I missed the different races.Overall I really enjoyed the story and am excited for Final Fantasy III.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first, I never played these classic final fantasy games back in the day, so my perspective is one free of nostalgia and I'm simply judging these as they are with some consideration for when they originally came out. I recognize that this game is not as popular as the others, and I can kinda see why, but I think most of these points are not quite as bad now in this pixel remaster version of the game. Here are the main problems that are actually annoying, even still:-Enemies proc their status effects 100% of the time on their attacks. This also bypasses immunity, meaning that items that say they protect against a status simply do not. This is especially annoying towards the end of the game where there's an enemy that procs instant death on every hit. This must be a bug but it's still present in the game even now so it's a major annoyance. The reason it's just annoying and not a deal-breaker is because these pixel remasters have quicksaving anywhere. So getting through areas with these enemies is not as bad as it would've been back in the day.-You have a 4th party member that is basically dead weight that gets switched out many times over the course of the game. Because of the way this game handles progression, these characters are often weak compared to your other party members and they leave too soon to ever have a chance to become useful. For all intents and purposes, you play this game with only 3 characters that matter.-Damage values feel chaotic and have a lot of variance, sometimes 17, sometimes 400.That's about it. All that being said, here are the good things:-Actually has a narrative, it's not going to make you cry, but it's there, and rather dark actually. Mostly just Star Wars retold as fantasy. Compared to the first game, whose story could be accurately summarized as "Crystals good, chaos bad", this is 10000% better.-Action-based leveling system. This is a neat experiment that basically has your party members gain proficiency with weapons and spells as they use them, rather than arbitrarily getting incrementally better at everything when they kill enough bad guys. This applies to stats as well, so getting hit raises max HP, using MP raises max MP, casting white magic raises spirit, etc. Cool idea and it works good enough. I like that it allows a lot of flexibility in terms of what your party ends up using, but once you're decently far, straying off of what you picked early on is difficult and you're better off just sticking to what you picked. This is by far the coolest thing about the game.-Actual dialogue, no choices yet, but you talk to people and learn keywords that you can mention to other people to progress. Rather simple system but there wasn't anything like it in the first game, so it's a plus.-Difficulty feels better balanced than the first game. Still pretty easy for most of it, but it did throw moderate threats here and there, and the final boss isn't nearly as stupid strong as the first game.Overall the remaster is good, but I do wish they would fix the status thing, that is lame. Otherwise the spritework and music are good, and being able to quicksave makes the worse aspects of this game palatable. Again like in FF1, I'm giving it a thumbs up because this remaster is (mostly) what it's supposed to be.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: While it's not the most well loved Final Fantasy, II always had a special place in my heart. I was keen to play the new version and see how they did it, and it's a blast. The skill leveling and gil drops have been balanced to not need grinding, although maybe tuned a little much as the game seems very easy (of course, this is a game I know backwards and forwards though, I know what to do an what to avoid, so I'm not the best judge for its difficulty).Graphically I do prefer the PSP version, but I see the appeal of this style and certainly don't mind it. The music also sounds incredible, the best its ever been. Aside from the aforementioned ease of the game this time around, I think mechanically this is a very solidly tuned version of the game. The quality of life improvements (on screen map, fast auto battles, party members unequiping themselves when they leave the party) are very much appreciated. So much so that even my beloved PSP version feels slow and cumbersome now. Extremely well done.What's not well done is the lack of additional dungeons added the various remakes, especially the Soul of Rebirth epilogue. That's not in this version, bizarrely, and it's sorely missed. Also of note, there's a lot of screen tearing when running around, which should not be a thing on a game with 16-bit style graphics in 2021... As a final note, the font sucks. Look into modding it out, it takes all of five minutes and makes the game much more enjoyable.I haven't mentioned the graphics because that's a matter of opinion. Compare the graphics of this and the PSP version, decide which you think looks better.All in all, it's a fantastic version of this game. If it wasn't for the lack of Soul of Rebirth, this would absolutely be my go to version of the game, even if I prefer the PSP graphics because the quality of life changes and updated music are just that nice. I would say I hope they patch it in, but Square is notorious for not adding content to or even supporting fully their PC ports, so take it as it is. It's still $12 well spent, to be sure.

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice FF2 remake. Its got excellent graphics and awesome music. Ribbon and some robes that protect against status effects I wish would list what they protect. Other than that, this is an excellent game and despite this issues and gets a 5 out of 5 from me!EDIT: The spell effects on screen are the same in every FF Pixel Remaster so far 1, 2 and 3. This is ok here as the first games did not have many effects and this can pass, but it is just plain lazy.Side note: If the music stops playing in game for battles and victory music then quick save immediately and exit the game. _childDocuments_.review: I'll start off by saying the amount of grinding I put into this game was beyond excessive and unnecessary. Killing the final boss on turn 1 was a real let down. At the same time though if you don't grind stats like agility you will have a very rough time of things. Some enemies even random ones will just eat you alive. Still, after my first time playing through FF II I overall enjoyed myself. The pixel graphics are beautiful, and the music is beyond epic. Especially as you get towards the final parts of the game. The screen tearing problem is easily corrected by forcing V-Sync on through your respective graphics card managing program. It's still somewhat annoying that you have to turn select 'borderless window' every time you start the game off, but hopefully it'll be patched soon. Story wise I surprisingly enjoyed myself despite the amount of back and forth. The keyword mechanic was pretty neat, and added an interesting way to learn or at least get hints as to where to go next. You can even learn a lot of lore when visiting a book shelf in a certain town in the late game. When traversing the world it's important to know WHERE you are going and HOW to get there. Otherwise you'll end up in areas with enemies that will eat you alive early on in the game. In a way I enjoy that as it adds a sense of danger to the world that you won't feel at all in the beginning. I remember taking the wrong path to Kashuan Castle or something and ending up dinner for some Vampire Girls. Confuse is a bad way to wipe, but it happened. Anyway, FF II is a fun, but also awkward game thanks to the leveling system or rather lack of one. Don't stress about grinding, and just enjoy the ride as you journey on to defeat the Emperor!

_childDocuments_.review: A decent RPG that, while not anything amazing, has elements that fans of the genre can find enjoyment in.Pros:- Story and characters. While nothing special, the story and characters are more complex than one might initially expect, and the writers do not pull any punches in terms of the stakes in the central conflict. Also of note, while he is simple, the main villain is so TENACIOUSLY evil that I couldn't help but be thrilled any time he showed up. - Music. As expected from a Final Fantasy game, the music is fantastic. The final dungeon and boss music, as well as the theme of the rebellion are the most noteworthy tracks, in my opinion.- Skill system. There are no regular levels, and instead stats, spells, and weapon proficiencies work similarly to Skyrim, where in order to improve something you must use it, with some slight differences. It is unique enough in a turn-based RPG that fans of the genre can have some fun with it.Cons:- Skill system. Unfortunately, the skill system is more shallow than it seems. Ranking up spells past rank 10 in combat seems to take a LONG time to do. I also noticed that I probably could have just spammed attack in the majority of fights and done just as well in the end, which kind of dampers the uniqueness of the system.- Technical matters. The stuttering I noticed in the Pixel Remaster of the first game are here too, though a little different. The stutter while walking was less obvious, but stutter during panning shots in cutscenes was pretty bad.- Extra content. This game seems to suffer the most from the Pixel Remaster not bringing back bonus content, as an entire parallel dungeon, boss, and story to the finale was not brought to this version that really enhanced the experience in other versions.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: This pixel remaster is a faithful recreation of the original Famicom game. Square Enix took great care in respecting the vision of the original.That being said, I think FINAL FANTASY II suffers from some practical gameplay issues. The leveling system is quite odd and actually discourages you from even trying in regular random encounters. Instead of leveling up through an EXP system, you level specific stats by "utilizing" them (i.e. HP stat goes up when you get hit). But why try in regular encounters when you will get most likely nothing out of it, and have to grind your stats some other way? There is no natural sense of progression. Furthermore, the dungeons have lots of winding dead ends that just require you to get into more useless fights.Despite this, FINAL FANTASY II makes some great strides in its soundtrack and visual storytelling. This game at least attempts to have a story which is semi-interesting compared to the first game's. If you're a FINAL FANTASY fan, I would give it a try, but it might not be for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II reviewVersions played previously: N/ATime to complete: ~20 hoursOverall Rating: 6/10Gameplay: 5/10Story: 6/10Graphics: 9/10The sequel to the classic NES JRPG, released in 1988, didn’t make its way to the US until recently. This pixel remaster provides a great way to play it, presumably with similar quality of life features that other pixel remasters provide. The gameplay is a unique spin on the classic RPG leveling system. Essentially, every character has a level with separate weapon types, as well as shields and spells. The more you use certain weapons or skills, the more they increase. In theory, this provides a great customizable experience. Quickly, I realized that it’s very hard to make a tank white mage, as magic interference prevents casters from using heavy armor without huge penalties to magic power. Whatever, I understand the balancing reasons behind this. Still, it’s a cool take on the classic leveling system and is heavily customizable, but it certainly could be executed better. It’s fun at first, but it quickly becomes tedious to level up new spells to make them usable, and towards the end, magic becomes almost obsolete. Also, some spells never seemed to work for me, mainly Esuna. The encounter balancing is abysmal, which is probably a holdover from the original, but it is frustrating to run into extremely easy enemies and ones that one-shot you in the same dungeon. While the gameplay is overall worse than the original FFI, the story is a step up, with the characters actually having names and simple backstories. The plot, while still a bit simple, provides more characters and plot points that make it feel more real. However, the plot fizzles out towards the end of the game, becoming a bit confusing and quite bland during the final part. It honestly feels like the ending was rushed. The graphics are beautiful, with the same small complaints of the default font and reuse of sprites as the first game in the series. Overall, this sequel is a slight step down from the first game, but it’s still a fairly fun and quick playthrough, with a more engaging story and a unique albeit somewhat poorly executed combat system. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the other retro Final Fantasy titles, but it’s not one that I would play if you haven’t been introduced to the series yet. Don't skip this one if you're playing them all in order like I am, but I wouldn't play it as a standalone game, and I don't think it's one I'd play again in a hurry.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be deterred by negative reviews. FFII is a great game, and this is its best version yet by far. The often lambasted levelling system has been streamlined somewhat compared to previous iterations, so you will definitely be strong enough at every point of the game by just playing normally. There really isn't any need to grind (unless you want to get all the spells you don't use anyways to absurdly high levels, but why would you).However, there are some mechanics that aren't very well explained, which can significantly influence your playing style if you know about them. Firstly, there's a magic penalty, meaning that magic will be a lot more effective if the caster doesn't wear heavy armor or uses certain weapons. But if your aim is to be as effective as possible, you should specialize your characters anyways, because the relevant stats are tied to specific actions. So you want your White Magic caster to cast white magic pretty much all the time, your Black Magic caster to cast black magic every turn, your Fighter to attack every turn. Also, using shields early on is a good idea for all characters, because evading attacks can improve the agility stat, which in turn increases evasion as well as the likelihood of getting preemptive strikes and less ambushes.On the one side this makes the random battle pretty samey, but on the other hand with the sheer volume you will be thankful for the Auto Battle feature and will be blasting through the dungeons in no time. Speaking of, the map added in the Pixel Remaster is a lifesaver with FFIIs dungeons. Just check the floor and you will instantly know where the treasures, dead ends and staircases are.The story is more serious than in FFI and FFIII and it has more interesting characters, even if the protagonists aren't all that developed. FFII has a great soundtrack, same as I and III, but where it really shines is in its art. It is by far the best looking game of the three first Pixel Remasters.

_childDocuments_.review: Bit of a mixed bag. On one hand, this remaster is great and definitely a most definitive way to play FF2 with extra whistile and bells. The basic game itself isnt' very good and I wouldn't normally recommend this to anyone unless they are a hardcore FF fan that's interested in seeing where it all began. This game is very important in term of Final Fantasy series' history on the whole series as many of classic FF monsters and monikor  we knew and love made their first appearance here like infamous Behemoth.QoL features are very nice and made this game very replayable, however there are still some pretty nasty bugs such as status hits triggering 100% of time and HP gain being very accelerated, 3 of my main characters' HP were easily 3-5x of 4th rotating party member.
