_childDocuments_.review: Finished Final Fantasy 2. Took me only 19 hours and sadly I had one great problem. The latter is a mix of local level up system and a minor confusion. In the very beginning of the game I got stuck in Fynn because I didn’t get how to get to the bar and decided to defeat one of those empire soldiers thinking he was blocking the path or something. As a result I wasted a few hours to level up my magic in random encounters, killed an empirical soldier and it made me too OP. This foolishness ruined the entire game for me. My party was so stupidly overpowered I didn’t even get to feel the majority of the bosses. And the last one…I killed him in just a few round and he barely left a scratch. All companions were babies compared to the main three, even the last one. What a shame…But this is still a good game. If not for my overpowering mistake I’d get to enjoy the vastly improved, dramatic plot which the first game really bad in comparison and even FF3 is not on the same level. The gameplay is the same, with leveling system being the only exception. Music is as good as before. Graphics are nice too. Overall, I really enjoyed it except the fighting which was too easy and as a result rather boring.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Final Fantasy II. It's a very flawed and brutal game, but I have always enjoyed its unique leveling system and its surprisingly well-told story given the limitations of the Famicom. While the Pixel Remaster does not include the Soul of Rebirth campaign from the Dawn of Souls and 20th Anniversary remakes, what is here is the most polished and accessible Final Fantasy II experience we have ever had, and I think that far outweighs the loss of the additional content from the previous versions.This game is still not one that I can easily recommend to everyone, of course, with its polarizing leveling system and its, frankly, diabolical dungeon design, but if you're willing to take up the challenge this game offers, I think you'll find it's quite an overlooked gem of the Final Fantasy series, especially now with all of the tweaks that make it smoother, faster, and easier to play than ever before.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: A Quest to complete every game in my collection that actually ends...Final Fantasy II attempted to introduce new features into the Series in their effort to grow the RPG Genre. Features that, ironically, a lot of new games utilize now such as the Skill Leveling. I can't say that it completes this - successfully - because a very substantial amount of the hours on this game were me letting the game play itself in order to farm the skill levels out. An action that isn't needed in order to complete the game since, if you play it naturally, you'll get everything you need to finish it from simply going through the story.It helped trivialize the game for me - on one hand - and fulfilled that RPG Power-Fantasy that lies within all of us. It also, however, was a lot of time that I could have spent doing something else.Do I regret letting the game auto-play itself until my Firion was at 99 in Everything but Stamina and Max Weapon Skills? No.Do I recommend you do this? No. If you wanted to make the game 'easier' and didn't want to struggle against the creatures you face. You can honestly just grind up one weapon of choice for each character and level up spells naturally as you do this. I recommend the Pixel Remaster of Final Fantasy II. It was, at-least from what I've seen, faithful to the Original while making some of the more grindy aspects less of a grind. It holds up as a first-time introduction to a story narrative within the Final Fantasy series beyond the 'Hey, your Heroes go do this' ala Final Fantasy I and is a good precursor to the amazing games that follow.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Quest to do em all. FF7, 6, 5, 4, 1 and 2 complete.I know the negative reputation this title has. I tried to be open minded. There are elements I love and elements I hate. So often in this title I kept thinking, 'this is a fantastic idea, but it didn't really work.'  I don't want to be too harsh either, I appreciate some attempt at experimentation. The limitations of the day.My thoughts- I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loved the levelling system. Particularly as I found ways to abuse it. The endless opportunities to customise a character, however, are offset by a time investment. I cannot believe I had to grind a 'poison antidote' spell multiple levels before it did its damn job. You'd be better off using items. I also made the mistake of giving every character a core set of useful spells as redundancy. In reality, none of them ever levelled because EXP was being divided three ways.- ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ endless dead ends and empty rooms in every dungeon. No fun in exploration in this game.- I was stunned by how much access to the world you had from the get go. Until I realised the game designers hemmed you in with powerful monster encounters as opposed to, say,  a mountain range. Attempts to explore often got me killed. No fun in exploration in this game.- Endless fetch quests. I'm used to having the world slowly open up to you as you progress in a FF title. Always returning to start for another fetch quest was lazy.- Storytelling was impressive. Constant back against the wall against an evil empire. Tragedy. The changes to townships as the war progressed. Much more involved NPCs and temporary party members. Probably simplistic by today's standards though, I thought it was impressive for NES in 1988. And a big step up from only a year earlier.  For the longest time though, I had the nagging feeling I was playing through a war story, not a Final Fantasy story. Lacking a mystical element to the world, endless horde of monsters notwithstanding. Of course in the final act, everything went straight to hell. - As always the Pixel Remaster is simply beautiful. The soundtrack never clicked with me as other FF titles.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate this game in a good way.  It's so frustrating it actually comes back around as charming.  Early game is tedious, you have to grind to get your characters to play the way you want them to.  But eventually you reach a place where you don't have to constantly be spamming whatever you are trying to skill up.  Otherwise, it is a massive improvement story wise from Final Fantasy 1.  I can't speak to the differences or improvements of this remaster, only that I enjoyed it after finding half a dozen guides to show me how magic penalty works.  I wish they had decided to show this very big penalty that affects combat so deeply, but I guess that might be part of the charm.  Inscrutable is the best word I can come up with to describe playing this game without a guide.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello friends,Today i will be reviewing the game Final Fantasy 2 Pixel Remaster edition. Unlike previous entries into the final fantasy games, this one tried some new mechanics, such as the  code war in learning new things in the game. This mechanic is not seen in other games in the series, and was used to test it to the fanbase in ff2. The leveling system is also different than in the other final fantasy games. This one uses a similiar system found in final fantasy 8 and in in saga games. Basically, you level up using weapons and skills. Each skill and weapons is associated to certain stats. For example, using swords increases your strength and hps. Using a wand increases magic points. Anyways, here are my pro/cons list:PROS:- First time on steam, Final Fantasy 2.- Different mechanics found only in saga games and later final fantasy games.- This version has a built in beastiary in the extras menu that is very good.- Nice music and pixel perfect graphics.CONS:- Some bugs are in this version. For example, if you miss some code words and do not learn them in a certain order, it can cause issues with progression in the game.- Some repetition is required if you want to learn skills and magicv up to max, with the exception to cure, which is very easy to level to max since you use it quite alot.- You can miss certain items and beastiary in the game if you do not use a guide to help you.Recommended since this is only way to get final fantasy 2 legitimately on steam. If you also are a big fan of the older retro games on systems, then i also recommend this as it really keeps the old pixel feeling of those retro games.

It made me not want to explore everything but I forced myself2) The map was a great idea but it should have probably had fog for the areas you haven't explored yet. _childDocuments_.review: FF2 has a lot of interesting ideas that it does completely wrong basically everywhere. Having a weapon skill system doesn't mean a lot when you can go unarmed and be more broken than any other weapon. Having a keyword system turns the game into say-everything-to-everyone to find where you're supposed to go next. Every dungeon has empty rooms that force you to endure enemy encounters trying to leave them. Every single enemy with status ailments has a near-100% chance of inflicting them. It's one of the most infuriating RPGs I have ever played and I never want to touch it again.

_childDocuments_.review: Decent version of FF2. I have several minor complaints about the design, but it's got some nice QoL improvements and the sprite work is really cute. Compared to the Gameboy Advance version:Pros: Text boxes open faster, the Sap spell doesn't seem to miss (grinding MP takes way less time), your weapon lv progress and stat changes are shown after every fight, stat bonuses seem to come by more often, and the back row now ALLOWS all weapons at half damage except the bow. Cons: No auto-run, no auto-escape button afaik, and the status screen no longer shows both stats/weapon levels and magic levels (you have to check the magic screen separately). The back row allowing physicals also means a set of 8 enemies can all physically attack you now, and you can target any of them.Ran across a major annoyance on the title screen key config menu, no way to restore defaults and I ended up using the mouse to assist me after half an hour of troubleshooting.

_childDocuments_.review: FF2 but worse in every way.Unlike Final Fantasy 1, I have only ever played this version on the Dawn of Souls GBA version.The extra content in FF1 on the Dawn of Souls version was some what pointless and not worth looking at.In 2, it's missing major aspects of the story, including a campaign featuring 4 specific characters that play a big part in the main story.Also, while grinding to the extreme in FF1 (PR) was pointless, due to no challenge requiring it, FF2 (PR) forces two heavy weapon and spell grinds.Not for any story reason, instead for 2 achievements. At no point do you ever need a spell or a weapon at level 16. There are no challenging enemies, no super bosses, no reason to even bother.Like 1, they removed some beneficial aspects, such as shield leveling, however they also introduced bugs all of their own.If you finish a battle by killing an undead enemy with a life spell, the game just soft-locks. You need to do a hard reset. As such, trying to ever use the "Life" spell in any meaningful way is a waste.For Final Fantasy 1, I said the Pixel Remaster version was fine and a good way to play the game if you want a version with achievements.For 2, no. The achievements are inane with a ton of missables and a pointless 16 level grind.Play the GBA version of 2 and you'll have a more fun time with better bosses, a satisfying extra campaign and not waste your time with grinding pointless levels.Just as an extra tip: If you do get this game and find yourself struggling with the 2 inane achievements. For the Weapon achievement, use 2 of the weakest weapons of the same type you can, find a strong enemy and then just spend 5-10 minutes hitting it for 0 damage, then use your other party to defeat it. Do that 16 times.For the spell, get a heal spell, stock up on ethers and/or elixirs, find a damaging floor and take a step. Heal everyone individually, then take another step.It's tedious as ♥♥♥♥, but that's what Square thinks you want.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing remaster of the least approachable FF game.  Play this if you've played the original before, or if you're a masochist, but otherwise it's pretty skippable.  It's also missing Soul of Rebirth which may rub some the wrong way but I think "more of the game" is the opposite of what this game needs.To be clear, this remaster is beautiful and is a great version of the game.  Screenshots don't do it justice.  The animations are crisp, the localization is good, some of the things that were broken in past versions seem to work now.  What more can we ask for?The issue is that the game is really divisive and not very approachable.  With that said, there were a LOT of really great and interesting (and influential!) firsts here:The first (last) Dragoon: The first appearance of the Dragoon class, albeit without its signature features, appeared here in "Ricard Highwind".The first skillup system: Anyone who's played FFXI will be familiar with the concept, but the idea started here; the more you do a thing, the better you are at the thing.  It's a weird, classless progression system that should mean the game is flexible and deep.  Unfortunately in practice hidden stats throw a wrench in it and the best way to get strong is to slap yourself in the face.The first real character development:  "Guy speak Beaver."  Snook-chit?  Chit chit.  It's not good character development, but it exists.The first (and last) time your status spells did anything noteworthy: Warp is the best spell in the game (Toad is less good in this one).Other first appearances: Holy, Ultima, Chocobos, Cid I think? (FF1's Cid was a retcon?)In conclusion if you're a fan of the series and kinda hate yourself, there's a lot of cool stuff to be found here.  Otherwise, skip right to 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by saying that I do like the Final fantasy series, the first game I played was Final Fantasy II (FF IV) on the SNES and have been a fan since then.  This game I really did want to like but to me it's just too repetitive...as if RPG's were't already repetitive.  But there's a lot of back and forth, you'll leave your hideout and head to a town complete a quest there and go back to your hideout only to be sent back to that same town for another quest that is a continuation of the quest you just completed.  The leveling system or lack there of is just for weapon skills and magic, I don't mind the leveling up of weapon skills there's a MMO that had that at one time and still does in it's "Classic" game.  However leveling up all your spells (if you choose to do that) can be tedious.  The music is great compared to what you would have heard on the original console.  Graphics are what I would expect to see on a 16-bit console (I rather like that look).  It's not a bad game, it does have it's moments, and some aspects of the game are interesting it's just not what I was expecting after playing the original Final Fantasy in the pixel remaster series.  I'll probably go back to it later and I might end up enjoying it, similar to the way I didn't care for Final Fantasy VIII and  picked it up years later and ended up enjoying the game.  Right now though FFII is just not very high on my list.  However if you're a die hard Final Fantasy fan then give this game a whirl it's worth playing simply to see some of the ideas they were trying in a sequel to the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: As a port/remaster, this FF2 is very well made. I have no issues on that end, the game looks great, the BGM options are great and it runs perfectly. I decided to give this a Not Recommend because the game itself is a step down from the original Final Fantasy in pretty much every way, in consequence failing as a sequel. While I do understand that the drastic changes implemented in this game kind of set the blueprint for what FF would become across the decades, a series without fear of changing the setting and gameplay styles (to different degrees of success), and I respect the courage that the devs had in order to make these changes after the massive acclaim of FF1 at the end of the day the results these choices had on the game itself miss the mark for the most part. The game is bigger, longer and has a slightly more developed narrative but this expansion serves no purpose other than to be expansive and in the end they just become bloat on an ambitious title. Everyone knows that the most controversial change implemented in FF2 is the leveling system. It functions more akin to what you'd find in an action RPG instead of a turn-based combat game, where the more a party member uses a weapon/spell/action, the more they become proficient in that talent. This makes the game absurdly grindy but truth be told, I didn't had much of a problem with the system itself. At first, it was jarring since I started this right after finishing FF1, but quickly I managed to focus Firion on sword and shield, Maria on bow and magic and Guy on axe/hammers. The game was grindy, yes, but not impossible to manage or annoying. That being said, if there's an area of the party and combat aspect of the game that definitely made no sense to me is the rotating fourth party member and the imbalance it brought to my party. At first, with characters like Minwu it was not as big of an issue, but as the game went on and the core three party members reached higher and higher stats, the 4th party member suddenly dropping in with an incredibly low HP/MP count in comparison made the character almost useless. This became fairly obvious in the Leviathan area when the dragoon joins in. I had all of my characters at over 2k HP and Maria at 300 MP and Ricard joined with like 300 HP and 3 MP. He was pretty much useless if he was not getting killed in one attack or two by the enemies. I don't really understand why the devs made this choice instead of just making two characters that rotate like Minwu at the early game and Leila or Ricard later on. The other big issue I had with this game is the awful dungeon level design. They are bigger than in FF1 but at the same time they are a 100 times more lifeless and lacking any charm. The dungeons are bloated to death with doors that go up and down or seemingly lead to chests when in reality they only contain empty rooms. Towards the end of the game, around the Mysidian Tower, I got fed up with it and just decided to give up on getting all the chests. This, combined with the grind and the increased encounter rate compared to FF1, made playing the end game areas tedious and a bit of a struggle to get through. The story of the game is seemingly more fleshed out than FF1's when in reality, it lacks the charm and fable-like magic of the first. The storyline feels like a power point presentation instead of a fable, where things just happen because they have to with constant twists that add absolutely nothing to develop the world or the characters. Even the villain, the Palamecian Emperor, falls incredibly flat in comparison to Garland and the amazing twist at the end of FF1.All in all, Final Fantasy 2 is an ambitious game made by creative and brave people that unfortunately fails as a sequel in every way a sequel can, from gameplay to level design to story. When I finished FF1, one of my favorite RPGs, I was already thinking of new party combinations for a future replay but when I finished FF2 I was only left with a sense of relief that I was finally getting this one over with before moving on to FF3.

_childDocuments_.review: Geez devs, you could have changed some of the battle mechanics that sucked like getting hit with the status effect EVERY time, instead of limiting the amount of power leveling available and how you can go about it. Because walking back and forth across every map screen 16 times to get from Door A to Door B isn't annoying enough, I have to cast every spell I want at level 8 or above 10,000 times. That was always a beef with this game. Even power grinding the spells was never something you actually wanted to commit to. I really didn't want to waste the time leveling anything in the magic department other than Cure, Esuna, and Toad. By a certain point that was easily the bulk of my casting with a good deal of Life and Warp as well. Otherwise you can pretty much auto battle through the game with a light armored Firion (or whatever his actual name is) sporting 2 swords and a light armored bare fist Guy. Maria(?), IDFK, Bottle Cap just sits back and either shoots the bow or casts Toad to great effect (Including most bosses and the first Emperor).Play this for a laugh and some self inflicted torment if you're into that sort of thing. The story progresses like whiplash happening at the same time as much broken glass and tree sap on EVERYTHING. Meaning there's a lack of cohesion. By the time you get your FINAL fourth character slot filled in... I let the bastard die right away and left him that way until I was done with the game. Didn't need him before, didn't need him after. Killed the final boss in 3 hits, while also failing to turn him into a toad twice in between before he was disintegrating. This happened on Auto-Battle. Really well balanced guys! Gotta save every battle or 15 steps through almost the entirety of the final dungeon, otherwise it's just, CAW CAW BANG ♥♥♥♥ I'M DEAD! ... and it is and will be just like that, regardless, SEVERAL times before you reach the end. It's just a matter of how much back tracking you want to do.As for the visual quality, since the Pixel Remaster seemed to be the focus here... HOGWASH!!! Who let that washed out color pallet through? Obscene use of black outlines. The pirate Leila looked more like a belly dancer than a pirate, and I choose to leave it at that.I expected MUCH better from a triple-A game company.Okay, leave it at THAT.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II has a problem. It just doesn't *feel* like a final fantasy game. For those of us that have played the earlier FF games, two was always the red-headed step child of the group. I attribute that to the more flexible style of the game. Gone are set classes, there aren't the jobs of later games. Oddly, FF2 brings to mind Skyrim. That's going to sound odd at first blush, but it's true. All of your characters can be 100% customised if you put the effort in. Levelling too is somewhat similar to Skyrim in that the more you practice a skill, the higher your proficiency. The more time you put into using your bow, the better that character will get. Ultimately, I think that this was the big problem. The way skills and magic levelled were ahead of the time. Perhaps it was too complex for us back in the earlier days of the FF series.That said, if you take FF2 as a stand alone game it can be an enjoyable experience. It contrasts with the original FF very well. The story isn't to everyone's liking, and party member four is a massive weakness (you invest and improve them and they disappear when you least expect it). FF2 is a competent game though. It's worth a playthrough to be able to see what the original devs of the series thought made an interesting followup to FF1.I should probably address this 'remake'. I have no fewer than four copies of the games FF1-6. I have them in original NES/SNES format, DS, Android, PS, and Windows. Personally, I preferred the earlier remasters for the Playstation. The visual style felt better, and the font didn't clash with the overall art style. The cynic in me feels like this version is just another ploy for money and not worth the investment.To those considering the purchase, I'd advise holding off if you have to choose between this and another game purchase. If you have plenty of spare cash, or are keen to complete your FF collection then do buy it. Just don't go in expecting this to feel like a good FF game. This is a fair-to-midddling RPG and an interesting historical look at what direction the series might have taken...what path JRPGs may have taken.

_childDocuments_.review: Often bundled together with the original Final Fantasy. Seen by many as the black sheep of the franchise. Mainly because of the way character progression is handled. There are no overall levels in Final Fantasy II. Instead, each stat increases individually depending on what actions are taken in battle. Using melee weapons will increase strength. Using magic spells will increase stats associated with magic. Weapon types and magic spells have levels and need to be leveled up as well. If it sounds grindy, that's because it is. Though, starting with the Game Boy Advance version, the difficulty has been heavily nerfed, to the point where you can play the game as any other RPG. In the original NES version, stats could actually decrease. This has not been a thing since the GBA version, thankfully. Pros- Remastered soundtrack supervised by Uematsu.- Auto battle feature that speed up battles.- Character sprites that are based on the sprites in the PSP version which in turn was more faithful to the concept art by Yoshitaka Amano. - Map screens for all towns and dungeons. Makes navigating more streamlined especially for FFI and II as they have maps with many nasty dead ends.- A "classic" screen filter that emulate the look of a CRT TV. Personally a must have for these sprite based games.Cons.- None of the bonus dungeons and super bosses from the Game Boy Advance and PlayStation Portable versions are included. There's no postgame content to speak of. You finish the story, that's it. - Some of the cutscenes from the GBA and PSP versions are not included.- There're are some performance problems. The screen scrolling isn't as smooth as it should be. I recommend that you play in Fullscreen mode, force V-sync and limit the FPS cap to 58 in the graphics card control settings.- Very small and thin font when you have the game language set to anything other than Japanese. You can do some quick modding by swapping the Japanese font file with a non-japanese one. This goes for all six games.Overall, this is a recommendation for first-timers. The most accessible version at the moment. Is this the best version of the game? Personally, it's either this or the PSP version. Some things are better in this version while others are better on PSP.Note: Final Fantasy II was designed by the same guy behind the SaGa series, Akitoshi Kawazu. The first SaGa game was released the year after FFII, for the original Game Boy.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy III didn't hate this game. As a fan of the Final Fantasy series i am glad i played this. But i would also never recommend this game to anyone i know.Final Fantasy 2 is infamous for its leveling system where the agility stat is king and you can only level HP by getting hit, Level up spells by constantly using them, attack stat by hitting enemies and agility by dodging.  The game does a terrible job at telling you the importance of this or how this system work, but if you were aware of it before you start the game, it is a system that can easily make you OP as long as you know what you are doing. Luckily the Pixel Remaster has done away with the «Levels decrease over time» system, so you don't have to worry about losing stats anymore.So because of the PR QoL changes and being aware of how the leveling system worked i personally didn't end up hating the leveling system, but if i went in blind and suddenly couldnt progress anymore because my stats were all over the place, i would probably hate it too.Dungeons are really bad in this game as they are built like a maze and have lot of trap rooms that leads to nowhere and makes you have to backtrack a lot. Its like a a frustrating amount of trap rooms, which is made even more frustrating by this games ridiculously high encounter rate on enemies. Like sometimes you can only walk 4-5 steps until you meet a new batch of enemies. The ridiculous amount of enemies i encounter when i would just travel or get lost in the maze-like dungeons ended up making me overleveld by default, so constantly meeting enemies that i would always one-shot really felt like a slog. This version of the game makes traveling dungeon better since you have a mini map, But you will most likely still be wandering into trap rooms and have to backtrack.  The console version has a fix for this where you can lower encounter rates and increase/decrease XP rates. But Square Enix being Square Enix has not given the PC version this feature.Story in this game barely exist, but it has more story then the first one. Thats honestly all i can say about it without entering spoiler territory on what little there is to spoil of the story.So in conclusion: if you are a big fan of the series in general, i say its worth checking out just to see re-occurring themes, enemies and some characters that originated from this game. If you just want to have a fun with a game or an introduction to the FF series i cant recommend this game at all. However! if you have already made up your mind and you are going to play it, please play the Pixel Remaster version as the QoL updates it brings is definitely worth it

_childDocuments_.review: I finally got around to playing Final Fantasy II, but I didn't like it that much. The story has more to it than the first game, but it's still pretty simple and forgettable. It was pretty fun at the start: magic and weapons level up as you use them, but in the later stages of the game, it takes forever for magic to level up. Also, you do a lot of the same stuff over and over again. Talk to the princess, walk to objective while fighting a bunch of enemies, navigate overly long and samey dungeons with way too many encounters, then return to the princess. It gets very repetitive. Still, the music and atmosphere are pretty good, but I would say this is probably my least favourite Final Fantasy out of those I've finished. I will give it a positive review though, because the Pixel Remaster makes it a lot better. You can turn off encounters if you feel like you've had enough for one area, you can speed up leveling and/or battles, and you can even switch to the original soundtrack if you want. For those reasons, it barely gets a nod from me.

_childDocuments_.review: FFII will forever remain a mixed bag until it gets a proper remake (which in my opinion it definitely deserves) and, unfortunately, this remaster/port is no exception. The Good: Smoothest leveling out of all the versions. I'm more than halfway through at the time of writing and not once had to stop to level any attributes. The music re-arrangements are beautiful, Uematsu outdone himself. The graphics are true to the spirit of the NES games with additional detail (water, smoke, effects) and look gorgeous. Auto-battle.Helpful map and Bestiary. You can save in dungeons. The Bad:Even though the leveling was rebalanced it is still FFII at its core, meaning all the problems the original had are present here as well. So mobs of debuff-inflicting and one-shot killing enemies, ridiculous encounter rates and the infamous skill leveling are all back. Cut content - the extra dungeon from GBA/PSP versions is not present for some reason and so far there are no plans to add it. Which is a shame, because the one here was actually not that bad. Verdict: I am probably one of the few people who actually like FFII with all its flaws, so take this recommendation with a grain of salt. Having played all versions of this game it is this remaster I am having the most fun with. The rebalanced skill leveling and auto-battle make the playthrough much smoother and faster, while the presentation is top notch and captures the spirit of the original. If you're looking for the definitive version of FFII, I would probably recommend the Anniversary for PSP. Yet, if you want to play through the main story to just familiarize with this artifact of gaming history, then this pixel remaster will absolutely get the job done.

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely an extremely solid, faithful remaster of the original game.  In terms of the remaster itself, there isn't much to say- it runs smoothly, the graphics are great, and the dialogue is very faithful to the original (from what I can remember, it's been 20 years since I've played the original). For the rest of the review, I'll focus on FF II mechanics specifically, but TL;DR- the remaster is great, and the game was ahead of its' time. Play it.To those mostly unfamiliar with FF II, it is a major departure from how FF I worked, specifically in the leveling department. Typically in a Final Fantasy, you get into random encounters, win, gain exp, and slowly level your characters up.  FF II is the same, up until the actual leveling- you instead level up individual weapons, stats, and magic. You do not have a "character level" per se, you will never have a team of "level 99" characters. If you've played Skyrim, the idea is exactly the same.  Get hit a bunch in battle?  Your health will probably go up. Auto attack a lot with Firion? He's going to end up with high strength. Also, the magic is quite different. Usually, your mage classes will start with basic versions of spells (Cure, Fire, Blizzard) that are low-cost, low-damage, which will be essentially replaced later with better versions (Cura, Fira, Blizzara) and so on. In FF II however, your spells themselves level up. This means that you never learn another version of "Cure", instead your Cure will level into Cure II, Cure III, and so on.  This is a really cool and straightforward way of spellcasting that not only simplifies the magic menu, it allows for the more useless spells in other entries in the series (such as Stop, Blind, and Slow) actually become quite useful if you devote the time into leveling them, as leveling up status effects give them additional chances to be inflicted (basically extra dice rolls). I'll note here that this leveling system can be absolutely and completely broken if you want it to- with a little (or a lot) of grinding, you can get your characters to ridiculous power levels and trivialize the entire game.The story is another matter however. It isn't bad, but it definitely suffers from being an NES-era RPG. The dialogue is typically very short, npcs don't offer much in terms of world-building info, and the side characters that constantly fill the 4th party slot kinda just come and go and you never really feel attached to them. The motivations for the main bad guy feel super generic, and [Final Party Member]'s motivations honestly make no sense. I'm okay with all of this, as I realize a lot of this is because of NES-era hardware limitations on memory, and expository dialogue takes up precious memory space, but just be aware that this is more about the gameplay and leveling systems, not the riveting story.Lastly, the random encounters.  Hooo boy. I generally don't whine and complain about random encounters (unlike most video essay tryhards), but FF I & II's random encounter rates are completely off the charts. This is simply to elongate playtime. Fun fact: I actually turned off random encounters using an emulator version just to see how fast I could run to the end of the game, and it cut the playtime down from about 20-30 hours to roughly 3 hours, and I'm not even very good at this game.TL;DR- Underrated Final Fantasy. Leveling system super cool & interesting. Story is generic but it's an NES game. Characters are mostly forgettable. Random encounter rate gets irritating. Music pretty good. 7/10 worth a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I decided to play this one after III and I. There's a reason for that. It's a chore. It's widely regarded as one of the low points of the series, and after spending more time with it, I can agree. I realised after a few hours that I wasn't having fun, and that the few good things it did were not enough to offset the bad.First the good:*This is the first game in the series to have characters with names. They even have limited personalities. The story is also interesting and character driven. The heroes aren't the heroes just because; they have an actual stake in ensuring that the Empire is brought to justice. The world itself has a grim, low-fantasy feel about it, absent of the lighthearted cheer of the other NES entries. Violence and death are as common as water, and the weak become swept up in the power struggles of the strong. The idea that all of this was squeezed into a NES cart back in the day is nothing short of amazing.*Character progression follows an Elder Scrolls-like formula, meaning that the party gets better at things the more they do them. You can completely tailor the abilities of the party to whatever suits you.Now for the bad:*The encounter rate is ludicrously high. I was averaging a battle every eight steps or so. It wouldn't be so bad if the battles were actually fun. Instead they're a grind. I ended up setting the party to auto flee every fight and hoped the enemies wouldn't get too many hits in before they escaped. Monster battles are the thing you do the most of in this game, but they're criminally lacking in fun.*The dungeons are large, sprawling mazes that are designed to annoy and waste time. This version has a mini-map that shows treasure chests and protects you from going down a corridor that leads nowhere. Unfortunately, there are smaller rooms that are designed in a way that makes it mandatory to enter to see what's inside. Ninety percent of them are empty. The game places you in the centre of the room for some reason, and the encounter rate is even higher, so you almost always get punished for exploring. It might sound small, but this choice of design is really quite indicative of the game as a whole. Sometimes, it feels like a punishment to play Final Fantasy II.These two drawbacks destroyed my will to play it any further. The good points mean nothing if I spend the majority of the game being annoyed.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the most accessible version of the game, though I think I'd still give a slight edge to the Dawn of Souls version just because the Pixel Remaster is way too easy. I mean, I'm glad that you don't have to beat yourself up like you kind of did in certain parts of the older versions, but I feel like you shouldn't be able to auto-battle bosses without grinding. To me, that's just too easy and easy is boring.I never stopped even once to grind until after I beat the game (just to get a couple achievements like max weapon skill) but almost every boss was dead in less than 5 rounds and it seems like you get HP up after every other battle. Although maybe that's because the encounter rate is through the damned roof which makes it even more boring being spammed by trivial enemies.This game was largely just an experiment with Square trying out a Learn by Doing method of leveling up stats and skills, and is often considered the black sheep of the series. All in all it's not a bad game, just different.

The port does its best to correct the issues with the character progression system; however, there's no polishing a turd.  The stat system is still incredibly tedious and takes fun out of the game.  In addition, the encounter rate in Final Fantasy 2 is nuts.  Prepare to spend hours crawling through short dungeons, fighting mobs of 6-8 enemies with varying weaknesses every ten steps.  Seriously, this game might have invented time gating in RPGs.  The story is interesting and I'm glad that Square took a risk and wanted to try some new things with the gameplay, but it just doesn't work.  The level of difficulty and grinding you go through for a wet ♥♥♥♥ ending just isn't worth it.  I would only recommend Final Fantasy 2 for diehard fans of the series that want to play every main title.

You get to listen to all the songs in the main menu and some of them are just so heartwarming. ⚫The auto-battle option is a welcome addition to a game like this. ⚫The UI is so good in this game. I had a look at the older UI that was used... yeah... this new, improved, modern UI is a much needed welcome for new players like me.⚫You can dive into the world of the game with supplemental extras like the bestiary, illustration gallery, and music player.⚫They took the class system in depth in this game. You can build around any weapon of your choice. Learn magic on ANY character. ⚫The friends lost along the way, shows how emotional the early games truly were. Yes it might not hit the same but to see how far the games have come since the originals... wow.⚫The level design/Dungeon designs improved drastically. Each new area looked stunning. My favourite area was pandaemonium. It looked amazing. ⚫They did improve on the "Where to go next" feeling a little.⚫Again, the same issue with FINAL FANTASY, at times, I felt lost. I was left roaming around the world map endlessly with no indication on what to do or where to go. ⚫Once I got the spell/Tome "Berserk" I was almost unstoppable. Then when I got "ULTIMA"... combined with "Excalibur" and "Berserk" the game was over. I could feel the enemies drop at my feet. Even all the boss's in pandaemonium dropped with my main character that used Excalibur and Blood sword. (You will know what I mean if you saw the boss rush in pandaemonium)(Thats all that is bad about the game really, nothing else. No joke)As a complete "noob" to the FINAL FANTASY games, with no knowledge of PREVIOUS games (1-13) this was an amazing journey for me and I loved almost every moment of it. I would recommend this game to anyone that likes turn-based games and the Final Fantasy series or to anyone like me, that's wanting to learn all these references and experience an amazing game series.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the story, graphics and the remastered music. This game set the stage for modern RPGs such as the SAGA franchise. This remaster makes the flawed stats system from the original Famicom verison much better.The main drawback to this pixel remaster is the removal of the side content that were available in the GBA and PSP versions. If you're a fan of classic JRPGs, I can wholeheartedly recommend FF2.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: It's Final Fantasy: Star Wars!While the story is anything but original, the characters in this installment have a way of making you quickly invested in their heavily Lucas-inspired plot straight away. Leaving the fourth party member slot for the occasional story-relative characters helps to show you where you could go with your three primary characters, whom you have total control over when it comes to how they play.Mechanically speaking, this game feels like a giant leap forward from both it's predecessor and its successor. You have the ability to take your three primary characters and make literally any party combination you could ask for. Want a priest who dual wields spears? Equip the character with the spears and work up their white magic spells! Want an arcane archer? Give 'em a bow and learn some offensive black magic spells! This was such a fun and free concept that was, unfortunately, abandoned for the far more limiting "Jobs System" to come in the next sequel.The Pixel Remaster does exactly what you want it to do: takes the original game, polishes it, and gives it modern conveniences to make it a more enjoyable experience for everyone in today's gaming sphere.Of the initial three Final Fantasies, this one gets my highest praise and strongest recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: A BLAST PLAYING THE "WORST" FINAL FANTASYFinal Fantasy II is notorious being one of the worst in the franchise. I've played it on the Gameboy once, the Dawn of Souls version and I can see aspects where it falters. Kinda hard to review old games because some flaws that I will state maybe come from its' old age and my perspective from a younger audience.One thing that stood out for me in Final Fantasy II either the Gameboy or Pixel Remaster version is that how bad the dungeon design is. Some dungeons (maybe all) have convoluted designs that just full on does not make sense. Why are there dead ends of corridors in huge castle? Why are there doors all over the place? And most doors will only feature TRAP ROOMS, which are basically an empty room which has a very high encounter rate and powerful mobs. Theres straight up a two floor level that I venture that are straight up full of TRAP ROOMS. Really a waste of time and didn't reward the players for exploration. Fortunately, the Pixel Remaster although feature trap rooms, lowers the encounter rate to a normal state.When it comes to exploration, some goodies and chests have these secret walls that you can pass through in order to get em. I did not know this until I opened a guide. I thought this mechanic was first mentioned Final Fantasy III where theres an NPC explaining where these walls exist. In this game, nothing was said about these walls. Story is kinda meh. I can see how this can be a good story if there are characterisation, fleshed out moments, and well-paced story telling. It felt like a fanfiction tbh. To be fair, this is one of the first attempts on bringing story in a Final Fantasy game. But Final Fantasy II still pales in comparison to its predecessor, Final Fantasy I, which has more of a simple story but has depth that leaves fans crafting theories about it until this day. In Final Fantasy II, the story is just... there.Done with the negatives, I like the progression system this game had. The closes thing I've played that have this progression system is The Elder Scrolls IV:: Oblivion. Instead of leveling up your characters to boost stats and overall become stronger, you level up the weapon you're using and magics you castin. All characters have access to all weapons and magics. And it depends on you build how your team is. Maybe a party member can have efficiency in swordfighting, but also possess deadly magics in its arsenal. Very customisable and overall very fun. Mentioning the soundtrack is great is like saying the sky is blue. NOBUO UEMATSU SHOULD BE WORSHIPPED.Overall, stressed out with the dungeons, didn't care about the story, but still had a blast.3/5
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Well, that was a bit of a ride.15-hour playthrough, played through this game in the past on GBA and PSP and generally pleased with this remake.Let me go through the pros and cons:Pros:-Grinding is made less frustrating thanks to the autobattle function + improved stat handling-Absolutely beautiful live orchestra renditions of the Final Fantasy II soundtrack-Easily moddable, so if you want a different text font it's easily achievable-The most straightforward, direct plot line of the early Final Fantasies-Guest characters add a lot of personality and flavour to the small world of Final Fantasy II, easily the most developed in the storyline-The emperor's a simple, but brutally efficient villain who provides plenty entertaining shenanigans-Kazuko Shibuya returns to recreate her original sprite designs into a semi 16-bit style, making this feel like a SNES FF2 with a similar sprite style to Final Fantasy 4 and 5-Minor, but it's interesting to see 16-bit recreations of NES enemy sprites over the previous version's inclusion of enemies directly based on Yoshitaka Amano's concept art-The chocobo theme is finally full length!Cons:-Autobattling for too long while grinding skills can create massive slowdown and frame drops for some reason-The default text font is butt ugly-The skill grinding can still be extremely tedious regardless of autobattle speeding things up-Minor gripe, but I found Battle Theme A to have a bit less grit to it than the PS1 arrangement-The main characters have dialogue, but zero personality-Difficulty can feel very uneven due to various quirks-The stat progression system lends itself to a lot of flexibility for the player, but is barely explained to the player at all-The airship is helpful, but only lends you full freedom when the game's already practically over-Guest characters have personality, but are often pitifully powerless compared to the rest of the party-There are items that claim to protect against instant death, but you get instant death anywayI still love Final Fantasy 2, and I have for years, but this remake definitely brought to light some of the more frustrating aspects of it.I do still heavily recommend going into it with an open mind, because the blessings more than make up for its faults.If anything, if you want to have the best time then look up how the game mechanics work and prepare yourself for building the characters you think would be most useful to you.The story and the guest characters are definitely the strongest point of the game to me, and the simplicity makes it easy to pick up and play without getting too bogged down in details like later FF games can be.People are right to express their gripes about this game, as is their right, but I can't help but love this flawed rushed masterpiece all the same.There are definitely some problems that could use some further tweaking, but the easily moddable nature of the Unity assets is a plus for that purpose if you want to personalise your experience.I do think I'm pleased, after all.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: This second game game in the legendary series features the removal of the class and level system in favor of leveling up specific skills by specific actions - you want more HP, get hit; you want a spell to get stronger, cast it more. It's got much better writing than its predecessor, meaning you are never stuck wondering where to go.  The plot is quite linear, but given the age of the game, that's fine.  Really, there are only 2 major flaws:1. While you can have 4 people in your party, only 3 are constant and the fourth rotates with the story and they generally come in much weaker than you, so you have to grind for a bit or be very protective of them.2. I saw an online guide that nicknamed this game "Final Fantasy Too Many Doors" and it's not wrong.  Dungeons frequently present you with a ridiculous number of doors to choose from, with no indication as to which is wrong.  The remained generally open into identical empty rooms and the only penalty for entering is an elevated chance of a random encounter.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II is a rather unique take on the Final Fantasy formula. In an effort to innovate, Square decided to opt for a Skill-Based experience system, something that would go on to shape the way we play RPGs to this day through games like Ultima VIII, Ultima Online, RuneScape, and The Elder Scrolls. While unique, the amount of grinding can be quite daunting and can be a turn off.While Square-Enix recently has been hit-or-miss with ports of their games, it seems the Pixel Remasters are pretty decent so far. The only issue is the choice of font being used for English. This can be remedied by replacing the font_en files with the font_ja ones. This forces the game to use the full-width English characters of the Japanese font rather than the Half-Width characters found in the English bundle.According to my research, this is the first time Final Fantasy II has come to PC and it's a welcome port. If you are looking for something different in the Final Fantasy franchise, a fan of FFII, or looking for something a touch different, I definitely recommend Final Fantasy II Pixel Remaster.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: People harping on the character progression in this game has become a meme, but I enjoyed it. While the Pixel Remaster has the option to turn off Random Encounters, I found myself preferring to fight instead, even in areas where enemies are far below my current Rank, due to how both persistent and random stat increases are implemented.The story is a bit bare-bones but conversations were generally more engaging through the keyword system than they were in Final Fantasy 1.The visual presentation of the Pixel Remaster is great and I found myself looking forward to upgrading my spells to see the attack animation change.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: This game is... yeah...I mean I liked some of it:The story was a nice change of pace, I liked how dark it is and how we can see the tragedies led out by the Emperor firsthand. I like the keyword system as it makes the game feel a bit more immersive and roleplay-like, even though the story isn't very good (I especially like how if you say to a guard "Wild Rose" they instantly know that you are a rebel and fight you, which is a nice touch). I like the leveling system, as it lets me build my team how I want to, like making Maria my main damage dealer and letting Firion cast all of the spells to heal. And, the music is fantastic, especially the last dungeon music.Only problem is that the game just isn't fun, at least for me. The dungeon and enemy design is incredibly terrible. There are so many dead-ends in every dungeon, but I just have to check and see in all of these rooms because there might be loot inside (but there usually isn't... usually... which is why I still check them). The dungeons are just built to waste your time. The enemy design is also so strange to me. There's this one enemy that just instantly kills anything it touches, and many more that do stupid things like it as well. The final boss was also super disappointing, and took (I kid you not) less than 50 seconds to beat. Just two pokes with a sword and he wets himself. The enemies in the final dungeon were more of a challenge than the boss itself! I was so excited to be able to use all of the abilities I've learned in the fight... but nope.I really cannot recommend this to anyone, as it's just made to waste your time. Leon sums this game's story and gameplay up pretty well as "Weak words, from the weak" lol.I mean, at least Guy speaks beaver.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: This is considered the black sheep of the franchise, but I believe that's not entirely true. Sure, the original Famicom game was somewhat a departure from Final Fantasy 1, but the spirit of the series is pretty much intact. The leveling system is weird, but it's not as bad as some people think. In fact, the system allows for a level of customization and specialization higher than its predecessor. Furthermore, the cast of characters is richer, although it means that some of them are cooler than others.This version, like FF1 before it, is somewhat an in-between the OG and the PSP remake, in terms of improvements and features. It lacks the bonus episodes from PSP, but offers new QoL features, such as bug corrections and useful maps. The music is astounding, and better than the Sony's portable version. I recommend this game if you have never played it before. Just be sure know what you are jumping into, as this is a classic JRPG.For new players, I can offer some hints to help:- you can correct the ugly font (just look for tutorials in the Guides section),- talk to everyone to collect and use the key words. It is important to advance the story,- don't stray too far from where you should be, as enemies can be extremely tough if you're not levelled enough,- try to specialize your characters, distributing magic and weapons in a way that somewhat resembles a classic JRPG team (fighter, black mage, white magic), but be smart and give Cure magic to everyone. The system allows for a high degree of customization, so abuse it.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I hate the Yes/No recommend as it makes it look like I hate this game.I've completely played through and thoroughly enjoyed the experience, right up to the last boss.Now, I didn't have any prior knowledge of basically the only way to beat the boss and sold the essential weapon since I didn't have a use for it beforehand. Now I can't technically beat the game unless I restart from the beginning and not sell it this time. Which I will not do. So, no, at this point I do not recommend a game that has impossible battles that hinge on a single item.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II was generally tied with Final Fantasy XIII as the weakest in the series.  I liked XIII better than VIII or XV and I hadn't played II until now.  I played the USA version of FFII (which was IV in the series) and then avoided playing the true II based on reputation and how old it was.  So the Pixel Remaster has given me my first taste of II and in this version, at least, I don't think it's too bad.  It has a terrible skill system instead of leveling and classes which, even in the remaster, makes it impossible to gauge if you are under or over-leveled at any given time.  And because you level up through the use of skills/spells, they turned up the random encounter odds and designed everything with long twisty corridors to force more and more fights.  So, I understand the opinions on this game.  This is definitely a more palatable version.I modded mine to use the PSX font and the GBA sprites/portraits and PSP battle backgrounds.  Looks fantastic.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: If this is your first time playing, you probably won't miss it.The Pixel Remaster is based on versions of the game before the Dawn of Souls (GBA) and 20th Anniversary (PSP) versions so you do not have any of the additional mid/postgame content. In just about every other game in the Pixel Remaster series, I'm fine with this. But Final Fantasy II is the only one that suffers, as Soul of Rebirth (The GBA content) is quite good, and you also lose the Arcane Labyrinth, which adds a little more lore, superbosses, and some fancy weapons to the game.That said, if you've never played Final Fantasy II, The game itself is pretty janky in design, with an exploitable character stat gaining system and an awkward proficiency-level system. However, since it requires much less time and commitment than traditional experience grinding, I find it easy to see this jank as endearing. But it is objectively pretty flawed, and I can understand why people might be turned off.For 1988, however, the game is pretty impressive. Believe it or not, the original Famicom version was even more flawed, and I think these later versions retain some of the jank for posterity.The story, for the time, is also very good. Final Fantasy II is one of the prototypical character-driven story-based JRPGs, and in spite of that, it's got a simple but well-executed story. Characters have compelling qualities and a reason to do what they're doing, and the climactic moments, for the time, feel grand and impressive.The game is very difficult. Enemies that can inflict status ailments with physical attacks have a 100% chance of inflicting that status ailment -  - and some later dungeons are definitely tests of endurance.If you especially like the SaGa series, it might be worth checking out, as I feel that Final Fantasy II was pretty instrumental in the conception of the series, especially the Romancing SaGa games.Other than that, I recommend giving a try, because if you can appreciate the game in spite of the awkwardness of some systems, it's really quite a fun, quick romp.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is one of the weakest Final Fantasy games.The random encounter rate is absurdly high through the whole game.The progression system is weird. There are not any character levels like what we're used to - characters gain stat ups after combat at what seems like random. There does not seem to be a way to track this.Weapons and spells gain skill points the more you use them. This is a problem due to how grindy the system is designed, and if you want to level up fast you are better off using the weakest weapons in the game until you are max rank with that weapon type. This also means that spells like Esuna, Berserk, Shell and Protect suck until you upgrade them a lot.The main story progresses using a password type system where you must MANUALLY commit certain topics to memory during conversation. If you don't, you won't be able to bring those topics up to advance the plot. Also there were several times when I completed an objective and had no idea what the hell to do. In FF1 you had to talk to people to gain hints at certain points along the main story, but the password system can obstruct that a bit.The party size is 4 characters, but in FF2, you may as well just count on there being 3 main characters. The guests are absurdly weak in comparison to your party when you get them and I found them pretty useless going forward without a lot of grinding. When they finally start getting decent, they leave the group and you get another worthless character.It's a shame, because I think with a little more QoL, this Pixel Remaster could have been a great game that fixed a lot of issues with the original FF2. While I'm sure it did in a lot of ways, it's still far from ideal.All in all, I would avoid this one unless you're absolutely certain you want to experience all the Final Fantasy games. I certainly gained more appreciation for all the rest of them after playing this one. (except for you, FF13)
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I have similar feelings about this as the first one. I'm amazed they managed to pack so much into an NES game in the first place. It is an expansive map with multiple companions, modes of transport, weapons and spells. It also looks beautiful and stands up remarkably well gameplay-wise after all these years. On the downside, getting lost and wandering onto the wrong part of the map is easy, and you'll get wiped out immediately. Also, how magic gets better through use gives me horrible flashbacks to the draw system in FFVIII.Like number 1, there is another mad difficulty spike at the end, but if you DuckDuckGo it, there is a simple way to even the battlefield.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: -- FF2 is a flawed game that I have a guilty pleasure for due to how cheeseable the stats system is-- Story is nothing to write home about, but not bad by any means-- I like the remastered pixel art, but let yourself decide on that-- Definitely recommend a guide for this game to prevent any confusion on story progression.  Definitely recommend guide if your going for 100% achives as there are missables.-- Unfortunate we couldn't get the extra content from "Dawn of Souls" I think that if your a FF fan looking to experience the whole series,  it's worth grabbing.  If your just a casual gamer looking around for a older style JRPG to play,  I think your mileage may vary.

_childDocuments_.review: For those that treat this one as the black sheep for having skill ups like Skyrim, I say give this a try. Even though you can cheeze it somewhat, there are still monster walls that require the normal RPG grind to get by, also it is fun to watch all your abilities max out. Once you notice you are no longer getting any more points on your weapons, you can switch it up to new ones. Fighting with 2 shields builds up your agi and your barehanded skill. Just remove the shields if you notice you are doing zero damage on your foes. The story for it being old, is pretty huge step up from FF1. Highly reccommend this to veteran's of the series.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game a lot, it's really good. The weapon/magic leveling system grew on me so much that I love it.  It has dialogue, NPCs are named and matter, actual story line, a few little cutscenes, a unique password system, a weapon and magic leveling system instead of gaining real levels, etc. I highly recommend it, just give it some time. Update: I love this game, it's really good.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get the hate. This was a fun game.Bows are not underpowered, use them if you like.You don't have to spam cast to grind spell levels.You don't have to hit yourself to gain HP (they fixed this, you steadily gain hp now).Dungeon enemy rate is not too high - just disable encounters if you don't want to fight.You don't have to use every keyword you know on an NPC - relevant keywords are now highlighted.Overall this was a fun game. I have nearly 20 hours on it, but I'm grinding post-game - I'd say it took about 15 hours to beat, but could have done it closer to 12 if I wasn't playing super casually (not using a guide).The only negative is the story (if you can call it that) - but keep in mind this was originally on the NES, and those games aren't known for their gripping storylines.I had a lot of fun with this game and its interesting leveling mechanics - reminded me of runescape or elder scrolls. Don't pass this up because of some youtubers throwing hate at this game, you'd be missing out!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: It's Final Fantasy II, so it's never going to be great, but this is probably the best way to play it. Just keep in mind what you're getting into.It's a shame because many of the elements are there that would make this a great RPG. It features a good story, albeit a barebones one, that clearly lays the foundation for games like Final Fantasy IV. From a historical standpoint, this is a very interesting game, and a clear sign that Square would strive to reinvent this series with every subsequent entry. The soundtrack is very somber and moody, fitting for the dire straits your party finds themselves in facing down the empire (though this is somewhat undermined by how much easier this version is that the other ports). The characters, while somewhat one-dimensional, are memorable and the designs are great. There's a lot of "historical" appeal here, seeing the evolution of mainstay series elements originating here, including some iconic monster designs and characters such as Cid. The PIxel Remaster treatment does an excellent job here, and the game looks and sounds great, and there's no denying I found it enjoyable to play even when I was just grinding through monsters.And that's kind of the problem: There's just not much here. There's the skeleton of something greater, elements that were impressive for their time and make the game stand out as noteworthy even now. The leveling system (which foregoes EXP and levels and instead raises stats based on combat outcomes like taking damage, attacking with certain weapon types, etc0, actually works really well in this version with the rebalancing that's been done, with one sole exception: Magic still takes way too long to level up. This renders most attack spells mostly useless, since you can only obtain them at Level 1. Without magic as a viable option in combat (unless you dedicate a character to spamming it every single battle to level it up), you're stuck just holding the Confirm button to hack away at everything over and over again. Even the ultimate magic, which I really, really wanted to use for thematic closure against the final boss, took an unreasonable amount of time to reach a level of power that would be on par with just attacking. This meant I had to take down the final boss (and pretty much every boss in the final dungeon) with the same cheap strategy that pretty much guarantees a win and undermines what could have been a pretty tense, harrowing fight.There's also lots of annoying little things like the zombie-filled "trap" rooms in dungeons. This is somewhat mitigated by the handy built-in game maps and auto-save, but these rooms were never a welcome inclusion in the original game either especially since undead enemies have the ability to drain HP with their base attacks. The game also hits you with a cheap shot around the last third of the game, where large mobs of enemies can inflict numerous annoying status ailments on your entire party all at once. Again, auto save mitigates this, but it's merely a bandage solution for a frustrating, player hostile design choice.All in all, it's just a bit dull to play, as you're running through (admittedly fairly complex, but linear) dungeons with frequent encounters. There's a large variety of enemy types for a game of this era, but it doesn't amount to much because you're mostly going to be auto battling through them and killing them in one shot, with the occasional strong enemy (or 5th/6th/7th/etc enemy you couldn't kill in the first round of combat) getting off an attack, maybe with some cool looking magic animations.If you're okay with all that, then I can say this version is worth a try if even as something light to play while you've got something else going on in the background. You could do a lot worse. However, it's hardly essential playing, and I'd really only recommend it to those who are curious about the evolution of the series and its earliest days.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Unlike FF1, the second game changes up a lot. For example, there's actual story now! It's not great, but it's enough to keep the plot going and guide the player towards the next goal. It's a NES game from 1988 after all. What changes the most is leveling system - levels are gone, it now allows you to individually level each stat (by certain actions like: attacking, dodging or losing health), weapon skill (by attacking) and spell (by casting). Sounds good on paper, but fails in execution. The best method of dispatching enemies is still attack spam, not to say that spells are useless, but they take a while to level, problem even more apparent with spells obtained later in the game, so ultimately you're going to end up with swinging a sword at the enemy repeatedly. As for your stats, they should level themselves somewhat well assuming you attack or use spells enough. However, if you're willing to grind there are unconventional methods to increase specific stats by for example: attacking your own party to increase HP and stamina or equiping 2 shields to level agility. Overall, like the first game, it gets too easy too quickly.But that's not the worst part - the combination of very frequent random encounters and dungeons designed to waste your time with multiple dead-ends and empty "trap" rooms is what takes away the most from the enjoyment. You will end up walking aimlessly around the dungeon triggering a fight every few steps. It's infuriating. This wouldn't be such a problem if encounters were interesting enough, but unfortutely - they are not. Oh, and most dungeons end with a "door puzzle". What's a "door puzzle" you might ask? A row of doors, one of which leads to the end of the dungeon, the rest are empty (which almost always guarantee an additional random encounter due to the game putting you in the middle of said room). Fun, isn't it?Not sure if that's a bug or not, but every weapon/enemy attack that applies a certain status ailment will trigger 100% of the time, unlike spells and abilities used by enemies. What it means that, if you don't dispatch enemies in the first turn, you will end up with some sort of status effect on at least one character. Pray that your characters have enough evasion to dodge any attack, otherwise you will end up with some "fun" situations such as: your party getting slowly killed because all characters got stunlocked by stun/sleep effect, your party killing each other because all characters got charmed, your party getting wiped first turn by a party of 6 coeurls in the final dungeon which have an on-hit instant KO effect regardless of health or damage done.Let's speak of some good things - like in the pixel remaster of the first game, the game looks really good and the music is awesome. I also like the fact that you can pretty much go anywhere from the start of the game. Yes, you will get pulped if you go to an end-game area too early, but I like when games do that. I can already see somebody grinding for hours in the first area and sequence breaking into high level zones.On the side note, the latest patch which came after I finished the game seems to significantly gimp dual wielding by "fixing a bug" that allowed your characters to attack multiple enemies if the first one died from the first attack.FF2 is not a horrible game... but it isn't a good one either. I enjoyed it to a certain extent, some people will really like the grindy nature of this game. I can recommend pixel remaster of FF2 only to the fans of the series or at least JRPGs that want to see the roots of the series. Otherwise, stay away.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Old school RPG game with some quality of life features to make it less tedious to play. However, as your characters improve and outpace monsters, the game can't challenge you anymore. I hope there's a hard mode. Treasures chests suck in this game and are almost never worth collecting. Melee builds beat magic builds and I'm not even sure how a magic build is viable, but there are monsters who can only be beaten with magic so it's required to have some. I like the characters and story. I enjoy the linearity. It's charming and simple and still fun.

_childDocuments_.review: FF2 is a game I feel is largely misunderstood. You can really tell they looked at 1 and thought of ways to improve it and took that chance. Let's put characters in with names, let's develope more of a political story in the world, instead of 4 characters let's have a solid 3 we keep the whole journey and introduce powerful allies you can play along the way, instead of having set roles let's let the player decide how they want to play and what roles they want to assign themselves. It can be confusing for some just starting to really assess that you should assign roles to be most optimal. Instead of leveling characters you level your weapons and spells by using them, as you do that your hp and other stats also increase. I feel this game has a lit of heart and ambition and I can see what they were trying to do. I'm sure due to the limitations of the nes at the time they couldn't execute all ideas properly. I think the issue for me was mostly not connecting with the characters or really caring about anyone. There is limited engagement of who and how people really are. I do feel this game deserves a modern day remake because I think all the things they want to achieve here can be done well.This also introduces a lot of ff tropes. Chocobos, Excalibur again, dark knights, dragoons, masamune. ultima, and pandemonium.Overall a great adventure if you take time to understand the flaws. 9/10
