_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II, even now, is the black sheep in the Final Fantasy series. After the first, it takes what was established and decides to see what boundaries it could push. It explores a more nuanced story that the first had to offer, more diverse magic, a password system to story progression, and so much more. But it doesn't get nearly as much love and, once FFIII came out, the game is completely overshadowed. However, not only to I disagree with most on the hate this game gets, I truly believe this game is slept on and is the best of the original Famicom titles.To start, but more-or-less beating a dead horse, the music is phenomenal. Each track stands out and really elevates the world and the battles you encounter to new heights. Unlike FFI's Pixel Remaster treatment where I find the new arrangements to be good, but preferring the original, here is more equal. I love the original score, but the arrangement, for the most part, brings every single track to a height it had not achieved prior. Some I prefer the original, but what is here is incredible.Visuals are what you'd expect. I find myself nostalgic for this and cannot praise them enough. You have colour swaps when fighting an upgraded enemy in their monster line. Unlike the original, some places (like the Castle Diest or the Jade Passage) have more life to them than before. Truly, very biased, but I adore the visuals.The story has it's dips of course, but for when the game came out in, I absolutely love the story. The characters have more going on than just a name to a face. There are highs and lows throughout your journey. There are certainly moments where you scratch your head, wondering why someone is acting a certain way or why the story took a took in one way to move the plot along. But overall, I find it quite charming.Now, the last but probably most divisive aspect to the game: gameplay. For those who may not be aware, FFII ditches the original game's traditional leveling system. Instead, it opts for a system where stats go up based on what happens in battle (i.e. if you take damage in battle, there is a chance you gain HP or if you use magic in battle, there is a chance MP and the corresponding stat, spirit or intellect, increase). I find this rather refreshing and a welcome attempt to try something new. But this does alienate a lot of people. You will even hear people joke about the game, saying it's the one which you have to spend hours hitting yourself to gain HP. But the game doesn't do anything unfair one bit. As long as the player has a game plan, or an idea what they want to do with their characters, then the stats should come naturally.I do want to note another aspect, which is more of an issue to bring up, is with the password system. I love the idea behind it, but I find it's a bit sloppy in terms of execution. For the most part, who you need to talk with and use a password, item, or gain another is simple. But sometimes it seems arbitrary and will have you scratching your head. It isn't a game killer at all, I do still find it charming, but can leave you a little frustrated if that's what you're stuck on.(I do want to note one thing if you're reading this! This game launched with some weird quirks to it and, luckily, many of them were patched out! However, there is one that does remain so just a heads-up! Casting Life on zombie-type enemies has a high chance of softlocking your game! There are plenty of other things your white mage can practice during battle and quicksaves really help to mitigate a huge loss of progress. But still, want everyone to be aware!)I love Final Fantasy II. From the moment I first played it years ago, to another playthrough on Dawn of Souls, it has always made me smile from how absolutely wonderful it is. And now, playing through it once more, my feelings have not changed one bit. It feels like a game with plenty of hurdles for people. So many, in fact, that I feel some people might get fatigued from it all, or just want to have a more traditional set-up. However, if you're willing to overlook the weird quirks of the game. To the leveling of magic, the leveling of stats and equipment. To the password system. You will unveil an absolute treasure of a title. A gem in a truly legendary franchise.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Its definitely a step up from the previous game but I will say the leveling system was a step down. Sure, it was different and unique from the generic leveling system in most in its field but having to level every single spell and weapon type separately by grinding seems like it was just there to inconvenience the player into spending even more time grinding. Although I hear in the original on the NES and some of the ports after that additionally to the weapons and spells, you also had to level armor by getting hit which sounds like a pain so I'm glad they removed that for this version. Although that's a complaint about the game I couldn't completely relate to, my real complaint is the frequency of the random encounters, it seems that every 5 paces/blocks you are hit with a random encounter, that means if you happen to get lost in a dungeon or go the wrong way while not paying attention you are in for a treat. On a better note, due to the frequency the game was a breeze to get through, I mean my main melee was at a whopping 8000 HP before the final boss which I also managed to take down in a couple of turns thanks to over-leveling.I guess they were testing the waters with the leveling system as FF and DQ were the pioneers of the JRPG format so they had to find a way to innovate. However, the game does deserve its props in the sense that it gave better character designs than the "chosen four" in the FF1 as well as giving them dialogue and some character building. The key word system was interesting for its time as a way to guide the player into where to go next as a lot of games during that time didn't really hold your hand with objective markers. The locations are always interesting as they have this sort of charm to them which makes for imaginative exploration.I wouldn't say its the worst game in the series as some people like to claim, that award easily goes to FF13. Overall, I enjoyed it and would recommend this to someone trying to play the classics.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this one is kind of boring and uninspired by today's standards.  The plot is painfully predictable, and the characters, while definitely more developed than in the first Final Fantasy game, are lacking in any kind of nuance.  The battle system is interesting for the era, in that it was a skill based system rather than experience based.  However, from a modern perspective, the system is incredibly easy to game.  On the other hand, that makes the game pretty easy to play without having to stop to do much grinding.Overall, playing FFII was an enjoyable process, and a fun bit of nostalgia, even if its not something I will likely ever play again.  If you're interested in a casual retro gaming experience, this is worth picking up when on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I can tell Square tried to improve upon FF1 with this game. In some areas I like the changes, in some areas the changes were not so great for me.The story is clearly an improvement. The 3 main characters actually have given names now, and have at least a tiny bit of back story. And I felt the narrative overall was deeper in FF2 compared to FF1.The new levelling system is both good and bad. Instead of your characters having levels, their stats grow based on what happens in combat. Get attacked and lose HP? Your max HP will increase after the battle. Use Fire magic a lot? Your fire magic spell level will increase after the battle. It's a bit like Skyrim, where what you do increases your stats over time. This can be a massive pain though, especially with spells taking forever to reach the top levels later in the game. When you gain access to a new spell, you have to use a really weak version of it for many, many battles to slowly improve it. And it really is a grind sometimes.I think I actually prefer the more standard and basic levelling system found in RPGs. It doesn't help either that your 4th party slot is filled with various 'guests', who start with barely any magic abilities and low stats. By the time I levelled up the stats and magic of the 5th or so guest, I was really tired of it. The characters in the 4th slot can be interesting and are used to flesh out the story and world, but every time  after I spent hours improving them was a major "FFS" moment.I did get stuck on the final boss for a couple hours. I was breezing through the final dungeon floors, but then got swatted like a fly by the big guy. It did feel a little bit lame to suddenly be faced with a boss that was extremely resistant to physical attacks and elemental magic. So unless you had been levelling up non-elemental magic to a high degree at that point you are kind of screwed. I was actually thinking about just not finishing the game, but in the end I stuck with it and grinded for a couple hours at the boss's feet to finally beat him.I very nearly gave this game a thumbs down, but on the most part I enjoyed playing FF2. I feel like the remaster on these games are surprisingly well done - there's beautiful music; sprites and graphics are improved while being faithful to the source games, and it's still interesting to see how the games have grown over time.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: No amount of quality-of-life improvements can make Final Fantasy 2 a good game.While the story is ambitious for something that was originally on the NES, it's not amazing but I recognize and appreciate the effort there, the gameplay surrounding it is a slog.  The game's infamous leveling system just isn't satisfying and necessitates grinding for certain spells to be remotely useful, plus the dungeons last an eternity on top of having absurd encounter rates.  It's just not fun to me.  The music is amazing but that goes without saying.Play 4 instead.  It not only has a slightly more complex story but also better gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I left a negative review previously before putting the game down, but recently I gave it a second chance. I've tried to enjoy this game, alas I still can't recommend it. Like I swear to god, every time I play this game, I discover another awful thing about it.What it does have going for it is that visuals are good-looking, the soundtrack is just as good as it is for other pixel remasters (in a good way), and I like that they based the main characters' visuals off the PSX version instead of the NES. The story is fine, I never felt that it was particularly good or bad.What I don't like about it is that it has some of the worst dungeon design imaginable, which is topped off with a fairly high encounter rate that makes dungeons consistently tedious. Almost every dungeon contains several empty rooms whose only purpose is to make you waste time. Some dungeons you might reach the end before realising that you needed to explore, so to proceed you need to backtrack through the frustrating encounter rate. What made me so mad is that certain dungeons do not allow you to teleport (possibly only the Dreadknought, the most irritating dungeon I have ever done) - I reached the end before it told me to backtrack allll the way to the beginning before I could proceed. At that point, my HP/MP are relatively low, and so I'm about to exit the dungeon to heal up before discovering it's blocked off because I did the thing I missed!! What the @$*%!, Square? I get they are going for an old-school feel but this is still something I couldn't bring myself to enjoy despite the nostalgia factor. They could've totally revised dungeon design the same way they made significant changes in other pixel remasters to make this a decent game, but they decided that the tedious dungeons were to stay. Bummer. Some dungeons have tons of encounters where your entire party gets constantly pelted with status effects but thankfully all spells can target everyone, including Esuna so that's a relief. However - Square decided that encounters of 5-6 enemies that stun you every single time they land a hit is a perfectly fine design choice, which means unless you flee in time, you have to sit through regular mobs just wailing on you. No warning whatsoever.Then sometimes the game throws you an encounter where the enemies spam a move that targets your whole party with a pretty high chance of petrifying them. I died in one turn. This is a game where you need to grind the one spell so you can cure that but you're SOL if your one character gets knocked out first. Even FF3 didn't pull that crap.Levelling up is somewhat fine in some regards but absolutely infuriating in other aspects. You can fight every single encounter in a playthrough (including when you mess up and have to backtrack), but chances are you'll hit a point where you have to fight giant enemies that take 0 damage from your melee attacks, and have no magical weaknesses so your spells do little damage. To make it worse - sometimes those encounters cannot be escaped from. Great!You have to grind in this game, as if the dungeons weren't grindy enough by themselves. You need to use your weapons multiple times in a given battle to gain any proficiency in them past a certain point; if you use them say, once or twice, you get nothing. There's times where there's little in-between 1-shotting enemies and doing 0 damage. By the time you've grinded enough to get beyond the 0-damage hitting, your other stats went up so high that the only way you can lose is when the game decides to stunlock your entire party (which it will).The frustrating encounters I describe plus the awful dungeon design make this game so unfun. No other Final Fantasy does anything like that. There's little to look forward to. Often you don't know what happened/what you need to do because the game isn't keen on giving you direction, or even a decent cutscenes. At one point you're supposed to take over a city but when you show up, it's like no one else on your side is there. You walk right into the boss with absolutely no one blocking your way, beat him up and suddenly you've taken over the city. Maybe this game was always like this but after playing other remasters, it's grating.Levelling spells isn't any faster and it's unfeasible to level up every potentially useful spell to the point where they are worthwhile. Spells only do decent damage against monsters that are weak to the spell's element; otherwise they quickly get supplanted by using melee. But you have to use them almost all the time to keep them useful. Learning new spells is underwhelming because it takes hours to bring them up to speed with your existing ones.It's ridiculous to the point where most new party members are significantly weaker than your main party by the time they join because they do not scale with how much you grinded. And once you get your melee characters past the phase of dealing 0 damage, the game seems to be pretty smooth sailing because they start obliterating everything. Sometimes magic helps but the bulk of the game is carried by my melee characters.I'm flabbergasted at all these design decisions. It's like the devs decided to make FF2 the sacrificial lamb for awful design decisions because NONE of the other games in the series are nearly as bad. It's a shame, because the art style is gorgeous and the soundtrack is a treat. The game is snappy. I can't tell if it was because I was still a kid and I would sit through even the worst of games when I last played this, or if they actually made it worse in the pixel remaster.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite a bit different from the first one if you are only now starting into the earlier final fantasy games. I really feel like they wanted a more dungeons and dragons feel with this and for me they succeeded. It is definitely less rigid then dungeons and dragons in this version but I think fans who enjoy wizardry and the like, might enjoy this game even if they are not final fantasy fans.  The Story is more in depth in this game since the first installment and you get a lot of first time monsters, classes, deaths, character development and difficulty along with a bit of open world. When I started the game you think okay all rpgs you go outside the main town and you grind till level 5 and then you make your way to the next area. Not in this game! There are no levels just skills so fighting and casting spells and all of it you do affects your stats. I ended up grinding for quite a bit before I made it into the next little town area and before I went in, I was like okay let me explore a bit to the left of second town. So I wandered a tiny bit and man I DIED! I got smoked and even though I grinded a bit more then what would be level 5, man I hit them for 0 and got a game over ! I actually ended up really liking that. I decided to explore the northern area instead of progressing the story and beat a few mobs with the blizzard spell I bought in the first town and just kept working those starter 3 characters. I checked the Bestiary and saw that some of these wizard guys had tomes and so did the ogre mages along with weapons! I was like wow I can get some really good stuff off these guys so I just grinded them till I got all the free spells and staves and shields and all of it. Even after I still could not beat these werewolf things but I was really getting strong and it was SO satisfying. Eventually I progressed in story a little and ended up going to Mysidia waaaaay early. I was able to buy all these great spells and even got a golden hairpin and some black robe or garb out of a chest in an area near Mysidia.    A lot of the fun I had was map exploring to see how far I can get and to open up the Bestiary further. I knew that the mobs would change past a certain point in the story so I wanted to have as many open as possible. I also was a little paranoid about it because the numbers of the mobs because they can change through story are not all lined up in a first time see order in said bestiary. When I saw empty spaces I was like okay did I miss something? So id explore a bit more and even with the guides on steam I found certain mobs earlier in zones then were mentioned which gave me a real sense of satisfaction that I got some of these off the list early. I did skill up my weapons off the green soldiers in the captured city which helped me to travel quite a bit for people who want to explore like I did. I think the best part of exploring the game was I never felt like it was a waste of time or I should just follow the path. It was nice to just be in this final fantasy world.    What made the game also really fun for me was that you could assign whatever spells you want to each character. So I felt like I was making my own classes and role playing the characters. Firion to me looked more like a ninja so I gave him a mix of things like yes he leveled up swords and it is what I maxed him with because of the blood sword, but I also gave him daggers and the Tomes of Toad, Fire, blink stuff like that. I gave Guy Thunder along with fist weapons and Axes and Maria all the elements but made sure she focused on Blizzard for my love of Shiva ^_~ Girls gotta have the Ice!   The spells improve on their looks as they move higher in rank as well as power so you feel a sense of progression while you are playing. Holy, Flare, Ultima, and the Warp spells in combat look really good as well as the base elemental spells. At certain points in the game some of the cave areas graphics made me think of my old super nintendo ff6 days. I think there was a lot of care and love put into this version of the game and I would recommend it.     I have only played this game once before on the Game Boy Advance as Final Fantasy I & II Dawn of Souls.  Now I will admit I do miss the added story of Dawn of Souls and I would suggest you check that version out as well if you can because you get to see original artwork alongside the characters commentary which I like. The sprites in Dawn of Souls are well done and just overall a very enjoyable version. I imagine you can find a video of the added story on Youtube or something if you do not want to play the game again which is understandable because Dawn does not have the speed battle option like this one does which can spoil someone pretty easily :D Read up on the additional story though if you liked this world!  If I had to say some sort of iffy thing about the game It would probably be how the weapons level up. There is a whole thing on it on the walkthrough. It is not game breaking just a little weird to use lesser weapons to fight higher mobs for gains. I got a weapon to level 11 by the end of the game and that was the highest I got it till I used the bloodsword to max out swords for the max weapon achievement. Also too my other main characters had level 10 weapons and did find and one I think even had 8 at the final boss so you will be fine! Though I did have 9999 health when I fought him. Muwhahah It is just a little wonky that is all.   I think my one more legitimate complaint if there is one is that I kinda wish your final fourth character wasn't even there. By the time you get the last person he does feel like an afterthought and I would have preferred Ricard or Leila instead back in the end party or of course the Badass mofo Minwu! Best White Mage ever!  It just felt like those characters were more in the story then the final character was. I think also too because I leveled so much that the final character did not really matter by the time I got to the end of the game and he kinda just filled the slot. I think that is why I wish one of the other ones stayed in the group or came back to it in the end. I had so many tomes in my pack and I didn't use them on the temporary characters because there was no need. I did put them on the final character but only a buff or two as an addition per round did much if anything. I leveled so far ahead of the last character that he fell short regardless why I would have preferred one of the earlier characters to come back as well as the fact that they were better characters and more developed. Overall Id say go buy it! It was worth every penny for me and i will probably play it again in the future with different character builds and spells leveled up. Replay value is hard to come by so give this one a chance!

_childDocuments_.review: Is good. (' ')bReasons to play this version of FF2 over the other ones?+ Stat increases have been improved to come much more naturally.  You can just play normally and it levels up at a reliable pace as you go. Grinding can be done normal style as well. No need to rely on the swap spell, micro managing your actions, or beating the crap out of yourself to get stronger.+ The music remixes in this version are simply the best. OST is so good.+ The auto battle system allows you to repeat your last actions. It is absolutely perfect for skilling up. This is the easiest version of FF2 when it comes to skilling up spells.+ The character designs look a lot less generic now. I love the updated looks for Firion, Ricard, Leila, and Maria. Everyone looks great.On the flip side, some major flaws of FF2 were not addressed;- The encounter rate is off the walls insane. In dungeons, expect to fight every 5-10 steps. Luckily, if you aren't feeling it at least fleeing seems to be easier than ever.- Skilling up magic is still a ridiculous ordeal, even with auto battle making it easier. Its quite a pitfall if you have OCD or are something of a completionist.- Those doors that lead to being caught in the middle of an empty room are still a thing. They usually throw a selection of 3-7 doors at you, and you better hope you pick the right one. The rest will waste your time and get you into additional fights.- The enemy designs are back to being based on the NES version. Not a terrible thing, but the PSP/GBA versions had made some of them look a lot more spiffy and those changes are now lost.Over all though, I do think that this will be my go to version to play FF2 from now on.

_childDocuments_.review: My first game was the original Final Fantasy VII when i was a child. Being able to replay this great game years later is a fantastic opportunity for fans of the final fantasy franchise.The story and combat mechanics are what you expect of a game built for the original Nintendo console.Playing through this series you can see the evolution of the franchise, Final Fantasy II has a unique leveling mechanic where your skills level up and not your character, imagine elder scrolls leveling way before elder scrolls. i loved how this leveling system worked even though it is flawed.It is also good to see them experiment with a unique conversation system (Key words, learn and Items) i could see the potential of what it could be although it is obvious why the cut it in later sequels.The music is great and the pixel art is very nostalgic.Highly Recommend for fans of the series but i would avoid if not a fan of final fantasy series or turn based combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II is quite the departure from the first game, and it gets a lot of flack for its design choices (or more accurately, the execution of said design choices), the most iconic of which is the skill leveling system replacing the traditional level up system.The Pixel Remaster version brings with it many quality-of-life changes that make playing through this game a fair bit more enjoyable than the original iteration. You may still prefer 1, 3, 4, 5, or 6, but I don't think you'll hate this game as much as you think you will. Worth the time.

_childDocuments_.review: FF2 100% Review:Hell. Literal hell. I now completely understand that this game was not meant to be 100%ed. In the time it took me to complete this game fully my children have grown up and had children of their own, leaving their poor father in the trenches to fight in a war he conjured for himself. This game has everything - missable objectives, a variety of things to level up, obscure mechanics, rare enemy drops, the works. In case it wasn't clear, there is no level 99 and I did not go for 100% achievements alone. I grinded up a total of 1024 magic levels, 512 weapon levels, and 5148 stat levels until every character was as strong as physically possible. I spent about 200 hours of my 218 just leveling magic and weapons on each character, bashing Guy in his poor, dumb head enough times to justify the brain damage the character suffers from. By the time I finished leveling fists on Leon, I'm surprised his brain functioned well enough through the fine paste it was grinded into to spit out his one line in English. By the end of it I could not tell you the plot of the game anymore, but I can probably draw the map of Pandemonium by memory alone now.If you want to play this game let me give you some advice - Learn to love the grind but not too much. I went through this so you - so no one - ever has to get this meaningless achievement of true 100%. Get cure, esuna, basuna, Ultima and all your buffs as high a level as possible, ignore most other spells. Just level 1 weapon and shields on each character (you have to use the worst weapon in your arsenal to level quickly). If you do go for all achievements, watch out for Dreadnought, Leviathan, Cyclone, and Castle Palamecia as missable locations (as well as some towns but mostly there's no chests in missable towns). If you go for 100% characters? Don't. Or have a good podcast available I recommend Cosmonaut Tabletop.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: On a journey to 100% ALL Final Fantasy titles on Steam~This is definitely a recommended game from me, but you need to understand it's not by chance that this title is selling so much less than Final Fantasy 1 on Steam (OK, maybe Stranger of Paradise helped too!).If I am to look at this through a lens of 1988, Square has managed to bake something incredible here, which has challenged levelling systems and equipment norms, and is even able to do so today! wow!This is why I also want to make clear that playing those systems today, in the way Final Fantasy 2 implemented them, unfortunately feels like a mess in every level...and that's a big statement playing this after Final Fantasy 1, which could not decide if it's Dungeons and Dragons limited spell mode, or drink-em-all potion/elixir spam!In this title your characters get to have (some) personality, which is sweet, and you still get to play mostly a party of 4. Although I will always like anything more than a 3-people party, the fact that you are locked into the 4th slot character slotting in and out of your party, without control of if, who, and when they come back, feels unsettling and super off. If I hadn't played this game before, I would end up building *Spoiler*, only for them to die and be replaced with another low-stat character moments after. Ouch! If you plan to 100% this game, I highly recommend the achievement guide posted by lylat on Steam!I hope I was able to provide some unique perspective for you, and able to help you decide whether you should play this game if you were on the fence!

_childDocuments_.review: A good remaster of a broken game.-: FF2 takes a different approach to levels compared to other FF games. The more you do a particular thing, the better you get at it. Use swords to improve your sword skill, use spells to improve your MP and magic, evade attacks to improve agility, and so on. At first, this seems like a great way to build a party in whatever way you see fit, rather than be confined to traditional classes. But in practice? Some weapons are consistently weaker than others, or rarely show up in the game at all. There is also an undocumented "magic penalty" (not described in-game, nor does it show up in any item descriptions or stats) where your in-battle magic damage is severely crippled if you're wearing any gear or have any weapons equipped. I'm not sure how anyone is meant to figure this out organically. I only learned about it after finishing the game and getting all the achievements, wondering why magic in FF2 seemed so weak compared to physical attacks. Why bother having a system centered around customization if you're going to punish most choices anyway?-: The encounter rate is extremely high. This makes dungeon exploration painful -- especially ones with multiple floors and long hallways. Turn a corner, battle. Walk five steps, battle. Open a chest... possibly another battle. Many pathways lead to dead ends, and there are lots of "trap" doors that lead to empty rooms where you'll have to endure additional battles just to get back out. This is normally fine if you're using the battles to build your stats, but in the event that the enemies are too weak to impact your numbers much, a lot of these battles will only waste your time and resources.-: Most enemies pose no real threat, but then you encounter some enemies that are more dangerous than bosses for some reason. Death Riders hit for massive damage, and enemies like Coeurls, Cockatrices, and Malboros have brutal status effects (stone, sleep, paralysis, confusion, insta-death, etc) that will always land even if their attacks miss. Those fights can very quickly go south. Bosses seem to be well-tuned for the most part, though the final boss dies in 2-3 turns if you use a certain weapon. All in all, when it comes to battling, I'd consider this an easy game with some balance issues.-: Surprisingly dark for a FF game. Lots of death and loss in this one. You've got a scrappy rebellion taking on a powerful empire, with a number of twists along the way. The main characters don't get much development, but I think the plot is reasonably good for its time, especially when you consider that FF2 was originally released in 1988 - an era where most games had very superficial stories, if they even had stories at all. Also, some elements in this game went on to become series mainstays: Cid, Chocobos, the Ultima spell, etc. It's always fun to see how those things began.-: The in-game font is a little ugly and can be replaced with some modding, but otherwise, the graphics in this game are terrific. Old sprites have wonderful modernizations, the inventory system is easy to use, the music is great, animations are colorful, the map systems and fast-forward/auto-attack systems are convenient, and the Quick-Save option is a lifesaver in tough dungeons. The Bestiary is awesome and very informative.-: I can't really recommend this game unless you're playing it for historical reasons like I am -- just experiencing it for the sake of being able to say you experienced it. A lot of the gameplay ideas introduced in this game didn't persist past this point, so if there was ever a main FF game to skip, this would be the one. It's almost universally panned as being the worst of the series. I'm still giving it a thumbs up because I think this succeeds as a remaster. They managed to take doody and turn it into something palatable, all while keeping its spirit in place - and that's not an easy thing to do! It's still an approachable game despite its faults, and I think that's a win overall.

_childDocuments_.review: I've always loved FF2. I realize most people do not. But I've probably replayed it more than any of the others, honestly, due to how freely you can customize your party. It's just so fun and satisfying to increase your strengths in any manner you wish, and this remaster makes that experience better than ever.I hope I don't get in trouble for this, but FF2 was the game that got me interested in emulation back when I was younger and perhaps not so scrupulous. This was before the game had seen an official English translation (in Origins). I had just gotten into computers and the Internet, and I loved Final Fantasy (the original, that is). I still have a printout of Zach Keene's FF1 walkthrough (dated July 1996, if memory serves; printed March 2000/2001) in a stack of notebooks right on my dresser. It was on the early fansite  (Nintendotaku) that I saw a link to Final Fantasy Fever, and on that website I discovered what was then called "FF2j". It all just sounded so cool, this game like my beloved FF1, that had never been released outside Japan. I just had to play it, and embarked on a frustrating journey to find the means to do so. Long story short, I was deeply engrossed from start to finish... sadomasochistic HP training, canceling hundreds of magic commands, and all.But enough background. What about this remaster? It's great. More than great, even, just like the others. The post-battle interface is markedly improved, showing you exactly what stats you gained and how you're progressing in weapon skill mastery; it adds to the satisfaction of increasing your abilities a great deal. One huge change is that, dual-wielding, even if you kill an enemy with your first attack, you'll go again and maybe kill another enemy too. I really hope this is not an unintentional glitch; please keep it, Square Enix! ^.^ It seems like you gain skill levels a little quicker too, and MP seems to build at a noticeably accelerated rate, which makes using magic easier.I adore the art that's more faithful to the original, even the creepy Balloons that aren't facing the party, but YOU, on the other side of the screen. O_O; I caught myself kicking and bopping during battles, which was highly amusing. In fact, I'm doing it right now as I write this review, listening to the DLC OST. Rows do not appear to be as restrictive as before; you can still be hit in the back row, and hit enemies in their back row.I also really appreciate the ability to change your lead character without the one in front of them having to die. This feature is in every other FF game, and it was incredibly odd that it was absent in the first place, but it's now been made right.The music, as stated, is awesome. It's like epic film score, and I make no exaggerations. The world map music is leagues ahead of the Origins version, and does a much better job of encapsulating the broken, tragic world FF2 takes place in. As with the other remasters, the first thing I did was listen to the entire soundtrack in the music player, and it even transcends into the realm of opera, with powerful vocals in Pandaemonium and the final battle. It truly feels inspired.Maybe I'm partial, but I really like FF2. I wish more people appreciated it. Maybe now, they will!

_childDocuments_.review: ｎｏｓｔａｌｇｉａ     ｉｓ     ａ      ｄｒｕｇUpfront - I like playing this game. I recognize though, the reason is that I was playing it in a time when this could actually pass for a decent game. Those days are long gone and remaster after remaster has failed to remaster much of anything at all. 'Pixel Remaster' with updated music is just too low effort. Every few years they trot out another remaster of each of these old FF games with minimum details to get the grognards and diehards shelling out cash again. The funniest, most blatant part of this is when the discussion page is full of arguments and theorycrafts on the changes because SE isn't telling you. While this is the first one of FF2 on steam, in order to prepare for the batch it comes in, they delisted some of the previous remasters so you wouldn't pay attention to a history of mediocrity.In case it wasn't clear at this point, this review is not based on nostalgia.  We deserve better, my fellow oldgamers.ｆｏｒ     ｔｈｏｓｅ    ｎｏｔ     ａｄｄｉｃｔｅｄThere is a reason that the term JRPG is synonymous with grindfest. The systems of many of these old games have the grind baked right into them. Grind is good sometimes but, not when it's somehow both simplistic and flawed. There's one important spell in this game. Everything before that spell is just preparation to make that spell more powerful. The game has a skill based leveling system where stat growth is dependent on using the right combination of skills, over and over, while wearing the right combination of gear.   For magic to be useful, you pretty much have to be naked. If you put caster character in the back row, they will not gain certain skills. If you use certain equipment, you will not gain certain skills. This is an issue when, remember, all the skill totals go towards buffing that one important spell in the game. You need a ton of gold grinding to increase the quantity of skills you have, in order to buff the one important spell. This leaves you pretty overpowered for most areas, rather quickly. The world is small and the story is driven by a fetch quest.  You will go to the same locations over and over to refetch different key words from the same,  uninteresting, small cast of npcs who have all the answers in their small, uninteresting towns.  The downside is that, while it's a tiny map, the encounter rate is about every seven steps. The 5th time you have to go all the way back to the beginning of the game, before the story is even halfway over, this gets pretty annoying. Pass unless you are guided by completionism, nostalgia or blind loyalty.

_childDocuments_.review: Ahh, Final Fantasy 2. The ambitious and bizarre sequel to Final Fantasy 1. I think this is a very odd game that is definitely worth playing in the FF journey. So why did I hit a negative review?There's a glaring bug right now in the Pixel Remaster version of FF2 (my actual thoughts I'll get to later) where all on-hit status effects have a 100% chance of applying. This means that any Cockatrice you encounter, if it hits you, will turn that party member to stone. Antillions do the same with paralysis. This means that any unlucky one hit results in that party member being locked out for the rest of the combat more likely than not. This makes the late-game a slogfest that ruined the enjoyment I was having with this game up until this point. (Square please fix this!)Moving to the actual remaster, it has all the quality of life changes from the FF1 Pixel Remaster - autobattle and such. The changes from the original, from what I gather, have made the weird grinding to get stat points up no longer necessary, though you can cheese if you still choose too. The custom building that this game lets you do (which apparently gets expanded on in the SaGa franchise) seemed daunting at first - anyone can do anything. My Firion ended up using dualswords and magic, Maria used a bow and magic, and Guy used dual axes. Leveling up spells can be an annoying grind (and if you want to 100% the FF games like me you gotta grind a spell all the way to 16 and a weapon skill to 16) and like in FF1 magic doesn't seem to scale well compared to melee. Moving to the story, this game is super ambitious for being nearly 30 years old. This is a dark war story, characters have personalities and fun quirks. One scene even made me laugh out loud. It's no Final Fantasy X, but I was surprised with how good the plot was. Ultimately, Final Fantasy 2 is worth playing for a fan who wants to do them all, but I can't recommend the Pixel Remaster at this time,

_childDocuments_.review: The gulf in depth and complexity of Final Fantasy II’s main story when compared to its predecessor is so vast that it's difficult to believe that the two games are part of the same series. Add in the fact that there was only a single short year between the releases of the two titles, and that level of improvement in such a short time begins to look almost miraculous. Unlike Final Fantasy I’s overly simple main story, Final Fantasy II introduces intricate narrative elements that would not only soon become the series’ signature but are also impressively detailed for the time period. From the very opening scene of the game, the player is thrown right into the fire to feel immersed in the hopelessness of a superior power invading one’s home. The tone for the rest of the game is set and the primary theme established: war is hell. The remainder of the game is all about combating the invading Palamecian empire as it seeks to bring all nations under its iron grip. From that point on, surprisingly complex subplots accompany and weave through the already convoluted nature of any politically driven tale. By modern standards, all of this is still quite basic, but still on par with many popular modern indie games. As an interesting side note, the crystals, a signature core of the very identity of the Final Fantasy series and main story arc of the first game, are entirely absent in Final Fantasy II. In my personal opinion, this is the category in which Final Fantasy II shows the most growth from its forebear. As with the main story, the difference in quality and scope is remarkable. Unlike Final Fantasy I’s vague prophecy serving as the only backstory for the Warriors of Light, the main characters in this tale have some realistic origins and individual identities within the overall narrative, making them much more relatable and easier to empathize with. Venturing out into the world at large also shows tremendous growth in the category. NPCs, important and inconsequential, also feel more individualized and unique than the primarily generic ones populating the first game’s world. With regard to major NPCs who are critical to the plot, they take on a far more active role and show personalities in the face of the struggles their world faces. This makes it much easier to become invested in them and their ultimate fates as you play through the story, a detail that was almost entirely absent in Final Fantasy I. As with the first game, NES hardware restrictions ensure that critical elements such as dialogue and the accompanying events are overly simplified, meaning even emotional events feel rushed and a bit wooden when compared to anything remotely modern. Despite such limitations, Final Fantasy II manages to fill its world with people who are far less lifeless than those of the previous title. With the first game, Nobuo Uematsu established himself as a legitimate musical genius and powerhouse. With a single game, Uematsu-san cemented his legacy in the annals of gaming history by writing a soundtrack full of pieces that have lived on to this day. After the success of Final Fantasy, Uematsu-san had a lot to live up to. In what would come to be an almost given in years to come, the master outdid himself and delivered a soundtrack that surpassed his first contribution. As with everything about Final Fantasy II, fans outside of Japan did not have the chance for the wonderful music written for it to become something steeped in nostalgia like the first game’s did. Not only is almost every piece extremely well-arranged to match the tone of their accompanying scenes, there are several genuinely gorgeous pieces in this OST. As is the case with all six of the games, the fully orchestrated Pixel Remaster arrangement of these legendary tracks is without question the best versions ever produced. Hearing the old 8-bit MIDI themes performed using real instruments and arranged for an actual video game environment is an emotional experience all by itself. As I have alluded to several times now, the limitations of early gaming hardware is evident in every title produced at the time. It was just not possible to do much visually. Developers had to find workarounds and tricks to create so much of these games that it's amazing they managed it at all. As a result, titles like this are quite static and repetitive in many ways, mainly stuck to hard set background levels and maps. Despite this, developers have long since mastered the art of getting the most out of pixel-based 2D games. This version of Final Fantasy II shows off that skill set to give us faithful and updated recreations of the original NES designs down to the smallest details. Where the Pixel Remaster chose to be a faithful upscaled HD remaster with regard to the art style, the PSP/Android version completely reimagined everything to create a much more vivid and detailed incarnation. While I understand and respect the decision to stay faithful to the originals, I feel that Square Enix should have used the PSP/Android versions as the model and built upon them. Even better would have been an Octopath Traveler/Dragon Quest I-III Remake style HD-2D build that took full advantage of just how far 2D gaming has come. This is without question the most controversial aspect of Final Fantasy II, and has been since its initial release. It is the main reason that many legacy fans consider it to be the “black sheep” of the mainline entries in the series. In my personal opinion, there is a good reason for this. Final Fantasy I established the series’ signature version of the turn-based system that became synonymous with the JRPG all the way into the mid-2000s. Final Fantasy II attempted to add levels of depth and realism to that system that were too far ahead of its time. In theory, using the Dungeons & Dragons model of dividing weapon types, armor types, and magic into individual sub-skills to be learned and upgraded independently seems like a fantastic way to add immersion and customization options. In practice, it fell short of the mark, instead turning it into a veritable confusing slog to reach max level 16 for each one of the skills and spells. On top of that, there are no character levels, meaning each character’s overall effectiveness is entirely dependent upon these skills. As gaming became more advanced, systems like this would essentially become the standard. Unfortunately, it was too ambitious for games so limited by the hardware of the time. I personally had to use the in-game boosts to make this system feel effective or bearable in any way. As with the original Final Fantasy, Final Fantasy II is enormous when compared to most every other game in the NES library up to that time. Even by modern standards, II still boasts as much game to consume and experience as most indie games of the present era. I find it amazing that the developers were able to push NES hardware and storage to a point to even be able to hold so much game on an 8-bit cartridge. The Pixel Remaster is 100% faithful to the original in terms of playable game, recreating the NES experience incredibly well, which is a double-edged sword. For players who specifically want an experience that is closest to the original NES version, this is the ideal version to play. The PSP/Android version added a wealth of post-game extra content I dearly wish had been added to the Pixel Remaster. The addition of an independent music player for the soundtrack and a gallery of Yoshitaka Amano official art are very nice touches, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II Pixel Remaster is an super easy version of one of the most unique Final Fantasy games.I always loved Final Fantasy II because of its new approach to the genre and its timless status. It is a very different game compared to the first game mainly due to its class-free RPG system allowing you to be what you are fighting with in your hand and also the very enjoyable adventure feature when you have to learn key words during conversations and then ask the learn words. It reminds me of the early Elder Scrolls games. Sadly, neither the class-free RPG system, nor the adventure feature would appear in any other future Final Fantasy game.NEGATIVES:So what´s bad about the Pixel Remaster version? Yes, I am beginning with "bads" because they are a majority here. The most crucial fact is that Square Enix released this game with mandatory easy mode that was present in Final Fantasy Origins on PS1 (you had to beat it one time to have normal mode unlocked) or Final Fantasy: Dawn of Souls on GBA. Items are cheaper, leveling the skills is faster, increasing strength does not affect intellect/spirit anymore so you can be any class you want and not be penalized whatsoever, the vast majority of your time spent with the game you are overpowered just like in Final Fantasy 1 Pixel Remaster making this game boring and overal pointless.More than 3/4 of the game you are constantly overleveled and battles ahead of you are just the most uninteresting fights at all. They just cannot harm you because they are too weak and you are too strong. Square knew it but instead of fixing the terrible balance, they just added the autobattle function so that you could not spent too much time with such nonsensical battles. Bosses in this game are super easy to to such an extent that they do not feel like bosses at all. In the original game you ran from battles because you did not want your characters to die, in this version you run from battles because YOU do not want to die from the coming boredom.Also, of course,  there are things which I did not like in Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster. The movement is about 30% faster which looks ridiculous, there are several save types - automatic saves, normal saves and quick saves which basically eliminate the original threat of being killed and having to start the whole dungeons completely all over again, there are minimaps even in dungeons which have to be manually switched off after every loading, in the world map the minimap cannot even be switched off, blur effect in the CRT filter is too strong and scanlines too thick, Balance-wise the original game was not perfect at all either, but this one is ever worse. For example they kept the infamous easy final boss fight which can be win with the Blood Sword with 2 or 3 hits, and on the other hand they kept his brutally high resistance against other melee weapons.As in the first remaster also in this I have been experiencing issues with my wireless Xbox Series Controller that just did not work at all. Some buttons did not work, some yes but with a lag lasting at least a couple of seconds. Fail that should have been fixed long ago...POSITIVES:The plot is very enjoyable and full of interesting twists. In addition, which is almost perfect, the game´s ending is not super happy like in movies from Hollywood. There is some bitterness in it after you finish the story. The game is also amazing at indirect storytelling which means that not everything visible on screen is immediately explained and in some cases you can even miss the explanation if not thoroughgoing enough in terms of exploring the world.As I said in the second paragraph, I liked the RPG system and the adventure feature often present in dialogues. It´s so fresh and Id be glad if it appeared someday in a future Final Fantasy game again! Thanks god they kept the system when armors/weapons affect your stats - every character can use and wear anything but it may affect your spirit/intelligence so your spells might not be as powerful as they can be if wearing specific armors.I love the design of dungeons. They are better than in the first game, they are like mazes, full of blind corners and empty rooms to which you often walk accross the floors or long corridors (only to return back empty handed). The best dungeon is the last Pandemonium, but also the Tower of Mysidia or the Cyclone dungeon are pretty good as well. The game becomes more enjoyable in the Tower of Mysidia and after it as now you can meet enemies that can wipe your party out because of various statuses like petrification or palayzation. I noticed that poison can be quite harmful. However because of the terrible balance, even these enemies are nothing in the final dungeon when you have so high HP and strength that you can easily beat them in 1-2 hits. The most dangerous enemies are Couerls that can hit you instadeath and destroy your party in one turn. However there is a bug causing you instadeath after such a hit even if you are wearing Protect Ring or Genji Armor which main purpose is to protect you from instadeath.The remastered soundtrack deserves its own paragraph as it is simply amazing! Nobuo Uematsu knows his music well and only he can remaster these classic songs/tracks the way he did it. The boss battle theme is breathtaking, the theme of Pandemonium now sounds like a Soviet battle march and the classic town theme is as lovely as ever.VERDICT:Due to the fact that the game itself is just a better and more interesting experience than the first game plus it has a very enjoyable story full of characters I am giving this Pixel Remaster a slightly higher score than I gave Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster. _childDocuments_.review: And here we are, continuing our grand journey through the Final Fantasy series. We have arrived at possibly the most infamous one of all, Final Fantasy II. While this game is not considered "bad" perse, a lot of design choices in regards to; combat, levelling and overall quality of life mechanics have changed how you can both play and enjoy this title.The story begins with our respective heroes: Firion, Maria, Guy and Leon, getting attacked by the Palamecian Empire and getting left for dead in their passing.The now three heroes, as Leon is missing for most of the game, are then rescued by the rebellion and are immediately told they cannot help as they are too young and inexperienced. They go off on their own to prove their worth, and in doing so, they immediately become stronger than 70% of the entire rebellion army and on their return, are now tasked with destroying the empire. In which they do with little effort for the most part.My primary concerns with the story is that it requires you to consume a lot of empty spaces with very little explanation. For the entirety, events will occur around you without any information provided as to why or how.And this leaves the overall story very confusing and shallow.Thankfully other than the confusing timeline and voids of lore, the story that does exist has been written beautifully, and flows exceptionally well.Character dialogue is immersive and allows characters to really grow on you, even if some are particularly short lived.For the most part FF2 plays a lot like its predecessor. It is a turn based combat RPG with levelling and magic, but that is where the similarities end. Levelling has been re-worked in an attempt to make the game scale better. You don't level your character as a whole, you level up their individual stats, and is granted on what appears to be an RNG system as you will often, for instance take a lot of health damage, which should level your HP, but no level will occur.Unlike the first game, status effects are 100% chances to be inflicted upon hit. This includes stun, petrify and instant death. If you accidentally come across 5 Coerls or Cockatrices in your game who have ambushed you (they get the first turn), this will likely be a game over for you. My only tip here is to save often, as items like Ribbon (which is supposed to grant immunity) doesn't work.For a majority of the game as well, you are short a fourth person, you are accompanied by 5 random NPC's who will join you from the world as you journey across it, but in terms of gearing up and levelling them it's completely worthless.When you finally get a permanent fourth member, they are so underlevelled that they get one-shot by just about everything.For the most part however, this game plays how you would expect from the rest of the series and shouldn't suprise you otherwise.Much akin to the first game, there isn't a lot here visually. It looks okay for its age, but isn't going to win any graphical awards. That's not to say the artstyte is ugly at all, as it is still quite nostalgically gorgeous, just don't go into it expecting a lot.The audio though, has been vastly improved from the original, seemingly done from scratch. Classic themes are back here with perfect touch ups to make them sound fresh and invigorated, which is what this game required.As I wrote with the first Final Fantasy review, the performance and specifications here are irrelevant considering the games age. It is safe to say you could run this game on a potato.🟧 No graphical options at all.RAM: 32GBCPU: i9 10900KA 3.70GHzGPU: MSI Ventus RTX 3080This is a tough one, as there is definitely a lot of nostalgia here, and the game is by no means that bad. However, some of the changes to the standard levelling formula, while they were done with best interest in mind, simply don't work for me here. Coupled with the existing bugs from the original where enemies can insta-kill your entire squad, I'd find it hard to rank this any higher. It's worth giving it a shot, but definitely wait for a sale on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is another fantastic remake of a FAMICOM classic! This is one of two games that the US never got to play on their original NES hardware. It was re-released in various compilations over the years, but for some reason, this one feels that it is finally the game was intended to be. Like I mentioned in my review for Final Fantasy, the soundtrack has been beautifully remastered into new arrangements that sound amazing. The updated visuals and effects helps really pop in this sequel and help tell the story with more grandeur. I really do feel like this game would have been in my SNES library had it been released for the 16-bit console.In this second game, you are starting to see elements pop up that will become mainstays in future installments. Most notably the character CID and Chocobos. The leveling system is completely different from any other entry in the series and will take a bit to get used to, but once you do, it is an awesome way to level the characters.This is probably my definitive version of Final Fantasy II. It is remastered from the original with nothing new, like the added dungeons from the GBA ports, added. I highly recommend this game if you are a fan of Final Fantasy or the JRPG genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Note that it is mostly a "neutral" review. It is also makes no sense to seriously criticize the game released in 1988. The port itself is great.I am just glad it is over and want to whine. The resistances mechanics in this game are insane. It seems like enemies have 100% chance to put effect on you with a hit. But at the same time there is a HUGE problem with protection items.You have like THREE types of item description which says "protects from negative effects" and even if you equip them all - you won't be protected. The Ribbon itself is almost useless now.  And you never know what resist it gives. For example, item may protect you from "physical negative effects like Stone". But for some reason, Paralysis is not a "Physical effect". I've actually never found an item which protects from it. The last dungeon is pain. There are several floors where you'll get encounters from enemies which one-shot you at any physical hit. You may get 6 of them at the same time or even get ambushed (instant Game Over most of the time). I have no idea how people were playing this without floor autosave. When i got killed by the final boss in FF3 (3D Remake) - i was like "well, gotta farm more" and "i need to rethink my party professions". _childDocuments_.review: I've never played any FF game until I tried Final Fantasy in mid 2023 and finished it in early 2024. I liked it so much I decided to try out every game in the franchise.  Final Fantasy II is just as playable and fun as the first one, but with a more involved story.  You still have four characters in your team, but there was a change up in that you start out with three, and the fourth team member will join then leave after certain quests are completed (make sure to remove that character's gear before that happens) to be replaced by a different character with each succeeding plot line.That was not the only thing that was changed up a bit.  Instead of one merchant selling things and one magic trainer selling spells, they were broken up into three merchants (one selling healing potions. another one selling sleeping bags, tents, and cottages, and another one selling herbs, all in the same shop).Also, your characters advance a bit differently than what occurred in the original FF.  They not only improve in HP and abilities, but also improve in uses of weapons and protective gear.Also, in FFII magic is learned by buying tomes then you learn the spells.The fights are similar to the way it was done in FF, but with different monsters, but still as challenging as before.I definitely recommend  Final Fantasy II, this game is well worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: A definite upgrade to the story compared to the first FF game and some pretty challenging parts to it too with some monsters giving you status effects that can wipe your whole party. Each weapon and spell you use individually levels up so you can spec your characters however you like!  Oh and the password system is pretty interesting too and definitely is its own special touch that which it adds to the RPG aspect to the game very well!  Characters are fleshed out a lot better and the villain always has an overarching presence throughout as you're playing throughout.  Certainly one of the more "eccentric" Final Fantasy games out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never been more bored playing a JRPG.However, if you're a major Final Fantasy fan, I'd still suggest giving this game a look because of how many series staples started here. It's one of the most important JRPGs for crafting story-fueled games, especially for when it came out in 1988. But, it's importance has lost it's luster over the decades.Despite being the easiest version of this entry in the series, it's archaic roots are too prominent to simply jump into. It took me a half an hour just to fully grasp the concept of the Levelling System. BUT, once I learned how to exploit it for my personal gain, I was able to barrel my way through this game within 15 hours after only a few hours worth of grinding.The idea of every party member being a blank state so you can decide what you want out of them all by yourself, it completely falls apart when everyone just becomes a Melee-focused powerhouse with Cure X for the rare situations when the enemy doesn't die in one turn. There's almost no fun to really derive from this Battle system, which is a shame when random encounters are probably at their highest in this entry. Most of this game is just letting the Auto-Battle button do the work and it's such a shame.The Story, being what it is for an NES-era title, is fine for what it is. It's really by-the-numbers for today's standards, but I'm sure this was something unheard of for NES/SFC games in 1988. Having all this dialogue in a game this short shows that they tried with making a more coherent and fleshed out tale.Finally, however, I cannot deny that the music was part of what kept me going. Uematsu's work still shines in this game's glorious new remixes and they're nothing short of fantastic.All-in-all, Final Fantasy II is probably not worth your time unless you're curious about the "black sheep" of the original 2-D series of Final Fantasy games. It's too different to really recommend you try if you're newer to the JRPG genre, and the story isn't exactly something that'll stand out for new or old genre fans. However, despite all of this: it's arguably the most important game in the 2-D lineup for the fact that it established so many pieces of the Final Fantasy mythos and world that it cannot be forgotten about because of it's bad gameplay.Its...divisive, to say the least.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty sure everyone knows by now, FF2 is the kind of game you avoid unless you're a Final Fantasy completionist.The leveling system is not very well explained, and there are many mechanics that simply are not mentioned, such as how monster level matters and is arbitrary per formation.Everything in this game exists to slow you down.  From the dungeon design, to the high encounter rate, to the dead end doors (which btw, some actually have treasure, so yes, you DO have to open every damn one).Final Fantasy generally has a lot of mechanics that allows you to minmax very quickly and take advantage of what exists in the game to blaze through, which a seasoned RPG player would know means that these games aren't as grindy as they're known for.  FF2 (JP) is one of the few Final Fantasy games that do not allow you to do that, and is one of the grindiest games, beaten by FF3 (JP).  Even if you are someone who understands the minmax, you will unfortunately have to deal with grind.Some caveats:  The Pixel Remaster allows for auto battling.  This means if you are wanting to beat this game for the sake of being a completionist, you can play this while watching netflix, I guessI recommend this game only for completionists who want to say "I've beaten every final fantasy game".  But since you have to beat 2 and 3 to do this, what will it cost?

_childDocuments_.review: 󠀡󠀡You know that hopeful sounding "item found" tune that usually plays when you get a power up in a Metroid game, or when you get an item in a Pokémon game? Imagine that sound playing while standing next to the bed of a man who just died literally a second before hand because he gave you an item as his body disappears. Imagine how out of place, immersion breaking, and oddly funny that would be. Final Fantasy II does this sort of thing not once, but multiple times throughout a single playthrough. The story is supposed to be taken far more seriously than the others in the franchise because of its "realistic portrayal of war" (even though said story isn't all that great, but then again, neither is the gameplay either), but at the same time, it does this while wearing a massive pair of squeaky clown shoes. And that's all without mentioning its completely broken leveling system or the unbelievably counter-intuitive keyword system. Look just about anywhere on the internet and they'll tell you to skip this one, which I would have to 100% agree.

_childDocuments_.review: GREETINGS FELLOW ZOOMERS, JRPG LOVERS or Final Fantasy enjoyers!After finishing Final Fantasy I (that's 1), I return! Now having finished Final Fantasy II !!!Are you worrying that you need to finish FF1 to understand or even play II?! Worry NOT! For FF2 is a standalone story not related to the first one in any way. If the first game proved to be too confusing, hard or just too lacking in direction and enjoyment, the second one will get your hopes up (I hope, haha!).The story is a great improvement over the first game. FF1 managed to be a very confusing, vague game with a wild story thrown in (time travel shenanigans that early?!). Fortunately, FF2 improves on that aspect by having a proper setting, a named main cast with some degree of personality and a direction beyond "you must save the world guys pls". Although the story while simple is still rather wild with many moments where a modern gamer would think "bad writing/storytelling" it still proved to be a very entertaining one! Firions special encounter with a certain entity and then Hilda, Guy speaking an unexpected language and Cid having an abrupt moment all proved to be very charming and memorable.The gameplay, although still the classic JRPG formula with lots of dialogue, dungeon crawling and menu navigation, has the combat and levelling system take a different turn from FF1: instead of having spell slots, we get the classic MP! But something strange happened... There are no levels. Your characters level up through mastery of the skills, actions and weapons they use. This system was more intriguing and fun to use than the standard levelling system, but it is quite a different system compared to the previous game.The addition of a dialogue system via keywords proved to be interesting, as the player is left with some agency to learn more about the setting, or mix and match to get pointers on how to progress the story.The visuals continue to be very pleasing, and often times it felt like an improvement over FF1; the battlemaps seem more varied, vivid; characters now have defining features and the main cast even has portraits; monsters still remain very detailed, and bosses look very intricate at times although I'm not sure if there is any particular improvement here, I liked all boss designs; but the effects do take the cake, very well animated and flashy.Music is absolutely banging, after completing the game I gave the original soundtrack (NES) a listen and I'm very glad all the music is still quite the same, only augmented with classical instruments. World theme is my favourite, with the final area theme coming to a close second.Overall, if you are like me and trying to work throughout over 30 years of Final Fantasy and enjoyed the first one... I can confidently say you will also enjoy this one.Fists OPSee you in Final Fantasy III, fellow enjoyer

_childDocuments_.review: Pass unless you're a Final Fantasy fan who wants to see the series roots, and even then maybe wait for a sale. 15-20 hours 20-25 hoursFF2 is a product of its time that hasn't aged especially well in quite a few design aspects. The leveling system is something that would have been far more interesting 30 years ago, but now is either frustrating if you don't understand it or easy to exploit if you do. The combat itself is fairly straightforward. Outside a few niche situations or extreme grinding, magic doesn't match attack spam and isn't generally worth investing beyond a few specific spells. This is doubly true if you don't realize certain equipment nerfs magic stats despite the game never reflecting this in the stats. On the other end, there's a weapon that trivializes every hard enemy in the game, negating most of what magic could ever do.Special shout-out to status effects. They rarely work for you without excessive spell grinding, yet always work when used against you - including 1-shot kill effects! There are several enemy formations that become incredibly frustrating because of this. Thankfully there's a great auto save feature that keeps you from losing more than one floor's progress!Fortunately it's never too difficult to know where you're supposed to be going, with a key word system triggering advice from prominent NPCs. The dungeons themselves have excessive amounts of empty rooms to bait you into extra fights - in a game with an already high encounter rate - but is a little easier to get around with the new mini map.The art style is the strength of these pixel remasters, and FF2 is no exception. The new art looks great and stays faithful to the original. The music remixes are incredible - some notable tracks being an underrated overworld theme and a final dungeon track that goes hard. Font is a complaint for many still, but don't let this keep you from buying. It's easily moddable with 5 minutes effort using one of several available guides.Don't expect a gripping story in comparison to modern games. That said, if you enjoy it as a product of its time, it can be perfectly serviceable. There are dramatic moments that fall flat due to a simple script, but the moments are there. A step up from FF1, but despite being in the RPG genre, it isn't anything to get excited about.If you have a tolerance for older JRPGs with archaic systems, this game can be enjoyable. This was my most enjoyable playthrough of the game despite my criticisms, but it remains a hard game to recommend to anyone that isn't a hardcore FF fan or absolutely wants to experience the entire series regardless.

_childDocuments_.review: I just played this after playing the Final Fantasy I Pixel Remaster (the Pixel Remasters were my first experiences with both of these games), and I really enjoyed it! As far as graphics, music, etc. are concerned, this one felt pretty much the same as the first one's Pixel Remaster (which I thoroughly enjoyed). The pixel graphics are really nice, the orchestral soundtrack feels great to listen to while playing the game, and the visual effects are subtle but coolAs far as the game itself goes, Final Fantasy II has a much better plot in my opinion: Final Fantasy I was somewhat straightforward (bad guy is tormenting the world, so collect 4 magical things to defeat him), whereas this one had a much more thought-out plot with characters you actually grow to care about. One thing that was frustrating, however, was that Final Fantasy II has missable monsters, chests, and even locations!! I was super careful on my first playthrough to hit every monster and chest, assuming I would naturally hit every single location along the way, but there was one super minor location (Rebel Camp) that wasn't important to the plot (i.e., I was able to progress fine without it) that counted as a visitable location. I had to start a new game and play through all the way to that point in the plot just to be able to visit it and get the achievement. I'm generally not a fan of missable game elements...Overall, this was an absolutely amazing game, and while I haven't tried out this game in other release forms (e.g. the PSP version), I really liked playing this on my 4K TV with a nice sound system, and I'm pretty sure this would be my version of preference
