_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II is a unique entry in the franchise that offers a refreshing departure from its predecessor while still maintaining the essence of what makes Final Fantasy great. As a long-time fan of the series, I found myself pleasantly surprised by the innovative gameplay mechanics and the emotional depth of the story.One of the standout features of Final Fantasy II is its character progression system. Unlike traditional leveling systems, where characters gain experience points to increase their stats, Final Fantasy II utilizes a skill-based progression system. This means that the more a character uses a particular weapon or spell, the more proficient they become in that skill. While this system can be challenging to master at first, it adds a layer of strategy and depth to the gameplay that is both rewarding and engaging.The storyline of Final Fantasy II is also a highlight. Set in a richly detailed world filled with political intrigue and ancient prophecies, the game follows a group of unlikely heroes as they band together to overthrow an oppressive empire. The characters are well-developed and relatable, and their personal struggles and triumphs add emotional weight to the overarching narrative.Visually, Final Fantasy II has aged well, with its charming pixel art style and detailed environments still holding up after all these years. The music is also excellent, with its memorable melodies enhancing the atmosphere of the game.That being said, Final Fantasy II is not without its flaws. The difficulty curve can be punishing at times, especially for players who are new to the series or unfamiliar with the game's unique mechanics. Additionally, the lack of a traditional leveling system may be off-putting to some players who prefer a more straightforward progression system.Overall, Final Fantasy II is a challenging and rewarding experience that is sure to appeal to fans of the series and RPG enthusiasts alike. While it may not be as widely celebrated as some of the other entries in the franchise, it is definitely worth checking out for its innovative gameplay mechanics and compelling story.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II Pixel Remaster is a remastered version of the original 1988 Nintendo Famicom (The Nintendo Entertainment System was known as the Nintendo Famicom in Japan) game in which Firion, Maria, Guy and a whole host of other characters fight to save the world from the Empire and the Emperor!If you have played any of the newer re-releases such as the Dawn of Souls version on the Game Boy Advance, then all extra content like the Soul of Rebirth that was featured in that version along with other versions of Final Fantasy II are not present in this Pixel Remaster version.The levelling system in Final Fantasy II works differently than any other game in this storied franchise. Instead of winning battles and earning XP that when a sufficient amount has been reached a party member will go up 1 level, in this game the party members level up based on what they do and what happens to them in a battle. This approach was supposed to give the game a more realistic setup to levelling and the logic is there - use a magic spell more and more and you will become more proficient at doing it. 'Practice makes perfect' as some would say. However this led to the system being unintentionally exploitable to make the game's progress far easier. That‘s why Final Fantasy II is regarded as being the 'Black Sheep' of the Final Fantasy family.But it takes alot of work, IMO, to be the black sheep of a long-time series and not be de-throned. It went unlocalized for a rather lengthy period of time, which meant when it finally did come it was being judged against games that came ten years or more after it. Memes about the game were established in the West before the game itself ever had a chance. Unfortunately, I feel like the FF2 Pixel Remaster has once again drawn the short straw. Of all the Pixel Remaster games so far, this is the one that loses the most.The list of differences with the Pixel Remaster when compared to the previous mobile version is almost identical to that of the first game. We’ve got completely new visuals that you may or may not prefer. (I LOVE THEM!) There’s a new version of the soundtrack that sounds outstanding. Gameplay rules hew a bit closer to the Famicom version in some ways than they do the previous remakes, though not significantly so. All of the content added in the various remakes has been left out of this game, almost as if this were the first remake of the original game. That latter point is a major blow to this game, in my opinion. It leaves me questioning which of the two versions I would actually recommend to someone if the choice was there, and I don’t think that’s really where Square Enix wants any of these remakes to be.Unlike the added content in most of the other games, Final Fantasy II‘s extras actually built on the game’s story in a meaningful way. It put you in control of a party of characters who had stepped out of the main story, challenging you to make your way through some tough areas with scarce resources. It served as a wonderful bit of closure for those characters, resonated well with the original story’s themes, and was a lovely ending for the narrative as a whole. Sure, the original game didn’t have any of this and it stood on its own feet just fine, but this is a rare case where I think after-the-fact added content actually made for a far better game.Assuming you can set that aside more easily than I can, you’ll find this to be a very agreeable version of a somewhat disagreeable game. It certainly looks, sounds, and plays sharper than the now-antiquated 11-year-old original app. This and the first game needed this refresh more than the others just on the basis of their age, and it’s good to see it looking so spiffy on modern devices. The content that is present in this version is certainly looking its finest, though I’m sure tastes on the chosen art style will vary. Would I buy this if I already had the original app and it was still working properly? Not unless I was a big Final Fantasy II fan or a completionist. But if you’re going to play the original Final Fantasy II adventure for the first time, this is an excellent way to do it.Final Fantasy II Pixel Remaster is a lovely remake of a game that people already loved or hated. Its strongest element is arguably its story, and that’s why I feel it’s hurt so much by cutting the excellent extra content added in the Game Boy Advance version. With that in mind, I think it’s best to stick with the old version of the game if you already own it and it still works. (Or rush the game in ~10 hrs with boosts activated like I did). This new version is more modern in its presentation and UI, and ultimately it will be the one that survives. It’s also the only one you can buy now, so if you want to play Final Fantasy II it’s this or nothing. I enjoy the game, but you will need to be willing to put up with its eccentricities if you seek to do the same.

_childDocuments_.review: The Pixel Remaster series is worth it for just the remastered music alone. And overall the QOL improvements are great (detailed in-game maps, mini-maps, auto-saves, quick-saves, inventory management improvement, Steam achievements). But these remasters really do a service to the old NES titles. The sprites and details are a big improvement on the originals. All that being said...I still hate this game. I hated it the first time I played it, I hate it now. This "Skyrim-style" leveling system was a failed experiment and this is arguably the worst game in the series. But...this remaster is still the best way to experience this terrible game today...so that's why it gets a thumbs up from me.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm 7 and half hours in as I'm writing this.So I'm not the biggest fan of FF2, but this version isn't good. The changes to this version makes the combat worse than any other version. The first and worst change was the rows. When you were in the back you couldn't be attacked at all by the enemy's basic attack, now you can and you receive half damage like in other games. I wouldn't have an issue with that but they still kept the enemy preferred targeting system which mean that Maria and Guy still get hit way more often than Firion or the guest member. Two issues with that. One, a lot of the enemies in this game have on-hit effects and they will trigger 100% if you get hit making some of the later enemies almost impossible if you don't know that they can either petrify or straight up kill you. Two, I like to make Firion the tank because the ambush rate is based on his agility(which is leftover from the NES version). And if he doesn't go that route then prepare for ambushes in the mid to late game almost all the time. Another change which i don't mind too much is you seem to gain HP very quickly. I think my main 3 members have 1500+ HP while the current guest has like 350 or so. In the NES/PS1 versions the guest character are actually useful but in this version they usually die pretty fast. So now you need to armor them up or give them all shields to help evade hits. But that is another thing I noticed. Evasion can be brought up too 99% easily but that only evades one hit and gaining actual evasion levels seems to be non-existent. So that can tie in with enemies having a 100% chance to inflict you with a status aliment and equipment that should protect you from those aliments don't work. There is a pretty nasty bug with the game. If you target an enemy with the Life spell while they are living and then they die from something else the game will lock up and nothing can be done. I have had to quit out a few times because I do a life spell at an undead enemy and then they end up getting kill by someone else and it just freezes it up like you need to Alt+F4 just to get out of it. Hopefully they fix the bug.Some good things about the game. The music is probably the best version of the soundtrack. It's still just okay but there is still some bangers on the OST. Magician's Tower is probably one of my favorite dungeons themes from the NES FF games.I recommend the GBA/PSP versions of this game. I personally like the PS1 version because once you learn how the game works it can be pretty easy.Edit: They fixed the bug where the enemies will have a 100% chance to inflict the status aliment they can on you. Now its still a high chance but if you are immune to the effect than it will no longer hit you. Also they made your Evasion amount(?) easier to level up. The number is suppose to represent how many hits you can evade with the percentage being how you will evade those hits. They also fixed some sounds bugs which I noticed in one area, can't remember where but it bothered me...Probably still won't play this version again. I like how the row system was originally.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, where to even start with this one...Okay, I get it. It was an NES game, they tried to experiment after Final Fantasy 1, I get that, but I've never seen a game get experimental and get LITERALLY EVERYTHING WRONG.Do you enjoy enemies having a 100% chance to inflict status aliments? Okay, how about we add those status effects to their physical attacks and ensure that you are ALWAYS getting hit with them everywhere you go. This can include paralysis so sometimes you get stunlocked for no reason completely out of your control, or INSTANT DEATH.Oh, but you can just avoid all that if you grind your shield rank, right? I suppose so, but have fun grinding that up, just like everything else in this game, grinding is not only encouraged, but REQUIRED. Every time you use a skill or weapon, or use a stat, you get more proficient in it. This includes your HP and MP, you want more HP? You're gonna have to take damage. Want to DEAL damage? Better swing your sword around aimlessly until it's properly leveled, and even then, enemies have insanely high defense, so most of the time your physical attacks will deal no damage, at least for the first half of the game. So then you'll need to upgrade your spells, which requires casting it an absurd number of times, which consumes MP, which you'll then need to rest at an inn to refill, and in this game inn prices scale, so the more your mp and hp go up, the more you'll be spending to refill them.This is all assuming your enemy doesn't just explode for no reason, which several of them do. Basically every dungeon in this game has bomb type enemies with high speed that spawn in large numbers that just self destruct and deal high damage to your party. Just like with enemies that have status based attacks, if you get ambushed, you will die, and it will be unfair.Speaking of dungeons, they are incredibly boring, poorly designed, have insane encounter rates, and have many, MANY, fake doors that set you right in the middle of a room with an even higher encounter rate.Mix all of this with an incredibly bland and boring story, and you have quite possibly one of the worst JRPGs ever made. I gave this game two full, dedicated playthroughs, got every achievement, and I cannot find a single good thing to say about this game, except that I don't have to play it again. Unless you are dead set on owning all of the games and playing them, this is an easy skip.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II was something of an experiment. There's a lot it did right though the same could be said against it. For starters, the level system. If you've heard anything about the game, chances are it's probably been regarding how you level. On paper, it showed ingenuity; cast/attack more to get stronger and tank hits to boost defence. The problem is you can exploit the system by having your party members attack each other. It will still count towards stat levels. It's a system that feeds grind addicts such as myself.Furthermore, the game's map doesn't have a hard limit on where you can go once you get the canoe(some exceptions like the Snow Plains). Instead, it uses difficulty barriers which can be punishing to someone on their first playthrough. Going too far to the left as soon as you leave the first town could easily pit you against mid-game mobs. The spawn map is a welcome addition because of this. You could argue they're only a problem if you go out of your way to break your stats.Trap rooms unfortunately take the dungeon design down a peg. The dungeons are littered with doors that lead nowhere, warping you to the middle of an empty room. Each step you take trying to leave yields a high chance for an encounter. I wouldn't mind it as much if there were only a few or if you got something out of it.That's not to say it's a bad game. I liked that Square gave it more of a fleshed-out story and identities to its main cast. It helped steer the future games in a better direction. I was a fan of the re-orchestrated OST especially on classic gems like "Rebel Army".

_childDocuments_.review: I dug it, honestly, minus the extra content that the previous versions included on the GBA and PSP, this was essentially the same, felt nice to play, same essential "leveling" system, it's not really a leveling system, as anyone who's played this game knows, stats go up as you use'm, Spirit goes up when using White Magic to make it more potent, Int for Black Magic, Strength for Fighting, HP goes up when you lose HP along with Stamina, though HP does also go up in regular intervals as well.Game's a bit longer than FF1 it feels like, or maybe that's just due to grinding, I spent about 42 hours on it, mostly mindlessly pummeling myself while also working, cause I didn't have to pay too close of attention to it while I did my work, that also includes a fair bit of time of the game just sitting there, doing nothing.Anyhow, if you like FF2, I'd suggest this version, if you've already got it on PSP or the Dawn of Souls copy on GBA, it's not a whole lot different aside from look and arrangement to music, but I'd say it's worth it.Editing after reading a few other reviews:I found a lot of complaints about the 100% chance to inflict status monsters when hitting your characters, I never noticed a whole lot of this aside from the hornets in the beginning, but since I learned about it so many years ago, you want to essentially build your main three up with as much evasion as possible. They can't inflict status when they cannot hit you. Agility helps raise evasion, and having high evasion with shields and cuirass gear helps raise agility, they go hand in hand. Magic Defense is the harder, lengthier one to build up I've always felt.Non-decreasing stats is more of a quality of life change than anything else, far as I see, it doesn't really take away anything from the game, there's already a little grinding you need to do to get going comfortably, but even then, it's not really required, you can shield and punch for a lot of the game if you want to.And I do have to say, I like how they did the 4th rotating member, whenever they leave the party, they also leave their gear with you, that was a nice change.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 2 is definitely one of the more unique titles in the series, but it is still a very enjoyable game.  It's one of my favourite games in the franchise. I really enjoyed my playthrough of the pixel remaster. This is probably the only game out of the 6 that I would recommend reading up on before playing though. It introduces a lot of different mechanics to the other FF games, and it is best to know how the game works before you play through this one. Regardless, I think this is the best version of FF2 to play.The pixel art is beautifully done. All of the main character’s art matches the Amano artwork as does the enemy sprite art. The environments are well done too, full of life and colour, and some are even animated for better effect. I can’t praise the art direction team enough. Music is another stellar aspect of this remaster. FF2 was always one of the more serious/dark Final Fantasy games, and this soundtrack really helps set the tone. The fully orchestrated tracks are REALLY well done, my personal favourites being the Rebel Theme, the Dreadnought theme and the overworld theme. The theme on Pandemonium is also very fitting. Nobuo Uematsu is a genius, what else can be said? The story of FF2 is a dark one, with very interesting characters. You will lose some of them along the way, which always leaves a void not only in the party but for the player as well. Now for money and EXP, it still follows the original game closely in this regard, but money is definitely more easily available. Levelling up spells and weapons is also much easier now thanks to the Auto-Battle option in battles. Speaking of which, the new spells, (especially Ultima) are GOREGOUS. They easily surpass all the previous versions of this game in term of spell appearances.Now for the extras. Having a music player is great, as is the option of having the Bestiary to check over. Completing this one was a bit easier than FF1, even the Iron Giant wasn’t hard to find (at least to me). The art present there is also very beautiful. Some things to note for anyone who might be playing this game:-	When you can, stock up on Antidotes, Crosses and Eye Drops. The early missions/areas in this game all have a LOT of enemies that can inflict poison/venom, blindness and curses on the party, and poison takes up a lot more HP here than in other games.-	When training your weapons, if at one point you notice the XP bar isn’t moving forward, or is empty, equip weaker weapons and attack with those. Weapons use skill points to level up, and using too strong weapons too early or on the wrong enemies can yield none, therefore no skill points. -	Unlike previous versions, no need to unequip anything from members leaving the party. Once they leave, their equipment will go back to your inventory.  -	FF2 while a great game, can punish exploration (to an extent) especially at the beginning. Follow the advice of the persons in the rebel base and DON’T stray far off course, or you will run into enemies that will pummel you. -	Use the mini maps to your advantage in dungeons, to get all the chests. If you see a chest behind a wall and no way to get to it, walk around the entire outside of the wall, you will find some hidden entry points. -	In the last dungeon, there is a very missable chest. Once you are on the floor with the 4 doors, take the first one on the left, and go all the way up to the top right room with a pillar/column in the middle. Checking the south-eastern wall in that room will yield a great treasure.-	If you want to fill up your bestiary, be sure to try and get every enemy in every area that you go to, and remember, once you enter Mysidian tower, and leave after getting the Ultima tome, enemies on the world map will change.I highly recommend this Pixel Remaster of Final Fantasy 2. Thanks Square Enix for this amazing remaster!

_childDocuments_.review: Damn. There it is. I FINALLY (almost) completed this game.I didn't expect this second opus to be that long, after completing the first one in 15hours-ish. That being said, it's the first FF game with an actual scenario, and it's interesting to discover that game when you know what games followed this one. It also introduces many things that remained in the next FF games, such as Chocobos, Malboros (and many others), and you get to meet the first actual Dragoon (Dragoon fangirl here).The leveling system is a bit confusing at the beginning, and everything isn't explained. I got through 3/4 of the game with a black mage who didn't do damage properly. Also, I finished the game with my weapons and spells far from being max leveled (hello to upcoming grind to get those two last achievements). Did I say confusing ? Yes. But not uninteresting. If you like doing researches like me, you'll enjoy trying to figure out some nice builds for your party.I wouldn't consider it as one of my favourite FF games, but I definitely enjoyed the ride.

_childDocuments_.review: I kind of feel bad, I don't want to hate on these games.  It's nice to have them available I guess?  So let's get the praise out of the way first, I think the art is a bit more consistent in this one than FF (player sprites, for example, seem to match the rest of the art style and look fine), and ... that's kind of it.  This isn't a hot take: Final Fantasy II just isn't very good.  It has maze-like dungeons, horrible treasure, awful level grinding, and poor balance.  In short, it's not a hell of a lot of fun to play and the port can't fix that.  It's here for completeness sake, but I can't imagine what you would do to fix this game.For example, it is novel that characters gain XP based on use (something the Elder Scrolls is known for).  Use a sword, gain sword XP.  Get hit, maybe your HP goes up.  Unfortunately it ties character leveling at least partially to RNG.  Magic suffers the most as spells are powered up individually, which means late game spells are useful only if you spend hours spamming them. My personal hatred is the treasure: very little is worthwhile to collect because it's typically a potion, small sum of gold, or an out of date piece of armor.  It is so rare to find something valuable, let alone useful.  Maybe it wanted to be more realistic, but it makes exploration unrewarding.  The game is also criticized for excessive backtracking and yeah: add that to the list.  Still, I will partially defend it: it worked for the narrative.  Returning to these characters did make them memorable.  I remember Gordon and Hilda, and knew the stakes and major players.  You can see the seeds of what Square would go on to do planted here, but it just isn't a fun game.While FF2 has it's fans, it is hard to imagine many people actually finishing this game.  I can praise Square for mostly leaving this one alone.  Unlike the FF remaster, this is an incredibly faithful port, and very true to the original.  I can at least argue it's a good way to experience it.  Unfortunately it's not a game I can recommend experiencing, hence the thumbs down.  The only reason to buy this is to have no gaps in your collection.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: First time playing FF2. It took much longer than I'd like to admit to figure out why my magic was so weak, so heads up the more gear you wear, the weaker the magic. Sounds obvious, but it is never imparted. In fact, the whole leveling system is a little bonkers...I'm not saying I don't like it, it just certainly is different! All-in-all, it was a classic Final Fantasy vibe and my recommendation is virtually meaningless since you likely already know if that is something you like or not! :)
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II is a radical departure from the first Final Fantasy games in some aspects and in others it is quite similar. The big change is that experience points and spell slots are out and in their place are a use-it-to-improve-it system of leveling and MP for magic. To get more HP you need to 'use' (read: lose) HP. To get more evasion, you need to evade attacks.Another big change for Final Fantasy II is that the story is a lot more prominent and the party consists of actual characters. There are even segments with guest party members to showcase different classes or ways of building a character you might want to emulate.The only real downside is that there is missable content if you advance the story too quickly. Reference material, such as a guide, should be employed for those wanting to get 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: While not being as good as Final fantasy 1, the game holds up in some spots, and lets loose in others. instead of a clean level up system, you get this system. If you use a sword, you get better in swords. You use magic, you get better in magic. which means you can easily break the game and only use your fists and they will become easily your best weapon. _childDocuments_.review: FF2 is one of these dark horse types of games. Many despise it but I personally rank it as one of the beat FF games ever. This is the game that honed in on character development within every aspect of its core. Everything makes sense from battle 1. Maria being in the back with a bow, Firion being up front with a sword and shield to Guy wielding an axe and leon having a sword and shield. This action shows their personalities. While Maria yes is being protected it makes since. She was Leon's sister and Guy and Firion were her adopted brothers. Naturally they would be protecting their sister and she would let them, her intelligence stat being higher at the beginning shows her growth she could achieve when pushed for black magic.As the story progresses and she loses her brother her determination does indeed grow to find him heightening her since to learn combat tricks to support her two brothers she still has present. Guy being the strong and silent tank being there to support his family in their older brothers absence. Then you have Firion the jack of all trades master of none at the beginning. With the most even stats showing that he is not only cautious but patient less brash than that of Leon who we get near the end.You have an array of side characters all with interesting stories and stats that to show their nature.The developers truly took their time to flesh out character development through every aspect from their abilities initially to their stats.The password system while some may find it tedious and annoying gives you a chance to flesh out more lore and give the series a way for you to influence the pieces of story you learn and see.It makes you explore the world and its inhabitants because you don't know on an initial play-through which npcs will be influences by these keywords.I believe FF2 while simple has some of the best character development in the series.From a game-play perspective the leveling system also offers you the most freedom.If you love the grind you can and you can make Maria wield an ax, and Guy become a monk if you desire. But, the beauty is you also can play the game as intended and see the growth as it progresses and know that the characters are growing as people too.Also the music is amazing!

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the best and most welcoming version of this game. The leveling system has been reasonably balanced to allow a smoother progression in weapon and spell proficiencies, while not making it stupidly OP. Enemies have been re-balanced as well and the whole game is just an overall pleasurable experience. Last time I beat this game was in the Origins collection. But this version is the easiest to complete. Aside from the achievement for visiting every location. Many of the locations are limited time through progression, so if You don't visit an optional location while it's there, you lose it forever and must start fresh. Same with any treasures in said locations. But the addition of the new map system makes finding them pretty easy. Overall, this is the best version of this Final Fantasy in my opinion and I recommend it to anyone curious about it. It's worth at least a try. And at $10 USD, you're not breaking the bank.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game multiple times throughout the years and this is a great port.  Not much really to say, it is FF2.  The only negative is that, paying for it I would expect better translation.  I think I've had better translation on an emulator.  It's not bad at all and isn't pervasive but I would like to have seen that polish.  Other than that, FF2 is a great break from the traditional type of JRPG without having to go to the modern action oriented battle style which I don't like.  For a grinder, FF2 can be an addiction.  Luckily for me, I got everyone to the highest stats in the game, and in the endgame, when I played it on the DS (I think that's the system that had the FF1/FF2 combo) .  If you haven't played it and you are a grinder, get ready for a lot of work to get all your weapons and spells to max level.  And, after playing FF1 PR, I have to say I absolutely love the map system now.  It lets me go for those achievements without having to track on my own.  It is a very good addition for those who are playing the PRs who have beaten all of these many times already.I definitely recommend this game.  Now on to FF3!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Ahh, the divisive one.Well, maybe not that divisive. Most fans actually consider this to be one of the weaker entries in the series. All mostly thanks to the leveling system. But it isn't all weak. In fact, it's actually a decent game in other aspects. Especially this pixel remaster, which does a fantastic job of presenting it. The leveling system leaves much to be desired, and I'm glad they scrapped it later, but you have to applaud the balls to try something new for a sequel. I always appreciate that mindset. You level the things you do. Attack with a sword; level sword. Get hit; level HP. Use magic; level MP and the spell itself. Newer games have done that and become successful, like The Elder Scrolls series which makes its living on it. Here it just doesn't come together. You still feel locked in to specific roles, much because of the likes of the hidden magic penalty stat for wearing gear. It makes sense, otherwise all characters can be identical master jack of all trades, but why it's hidden remains a mystery. Even in the remaster. And it forces you to make fairly pure mages and pure fighters. Well, kind of. Just make sure the mages rock bare fists in the front and they will decimate enemies all the same. I guess that's a battle mage/monk in some sense. Still, if you don't use magic you don't level it. So, either you use it all the time, or have to grind levels for it specifically when you need it. Since leveling isn't that hard and doesn't take up an abundance of time, it's ok to grind for it at times, but it's still annoying and a bad system for magic in an FF game where you mostly use magic when you have to,. Here it's balls out magic all the time on every ragtag enemy just to level it.As far as fighters go, you might be tempted to use dual wield just for the extra damage, but the shields are imperative at times to get your evasion up. Believe me, evasion is more important than HP and defense. Enemies have an annoying habit of having 100% status effect chance on hit, which can devastate in seconds. Don't get hit is the key.The story is kind of whatever nowadays, but the fact that you had named characters and party members swap in and out during the story was new and very interesting back in the day. It's also more involved than the first game, so they made quite a few new stabs at the delivery of it for its time.When it comes to presentation the game shines, especially this version. The original had amazing music and here in the pixel remaster we get a new arranged soundtrack that sounds superb. There are some real bangers here as per usual with the series. The pixel graphics works wonders and stays true to the original. It plays snappy and has a lot of quality of life improvements.Overall this package is a very good one. The game itself leaves something to be desired, sure, but most people who play it nowadays do so for the nostalgia or for the historical context as fans of the series. This is probably the best version of the game to play. And it's still a decent game that is totally playable, just make sure to read up on the level system a bit beforehand to give you less of a headache later.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: This game introduces a new leveling system over FF1. the more you use a stat or ability the more it levels up. Your PCs do not have their own character levels only their stats do. This makes the game so much worse when it comes to grinding or trying to level up specific things. I major change I liked this the loadout system allows you to equip 2 weapons. I would advise you teach your characters how to dodge first by equipping a shield and leveling dodge. otherwise everything, but the leveling system is an upgrade of FF1
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I had this game back on the PSX from FF Origins, and it was always difficult to get into because of it open nature and cryptic leveling system. The Pixel Remaster simplifies the leveling to make it less intimidating, and while that might take away some challenge from the original intended experience, I think it makes it more accessible.The sprites for your playable characters look better than they ever have, matching the character designs perfectly! While it may not be as character focused as later Final Fantasy games, this is the first time the series had any focus on character. These character moments I personally found to be memorable, because FFI and FFIII feel super dumbed down by comparison.The story surprised me with it's scale and dark tone. Even the remastered music has a fitting tone that separates it from the rest of the classic FF games, and has much more in common with Final Fantasy Tactics. As you go through the game, you witness A LOT of death and destruction. I swear if this game was made nowadays, it would have Game of Thrones levels of pain and despair, and I'm kinda here for it. My one MAJOR COMPLAINT which will hold me back from repeat playthroughs, is that the random encounter rate is way too high. Approaching the midpoint of the game it truly becomes tiresome to get into battles, especially with all of the dead end rooms dungeons have with the sole purpose of wasting your time and wearing you down. But other than that, I had a wonderful time playing this game, and I'm glad to have finally been able to finish it!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game with many, many flaws. The pixel remaster and access to maps online makes these flaws easier to overlook, but they're still very much there.First of all, the magic system. Each spell (and attribute, for that matter) has its own level, and the only way to raise that level is to use the spell. This means that, even after the game ends, if you teach your character Fire, for example, they start from level 1 and have to use Fire over and over again to increase the damage of that spell. While in theory a very flexible system, this leads to lots and lots of grinding for basic spells. This same logic also applies to health (though there is a booster on by default that increases your health every few battles), SP, and weapons. This is amplified by the fact that the calculation seems to be broken, so odds are, you'll be finishing the game with your most used spells around level 8-11.The second thing I want to mention is the dungeon design. Final Fantasy II  to waste your time. Almost every floor of every dungeon has a door that leads to an empty room, and in the original game, the tiles in these rooms would trigger a random encounter . The game's dungeons are largely centered around these trap rooms, making dungeon design extremely boring and ends up being a maze made to waste your time.However, at its core, it's still Final Fantasy. I had a lot of fun trying to make Guy deal a ridiculous amount of damage on each hit, and the freedom in being able to teach magic to anyone, although genuinely broken in a bad way, had me experimenting up until the last few hours. I had some fun, but I will probably never play this game again.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: FINAL FANTASY II is the only opus of the Pixel Remaster Collection that I recommend you to skip, unless you like pain.Even though the Job leveling system is quite unique, even today, the story & characters are not interesting at all and the game is filled with bad ideas and design flaws that are gonna make you waste a lot of your time. Honestly, play the intro if you are curious, but just launch the III instead.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to play this once just to finish it. So far, I am not liking it very much. The reasons have been said many times in other reviews.So why the recommendation? Because it is so odd. From fluctuating inn prices, figuring out gear penalties, strategizing where to build stats, figuring out what ailments are temporary and permanent, there's a lot to digest. Some of these elements would be used in other installments. So just for the history alone is worth it. Sure, you can play the other versions. I am not bashing them. The way this remaster was done makes it worth the slog and the flaws.I am sure many will disagree with me. That's OK. This is not my favorite, but like I said, I just want the satisfaction I actually finished the game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite FF games... but this remake is not FF2 at its best.I would say skip it, but they pulled all the other versions. Sad cash grab? (..and by getting this, I understand I'm part of the problem.) So if you need your FF2 fix, and have no options, try to get it cheap?Did not like the "freebie" HP upgrades that randomly popped up after battles, and how they changed the skill/magic upgrades. The graphic updates are far below other remakes, and other than the music, this really is nothing special.PSP vers and its reissues are still the best way to enjoy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Another Final Fantasy game thats been released multiple times. This is not the best version of this game imo. Even if it was the best version, this is the worst game of all the final fantasy main line games.Also of note, there a bug/feature where enemies apply status effects 100% of the time if their attack hits at all, even if it does no damage. When enemies are just envenoming you its an annoyance. Later on though enemies stun/sleep/petrify/confuse/mini or just straight up kill you. I had 99% evasion which should be the way to counter this but you can only evade 4 attacks and enemies are attacking up to 12 times.On the plus side this also works in your favor when the sleep sword and curse (ancient) sword cant be resisted by enemies, so you can sleep lock every boss including the final boss.Also they removed stat decreases so you can have hybrid mages and physical attackers. Make sure you look into magic penalties based on equipped gear though. Its not explained in the game and has a huge impact on viability of magic.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: As a part of the whole Final Fantasy series it is a must. Every fan of this series should try it out. But the game is old and you need to be aware that the graphics are just pixels and it is only the second title in the series. So the story isn't anything amazing, just the usual "Let's save the world". The gameplay quickly becomes repetitive when you can't make few steps without starting another battle. However, I liked the new mechanics for leveling up. It was an interesting thing that brought a bit of strategy to developing your character. So the game gets a great plus from me for that. In overall, I enjoyed the game but I am a fan of FF series and I admit that this game is not for everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: The second Pixel Remaster is another home run, in my estimation. Quite possibly the most enjoyable version of FF2 as far as a casual playing goes. Of course, that isn't to say it isn't without it's problems. So lets go over the bad before we finish out with the praise.1. As with the first game, the price is a bit ridiculous. It could be a bit lower.2. Status afflictions in this game appear to be bugged. Enemies will basically hit you 100% of the time with them if their hit connects at all. So any time a flower hits you, you're guaranteed to be confused. This, for the most part, isn't THAT bad. But it becomes a pain in the final dungeons where you're confronted with a specific enemy that instantly kills you upon touch, and you have to fight five of them and they get an ambush and whelp you're basically dead. If this is working as intended then I suggest the intended method is stupid.3. I ran into two bugs while playing the game. The first is after a late game cut scene the game just froze mid scene and I had to reload an old save. Thankfully this didn't repeat. The second is that it seems on rare occassions the game just simply doesn't acknowledge an opened chest or what have you. I've seen people reporting that they grabbed the Ultima Tome and the game didn't count it as an obtained item for the achievement. I myself played with a guide (as I was doing the bestiary) and after getting every chest in the game I noticed according to the achievement I was missing 10. Then a few minutes later it said I was only missing four. And then finally three. There's a bit of a delay between you doing something and the game acknowledging it. So if you were to open something but then save and quit before the game acknowledged it, then it might not actually count. So be aware of that if you're achievement hunting.Now with those out of the way, lets talk about the positives. The first is that they've removed two very annoying parts of the vanilla game. The first is that there were rooms where you'd enter and every single step you took was an encounter, and it'd spawn you directly in the center of said rooms. It was annoying to say the least. They've removed the every tile encounter, and instead they just act like normal encounter rates. The second change is that you no longer LOSE stats when raising skills. So you're no longer pidgeonholed into being a pure mage or a pure fighter (or doing a combo but being meh at both). You now have a sort of Elder Scrolls way of dealing with the game that lets you level every character the way you feel is necessary. I can understand some might view this as a negative as it does make things a bit too easy at times (although the 100% status affliction rate tends to even that out late game), but it makes things a bit less tedious.As with FF1 PR you also have the mini map which was a great feature there and remains so here. You have the soundtrack, design art, and all those bells and whistles. Overall if you enjoy the game this is probably the definitive version of it, or at the very least on par with the PSP version. It has a couple of annoyances, but overall I have to recommend this with the same caveat of waiting for a sale to mitigate the ridiculous price a bit.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: It's actually insane how this game came out a year after Final Fantasy 1 cause Final Fantasy 2 is very different from it's predecessor. There is more of a story, the protagonists have character and this game is shockingly dark especially since this game out on the famicom in 1988. This game is considered the black sheep of the first six Final Fantasy games but I honestly had a good time with this game and I didn't mind how the battle system worked. Also this game introduced being able to ride chocobos, ultima spells as well as the Dragoons that became series stables. This game also went and created an entirely new series called SaGa as the director of the SaGa series worked on Final Fantasy 2. Only thing I didn't like about FF 2 was the constant dead ends in dungeons that got old really quick.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Very different leveling system from the first game, which some people apparently do not like. However I thought the leveling system was interesting and enjoyed 100%ing the game. There were a couple of small grindy sessions for 100%, but those can be sped up using the in-game boost cheats (which I'm pretty sure don't disable achievements). The story is better than the first game, and the music is very good. Definitely recommend at least trying it out.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: The best way to play the most underrated Final Fantasy in the series. Is this game great? No. But it has some really interesting ideas, and in terms of story it's such a leap forward from Final Fantasy 1 that I can't help but love it. The music is top notch, and the visuals in the Pixel Remaster are great as well.I'd definitely reccommend this over the GBA/PSX/PSP versions or god forbid playing a NES rom hack.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Huge downgrade compared to the first title in the series. Bland story, the new weapon/spell skill levels are an annoyance as well as the ask/learn keyword system. And having achievements linked to said systems is even worse. Having achievements that require you to cheese/grind something that is not meant to be part of the natural flow of the game is plainly bad design (spell cap was ok, but weapon cap grind is yet another annoyance). Not worth its price imo.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: It is a solid Final Fantasy game. I don't know if I like it more than the original (FF1), but it definitely has more story, with some dramatic moments. The password system for learning and asking NPCs about keywords to learn about the game is intuitive. The level up system is more like an elder scrolls game--wherein your skills increase by use (be it active or passive). Some people don't like that, but I think it is pretty neat. That allows you to play your different characters however you'd like.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: This is truly my favorite version of FF2. Like the Pixel Remasters for FF1 and FF3, I'm loving the classic NES/SNES character sprites and the updated soundtrack supervised by composer, Nobou Uematsu! Admittedly, I kind of miss seeing the CG cutscenes that were used in the opening for the PS1 and PSP remakes, but it's something I'll gladly overlook. Also, as with the Pixel Remasters for FF1 and FF3, the game runs kind of choppy in the first town (and possibly other towns), but is not really a deal breaker. Just a minor issue that I hope will be fixed later. Aside from that, I'm quite satisfied!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I was debating whether to give to this game a negative review and I chose to rate it as positive. First, I appreciate the work put into remastering this game, I can say it works almost flawlessly (I run it with Vsync turned ON from the Nvidia control panel). Second, the soundtrack is a masterpiece, like for the first FF1 PR. Third, the story is good, like any FF game.What I don't like is the gameplay, it is just boring, this game certainly shows its age. The problem is that almost all the battles which end with no XP feel useless, since the only XP is given for leveling spells and weapons. Another issue, the spells are kind of broken in this game: besides some certain enemies, almost all the elemental attacks are ineffective in this game, compared to FF1 where the elemental attacks were very useful and worth using. And, finally, like in FF1, I got used to not using any spell besides the elemental ones because, almost always, they ended up in a miss hit. Sure, there may be some useful ones but with the lack of a proper manual, it becomes a chore to use them all just to discover a spell good for a particular enemy. Add to this the empty rooms (I think 99,9%) and the incredibly high encounter rate and you end up with a game which feels like a job waiting to be finished. I didn't finish the game, I don't feel like going forward, maybe another time.I have one request to Square Enix: please give us an option to completely disable the mini map inside the dungeons, it just takes away from the thrill of adventuring. The auto battle feature, on the other hand, is a totally useful QoL feature. And please, for each PR game, give us the manuals (which I would say are mandatory for a correct understanding of the mechanics), I don't understand why these were not included with these releases.Do I recommend this game? Yes, it is something special and I support remastering/remaking good old games, plus it is worth playing for the story, music and setting, but the gameplay is just plain bad which makes the game to feel boring while playing. All in all, I would say it is a must-have title in any gamer's library.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: FFII is FFII, and Pixel Remaster makes no apologies. If you like FFII, this is a great version to play. A very early incarnation of the concept of levelling individual abilities and skills based on using them, rather than set bulk improvements at set exp increments is the biggest change between FFII and its brethren. FFII also experimented with an idea of learning and bringing up keywords/key items in conversations to progress the plot. FFII was a bold experiment, probably spawned the SaGa series, and is likely worth a shot by anyone who likes the series. This is my favorite way to play it.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II is a frustrating, tedious mess regardless of version. Its lofty ambitions and groundbreaking mechanics are staunched by its utter lack of ability to execute them.The idea of training in individual stats rather than gaining character levels was novel in 1988, as was the concept of improving your ability to use certain weapons and magics. It's a system that promises endless customization, but in reality you'll be sticking to one set of weapons and a handful of spells per character or be forced to grind MUCH longer than anyone would have any reason to. Rather than a party of freeform Jacks-of-All-Trades, you end up with a slightly looser class system, akin to the first game.Combine this with dungeon design centered on wasting your time, a lackluster attempt at character writing, and the fact that at any given time you're either immensely over-or-underpowered, and you have a recipe for an RPG I NEVER want to touch ever again.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: FFII attempts to take the franchise in a different direction, away from classes and choice. You are given 3 main characters that are essentially interchangeable stat wise with the only real difference being their name and sprite. Here comes the first big problem - your 4th party member is a guest party member for the majority of the game.Second problem - the way you progress your character is very odd, its done by becoming proficient at using the various weapons of the game, its a cool idea in concept but i believe it was pulled off badly in practice
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this after beating both the first and second games in the series.There's two kinds of people when it comes to these Pixel Remasters:A) The people will appreciate their time with these, and also the remastered Original pixel work and AMAZING remastered soundtrack. B) The people who want these to be the PSP/GBA/DS remakes with the extra concent, etc etc.All I can say to those people is, please give the Pixel Remasters a shot.I would feel bad if you missed out on an amazingly genuine Final Fantasy experience.Step into these good good waters.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: This would have probably been miserable to play regardless, but doing it right after FF1 made it even worse. I do acknowledge that a lot of ambition went into making this game, but while some of the core ideas were solid, most of the execution felt quite poor and led to almost constant frustration throughout the runtime. I guess this sometimes comes with the territory when you try to experiment and offer something completely different. Like many others my biggest gripe was likely the progression. Maybe not even so much the mechanics of how it worked, but rather the way it constantly made me feel. The game sells the progression as what is essentially ultimate freedom - the more you use a certain ability the more it levels up and all equipment can be used without limitations. It should feel very natural, but instead it caused an almost constant feeling of dissonance for me. I felt a need to always use abilities I did not need in my current encounters just so I could level them up for future battles where I actually needed them. This made everything feel very hollow for me. There's so much choice with cool magic, but realistically you need to pick 2-3 favourites because unless you spend the time casting something constantly it will be relatively useless. In addition to this many of your characters stat upgrades are somewhat random. If you get hit enough your health may increase a little after the fight. Same with dodges, MP and probably a few more things. The added randomness and removal of actual levels ended up almost completely removing my excitement at seeing my characters progress. Naturally not loving both ability progression and stat progression meant that combat started feeling incredibly hollow after a while. Which brings me to the next point. There's so damn much of it. There is a random encounter approximately every 4-5 steps you take. In addition to that the dungeons in this game are about twice as long and filled with maze like dead ends and confusing stairs. Two things that absolutely do not work together. I would have liked to explore the maze, but there's a constant feeling of being penalised with 10 random encounters any time you take a detour. Since progression seems to be the keyword for my little rant here I'll also add that map progression took a massive dive in this game. In Final Fantasy sections of the world map were unlocked in clever ways to guide the player more naturally and offer a sense of being on an adventure. For the most part this is gone in FF2 and the majority of the world map is open from the very start which removed a lot of the sense of wonder I had while playing the first game. I have more gripes, but I figure I've already ranted enough about my experience and probably come across more negative than the game perhaps deserves. The biggest praise I can give this game is definitely the music. Nobuo Uematsu is a genius and listening to the iconic soundtrack made everything a little more bearable. It also looks amazing and I love all the sprite designs. The story - while not being perfect - strives to be a little darker which was interesting to see. It's still not something I want to judge too harshly in these early games which is a whole conversation of it's own, but they are getting closer to crafting a proper narrative. FF2 also introduced a lot of series staples like the Chocobos so it was cool as a fan of the franchise. It might even have more iconic elements than the first game as far as the identity of the series is concerned. I just wish that I had enjoyed the actual gameplay more.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: The game is boring until the last two dungeons where out of nowhere magic is suddenly useful for the last 3-5 hours of the game. Story progression locks you out of certain chests as you can only get them at very specific points in the story. This feels like the kind of game that you don't play right until you've made all the mistakes and failed over and over. I don't know about anyone else, but I'm not a fan of that mindset existing in slower paced rpg's. Souls games? Sure. This ♥♥♥♥ that moves at the speed of paint drying? No. It's too grindy. The main characters aren't really likable unless Guy speaking to animals is your thing. The plot in the climax seems really jerky and disconnected. And the progression system is tedious and adds to the grinding. I have come to realize that this game needs more than a pixel remaster to be enjoyable. I do NOT recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I had never played this before, it was really interesting and different.  Remastered graphics were excellent.  Again, the soundtrack was incredible.  Such a difference in systems from FF1.   Played Firion (dual wield sword, full armor, white magic), Maria (knife/staff, low magic penalty armor, Black magic),  Guy (dual wield axe, low magic penalty armor, white magic).  Game did not feel very difficult at any point and didn't feel the need to overly grind which was surprising.   Did the font mod on this one also.. a must.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start by saying I completed and got all the achievements for this game, but this is the only Final Fantasy game I haven't particularly enjoyed. The Skyrim-esque levelling system I can deal with. It's not ideal but it worked I guess. What I can't deal with is the way random encounters and debuffs are handled. The encounter rate in dungeons feels extremely high, so you're in a battle every couple of steps. Add this to the fact that if an enemy has a chance of inflicting a status effect on you with a hit, that status effect seems to be a 100% proc. This means you can be ambushed, have petrify/death auto inflicted on every party member before you can even select a command. Game over. This is nothing more than completely artificial difficulty - artificial because the game isn't difficult at all thanks to autosave/quicksave feature - so really the word for it is just "tedious". Oh, you got ambushed and wiped before you could do anything? Well reload the autosave and hope you don't get ambushed this time. I got my money's worth I guess but I would avoid this one unless you have nostalgia for it or are just a completionist like myselfTLDR: don't buy unless you are a big fan of the series and just want to complete them all
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure why it says 10.3 hours for me, I must've experienced an ISP outage or something.  My hours should be somewhere around 20.Awkward design having to travel from one corner of the map to the next just to turn around and travel back, but outside of that, fun game.Having to rotate a 4th character consistently was pretty bizarre but nothing google and preparation couldn't help me with.I'd recommend this game if you enjoyed the other early FF games.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this. The most satisfying thing is that the you level up your skills organically, and there are no official classes. Any character can wear any gear and learn any spell.I did have some gripes. I don't know if I was overlevelled, but the game was very easy. I spent 2/3 of the game on auto-battle, reading Reddit on my other monitor. Also, magic was pathetically weak beyond the early game. Every time you get a new spell, you have to level it up individually. By the end, my martial characters were doing 2-3 thousand damage per turn, and my caster with level X Ultima did about 500 per cast.Still, enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: The real world impact this has on your life cannot be understated. With hope you leap into this game as in life with captivated eyes and wonder of what might be. Through the journey your understanding of reality breaks into millions of shattered grains of that previous hope as the game, as in life, destroys any last bastion of your sanity. With pain and anguish you learn the truths that were only meant for late night game coders and a candlelit science hidden in the backrooms of your parental figures darkest nightmares. Great game though! Enjoy the journey!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Solid! It's definitely not a great game, but it's worth it for the history and innovation - there were a lot of cool ideas with this game, even if most weren't actually realized very well, so it's cool to play through just for the experimentation and to explore what the devs were trying out. _childDocuments_.review: Though one of the easiest renditions of FF2 from a gameplay perspective, it's also one of the most accessible. I didn't even have to grind/have my party slap each other silly to get stat increases to weather through the game like I did on my other playthroughs! More so than FF1's pixel remaster I feel, FF2 benefits greatly from the revamped spritework and overhaul of the soundtrack. Easily the definitive version of this game from a presentation standpoint! I had a lot of fun revisiting this title and taking everything in.I do have one gripe though... and I'm honestly not sure if this should be read as a criticism of the game's original design or a bug in the current version of the remaster. Enemy regular attacks with status effects are 100% guaranteed to land those status effects on your party - all it takes is a single hit that doesn't even have to do damage to you. This would be fine honestly, it certainly keeps things interesting and you on your toes. But instant death and stone are among those guaranteed status effects, and much of the equipment that is described as guarding against such effects do not appear to work. All 8 times I game-overed while playing this was because of these two issues compounding; sometimes you just get that unlucky with certain encounters. This is mitigated somewhat by check-pointing everytime you enter a floor/room. Certainly not a deal breaker, but in a game that's already promised to be a better balancing of the original game, these apparent quirks either come across as intentionally mean or unintentionally overlooked - I'll let you be the judge. Without giving too much away, shields are very good in this game, and betrayal fangs work very well against a certain late game cat enemy that's more efficient at killing you than the final boss is when it shows up in high numbers. If you get stuck that is.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a hardcore Final Fantasy fan but haven't played this game, then I'd say play it to experience the game. But get it when it goes on sale. For everyone else, save your money. It's not worth playing this game. The story is nice though, so maybe read about that on the fan wiki.I avoided Final Fantasy II for the longest time because I was aware of its "use-based" system. And for a video game RPG of the time, it is pretty innovative. However, its execution is less than stellar. While I haven't encountered a case of "the system screwed me over," some aspects of it feel like it needs a lot of work. However, this is the least of the game's problems. A bunch of other design decisions were made that make the game less than fun to play than the other classic Final Fantasy games.What I liked:* The same QoL updates, bug fixes, and such like in Final Fantasy I where applicable.* The story, while simple, is pretty engaging for a late 80s RPG.* This is where most of the Final Fantasy staples, like Chocobos, Cid, some enemies, and teenagers fighting against an evil empire, come from.* For the most part, stat growth isn't actually that bad. I would argue that the way it's balanced prevents the need to grind.* It's pretty easy to simply "Brute force" your way through the game after a certain point, for better or worseWhat I didn't like:* Random encounters are still plentiful as ever. Because of this, if I'm steam rolling through enemies, it becomes more of a hassle to go through a dungeon. In other Final Fantasy games, I might do the battle because every bit of XP counts. But in this, you might get some stat growth, but not enough to do every battle.* While the weapon skill growth system isn't that bad, the magic growth system missed out on the balancing act. Leveling up magic is super slow. I was towards the end of the game and none of my spells were half way to the maximum level of 16. Most of the offensive spells were floating around 4. The problem with the magic skill growth is it depends on the enemy's "rank", which for most of the game you'll encounter at most rank 5-6. So if you want to grow much higher than that, you're going to have to spend time grinding those spells.* Points to grow skill levels don't overflow. Once you've used the weapon/magic enough times to level it up, it stops growing until the next encounter.* Practically all of the spells are useless until level 3-4.* Casting spells on multiple targets is equally useless.* Enemy attacks can apply status effects, as early as the first encounter. While some of this can be annoying, later enemies will start applying status effects that are basically a game over condition if everyone gets hit. The problem is that unlike later Final Fantasy games, certain status effects like Sleep and Confusion don't go away when the character gets hit. Worse yet, the status effects can be re-applied. Spoiler alert: Malboros when you encounter them don't kill you with Bad Breath, they kill you because they paralyze your whole party and there's nothing you can do about it unless you get lucky and they miss enough. If it wasn't for Quick/Auto save, I'd probably would've rage quit at certain parts.* The dungeon design gets frustrating. Later dungeons litter themselves with fake rooms and pointless treasure.* The "Learn/Ask" dialog system while interesting in theory, ends up being a pointless gate keeper to progress the game.

_childDocuments_.review: As with the first game, this one looks and sounds fantastic. The graphics are clean, and the sprites are gorgeous. The orchestrated soundtrack sounds beautiful, creating an immersive experience that fans and newcomers alike can appreciate.The story and characters are surprisingly deep for a NES game. So many characters die over the course of the game, and the Emperor is a straight-up mass murderer. This depth in narrative was groundbreaking for its time and still holds up well.The unique leveling system is actually a lot of fun to use when it works properly. It offers a lot of freedom in how you build your characters, and the fact that everyone can use every weapon and spell with relatively equal effectiveness is awesome. The humor also shines through, something I didn’t really notice in the first Final Fantasy. In the early game, I was engaged with the combat and liked the leveling system. By the latter part of the mid-game, I was nearly invincible with just auto attacks and all my party members dual-wielding. Then the game turned into auto-combat mode except during some boss fights where I had to use some buffs before turning on auto battle. It got boring.Regarding gameplay, the encounter rate in this one is, wow, too much. I couldn't walk 10 steps without triggering a battle. It felt like I was constantly interrupted, which made exploration a chore rather than a joy. The dungeon design and encounter rates made a lot of the dungeons really frustrating to navigate. TL;DR; 7/10. Its music and visuals are stunning, and its story is impressively deep for its time. However, its progression system and encounter rates can be frustrating, making the gameplay experience uneven. If you can look past these flaws, there's a lot to enjoy, but it might not be everyone's cup of tea.

_childDocuments_.review: !!Before the review, I need to point out that the devs added mandatory screen flash on crit. If you're epileptic, avoid these. It gets really irritating sometimes.!!Right after playing FFI, the story here is leagues better.Sadly does not include Soul of Rebirth content from the GBA... but let's be honest that'd just introduce a whole pile of extra grinding. Oh right, yes, about that...The quirk with this game is that it's *grindy* beyond all comprehension. Every single thing can be grinded for hours and hours by laming it out in battles (I mean that - blasting through encounters is not how you gain exp - the more time you waste the more exp you may or may not gain toward specific stats, weapons, and/or spells).There's really no difficulty here once you treat this game as a stat management grindfest.With no standard level system to hold you back, the potential is absurd - in a good way, if you're into that.Wait, why am I recommending something so grindy? Because the worst part (spells) can be boosted to 4x speed. You should do that. Look at my play time - I did a boosted run and decided to try an unboosted run where I still grinded everything to specific levels. Just... turn on the 4x spell exp boost. Everything else is fine and if you're having issues it means you're just failing to understand how the exp systems work.Oh, the systems... I guess I should bring something up. I tried looking up formulae and found incorrect information regurgitated everywhere, hopefully because what I found applied to an older version. I'll just give the two most important ones that I used right here. Surely it'll help to have the correct information for this version in one more place.Weapon: Enemy Rank - Level + AttackIf Weapon Exp>0 Then add +10 to Weapon ExpRegardless of how many hits, or no hits at all, one attack command counts as 1 toward AttackAttack is doubled by dual-wielding the same weapon typeDual-shield gives experience as if using Unarmed and a ShieldSpell: Enemy Rank - Level + Casts +2Enemy Rank is the Mean Average of all Enemy Ranks present in an encounter, rounded down.Enemies fleeing can cause issues since they're removed from the average (unless they were the only enemy).There is no double cast effect in there, and no it's not +3. Again, look at my playtime. I've been keeping track of my exp externally and comparing it with the game during my unboosted playthrough. Everything matches up and has been matching up for all the hours.If you want double (or rather, quadruple), the boost option that I recommend applies afterward, to the final result.Turn the 4xBoost on, for spell experience. For the love of being able to enjoy this game, because it's actually really good if you're not standing there flailing your arms casting the same thing to no effect for combined hours (and I mean *hours*).Seeing that... you should have an idea of what you're getting into. This isn't just a game with a single exp bar per character with simple levels no no no. You're not getting into that. If this isn't your thing then it's time to run away.If you're intrigued and want to start building the characters up, give this game a whirl.Final note: Contrary to popular belief, you do not need to attack your own party members, unless going for absolute max everything, but even then you'll only *need* to do it for specific spells, to be honest.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this on Steam Deck, and it worked perfectly fine.Final Fantasy II is an interesting game; it is both a sequel to the original FF and a re-envisioning of the formula. Some things are very similar: certain spells, items, monsters, airships, etc. And some things are completely different: namely the leveling and spell systems, and the more fleshed out story. These new elements are very hit-and-miss, making the game very devisive.Let's start with the gameplay. The main element people hate on the most is probably the leveling system. Rather than gaining XP and leveling your character, you level up individual stats and proficiencies by using them: hitting people with spells levels up that spell, losing HP increases your max HP, etc. This isn't unheard of nowadays - this system has since be popularized by the recent Elder Scrolls games. And its main strength is its main weakness: your characters end up fitting into a certain playstyle. While it gives your characters... well... character, it also pigeonholes them into roles, and when a new enemy does a thing that you aren't prepared for, you might have to go back and grind lower level enemies for a couple hours. As an example, I had Basuna leveled up to level 2 to combat off poison, but mostly ignored it. When enemies started destroying me with the Stun status effect, I had to then backtrack and just start randomly casting Basuna to get it up to level 4 or so. (And speaking of spells, all spells can be cast one single or multiple targets at once... a fact that I swear the game neglects to inform you about). All and all, I really enjoy the gameplay, but at times it is either a 9+/10 or a 2-/10.The story is very interesting, albeit littered with tropes. There's this rebellion against an evil emperor going on, and all the characters have names, roles, and simple motives. It is more engaging early on compared to the previous FF, but things get way duller that FF1 by the end. There's also this idea that your 4th party member changes based on the story - but it always seems ham-fisted, and they are ALWAYS underleveled. So you might need to grind them up for the next dungeon.The dungeons are by far the worst part of the game. At the beginning of the game, they are fine - some even have you revisit them in not-annoying ways. But by the end, you will be running around a giant maze, bumping into walls to find hidden opening to get a chest. Some dungeons have a HUGE annoying spike in difficulty. And the last dungeon starts out hard, gets EASIER at the end, then the final boss comes in and is ridiculously overpowered and annoying. All in all, Final Fantasy II is definitely a game worth checking out, especially if you are a fan of Skyrim but want a retro JRPG. The game is interesting, and I had fun
