_childDocuments_.review: To begin this review, I will state that I enjoyed this game.  However, I don't recommend it for a couple of reasons that BUGGED me I'll get into within the Cons section later on.Let's start off with what I consider some positives of this game!PROS:Final Fantasy II is notorious among the other Final Fantasy games for having a different way of leveling up.  Your characters level up based on what weapons you use or what spells you cast, plus you can equip anything to anyone in the game. This is interesting because you can make your party anything you want!  An example of this is your dedicated healer, otherwise known as your White Mage.  In this game, you can make them a durable White Mage by giving them that brand new set of Golden Armor you just found, or make them a powerhouse who can heal by giving them that there Winged Sword!  Whereas in the other titles, most of the casting classes (or "jobs", if you will) are generally restricted to cloth armor only and aren't capable of using certain weapons.Square, back in the day, tried to have a more narrative-driven story with an actual main cast of characters who aren't just blank slates compared to the first Final Fantasy, and it's not too terrible.  This was a foundation of a trope within the series that boils down to "Empire evil!  Go stop them!" that we tease in future entries.  Granted, it's far from perfect by all means, but I feel that it's still enjoyable.  If anything, it's a nice little trip down memory lane.The music in this particular Pixel Remaster is my favorite soundtrack thus far in the PR series.  I fully admit that one of my main weaknesses when it comes to music in a video game is throwing in some good choir.  The final dungeon and final boss tracks of this game do just that, which makes them sound so much more epic compared to previous renditions of the same tracks.  (At least to me, anyways)The pixel art for the battle scenes is a spot-on remastering of the original Famicom version, and it looks absolutely amazing.As with all the other Pixel Remasters, the game's UI automatically changes based on what control scheme you use.  I've personally used the keyboard, XBox controller, and Playstation controller.  I am unsure if it adapts for the Nintendo Switch Pro controller, but maybe I'll test it out sooner or later.CONS:The leveling system that I praised earlier is a double-edged sword.In my initial playthrough of this game, I didn't have a "dedicated class" for each character.  I pretty much just made everyone a hard-hitting Paladin, for lack of a better term.  Everyone had high damage-dealing weapons, really good armor, and Cure/Esuna (as the latter spell effectively replaces Life at higher levels).  This made the game very trivial, save for a couple of areas I'll get into with the last con.My second playthrough of the game, I chose to have a "dedicated class" for each character, and it did bump up SOME of the challenge, but not by much (again, except for the couple of areas I'll mention at the end).The random encounter rate in this version of Final Fantasy II seems to have been jacked WAY too high.  In every single dungeon or the overworld, I was getting into a random battle every 3 - 5 seconds.  Compared to other versions of Final Fantasy II, this is absurd.  I understand that the only way to level your characters is to get into battles and actually do things (go figure, right), but after you hit certain levels with your weapons or spells, the lower ranked enemies don't grant any experience.  So it felt like everything just came to a crawl in a whole lot of areas where my patience and sanity were getting checked.Some people have complained about the text size or spacing, but that hasn't personally bothered me.  It could be due to them playing at higher resolutions and the text is too small, but I can't speak for everyone who had the issue.During my two runs, any time an enemy has an attack that inflicts a certain status ailment, such as stun or instant death, it had inflicted that status effect 100% of the time on their target.  This was even when I had equipment that nullified or resisted the status effect.  Granted, the only enemy in the game that this didn't happen with me was a Malboro...for some reason.I'm unsure if this was due to a programming oversight or not, but it didn't make the game any better for it.  Compare this version to previous releases of Final Fantasy II, where if an enemy inflicts stun on your character, it would inflict it once.  If your character was already stunned, it wouldn't re-inflict the stun stat again.  This game, however, does re-inflict the status.This was one of the two hurdles of the game that made it unnecessarily difficult.  I had gotten into an encounter with some enemies that inflicted stun on my whole party and it was a long, drawn-out wipe because I was effectively stunlocked to death.The other hurdle was similar.  In the final dungeon of the game, I was Ambushed by a group of a certain enemy that inflicts Instant Death when they hit you. Needless to say, 6 of them versus 4 of us = Instant Wipe.  (For those of you who have experienced this first hand, I apologize for any potential PTSD I may have caused).Now for the two bugs I've found in the game that were still active as of 06/17/2022, almost a year after this game released.  Please note that BOTH caused Final Fantasy II to freeze up, forcing me to close out the game and restart it.The first bug involved an encounter with 4 Antlions (that inflict stun with their attacks).  I downed two of them and they downed two of my party members.  I managed to put one of them to sleep with the Sleep Blade, but they still successfully stunlocked me.  The Antlion that was still awake decided to dip out of the fight (probably due to it leaving the oven on), thus causing its buddy there to continue sleeping while Firion and Guy were helplessly stunned.  The battle locked up and I let it sit there for over twenty minutes, clinging onto hope that it would fix itself.  But it never did...The second bug involved my healer casting the Life spell on a group of undead enemies to kill them instantly.  The game, again, locked up and did not progress forward at all.  Firion just stood there like a deer caught in the headlights and forgot what to do next.After researching this, I found that if the only enemies left are a group of undead, you cast the Life spell on them, and it successfully kills ALL of the remaining undead, the game doesn't know how to comprehend this level of madness and locks up...Considering this game is almost a year old and these issues still exist, I have a feeling that Square Enix won't be patching them out.  They're relatively easy to avoid (especially the Undead one), but the fact that they're still in the game bothers me on a personal level.FINAL VERDICT:I enjoyed the game, but unless you're a huge JRPG fan or Final Fantasy fan (or both!), I can't fully suggest it for newcomers to the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Can we please get an "Ultimate FF[Number] Remake" that combines all remake content and artstyles into one singular game? FF2 PR is a remaster of the original FF2, meaning it does not include content added in earlier remakes of the original title, which may not be a huge deal for everyone, but does bother me as I don't like missing out on content, and it may be a bit confusing to consumers what exactly they're getting here. I'm aware remaster =/= remake, but honestly a project that seeks to combine all versions of the final fantasy games into one convenient entry would be preferable. FF2 is probably the easiest final fantasy game you will ever play, and honestly I had more fun with it than FF1 because of the system behind that. In this game, everything increases based on usage. Your stats, skills, and magic all increase as you use them and thus you get a system in which everyone can be proficient at everything and anything if you're willing to grind it out for long enough. Sadly, while this experimentation is fun, this game was not at all designed in a way to combat the most obvious problems such a free system would provide. It doesn't take much to realize that you can sacrifice one party member attacking the enemy to instead cast a useless spell in the encounter to increase it's usages for when it'll be useful later. Or purposely allow your characters to take damage so you can heal them increasing heal's potency and usage count too AND their health pool. The enemies in the game don't really use this freedom against you and even with a minimal amount of grinding, you'll be stomping through most of them. Grinding honestly makes the game even easier than it already is with the only thing slightly ailing you being enemies casting status effects. It's a shame that wasn't fleshed out more because it really is interesting for all it's faults.When it comes to the story, there isn't much to speak about other than two things. The first thing being the absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ shenanigans that happen with the 4th party slot. Your 4th party member is mainly a temporary spot held by different characters throughout the story, and honestly, I like it as it keeps the game fresh and lets you see more of these plot-relevant characters, even if it can't do too much with them. It makes the journey feel a bit more varied and adds a sense of realism to this world. They aren't just NPCs watching you do all the work, but fellow allies constantly joining your party to assist your quest, it's good and I wish more games tried doing this with their side characters.The second thing being the addition of "Passwords" which are just highlighted colored text in conversations that you must learn to add to your collection, and then use on the right NPC/place to progress the story. There's no real consequence or benefit to getting the password right or wrong as you can always pick each word on the list to every NPC until you find the right thing making it mainly pointless other than signposting who/where you need to talk to/go to next. I don't really like it and I'm glad it was scrapped in future titles.Overall, the gameplay in this one is a bit wacky and the story isn't all that interesting, but it's pretty short even for full completion and I can't really say it left me feeling annoyed or disappointed. It's just a short, interesting little RPG thats also worth experiencing if you want to see the earlier Final Fantasy titles.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite all the effort Square Enix put into this Remaster, I still cannot recommend this game to ANYONE...and that's a damn shame.To start with, let's focus on kind things I can say about the Pixel Remaster of Final Fantasy's most infamous title. They finally managed to fix the skill leveling system. Increasing your health and stamina no longer requires you to bash yourself in the head. The leveling of weapon skills now feels natural, increasing as you'd expect it to you as you fight stronger enemies. Leveling shields, and therefore evasion, and therefore Agility, is no longer based on luck. Leveling magic is slightly less painful than before, but still feels underwhelming. Magic doesn't feel impactful until it's extremely high level, and even then it will pale in comparison to most leveled weapons or your bare hands. At least Ultima is no longer glitched. If none of that were enough, the music is hauntingly, beautifully remade in this version. The orchestrations somehow turn some of the worst tunes in franchise history into legitimate pieces of music, and that's not something that should be ignored.Unfortunately, that is where my positive words end. For all the effort placed into fixing FF2's most famous problem, it seems the team forgot to fix all of its other crippling flaws. The encounter rate in this RPG is far too high even for games of its era. It's easily twice to three times as frequent as the original Final Fantasy, a game that basically lived and breathed random encounters. While already frustrating in and of itself, it's compounded by the fact that regular enemies are never challenging. The game constantly throws weak cannon fodder at you, slowing the pace of the game down and forcing you to deal more with annoyance than threat as they inflict resource-draining status effects on you. Boss fights are only notable because of their hilariously overweighted stats, causing characters that were once hitting for 200+ damage to hit for single digits. I suppose this could be an argument for leveling your magic, but as previously stated, Magic is underwhelming in every other instance.Then we have the dungeons...though I hesitate to call them that. The dungeons in Final Fantasy 2 seem to be ripped right out of the pages of an amateur Advanced Dungeons and Dragons DM. The very first dungeon of the game is a winding labyrinth 5 floors deep full of enemies that have nothing to do with area or the story at hand. Said floors are populated by doors that more often than anything, lead to dead ends that start you off in the middle of a closet, six steps from the exit, just so you have a chance to get another encounter before leaving. Of course, ONE of those doors is actually the way forward, so you'll be forced to check them all to get lucky. Resources are scarce and rewards even scarcer. There's no joy to be had here, and it's only the first of many, many dungeons in this game. It is a sign of all you have left to look forward to, which bodes ill for the rest of the experience.Anything else I could say would simply hammer in the points I've already made. Everything about this game compounds in on itself, making the experience worse the longer you stick with it. It tries to wear you down more than it tries to let you play it. It is an exercise in perseverance more than a video game. If you enjoy tormenting yourself and grinding yourself against a system that is TRYING to defeat you, then PERHAPS you might find some entertainment in Final Fantasy 2. Sadly, I cannot, and I don't believe most people will. This is the ONLY Pixel Remaster I do not recommend. Stay far, far away if you value your health.

_childDocuments_.review: Aaah...Final Fantasy II. The Final Fantasy that the internet hates...I highly recommend Final Fantasy II: Pixel Remaster for those who have never played it and/or those that missed the original Final Fantasy II on the NES. Having played both I will say, without a doubt, that Pixel Remaster should be peoples' first choice. Especially with recent patches, where people can regulate and balance the difficulty as they wish.  FF2, regardless of version however, is notorious for its high encounter rate(especially in dungeons!) and an open-ended or"weird" leveling system. The original NES version reportedly contained quite a number of game-breaking glitches. To me, it is these aspects of FF2 that gave it its, imo, undeserved reputation. However, Final Fantasy  II: PE has largely solved these issues with one, being a much better and technically sound game than the original. And two, an in-game mechanic to balance difficulty and rewards.Now let me get to the good stuff. One thing I appreciate about FF2 is its dungeons. To me, they are pretty much the 'meat' of the game since most of the in-game progression takes place inside of them. The story, although minimal (rebel army vs empire), is serviceable and well-presented. The rotating cast of characters is actually an interesting aspect of the game that I like. Also, (get ready...) yes I like the leveling system. I would argue that its biggest flaw, the potential to create game-breaking characters, is also its biggest strength.

_childDocuments_.review: FF2 has a decent story, some flaws, tweaked gameplay, and a great re-orchestrated soundtrack. Overall it was pretty enjoyable.There are some flaws that mar the experience from time to time. You primarily have 3 party members, so your 4th will always be under-leveled. This is both an interesting approach, but is not as efficient in the long run (read handicap). The other element is that late into the game, there are some enemies (2 in particular) which are flat out broken, so avoid them in packs if you can (great malboro, coeurl).The gameplay has been adjusted in a few ways to remove some of the grind that was part of the originals (you'll still have to a little). This is a net positive in a game that clearly you need to grind in to progress.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II is an incredible departure from the first game, and I mean this in the best possible way. Rather than retread old ground, the second game in the series sought to make its mark both in mechanics and story, while bringing us eventual staples of the series, like the beloved Chocobo.First, unlike the first game (and most other Final Fantasy games), the leveling system responds to your actions in battle. Much like RPG's that wouldn't come out for another 20+ years, if you want to be a mage: then use magic. If you want to tank hits, then you have to get hit. The party does not earn flat "experience". Instead, they gain proficiency FROM their experience.Then, there is the story. Of course, being the newer game, a more robust story is expected. However, Final Fantasy II is anything but a light hearted adventure. At it's core, this is a story of war and loss. This is the first time in the series, and certainly not the last, that we explore tragedy in our heroes adventures. In order to achieve victory over evil, inevitable sacrifice must be made. These sacrifices come in loss of life, but even more compellingly: through the loss of a WAY of life.In all of Final Fantasy canon, this game is usually a forgotten whisper. Part of a cliff note on the way to the more successful Final Fantasy IV. But do not be fooled. This game was bold and it is full of heart. I had more feels for 8-bit pixel characters flickering into nothingness than I have felt for AAA sagas that spared no expense to animate every shed tear.This game stands shoulder to shoulder with the first, not as a clone, but a companion. Join Firion and company on their campaign against the empire. If you don't stop them, who will?

_childDocuments_.review: This is, to me, the best version of this game out there right now.  I've played the NES, PS1, and GBA versions of it.The leveling system for weapons is simplified (arguably too simplified if you ask me), the music sounds great, and the auto-save is a very nice feature to help combat the large amount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game throws at you.I don't know if it works like this in this version but in previous games your chance to be ambushed was determined by Firion's Agility, and even with 90+ agility I was regularly getting ambushed.  That in itself isn't a problem, the problem is when you factor in the game's other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.Any enemy that can inflict a status ailment on hit has a 100% chance to do so.  So when you're ambushed by a group of enemies with status ailments, it can be a situation where you're simply ♥♥♥♥♥♥.  This happened to me at least 10 times, with ambushes that nearly led to me being killed due to simple bad RNG happened many more times than that.  In the final dungeon alone I died 3 times to ambushes from enemies who had a 100% chance to instantly kill you on hit.Leveling Magic is about as easy as it is in the GBA version, which is to say it's still a pain.  I know there are cheese strats but unless you look them up you're unlikely to stumble onto them (and I didn't want to use a guide for cheese strats).  So without cheese strats magic was mostly worthless.  Early on it was ok against some enemies, but late game I used 4 spells: Cure, Esuna, Haste, and Berserk.  I enjoyed my time maybe halfway into the game, but after that it was tedious.  I only beat the game because I'm stubborn and like to beat all the versions of Final Fantasy games.  If you feel the need to beat a version of FF2, this is the easiest one, but that's the only real praise I can give it.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone initially cautious about diving into the "Final Fantasy 2" remaster, I was pleasantly surprised by the end of my playthrough. The game's unique leveling system, a departure from the familiar systems of other FF titles that might be better known, allows skills like weapons, magic, and armor to level up individually based on usage as opposed to an overall character level. This mechanic, initially a point of concern due to perceived difficulty and grinding constantly reiterated when this game is mentioned, turned out to be an unfounded worry.Despite not being a seasoned RPG player, I found the system neither cumbersome nor detracting from my overall enjoyment. The remaster offers a refreshing experience, retaining the charm of a classic JRPG while breathing new life into its visuals. Don't go overboard grinding away, or cheesing it with any strats you might see commonly recommended because its simply not needed. Min max if that's your thing, but don't feel you need to in order to just sit down and enjoy a playthrough.Some con's I suppose, and there always are. The encounter rate is kind of absurd, somehow I lived with it, but I didn't love it. There are mods that can assist in reducing the encounter rate, or even disable/enable encounters full stop. It also has all the same issues as the other pixel remasters in that the walk speed is incorrectly mapped resulting in stutter, again there is a mod that can allow you to resolve that and I would recommend it if you notice this and are bothered by it.It may not be my game of the year, but for fans of JRPGs who can appreciate the aged yet updated art style and classic JRPG styled turn based gameplay, this "pixel remaster" is definitely worth your time if you go in with those expectations in mind.

This review could be a 5,000 word essay listing out all of the stuff that's wrong, but I don't want to spoil the game for you. _childDocuments_.review: FF2 is both a step up and a step down from it's predecessor. It's much bigger than the first game and the main characters this time around have personalities and actually interact with the world around them, instead of just being spoke at.What it doesn't do well, however, is the gear/levelling. You're tasked with levelling up weapons and spells individually, rather than just getting stronger yourself and then upgrading your gear. This results in a bit of a grind if you want to swap your characters weapons or "classes" around mid/late game as they're basically useless until they level their proficiency up. This couple with random stat upgrades which, if memory serves, isn't really explained all that well...levelling just felt confusing. But I was making progress, so it is what it is. The game built up to a good finale and after spending some time grinding those last few achievements I managed to 100% the game in around 17-18 hours which was a pretty big up from the 10-11 the first game took. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: The infamous Final Fantasy II.  This game served as the introduction to a lot of iconic Final Fantasy staples.  The pixel remaster is a fantastic way to get into this title although similarly to FF1, a lot of the fundamental issues with the original game still carry over.Good things worth noting include the visuals, amazing soundtrack, original cast (despite being underdeveloped), and to provide a controversial opinion - I actually enjoy the progression system.  Although it is understandable why the progression system is despised by so many, but I found the leveling to be enjoyable.  It is nice seeing your stat numbers go up every few battles, and makes random encounters feel more rewarding when trying to crawl through the dungeons.With that being said, there are a lot of things that justify an unfavorable opinion.  The encounter rate is insane, status ailments still land 100% of the time against your characters, the fourth party slot is constantly changing which makes it difficult to reach full potential, and the game feels like it drags a little too long near the end.  Despite completing the game in 21 hours including achievements it does feel pretty slow.  I am giving this a recommendation for massive fans of the franchise, but won't recommend it for casual RPG fans.  The game has a lot of neat ideas, but suffers from balancing issues.  Most encounters will range from being very easy to feeling cheaply difficult (mainly due to status ailments).  There is still plenty of fun to be had in the exploration, simplistic story, and watching your characters grow into power houses.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of unfair reviews spanning over many versions and decades of the game's existence.I think mostly all of the bad reviews are just recycled from other bad reviews they've read and self-fulfilled them in their own gameplay like a prophecy.I will briefly review this game through a proper lens, as an RPG made in 1988 as the American sequel to the first FF title in the series. But I will review the experience playing specifically this version of the game. So no jabs based off of bugs that were solved decades ago in the GBA version and now. Form your own opinion before you buy.===============  Leveling System===============This is where most everyone says this game fails. To put it simply without having to read a long guide, instead of your characters leveling up traditionally, by character level going up and subsequent stats like HP and DEF going up in the background proportionally to your character/class. In FFII, your characters level up each stat, weapon, and spell individually from each other. There is no 'experience' rather, these stats level up by the amount of times you use them in battle. Regardless of the strength of the enemy you're fighting, each attack counts towards leveling up your weapon/spell regardless of how much damage you do or if you miss. In theory, you could level up all your spells and weapon types to the max (16) off of goblins before you progress the storyline at all. You do not have a class, so each character is a blank slate with slightly differing stats (Maria has more Spirit for example, making her a better white magic caster early) but you can format your party any way that you wish, have a black mage dual wielding axes and wearing full armor at the slight cost to magic accuracy but gain a lot of versatility and survival. Stats like HP, DEF, and MP level up under their own conditions, but will raise naturally with your chosen playstyle.People say that the fastest way to level up HP is to have your party members attack each other. This is because HP leveling up is based on how much damage you take in battle, take more damage and survive the battle, you have a higher % chance your max HP will increase after the battle. For decades, the 'pro strategy' was to get in a battle with a weak enemy that deals 0 damage to your party and then attack your party members to the brink of death, win the battle, go to an Inn and repeat. People feel the need to do this because they want to be more survivable, but they don't have to do this, it is just an option and I'm here to tell you that it is a BS waste of time. That method is the fastest way to level up max HP but at a great cost, many bosses and even overworld enemies deal %HP as damage up to a certain point, so if you don't have the same damage to match that then you're damning yourself to battles where you need to constantly heal. That's because your stats like ATT specifically raise incredibly slow when you attack your own party members. People don't realize this and they feel like the leveling system is a burden when in reality they made it a burden on themselves by abusing a fringe leveling method.There is another one, spamming teleport in town, using cure to heal the caster for HP lost by using teleport, then walk to an Inn and repeat to fast level cure and teleport. This is embarrassing that so many people actually think that is worth your time, but people even review the game poorly because of it. Test it out for yourself and you will see how much slower it is to just using teleport on enemies in the overworld like the traditional FF player would do. Instead of using teleport once, then cure, then walkinto an Inn, cutscene, then repeat is only one teleport cast every minute, while in battle you can use it like 12 times a minute. The things people hate about the leveling system are so self-inflicted.Pros- Leveling system offers astounding freedom and truly rewarding moments of experimentation- For 1988, this was a great crack at an open world. There are of course areas you can reach only to enter and have a locked gate staring your party in the face. But some areas like Fynn Castle still has encounters on.- Open world offers a fun challenge for daring players who like to hunt for items they have no business having yet.- Dual wielding finally makes physical characters capable of slaying more than one mob per turn, pair that with another one or two physical characters and you can clear many encounters in one turn.- Experience gained by times used regardless if it misses allows for easier party change-ups on the fly (I trained axes on a whim with guy and got it to level 8 by the end of the dungeon)Cons- Keyword system is a bit weak. It isn't something anyone really gets stuck on, if you don't know what to do next, just try a bunch of keywords or items with the princess or gordon, chances are the most recent word you learned is what you need to say to progress, and even then it only takes about 30 seconds max to try every word in the game. Its just a weakly implimented system that can only be used on key npc's and seem like it could be scrapped for a linear dialogue experience like FF1. - Dungeon designs are.. very testy. You need to be patient, many dungeons are maze-like and far from linear (often having to backtrack a few floors and go back down a different way) and there are many dead-end rooms with really high encounter rates. This is obviously meant to force the character to train or to kill off the player and force them to train elsewhere or rethink their party. But there are better ways to go about that in retrospective.- The fourth party member is ever changing until the end of the game, and boy are they pretty damn useless and not worth investing time into because you will eventually never use them again. I often just left the fourth member dead and found that the dungeons were so much easier without them. The fourth member should have stats based off of yours in my opinion, that way they are an actually welcome addition. Minwu is an exeptionm though, whose vast library of spells gives you a fun taste of how powerful a white mage can be.- Plot was supposed to be dark and have character arcs but its boring. Deaths are really orchestrated beforehand and you aren't invested enough in the characters to feel much of anything. It is really up to your imagination there.- There is a sword you get towards the end of the game, Blood Sword, that is so stupidly overpowered that the final boss and dungeon is pitiful and mundane. Extremely anticlimactic, I could see this being a good thing if i really went out of my way to get the item, thru missable dungeons and such, but you can just talk to someone and get it.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent sequel built upon great foundations. This time they actually added character dialogue and a more in depth story. I was also very surprised to see that the leveling and class build systems were completely removed and replaced with something else entirely. It was interesting to see that the basic xp-level up system was replaced with an early version of the skill system you would later see in the Elder Scrolls franchise. This was mildly annoying to learn at first, but about a 3rd into the game it really allowed for in depth variety and customization for each party member. The only complaint I have really is the constant cycling of the fourth party member, it adds for an inconsistent experience. Some are really good and broken while others are complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (Leon). Overall, Recommend to newcomers and those familiar already.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok first of all this game is not bad at all.....I def can see why people may not like it since it does not follow the traditional level system of JRPGs.  Square took a different approach to this game with the player making the characters into whatever they want since the character skills increase the more they use them. So if you give a character a sword and constantly use the sword then the character will improve with swords and get much stronger....same thing with armor and magic...if you use a lot of healing magic then you will be stronger when using white magics. Back when this game originally released players complained that the game was broken since you could increase your characters stats by simply attacking your team and healing them (Thus maxing your Health, magic, attack and other stats) but in the pixel remastered it def didn't feel like that was needed to be done in order to get through the game and enjoy it, when I played my characters stats went up pretty well with a bit of grinding but nothing extreme.The story def improved in this game compared to the first Final Fantasy. You play as a group of young warriors who join a rebellion in order to stop a power hungry emperor and his empire from taking over the world.  Throughout the game different warriors will join your team to help you stop the empire and take back towns and land.  The only problem I had with so many different party members joining your team throughout the story is I never fully could get attached to them since they wouldn't be with your team for long and every time a new member would join you had to level them up a bit for them to be useful (you would finally get your last permanent party member  right before the end of the game and they were way under leveled).Overall the game was fun and improved on somethings from the first Final Fantasy game. Though the level system is different this is still a fun JRPG and should be played.

Or you can skip it. Up to you.

_childDocuments_.review: I just beat the game and now want to include my thoughts about this controversial game.Excuse the poor structure of the review but it's like 3am when writing this and I just wanna get it out there. First of all the concept of a 4th switching party member. You're always missing a 4th fixed party member until the very end. The idea is good but the execution is really bad. The characters are really weak compared to your group and mostly even get one or two shot by random encounters which just makes them useless. I didn't even bother reviving my 4th crewmate half of the time. You can't use them except for melee combat unless they come with a spell or two equipped which is negligible compared to your party of three. Equpping them with gear only helps a little with this problem. So overall this game has to be played as a party of three, which is fine since it gives the game a different dynamic too.The skill system is a cool concept too. You pick what you like and start improving in those areas. Like broadswords? Use broadswords -> get better with broadswords -> do more damage with broadswords and so on. The same goes for the spells in the game. The game has oh so incredibly many more spells than the first game it's awesome. The remaster makes all of the spells look really cool too but sadly the character system hinders you in using a lot of the spells you can get. Since all spells you learn start at level 1 which makes them useless later down the line - buffs are marginal, debuffs miss 99% of the time, even when leveled somewhat. It's just easier to melee mobs unless they're very resistant to melee attacks. I gotta say though the leveled spells don't just improve in damage but also in visual effects. Every three levels or so your spells become visibly more powerful and it's really cool to see spells just become flashier and flashier - this can be experienced in the very beginning of the game already. It's neat. They nerfed AOE damage heavily though which is understandable compared to the first game but still using AOE in this game is practically a waste of mana. I only did it when actually trying to level spells cuz I knew I could use about 10 more spells than I usually would. Because of the skill system in the game the encounter rate is really really high with enemies. You need the "xp" to level your skills but that makes it that you have to fight every 3-6 seconds which makes travel horrible.This ties in the next two major flaws I have with the game. - I felt my time actually wasted. The dungeons in the game present you with a lot of doors, which are an effort to get to and then usually have NOTHING behind them. I would say like 90% of doors the game has are pointless to have you encounter more enemies and "waste" your time. - Same thing goes for chest loot. It might just be me but in the first game I felt like many chests had interesting items in them. This game gives you either rarely a good weapon or armor piece for making a pretty big detour from where you actually need to go for a, for example, regular potion. It made me not wanna go open chests anymore because I'm sorry but I don't need a single item of Ether or a regular HP potion. It feels like just another way to "waste" your time with more encounters. The story is okay - it's nothing major but there is some storytelling going on, more than the first game but still very basic. Was okay though. The addition of a map and also quick safe as well as auto battle made this game a lot more enjoyable because these games really need it. That's about all I've got to say. I'd say it was interesting to see and I liked the concepts but I can really understand why this game is not very liked. TLDR: If you want to play this game be prepared for a very very grindy experience where you feel like the devs actually tried to stretch your time with many doors to check and many not so useful chests to open. I would still recommend it if you enjoy the final fantasy universe and want to experience the whole genre and where everything began to grow until today. Final verdict 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Well, they finally did it. They finally made FF2 a good game. After 36 years of desperately trying to rebalance the horrendous original, they finally succeeded. Is it perfect? HELL no. But beyond a complete and total reimagining, I'm not sure what else they can do at this point. This turd has been polished to a mirror sheen, and honestly? It's good. Not great, but I might even be tempted to say this is superior to FF1 now. Before the most recent update, such a statement would've been heresy.Now, things like stat growth and overall difficulty were balanced a long time ago with the GBA and PSP versions. People gripe about those things to no end, but they were...pretty much fixed 20 years ago. But that's not FF2's biggest problem. Oh no. The two biggest issues were the magic leveling/grinding, and the dungeon design.Magic leveling is a cinch now thanks to Auto-Battle and the Boost function. So if you're at the end of the game and need to get Leon up to speed, doing so doesn't take long at all. Just crank the boost to 4x, set every other party member to Defend, and let the auto-battle go. It's that simple. In addition, Magic Interference is now fully displayed, instead of being an invisible stat. I had no idea it was even a thing prior to this version.The dungeon design is still garbage, but you no longer need to worry about dead ends thanks to the map, and, thank god, you can turn off random encounters. That means if you walk into one of the dreaded "monster rooms" by accident, you can just turn off encounters and walk back out. The ways you can tailor the difficulty to your liking here are actually very nice. Some may say this version is a cakewalk, but I'd rather play a cakewalk than the nauseatingly tedious original.Key terms are no longer a pain in the ass as the ones you can use are now highlighted in red. Dual-shields is now a viable strategy since you can still use your fists with that setup. Setting someone in the back row no longer gimps their HP. There are so many little fixes under the hood, and they all serve to make this the best version of FF2, and the ONLY version worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: is not a good game.I can think of only two reasons that somebody should play this game:1) They want to be able to say "I've played all the numbered  games!"2) They want to make RPGs, and want to experience a bad oneComing straight from playing , the first few hours of  were very surprising.  It has a lot of good and innovative ideas: one of your slots is reserved for companions that rotate in and out as the story progresses; characters aren't bound by a specific class, and can learn/equip anything you want; there's a keyword system allowing for (primitive) dialogue branches; and abilities/stats increase with usage.  Wow!Unfortunately, it all quickly falls apart.  The mechanics are good ideas on paper, but aren't fun.  The rotating character isn't worth leveling at all, because you know they'll leave shortly.  Your characters quickly become locked into whatever soft class you chose at the beginning, because it would take too long to train them in anything else.  The next step in the story is often unclear, and progression is locked behind learning certain words.  All strategy is removed from the game, because you're rewarded for spamming the same attacks and abilities over and over.Oh, and status effects are 100% effective, which doesn't make any sense.  An enemy ambush can wipe you out before you have a chance to do anything, and you can put the final boss to sleep so it never takes any turns at all.My recommendation is to skip this one and play the others instead.

_childDocuments_.review: FF2 has a lot of problems:- The first 2/3 of  the game are very slow going, boring dungeons, too many fetch quests- The abundance of empty rooms drove me nuts- The leveling system is confusing at best- The enemies are a strange fit (Zombies on airships, really?)- The first 15 hours or so it is too easy and only then I really had to learn the mechanics of the battle system... but... in the last 1/3, the story comes together and things happen, all of a sudden the design of the dungeons was much more fun for me and after fighting through the last dungeon and killing the final boss at 2:30 AM I had a great time! :-)

_childDocuments_.review: It's basically the same as the first game but with major changes. First, NO MORE LEVEL UPS! Sounds like a bad thing right? Nope. You can become overpowered and make the final boss feel like cakewalk if you just grind. Second, you can use more weapons like spears, bows, axes, lances, sword and canes. Though you usually just want the axes, spears or swords. Third, magic is learnable by mostly everyone and you can level them up like weapons too. The only "bad" thing about this game is that it's too easy!!! But the story is great, so is the soundtrack. I give this a 7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I definitely get why people don't like this game. I think it's enjoyable though. The leveling system is strange but it's easy enough to grind and get overpowered. I liked the story. It's simple compared to the later entries, but it was pretty ambitious for the time. And like all of the Pixel Remasters the soundtrack is amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately there have been some choices in this game which make it really tedious to go through. Monsters that can apply unavoidable (unless you get stuff like Ribbon which doesn't appear until the end of the game) debuffs that can render your party immobile just to sit there and watch them die, the whole leveling of weapon skills and spells making a lot of gear and spells useless because everything starts at level 1 regardless of when you find it and the fact that the optimize feature doesn't work for casters. Then there's also a hidden mechanic about Spell Penalty on gear which is invisible without mods and not explained at all in the game.I'm quite the Square Enix fan but this game was just horrible to play. The only reason I finished it was for the achievements but otherwise I would have quit a lot sooner.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II is not as bad as everybody makes it out to be.  I loved this game with just a few exceptions such as the weapon leveling, Coeurls, and rare encounter chance being 1/64.  Overall the game is amazing it really didn't take long to get overpowered before the game was over and I would def say play this and experience it for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy II is the first Final Fantasy game that didn't have classes in it. Unlike 1 and 3 it is very story-rich, and I was surprised at how they walked that back for 3, but then 4 and onward went story-rich again. You play the role of 3 Orphans whose parents were murdered by the evil empire. Instead of having classes like most FF games, you have a variety of skills related to weapons, and each spell is its own skill too. You cast a spell's level equal to the skill level of said spell, so if you have fire leveled up to 16, it costs 16 mp and is Fire 16. It does the equivalent damage of a 16th tier fire spell, which can be absolutely devastating obviously.This is the mold in which all future FF games were cast story-wise, with 3 being an odd hiccup along the way where they made something more like 1 again. Great game, and maybe one day I'll actually finish it.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: 100% in about 15 hours with turning off encounters occasionally.FF2 is an improvement over the first in some areas but a huge step back in others. You have somewhat actual characters now that can speak occasionally but that is pretty rare. The leveling system is a mess something you'd be more likely to see in a Saga game. You also have a rotating 4th member of your team the entire game so you are constantly releveling someone. The skill/magic system leveling is broken you'd never naturally max weapons even with a 4x boost without knowing the trick. Unlike the first there are missables if you are going for all achievements.At the end of the day you can still just auto battle with weapon attacks and do just fine. Helps to buff at the end of the game to speed it up. Offensive magic peaks early then falls off significantly.It's an interesting experiment but I would never want to replay this game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Some of the dungeons can be a bit confusing and annoying, even with the maps, and the skill leveling system is a little more complicated than it needs to be - ok it's a LOT more complicated than it ever needed to be.That being said, it's still a fun game, long as you manage to figure out where you need to go, so you don't have to wonder around too much fighting the random encounters.The "free-form class system" (that is: the ability to assign any spell to any character) and the little "key phrases/objects" system are both nice touches.Be careful though, certain areas on the map have enemies that are far too dangerous for a good chunk of the game. You probably will take a bit of a beating trying to figure out where to go...or rather, where you're not meant to go.I was warned about the leveling system not being very well-liked by fans, and while I do agree, as I've said above, it did actually grow on me a little. My recommendation is, just play the game normally, and only stop to grind if you run into a dungeon you can't seem to get through. If you worry too much about "raising your numbers" you're going to have a bad time.As for the price...I think there's enough "game" here for 11.99 euro, whatever the other currency equivalents are.Enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Loads of bugs. _childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended when on sale or for those who want games for historical purposes or for special challenge runs.FF2 has some good ideas with an Elder Scrolls system of learning by doing, but for a regular playthrough it feels a bit off.  I imagine this would be much more fun for a speedrun or if you enjoy putting certain challenges or restrictions on yourself.The dungeons are the biggest issue with lots of empty door rooms that just pad time, and nothing to really interact with side from later game damage tiles. _childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Oh god no.I played and completed this game within 24 hours after beating the first. It made some improvements, and got a lot wrong. I'll start with the good before going into the bad, which there is a lot of.The story is improved from 1. It makes sense and the overarching objective is made clear: defeat the empire. Basic story, but some good plot points. Think Star Wars, with rebels and empires. The game takes away a party member, which adds a dimension to the story telling. You don't feel like a force of nature, with characters directing it to progress the story. You get a few characters come and go, which adds the feeling that you actually have allies, rather than turning up, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ up and leaving. Characters actually recur, and going back to Altair after every quest makes it seem important in the grand scheme of things.Now for that bad. There is a lot.The progression system. What a downgrade! The classes have no personality. You can become proficient in any skill. Of course, there are limitations such as stats, but it feels like it is there to bolster the broken progression system. Each time you use a skill, you get experience in that skill. You then level up those skills and gain stats corresponding to the skill. There are no party member levels. This is where it gets annoying. The other form of progression is equipment. Anyone can wield anything. So if you have a sword fighter and can't obtain a better sword in a while, that character does not progress. Their damage output plateaus until you finder a better sword. To combat this, I grinded every weapon class on every character to max level, so I could equip what I want when I found it. This made the game very grindy.  You gain stamina from taking damage, leading to situations where you attack your own party, just to level it up. Magic is slightly different. Every time you level up a spell, it gets more powerful, and you SOMETIMES gain some MP. The MP cost goes up. Say you have 10 MP. If you use one spell for 1 MP, and level it up, it goes to 2 MP, and you may gain some additional MP, up to 15 MP. Before you could get 10 hits off. Now you can only get 7. MP progression should be uniform with the cost, if not outweigh it. As spells level, you should AT LEAST be able to cast the more powerful version as often as the lower level. Instead you have to spend more Gil on restoring MP. The solution is to spend Gil to get more spells you are never going to use and level them up to increase a party member's total MP.  You have to do this with every character, to get the best stats, and you just fall into having 3 core classes in the end. Why would you not just have distinct roles and classes with a separate progression curve? It gets worse when you have to constantly switch out the 4th slot for whatever story character is coming with you, otherwise they are just an item mule from being under-levelled. It feels like all this was to get player to play longer and use all spells. It is artificial game length.Speaking of artificially lengthening the game, next is level design. It sucks. There are empty rooms. These serve to trick the player into going into them, spawning them in the middle of the room and taking more steps in a dungeon, leading to more encounters. It would be alright if they had loot as it serves as a reward for exploring. But they most often don't. The worst part is, the longest path to a door is always the correct one. If there are 3 doors in a level, the one furthest away will be your objective. If your system can be beaten after a few dungeon levels to learn it, it is a bad system. There is also this stupid trick they do where there are multiple doors and one leads to the next level, while other are empty. Yet more design to lengthen the game.The landmasses are also designed to purposely build long paths between objectives, increasing encounters. This is annoying because you often have to return to Altair after every mission, which means lots of encounters after barely surviving a dungeon. This is so bad, the series stable, the Chocabo was created to zip from the far side of the map to Altair without them. Such an iconic mascot is due to poor level design. You also unlock ships and airships too late in the game. Airships can be paid for from a central town, making it slightly better, and for once, a good design choice. But the game seems very linear due to obstacles where a vehicle is require to progress. I'd much prefer to unlock these earlier but put limitations on where they can land, like the first game restricting ships to ports, or the airship to certain tiles.To finish on a high, the new "Ask, Keyword and Key Item" is pretty good. The party can obtain information and ask previous NPCs about it, leading to some rewards for those who go out and look for greater context.Overall, a downgrade from the first game, which was only alright.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy...Where does one start with Final Fantasy II? It's not perfect? Yeah, let's go with that. As a bit of lightning fast history, the NES version of this game was nothing short of an utter mess. The well intentioned leveling system the designer from who would later go on to create the SaGa series, did not come together as well as it probably seemed to on paper. Flash forward and this game has been ported a great many times. From PSX, to GBA, to PSP and finally this Pixel Remaster. Most iterations have made small tweaks to the system to create a more streamlined experience. In Final Fantasy II you do not level up in a conventional manner. You instead gain stats based on the action you take in combat. In the NES version this would often decrease an opposing stat, but either way it was not quite a smooth incline of difficulty from the start of the game to the end of the game. I'd say by the GBA version this had largely been fixed, but in the Pixel Remaster I think it can be said that Final Fantasy II can now be called an enjoyable experience with a couple of irksome traits.It was often said that the best way to gain stats in the earlier versions was to just beat up on your party so you were always fighting something of relative strength to you. I'd argue that this is a pointless method, at least as of the pixel remaster. Play and fight and you'll soon be balanced correctly, maybe even overpowered, without the need for any tricks.That said, if you're someone who has to do everything in the game then Final Fantasy II might rub you the wrong way. Leveling magic and weapon skills all the way to the cap still takes a lot of grinding for arguably very little payoff. The game difficulty just isn't there to justify it. Visually I find the game quite appealing. Some prefer the sprites from earlier ports, but I think this is mostly preference. The pixel remasters, for better or worse, keep a level of consistency that can be comforting to play. Not to mention that it's fairly mod friendly, so you can clean up some edges like the font or UI, replace the sprites and so on. Sound is wonderful. If you're looking for 8-bit sounds you'll need a mod but the arranged OST for ALL the pixel remasters are quite something to hear. Final Fantasy II also has some of the most underrated music in the franchise i'd say. A very strong point.Story wise...Dark, very dark for it's time. Will it have you on the edge of your seat throughout? No, it's based on the script of a NES game in the end. It does however do surprisingly well. It took FFIV to unseat this game's general plot if you ask me. It's not going to move you to tears, but it will have you rooting for your heroesWhile you are missing the added content from the GBA and PSP ports, I'd say the Final Fantasy II Pixel Remaster is the best overall way to go about playing this bold game. If you've played some of the early FF games I would give this one a chance to warm to you. It will have several things you wish it had handled better, but I think calling this the black sheep of the Final Fantasy series is becoming less and less accurate with each new version.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the FF1 Pixel Remaster, the new music sounds fantastic, and really breaths some new life into an old game. I've been very close to beating this game many times before, but this was the first time that I finally followed through with it. FF2 is usually at the bottom of most people's lists when it comes to Final Fantasy, and I can understand why. My biggest gripes with the game are fairly minuscule, I wish they had used the sprites from "Dawn of Souls," leveling can be a chore and a half (thank you, auto-battle), and I just can't bring myself to care if some characters die because they weren't around long enough to care about them to begin with (Ricard is the homie though). But, for it's flaws, I respect that it tries to stand out when compared to its predecessor. This introduced the revolving party members that would be used in most Final Fantasy games going forwards. And, this was the beginning of the job systems.Is it a perfect RPG, nope. Did I enjoy myself and can I say that completing this game was worth my time, yep. And that's good enough for me.

_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Relative to its immediate predecessor Final Fantasy II doesn't feature archetypal characters that specialise in a given area/style. Each character can cast magic or fight in melee/range freely even though the base stats do tend to favour one over the other. It takes little time to adjust their stats as you see fit once you get the hang of the level up system (The more you do a particular thing, the better you get at it). FFII also lacks a more traditional leveling system, instead allowing you to level each individual stat, weapon type and spell. This is also where there started to be more of a focus on the narrative that gets repeated in various other installments as well as giving your party members, and side characters, personalities in addition to some form of a story arc.One pitfall that I found grating was that while your party is comprised of 4 characters, the 4th character is in constant rotation throughout the game. Meaning whatever investment you put into them is only temporary until they either rejoin, or permanently leave your party, taking whatever you had given them.Overall though, I found the game to be fairly enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Steam really needs a neutral option for reviews because my thoughts on this game are more complex than a thumbs up or down. I'm giving FF2 a 'recommendation' only because I think this is the best possible version I can imagine of the core game.Final Fantasy II has a reputation for being one of the bad games in the series largely because of its grind-heavy leveling system. Instead of following a traditional level-based system where stats increase after crossing thresholds of experience points, each stat levels up based on use. If you take damage, your health points might get a boost after the battle. Same with magic as using spells will increase the stats that calculate magic damage. Weapons and magic spells work similarly with weapon types and individual spells leveling up after you use them a set number of times. But it makes the game very grindy because there feels like there's an element of randomness to stat increases. For example, Maria was my dedicated spell caster, firing off spells 60% of her turns. Firion was my back-up mage for healing and some other buffs. Magic use should make MP go up, yet for most of the game Firion's MP pool was much higher than Maria's despite using magic much, much less frequently. Other stats seemed to increase with greater consistency and frequency. And that is what saves the game: it is very grindy, but it is far less grindy than the prior versions I've attempted to play. You have to give Square Enix props for sticking with the unique leveling system even though few people seem to like it. With this version, they've at least made it tolerable.But that isn't this game's only problem. Dungeons are tedious. They aren't too awful at first, aside having a series of doors one of which is the exit and there rest leading to empty rooms and random choice determines how many you have to go through, but by mid-game, they start to get down right nasty. The mid and late game dungeons are expansive multi-story labyrinths where you might go down a stair case only to find out two floors later it funneled you to a dead end. And it stings bad to have to backtrack and find the right route because the enemy encounter rate is through the roof. Many times, especially in dungeons were you can get ambushed by mobs that inflict status aliments that essentially spell game over if you don't slay them before they take their turn, they tested my patience. Thanks to the generous auto-save, you don't lose too much progress. A very good thing because there are no save points so in the original if you got game over, you had to start all the way back at the beginning. Is there anything good about this game? It has historical significance as the first story driven game in the series and if you put the plot beats down on paper they sound pretty good. But this is an NES game at its core so nothing is really developed in detail. The orchestrated soundtrack really slaps so I spent a lot of time in the music player. I'm really glad I found a version of this game I could play to the end just to say I experienced FF2 and could see how this game influenced FF4, which I see now is basically this game with a more straight forward leveling system. But I can't recommend it for anything other than historical value is faint praise at the end of the day.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I thought the claims about the bad leveling system were exaggerated, but I was wrong. My characters who had been using melee the ENTIRE TIME suddenly stopped gaining levels in their weapons for a weirdly long time. Guy was sitting at level 3 axes for forever. And I was even doing extra fights by looking around the world. Then I get to the first boss and the majority of their hits are hitting him for a whopping ZERO damage. In a game where you're supposed to gain xp by using specific weapons and skills, my dudes who had been doing melee with the same weapon the ENTIRE GAME can't even hurt the FIRST boss. I did some research on it and apparently they need to get a minimum number of hits on these early game monsters per fight to keep leveling. So basically I need to have one dude do all of the killing per random fight in order to keep leveling melee, while everyone else sits around jerking off and defending against monsters they can one shot. ABSOLUTELY NOT. I'll pass or just use the cheaty booster I guess

_childDocuments_.review: This is already one of the lesser Final Fantasy games. The dungeon design is horrendous (though this is somewhat mitigated by the remaster's map feature) and there's way too much backtracking. But this port also brings back the feature from the NES version where heavy armor and weapons weaken your magic, and it never bothers to tell you this. There's a solid RPG buried deep underneath if you can stomach the frustrating stuff, the music is great, and the plot is full of heavy themes that I appreciate, but all in all, speaking as a huge fan of the series, you can feel free to skip this one.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I tried so hard to like this game.I really wanted to like this game.It flat relies on some things I think are really bad gameplay:1) skill improvement requires grinding the skill against enemies. This means that to get good at skills, you'll be doing a lot of "explode more enemies than I need to to finish a dungeon, because if I don't have max rank later our party will be useless" - Sometimes this also requires grinding a spell that appears to do -nothing- on initial cast until something changes.2) it relies a -lot- on instant death mechanics as a "challenge" in fights, meaning sometimes you'll be repeating a floor repeatedly hoping they miss in endgame. (and remember: the old NES version of this didn't autosave on every floor. Imagine having to redo the dungeon repeatedly!)3) it relies, again, a lot on shuffling your last party member slot as part of the plotline, meaning you'll always have someone who's underdeveloped and well behind the party curve unless you stop and grind them up, every single time.4) suddenly the final boss, who heals for most of the damage he deals on autoattacks, and has so much defense that your guys who were dealing thousands of damage on autos are dealing less than 100 on autos, while he heals for 1500 per round from his attacks.Taken on the whole, there's a lot of good moments and nuggets in this game, but the grindfest and rng and misery of the combat system taken as whole just wore me down.  I won't be finishing, and I can't in good conscience recommend it to -anyone-.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 2 is probably the most tedious, most frustrating and most grindy Final Fantasy I've played in this Pixel Remaster collection. Because of spell level grinding. Final Fantasy 2 is awful at wasting your time. I don't know how bad it used to be in the NES version, but it has not been improved enough in this Pixel Remaster. You will cast spells hundreds upon hundreds of times, regardless of whether you actually need to or not, just to gain spell levels. Why you might ask? Because if you don't, your spells will be worthless. Low-level spells do pitiful damage and status-affecting spells will always fail, so you're just wasting MP unless you level them. Even if you do level the status-affecting spells, there's a good chance they won't work properly anyway.To make matters worse, the spell design is awful and is filled with tons of useless and/or redundant spells. You don't just have 1 spell to paralyze target - you have multiples, such as Stun, Sleep and Stop. Each spell does exactly the same thing but it affects a different resistance. So if you want to be able to paralyze enemies, it's not enough to grind out levels for 1 spell - you have to grind out all the different versions individually.When I found the Flare or Holy tome and it did 28 damage instead of 8000, my heart sank. I tried grinding for hours to improve its damage, but it just never compared with my basic attacks. This is awful design. The reality is, basic weapons will always do more damage than your non-elemental spells like Holy or Flare, even if you invest 100% of time leveling them. Because you can equip 2 weapons at the same time, you will always do more damage and you actually better action economy because that damage is spread out across 2 attacks. Flare and Holy simply cannot compete with this, and so they are just bad spells.Even in cases where there are enemies that can only be damaged by spells, Holy and Flare don't do enough damage - you'll still need to take advantage of elemental weaknesses. So spells like Fire, Thunder, Blizzard and Scourge are actually the only damage spells worth investing in.There is a spell called Ultima which is capable of doing real damage, but the reality is, it takes so much investment to raise it's damage you're still better off using weapons for your own time and sanity.Secondly, weapon leveling isn't much better. It's certainly fine to beat the game - you'll probably finish the game at level 11 out of 16 weapon levels for the types you've been using. But good luck getting that level 16 weapon achievement. I never attempted it, but I'm guessing it must take hours and hours. No thanks.Thirdly, one of the reasons for spells doing poor damage is that many pieces of armor will significantly negate your spirit or intelligence. There's no way to know that this is happening unless you are told to look for it on the Final Fantasy wiki for FF2. Sadly, I found out that a pair gloves or a helmet was negating 40% or so of my spell-casting power. If you do play this game and plan on using spells, make sure you research this. Again, I just want to stress what a horrible design this.Lastly, there's a bug in the game where enemies can inflict status effects onto your characters with physical attacks, and if you don't evade the hit, the status effect will get applied 100% of the time. This means that if you are ambushed by 4-6 enemies that can turn you to Stone, Paralyze you or even instant-OK you, it will be game-over if most of your characters did not evade these hits. This is a huge bug and you will have to grind a lot to get the type of evade stats that you need to ensure you don't die to stuff like this.To make matters even worse, Protect Rings don't actually protect against Death. The Coeurl's in the final dungeon still instant-OK you despite having it equipped. Ribbons don't seem to protect against much either. I actually got one very early as a lucky drop against that Lamia Queen boss in Hilda's room and it did squat for me all game. I equippped ribbons on 3 out of my 4 characters and it didn't protect them against sleep, confuse or instant-death attacks at all. Square Enix has to fix this!!!Overall, unlike the other pixel remasters, FF2 just isn't fun to play - even with all the quality of life updates. They just didn't go far enough and there's just way too much grinding. The 100% status effects that can cause instant game-overs, and all the spell grinding you are forced to do just completely kills the game for me. I've probably died 6-8 times due to these type of game-overs where enemies ambush you and there's nothing you can do due to the 100% status-effect bug.I do not recommend FF2. It's the only Pixel Remaster I strongly suggest you avoid getting.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: I first played this with the Dawn of Souls pack on the GBA.  This version included a post game campaign made up of the 4th party members you lose over the course of the main game.  While it is more of a loss than the random dungeons of Final Fantasy I, as there is actual story here, its still not much.  Instead of random dungeons, you get the last two dungeons mirrored and palette swapped.  In addition, there was a single town and a side area with one boss.  You aren't missing anything a skip through a YouTube playthrough can't provide.Final Fantasy II is one of the more unique installments in the series.  Rather than leveling up via experience points, party members gain stats based on use.  This includes using different weapon types and individual magic spells leveling separately, and tanking damage increasing health.  Problem is, the point you get from enemies does not increase at the same rate as your party.  This makes the best way to improve your characters is to attack themselves.Other problems include the aforementioned 4th player character rotating as the plot demands.  This generally makes them much weaker than the 3 that are consistent.  And since they will eventually be lost as well, there isn't much reason to bring them up to par.  Dawn of Souls alleviated this a bit by letting you import them as they were from the main game, but as said previously, its not worth playing.As it stands now, Final Fantasy II is okay.  I would put it last out of the NES trilogy.  The alteration to the level up process was a neat idea, but doesn't work as well as it should since it's so slow.What kills the recommendation currently is the change to on hit effects.  Like many other RPGs, monsters can inflict status effects like paralysis on hit.  And by can, I mean will 100% of the time.  This includes death, killing a character instantly.  This means you can quite easily lose an ambush, or even a regular battle with a slow party, without getting the chance to do anything.  Although there is an autosave every floor, and a reusable quicksave, you shouldn't have to rely on it just to play.  Until its changed, I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 2 has a pretty solid story for an NES game. It's not going to change your life or make you think extremely deep thoughts about the nature of society, but the story itself is just a nice fantasy adventure that you would expect. Though regarding the story, it does cover death a couple of times which genuinely surprised me for a game such as this, and the topic was handled pretty well. For the gameplay, i'm not the largest fan of how the combat system works. The upgrading system is a bit annoying and just feels downright tedious, but it was enough to get me through the entire game if it means anything. One tip i'll give you, the game itself never felt too difficult for me personally BUT I highly recommend upgrading all magic for the final boss, i had basically just one mage at the end of the game and physical damage did almost nothing to the boss so the final boss for me was really difficult. Also, the game has a party of 4, but the 4th player switches out from time to time, and they'll often have less health than your main characters and all but one will have basically no good magic, so by the time you get your last party member it takes forever to upgrade their magic, but again the game never felt so bad that i couldn't play it. The game is short enough to where you can bog through it to see the story, but even then the story isn't nearly as good as ones that come after it (doesn't mean it's bad, just nothing mind blowing) to be honest i think the only reason to play this game would to see final fantasy's legacy and where everything started, (which is why i'm playing through all of the pixel remaster games) because you can really see elements from the future games in this one, and i would definitely say that the roots of all of those things in the future are interesting to see. As a game itself it's not that bad and it is relatively cheap, so if you want to play some okay combat with a decent story and pretty good music, then this is the game for you and i do recommend it. but if you don't care to see the story or suffer through the tedious dungeons, then maybe just listen to the soundtrack online.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Decided which way to vote this game was a challenge. This being my third playthrough of Final Fantasy II (first being on PS1, then on PSP) I was familiar with the mechanics and generally remembered the story. However, out of the main games, this is my least favorite for many reasons, but there is still certain quirks about it that can be enjoyable.Firstly, Final Fantasy II was trying to be Final Fantasy, but doing almost everything different which made it a very divided game. Some people love it while others hate it, but I am in the middle. The story isn't too bad, but just so much backtracking to places without much restriction on exploration or sometimes the destination isn't clear because of the map layout. However, you are Firion, Maria, Guy, and a random 4th member that changes throughout the game's progression. You are orphaned and join the rebellion to stop Emperor Mateus from destroying the world. You basically go to different towns to do recon missions or info gathering then head back to the hideout. This makes the early game a little dull as you go far away then run back (unless you pay to take the boat or airship which is more expensive the farther away the destination.) over and over for most of the game. About the time you get the boat and airship is it less tedious and you go from one location to the next with little backtrack.Anyway, enough about what you already know. What is different? Just like the other Pixel Remasters, the music has been rearranged, an improved map for the overworld and locations have been included. Auto-battle and cursor memory are also helpful. The bestiary, entire soundtrack with other improvements have been made. Unfortunately, despite these improvements, it is still Final Fantasy II which means you will be either dreading the grind ahead or just having fun finding out how broken you can get. The leveling is faster in this version, which is nice, but it is still horridly unbalanced for numerous reasons that have been stated to death at this point.For me, I chose to grind a lot because of an issue with this version; on-hit effects. Like many other Final Fantasy games and other RPGs, enemies can inflict status ailments on-hit. Unfortunately, in this version those percentages have been set at 100%. I thought I was crazy until I fought later enemies with on-hit confuse, sleep, stun, death, and many other annoying ones. I consulted the forums (yeah, some people claim it is intentional) and then played the other versions. This was not present in the other versions otherwise, I would have grinded much more and would have used certain weapons more. I say that because this bug affects you as well. More specifically, the Sleep Sword is broken as it does sleep on-hit 100% of the time. I do hope they fix it, but you can always grind a ton and use certain weapons to use it to your advantage.In closing, I had fun playing it again as I had much more knowledge this time around and the modern improvements made it faster, but the leveling is still my least favorite.
