_childDocuments_.review: This beautiful rendition of Final Fantasy II falls short of being enjoyable because it is also a faithful rendition of Final Fantasy II. As with other Final Fantasy Pixel Remasters, the visuals mimic SNES Final Fantasy titles, with a touch more shine. The character sprites use the additional color depth to bring some of Amano's vision to the originals.The music is gorgeously arranged. The overworld theme, especially, is a cinematic-quality beauty.I enjoy the story, too: this is the first Final Fantasy with character development; I find Prince Gordon's character arc particularly gratifying. The plot takes troubling turns, and yet also has its moments of victory. Many places change as the plot advances; the enemy's and heroes' actions feel consequential. Also, Final Fantasy II has some firsts for the series: first chocobos, first Cid, and first malevolent Empire.Unfortunately, these good points don't save the game from its deeply flawed gameplay and map design. The game's open world fits poorly to its linear story: the first warning that you're going the wrong way is that you encounter monsters much too strong for your party to handle. But this is forgivable compared to other flaws.Final Fantasy II makes an early attempt at flexible character advancement. Unfortunately, it's overly granular in a way that isn't fun. Each weapon type and spell advances individually, and in many cases, one barely differs from another. Meanwhile, HP and Agility would make an interesting difference, but have no clear way to focus on their advancement. Thankfully, advancement goes quicker in the Pixel Remaster than in the original, and stats never decrease. If anything, large portions of the game are too easy! At least this gets the gameplay out of the plot's way to an extent.The game's most serious flaw is its long and tedious dungeons. Each stretches on for 1-2 hours of play, usually without any character interactions or plot points until the end of the dungeon. The empty square rooms behind most doors get particularly grating. Warp and Teleport spells, plus the Pixel Remaster's auto-battle feature, help speed things up, and the Quicksave feature is a vital modern touch. But it's still a long slog.I struggled with whether to recommend this; it meets its goal as an aesthetically pleasing and faithful remaster of Final Fantasy II, a game which has its good points. It's a shame that it remains tiresome to play.If you want to experience every Final Fantasy game, pick up this game or watch an abridged video of someone playing, depending on how much you value your time. If you're looking to kick back with a fun JRPG, I'd advise skipping this one.

_childDocuments_.review: -Finished game review edit-First a caveat: enabling vsync in video card drivers fixed the screen tearing issue for me, but it did not for some people I know once they switched to full screen. I also ran into bugs where battles would occasionally start to slow down to 2fps even when nothing was happening. Rarely, but it happened a few times.The complete audio and visual overhaul made the journey an enjoyable one. The quicksave is revamped so you can use it to save mid dungeon or before that boss. The story, although not as developed or personal as say FFVI, was taking huge strides in that direction: main characters don't always do the right thing and some perish. It is of course, told with minimal text. The end result feels like the outline or sketch of a possibly much better story, presumably if more storage space had been available back in the late 80s.The difficulty is unbalanced at times. Expect extremely easy periods followed by difficulty spikes, and long dungeons that are far more challenging than the bosses. And about that final boss...  Also, I had no problems multiclassing--in fact it's kind of necessary in this game.Grinding was minimal. However with the lovely pixel art environments and music, turning down the high encounter rate would have improved the atmosphere, But hey, it's an old RPG.Skill and magic leveling has its ups and downs. The proto elder scrolls (use it to level it) system is neat, but I found myself skipping a lot of new magic toward the end of the game, because you'd have to level it quite a lot for it to be useful. And it wasn't necessary. It's more for completionists.You might enjoy this game if you are curious about 80s JRPGs, retro games and so forth. As far as remasters go, this is how you do it right (even if the game is a bit quirky), so this has left me looking forward to the rest of the pixel remasters which have much stronger entries. If you decide to try it, just watch out for the vsync issue while you have time to refund.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: There's little that I can say about this that other people haven't. But I'll give my honest thoughts.Final Fantasy is somewhat synonymous with storytelling today. But this game has little to no story whatsoever. It's basically giant dungeon crawl after giant dungeon crawl.This game gets a lot of flack for the leveling system, but honestly it didn't bother me. If anything it allowed for deeper customization of your party / characters.What I did not like, however, was just the sheer amount of combat. This game has higher amount of random encounters than any other game in the franchise. In addition, the dungeons are simply massive and purposefully confusing. But if 'fixed' that, there would be nothing left of the game.To make matters worse, it's not balanced well at all. At one point I was fighting 6 enemies, each one of which did a melee attack the stunned. They ambushed me, and stunned my entire party. I could not give a single command before I got a game over, which took over 10 minutes.I love the other Pixel Remasters that I have played. But I'll never play this one again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is probably the most controversial one in the series. Some people just like it BECAUSE of how quirky and abusive the leveling system is. I am not one of these people. Seeing as I recommend it anyways, this review is based on whether or not this is a good version of this game to play. They made everything cheaper, so you don't have to penny pinch as much in the early game. They also gave everyone 10MP at the start of the game instead of 5. These two things help get you past the most annoying part of the game. Outside of that, this game is basically every other version of FF2 out there. Teach Maria spells and have her cast them on your entire party to increase your HP and MP until you have a few thousand HP on everyone and a few hundred MP, and then beat the game. Don't play this game. If you want to play it anyways (like I did) this is probably the best version of the game to play. This game has been a nightmare for me for 15 years. After I get all the achievements/ get bored of trying for the achievements in this game, I'm never playing this game again.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to take my time with this one before putting up a review. This isn't the first time I have played FF2. Everytime I tried it ended in the same outcome: this is the worst RPG ever made. (And trust me..i have played a lot of RPGs.) So, instead of my usual test drive and then a review, I waited until I got all the way through it.Did my opinion change though? Well, viewing the thumbs down...it appears not. But it did get better in this version.There are two big issues that have plagued FF2. One everyone is very aware of, and was fixed. The other issue....well lets list them both:1. The level up system - It has always been the big problem with this game. It makes sense but not many people like it. We are used to leveling up after set xp...instead of what we do in battle. Thankfully this version fixes one of the big issues with this game: acquiring HP. To attack yourself to gain HP in the past was ridiculous. This version HP rises over the number of battles you do. Kudos to this version for fixing the whole system. But...2. You go the wrong way....you die - This was not fixed. And this is the real reason why I hated this game so much. I wasn't crazy about the level up system, but if you step in the wrong area, then your game ends...that infuriates me. You can be in one area with max weapons as high as they will get, one hitting everything...and then take a step in the wrong direction and go straight to 0 damage hits and getting one-hit killed. This was not fixed.I know what you are probably thinking: this is standard if you go the wrong way and encounter stronger enemies. But RPGs are good at hinting you will encounter harder enemies. The first Dragonquest used bridges to signify you are going into a new area with new monsters. Final Fantasy split them up by islands or dungeons. This one does neither. it is like constant peninsulas of power popping up as just normal areas, but instead of doing little damage, you will do nothing...and get hit hard. Very hard.Don't believe me? Do this then....fight around the first city until you get your weapons to level 3. Then head west and north...you will encounter a swamp. Stay south in the swamp, and you will be one hit killing everything. Then head a little north still in the swamp, and the monsters change with no break in the area....and you will go to hitting for 0 damage.Or head west from the starting city and south where the forest ends. You will now encounter enemies that are FAR stronger that you can possibly imagine to be. But you won't know this until it is way too late.Or even go into the city where the first castle is located. Talk to a guard. Congrats...you don't have any chance of winning.Once you get past this in the beginning..it will get a lot smoother. But that doesn't make it ok. This has always been bad programming....and will always put this game in the bad RPG category.However if you are going to get the whole set...it is worth playing through. I wouldn't recommend getting it by itself though. So if you are already planning to get 1-6....just go for it. There is still a lot of fun in the game. Just know where to walk..and when to walk there.

_childDocuments_.review: I am happy that Square Enix decided to remake this game along with the rest of Final Fantasy 1-6. However, I would not recommend to play this game unless you are a die-hard fan of Final Fantasy.PRO: The gameplay was alright, nothing unexpected. Despite the infamy of having to level individual stats, it was very enjoyable while listening to music or podcasts. If you feel like you need to grind, I would recommend just relaxing while doing it for a good time.CON: There are moments where you should just expect an insta-death, especially late game in the final dungeon. I wouldn't even call it hard, just simply dumb mechanics that weren't fix, and it really takes you out of the game experience. This wasn't a leveling issue, as I was still running into these issues and was able to kill the final boss with ease.PRO: The keyword system they used was interesting and definitely nice to see more attempts of variety after the Final Fantasy I.CON: The traveling back-and-forth to the main town got annoying after a while. This isn't a major complaint, but something that you definitely as you progress through the story. They keyword system, which innovative wasn't that great.SCORE: 4/10PRO: This arguably the first "scripted" story in the Final Fantasy series, with more serious dialogue, and basic "cutscenes" that is definitely something to appreciate.CON: Overall, the story is alright. While it tries to draw you into specific moments, I felt it was lacking.SCORE: 5/10PRO: Overall, the music was great. No complaints.SCORE: 7/10PRO: Overall, the graphics were great. They did a good job keeping the original style while improving them for this remaster.SCORE: 7/10I think what really made this game suffer was its gameplay. While innovative, it definitely made it more annoying, and there other gameplay issues outside of leveling that were significantly annoying, even in the late game. There were also story choices, like going back into the town repeatedly, that made a lot moments feel more like a chore.While I can appreciate this game in its place in the Final Fantasy series, I wouldn't recommend playing this unless you are a die-hard Final Fantasy fan and want to play all the game.SCORE: 4/10

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game many times before on Famicom, PS1 and PSP and I probably enjoyed myself the most on this playthrough. _childDocuments_.review: With this being my first ever play through of Final Fantasy 2, I was pleasantly surprised but also left a little unsatisfied. The game play is more interesting than FF1 with a new leveling system that rewards being consistent with your weapon and magic choices. Although it is easy to become over powered in the early game with a little bit of time and effort, enemies eventually gain attacks and abilities that can wipe your whole team before you can even do anything about it, even with overpowered gear and abilities. One of the reasons for your characters being overpowered was due to only having 3 permanent party members with 1 consistently rotating party member that is always under leveled and will more than likely leave after one dungeon. This leads your 3 permanent party members virtually doing the work of 4 since most of the time I would let my 4 member just die and never revive them. Overall the story I would say is a lot more interesting than the FF1. Rather than a simple premise of the heros of light going to awaken some crystals, although classic, becomes a story with some twists and turns revolving around a country of rebellion. The learn and password system allows for easy story progression of you get stuck and will explain some of the lore and reasoning for some of the characters choices. In conclusion, I would give FF2 pixel remastered a 7/10 due to the updated graphics and quality of life upgrades like unlimited storage and auto battles. Where the game lacks is in its rotating party members and the inconsistent leveling/ power creep.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first played  a long time ago, I HATED the stat-grinding system, so much so that I dropped it before I even got to the first dungeon. In fact, I got used to it. That said, I'll take a traditional EXP leveling system any day. The cast of characters in this game are pretty flat compared to the ones in the later  games. Overall, it's not a bad game, but it's still by far my least favorite entry in the main series.

_childDocuments_.review: FFII gets a lot of hate, but it is not at all bad. _childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: A very divisive game, but I enjoyed the leveling system. Skyrim copied it and apparently that's a good game by 2011 standards. Tom Howard didn't hire me to say this, but FF II "just works" when it comes to leveling. Want to be a fighter? Sure thing go ahead. Want to be a mage? Just fling spells and you'll figure it out. Sure you can hit yourself over and over again for easy exp, but that's part of the 1988 goofiness. In all honesty there is no point in even leveling because the blood sword deals damage as a percentage value, which apparently means 9,999 damage against the final boss even if you haven't leveled up. There also is this very creative Ultima spell that levels up based off of every skill that you have leveled. Feel free to use it if you want to make the most out of what the game has to offer. If you don't or if you don't have that much time, then just use the blood sword to cheese the game in record timing. Either way works and both methods are a good time.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: A great remaster of a busted game.Since its release in 1987 FFII has had numerous re-releases, each serve to make the game marginally better, like adding full saving and removing stat-atrophy but still unable to fix the game's fundamental issues. The Pixel Remasters ups the artwork and OST once more, and adds a checklist feature, auto-battle, and mini-map.PLOT: I'll give the game credit for having an original plot, a consistent antagonist, and not ripping off AD&D. Sadly it did come a console-generation too early so none of the characters are all that developed, outside of Firion being a virgin and Guy speaking Beaver. The moment you get the airship is a wet fart since there's no new music, no new places to go to, and half the places you could go to get nuked before then.PROGRESSION: A system where your core stats increase after every battle is a good idea. A system where you have to manually level-up every weapon-type and magic-spell for them not to be useless is a terrible idea. This progression was better done in the later Saga series though its utterly botched appearance meant it never returned in Final Fantasy. What's the point of buying a Flare spell in the last dungeon if it's completely worthless unless you grind?DUNGEONS: Absolutely irredeemable. About two-thirds of the game's maps are sprawling dungeons with high encounter-rates, branching paths that span multiple floors, and numerous doors that lead to rooms containing nothing but an enemy ambush. FFI's dungeons felt like a product of the time, FFII's dungeons are actively horrible and date the experience far more than I or III.ART & MUSIC: They're fine, but nothing remarkable.CONCLUSION: FFII is hard, oddball, experimental, and ultimately not rewarding. You can safely skip this one as none of its innovations continue into the rest of the series, and the concepts it did introduce are done better in the immediate sequel, the excellent Pixel-Remaster of Final Fantasy III.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was honestly way better than I expected it to be. For starters, the music is amazing.I played FF1 and FF3 (3D version) before I played this game and the story in those were really bad and basic. So considering that this was made before FF3, I expected it to also be really bad. To my surprise, the story was actually pretty good! Multiple characters died, cities were destroyed, and the dialogue had much better writing than FF1 and FF3's. That being said, you could definitely tell that at the time they were limited on how much dialogue they could put in. It felt like they were trying to tell a much more complex story, and multiple times had to limit what would normally be a 5 minute cutscene to just a few lines of dialogue. If this game was given a full remake and didn't have those limitations, the story could be really good.One criticism I've heard of this game, and I'm sure you've heard of it as well, is the leveling system. You level up every spell and weapon type each time you use it. You also level up your health each time you get hit, however, in the pixel remaster you automatically gain more health after a certain number of battles, which apparently was not in the original. This common criticism is actually a positive in my opinion. You're not restricted to different classes, and you can really customize your builds to your liking. You want someone who can dual wield axes as well as heal? You want the entire party to able to heal? You want someone to fight with a spear but also cast a lot of fire magic? You can do that. Any spell and weapon can go to any character.I do have some criticisms of this game, though. At the start of the game you can rename all 4 main characters, however, one of your main characters (Leon) is not usable or involved in the story until the very end of the game. It then basically makes him a side character, even though he's presented as a main character at the start. You'll frequently have various other characters fill the 4th party member slot, although you can't name them and some of those characters you'll end up using more than Leon. So if you name Leon after yourself, well, that's bad news for you. Another criticism I have of this is the final boss. He can do melee attacks which can drain up to 5,000 of your health (at least that's the highest I noticed) and for context, the max health you can have is 9,999. This attack then REGENERATES the boss' health, while the best weapons in the game will only take out a few hundred of his health because of his high defense. Maybe that would've changed if I grinded for hours. Thankfully, there's 1 weapon in the game (the Blood Sword) that drains a ton of his health and restores it to your party member. With this you can beat the final boss pretty easily. However, there's no in-game description telling you any of this, and the weapon itself says it does less damage than some of the other swords you'll have. I only knew about this because of an online guide I was using. What's worse is that you can completely miss the chance to get this weapon if you don't talk to a certain character at one point in the story, and if you happen to sell this weapon there's no getting it back. I don't think it's even possible to beat the game without that weapon.TLDRPros:1. Good music2. Good story3. Good build customizationCons:1. A renamable character is presented as a main character, but only appears at the end of the game.2. Pretty much impossible final boss if you happen to miss or sell a weapon, and no in-game description to suggest that weapon is important.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a mixed bag but I would say it tends to be more frustrating than fun at most points in the games. It seems the game loves to waste your time with bizarre game play choicesPros:-Amazing OST-Lots of freedom to build your party how you see fit-Nice visuals-Guy and LeilaCons:-Way too many dead ends that serve no purpose. In a RPG you want to explore but the game punishes you for it with empty rooms 95% of the time.-Encounters are way too frequent which destroys the pacing-Enemies can stunlock and instakill. If you are ambushed by a certain enemy type that can do this, your party will most likely be defeated-Status aliments afflicted on you is way tot frequent since its at a 100% rate to succeed. Also most of them don't wear off so it can lead to the dreaded stunlock mentioned above-Your party is always changing which sounds like it could keep things interesting but all it does is force you with an under-leveled character. Then once you start to level them up and get use to them in your party, they take them away and replace them with another under-leveled characterOverall I enjoyed the game but the negatives outweigh the positives imo

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by saying that I love Final Fantasy, and I have a special appreciation for the original Final Fantasy on the NES. That being said, I hate this game and it disgraces the entire series, including its predecessor. I hate its dungeons, with these fake rooms that you spawn in the middle of and force you to fight 50 enemies as you crawl your way out. I hate most of the music, the dreadnought theme is repetitive and I find the overworld theme to be sappy and obnoxious. I hate how all of the bestiary entries are in order of their type and not around when you find them, leaving these large gaps in between each (this wasn't a problem in the previous pixel remaster?). I hate the shallow and meaningless characters that pretend to have personality, that I'm supposed to feel agency for and attached to. I appreciate the darker tone that they were going for but it just doesn't communicate its ideas very well, with these side characters introduced to us only for them to die only an hour to a minute later. And its progression system, leaving you with these lopsided party members that have little merit unless you ruthlessly grind for 5 hours.This game is an important entry that introduced a lot of the mainstays for the fantastic games to come. That being said, if Final Fantasy II's one redeeming quality is that it makes every other one in the series look better, its probably not very good. Especially not for the outrageous price; I only purchased this remaster through the bundle that came with the 5 other games that I actually wanted to play.

_childDocuments_.review: In terms of faithfully recreating and building off of the existing game, the pixel remaster does a fine job of bringing that classic final fantasy 2 experience to modern gamers. Unfortunately the classic final fantasy 2 experience is agonizing and miserable. The first game in the series to have a followable story, does a surprisingly decent job of building a world and characters in it, but the gameplay has aged horribly. I took a three month break from playing this game right at the final dungeon because I found it so frustrating. After spending a few decent hours trying to engage in the game's combat system I found that after the 10th random encounter I would just auto battle, and then continued to do that for the entire game. By the end I had some weak magic spells but still managed to mostly get by until the final dungeon where I had a 30% chance to wipe on a single enemy turn, but then I killed the final boss in two hits so I don't know where I stand on this game. Frustrating experience that I do not intend to seek out again.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY II

_childDocuments_.review: Do yourself a favor and give this one a pass.First off, yes, I cleared it. And, yes, it had some good things, the main one being that unlike 1 and 3, FF2 has a story you can actually care about. Alas, the negatives outweigh the positives for this game, something that could have been easily avoided if only the devs had playtested it. Even once.Nevermind the blatantly obvious typos and mis-translations in the English text. Or the non-game-stopping but easy-to-catch, easy-to-fix bugs that were left in the game due to sheer laziness on the part of the devs. These could still be forgiven. The problem is in the combat system. Encounters are so frequent in the dungeons that you literally spend more time in combat than exploring. Yet these battles are ludicrously ill-balanced.Magic spell damage is so low that even at maximum level, the most powerful spell in the game is weaker than the weakest of physical attacks. Yet some enemies can only be damaged by magic, so you can't just avoid training these super-weak spells.Your physical damage against enemies is so unbalanced that most of the time you will either deal enough damage to 1-hit-kill your enemies, or deal 0 damage. Rarely is it anything in between.Level bosses are so weak that by the time you are strong enough to get through a dungeon, you can usually finish the boss fights in 1-2 turns. The ONLY exception is the final boss, which is the opposite in that it is exceptionally over-powered to the point that you will need to carry in a ton of expensive healing items if you want to defeat the boss without spending hours leveling your characters at the end.Enemies that have additional debuff effects to their physical attacks (eg. stun, sleep, death) will apply those debuffs to your characters 100% of the time, even if they deal 0 damage. This means that weak enemies can and frequently will stun-lock your whole party, but because their physical attack damage is so weak, it could take 10 minutes before they kill all your characters as you sit there unable to do anything. The only recourse is to literally force-quit the game and reload. In the latter half of the game, you will need to save after every single battle, as this happens ALL THE TIME! (Additional: The screen resolution config is never saved, so every time you start (or have to restart because of stun-locking) you have to manually re-configure the screen resolution.)Seriously, avoid this game. It's not worth the frustration.

_childDocuments_.review: In FINAL FANTASY II, a malevolent emperor has called upon monsters from a demonic realm to take over the world, ending what seemed to be an eternal period of peace. Thousands of lives succumb to their attacks, leaving many children orphaned. From the destruction rise four young survivors who will take it upon themselves to stop the merciless ruler and avenge the death of their parents. This all-new anniversary edition contain the best treatment of the classic RPG and features all-new character art, updated graphics, new dungeons, full 16:9 widescreen presentation and an updated camera view that gives players a new vantage point. [Square Enix]

detailed_description: FINAL FANTASY I-VI Bundle Purchase the bundle now to receive all soundtracks and wallpapers from FF1-6! Soundtracks and Wallpapers will unlock in line with each title’s launch. See individual store pages for details. The games that inspired a generation come to life once more, in the ultimate 2D pixel remaster! Purchase the bundle and receive FINAL FANTASY FINAL FANTASY II FINAL FANTASY III FINAL FANTASY IV FINAL FANTASY V FINAL FANTASY VI This bundle lets you purchase all six games from FINAL FANTASY 1 to FINAL FANTASY 6 at a discount price. It also contains a sound track, featuring total of 20 tracks and total of 14 unique wallpapers. Enjoy universally updated 2D pixel graphics and the beautifully rearranged soundtrack. Gameplay is improved with modernised UI, and extras such as a beastiary, illustration gallery and music player allow further immersion into the world of the game. ＊These games are newly developed remaster editions based on the original titles. Some of the changes and additional elements found in other remakes of these games are not included. ■ Beautifully revived with new graphics and sound! Universally updated 2D pixel graphics, including the iconic FINAL FANTASY character pixel designs created by Kazuko Shibuya, the original artist and current collaborator. Beautifully rearranged soundtrack in a faithful FINAL FANTASY style, overseen by original composer Nobuo Uematsu. ■Improved gameplay! Including modernized UI, auto-battle options, and more. In his search for the crystals, Cecil must travel over land, under the ground, to the Land of Summons, and even to the moon. _childDocuments_.review: Oh yes, this is it people. This is peak FF right here. A lot of people bang on about how great 6 is but for me, 4 is the one that sits in the treasured place in my heart. 4 marked such a big shift in what FF was. The scope seemed grander, the ATB system expanded the combat, the characters had more personality and even the story was becoming more than just Warriors of Light get Crystals. It's still very crystal based though. :)It also finally had one of those sacrifice moments that actually felt sad. It might not be quite as tragic as Aerith's death but the Palam/Porom moment always stuck with me and made sure this game continued to resonate with me long after playing it.As for pixel remaster quality. Once again the sprites and music are on point, perfectly nailing the feel of the original with a modern upgrade. It seems there might only be one area for concern.I've seen some other reviews calling out the difficulty. I haven't got far enough in to fully test that yet. If enough people raise their voices perhaps Squeenix will patch it? We can hope. Even if it is too easy I still couldn't thumb it down. FF4, best FF.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty much exactly what you probably want. The original game with modest but appreciated improvements that make it more fun to play today. What every remaster should be, really.The orchestral soundtrack is truly amazing and maybe the best part for me, but don't sleep on the redrawn pixels. They look like your memories at first, but compare them to the actual SNES game and you'll be blown away. Only quibble I have is the CRT filter is a little strong, but you can use one from Reshade instead if it bothers you. I do recommend some kind of CRT filter, especially if using a large monitor like me, as the games weren't designed around you seeing every individual pixel clear as day.I have been pretty much a PC only gamer since 1994 or so, but I have a ton of nostalgia for the NES and SNES games I played before that. This remaster satisfied that nostalgia while also holding up as a fun (if simple) game and story. I wouldn't hesitate.

_childDocuments_.review: The first title in the series to come out on SNES. This is also the first game to introduce the "ATB" battle system. I'm not the biggest fan of it, because it forces you to select stuff (for example spells) faster when in battle. Though it's not game breaking and in this version I believe you can slow it down.The story is much more character-driven and deeper, kind of like in FF2. The enemy encounters are not so tiresome just like in FF3 but the enemies and especially the boss fights can be challenging. The music is great and the graphics are more detailed (probably because the upgrade to SNES) but still the same style.I do like that the character job/class is now fully tied to the character and to fit the story. The story/gameplay is also more linear but that's not a bad thing.It seems that this game has a direct sequel/dlc called "After years". Don't worry the game doesn't end in a cliffhanger even though it has a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: The short version of this review is, this is the best version of FFIV you can get easily today, and while the game isn't the best in the series, what you get for your money is a pretty absorbing and fun adventure.To elaborate on how it compares to other versions (SNES/SFC, PS1, GBA/WSC):* The script is not the shoddy SNES one, it's closer to the other versions (but retranslated again, I think? I'm not an expert on that). This means in the intro there's no dialogue in Mysidia, Cecil broods a lot more, there's a package instead of a bomb ring, and the "spoony bard" line as usual has been inserted but it's the first thing Tellah says instead of the third. Meh.* The most obvious change is the difficulty is significantly easier - experience is earned faster. Is this bad? Not sure, the game's fairly slow-paced anyway.* Identical engine to the other remakes, including how if an enemy is killed it auto-targets the next enemy instead of a random one (like other versions, from memory).* Graphics are obviously mostly the same as FFIV Advance. Character portraits aren't updated so look rather dated.* Gameplay is otherwise the same.For those new to the game:* Compared to the 3D remake, I'd say this is the better game. Put simply it plays better and there's less time spent standing around.* Compared to the other 2D versions, this is about the same as the GBA one in quality. That version has a few other features, but I still feel like this one's just as fun. The SNES (US) version is pretty hideously outdated by comparison. I did play through that version decades ago, but there's no going back for me.This is my preferred version overall. It's not perfect (notably there's graphic tile bugs that will probably get patched out soon, and a few places you can soft lock, but there's autosaves to protect you there) however it's the most accessible version in a long time, and it won't bore you to death like the 3D remake. I think my biggest qualm is the full price is steep for an old game, but at 20% off it's much easier to swallow.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: Classic game. Set the basis for future Final Fantasy games, arguably more so than 1-3, introducing the ATB system. The characters are fun and memorable, though the games formulaic reliance on characters "sacrificing themselves" to make room for other characters can weaken moments that should otherwise be extremely emotional. Cecil is a great protagonist, and his relationship with his allies, Rosa, and especially Kain are a highlight of the game. The game makes you feel bad for this man.One thing that surprised me is the low difficulty of the game. If you've played a lot of jRPGs, you may be caught off guard by the simplicity of the encounters. This is hardly the games fault; it's an old game, and future games were heavily inspired by it, so many of it's bigger tricks would go on to be cliches in later jRPGs.Overall, I recommend this game. if you're looking to play the pre-7 Final Fantasy games, this game offers a very comfortable jumping on point.

_childDocuments_.review: +Sprite work is handcrafted and emulates the original +Music has been remastered and elevated from the original tracks+Achievements and trading cards +Art gallery and music gallery +Mini-map and QoL features +It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Final Fantasy IV--the definitive Final Fantasy--2D again at last-Missing content from other versions (this version is based on the original SNES version)  -UI and font are lackluster-Not as comprehensive and definitive as the PSP release (will we ever see the Interlude content on another platform?)-It isn't Final Fantasy VI Final Fantasy IV is the most important Final Fantasy title. More important than VI, VII and any other that came after it. Perhaps not more important than the series inception with the original, but it is huge. This game is when the soul of the series began. This is the Link to the Past of the series. The Super Mario World. The Dragon Quest III. This is THE Final Fantasy. Like Link to the Past, Super Mario World and Dragon Quest III, Final Fantasy IV took everything that worked from FFI-III and threw it together into an ambitious debut on the SNES. From the job system from FFI and FFIII to the focused narrative and characters of FFII to the large amounts of secrets to uncover from FFIII. Final Fantasy IV was when we started seeing the drama and character development we would love within the series. There is an attempt at romance with Cecil and Rosa (love triangle if Kain is included). The characters in the game all have differing relationships with each other, leading to interesting drama and dynamics. Palom and Porom don't trust Cecil because he murdered people from their town. Tellah hates Edward at first. Golbez is related to Cecil. The series is largely known for its character moments and drama today, but FFIV solidified it!  The world feels far more lived in than the previous entries. Rosa has a home in the village of Baron. Cid does as well. The NPCs respond to you as the Red Baron captain when you talk to them. There is a mix of people believing in the king and doubting him. There is a weight to Cecil's role as a dark knight. Every job has a place in the world of FFIV. There isn't ever giant lore dumps either. The lore and world is built organically within the narrative. Okay, maybe the Lunarian stuff is a lore dump, but most of the lore is built within the narrative in an organic way. And many of the places all contain differing cultures as well. This is where it began. The system that so many classics would use. The same system that Final Fantasy VI and VII would use. The same system that Chrono Trigger would use as its base. And not only did it influence many Final Fantasy titles, it was a large influence on the JRPG genre.  Most games had been traditional turn based, but Final Fantasy IV sought to provide an action-heavy battle system that felt...well...active. And it works really well here. There is a balance to the game play in Final Fantasy IV that Final Fantasy II and III struggled to have. Because of set jobs and set party members, FFIV is always designed in a way that makes sense for those jobs and party members. Rather than having to account for different use of jobs. Final Fantasy IX would be similarly well-balanced. Cecil is 20 years old. He isn't a teenager. He is captain of a military unit. He instigates murder to get the crystal in the opening moments of the game. Cecil is still unique in JRPGs even to this day. We wouldn't see a protagonist like Cecil again until FFVII with Cloud Strife, whom is 21. Cecil has a strong character arc in this game that remains one of the most memorable within the series along with Cloud Strife. And this development happens through character interaction and connections. Rydia helps Cecil grow. Rosa helps Cecil grow. Palom and Porom help Cecil grow. Tellah helps Cecil grow.  Final Fantasy IV was a trend setter. Not all those trends were positive. One of the most negative trends was the surprise villain, which is also part of FFIII, but not as heavily. The villain in FFIV is rarely hinted at. It comes out of nowhere. Also, while the game has a great story for the time, the characters can't compete with FFVI. And the sprites remain less expressive than the FFV and FFVI sprites (and Chrono Trigger). This remaster isn't definitive and won't be as it is lacking the extra content that was previously added. No GBA additions. No Interlude. A shame considering the Interlude bridging the gap between After Years and IV has remained on PSP. The UI and font are somewhat lazily done. That said, the music is fantastic, featuring remastered songs that go above and beyond in recreating tracks in the game. I am not 100% on boars with some of the new tracks, but I am in awe overall at the quality of music. I also know some people dislike the sprites, but I actually highly enjoy the sprites. I can tell that there was an effort to replicate the original while including more detail. This isn't a port. It IS a remaster. There was work and effort behind this. So, overall, I think the remaster is good. It isn't perfect and won't please everyone. But I think it is a good opportunity to play Final Fantasy IV again or even for new players of FFIV. All in all, I recommend this port! And who knows? Maybe we will see other pixel remasters down the road like After Years and even better: the Dragon Quest series (DQ1-6) on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: The Pixel Remaster of this game is absolutely stunning! A positive review to support future endeavors similar to this series of games handled with a clear love for the classic titles with fresh life breathed into them.That said, overall for my first experience with FFIV I was left unimpressed. The story writing is pretty bad, in my opinion. It has its moments but every significant plot point felt either too obvious or so heavy handed that it failed to strike a single emotional cord with me at any point. Every character virtually has the same exact motivation for their journey that they're honestly interchangeable at any point to the same effect - and the fact that you're teased with a cast of characters with unique roles to fill, only to be shoehorned into using specifically the five "most important" characters by the end really feels like a slap in the face. There's a lot of cliche under the hood and the writing is overall miserable as well, with a lot of things happening that merely happen because the plot needs it to happen to advance. The twins were genuinely the most interesting to me, but they're very quickly removed from your party and remain absent for the remainder of the game.Not to mention the twist at the end felt... Really wasted. Sort of a twist for the sake of being a twist, with no real weight or consequences to it. A plot twist should be transformative and change how you view the previous sequences in a story, not just slapped on for shock value.Still, it's an older game and they hadn't really dipped their toes in immersive story-telling in the FF franchise yet. FFI and FFIII barely had a story to speak of with self-insert characters, and FFII was their only real experiment with a narrative driven FF so far - which was written in a vastly different and more mature style from what they later developed. However, the PR also made the game incredibly easy and makes it incredibly difficult to not be over leveled and easily overpower every boss in the game, leaving it with very few selling points for me personally.I'd recommend picking it up for collection sake and to experience the game for the first time, as it's still a fun playthrough if you have about 15-20 hours to kill, but not if you have alternative means to play the game or have played the game before - or just get it to support the Pixel Remasters in hope Square takes note that actually putting effort into their re-releases is appreciated by the fans!

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first title in the Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster Bundle that I didn't feel as enthusiastic about.  I do like and recommend it.  It plays well and has all the features I-III did.  It has a great soundtrack!I wasn't expecting the same exact style as the I-III NES versions.  I thought that they would have their own updated style and then the SNES ones would have been upgraded a bit more.  The use of the same animations/visuals for the spells gives the game a really different feel than I had when originally playing the game.  I miss the SNES animations for some.  This also the first of the bunch to have some mega grindy parts, also tied to achievements. Though that is at the end of the game and optional.  The fact that you don't have to stop and grind at all the entire game and still be overpowered lets you go through so much faster.  I didn't realize how short the story was.  It did allow me to get a better sense of how everything tied together.This is making me wonder how FFVI will turn out.

_childDocuments_.review: This was the first Final Fantasy game I've ever played back in the day, so the price is worth the nostalgia.I like the faster leveling of this new version, no more hours of pointless grinding just to progress the story. Addition to that, I set the battle speed to run at max so overall the flow and pacing of the game is really good. There's really no point in the game where I have to stop and grind for levels. It used to take me many tries to beat the summons. And being an adult now, it's not the case anymore. I can quickly see the enemies' attack pattern in a couple of tries and came up with a strategy right away. I also like the auto save feature where when I die, I don't have to start from my last safe point, which can be miles away during the last dungeon.The map location indicator is another make-life-easier feature. I used to wander around the world map for like 10 minutes looking for a town because I got lost. Now I can go from point A to point B in seconds.When Final Fantasy 7 Remake came out, I was blown away by the depth they've added to the world and characters, and I was wondering what if they remake FF4? But after playing this game again and actually reading the correct translation, I was like "nah" lol. Even though the FF4 story was not as dull as the first three games in the series, it was still pretty cringy to say the least, and the characters were all so empty. For example, when Cecil visited Mysidia in quest to become a Paladin, the chancellor sent his two pupils to go along with him, which later revealed that they were spying on him. This part here does not make any sense. If they think Cecil is dangerous in the first place, wouldn't they worry about their little kids getting kill for spying? If this game does get a remake, there's going to be a lot of rewrite on the story just to make it make sense.So overall, this game is good for the nostalgia or just to experience a retro game if you're playing for the first time. Don't expect much beside that though.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: In my reviews of the previous Final Fantasy games, I gave different recommendations depending on how much time you’ve got for gaming, because Final Fantasy I, II, and III are fine games in my opinion, but they’re not that great.Final Fantasy IV, though, is a whole different story. It takes the series to the next level. The story is great, and for once, the characters actually have interesting personalities! That’s something the older games were really missing. The gameplay is solid, and everything runs smoothly. If you’re into jRPGs, you should really try this one. It's simply a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: Game looks incredible. The water and spell effects would have vaporized any SNES or GBA that tried to render them. EXP requirements for leveling up have been halved, so far less grinding is required.However, the game is mechanically shallower than the 3DS version, as the 3DS version has a bunch of changes to make the combat more dynamic and interesting. This version adheres to the original mechanics, which is great if you're looking to revisit this game in more or less its original form, but the 3DS version has a lot to offer too.Recommend both, prefer the 3DS version for mechanics, but this one looks a lot better.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sorry, but as a long-time fan of this game, I cannot recommend this version.Pros:-Pixel Art looks great-Soundtrack and Sound Effects are spot on-Quicksave function, 8-way movement, Dashing,and other quality-of-life improvementsCons:-Difficulty has been reduced to the point of absurdity. This version is even easier than the American FF II release for the SNES.-Screen tearing and lack of V-synch is a major issue. Especially for some flashing visual effects. I would strongly recommend against playing this version if you are Epileptic or otherwise light-sensitive, at least until a V-synch feature is patched in.Overall:The difficulty reduction is just too much. The game I love is in here somewhere, but, this resembles little the game that challenged me and my child's mind back when I first played it. As an adult, I've played almost every other version of this game, and I still found them challenging and engaging. This version, I just tear through everything like it is made of wet cardboard. The primary feature of this game is its difficulty, and frankly, even with Active-time battles and battle speed on high, I just don't see any.The flashing effects alone on a 60htz screen will not be a problem, but, say, a 75htz or 144htz screen, with a lack of V-synch, can cause serious issues. And I am honestly concerned for the health of people with mild epilepsy who choose to play this game, as-is.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: I did enjoy the story mostly and the revolving cast of characters added a grand scale to things, though with it comes the lack of any customization in your party and character classes(which is kind of a main draw of jRPGs).  I did not like the "sad" moments for the sake of adding drama only to take it back 100 times.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: Very similar to FFII in that you play as predefined characters that have distinct personalities, with story and worldbuilding as a major focus. I prefer this a lot more than the way that FFI and FFIII approached characters, and I'm glad that they seem to have stuck with it going forward.The ATB combat is a huge downgrade from regular turnbased in my opinion, as the added pressure takes away a lot of the time you would take to think of a strategy. This is especially bad considering how hard the bosses in FFIV are compared to the three earlier games. In the same way that it would be horrible to play a version of chess where your opponent can take their turn while you are still in the middle of yours, ATB combat feels bad. Even though I prefer the classic turnbased combat of earlier games, FFIV is definitely the best in the series so far. The world and characters really carry the game, and I suppose that's why they lean into this aspect more and more as the games go on.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: Very faithful to the original. The new OST slaps, and I prefer Shibuya Kazuko's updated pixel art. While most art stays true to the SNES, spells and various cutscene effects have a modern take. Cave Magnes sparks with magnetic energy. Fans whir in the Tower of Zot's flooring.Like all the Pixel Remasters, we have dash and auto-battle features.About story complaints: y'all, it's not a good story. It never was. All the remaster can do is modernize the dialog a bit. They can't fix the story. They can't fix how short the game is. FF4 was rushed out in 1991, barely a year after FF3's NES release. Appreciate this for what it is: a Super Nintendo game from 1991 faithfully "pixel remastered" with a few modern conveniences.There's a bit of a decrease in difficulty:- Battles have a significant EXP bonus.- Monsters act a bit slower now, especially at the start of combat.- Auto-battle makes battles less tedious, so you're more likely to gain more levels. I remember running from many battles in the original because the random encounters were so obnoxious.However, without spoilers, certain encounters and bosses *are* notably more difficult. Not many, but definitely a few surprised me.If difficulty concerns you, flee from more battles than usual.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: Final Fantasy IV is my all time favorite RPG. This doesn't mean I think it is the best RPG, or the most polished, but it is my favorite. *SPOILERS throughout the review* Let us discuss the pros and cons:First, the music. Good gravy the music. It is perfection. There is no other way to describe it. The music is the only thing that will not disappoint you throughout the game. From the first song to the last, you'll be impressed and in love with the music.The graphics are great. There are parts of the game where you look and see "damn, they upgraded that part" (most notably the water graphics when on the boat). There are small issues here and there (forest tiles) but these minor things do not really stand out to me? I don't go looking for them, and I really don't notice them like others do. but the forest tiles do stand out. Gameplay is classic ATB. You can change this to however you want, increase battle speed, minor tweaks like that to try and get the game to suit your needs. Darkness is here (Cecil's DK ability), Tellah has Recall, and other characters have the abilities that were removed in the FFII (US). The pros are basically this: The music is better, the gameplay is improved and things are added that were removed in the FFII (US) version, and the graphics, overall, are better. Plus, you can always downloaded mods to fix some of the tiles if it upsets you that much.Now...the cons. And this is a big con. I struggled picking to recommend this game or not. But I just....I cannot recommend it in the way it is presented.  Why?The difficulty. The game is ridiculously easy. Apparently characters only require half the XP from the original version. So you level twice as fast. But, you might say, wasn't the SNES FFII easy?  Well, yes, and no. It wasn't *this* easy. And I think the FFII US version was just simpler, not easier. I could be wrong. Here's a few examples, from different parts of the game: (Disclaimer: I did not grind in anyway. The only time I got off the story line path is when I went to Land of Summoned Monsters and Sylph Cave as soon as getting the opportunity to do so, which is right before the Sealed Cave). The four fiends offer little to no resistance. Scarmiglione was a pushover and offered no threat. Cagnazzo died within a few turns (he didn't even get to use his abilities). Barbariccia was the more difficult one due to lack of magical weakness exploitation, but she still died pretty quickly.  Rubicante didn't really do much except cast Fira a few times then die. I think he even cast Blizzara on himself (which he does when his flame cape is up, so he can absorb it, but he did it when his flame cape was down, so he damaged himself).  He died pretty quickly. The Demon Wall encountered in the Sealed Cave? Just as an experiment, I decided to just auto attack this boss. No magic. No buffs. No jumps. Everyone just attacking. And it died in a few turns. Now, in every version of FFIV that I have played, this boss is a sort of DPS check. If you don't know what you are doing, or are underleveled, he will crush your party and kill you.  And he didn't do anything to me. I set the battle to auto. All my characters attacked. And he died. Odin.  Odin, like Bahamut, would set a countdown, and if the time limit came up, he'd kill everyone.  Odin died in 2 rounds. He didn't even get to put his sword up to start the countdown.Some people on have reported they have skipped entire boss phases because they do too much damage and kill them before the change. The difficulty in this game just does not make it enjoyable for those that have played FFIV in anyway before. In all honestly, some random mob encounters are more difficult than the bosses they guard (some of the later enemies have auto-counter attack). Since you gain so many levels so quickly, sometimes you just don't need to fight any of the encounters in a dungeon because either you are over leveled or it is just a waste of time. And there just is no reason to do anything in random encounters besides attack. Rydia can't cast her magic fast enough before the physical damage dealers kill 2-3 of the enemies in the pack of 4, so her AOE summons/magic just hit one mob. So why the hell did I cast it if it wasn't needed? And this is throughout the game.Even if I never played other versions of FFIV, I'd be really disappointed and upset over the difficulty. I'm not sure why they decided to make leveling twice as fast, but....it just ruins the game. When you can simply auto-attack one of the more difficult bosses in the game, it just sucks all the fun out of the game. I'm not saying an easy game can't be fun, but when  you remove strategy and game plans, you basically just have an autoscroller game that plays itself. If you played other FFIVs, you'll play this game and feel nostalgia, then disappointment as the nostalgia wears off and enemies and bosses just melt from damage.If you never played FFIV before, I would suggest buying the 3D version instead. And it pains me to say that. I love this game. But I don't love this version of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 4 takes elements from prior instalments and adds onto them to make a decent product overall. Starting with the story, this is the first fleshed out story that the series gives us, packed in with some character growth, and world building that takes it to some unique places. This is also has the first cast of fully fleshed out party members, each with their own distinct role and characteristics. There are still some issues however, firstly this game takes the FF2 method of having a rotating party of rotating characters that are forced out for various reasons, meaning you don't have the "true" party until just before the final dungeon. However because the game does not also share the FF2 levelling system, it is nearly not as bad. Depending on what your preferences this could easily be the best of the four, however in my eyes it falls slightly short of its predecessor (FF3) but is still a good game to get into.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy's first dive into a more serious story is quite successful. While Cecil could be a bit dull at times and the story was nothing groundbreaking by modern standards, for the time it truly was something special and still holds up as an enjoyable experience today.Cecil's journey from Dark Knight to Paladin was interesting and the rotating cast of party members kept things enjoyable. My only grips would be that some party members were vastly more useful in their abilities than others and there are a lot of moments where your party feels "incomplete" due to missing a certain type of party member. It is also very easy to get lost without a guide, though not as bad as the earlier games.Overall, a fun experience for fans of older RPGs who want to see more modern storytelling.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished this ages ago and just forgot to write a review, so here it is. With an average completion time of 20.5 hours, Final Fantasy 4 is what I believe to be a good introduction to the series for the modern audience. The only other Final Fantasy title I'd finished prior to this was 15, which is an action game. Final Fantasy 4 is the first real turn-based game I played and enjoyed in my 22 years on this planet.If you think Final Fantasy is a hard series to get in to because you "don't like turn based games", well, grow up and expand your taste in games like I did. Final Fantasy 4 is a masterpiece and I understand why it is often regarded as one of the greatest video games of all time, a pioneer in the RPG field. I'd recommend this game as a gateway into the series, as luckily not many Final Fantasy games relate directly back to each other unless specified (13, 13-2, Lightning Returns, 10, 10-2 etc.), and Final Fantasy 4 even has a sequel available! Square Enix games often go on sale on Steam, but majority of the older Final Fantasy games are multi-platform compatible now, so there's nothing stopping you from picking it up.Overall, I'd list Final Fantasy 4 as a game I really, REALLY enjoyed, and maybe one day I will play the sequel and other titles in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic version of the game. The reduced XP requirement per level makes for a much better pacing. FF4 retains its challenge but just makes it easier to move forward if you hit a wall.  As for the game itself and how it holds up in 2022 as an RPG. The first half of the game is a masterclass.  Great storytelling with good tension and some great moments.  Characters are built up reasonably well and show their motivations clearly.  Its a truly fantastic time.  Enter the second half of the  my opinion the story falls apart and the quality of game play goes down hill.  This was fine for its day but it did not hold up well for me. Still this downgrade doesn't ruin the game it simply takes it down a peg.  6.5/10.  This pixel remaster did a fantastic job with it.  It's my favorite version of the game to play through again.  Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the greatest games of all time remade. Of all the versions of Final Fantasy 2 (4) out there this one is the most similar to the original Snes Port. The pixel remaster features new music, new backgrounds, new graphics. ProsThe music is excellent. Its a clean walk down memory lane if you've ever played this game before. The story is the more visceral Japanese ported version that was on ps1. All the extra moves for the characters are present, like Dark knights shadow move etc. Auto Attack feature which is included in all of these pixel remasters really speeds up battles. Not a con for me, but I should note that the game is very easy. I'm old now and I just wanted to relive the games I played in my youth. My recommendation if you want more of a challenge don't use the auto attack. You also don't need to sit and grind out levels like in the original version in certain areas. You can just play through which is nice.Meh The graphics are only slightly improved imo. They look nearly the same, And that's just okay for me. The sprites are very very true to their original forms. I'm sure if I could hold both versions right next to each other you could certainly tell the difference but its really close. The good in this is that they paid attention to the details in the world tiles the maps, and fight scene backdrops those things are vastly improved.ConThis is a jab at ALL of these pixel remasters. And this is something I am disappointed with because its just laziness to be honest. All the magic effects are exactly the same in these pixel remasters. Meaning Fira graphically is exactly the same graphic animation from Final Fantasy 1 remaster. Its really not right that they were THIS lazy and they couldn't redo the basic spells to match each games style. I cannot verify if this is also the case with ff2 and ff3 remasters since I haven't played those yet. With that said the magic graphic animations are EXCELLENT.I gotta take a star off for the magic effects not being properly ported over from the original FF2 (4) game. Its enough that they made all the menu systems exactly the same across these pixel remaster games which is actually a pro, but it looks not so good, but it works very well. Function over form I guess. One thing that they removed from the original is the ability to change the menu background color. I was slightly disappointed with that as well since I always changed that to a darker blue or black. I highly recommend this game for anyone who has played this game in the past and for anyone who never played it before. It is an absolute pleasure to play and explore.

_childDocuments_.review: (EDIT - Review has been updated to reflect changes in ver. 1.0.2)'Final Fantasy IV' has seen more re-releases than almost any other videogame in history, yet it persistently eludes perfection. You likely won't be fully satisfied when it comes to the Pixel Remaster, but 'FFIV' remains a timeless classic, and there's enough new here to warrant buying it. At least if you haven't played a few of the previous ports.THE GAME:'FFIV' often gets eclipsed by later 'Final Fantasies' like 'VI' and 'VII', but its influence on videogames can't be overstated. It invented the ATB battle system, and was one of the first RPGs to have a cohesive story and playable characters that were more than just blank slates. It's a fun, easy-going sword-and-sorcery adventure that won't win any points for innovation or originality by today's standards, but doesn't get bogged down in overly-complex melodrama like more recent 'Final Fantasies.' It also contains possibly Nobuo Uematsu's greatest soundtrack. Since its initial release, I've probably beaten this game once per every year it's been out (30 years at the time of this review).THE PORT:The music in this game has been completely revamped and expanded with modern instrumentation. 'FFIV Pixel Master' is hands down the best-SOUNDING port of the game, and this almost makes it worth the purchase alone. Field sprites have been upgraded with more accuracy and detail (Kain's field sprite now has turquoise armor instead of navy, matching his battle sprite, Yang's mustache is much more visible, etc.) Surprising new field graphic effects like waves, explosions and beams have been added, giving the game the most polished look it's ever had. Areas that were previously just palette swaps of eachother come alive with things like creeping fog and blowing sands. This is perhaps most striking in the infamous Lodestone Cavern; Random electrical bolts run down the walls and the screen will occasionally blur, making it much more obvious you're venturing within a magnetic field. Other quality-of-life improvements include displaying stat increases when a character levels up, the ability to walk in eight directions, tighter inventory management, quick save, and a smarter auto-battle.Negatives? Yes, the font is horrible. I recommend downloading a mod to upgrade it. Known bugs as of the 1.0.2 update include some glitched audio cues and a couple of minor visual errors (most notably, Edge's Throw animations are missing). What we will most likely never see fixed is the game's missing extras. All the bonus content present in almost every port since the Game Boy Advance version? Yeah, it's gone. That includes all the CG cutscenes, 'Final Fantasy IV Interlude' and 'The After Years'. All of these items were included in the PSP version and could've easily been included in 'Pixel Remaster'. Fat Chocobos are rendered completely useless, as inventory space is now infinite. Stat DEcreases are also gone which, in the case of party members like Tellah, actually helped show that these characters were changing (in Tellah's case, demonstrating his age catching up with him).THE VERDICT:'Final Fantasy IV Pixel Remaster' is essentially what the original 'FFIV' could've looked like had it'd been originally released on the PC-Engine instead of the SNES. As with the other Pixel Remasters, this port is likely the product of a backlash brought on by some of the questionable aesthetic choices of the mobile remasters. I bought 'Final Fantasy IV Pixel Remaster' knowing I was likely going to be at least a little letdown, but I'm a sucker for 'FFIV', and I haven't played the PSP version. There are definitely some glaring issues with this port, but so too have their been in pretty much every version of 'FFIV' to date, so I guess nothing's truly changed.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah yes, Final Fantasy 4. Others may have surpassed it technically, but it is still my favourite Final Fantasy. This was the first game I played where the characters were more than just vacant, blank slates sent out on some generic quest. Sure, the game has crystals, dragons, princes, princesses and all the other typical JRPG trappings, but every character had their own personality, motivations, and agendas. I still think the characters rank up there with any other Final Fantasy. It was a huge leap forward from FF1 (of course later when I learned about FF2 and FF3, it was somewhat less impressive, but still…) and this was probably the first time I found myself emotionally invested in a game. I recall getting angry walking among the displaced residents of Eblan or feeling happiness when reuniting with old companions along the way. The plot was like Shakespeare to my tween mind. Sure, with the benefit of 30 years maybe it is not as impressive as I remember, and some of the more interesting dialogue appears to be the result of a dubious translation. But, dang it, I think it still stands the test of time.The 3D remake was cool and all, but it was a different game (to some degree at least). So, getting an official PC release of the original is pretty awesome if you ask me. The updated graphics and music are icing on the cake.Also, I like the font.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: I came to FINAL FANTASY IV (Pixel remaster) with some knowledge about the game, like gameplay mechanics and a bit of story from FF, FFII and FFIII. I have recently just completed the first 3 FF (pixel remastered) games and I loved every moment of those games. After completing each game I moved onto the next game with even more knowledge on how to play and what I am looking for on each game for items and such. When I came to FFIV I was a bit overwhelmed by the new "flow of time" combat but I quickly adapted to it and by the time I finished the game... I wanted more. Final Fantasy IV is STELLAR. PHENOMENAL. GORGEOUS. STUNNING. A WORK OF ART. This has got to be the BEST story driven FF game I have played to this date. ⚫Again, like all other FF games, the soundtrack was amazing. You get to listen to all the songs in the main menu and some of them are just so heartwarming.⚫The auto-battle option is a welcome addition to a game like this.⚫The UI is so good in this game. I had a look at the older UI that was used... yeah... this new, improved, modern UI is a much needed welcome for new players like me but I do understand why some people want the original SNES version as an option.⚫You can dive into the world of the game with supplemental extras like the bestiary, illustration gallery, and music player.⚫They added the ability to "Target all enemies" or "Target all allies" with black magic spells or white magic spells. You no longer need to use multiple, say, lightning spells to kill a group of water monsters. 1 spell, target them all with lightning and BOOM, all dead. Saves you having to wait 3 rounds to kill 3 water monsters.⚫Final Fantasy IV also adds in the "flow of time" during battle. As you battle you see your little bar going up for when you can attack, if you take to long during your turn you will see that time keeps flowing and the enemy can keep attacking you. This was a major improvement in my opinion. Made the battle's feel more real and it also showed you when its your turn to attack.⚫The level design/Dungeon designs improved drastically again. Instead of only having one map to explore they added in another MASSIVE world below you that you can explore and THE MOON. Each new area looked stunning and unique. ⚫The hidden items around towns and secret chests return in this game with a little twist... they aren't that easy to find anymore. They made it so you run around searching the towns, caves, dungeons e.t.c looking for hidden walls and items. Before, it lacked that creativity to me but FFIV fixed that feeling and actually pushed me.⚫This game has some of the most memorable villains, characters and fights I have seen too. Ranging from the absolutely DEVIOUS Rubucante to the master Dragoon Kain. I do not think I will forget these 2 anytime soon.⚫From the start of the game the story had me hooked instantly. There was no silly side bits that would make you lost and the games story was AMAZING from start to finish. ⚫They improved on the "Where to go next" feeling DRASTICALLY with this game. I was never lost at all. With this being more of a STORY based FF game, you always knew where to go next if you read the dialogue. They tell you "Head east to the town of ....... " so you go east, do the story and then it tells you where to go next. All while exploring too. Amazing. ⚫Now, I do not know if people actually cared about this but theres a little room in a pub thats a developer room. I had to look online to see what this was and I am sad to say that it was indeed an easter egg that was removed from the PIXEL REMASTER of FFIV. "So if you're looking for the Developer's Room in here, it's found via a secret door in the Dwarven Castle pub. Here, NPCs representing FF4's staff can be found. However, it's been removed from the FF4 Pixel Remaster version"  As a complete "noob" to the FINAL FANTASY games, with knowledge of 1-3 and no knowledge of 4-13 this was an amazing journey for me and I loved every moment of it. I would recommend this game to anyone that likes turn-based games and the Final Fantasy series or to anyone like me, that's wanting to learn all these references and experience an amazing game series.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV has not been the first Final Fantasy I played. But it is the only title in the franchise so far that I’ve played more than twice. In fact, this Pixel Remaster playthrough has been the… fourth playthrough, I believe. As I’ve previously played through the original “Final Fantasy II” release, the unofficial translation of FFIV, the Final Fantasy Chronicles release on PS1 and the Final Fantasy IV Advance version on the GBA. I’ve also attempted to play the 3D remake for DS, but extremely disliked the visual style and changes to the game. Hence, why I was so excited about the Pixel Remaster version coming – hopefully the “ultimate” remaster of the original version of the game, available for generations to come. And this version is pretty much exactly that.Final Fantasy IV feels like the first game in the series, where everything clicked together just right. In many ways, it remains the “quintessential Final Fantasy” and a perfect introduction for anyone who has not played the series before. It has a strong story focus with lots of memorable characters and events, now presented in a more “cinematic” way than it was possible in the previous games. It streamlines all of the ideas of the previous titles in the best possible way, allowing you to enjoy the adventure without thinking too hard about the mechanics behind it. Even the soundtrack, that is always good in Final Fantasy games, feels especially memorable and amazing.Of course, the streamlining could be taken as a negative too. You no longer manage your party as much as you would in previous games – all of them have their own jobs/classes assigned and all you have to do is gain experience and level up, the skills and abilities will unlock on their own. There’s only one “gimmick” dungeon and even that one is pretty simple to go through. All while the requirement to think very tactically about using each class and each spell or ability comes up very occasionally, during the trickiest fights. Most of the time, you can just attack. The party size in IV is the largest of all numbered single-player Final Fantasy titles too, with five controllable party members, which also makes it considerably easier to manage the flow of the battle and turn the tide when the party members start getting incapacitated in any form. Personally, this never bothered me, as Final Fantasy IV is a fun story-driven adventure first, and a jRPG second. Which is why the fact that Pixel Remaster rebalances the game even further is more than fine with me.Now, the story of the game isn’t particularly deep or complex, and it even reuses some of the twists and ideas from the previous games, with some very direct references to Final Fantasy II. This is more of a young adult fantasy adventure story than anything, but a well delivered one. And, arguably, that’s what most of the Final Fantasy stories are like, with more complex plots and characters being an exception rather than the norm. It also feels smaller in scope compared to the previous game, but yet again – most of the games in the franchise are.There are elements of the game that have never been great and are not changed by the Pixel Remaster. The final dungeon, for one, is still a pain in the butt, even with the return of additional save points from previous ports. If you’re a completionist, you will be happy to hear that items like “Siren” can be purchased in a shop added in the previous ports and the chance of some enemy drops have been increased. And with the quick save ability you can always retry if you run out of this item. But you’ll also be sad to learn, that this doesn’t make the item grinding any less annoying, just potentially shorter.That said, if you aren’t aiming at doing everything the game has to offer, it’s unlikely you will have to grind or will find many troublesome parts (apart from the final dungeon, I suppose) that can detract from the enjoyment of the adventure. The rebalanced level gain feels just right for that (and if you want to grind, it’s less tedious now too) and I’m glad it’s here. Also I’m very glad that none of the additions from the latest ports, like new dungeons and ties to “The After Years” are here. The flow of the game is exactly as it was in the original version with most of the script sticking to the original Japanese version lines (they did keep the “Spoony Bard”, I’m happy to note). I can see some lamenting the lack of those expanded mechanics and ideas, but personally I found them to be annoying and superfluous.In case it’s not obvious, Final Fantasy IV is one of my favorite entries in the series. And Pixel Remaster version is exactly what I wanted to see. The game, in my opinion, remains one of the best candidates for “your first Final Fantasy experience”, with the remaster making it even more enjoyable. And even the new arrangements for the soundtrack felt so perfectly close to the original, despite being enriched with new instrumentation, that I never felt like I wanted an option to switch to the original soundtrack (even though I still feel like it should be a thing in these remasters). I loved replaying FFIV yet again and cannot recommend this Pixel Remaster version enough.
