_childDocuments_.review: My Final Fantasy journey continues! Easily the most story-driven so far, and more engaging on that front. I do not care for the mixed system of turn-based with the action timers, which is far less satisfying because you're navigating the combat menus while the clock keeps ticking. So the game mechanics are worse than 1-3 on that front. However, it was nice to see the staple from later Final Fantasy games show up the first time with Summons. The constantly rotating cast made for more interesting story, but was a bit annoying as well, however it's not done so much that it ruined the game for me. The music is absolutely my favorite of the four, and the remastered tracks really help. 4 is one of the "big" ones and I can see why, I just don't like the stupid action bar during combat. Either go full turn-based or full action combat.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: This game was kind of a blast, this was the first game in the series to have that real "Final Fantasy" feel to it.  From the gameplay to the story this game truly was a HUGE step in the right direction for the series. The gameplay is honestly incredible, first using the "Active Time Battle" system it makes fighting enemies so engaging (and stressful lol) it also requires a lot of thought into what tactic you're using at any given time.  Each time there is new enemies in a dungeon or when facing a new boss you have to really figure out the best way to attack and how to time each attack accordingly, the battle system of previous games i really liked and found to be fun, however here battles are just simply less "clunky" then previous entries. I also am in love with the presentation with this game, the music is honestly breathtaking in many places (when the boss battle theme comes on you know im bustin it down) there are so many stand out tracks in this game made all the better by the orchestral arrangements. I also love the artstyle although if your playing all these games in a row it might get a little stale looking at the same kind of graphics for each game. Sadly the only part of this game I think is objectivly weak is... the story. Now that doesnt mean I think it's bad by any means, the previous games only had "story" as an excuse to get you from one place to the next. With this game though, it actually has an actualized plot that you can follow along to and characters that are supposed to be interesting.But the story just feels not fleshed out... In the slightest. some of the characters are interesting, but a lot of them are very dull and generic. There are no moments with the characters that makes me care about them, with only a few exceptions. The plot just has too many cliches with no substance, there are some interesting moments but they are far and few between honestly. despite all of this I think that the game is great one to play through for those little cool moments of story, and sick gameplay. Even if there are moments that kick my ass, there many things that really make up for it.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Like everyone else, I LOVED the music.  It is definitely a great improvement while keeping the spirit of the original. I know its an old game, and it is supposed to be pixelated, but the pixelation is way too overkill.  The original game actually looked a lot better and I prefer to play that game even without the Quality of Life improvements.  Also, a lot of the original animations were replaced, the new ones are meh.  I really loved the original animations (or Sprites) and don't like the fact they replaced them.The translations are also terrible.  Spells are renamed and oddly, what is wrong with "Lit" and "Fire Bomb"?  Part of the story is also translated terribly. _childDocuments_.review: FF4 was always celebrated for being a challenging RPG.  When it came to the US on the SNES, Square (rightfully) assumed we were all idiots and toned their game down a few notches so it wouldn't be quite so difficult to American audiences.  Future releases not only bumped the challenge up to the level it should be, it also added substantial extra content.FF4 Pixel remaster not only omits all this extra content, it dumbs down the difficulty of the game even further than the original SNES release.  You only require half the XP per level, so you essentially level twice as fast.  Once you are a couple hours into the game, you are now overleveled the point that none of the bosses even present the slightest challenge.  You can literally set the game to auto battle and win against most bosses.  The new music arrangements and the prettier spell effects are nice enough, but if you paint a turd gold, it's still a turd.If you want to experience FF4 (and you should), go buy the 3D remake.  It will challenge you and give you an overall better experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV is a big evolution for the series' story and characters. _childDocuments_.review: I'm no stranger to Final Fantasy or the Active Time Battle system, but this is chronologically the first in the series to use it, and definitely the worst implementation I've ever encountered. If you need time to think, that's too bad, because you can't have a command window open that isn't magic or items without having the enemy timers ticking frenetically away. With up to five characters to rapidly make decisions for, it can make it hard to enjoy the fights or even know what is going on.The story isn't bad, but FF9 delivered a much more satisfying version of basically the same plot.The encounter design is garbage. It's one thing for random encounters to include creatures that are just too much hassle for one reason or another: Constantly healing to full, instant death attacks, etc. It's not hard to escape random encounters. Gimmicky boss fights that are over-tuned to the point of one-shotting characters who can breeze through the rest of the dungeon even when responding to the gimmicks correctly? In a dungeon where you can't replenish your items or leave without defeating the boss? Even allowing that the 90s were a different time, some things just aren't acceptable.If I had played this when it originally came out, I might have dropped the franchise permanently.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: These remasters are not Super Final Fantasy Turbo HD Remixes, but they are cozy, pixel-sharp, have absolutely gorgeous new soundtracks, and play well.Honestly, the best part is how many people will complain about "missing content" that, before they announced these, they would have called "superfluous content from the handheld releases" - just being contradictory - or those that don't know how to use a computer and need to have this on a console. It'll obviously get a console release when all 6 are out; I'm happy with the first-on-PC approach, myself.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really nice version of one of THE classic JRPGs of the 1990s with an outstanding rearranged soundtrack! If you're looking for a straightforward, story-focused playthrough with great characters and narrative, look no further.One small negative is that they left out the additional content of the GBA version, but since I played the SNES version first, I got a lot of good nostalgia from this. And you can load your save after beating the final boss, to complete more achievements if you want, which is a nice bonus. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED, unless you're looking for challenging combat, then play the 3D remake of FF4!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: While Final Fantasy I got me into experience-based RPGs as a child, Final Fantasy IV (known as II at the time in the US) sealed the deal. This was the love of my youth and gave me an appreciation for classical music...if not gaming music in general. Compared to games of the time, the characters were older, well-developed and the storyline was more mature. My review below is thus made in comparison to the SNES version, as I never played Japanese, expansion or other remake versions. While the game is close to my heart, I don't have rose-tinted glasses. The original had a lot of issues, though it was also groundbreaking for RPG and FF mechanics and story quality moving forward.If you loved the original, you'll probably love this. If you never played the original, this game may not have aged well and the bugs I experienced with the October 1st, 2021 patch may make things worse.+Improved graphics.+Improved and faithful music.+Art book and bestiary built into the game.+Still contains a full serving of spoony bards.+Characters that leave party return all their equipment.+A few additional abilities and items not in original US version.+Item descriptions, including on-use effects.~The EXP required to level has been halved, making the game more casual. I personally was happy with the original game, which I didn't find grindy at all, so I modded the original EXP tables back in.~A modern font is used to comply with iPhone apps. There's an easily-available mod to use FFVI fonts, though.~Combat is generally trivial except for the increasingly common number of enemies that counter-attack your physical or magical attacks - often with unusually high damage. A few enemies and bosses in the final dungeon can still wreck your face if unprepared.~Doesn't have the additional content from other re-release versions.~Developer's Room has been removed (though it wasn't in the US release in the first place).~Minimap, area maps, autobattling, sprinting, diagonal movement and quick saving are all new. However, you can disable or simply choose not use them.~Environmental objects you can interact with have a little popup when you're next to them. You don't need to spam your interact key/button on everything in the game now...just walk near.~Would have liked the option to play the original SNES music, as much as I like the remastered.~Attack animations are slightly different. Mostly noticeable on dual-wielding characters.~Missable achievements.~The patch that hit today apparently raised the drop rates for some achievement-related items. I can't say how well they worked since I only had about an hour of playtime left when the patch it. Tying achievements to the frequently and ridiculously low droprates in this game was a bad idea. -Minor translation updates are included, but renaming of the package that goes to Mist completely spoils the upcoming event.-Had to manually modify my NVIDIA 3D settings to enable VSync and stop screen tearing.-Nearly impossible to organize your inventory with the changes they made to it. Also, no need for the fat chocobo anymore.-The mouse cursor doesn't disappear when not in use unlike just about every other game out there.-Strangely long load times for what you'd expect to be a glorified SNES emulator.-Healing from the menu is laggy and lacks feedback.-Weapon/armor comparison doesn't show all stats and can give you bad advice.-Starting autobattle too early softlocks the game.-Today's patch frequently soft-locked my game when battle started or even when exiting the bestiary. I only got through things by using Quick Save.

_childDocuments_.review: In their "Pixel Remastered"- series Square Enix polishes the graphics and the OST of the Originals, but otherwise stays truthful to what those games were - game mechanics, dialogues, etc. stayed the same. Final Fantasy IV took a step up to its predecessors in terms of character development. In FF I and FF III the character did not even have own names and not even a story. They were characterless figures running through a plot. In FF II the characters had names, but their stories were  thin. FF IV is a major change in this regard, giving their characters background story and character development. This is the reason why Final Fantasy IV plays a major role in the evolution of the franchise.But by no means is FF IV a masterpiece of storytelling.  We are talking 1991 standards here. Back in the day the story felt revolutionary - but from today's perspective FF IV tells an odd story with flat characters. The game mechanics - sadly - are not as good as in FF III, which had the generally well working Job System. In FF IV your characters have preset classes. The Dark Knight deals a good amount of physical damage, the White Mage is a good healer, the Black Mage can cause magical damage, etc. Sadly you are not flexible with your party since you cannot switch any party members - and the game really suffers from that. Therefore, I can only recommend this game to fans of the series. If you are such: Go for it. You will not regret the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV, imo, is the first FF to really introduce a deep, emotional storyline. With this game's great characters, great traditional jrpg story, and amazing soundtrack, Final Fantasy IV is easily one of the best in the series. I highly recommend! And, of course this is all just my opinion and we all have one, but if you're a fan of FF or just beginning to start the series for the first time, do NOT overlook this gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV - Pixel Remaster it's such a nostalgic trip, especially with the intro of the Active Time Battle (ATB) system.So, let's talk characters. Unlike some of the earlier games, where you could mold your characters into whatever you wanted, FFIV sticks them into specific roles. Each character has their own thing going on, and they grow into these roles in ways that feel really unique. The story it's your classic hero's journey, but it’s surprisingly deep for a game of its age. It’s simple, but each character has personal goals and motivations that add layers to the narrative.Gameplay-wise, the Pixel Remaster makes things a bit easier, which is great if you want a more relaxed experience. But, here's the catch - if you decide to do a bit of grinding, you can easily get overleveled. This can make some boss fights less challenging. It’s a bit of a bummer because you miss out on the unique tactics you'd need in the original versions.Now, about that ATB system—it’s a bit of a mixed bag. On one hand, it adds this cool layer of urgency because enemies can keep attacking if you’re slow to make decisions. On the other hand, it can feel clunky, especially when you're waiting for a spell to go off. It's definitely different from the turn-based system in FFIII. But, as clunky as it feels sometimes, the ATB system does have its charm. It allows for more dynamic battles and keeps you on your toes, which I’ve grown to appreciate after some time.One thing I absolutely loved was the mid-dungeon checkpoints. They’re such a lifesaver! You can grind a bit and then take a breather without trekking all the way back to town. It’s a small quality-of-life improvement, but it makes a big difference.Overall, the combat is the highlight of the game. It's engaging and, for the most part, avoids feeling repetitive. FFIV was a pioneer with the ATB system, and while it’s not perfect, it introduced a sense of real-time pressure that made battles feel more intense and immediate. Even though you can't customize your characters' classes, figuring out how to best use each one in different situations feels like solving a puzzle, especially with the mid-game bosses. 8/10

The auto-battle option speeds up battles and is quite clutch for grinding. The run button is also a great time-saver. The on-screen maps make navigating and finding treasure a lot more streamlined than they could have been. The graphics in the game work just fine. I think they're a solid midway point between the original Super Famicom graphics and the PSP version's graphics, which were quite stylized by comparison.I know there are so many versions out there, but I can easily recommend this one for new players because of the quality-of-life features, shorter length, and a presentation style that feels true to the original while being modernized in some really nice ways.

I find the new fonts fine without having played earlier releases, but I understand those that prefer the old one and would prefer at least a toggle. Luckily the modders were on it day one. What it has an option for, however, are the button prompts: it's not as common - even among brand new releases - as it should be to have both Xbox and PS prompts available for choice by default.It's pretty much what I expected from a classic's remaster. Recommended if you're looking for that oldschool JRPG experience available out of the box.

_childDocuments_.review: Another Pixel Remaster is here, and you know what that means. Get ready to perform your own Day 1 patch. You’ll need to, at minimum, do a font fix and a fix for the forest tiles on the world map before you start playing the game. The guides section will help you out with these. I love Final Fantasy IV. It’s my favorite 2D entry in the series. And so despite the many issues with the pixel remaster, I still had a great time playing it. If all you want to do is play the game in the easiest way possible and get a solid dose of nostalgia, this version is fine. It’s for that reason that I’m just barely giving this a positive rating. The writing and translation work is very good. Visuals are solid- not as extensive as what was done on FF1-FF3, but the widescreen presentation is appealing and the game mostly looks very good if a little too bright. The music remixes range from quite good to downright puzzling, but I was able to adjust to most of the new music without issue. It’s nonsensical that there is no option to switch between the original and remixed soundtracks, but the Pixel Remasters are not known for being thorough with the options. The difficulty is far too low- unless you run from a large number of battles, you will quickly and effortlessly outlevel the entire game. It’s possible to miss out on the unique mechanics in certain boss battles entirely because you just defeat them too quickly. This is the worst issue with this, and all of the other remasters. FF4 was not an extremely hard game back in the day, but you shouldn’t be able to mindlessly auto-battle your way through the final dungeon of all places. A first time player should make every effort to play the original Super Famicom version translated for the best possible experience. But if you want the quick FF4 revisit experience to squeeze in during your 40 hour work week, there are worse ways to spend your money.

_childDocuments_.review: A Timeless Tale of Heroism and Redemption - Final Fantasy IV ReviewIntroduction:Final Fantasy IV, a seminal entry in the long-running franchise, has captivated players since its initial release in 1991. With its engrossing story, memorable characters, and innovative gameplay, this classic RPG has stood the test of time. Developed by Square Enix, the remastered version of Final Fantasy IV brings the beloved adventure to modern platforms, allowing both long-time fans and newcomers to experience its magic. Join me as we delve into the world of Final Fantasy IV and explore its strengths, weaknesses, and enduring appeal.Graphics and Presentation:The remastered edition of Final Fantasy IV showcases beautifully updated visuals that retain the essence of the original while introducing enhanced character models, vibrant environments, and impressive spell effects. The meticulously designed world immerses players in a rich tapestry of diverse landscapes, from lush forests and ancient castles to foreboding caves and sprawling cities. The attention to detail and artistic flair breathe new life into the game, creating a visually stunning experience that captures the imagination.Gameplay and Character Development:Final Fantasy IV introduces several groundbreaking gameplay mechanics that have since become staples of the series. The Active Time Battle (ATB) system revolutionized turn-based combat, injecting a sense of urgency and dynamism into battles. Players must make strategic decisions quickly, as the enemies and allies act in real-time. The introduction of character classes, each with their unique abilities, adds depth and variety to the gameplay, allowing for diverse party compositions and flexible strategies.The narrative-driven gameplay of Final Fantasy IV unfolds across a series of emotionally charged story arcs, filled with dramatic twists, political intrigue, and personal redemption. The characters undergo significant growth and development, with memorable personalities and motivations. Cecil, the conflicted protagonist, undergoes a compelling journey of self-discovery and redemption, surrounded by a cast of colorful allies and formidable antagonists. The narrative's emotional depth and thematic resonance make it a standout entry in the series.Music and Sound Design:The remastered soundtrack of Final Fantasy IV masterfully combines the original compositions with updated arrangements, striking a perfect balance between nostalgia and modern musical sensibilities. The sweeping orchestral scores heighten the emotional impact of key story moments, while the energetic battle themes enhance the intensity of combat encounters. The sound effects, from the clash of weapons to the casting of spells, are meticulously crafted, immersing players in the world and adding weight to their actions.Enhancements and Extra Content:The remastered version of Final Fantasy IV introduces various enhancements and bonus content. The inclusion of voice acting brings the characters to life, adding an additional layer of immersion. The improved graphics and interface enhance the overall visual experience, making navigation and combat more intuitive. Additionally, the post-game content, such as bonus dungeons and optional boss battles, provide extended gameplay and rewarding challenges for dedicated players.Conclusion:Final Fantasy IV, in its remastered form, remains a shining example of the genre-defining RPGs that have made the series legendary. Its captivating visuals, innovative gameplay mechanics, and emotionally charged story continue to resonate with players. Whether you are a long-time fan or a newcomer, Final Fantasy IV offers an unforgettable journey of heroism, redemption, and personal growth. With its timeless appeal and enduring impact on the RPG genre, Final Fantasy IV is a must-play experience that showcases the brilliance of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR this software is hands down the best version of FF4 to RE-play the game. Every single piece of criticism (notably lack of features, voice acting, being forced to fight harder bossfights and grind bc of that, graphic/animation bling, cinematic  pacing) is actually at the same time very valid and irrelevant... if you revisit the game and not play it for the 1st time.for the first playthrough i -> together with the majority of reviewers, recommend you playing the 3d remake on steam, favorably with an xbox controller, on hard mode for the "true" experience. if you are an adult who actually has better things to do than spending an extra ~10-15h on the most boring parts of this game in order to attain a *slightly better* experience during eg bossfights, cutscenes etc  there is nothing wrong with you going immediately for this version. if you are like me and the game is essentially burned to your head anyway you wont miss anythinng really. most significant is again that i can probably 100% this game in less than 20 hours without sweat. yes that is partially due to some neglectible npcs and achievements being removed but the overall user experience is drastically improved, from faster dialog speed to better combat automatization its just glaring. so essentially the only crowd not pleased by this are 1.) people with  alot of time who want the best introduction playthrough and 2.) people who wanted the definitive version of FF4 and are disappointed because this is missing a few pieces in order to be inherently favored by the most hardcore fans.

_childDocuments_.review: Still a great game, in one of its best looking shapes. Yet I would have left the difficulty level untouched. With the new balance you can beat the game with virtually no challenge at all, which is a shame. My memories of this game are mainly made of great boss battles which are now nowhere as challenging as they were back then. Could it be that I am only grown better? Most likely it's not only that. Still, great edition of a great game (and epic new version of the OST).
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: New review having beaten it last night.The game might start out feeling it's not as fun as the others since some of the earlier characters like Tellah and Edward aren't quite as good as main character Cecil, or Kain or Yang. But the game becomes more enjoyable as it progresses.My only real complaint is that most new characters you get are way underleveled and might take quite a bit of level grinding to get them up close to Cecil's level. But characters that leave and rejoin are always around Cecil's level when they rejoin. If you don't mind that, the game can be very enjoyable.I initially gave it a negative review for the apparent inability to run from battle, but I later found out you are able to do so by holding 2 and 3. Aside from not saying anywhere how to do this, running from battle is very easy in this game as you immediately run as soon as one of your characters is able to make a move (other games they often take a long time resulting in several hits from the enemy you're not ready to fight, and in II, at least PSP version, you can't run from enemies who are stronger than you), which is very useful in the last stretch of final dungeon where Behemoths are encountered almost every battle.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first 16-bit game in the series, and it shows. Playing them in sequence makes it clear that this was a big step for the franchise, with better graphics, music, and a much richer story. In fact, this was one of the best stories in RPGs at the time, and even today it inspires modern games. Characters are charismatic, and Cecil's epic adventure is emotionally rich.Having played the original SNES game and the PSP remake, I can say that this one is a lot closer to the 16-bit version. Graphics are very similar, although different, and it lacks the bonus present in both portable versions. In the case of music, this one is the best version, with an amazing soundtrack. All in all, this is a good version, better than the 3D remake for the DS (in my opinion).For those playing for the first time, I offer some advices:- the game can be hard at the middle portion, when you won't have a reliable healer for some time. Buy a lot of items for regeneration,- grinding is not necessary, but it can help in some situations. Try to gain at least 2 levels every time you reach a new dungeon.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: An iconic classic with a fresh coat of paint! I prefer this over the previous releases of this game - this version feels like how it should be experienced. Almost like Octopath Traveler in terms of slight graphic upgrades (though not quite as polished as that). The standout for me is the updated soundtrack, it really does this beautiful soundtrack justice. Overall I'd say this is the best iteration of this game so far - play this version!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: I love Final Fantasy IV. If you want to get into the classic (pre-PS era) games but don't know where to start Final Fantasy IV pixel remaster is a good place to start. It focuses more on story over mechanics, the game isn't too hard (like Final Fantasy III or earlier), the game can literally be completed by simply grinding it out because abilities are generally learned on level up. It's a really solid story.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 4 is a good, simple game. It's not a great game, but it's definitely a game worth your time. The plot is basically the classic hero's journey of fighting evil and overcoming great odds, and it's actually really refreshing to play this kind of game in an age where everything has to be deconstructed. Every character these days is this weird, ironic Marvel character who has to say a funny line every 10 seconds. This kind of writing is so inflationary these days that the old traditional hero's journey is actually kind of refreshing to experience (which is pretty funny, to be fair).It's also a good game if you're interested in the history of Final Fantasy, because this game started a lot of trends for the franchise, at least until Final Fantasy 9, like the Active Time Battle (ATB), getting rid of jobs, focusing on character specialities (except for FF5) and therefore also focusing on a much deeper character story than just an adventure type game. All the things you love about FF6,7,8 and 9 started with this game, so it's a very interesting game to experience if you're a big fan of the franchise.I think the price is a bit much though, so get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think a lot of people will tell you not to play a classic game. That being said, it's a generic RPG. You can't  choose classes, there is no skill tree or much item selection, party members leave on you randomly. The game is fairly compact but it's still story driven, so you can entirely skip over parts if you just follow the story and don't check everything before you go to the wrong place. The ATB system feels very unfair: Enemies take turns after you already locked in your move and kill your healer or mage who take ages to carry out their turn. You can turn random encounters off and increase XP, and as far as I'm concerned, there is no reason to play the game as it was intended. If you get to level 50 near the end you just get bodied, and if you throw in 20 more levels it's just trivial.  Try it if you're interested in history, otherwise I wouldn't bother.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV brings much more compelling writing to the series. Characters now have some actual depth to them. Even the player characters are memorable, unlike previous installments. I would go so far as to say that FFIV is more story-focused than combat-focused at times. There are secrets, scripted battles, NPC dialogues, and so much more waiting to be discovered. You also run into situations where  but it feels so much for satisfying and story-driven than the way FFII handled it. Unlike FFII, it feels like it matters.The move towards character and story-focused gameplay results in a cast that you can actually feel complex motions about (complex for a 90s JRPG) and it doesn't feel at all out-of-place when playing it. It also means that there are some genuine twists in the story.This game is a joy to play whether you're already a current fan of the series or not. I would say that if you're trying to introduce someone to the early Final Fantasy games then I would show them FFIV first. FFI is rough around the edges, FFII can be frustrating, but I think FFIV is just right to get someone interested.

_childDocuments_.review: I played and platinumed all six Pixel Remasters, and wrote six weird rambling reviews! Read them all for comparison and context, or skip to the one you came here for!This is the most barebones of the series, no pesky characters or plot to get in the way. Kill some enemies, level up, next town, new gear, next dungeon. It is also probably the second easiest. Not going to complain! Short, sweet and to the point. Just over 18 hours for all achievements. You start out with your four nameless, silent,  little pixelated heroes and choose a class for each of them. I chose warrior, “thief,” white mage, and black mage. I did some research and as far as I can tell “thief” is Japanese for what roughly translates to “broke-ass warrior.” I would recommend new players to opt for two full warriors as to have a party of 4 instead of the 3.5 that I ended up with. Sure, his defense, damage, HP, and set of equipable weapons were all worse than my warrior, but his agility was slightly above average, so I had that working for me!Level-ups come in the traditional way, classes are well defined, spells are bought at shops. Instead of having a global MP pool, each tier of spells has a limited number of casts (recharged by items or at an inn).Music was good, but nothing remarkable. Verdict: 3.5/5 “thieves” This is the weird one where you level-up a skill or weapon by using it repeatedly, Bethesda-style. There are no classes or jobs per-se but each character gets good at what they have been doing. It’s not my preferred way of doing business, but I didn’t mind too much. For their second entry in the series, they actually bothered to have some sort of plot! There seem to be people in the world who have lives, roles in society and care about stuff. You have your war, an evil empire, and a magical tornado, oh my! Your “characters” however are just pixelated bundles of stats who barely speak. That’s fine, just swing those hunks of metal and wood at the things I tell you to swing them at. Uh, Maria… your bow is pointing the wrong way. A pretty easy entry in the series, with a weird difficulty spike at the end, but even that wasn’t too bad. You can quick-save between fights. Buy your spells at town. Cast them with a global MP pool this time. Cost is based on how much you have leveled the spell. (Spells are are trash btw in this one, but a few enemies are highly resistant to physical.)Again, music was par for the course.Verdict: 3.5/5 evil empiresOur third entry here seems to be the birthplace of jobs. A job is like a class but a bit more focused and you can swap in out of them at any time. Your job levels up independently of your character level, but character level has much more barring on your effectiveness, so you are encouraged to bounce around jobs from time to time. This was definitely the easiest of the six games, and just barely the shortest, clocking in at about 18 hours for 100% achievements. Auto-battle, Hello. Much like the first, the story is bare-bones and player characters are just stat-sprites. Just bellybuttonless palette-swapped clones who occasionally grunt. The magic system is the same as the first game. It’s probably the weakest entry in the series, unless you're into the whole “brevity” thing… man.I caught some of the music, but to be honest I was listening to the Cyberpunk 2077 score for much of this game. A little weird, I know…  Moving on!  Verdict: 3/5 floating continentsOh sh*t, here we go! We have characters, they live, they love, they suffer, they grow. Romance, betrayal! Ok, sorry, let’s start over. The third entry takes a big leap forward in terms of characters and story, as in, it has them. You have your  main characters and then some guests that come and go. Jobs are gone, and the characters each have a set, permanent class. The classes are well defined with unique abilities and equipment sets. Spells, for those who can use them, are learned naturally through leveling. This is probably the second best game in the series. Challenge and length are moderate. The story, characters, and destinations are all well above average. Some extremely unforgiving RNG from the original has been toned down significantly for those of you interested in treasure-hunting all the treasures huntable. The music takes a big step up at this point in the series. The moon music is strange yet awesome. The “giant” music is epic and gorgeous. Could it be that this is just the nostalgia factor due to playing this game as a wonder-filled, wide-eyed child? Nope! Verdict: 4.5/5 spoony bardsJobs: checkAcceptably life-like characters: checkHigh concentrations of chocobo: checkVerdict: Not yet? Ok. This is the hardest game in the series, and second longest. We’ve jumped up to almost 57 hours for all achievements! *sigh* What am I doing with my life?  Annoying status effects abound in the later dungeons (where are those damned ribbons?), and optional superbosses make their first appearance! Think Ruby and Emerald in FF7. As mentioned above, jobs are back. And how. There’s a ton of them, and you’re going to master every bloody one if you want that final achievement. Yes, even the geomancer! Especially the geomancer!! One really great thing is that you can master certain abilities or passives unique to one job and then “equip” it on another job (one at a time only). Buy your spells at the local grocer. Standard MP pool is present. If you enjoy a grind and a challenge, this is the one for you. The music quality remains high, especially on a certain larger-than-normal bridge, and when fighting one not-so-mysterious swordsman.  \m/Verdict: 4/5 cartoonish, one-dimensional villains We made it. Here we are at what is definitely the crown jewel of the Pixel Remasters. Maybe even the best RPG of its era? I would still argue for Chrono Trigger, but elder millennials and gen-xers of good faith can disagree. Where to start? We have a massive cast of memorable characters (including the best villain of all time), romance, comedy, tragedy, and the best spectacle and story-telling in the series. The locations, the towns, dungeons, forests, and factories really come to life through excellent art direction and detail. And the music is stellar! “But this isn’t the end of the review...” Don’t care!Note: Some reviews mention a strange rainy town filled with thieves and liars. Never heard of it. Not in this game. My only gripe with VI is the class system. There really isn’t much of one. Every character has a unique ability, but equipment sets have huge overlap, and characters are frequently rotating in and out of the party. So you never feel like you have clear defined combat roles. Really, it’s nitpicking though. This is the longest of the games, though it ends up feeling appropriate. Difficulty is middling.Now, I know you're dying for me to tell you how magic works in VI. Well, dear reader, for that you will have to subject yourself to a fairly minor spoiler.  Well, that’s it! The music is amazing. The overworld theme, the blonde’s theme, the villains theme. And the town that doesn’t exist has terrible music!Verdict: 5/5 16-bit laughs, 5/5 opera-loving octopi, 5/5 B-day suits. I can’t decide!

_childDocuments_.review: I love FFIV: this version is visually appealing and the re-recorded music tracks are great. However the difficulty is lowered to the point this version of FFIV is a walking simulator. This is Square's first real story for an FF and it shows as the years have gone on, it's full of plot armor and cheesy one-liners. Without any difficulty to slow down the pacing of the narrative, all of the minute flaws of the narrative are in the players' face. The 3D version is still my preferred version to experience FFIV. I hope Square will patch this game to bring over the difficulty balance from the 3D version. (I don't mind not having Rydia get one-shot outside of Kaipo, but after the first boss fight with Rydia she has enough levels/HP to survive encounters). Ideally the difficulty should pick up when Edward is in the party. And after Antlion take on the difficulty of the 3D version.Is it a running meme at Square that every other release of FFIV needs diluted difficulty? Hardtype (Chronicles release US) had an engaging difficulty, the 3D version had multiple options for difficulty. It's a little sad to see the latest release of FFIV being a walking simulator.

_childDocuments_.review: They continue to do a great job with these ports.  The orchestral music is the star of these Pixel Remasters in my opinion, and it remains true with this game as well.  Some may have issue with the fact the player levels more quickly in this version, though I still found the final boss to be a massive threat anyway.  I did not go out of my way to grind other than picking up things that could be missed to complete all the achievements and exploring each area.  Farming for the ultimate equipment absolutely did over-level me to an extreme degree, but the resulting equipment trivializes the game anyway too.Regarding bugs, they patched the most pressing ones and I did not have any significant issues playing.  That said, there's really absolutely no excuse for lack of in-game v-sync settings and apparently the way it scrolls can cause some stuttering.  I forced v-sync on in my GPU settings and got used to the remaining quirks immediately, but it would be nice if they fixed that in all the Pixel Remasters.  The soundtrack overall is fantastic, and remains the highlight of these Pixel Remasters for me.It's a real shame they aren't bringing over the bonus dungeons and other content from some of the other 2D releases, but this is still a fantastic version of the game anyway.The 3D remake is still fantastic and remains (by design) the hardest version of the game.  I recommend both of them, and would have difficulty choosing between them exclusively.

_childDocuments_.review: I fondly remember playing the FFIV remaster on the GBA as a teenager in the late 2000's.  So how does the FFIV Pixel Remaster hold up?  Especially when compared to my continuation from FFI, II, and III?  Well, it is indeed as epic as I remembered, though the pros and cons of this entry generally end up being the same thing depending on who you ask, and what you value most in a Final Fantasy.While it has it's cliches, there is more story development and dialogue in the first hour of FFIV than the first three FF games combined.  It can get aggravating having characters join and leave the party frequently, almost arbitrarily, but they are moved in and out fluently, and the PR does let you keep their equipped items. Because of how well scripted your characters are, your team composition will look almost identical to someone else's at any given point of progression. Also, all-in-all, this entry isn't particularly long; with a guide, it is easily 100%-able in about 20 hours or so, though without a guide, you could easily spend double that time.So what's the big deal about this entry in the series then?Well, story and exposition needed to convey a fantasy game is actually here, and it's great, especially for its time. This Final Fantasy finally conveys some serious emotion, and combined with an absolutely amazing music direction, creates powerful and memorable scenes. From a Pixel Remaster standpoint, this entry is also the first to (in my view) have some genuinely difficult boss battles, which is a plus, though keep in mind bonus content from prior remasters, which was usually the source of very difficult fights, are not included in this release; given the sub $20 asking price, and focus on preservation of the original game, this was not a big deal to me, personally. While shorter than II or III to 100% (after some rare drop rates were increased in IV) the quality of the overall game direction is greater.While FFIV may only seem like a slight step forward in terms of gameplay, it feels far more refined and direct, and thus more fun to play. The narrative is light-years ahead of the prior three entries, and far more memorable as a result. I can't deny the nostalgia from my own perspective, but I also can't deny how great it felt and refreshing it was to play after the first three entries, which focused more heavily on gameplay over narrative. While FFIV is not the 'Hamlet' of JRPGs, it is still a legendary RPG and among the best FF's, deservedly.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV, yet another fantastic entry in a fantastic franchise (and just as I'm typing this I realize the unintended pun). By now, if you've been playing these Pixel Remasters, you should be familiar with the basics. Graphics are obviously 2D, and gameplay remains mostly the same, as it's a classic RPG with turn based combat. However, this game introduced the ATB system, or Active Time Battle, which I was already familiar with from playing Final Fantasy VII.The way ATB works is that each of your characters has a gauge that fills up overtime. When that gauge is filled, you can perform an action, be it attacking, using items, or casting magic. So, it's like turn-based, but not quite so. Enemies most likely use a similar system, although you can't see their gauge. Another interesting gameplay aspect is that now many enemies counterattack certain actions with a special move; some enemies might react against physical attacks, casting spells immediately, or might use powerful attacks whenever you use magic, so there's this whole deal about figuring out the best way to approach a battle.Another change is the party system. First of all, you can now have up to five members, instead of four. And, like Final Fantasy II, your roster will be changing throughout the course of the game until settling into the final party. The leveling system remains similar to previous games (minus II); after each battle, you get XP that helps you level up, and whenever you level up, stats increase. Something new, though, is that spells aren't bought, your characters learn them either through story events, or leveling up.Now, getting onto the story, while previous games already have a mix of fantastic elements and some minor science fiction, this is the game where things start getting really weird. Without getting into a lot of spoiler territory, you'll be facing fantastic creatures like dragons, as well as technological monsters like robots. The story itself is also filled with twists and turns, as it begins with Dark Knight Cecil questioning the actions he's performed lately in the service of his king. It's probably a bit silly and overdramatic in parts, but honestly, having played several Final Fantasy games now, I love them for the overdramatic and silly.The soundtrack is once again great, with remastered tracks, and graphically, well, I already said it above, don't expect many changes from the previous Pixel Remasters, besides some updated sprites for enemies. The charm is in looking retro.All in all, this is yet another Final Fantasy game I can easily recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, yes, I do recommend this game, but mostly for the nostalgia and the fact that you don't need an emulator and hope you can find a working ROM to play.  Comparatively, I don't know if, "remastered," is really the word for what this is, since most of it looks and plays almost the same.  In any case, here's my comparison to the SNES version.The good:By comparison to the original, the effects during the spell-casting, summoning, and plot based scenes, got a MAJOR upgrade.  The cut scene for when Leviathan attacks the ship, for example, is way better than the original.  There were improvements to some of the BGM as well, and the menus are clear and sharp.  The ability to track how many chests you've found in each location is a nice touch.  It's also kind of cool that you can scale the mini-map as needed.  And unlike the original, diagonal movement is possible, to make traversing areas much quicker.  As far as the individual characters in combat, I'm not sure if this is an improvement or not, but it seems some of the characters have additional skills.  For example, Cecil starts with an AOE attack called, "Darkness," Edward has a, "Heal," ability, and Tellah has the ability to recall spells he forgot.  This ability disappears after Mt. Ordeals.  These new abilities can sometimes be useful.The "meh":  The names of the spells have all been updated to more recent incarnations (reflect instead of wall, etc.) so if you're expecting to see all the old ones, don't.  Many of the enemies, lots of Cecil's gear, and several bosses, to include the Elemental Fiends, have received name changes.  Kinda weird, but again, meh.  Some of the dialogue is also different and feels a little off in spots, but in others, weird bits that felt poorly worded before now read more fluidly.The bad:During the Prologue, all of the dialogue between the Red Wings crew and the wizards in Mysidia has been cut out.  While it doesn't significantly affect the story, the end of the scene where Cecil lowers his head in shame would actually have context.  The first plot point you embark upon has had several details substantially changed.  Originally, you're commanded to "hunt the monsters of the Misty Valley," and you're given a "package" to deliver to Mist Village.  In this version, you're told to go kill the dragon in the mist cave, and you're given a "bomb ring" to take to the village.  This ring remains in your inventory even after destroying the village.  The way the enemies die is completely pixelated by comparison to the crisp linear dissolve circa SNES.  If it was done well, it could've looked pretty cool, but this piece specifically, looks like a rushed, ill-contrived visual effect.  Oh, and Scan doesn't work properly.  It only shows you the enemy's HP and a weakness, but apparently we don't get to see the enemy's MP anymore.  WTF, Chuck?!All in all, it's every bit as good as the SNES version, although I'd have liked if they made the characters look just a little better.And mind you, much of the above is flavored with my own opinions.  If none of that matters to you, and you're gonna play because you love the game, then you'll love the enhancements, and you'll get all the joy in reliving the adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: I just crushed this game in twelve hours. I don't remember it being that short, but maybe it's because it's been an entire three decades and I'm better at games now. To me this was a life defining game at the time, and it still holds up. Even through decades of technological advancements I can confidently say this game is a better game than Final Fantasy 15. You know why? Because it was a complete game, no DLC ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. We bought it at the store, jammed it into our SNES, and got sucked into the bright, beautiful pixel graphics and peak Nobuo soundtrack with our young impressionable minds, and were blown away. I realize now a few of the characters were one dimensional (Yang and Rosa, maybe a few others in spots) but it wasn't as much about the personalities as it was what the characters themselves went through. They improved on this quite a bit in FF6, but this was the first time we really got that trademark Final Fantasy narrative drama of loss and redemption. If you liked the original's graphics then you should appreciate the the updates done in the pixel remaster, since it was the original artist that came back to redo them. It's just a feast for the eyes, especially with the fluid new spell animations and water/fire effects. Same with soundtrack, it's like Nobuo came out of retirement to bend you over and spank you with the nostalgia paddle by bringing in a full orchestra to sonically improve these already perfect melodies. It's literally a dream come true.More complex doesn't always equal more fun. Sometimes you hit the sweet spot, and maybe it is just the rose colored glasses talking, but I feel like this era in the series (and Final Fantasy 7) hit on it perfectly. I bought the whole bundle to support bringing these sorts of games back (Chrono Trigger next please?) so I wil play FF5 when it comes out, but what I'm really waiting on is to replay FF6 with the new graphics and soundtrack.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: I played both the FFIV Pixel Remaster and the FFIV 3D remake side-by-side for good comparisonsMuch more fast-paced than the 3DR, also combat is simpler as well.  Not as cinematic (like the other PR FF games that came prior)Compared to the titles I played prior (1, 2, 3 PR and 3 3DR), combat changed a lot. Instead of it being a full turn-based experience, it has an action bar that fills up and when filled you'll get your turn for a character after other PCs/enemies who had action bars fill prior. Honestly a very clunky mechanic, in both variants of FFIV that I played. When casting spells, there is an invisible "Castbar" that has to fill as well, this was only apparent to me as this castbar is not invisible in the 3DR version of FFIVStory was a massive improvement compared to the titles I played prior, for the first time in this series I honestly cared what characters were doing what and what was going on. The games seem to get better about this as I go through the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV came out in the US in 1991 as Final Fantasy 2 for the SNES. I was a 10-year old boy, but boy did this game influenced my tastes in games for decades to come. Every JRPG that came after, I just had to compare it to FFIV.FFIV is the quintessential hero's journey. It's packed with a lot of life's lessons for any one 10-year old boy to learn. Friend becomes enemy, enemy becomes friend, morality vs loyalty, betrayal, third-party love situation, the limitation of life in old age, spoony bards, the duality of man, and journeying through self-discovery when the protagonist, Cecil, finally learns who he is and where he's from. This port stays true to the original Japanese version with a lot of QOL improvements that makes the game easier to enjoy 30 years later. The 4x exp/gil boost is a welcomed addition along with the fast-forward feature. It's a beautiful game that deserves it's place in history as one of the greatest JRPG ever made, with a legendary story about the human experience that resonates to this day.

_childDocuments_.review: It set the narrative template for all Final Fantasy games to follow.  While still simple, the story has a strong thematic core around its main character’s redemption arc that sets it apart from most games of the era.  They’re all familiar tropes, but the characters have enough personality and inner conflict to be memorable.This is often the game I recommend as a starting point for the series, especially if they don’t want the 40+ hour commitment of later entries.:- Maybe one of the best paced FF games.  It only takes about 20 hours to complete, including most side-quests.  It rarely gets bogged down by grinding or back-tracking.  You can accomplish a lot in a one hour-sitting.- The many, many plot twists that up-end everything you thought you knew about the world so far.- Simple but rewarding side quests.  There are several optional summons that are worth going out of your way for.- Doesn’t really need to be said, but great music elevated by the orchestral remaster.- I prefer it over the 3D remake because the combat and dungeons are much faster.  Some people complain about the optional dungeon being absent, but I don’t really consider a big, grindy dungeon to be compelling content.:- Typical of a JRPG, the story starts strong and gets sillier and sillier as you go.  It didn’t bother me when I was 10, but in a modern context you’ll recognize a lot of JRPG tropes.- While the character stuff is great, the individual plot beats and objectives get repetitive.  There will be points where you’ll be like “didn’t we just do this?”- Fairly easy except for a couple spikes in difficulty where it feels like your best option is to run away.  You will get stuck with an objectively bad party at points (like 3 mages and 1 warrior bad) and the game slows way down as a result.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: While it may not be the most complicated or difficult RPG, Final Fantasy IV offers great gameplay and a story full of twists and gripping moments, albeit littered with the occasional cliche. There were times I was running from battles just to get where I was going to advance the story (if I was adequately leveled of course)!Final Fantasy IV is a JRPG that follows the ATB system - you wait for a gauge to fill, and your character can act. Whether or not the enemy acts during you picking your options is up to you - there is a Wait option and an Active option. For newcomers, I would recommend using the Wait option - when you set the ATB to Wait, while you're targeting your enemies or allies, the enemy's ATB gauge will not fill. Final Fantasy IV does not require a steady grind if you just want to play the main story; there are some challenging bosses scattered through the game, but if you are battling your way through the dungeons presented and updating your equipment regularly, there shouldn't be much of an issue!The only gripe I have with the Pixel Remaster of FFIV is the omission of the extra content that Final Fantasy IV: Advance and Final Fantasy IV: The Complete Collection offered, particularly in the form of the Lunar Ruins and the party swapping option. If you'd like to read more about the total differences between the many different versions of the game, click . The Pixel Remaster is still not devoid of content, however - not in the slightest! There are still plenty of secrets to be found by exploring the world.This game is a classic! I would definitely recommend playing this version and then maybe branching out to FFIV: The Complete Collection or FFIV: Advance to try the extra content - better yet, there's a whole REMAKE of this game (originally released on the Nintendo DS) that is widely renowned as much more difficult with new gameplay options and even a New Game+ feature! This is a great starting point, though. Check it out!

Which was great at the time, but in today's age this game plays really poorly. If you want to try ff4 and want a fun game play experience and not just a nostalgia trip, then I would recommend playing any other version of ff4 than this one. _childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV is a richly diverse world and story of love, betrayal, heroism and loss, which succeeds where FFII failed. The characters' chemistry is a real testament to how it would progress in years to come, as well as the soundtrack being made up of the first memorable arrangements in the series.  In terms of gameplay, FFIV introduces the Active Time Battle (ATB) system which, in itself, is the most innovative feature, and would be a formula used again and again in later titles.  I've been replaying the series in order from the start, and in my honest opinion, as much as I respect and enjoy the first three, FFIV is where the narrative enters a whole new level. With FFIV's release in 1991, the bar was raised phenomenally.  I couldn't recommend it enough!  Right ... onto V!

_childDocuments_.review: Things I liked: * The new character sprites look great and I love them. They're detailed and I feel like I can actually make out faces and features. * The monster sprites look just about the the same as I remember from the original SNES title. * The translation this time is great. The heavy moments actually feel heavy and everyone's motivation comes through. I feel like I understand the story a lot better than when I played on the SNES years ago. * Quality of life features - Auto Battle is great. Running in towns and dungeons is nice. Infinite arrows. * Edward still stinks. Things I didn't like: * Spell animations. Fire/Thunder/Blizzard/etc are all reused from the 1-3 Pixel Remasters. And a few others. I remember SNES IV having some unique looking animations and was disappointed that they recycled from the other games. * The font. I don't like it and replaced it with something I like. I feel bad that mobile players don't have this option. * The forest tiles. Yes, it's an easy fix for me, but it's lazy for what's supposed to be a premium game and EVERYONE was screaming about it since the previews came out. Random Thoughts: * Cecil having his Darkness ability as a Dark Knight was neat, but didn't really make the game easier or better in any way. Nice touch, but whatever. * If you've never played the game before, this is a great way to experience it. If you're an older player who grew up with the SNES version, you might not get as much out of aside from a nostalgia trip. There are stronger entries in this series (can't wait for 5 & 6).

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game to anyone who I know liked it when it first came out.Much of the music is a massive improvement.  A prime example was the last boss fight music.  It went from being an odd waxy sound in the original to a fast paced choral and instrumental piece.  Unfortunately, not all music was handled well.  The worst case scenario that comes to mind is the ending.  The credits run super long and when the original end music ends, rather than go to the original's prelude music, it plays the overworld music.  It then does not transition to the prelude music when the credits end, it just keeps playing the overworld music.  It feels pretty lame.  I did notice that they let you move most end text at your own rate, but it caused the transition from the first end music to the second not flow smootly.Graphics are, for the most part, nicer.  A lot of spells are much more interesting and epic.  There are some cases where it just falls apart.  The removal of any sign of Edge throwing something was pretty meh.  Directly related to that, his sprites feels like it has no contrast to it at all.  I can understand why some people do not like the changes that were made.  I can understand that it was needed due to going from CRT based graphics is modern monitor.  But, yeah, it looks like Edge is walking around in a bed sheet.Gameplay is pretty good.  Diagonal movement is nice, as is the option to move faster.  The sped up auto attack option in combat is nice for stretches where you do not need to worry about strategy.  I can tell the game is sped up though as I just beat my previous best of 16 hours by 4 hours.  So, yes, I did the whole game in 12 hours.  This is even with some of the combat being the Japanese version.Overall, it is a good version of the game.  It is just unfortunate that they skewed some things in weird ways that makes it jarring if you played the original.Some last notes, there is a bug even at this time where you need to restart your computer because it starts taking longer and longer to release you to move after scene changing.  Another oddity was when I was abusing the mech dragon summoning in the giants to get lots of levels fast.  The game almost crashed once.  It must not like giving you 3 or 4 levels at a time.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 4 is far and away the best game of the series yet with a comparatively amazing story after the first three titles and brings along with it plot twists that actually got me, given that the Pixel Remaster Collection is my first proper experience with the original six games. The way the characters were given classes and the original type of gear customization options, like for example being able to carry only one weapon per character brought back the feeling of simplicity from the very first game whilst maintaining all its depth with the very much more story driven approach of this sequel. Next to point out is that the game is way more difficult than the ones prior, at least until endgame if you don´t grind. As always retro FF also looks visually charmful and pretty, so same for FF4. I was just overall surprised and impressed with the creativity that flowed into the game, offering a strong contrast to the usual same generic narrative of FF 1-3 as well as even the environments the player finds himself over the course of the playtime offering rather strong variety and the grand scheme of things. _childDocuments_.review: As  was the first  game that was released on the Super Famicom instead of the Famicom, I was wondering how different it would be. Of course, thanks to the graphical updates of this Pixel Remaster version, there’s not much of a difference in looks compared to the other remastered versions. But would the story presentation and gameplay be enhanced by the improved hardware the game originally released on? Would it be a generational leap for the franchise?The answer to that question is … not really. Instead,  is doing what its predecessors did: some drastic changes and otherwise more of the same. When I reviewed , I , arguably the biggest change it offered. And ? It dropped the entire job system; jobs are now unchangeably tied to each party member instead. The big gameplay change here is now an “Active Time Battle” system (ATB) instead, which would consecutively be featured in later  titles as well.In the case of this  Pixel Remaster, ATB basically means the same turn-based combat found in the three previous titles – except that a character can only act once their ATB gauge is filled. The recharge speed of the ATB gauge is determined by the character & game speed. By default, the game uses the “active” ATB mode, in which time moves on even if you’re navigating item menus. There’s also a “wait” mode, which stops time while navigating menus. Unfortunately, the game does not tell you about these two modes beforehand but for everyone who wants a more classic turn-based experience and some time to think, I recommend switching to “wait” mode.Personally, I think ATB makes for a nice change, as it makes battles feel less static. However, I do wish there was an option to see the enemies ATB gauge as well in order to make better estimates about the timing of your own actions – am I going to be able to heal before the next attack or should I already prepare reviving? Additionally, navigating spells and item menus can be quite time-consuming the longer you play the game, as those lists keep on growing. The “wait” mode helps with that but that’s only if you know about its existence beforehand.  The second bigger gameplay change  introduces are boss phases – and it does make heavy use of that. Bosses can now change their behavior throughout a fight – we also had something similar with Hein changing his elemental resistances in  , but  heavily expands upon this idea. Even the first boss in the game changes phases already, though it’s more of a tutorial to teach you the idea.These behavior changes do make bosses more interesting as keeping up with the changes is rewarded with dealing high damage. However, due to the ATB nature of the game, it can be quite hard to predict attacks correctly – an ice spell you began casting when the boss was vulnerable to ice damage might only hit once the boss can be healed by ice attacks.The last big change of  would be one concerning the entire party – which can now consist of up to five members instead of four as the previous games. Though, as  likes to give and take away party members quite often (not as often as  at least), you’ll better get used to work with different set party combinations – remember, the vast job system of   has gone.As for the rest of the gameplay, it’s basically the same as the three previous  games. An overworld with dungeons mostly explored as part of the story, a lot of random encounters and vehicles/new zones that are unlocked throughout the course of the game. There’s a bit more optional content offered in , mostly concerning unlockable summons, but it’s still mostly about just going through the story. The bonus dungeons from the GBA/iOS versions of  are .What unfortunately didn’t benefit from the original jump from the Famicom to the Super Famicom is the story presentation. Apart from some story battles the game plays for you, cutscenes are still rare and – more importantly – dialogues still short text boxes. While  does feature interesting characters, they all suffer from being very one-dimensional thanks to the few lines of dialogue they got. Of course, thanks to modern standards, this verdict is partially influenced by the expansive writing games feature today. But even while I liked certain character dynamics (Palom & Porom!), I can’t help but feel that most of the story still falls flat simply because there’s no room for the characters/the events to develop. The final villain especially feels thrown in instead of naturally developed. That said, the story is noticeably becoming more complex with each title in the franchise so far, which is definitely an improvement.Lastly, let’s go over the Pixel Remaster improvements again. Just as I praised in my previous reviews, the additions made by these remasters are all great: an auto-battle option, a bestiary, maps for all areas, a faithful graphical overhaul and amazing rearranged music – I wouldn’t miss any of them. Unfortunately  also features heavy screen tearing when played in fullscreen mode – similar to the other Pixel Remasters. To fix this, simply go to the NVIDIA Control Panel, select the game and turn on "V-Sync" as well as "Triple Buffering".Concluding,  is another early entry in the franchise that offers some big changes but also keeps much the same. As such, similar to the previous Pixel Remasters, I recommend using a minimalist walkthrough such as  to get help in case you don’t know where to go – or want to make sure you get all missable treasure chests. As this game is also once again not offering much in terms of tutorials, you might also want to look into the  for the SNES version of the game (initially called  in North America). That said, if you’re new to RPGs, this isn’t a great place to start – choose a more modern RPG to ease you into the workings of the genre first.

_childDocuments_.review: GREETINGS GAMERS FROM ALL AROUND THE WORLD AND FINAL FANTASY ENJOYERSI have returned, this time having completed the fourth entry in the Final Fantasy series, Final Fantasy IV aka FF4!Finally having dealt with the embodiment of darkness (which was pretty hot, not gonna lie) in FF3, it was nigh time for me to embark on the journey that is FF4.Similarly to previous installments, this game is a standalone entry and self contained story in the series with recurring themes typical of a Final Fantasy game: that one guy named Cid that has something to do with airships, chocobos, Black & White magic, elemental Crystals, Dragoons and the list goes on.This time around, the cast is named yet again, thus more in the vein of FF2, rather than FF1 and FF3. Our main protagonist is Cecil, a Dark Knight serving the kingdom of Baron and the game opens with a mission gone rather not as expected. As far as the plot goes, it's definitely a Final Fantasy-esque story, full of twists and turns for you and your companions where you eventually beat up the big bad guy and emerge victorious, thus saving the world! Compared to FF3s rather whimsical and wacky tone, FF4 turns in for a more serious, heartfelt story, although not completely devoid of comedic moments (such as when Cid hangs out with you). Overall the story was enjoyable and I preferred this plot more than FF3s.The cast is full of endearing and interesting characters (such as Cid with his very upbeat attitude or the flippant Edge) and our main character, Cecil, proves to be rather complex as well, making him very compelling from the very start of the game. The game retains the typical FF mechanics until now with one single major change: the introduction of the Active Time Battle system, known to some by its acronym the ATB. This is a massive game changer, as now all characters have to charge up their turn before making an action and unfortunately for the player, the enemies can attack as you decide your next move, even multiple times! As such, a much more hectic and engaged approach to combat is required. Thankfully, the pixel remaster edition will let you to slightly tweak the system by activating the wait option: all combat pauses as per a typical turn based game when selecting spells and items. As far as difficulty goes, this was more in line with FF3, with no particular cheese strategies but not ballbusting or gimmicky aside from the final boss requiring me to grind an additional 5 levels for my party members in order to take it down. A rather streamlined and balanced experience with segments that range from easy to challenging for a casual gamer like me.Visuals! Similarly to the previous Pixel Remaster entries, FF4 PR has a beautiful pixel art style, with great backgrounds and spritework. I've looked online comparing the original, mobile and this versions sprites and I have to say these are the prettiest, with a similar feel to the original game. Similarly to FF2, our main cast even have portraits in the main menu, which is a neat feature I appreciate. As usual, the spell & battle effects take the main slice of take with their flashy and over the top visuals (meteor & Bahamut in particular are very cool).Music is as usual, phenomenal. I gave the original soundtrack from the SNES a listen and I can confidently say that they managed to capture the same feels with this new soundtrack. In some story segments, the tunes absolutely enhance the entire scene, making some of them unforgettable. Favourite tracks: Overworld theme, love song, sad song, land of summons theme.Overall, I think FF4 is a strong entry in the Final Fantasy franchise. The story is great, a very interesting tale of betrayal, forgiveness, faith and ones mission. To think such a great story was in video game format 30 years ago is very impressive. In my opinion, if you want an "og final fantasy experience" this would be the first game I'd recommend as it encompasses everything that I think makes Final Fantasy well, Final Fantasy.I wholeheartedly recommend this game both to people looking for their first entry to FF series and to people on the edge on whether to continue playing the series after finishing (or dropping) FF3.So long and see you in Final Fantasy V my fellow JRPG aficionados and Final Fantasy enjoyers, thank you for reading.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:-Memorable story and characters-Fantastic redone soundtrack-Gorgeous new 2D visualsCONS:-Terrible default font (Can be easily solved with readily available fanmade fix)-Dualsense controller support requires third-party software like DS4WindowsOTHER:-Does not include bonus content from later releases, as it's based on the original SNES versionFinal Fantasy IV still reigns as one of the best entries in the series. It's a breezy entry as well, clocking in between 15-20 hours depending on whether or not you complete the couple of lengthy sidequests or do some grinding. The game's pacing is on point, constantly moving you to new locations and giving you new things to do. The story is simple, but done in a way that's charming and even has a few surprising plot twists along the way. The characters are memorable as well, as they're all pretty useful in battle and their banter between each other is fun and likeable. Grinding is almost nonexistent as the game's pacing consistently keeps you fighting enemies that are just about at your level or just slightly higher, meaning you're always getting pretty good EXP so long as you don't run from battle super often.If you're new to the series and looking for a good spot to jump in, this is a perfect place for beginners. It's easy to pick up and play, there's always something interesting going on and it's a breezy playthrough for those who don't have hundreds of hours to spend.

_childDocuments_.review: Played it because it is historically significant, and it was fun to see where the signature Final Fantasy penchant for theatricality and melodrama originated. While it is charming in the retro sense, do not go in expecting a well-modulated plot. Characters die, come back, pledge loyalty, backstab etc There is just so much incessant flip-flopping it kinda destroys any sort of emotional impact any of those moments have. But I was willing to tolerate the absurdity because I can acknowledge FFIV was probably one of the earliest, if not the first, to introduce involved plotting of this sort in games at all.Highlights of this version would be the absolutely fantastic rendition of the original chiptune music (Overworld theme, Theme of Love, Rydia's theme and Troian Beauty are S-tier FF tracks), some decent remastered pixel art, and what I think was a less grindy EXP curve (this was plenty grindy enough for me already).

_childDocuments_.review: Once again, the Pixel demake (it actually has even less content'n the OG JP version so yes, it's technically a demake) is a mix of the old and the new, but this time it's a bad mix.  It took the "difficulty" from the OG NA version (or rather, complete lack thereof), but re-added the skills, items, and other goodies from the other versions, effectively making it even more braindead easy, to the point where all bosses die within a turn or two and cannot remotely harm you unless you just never use heals (which you really don't need to).  They also boosted the exp and drop rates, made it so you learn spells a solid ten levels earlier (don't need to grind to learn Reflect for the Sealed Cave anymore, chances are you'll already know it before you've even entered the Underworld), and you just generally deal more damage and receive lessAnd unlike the other Pixel remakes, it's not even worth getting for the new orchestral rearrangements, since it's actually worse, this time.  They absolutely butchered Edward's Song, and removed the fart noises from the moon theme, effectively making it less alien, and more threateningIt's just... a dull experience that's somehow even worse'n the original, and IV wasn't exactly a good FF game to begin with

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV is as close to perfect as a video game can get. What I mean by this is that it has zero fat. It is absolutely, 100%, perfectly-paced. Its memorable characters, great battle system and soundtrack shine and make it stand out as when Final Fantasy became a truly great franchise. Even compared to later games, even compared to the game directly after it, FFIV is such a special game. It's a true masterpiece of the medium of video games and a must-play for anyone interested in JRPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: With the latest update to this game, I can safely say this is the definitive version of Final Fantasy IV.
