_childDocuments_.review: Ever since beginning my journey through the Final Fantasy franchise over two years ago, there was no title I dreaded playing more than Final Fantasy IV. Being the only entry in the series I had played before, I went into FF4 with no small amount of nostalgia - and though I played it too long ago to remember many details about its narrative and characters, I could vividly recall the visuals, the music, and the emotion held within this 15-hour RPG. I remember absolutely falling in love with it, and so I was worried that the game wouldn't hold up. Being the first game in the series to really hone in on the narrative aspect of the RPG genre, there was plenty of reason for FF4 to make mistakes with its pacing and characters - it would have made sense if it sucked. Thankfully, my worries were unfounded. Final Fantasy IV feels reminiscent of a soap opera - every narrative and character beat is steeped in melodrama and overwritten to a degree that might cause other narratives to drown in exaggeration and lose all meaning. Every line is written as though it's the most important thing in the world, every conflict is settled through either a fight or a sacrifice, and the tone of the whole story is nothing short of bombastic. That said, with the visuals of the game being so simplistic, the intensity of the writing actually serves to compensate for a lack of other emotional indicators, balancing a boring presentation style with its excess, and keeping the game interesting. Every character has something to do in the narrative, and the large rotating ensemble cast is always entertaining and compelling. The result of this tonal balancing act is a surprisingly emotional story. Aided by an excellent soundtrack and a healthy dose of nostalgia, Final Fantasy IV manages to deliver a truly compelling narrative - surprisingly so, considering its simplicity. The world Cecil and Co. explore throughout their journey is impressively vast too, featuring double the content I was expecting from the game. For its epic journey and memorable characters, Final Fantasy IV earns a 7.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably my least favourite of the SNES final fantasies, although it is still reccomended.The ATB system has aged quite well, though I think the five party members in this game can be a burden sometimes.The story in this game is better than the story of FF5, but still not as good as that of FF6. _childDocuments_.review: Yes, I'd recommend the game but not to just anyone. I'd recommend it to casual players who just want a walk down memory lane but may not have a a ton of time to play. First thing I can appreciate is the addition of the sprint button, it makes it seem as if you were given a pair of sprint shoes (FF6 relic) but still makes it more of an option of how you play. These types of changes are a plus. I played the original SNES version many times through as a kid so it was great to hear the remastered audio, the music is rich and very well done, though I believe you'll have a much better experience with a set of headphones or a good quality audio system. The graphics are a welcome update that stays loyal to the original pixelated style, graphics are updated to be smooth (although I personally experienced a lot of screen tearing, that was distracting at times) but did not interfere so much that the game was unplayable, it was annoying though. There are a couple of gripes I had that you'll see mentioned in many other reviews, specifically the difficulty and leveling. Difficulty seemed to be set to very easy, and I'd like to see an update that allows for increased difficulty from the options menu, one example I can think of is my party was only wiped out twice in game, and both times were on Bahamut without a full party. No other enemies were able to defeat my party.  As for leveling it seems the devs opted to lower the XP requirements significantly. I was able to max out every character to 99 with very little resistance, Another gripe I have is the hummingway cave doesn't seem to have the sirens for sale in this version. It's a minor gripe that could assist with completion of achievements, but still it would be nice to be able to spend the ridiculous amount of gil on something useful. I'm looking forward to seeing what the modding community does to breathe some new life into this game, and taking that into consideration if this game gets mods then I could recommend it, but I think (and it's just my opinion) that my decision to buy this game as it is right now would hinge heavily on whether the modding community will be allowed to do their thing. In it's current state, as a fan of the original I say sure, go ahead and buy it but only with the hopes that some updates or mods will fix some of the issues addressed. The nostalgia factor is still there and the audio experience is so good I was able to overlook the negatives, for now.

_childDocuments_.review: Just awesome. Definitely the best way to experience the original game presentation wise. I guess it's easier (other reviews have mentioned you level up 50% faster than the original, I have not looked into that to verify), but as someone who likes to 100% these games I'm always way over-leveled anyway and didn't really notice. A hard mode option would be cool but not something I'd expect.Aside from difficulty, the game is very true to the SNES original, specifically the Japanese release. There are many abilities that were stripped from the NA release (roughly 1 per character) that have been included here, so that was fun to experience for the first time. The maps are a welcome addition (same as the previous pixel remasters).If you liked the original SNES game and want to experience it again, or if you're new and want to experience the first SNES Final Fantasy in the best way possible, I'd highly recommend this version.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: + The Pixel Remaster graphics are predictably gorgeous+ Compared to Pixel Remaster 1-3, this had the best story so far, although I contend it's far worse than its reputation would insist+ They kept "Spoony Bard" in the translation+ Just as predictable as the visuals, the remastered soundtrack is the best this entry has ever seen+ I still love Auto-Battle; it's a dream for grinding+ The more modern UI is a dramatic improvement on the original game's+ There isn't just one World Map to frolic around in; there are three+ The spell and summon animations are *chef's kiss- The writing has aged poorly, and is mostly awful, let's be honest- The tone is all over the place- I'll go against the grain and admit that I didn't care too much for this cast of characters, and never really have; with few exceptions, I found them to be largely forgettable and unspecial- The difficulty felt heavily nerfed, a worrying trend of the Pixel Remasters; there were at least two challenging dungeons in the Underworld, but my party seemed to breeze through everything else with surprisingly little grinding- The optional summons and Adamant quest line can all get @#$%-ed; even though the devs have reportedly patched the drop rates, these take forever and drive me nuts as a completionist (still working on these as of this writing)- FFIV does too much; you go to the underworld, the moon, you ride a whale spaceship, you invade a giant robot, there are aliens, etc. It gets carried away with itself and frequently feels silly and unfocused

_childDocuments_.review: ### Update 2024/06/01There were a couple of updates since my review. First of all, you can now switch between the original and the remake soundtrack. You also can switch to a more fitting font. Those two things already let the game fell much more atmospheric and far less like a bad mobile port. They also added the possibility to multiply the exp you can get by a lot. So, becoming completely overleveled and steamroll everything should be easy now if you don't like the balancing of some enemies. You also can deactivate random encounters. Those things are far away from a good rebalancing. The game is still 95 % of the time far too easy and then suddenly everything around you explodes and your whole party is dead and you don't know why (if you don't change the difficult sliders, if you increase exp the game is 100 % of the time far too easy). But the game is now atmospherically and good playable. I appreciate that they took the time to fix these issues (on the other hand, it's still an impertinence that they released the game in this state for this high price). Objectively the game is now a thumps up. Even if I still recommend the 3D remake if you want the better game, this pixel remastered is only for "historic" or nostalgic reasons interesting. Balancing, content, storytelling - everything is better in the remake.### Original reviewIf you don't love the pixel art I don't know why you should play this. Everything this has the 3D remake has also - and more. I also don't really get a nostalgic/retro feeling because you don't have an option to use the original soundtrack. (Instead the game uses the soundtrack from the 3D remake which is great but why I can't simply change it if I want the 1991 feeling?)But the biggest minus is the balance. People say "the pixel art version of Final Fantasy 4 is the easy one, the remake can be very difficult". That's simply not true, the pixel art version is the "developer trolls you"-version. In 50 random battles you can just press x or use the auto-attack feature. You don't really play you just watch the game doing everything by itself. Even some boss fights are that easy. But then - in one of 50 battles - a random encounter will kill your whole party because the enemy casts some spells you can't counter or don't know how. (And you can't learn it because you don't get information about you enemy until you kill him.) And because these encounters are random you don't get a second try/chance to prepare yourself. It's really horrible if you have such an encounter when you didn't have the possibility to save for a long time (which is not possible in dungeons - only on special occasions). You watched the game 30 minutes playing itself and suddenly you whole party dies randomly and you can do the same thing again.Only chose this version if you want shorter dialogues and absolutely love pixel art. The 3D versions has everything that this version has and more (and btw at least the Steam-version has an easy mode so it shouldn't be that difficult - I finished it on the "original" hard  difficulty and was less frustrated than with this version).

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to believe that this game is over 30 years old with how gracefully it has aged.The combat, which features the first ever appearance of the ATB system we all know and love, is exceptionally engaging and continued to be fun throughout the entire game's duration. I would recommend reading some guides for the final boss though, as there is an extreme difficulty spike which requires an airtight strategy.The story is also absolutely astounding, especially so for its time, and it kept me hooked throughout the entire runtime of the game.Alongside the positives of the original game, the remaster was executed masterfully, bringing the original game into the modern era without losing any of the original charm; In particular, the music in this game was redone spectacularly, and I couldn't have asked for a better auditory experience. I personally would easily consider this the definitive Final Fantasy IV experience.This game is an absolute must-play for any Final Fantasy fan, or any JRPG fan in general. Put this one on your backlog.

_childDocuments_.review: Of all the Pixel Remasters, FFIV was probably the one I was most reluctant to play. For most of my life I've called it my favorite game; it hit me at the perfect time in both my personal and gaming life back in the 90s. The stories and memories I have from FFIV (II back then for the SNES) both in-game and in real life where my friends ​and I would talk about the game for weeks/years, I will hold with me for the rest of my gaming life.So naturally I was hesitant to ruin those memories by playing an adaptation, flawed as the SNES version was, and I never bothered revisiting the game through all its releases since then. But as soon as I booted up the Pixel Remaster and heard that re-orchestrated Red Wings theme, I knew it was the right choice to play it again, nearly 30 years later.As against the redesigned sprites as I was, everything just fit so well together with this release. The colors were more vibrant, the backgrounds more elaborate, and the spell and other effects were taken to the next level with modern, FFRK-ish reinterpretations. And the music, man the music. I've owned and listened to all the official FFIV soundtracks and arrangements (yes even Celtic Moon), but this re-orchestration was a feast for my ears.I relived my childhood through the vivid aural assault of this soundtrack, from the marching beat of the opening Red Wings sequence, to the techno futurism of the Giant of Babel, to all the emotional strings pulled and played by the final battle and the epilogue. Hell, even acquiring Excalibur had an amazing theme playing on Cecil's/the Red Wings leitmotif. The soundtrack isn't the only reason to play this version, but I will say that it's 5000% the best one.On a personal note, getting 100% on this game is one of my most important and treasured achievements, since I finally got to find every secret and fulfill every activity I never got to in the original, from acquiring Yang's wife's knife to trading in the Pink Tail. It's also extra sweet since I finally get to beat it with my adult grinding powers on a "Hard Type" version of the game.I'm thinking of skipping FFV because it's one of my least favorite FFs, but holy airship did this make me excited for FFVI and what the new pixel art and music has in store, plus it's another game I haven't revisited since the 90s. If The Final Battle was already this good, imagine Dancing Mad...Final Fantasy IV is and always will be my favorite game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY IV

_childDocuments_.review: I will preface by saying that, as a kid, I played Final Fantasy IV on the SNES a ton and the game's story, characters, dialogue, events, and music are pretty firmly etched into my mind. So, with that as a backdrop, I can say that i have mixed feelings about this Pixel Remaster.Now, I can admit that some things I dislike about this game are nit-picky and simply my personal preference - dialogue changes, character leveling changes, changing the sound Kain makes when he jumps, the look of forests on the map - but there is something very specific I am unhappy about... and that is the soundtrack. Now, if you never played the original SNES version of the game, then the soundtrack shouldn't be an issue. In fact, on it's own, the soundtrack is actually pretty good. However, when compared to the soundtrack of the original SNES version, this remaster took a step back. Quite simply, it isn't as good as the original. Specifically, if you look at the three main tracks (main theme (map), boss theme, & four fiends theme), they just don't have the same feel - check them out on youtube. The original gave you a feelings of drama, importance, and epic-ness. The remaster gives you a feeling of hugs and friendship... it just isn't the same.Take the boss theme for example: in the SNES version, you hear the boss theme and think "damn, sh*t's about to go down", but in the remaster, with the use of an electric violin as the main instrument, you now think "they're about to have a ho-down". For me it ruins the aura the important encounters and situations you find yourself in, particularly boss fights, fiend encounters, and traveling across the map.But, all in all, I still have to recommend this game. I have had zero crashes, glitches, or other issues and, aside from the only real issue I talked about, it is a pretty solid "remaster" of a beloved OG Final Fantasy title.

_childDocuments_.review: This absolutely scratches the itch i want in a remaster. Final Fantasy 4 is a Classic that has few rivals i can genuinely see why square japan skipped 2 and 3 coming to america and finally sending this. it was a true next step in the Video Game Jrpg. it was the first game in the series to have a Distinctive MAIN Character where as the focus used to be on a group of adventurers, IV grasped the concept of the story of a character growing and becoming a hero with help of friends along the way. the story is solid and provides all the proper elements, including humor (albiet a little campy for this day in age), drama, action, suspense, and yes even Romance.  the cast of characters are all fairly class based and you can see how while it is a jump in Final fantasy style that it was crafted based on its predecessors. Though it is one of the better Crystal story games it does stray from the importance of elements, it mentions the overworld crystals having elemental affiliations (water in Mysidia, fire in Damcyan, Wind in Fabul, and earth in Troia) but thats as far as it goes. there isn't mention of any of the underworld crystals having anything to distinguish themselves from one another. but over all the game play is excellent with memorable battles and the first time we see ATB system come into play.  now that being said.  this Pixel Remaster gave the game NEW LIFE! everything was more brilliant and varied! i think of the original graphics which where nostalgic but i see a layer of almost dull patina on them now. i am not a huge fan of the take over of spell naming that began in FF8 but it is what it is. there are wonderful exploits that have been left in the game while other more game breaking exploits have been removed which is reasonable. the remaster overall is Truthfully without flaw the negatives are absolutely personal preferences and hold no bearing on the overall quality.  my only suggestion to the staff is this would have been a FANTASTIC oppertunity to add some additional story perhaps flesh out more of the world add some side missions but thats personal again. buy this if you love Final Fantasy.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great remaster, and well worth the buy if it's your first time playing the game. The game play is fun, albeit random battles interrupting exploration can become tedious, something I know will put a few of people off, but the story is one of my faves of the series and worth trudging though the random battles.However the game's lacking in content outside of the main story, there's the bonus art and music player which is nice; but content added in the GBA ports are absent here, as well as in the other remasters, and I don't understand why they didn't add them. I know that these remasters are just based off of the original releases of the games, but it would make the price so much more worth paying, and could attract people who've played the games before, and want more out of the game as well as easy access them. I myself bought the game because I wanted to experience the game again, and being on steam made it easier to access, but I felt let down that the content ended with the main story.Overall, the Game is worth it if you just want to play the main story or it's your first time playing through, but if you've played the games before or just want more out of the game I'd recommend the GBA ports, but if we get them (or at least the extra content) on current platforms, I very much doubt.

_childDocuments_.review: So, Final Fantasy IV is back with this Pixel Remaster, and wow, it’s pretty darn good! If you’re a fan of the old-school JRPGs, you’re in for a treat. SquareEnix did a nice job of keeping what made the original great while adding just enough polish to make it feel fresh.The Good Stuff:	•	Visuals: The pixel art is beautiful. It’s like they took the original game, dusted it off, and gave it a fresh coat of paint. The colors pop, the backgrounds have more depth, and the characters look great. It’s like the game you remember, but better.	•	Music: The remastered soundtrack is pure gold. Nobuo Uematsu’s music has always been iconic, and the new arrangements really hit the spot. Plus, you can switch back to the original tunes if you’re feeling extra nostalgic.	•	Gameplay: They’ve added some nice quality-of-life improvements. The auto-battle feature is super handy for grinding, and the rebalanced difficulty feels just right. It’s still challenging, but not in a frustrating way. The interface is cleaner too, which is always a plus.	•	Story & Characters: The story is as awesome as ever. Cecil’s journey from dark knight to paladin is still epic, and the characters are well-written and memorable. The plot has some great twists, and it’s full of those classic JRPG moments that hit you right in the feels.Steam Deck Performance:	•	Runs Like a Dream: If you’re rocking a Steam Deck, you’ll be happy to know Final Fantasy IV Pixel Remaster runs flawlessly on it. The game’s lightweight nature means it doesn’t stress the hardware at all, so you get smooth gameplay with no hiccups. Whether docked or handheld, the performance is solid.	•	Controls: The controls feel natural on the Deck, and the layout is perfect for this kind of game. The touchscreen is a nice bonus if you want to quickly navigate menus, but the buttons and thumbsticks work just as well.	•	Battery Life: Because the game isn’t too demanding, you’ll get great battery life. You can easily squeeze in several hours of gameplay without needing to recharge, which is perfect for those long gaming sessions on the go.Overall:If you’re a fan of Final Fantasy IV or just classic JRPGs in general, this Pixel Remaster is a no-brainer. It’s a solid update that stays true to the original while adding some much-needed modern touches. And if you’re playing on a Steam Deck, it’s a match made in heaven. Definitely worth picking up, whether you’re revisiting the game or playing it for the first time. It’s a nostalgic trip done right, and now, you can take it with you anywhere.

_childDocuments_.review: I played a few versions of Final Fantasy 4 growing up, the US version on the Super Nintendo, the GBA, the DS, the PSP collection, and now this one. This version has a bit going for it, but also some problems, mostly with bugs and design decisions.  It's not particularly my favorite version, and I would go as far to say that it is inferior to most of them.  Despite that, I would still recommend this game to new players, though only them.  Veterans of this game would best find another version than this one.The music is very beautiful and it's of top quality with the previous Pixel Remastered versions for the most part, though the horn at the beginning of every battle and boss fight was jarring to the point of hilarious.  I haven't had a good laugh since Sonic Unleashed. I also found the game to be extremely easy.  All the hard fights I encountered from previous versions barely required any work to beat in this version. I didn't have to grind at all and I just managed to defeat Zeromas with not too much trouble in between.  I found it quicker to finish than the previous games I played, even quicker than Final Fantasy Mystic Quest, a game designed to be easy.I noticed the loading time between Towns, Caves, and Overworld is not as seamless as the previous games or in previous versions.  I also noticed the Hovercraft and Chocobos are much slower than they were originally, though these are minor grievances since you barely had to use them.  The forest tiles were a little broken, and of course the font still looks bad.  There also weren't any shadows on the enemies or any flying animations present in this game, which I thought was a real shame for upgraded graphics not to give them a little more life.  I also didn't care for the lack of message windows showing when an ailment was inflicted on a monster.  It was hard to tell when a monster was affected by paralyze or sleep, because there was no indication of it working or not when it came to weapon abilities.  Speaking of which, Edward's hit rate was even worse in this version and he was even more dead weight than usual as none of his abilities were effective at all, though that's just my personal taste since you only play as him for an hour.I saw some slight bugs playing the game, like when I inflict confuse on monsters and yet they can still cast magic on my party just fine.  Also I don't know if this is a bug, but my osmose didn't work on the mages, though they can absorb my magic. I never had it work for me at all.  There was also a point where my cursor had trouble picking the monster i wanted and sometimes the cursor would disappear.  I hope some of this stuff gets fixed in development.  It didn't ruin my gameplay, but I felt it took me out of it. Even though I'm fine with not seeing any extra content in any of these remasters,  I still feel the ones in Final Fantasy 4 would have really added to the experience, like the party swapping mechanic and extra dungeons. Honestly it not a deal breaker for me to have it not included, but maybe they will add it down the line.I grew up with this game and I still found it very charming from beginning to end playing this. That being said. I just hope they fix the bugs I encountered playing it.  If you are looking for a definitive version of this game, I'd stick with almost any other port.  But if you need a game easily accessible and want a fun stroll while playing a charming RPG, then pick this up, but when it goes on sale.  You'll be glad you did.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a decent amount of this version of FFIV up to the Tower of Zot, so I feel like I'm now in a position where I can give my opinion on this pixel remaster. With that being said this is a very faithful recreation of the SNES version of FFIV with a modern flair. The pixel artwork is immaculate, maybe the models could use a bit more personality but they still look very nice as is. Water, spell animations, and other environmental effects pop in a way that adds more visual flair without looking out of place. Overall visually its very pleasing to look at as you play.I believe SE was trying to recapture the "child-like" wonder of how people growing up experienced these games which they've succeeded here with this pixel remaster of IV at least. I haven't gotten a chance yet to dive into the other ones so I can't comment on those. Also the remastered OST sounds great as well. The presentation as a whole is nice aside from the font which I quickly went ahead and modded. Some potential cons would be the lack of the extra content introduced in the GBA and PSP versions of the games. Also to consider is there isn't any voice acting like in the 3D version which takes a more "cinematic" approach to delivering the story. I'm not entirely sure, but this version does seem a bit easier than previous versions. It feels like the EXP you receive is a bit more generous in the amount than in the past which makes leveling quicker (Personally I don't really mind, but you may find yourself often overleveled if you intentionally try to grind a lot). Therefore you run into many situations where your party is so strong you don't need to strategize too much and can sometimes steamroll Boss battles with little agency. Lastly I have seen a little bit of screen tearing but not enough that it bothered me or took me out of the experience, I just feel it's worth mentioning though.At 17.99 USD it isn't exactly cheap for an old RPG that can enjoyed in so many other ways across multiple platforms. However if you want something closer to the original version but spruced up with some modern quality of life updates it almost doesn't get better than this. If your backlog is already large then wait for a sale of this down the road. If you want the most "complete version" of FFIV content wise then the GBA or PSP versions are your best bet. Touching real quick on the story, it is serviceable and definitely feels like a product of it's time. At least the localization seems to be much cleaner this time around. Considering when this scenario was originally written and the landscape of videogame narratives at the time it's impressive. A lot of JRPG narrative staples and tropes that we see today have originated from this game which is the biggest compliment I can give. FFIV is probably the most accessible of the classic FF games with some of the most iconic characters of the series with Cecil, Kain, Rydia, and Rosa to name a few. I believe Cid made his first playable appearance in this title as well. The story itself is one of redemption and self-discovery with the crystals playing an important role as with many of the classic Final Fantasy stories. I don't know if this is really a spoiler at this point, but you get to go to the moon in this one.Overall It's nice revisiting classic games like this in this type of format. I don't really remember most of the details of this game since I haven't played through FFIV since the GBA days when I was a kid so rediscovering forgotten story beats has been fun. The FFIV pixel remaster is worthy of the FF branding, and whether you decide to pick it up now or further down the line I believe it's a game worth your time.Edit: Part of why I'm playing through this is because Endwalker for FFXIV is coming out in a few weeks, and there are many references to IV in the upcoming expansion. So I'm trying to brush up on my general FF knowledge base so I can appreciate the homages it's making when I finally get to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: I am heavily partial on Final Fantasy 4 as this is one of the first SNES games I bought with my own money as a young kid & it is still one of the best told Final Fantasy stories. In 4, the narrative is taut, even if portions aren't very realistic (I'm looking at you dirtbag Kain) &/or come across as cheesy. The gameplay is straightforward and builds upon the exceptional turn-based combat that made FF into a juggernaut it is today. The 4th game is the first entry featuring ATB and when I was young this made such a huge impact on the flow of combat that FF4 is a staple game for any RPG enthusiast in my opinion.The Pixel Remaster cleans up some of the badly translated dialogue from SNES FF2, and improves a number of the "scenes" by improving spell effects shown on the field/map screens and polishing the pace of dialogue on some of the less-sensible parts on the original cart ROM. The music is exceptional, and combined with the sound improvements make for the best way to experience FF4 in its pixel form.

_childDocuments_.review: "Final Fantasy IV," originally released in 1991 for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES), is a landmark title in the Final Fantasy series and a seminal entry in the role-playing game (RPG) genre. Developed and published by Square (now Square Enix), this game introduced many innovations and narrative depth that would become staples of the series. Story and Character DevelopmentRating: 10/10 - Masterpiece"Final Fantasy IV" is renowned for its compelling story and deep character development, a significant evolution in storytelling for video games at the time of its release. The game follows Cecil, a dark knight who embarks on a journey of redemption and self-discovery, challenging players with themes of honor, betrayal, and love. The narrative is richly woven with memorable characters, each with their own backstories and arcs that contribute to the game's emotional depth and complexity.Gameplay MechanicsRating: 9/10 - ExcellentThe game introduced the Active Time Battle (ATB) system, a departure from the traditional turn-based combat of earlier RPGs. This system adds a real-time element to battles, requiring players to make decisions quickly, which significantly enhances the dynamism and strategy of combat. The diverse party members and their unique abilities encourage players to experiment with different strategies, providing a satisfying and challenging gameplay experience.Graphical and Audio PresentationRating: 8/10 - GoodFor its time, "Final Fantasy IV" showcased impressive graphics, with detailed sprites and vibrant environments that brought its fantasy world to life. The game's visual storytelling, especially in dramatic cutscenes, was groundbreaking. The audio presentation, composed by the legendary Nobuo Uematsu, features one of the most memorable and emotionally resonant soundtracks in video game history, elevating the narrative and gameplay experiences.Overall Impact on the RPG GenreRating: 10/10 - Masterpiece"Final Fantasy IV" had a profound impact on the RPG genre, setting new standards for story-driven gameplay, character development, and strategic combat. Its introduction of the ATB system influenced countless RPGs that followed, and its narrative depth demonstrated the potential of video games as a medium for storytelling. The game's legacy is evident in its numerous remakes and ports, each seeking to introduce this classic tale to new generations of gamers.Overall Summary and ScoreOverall Rating: 9.25/10 - Exceptional"Final Fantasy IV" stands as a monumental achievement in the RPG genre and video gaming as a whole. Its engaging story, innovative gameplay mechanics, and emotional soundtrack combine to create an unforgettable experience. While its graphics may seem dated by today's standards, they remain charming and effective in conveying the game's epic scope and intimate moments.Recommendation: Must-Play for RPG fans and those interested in the history of video games. "Final Fantasy IV" is not only a pivotal game in the Final Fantasy series but also a timeless classic that continues to inspire and captivate players.

_childDocuments_.review: As a retired FF4 speedrunner and long time fan of the FF franchise (all the way back to the first one on NES), this remake was worth the playthrough.  I almost all the achievements and probably 98%'d the game in about 9.5 hours -- fighting every battle, no running, no continues, no game overs.  Some observations:- Diagonal walking is a nice touch.  No real advantage, just a quality of life thing.- All the SNES glitches have been fixed.  So no Mist Skips or GP underflowing.- The difficulty is definitely toned down a whole lot, even more so than the OG FF4 SNES US version (FF2).- The music is beautifully remastered.  Felt like a modern touch to the original tracks.  Awesome.- They changed up the order of the Four Fiends battle.  Nice unexpected switch up.- I like that the devs are still patching the game -- that's kinda cool to me as a long time fan.Now with all that said, I don't think this game has replay value beyond maybe 1-2 playthroughs for old school players.  The biggest challenge would be trying to get all the "Steam achievements", but the game doesn't really hold a challenge.  This is a true remake of the SNES FF4 game, not the PSP or NDS versions that came later.  There is no post-game quest like on the PSP/NDS versions.If you are a new school gamer and didn't play the OG version of this, you are probably better off finding the PSP version (the best version in my opinion in respect to quality of gameplay, graphics, sound, music, replay factor, etc.) or even the NDS port to PC ("3D remake") before this one.  If you are an old school gamer and don't have the OG on a Nintendo based console somewhere and you just want to feel the nostalgia of 1992 over again, this game will give you that...  for one or two playthroughs.So, would I recommend it?  Yes, if you just love the franchise and want to feel young again for a playthrough or two.  No, if you've never played this title -- go find the PSP version, you will thank me later.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished Final Fantasy 4. Took me only 19 hours (and there was plenty and afk and pointless travelling). Honestly have mixed feelings. I like that the developers decided to return to the idea of named characters with real identities and backstories from FF2 while dropping the leveling system which was probably for the batter. As a result FF4 is basically a mix of 2 and 3. You don’t create your party members and can’t even change their jobs (classes). Initially I was a bit alienated by this approach since it’s not what I was used to. At lest in FF2 you could turn any character in what you want him to be (even though they have some starting preference and canon proficiencies). Here you start with your main hero Cecil already being a level 10 dark knight and can’t change that. As I said this felt a bit off coming from previous FFs but in the end the game won me over. The plot is more personal this time, all characters have their own reasons for joining you and keep leaving and rejoining your party at different moments which really makes them feel as real people rather then your mindless pawns. Also there’s a lot of them and your party is constantly changing (except the main hero) but the game always makes sure that you have a balanced group with at least one healer, so it never feels irritating. Also the plot is a lot faster so to day. The pacing is very quick one action of great importance comes right after another, your party is always moving, visiting new kigdoms, changing etc. Even felt a bit too fast in the beggining (again that's me coming from FF1 and 2)The gameplay is a big step up. With active time battle system, unique abilities for each character (some even havemore than one) and improved, more interesting battles (especially boss battles) this game is really great to play. Some call this the best of early FF and I almost want to agree, but there’s still this little something that I can’t quite put my head around and it prevents me from agreeing wholeheartedly. I guess it really is the best, simply because it combines the best elements of previous 3, but still. Maybe it’s a matter of not being able to create and control your party, maybe it felt more like me being a driver of their story rather than making my own. Maybe those empty husks from FF1 and 3 made it easier for me to self-insert or something like that. Should probably give it some time and see what the aftertaste will be like, but for now I can it the best of four only half-heartedly.

It looks terrible. The Under-world is much better. -Cecil's new sprite for the map portions looks terrible for the Paladin. Looks like he has a gut, lolz.0/1 -Copy and Paste antics. Lazy editing. I'm harping on it.-Red Wings and Baron Castle Trumpet sounds are quieted down and have a lessened effect on power and prowess.-Factually the changed music does not fit the game for these instances which is a shame.-Treble and Bass have been severely dampened. The original SNES had a glitch in the music portion and when sounds were played some would sound much louder which gave the trumpets a nice blaring sound that caught my attention nicely in the SNES version. _childDocuments_.review: I have a long history w/ FF4 going back 30+ years and MANY remasters/re-releases/etc.The pixel remaster of FF4 is how I believe Squaresoft wanted this to land in the west back in 1991. The translation is much more streamlined and localized. They left in the "spoony bard" line which is fantastic and a nod to its roots. Unfortunately, they pulled the Dev Room from this release as well. I played this on my Steam Deck. The experience was flawless. I've had MUCH WORSE (here's looking at you FF Chronicles).Soundtrack is redone and sounds fantastic. I wish they had an option for the old school soundtrack.One of the BEST things they added was the "classic" mode for the display that emulates the scanlines on a normal tube-tv (10/10).The game seems to take a little while loading (may be my version of Proton). Afterwards performance is a 10/10. No framerate issues, no lagging, no latency issues w/ an external XBox controller. This plays awesome on the dock.Bestiary and Music Player being added are a nice touch.The auto-battle feature is DEFINITELY welcomed in some circumstances around end-game.This is a faithful port of the SNES/SFC original and anyone that's a fan of it will likely be happy with it.Honestly, this is my third favorite release (which isn't a bad thing!). The PSP FF4: The Complete Collection is by FAR the best way to play this fantastic game. I wish Square would release that on Steam. The second being FF4 Advance on GBA -- because of all the bonus content.This release is well worth your money and time regardless of other releases. If you want to enjoy a classic JRPG from the SNES/SFC era, this is it.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this is a good port of the original SNES release of the game (that means the PSP additions are *not* present).  The visuals are very similar, but generally enhanced.  Visual effects are significantly improved.  Audio is remastered and substantially better than the SNES.  The translation is cleaned-up, though iconic lines remained untouched.Pretty much all grinding has been removed from the game, which is contentious: some people think this makes the game more enjoyable, others think it makes it too easy.  Regardless of the easier levelling, the game is definitely easier due to enemies being so much slower than you --- I beat many bosses with them only acting a single time.At the end of the day, Final Fantasy IV was never the most challenging in the series.  It was remembered for its story and characters.  These all come across just the same as ever.  I doubt I would suggest this as an entry point to a new player, but is definitely worth existing fans buying.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing I-III I feel like IV had a drop in quality, though some of it is personal preference. The artwork remains solid but there are quite a few things I feel they got wrong here.The game is way too easy, and I don't just mean easy, I mean EASY. I never once stopped to grind and not a single boss even came close to a challenge. I even started teleporting out of dungeons or warping to previous floors in an attempt to avoid as much xp as possible from walking back out of dungeons.As soon as I got the "Magma" airship in the underworld I skipped three dungeons ahead and went straight into the Sylph Cave, the game is that easy. I remember in older versions having to grind just for Rosa to learn Float but she had it way before she needed it here because the game showers you in xp. You're supposed to go to the Sealed Cave, then the World of Summons, then finally Sylph Cave. But that's how easy this version is. The first thing I did when I landed on the moon? Straight to Bahamut without a problem.I even tanked TWO Megaflares from Dark Bahamut in the Lunar Ruins because I forgot if you summon Bahamut on him he counters with Megaflare. So it went Megaflare (bosses opener) into Curaja(which only healed a little over half of Megaflares dmg), into a 2nd Megaflare and only Edge died from the 2nd one and still finished the fight after such a screw up.One more thing to add about combat is the lack of a cast bar like the PSP version had. In that version, your ATB would fill up Yellow, then if you cast a spell it would fill up in Green to show you the spells cast time. That's not in this version for some reason.The music in this one also took a step backwards which is a real shocker for a FF game. I dunno what this Jazz theme is they had going on with IV but its awful, especially that surprised trumpet sound at the start of EVERY. SINGLE. BATTLE. It kills the atmosphere completely and it's even in the boss tracks as well, though a bit quieter. Even a few of the more "epic" tracks like the final dungeon music seem a bit toned down.It's still not a bad game, but if you want to play Final Fantasy IV, then this one should only become an option if you can't get your hands on the PSP version, which is by far the best.

_childDocuments_.review: The Before Review*Just got it, am at FabulThe After Review will be when I've beaten it (to see if anything's changed)The music is the #1 reason to buy this game.  You'd pay 20 bucks for a CD in 2010 (worth about 24 in today's dollars?).  This is 20 bucks in today's dollars (or less if on sale), and you're getting intimate studio time with Uematsu.  I disagree with several of his decisions as far as modifications to some scores and instruments used, but I digress.  No one ever paid me more than twenty bucks to music for them.But the music is done absolutely top tier superb.  It pays great respects to what we had to imagine when playing the MIDI-laden original.  He gets to add soft edges and rippin' booms now.  And it's pretty much what you've imagined if you're like me and can hum/whistle every single score from FFII/IV on demand and have tried to tinker with the scores yourself.He could have flat-out done this with an orchestra, but he clearly wanted to keep some of the digital art intact.  After all, the original was literally all 1's and 0's compared to what they do now with games.  The visuals. . . exact same thing.  Everything is almost exactly as you remember it, but they brought life to the art with water animations and effect-overlays (looking at you cloudy dust in antlion chamber).  They put stupid amounts of details in the most obscure things that I wouldn't blame them for totally overlooking.  Before you agree with me, go to the ocean and see if you can find the sun in the water.  THAT MUCH RIDICULOUS DETAIL INTO THINGS WAS PUT!  Fan.  Freakin'.  Tastic.The gameplay:  Terrible.  When I played FFII, I was 12/13 (the year it came out).  I did not pay attention to metas.  I did the same strategy over and over for each playthrough.  I had no  idea what half the stats and items actually did.  And I never used magic buffs.Now?  Same thing but mostly on Q.  They gave Bard a spammable heal for example.  So once I picked him up and got holy arrows for Rydia and Rosa, I was literally able to put everyone on AA mode except Bard, who spams randos from his spammable rando harp effect (also new to me as I recall??. . . I thought we used to rely on the stats on his AA for the debuffs. . .?).And I say terrible with a total grain of salt here.  Because I literally am playing this game to feel like I am spending time at my Grandfather's house back in the day when I used to play this.  I've played the game so many times on so many versions, I don't  need to worry about how hard or easy it is, because this is quite like a book for me, or a movie, or any of that.  All over about 30 hours of my life, almost like a book.  With a story, so much more like a book.So now, I just put everyone on AA-duty Q-mode (that's the autoplay feature they added), and I spend more time looking at the maps, the damage from the various comps of mobs I encounter so I can swap my Q-mode as needed, which isn't often at all tbh; and listening to the boss song for as long as I can.WHICH SIMPLY ISN'T VERY LONG AND THAT MAKES ME KINDA SAD AND MAD.  At least the boss fights could be challenging.  But autopilot?  On one of the best songs in the game historically in my expertly stupid opinion?  In the best format it's ever ever been ever?  If I had one gripe, it'd be that.  Nothing feels epic about a boss that goes down three turns in on AA mode; and I am about 90% certain there's some bad programming with Q-mode in general because I notice my 6 Vs. Me fights, I get about 2.5 turns per mob turn.  ATB seems clunky, to be honest.That's fine, SE.  I'll just park outside and wait for the (emotionally, perfectly executed) sad trumpet music to play.  Because you did a bangin' job on that track, too.  And I used to hate the main outside theme.BEFORE PLAYTHROUGH REVIEW SUMMARY10/10. Get it for the feels, or if you just want an OG RPG to doodle about on.  But gonna let you yungin's down easy here: you'll never get the full value of this game that the older farts can, because we play this game kinda like how we tell people where we were on 9/11.  It's got some serious attachment that you missed out on because your AAA games today have dominated every ounce of your imagination to the point you've likely never had to fill in all the details of a pixel game AND FEEL LIKE IT WAS THE ABSOLUTE BEST THING EVER (like we'd play this game and find ways to pretend it was all CGI-quality, and that the music production was at least as good as the hits on the radio) when you can look at it now and go, "Wow, just a buncha dots on a screen I got all excited about in my youth."BUT IT WAS THE BEST DAMNED TIME FOR THE JRPG.  And they give us this kick in the nadstalgia.  And I just wish you could experience this the same way I am.But what I want to say in my conclusion is this: the game, given the ease (which really changes the dynamics of playing it), is almost what I'd call a 3D Audiobook.  It's purely a visual/auditory and to some degree literary indulgence, with some command input from the AI (that's my way of making a joke about us, but idk if it worked).All that.  (Plus 100% More Nostalgia).  For less than the cost of a CD 12ish years ago.  When some of us still bought them sometimes.Yes.  Sign me up.  And 3/6 comes out just in time so I can go down that Memory Lane.

_childDocuments_.review: Introduction:The first Final Fantasy game that I ever played was the so-called "Final Fantasy II" on the SNES, which of course we now know was actually the fourth game in the series, but it was the second Final Fantasy game to be released in the North America, so that's how they titled it domestically. However, I think that was just about the best game to start with, as it's when the series had really hit its stride, establishing many of the elements which would become mainstays in the Final Fantasy games. Final Fantasy II (i.e. IV) was the game which got me into the series, and as such holds a special place in my heart. Alas, even I must admit that the original game has aged poorly, and has been greatly improved upon in subsequent revisions of the game, thus rendering the original release objectively the weakest example of FFIV. So when the Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster games were announced, I had presumed that they would use the improved/enhanced versions of each game as the basis for each Pixel Remaster. Unfortunately, that is not the case, which is a bit disappointing, but that begs the question; what changes were made, how was the game improved upon for this release, and how does the Pixel Remaster compare to other versions of the game?Visual Presentation:As the subtitle "Pixel Remaster" suggests, the classic visuals of the original game have been faithfully recreated in pixel art, which gives the game an appearance which is simultaneously nostalgic yet fresh, as it is visually similar to the classic 16-bit graphics of the original game it was modeled after, yet the pixel art is obviously much clearer and more vibrant. Personally, I prefer the enhanced visuals of the Game Boy Advance Remake, the aptly named; Final Fantasy IV Advance, so it was slightly disappointing to me that they chose to recreate the visuals of the original SNES release when the enhanced visuals of the GBA remake were just plain nicer, yet still featured that classic 2D look. Regardless, the game looks wonderful.Audio Presentation:Not to be outdone by visuals, the remastered audio of Final Fantasy IV Pixel Remaster is to my ears easily the best version of the original soundtrack yet. The classic chiptunes of the SNES release have been recreated with modern audio and musical instruments, making this the definitive version of the FFIV Soundtrack. Not only do all of my favorite tunes from Final Fantasy IV sound better than ever in the Final Fantasy IV Pixel Remaster, but my absolute least favorite, the dreadful Mysidia tune is no longer offensive to my ears. No longer does it sound completely awful to me, as it did in literally every other release. It sounds alright, and I'm no longer annoyed by the sound of it to the point that I have to mute the audio whenever I enter Mysidia.Gameplay Mechanics / Content:Fortunately, the classic gameplay has remained unaltered, and thus plays exactly as it should. It's a simple, turn based, JRPG with the classic Active Time Battle (ATB) system which makes it a little more fast paced, exciting, and challenging than your standard turn based JRPG battle system. In addition, a number of Quality of Life improvements have been added, such as a detailed Level Up subscreen after battles, Arrows no longer being a finite resource which the player must keep stocked up in their inventory, abilities which were removed from the original SNES version like Dark Knight Cecil's Darkness and Rosa's Pray have been restored, and item drop rates have been adjusted to make obtaining rare random loot less frustrating to obtain. Unfortunately, the additional content from Final Fantasy IV Advance is notably absent, and therein lies my major criticism of this release... The decision to maintain the classic visuals of the SNES release over the enhanced graphics of the GBA remake for the sake of nostalgia is understandable, but to leave absent the additional content which was unintrusive as well as completely optional is just lazy and dramatically reduces the overall quality of the game. Furthermore, the level of difficulty in Final Fantasy IV Pixel Remaster has been greatly reduced. It takes precisely half the amount of experience that it did to level up in the original, and there's no way to increase the difficulty. As a result, the game is substantially shorter in length than other version of the game. I was able to beat the game in just over 23 hours at a relaxed pace, which don't get me wrong, isn't bad, but a completionist run of FFIV Advance can easily last up to 60 hours! Granted that I didn't do a completionist run of this game, unlocking all the chests, finding all the hidden items, etc, but I did all of the side quests and completed the game in just over 23 hours, so I can't imagine a completionist run lasting more than 35 hours tops. So it's nothing short of a disappointment that they neglected to recreate the additional content of what many consider to be the definitive version of the game when they made this remastered version.Story Presentation:Once more, this is merely a recreation of the original SNES release, meaning all of the additional cutscenes from subsequent re-releases are completely absent. You won't find any of the additional cutscenes from the PSone, GBA, or DS versions here, regardless of how easily they could have been adapted in this versions artstyle. In fact, just about the only way that the story differs from the original SNES release is that they thankfully didn't opt to faithfully recreate the terrible English language translation of the original, save for of course the iconic "Spoony Bard" line which has appeared in every English language release of the game. Forget about experiencing the Interlude from the PSP remake, as well as The After Years in this release. This is the story content of the original SNES release with a better translation, nothing more.Final Verdict:Final Fantasy IV Pixel Remaster is a faithful adaptation of the classic SNES release known as "Final Fantasy II" in the United States which will appeal specifically towards those who desire a stroll down memory lane and nothing more. Those who are more accustomed to enhanced versions of the game are bound to be disappointed by the absence of the additional content which expanded upon the game as a whole. This is by no means the definitive version of Final Fantasy IV, nor even a complete version of the game by any standards. So those who wish to experience a more complete version of the game, I recommend that you stick with Final Fantasy IV Advance for the Game Boy Advance. For those who wish to experience the definitive version of the game, I recommend that you seek out Final Fantasy IV: The Complete Collection on PlayStation Portable. Again, I cannot stress enough that this is by no means a poor game, in fact it's practically perfect for what it was intended to be, a faithful remastered version of the original game. However, I have to remain true to myself, and as a longtime fan of the game, it is a disappointment because it could have been much better. Had they included more of the additional content from past revisions of the game, then this could have easily been the definitive version of the game which retained the classic look yet included all of the nice little additions/improvements to the game which have been made over the years. So in conclusion, to me it's a 6 out of 10 experience, but for others it could easily be a 10 out of 10, you be the judge.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first one that truly feels like classic Final Fantasy. It includes most of the classic elements we've already seen in at least one of the previous three games, such as ancient high tech civilizations, chocobos, recognizable character classes and skills, an evil ruler that's actually corrupted by an evil entity searching for the elemental crystals for its own gain, and several modes of transportation including airship variants. Mechanically, the leveling and XP system is again tied to your character and there's no jobs or skills to level individually, though some characters do change classes at some point as part of the story. You have HP and MP and they level with your character and you no longer have to buy spells and learn them because they are unlocked by normal advancement, so it simplifies things a lot, while retaining the same equipment and item mechanics as the previous three games. As for the story, it goes back to what FF2 was doing but further develops it, with a more complex story and more developed characters, starting with the protagonist, Cecil the Dark Knight, who starts out working for the bad guys but has a crisis of conscience and switches sides, and a party of up to four additional characters from an extended cast that cycle in an out of your main group depending on at what point you are in the story.  All in all, an excellent game and my favorite in the series so far. I'm also curious about the later 3D remake, which I'll be sure to play in the future.

I'm definitely looking forward to another play through, and I'm tempted to try and get 100% of the steam achievements, something I never care to do.The story is whimsical and quite good if you are comparing it to the story of FF1,2 or 3. The characters are endearing, and there are plenty of twists and turns. It's not the greatest story ever, but there is something special about it.I'm not sure if this is the "best" version of FF4, but I'd highly recommend this if you are trying to play it in it's original pixel glory. The FF4 for DS is also excellent, with some really fun changes. Beating this makes me want to go through and play that 3d DS remake. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: The first FF game of the series I can recommend to a broad audience. The story of FF4 is legitimately interesting and the characters have some timeless charm that even modern RPGs can sometimes fail to emulate. The combat has improved significantly, and the addition of Active Time Battle (ATB) was no small part of it. Combat feels more engaging, although admitted still not a tactically rewarding experience. There are tricks to certain enemies, but there are only a handful of "tactics" to overcome these challenges. To their credit, the pacing of the game is way better than in predecessors and you generally have finished an area by the time the enemies there start feeling repetitive. The story is definitely the spotlight, and the creators seem careful to not hide it behind endless grind sessions.It's important to note that not everyone is going to love this experience. Although the plot is very good by the standards of the time, emotions can be very hard to portray via text and a dozen character poses. Some imagination is required, and to their credit the music does assist in painting the scene. However, the game is littered with tons of cringe-filled lines that the JRPG genre is well known for.The customized experience of previous games is also entirely removed from FF4. Although this makes the narrative more logical at times, you may miss the ability to develop your team around your favorite strategy. I'd argue it is worth the price, but it could be a sticking point for some players.Additionally, FF4 is rarely challenging, which may be off-putting for old-school players expecting to put some work into the game. In addition to the relatively simple "tactics" of the game, the leveling curve is generous and makes it pretty easy to progress without needing to grind levels.If I were to recommend just one retro FF game, it would not be this one. However, you could certainly do worse for $15-$20. If you just want to dabble in the series, I'd recommend waiting for FF6 and coming back to this if you enjoy the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Another walk down memory lane for me. This was the game that really got me into JRPGs when I played it on the SNES as Final Fantasy II. This version has some of the features I think they took out of the original Japanese version when they released it in the US, but doesn't have some of the extras you get in some of the more recent ports and editions, like extra dungeons and such. Graphically it's not much different from the original, since this is about the level of graphics they're shooting for. Mostly the spells have some nicer effects. The music has gotten an update, which I have mixed feelings about; I kinda missed the original sound of the SNES soundtrack. They also improved the localization of the dialogue from the original, although it's probably familiar to anyone who's played any of the other adaptations. "Spoony Bard" of course, is still there. The story is a little simple, although it was really cool when I was 10. The battle system has moved on from the simple turn-based mechanics of its predecessors in favor of an "active time" system, where enemies and player characters have timers that determine when they can act, and enemies will continue to attack even when you're deciding what to do. Another new addition compared to the previous three games in the series is characters having fixed classes and special abilities. Difficulty wise, I didn't have any real trouble; it felt a lot less grindy than the original, I was more or less able to proceed at a constant pace through the game without too much pausing to beef up. As with the other Pixel Remaster games, they have an auto-battle feature that helps speed things up in those situations. I also managed to 100% the game without much difficulty, even with the ones that require a bit of RNG for loot drops. Maybe I got lucky.Anyway, most of your are probably familiar with this game. Buy it to relive old times or to experience an earlier game in a series you love. It's a decent value if you buy the whole Pixel Remaster series on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A great short story with strong characterization but weak gameplay.Final Fantasy IV is the first game in the series that really  like the grand stories told in later games. Characters are memorable and all stand out, could definitely have been longer, but it's a good few evenings. Gameplay is definitely a step down from the versatility of FFIII, but it kind of works in its favor at least in how linear the game is. Of course, it's going through dungeons and finding chests. This version isn't very difficult, but it's tolerable for how short the total experience is....Somehow this game made me tear up a few times. The story has a limited scope with its smaller party but it really utilizes its characters very well.

_childDocuments_.review: I love everything about the pixel remaster except for one glaring issue: the difficulty. It's brain-dead easy. I've played every version of this game throughout the years, and yes, the North American SNES version was also easy. But you could hire a chimp to press buttons and speedrun to the end of this game without dying. It's ridiculous. Square doesn't usually fix their games so we have to rely on modders to hopefully make a slightly more challenging version. Until then I'm shelving this one.Update: I found a mod that corrects the starting Experience, along with the Experience required to level up (in the VG Research and Modding Discord). The game now plays at the correct difficulty and I love it. Keeping this review negative in hopes Square fixes this game themselves along with future games.

_childDocuments_.review: This version is okay, but as a person near 40 with serious nostalgia attached to this game, they've done a lot of fixing what wasn't broke. Remaking background art, adding 3d effects to spells, transparency layers and light reflectivity on the water. I get it, I'm not the whole market for this. To be honest I don't even hate all these changes, the spell graphics look kinda cool, the arranged soundtrack hits really nice. There's  QoL cheats in the options for more XP to reduce the grind, turning encounters off when you feel like it, and I'm using the hell out of them. However....If you want authentic gaming history, you'll need to play the original release somehow and not this.  We found the secret passages by pressing direction buttons against the walls. In the snow, for 5 miles, uphill both ways. If you want it like it was, you play it blind, because we didn't have internet at home to look things up.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a long-time old-school FF fan and I played the original SNES Final Fantasy II. I must have beaten it over 10 times at the time. It was the first RPG on consoles to have characters thoroughly developed with an engaging plot that was going beyond 'beat the bad guy and his henchmen to save the world'. And this one also harbours my all-time favorite character in FF series... Kain. So yeah, I do have a certain bias toward this one game. I'd like to add to this that for people who loved FF9, 4 is basically its grandfather in many ways. Like its later sibling, classes are locked on every character and they can't be changed at any point in the game (with one particular exception that I won't spoil.) One particular flaw, and big one as that, is classes are not balanced at all, and I don't think it was intended to be from the start. For example, the bard character is not good at anything. And by that, I really mean ANYTHING at all. But it's all right because characters come and go. At no point in the game you will have freedom of choice on who to choose to be in your party. Characters just come and go. Is it a bad thing? I think it's debatable, but my opinion is that this design decision was meant to give more freedom on the narrative for the developers.  I won't go into details for obvious reasons, but for new players out there, you will come to understand what I mean as you play the game. With that said, this Pixel Remaster excels in recreating what the original was. The locations, the game-play, and the abilities remain unchanged as far as I can remember. Having not played the GBA release, I can't comment on the omission of the additional content. If you like the older FFs (everything before 13, except FF14), chances are you will love this one. It's also fairly short. You can breeze through it in about 20 hours. At this time of review, the horrible font can finally be changed to one mimicking the original. The same goes with the music. You're now free to switch at any time between the updated soundtrack and the original MIDI OST. And with that, enjoy the game. Great ride and great nostalgia for old-school FFers like me.

_childDocuments_.review: Versions played previously: SNES (Emulator)Time to complete: ~21 hoursOverall Rating: 9/10Gameplay: 7/10Story: 9/10Graphics: 9.5/10This game holds a special place in my heart, because I was introduced to it by my dad, who had a collection of ROMs of games he played in his childhood. It was also the first Final Fantasy game I ever beat. I was excited to see how the pixel remaster improved on the game, and it definitely delivered. The gameplay is a simple ATB system, with fixed classes and abilities learned based on level. In that regard, it’s not the most creative FF battle system, but then again, sometimes creative doesn’t equal good (see: FF2). Still, the gameplay is solid. Maybe a bit boring or unintuitive for someone who’s used to modern games, but I think it’s super fun. It’s helped by the pixel remaster features like auto-battle and quick saving. The story, though unchanged entirely from the original, is even better than I remembered from when I last played this game, several years ago. It’s slightly predictable in parts, and maybe the nostalgia factor is what makes me rate it so highly, but it’s a beautiful story with an abundance of nuanced characters and character development. I was skeptical at first of the pixel remaster’s graphics changes when I first saw them, but in the context of the game I think they’re beautiful. Also, this game doesn’t suffer from the same issue as some other FF pixel remasters where some sprites and animations are reused, at least not nearly as noticeably. In fact, the only complaint I have about the graphics is that the default font should be the classic option instead of whatever ugly font the modern option is(This goes for all the Pixel Remasters). Overall, a wonderful game, as good as I remembered, with many improvements in this port. Pretty refreshing, considering Square Enix is usually known for good games with terrible ports.

_childDocuments_.review: I would say, more or less that the game is good. It's a fine RPG, the story and characters aren't mind blowing but they're good enough. I don't think I need to elaborate to much on the pros, many others have sang its praises. Instead, I'll tell you that issues the game has, and why I would recommend it anyways.I think it's worth noting that the original FF IV was made in 1991, and it shows. The tutorials don't really exist, you're supposed to get that from random NPCs. However, it's really a big difference being shown in the menu compared to being told in words, and as a result I didn't understand quite a bit of the game interface till I had almost completed it.The game isn't always clear on where you go next, but expects you to figure it out. Sometimes I do manage to figure it out, based on thinking "What would Cecil (our main character) do?" but sometimes that's not enough. In fact, one time it was completely contradictory to what one would logically expect. Eg. At times I would just try everything and hope it would progress me, and that would eventually work, but I found that very frustrating. Later after a while of not knowing where to go I just looked up a guide, and that made the experience more enjoyable. Thus, I recommend you play this game with a guide, for when you can't figure out where to go for progress next.Second issue I have is with he music. Now I know that there is much praise for this remaster's music compared to the original, and briefly listening to some of the original tracks I would agree. However, perhaps this is a relic of the old version, I don't find the music adaptive enough. There are times where I think it would have been much better to change the soundtrack or perhaps have no music at all (to make it feel ominous) and they just don't, and it feels like a missed opportunity to me. The best example would be when  I like this game's music, but I think it could be much better used.The game occasionally crashes, so you know what they say about JRPGs: Save early, save often. When I don't, I lose a lot of progress. Very sad.On the whole, I don't actually think it's an amazing game. However, I do reccomend playing this, if only to appreciate how much better game design has been since 1991, and because this introduced many elements of Final Fantasy. Of course, that's not all this game has to offer, it's enjoyable, it's just that it lacks some of the quality of life things that I'm used to in modern games, and I've had more fun with other games as a result. Still, I don't regret playing this. It's just that I would not recommend it if I was just looking for fun, I think there's better fun out there today. But the story is nice, the pixel graphics give good nostalgia and are done very well, it's a great way to experience this 1991 game, and it's a window into the past, to see what games were like and how far things have come. Though I enjoyed the game, I enjoyed what the game was far more, and if you're that sort of person I think this is a good game to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I had never played Final Fantasy IV before despite being a long time Final Fantasy fan (a travesty, I know) but with the highly anticipated Endwalker expansion coming to Final Fantasy XIV I wanted to understand all the FF4 references, so I decided to get this wonderful pixel remaster. Pros: Remaster of a fantastic and much-loved gameGreat music! Good story; I gasped once or twice in the story when certain things happen; such as The Thing that happens shortly after you fight Cagnazzo...) or the scripted fights between certain characters. Nice Pixels!Cons:1) While the music is amazing, the vast and sweeping orchestral suites don't really seem to fit the retro vibe of the pixel art style imo; I think they let you switch between the old and the new which is cool; but perhaps like, some kind of modern-yet-retro inspired reimaginings might have been a cool idea? Like still orchestral but with a synthwave edge to them or something? 2) This is coming from someone who never played the original and heard for decades how the the story in FF4 is one of the best in the franchise'; but as a first-timer the story moves at a break-neck pace, important developments happening one after another in quick succession with almost no room to breathe or getting proper build-up. Or there are moments with seemingly no sense to them. For example(spoilers), after being lost at sea you randomly find Yang again hanging out in the bar in Baron, but he's (a) been mind-controlled somehow that is never explained, (b) carrying a skeleton key to the Baron Castle?! despite being a mind-controlled servant kidnapped from an enemy nation, (c) made the leader/superior officer of a group of Baron soldiers despite being a kidnapped mind controlled slave from an enemy nation, and (d) easily freed from ill-explained Mind Control by just beating him up a little, which begs the question of if he's so easily freed why was he put into a soldier group meant for combat at all? But I get it, it came out in what, the early 90s? FF3 is a super bare bones story where the main characters had literally no character at all; and FF5 was a well-paced story with a small but intricate cast of characters with well-fleshed out stories that had room to breathe; so naturally it would make sense that FF4 would fall in the middle between the two. A product of it's time, a stepping stone to improvement and evolution. 3) Some characters seem inconsequential gameplay wise; and I miss the job system of 3 and 5. You get many many characters throughout the story and they are constantly leaving and rejoining the party like it's a revolving door; characters like Cid seem to have no real point or strength (keep in mind im a filthy casual who usually doesn't look up guides or the most optimal way to do stuff, i just play and learn intuitively); he just swings his wrench and has Libra as a job skill. But hes only in the party temporarily, so his limited utility is only available to you for a brief period, which makes sense why he doesn't seem to have a point? While he was in the party, I just basic attacked with him 90% of the time. Then he was not in the party and it was sort of like, oh good, if someone else comes along they might be more useful. Anyway. It just makes me miss the more stable party of FF3 and FF5 with the traditional FF Job systems that allow you to choose what actions and abilities you have at any time, and level them as you see fit, and losing a character doesn't lose you their job actions, if that makes sense. This is an overarching critique of FF in general actually, in that I prefer the games with the job system over games like ff4, 7, 8, etc where characters are tied to one way of fighting; i know its part of their character and stuff but sometimes it feels so limiting, and if that character leaves the party they take their utility and special abilities with them (which in the case of 7 was intentional and story-relevant, which makes sense but....anyway ill stop talking) Conclusion: All that being said I still found myself gasping over certain story developments I was not expecting, and feeling attached to characters I have known about for decades from ancillary media like Dissidia and the TCG, etc.; falling in love with the music; really enjoying getting into the groove with combat, and really wanting to know what was going to happen next, or what was going to unfold in the plot. OVERALL a great classic game that any fan of Final Fantasy or RPGs in general should check out. See you in Endwalker!

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy IV was something of a turning point for the JRPG genre back in 1991, one-upping Dragon Quest IV's increased emphasis on character with a tightly-plotted games with a dizzying number of plot twists and turns for a game of its time. In spite of this, the game remains very briskly paced, especially compared to future games of its genre, and doesn't overstay its welcome. It also introduces the series' trademark active time battle system, introducing real-time elements to what was a turn-based system and increasing the tension of any given battle. The on-rails nature of the game can be frustrating at times, but for the most part, it holds up quite well, especially with this remaster treatment.
