_childDocuments_.review: I've never played FF5 before; heck, I've only played 7, 10, 13, 14, and 15; the pre-3D era of FF has eluded me. With that in mind, I want to say that this port is wonderful for accessibility. I want to say this game is charming and worth playing, and has a lot of depth to take advantage of. After nearly 12 hours however, I have two big issues that completely destroy my ability to recommend this game to people:1) Consistent input softlocks. Whether on controller or M+K, you can and will enter a situation where combat menus stop receiving any input, effectively trapping you. If an enemy flees and your entire team has full ATB, that's a softlock- you're stuck celebrating your foe's absence forever. Opened up a menu while an enemy attacks? That's likely a softlock. Used the scroll wheel on the mouse in the magic menu? Probably a softlock. Controller briefly disconnected? Softlock, no swapping to M+K in a panic for you. This is the one that ruins my ability to recommend the game in its current state to anyone.2) The random ATB starting charge seems like a fun shakeup... at first. But after playing with combat enough, you discover it creates a menuing chore. When more than one character has their ATB ready, your menu defaults to whoever got it first (or in a tie, the uppermost character I believe). Because the ATB amount each character gets is random, you don't know who is going to get their ATB first in combat; this can create moments where my monk lets loose a Kick attack when I thought my Beastmaster was about to be next to use Control. If the character you want to make the opening move with is LAST in the ATB RNG, you have to press the "swap selected character" button 3 times and wait for the menu to catch up. All the while, your opponents get to keep throwing out attacks for free because you do not pause while in the main combat menu- only the submenus. M+K might support being able to choose a specific character to swap control to (I haven't tried, honestly), but controller is up Ship Graveyard creek without a paddle. It feels awful and it is a constant problem in random encounters, to the point where I just spam the Attack button until I get the character I want. This one is a touch petty but, c'mon. There are workarounds.Phantom 3) I can't speak for myself on this one, but I've heard this port is absolutely full of gameplay glitches too. It's all hearsay and rumor, stuff like "Regen doesn't work," "Reset completely breaks boss fights," "the map is straight up missing icons for locations," and so forth.I also hear they're ironing bugs/softlocks out and making them a priority, which is a big plus. But at launch, this is an unacceptable state to release the game in. The "lose all control and stare at a command menu forever" softlock is so common, so easy to trigger through normal play, that I really believe that playtesting wasn't even considered. I triggered my first one in two hours! Come back to FF5 once these are patched, whenever that is.UPDATE: I believe I have identified why the input softlock occurs... not saving after many room transitions. I suspect it's a hitch with the Auto-Save system. So long as you manually save every 8 minutes or so, the glitch just stops occurring. Try that if you're having trouble!DOUBLE UPDATE: How... how do you bungle up the world map on the top right. Without going to into spoilers, let's just say the world map pre and post a disaster is swapped. Something is missing that should be there pre-disaster, and likewise something is there that should be missing post-disaster.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V holds up really well, and feels like a refinement of everything good about Final Fantasy I-IV. Unless you're just used to this game's SNES or GBA aesthetics (I am not) the Pixel Remaster is a fine way to enjoy this classic JRPG!That said though, it *is* a Square Enix PC release, so technical issues are to be expected. The worst: when facing the gargoyles within the ocean rift in the merged world, the game froze up and had to be forced to quit multiple times. I fixed this issue by going to a different area, fighting a bunch of different enemies, and then coming back. After looking into it, I never saw anyone else with this issue, so who knows!Other than that, the minor annoyances: sometimes the game takes a while to load after launch, sometimes battle scenes take time to shift (i.e. if you were fighting enemies in a forest area then enter the desert, the first desert enemies you encounter may briefly load with a forest background), and the ATB gauge doesn't seem to increase smoothly in some busier fights,Overall, I think the work Square Enix has done with the Pixel Remasters to recreate these games for modern platforms is pretty cool, and this is a fine way to experience a very good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Aside from its recognition of a third gender (pirate),  is my least favorite of the franchise.  However, this iteration of it is easily the best one available so I'll cover why before dragging it.+ BoostPost-release (I think?), Squeenix has added "Boost" to the configuration menu, which allows you to adjust experience, gold, and ABP (skill points, effectively) up or down by various multipliers.  The Pixel Remasters nerfed the difficulty substantially, so 0.5x experience feels like a more traditional playthrough for me, but the lack of ABP always has necessitated a big grind if you want to master jobs.  A 2x and 4x multiplier option is a welcome addition.+ SoundtrackEveryone loves the hype of the new "Big Bridge" theme and that's fair.  Myself, I hated all previous iterations of the upbeat town theme (Harvest) as they were all way too loud and the chiptune instruments made it worse, whereas this version uses some woodwinds and normalizes the volume.  Lovely.+ TranslationFFV never got the official Ted Woolsey treatment (near completion, but unreleased) and a lot of what we had to go on early on were fan translations.  A couple of variables in the game is that you have a pirate character (some prefer to really amplify the pirate talk) and the cast as a whole is rather goofy, which allows for some liberties in how you render it.  The GBA version for example had an obnoxious number of dated pop culture references which didn't make sense in context.  This one still makes a few of them (there's a Simpsons reference from 1993) but steers more towards what I sense is literalness, which would help it avoid looking dated.  The peculiarities of the world probably would have benefited from Woolsey giving them a particular flavor, but I doubt we'll ever see that.- No Bonus DungeonsThis is more of a problem to other people than it is to me although I have to concede that I did use some of the new job classes.  Bonus Dungeons came about during the GBA era re-releases and generally provided superbosses and new ultimate equipment, but there were some attempts to provide more features unique to the game.  They were as follows:FF: Nada.  Zilch.  Nothing.FFII: Bonus dungeon for character redemption.FFIII: N/A. First NA/EU release was the 3D one for the DS that broke the class progression.  Like FF, all you really got was some new bosses.FFIV: Ability to bring different teams in to face final boss.FFV: Four new classes.FFVI: New magicite / spells.IMO, the bonus dungeons were soulless grinds that added little to nothing to the narrative, but I can see why some people appreciated them and I liked the extra materials in the final three, just not the dungeons themselves.  This also provides Squeenix an out to release an even-more-definitive edition later.- No Amano PortraitsTo summarize, odd numbered FF games 1-6 were focused on customizing your classes and that didn't really fit with the set portraits available in the even numbered ones, where your teams mostly occupied the same role throughout the game.  One concession I'll make to the GBA and iOS versions is that they used the portraits from series illustrator Yoshitaka Amano to give a profile of who was talking, including characters outside your own party.  PR just color codes the names of the speakers.  Weak.As for why I don't like the game, this version fixes a lot of the play elements that made it a chore previously (notably, the ABP grind), so I do endorse it if you want A version.  My main complaint is that the writing is inexplicably weak compared to IV and VI.  Final Fantasy IV had twelve characters and VI had fourteen.  The fifth entry in the franchise limited itself to five playables and all of them are less distinctive than any of the other twenty-four with the exceptions of Gogo and Umaro who aren't even required for the plot of VI.  The world has less of a sense of geopolitical history compared to the SNES titles (and possibly even II).  While IV and VI have major thematic overtones, V coasts on a sense of adventure that allows for a series of random events to be threaded together.  Probably the dumbest part is that the antagonist, Exdeath or Exodus or whatever your twelve-year-old cousin thinks is cool, .  I get that you probably can't go big all the time, but this is probably the smallest they ever went.  I'm not sure why it's so beloved by its creators given the seeming low effort involved but it's not among the JRPGs that's going to make you feel ways about stuff.

Story is not 'deep' but has a lot of charm, villains and supporting characters alike have good banter.Music is all fantastic, played the game to hear 'battle on the big bridge'Other great things :  - Frequent checkpoints encourages experimentation on harder foes- All jobs have some skill that can be incorporated into your set-up making it fun to play with options- Difficulty and pacing are perfect, physical skills never wear-out their welcome and a character who is the primary healer may become the DPS a few hours later.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is the pinnacle of the series game design up until this point. All the pros and excellent features of previous games return, and almost all of the negative features have been removed (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ATB still here). The first thing that made me hype about this game is that the FF3 Job system finally returns in a sequel but VASTLY improved upon. In this game each time you rank up a job (earning ABP), you permanently learn a new class ability on the character itself. It is stored in a talent bank; and upon changing to a new job, you can slot it into the bonus slot on any other job you want. This allows for an extremely in depth  class system. You can have mages with swords, mages that can cast every school of magic, Dual wielding knights and more. This game also shocked me with it's story presentation. Actual full length cut scenes with the models, and an in depth backstory behind the world and what happened in it for once. An exponential improvement upon what FF IV was working towards with expanding world building and characterization. Interpersonal relationships between the party help make the story vastly more interesting and keeps you engaged throughout mindless grinding. The best villain so far KING EXDEATH made me always wonder what would happen next. I always felt like some of the main villains in previous games didn't really have their motivations or characters fully revealed and fleshed out, so I very much liked learning every little thing about him and why he wanted execute his plan. The only complaint I have about the game is the continued inclusion of ATB. In a turn based game, especially a JRPG, I don't particularly enjoy having my turns timed before the enemy attacks. It gives me WAY less time to stop and think about what the next best move is. ATB won't hurt too bad for the first half of the game, but once the bosses start getting kind of out of control (), this is much more of a problem. Overall, I recommend this game to anybody. If you are new to Final Fantasy, I recommend you go from 1,4,5. Seem to be the most interesting in story engagement so far.

_childDocuments_.review: I've already gave a thumb up but how good is FFV and why?:If you are familiar with other famous FF titles, FFV is simpler and more adventurous. Its simplicity, along with its bright main color tone, makes the pace brisk and keeps players feeling more relaxed (compared to the darker vibe of FFVI). For someone wants a simpler, adventurous but still imaginative entertainment experience, FFV is the best choice among the whole serie.:I can say FFV's job system is, standalone, already the most polished one. Unlike FFIII, which has fake freedom in its job system (because many scenes have a tendency of "what character should be used?"), FFV provides true freedom to determine your playthrough. Compared to later titles, FFV's job system is polished and clean. By "clean," I mean that FFV's jobs don't couple other properties (for example, FFX's jobs couple character special abilities or their fixed weapons), and each job is simpler to understand and has obvious functions.Think about it—most 4-job fiesta runs happen in FFV. So, how good is FFV's job system?:How can I describe FFV's unique sense of adventure? Let me use the feeling that FFV's soundtrack gives to describe it.When it's adventurous, we want it simple and brave, driven by dopamine and our instinctive courage. We don't need it to be speculative, to pursue reasonableness, or for the character’s behavior to be worth pondering. We just need to dive into an adventure (but it has to be imaginative). The color scheme, the simple character guts (simple doesn't mean they're naive), and the simple music hook the player. Particularly, the music in this game can make you feel the sense of adventure in just a few seconds (it still follows the principle of being simple, and it hooks me well). For example, I compared many titles' combat themes. In many other titles, it took me 20-30 seconds to slowly get the vibe of the combat theme, while in FFV, it took me 5-8 seconds. This kind of simplicity and inspiration runs through FFV's music, storyline, and characters. I believe this is the principle behind the unique sense of adventure that FFV provides.When this is a game about adventure and saving the world, many artworks fall into clichés, but FFV has its own imagination. _childDocuments_.review: It's FF5 so ofc it's good, however I was extremely disappointed to learn that all the GBA bonus content was missing from this version. I know I could avoided this entirely by just doing some additional research on what the Pixel Remaster included, so this on me, but it was still a disappointment to find out because the Sealed Temple and 4 additional jobs were definitely some of my favourite additions in the GBA release. Another thing that also bugged me, was the fact that dialogue portraits aren't a thing. I find that they really helped to add a lot of personality to the dialogue overall in previous versions, whereas in this one because there are no portraits it now just makes everything seem like throwaway NPC dialogue. I could mod them in, but I don't think something as simple character portraits should require modding in the first place.Some of the spell animations have also gotten worse in my opinion. Roulette now just appearing instead of actually playing the roulette animation, Fire/Fira, Flame and Thunder scrolls for example. This is admittedly very minor, but it still adds to the overall experience.I still enjoyed the game a lot, the upgraded soundtrack and overall updated spell animations were wonderful. However, I wouldn't recommend this version of the game unless you're just not a fan of the GBA release and all the added content that came with it. Otherwise it's still FF5, so you're definitely going to enjoy it, but for persons like me, the game just feels incomplete. TL:DR - If you don't care about GBA release content, go for it. Otherwise, just stick to emulating the game, and if you do want to buy the game despite this, do so when it's on sale for less than $10 is what I'd recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Just to preface, FFV introduced a lot of staples to the already-prevalent FF franchise back in '92. When Square was releasing FF in the west, they chose to skip this game along with FFII and FFIII; deeming it too hard for westerners. When it did release in '99 for NA(EU/AUS in '02) as part of a PS1 anthology, the time gap had taken its toll, making it something of a dark-horse within a series now populated by much bigger titles. It didn't help that the PS1 version had save and performance issues.     The first and foremost addition it gave us was the robust job system; a notable upgrade to FFIII outside of just additional jobs. FFV allowed you to use abilities from one class while being in another class. The possibilities were endless(well not really but still!) Some of the classes would come back such as the Samurai or Blue Mage; if not in name, in ability.)     The plot follows a similar formula to I, III, and IV in that you're warriors of light tasked with protecting crystals from an oncoming threat to the world. There are some moments that fall flat or feel rushed but the story's definitely in-depth. Sort of a bittersweet middle spot to the pre-3D FF era.     This remaster does wonders for not only the sprites but the UI. Heaven knows SE was sleeping when they decided to port over the mobile version originally. While I did like the portraits when the characters spoke, I'd still say this is probably the definitive version now, toppling the GBA. In my book, it's still a must-play!

_childDocuments_.review: FF GOAT!!!!!This is it, this is the best one. Plot is great, lot's of great storytelling elements and plot/gameplay allusions that are not obvious on a first-time playthrough. Great cast and overall story, the one criticism I'd say is that the main antagonist is underwhelming in the long run which is disappointing following FF4's antagonist. FF5's main antagonist doesn't get much characterization past being evil and their backstory isn't very compelling. However, this is minor when considering the amount of growth and characterization that the main cast of protagonists receive.THE BEST JOB SYSTEM! Clearly I'm biased, but FF5 has the most fun gameplay of the original 6 FF games IMO. There is an insane amount of combat potential between the almost unlimited job and ability combinations available. Similar to FF3, FF5 debuts more series staple Job archetypes such as Blue Mage, Mystic Knight, Dancers/Bards, Samurai and others. There's a buttload of secrets & optional content, once you pass a certain point in the game you can choose to either make a beeline straight to the final boss or take your time and solve some of the secrets of the world or tie up some plot-related loose ends in exchange for rewards and power ups. Despite being one of the more convoluted FF worlds to navigate, FF5's overworld is one of the most rewarding.Honestly, I just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love this game. It's my favorite mainline FF game because it allows so much freedom and creativity on how you choose to playthrough the game. You can play through the game 1000 times and each playthrough will be unique. You can do challenge runs and limit how you play the game or if things get too hard you can be a dweeb and find a strategy to cheese almost any boss fight. This was also the last mainline FF game to feature a medieval fantasy setting until FF9 temporarily returned to form (I'm one of the people that prefers this type of setting). If I had to recommend just 1 FF game to play it would be this one. Fun Fact: This game was released in 1992 which was the year I was born.This game introduced the most powerful cheese in all of FF, Gil Toss.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V, developed and published by Square Enix, has stood the test of time since its original release in 1992. With its recent resurgence through remakes and re-releases, it has once again captivated players with its engrossing storyline, deep character development, and engaging gameplay mechanics. In this review, we'll delve into the various aspects that make Final Fantasy V a timeless classic in the RPG genre.Storyline:Final Fantasy V introduces us to a world where the elemental crystals hold immense power and maintain the balance. As the protagonist, Bartz Klauser, embarks on a quest to protect the crystals from an impending threat, he meets a diverse cast of characters with their own motivations and backstories. The game's narrative is rich, filled with twists and turns, and explores themes of friendship, sacrifice, and the consequences of one's actions. The characters are well-written and grow throughout the journey, making the story emotionally engaging and memorable.Gameplay:The gameplay of Final Fantasy V combines traditional turn-based combat with a deep job system, which allows players to customize their characters' abilities and roles. The job system is the game's standout feature, granting players immense flexibility and strategic depth. With over 20 jobs to choose from, each offering unique abilities and playstyles, the possibilities for party customization are vast. This system encourages experimentation and allows players to adapt their strategies to overcome various challenges, making combat consistently engaging and rewarding.Exploration is another strong suit of Final Fantasy V. The world is expansive, offering a plethora of towns, dungeons, and hidden treasures to discover. The ability to switch jobs on the fly enhances exploration, as certain jobs provide specialized skills useful in navigating different environments. The game strikes a perfect balance between linear progression and open exploration, ensuring a sense of adventure while maintaining a coherent storyline.Visuals and Audio:Visually, Final Fantasy V has seen significant enhancements in its remakes. The original pixel art, though charming in its own right, has been upgraded to more vibrant and detailed graphics, breathing new life into the game's world. The character and enemy designs are iconic, and the environments are beautifully rendered, showcasing the game's imaginative setting.The soundtrack of Final Fantasy V, composed by Nobuo Uematsu, is an absolute masterpiece. From epic battle themes to emotional melodies, the music enhances the game's atmosphere and emotional impact. The remastered versions offer even better audio quality, ensuring a delightful auditory experience.Conclusion:Final Fantasy V remains a timeless classic that continues to captivate players with its engrossing storyline, deep character development, and innovative gameplay mechanics. The combination of a rich narrative, a robust job system, and an expansive world to explore creates a truly memorable RPG experience. Whether you're a long-time fan or a newcomer to the series, Final Fantasy V is an adventure that shouldn't be missed. Step into the shoes of Bartz and his companions, and prepare for an unforgettable journey that will leave you craving for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, probably the single best gameplay among all the classic Final Fantasy titles. It's not aggressively awful or trope-heavy, but it lacks any and all impact or bite. It's there, it's mildly amusing, it does its job, but nothing more. Gilgamesh is great in this though.Definitely recommend checking the game out, especially if you're into challenge runs or the like! As classic JRPG gameplay goes, this one is absolutely up there near the top.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve been a fan of the Final Fantasy series since was a little boy, and Final Fantasy V has always held a special place in my heart. The Pixel Remaster does justice to the original while breathing new life into it, making it a must-play for both veterans and newcomers.The updated pixel art is gorgeous. Characters, monsters, and environments have never looked better. The new visuals stay true to the original while being more vibrant and detailed. And the reorchestrated soundtrack? Absolutely stunning. It captures the essence of the classic tunes but with a richer, fuller sound.The job system is as fun and deep as ever. The remaster doesn’t mess with what made the original great, but it does add some nice quality-of-life improvements. The UI is smoother, and there’s an auto-battle feature for grinding (a lifesaver). The save system is also more forgiving, which is a big plus.If you’re thinking about playing this on the Steam Deck, go for it. The game runs flawlessly. The controls feel natural, and the pixel art really shines on the Deck’s screen. Plus, being able to play this classic on the go is just awesome.This is how you do a remaster. FFV Pixel Remaster is a fantastic update to a classic game. Whether you’re playing it for the first time or reliving the adventure, you won’t be disappointed. Highly recommend, especially if you’ve got a Steam Deck.

_childDocuments_.review: *** I can conditionally recommend this if you're into FF games but if you're looking for a stand alone game to play in the Pixel Remaster series, there are better choices. ***I've been playing the Pixel Remaster series in order.  FF5 is combo of FF3 and FF4: it has the flexible jobs system of the former and the characters + story of the latter.  A winning combination right?  Well ... hmm.  I feel like the character and story elements of FF4 are better than FF5.  And, part of me liked the simpler job and leveling systems of FF3... maybe there was a tad too much to do in FF5.  There were points in the game where to achieve something, you had to have had a character master a particular job or skill, whether or not you were interested in it.  The other thing was that FF5 added even more magic varieties beyond white, black, and summoning.  Now we have Blue (monster magic) and Time (parts of white & black from other games).  Still though ... summoning was king and even though it was fun to hunt down monsters to control and learn blue magic skills, with the exception of a couple of spells, it didn't feel worth it in the end.All told it took me 60+ hours of play time to get through FF5 whereas it has been 15-30 hours each for FF1 through 4.  The game did feel like it was dragging on a bit but maybe that had to do with blue magic hunting and job leveling.  Also, the difficulty level of this game felt much greater than that of FF1-4.Is the game worth playing if you are FF fan or want to, like me, run through the Pixel Remaster series .... sure.  Is this game worth playing as a standalone? ... that's where it gets murky.

The plot also isn't as involved as in the other SNES entries, but it's a great palate cleanswer between the darker moods of IV and VI.

_childDocuments_.review: Versions played previously: SNES (Emulator) - partiallyTime to complete: ~29 hoursOverall Rating: 9.5/10Gameplay: 9/10Story: 8/10Graphics: 9.5/10This is the final game in the series that originally never got a version in the US, and it’s the first one that I don’t understand why. I was expecting this one to be a bit of a flop, sort of like FF2 and FF3, but I was left disappointed that this never got a real SNES release. The gameplay is the most fun of the first five games easily, taking all the good parts of the FF3 job system with none of the flaws. Unlike FF3, in this game you can actually make some amazing combinations of jobs, and even most of the jobs that seem “useless” are actually helpful sometimes. Additionally, the ability to mix and match skills from different jobs provides great replay value, and this is the one of the first five I’m most excited to play again. As for the story, I was shocked at how good it was, considering I’d heard it was one of the less serious FF games. It is truly the Saturday Morning Cartoons of Final Fantasy, but that doesn’t mean the plot is bad. Despite being slightly predictable and a bit on the nose, (the villain is named Exdeath, seriously?) I found myself falling in love with the characters, and I was really affected by the twist near the end. It wasn’t quite the epic tale of FF4, but it was really good. The characters all have good nuance and development, and they’re all interesting with the possible exception of Bartz. The graphics, like the rest of the Pixel Remasters, are amazing. Like the other games, the only drawback is the reuse of some sprites and animations from the others, which seems a bit lazy but overall still looks pretty good. Anyway, it’s definitely an underrated FF game, and I highly recommend playing it, especially if you like retro JRPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V - Pixel Remaster has one of the best job systems in the series so far. The way you can mix and match abilities from different jobs is super fun. It’s simple enough that you’re not overwhelmed, but there’s still a lot of room to experiment. It feels like you can try just about any combo and make it work without totally wrecking your party’s balance. FFIII laid the groundwork, but V took that and refined it to near perfection. You get most of the jobs pretty early on, and the game basically dares you to experiment. It never punishes you for switching jobs around, which I love. Want your white mage to become a ninja? Go for it. The flexibility is amazing, and it’s refreshing that you don’t have to worry about min-maxing your stats every level up. Plus, the costumes? Delightful. Each job class has its own look, and they’re all so fun to see.Story-wise, okay, it’s a bit lighter compared to the more dramatic FFIV. But honestly, that’s part of its charm. And even though the plot sticks to that "warriors of light" formula, the party interactions and their personalities really shine through. They feel like a family by the end. And there's Gilgamesh! That guy steals the show as the comic relief  who keeps popping up. Every time he’s on screen, it’s gold.Another thing I really appreciated is how well-paced the game is. No random difficulty spikes that force you into a grindfest for hours. The dungeons are mostly short and sweet, with enough variety to keep things interesting.Gameplay-wise, this game holds up incredibly well. It’s insane to think it came out in 1992 because the way it handles job swapping and skill inheritance feels way ahead of its time. The level of flexibility you get is nuts – you can give your knight some black magic or have your monk whip out a sword if you want. And the boss fights? Some are susceptible to instant-KO moves or status effects, but others have these wild mechanics where they shift their weaknesses mid-fight. You can’t just brute force your way through – you actually have to strategize.Now, the downsides. Leveling both your character and job levels takes forever. If you’re aiming for 100% completion, brace yourself for some serious grinding. Hitting level 50 with all characters or mastering every job is borderline impossible without spending hours grinding. Plus, there are a bunch of missable enemies and chests, which can be super frustrating if you’re a completionist.TL;DR; Final Fantasy V is easily my favorite so far. It has a brilliant job system and some of the best pacing in the series, even if the story’s a bit lighter and the villain’s not amazing. Lovable characters, flexible gameplay, and a surprising amount of depth for an old-school RPG. 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Of the 3 SNES FF titles Final Fantasy V may have the blandest story, but in my opinion it is the most fun.The job system, originally introduced in Final Fantasy III, is finally perfected here.There's plenty of jobs to choose from, most of which offer some great unique power ups and abilities, and having so many jobs to level up really gives you a lot to do. God I love stealing enemy skills!The story is your basic catch the crystals though the villain this time at least has a bit of a personality and a couple of the characters have a nice arc. You get new jobs before you run out of things to learn from the previous set and it functions perfectly on my Steam Deck.I've been looking forward to this one and 6 the most since I grabbed the Pixel Remaster set. I won't at all mind grinding out every single achievement!

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, this game is way longer than all previous entries. A lot of that goes into grinding, mainly character- and job levels. No Secret Summon Spells this time, for the better in my opinion. Standing out like previously are the slowly evolving, charmful retro visuals with the advance of the series. The story in this part is once again leaning on the simplistic approach of the first three Final Fantasy games, however with a lot more depth introduced, similar to Final Fantasy 4. The story in a closer look is enjoyable and the characters likeable, even though really far stretched out to the point of it challenging my patience a bit. I sat through it nonetheless, no regrets at all. In matters of character customization the game took another step forward, allowing more diverse team composition through the ability to equip a skill from a mastered class to your current one and keeping around all the best qualities of the equipment system from my earlier favorites of the franchise. Furthermore I really enjoyed the indivudal sprites for every characters job classes, had me regularly excited to unlock new jobs and see the visual designs. Following all that Final Fantasy 5 also has my favorite original soundtracks of the whole series so far, which carries the game as a whole to another level and makes the playing experience a lot more pleasant towards the later portions. Even through partially tedious grinding I found myself considering this as my current favorite, tied with Final Fantasy 4. Though having similar if not greater depth to the story than FF4, I do probably still prefer the fourth entry for hitting what I consider my sweet spot for length of the game, feeding me a decently intricate and well thought out story in a more digestible size. FF5 feeling too long might just my personal taste to be fair, considering that admitingly nothing felt like senseless filler and every cutscene and quest felt like it had its clear purpose. In finishing words I`d say that Final Fantasy 5 is a very enjoyable game, best experienced in shorter sessions due to its impressive overall duration. I´m not sure about calling it my favorite but I definitely thoroughly enjoyed my time with it from start to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is the classic and many would argue the quintessential game of the SNES era. If you've played classic Final Fantasy then you know what to expect: your characters lined out on one side with enemies on the other playing out pseudo-turn based combat. The gimmick of FFV, however, is that you gain skills and abilities by playing as (and mastering) different classes that you obtain throughout the game. You can then mix and match to create useful synergies in the early game and absolutely broken combinations by the late game. Something like a Knight with White magic to make a paladin hybrid to a dual wielding tornado of death that attacks 8 times and can add spells to their weapon strikes. That adaptability is key to enjoying Final Fantasy V.The story is classic Final Fantasy: world ending villain appears and everything changes. Four Heroes of Light gain the powers of the crystals to fight back. Nothing new under the sun but the simplicity of the story is part of its charm. It really serves the gameplay more than anything else.If I have one complaint its that the encounter rate is a little out of whack in this entry compared to others, even earlier games like FFIV. By the late game enemy encounters feel about 2-5 steps too early and those dungeons feel more tedious as a result. Running is always an option, but you'll want the resources from battle to stay competitive as it progresses.All in all this is a wonderful game and fans of tactical combat with lots of diversity in classes should give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: This version does not have the additional content found in the GBA and Mobile versions, but I still think it is a great experience.The redone music is a real treat, and the upgraded backgrounds during battles are also very nice (especially in ExDeath's Castle after the illusion is removed).The colors and graphics are sharp, as are the new cutscene animations (ie. crystals shattering, etc.).Some features included in all FF Pixel Remastered editions:►Hold down B (on a Nintendo-type controller) to run, and in this game when you learn the Thief's Sprint ability, it makes you run  when you do this. Granted, I find both of these can make your character run a little too fast, and you might make mistakes in some situations. For example, when you are trying to escape Castle Karnak before it blows up while getting every treasure chest and learning Aera and Death Claw on your way out, your character might dash past turns you meant to make. Update: This was patched on Nov 24, 2021.►Auto-Battle feature, this is nice.►Quick Save, which can help in some situations. For example, in Barrier Tower, you might miss the Red Dragon for your Bestiary from 2 potential treasure chests. Quick-Saving just before opening these chests can save you time if you need to reload saves to get both the Yellow and Red Dragons for your Bestiary.This version also does not have the best translation/dialogue. For example, when you first meet Sage Ghido in his cave, Faris will say (and I quote) "By the briny beard of Neptune". I personally really don't like this (although, this is still an amount better than the PS1 Anthology version's translation, overall).Though I see most reviewers will direct your attention to the GBA bonus content missing (which I also wish was present), as well as the bugs, I personally feel there is an underlying issue with FFV that exists with every version of the game (including this one). And that is, when playing, you'll often not know what to do next, and the game just does not "tell" you where to go next, far too often. I understand this is to encourage exploration, and to try to make the experience less linear, and to not "hold your hand", so to speak. But I really think this game would benefit greatly from a dialogue option where your team discusses where they should go next in some cases. A good example is in the DS version of Final Fantasy IV. There is an option in the menus where you can open a dialogue with your team about what you should do next, and where you should go. This feature also existed in Phantasy Star IV on Genesis, to name another JRPG. You see, there is nothing wrong with having something like this in any JRPG, and it is not a sign of weakness if you need this, let's say, because you took a long break from your game and need a reminder of where you are currently. I feel it is a missed opportunity that this feature was never added to this game especially. For any version of Final Fantasy V, I'll never give anyone a hard time for needing reference materials, like a walkthrough for example.Granted, the monster designs are brilliant, creative, colorful, and diverse, and the different ways you can take down bosses (especially with !Blue magic) is just a joy to experience! Make sure you use Aqua Breath on the SandWorm boss in World 1, use LVL.3 Flare on Exdeath in World 2, and Use Death Claw on bosses Byblos and Dragon Pod to bring them down! There are MANY other examples where you can make fools out of bosses in this game, which just enriches the experience! Possibly my favorite, use !Sing with Romeo's Ballad to cast Stop on super boss Omega! Granted, the Stop only lasts like 2-3 seconds, so if you have 3 party members !Sing Romeo's Ballad, while 1 person does !SpellBlade with Thundaga, Omega becomes a toaster.I personally think the Job system is better here than it is in Final Fantasy Tactics (no joke). This is because of the passive abilities you get for mastering Jobs in FFV.I am grateful for this Pixel Remastered version, even though it is missing the GBA bonus content, and even though it can still leave new players lost unless they don't mind spending long evenings exploring, or referencing walkthroughs.***Some points about my review above:►I completed this game and earned every achievement, and I really took my time. This includes mastering every Job, and Finding every !Blue spell, defeating Omega and ShinRyu, getting every Treasure Chest, going to every Location, etc.►I am not a Speed Runner. Although I occasionally enjoy watching speedruns, I myself never try to speed run through a game, as it ruins the experience for me. I much prefer a slow burn. I understand this version of FFV has some notable bugs that (to my understanding) can ruin the Speed Run experience, but I only experienced one bug, although it was considerable. When I used !Steal on the same monster enough times, it stops working. After just 1 "Couldn't Steal", it will eventually start saying "Nothing to Steal" on subsequent !Steal attempts on the same monster, even though I never successfully stole anything in the first place. I was farming Ice Shields from Numb Blades on the Island Temple in the Merged World, as they really help against ShinRyu.This is the 4th version of Final Fantasy 5 that I've completed (also mastered every Job, defeated all optional bosses, etc.). Listed below are the versions I've done this before:►The original Super Famicom version, with the RPGe English Translation Patch.►The GBA version with the Sound Restoration Patch. Includes the additional Jobs and bonus Dungeon reachable via submarine, after ExDeath.►The Steam version previous to this one, which was a mobile port. Also includes additional Jobs, Dungeon, and the infamous character sprites. For this version, I only completed 87 of 96 achievements; as I didn't get everyone to lvl.99, I didn't clear the cloister of the dead, as I really had enough of this version after over 125 Hours.I've also played (but never completed) the PlayStation 1 version (Final Fantasy Anthology) a very long time ago, as the loading times and translation of that version just turned me off far too much.I'll kept all these versions in mind, as I wrote this.

_childDocuments_.review: I was sceptical at first but it's easily my third favorite FF game now. Here is how I'd rate it:1. Music: Pretty much the same as in every Remaster. It's ok, it sets the atmosphere but nothing special. 7/10.2. Graphics: Hugely improved. Actually looks very nice, I especially like the battle animation of the spells and Summons. Feels very impactful and strong. 9/10.3. Story: Basic premise. Gotta save the world from an evil overloard threatening to destroy the world. The world and characters are at least interesting enough to keep you playing. Might have been great at that time but very clichee and overused nowadays. 7/10.4. Gameplay: This is they main selling point. Easily the best job system ever, even better than Bravely Default in my opinion. It's a lot of fun to switch around and experiment and finally get it all together at the end. Lot of interesting skill and abilities to learn and master and you always get something new and cool until the end. Easily a 10/10.So overall a 8.5/10 for me. If you like classic FF and turn-based JRPGs with job systems then I think this is a must play.

_childDocuments_.review: This remake reminds me of why I first loved JRPGs in the first place. It's also the first time I beat FF5.The sheer amount of character customization is top-notch, even compared to other Final Fantasies where you pick your classes. The story is lighthearted and fun, and there are plenty of creative and interesting mechanics in both random battles and boss fights. The game script is very similar to the GBA release of Final Fantasy 5. And of course, the remastered songs are still amazing, like in the rest of the FF Pixel Remasters. Final Fantasy 5 is also the game where a few series staples debuted. Time Magic and Blue Magic are rather potent here, and the Chemist's ability to mix two items is lowkey powerful. Let alone the debut of classes such as the Samurai, Bard and Dancer. Git gud and grind enough, and you may be able to master the Red Mage's Dualcast (also debuting here) and the Ninja's Dual Wield. It's entirely possible to break the game's difficulty over one's knee, with enough devotion and the right combinations... which is also why not one, but two superbosses can also be found in the final dungeon.Those who have played FF5 Advance on the GBA, or the now-defunct mobile port, may be disappointed to know the added content and four bonus classes aren't here. This is standard for the Pixel Remasters beyond FF1 PR -- they're a more purist experience in terms of content. Other than some minor quality of life tweaks, nothing changed a whole lot in this one. But that's not a problem for me, because the original FF5 is where the series first got really, really good. It's hard to polish up perfection, right? ;)
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first chance at playing this Final Fantasy. 3,4,5,6 are the only ones i never got a chance to play as a kid. And as a adult i didn't wanna touch the horrible Mobile ports as they just don't look the same. After playing this pixel remaster i've got to say i LOVE it. The music is by far some of the best final fantasy music ever, the new Vocals to some of the OST's are just amazing. The job system is really fun ever more so than the FF3 DS remake. I was so shocked to see that FF5 was the series first for a lot of things, Omega, Gilgamish, Blue Mage, Level 5 death, ect. I fully recommend this game for any fan of Final Fantasy.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite version of Final Fantasy V ever released. It looks great. The script is very good. The soundtrack is excellent in a way that none of the Pixel Remasters have yet achieved. It just feels like you're listening to the soundtrack from Final Fantasy V. This game feels like the reason why they wanted to remaster these games to begin with. Like every decision has been made in service of Final Fantasy V first and applied to the previous games as best as possible.A really fun Final Fantasy experience. Recommended but definitely replace the font.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is fantastic. The job system alone gives this title immense replay value and surprising strategic depth. The story is cliche but done in such a fun way with enjoyable characters it still leaves you invested.But this port is incredibly unstable. Multiple fresh installations on multiple machines have all had the same issue; random slowdown leading to softlock. It doesn't matter if it's Intel, AMD, NVIDIA, Windows 11 or Windows 10. The game is still running, music playing, but utterly and totally unresponsive. The only things that have worked to break the lock is to change the party's entire equipment and jobs. Which basically undermines the entire premise of the game, and only seems to work some of the time.Further to that; I quick loaded a save from shortly before a boss fight which softlocked. Upon loading, the boss fight... did not trigger. I just walked past where the fight should have happened. The fight simply didn't occur. That was one way to get past a bug, but glitching through a different glitch is a very unsettling way to play.It's effectively unplayable in the current state. Avoid until this game has been patched.Very, very disappointing considering the stability of the previous titles in the pixel remaster series.

_childDocuments_.review: The Final Fantasy Pixel Remasters offer players a great way to play old school Final Fantasy games in a near-pure state, with some improvements: mild gameplay tweaks, old bugs fixed, and a graphics update which is a bit more palatable for the modern gamer (as well as having a cohesive look among the titles). None of the Pixel Remaster games have the additional content from each game's re-release, but that doesn't bother me.My only gripe overall is that Square Enix hasn't addressed the font issue. It  easy to fix on the user's end, which is great, but with the amount of comments on the font since the first PRs came out, and no change on the developer's end, is a bit disappointing to me.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm honestely not used to praise SquareEnix for their remasters - given my experiences from their previous steam versions of FFs, Chrono Trigger or even the most recent Chrono Cross blunder. But as they say: give credit where it's due.The game original style is preserved perfectly - a beautiful pixel art that looks great even on 4K displays. The UI is no longer so cumbersome, it's modernized and very pleasent to use. There are no issues with input delays as it was the case in the previous steam/mobile versions. Everything feels responsive and userfriendly.As for the music: the original one was great - but gosh how well it sounds right now with this instrumental arrangements. Few tracks worth mentioning: "Legend of the Deep Forest", "The Day will Come" or "Reina's Theme". 5th Final Fantasy was always the least liked one from the SNES era for me. But, this remaster really makes the game shine and I had a really great time playing through it. I think that this a perfect state for the game to be preserved.This is a remaster worthy of Gilgamesh!

_childDocuments_.review: Breaks my heart to choose "Not Recommended" for my second favorite Final Fantasy, but it's just in too rough a shape.Final Fantasy V is an excellent game, and this version has the potential to be great, but the ridiculous amount of bugs just sour the whole experience. During my playthrough, in a couple of instances the game became almost unplayable, and in more it was heavily marred by the bugs.To list some problems, events are sometimes not triggering/appearing, certain ability combinations are causing persistent problems where battles become softlocked even after reloading a save, abilities aren't accurately affecting attributes and certain spells and equipment don't function correctly.The visuals are nice, if a bit too bright and washed out compared to the originals. Once again, the music is fantastic, arguably the best thing to come out of this entire remaster series.I'm earnestly hoping that there is a future in this world where I can safely change this review into a Recommendation, but for now I'd recommend to skip/wait instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I have read somewhere that this part is not really cherished by many fans of final fantasy series, I don't really understand that. For example FFIV had preset classes, and I didn't like it at all.Secondly the characters and the storyline are even further improved from its predecessor. They start to feel like fully fleshed characters, even though their backgrounds are not really that interesting, the game offers even a meaningful change of characters in your party, and the cutscene about it really conveys alot of emotion.The battle system is vastly improved, there is a blue mage job that gets spells from enemies, beastmaster can catch enemies like in pokemon, I could go on and on. _childDocuments_.review: Pros:The soundtrack. Just... wow. This is now the best version of FFV. The delisted version had four bonus job classes and a bonus dungeon that extended the endgame. This version omits that material. The soundtrack more than makes up for it.The job system. Speaking of job classes, this game has one of the most engaging progression systems I've ever seen. It has huge potential to customize. It allows you to quickly retool if you fight a boss or run out of MP. Using "Freelancer" (or the hidden class) in the endgame gives you the stat bonuses and passives of all job classes you've mastered. Job level is often more important than experience level.Auto battle. All recent Final Fantasy re-releases have had this in some form. I grind levels, gil, and ABP while riding a stationary bike, folding laundry, sitting through something boring...Cons:The plot. Four heroes of light seek four crystals and many more mcguffins as they quest to defeat the evil dark lord. If that is a spoiler for you, you are a Final Fantasy n00b. Let me redirect you to Final Fantasy 6 (not available on Steam at the time of this writing) or 7. They are way better. Or 4. It had five heroes and plot twists.The characters. Bartz is an immature jerk. The others can only be described by their relationships to one another. The awesome job system actually hurts here because any character can have any job, so characters are identical in combat beyond small stat changes. Unfortunately it doesn't get any better once the sweet battle music fades away.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - If you're a fan of FF5, stay the heck away. If you're not, STILL STAY AWAY. STAY FAR A-BLOODY-WAYWhile visually the game looks nice-ish as a "remaster", the game seems to have been un-broken and re-broken in comparison to the GBA version of FF5 (despite using the same but slightly-altered translation and re-positioned sprites that were in said version due to its tiny screen.) For those who love playing this game, especially for Four Job Fiesta, you'll find yourself even more frustrated than if you were playing the old Playstation version.This is also not something I would recommend to someone new to FF5 because you'll become incredibly frustrated with how the game plays as it is, and to be fair the story of FF5 is really bare bones compared to previous and future installments. The remaster especially, though, is full of not simply nitpicks but actual mechanical issues. Even the "new" UI looks like an amateur flash game maker did it. The dissonance of quality is too jarring to be able to overlook it, which is a shame since the remade chipsets and sprites actually look pretty good/crisp.If you're thinking of buying this because it's cheaper than looking for other versions, please don't. This remaster kick Squenix has been on is basically just half-arsed murderizing of old, beloved FF games. Please just go find an old copy somewhere at a store or website, or better yet [REDACTED] because this "remaster" is just insulting to people like me who have played FF5 so many times for Fiesta that the changes and mess-ups are just grating. It's better not to feed the monstrosity that thinks the only FF worth properly remaking is 7.

_childDocuments_.review: The best way to play FF5 imho !- SFX and VFX were modernized while still being pixel-art and very well integrated. - The (optional) rearranged BGM is absolutely epic, besting the original SNES BGM, which was already epic !- A classic pixelated font is available to replace the horrendous default "new font".- Boosts help you re-enjoy the story without having to spend a huge amount of time grinding for EXP/AP/GIL.- Re-balanced bosses and mobs that make the game more challenging by default and call for more creative use of the many available jobs for your characters

_childDocuments_.review: + The most famously vibrant of the fist six entries is even more so here; absolutely gorgeous game+ Splendid, remixed and remastered soundtrack; this one really isn't talked enough about, and I found it to be one of the strongest in the Pixel Remaster series+ Characters are much more expressive+ With the notable exception of Cecil's character arc in FFIV, I contend that V has the best characters and story thus far; purists often rag on this entry for its levity, but it knows when to inject a little emotion just as well as games like II and IV that game before it+This game is FUN; really, and truly fun+ The job system is widely celebrated for a reason; it's endlessly malleable and generously rewards experimentation+ The dungeons are so much more creative and unique as compared to I-IV, and by a country mile+ The side content is actually challenging and varied, in a way that modern entries to the franchise oblivious to+/- If you grind a bit and go hard with some of the party combinations in the end-game, you can cheese FFV until it absolutely breaks- Exdeath the Splinter- The Dragonball Turtle Fight- Getting all of the Blue Magic can be intensely frustrating, which can be maddening for completionists like myself

_childDocuments_.review: FFV is a weird game. On the one hand I love the gameplay in this, but the plot is sooooooooooo boring. Back in the day I played this game multiple times, and I had the same opinions about it back then that I do now. The job system in this game is very fun. Getting to mix and match everything, getting to play dress up with the characters, and finding fun ways to combine equipment with those skills. It's just a fun game to play. The battles in the game are interesting too. There are boss fights that require some strategy to over come, and if you try to face tank them you'll get punished. They aren't the most in depth fights in the series, but it's just enough to be interesting. I've always enjoyed playing this game.I have never liked the plot though. The plot of this game is incredibly boring. SO BORING. Maybe some people could like it, but I definitely do not. I didn't like it when I was a kid, and I don't like it now. The hardest part of this game is slogging through the plot. Now that I've played FF4 I kind of like this game's plot a bit more than that, but I don't particularly like the plot of either way very much. Especially since FF6 exists and that plot is solid. It makes FF4 and FF5 look like rough drafts by comparison. If you like Final Fantasy games with jobs systems the game play of FF5 is pretty fun. I like it better than FF3 in that respect, but it's no where near as much fun as FF12 or FFTactics. Just a nice thing to play on a lazy afternoon. If plot is important I really don't recommend this game at all. If you can't look past a bad plot might want to skip this one. If you mostly just play to kill monsters and have fun experimenting with game systems this one is pretty good.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I'd say this one is to FF4 what FF3 is to FF2 in the sense that it's a clear improvement in many respects but for some reason decides to take a step backwards in a few aspects. The storytelling and cut-scenes are much more detailed than in the previous game and the characters have more detailed animations too, as well as the environments looking a bit better. It's a more focused story with just a small group of characters that get more time in the spotlight and you don't have a revolving cast of side characters that pop up for a while to help your protagonist. Character leveling, XP, MP, items and spells/skills are what you'd expect from previous games, and the usual elements are present (chocobos, airships, magical tech, elemental crystals being corrupted by evil entity and putting the world in danger, etc), but instead of having a character class tied to a specific character, this game brings back an improved version of Jobs, which you can assign and re-assign freely and are leveled in parallel to your character level by using ABP's instead of XP.The only thing I didn't like much is that the jobs system makes grinding necessary in order to really be able to take advantage of it, and that some dungeons kind of overdo the maze/puzzle gimmick for my taste. Very good game, anyway. I liked the story and the cast roughly as much as the cast and story of FF4, which was my favorite game in the series so far.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: The Pixel Remaster of this game is amazing, before this I loved to play the GBA version. _childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is absolutely an under-rated title within the Final Fantasy franchise. Taking the best from past titles, such as Final Fantasy IV's ATB gauge and narrative story, or improving upon mechanics like Final Fantasy III's job system, it makes Final Fantasy V a fun and rewarding experience the entire way through.I can not praise the job system enough. While Final Fantasy III gives you the ability to swap jobs and try different configurations, Final Fantasy V rewards you for experimenting, allowing you to keep abilities learned from leveling other jobs, and letting you experiment with your favorite jobs on how to improve them. This could be as simple as making a White Mage with Time Magic and a Samurai with Two-Handed, to a Berserk Bard or a Freelancer that calls random summons and animals.There is also so much more content in comparison to the previous games. You can get all the summons, fight Shinryu and Omega, or just work on getting all the abilities and Blue Magic spells.The gil costs are also significantly better, and buying spells allow your entire party to cast them instead of just a single member. This only one example, but there are other overall improvements from the past games that just make it so much smoother of an experience.8/10While I don't find the story as enteraining as Final Fantasy IV or VI, it is still entertaining with interesting characters, with a lot more cheer than seen with many other games in the franchise before and after.6/10Overall, FFV is a fantastic game, with amazing mechanics that honestly haven't been explored enough in the series, and while it isn't the strongest game in the Final Fantasy series, it certainly is a hidden gem for many players that makes it worthwhile.Overall, I would give the game an 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't Final Fantasy V. And that's not being a gatekeeper, it's the exact same combat as the rest of the Pixel remasters. This may seem like it'd only effect small things(like using rods from your inventory). But this completely alters the atb system by adding random atb start points. This means the difficulty of a fight can be completely decided by what rng seed you get, for every fight. That's not how the balance of V was designed.In addition, the game somehow looks and controls worse than the mobile port. Hell, even the auto battle feature is worse AND slower than the mobile version.Id say the only thing this port does better than the mobile version is the music. The Music is legitimately amazing.Basically, buy the mobile version or the GBA version if you think the mobile port is too ugly too.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V Pixel Remaster is a faithful remaster of the original game and altogether with Final Fantasy III Pixel Remaster the best Pixel Remaster released so far. After the overally weaker Final Fantasy IV, Final Fantasy V brings back a real RPG gameplay and much nicer graphics. Final Fantasy IV Pixel Remaster felt rushed, but it is a completely different situation with Final Fantasy V Pixel Remaster. And although there were several bugs reported, many of them have already been fixed by the official patches.I am glad that Final Fantasy V Pixel Remaster was not affected by the weird decision to make these games easier and the difficulty is basically the same as in the SNES or PS1 version. Though it does not mean it is automatically perfect. No, it is far from being perfect. Final Fantasy V itself was always an easy game, especially in its first half as bosses had too little HP and common enemies were just coffin fodder. It is a pity as those boss fights were designed nicely, but the fights end earlier than become more interesting.On the other hand, talking about difficulty in Final Fantasy V is a bit tricky. Since you have the famous Job System in your hands, it really depends on your jobs and unlocked abilities how much difficult battles can be. Let´s say, if you have a traditional party consisting of a warrior, a black mage, a white mage and for example a thief - basically your stereotypical RPG party - difficulty will not be too high in the first half, but later on it will definitely increase with much more difficult boss fights and even common enemies.Yes, Final Fantasy V is about the job system. This is actually the last real RPG when it comes to the Final Fantasy franchise. There are 22 jobs and every one contains a few skills that can be applied to other jobs and this is when magic happens. Thanks to this simple but very effective system you can be a black mage who can wield Excalibur, or a white mage able to cast Firaga or a ninja who can summon Bahamuth. Another great thing about Final Fantasy V are the dungeons. Almost every one is beautifully crafted, with many passages, dead ends or rooms you can enter. Their design is fantastic, clever, maze-like and very interesting. Especially the dungeons in which the tables that allow to unlock the ultimate weapons close to the end of the game are amazing! The last dungeon is a bit underwhelming to be honest. It is not very exciting or interesting.I love the story of the game. Once again there is the theme of crystals, there are the Warriors of the Light. Final Fantasy V is one of the funniest FF games ever made with a lot of jokes, funny situations and laughs despite its dark premise. Well, maybe just the main villain Exdeath does not reach the heights of Golbez from Final Fantasy 4 or Kefka from Final Fantasy 6. However, the game lacks of the indirect storytelling that was amazing in Final Fantasy III. There are just a few NPCs that can tell you something about the lore and world and there are basically no books to read in order to gain some knowledge. This is a big minus from me as Final Fantasy 1 - 3 were fantastic in this.Graphics are very nice, all the added details are beautifully crafted and they added life to many scenes. I have a big complain against the world map which is directly taken from the GBA version (just like many monsters´ sprites). It looks bad, it is too bright compared to the rest of the game and it has no atmosphere. Just like in Final Fantasy IV Pixel Remaster. Of all Pixel Remaster games released so far, Final Fantasy III Pixel Remaster has the best looking world map.Music is perfectly remastered. As in previous Pixel Remaster games, the remastered music is the best thing in this remaster as well. No, they did not butcher A Big Clash of the Bridge - it is fantastic! I have to say that in my opinion the battle theme sounds a bit flat compared to the rest of the soundtrack.Final Fantasy V Pixel Remaster proves that Final Fantasy V belongs amongst the best Final Fantasy games ever made. It was the last Final Fantasy directed by Hironobu Sakaguchi, which on one hand is a sad statement, but on other hand he created one of the best his games.80%

_childDocuments_.review: Writing is the weakest since final fantasy 3. _childDocuments_.review: Mwahahahaha!!!  I disguised myself as a tiny splinter to bring you this early review!!!- Music is God tier like all of the other ports.  I hear some complaints about the "battle theme not having enough bass" but it still sounds decent.  The boss theme took major steps forward.  I remember hating the obnoxious abrupt beginning "DUNNN DUNNNNN" of the original boss theme, but now it sounds more smoother during the intro which let's me appreciate the piece as a whole.  Battle on the Bridge, and Decisive Battle are both top tier battle themes.  All dungeon, overworld, and character themes are beautiful as well.  All in all this soundtrack improved majorly on what was already a good playlist.  Although if you already own the GBA version then it may not be worth it for the music alone since this version is missing extra content.- Gameplay this is among one of the best of the old era Final Fantasy games.  The job system makes a glorious return only this time you can carry over one learned ability from ANY other job.  Want a black mage that can steal?  Its possible.  Want a knight that can use time magic?  Its possible?  Want a bard that can yeet your expensive weapons at the enemy with throw?  Its possible, but I don't recommend it.  Pair this integrate system with equipment optimization then you got yourself a solid JRPG.  Grinding becomes enjoyable when you are frequently learning new abilities for each job.  Makes it exciting to see what the next unlock is going to be.- Content isn't lacking too much either.  There is a fair amount of side optional, and misable content.  Additionally there are two "superbosses" that give you a decent challenge in the endgame.- Story is cheesy at times, but its a fun adventure to follow.  There are some sad, and dark moments weaved in during the second half of the narrative so you do get a rounded story.  With that being said, a lot of the storytelling complaints are valid as many of us see this as one of the more "game play" oriented entries to the series.  I still loved the events that unfolded personally, but it won't be for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: [REVIEW UPDATED]Full disclosure: I haven't actually played the game yet. I've just been looking at the gallery and listening to the soundtrack for two and a half hours. And I felt compelled to share my sentiments. This is special. They preserved the original title screen and opening, and it's just plain gorgeous. I never knew FF5 had such beautiful and charming art as I'd never seen most of it.And the soundtrack... I just want to say, many years ago, when I first played FF5, I envisioned within my head a full orchestration of the 8-minute Ending Theme, not knowing if it would ever become a reality. And today, it has. Not only did it become a reality, but it passed with more flying colors than the Famed Mimic Gogo himself.Looking forward to diving in![UPDATE]Played a bunch, it's immaculate. The game looks gorgeous, I say it again and again. The soundtrack is shockingly soothing, rather than loud and boisterous. I've died quite a few times, so I certainly wouldn't say it's too easy. Can't wait to get further![UPDATE 2]After finishing, had a few more comments. I was quite shocked that the original difficulty was preserved, and it was a bit maddening at times (especially vexing after 4's PR was essentially the EasyType). There are some bugs, though I only encountered a few, including the Quick spell malfunctioning occasionally, and Gold Hairpins not working quite right. My game also locked up once, when mimicking an action in the final battle. It was annoying, but none of this hampered my overall enjoyment. The raw difficulty did, more so. It's still a beautiful game, but after years of playing games with watered-down difficulty, I'd quite gotten used to it... so this game's difficulty level definitely came as a surprise.There are more serious glitches I've heard of, though, including a missing boss and the Beastmaster's !Control ability corrupting save data. I only used it a few times for some Blue Magic, on Faris, and I never used the !Catch ability, which I heard can also create problems. It's mostly fine, though... but definitely keep some backup saves, just in case. [EDIT: These glitches have been fixed in the recent patch.]As I said before, the nostalgia really hit me while listening to the soundtrack and looking at the artwork, and also at other times while playing through the game. If you have any attachment to FF5 whatsoever, you should absolutely play this. Even if you've never played it before, it's worth picking up, but be aware that the level of difficulty is much higher than any of the other early installments.

_childDocuments_.review: Story Time!After having a great time with FF3 Pixel Remaster for the first time ever I was super hyped to dive into FF5 which is said to have truly improved the job system.  I've played FF5 before and ranked it rather highly on my favorite FF games (6th place) a decade or so ago. I'm sorry to say my hype for this game was let down.  FF5 triggered the need to min/max and grind for power in its job system where FF3 had me playing the game naturally.  FF5's story was also a total let down and really doesn't hold up well.  After playing FF4 Pixel Remaster I expected a lot better but this was pretty weak. In addition the best way to build physical attackers in this game leads to a long drawn out unskippable animation which kills the pacing and flow of combat.  Its FF5's equivalent of Knights of the Round...making each attack take about 10 seconds to resolve for the rest of the game where up to that point they would normally take 2 seconds.   You notice it...and it adds up over many hours of gameplay remaining.So why the recommendation?  FF5 still has strong game play despite the above complaints.  They do a clever job with the Freelancer and Mime end game balance.  The way classes fold into those two options is really smart.  Several of the classes are better balanced and more viable than you might think...this game has great potential replay value if this stuff really lands for you. While story is weak its also not actively horrible.   The music in this game is very good.  Better than I remember for sure.  5 / 10 by 2022 standards. The game gets a passing grade.  I enjoyed FF3 and FF4 pixel remasters more but this was worth experiencing.

_childDocuments_.review: played and finished the original Steam port of Final Fantasy V a year or so ago, so I simply copied and updated my previous review. Hence why it might look similar for some people--First, I gotta say, I first played Final Fantasy V at least 17 years ago on SNES, and yeah, this game really shows its time. It's by far one of my favorite Final Fantasy ever, one that made me love the whole franchise. This port just revived my love for it!  FFV featured a really great women representation: Faris being a great pirate leader, courageous and determined, just a bit selfish at first. (Her being a girl is kinda a spoiler, but the game makes it so obvious, even younger I was suprised they thought she was a man... oop)There's also the reckless princess, Lenna. She's barely sexualised, has a lot of devotion towards her mission, despite her daddy issues.Then, there's Krile, who's 14, and yet really smart and strong.Final Fantasy V is the opus that actually mastered the job mechanics in the series, and for some reasons, the last one in the mainline games with it. It's just so fun to tinker around with it, so many many options are available... at the cost of grinding.You can basically change all of your possible attacks so your character can suits to any playstyles. I spent hours and hours trying to make new combinations.Being a game from the 90s, there's a lot of grinding involved; Job levels, character levels... It's honestly the worst part. Modern, and more popular Final Fantasy ports has boosters / in-game cheats to circumvent having to grind, making them more paletable. In this new remaster, it features auto-battles and you can set battle speed, making a good chunk of the grinding much better. My only issue is the lack of boosters/cheats, I used a cheat sheet (yet again) to make the grinding much more simpler.Compared to the previous port, the graphics are really gorgeous, it respects well the original style, and it feels and looks just like I remembered, except it's not and it's much better than the original. The music does sounds a bit different, but I quickly got used to It, and it's so much better than before. So glad they remastered the whole soundtrack. Lots of issues I had with the original port are nowhere to be found. No issue with the battle speed and text speed, no controller issue to be found too. The only thing that pissed me off a bit is having to quit the game every time I wanted to look at the bestiary, but that's such a small price to pay for such a great port. Especially compared to what they did before it. The original additions of the GBA version are nowhere to be found here, which might be a bit of a problem for others; for me it's totally fine since it was the most boring content in the game. Except maybe the two new jobs, but you unlock them right at the end of the game, so I never really took the time to thinker with them. Supposedly it makes the whole game broken, which is more reason for me to not try them.It's by far the best port of Final Fantasy 5, minus the font issue (that can be super easily fixed) and it feels like the definitive edition of it, finally. I'm so glad I got to enjoy it in this shape, for once. I definitely recommend it to anyone who never got to experience this classic JRPG, and all those who played it back then in any other shapes. I just love Final Fantasy 5 and I'm so happy it's available legally in a much better package than ever before.

_childDocuments_.review: Is Square deliberately trolling here? Serious question given some bizarre decisions. When the HD Remaster of FFVIII came out I thought Square-Enix had finally realised how little they had to do to earn my money. Just release something at least on par with what I can manage on an emulator and I will pay. License the damn emulator and make someones ROM hack official. Do not mess with the art style too much, do not fiddle with the sound files beyond making them playable. And that leads to the core of what hit me as wrong here. After you get through the games initial menu (which seems to be faithfully playing the og start screen score) you suddenly hit the fiddling about. The FFV score seems to have been retouched... why?!?!?! You've basically admitted at this point, by deliberately returning to pixel style graphics (rather than the prev abortive attempt at inserting a bastardised version of the concept art for characters) , that people want it plain retro. Why then mess with one of the classic scores of the era? Is it to justify all those concert album re-recordings or something? You don't need to. Then the graphics themselves; why in this day and age would you have such a bare graphics filter page? Why no v-sync on a game that clearly needs it? Any emulator would give me that option. And the text; og massive boxes... with text that looks ludicrously small in it. The lack of really basic things like being able to switch to original score, change the awful font size, or fix screen jagging makes all the nice concept art and music player stuff icing on a turd... just; why?I'd love to be able to tell you Square got it right this time. They didn't, and I don't understand.
