_childDocuments_.review: FF5 has probably the best realized job system.  Each job lets you learn unique techniques that you can mix-and-match with other jobs.  You can go very in-depth with this and build the perfect party for your playstyle.  This also makes it one of the grindiest games in the series :\:- The jobs system is a neat idea on paper. It's a lot of fun near the end of the game to switch to the default class and have all the passive techniques carry over. Major power trip.  It’s like playing a game in the 90s and turning on God Mode.- No spoilers but the late-game map is so cool and something I wish the series experimented with again.  You can tell they were already experimenting with the expected formula.- One of my favorite versions of the chocobo theme.:- So. Much. Grinding. This is the natural tradeoff of having two dozen jobs with about 10 learnable skills each. While you don't have to grind, not doing so means you’re missing out on what makes the game unique. Let me put it this way, I completed like 8 FF games in about 2 months. This one took me 2 months by itself.  It just became such a chore to complete.- The story is a big step back compared to FF4. Almost all the characters are as shallow as they come (the villain's name is Exdeath). It's honestly shocking this was supposed to be the series' big SNES debut before FF4 got reworked.- While not bad, the music doesn't live up to the standards of the series. Even FF2 and FF3 have some great soundtracks that were incredible given the time period. This soundtrack is...merely serviceable.- There's one particularly mean quest near the beginning where you think you screwed up and missed out on a job, but you can actually get that job back about 20 hours later. Screw that quest.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not going to say there are literally zero differences between this and the SNES version, because that's not accurate, but there are a lot of things that Squeenix could have done with this game that made a whole bunch of people angry when they did it in the other games, but would have actually been *extremely nice to have* in this one. FFV and VI use very similar mechanics under the hood to handle combat, but VI had the benefit of an extra year of development time to clean up the damage formulas, refine the math, and remove some odd behaviors that appear in V.Instead of rewriting the intended algorithms in this new game engine Squeenix is using, which actually would have been some really easy, straightforward math in a modern programming environment, the devs made the extremely odd decision to painstakingly reproduce weird and obviously unintended game mechanics. Oh, and in classic Squeenix style the game is horribly bug-infested right now, with the Beastmaster job in particular doing some really wild and random stuff.Right now? Definitely don't buy the game. Buying the game right now is the worst idea. Buying the game later, even if it's a weird SNES clone right down to the bad 16-bit computer math? If you've never played it before, maybe do that before the Four Job Fiesta next year. That could be fun. If you have played this game before and can still play this game in any other form, just don't buy this game. It's not literally the same game, but any good, significant change that could have been made has mostly been skipped, and most of the other changes just seem kinda niche.

_childDocuments_.review: After I and III's job systems came V. V's job system might very well be my most favourite iteration of a job system in Final Fantasy. There isn't much to dislike when it comes to FFV personally. If I were to nitpick, I don't really like how the Pixel Remaster took out the extra content from the GBA release. V was the first Final Fantasy game to introduce a timer. It's really great because it gives you a sense of urgency that you never really had in previous FInal Fantasy games.I love the freedom FFV gives you. You can use pretty much any combinations of jobs you'd like. Unlike III which don't really encourage job experimentation, you are not neutered when experimenting because of two things: the separation of job and character levels, and secondly you can still use abilities from other jobs you already mastered. in terms of what you can do to beat bosses, status ailments, HP reducing spells, and level manipulating spells are all viable strategies for you to tinker around with. Some bosses are even instant game overs if you are unprepared. FFV gives me Megami Tensei vibes, as strange as it may sound since it forces you to strategize for boss fights. I love games like this.Oh, did I not mention the soundtrack was amazing at the right moments? I'm not the biggest Uematsu fan, but some tracks like Battle on the Big Bridge and Lenna's theme are amazing.----------Due to how unique V's approach to the job system and boss fights are, FFV unexpectedly became my favourite Final Fantasy from I-VI. It truly stands the age of time and I dare say this might be one of the most replayable Final Fantasy entry due to the freedom it gives you.

_childDocuments_.review: Encounters were too common and they ruined the fun of the game. I couldn't explore because of them, I couldn't figure out the story because of them, I constantly got lost because of them, if not for the Pixel Remaster letting me turn encounters off I probably would still be playing this game after 240 hours and not beat it yet.The battle system is amazingly unfair and there's more wrong with it than right. I think they tried to make players more incentivized to use mages this time around compared to FF3, but everything they did in the name of that goal seems to just make the game feel unfair.I never felt truly at home with any of the characters in this game. It was interesting to see how it may have inspired a bunch of future games but playing it merely satisfied my curiousity, not my thirst for fun.The music was horrible, like why is the battle music so annoying after a while? Got on my nerves and there were quite a few songs I didn't like. Also wasn't a fan of the way they drew a lot of the pixels for the youngest party member.I didn't feel like I was beating the game fast enough with how little ABP I was getting so I had to turn that booster for it on(I suppose I'd feel differently if I never skipped battles but at that point they would have been so disruptive i'd have casually soared to level 99 with maxed out Jobs). And if I hadn't done that I still would have beat the game much more slowly, to the point that I don't even want to think about how long it would have taken me to beat the game. There's a difference between testing the player's patience, and trying to make them lose their mind by not allowing them to play the game!Gilgamesh really salvages a lot for the story's rating here and there are some other interesting characters here as well, all of which would be interesting to behold voice acted. Only problem is the story is locked behind the exploration and progression which were done very poorly this time around so if you only want high quality RPGs, I'd look to Bravely Default 2 instead. I played that game on the Switch, so you wouldn't see my review for it here. but I'll score BD2 for you as well since I suppose you're curious what I rate it.Exploration: 1/5Story: 4/5Progression: 2/5Art: 2/5Battle: 2/5Bravely Default 2 ratings:Exploration: 5/5Story: 5/5Progression: 5/5Art: 4/5Battle: 5/5

_childDocuments_.review: I have become wiser with age and prefer to enjoy the story and experience good gameplay. This game is from a different time where RPGs were unforgiving and reminds me of FF1, where you can get into battles and areas your party does not belong and can get wiped out. Time is a luxury, and I do not want to spend it grinding.The game feels like I need a strategy guide to hold my hand, or I will suffer through it. Jobs are just a chore as you figure out what combination is best; it is tedious and requires learning how to cheese the game--such as being a Samurai to toss Gil to multi-kill a boss.Final Fantasy received polish with FF6 with the forming of parties and an extensive roster with specific classes/abilities already defined. And instead of jobs being thrown at you from a shattered crystal, FF6 characters joining the party balanced the game and flowed with the story. You did not have to worry about mixing, matching, and grinding jobs and abilities. The nostalgia for FF2(US) and FF3(US) helps me get through the quirks of those games. But FF5 can remain the lesser-known FF as it does not have the charm of the previous game and the next game in the series. Yet, I am pleased with making it to the Big Bridge, which it is mainly known for.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the definition of a mixed bag, but ultimately falls with more in the "against" column than the "for" column.It looks nice enough in modern resolutions, the colour palette seems to have been brightened up a bit, the music is good, as you'd expect of Nobuo Uematsu.The story however, is paper thin. Story is a huge reason you'd play a Final Fantasy game, but this story is as basic and predictable as it gets; a pure good vs evil tale with no depth or nuance. There are some a few moments of humour where the translation shines, but for the more part, the story is like something from a children's book.If not for the story, then you'd be here for the gameplay, but this is where the game really falls apart. This game has the "job" system where characters aren't really set into a particular role, but can be trained into pretty much anything through changing their job class. However, there is an overwhelming number of these, many of them are redundant and grinding them to level them up takes forever. In general, grinding for experience and the points to get the jobs levelled up takes way too long outside of a few select areas.Much of general fight encounters are easy, but way too numerous. You can't take 5 steps in a dungeon without a fight starting, which is a pain when the dungeons are so maze-like. Exploring the over-world is a chore because the fights are so frequent. The over-world area is quite empty, but also big enough to take a long time to traverse, which again is boring when the game is very vague about where to go at certain points in the story and there are so many random encounters.The boss fights are mostly bad as they are based around gimmicks. Many of the bosses in the game are built to resist basic attack and magic strategies, instead the developers seem to want you to equip a select set of gear and classes to counter the boss, which is great unless you missed a particular spell, summon or armour set, or you didn't level up a certain job class.Ultimately, the game is good for nostalgia and it is cheap, but it isn't much fun. Don't expect the level of quality of story or gameplay that you'd find in a later FF game and maybe you'd enjoy it. If you played it back in a the day and liked it but didn't love it, maybe give this a miss. If you have never played a FF game, don't make this your first one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the Final Fantasy that I started when I was much younger but quickly abandoned after starting it up. To be fair, I had just finished FF IV which has probably the second greatest story in the pixel final fantasies, so the bar was already very high. I rode a wind drake and found a crystal and the characters just didn't grab my attention in the same way. I found the plot boring and I had no desire to see it to the end. Revisiting V after this long hiatus in the pixel remaster I can say the needle has moved slightly in the games favor but I do not think I'll ever run through this game again. Pros: They brought back the job system in full force as it was in FF III which was fun to an extent but so many of the jobs you're left looking at going what is the purpose of the "dancer" job or why put effort into leveling this up when it doesn't greatly benefit the final Freelancer stats? The final dungeon was not a kick in the balls to get through which was appreciated. There were some decent character interactions? Cons: The story, some will love it and not agree that it isn't strong but I just did not care about the adventure or the character development or the dumb quips from a recurring foil to the gang. The ever growing jobs list that could have been thinned significantly. That's about it. Final Fantasy III had a fun idea with the job system and Final Fantasy V really took it, and did not expand on it in a significant way. Final Fantasy IV and VI have much better stories with characters that you actually see develop and care about so I ask why bother when others in the series do it better. Is it a bad game? No. But would I recommend someone play IV or VI instead? Yes.

_childDocuments_.review: Aside from Final Fantasy II, I've played through all of the Pixel Remaster releases up to this point and thoroughly enjoyed them. Even if I found FF III and IV to be a bit easier than I would have expected, I still had fun playing through them (and, in IV's case, enjoying the story again). Like most folks playing on PC, I modded the font to be tolerable, which helps a lot, and used an Xbox-compatible controller (which IMO is vastly superior to playing on keyboard).This quality of this release of FF V has been great so far. From a remaster perspective, V keeps up the same level of quality as the other releases. Sprites and maps look great, with a few exceptions; some of the Kick animations, for example, are janky. The spell effects are largely reused from prior releases but still look and sound exceptionally retro and crisp. I'll be somewhat upset if the remaster of FF VI doesn't use its more iconic spell effects and sounds, though. The font is... well, at least it's really easy to mod. Overall, however, each of the Pixel Remaster releases have been well polished and fun to play and FF V is no exception. So why do I not recommend this game, then?The fifth in the series is one of the few I haven't played to death over the years—not even on the PSX or GBA re-releases. I dabbled, of course, but never committed. This time, I figured, I had to keep up the momentum of playing through the remasters. I settled in for a few nights of FF V and started immersing myself. Unlike FF I, III, and IV, this one is kind of frustrating. Sure, all of them have their quirks, but usually a well-balanced party and maybe a tiny bit of level grinding will get you through. FF V, by contrast, seems to have several boss fights, especially in the middle of the game, which punish your decisions with predicaments you couldn't have seen coming. See, the job system here is really cool. Its evolution from the system in FF III makes leveling multiple jobs much more rewarding. You're less encouraged to specialize here, especially since your stats aren't affected by your job at level-up anymore. Instead, your job's stats are sort of "merged" with a character's base stats. You can equip abilities from multiple jobs at the same time, so creating hybrid combos is both exciting and useful.However, there is no easy way to grind job points (ABP), at least not in the first half of the game. If you're playing casually, you'll reach a point where most of your characters have some kind of rough specialization. Maybe you've got a couple of casters and a couple of physical-focused damage dealers. At this point, your jobs likely need 100 ABP or more to reach the next level, and non-boss fights only give 1 or 2, so you've probably leveled your jobs about as far as you're going to until you progress the plot some more.If you're like me, you try not to read walkthroughs or guides for these games. So when I got into a fight with a boss that shifts its elemental resistances, I brought Mystic Knights (can change the elemental property of their sword), a Red Mage, and a White Mage. It worked great! Until the final phase of the fight where it becomes completely immune to most elements. Suddenly none of my characters could deal damage... at all. I had made the mistake of not picking up a couple spells, trying to save gil—equipment gets expensive since you're trying to keep enough on hand for various job combos—so my Red Mage didn't know anything except fire, ice, and thunder-elemental damage spells. The White Mage had the Healing Staff equipped, and you can't "turn off" a Mystic Knight's enchantment once one is applied. It was only when I switched my Red Mage to a knife mid-combat and had him physical attack the boss for 120 damage per turn that I eventually killed it.Right after this, the plot caused my Red Mage character to leave the party. He was also my primary summoner. Then the game put me in a fight where I needed to kill 6 enemies all at once lest they self-destruct and wipe out my party, or resurrect all of their allies. I died a few times before switching a couple characters to monks and kicking them all to death (though self-destruct still wiped me a couple times after that). After that, I was faced with a boss which simply output too much damage for my 3-person party to survive. In all of these scenarios, the obvious answer was to grind some more. Grind for ABP to teach more characters Red/Black magic and summoning. Grind for more levels to get the HP necessary to survive more turns. Grind for more gil so I can just spam Zeninage to kill everything. To be clear, I had already spent a good 2-3 hours grinding earlier in the game; there's a cave where you can reliably find easy-to-kill enemies which give 2 ABP per fight. This is where I gained several job levels across multiple jobs for all my characters. I just didn't have the  combinations.Any single one of these fights would have been fine, but this was 3 fights in a row. It indicates a difficulty spike in the game where it expects me to grind more, fight and die a few times to find the right combo, and then try again. I checked out some guides and all of them wanted me to have apparently gathered several blue magic abilities and to just know where those are useful (e.g. Level 5 Death requires you to know the enemy's level).Obviously, I am to blame for these failures to some degree. Had I not focused all my Red/Black magic onto the one character that left the party (not that I saw it coming), I could have used it to kill those 6 enemies faster, for example, instead of relying on the relatively low-damage Kick ability. However, together these fights left a sour taste in my mouth for the game. Myself, I'll probably pick it back up and power through it. I'll give in to what the game wants and either grind myself silly or read a guide to know what kind of arbitrary BS the next boss will expect me to use to defeat it. But what about the next person like me, who maybe also hasn't played FF V but isn't as much of a fan of the series?For that person, I recommend a skip of Final Fantasy V. Play VI instead, a game with a (subjectively) better story and which is also much more forgiving in the way it allows you to customize your characters, though not without its own tricky and unintuitive systems.

_childDocuments_.review: This game asks a LOT of you compared to basically every other mainline Final Fantasy title. You really have to immerse yourself in the job system in order to succeed, and you'll run into several difficulty walls (i.e. bosses) that sometimes require teleporting out of the dungeon, looking up strategies online, and grinding up experience with certain jobs so that you can retry the boss with a specific-to-it strategy, or grinding up large amounts of gil to purchase rings that make a particular fight doable. If you're hoping to be able to just pick whichever roles you want for your characters and coast through the game--like you largely could in III--be advised that you will run into a lot of problems, especially at the last boss, which is almost impossible to defeat without a large number of mastered jobs and very clever uses of specific jobs and skills. The game also continues some of the bad game design of the first four games, like too-frequent enemy encounters that constantly grind away at your resources in a frustrating way that feels overly punishing and frustrating. The best way of dealing with most combat encounters when you're in a dungeon is to simply run away from most fights, which is as easy to do as it is cheesy. As long as you grind a bit to make up for the lost experience, it's the most sound strategy for advancing through dungeons, especially the ones that are labyrinthine and full of annoying traps and confusing, branching paths.The game really wants you to immerse yourself in its systems, to really sink into them and master them. Unfortunately, I only enjoy investing that kind of time when there are other hooks driving me, like a great story (this one's is so-so), great characters (this one's are cute but unremarkable), and various and fun systems of progression to keep the dopamine dripping (other than the job system, this game basically has none of these beyond filling out the bestiary). Now granted, I loved Final Fantasy I and III, which are pretty threadbare in terms of content, but they are brisk and move along at a rapid clip, easily doable in 10-15 hours each, so they don't overstay their welcome long enough to notice their lack of systems and progression models.Only get this if the idea of the job system is really appealing to you. Some people absolutely adore this game for the job system, and great for them. But if you're like me and prefer your JRPGs with more story and character focus, then try IV or IX (my favorites, the latter of which is brimming with great content and fun things to collect and do), and if are looking for a more "classic" Final Fantasy experience but don't want to get bogged down by this game's sizable time-demands, then try I and III, which are adorable, nippy little games that come and go quickly, long before they overstay their welcome.Despite all this, you might love this game. Some people consider it their favorite. People whose tastes fall more in line with my own should consider this review a note of caution.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you know what four job fiesta is? Boy, do I have a good reason for you to buy this game.As the quintessential realtime turn based replayable RPG, Final Fantasy V is about as generic as it gets these days. You follow the story of Bartz, who has to figure out why people keep showing up around meteors, and you end up saving reality. As you advance you unlock jobs for your characters to gain new abilities, and herein lies the depth of the game: there are so many ways to combine these jobs and abilities, you can spend a lot of time and complete the game without seeing all of them.The Four Job Fiesta is an anual event where people donate to charity and played the game in a challenging form, limiting the jobs they'll have access to. This gives a whole new perspective because strengths have to be played to their max while weaknesses need to be played around, and it's incredibly fun. Most of the time I have in this game is just playing those events year after year.Previous releases of this game have had more content, but this is just a remake of the original game, no additional dungeons, jobs or monsters. That's fine, the game has plenty to do as it is.

The boosts for experience, gil, and ABP are great additions to balance this game out when you inevitably have to grind. This is definitely the best version of Final Fantasy 5, hands down!

_childDocuments_.review: I am embarrassed to admit that even though I have owned the PS1 Final Fantasy V release since it came out, this is the first time I have played V through to completion.  And it was a nice time.  Nothing in the game is a revolutionary jump for the Final Fantasy series, but it all comes together to create a fun and breezy experience.Playable with some limits on the Steam Deck, although once again name entry is a bit of a chore (which could have been mitigated with an extra keybind of A = Enter). _childDocuments_.review: You should play Final Fantasy V if you enjoy classic JRPGs and want a rich, rewarding experience. Here are a few reasons why:Job System: Final Fantasy V is famous for its robust job system. You can customize your party by choosing from 22 different jobs, ranging from standard classes like Black Mage and Knight to more unique ones like Dancer and Time Mage. It offers a lot of flexibility and strategic depth, allowing you to mix and match abilities from different jobs.Replayability: The job system also makes the game highly replayable. You can experiment with different job combinations on each playthrough, offering new ways to experience the game every time.Classic Story: While not as complex as later Final Fantasy titles, FFV offers a solid, charming story filled with adventure, friendship, and sacrifice. The tone is lighter than FFIV or FFVI, but it still has its emotional moments.Challenging Battles: The game has a nice balance of challenge, especially if you're looking to optimize your party's abilities. Boss fights can be quite tough, requiring careful strategy and understanding of the game's mechanics.Soundtrack: Nobuo Uematsu’s music is iconic, and FFV’s soundtrack is no exception. The music perfectly captures the spirit of adventure and tension throughout the game.Legacy of the Series: If you're a fan of the Final Fantasy series, playing FFV lets you see how the series evolved. It stands as a key bridge between the earlier games and the later, more narrative-driven entries.If you love character customization, strategy, and a classic JRPG feel, Final Fantasy V is definitely worth your time!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: This is what I'd consider to be the best classic Final Fantasy game - although I haven't played 6 yet, so I may change my mind, but after playing 1-4, this is where I stand. There are so many different classes to choose from, and there's no penalty to switching classes at any time. Something about leveling each class and making your Freelancer and Mime classes super powerful is just so satisfying. You can tell that square really wanted you to figure out the combat system so you can really have fun breaking the game. The characters are all really great as well, each character has a trait or an aspect that makes them really endearing, and the side-characters are all pretty cool as well. Gilgamesh is my dawg, don't ♥♥♥♥ with him.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Solid sequel with a stronger focus on storytelling and character development. This was a really solid entry following up FFIV. This was my 6th FF completion, and 9th game played. It didn't bring a whole lot new mechanically, but the story telling, world building, and character development were a step above. Felt a lot closer in tone to my first foray into the franchise (FF7).This entry, like most of the other classic titles, focuses on world crystals that are being destroyed and four heroes who need to save the world. Even though the high level strokes of the story are the same they did a stellar job telling a unique story, with some deep world building, and strong characters. You take your party on a journey to undo the damage a dark force is trying to unleash on the world. There are numerous twists and turns that I was not expecting and was pleasantly surprised by.Gameplay wise, you explore the world to complete the main quests and any side quests you can encounter (mainly unique items, magic, and summons). Character customization is mostly the same from FFIII. You have a job and you level that job up through combat, and you purchase magic at the shops. The jobs did feel a bit more unique and varied though. I was able to level up almost all of them by the end of the game which was pretty cool.One thing this game leaned more heavily into was the "cinematic" scenes and dialogue. The characters felt very alive with their own personalities. Animations were also a big step up.The overall feel of the game was pretty amazing. It's definitely on par with my experience in FFIV which has been my favorite so far in these classic titles.I played the game entirely on Steam Deck. It ran at 60fps/60hz with no issues. It sips battery so you can get some long play sessions in with this one. The game took me a little over 42 hours to beat and it was well worth it. Overall, this was a very solid entry in the series. The storytelling, world-building, and character development was top notch with some solid gameplay that didn't get too grindy. Highly recommend if you are a fan of the series at all.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: V’s offered pretty good job system. This system allows the player to choose between 22 different classes for each of the four characters. It also offers the possibility for the characters being versatile with more than one skill from all of the classes. The story and the characters altogether were interesting. I can say I really enjoyed playing this installment.

_childDocuments_.review: Much better take on the job system from 3, and it shows. It's a blast to jump from job to job to maximize your performance in the late game. Unlike in 3, you can use abilities from one job in another, so it feels less jarring or punishing to switch into a job just to nab some abilities. Worth the money spent, got about 25 hours on my first playthrough, and if you're the type to mix things up on subsequent playthroughs, you can really stretch this game's playtime out as long as you want to.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never actually finished Final Fantasy V before now. Before the mobile version, and this version, the only way I could have done would have been to try finding the GBA release which, even when it was new, was difficult to come by. There was also an international release on the original Playstation if I recall correctly, with a hilariously bad translation. Anyhow, what I like about this game is how it nicely mixes the gameplay of Final Fantasy III with a story that's somewhat more in line with Final Fantasy IV. Your party grows and can access more jobs as they find and attempt to preserve different elemental crystals. I like how mastering a job applies a permanent buff to the Freelancer job, which keeps that one in your mind as an overall end-goal when it comes to the Job Grind. There aren't as many instances of needing to use magic to travel around dungeons as there were in Final Fantasy III, but it's still present from time to time. I quite like how the tone of the game is pretty lighthearted for the most part, but it's able to nicely mix in more serious character moments. I think a moment involving Lena and Hiryu might be one of my favorites from the series, and if you manage to get Gilgamesh to the endgame, his last scenes left a surprising impact too. As for the combat, it's the kind of turn-based JRPG thing one would expect from the first 10 Final Fantasy games. It's a bit flexible in that you can change the speed and change whether or not you want it to be more active or more turn-based, but overall it still feels quite a bit easier compared to the older versions of Final Fantasy V that I've played. It wasn't as easy as the Pixel Remasters of Final Fantasy I or II, and I can't speak for III, IV, or VI, but it would have been nice if this was a more challenging game. I think I might like the way the old version looks more than this version, I think it's also worth pointing out that the old version has more content in the form of an extra dungeon, about 4 (maybe 5) extra jobs, extra bosses, and more achievements. It's also likely that the old version will get pulled from Steam if it hasn't yet been so since neither that version nor this version is going to be getting a price cut any time soon, I strongly recommend getting *that* version instead of this one. By the time I was ready to take on Omega and Shinryu, my party was strong enough to mulch them with 8-hit Rapid Fire physical attack combos, and mimicry. On the one hand, I enjoy grinding to the point where my party is more or less unstoppable, but I understand how anticlimactic that kind of thing can be.Something else I want to point out are games like Dragon Quest 3, Star Ocean 2, and Octopath Traveler: games that take the SNES pixel art style but blend it more with modern sensibilities in terms of lighting effects, more detailed backgrounds, voice acting, spell effects, etc to make for a much more visually interesting versions of classic games. Out of the Pixel Remasters I've played, this is my favorite but there are fewer other versions of Final Fantasy V to compare this one to. Even so, this version has some great quality of life improvements that set it apart, like full dungeon maps and counters for things like treasure chests and hidden items collected. I also really like how I can switch the language, unlike with the old version, but admittedly that's not a feature many people are going to look for. If you're concerned about English translators with a chip on their shoulder though, it's worth taking the time to try learning Japanese to side-step people like that and their agendas. Even if Square makes a 2DHD version of this game, and the other old Final Fantasies, there's value in playing this version, and I recommend it. There are really good character moments, the combat and progression was engaging to me, but I can't speak for the translation but I'm positive it wasn't as hilariously bad as the 4Kids-esq old version you can find on Steam or the even worse but funnier versions from older console generations.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, Final Fantasy V—a title that might have you scratching your head if you're from the US and trying to piece together the franchise’s quirky numbering system. Yes, it's the fifth installment of Final Fantasy, but if you're confused thinking, "Wait, isn't Final Fantasy VI also Final Fantasy III?" you're not alone. There was definitely some identity crisis in the early days, like a teenager trying to find themselves but with way more chocobos and crystals.Now, onto the game itself. Final Fantasy V might just be the hidden gem of the series. It starts off with a happy-go-lucky vibe—think Saturday morning cartoons with a side of magical crystals. But don’t get too comfortable, because it soon takes a nosedive into darker, eerier themes faster than you can say "Gilgamesh." It's like starting a book with fluffy bunnies and rainbows only to find out by chapter three that those bunnies are actually part of a cult.The music? Oh, the music is an experience on its own. It perfectly captures every mood swing of the game. There’s triumphant, heroic tunes that make you feel like you can take on the world, and then there are those chilling, dark compositions that make you want to double-check that your door is locked. Seriously, the Exdeath chord progression still gives me chills—it's like the soundtrack is saying, “Prepare to meet your doom!” in the most melodious way possible.Overall, Final Fantasy V is a must-play for any fan of the series. It might be a tad more challenging than, say, Final Fantasy VI, but that’s part of the charm. The newly updated version has made it a bit more accessible by adding ways to boost experience points, among other tweaks. But don’t be fooled—the final boss still requires a bit of prep work. Think of it as the ultimate test of your RPG mettle.So, grab your sword, gather your party, and dive into Final Fantasy V. It’s a wild ride of emotions, epic battles, and, yes, some serious identity crises—but isn't that what makes it all so fun?
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: 100% in 31 hours (28 on save) using a guide (for missables) and turning off encounters occasionally. Some very annoying achievements and a lot of missables so a guide is highly recommended. Had to grind for mastering all jobs, level 50 and 2,000 enemies killed. Would highly recommend using 4x AP the entire game since you only get 1 per fight and there are a lot of fun classes to use. Leveling jobs end game is simple it's not a matter of need it's just more fun.FF5 further refines the job system from 3 but isn't fully perfected until Tactics. Unlike Tactics where you can pick from 5 categories to equip skills here you only are given your main and a secondary. But that secondary could just be a passive which limits your options. You can use your starter class which lets you pick any two things and you will have the innate passives of mastered jobs which is nice. But that is a very late game thing and I found myself not using what I really wanted just to learn/equip something.The story isn't that deep but is enjoyable. The cast has some personalities and doesn't have a revolving party like the previous game.I do find V much harder than the previous games. Although many enemies do have weaknesses that can be exploited if you fully take advantage of the job system. The final boss wiped the floor with me unless I used generic strategies but I was only level 39.This is a great game and I would highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome, those of culture, to the best Final Fantasy. After the quite serious affair of FFIV, this is a tale of four awkward nerds of varying competence who are thrust together in a quest to save the world from ecological disaster. This is Final Fantasy chancing upon you at a bar and reminiscing a few drinks deep, "Man, we'd really send you into a dungeon for any random reason we could cook up that day, huh?" The lighthearted tone and some of the terribly sparse stretches of plot tend folks to consider this one of the "weaker" entries, but the sheer versatility of the job system is simply not to be missed.Bartz is a wanderer whose travels take him to the kingdom of Tycoon. There, he meets Princess Lenna and Galuf, an amnesiac found dazed near a fallen meteor. The winds of the world are weakening, wreaking havoc on travel and weather, and Lenna intends to find out why. Galuf doesn't remember much, but Lenna's talk of the Wind Shrine and the crystal within seem to jog his memory ever so slightly, and so their paths align. But with the winds stagnant, there's no way to cross the sea to the Wind Shrine--except by the boat of pirate captain Faris, towed by a sea monster...Thus begins a tale rife with levity and vigor. The real fun, of course, begins at the Wind Shrine, and redoubles at the other elemental shrines around the world. There, the party is bestowed a series of "Jobs", character classes which confer different abilities and available equipment unto them. Characters' jobs can be switched any time out of battle, so the party can be freely customized to face that next dungeon and reconfigured again just before the boss, or you can build a formation of your favorites. In this way, FFV bears similarity to FFI and III, but where V evolves is in Abilities. By sticking with a job and accruing Ability Points (ABP) from winning those now-famous Active-Time Battles, characters can gain "job levels", which unlock various active and passive abilities from that job. Some represent the job's innate powers, so that you can then freely mix them with another job. (One example given in-game is giving the curative White Magic to the tanky Knight--it's like Cecil's still here!) Some abilities are only available by leveling up jobs and learning them in this fashion, such as the Beastmaster's Control. Through this system, you're allowed to build the party of your dreams, pretty much whenever.For some, this will be a drawback. Those who prefer the specialized characters of FFIV or VI are going to chafe at the blank slates that are Bartz and friends. It's also sort of a shame that there's no way to, like, save and load particular configurations of the party. That's never been a feature in any version of FFV, but it would have been nice. There isn't a whole lot in the way of...hm, okay, so in some other Final Fantasy games with similarly customizable characters like VI, you have something like the Espers' level-up bonus, where you have influence over the long-term growth of a character. V doesn't really have that. Yes, each character levels up jobs and learns abilities separately, and fully mastered jobs do pass many of their passive abilities and stats to the character's default "Freelancer" job. But then if you were to master every job with every character, they would always turn out the same, you know what I mean? Some folks might not like that.For a series now so famous for storytelling, this particular game represents a conscious step back from that. There is intrigue and drama to be had here, sure, but that doesn't really pick up until about a third of the way into the game, and even then, it's still undercut by the lighthearted mood often supplied by the cast. Bartz himself is a joker, a goof-off, kind of an idiot...he's so not your typical FF protagonist that he outright declines to travel with the others at first, just because he's not headed that way. And ironically, his companions may very well get more character development than he does. But these developments are positively drip-fed; many of the cutscenes are interested in telling you where to go next first, and then maybe after that they'd remember to give someone a short monologue, maybe. And just when the writing of the main cast begins to hit its stride, you start meeting Gilgamesh, a clown and a half who steals every scene he's in.Final Fantasy V is definitely in an odd spot. It's not in line with what IV and VI are trying to do, but it's blazed its trail upon the series all the same. It's sort of an evolution of I and III, while also being sort of tongue-in-cheek about how they worked. The Job system would find purchase in the Tactics spinoffs and the online ones, and other now-famous parts of Final Fantasy like Blue Magic got their starts right here. But it's also trying to do its own thing, a tale of four people who are vastly ill-equipped to save the world, but they have to step up anyway. It's a game where most of the bosses can be trivialized through a few key abilities, which feels like a joke all its own. It's a game where the characters are surprised to find sea monsters in the sea, but don't bat an eye when a ship is full of killer robots. It's a game with a ton of, like, one-time-only sort of things that can be missed, which is going to drive you nuts if you're trying to find everything for the achievements. Final Fantasy V probably doesn't resemble the vague image most people think of when they think "Final Fantasy"--but back when it first came out and there were only the other four, it would have seemed quite in line with them. But it's the sort of "in line" of a kid who acts up when the teacher's back is turned, and who abruptly snaps back into place when the teacher turns to look their way. But above all, Final Fantasy V is a game you can come back to again and again, and a game that succeeds on its own merits.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is hilariously convoluted and quite a bit cliche (at least by today's standards), and the number of deaths in this game would make George R. R. Martin weep, but overall it's not a bad game. There's a lot of customization you can do with the job system, depending on what you need at a given time. I would recommend having a second character get a few levels into jobs you have maxed with another character, just for an extra bit of wiggle room as far as abilities go, but even if you keep it one job per character, it won't be too much of an inconvenience. I'm currently 45 hours into a game, and I'd estimate that I'm about 2/3 through the story, so for those who enjoy a longer playthrough, this is perfect. Compared to other FF titles, it isn't even that grindy. Level progression is handled very well, and I haven't really had to grind levels to keep up with the mobs/bosses. I did grind out all of the jobs once I had all of them, but I did it in an area with high AP low XP, so my levels barely increased. Unlike, say, FFIV where I had to grind for about four hours to reach the level 70 achievement requirement, I'm confident that I'll reach the level 50 achievement requirement for this game just through natural game play. So yeah, if you're a fan of JRPGs and/or FF in particular, I'd highly recommend playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this one a lot, I think the story is really fleshed out and I think they perfected the jobs system over III. My biggest gripe is that a lot of bosses have nonsense gimmicks that feel like they're in place to counter over-grinding. The three freaks is a good example. I played the whole thing with a 4x exp boost because I struggled with bosses 3 hours in so take this review as you wish.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I believe this is the most annoying of the Famicom/Super Famicom Final Fantasy games (I-VI) because of the puzzle dungeons, and the fact that there's a particular job/ability you need to use for many bosses.  If you try to make it through this game without help from strategy guides, it can be very frustrating.  Pixel Remaster at least allows quick saves and autosaves, to make it less painful than the original.  That being said, the job system is fun, and the multitude of jobs available, and abilities available, give the game great replay value.  My second time trying to make it through the whole game of Final Fantasy V, I did use strategy guides, and had more fun trying to see how minimally I could change my group's jobs/abilities, to defeat the bosses.

_childDocuments_.review: Fine version of FF5 with lots of quality of life enhancements. They added a new font with an update, so the game's text is no longer an eyesore without mods. As for FF5 itself, it's among the most fun and addicting games in the entire series. _childDocuments_.review: "Final Fantasy V" stands as a shining gem in the illustrious Final Fantasy series, celebrated for its innovative gameplay and captivating narrative. At the heart of its brilliance lies the iconic job system, a revolutionary mechanic that has left an indelible mark on the RPG genre.From the moment players dive into the world of Bartz Klauser and his companions, they are introduced to the intricacies of the job system. Offering unparalleled flexibility and depth, this system allows players to customize their party members' abilities by assigning them various jobs, each with its own unique skills and attributes.The beauty of the job system lies in its simplicity and complexity simultaneously. On the surface, it offers a straightforward means of character progression, allowing players to switch jobs at will and experiment with different combinations to suit their playstyle. Whether you prefer the brute strength of a Knight, the arcane mastery of a Black Mage, or the nimble agility of a Thief, the job system ensures that there's a class for every preference.Yet beneath this simplicity lies a staggering depth. As players delve deeper into the game, they'll discover the intricacies of job synergy, learning to combine abilities from different classes to create unstoppable combinations. The possibilities are endless, offering a level of customization rarely seen in RPGs of its time.But it's not just the gameplay that makes "Final Fantasy V" shine; its narrative is equally captivating. From the lighthearted banter between party members to the epic struggle against the nefarious Exdeath, the story is filled with memorable moments that will keep players engaged from start to finish.And let's not forget the music. Nobuo Uematsu's iconic score perfectly complements the adventure, evoking a sense of wonder and excitement as players journey across the vibrant landscapes of the world.In the end, "Final Fantasy V" is a testament to the enduring legacy of the Final Fantasy series, showcasing the innovation and creativity that has made it a beloved franchise for over three decades. And with its groundbreaking job system, it remains as fresh and engaging today as it was upon its initial release. Whether you're a longtime fan of the series or a newcomer looking for a classic RPG experience, "Final Fantasy V" is an adventure not to be missed.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I was NOT expecting this game to be as good as is was seeing as nobody talks about it. While it could be quite goofy at times, it knows how to take itself seriously which is much appreciated. While I'm still not a fan of the ATB system, the return of job classes made me so happy, not to mention how much you could customize your party because of the job system allowing you to carry over abilities from previously used jobs. The music as usual is nothing but straight bangers, Nobuo Uematsu brought the heat once again.As for the story, it did start abit slow, and has some of the cliches you might expect from Final Fantasy as this point, but that didn't make it bad or uninteresting. By the halfway mark I found myself really caring for the cast of characters and when bad things happened to them, I felt for them. Up to this point a Final Fantasy game hasn't made me cry, 5 changed that. Without spoiling it, the final scene is what did it for me. If you know you know.Beautiful game, great characters, music, artwork, everything, just a tad predictable and the world could be kind of boring at times. 8.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: One of the things I really appreciate about the game is its incredible sense of adventure. Right from the get-go, you're thrown into this intriguing plot about the crystals that keep the world's elements in balance, and when they start to shatter, the whole premise just instantly grabs you. It's a classic setup but executed with such charm and enthusiasm.The characters are another huge win for me. Bartz, or Butz depending on the translation, starts off as this carefree wanderer, which is a refreshing change from the often more serious or destiny-bound protagonists you see in other RPGs. Then there’s Faris, who's just so cool—her reveal as a pirate captain was such a fantastic twist! The interactions between the characters, filled with humor and heart, really make you care about their journey and the friendships they develop.But honestly, the absolute standout feature has to be the job system. It's so flexible and allows for so much strategic depth. I had a blast experimenting with different job combinations and seeing how different abilities could synergize. It turns every character into a Swiss Army knife, capable of adapting to various battle scenarios, which keeps the gameplay feeling fresh and engaging. Plus, mastering jobs and unlocking new abilities gives you a real sense of progression and power.The music—oh, the music! Nobuo Uematsu is a genius, and the soundtrack in "Final Fantasy V" is proof. Tracks like "Clash on the Big Bridge" are not only iconic but elevate the excitement and emotional impact of the battles and story moments. The music has this way of perfectly capturing the essence of adventure and the emotional stakes involved.And let’s not forget the visuals. Even though they’re from the 16-bit era, there’s a lot of creativity in the character designs and the world itself. The pixel art is charming and has aged quite well, contributing to a nostalgic yet timeless aesthetic.All in all, "Final Fantasy V" strikes a fantastic balance between compelling narrative, strategic gameplay, and artistic presentation. It might not get quite as much attention as some of its siblings in the Final Fantasy series, but it’s definitely a gem.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: The Single Greatest Job system of any video game ever. You literally get to craft your characters from the ground up. Anyone can be your healer. Anyone can be your mage. Anyone can be melee dps. Anyone can be your tank. If you grind, everyone does everything. Phenomenal progression design. Levels determine HP/MP, classes determine the other stats. Blue Magic was the coolest execution of Magic to date. Lots of tech around blue magic and enemies.Music was the best score of the first five pixel remasters. Plot was strong but lacking in a few points. World(s) design was excellent and interesting. Characters were fun and had good development. New mechanics abound. Fights were harder to put into autobattle since the game is no longer simple.Recurring characters returned such as Cid. The typical crystals story line continued but in a newish way. A magnificent entry in a magnificent series. A little grindy for 100% players but not as bad as FFX.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Playing through all of the pixel remasters for my first time through the series. This game was an incredible ride. The job system is perfected from the first iteration. The amount of customization is so much fun. The game is actually fairly challenging at points which really encouraged me to engage with all the different systems. The story while not aiming to be as serious as 4 was actually pretty enjoyable and funny at times. The characters are all great. With the longer run time and added challenge and complexity this entry really felt like an adventure and I highly recommend it! Also you fight an evil tree.

_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: This experience was great, Final Fantasy 5 offers so much in terms of gameplay variety that many people who are very accustomed to rpgs will love, however to be completely honest, if your new to the series or just rpgs in general. I'd actually advise avoiding this game. I'll get into why but first I'm going to explain what the gameplay is like.First of all, the job system is incredible,  the sheer amount of variety is almost overwhelming with how many options there are. you can choose one of many classes, but not only that you can learn specific abilities, and mix and match them with other jobs. This makes strategy super fun at times as you need to really lock in on what your party is made up of. But on the other hand, it does get a bit frustrating having to switch characters constantly to see what can fight the most effectively, a lot of trial and error is required in order to defeat some bosses, which at a certain point was just annoying. This really isn't a game where you can just stick with a set amount of classes and just roll with that for the whole game. My mistake was that I didn't put a lot of variety into my parties and ended up only mastering a couple of classes by the end, making the final boss for me extremely difficult. but, through all the pain and annoyance this game put me through, it was so satisfying when you finally find out the winning strat, this was especially the case when I beat the final boss. lets talk about the story, while simple, I just find it to be charming, yeah the characters are kinda one note. But it reminds of ff1 story as that game was very simple yet I felt to fulfilled by the end of it, and its the same for this game as well, sure because of its simplicity its not as memorable or impactful, but I feel as if that's not what they were going for. the graphics obviously look great and so does the music (even tho the soundtrack isn't one of my favs of the franchise) there are stand out tracks like "Dear Friends." All in all it's a great game with whole heck of a lot to do, I do think it goes on for a little too long tbh, Id prefer if it was maybe 3 or 4 hours shorter bc it kinda became a slog at the end. But I still like it and feel it's just as good as its predecessor. 8/10

Granted, the extra jobs, as busted as they were, would have been a fun edition, but the QOL, updated soundtrack (FINALLY), and general cosmetic updates make up for that. _childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is a weird one for me to place, but I do recommend the game. However, the game's narrative is rather weak when compared to Final Fantasy IV and even VI. That isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it is noticeable during several moments which makes the game feel like it probably drags on a bit longer than it needs to.

_childDocuments_.review: This is more or less the classic 2D RPG, but with a twist. You will still have party members with a certain class, but you can switch at any time and keep one old ability. This is a little bit unfair because the mages can have 2 full pools with spells and the fighters can pick ONE extra action. Still, the fighters are pretty good, though a bit boring. It pays off to switch jobs/classes, but after you went through the ones you like you're fighting with one hand behind your back to learn more skills! Of course you don't have to, but it makes the game more challenging. At the end of the game you can combine whatever skills you like and have a blast. I've said the same thing about FF6: It's a fun and easy system, but it does make your choices less meaningful. The difficulty is all over the place. Some optional bosses can hit you like a truck, but I didn't find the required encounters that hard for the most part, especially with the build I had. The mazes are fairly simple, so the random encounters don't feel that bad. In terms of gameplay the best FF so far for me. It's a bit more simple and fun and you don't need to worry about a dozen other party members that are underleveled.

But when they do show up its exciting. This story is ok, better than most but not as good as 4. They really try to be more light hearted and comedic in this one. _childDocuments_.review: Probably my favourite Final Fantasy game so far (at least until I hit the later games). Meshing together the character and party malleability of Final Fantasy II, refinements to the job system introduced in Final Fantasy III, and continuing the use of the Active Time Battle system from Final Fantasy IV results in one of the most enriching experiences I've had with numerous possibilities on how to tackle certain problems.High recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underrated title. This Final Fantasy is largely similar to FF3, but with updated gameplay and combat that feels closer to FF4. So what does that mean?  Taken from FF4, the ATB system is here, adding a dynamic to combat not seen in the third title. Like 4, spells are based on a mana pool, as opposed to the spell change system in 3.What makes this game more similar to 3 is the job system. Your team of four can flexibily and openly play any one of 22 jobs, and you can even pick a secondary skill from other jobs that character may have leveled up. Jobs have their own leveling system, separate from character levels- which, are also here. All in all, it's a wonderful system. This game is one of the most difficult games of its random battles games. I'm still working on an optional boss, and the final boss took me a few tries - by comparison, I beat FF6 without a single death. Not so much here.The story is fun, and whimsical, with some pretty funny moments. Exdeath is a solid villain but isn't super memorable. There's another villain you encounter quite a lot that's far more memorable, here. All said, story isn't this game's strength - which is the only thing holding this title back from being recognized as a classic Final Fantasy game.In short, if you like any FF game, play this. If enjoy JRPGs, play this.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Oh, let's dive into the enchanting world of Final Fantasy V – a game that has woven its magic into my gaming heart. Now, before I delve into why it's my second favorite, let me take a moment to shine a spotlight on my ultimate, the often overlooked gem – Final Fantasy Dimensions. That one holds the crown, but we're here to talk about the brilliance of FFV.Final Fantasy V is like a symphony of gameplay and storytelling, and it sits proudly as my second favorite in the Final Fantasy lineup. The job system is the real MVP here – it's like a playground of possibilities. Switching between classes, mastering abilities – it's a strategic delight that keeps you engaged throughout the journey. The characters, a quirky ensemble of adventurers, each with their unique charm, make you genuinely care about their quest.The storyline is where FFV truly shines. It's this epic tale with unexpected twists and turns that keep you on the edge of your seat. What sets it apart is the perfect blend of drama and humor injected into the dialogue. You can't help but chuckle at the witty banter and fall in love with the narrative's charisma.Now, let me divert the spotlight for a moment to my absolute favorite, Final Fantasy Dimensions. It's the unsung hero, the hidden jewel that doesn't get the attention it truly deserves. The dual-world concept, the intricate job system, and that nostalgic pixel art style – it's a nostalgic trip that pays homage to classic RPGs.What truly sets Dimensions apart is the emotional depth of its story. It's not just an epic journey; it's a personal quest that tugs at your heartstrings. The music, the narrative, the characters – they come together in this magical symphony that creates an unforgettable experience.So, while Final Fantasy V holds a special place as my second favorite, Final Fantasy Dimensions is the undisputed champion of my Final Fantasy journey. Each Final Fantasy game is like a unique potion in a grand alchemical experiment – they revive your love for RPGs in their own distinct and magical way. FFV and Dimensions are like two sides of the same crystal, each reflecting the brilliance of the Final Fantasy legacy in their own splendid manner.

_childDocuments_.review: FF5 is more of a iteration on FF3 rather than FF4. Combat works similarly to FF4, it's using Active Time Battle system. It features a job system similar to FF3, but significantly improved. You can effectively mix and match different jobs by learning abilities on a specific job and putting them on different jobs. There are also many new jobs. All of this makes the game very replayable. The story is pretty goofy and light-hearted. I wouldn't call it "bad", it has some strong moments, but it doesn't takes itself very seriously. The music is great. It's this game that brought memorable tracks such as Battle on the Big Bridge which was fantastically remastered for the Pixel Remaster.I'd say it's definitely worth the time and money, as it is most likely the best Final Fantasy in terms of gameplay out of the first 6.

_childDocuments_.review: WHY HELLO THERE, my fellow Final Fantasy enjoyers, JRPG consumers, FF IV conquerors and gamers from all around the worldUpon defeating the spirit of raw hatred itself in Final Fantasy IV, I embark on my newest journey: sailing the Final Fantasy V seas as a Freelancer!As the before installments, FF V is completely standalone and isolated from the previous Final Fantasy games.As per the now established formula, some concepts are recurring: Chocobos, elemental Crystals, that one guy named Cid who really likes airships yada yada, you know the drill.Yet again, we have a named cast, starting with our traveling protagonist Bartz and his chocobo companion Boko. Throughout the game you meet other charming characters like Galuf, Lena, Faris and Krile to build up your party. Their interactions are fun, and throughout the game a rather charming and endearing tone is set, much less grave, sad and melancholic like FF IV was. A welcome change, imo, after such a heavy game, a lighthearted one definitely works. Our new villain is a man in a tin suit that laughs in an exaggerated way and mocks the party at all times, unlike the practical Golbez of few words from IV. By the end you truly believe the Final Fantasy was the friends we made along the way with how charming Bartz being a doofus is, how Galuf breaks some tropes, how Gilgamesh keeps appearing (ARGH!), or how Faris' secret is revealed.That doesn't mean the game is devoid of serious or sad moments, however. These moments are even more accentuated due to the lighthearted tone of the game, so when ♥♥♥♥ goes down, it really does. I think it is a good example of good storytelling and setting moods.Gameplay & mechanics! The job system returns from FF III, along with the ATB system from FF IV. Personally, I rolled my eyes the moment I saw the job system but that feeling was quickly tossed aside: this time around, the system is much more improved, less gimmicky and more useful. The penalties for switching jobs are basically nonexistent so it feels a lot like the game encourages you to experiment with various jobs. Some abilities that you obtain by leveling up the job, can be used in the ability slot to use it outside the job, leading to wacky, practical or downright broken setups (Dualcast Summoner, looking at you). Rarely did I feel the need to use a specific job to progress, unlike FF III where some parts of the game were gated by using specific jobs for the boss battle or area.As far as graphics go, FF V seems more colorful and vibrant compared to FF IV, most likely because the tone is lighter as well. The spritework is also good as expected of a Pixel Remaster entry. Every character has a different outfit for each job (which is very neat), ranging from cool to cute and some even being wacky. As usual, effects are the wildest and flashy.Not much to say in this department that hasn't been said in previous entries, although it's a shame our protagonists this time around don't have portraits in the party menu.Music! As usual, FF V gets a really neat soundtrack, remade with real instruments and fully faithful to the original SNES soundtrack. Some absolute bangers present in this entry. In no particular order, my favourites are: Battle at the Big Bridge, The Dawn Warriors, Reminiscence, Beyond the Deep Blue Sea, Sorrows of Parting, Slumber of Ancient Earth and very close to being my top favourite is The Final Battle, what a banger.I personally recommend this entry in the Final Fantasy franchise. It was probably at this point where they finally nailed a perfect balance between wackiness and serious storytelling, with compelling character interactions and not just a melancholic story that you are looking forward to see unfold like IV along with a job system that encourages the players to experiment and find their own playstyle.Give it a shot, it's fun.[job changes to Monk and slices the review with Katana] see you in Final Fantasy VI, adventurer.

_childDocuments_.review: As an early to mid-teen during the 16-bit era, I absolutely loved Final Fantasy IV (II) and VI (III). I played through them both more times than I can remember. I knew all the secrets, I leveled my characters to 99, I poured over the Nintendo Power guides. Of course, since it didn't officially release outside Japan until 2003, I never got the chance to have the same experience with Final Fantasy V. Sure, I tried to get into it several times over the years, but it always seemed so lackluster compared to IV and VI that I'd quickly lose interest. Fast-forward 20-something years. I'm now in my 40s and decided to give Final Fantasy V an honest go with the Pixel Remaster. After about 40 hours I finally finished it, and I can say that it was worth the money and the time invested. First of all, Square did a great job with the Pixel Remaster updating the graphics and sound to modern standards, but not so much that you can't tell that it was originally a 16-bit game. As for the game itself, well, the storyline isn't nearly as epic as IV or VI, but that doesn't mean that it's bad. I think I read somewhere that Square's plan for the FF games was to make the odd-numbered games more gameplay/battle focused, following the "4 warriors of light" format of the original game, while the even numbered games would be more story focused, though one can argue that approach went out the window with Final Fantasy VII. Either way, expect a few twists and turns, but don't expect a masterclass in storytelling like IV or VI, if you've played those. Where the game really shines though is it's mechanics, notably the famed Job system. Take some time to wrap your head around it, and you can create immensely powerful characters. You can go with a tried and true Knight / White Mage combination, or really buck the trends with something like a Bard / Dancer. Not every combination (or single job for that matter) is as viable as others, and while there are truly overpowered job combos, the game lets you build what you want, providing ample support for all the jobs. This was what I had the most fun with in my play through. Trying out the different jobs, figuring out what worked and what didn't, and ultimately coming up with a plan for each character. I did do a bit of AP grinding to level up jobs, but not much. Maybe a couple hours worth. Once I was set with jobs about 3/4s of the way through the game, I finished up the the story. I finally beat the final boss with my characters right around level 40. I never felt the need to grind experience, though I did skip a few optional encounters like Omega. With my job selections and the aid of some amazingly overpowered gear (*cough*Chicken Knife*cough*) I breezed through almost all the encounters. Frankly, I found the game to be a bit too easy if anything.Anyway, while I had a good time with the game and I'm glad that I finished it at least once, I'm not sure that I'll be back for a second play through. Maybe some day far into the future. However, I will now be buying the rest of the Pixel Remaster series and reliving some childhood nostalgia.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's another stop on the journey of Final Fantasy fans eager to revisit the earlier games or experience them for the first time. Final Fantasy V was the only one of the SNES-era games not to make it to the US when it was originally released. Story-wise, I can kind of see why. It seems a bit more meandering and less cohesive than the previous installment. It has the usual "group of heroes band together to fight an evil power bent on world destruction/domination" with crystals, chocobos, airships, moogles, and a guy called Cid.Like Final Fantasy III, FFV uses a job system. Jobs unlock as the story unfolds, and each job has unique abilities. Winning battles gains experience that allows your characters to master skills from each job so that they can be used while equipping other jobs. And mastering each job adds its innate passive abilities to your default "Freelancer" job, making it more powerful as you advance.Like the other Pixel Remaster games, FFV has a few nice quality of life additions, like a quick save feature that basically allows you to save anywhere, the ability to adjust battle speed, as well as an auto-battle feature to make grinding less tedious, and it's a pretty grind-heavy game if you want to 100% it.Difficulty-wise, the game can be really easy in places to extremely hard if you're not using a walkthrough. Some of the boss battles and strong enemies can be difficult unless you're using a specific combination of jobs, skills, and equipment. Play it if you want to experience a Final Fantasy game you probably didn't get to the first time it came around.

_childDocuments_.review: I got a disclaimer to say about this review, Final Fantasy V is the first one I played and I firmly believe that this is a series where everyone enjoys the first one they played the most. I revisited this series so I could take another view on this games and see if my opinions on any of them have changed in the years since playing them last. Every time I've done this, Final Fantasy V always ends up being a little more ahead than the others. For newcomers I'll say it's absolutely worth checking this game out. The game is very huge and full of content for it's time (I'd argue it having more than later 16 bit games like Chrono Trigger), and while the job system seems daunting at first it's really easy to pick up on and encourages experimentation with no drawbacks. The story is a lot more lighthearted and goofy than the stuff that comes before or ahead, and even pokes jabs at the way FF2 and 4 contrive ways to change your party configuration.For people who played the older versions, there's no GBA stuff in it so it's really a make or break issue for you there. I hated the mugshots because of how much the concept art clashes with the in game art, and the exclusive classes are obtained so late that it feels like a bit of a missed opportunity. But I think with this pixel remaster in particular they went extra hard on the music because it sounds so good in this version, and of course affects a lot more of the overall experience. I think it's worth replaying the game just because each time I do I find a new way to break it.And now, I must slowly and unskippably trudge through the snow to play the last game in this collection...
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is an interesting game. While FFIII has the job system, FFV takes it up a notch. It features 22 jobs, with each having unique skills that can be equipped to other jobs after reaching a certain level. In theory, it makes you think about who you're facing, what jobs you have, if they work well with each other, etc etc. The only problem is that some enemies (even bosses) are easily taken down without much thought. For example, during the final boss, I just equipped 4 of the same jobs and tweaked their abilities a bit, and the boss was taken down pretty easily. As for the story, it was pretty unremarkable. It was interesting enough to keep me entertained and had some great moments. Two things I did not like at all: Missables and Achievement Hunting. You HAVE to follow a guide if you don't want to replay the game multiple times for the missables. Mastering all jobs sounds easy enough because you level them up as you play the game. I misinterpreted it as mastering all jobs, no matter the character. Oh boy was I wrong. In reality, you NEED to master all jobs with one character in order to master the Freelancer job. EXP grinding for level 50 was absolutely brutal. This port of FFV doesn't have certain post-game dungeons like the Advance version does, so you'll have to resort to spending hours in a spot just grinding everyone to lvl 50. All in all, I rate this game 7/10. It would've been higher, but the end-game stuff absolutely drained me.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is a solid entry in the series. The complexity and flexibility within the job system is a real highlight of the game. The story and characters are pretty good, but the narrative is a little weaker than some other entries. If you want to go crazy with the job system and experiment with trying to cheese fights, this is a lot of fun.
