_childDocuments_.review: So I installed a few mods to fix the text and add portraits to text boxes (and replace the meteors with the moon from Majora's Mask).  I participate in the Four Job Fiesta every year, and I used this version this year (Dragoon, Bard, Mystic Knight, Summoner).  Having also played the PR for FF6, I feel pretty much the same way.  Love the  wide aspect ratio, new spell animations, music, like it's all great.  Having played the Fiesta for a long time now, not having a real turbo button did make this feel like it dragged out a long longer than I'd prefer.  And I REALLY wish you could use the D-pad for walking instead of the analog stick.  But aside from that, I can recommend this for both casual play as well as the for the FJF.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: An adventure full of heart and excellent, diverse gameplay. My favorite FF gameplay besides X-2. While the story isn't nuanced or deep, it executes a simple premise well with some genuinely emotional and impactful moments. The status quo of an otherwise simple story is also shaken up several times to keep things interesting. This is an easy recommend to any turn-based fan.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very iffy about final fantasy games, 1 I loved, 2 ehhhh no thanks, 3, and 4 were okay, 6? best left unsaid considering the love for it, 7 was and still is outstanding, 8 was a hard pass, 9 great, 10 okay and I'll leave it there you get the point, FFV? Is one I super enjoyed 7 being my favourite I'll say 5 is a real close second, with some fun mechanics, a surprisingly good story and a lot of heart to it, I'm happy I finally got to play FFV and enjoy what it has to offer dood.Okay onto the meat of it, kinda weird because I'm sure most peeps will know what this game is like but for the initiates who like me never played it before? This'll be for them, okay so for starters as you can imagine it plays in battle like a typical FF game, using the ATB system your meter fills up and you take your turn at which point you choose from a list of moves, simple enough but wait there's more! As each character can learn abilities/spells but are they unique? I'll explain that next dood!So here's what makes FFV both unique and frankly quite awesome and that's the fact that you can choose from classes, what's that? Just sounds like FF1!? Hahaaa! That's where you're wrong dear reader! As you see your characters can choose classes whenever they like, they even expand over time and you can equip another skill in your second slot, want a black mage summoner? Me too that's what I did, a healing time mage? I did that and of course as you master classes all the abilities and bonuses become usable by the freelance and last class you find, allowing you to create and mix and match your styles of play, it really made for a crazy yet fun time dood.In terms of difficulty? This is actually one of the easiest FF games unless you're going for the super bosses and as we all know the FF devs love to make those absurdly difficult XD otherwise you can easily make yourself overpowered or you can make yourself less overpowered but look cool in one of the many outfits for each class, although you'll be stuck using those class movesets, honestly I would have liked a costume choice option in this day and age but eh guess they are keeping it as classic as they can dood.Music is remixed/higher quality? versions of the original and frankly all sound great, the visuals are great too ranging from the sprites in combat and the world itself, it was a treat to traverse and it makes me wish it had a NG+ but sadly it was not to be so, a lot of quality of life they could have added but even so it was still fun dood.There's not really anything else to talk about but personally? I think this game is definitely one of the best ones done in the main franchise, the diversity of playstyle, the story, the music, it's all just great to me, it deserves a lot of love and if you weren't sure about it I would say give it a go, I certainly loved every moment of it myself and if ya buy it? I hope you do too dood ^-^
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I first played this game over 20 years ago and I've owned every version of it, even the defunct mobile version port... The game still holds up wonderfully after all this time. And going back to it, I always discover something new.This is quite simply the best Final Fantasy game. The job system gives it a huge amount of replayability and can break the game wide open. This also means that through the job system you can make the game as challenging or easy as you want, and it allows for so many creative solutions to the situations in-game.And the music... The Pixel Remasters have done a good job overall, but on FFIV I thought the best tracks were kind of botched. But on this one, the opposite happens: Battle on the Big Bridge is more hype than it ever was, the Merged World theme is tear-worthy and the final battle themes are amongst the best music I have ever had the privilege of enjoying.Even if you skip the other PR's, don't skip this one. This game is worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe the plot isn't as deep as Final Fantasy IV, but Final Fantasy V is a game slathered in fun and whimsy and served on a bed of a terrific job system. Mastery of multiple jobs is encouraged as you can have two equipped to each character (get that Summoner job on your big hitters as soon as you can). There may be better stories in Finals Fantasy past and future but I don't know if (outside of the mmos) there was ever a better job system.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy THE EXTREME.  After several redundant renditions of basically the same game, Square invented something which is basically the prequel of today's FFXI Online.  An open ended, choose your own ability buffet of Lego building inventiveness it sets the stage for Miyamoto Musashi's own idea of Void.  In the void is virtue, and no evil. Wisdom has existence, principle has existence, the Way has existence, spirit is nothingness.  By far the emphasis is on THE WAY HAS EXISTENCE which is basically Taoism.  Basically, in this game you have to build against [nothingness] which is the objective of Exdeath Exodus.  Years later, post FFXI, FFV does in some ways put 11 to shame in the sheer swath of creative choices.  A Dancer with Bard ability singing about Romeo?  Check.  A Ninja dual wielding Knight with custom items?  Check.  Despite the removal of V because of its too complicated for Americans label, this game is brilliant and perhaps America has caught up to the global stage.  To add a brilliant touch of charm, the game itself and some of the characters (Krile especially) carry this Sailor Moon style of the time which is very elusive, yet attractive.  Our usual tired formula of Town then Dungeon is tilted as convention gets trashed in favor of survival alternatives.  More than anything V provides an EXTREME look at what Final Fantasy could have been... a Sailor Moon flavored rendition in ultimate possibility.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the first 4 games pretty much one after the other, i'm starting to think this isn't the best idea.However, this doesn't mean final fantasy 5 isn't good. I am a bit annoyed that certain jobs have a higher requirement of ABP  than others...but I will say this: it is worth getting them leveled, because for most of them, the abilities they give you on mastering them are pretty good (there's also an achievement for mastering all the jobs so...)I'm technically not finished with the game, but I am on the final dungeon.I've also not played for 68 hours exactly, more like 50something, according to the ingame timer, not steam.The story made me angry and anxious at a couple  the best way.One piece of advice though: i bought this series one game at a time, and if you're going to do it that way and wait a few weeks or months between buying each game, then fine. But, if you want to play them all one after the other, buy the entire bundle: it looks like a lot of money in one go, but it is cheaper in the long run, not to mention that considering what AAA games cost these days, it's really not that bad...Anyway...i'm taking a break. Enjoy... :)
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the most overlooked entry in the Final Fantasy series, considering its quality. All because it didn't release outside of Japan back when it first came out and that it was going for a more lighthearted story. For some people, Final Fantasy must be a serious affair all the time. This game features the job system that originated with the first game and was improved with the third game by allowing you to change job at any time. With Final Fantasy V you can mix certain abilities from one job with another job. Cross-classing, in other words.Like all the Pixel Remasters, this version lacks the bonus content that the GBA and previous Steam version had. It can be a bummer for series veterans but inconsequential for everybody else.Highly recommended for newcomers to the series.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V...probably the most forgotten about in the series, or at least the first 10 games. It had the unfortunate luck of coming between two of the biggest of the series and never coming over seas to the SNES; but I think there are other factors that makes it forgotten.Lets get those out of the way:1. The dungeons don't really feel epic. Final Fantasy is good about having rather large dungeons to explore, but this one the caves and dungeons always felt tiny and uninteresting. There is a little too much "single room where you run around the center walls from a stairwell that comes out of it in the south to one going up in the north" or vice versa.2. There is missable stuff that feels basic to the series...like possibility of missing the Shiva summon.3. Compared to the mood of IV and VI..this feels a little too lighthearted and cartooney. But FFV is still an amazing game, and has a great Job system attached to it. Like III, there are so many classes to go through, and so many ways to handle your opposition...you can play with a different experience and feel each time.After the heavy mood of IV, this is a good one to just relax to and have fun with it. It probably won't end up as your favorite, but it won't end up as your least favorite either. It is pretty much in the middle of the deck.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: The one that got away, this game would have blown my mind as a kid if it had actually released on the snes.The job system is really amazing and gives you the ability of each playthrought to be as new or refined as you like.This pixel remaster is definitely one of the better ones with much improved music and graphics, the difficulty however has stayed similar so prepare for a rough time at certain parts of the game,
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: This is the least story driven SNES Final Fantasy. I would not recommend it for those who are looking for a narrative driven experience.This game may have the best customization of any final fantasy in my opinion. The class system is quite brilliantly designed, and especially in the late game after you unlock the Mime class. I love the way this game lets you build characters, with some very powerful combinations. You also have all the classes at a very nice point in the game, that lets you build your characters very well timed for the end boss.Something I would like to address is the difficulty of the final boss. This is potentially the hardest final boss in the game, and can pin some very bad status effects on you that can make you life very difficult. even with well built characters, this boss can absolutely destroy you because of the number of status effects it can throw at you. This boss is very fun if you're willing to put up with a challenge, but you may not enjoy the final boss as a casual player.On the topic of the story, this game is highly lacking. It tries to have a concise narrative, but it just feels as if it falls apart very quickly. There are some nice moments that feel quite powerful, but most of the story is built only to allow you to progress through the game.I would give this game a 7.5/10. mainly for the story. It may seem harsh to get rid of so many points for a bad story but in a game like final fantasy, the story makes a very big deal. I would recommend final fantasy 6 over this game mostly because of the story.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: The SNES era of FF was my favorite and while I'm not a huge fan of the art-direction change in these remasters I still enjoyed the game just the same and will always support some of my favorite games from my childhood. With that said, the combat is incredibly easy compared to the OG games, so be prepared to absolutely steamroll everything.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: My personal favorite of the classics in the series barring FFT. Usually the most maligned of the lot simply because it's the one people are not nostalgic for, go figure!There's a lot of jobs to try and customize your party with with none of the obnoxious mechanics such as stat growths that other games have these days, and it's never hard enough that you feel like you have to stress about minmaxing or your composition, so it's just a good time. The story is fun and doesn't overstay its welcome, but still has its emotional moments, and the OST has a lot of good tracks.I personally would recommend modding in the SNES fonts since they look great in these games, they also work for all the other 5 PRs. As well as the SNES OST or the Synthetic Origins OST based on preference, as I feel the orchestral remaster missed the mark in quite a few songs (such as boss battle), but other than that it has been a great way to reexperience this game.Please don't skip this one!

_childDocuments_.review: After playing all six of the Final Fantasy Pixel Remastered games, this one stood out to be one of my favorites as it has improved upon the storytelling compared to the previous installments with enjoyable gameplay mechanics like the job system that . _childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: This is the one to play if you want the core, classic Final Fantasy experience. Of all the features that are sprinkled throughout the series, FFV has the most of them. The most types of magic, most jobs, most forms of transportation, (VI has the most summons), it's got it all.Final Fantasy I has jobs and 4 heroes. The setting isn't too crazy.Final Fantasy III has interchangeable jobs and a crazier setting.Final Fantasy V has interchangeable jobs where abilities learned from one job can be used in other jobs. The setting is the most crazy.Of the first 6 games, I,III, and V feel the most like the same series. II is great if you like the SaGa series. IV and VI are great if you want more narrative/character focus, but they do deviate from the core experience (still amazing in their own right). Beyond VI, the primary artist and general mood changed to the point where it doesn't feel like the same series anymore. Less fantasy, more anime/angst.Is the Pixel Remaster the best way to experience FFV? Not quite, but close. The content added in the GBA version is missing, but I think the game is fine without it. The awful overly-bright colors from the GBA version is here though, so you may want to mod it to look more like the SNES version.

_childDocuments_.review: Online chatter would tell you that FF V is the unfortunate step-child sandwiched between the groundbreaking FF IV, and the magnum opus FF VI. In some ways, this holds true. IV and VI prioritize theatrical, character-driven storytelling over V's less exciting return to the usual Warriors of Light against the Big Bad setup. But I happened to enjoy V far more than IV (and what little I've played of VI) for some key reasons:> the game is goofy and lighthearted, without losing its sense of tension when it needs it> the gameplay with the Job system is fantastic, and makes FF games with locked in classes feel quaint> actually commits to its character deaths without chickening out (*shakes head at FF IV*)> has GligameshThe only negative I can think of is that the last act is very thin on story events and is mostly dungeoneering and powering up for the final confrontation. Which is fine, but is a sharp contrast to the first two acts, both of which which broke up the gameplay with the novelty of new locales and humour.

New pixel graphics and remastered music add a little something as well.  Great for those who want an experience close to the original, or someone coming into FF5 for the first time.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: FFV finally has a port that allows the game to truly shine. Long ago were the times of fighting Y Burns and Karl Boss in the PSX version, dealing with the limitations of the GBA, or the misguided HD remaster of the initial Steam/IOS release. The PR offers a reworked soundtrack that is simply a treat to hear, and graphics that stand out above the muted palette of the original. With a custom font package, the interface is a welcome evolution over the stale mobile-port style that plagued the earlier remasters.The game itself is probably the most mechanically robust game from the 2D era, using the famous job system that first debuted in FFIII. Once acquainted with it, there is much fun to be had in figuring out clever ways to combine abilities, with ridiculously powerful builds that can result from exploting its depths. The story is somewhat sparse, however it does pick up in the second half, where its execution is enough to show that Square was learning how to integrate plot and gameplay into a cohesive whole.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. It feels like it builds upon everything that FF1 and FF3 focused on and improves it considerably. Unlike FF4, the story takes a back seat to the gameplay. The narrative works in its own right, but certainly leaves a bit to be desired, especially after FF4. It works in this game though because the gameplay is just THAT good. There are more than 20 jobs and over 100 abilities to learn from the variety of jobs available. This makes the gameplay incredibly flexible, allowing you to change your party composition at will to fit your preferences. You want to play a knight who knows time magic? Go ahead. You want your white mage to master black magic? Go for it. There truly is going to be no two people who play this game exactly the same. The amount of options puts even modern JRPGs to shame. Because of this, this game is just FUN. That's all I can say. If you like JRPGs, you cannot have a bad time playing this.8.5/10 - V, IV, III, I, II

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is a beautiful game that embraces wholesome fantasy entirely. The villain isn't complex, the characters are all nice and good people, and you know the ending will result in the world being saved with everyone living happily ever after.The job system is the best the series had seen, with experimentation rewarded with bonuses to the characters as a whole— there's definitely ways to abuse the system, but if you're completely blind, you'll most likely have a completely different party setup than me. The end-game is great, with half a dozen optional dungeons and a few bosses that offer a good challenge with good rewards. Is Final Fantasy V groundbreaking? Are the characters deep and complex? Is the story deeply engaging and intriguing? Nope, and sometimes that's good enough.

_childDocuments_.review: FFV has always felt like the forgotten entry of the golden era of Final Fantasy, despite being extremely well regarded. Part of this is being sandwiched between two very strong, memorable games, and part is due to the game never really getting a definitive western release (the GBA version and its awful music being probably the closest). For some reason I’d never actually gotten round to playing it either, which does mean that this review is entirely free of nostalgia.The pixel remaster is something of a mixed bag. I like the updated music and graphical effects, as well as the quality-of-life features (a quick save, autosave and auto battle). However, the juddering while panning, especially during cutscenes really detracts from the presentation even if you do get used to it eventually. The font is absolutely dreadful too, but replacing this is a five minute job that works across all pixel remasters so I certainly wouldn’t call that a deal breaker. The biggest omission is the extra dungeons from the GBA and mobile ports, which really does stop this feeling like a definitive edition.Out of the SNES games FFV does feel like something of an odd duck. FFIV and VI are primarily narrative driven games, with some of the most iconic characters and moments in the whole series. FFV’s narrative by comparison is really not the focus here – in fact, I’d go as far as to say it’s utter fluff. Your party might as well have come free in cereal for all the charm and personality they exhibit. The story is absolute boilerplate fantasy with a villain that is only memorable for being an evil tree and one particular absurd meme moment.   But in terms of mechanics and dungeon design, FFV is one of the strongest in the series. The job system allows for an enormous amount of customisation and optimisation, and it is a big improvement over FFIII. Yes there are the well-known broken combos, but you’d be surprised at what combinations of jobs and abilities end up working together. While I wouldn’t say all classes are made equal, all of them at least offer something interesting. Due to this level of freedom offered to the player, the devs really pushed the boat out in terms of boss design. Nearly all of them offer some kind of interesting mechanic to keep things fresh, and unlike FFIII you aren’t forced into particular strategies or classes. The dungeon design is also some of the strongest in the series, treading that fine line between satisfyingly complex and being a confusing slog. Sadly like all the SNES FF games the encounter rate is absurdly high, and unfortunately there’s no way to turn them off. I find my tolerance for such things has waned over the years, and even if battles tend to be very short the constant barrage of interruptions can get exhausting. The option to tailor your encounter rate was a feature nearly a decade ago in FFV’s spiritual successor Bravely Default, and it’s a shame to not see it backported.Bravely Default also highlights another issue that really isn’t the fault of FFV – namely, that every game that took inspiration from FFV’s job system added their own twists and complexity, leaving the original looking a little barebones in comparison. Make no mistake, Bravely Default and Bravely Second are absolutely the superior games to FFV in every way that isn’t dungeon design – better mechanics, better graphics, better characters and a better plot (even considering the first game’s notorious last third). If you have access to a 3DS I would strongly recommend them. Just don’t bother with bravely default 2 on steam. It’s not good.Coming back to FFV was something of a breath of fresh air, especially after recently slogging my way through FFXIII and FFXV. I forget how brisk and tightly paced these older games are, with absolutely no cruft. I did nearly everything in the game, including around five hours of unnecessary job point grinding and getting all the blue magic and summons. This took around 35 hours, and it could easily be done in 25.  If this the Final Fantasy you forgot to play (and statistically it is), give it a punt – it’s easy to see why plenty of people rank it as their favourite.

_childDocuments_.review: I've always loved this game.  The sheer volume of job classes available and techniques you can use to tackle your foes.  You can play to your own style or try out new ways every time you start a new file.   While it doesn't have the story depth of its predecessor and successor, it is still fairly charming, with fun characters.  And a few surprises along the way.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is probably my favorite in the series, but I don't think the Pixel remaster is the best version of it.First off, the gameplay. Words cannot describe how much fun this one is compared to its predecessors. FFV has a job system like FFIII, but is leagues better in every way imaginable. The variety of jobs is just incredible. You get your basic Knights, White Mage, Thief, but you also get Blue Mage with its creative way to learn magic from enemies, Mystic Knight with its ability to imbue weapons with elemental attacks, and even Chemist with the ability to combine items on the fly to make various effects. And after you level up each job, that character will learn an ability that can be used with any other job in the game. There are so many possibilities of job combos that there are still some that I probably haven't seen even after playing the game twice! (This system is also what inspired things like Bravely Default, one of my favorite games ever made)The bosses are also super engaging, forcing you to learn their attack patterns and come up with a strategy, especially the game's two superbosses. There's also a ton of optional content which is super nice.One issue with this version of the game, is that it's missing some content. There are some missing jobs that were in the GBA version of the game that I wish made the cut here.However by far the biggest complaint I have is the achievements. So each remaster has Achievements for getting every chest in the game, hidden item, and location on the map. And I swear to god they the worst here. Many dungeons are one-time-only, meaning if you miss a chest, you better pray that you saved before hand. And there is no easy way to know were you haven't been, since so many of them get locked out after key points in the story! I ended up giving up on getting 100% on this game, just due to how obnoxious it all is.Still, I love this game and what it has to offer, and I'd recommend any Final Fantasy fan to give it a chance. Just don't go for all achievements lol
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: FFV is one of the lesser-known Final Fantasy games, but it's just as awesome as its lineage would have you believe. Combining the tried and true JRPG formula with a completely overhauled job system, this game gives you the freedom to set up your party juuuuust the way you want them. For min-maxers or tinkerers, this game is a dream come true - and in some cases, you will definitely have to do some tinkering, as some bosses demand certain mechanics or playstyles. Then you add on the Pixel Remaster graphical, audio, and UI upgrades, and you have a stellar game on your hands.The only negative thing I'll say about this game is that I'm not a big fan of the translation used here - there are a few too many in-jokes or pop culture references for my liking. They're not everywhere, but when they cropped up they really took me out of the moment.But all in all it's still a fantastic RPG with an incredible job system and fun, engaging battles all the way through. Easy recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: The re-orchestrated soundtrack sounds great as usual. Although I don't know if I like the music as much as I did IV's. The humour in this entry is a nice addition which does liven up the slower paced moments in the story. The whole adventure feels quite a bit longer than some of the other entries though I did start to feel like it was a bit too drawn out despite how well developed the story was.The gameplay is another interesting take which lifts the job system elements from III. This game refines the job levels to be a little easier to max out jobs with ABP instead of regular experience and with lower job level caps. _childDocuments_.review: I'm used to the SNES rom that was hacked to be in English, and overall it's a really nice remake. It does not include any of the special features from the GBA version (like the extra jobs). It's really a remake of the original.The graphic improvements were nice, but the music quality improvement in particular is especially good. I also really appreciate the language selection feature (I played through in German).My only complaints are pretty minor. Sometimes button presses do not go through, and I've made a few wrong actions in battle because of this.During battles in the original version, you press right and select "defend", or press left and select "row". In the Pixel Remaster version, you press either left or right to get to a second menu, and then you select either "defend" or "row". It's disorienting coming from the original, and I sometimes select "row" when I meant "defend". It's a bit difficult to explain, but if you're used to the original, you'll notice this immediately.

_childDocuments_.review: I've really enjoyed playing through the Pixel Remastered Final Fantasy games, and Final Fantasy 5 has been my favorite one so far (haven't played FF6 Pixel Remaster yet). The soundtrack is absolutely incredible, the quality of life options within the game, such as the mini map, auto-battle, etc. are great, and in my opinion has one of the better plots to a Final Fantasy game. However even with all the praise I have for this game, there are a few things that I wish were updated or fixed  that would make this game 10/10 for me.1. Move Bestiary into Configuration Menu: Having the Bestiary only accessible in the main menu of the game and not within it can be quite annoying if you are someone like me who likes achievement hunting and want to check that I've fought every enemy and have to save/quick save to go to the main menu to check what enemies have been recorded. 2. Game Play/Soft-Locking during Auto-Battle: I've had this happen a number of times while playing this game and repeatedly during an auto-battle with Unknown (Bestiary #168) in the Great Sea Trench. There are 3 enemies and when one of the three is defeated it will respawn. You can auto-battle here and grind for a lot of EXP and Gil (APB is only 4, so not good for grinding Job Levels). However, whenever trying to do this, the game will soft-lock in battle after about 15-20 minutes. The battle music will still be playing, you can turn auto-battle off and on but the attack bars will remain frozen, you can't input any commands, and if you try to flee from battle, it will just put the characters into a run animation. I've also had this happen on other battles while using auto-battle, but this is the one I've been able to repeat.Overall I would still say this is a great game worth playing if you like JRPGs, Final Fantasy, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: FF5 is the first game that really feels like it ticks all the boxes for what we've now come to expect for a Final Fantasy game.The job system introduced in FF3 makes its return in a greatly improved form, it's not perfect, but it's good enough that it definitely justifies its existence as a feature, something FF3 didn't really manage. The 'ATB' real time battle system returns from FF4, and it works for this game given the various ways turn rate can be affected. Jobs feel hit or miss, there's some notable must haves: Monk, Ninja, Ranger, etc. Some jobs feel bad, Berserker, Geomancer, Beastmaster, and Dragoon come to mind (I like Jump as much as the next guy but it feels so limiting in this game and there should be more to a job than a single ability, okay?). The jobless/'Freelancer' class gains the intrinsic perks and highest stat bonus from all the jobs that have been mastered on that character. This does allow for some depth, but this is not explained well or really at all by the game. The aforementioned stat bonus inheritance will not be clear to you what that means or even that it exists unless you read about it online. The game would benefit greatly from being forward with what is implicit to jobs and furthermore what is transferred to freelancer and what is not, since not all abilities are. You will almost certainly spend a non-trivial amount of time grinding abilities for specific jobs, I don't really like how long this takes. By endgame, you're basically only using Freelancers since the power on offer there is way outclassing any specific job. This job/combat system is good, not great, but good. This is the highlight of the game to me so I spent the most time talking about it.The plot is pretty forgettable, honestly. Evil bad guy is evil and wants to destroy the world because evil. The plot may be weak, but the world itself is probably the most interesting of these first 5 FF games. They do some cool stuff with the world that wasn't really done yet in FF, so that's neat. The characters are what I would call bare minimum to be actual characters. They have 1 or 2 personality traits but they largely don't matter and are mostly just trivia. Lenna probably has the most interesting and well-defined character trait. My biggest complaint with the characters isn't really that they're bad, but that the plot wouldn't meaningfully change if they were different people. There's one or two notable exceptions, but it's largely true. The game definitely acts like the plot is more dramatic and interesting than it normally is, but it's trying at least. There's a couple touching or sad moments that work but most of the time the scenes felt like window-dressing to pretend like these characters matter to the plot, which again I would argue they largely don't.Music is alright, honestly I think I liked FF4 more. I don't think I'll remember most of the music in FF5. I still think about FF4's boss music because it's SO good. Nothing like that in this game.This one is pretty long too, it took me twice as long to beat the game to my satisfaction (All optional bosses, most of the job abilities I wanted) compared to all 4 previous games, which were normally clocked in at 20 hours or so for the same general level of completion. The game is okay, and I'm glad I played it, but I don't ever want to play it again. FF4 had simpler gameplay but better plot and characters, and didn't feel like I was required to grind as much as this game wanted me to. That being said, this is probably the template. All the pieces are there, they just need to be 2X better, and this game is probably masterpiece tier. Speaking of, I look forward to playing FF6 and Chrono Trigger next.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like where the Final Fantasy series really starts in force. Final Fantasy V is probably one of the most well-balanced RPGs I've ever played. The game, which took me over twice as long as any other preceding entry in the series, but still manages to never get boring, is consistently challenging the entire way through and encourages you to try new strategies and keep switching up your approach. And the job system, as good as its been so far, really caters to this. Every single class seems viable and good in different situations, and the achievements pushed me to master them all. Figuring out different combinations of jobs and abilities was a lot of fun. The battle system is basically the same thing as in FFIV, but it works even better here because the fights are just so damn polished. There are two new types of magic joining white and black: time magic, which can effect the timing of your turns among other things, and blue magic, which you learn from enemies. Blue magic in particular was a really fun addition, acting as a unique sort of collectible that had a lot of impact in game, as blue spells are often pretty powerful, and some were difficult and fun to obtain. Some grinding is needed for 100% completion, but its not too much and it was generally pretty engaging. The story is great, characters are fun and you actually care about them. Thus far, this is probably the best one in the series hands down, though also the longest, so it's more of an investment than the four entries before it. If you liked the other games in the series, definitely don't skip on this one!

_childDocuments_.review: Going into FF 5 blind I had very low expectations. I hadn't heard anything about it except about the more refined Job system and Gilgamesh existing. Not only that but a lot of reviews talk about bugs and crashes. The game also seems to be the least reviewed out of all the pixel remaster games as of this writing. I was expecting a relatively frustrating experience before getting to the highly praised FF 6.Am I glad that I got proven wrong. Out of all the FF games I have played, FF 5 is easily one of my favorites at this point. And in chronological order it is a huge step up from anything that came before it. In a way it feels like a love child between FF 3 and 4, creating a mix of some of the best parts of both games.The job system is not perfect but it is MUCH more refined compared to FF 3, you can mix and match jobs much easier. Swapping on the fly is much simpler and you are never truly forced into running a specific class (with very few exceptions). Jobs are expanded and have multiple new abilities and actions that they earn through leveling up, there are even proper text boxes providing explanations for all the different actions and classes. They even added different sprites for each main cast member for all of the different jobs! All of those QOL features and improvements make this a much more fun and open job system experience compared to FF 3.The amount of content is huge in comparison to the last 4 games. This is the first time where I felt like my decisions mattered a ton for the fights. Exploration gets rewarded and there is a lot of really cool optional stuff that you can just completely miss if you don't take the time to take in the world. It is much less linear compared to its predecessors and expects you to put in effort to find your own way of playing through the game. Its easily the hardest out of all the pixel remaster games up until this point and I died many times trying to figure out how to beat some of the bosses, try slowing the game speed if you are also struggling like I did.The game really expects you to immerse in its world, there are a lot of moments where I felt like I was completely lost until I just stumbled on the next story objective or started to finally figure out the combat. Most of the time this works out and it creates for some really engaging story moments where you really feel the desperation due to how unexpected some of the boss fights can be. The fights in this game in general feel like they try a lot of new and interesting ideas. The general story isn't anything incredible but it has some incredibly emotional moments, and one of the most charismatic and fun side villains I have seen in any RPG. I love you Gilgamesh.The one big negative I had while playing the game is that the dungeons can feel like mazes, and it feels very similar to FF 3 in how much it feels like a war of attrition. Your resources are worth a ton and it can feel really tedious to explore as much as I did and still sometimes have to waste a ton of resources to kill some relatively simple mobs. Some of these dungeons also use a lot of new gimmicks, and sometimes that just results in some really frustrating and tedious dungeons.The music is also a bit of a let down compared to FF 4. A lot of it is still great but there are a lot less stand out tracks, the ones that do stand out REALLY stand out however, creating for some incredibly memorable moments.The earlier mentioned bugs/crashes is something I only barely noticed. I had no crashes and the bugs I did see were some collectibles that didn't properly get shown off. For the rest I had an extremely smooth experience.The last thing I wanna talk about is the main party, it is a much smaller scale party compared to FF 4. But there is a lot to be said about that size. This party felt so unique to me, and I think that is partially due to the story, but I think the biggest reason is because of the job system. Every party member ended up serving a super unique role that I made myself, and that ended up creating a big identity for all characters in my head, it was super fun to watch the story of these characters and see how they grew in game from a mechanics perspective.FF 5 expects the most out of its players compared to any FF game before it. But in turn it rewards you with a really robust world, a very replayable experience, a fun combat and job system, and a simple but fun story. It might be one of the most overlooked/underrated games in the series, this is the easiest recommendation I can give out of all the pixel remasters up until this point, it still holds up really well and is a ton of fun. Lets hope that FF 6 is as fun as all the praise it gains.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to start? I originally played FFV on the PS1 maybe 15 years ago, and got stuck against Exdeath. But now I've got a PC, I've been replaying the series from start to finish, and I must say... I done him in this time. But there's a downside; even though I managed to finally complete it - after hours of almost chucking my PC out the second floor window - I didn't enjoy it as much as I did years ago.  I still recommend FFV to anyone, as I know it's a lot of people's favourites, and those people must also enjoy having high blood pressure, but to me, by the second half of the game, it felt like a chore. The difficulty is astronomical compared to the first 4 titles. In fact, probably compared to most in the series. In a nutshell: FFV is hard. Incredibly hard. And it takes the enjoyment out of it at times.  That being said, I commend yet another retelling of the Warriors of Light story from I and III, but this time with a well-balanced and strategic job system which gives credit to countless jobs and strategies you would never use in III.  It also saw the introduction of Gilgamesh and Moogles, and injected a lot more humour into its story than the others.  All I can say is play it. But remember: Spellblade-Dualwield-Rapid Fire.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic. Best one so far imo out of the first 5.I love the changes to the job system from FF3, you level up jobs so you can use their skills on other jobs almost cross class style and lets you combine some really powerful abilities together and make other jobs stronger. You can swap to any job and not feel like the strength of that job is diminished because it is level 1 because your stats come from your character level instead. I loved looking at each ability I mastered every level up. There also wasn't the cheese you had from FF3 where you could just sit and defend to level up your job since the ABP was determined by the enemy. Also, having the option to play Mime and Freelancer at any point and be able to equip 2-3 things instead of just 1 was really nice too.The story was the best so far, the villain was so much better then 1-4 games. There was also no annoying character swapping. It seems like each game has been an improvement in some way and they brought all of the good things from 1-4 into this game without any negatives that I can think of.Off to play FF6 :) I wonder how it will compare!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I love this entry in the franchise, easily in the top 5 and possibly in my top 3 behind 9 and 6. Not quite as serious as the entries its sandwiched between, but still serious enough with a wonderful villain. The job class system from 3 makes a return, with improvements to help you customise your abilities in combat. The jobs, whilst looking similar, also look different for every character, which is so much better than 4 characters in the same job class all looking like carbon copies of each other. 5 also has the first version of the blue mage (and possibly the most broken version, it can turn so many bosses into a joke if you know what you're doing)The characters are fun, the soundtrack is as always, a masterpiece (clash on the big bridge is always an amazing track, regardless of whether its the original, the pixel remaster version, or the versions from 12, 13-2 and 15, and any other versions). Truly a charming fun game
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best FF games, not only highly recommended, but an essential.  Does suffer at times from feeling like the middle child of FF4 and 6, battles aren't quite as fluid as 4, things aren't as beautiful as 6, and there is a mix of assets from the game shared by each that really shows the tweener aspect of this game.  Has it's own developed sense of humor that wasn't quite present in previous installments, epic soundtrack and strong cast of characters that have great developmental moments through out the game.  Despite the battles at times feeling a bit clunky, the battles you fight are better designed than in previous FF games and it shows, and tends to be better balanced than 6.The game does at times drag, and suffer from getting repetitive, you will see several scenes multiple times, but overall there is a lot of content in this game, and start to finish took me longer than FF15, so there is no shortage of content here.  There are also plenty of extras after the game is over to keep you busy.Overall this is one of the best entries of Final Fantasy, and any fan should pick this one up, it's top tier and pretty much any fan who gives it it's due will find it an instant classic.  In regards to the Pixel Remaster specifically, the soundtrack is very nice and has some great renditions of the original soundtrack.  Most of the upscaled tracks sound fantastic, with some even improved!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Well worth the play through, especially for those who havent played before or old veterans.Lots of reviews out already but all in all this is solid.There are a few things that could be fixed, targeting, minor glitches, ect, but this is all around a good 9/10 for me.Game: 8/10 - Fun to make the characters how you want and the mechanics are mostly solid. I only had 1 crash ever, no clue how some others have had problems, I never saw anything major at all.Challenge: 8/10 Can go through the game, be strong, and still RIP on some bosses. This is good! Its not a walk in the park and bosses and challenges feel like challenges. Very well balanced. Music: 10/10 - This could not be better. Its beautiful. Hands down top-notch quality.Story: 8/10 - Good story, could be slightly better, but it was great back then and still holds upRemaster: 9/10 - Very well done. They worked hard and it shows.You can get a huge amount of hours out of this game and plenty to do. Give it a go if you have time!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty good version of FFV (thank god too cause the old Mobile ports looked like ass) with tons of quality of life.Only real thing is that this version (same with Final Fantasies 1,2,4 and 6) is lacking are the extra GBA content which was weirdly left out. If you want what FFV was like back on the Super Famicom but with less grinding, faster load times and fights then here you go. If you want the new jobs and dungeons the GBA version added, well sadly you are out of luck. That being said I'd still recommend this if you want job, heartfelt JRPG with great music, a really fun job system and overall fun gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I'm biased because FF5 is one of my favorite part of series, and game overall.After all disaster ports and poor translations at last is something good. Quality of life improvements, like saving at every room, made this game easier than original, SNES version. Music is amazing. There were moments when I paused for a while, just to listen the remastered tracks. Graphics and special effects are ok. I don't understand why Pixel Remaster doesn't use classic font, but it's not game breaking and you can google how to fix it. My biggest critique is about ending. If you played SNES version you know that credits are timed. Character stats have "epilog" of ending theme and  last, bombasting notes are hitting just as you see "The End". After taht you heard some quiet melody. It was emotional moment, and makers of this version of game didn't care. Credits are longer than music, so ending theme ends during cast rolling, after that you get just main theme. It was disappointing to me. Ending in game is one of most important moments, and you will remember it. Apart of that, this is version you should play if you didn't play original, SNES version. It's amazing game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I was very satisfied with this game.  Overall this game is in my top five for the entire series.  As far as the pixel remaster was concerned it was about what I had expected.  The music was perfect, the graphics looked great but still very comparable to the original, the difficulty was also about the same as the original as far as I can tell.I do miss the extra content from the advance and mobile versions of this game, hopefully there will be DLC add ons for this in the future.  My only complaints are the same that I have had with the other pixel remaster games.  Why isn't there a build in font choice?  Why are the backgrounds only blue with no customization?  These two small things should be easy to implement and would go a long way to player satisfaction.Overall my complaints are small compared to how great this game is.  I enjoyed myself very much and will play it again in the future especially if there is DLC!!!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: It's the "comfort food" game of the SNES trilogy (4,5, and 6). The story is not as good as 4 and 6 but the gameplay is arguably the best of the 3 thanks to the job system. It's just a fun RPG to mess around and make all sorts of busted job combinations.As for the port itself it's a major improvement over the godawful mobile/steam port from years past, however it does has some issues. The biggest one is that unlike the GBA port, this one is a straightforward recreation of the original therefore all of the extra content from the GBA port is not present here. Also worth noting is that the soundtrack is entirely remastered and while I do enjoy some of the recreated tracks, I do wish that they could have provided an option to listen to the original soundtrack. Lastly, the default font is honestly pretty awful. Thankfully you can easily mod it into something that is more pleasing to the eye. Overall despite it's faults, this is a solid way to play FFV and I highly recommend it.8.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I never played this game in its original version. My favorite was always FFIV. Playing this now as an adult, I'm just delighted by all the little details. I love the class system. I could do without how much of a pain the Red Mage is to master, but I think Dualcast was worth it in that final battle.The game is grindy, but in a fun way, I think. I liked the main characters and had a lot of fun following them. This game was also super plotty. You have three worlds to go through, tons of backstory. Yes, some of the plot could be laid out a bit more delicately, but I honestly had a ton of fun.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Nah, the screen-stuttering is too much. I've tested on every platform now, and while the community seems to be accepting hardcore scroll-stuttering (VERY jerky motion of the scene whenever you move around any scene) as if its ok, The truth is these games move like garbage, and not enough people are raising a fuss about it.This is not an FPS issue. It happens on PS5 and Switch just the same. The Devs coded the movement wrong and it is well documented. it is present on every title and every platform, and low-key cited in many reviews. It really throws the experience, and the frame pacing was more smooth on PS1. I simply cannot accept this. Its too distracting, and making the Pixel Remaster trilogy run SMOOTHLY should've been a top priority. Modders have tried to fix this for 5 and 6 on PC, but consoles are hosed, So, much like FF6, here is a game that looked and ran better on the 10 dollar Mobile port, pushed out as if it is honoring a legacy of pixelly graphics... but missing many features and even the quality of previous versions.Look, Final Fantasy is of course legendary. 5 is a decent entry if you really like the job system- but, if you are reading this as a new player, and you want a compelling story and "FF experience", skip straight ahead to FF6, the crown jewel of the 16 bit era. Also, if you are at all sensitive to stutter, you might want to look up the mods that address this amateur programmer stuttering effect.FF5  DOES have a nice updated score, so shouts to the music team, as usual. However, they chopped so many features from that the PS1 and mobile ports gave us. We are talking about bonus dungeons and side quests, core FF stuff, left on the floor. A common theme is that they want to 'preserve the snes experience', but it seems like they do so in ways that require less work and deliver the least content to us (bonus dungeons were not killing anyones nostaliga), and cant even give us the pleasant motion experience you might find in the dozens of indie rpgs born from FF.I have to give this a BIG thumbs down until they patch the 80 on 60 movement stuttering, its extremely unpleasant, reported all over the internet, and whoever QA'd this Remaster needs their eyes checked.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Another nice pixeled remaster of one of my favorite series.  The job system is back from 3 but this time it is much better.  So much customization in this game, or if you arent into that you can just pick a class and go with it.  I mean this game even spawned a yearly event in the four jobs fiesta.  The music in this game is awesome just like the other remasters. Cant wait to complete this so I can move on to 6.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: The remaster of FFV overall is pretty good. It's got a solid story, combat is more nuanced in part because the job system is still great. But there's one big problem I had that really soured my experience. The Music.The music in FFV is pretty iconic, but unfortunately the team was put in a really tough position. There's just so much more of it than earlier entries that in the end, much of the music uses virtual instruments and are not a live recording. And it's painfully and frustratingly apparent.When it's recorded you can hear the brilliance, particularly in the certain tracks (gilgamesh, end credits). But where its VSTs, boy does it feel flat and restricted (castle of dawn), and that's so unfortunate as its so good at its core.But maybe you won't be bothered by that. :)
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V has always been one of my favorite entries in the series and the Pixel Remaster version does a lot of things well. While it's not a massive graphical upgrade compared to previous releases, this version adds a lot of added conveniences, such as speedier battles, an incredible new OST, and none of the lag and slowdown that hindered the GBA version (the version that I have played for the last 15 years and was the preferred version of the game for many). There's also a lot of small details and updates to appreciate for those who have run the game many times before. Mostly things you wouldn't think twice about, like some of the more obtuse story triggers beings more streamlined. One example of this is that, after clearing the Barrier Tower, you don't have to wait around for Galuf for a minute or two. Or not having to wait for the rope to be lowered in the pit in the third world. The Alte Roite battle triggers in the final dungeon have also been made easier to dodge, which is another welcome change. Little things here and there like that go a long way.Some bugs definitely hold the experience back, however. The Famed Mimic Gogo bestiary bug that was introduced in the January update will be sure to frustrate completionists. I also had a battle freeze on me entirely in the final dungeon when I used auto-battle, which I understand has happened to quite a few other players as well. There's lots of other small bugs here and there and I'm hoping Square-Enix hasn't ended support for this game and will fix them.Overall, it's my favorite version of FF5 to date even without the extra GBA content and is the best of the Pixel Remaster series so far. Hopefully there are more bugfix patches on the way so that this version can be the best version that it can be. With that last bit of polish, it could be definitely be the definitive version of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: This is my least favorite final fantasy game. It has charms like the job system, similar to 3 but with abilities that chain together and work better. Some of my favorite JRPGs use FF5 inspired job systems like final fantasy tactics and Octopath traveler. The problem with ff5 is that it wastes your time, is the grindiest of all the games I've played so far even with the Pixal remaster boost system I find myself grinding. Dungeons waste your time with traps that make you fall through the floor and backtrack. powerful monsters show up out of no where, over leveled for the area and kill your party outright. if it wasnt for quick save, auto save, monster encounter on/off and boost system, I wouldnt even have played as much as I did. I am trying to beat every Final fantasy game. and when I beat this one, I dont think I will play it again.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Great remaster of the SNES original, which never came to the west. Fun characters + gameplay and a stellar OST! The only negative I found: the last dungeon and final boss are harder than they needed to be, forcing you to grind EXP & Job points, which I never had to in this version before that point (or EVER in older versions of this game). Still, recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what an amazing game! I'm a huge Final Fantasy fan, and I'm playing through all the Pixel Remasters, but out of the pre-FF7 titles, I had only previously played FF6 (I'm super excited for its upcoming Pixel Remaster!). I've been playing them in order, and they just keep getting better! This is very much like the other Pixel Remasters: nice quality-of-life features, amazing music, great visuals, and all around just a great time. As far as the game itself goes, FF5 seems to have the most fleshed-out and well-developed story/characters out of FF1-5, so I was a little frustrated that they're still obsessed with "all-powerful crystals". My first exposures to Final Fantasy were FF7 and FFX (my favorites), and I'm so glad they didn't use the exact same "crystal warriors" theme all the other ones so far have been usingOverall, I highly recommend this version of FF5! It's an excellent port, and it looks really nice on small and large displays
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Played up to the 5th pixel remake, 6 has yet to be released, but this is far and away my favorite of the bunch so far. Only one crash that I was never able to replicate (it was super weird and specific so I didn't worry about it), the music is great, the job system is absolutely amazing and gave me incentive to grind so I could smash the final boss with little to no difficulty, even the story is pretty great considering the time period. I still think 4 has the best story thus far, but 5 beats it in every other aspect. If you play any of the remakes I highly recommend this one over all the others (6 could easily be better but have yet to play so idk)
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I had played through this game once before (the Super Famicom version with a fan patch) and I remember not liking it very much. After playing I-V of the FF Pixel Remasters, I can say that this is still the one I like second least (FFII has atrocious gameplay, but I love the music and the events were really cool for that era),I would still very much recommend this game to fans of JRPGs, especially if you value flexibility over narrative. This game allows you to create a fully custom party and they give you plenty of cool jobs to play with. I actually liked the fun and kooky characters more this time around, even though the story is very light and kind of thin. It feels like a giant step back after FFIV. My main complaints are two-fold: 1. Unless you force yourself into a challenge like the Five Job Fiesta (very recommended), you will end up choosing the best abilities for your team and ignoring everything else. By the end of the game you cast one or two spells and rapid fire with your members that you steer towards physical combat. This system shines when you need to puzzle your way through a tough boss by putting together a team of unique specialists, but it really sucks once you have sussed out the strongest party and have no where to go from there. The other games dodge this by giving each party member something unique about them. This game only has the slightest stat difference between the four party members,Also, the way this game handles status effects is really antiquated. It somehow feels worse than both FFIII and FFIV! Even with the all powerful ribbon, your party can be confused and turned into a damned zombie (the worst status effect in the history of games). The zombie effect turns your party member against you, can't be cured by anything but holy water, and drops your HP severely even when cured. It's annoying as hell and you have to give up your one accessory slot if you don't want to have it ruin your day. It's not like this game is that difficult, but the monsters and some of the design choices make it annoying.Personally, I think status effects are bad in most Final Fantasy games because they are so effective on the party and so worthless on enemies, but that's not specific to this game. I think FFV is a good game. Maybe even a very good old JRPG, but the lack one of those classic stories like IV, VI, VII, IX, and X just makes it feel like a lark rather than a must play.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: This is where the Pixel Remaster idea starts to really fall apart for me. Final Fantasy V Pixel Remaster looks OK, but really not much better than the original. It looks better than the horrible old version on Steam, but so does anything. This game also has a few really annoying bugs tied to achievements, so if you're the 100% achievements type, maybe double check the patch notes before committing to this game.At the moment of writing, the most prominent issue is the Bestiary bug where certain bosses or special enemies fail to register properly. This may be fixed in a future patch, but it should have been fixed already since the game has been out a while. I may amend my review if they fix it (if I can remember, lol)Alright, enough about that.Final Fantasy V is the evolution of Final Fantasy III. It has a frankly massive job system that lets you mix and match abilities to create fun setups for your characters. It lacks the extra jobs from the GBA/old Mobile/old Steam release but I'll be honest, it doesn't bother me. This is just pure vanilla FFV, and if that's what you want then you'll be happy.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: It was nice revisiting this one.  The job system was definitely starting to shape up, but I still always get the urge to play Final Fantasy Tactics (NOT ADVANCED!!) as it was my favorite way to play with the job system before FFXI.  The quality of life conveniences were again very nice as it let you cut through a lot of the time sinks.  It changes the feel a bit and will make it a different experience for a new player, but easier for those revisiting.The story in this one seemed to fall apart or be forced/rushed toward the end for me, but I still liked it.  It really leaves me with a want for a good FFT remake. :)
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: The game runs great from a technical standpoint. The only issue I ever had was there seemed to be a slight hiccup during the battle phase where the screen would pause for a second or two. Not sure if that is my computer or the game. I didn't have that happen with FF I-IV so I am not sure. The "speedup" feature is most used for this game out of I-VI because this game feels to be the most grindy out of the 6 games and the enemy encounters seem to be far more frequent in this game than in the other FF games. The music and visuals are very clean and look/sound amazing! These pixel remasters are a GREAT way for fans of FF to go back and play the earlier games without having that nostalgic factor.Now onto the game play and story aspect of my experience. The story is good compared to the earlier games (excluding FF IV) but seems a little drawn out at time. There are moments where you feel like "can we wrap this story up already) but considering how they were starting to transition from games with little to no story/character development to games with a lot of it then I can understand why they were so ambitious. The characters are decent compared to others from the series. The main character lacks more than the supporting cast does. Finding what you are supposed to do next can be confusing at times if you haven't talked to every NPC in a location to find out a hint on what to do next which is good and bad. Again, it goes back to the drawn out aspect of the game. You feel like they are sometimes recycling content in the story just to make the game longer without having the richness to why you are doing it. I hate to admit that I found myself at the last 10 hours of the game saying to myself "when is this going to be over." The updated job system from FF III is something a lot of players loved and I did initially as well BUT it became a very tedious task to continuously swap jobs in and out for certain dungeons/boss fights. I felt the need to grind to get jobs where I needed them and It made my game play go from around 30-35 hours needed to beat the game to around 54-ish which seems crazy that I spend so much time doing that. I did not enjoy doing that during the second half of the game and that is where I probably burnt myself out with this title in FF series. If you love grinding then this will be your favorite game in the early FF franchise. I have a love/hate relationship with FF job switching out games in the series so just to let you know where I stand. Overall, I enjoyed this game when it was over and have more fond memories of it now that I have finished it. I would rank the early titles (in my opinion, of course) as (from best to worst) IV, I, II, V, III. I would highly recommend this title if you have never played through it at least one time but I do not know if I will play through it again in my lifetime lol.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: About a couple of hours into the game and man, this is exactly how I remembered it! The update score is a huge plus and the visual style is exactly how it should be. I honestly was nervous when I first saw these pixel remasters announced and hesitated at first. But I figured if I was gonna try one out, it might as well be FFV. This was my favorite in the series for a long time. Very good first impressions.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: A faithful recreation of the old, quirky classic. I appreciate the quality of life improvements, and I also like that the pixel art is still here. If there is a way to turn off random encounters (as in other Final Fantasy remakes/remasters), I have yet to find it, as the random encounters do get a bit repetitive. Still- a great game, and totally worth your time if you're a Final Fantasy fan.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game. I had never fully played through FFV. Tried a long time ago on PS1, that wasn't a good experience. Tried it on GBA emulation, was digging it but didn't finish. This experience with the Pixel Remaster was very positive. I thoroughly enjoyed it! Loved the presentation of graphics and music and sound. I heartily recommend this as a great way to play FF5.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Remake is mostly well done. I could have used a -little- more in the way of modernization for the pricetag of such an old game (perhaps a bit more from the auto-battle. A few more graphical and UI changes may be welcomed), but it does it's job. I prefer some of the fan translations from the height of the emulation era, but in this case too, this remake seems adequate at the least.The game itself is still awesome. Revolutionary job/class system. Good story. Lovable characters. Hatable villain. One of the best of the Final Fantasy franchise in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: In this edition of Final Fantasy, the Job mechanic is introduced.  There are plenty of other places to read to understand what that is, and in my opinion, it is a GREAT addition to the series.  While the story is a little thinner and lighter-hearted at times than Final Fantasy IV, the game mechanics are the same or better.  If you are a fan of the Final Fantasy series, I recommend this installment.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: (This was the last FF game of the main series I hadn't played. I can finally rest in peace.)I'm just going to give some feedback for the devs since there are more than enough reviews of FFV out there.For the love of god, please add an option allowing to choose between the current font and a pixelated one. The smooth one clashes with the pixelated art style. This is actually also the case for the intro that - for me - was just too smoothed out. You don't have to remove it, but please add an option where you can choose.In general, this game could use more configuration options. While the soundtrack is fantastic, I would have loved to switch to the midi soundtrack in between. I would have also loved to modify the textboxes by adding character portraits.Now I know that there are mods for this - I did actually use some of them - but it just felt like modding things that should have been in the vanilla version to begin with.Overall, it's still a good version to play.Thank you for that. It was money well spent.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: First time completing FFV:Fantastic game and a huge step up for the franchise (compared to predecessors). Gameplay is well thought out and executed—maintaining entertainment throughout the entirety of the game.IMO, this is the first game to feel like a true Final Fantasy and should be considered the start of the "Golden Age" of the series.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: In terms of gameplay and graphics, this is probably the definitive version of Final Fantasy's fifth installment. I've played the GBA version, and I do like the added content in that one (which is not in this version), but for those looking for a fresh take on the original, this one is the way to go. The retooled graphics are beautiful, and the new musical arrangements (overseen by Nobuo Uematsu, himself) are absolutely godly! Definitely worth playing for veterans and newcomers alike!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I like this version alot. I don't like the way the base game though. I recommend mods for sprites, menu, and fonts if you prefer a more retro feel. The job system is very deep and allows for some crazy combinations if you enjoy old-fashioned grinding. It does not include any bonus content added in previous FF V releases but I don't mind that at all.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy 5 is my favorite game in the series, and this is pretty much just another version of it, so I'd recommend it.  That said, I wouldn't say it's my favorite version of the game.While the music is great, it has a lot of stuttering which can feel awkward at times.  It also lacks the added GBA content, which imo isn't great but it's still a bit sad not to have it.  The auto-battle function is nice, though.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: It has been many years since I played the Game Boy Advance version of FFV. I had previously imported the Super Famicom version and played some of the troubled Playstation game. This Pixel Remaster version is my favorite so far. The excellent music and the graphical flourishes here and there really add to an overall very polished presentation. The game feels solid all-around, and the Job system is one of the best character development mechanics the series has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I seriously considered skipping FFV in this series of Pixel Remasters, simply because I finished the GBA version a few years prior. FFV is also not high on my list of FFs, and I was certain that that wouldn't change with this release, especially after getting burned out on both FFII's "unique" and FFIII's similar job systems.But after all was said and done, I can honestly say this game was so much sweeter the second time around, especially in light of the standardized Pixel Remaster UX and UI, the redone and more vibrant visuals, and of course--of course--the music. When I first ventured to finally finish FFV after literal decades since the first fan translations came out, my main reason was to get to and play through Clash on the Big Bridge, one of my all-time favorite Nobuo Uematsu pieces. I had a similar goal going into the PR, but while I came for that track in particular (and sweet baby potatoes is it one of the best versions yet), I walked away with so much more thanks to the rest of the soundtrack.Everything felt more...alive. I had more fun grinding out jobs, paid more attention to the art, and did more of the arcane FFV tasks like finding that damn Stingray or all the quirks involved with collecting all the Blue Magic. And since this was my second trip, it was awesome knowing and breaking the game with combos like those with Rapid Fire and Mimic. The ending also felt different this time. I wasn't expecting this version to change my mind or heart because I'm not a fan of how generic FFV's main plot is, but man, when Dear Friends hit, it hit me like a bag of chocobo eggs.My opinion about FFV as a whole hasn't changed. But like all these Remasters so far, I'm grateful I got to experience it like this, in one of its best incarnations yet.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: First, I have to be a little forgiving about the bugs.  I forgot just how MASSIVE this game was.  I'd say it's just as big as Final Fantasy VI, so the fact that they were able to get it out as close to the other remasters is pretty damn incredible.  I would say that once all of the bugs are patched up, this will probably be the best version of the game.  Now, as for my thoughts on the game itself:I thoroughly enjoyed playing this game back when I played the SNES ROM translation and again with the Remaster, but my thoughts are the same: it will be a long, long time before I play all the way through it again.  This game is PACKED.  There are so many monsters to find and so many collectibles, and the jobs...there is such a wide variety of abilities that you can mix and match.  The best word I can use to describe this game is "overwhelming," and completing all of the achievements felt like a marathon.As far as the story is concerned, this is Square taking the four crystals formula and squeezing every last drop out of it.  It's no surprise that VI deviated so much from the ones that came before it, because this one took the tried and true story tropes from before and ran them into the ground.  That said, the characters aren't bad, but the heroes and villains are pretty one dimensional.  This game's story is pretty forgettable, but...The story is not what this game is known for.  It's the gameplay that makes this a gem.  They took the jobs system from III and went wild with it.  In the end, if you can grind it out, each of your characters can have access to 74 different abilities, which can be mixed and matched to your liking.  If you want to fashion a Dragoon Thief, you can do that.  Or how about a Blue Mage Ninja? Or a Berserker Monk? Sword-wielding Bard?  It's truly insane.  My only gripe is that this game is so packed, most likely you won't max out all of the abilities until literally the second-to-last room of the game.  Still, the fact that you get a constant stream of new abilities and passives while leveling throughout the entire game makes grinding so much fun.  One complaint often made about this game is the difficulty level.  It's true, many of the bosses and mobs are very challenging, due to the different types of status effects and one-shot mechanics.  However, if you use the abilities properly, you can come up with some cunning strategies that can kill many bosses in one-hit or with your characters on auto-pilot. That's the beauty of this game.  There's so much customization and strategy involved. By the end of it you are so mesmerized by the gameplay that you almost don't even care about the story.  All of that said, this game isn't for everyone.  This is NOT an entry-level Final Fantasy game.  Despite how much fun I had playing it, I can really only recommend it to people who enjoyed the other games and are looking for more of a challenge.  It's an incredibly special game and the last of its kind from that era, but I could see someone who is relatively new to the series getting overwhelmed and turned off. FFV would rank higher on many lists if it had a stronger story, but it's still a very high-tier Final Fantasy title due to outstanding game design.  If you've never played a Final Fantasy game before, revisit this one later.  If you enjoyed IV and VI, you will certainly enjoy this game.
