_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is my favorite. It reintroduces the job system from 3 and greatly improves it; encouraging experimentation without forcing it like 3 does, and allowing party members to dual-class and eventually tri-class when leveling more than one. And with 23 jobs to choose from, there's a lot of build options, and damn near all of them are viable.FFV is also a great starting point for the franchise, as it's the closest thing to a 'standard' Final Fantasy game. If you ask someone who's never played a FF game to conjure one up in their mind, V is probably the closest to what they'll think of. For a long time my recommended starting point for FF was to play IV and V back-to-back, and I still think that's a great way to experience it; even though now I'd say just start with the pixel remasters and play them in order.It's definitely not perfect though. There's exactly two dungeons (one of which is optional) where I was actively not having fun, and it does a common FF thing where it's fairly easy up until you reach the final boss, then it becomes wtf hard. You also essentially  to level at least a third of the job list to have the required stats for the final boss, and It  doesn't have the bonus content from the GBA release. Lacking bonus content is the case for all the pixel remasters, but V is the only one where the missing content makes me sad.That said, FFV is fantastic. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Back when I was going on my Final Fantasy spree in the early 00s, trying to play all of the titles in the series, being late to the party myself, FF V left me conflicted. On one hand, I remember enjoying the vast majority of the game and the way the Jobs (character classes of FF series) were handled. On the other, I also remember serious difficulty bumps, most notable one being the final boss that I simply could not defeat no matter how hard I’ve tried, which lead to a long and exhausting grinding session, before I was finally able to finish the game. Yet, with recent years Final Fantasy V has become a very popular entry, leading to really cool charity events like Final Fantasy Four Job Fiesta, and I was curious about replaying the game myself.Now with the Pixel Remaster version available, I was happy to see that my opinion on the game became more positive.Final Fantasy V is a curious title in the timeline of the releases. After IV has simplified things by taking out a lot of player choice with different systems and upgrades and focusing far more on the story and adventuring, while also being partially a revisit to a lot of the concepts from FFII, V is very much a return to the ideas of FFIII. You have a party of 4 people again and most of these people are unchanged and available throughout the entire game. They all start at a default class that has no special abilities and after some story events get more and more Jobs they can switch to at any point.Unlike III, every job is completely unique, so there’s no definitive progression that you aim for – you will never get a better White Mage or a different Bard, the abilities are unique to those classes only. However, every Job can be “mastered” after leveling it up to the maximum level. And every level of the Job makes one special trait of said job (either active or passive) available to be equipped for other Jobs. And that means that while all jobs are unique, you still can switch a Job to adapt for the situation, while not necessarily loosing the ability from the other class that you enjoy using. And also gives you the endgame incentive to master all jobs, which will, in the end, make your character incredibly customizable.Going for that, though, is pretty grindy. You can avoid most of the grind if you’re not interested in lots of optional challenges and unlocks, of course, like beating the two extremely tough superbosses (the first time these appeared in the series), but there would still be a few moments where you might feel slightly underleveled and underprepared for the encounter. Like that final boss fight that I’ve had so much trouble many years ago. Unfortunately, some of the obnoxious and grindy parts, while still optional, can happen pretty early on, like one timed section which isn’t difficult to just go through, but is ridiculously difficult to go through, while grabbing all treasures and getting all bestiary entries. It’s not a fun part of the game and I almost wish they’d up the timer at least in Pixel Remaster version. But that’s not the case and, in fact, I didn’t feel that the game rebalanced much if at all. Which isn’t surprising, I suppose, given how popular the original version has become for the challenge runs.I haven’t been talking about the story much, because it’s not that engaging for the most part in this one. Despite characters being considerably more nuanced and interesting in comparison with IV. The overall plot seems like a strange retelling of the Silmarillion, except mixed with the usual Four Crystals of Final Fantasy. And I probably shouldn’t be saying “usual”, since this was the last title in the series until FF XV to really focus on the Crystals and sometimes to feature them in a recognizable form at all. Either way, most of the time FFV isn’t played for the story, but that said, the game has many memorable moments and characters. And it also really pushed the expressiveness of the characters and the cinematography of the scenes for the franchise. The character of Gilgamesh is wonderful, going beyond a comic relief rival he’s at first presented to be. And the ending sequence in the game is genuinely moving and well delivered. But again – most of the time, you forget that the plot is there because it’s pretty simple and the characters have very simple motivations and needs.I’m glad that I’ve replayed Final Fantasy V, even though it remains not an entry I would name among my favorites. For a fan of jRPG mechanics, this is a gold mine, as you can challenge yourself with crazy party Job combinations and still be able to go through the game. For a fan of stories in Final Fantasy titles – it’s not the first choice for you. But it shouldn’t be the last either. I really liked the Pixel Remaster of Final Fantasy V, and you should check it out as well. Just be aware that it will take you at least twice as long as IV to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing off and on since release and have read quite a few bug posts, but in my 42 hrs I've only encountered a few minor things. Like if you're selecting magic from Spellsword, sometimes the cursor won't show up when you select your character to enchant, and if you finish the command the enchant won't work so you have to cancel back into the menu and re-select the magic to make the cursor appear. There are also a few instances of the Heal Staff not healing an ally even though it plays the hit animation, it just skips the heal (it's not a missed attack). The only other thing, and this seems a bit ridiculous, is that increasing your Weight stat by equipping heavier armor is shown as a Green (Good) stat instead of a Red (bad) stat. The higher your Weight, the slower your ATB charges so increased Weight should be shown as Red not Green.That said, they did a round of bugfixes not long after release and they are (as of the time of me writing this) working on a second round of bugfixes.Other than that, I think this one has been the best of the Remasters so far, slightly ahead of III. The graphics are exactly what you'd expect and not only did they deliver on the music, but there are some tracks here that I like more than the originals (The overworld theme for World 2 being a standout for me). They also didn't dumb down the difficulty like they did in some of the other remasters (though there are plenty of ways to break the game with so many class abilities being available).I've always been a fan of V from way back when the only way to play it was an English translated ROM, so maybe I'm a bit biased, but the PR doesn't disappoint.

_childDocuments_.review: POTENTIALLY THE BEST CLASSIC PIXEL FINAL FANTASYThis game slaps ass. I don't know what to say. A good thing I never really heard how good this game is before, because this game is very fun to play.Final Fantasy V is the fifth main installment of the Final Fantasy franchise and this is the Pixel Remaster Version which provides quality of life changes like auto battle, a world map, and more. I haven't played the past especially the original SNES version but I heard that this version is a much easier diffculty. Like baby-mode, which I disagree. This game can clap some ass if you're not prepared. Although this is how I think of the Pixel Remasters, coming from someone who never played the original version.Moving on to the game, I love this game. This game tone down abit its tone, story, from its predecessor, Final Fantasy IV, which has more serious and dark tone in its story and world building. In that game, people die left and right. Final Fantasy V took a more light-hearted and charming route, ramping up the comedy but still have some dark moments. I love the story. Many memorable and funny moments and character. I do admit at first I thought the characters are gonna be much inferior and forgettable than the last game which has more iconic characters like Cecil the Dark Knight, Kain the Dragoon, Rydia the Summoner. I also thought the jokes are gonna get on my nerves since my falling out of the MCU movies recently because of its overabundance of jokes. But I was wrong. I love all of the characters, iconic or not. The jokes land since the story never really took itself seriously. But when it wants to take it seriously, there are no jokes to ruin it. I love it.I'm gonna touch on the gameplay now since we're at this part. Final Fantasy V took Final Fantasy IV's combat system and Final Fantasy III's job system and mush it all into one package. You play as four characters that can each hold one job. Leveling up a job can give you access to a specific ability from that job which can be used in other jobs. I don't know how to explain, but think of you want to be a Black Mage but at the same time a Knight. Since you can't hold a sword as a Black Mage like a Knight can, you can level up that job and access its ability. Once attaining it, switch to the Knight job and voila, you can now access Black Magic at the same time being a sword wielding knight. This type of customisation can breed to a variety of playstyles and ways to play the game. Other than the enjoyable combat and job system, this game introduces the superbosses. I'm not quite sure if they are present in FFIV but this game have many superbosses that can give gameplay-changing rewards. I do admit I haven't beated them all yet at the time of writing this but I will try and fight them. Especially that pesky OMEGA. I've beaten your ass in FFXV and I'll beat your ass in a turn-based way that you'll never see the light of day again.It felt like the song and soundtrack found its footing in this game, creating a whole new identity for FFV. I've played some newer titles like FFVII. FFXIII, and FFXV and each of them have their own unique soundtrack representing them. This game, FFV, is the first one to have its own identity when it comes to soundtrack unlike past games where their default soundtrack is the Prelude and their world themes is what represent them. The soundtrack slaps ass is what I'm trying to say. NOBUO UEMATSU is a beast.I'm having trouble thinking of its flaws since I love all the characters which at first I thought is going to be forgettable. Probably I can say is the villain of the story which is cartoonishly evil and sometimes hilarious. But that doesn't count since the story itself didn't take itself seriously, like the villain itself. I love all the characters including the villain of the story here.Tldr: Charming, funny tale of adventure. A very enjoyable game. Overall had a blast of a time.5/5Edit: I changed the title from "THE MCU OF FINAL FANTASY" to a new title because I'm not really proud of the old one. The old title felt more degrading this game rather than praising it nowadays.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is a game I've tried to complete a fair number of times over the years but I didn't get super far and it never really clicked with me. But on the release of the Pixel Remaster I finally decided to hunker down and do it, and it was a truly joyous time. I can't make a lot of comparisons to the SNES version as I don't know it as well as I do the other series entries. If you've played the other Pixel Remasters, you have a very similar set of pros and cons here. You'll need to manually fix the font before you begin playing and there are some choices that some fans will enjoy and some won't. It's far from the visual train wreck that the previous PC and mobile releases were, though. Regardless of imperfections, the quality of the original game shines through. Despite a slow start and a few small bumps along the way, the game is excellent and a far better showcase of the job system than Final Fantasy III. Most of the classes are very viable or offer something worth getting to use with another class. The system is just plain fun to mess around with once you get into the possibilities. It's not always well balanced as there are some completely overpowered tactics, but through normal play that isn't an issue.The story is not as epic and captivating as FF4's but I still found myself emotionally attached to the main characters and enjoying their hardships and victories. It takes a while to ramp up compared to some of the other FF titles, but there are some truly fantastic scenes that any retro RPG fan will enjoy.Strongly recommend playing either the SNES, GBA or Pixel Remaster versions of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the best version of Final Fantasy 5 I've ever played. To compare it with the other PC version which is just ported from Mobile, this version blows it out of the water in its faithfully pixelated aesthetic and UI. Not having the extra content is a bit of a shame, but believe me when I say, the quality and faithfulness of the base game is far more important since that is what you'll spend the majority of your time playing. On top of all of this, the game has a fully recreated soundtrack which is a massive over all improvement in sound quality and overall enjoyment. In most songs, the instrumentation is much more diverse sounding and interesting. The only track I'd say that didn't see as much improvement would be The Decisive Battle. _childDocuments_.review: My first experience with FFV was the PS1 version and back then I didn't like it nearly as much as IV or VI that I had played on the SNES. Looking back my views might have been biased by the PS1 load times or other issues.Trying it again now and finally beating it I think this might be my favorite SNES Final Fantasy game and one of my favorites this series has to offer. Compared to its direct predecessor FFIV you can see a ton of impressive improvements to gameplay variety in the job system, boss difficulty and mechanics, and interesting graphical effects.The story is a typical 'save the world' narrative but it works because the game doesn't take itself seriously and is just a fuzzy feel good kind of game. The music is excellent, as would be expected by an Uematsu game, and the remastered tracks sound great to me.The remaster adds some gameplay functionality that make the game more convenient to play such as quick saves, auto-combat, and accelerated battle speed. It's easy enough not to use these if you want a more authentic experience but I appreciated them.The only thing that's missing is the extra content from the GBA version but after reading about it I don't think I missed out on much.It's not perfect (you probably will want a mod for the UI) but it's a great remaster and I wouldn't recommend playing any other version.

_childDocuments_.review: Great, great, great game!I've had an overall great time with this Pixel Remaster and almost everything seems to have been done right.This is a great favourite, so I'll give y'all a short rundown of the pros and cons here.Pros:-Great revised pixel art that's mostly consistent to the atmosphere of the original game while freshening things up pretty well-Some timing issues from earlier versions (especially the mobile remake's intro) have been mostly corrected-The original title sequence is intact! Mostly, just lacks credits.-Great rearranged soundtrack!-GBA translation with some minor updates, which has a great sense of humour-The original difficulty is mostly preserved, with some minor balance tweaks and bug fixes-Some graphical glitches present in the screenshots on the Steam page got fixed on launch day, that's a very appreciated effort!Cons:-The rearranged soundtrack is great, but the sound mix feels a bit rough and unbalanced at times.-The standard font is uncomfortable to read as usual.-Sometimes the mode 7 stuttering gets so bad it actually makes me feel almost nauseous, especially with an airship. I don't know how the stuttering got worse, but somehow it's happened and I greatly desire a definitive fix for this problem that's plagued the pixel remasters from the start.-The updated pixel art is pretty nice overall, but the differences can be so subtle it almost feels pointless at moments.-The old mobile version got scrapped in favour of this, with no crossgrade discount for those who owned it earlier. That just feels dirty, even if this version is mostly better from a technical standpoint.Overall I had a very good time with this remake of Final Fantasy V, probably the best I ever had.But I can absolutely feel the frustration of those who put money into the earlier mobile port that came to Steam that never had any support of any kind, to the point it was a dysfunctional mess from the start and only got worse later on.I'm not calling this a ripoff, but it does beg the question of why Square Enix even bothered with porting the mobile version to this platform if they were eventually just going to dump it.

Plus it gave us the lovable recurring villain that is Gilgamesh!FF5 is a masterpiece that holds up well to this day. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy V is one of my favorite games ever. Its just a really good game and I have probably beaten it more than any Final Fantasy. This is a great version, the music rocks, the pixel art is great and the spell animations for the most part are top notch. It beats the pants off the previous Steam version.Some of the downsides of this version is they got rid of the post game dungeon. It was pretty cool to have in some of the other versions but its not a deal breaker, it always felt pretty tedious going through the post game dungeon. Another thing that sucks is they nerfed some of the quick kills on some bosses, no more dark shocking, then Level 5 death on Atamos or death by math on pretty much any boss past the second world. The extra jobs from the GBA and Older Steam version is also gone but those are not as good as the base game jobs. One last nitpick is some of the achievements are a little grindy or tedious. Like mastering all jobs or picking up every hidden item, you basically need a guide for completion because some areas are closed off after getting though certain parts of the game.But, other than that, this is an awesome version, and unless you are really into speed running, I think this is probably the best version to get into. I love the job system in this game. There are so many broken combinations this game can be as hard or as easy as you want it to be, and it really encourages you to tackle some challenging bosses by mixing up your party composition and its awesome.Is Final Fantasy V the best in the series? No, that would probably go to VI, VII, IX, or X. But Final Fantasy V is just so much fun.If you are looking for a good length classic JRPG with a ton of heart, you can't go wrong with this version.

_childDocuments_.review: This remaster is not complete, you can tell by the inconsistencies in animations (ninja scrolls for example), the various bugs, soft locks experienced by others.  The pacing of this remaster is a bit out of sync.  If the the intent is trying to replicate an experience akin to that of the super famicom version, then this is an abject failure.  Patches should be in order to complete this remaster, but I'm not holding my breath.The only positive is that this is simply a "better" IOS port but without the extras which makes it playable on this platform, but for 15.99 people deserve better when a dev has so much to work with when it comes to 20+ year old content.Hope and pray they don't apply the same work ethic they did to this and FFIV to the FFVI pixel remaster.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: I'd forgotten just how long this game is.  Another solid entry for the Pixel Remaster series, the Uematsu-rerecorded soundtrack is baller, the gameplay systems are smooth, and all the completionist-lite "what did you get vs what did you miss" information systems are here.Thankfully, there's no "Pink Tail" or "hidden Summon" nonsense in this game like in IV;  It's much more accessible.  For those of you trying to 100% the game, I recommend creating a save before the end of the first and second world in case you find that you're missing something that didn't make its way into the third world.The characters are goofy, especially the primary protagonist 'Battsu', the antagonist 'Exdeath', and the antagonist's trifling crony, 'Gilgamesh'.  This is ultimately a long, big, feel-good adventure where Square paid homage to Final Fantasy's origins before beginning their inexorable drift away from crystals and classes.Final Fantasy 1-5 are 100%ed; Waiting on my favorite FF of all time to finish up the retrospective!

If so you'll probably enjoy this version. If you're approaching this from the perspective of a new player then I guess the question is "do you like completely customizable jRPGs?". _childDocuments_.review: It's a great version of the game but due to some critical bugs, I'm not sure that I can call it the definitive version of the game. I love Final Fantasy V and would recommend it to anyone with even a passing interest in JRPGs. I especially love the job system. However, be wary of these critical differences that would potentially make it less worthwhile than the other versions:* Chicken knife duplication bug that makes Ninja quite powerful* All equipment that grant buffs such as Reflect, Haste, so on expire upon being replaced with another status (Death, petrification, etc.). This means that borderline necessary equipment such as the Hermes Sandals are broken against the player's favor.* The ATB gauge has random starts at the beginning of battle, making agility almost completely useless in grindingI would call the advance version a superior definitive edition, but this also does a lot of good things! These bugs will most likely get fixed with time, or at least modded out.* Autobattle* Good soundtrack* Nice animations* Campy Exdeath dialogueThis game's story is like a saturday morning cartoon. The gotchas and intrigue are nice.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best ways to play Final Fantasy V in my opinion. Yes, the bonus content from the GBA version is missing, and that's going to be a deterrent to some, but if you can live without the post-game dungeon like I am, this is perfectly fine. What matters is the core gameplay and fun Job System are still there and as enjoyable as ever. I found it easier to experiment and swap abilities on the fly between battles since I could rely on Quick Save or Auto Save and could painlessly switch Abilities without having to go through the whole Job menu and have to redo my equipment setups.The presentation is great, just as the other pixel remasters are, but I think this is the one game in the series I've played so far where the remastered graphics and especially music are preferable to the original. There's something about the Pixel Remaster sound font that works really well with these compositions. The localization works really well, too: it's the same as the GBA version, adding a lot of lighthearted silliness to a game world that really benefits from it.This one also feels a lot less toned down difficulty wise than the other pixel remasters. FFV was never a difficult game per se, as it was open ended enough that you could beat it with nearly any job combination, but that works in favour of the game. It's completely doable to pick 4 random jobs and make your way through this game, and it's highly encouraged.There are a few bugs here and there that I came across, most notably a few boss encounters; I was able to somehow skip one minor boss only to have it show up later when I revisited the dungeon, and a certain timed boss fight in the last third of the game that's supposed to trigger a Game Over if time runs out... well, the game lets you fight it again without the timer resetting. I also experienced a soft lock during my first attempt at the final battle, but that may be due to me toggling auto-battle on/off for high speed. Nothing major, but something to be aware of.There's also a couple of subtle improvements and changes that I feel are worth mentioning. There's a certain superboss near the end who is now much easier to "avoid" if you don't wish to fight it. Most of the "timed" story scenes no longer require you to wait and just require you to interact with an object or talk to an NPC. The little telltale "pauses" in certain battles that serve as cues for certain bosses to change form are a bit harder to spot as the battles feel a lot "smoother" than the SFC version.My only real gripe is for completionism sake, it'd be much easier if the Bestiary was accessible through the menu while in-game instead of having to jump back to the title. When you're hunting down missable monsters, it's a bit of a pain to have to save, quit, load the bestiary, note down what you are missing, then start again. There's also the stuttering as you move along maps, but that's not a huge issue.Overall, absolutely recommended if you're looking for an excuse to play Final Fantasy V again, and a great version of the game for newcomers.

As for the difficulty, they seem to have buffed some of the bosses that needed buffing, and nerfed some of the bosses that... didn't really need nerfing so again, you win some you lose some.  Plus once again, they've somehow introduced some new bugs and glitches in this version but this time, they're actually working on fixing 'em, which is encouraging considering they just abandoned the other Pixel games the moment they got released; it's good to see FFV get some love...now if only they'd add the darn extra content, so I can get some semblance of a real challenge in this game

_childDocuments_.review: This is an awesome, often overlooked entry in the series, and I think this is definitely the best of the pixel remasters so far.Final Fantasy V is one of the entries that got lost in the shuffle. During the SNES days, it was a Japan only title, and when it finally made it over to West during the Playstation 1 era, the first port was not warmly received. It was a 2D game in a 3D era, further dragged down by the fact the port itself was not very good. The translation was cheesy, but not in a good way, and it had very long loading times between screens. FF5 is something of an oddity for a SNES era Final Fantasy. Sandwiched between arguably two of the series most depressing entries, It is mainly remembered as being a light-hearted adventure that is also light in narrative weight. But I don't think this is true. This a game where a lot of its personality comes from its humor, and its not that it's relatively straight forward story is lacking in plot twists or dramatic moments. I think it's just this is game that is defined more by its humorous scenes than its tragic ones.And that humor really shines in the pixel remaster thanks to an excellent script that had me chuckling many times. The music is also perfect with an orchestral score that is easily my favorite of these remastered soundtracks. The real star of this game is the jobs system. Much like Final Fantasy III, the characters can switch job classes freely throughout the game. But FF5 takes it one step further. As you battle the various monsters in your quest to save the elemental crystals from a mysterious evil bent on their destruction, you earn skill points that level up your job class in addition to experience points for your character's base level. When you level up the job class, you learn skills related to that job. Jobs come with a variety of passive perks as well as abilities you can use in battle. One of your two ability slots will always default to the special ability for that class, but the other slot is free for one ability of your choosing.This potential for mixing and matching is where the game really shines. You can come up with some crazy combos. Here's one of my favorites: mastering the archer class gives you a skill called rapid fire which allows you to hit four times per turn. Combine that with the monk who hits twice per turn with their bare fists. I was dealing an average of 1800 damage per punch, even more when monk dealt a critical hit. Now multiply that by 8 hits. I was steam rolling bosses in the final dungeon with this build. Unlike the other pixel remasters, the difficulty has not been downgraded very much if at all. This version is still quite challenging, and you are going to need to deploy clever tactics to get through its many hard dungeons and boss encounters, even if just by your fingernails. I spent over 30 hours on my first play through. While I believe it is appropriate that this entry was not streamlined like most of the others, keep in mind that this makes the game grindy and slow at times as you cleave your way through hundreds of random battles to master job abilities. But that's the way I like it, and I am really looking forward to the Final Fantasy VI remaster.

_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: It's amazing. The visuals and animations really perfected this game, while the interface made it really easy on the eyes and fingers. I feel this is the best way to experience Final Fantasy V at the moment. What I still like the most is the job system, which is very addicting and, thanks to the visual upgrades, very easy to maneuver around and play while enjoying all of the jobs included. The addition of a quick save function and auto save does make the game easier at times than it could have been otherwise but you will have difficult battles none the less, which will require thinking about what jobs you are using and what strategy you should employ. You can choose between wait and active mode (I chose active because of added difficulty) and that is a welcome option here because the combat feels really fluent in both cases. There are drawn maps for every location which is both beautiful and useful, and it doesn't hinder the joy of exploration too much. The treasure tracker makes it easy to know if there are any hidden items in towns or dungeons you visit.For the remasters of older Final Fantasy games, I waited most for this one, because it is definitely my favorite one and I am very satisfied with the result. I feel like I could return to this and play endlessly.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: All of these pixel remastered games have been great. This is the second in the entire pixel remaster set that contains the jobs system. What's great about this system though is that you get benefits for each job level that you advance which carries over into other jobs. So you could have a black mage that does the dragoon jump, or a knight that punches with their fists etc. Many jobs from FF3 Pixel Remaster are not in this one, as this one has some new jobs such as blue mage and time mage. Soundtrack is always amazing, the graphics are nicely done and the job system is fun. Highly recommend this.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY V

_childDocuments_.review: As per all the previous pixel series, the graphics/music/quality of life changes are great. Job system is interesting. After playing FFIV, the story and characters in this game are a pretty big letdown. I am 3 hours in, the main characters seem to have very generic and boring personalities and you are presented with very little back story or struggle the characters are going through to make you care about them. As a result, when things that are supposed to be dramatic happen, I felt little or nothing. Overall, if you like Final Fantasy, I would still recommend it.

name: FINAL FANTASY VI
detailed_description: FINAL FANTASY I-VI Bundle Purchase the bundle now to receive all soundtracks and wallpapers from FF1-6! Soundtracks and Wallpapers will unlock in line with each title’s launch. See individual store pages for details. The games that inspired a generation come to life once more, in the ultimate 2D pixel remaster! Purchase the bundle and receive FINAL FANTASY FINAL FANTASY II FINAL FANTASY III FINAL FANTASY IV FINAL FANTASY V FINAL FANTASY VI This bundle lets you purchase all six games from FINAL FANTASY 1 to FINAL FANTASY 6 at a discount price. It also contains a sound track, featuring total of 20 tracks and total of 14 unique wallpapers. Enjoy universally updated 2D pixel graphics and the beautifully rearranged soundtrack. Gameplay is improved with modernised UI, and extras such as a beastiary, illustration gallery and music player allow further immersion into the world of the game. ＊These games are newly developed remaster editions based on the original titles. Some of the changes and additional elements found in other remakes of these games are not included. About the Game A remodeled 2D take on the sixth game in the world-renowned FINAL FANTASY series! Enjoy the timeless story told through charming retro graphics. All the magic of the original, with improved ease of play. The War of the Magi caused magic to disappear from the world. A thousand years later, humanity relies on machines - until they find a young woman with mysterious powers. The magicite system allows players to customize which abilities, magic spells, and summons the party members learn. All the playable characters have their own stories, goals, and destinies. Journey through their interwoven fates in this sweeping melodrama. The pinnacle of the FF series at the time of its release, FFVI remains critically acclaimed and beloved to this day. ------------------------------------------------------------- ■Beautifully revived with new graphics and sound! Universally updated 2D pixel graphics, including the iconic FINAL FANTASY character pixel designs created by Kazuko Shibuya, the original artist and current collaborator. Beautifully rearranged soundtrack in a faithful FINAL FANTASY style, overseen by original composer Nobuo Uematsu. Reimagined cinematic-style opera scene, complete with newly recorded vocal performances. ■Improved gameplay! Including modernized UI, auto-battle options, and more. Switch the soundtrack between the rearranged version, created for the pixel remaster, or the original version, capturing the sound of the original game. Now possible to switch between different fonts, including the default font and a pixel-based font based on the atmosphere of the original game. Additional boost features to expand gameplay options, including switching off random encounters and adjusting experience and magic AP gained multipliers between 0 and 4 Dive into the world of the game with supplemental extras like the bestiary, illustration gallery, and music player. (This remaster is based on the original 'FINAL FANTASY VI' game released in 1994. Features and/or content may differ from previously rereleased versions of the game.)
about_the_game: A remodeled 2D take on the sixth game in the world-renowned FINAL FANTASY series! Enjoy the timeless story told through charming retro graphics. All the magic of the original, with improved ease of play. The War of the Magi caused magic to disappear from the world. A thousand years later, humanity relies on machines - until they find a young woman with mysterious powers. The magicite system allows players to customize which abilities, magic spells, and summons the party members learn. All the playable characters have their own stories, goals, and destinies. Journey through their interwoven fates in this sweeping melodrama. The pinnacle of the FF series at the time of its release, FFVI remains critically acclaimed and beloved to this day. ------------------------------------------------------------- ■Beautifully revived with new graphics and sound! Universally updated 2D pixel graphics, including the iconic FINAL FANTASY character pixel designs created by Kazuko Shibuya, the original artist and current collaborator. Beautifully rearranged soundtrack in a faithful FINAL FANTASY style, overseen by original composer Nobuo Uematsu. Reimagined cinematic-style opera scene, complete with newly recorded vocal performances. ■Improved gameplay! Including modernized UI, auto-battle options, and more. Switch the soundtrack between the rearranged version, created for the pixel remaster, or the original version, capturing the sound of the original game. Now possible to switch between different fonts, including the default font and a pixel-based font based on the atmosphere of the original game. Additional boost features to expand gameplay options, including switching off random encounters and adjusting experience and magic AP gained multipliers between 0 and 4 Dive into the world of the game with supplemental extras like the bestiary, illustration gallery, and music player. (This remaster is based on the original 'FINAL FANTASY VI' game released in 1994. Features and/or content may differ from previously rereleased versions of the game.)

More in the second half for me. My save file would not load once so I had to ALT+TAB to end the process and restart steam for it to work. _childDocuments_.review: I have replayed this entry for many rounds, from SNES, to GBA, to 2014 version, and the current pixel remastered version. Everytime the experiences are very fresh and new. In PP, I can still found a new scene that I haven't explored yet ! The replay values include the character customization (if you can withstand the difficulty to train in early phase), experiment with different jobs combination, and revisit the incredible story (there are some stories you need to explore by yourselves, as the game do not explain everything to you, very subtle, not over-explaining, which is a good way to let us imagine the backstory of each characters and events). And mastering Gau is the best way to replay!As for the gameplay, I didn't grind and farm much, just proceed with the dungeon with proper character, magicite, and equipment management. It is much challenging and fun to battle the boss when your level is not too high (challenge Kefka between level between 35-45, his Havoc Wing can make you almost die). FULLY UTILISE THE ATB SYSTEM for advance player (make it "ACTIVE" mode!). This mechanic need you to strategize before battle, think and take fast action during battle. Another best mechanic in FF6 is the shift character function (Z key) during battle (need "Active" mode), which add another layer of battle strategy and adapt to different circumstances.Downside:- The character customization is like a double-edge sword (if you can withstand the difficulty to train in early phase).- SInce PP is based on SNES version, not much post game contents.- Some contents in the GBA version (and 2014 version) are not included in this game 🥲

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best JRPGs of all time. If you asked me what my favourite FF was, I'd probably answer 6. A classic by all possible accounts, hugely influential and pretty much universally beloved, even by people who aren't fans of the genre. It has a freaking opera scene written for it (which received multiple adaptations), the design of the final boss seems to reference Dante's Divine Comedy... it is, without a doubt, a masterpiece.Right?Full disclosure: this is not a review of this particular port of FF6. This is a review of FF6 as a whole, written for someone who's yet to experience this journey, and is on the fence about getting it (so no spoilers). I played the game three times. Once as a teenager, once as a young adult, and just before writing this - but this time with an observer, so I could see how someone who doesn't have any nostalgic connection to the game would react to its powerful scenes.The verdict of this little experiment is: it's a very mixed bag of a game, with lots of unfulfilled potential, strange design decisions, stunted writing, story that makes surprisingly little sense, underdeveloped characters... but with some undeniably amazing music, a fun battle system and some very tight pacing in the first half of the game. In other words, I think you're better off playing something else, unless you're interested in FF/JRPG history.FF6 is pretty unique as it has no less than 14 playable party members (3 of which are optional), and not one of them really feels like the definitive protagonist. Due to the way the story is presented, you can choose anyone you like to be the lead, and it will still make some kind of sense. But this approach introduces more issues than it's worth.For one thing, it simply doesn't allow any real personality or personal growth for any of the characters. What, that's nonsense, I hear you say, Mass Effect 3 has ~15 party members and all of them are distinct and have personal arcs. The problem is that FF6 is an almost 30-year-old SNES game, storage space was limited, and the script is somewhat short at ~25k words (GBA version; for reference, FFT has ~80k, FF10 has 120k, and Mass Effect 3 has a whopping 430k). As such, most characters have maybe 5 scenes defining their personality, and... that's it.Usually, these scenes are very short, but some are essentially mini-chapters of the game. I don't necessarily hate this: in fact, the script's brevity keeps the game's story moving at a very satisfying pace - I'd say it's the game's greatest strength. And besides, it's possible to tell great stories in just a few words.But FF6 doesn't do that. Instead, the characters are (mostly) static, archetypal, their relationships to each other almost nonexistent (there are exceptions, but even then they're rather shallow). Which is very strange, because I could've  that this game had deep, interesting characters! Maybe it's because of their expressive sprites?I suspect this game's script is a little like pixel art. Because it's somewhat lo-fi, a lot of the engagement comes from your mind filling in the blanks. This might've worked in 1994 - or rather, it very much did work in 1994 - but in 2023 we established that games in fact  have detailed, mind-bending stories even while still being told mostly via text, as f.ex. Disco Elysium has shown (over 1 million words, for the record!)The writing is somewhat dry, but functional. They could've expanded the script in this remaster, fleshed it out so it's up to standard in 2023, but they didn't, and that's also a respectable decision - keep it the way it was. In general, it's okay if you don't have high expectations - the first half of the game reads like a passionate amateur story. It introduces new characters, concepts, some minor worldbuilding... even some drama. Sadly, some things got removed from the original version (e.g. at a certain point, one character is getting beaten up - but they got rid of that, and it really diminishes the power of the scene). Still, it's enjoyable and it just flows - the gameplay mixes with the story well, even if the story's rather light on things like foreshadowing, themes etc. Then, there's a plot twist. It's a pretty good plot twist; or so does everybody say. Including myself. But seeing it now, after all this time, yet again... it's still good, but not  good as I remember.And then the story just kind of... leaves. The game loses its main narrative arc, only to regain it at the very end. Instead, it opts for multiple smaller stories. Alas; they're also quite shallow, often don't make much sense, the writing is somehow even worse. It's best to think of them as excuses for you to explore the world and do dungeons, fight bosses, collect treasure. Now, Chrono Trigger did the same thing - except in CT's case it happens literally right at the end, it's very "sidequesty" and there's less characters, so the narrative depth of those escapades can be a bit higher.To give you an example of why I consider this game's writing bad - at some point, you meet a character who used to be your friend. He's depressed, drinking his days away, saying that he lost his dream, there's no point anymore. Then, your party leader asks: "Have you tried... getting a new dream?". And the punchline?  He just says "wow, I didn't think of that! Thanks! Let's go!". This approach to mental issues is so common and unhelpful  that it's become a bit of a meme in neurodivergent circles. "Wow, thanks! I'm cured of depression!"Or there's this gem. One of your characters is a confused young woman who for some reason is obsessed with figuring out what love is. There is no love interest, there is no real reason for her to be obsessed with it, but she makes this conundrum her entire personality. This might've been seen as deep and poignant back then, but now it just makes you roll your eyes, especially since the payoff to this whole arc is weak at best.This one's alright. It's a bit weird, some characters feel completely overpowered compared to others, but it works somehow. There's a lot of depth to the battle system: status effects, different kinds of instakill abilities, elemental resistances, and every character has their own battle command. Locke, the thief, can Steal from enemies, Sabin, the monk, can use Blitz attacks, Shadow, the assassin, can Throw shurikens and so on. I've seen complaints that this game is too easy to "break open" - but that's only the case when you read about the enemies' weaknesses as well as ability combos online. On your first playthrough, I'd say you're going to have just enough of a challenge - especially since this version is rebalanced somewhat, making the game harder. I still wouldn't call it "hard" per se, just don't expect to steamroll everything without trying.Oh, and the game has random encounters - and you can't turn them off. There's an item that prevents them from happening, but that's rather late into the game, and I wouldn't recommend doing that due to EXP loss.Writing this has been hard. Taking apart a work of art that I considered an absolute masterpiece for the majority of my life, knowing full well that I'm going to piss off a lot of people... well, I think that looking back at what you used to enjoy some 10-20 years ago with a fresh, critical look is something that we all should do sometime. That's the main reason why I did it.FF6 definitely was a masterpiece, back in the day. Influential, innovative, fresh. But since then, a lot of better games have appeared, ironically also because of FF6's influence. Perhaps it's time to stop dreaming about the lost past, and start looking towards the future. It's what Grandpa would've wanted, isn't it?

_childDocuments_.review: The praises levied towards this game as being one of, if not the, best final fantasy game are completely justified. I'd never played this game prior to getting this pixel remaster on steam, but even now, as an adult that never played the original ever growing up, I can say this game is incredible. It's still not my favorite, since I don't think it will topple 10 from that throne for me, but it's certainly an amazing game and it definitely rivals 9 and 10 as being among my favorites in the series. The characters are amazing and the story told is gripping and awe-inspiring throughout the entire playthrough. It's admittedly not perfect, as I found that there are some unfair things that come up during combat (because it's a turn based RPG and those things happen), the most egregious example being enemies freezing your entire party, and then you can't move and they proceed to wipe you out before you're able to move again. However, those moments are few and far between, and generally, the gameplay is solid throughout. If you haven't played 6 yet and you're a Final Fantasy fan, do yourself a favor, this game is seriously amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY VI

_childDocuments_.review: I originally played this one when it came ot as "Final Fantasy III" for the SNES and I loved it. Re-playing it now it feels like the same game in a way the other Pixel Remakes don't quite feel the same to the original, maybe because this one was kind of the bridge between classic and modern Final Fantasy and it didn't need too many modifications to look better, since the original came out late in the SNES's life cycle and looked pretty good. Compared to the other FF Pixel Remakes, the character sprites are noticeably bigger and have more diverse animations. As for the story, well, it's a classic and the first time the series moved away from the traditional medieval fantasy in favor of the more high-tech setting you see in most Final Fantasy games to this day. The story and characters are the most detailed they've ever been up to this point in the series, and the game does a great job of keeping most game mechanics and systems from previous entries but tweaking them a bit. This is probably the most famous of the first six games, and it still holds up to this day. A classic in every sense of the word.

_childDocuments_.review: 9.5/10Final Fantasy VI is the game that I was anticipating the most not only of the pixel ff games, but of ALL of the ff singleplayer games... and man did this game not only meet my expectations, but it really exceeded it imo.StoryI know that the story was going to be good, but wow was it AMAZING. The whole game has two halves of it, the idea of bonds, war, and the consequences of the actions people take just to win a battle in any mean necessary like poisoning an entire castle. The second half however is when the game's main meaning truly kicks in, losing someone, and dealing with that loss. This was when the game's story TRULY became magical, and while both acts I equally love, the idea of overcoming loss, and how there is meaning in life is what will stick to me whenever I think of final fantasy VI. It is just wonderful, and if I had to complain just a little bit, it would be that the section where you split into three different scenarios was a bit of a story halt, and some character's introduction like yeti or that mimic were just strange imo. However I still LOVED the story and just wish I could actually re-experience it again.CharactersThis was the first time in a Final Fantasy game where the characters were not only amazing, but were TRUE characters and not only had their flaws and story development, but own themes, tragedies, and overcoming those tragedies. While some of the older FF games had character, they are nowhere near as close of character quality and development as in FF6. The game even takes breaks in the story simply to develop the character, which some may see as filler, but the scenes were so damn good that it made me care for them so much more. Nearly all of them experience loss in some form or another, and watching their journey overcoming it brought a tear to my eye in many moments in the game. Terra's goal searching and trying to figure who she is, Celes and Locke's love conflict and overcoming their loss, Seltzer's attempt of forgetting her love one's death by attempting replacement, then finally accepting her gift were beautiful. The only complaint I have of the characters is that not everyone is treated equally in terms of character Development. The game doesn't have a main character, as the mc is whoever you think should be the main character, however some characters like mog, mimic, or the yeti were simply given very little character, which sure they are side optional characters, but strago isn't given nearly as much care for his development like the others, which maybe due to them wanting focus on others, but is something to point out.GameplayThe ATB system returns, and while the class system does not return, it is replaced by individual characters having much more unique skills, which was an amazing choice for how the game works, as their skills were not only something only they can do, but it was their character, like seltzer having an actual slot machine as his skill, using randomness to achieve his goal. Not all of the characters are balanced equally, as some skills are just kinda worthless, like sure Celes has the ability to soak any magic spell, but it doesn't soak ALL spells, and why bother when the best attacks are magic, and it even soaks YOUR spells. Meanwhile Terra gets a skill that doubles her magic output. While yeah it isn't all equal, they each served their role and I found use in every character... except that yeti and mimic they just suck cause you can barely control them. Lastly I love the ATB system so it is a huge positive for me, if I were to talk about how it is used in ff6, it flows much better due to the active time bars moving even while animations play, which used to pause in older ff games. It is a huge improvement, but kinda hurts itself in endgame, as everyone's speed are so fast, and animations are so long, that it kinda turns into a queue system as by the time an animation plays yours or the enemies are already ready to attack. Still, I loved the combat in this game, and mainly complain about that part and some bad skills, also buffs and debuffs are much less important due to that reason.Musicwow, the music in ff6 was just... perfect. Not only did it have the standout songs, like most FF games, it however had THE standouts songs AND overall music was just AMAZING, while usually older FF games, it has the highs and lows. I could easily listen to the entire ost, and listen to it again, maybe even shed a tear cause its that damn good. Terra's Theme, Magitek Factory theme, Locke Theme, Searching for Friends Theme, Kefka's many boss themes, Seltzer's Theme, I can go on and on for how many of the songs I just LOVED. Each character having their own theme, but also having variations for the story to have an epic, and a sad version which is simply AMAZING. Just listening back to them can make me cry, and the battle theme was AMAZING in this game, including the boss theme man it was too damn good.Boss Design, Dungeons, and DifficultyThe Bosses in this game were actually pretty good for a turn based, some of them like Ultros were always a treat to encounter just to see their funny dialogue. Mechanic wise the bosses had pretty fun things you had to worry about, instead of just spam A to win without strategy like the much, much older FF games. The boss designs weren't FORCED mechanics like in FF3, but they still had those few oddballs that had more annoying mechanics, usually those who had magic reflection + multiple enemies, and doom was kinda annoying, but overall I liked it. Dungeons were also really amazing, especially as they had a ton of unique songs just for them, and had much more variety in their designs, only didn't like the Floating continent, and while I did enjoy the separate party dungeons, I do think they could def be improved but were held back my hardware limitations. Difficulty was also easily in a sweet spot for me personally, where it felt hard but doable. Obviously not SMT or Souls game hard, but felt like a nice touch of hard instead of being too easy where I auto-battle most of the way through like the nes FF games.Nitpicks/Last Positives-Kinda wish Relm and Strago's Character were more developed, they were introduced a bit too late in the story and aren't given enough love like the other characters.-Relic system is good, still prefer class system but for this game it makes sense, def super fun to play with an experiment but the broken combos were the most fun to work for.-Kinda Wish Esper system was a bit tuned, the level up bonus for example could be done without as it allows you to make non-magic users, also broken magic users which kinda dislike for story reason. - I can't express how amazing the characters were in this game alongside the story, EASILY the best part of FF6.- I wish this game got the remake instead of FF7, but it makes sense since pixel art still holds up while early 3d is ugh, but I still like the small bits where they used hd 2.5 like the opera scene THAT was amazing.ConclusionFinal Fantasy VI is EASILY the best pixel final fantasy game, and a contender for the best single player Final Fantasy game period. The Idea of how do you deal with loss, the characters, sooo much of this game was near perfection. The only thing holding it back are the nitpicks and issues that add to it not being a 10/10 game for me, but a 9.5 is super nearing that anyways so it doesn't matter. If someone told me this was their favorite game of all time I wouldn't blink twice, and I easily recommend ANYONE to play this game if you are a seasoned FF or a newcomer to the series, as it will tug your heart strings at least once.9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun with a great modernized soundtrack, and the art style (minus the brighter world map) is faithful to the SNES version.It's pretty buggy at times. The audio on map changes doesn't always fade in/out and rather just starts playing on top of the other song, but only sometimes on some instances. Also there seems to be missing music in areas where there should be music so it's just dead silence for a few minutes. Also, some of the sound effects and background sounds are awful. Worst I've ever heard. The wind BGS, the fire BGS, and the magitek/ chocobo step sounds come to mind. They are wretched. Obviously the font is still the small skinny font, but that's easy enough to fix. There are graphical errors where the player will appear underneath upper level assets (south figaro has 1). I found a few of the relics don't function as described either. The biggest issue by far is the screen tearing. It's BAD - diagonal scrolling is like a jittering earth quake (esper flashback), but you'll notice it from walking or running around towns. It's easy to spot. Also, loading seems to have an odd delay. You load the game, the map loads, the music plays, and it's like 10 seconds before the game let's you control everything. Also, small gripe, but the placement of the choice selections are a mess. Sometimes they're up top with a message window, sometimes they show up on the bottom for no reason. Sometimes you have to press *litterally any button* to advance the text to show it, sometimes they just show up automatically without your input.I know I've gone on a bit about what I don't like, but the thing is. It's quite likely that Square will patch most of this stuff out and fix it. I played for a solid 10 hours today and truly enjoyed the time. The clean graphics and beautiful soundtrack, being wide screen, it all does make it feel like a fresh game. Out of all the Pixel Remasters, it's the one I've most enjoyed playing though. Happy gaming everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY VI

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of this game ever since it first released in North America as Final Fantasy III, I now regard this as the definitive version of the game, with a couple of caveats. First, it doesn't have the new Espers introduced in the Game Boy Advanced version, or the Dragon's Den bonus dungeon. I personally never felt those additions to be essential to the experience, but players of the GBA version may miss them. Second, prepare yourself for the Opera House scene. The rearranged orchestra is great, and visually it's never looked better, but.. well, I'm hesitant to provide more details than that, as it felt like it was meant to be a surprise. You will have to take my word for it and judge for yourself when you hear it.Finally, I highly recommend taking the time to download one of the many mods available to fix the font. There is one available for the SNES version's font that is superb. I only ran into one potential issue, where at a certain part of the game one of the longer dialogue prompt choices was cut off because the default font is quite a bit smaller than the one provided by the mod.Overall, I was pleasantly surprised with how this version of my favorite Final Fantasy ended up. The new orchestral arrangements of the songs are excellent, the backgrounds during battles have never looked better, and--with sincere apologies to Ted Woolsey's fans--the localization this time around is absolutely spot on. Must play.

I myself have not used the boosts on "My" game however I am showing my younger son who has recently takin an interest in turn based RPG games and showing him my all time favorite RPG game from my childhood. The boosts have come in handy for his shorter attention span and help remove "The boring parts" so that he is more engaged. Minus one point for changing from its original form with no option to revert it to its original form. A must buy for any fan of the series.AAAHHH! Son of a (K-word here),Submariner, Sand-worm!??? _childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy VI is a certified classic and this is the 5th new version of the game. This version of the game is probably one of your best options for experiencing the game if it is your first time. Prior versions have had issues like some censorship needing to be applied to the localization of the original SNES release,  the extremely long loading times of the Playstation release, the reduced sound quality and oversaturation to compensate for the lack of a backlight in the GBA version, and the prior Mobile/Steam port having a really bad UI design and terrible redrawn graphics. This version tries to stay faithful to the original vision of the Japanese Super Famicom release which means the bonus items and dungeons from the GBA version are not here, but in the place you get a better overall presentation. The soundtrack's recompositions are amazing and really enhance this version of the game's feel, at times the added graphical effects look amazing, especially when it comes to things like water and fire in towns, and the Opera gets a complete facelift with HD-2D elements being introduced, and the Opera even has vocals in multiple languages (although you cannot change the audio language on its own, it is tied to your text language). These added flairs are a welcome addition, although there are a few issues when it comes to the new presentation.  The Overworld seems to be based on the GBA tileset which leads to the issue of oversaturation, as the greens of the grasses pop out way too much compared to the subdued darker shade that the original SNES version used. The opening credits when Biggs, Wedge, and Terra march to Narshe are also removed which looks rather awkward as those credits helped add to the cinematic feel of this opening in the original, while in this remaster it looks really damn good, but some of that cinematic quality is lost without the credits being there, leading to an awkward feeling 2 minute trek across the snow. This may be a dealbreaker to some people but some censorship that was in previous versions of the game have been carried over to this new version. When you first meet Celes, the sprite of her chained to the wall and the animations of the guards beating her are removed from the SNES version. This was a carryover from the GBA version and was originally removed due to CERO restrictions which would bump up the game's age rating and would limit sales in Japan. Presumably this was carried over for the same reason. The one armed salute from Gehstalian generals in a flashback scene have also been removed and replaced with a two armed one to avoid potential Nazi connections. The Siren Esper also is censored in this version, using a sprite similar to the old mobile and steam port with a short skirt to cover her butt. It does not seem like any of the other sprites or any other story sequences were censored, but just keep these in mind if this could be a dealbreaker for you. Most of these are very minor or have understandable reasons so it really shouldn't effect the gameplay experience.The enhanced gameplay from the other remasters is present in this version with autobattle and the minimap, which can be pretty useful for level grinding and for navigation.  Overall this remaster is a good product and a great way to experience this game for newcomers and old time fans alike, just keep in mind some of the minor issues.

_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY VI

_childDocuments_.review: This the first in the series where I loved every single character and their own separate story arcs. It's also the very first to move away from crystals as a standpoint, and it created a much deeper, emotional ride than its predecessors.  Final Fantasy VI sticks with the successful formula of the ATB Battle System, but this time with the aid of Espers - which in my opinion - were implemented in the perfect way. You don't need a job system to carve your characters in a certain light; the Espers allow you to head them in whichever direction you want, teaching them the magic they will need to fill a certain position in the party.  FFVI also has the largest cast in the series, and you would think that some would feel forgotten about, but they don't. Each has their own unique story you can unravel, if you're willing to invest the time in to finding every scene and secret.  And last but definitely not least, the music has taken on new life, and is completely mesmerising, just as it was in the nineties.  Ultros for Prime Minister!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY VI

_childDocuments_.review: Whoever is doing the soundtracks for these pixel remasters is psychotically in love with trumpets, violins and electric guitars. FF4 remake had that godawul cat-screeching/elephant noise trumpet to start every battle. They toned that down a bit here but decided to add it in a few lines later and make it just as annoying and pronounced. Once you hear it, you cannot unhear it, so have fun with that in EVERY BATTLE. God i just listened to it on youtube again to make sure I wasn't imagining it and yep, it's just absolute garbage.The mini-boss/boss battle theme "Decisive Battle" ditches the trumpet for some Lindsey Sterling-eqse violin, which isn't THAT bad, but throw some glam rock guitar playing in at the same time  What in the world is going on with this? It actually sounds like two tracks playing on top of each other and it is AWFUL. Just straight up rotten.Atma weapon theme sounds distant and suppressed. Dancing Mad has the most uninspired vocals I think I have ever heard in my life. The weird midi pseudo voices from the SNES version have more personality to them, somehow.All the other themes....I think they are pretty good for remasters. No major liberties taken with them and they do, for the most part; they sound like updated versions of the originals. So why a negative review just for the music? Because everyone knows that in the annals of video game history FF6 is one of the best soundtracks of all time. It was an absolute watershed accomplishment for sound in video games and the tracks you are going to hear the most (the battle themes) are the ones they messed with the most. They are awful. It's like if you took the Mona Lisa and drew a mustache on it for real. Some people would be like "wow it really adds a lot to the picture, gives it a different perspective...maybe Mona Lisa isn't female after all?!! Makes you think huh!? wow what a bold and amazing change they made to it, it really modernizes the art and makes it more of an enigma than before!" and as insane as that sounds, that's the exact same thing you get with people praising these awful new themes. Can't wait for the modders to replace the soundtrack with the original. Until then, not wasting my time with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy VI is not only one of the best games of the Final Fantasy series and of all RPGS in general but also one of the best games of all time.The visuals and audio that are still incredible 30 years later after the original release, fortunately Pixel Remaster faithfully gives a few tweaks to both but never intruding in the art and music direction too much that it would distort the original and under the guidance of the original authors and for sure the music in particular will stay with you for long after you play.The main story is great and the game starts with one of the best openings in a game and throughout it always has a clear goal that never gets dull since they were wrote it in a way in which they weren't afraid to go from deep serious moments to lighthearted and even funny but in a thoughtful way rather than a quippy mess as the way they write nowadays that you can never get a scary, tense, serious or thoughtful moment that is immediately ruined by a stupid quip that nullifies all that came before.Due to this approach mentioned above, it lends the game to be full of iconic and memorable moments, from supplexing a phantom train, to unexpectedly singing in an Opera, to fighting an annoying talking octopus monster in the sky, to experiencing for the first time the most iconic laugh in gaming, fortunately it never stops having these small fantastic moments in the main story, while in parallel it gets to explore all the side stories and subplots of our full cast of truly diverse and fleshed out characters all with their destinies and past beautifully intertwined in an organic way in which everything gets resolved neatly at the end.Definitely a must play experience for all fans of Final Fantasy, and for fans of RPGs in general and even for other players it's worth at least a try to see if it might spark and connect with you and lead you on forward to this fantastic adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY VI

_childDocuments_.review: Leagues above the "RPG maker" port they released a while back, with a lot of quality of life improvements along the way (minus that awful font).I don't think it's the definitive version of FF6, but it is the best version outside of the original SNES. As for the game itself, it's one of the best JRPGs ever made. You should play it.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY VI

_childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy VI is often viewed as a bit of an outlier in terms of its story; it doesn’t rely on the formulaic Crystals, nor are players controlling destined Warriors of Light—in fact, it is one of the design philosophies that FFVI isn’t even supposed to really have a singular character that could be pointed out as the game’s protagnist.At the very least, the game opens with players controlling Terra. A mind-controlled soldier of the Empire that is on a global conquest, brutally invading and annihilating any resistance to its Magitek regime. Very early on, however, Terra manages to break free after coming face-to-face with an Esper and is then introduced to the organized resistance group Returners, from which a grander story of both resistance against the Empire, the nature of the Espers, and the schemes of the antagonist Kefka unravels.I do not think that FF usually features fantastic writing, or usually they come with large caveats, such as FFIV featuring really gritty scenes of self-sacrifice but handwaving a lot of it by involved characters miraculously still surviving. FFVI is a nice exception to this—both its main plot and the surrounding sidestories are exceptionally well developed. Nevertheless, I don’t agree with the praise that Kefka usually receives—evil, truly just evil, characters are difficult to write, and Kefka himself, while I understand that his role in the story was curated with this sort of archetype in mind, remains disappointingly underdeveloped, with merely a single, optional dialogue even referencing as to how he became as deranged as he is.The second aspect to the quality of the writing, which is also mirrored in some gameplay elements, is that the comparatively large cast of playable party members aren’t also equally sharing in story content, and the difference is a little gross. Characters like Terra, Locke, and Celes may all be considered the “main” character, sure, but equally there are a bunch of characters that get little to no content whatsoever. Gau, for example, is an early character that you meet even before some of the last “main” characters, and he receives a single scene centered around him very late in the game.In essence, I think that there simply are too many characters within the main cast, which leads to a lot of them feeling underwhelming. The antagonist is a little ill-defined and ultimately can even ruin some more serious and twisted moments of the story, and it feels like enjoying Kefka and his role as the antagonist hinges a lot on the player going out of their way to interpret more into him than the game shows by itself. FFVI is a very classic Final Fantasy—while it doesn’t feature a job selection, it keeps the ATB gauge, which is a system to determine turn order in combat while also allowing for a more active combat style rather than just selecting your action with no concern to the enemy’s actions. While normally, I would consider the lack of customizeable jobs/classes as a bit of a negative, it is one instance where the large cast of party members works out in FFVI’s favor, at least mostly, as each of the recruitable characters comes with their own unique ability around which players can then customize their abilities. The big issue I have with this is that a good number of characters are very weirdly designed. For example, one party member is an archetypical Blue Mage, a class that learns skills from seeing enemies use them. He functions exactly the same here—and then you have a second character, ostensibly also a Blue Mage, though he only learns enemy skills if you fight them in a special zone of the game, then he vanishes for a few turns before returning. It’s a Blue Mage with extra steps. I take a bit of an issue with this, as many of these, especially optional recruitable characters, come more across as poorly thought-out gimmicks than full-party additions.Something Final Fantasy VI excels at still is optional content, as the game is broadly split into two major chapters, the second one being rife with optional dungeons, sidequests, and secrets to hunt. It does make exploration feel the best out of all Final Fantasy games that I have played so far, and I am happy to extend similar praise to the dungeon design—gone is the linearity of the early titles, but it hasn’t gotten so deep into the gimmicky designs of the later titles that they become actively tedious to play.Balancing is pretty solid as well. I never had the impression that I needed to grind to continue the story. Some gear combinations are incredibly overpowered but aren’t easy to figure out necessarily, as the game has an odd tendency to only list the full effects of an accessory in a different description window. Stat growth is also handled a little bit differently to other Final Fantasy games. Upon leveling up, HP and Mana are the only stats that increase, whereas Strength, Magic, Speed, etc., are based on the Esper / Summon this character has equipped. This is an okay system that incentivizes frequent experimentation with Espers, which hooks also back into how abilities are acquired, but can also feel a little punishing early on when the player does not have any Espers to equip and thus may feel like they are “wasting” their level ups.Finally, while I usually do not consider achievements in my own reviews, I figured to mention that the game is a bit nightmarish for completionists due to a single achievement that is entirely based around RNG. In fact, this entire review right now is being written while I’m going on seven hours of auto-battling for it. Fun.Fantastic. Having played and dropped Final Fantasy VI multiple times in the past, I was utterly blown away by how much of a glow-up the Pixel Remaster version gave the game. I won’t go as far as to say it looks , but the quality of the sprites, backgrounds, and especially the visual effects for spells is fantastic.Sound design between music and the various sound effects is equally improved and even features voice-acting during one iconic sequence. Overall, just as phenomenal as the visuals. A final very nice addition is an immediately accessible gallery in the main menu, featuring a selection of concept art to browse as well as a music player.While the game ran overall very well, I also did experience two instances of the game softlocking after combat, wherein it would just not accept any further inputs while also not ending combat, forcing me to restart the game back into the main menu.As I slowly go through the remainder of Final Fantasy games that I have yet to finish, I keep being positively surprised by titles I had not given a proper chance in the past. Final Fantasy VI in particular was not a title I had high hopes for, but after a reasonably slow start, it swiftly developed into what I would now consider to be the best mainline title of the series. The base game alone features a fantastic story, strong main character writing, and now also amazing presentation thanks to the Pixel Remaster.
