_childDocuments_.review: Title: Final Fantasy VI: Mastering the Art of Magic in a World of ChaosFinal Fantasy VI, a crowning jewel of the RPG genre, showcases Square Enix's unparalleled ability to craft immersive worlds, compelling narratives, and innovative gameplay mechanics. Released in 1994, this iconic title continues to captivate players with its rich storyline, memorable characters, and groundbreaking magic system that revolutionizes the way we interact with the mystical forces of its universe.At the heart of Final Fantasy VI lies a captivating tale of rebellion, redemption, and the eternal struggle between light and darkness. Set in a world ravaged by war and oppression, players embark on an epic journey alongside a diverse cast of characters, each grappling with their own inner demons and personal quests for freedom and redemption. From the stoic Terra to the valiant Locke, the enigmatic Celes to the lovable Mog, every character brings depth and complexity to the narrative, forging deep emotional connections with players as they navigate the trials and tribulations of their journey.Central to Final Fantasy VI's immersive experience is its innovative magic system, which offers players unprecedented freedom and flexibility in harnessing the power of the elements. Unlike previous entries in the series, where magic was often limited by MP (Magic Points) and spell slots, Final Fantasy VI introduces the concept of Magicite—a magical substance imbued with the essence of powerful beings known as Espers.Through the use of Magicite, players gain access to a vast array of spells and abilities, which they can customize and master to suit their preferred playstyle. By equipping different Magicite to their characters, players can learn new spells, enhance their stats, and even summon powerful creatures to aid them in battle. This dynamic approach to magic not only adds depth and strategy to combat but also encourages experimentation and creativity, as players explore the countless possibilities offered by the game's expansive magic system.Furthermore, Final Fantasy VI's magic system is seamlessly integrated into every aspect of the gameplay experience, from exploration and puzzle-solving to character progression and storytelling. Whether you're using magic to uncover hidden treasures, overcome environmental obstacles, or unleash devastating attacks on your enemies, the versatility and potency of the game's magic system never cease to amaze.Beyond its captivating narrative and innovative gameplay mechanics, Final Fantasy VI boasts stunning visuals, evocative music, and meticulously crafted environments that immerse players in a vibrant and immersive world. From the bustling streets of Narshe to the ethereal beauty of the Esper World, every location is brought to life with breathtaking detail and artistry, creating an unforgettable experience that transcends the boundaries of time.In conclusion, Final Fantasy VI is a timeless masterpiece that continues to captivate players with its gripping storyline, memorable characters, and groundbreaking magic system. With its innovative approach to harnessing the power of magic, this classic RPG remains a shining example of Square Enix's unparalleled creativity and vision. Whether you're a longtime fan of the series or a newcomer to the world of RPGs, Final Fantasy VI is an unforgettable journey that deserves to be experienced by all.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a reasonable game. I'm choosing to NOT recommend it on the grounds that you're most likely interested in it because of the rabid fan love for it that I think is honestly massively overblown and will let you down.FF6 isn't terrible, and the improvements it brought over the other pixel games are clear. It's probably the king of the pixel era! If you were a kid or young teen in the mid nineties playing this on release you're going to have had your mind blown. It might have been your first game with "mature" storytelling (or at least... with some occasionally strong themes such as suicide) and you'd probably end up thinking the world of it. You'd probably keep talking about it on the internet into your adulthood like it's the best thing ever.But I don't think it is. I'm familiar with lots of the other FFs, including two of the other pixel entries (1 and 4) and wanted to come back to see what all the hype was about! What did I find? Well... 6 has a fantastic twist in the back third in which and it plays with the concept of who your protagonist is in fun ways. Some characters have reasonable arcs.But that's about it. Beyond the simple fact that it's dated and a bit janky here are some of my less happy opinions:* There is a huge cast of playable characters, but most don't get great stories (or even stories at all when it comes to the secret ones near the end)* The balance is scattershot and the mechanics often don't feel very satisfying. FF1 lent on grind, sure, but it felt like a very coherant gameplay experience. This one is all over the place.* Kefka is an utterly uninteresting antagonist to me. I'm sure if it was the mid nineties I'd have eaten it up, but at this point in my life I'm unenthused by this archetype.* The setting initially projects quite a lot of history and depth, but actually ends up feeling rather shallow.I don't particularly recommend this port, either, as it looks like the GBA edition had a lot more fun content we're missing here. I get that's the point of the pixel remasters, but that doesn't make this a better product. GBA has some art style issues but if you can look past that (and you probably can if you're playing 30 year old games in the first place) then the actual content underneath is clearly richer, with additional summons, dungeons and superbosses.This game is just... alright. A solid 5/10. I don't regret playing it because now I understand the references in other media better, but that's about it. For me I'd personally that say that FF4 was a better story experience from the pixel era, and FF1 was a better gameplay experience.I respect that some people love this. Square accomplished some amazing effects for the SNES. The opera scene, music and theatrics are standouts. Reviewed in the mid nineties this thing was definitely great. But for a newcomer coming back today it's an easy skip.Don't trust the hive-minds nostalgia this go around.

_childDocuments_.review: In my youth, I played Final Fantasy VI Advance for the GBA. I remember fond memories of playing it for hours before having to save and go to bed. As I was born the year FFVI came out, I never got a true opportunity to play it till the GBA port years later.And in my honest opinion I can firmly say, despite the bugs, despite the only crash I had about 17 hours in my play through, this is a very solidly made game and one of my favorite JRPGs of all time.I reiterate that even though I played the GBA port, this pixel remaster is phenomenal and a wonderful time sink. As of writing, I only have about 18 hours of current playtime, and I have not been disappointed. Although I am far from a games journalist, I can attest that this may be the best version of the Final Fantasy VI to play in my opinion.All in all, a solid 4.75/5

_childDocuments_.review: To me, this felt like both the natural culmination of the original pixel games, and a new standard for future games to go by. On a narrative and gameplay level, this game is very linear for the first half. After a major plot development halfway through, it goes entirely open world and has the best world the series has to offer up until this point. Jobs are out, but are replaced by the equally in depth magicite system. Espers and gear relics you can find serve as a way to give characters certain builds and abilities. It felt like a more complex rework of the FFV job system. The narrative for this is the first I can still stay holds up really well after all this time. I actually want people experience the characters and the plot developments in this game. There are now up to 12 party members that can be obtained, and over half of them have complex backstories and character arcs/development throughout the entire game. If you seek to do everything this game has to offer, it will give about 40 hours of a classic 90's JRPG experience. I Highly recommend to anyone that is a fan of turn based games.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Thought : Inferior to the original. If you have access to that, play that.  Not a horrible game if it is your first time, but I would wait for a huge discount.  Edit: I am getting used to the new graphics, but there is still something in each new scene/area that is just different enough to stand out in a negative way.  The lingering, loud, repetitive sound affects. Even the soundtrack changes in certain areas changes the feel of that area.  The size of the chocobo to the map being so off that you can't even move through many areas. At one point I was going to write down everything, but after seeing all the positive reviews (though a large portion of people don't even have the very first achievement in the game for getting through the first mine section ... suspicious) I realize that if you play this game for the first time you might not notice all the changes. But know that you aren't getting the same experience you would have if playing ff6 for the snes for the first time.OMG ...  my first reaction is so negative.  I'm going to revise my review when I finish playing it, but wow.  Unlike the other entries in the pixel remaster series, this one is the first that feels like a HUGE downgrade.The maps are completely different dimensions being zoomed in, but at the same time squished down to seem so much smaller in size/scope, while at the same time the sprites are larger and elongated. It feels completely different from the original game in a bad way.  The detail of the maps are also downgraded (i had to fire up my copy of ff6 for snes just to confirm I wasn't imagining things).The battle effects, battle backgrounds, and soundtrack are upgraded, but it really doesn't make up for the sprite changes.  The sprites seem like they were just pixelated versions of the original that were redone in a poor quality.  It literally hurts my eyes looking at them ... again I loaded the original and they were 100 times better.  I have no idea how this made it past Quality Control. This is something that is, like the map issue, always present in the game. =/The first 3 pixel remasters (1,2,3) were huge upgrades and very well done in relation to their original, the second 2 ( ff 4 & 5) were minor upgrades, but this one is very disappointing.

With the QoL changes (Quick Save, Auto/Speed-Battle) and the portability on the Steam Deck, the only people who won't love this are graphics snobs or those with an aversion to grinding. 10/10 game!

_childDocuments_.review: The last of the Pixel Remasters, Final Fantasy VI is a solid addition to the lineup. It has everything that made the original game fun and engaging, and refined it for modern systems. The music is solid, the gameplay is good, and the visuals are top-notch for a beefed-up SNES game. Of all of the Final Fantasy Pixel Remasters, this is perhaps the quintessential one. It's the apex of Final Fantasy before the Playstation era, has a big world, interesting characters and events, plus a lot to do. For anyone who enjoys JRPGs, this is well worth your time!

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a lot of JRPGs. A lot. Most of the Tales Series, Xenogears, Xenoblade, etc. And most importantly for this, every main Final Fantasy entry (and most of the various sequels and prequels attached to them). And while I would still say that, for sentimental reasons, Final Fantasy X is my favorite, no other game in the genre has topped Final Fantasy VI in terms of quality. Hell, you can argue no other game period has. Everything is a pure masterpiece. The graphics are artful. The bosses and fights are fun, with the right touch of difficulty. The ensemble cast of characters have a wonderfully wide variety- both in terms of who they are and how they play, with each having special skills. The music is some of Uematsu's best, proving why he is a modern day composer who should be counted alongside the legends of the past. Where it shines most though, is the story. A rich narrative with plenty of comedy, drama, action, you name it. A massive adventure spanning the world, in both it's Balance and Ruin forms. And of course, an iconic villain driving it all.As for the specifics of this remaster, it returns to the more classic style of graphics compared to the frankly ugly version previously available. But now somewhat cleaned up and, importantly, optimized for modern, widescreen displays. The new recordings for the music might make some who played the SNES version miss that console's chiptune sounds, and I've seen people who are unhappy with the font. But these are ultimately small things that do very little to mar this update of one of the video game medium's crowning achievments.

_childDocuments_.review: I did not finish this game. The biggest issue is that the story has no drive to it; it does not give you a good reason to keep playing. It lacks a nuanced main villain (the villain is evil because they like having power); dialogue is very sparse and thin making it hard to see the characters as being unique rather than generic; and the second half of the game lacks a plot whatsoever. Mechanically, the game is fine (except that characters not in your party receive no experience, and you need the entire party for the last dungeon), but the storytelling is a big disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: This version is good, but there is none of the extra content from previous ports/remakes.The music is a mixed bag. Synths sound better, but percussion and drums sound worse. Some songs are better than the snes version, others sound worse than the GBA version. Phantom Train is an example of a great remastered song, Devil's Lab is an example of a poorly remastered song.Like the other pixel remasters, there is frame stuttering, font issues, and the tilesets are brighter.*Recent patch has fixed below issues. leaving this part of the review in-tact, as it took 2 years to fix game breaking bugs*I can't recommend this version until they put some thought into combat bugs. The battle engine is broken to the point where you'll be softlocked out or will experience a few bugs your first playthrough.The jump command is unusable, avoid it if you don't want the game to be locked (insta death, re-revive, and a few other commands will freeze the game). The destroyer rage is broken, it will also freeze your game intermittently.The Vargas fight sequence script has been convoluted and is bugged. You need to wait for a prompt before you should blitz this version.Whelk fight will soft lock under certain conditions where Terra is k.o'd.Game breaking bug that forces you back into the world of balance while in the world of ruin via Albrook.Esper swapping is bugged.Magic tower has a bug where if Ultima wipes your party, everyone will still be dead but you'll still reach victory conditions. You can go through a ton of battles with everyone dead, there will be no loss condition since everyone is dead.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally released back in 1994,  is the last of the first six mainline entries that got the  treatment. And as with the previous remasters, the overhauled graphics & music as well as the gameplay additions (maps, auto-battle option) are well-appreciated. That said, the   from the GBA version were not added, unfortunately. But as I already detailed my thoughts about the  upgrades in my , I want to move on to talk about  itself.In a   was actually voted the fourth-best mainline FF title – and the best out of the six 2D-era games. And while I can’t confirm the former, I can definitely attest to the latter.After the iconic intro sequences (which is missing the credits in this remaster, for some reason) concludes, one thing immediately comes clear:  is departing from the high fantasy setting of the previous  titles. While each of them featured more and more technology,  goes one step further and introduces Steampunk elements like Magitek. Those Steampunk influences remain smaller than I admittedly hoped for, as the rest of the games mostly remains high fantasy, but they’re an indication of the direction later  titles would take.But even with some Steampunk elements,  stays true to its predecessors and features a turn-based, Active Time Battle system. Unfortunately, the great job system of  with its many customization options is gone. Instead, we’re back to the job system of , which means jobs are unchangeably tied to each character: Only the monk character can use monk skills and so on.Considering how many permanent party members  offers (in total!), this is an understandable change – but those who were hoping to create more game-breaking skill combinations might be disappointed. The  version of summons, Espers, offer a little bit of customization – they’re used to teach magic and offer different bonusses on character level-ups.This is nice in theory but annoying in practice: You’ll constantly switch around Espers when characters are about to level up in order to raise their stats to your liking. However, Espers are also used to teach your characters magic: Once an Esper has been equipped, your character slowly learns their spells while fighting. But as the spells you want to learn and stats you want to boost are usually not shared by the same Esper, you’ll end up constantly switching Espers around in order to level optimally. That’s quite a hassle and could’ve been solved by allowing you to equip two Espers per character – one for magic, one for level-up stat boosts.Anyway, apart from the changed job system and the Espers, the gameplay of  is business as usual. Random encounters, dungeons, an explorable overworld, lots of (sometimes missable!) items, bestiary entries and chests to collect. It worked well in 1994, it works well now. However, especially those going for all achievements are going to run into some annoyances - like the tedium of getting all Blue Mage Spells, Rages and Slot results, as some are really RNG dependent.As such, I would recommend a . But even those not going for all achievements should consider checking it out, as  offers more optional content than before – the problem here being that some of it is obscurely hidden.I’m serious, even entire Espers and playable characters are unlocked in such a weird way that I doubt most players are going to find them on their first playthrough. I’m all for optional content that’s not thrown into your face but hiding an Esper in one random air tile that changes after each battle? Betting that one special item in order to fight the one bestiary entry in the Colosseum? Upgrading the contents of some chests later in the game but making others permanently missable if not acquired the first time? Come on, really?In terms of story,  finally offers a decent antagonist, which is not only introduced early on but also gradually turning for the worse. I do wish they received more screen time though, as their motives are ultimately still explained by just a few sentences at the end of the game. Nevertheless, they’re definitely the most memorable antagonist yet, not only thanks to their iconic laugh.The story of  focusses more on its huge cast of playable characters, even introducing scenarios only featuring select party members. I really enjoyed my time with most of the cast and even had a few good laughs thanks to some great dialogues and character moments. However, it’s also quite noticeable that the game doesn’t treat its characters equally. While some even receive multiple backstory sequences, others are basically ignored once introduced (especially the optional characters). Considering the huge cast of playable characters, I wonder if it would’ve been better if some of them were just cut.I also feel like the tech limitations of the time are stopping the story of  from achieving proper depth. While characters do receive backstory events and developments, I feel like many of them are still one-dimensional by modern standards. The story presentation is once again improved but characters still suffer from being simple sprites with few animations and dialogues remain short. This is hardly the fault of a game from 1994, just don’t expect  to be up to modern standards simple because it’s the last of the 2D-era games.Anyway, for all these criticisms in terms of story, I feel like I also need to point out that  features some of my favorite locations in the franchise. Apart from the usual caves and towns, there are some great scenes set on a Phantom Train (which can be suplexed!) or even an opera. I was also surprised how dark the story was at times, featuring scenes that would genuinely grueling if the game was ever remade in 3D.Concluding,  is definitely the best out of the 2D-era  games. It holds up surprisingly well, even after almost 30 years since it’s release. If you ever want to play one of the 2D  games, this is it. And if you don’t, at least listen to the soundtrack, which is truly phenomenal. , here linked in its  concert rendition, is just one of the many great tracks this game offers.

_childDocuments_.review: So I picked up the game for 20% off after hearing about the update. The classic text option was the main selling point for me, and was what kept me from buying it before. I just got to the point where I get Cyan in my party for the first time.I like the new sprites and the widescreen format. The battle run more smoothly no having to wait for a defeated enemy to fully disappear to start the next attack, and the auto-battle function takes away a lot of the tedious aspects of the original.Definitely the biggest improvement over the original game is the soundtrack, which sounds great so far.My main complaint is the lack of portraits in the dialogue boxes, but that's hardly a major issue and can apparently be fixed with mods anyway.Other than those points, being able to disable random encounters and adjust the experience and magic point rates can be fun, especially if you're going for a low-level or other type of handicapped playthrough.I've noticed one difference in the actual maps so far, unless I'm remembering it wrong there's a bucket in the area with the save point just before Ultros that restores your party; I assume the devs took measures to make sure players aren't accidentally soft-locked at points-of-no-return by being stuck with a nearly dead party with not magic points or healing items.

_childDocuments_.review: As a person who is a big fan of FF6 and considers it as their favorite game of all time, I had a great time with this version. Even if they didn't include the extra dungeon, Espers, and bosses from the GBA version when they clearly had all the time for it if they had the time to add 2DHD assets for the entire Opera scene WITH voice-overs (which was great IMO), AND the delay from last year. It is VERY obvious they gave much more effort to FF6 compared to the other pixel remasters.The visuals in my opinion, is really good. From the character sprites, the backgrounds, and the new re-drawn magic spell graphic effects. At first I was skeptical with it when they first showed the new character sprites, but the more you play, the more you'll appreciate it. I actually even prefer the new character sprites to some extent over the original. There are valid complaints about the overworld and battle backgrounds being overly bright. Personally, it didn't bother me in the slightest but there is a mod to fix/replace that. Same goes for the character sprites to replace it with the SNES sprites or even the T-Edition sprites. OR maybe you like the PR style and have noticed the lack of detail on the sprites. Which I then suggest "Pixel Reprisal" mod which is honestly a must-use if you ask me.The soundtrack is actually a  deal for me when it comes to FF6, and the new arrangements are OK. I still highly prefer the original SNES OST a lot, and its not even for nostalgia reasons. Some tracks just doesn't have the same impact because of the instruments they used. I personally don't like what they did with Terra's Theme (Overworld theme), the battle music, boss themes, and final boss themes. But I did like what they did with Narshe's theme. I don't entirely dislike the arrangements but if you aren't satisfied with what you hear, there is a SNES OST Mod available or an alternative called "Synthetic Origins" which serves as a great in-between for SNES and the new arrangements (Can be found on the Discord/Nexusmod link below).There are some improvements that I've noticed:- A more detailed minimap including a full view (which the rest of the pixel remasters have)- You can change anyones equipment anywhere even if they are not in the party. Which saves a lot of time having to go back to the Airship and swap equipment/espers with characters.- You can select Cyan's Bushido skills instead of having to wait like in the original version to get the one you want, which is a HUGE improvement.- Sabin's blitz are easier to perform for people who can't do fighting-game command inputs (lol). You can select them and it displays on screen what you have to press whereas in the original, they don't show you anything unless you look in the Ability list in the main menu. Messing up the inputs just resets and makes you do it again. You can even press them individually and slowly. Personally, I find this weird because when you do a circle motion input for Phantom Rush, Razor Gale, and Fire Dance with an analog stick, the game doesn't register the inputs fast enough and stops halfway. In the original game, this wasn't a problem at all. I've also noticed some neat touches and other minor things that were changed/added such as:- Refill Buckets in some areas where you are locked out from going back. Probably to prevent softlocks if you're underleveled or out of items. (Ex: before fighting Ultros for the first time and before fighting Shiva and Ifrit in Magitek Facility)- The scene where you rescue Celes from her Cell was censored as many have found out. They removed the Guards hitting Celes like 4 times.- Zozo buildings in the background when you go to Mt. Koltz in World of Ruin.I didn't experience many bugs that others have except one where another party member performed Mog's Dance instead of Mog himself (which was pretty funny). They seem to be fixing these bugs along the way at least. If you want a more detailed comparison, watch AustinSV's video on Youtube where he compares every version including bugs and other things. I think he did a good job on it.Other than the extremely necessary SNES Font mod and the ones I mentioned before this, I used and/or recommend:- Better Speaker Boxes or Embedded Speaker Frame (Can't use both since its not compatible)- Nintendo Button UI prompts because I hate Xbox Button layout (Personal preference)- A reshade mod that color-corrects the visuals- A nice Celes sprite mod that I used late in the game that makes her look more like the original outfit that Amano drew. (Personal preference)- If you want to increase game-speed even further than auto-battle for grinding purposes or disable encounters, there is a mod called "Memoria" on github which adds a keybinding for them.There are a bunch of other useful UI/Visual/Audio/Font mods in their  and . Although most of them get posted in their Discord first. I recommend browsing through it after playing a bit of the beginning. Just know that some mods may not be compatible with other mods.TL;DR: It sucks that it doesn't have the GBA content but if you don't mind that like myself, then this version of the game is good. If you're a purist, then obviously don't buy this. Lots of quality of life and minor changes other than the ones I mentioned. Use mods to make your experience better.: Theres now a great and helpful guide for mods in the  tab explaining how to mod it with a list of mods as well. I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: The pixel remaster graphics look absolutely fantastic and are well worth the price alone.The updated music is very well done and keeps the feel of the original music in almost all cases.What I would like to see is an option in the game to choose a different language's opera scene. Example, I want to play in Spanish but hear the Italian opera version. I am sure a mod will come that will allow something like this.The difficulty, random encounter rate, damage, price of items, gil collection rate, and more have been modified to make it easier to pick up and play for first timers. Given I am now in my 40s and have responsibilities, sadly, having developers respect my time is great. For those that want a more original feel though, it would be nice if they returned the rates of all of the above with a menu selectable option.There is also a question of some censorship. Celes doesn't get hit in this version (she hasn't in a long, long time anyway, but it IS different from the original). The soldiers do a dual arm salute instead of single. _childDocuments_.review: A good game with nice updates to the graphics, special effects and redone music.  The pixel art updates, especially some of the detailed backgrounds (like the distance backdrop of Narshe beyond the overlook) and ambient animations (like for lake and river water) were some early on treats, not to mention the beautiful spell and attack animations and crisp enemies.If all of the pixel remasters are this lovingly gone over, then we're all in for a real treat- an excuse to give already great games another spin in a fresh feeling incarnation.I noticed there's some quality of life features that are quite context specific that really take the annoyance out of those spots - signalling strong attention to the player's experience, everywhere - which also will make a replay of these classics focus on the fun.  For example, I always hated getting stuck in the tunnels under South Figaro when leading Celes to safety, but now, stepping out of sight into the shadows in the basement highlights possible routes thru the dark to guide you, so you can navigate thru this early area of the game easily.  Perhaps that removes a bit of challenge the old game had, but it also removed a lot of silly frustration.  You can nab the chests and escape onward to your adventure instead of being trapped in endless fights trying to escape from a mistaken turn into a dead end you can't see.  I also think the party were healed and re-equipped automatically at points that weren't in the original game - as if to prevent the party from going into a fight unexpectedly after being reunited or just after a cut scene.  (And yet important cases where a character is SUPPOSED to be missing most of their gear, like when you take control of Locke and later Celes during the South Figaro scenario, are still honored.  They seem very careful as to what they updated to be more fair and enjoyable to the player, without hurting the original flavor and flair.)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good remaster. It's not perfect. But if you have never played Final Fantasy VI and you don't have a gameboy advance or super nintendo, this is the best you are going to get. I like it overall, they use the better translation (though it's less amusing), the music is an improvement for the most part, and the game looks great overall. In that sense, it does exactly what it is supposed to do. I have played Final Fantasy VI on just about every device imaginable, and this one is by far the most accessible and the most modern. Some things I don't like: I don't care for the font (as others have stated). I don't think it takes away from the story, but it's just so awkward that it stands out completely. I think the scanlines could be better. They do a pretty generic job and it doesn't quite achieve that old school crtv feel. The missing credits in the intro is pretty bewildering, and if it is your first playthrough, that whole sequence with the mechs walking in the snow for two minutes is more awkward than it used to be. None of the cons take away from the overall experience though. You are going to hear a lot of people tear it apart though, and the majority of those people are veterans to the game. That's why I really recommend this game to people who haven't played it and have been wanting to, or veterans like myself who still want to play the game and understand what they are getting. People are going to think their first experience with the game is the absolute standard to experience this. Don't let that deter you. The important aspects of the original: the combat and the story are retained here. Play it for that. Also you can suplex a whole train.

Granted, the singer for Celes's part wasn't THAT great, BUT, Celes wasn't a trained singer, and the person doing her part sounds like  a trained singer trying to sing for an inexperienced opera singer, so it absolutely works out! _childDocuments_.review: The original FF6 for SNES is one of my favorite games of all time, and the pixel remaster is decent. That said, there are a few missed opportunities and weird bugs that hold this version back from being the new definitive version of the game. Nothing game breaking for the most part - although I have soft-locked myself in combat a handful of times due to an interface bug that causes character actions to break sequence and hang up searching for an animation that doesn't exist.The new OST is somewhat underwhelming in my opinion. Some tracks, like Narche's theme or the end credits sound fantastic. Whereas the final battle with Kefka or 'Searching for Friends' both kind of fail to deliver for me and made me miss the chip tunes.The updated features like the bestiary are okay; but having to use them on the main menu ruins any kind of in-game usefulness they may have. Speaking of interface, there are a couple areas that the devs sort of whiffed IMO. Menus are no longer customizable, the font choice is awful and the equipment details view is honestly way better on the SNES version due to the complete lack of useful information in this version.Lack of expanded content from the GBA version was disappointing but not expected - this has been the treatment with all the other pixel remasters. It may sound like I'm being rough on this version, and maybe I am. Again, this was another opportunity to create a definitive version of FF6 and the devs kind of missed the mark IMO. Is this version BAD? No, it's perfectly serviceable. For the price point, it's pretty good. Though, I can't help but be kind of excited to see the ways that the modding community inevitably spruces this one up.

_childDocuments_.review: GREETINGS FINAL FANTASY ENJOYERS, JRPG lovers, gamers from all around the world!Having finally beat the evil tin can man and saved a merged world in Final Fantasy V; it is time to embark on the next iteration of the Final Fantasy series, Final Fantasy VI (FF6)!Boy, what an absolutely phenomenal game this is.I think this story is best experienced firsthand as it's got very interesting beats and points that shouldn't fail to entertain or immerse. The first scene of the game starts with a dark and brooding cutscene, setting the appropriate tone for this entry, quite similar to FF4. My initial impression is that it's FF2 but more expanded, but I was proven wrong early on. It also has a lot of drama and/or dramatic influences and it's very blunt about it.Unlike the previous entry, the cast is rather large! If you do all the quests your cast should top at 13 characters I think (at least that's how many I had). Each of them is rather unique and they even have their personal backstories integrated into the story or via some sidequest when you acquire them, all neat stuff. They're all great characters, I love them all dearly :)Rather early on you unlock quite a lot of them and you can mix and match your party however you see fit, which is great but also kind of a bog as you still need to level everyone, as the game requires multiple parties to progress sometimes.As far as gameplay goes... Once again, FF6 departs from FF5 job system, with each character having a predetermined job specific to them.Cross job skills are no more, and instead relics make an appearance, which are basically accessories that add abilities, statuses or enhance your already present abilities, like turning Steal to Mug or granting 100% accuracy.Another new addition is the summon system, which now everyone has access to. Depending on the summon equipped, levelup stats are influenced and the character can unlock that summons spells. Basically everyone can be a healer now, which is neat!Additionally, every character has their own unique mechanic such as: Terra's trance which powers her magic, Celes' runic which absorbs spells for healing or Sabin's martial arts that require button inputs. This more or less makes each character different in playstyle and how you approach the summon system.Visuals this time have a lot more details, showing how FF6 was a late SNES era game. This time around Pixel Remaster actually has some noticeable additions: most striking being the Opera scene, completely different from the original game! It was really good!Another yay is that character portraits are back, yet again by yours truly Amano Yoshitaka! WOO!The game overall is very pretty and I think for any 2D JRPG the level of beauty FF6 achieved should be their baseline.Music is great, absolutely banging in fact! A lot of the music, similar to the story, is more "fine arts" in my opinion. My favourite pieces are the Opera song, Terra's theme, Cyan's theme, Celes' theme and the train area song.Overall, if FF4 is too old for you, FF6 is a must play if you want to at least experience the Final Fantasy series at one of its apexes."X Y down up!" [meteor strikes this review] I'll see you in Final Fantasy VII, soldier.

_childDocuments_.review: FF6 is commonly referred to the best retro Final Fantasy game. But how does it actually hold up to its predecessor?FF6 moved away from the freedom that FF5 gave and moved to a much simpler system for learning magic. It no longer uses a job system, but equipping summons/Espers will give you progress towards learning magic. Some espers will also give you bonus stat during level up. Unfortunately, this means there is a 'correct' and 'wrong' combination for stat growth and you are encouraged to micromanage your Esper when you level up. At the end of the day this really doesn't matter because FF6 moved away from interesting boss fights design like in 5. Boss fights in FF6 boils down to spamming your strongest attack spell over and over again and occasional healing and buffing here and there.Each character are now given more individuality in the form of set job abilities like FF4, but with the freedom of learning any magic. On paper this sounds great, but at the end of the day only certain characters really shine while some of them are downright terrible to use. Like FF5, the fact that FF6 Pixel Remaster removed the bonus content found in the GBA version might also make the Pixel Remaster a sidegrade.FF6 took the timer concept that was first introduced by FF5 and made great use of it to increase the sense of urgency. Along with timers, FF6 had so many dynamic elements that were never seen before at the time. Just to name a few, you have enemies that move in the map that you can intercept and the introduction of minigames.FF6's emphasis on splitting your party really gives me massive Octopath Traveller vibes. It's crazy how much FF6 does it better than even Octopath Traveller did nearly 30 years later. It's impossible to detail what I like about FF6's story structure without getting into spoilers. But I like how much of it is baked within the gameplay itself.----------FF6 is truly revolutionary at the time and still very much holds up. It's very cinematic which we'll see its successors take to the next level. Unfortunately when it comes to the gameplay standpoint, FF6 is a major setback from FF5 with its job system and amazing boss fights. Despite this, FF6 remains an enjoyable cinematic experience worthy of its reputation.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: -Most graphics are upgraded and crisp, especially pre-rendered backgrounds in battles and cutscenes. Mode 7 sequences are much improved.-Extremely accessible way for anyone to enjoy this classic, legendary Japanese role playing game.-Reasonable price point ($15-18)-Most of the music has been overhauled with real instruments instead of midi ones. In most cases, this is a wonderful improvement, but not always.-The revamped opera scene with recorded vocals is probably worth the price of admission.-The "auto battle" feature isn't inherently a "fast forward" or "fight endlessly", but slightly increases the speed of the battle and makes characters redo the last command they carried out. This does make some things a little easier, but only works in battles, so a true fast forward option would have been ideal, but this is still pretty good. -Worth mentioning I suppose, I was pleasantly surprised to see much of the censorship removed - "Holy" is a spell, cafes are pubs, the enemies with cigarettes have smoke coming off of them, the Goddess statue's woman is nearly nude, etc. Usually you'd need to play the Japanese version to see all that.Cons:-On the topic of graphics, much of it almost looks worse? The character sprites are hit or miss. -I find the zoomed in camera/field of vision off-putting, though I am used to the way the original looked.-Most of the menu/UI is going to take some getting used to. It's not as intuitive as the old game. There is NO option to change the color of the text window or size of the text, and it comes with a boring blue color and small font. I don't see any excuse for this. Like this is unacceptable. -There's some input lag during battles, which you get used to, but I found the instantaneous input on the SNES superior. As someone who practically speedruns these games, I like the controls at the same speed as my brain. -All of the battle theme remixes are not as good. Normal, boss, super boss and even Dancing Mad are better in the original game, but they aren't HORRIBLE. Slightly disappointed, but might just be me. -Sadly, I think the classic, legendary overworld music in the World of Balance is not quite as good. I think anyone who grew up on FF6 can be moved simply by hearing that song. -When bosses die now, they kind of just fizzle out. Originally, you'd hear two very crisp crack sounds, along with a flash, and then it would slowly sort of burn up. It was over the top, and awesome.-For some reason, the steal success rate plummeted. -You have to leave the game to view the bestiary. This is incredibly inefficient.-Some slight "nerfing" complaints - They removed the scene where Celes gets beat, the Magi Master no longer casts Ultima as a desperation attack, you can take your sweet time entering Blitz commands, etc.-No character faces while speaking.Overall, I lean slightly toward recommending you play this, but not enthusiastically. I am UNDOUBTEDLY a Final Fantasy 6 purist, as it has been the greatest game I've ever played since Christmas 1994. What bothers me probably doesn't matter to most people! If you are not into downloading emulators and ROMs, I think this is a fine way to experience the game. I would still have to say the Super Nintendo version is superior, ever so slightly. The only reason I would say to skip this is if you are dead broke and would miss the money spent, or if you don't enjoy JRPGs, or aren't sure if you do.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm emotionally spent after completing this game. I felt all of the good vibes and progression from the first 5 titles coming together to build up this masterpiece! As good as some of the previous titles were, they all walked so that Terra, Locke, and the gang could soar!!I previously thought FF4 to be my favorite story among FF Pixel Remasters, but after taking everything in, it's only right to give that title to FF6. The game delivered a fulfilling story for such a wide array of unexpected characters! The game knows how to pace itself and has especially good timing when inserting (excellent) scenes for comedic effect—something that was really developed in FF5. Some storylines went deep while others only touched the surface for the sake of mystery and exploration, but at the end of it all you get a plethora of well-done romanticized plot lines that joined together a ragtag crew of rebels and misfits on a beautiful quest to save the world!! As is the trend with the PR titles, the combat in 6 is a direct improvement from its predecessors. Instead of the largely temporary rotating cast from 2/3/4, we get 14(!!!) playable characters that stick around near the end and lend combat styles that are unique to each other. This freedom of choice is a large departure from previous titles, but it is a welcome change that did not feel like a half-baked design choice considering how deep you can go mechanically with more than half the cast. Whether you're a fan of the agile Thief (Correction: Treasure Hunter!!), Blue Magic, Dragoons, or Martial Artists, the game's got you covered!With regards to the soundtrack, I also think that FF6 has the best OST among all remasters. There are a few tracks in FF6 that really deliver a range of emotions starting off on melancholic notes and evolving into a progressive and hopeful message. Several of these tracks fit perfectly with how some character arcs are told. Terra's Theme really separates itself from other opening themes in the FF universe.I can't believe I'm now finished with the entire Pixel Remaster set. It was truly an epic series of adventures and probably the best value for my money in recent years. As someone who wanted to start off this year rediscovering my JRPG roots, FF1-6 was an excellent choice. Thank you Square Enix for topping off my lovely FF experience with FF6—an absolute masterpiece!!

_childDocuments_.review: What is "Final Fantasy VI Pixel Remaster"?Well, obviously it is the Pixel Remaster of Final Fantasy VI, or in the United States Final Fantasy III (SNES). This review necessarily has to contain some spoilers, so please just get the game (possibly on a sale) and play it instead. I fully recommend it!The controls allow you to easily access everything important thanks to the menu system, an idea that originated in Dragon Quest I for the NES and was quickly adapted by nearly all JRPGs. Combats happen in kind of real time, similar to Final Fantasy V. The game also can be played with a keyboard.You can save at any time in the overworld, or at predetermined save points in dungeons. The Pixel Remaster also added a quicksave functionality that does NOT delete the save upon loading, so you can have one save at any time now in addition to the "hard" saves. Entering any new room also creates an autosave (like the quicksave, the autosave also is always overwritten with the newest one).During the story you will be able to learn magic with every one of the   characters.. The storyline is where the game truly shines. The Empire wants to rule the world, and Emperor Gestahl has devised a plan to control the world with Espers, of which Terra is one. What are Espers? How can Terra overcome the odds and save the world from the Empire? And - if you heard some things about the game before - why does this include ? This and much more is figured out by you as you play the game. You start out in a cold city named Narshe, After around an hour or two the game splits into three paths or "scenarios" that you will all have to play out. The story is one of the strong points of the game, as is the gameplay, the music, the... well... everything except part of the menuing and .Like almost every Final Fantasy game, there are missables and one-time dungeons, so using a guide is advised for 100 percent completion. The updated map system from the Pixel Remasters allows you to see how many items and treasures are left in a specific location. But some things you can discover in the world would require some exploration skills.The gameplay is typical Final Fantasy: New ideas meet the solid battle system. This time you have multiple ways of fighting at your disposal, an idea that originated in the job system in Final Fantasy III and was perfected in Final Fantasy V.  For example, you can use tools to inflict damage and even instant death, or do so with "bushido" techniques.The music, as said before, is again absolutely masterful. Nobuo Uematso by the time of this game had absolutely perfected his skills. As just one example from very early on, Terra's theme is one of the most memorable not only in this game but in video game history.The graphics are a great update to the SNES graphics while still staying rather true to how the original should have looked like. Final Fantasy VI was the last 2D entry in the series, Takahashi, Shibuya, Sasaki,  Inazawa, and Tanaka created a wonderful 2D pixel world that looks even better in the remaster. For more background information - pun intended - you can see this interview: The gameplay is what you expect from a Final Fantasy game. You run through the world, gain experience from random battles, level up, and experience a story that you will think about long after playing the game. The Final Fantasy series never spared any of its characters from death, so you'll always be on your toes about if the story will kill off one of your main characters, any NPC that grew on you, etc.When you are a bit through the game you get to an "auction house" and a "coliseum", minigames  that allow you to get some better items.Speaking of items, you can equip two relics again, similar to Final Fantasy V. This will lead you to nearly always being able to equip an item that gives you an answer to the task at hand as well as giving your characters a permanent (as long as the relic is equipped) bonus effect (I chose haste).As you explore the world, conquer dungeons, fill up the bestiary, the gameplay is rather linear, but eventually it will open up and you are in an open world where you can do things in the order you want.There would be a lot more to talk about that makes this game great, but it would necessarily have to contain big spoilers. Instead, let me just add one last thing for those in the know: Yes, that move still works against that boss in that forest. Some unintended features are so good they are better left unfixed. And thankfully this is one of those occasions.The length of the game is around 35 to 50 hours if you go for 100 percent completion. I needed almost 41 hours.Do I recommend the game? Well, the first half of the game was a 12/10 for me. Especially that opera scene. Just that alone is worth playing the game. The second half got worse in my opinion, but was still a solid 8/10. I guess after playing five other Final Fantasy games before the gameplay just wore out on me.Recommended? Yes, absolutely! My favorite, after all is said and done, among the Pixel Remasters is Final Fantasy V for the gameplay, but Final Fantasy VI for the story and... did I mention the opera scene? I think so. But just in case I forgot my previous mentions: There is an absolutely amazing opera scene. So if you don't have the game, get it on a sale, or the entire Pixel Remaster collection. They are all great, except maybe Final Fantasy III.And if you have the game, why are you reading this? Install it and play it!

_childDocuments_.review: What makes this unique to the series?This was the pinnacle of 2D Final Fantasy.  The story is memorable, the villains instantly iconic, and the mechanics go way beyond the typical JRPG menu options.  There's a reason this is often mentioned in the same breath as Chrono Trigger.Positives:- The story and setting is one of the most unique in the entire series.  You've probably fought against an evil empire before, but have you done so in mecha suits in a world ravaged by magic wars?  The many plot twists are up there with FF7 in how well they're pulled off.-  Some of the best end game content for its era.  There are 13 playable characters in this game, including 3 secret characters.  There are multiple optional dungeons that require planning to get through.  It gives you just the right rewards to want to see everything the game has to offer.- The replay value is also fairly high because there's a lot of optional (but incredibly rewarding) character scenes you can miss.  I've replayed this game a few times and some of the stuff you're more likely to find in later playthroughs are mind blowing.- I thought of all the Pixel Remasters, this would be the one with the smallest upgrade.  And that's true for the graphics, but the soundtrack got so much love here.  They completely re-did the opera scene and pulled in the full orchestral score from the Distant Worlds concert.  When I got to the end credits, I had so much more appreciation for all the different character melodies that were brought to life by the new arrangement.  Just *chef's kiss* perfect soundtrack.  I'm getting the OST.Negatives:- I've played this so often, I actually wish I could just skip combat at points and go straight to the next story beat.  It's not that the combat is bad, but wish the narrative pacing was faster.- Later FF games handle character development better.  Every character gets a chance to shine, but by the end you have so many of them and the game has to work with so many different possible combinations that their personalities disappear for long stretches.- It's not the worst final dungeon, but it is obnoxious when they hide some optional quest content in an area with no way to unlock permanent progress. I had to go through that thing 3 times because of party setup mistakes I made at the beginning.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm leaving the old review up for posterity, and as a reminder when reading user-posted info online - trust but verify. Once I finally made it to the continent, the difficulty did not decrease. Up to that point, I was trying to play through with no extra grinding, but once I finally accepted that the game wasn't letting up anymore, I turned the ATB to Wait and the Exp/Gil/AP boosts from 1 to max. It's not how I wanted to play it, but I also didn't want to spend multiple hours grinding.I know this remaster fixed many of the bugs from the original SNES release, but it's like they didn't playtest everything.

_childDocuments_.review: Long ago, the War of the Magi reduced the world to a scorched wasteland, and magic simply ceased to exist.A world of technology, ambition, and conquest. Of forbidden magic, twisted by the Empire. Of love for those lost, and those found. Of forgotten families, and forged bonds. Of hope, and despair.Final Fantasy VI is a lofty game, and it's no surprise so many people love it. It's evident that every lesson learned in the earlier entries of the series has been put into this masterpiece, and it shows; cinematics far and beyond anything the other games had seen, dungeons that offer unique challenges and special set-pieces, and a huge cast of characters that all have their own personal arc.Increase the random encounter rate too high or introduce nothing new to the player, and it can feel like a slog. Decrease the difficulty, and combat loses all its depth. I think Final Fantasy VI, in it's first half, has near perfect pacing. Companions with their own unique mechanics, dungeons in unique locations, and it's just camp-y enough that it's constantly exciting. And then there's the second half of the game. The first half of the game is extremely well crafted because they actually finished the first half before they expected, so they tinkered with the narrative a bit and extended the game (according to Famitsu's "24 Years Since the Release of Final Fantasy VI - Looking Back At The Passion"). While I enjoyed the second half, it falls back on the formula Final Fantasy V established, which was a ton of end-game dungeons that serve as challenges with a few drips of story, lore, and fantastic rewards.Final Fantasy is a franchise that likes to experiment and flip back and forth on ideas, and there is no better example than VI's characters. In Final Fantasy V, everyone that was good, was obviously good, and the evil, obviously evil. Here... not so much. Final Fantasy VI is complex; there are 14 possible party members, with ten (eleven?) main characters that have real mini-stories attached to them, and while there's only so little screen-time for each character, I was really surprised with how much characterization present, either in the animations, dialogue, interactions, or quest-lines. Locke in particular was very well done, to the point that only a four minute cutscene made me tear up a bit. It's really solid for what it is, and while I love  getting to know characters, the larger cast and focus on enriching the world makes up for it. The game's also very funny in a way most games can't be, as sprites jump around the screen, chase each-other, and emote every one in a while.And then there's Kefka. It would be an incomplete review to not mention him. It's difficult, because I don't think I  him as a villain, but I really enjoyed his presence, because he's always entertaining. I actually think he's a very surface-level villain, as there's only one throwaway line from a random villager in Vector that addresses his past and just about nothing else. He never made me reflect on the decisions of the protagonists or consider his point of view, but compared to the rest of final bosses in I-V, he's fantastic (even though that's not saying much).While the introduction of the Esper system was initially exciting, I think it falls flat in the second half of this game. In Final Fantasy V, each character could freely specialize into any job, and they'd gain bonuses based on each job that would result in permanent character upgrades; in Final Fantasy VI, each character can equip a magicite, and they can learn that magicite's spells as well as increase their attributes on level up (for some). The issue is that this system becomes very messy at end-game, with characters losing their combat personality as just about everyone should have Cura, Raise, and a myriad of other spells just to make life easier.In my playthrough, every character was an amalgam of spells, and while characters like Sabin and Setzer maintained their usefulness with their unique abilities, the vast majority didn't. I personally really enjoyed having Bartz be my melee-focused character, jumping between Monk, Thief, Mystic Knight, Ninja, and Samurai. Other than Terra and Celes, who were mages first and foremost, everyone else was just an assortment of random useful spells and abilities, which was much less enjoyable. On top of this, the end-game of Final Fantasy VI's magicite requires quite a bit of grind. Want the best spells? Kill this end-game dragon or boss, then farm enemies for a long time because the acquisition rate for every single spell is x1. I don't really have the patience for unnecessary grinding, so I was left with spells that did the job, but weren't entirely impressive. It's not like it needed to be said again, but Final Fantasy VI is a masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly the definitive version of Final Fantasy VI as they fixed many of the bugs that existed in the original. In short, this is worth grabbing because it plays differently than the original enough that certain fights play out differently and overall the game feels different, but the same, if you get what I mean.For example, in the battle system, they've finally fixed the issue where if two characters attack the same enemy and the first one clears it, the second one will move on to another target. In the SNES version, the second character would try to attack the monster that isn't there anymore and would just miss. You basically had to learn how many hits each monster would take and carefully choose your targets.Next, Sabin's Blitzes have been made easier than ever. Now you are given multiple chances to enter the right input, and it tells you the inputs on screen.Cyan's Bushido has been improved a huge amount. Instead of sitting at the menu waiting for it to charge, it now charges quietly in the background so you can execute other actions.Evasion now impacts the game, and it is noticeable.There are other battle changes, but those are some of the big ones. Beyond that, the soundtrack is the best version of FF6's OST I have heard. It brings a new level of atmosphere to the game that wasn't present before - especially if this is a nostalgia trip for you! The QoL changes (fast forward battle system, swapping Espers, sprint button, etc) were all thoughtful and don't take away from the game.Overall, the changes and fixes done were carefully considered and it is clear the objective was to further the game towards the design objectives set out when it released in '94. The SNES version feels somewhat incomplete by comparison now - but that isn't exactly accurate since it was the only version we knew for so long. Standing side by side, the pixel remaster shines and is a worthwhile playthrough even if you have the original. In fact, if you loved FFVI, you owe it to yourself to experience the pixel remaster.

_childDocuments_.review: This would be an easy recommendation if it didn't lack the GBA content, but alas, I have to sacrifice either a control scheme that allows me to swap between party members, or a solid dozen hours of content.Also, the weird bugs are a problem too.This game, most of all, had the best GBA content, and it's a shame no one's figured out how to mod it in yet. While the content being absent hurts for the other games too, it hurts the worst for FF6 when the GBA content actually includes a cut boss from the SNES version.I was fine with FF1-3's Pixel Remasters, because every single re-release played very differently, and FF1 and 2's PR releases are the only versions of the game, with the original unmodified gameplay, and without the plethora of broken and flat-out not programmed mechanics present in the NES and PS1 versions of each. As much as I would like to see the Dawn of Souls areas, I'd imagine the gameplay differences would necessitate a full rework for each game's DoS content.FF3 on the other hand, is a more complicated story. The ideal version of that game would be a totally new version containing the dialogue, characterization, and art direction of the DS version, but with the gameplay, difficulty, and mechanics of the NES version as an option, alongside the DS version's gameplay. But short of that, just making both versions separately available is good enough. Which they are.FF4 is also a complicated story with a lot going on, but the PR version's a solid replacement for the SNES/PS1 version, and the GBA/PSP/DS versions all have their own quirks. Generally, I think the DS version, like FF3, stands separately, and well that's also still on Steam. The GBA and PSP versions, have more content, but are otherwise worse in every way, and unlike FF5 and 6, don't have enough to make those versions worth playing over the DS version. Square COULD have remedied that, but chose not to, however what I consider the definitive version of FF4 is still on Steam.FF5 and FF6 both added a sizable chunk of content in the GBA versions, that is entirely absent here. Entire jobs are missing from FF5, and FF6 GBA had one of the greatest post-game dungeon additions to any rerelease, of any game, full stop. Despite that, the GBA versions weren't without many, many problems, to numerous to discuss here, and the Pixel Remasters were a perfect chance to make a real definitive version of both games. And Square WASTED THE CHANCE.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautifully done Remaster of one of the best games in the Final Fantasy series.  I'm sure everyone knows this, but in case you don't, this is the game that was originally released in the US as Final Fantasy 3 for SNES.  It is one of the best games in the series, if not the best.It is not a port of the original game, so if you, like some of the negative reviewers, are expecting it to look, sound, and feel identical to the original SNES game, this is not for you.  If you're looking for a game that's faithful to the original that makes some changes (some are improvements, others maybe a little less), then this is what you want.I always had to play this 2 player for SNES because I could never master Sabin's blitzes.  I don't know why.  In this version, you pick the blitz that you want, the combination appears on screen, and you put it in.  If you mess up, it starts over, rather than failing.  It's a much improved way of doing it.  Sabin's Bushido is likewise improved.The best improvement, in my opinion, is the ability to run.  Remember having to use a relic slot for Sprint Shoes?  Now just press and hold 'B' on your game pad (or whatever button on your keyboard) and your characters will sprint.  Let's you easily change between running and not without having to use up one of your Relic slots.  Don't want that?  Sprint Shoes still exist and work the same.I'm not a very musically inclined person, but the music seems very similar to and faithful to the original.  There are some changes, but very similar in general.Overall, a great Remaster and I highly recommend it.  You can't go wrong with FF6.

The characters are so much fun and offer variety in combat, the remastered soundtrack is great for the most part, and the storyline still resonates even after the series' more cinematic entries. _childDocuments_.review: Final Fantasy VI is a masterpiece. Where FFV was goofy and didn't take itself very seriously, FFVI is a sprawling epic with the most playable characters across the entire mainline series. Everything is refined and perfected in this entry.The story is quite good, by far the best up until its time. I love all the characters and their journeys, even if some characters have a lot less to do than others...  but in the end I was left satisfied and knew most characters quite well. The magicite system is in my opinion better than FFVII's materia system but worse than the jobs in FFV. I dunno, something about the changing outfits just makes me love FFV's jobs. That's not to say magicite is bad though, I absolutely love it. Sure, you don't get many at the start but later in the game the options are endless and you can build characters however you like.As a remaster this game is also very good. Everything is a bit brighter than I would have liked, but that can be fixed with numerous mods. Speaking of mods, there are lots. I personally use the Moogles and Mods discord for finding mine. However, mods are by no means essential and you can easily enjoy this amazing game without any at all.Between all the 2D Pixel Final Fantasy games this one blows them all out of the water. Please, please play this if you have even a passing interest in RPGs. You will not regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic version of Final Fantasy VI.  I only played the SNES version of this game a long time ago, so I didn't feel like I was missing out on anything even though I'm aware that the GBA/Mobile versions have an extra dungeon and this version doesn't. This version is actually more challenging than the SNES one since you can't abuse the Vanish/Doom bug anymore and monsters seem to use their special abilities more often.  However, the player also gets advantages such as Cyan's Bushido bar not needing to charge during his turn, high speed walking (even further enhanced with Sprint Boots), and auto battle that helps with grinding things like exp or decursing the Cursed Shield.  The new music is fantastic and I love how they use actual voices for the Opera segment.  The graphics look great for the most part, though they are a bit too bright at times.  This is mostly noticeable in the overworld.  Also, I'm happy that the classic look of the characters has returned instead of the chibi versions in the mobile port. This was an excellent stroll down memory lane and it's still one of my favorite games of all time.  If you haven't played any of the old Final Fantasy games, you can't go wrong with this one.

The new spell effects, attack animations and "HD-2D" sections are a fun way to modernize some of the more dated effects and mode7 cutscenes. _childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I (really) played FFVI and I finally completed it. Generally, I am not a fan of 2D Final Fantasy and I abandoned every of them (sometimes close to the end) aside from FF1 which I completed on PSP. Why ? Well, even if I started to play on Sega Genesis, I am pretty easily annoyed by veryy long RPGs with basic plot and dialogs. There is a before and an after with FFVII. This one is however better than all other 2D games in terms of overall direction. The main setting and plot is close to the original game actually but with more details and overall development. The pixel art/technology is beautiful (some areas are magnificent) and the music is divine (I love this variation of the FF theme, Terra theme, etc.). Now the story and characters are somewhere in-between the PSX trio and the pixel era, maybe closer to the second one however. Dialogs are a bit lacking and the great story somewhat falls short in dramatic events. But on the other hand, many of them - the most important one - are really well directed - maybe not memorable for me at the present time because I am old - but I can imagine how they can catch children memories.I also like the concept of this episode : there is not really a single main character and the gameplay makes you play different groups or characters as leads during the adventure. The break between twio parts of the games also change the way you explore the world. And the atmopshere of the two parts are very different and well rendered.This concept translastes into the gameplay with unique characters abilities : everyone has a special command which can translastes into several sub-commands (blue magic, etc.). Most of the time it is a hit, sometimes it's a miss (but I do not doubt that it will appeal to a niche). You can also transform your commands with equipment, the game is so very rich.If we keep talking about gameplay, fights are generally interesting with unique bosses but after getting ultima and stronger abilities it becomes spamming. The content is quite huge and there is a lot of gameplay variations. I must confess that I ignored most of them (I completed the main sub "quests" but not the longer activities) but FFVI is really rich in terms of content and I must recognize it.Overall, the game is a great work of art, a bit plagued (less than other 2D FF but still a little bit) by the good old random-looking dungeons and numerous random encounters (which you can reduce to 0 later with an object, buit really later) but not enough to ruin the experience. Maybe the real missing part is the lore, you have a small catch about it but the towns, the details about the empire etc. are very lacking. Even in terms of art, the game did not really capture their essence fully.To close this small review, a small comment about this version and Steam Deck play. First, the Steam Deck experience is perfect. The minor incompatibility which makes it "Playable" and not "Compatible" is that you must call the mouse to accept new characters namings. Plus I experienced maybe one or two crashes some weeks ago but I never experienced them in the second part. This verison specifically has some minor issues : if you play full screen, there can be a weird screen tearing then you must play with bordeless window (only on TV, Steam Deck was OK). Seconsly, the game must load itself in the RAM and you wait weirdly frozen with  "Loading..." text like 30 seconds or more whatever storage/ram you have at every launch.  This is minor but at this price for a SNES game, this could have been better polished. This will not transform my review into a negative one but I must note it.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought FFVI on the SNES at age 13. It quickly became my favorite game of all time. I read through the official strategy guide hundreds of times. I bought the 3-disk soundtrack and played it when I was feeling lonely, lost, or depressed. It didn't solve my problems but going to this game and its wonderful cast of characters allowed me to escape for a couple of minutes.I have not visited this game since the 90's. I was completely overwhelmed and started tearing up when I heard the overland map's music. The way this game instantly transported me back to a time where the world didn't seem as ♥♥♥♥♥♥, where I had my whole life in front of me.... cannot be replicated. Middle-aged now, I will always hold this game close to my heart. The redone music alone was worth the price of admission for me. I have encountered zero bugs as of The Floating Continent. There have been many quality-of-life improvements in this game over the years, although I am not sure which ones are exclusive to this game. I recommend this game, but recognize that those without powerful nostalgia will not get what I got out of this. For those in my shoes, it's hard to imagine a better version.

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings back all the feels. With the revamped soundtrack, and vastly better sound equipment the opening theme just drove chills down my spine. _childDocuments_.review: This game is SquareSoft in their prime. Pure SNES-era surrealism🤪: I've had a fistfight with a sentient steam train that takes people to the "afterlife"; travelled 600 miles via a gulf stream with only one Victorian-era diving helmet and three party members, all while whacking underwater creatures about the gills; and was propositioned in a bar by a courtesan who referred to the members of her décolletage as "Humpty and Dumpty" . . . Square thinks that all they need to do to make their games sing again is crib the vague steampunk/high fantasy aesthetic of their older titles and apply them to same morose, lugubrious, insipid nonsense narratives they've been peddling since FF8, and that's not what was good about their older games – it was the surreal madness of a fever dream combined with interesting locales that had no business being in the same world as one another that made the experiences unique and interesting. Final Fantasy VI is an example of the very best Square had to offer in their heyday, and I fear we'll never see another game of similar quality from them again😔.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, if you're a fan of the GBA reboot and subsequent versions, this is pretty much a rehashing of those for Steam.  I've seen little or no difference between them and this, therefore, you'll enjoy it.If you never spent time playing those, for a variety of reasons, such as you didn't like the reboots, maybe played the crap out of the original and didn't touch any newer versions for lack of time, lack of gaming platform the reboots were on, etc., then don't bother with this one.  Go get yourself an emulator and a ROM of the original, and don't waste your money on this steaming pile of excrement.Like all the reboots before it, the re-publishers have changed names of things, so there's a lot of re-learning of Gau's rages, relearning of spell names and weapons, and that sort of thing.  I also didn't like how some of the mechanics were, "remastered," such as the tried and true Vanish/X-zone, Vanish/Doom, and the fact that the Black Belt relic now takes away a character's turn when attacked, unless you're actively assigning that character an action.  Apparently, "Life 3," which is now called, "Reraise," doesn't work properly at all, either.  For example (since there's no longer an insta-kill for the Intangir), just TRY using Gau's Destroyer rage in the battle with an Intangir.  He'll use Reraise on at least one member of the party.  When the Intangir kills a lower-level party, the Reraise will have, "No Effect."  This shouldn't be possible.  Further, you can cause the game to freeze in any battle pretty easily.  Say a member of your party is really low on health, and you attack that character with another character wearing the Genji Glove.  The first strike reduces that character to zero.  The second strike puts the character back on his/her feet at zero health, and the game will freeze.I'll update this again when I find what I'm sure will be more reasons NOT to spend your money on this game like I did.  Really wishing I didn't go in for the nostalgia thinking this would be like the original and not just another crap reboot.
