_childDocuments_.review: Like many other people, my youth was shaped in part by Final Fantasy 6. At a time when Mario and Sonic were dominant, FF6 showed me that video games could tell complex, emotionally affecting stories and present rich worlds full of well-realised characters. Kefka remains my all-time favourite villain, and some version of Dancing Mad has lived on my playlist rotation since the early 00s.I was never satisfied with any of the post-SNES releases, though; the GBA version had more content and some visual upgrades, but vastly inferior audio. The Playstation release had some neat cutscenes, but it was plagued with load times. The mobile/PC port preserved the audio, but the visuals and interface changes didn't click with me. This version tries to marry some of the best elements of previous releases, and succeeds to a degree, but with some caveats. Let's get the bad out of the way first.  The retina-searing overworld map. This is the elephant in the room, and I'd love to know what the reasoning was behind the inclusion of the GBA maps over the SNES versions. The Veldt looks like an ocean of Mountain Dew. The World of Darkness map is less egregious, but still too bright. Thankfully this is easily modded out, and I highly recommend doing so.The font. I'm no Graham Stark, but I feel the need address this. The font is small and squished and just plain boring to look at. As a result, text boxes are left with a lot of empty space at times. It seems like a nitpick, but considering how much reading this game requires, it's affected my enjoyment more than I expected.The censoring. Specifically the change to the imperial salute during a flashback and the removal Celes's beating during her intro. Is it the end of the world? No. Is it idiotic and unnecessary? Yes.Bugs. From Gau auto-missing melee attacks to jerky NPC movement to Mog spinning when he stumbles but not when he successfully dances, there are a lot of them. Other reviews have listed many more, but thankfully the devs are working to iron these out.Little things. Man, I used to smirk when Mog stumbled. He'd bounce back to his feet and stay frozen for a second, presumably in embarrassment, before rejoining his friends. It was adorable and full of personality. This still happens, but... it's off. The timing's just not right, and his new sprite doesn't convey quite the same emotion. There are a number of moments like this. It's not all bad, and some things are surprisingly spot-on(Sabin and Gau's little dance during Gau's intro, Cyan spin-hopping around during Flurry, and Celes rhino-charging into the dressing room before the Opera come to mind), but for every moment that's faithfully recreated, you'll find one that's just a bit off, especially if you're a longtime fan like me. It's not a deal-breaker, but it's noticeable.The soundtrack! This is 100% of the reason I bought this product, and I am just floored. When I was young I was lucky enough to know someone who owned the OST album and let me copy it for myself, and believe me when I tell you I wore that tape OUT. We've been treated to a huge number of remixes and live recordings since then, and while I love most of them, especially the tracks from the Distant Worlds albums, I've often found that they change the tone or style of a given track in a way that doesn't quite evoke the same feeling as the source material. Obviously this is the point of adapting and remixing, but I didn't want to spend the whole game listening to a soundtrack that didn't fit the action, and this caused me to hesitate for a few days before taking the plunge. If you're on the fence for the same reason I was, then let me put your fears to rest: the new soundtrack is nearly perfect. It updates the sound of the original with live instruments while preserving the tone and style very well. Many tracks also have a second loop too, which adds variety. Standout tracks for me so far include Grand Finale, which plays during the on-stage battle with Ultros at he climax of the Opera, and On That Day... which plays in certain towns in the World of Ruin. As of this writing I haven't beaten the game yet, but I'm confident I'll enjoy Dancing Mad and the ending themes.It's not  perfect, though. Metamorphosis, which plays at key climactic moments, sounds a bit tinny, and the first note of Cyan's theme is rather jarring. Like, I understand what they were going for, but it just kinda punches you in the ear for a split-second and that always breaks my immersion. Overall though it's exceeded my expectations so far.QoL additions! These range from auto-battle to a sprint function so you don't always need Sprint Shoes equipped. So far my favourite of these is a quick-save function that can be used anywhere in case you die. It also seems to auto-save in this slot whenever you enter an area. Others have complained about Sabin's Blitz inputs, but I don't mind this at all since I could never pull them off reliably as a kid. Removing Cyan's Bushido timer is a double-edged sword(ha) though; Cyan still waits to perform his attack, but now you get to use your other party members in the meantime. I didn't like this at first, but given how much harder the game seems now, I understand why it was done. Speaking of which...Challenge! I've seen lots of other folks complaining about this, but I'm actually enjoying the wonky balancing. FF6 was always easy to cheese through, and it's kind of a nice change of pace to be struggling at times. Admittedly it feels weird: bosses will attack relentlessly at first, only to stop entirely when you're down to a single party member, or when your whole party is stopped/frozen and unable to act. It doesn't exactly feel fair, but it certainly makes for a less-mindless combat experience where equipment and relic choices matter a lot more. I understand why this might be a negative for a lot of folks, but I found it weirdly refreshing.Visuals! World map and Mog-dancing aside, the new sprites actually look pretty good. They're not a huge departure from the SNES sprites, but they're slightly more detailed and vibrant. Kefka's sprite is a clear stand-out; his colourful outfit and makeup are clearly communicated, although there is a small visual bug that causes his pants to switch colours when he shakes his head. Besides the characters, small visual flourishes like shimmering water and more environmental animations make the game more interesting to look at, while the iconic Opera scene has been gussied up with a bit of 3D rendering that makes it stand out all the more.Overall, this is an enjoyable update to an old classic, but it's tough to call it the definitive version. The new soundtrack does a lot to lift it out of the mire of its flaws, but there are ways to experience this game that are better balanced, more stable, and won't damage your eyes every time your party steps outside. That said, for me at least, the soundtrack alone was worth the price of admission, and playing through the game with this fantastic new soundscape has made me feel like a kid again. If you think you'd feel the same way, then this is an easy recommend from me.

_childDocuments_.review: I would absolutely recommend this game.  After all, it's Final Fantasy VI, which is a classic.  HOWEVER, there are some things than should be noted that, unlike the other PR games, are a step down.//Good Things//- Quality of life changes, especially auto-battle, which helps make leveling up/grinding a whole lot easier.- Mini-map, which has helped me find things that I have never found before in this game, and I played it when it came out of the SNES.- The soundtrack is beautiful, and the remastered soundtrack does not disapoint.- The dialogue is for sure a lot cleaner than the original.//The Bad//- Despite some of the improvements, some things just don't look right in the PR.  In fact, some things look better in the SNES original.  Character movements are choppy a lot of times, along with any non-static backgrounds (see Desert/House Fire level).  It just baffles me how these things look worse.- Some quality of life things from the original games are MISSING, such as un-equipping all party members when there is a story related split, the missing hook from the Magitek Factory that allows you to escape from Ifrit and Shiva's room, the VERY slow split battles in the Narshe mines and fields.  Some details are also just not included, like how Strago no longer has a blue triangle when he casts Lore magic (and it is the generic white magic cast).- There are also some bugs with the game that I have found, mostly surrounding auto-battle.  Some examples include Gau's Rage command not working and Gau just using a regular attack (it should be noted he still cannot equip weapons), and Mog's dancing in conjunction with Setzer's slot command caused Setzer to attempt to cast Mog's dance spell and the game locked up and had to be reset.While the game overall is fun and there is plenty to like, there are also a handful of noticeable things that just look unpolished compared to the SNES version that I hope are fixed in some sort of patch.  If you are buying this game expecting a superior, or even in some ways BETTER, experience to the original, you may be disappointed.  However, if you are buying this for some FF6 goodness, then this will be more than suitable.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll give a quick TLDR: This game is excellent, and that’s coming from someone who has never been a fan of this series or any of the other gamesHave you never played or barely played a Final Fantasy game and are wondering whether or not this 20 year+ JRPG is gonna be your thing? Well then my fellow FF noob let me preface this by running through my experience with the FF Franchise. I have played final fantasy 1 for maybe 20 minutes via emulation, FF10 for probably close to 2 hours, FF12 for 30 minutes, FF13 for maybe an hour, and Lightning returns for less than 10 minutes.I have played FF14 and 15 for significant amounts of time, but they are so different from these other FFs that I’m not even going to count them, and I didn’t even necessarily like FF15 despite the time put into it, but you get the point. I am not a fan of this franchise, and any dip into these games are purely to satisfy my curiosity. I have no nostalgia for FF and no biases. So I am here to tell any fellow FF noobs that this game is amazing and totally worth your time.The character options you have are actually unbelievable for a game that came out in 1994, shaming even some modern RPGs. Espers, relics, abilities all help you make the characters the way you want. There is little to no grinding required if you just Superpower like 3 of the characters (make sure one is Celes for the love of god, you will thank me later can't say why) and the few times I did grind were voluntary. I WANTED to grind because of some of the rewards you can get with Magicite especially to give Ultima to Terra, or to get the Paladin's shield(idk if the latter was worth it lmao)Equipment feels super important and I found myself often switching optimal gear for gear with relevant abilities or immunities to help me with certain sections of the game, especially boss fights, and there are all sorts of hidden uses and synergies for items equipment and enemies. It was always a thrill to discover something new or to have a train of thought lead to rewarding results. As a single example, there is a spell called stop. The spell stops your target from acting due to the spell warping time around them and making them appear frozen in place. There is also a spell called haste which makes your character act faster... but by warping time to make them appear super fast. If you haste a character with stop, it cures stop and makes them fast. So good. And there are many MANY other interactions like that. Sorry if these are common for Final Fantasy games and I'm just spouting old knowledge as new, but this is my first 'true' final fantasy remember, and I found these interactions to be truly wonderful.Also there are 14 total recruitable characters and all of them feel unique by having separate abilities with widely varying usefulness, but the Espers can fix characters you like that have weaker abilities. These can vary from Power boosts to move steals to an entire separate magic system, and early on it will define who you feel is most powerful or most desirable to have in you party. Speaking of Party, this game handles parties in a way I have never seen any other game. Not only do you control multiple parties in a few separate instances, but at one point in the story, the entire group split up for you to follow 3 different parties as they try to reconnect to each other. One of the absolute stand out moments for me in the game was the screen where you had to choose who to follow. I thought those characters where just going to reappear later in the story, but you straight up follow all 3 journeys and you get to see a BUNCH of new characters and places through each.This may be a good time to talk about the story, which again, for a game made in 1994 HUGELY suprised me. Unfortunately, the main twist of the game was already known by me pure by reputation, but I am kinda glad because I would never have even considered playing this instead of the likes of Bravely Default or a Tokyo RPG Factory game. The story is fairly dramatic, but sets a good tone to expect that as the game starts. The drama itself is inconsistent, but overall I feel it's really really strong for a game from 1994. Cyan, Terra, Celes and Locke where all my favourites for story, and some of them can get quite dark and 2 in particular gave me pause. My jaw was on the floor. 99% of all characters have some sort of terrible backstory, but amazingly the backstories of each provide motivation for characters to join, and as they grow and move past these backstories, provide FURTHER motivation to power through to the end of the full journey. Incredible.Really the only thing I didn't like was one of the villains, Kefka. He is one of those bad guys where suffering and destruction make him happy, and to further traumatise or humiliate some one will ALWAYS be his priority with the exception of more power. He starts as a henchman which seems more appropriate, but eventually is able to go toe-to-toe with some pretty powerful characters, even being able to one shot espers at one point. Maybe I'm missing something, but the power gain seemed out of nowhere and annoyed me as I anticipated his demise. And this is all BEFORE the floating continent. His motivation turns out to be extremely nihilistic, it just makes you wonder what he's going to to after he gets what he wants. It's like the usual "Take over the world" bad guy where you think "Why? To do what?" and it's never brought up.Other than that though I had a great time from start to finish and there is SO MUCH more I could talk about but I'm really bad at explaining it all and I feel like I've spent way to much time already on a damn steam review haha. So if you are still here and still reading congrats and you should buy this if anything I said interested you, because it really is an amazing JRPG, and will no doubt lead to many other amazing JRPGs I have overlooked or found inaccessible over the years. HIGHLY Recommended

_childDocuments_.review: Holy lord, this game is my absolute favourite Final Fantasy (shared first place with FF9) and this version is the best. I've played the original SNES-version, the PSX-version (that's the first PlayStation for you youngsters), the Android-version and now this one. It by far outclasses all other versions. The simple reason is that the added extras, from GBA version that are also on Android, doesn't give me much value, instead this version gives me the most beautiful pixel work I've ever seen, together with a total masterpiece of musical renditions of all songs. On top of that we have auto-battle, cleaner interfaces, improved dialog, auto-save (if you die you can restart from entering a cave), and many other minor quality of life improvements. Blitz are now even simple to input as the commands are show during battle and are remove individually as you input them. Every inch of this game feels genuinly remade with the most love possible.Ever thought about FF6, or revisiting it? This is the version! Love pixels and JRPG, this is by far the best Final Fantasy in the pixel-era. It plays just as well today as it did all those years ago, perhaps even better now.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright you young whippersnappers who are all up on the hippest newest game jive but don't know your roots, here it is (by the way, I'm posturing - I'm only 39).  I spent hundreds of hours on this game in my teens in the 90s, way before hours were tracked online or before time tracking could go over 99 hours and 59 minutes.  It is one of my favorite games of all time.I'll denote the things I've noticed in the order I noticed them and whether I appreciated them or not:1. The graphics are amazing and I immediately fell in love with the redesigned spells and effects.  Just like when I was a teen, I can't wait to see how each spell looks. Love this.2.  The music is a bit harder to hum along to due to increased complexity but with that comes increased quality so I can't really complain.  Ambivalent about the music.3.  Kefka's laugh is unchanged.  I would have been pissed if this wasn't the case.4.  The phantom train is MUCH more difficult than I remember - it immediately uses an attack which is essentially Bad Breath on your entire party, and uses that move often afterwards.  I kind of hated that battle because of it.  It was less of a battle and more of a RNG attempt to avoid imp, berserk, confuse, and doom.  Didn't like that much but after a few "rolls of the die" I got past it. EDIT: I think I just hella rushed through the game (in my attempts to not level up too much before Esper stat bonuses).  I was level 19 with Celes when I arrived in World of Ruin later.  So it's probably not harder than it was.5.  Some of the dialogue is improved, some of it is a bit less clear than I remember.  Some word changes make the story have less effect for me - it's hard to describe exactly what I mean but for example, there's a time when Sabin asks Cyan "Is that your family...DEPARTING?!" in the original version.  But in this version it's changed and it just doesn't have the same meaning as "departing."  Overall it's probably an improvement over the original game, but I've only played four hours so far (I just got the three parties back together for the first big battle of the game).6.  There have been some obvious political correctness changes.  I don't know how far they extend but I'm four hours in and noticed that during the scene where Celes is chained to the wall, they no longer beat her as they did in the original version.  I can't tell if this is an attempt to make the game friendlier for younger audiences or just political correctness making the storyline less believeable.  Think of it as if you're watching any dramatic movie.  The gender of the person being beaten doesn't matter - it's just story.  And I'm not saying this specific change is good or bad.  But it definitely feels weird for the animations to be missing while the dialogue remains.  I don't know if people who haven't played the original version would notice anything strange about the scene or not, though. EDIT to this one: Later on, there's a part where Gestahl smacks [someone female], so the person who replied about the restraints must be correct.  You learn somethng new every day!7.  Quality of life changes such as cleaner menus, better naming, an on-screen minimap, quicksaves, autosaves, auto-battle, visual cues to hidden passages, and more don't offset the difficulty of the game.  Actually, because of the increased framerate and responsiveness of the game, some of the bosses are quite a bit harder due to their speed.  Tunnel Armor is very fast with the magic now and if you delay at ALL in casting Runic it will one-shot you.8.  Some of the cutscenes' animations are a bit janky now because of the speed at which the game moves and the resolution of the screen, but it's not so bad that it ruins the experience for me.  9.  Things which were trade secrets when the original game came out are now told to you in-game, which is nice.  I remember how I had to learn about the secret low-HP basic attacks from a "Secrets of FF6" book I found at Tiger Books back in the day and NO ONE knew about it.  But now they tell you in the training room...so that's nice. :)  Although I do miss the old days before the internet and data mining when games retained their mysterious secrets long after release.10.  In the original version of this game, upon death you were sent back to the last point at which you saved, but you would retain all XP you had gained in the meantime (but not gold or magic point progress).  This was a workaround for the problem that occurs when you progress too far into a game without leveling up sufficiently and find yourself saved right before a boss that you have no chance of defeating.  This feature has been removed from this version in lieu of a quicksave feature.  Both have their ups and downs.  The quicksave is nice at times if you know the progression of the game (luckily I do).  But new players could easily get hosed by saving right before a boss and not being able to back up and level up more when they find it too powerful (the worst-case scenario of this is you have to start the game on a new file).  I will tell you that I made the mistake of saving at the save point right before the minecart escape scene, and I had been rushing through the game so I wouldn't level up too much before getting the Espers with +2 stats per level.  The boss of that scene wiped the floor with me several times because my characters had <500 HP.  Eventually got past it though.11.  In the early stages of the game the auto-battle isn't too useful and will almost certainly get you killed, but later on when everyone has some good abilities to rely on, it's the bee's knees.  When I needed to grind up some levels before the gate to the Esper realm, I fell in love with it. Get three characters using good offensive moves and one spamming a cure spell, and you've got a good leveling setup (and it animates at double speed!)12.  There's a glitch in the Veldt where your team's moves don't get reset when Gau appears like they should, so he gets hit and runs away when he shouldn't.  It seems to work correctly when you have auto-battle on, sometimes.  I am almost certain this is not the original functionality because I don't remember having to count the number of moves I used to get him back in the old days.13.  Vanish/Doom doesn't work anymore :(  Intangirs are annoying and not worth the time because of it.  I can't imagine I'm going to have fun with Brontosaurus either.  But it has forced me to actually fight some of the enemies I used to skip because they were annoying.  I've actually (kind of) enjoyed that.14.  World of ruin has a pretty sunset :)  The increased color spectrum of the game shines when you first wake up in the aftermath.15.  Couple of minor bugs I noticed - if you have your cursor settings on "Memory" it will no longer reset them when you change from offensive spells to defensive spells or vice-versa so you may accidentally heal an enemy or use offensive magic on an ally.  And if you leave the floating continent from the midpoint where you can board the ship, and then land on it again, you'll never stop hearing the airship fan sounds (outside of combat) until you reload the game.  Both pretty minor.Overall I'm thoroughly satisfied with my purchase so far because the revamped spell animations alone are enough for me.  I can't wait to finish the game from the beginning for the (who knows how many but over ten)th time.

_childDocuments_.review: One of those classic JRPGs that gets a lot of love for a whole lot of good reasons. After finally checking it off of my backlog after half of my life, I can confirm that the game deserves the love that it gets and it feels way ahead of it’s time. The latter half of the game is somewhat an open world game, which is a nutty concept for an SNES game released in 1994. It’s such an incredibly well-done experience and it makes sense how they evolved from this to releasing FF7.I think that if you’re able to stomach JRPGs from the 90s and don’t mind the awkward translation or hilarious balance, this is a damn fine way to spend your leisure time. I feel like it is worth approaching this game with a guide to avoid random pitfalls that games from this time period are known for, and also to not miss anything. Be warned that you have a lot of grinding ahead of you, but do know that there is a battle speedup option.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't encounter much in the way of new bugs . Even a couple from my snes cartridge of "Final Fantasy III" were not present in this launch. But, that was totally expected he's recomposed these songs many times over the years for various showings. What is new is that the opera scene is completely voiced in English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Japanese, and Korean. I created a save right before it and listened to each. My wife speaks both German and Korean--we both enjoyed those recordings a little more than the English as something stand-alone. However, I think they nailed the impromptu performance given by a military general best in the English version while still making it something less than silly like stage fright or whatever.  Overall, I was very happy with the game. Is it hands down better than what can be accomplished through modded roms for SNES and GBA emulators? No. But. this is a legit way to get what I believe is a great experience. My only knock to it at all is when I first load up the game despite it being installed on an NVME ssd there is a little loading buffer that takes 2-3 seconds before I can actually take controll of the characters. Otherwise, loading times for anything else are if anything more seamless than my snes cart. The game itself is a wonderful classic close to my heart and I do hope to see a 2.5HD remake hit PC someday.

_childDocuments_.review: I've heard many people in my 21 years of life say that this is "the greatest jrpg of all time" and other things to that affect, same with FF7, and although it took me a long time to get to this game. I finally understand why. Every moment, all characters dialogue, all feels so immaculately written, and the gameplay is fine crafted and fantastic even to this day. The game makes quite bold decisions in storytelling for SNES-era gaming, for example, a few hours in, many characters are split up from their party, and you are given a choice to pick which one to split off to and explore first, and they all eventually meet back up, it's kinda GENIUS!! And every character in this game actually has a ton of depth, and emotional heft. Terra is a wonderfully written character, and is also the closest thing this game has to a main character, and her struggles are told beautifully through the games writing. I'd say half the party members have just as much depth as Terra!! I don't even wanna go into it but FOR REAL, this game tells a GREAT STORY. The games main villain is despicable, like comically evil, and it's perfect. I can't really think of too many non mechanic things this game does wrong, other than pacing in the 2nd half (but it's really not that bad). This game is the Sgt Peppers Lonely Hearts Club Band of video games, or something to that effect, it's a landmark, and i'm glad I can finally appreciate it. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve been a fan of Final Fantasy since the first title in the good ol’ SNES days, so when I heard about the Pixel Remaster, I knew I had to dive in. Right now I am playing through all FF Titles on Steam and I have been putting in some hours in FF-6 again. so here’s my take.Pros:- Faithful Visuals: The updated pixel art is beautiful. The remaster keeps the charm of the original while making everything look crisper and more detailed. Characters and environments feel more vibrant, and the new lighting effects add a subtle but nice touch.- Orchestrated Soundtrack: The re-recorded music is simply stunning. Nobuo Uematsu’s compositions have never sounded better. There’s an option to switch between the original and the remastered soundtrack, and I found myself switching back and forth just to appreciate the differences.- QoL Improvements: Auto-battle, faster walking speed, and an updated UI are welcome additions. They make the game feel more modern without compromising the original experience.- Story & Characters: Still top-notch, still think FF-6 is the worst title in terms of Story & Character. Its still top! But the other titles are way better! The narrative is as gripping as ever, with unforgettable characters and moments that hit you right in the feels. Kefka is still one of the best villains in the series, while being a total Megalomaniac. Cons:- Font Choice: The new font is a bit of an eyesore. It’s too clean and modern, clashing with the pixel art. I found myself wishing for a more classic-looking font. You can mod it, but it’s an extra step that shouldn't be necessary.- Brightness Issues: Some of the backgrounds, especially in darker areas, seem too bright compared to the original. It doesn’t ruin the experience, but it’s noticeable if you’re familiar with the SNES version.- No Extras: I was hoping for some new content or behind-the-scenes extras, but this is a pretty straightforward remaster. Don’t expect any surprises if you’ve played the game before.Overall:The Pixel Remaster of Final Fantasy VI is a fantastic way to experience one of the greatest JRPGs of all time. Despite a few minor issues, the game remains a must-play, whether you’re a veteran or a newcomer. Just be prepared to tweak the font if you want a more authentic feel.Played it on Steamdeck BTW, runs great. Throttle Settings down and you have 9hrs+ Battery Life.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid port of an all-time classic RPG. It is light on features, the camera tends to jitter when moving, and the UI is kind of ugly. For me, it's still the best way to play FF VI. Here's why:PROS:-The soundtrack has been lovingly recreated with new fonts and electronic orchestration. Some may prefer the original, but I really like how it has been updated.-The "auto-battle" feature speeds up battles--by toggling it on, your characters will automatically perform the last action they did. If you want to assign a new action, simply toggle auto-battle off and give them a new command. This is a huge time saver, especially when you can avoid re-entering the same commands for Sabin's blitz.-The pixel art looks good in native resolution.-The "Opera" scene has been updated with a vocal performance that is charming and adds to the experience.-Extra art and music player are appreciated.CONS-The original soundtrack is not available as an option.-The pixel art is noticeably brighter/lighter in color than the original game. Some say too bright!-The default UI text is an ugly Arial (check out mods if this bothers you like it did me!)-The ATB meter wiggles weirdly and looks bad-Any time the camera moves during a cutscene (sweeping shots or shaking camera) it is jittery and looks bad. CONCLUSION:This port is low effort in some respects, but well done in others. For me, the auto-battle feature, crisp new soundtrack, and sharp visuals make this a great way to play a classic. Plus, one of the best parts of the game--the opera--is enhanced. Celes, with some vocal training I think you could really make it as a singer.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a SNES classic, one of the greatest RPGs of its era, and one of the best Final Fantasy games. And this port is the definitive way to play it.While the original SNES port had its charges, its translation was lacking in places, causing some subplots and characters to be diluted. PR's script is based on the GBA with a couple of touch-ups, allowing the story to come across much stronger. While some of the most memorable one-liners are missing ("son of a submariner!"), the story is overall intact and still holds up, with a memorable cast of characters, a deep and intricate story, and themes about despair, hope, life, and love, that resonate as strongly today as ever (XIV players will find some of Kefka's lines strikingly familiar)The graphics are fantastic. The one smudge is that the world map is WAY too bright, but nothing mods can't fix. Otherwise everyone looks just as good as the SNES or better. IMHO the character sprites are just as good and they more closely resemble the characters' iconic designs they use in other appearances these days. The field graphics are touched up in small ways that add a lot to the atmosphere, like Zozo having graffiti on the walls and broken windows, or Narshe having some of the barrels lying around frosted with snow. Attack animations are recognizable in both visuals and sound; Firaga shoots a massive fireball at enemies that explodes, Blizzaga creates a pillar of ice around them that shatters, Ultima is still the iconic glowing blue sphere of energy, etc.Gameplay is identical to the original, unlike other PR ports there were no major changes to make the game easier, and VI is already pretty easy. What changes they did add are simply quality of life improvements - after a point (I believe when you get the airship) you can view everyone's equipment when they're not in the active party and change their gear anywhere, anytime. You can view if a character has mastered all an Esper's spells or not, and if you try to equip them with an Esper equipped on someone else, the game will let you do that and unequip the other character. The main menu shows you equipped Espers and experience remaining to the next level up. The victory screen shows you the stat boosts characters gain at level up, including the ones from Espers. All these little changes make it much easier to keep track of everyone's skills and equipment and grow your party.The only major change to difficulty is a mercy feature: some spots have pots of healing added to them to fully heal the party. But there's maybe only half a dozen throughout the game, and they have two things in common. One, they're near save points, but any player who is properly prepared will always have a Tent; and two, they're in areas a player can't backtrack out of (at least not easily) and thus if they can't progress, they could be softlocked. So I understand the devs tossing players a free heal in spots where they need it in case they don't have a Tent. The original FF6 actually did that all the time, just in discrete coding rather than a visible pot next to the save point.Other QoL features are here - a map with marked locations, which also tell you how many items and treasures there are to find, a bestiary, a minimap, visible secret passages, auto-saves and quicksaves. Some areas had small indicators added to make navigation easier, particularly the Magitek Research Facility which has caution stripes around pipes, lights added above doors, and has a tweaked palette to make environment features pop a bit more. I don't mind this, some areas in FF6 ARE difficult to navigate, and these touch-ups are unobtrusive.Finally, it goes without saying - the soundtrack is magnificent.The shortcomings of the port largely come from glitches. Some character animations don't play properly in battle (sometimes Mog doesn't do his spin when dancing, characters don't step forward and back properly under certain circumstances), the game freezes sometimes (I've never had it crash, but I know other players have), and there's a bug people found to exploit with Gau to duplicate items. But it's nothing I'm sure can't be patched by fans or Square Enix. The loss of GBA content is mourned but it doesn't hurt the game, this is still a complete and finished game that is just lacking that post-game challenge.Final Fantasy VI was delayed from the promised 2021, and it's obvious it was delayed because Square Enix knew how important this game was, how much players were looking forward to it, and that they had to hit a home run with this remaster.  And they knocked it out of the park. The flaws are minor and excusable, especially in light of how great everything else is. Again, every aspect of this game is just as good or better as the iconic SNES port, and it outshines the GBA port and previous mobile/Steam port with superior sound, graphics, and performance. And if you feel there are elements of the game that should be improved, there are always mods and it's going to be easier to mod this port than any previous ones.If you've never played Final Fantasy VI before, there is no better time or way to experience it than this.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I finally buckled under and bought myself FF6:PR (and have since finished it twice,) I hesitate to give it a blanket recommendation knowing full well a more complete GBA version persists out there. The QoL improvements and superior sound quality isn't really enough to justify the price tag, censorship, inability to skip cutscenes, and exclusion of the GBA version's bonus dungeons and espers. In that sense, this really is a relatively straightforward re-re-repackaging of a great but pretentiously overpriced classic. The PR is better suited to players accustomed to modern grinding options and older fans who have a neurotic itch to finish each and every version of their favorite game. Meanwhile, the rest are probably better off waiting for either a steep discount or, more unrealistically, DLC bringing back all the cut content (i.e., FF6 GBA version > FF6:PR).

_childDocuments_.review: I first played Final Fantasy III on the SNES about two years after it launched. I was 15. It very quickly became one of my all-time-favorite-games and to this day I still enjoy it. Admittedly, I never got to play the GBA version, but I don't feel like I'm missing anything. I played the PS1 version, and I liked the new cut-scenes, but I remember the loading times being crazy long for a disc port. I tried the old mobile version and I honestly couldn't play it because the action menu would cover the entire screen while the background is playing out, making me feel like I'm missing out on the action as it unfolds.This version, the Pixel Remaster, seems to be very enjoyable, and the closest compared SNES version to ever hit the market. It includes the "correct" translation version of the character dialog. However, it also includes the US version SNES release censorship as well. The scene with discovering and releasing Celes, for example, is so heavily edited in the PR, even over the SNES US version, that many people felt it was overreaching and misplaced for western audiences.I've played this game several times over, both SNES and PS1 versions, and I'll say this...This version is obviously the best looking adaptation. The game just "pops"Pros:Overall better textures and atmosphereGood ambient sound/noiseSeveral small QOL featuresIncredible SoundtrackAuto Battle can be a life-saver for grinding levelsGeneral Maps Available for most areas by defaultAuto SaveQuick SaveCons:Lots of screen-tearing, especially during Over World travel by footCombat Commands negated by random enemy actionsRandom Frame Drops, but particularly bad during spell/lore castingPoor performance during City explorationAudio sync issues during cinematicsRandom crashes while loading new saveI absolutely love this particular installment in the franchise, and growing up with it as a kid, it'll always have a special place in my memory. I appreciate this game for everything it is, and more... what it means to me, personally This game got me through some tough times. While I understand FF7 is the popular kid in the room, for being the first 3D game in the series, *everyone claps,* I feel like FF6 would be the seemingly mature, quiet, yet loud when comfortable kid. The guy that likes dark humor, yet tries to remain tasteful. R rating!This is a game best played blind. If you've never ever saw a thing about this game, as old as it is, it is VERY worth the exploration. This is considered an ALL-TIME-CLASSIC. Not to be missed by anyone, even the casual gamers.If you like RPGs even a little bit, this game is for you!!!!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit mixed on FF6 but if you like old JRPGs it's worth a play. I highly recommend modding in the SNES font because the new one is jarring and seems to leave text fields to be practically empty as they were meant for the large and bold original font. If you want to play a SNES JRPG, play Chrono Trigger, if you've already played Chrono Trigger then go ahead and give FF6 a try.FF6 has a lot of good and unique ideas, like giving every character their own special gimmick, but they are done a bit unevenly. Blitz is a top-tier special command, it has it's own special input and it's stupidly strong by not using MP. Tools, another top-tier special command, great, doesn't use MP, no notes. I get why Throw is the way it is, but needing to expend an item and being able to throw weapons just makes it annoying to use, and you can't really go fast or you'll accidentally throw something useful. The other chunk of abilities wouldn't be bad on their own but take a decent amount of investment (like Rage and Lore) to be really useful when Sabin has just been punching the living daylights out of everything while his brother one shots things with a chainsaw with no MP used up and no control of the character lost. I like that the game wants you to use all of the characters and makes them different to incentivize trying them out, but the lack of XP gain for people not in the active party is a drag. I realize this is SNES era so a lot of that quality of life stuff wasn't around yet, but so is Chrono Trigger and it does have XP gain for inactive party members. The lack of XP share would be less of an issue if the last dungeon didn't require you to have 12 party members ready to throw at end game bosses, which also starts making the quality difference in their abilities really stand out. Visually I like SNES era JRPGs as well polished spritework and that holds true here most of the time. A few areas are a little visually busy in my opinion and it makes navigation harder than it has to be, but overall it looks great. The soundtrack was always good and the pixel remaster versions are solid.For this port itself, it seems odd that it doesn't have all of the GBA port bonus content but it doesn't. I had some weird bugs in the last dungeon, a few times while grinding I had enemies just refusing to die even well after passing their HP. No idea why those Great Behemoth's HP broke but they sure did. I also had it get into an invalid state when starting the last phase of the final boss where animations were moving, music was playing, the combat hud was there but no one would do anything. I had to quit and do it all again.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best final fantasy in my opinion.This game is more story driven then either of the other SNES final fantasies, and has my personal favourite final fantasy villain. The villain in this game is overshadowed by Sephiroth from FF7 frequently, but I think the main antagonist in this game is the best example of insanity in the FF series.This game has considerably less character customization than FF5, but it still has quite good variety. The esper system is sort of like the materia system but slightly less open, and a little bit more committed. This game is overshadowed in specific fields, but nothing in this game is worse than mediocre. The story is the high point, and I recommend this game for a number of reasons, but mostly that. The depth of combat is also the most balanced of any of the final fantasies up to this point. There are still a lot of status effects, but a lot more of them actually make sense to exist. There are none that exist to be gimmicky, other than your odd few. Combat in this game feels great either way, and I do not think these oddities take away from the experience.Overall, this game is in my opinion the best final fantasy, and I would rate it at a 9.5/10, mostly because of the story. The only place it really loses points is with the esper system, which while good, is not as good as some others. This is the only real place the game is completely overshadowed. This is my most highly recommended FF game.

_childDocuments_.review: Bottom line: The FFVI Pixel Remaster is a fantastic take on the originals that does not radically change the formula but adds subtle updates to make the game look and sound like you remember. Fans old and new should definitely give it a shot.The Long Version:Final Fantasy VI is comfort food for me. As a 13 year-old queer teenager in 1994, the story and characters of FFVI had a profound impact on me. To this day the SNES original is one of my top five games of all time. There are only a handful of other games that have had such a ttransformative effect on my life. To say that I love the base game is an understatement of epic proportions.When I heard about these Pixel Remasters I brushed them aside. Why "remaster" something when your aim is to make it as close to the originals as possible? Why not just play the originals? It's not like finding a modern way to play them is hard. Well, after about 10 hours I get it. The changes and updates here are subtle, but go a long way to make a slightly new experience for old fans while also providing the optimal way for new players to experience these timeless classics. Graphics:Rather than redraw the sprite work like in the mobile release from a few years ago, Square took the original chunky sprites from the original but added in a subtle upgrade in color depth. At first it's hard to tell what's different, but then it sets in - Edgar has more gold trim on his clothes and different colored boots, for example. Sprites are also a bit bigger overall, and on a 55in screen the whole of the game has a slightly zoomed in effect. It's a little jarring at first, but after an hour or so you get used to it. Backgrounds saw a similar upgrade to color depth, and some backgrounds got a slight 3D treatment to enhance the effects. For example: In your escape from the Returners Hideout on the raft ride, the battle background on the raft has some subtle 3D effects applied to the water to make it undulate and ripple, but it doesn't remove the feeling of the original game. Other touches include upgrades to lighting in towns and dungeons that add more atmosphere. The most noticeable is in Zozo where all the signage now has a soft neon glow - the edges of the neon signs spark and pop and soft purple lighting floods out of the windows in the dark buildings. These subtle upgrades lend credence to the "steampunk" atmosphere the original designers were going for. Again, it's all very subtle but welcome, and doesn't look or feel at all out of place.Music:Uematsu oversaw the music production here, and like the graphics it's a subtle upgrade that adds a bit of extra instrumentation. What it sounds like is he took the original samples the SNES OST is based on, but now they are not compressed to ♥♥♥♥ to fit on an SNES cart. While the compression the SNES sound hardware uses has its own charm, and these new tracks in no way replace the originals, they are an excellent accompaniment to the original design that long-time fans should appreciate. A few tracks like Forever Rachel and Zozo also got a slight extension which adds even more feeling and emotion to each track. This is the aspect of the game I was most worried about, but I've fallen in love with these new mixes. I don't "prefer" them to the originals, but the work the team put in here is to be applauded.Gameplay:The auto-battle option is the standout feature here. Not only does it increase the battle speed by 2x, the game saves your input commands between battles! Basically, you can enter a battle, enter a string of commands for your party, then turn on auto-battle. Your characters will continue to use your last string of inputs on every turn, and those commands carry over into all other battles in the same area. It's almost like setting up little "gambits" (like in FFXII) and watching your minions perform their AI dirty work against the Empire's hordes. What's even more awesome is that complex inputs like Sabin's Blitz commands only have to be entered once. Once the auto-battle is set, he'll repeat the move every turn. Setzer's roulette will still randomize every turn, though, and Cyan's sword arts will still need to charge - so that doesn't break the game or anything. The auto-battle makes grinding a BREEZE! This is very, very welcome addition to the game.Overall:There are a litany of other small changes here and there. I've used the word "subtle" many times in this review, but that is the most apt word I can think of to describe the changes made to this modern edition of one of the true all-time classics. For purists, you can play the SNES original easy enough these days - so there isn't any point in complaining about anything this game is missing or changed - go play the original if that's what you're after. For the rest of us, though, this is a stellar update to one of my very favorite games of all time and I encourage all fans new and old to give it a shot. I think you'll be surprised.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't begin to explain how amazing Final Fantasy VI is all on its own.  The story still holds up.  The characters are still memorable.  The gameplay is still enjoyable.  The music has been, and always will be brilliant.So the real question isn't "is Final Fantasy VI recommended" because that is always going to be a yes from me.  it is instead "is this version worth playing" where the answer can be a little bit more nuanced although in my personal opinion I do think this version is still an excellent way to play a great game for both first timers & veterans.  With that being said I still think there are aspects to the original & GBA version that make them better depending on what the players themselves value.For example: I do prefer the sprites from the original game much more.  That doesn't necessarily mean that these sprites are bad.  In fact the designs in this version is still really nice.  I just preferred the original in comparison.  The GBA version also has bonus content that this version doesn't have.  While it can be argued that the bonus content "isn't necessary" I do think its exclusion is still a negative that justifies critique.  The rearranged music is incredible as well.  Its impossible to say if the original soundtrack is better, or worse because each track would need to be looked at individually.  Although from everything I've heard so far the soundtrack in this version still does the game incredible justice.  The achievements are well implemented similar to the previous pixel remasters.  Definitely worth going for a 100% although a guide is recommended if you decide to do so.I can understand if major fans of the original are not fond of this re-release.  Although I still proudly give this my stamp of recommendation because it does an excellent job presenting the masterpiece that was the original game.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I really loved Final Fantasy 6. Fantastic game. The characterization of FF6 is top-notch, and manages to make the party very likable. FF6's world stands out from many others in the series due to how absent magic is. I do think some characterization is a little undercooked, however, even if I like many of the characters, but I'll cut some slack for the time. My main critique is the Esper system, which is cool on paper, but making it so your stats are gimped if you level too much without them really sucks. Once I was able to grind, I freely did so, but that was extremely late in the game. Espers are probably my least favorite system in the series, and I kinda prefer having characters be more specialized or playing to their niche.But regardless, Final Fantasy VI is legendary, and is iconic for good reasons, and it makes that clear even with how old it is. I'd recommend the Pixel Remaster though, since it adds QoL features (such as turning off XP so you don't overlevel) that'll make the game more tolerable in the modern age.Score: 94

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this on the SNES, GBA, and the old PC version (with the super wonky graphics), and this port is pretty good overall, with some let downs here and there. PROS: The overall pixel remaster looks great on a 16:9 HD monitor, better than an emulated SNES or the old PC, by far the best looking version. Also, easily the best music. The overhaul on the music is still very much in the tradition of the original, just with better samples for certain instruments. Terra's theme, for example, now has a decent panflute sample that pulls it out of that really flat SNES sample sound. Also, plenty of Quality of Life upgrades, like Auto Battle (perfect for grinding), and the weapon and armor stores let you not just compare equipment, but you can equip, remove, and sell the old stuff all in the same menu. Another huge Quality of Life addition is the option to boost your rewards from combat, to lower the amount of overall grinding. The 2nd half of this game is a LOT of grinding, so it helps quite a bit. I think the biggest plus is that the game still feels very much like the SNES version, with the upgrades just enhancing what made the SNES version great. Not a ton was touched, but what was upgraded doesn't pull you out of the FFVI experience like, say, the PC port, where the menus and graphics were just completely different. CONS: I'm still only a few hours in, so this is what I've heard not experienced, but, apparently this doesn't include the GBA additional content. Honestly, I don't remember what that was, because I mostly played the SNES version, but still, strange that they wouldn't give you everything. The game is also a bit strange with scrolling screens. It's choppy, and noticeably choppy. Not enough to really be annoying, but still, weird that it would be an issue. Apparently there's a little censorship, or changing of content, to remove some of the more controversial elements, such as Celes being punched. I don't know, kinda find that...weird. I mean, they don't want to show a guard punching her, but then you'll get into combat and a guard is trying to flat out kill her...just a weird call. OVERALL:It's a great PC version, which is what I've wanted for a while. Yeah, I could emulate the SNES version, but you know, this game is worth my $$$. If this is a game you've played multiple times, and love, you'll probably really enjoy the upgrades, and the price is completely reasonable.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who hasn't dabbled very much in the 2D Final Fantasies, going back to FFVI ended up being a fantastic experience, and (in the absence of knowledge of other versions) I felt like the Pixel Remaster represents the game quite well. Final Fantasy always has had a tendency to change game mechanics pretty significantly between games, even going back this far, and VI's primary gimmicks of espers and a simply enormous, fully modular party make it a very strong entry in the series that allows for a lot of variety across playthroughs, even if that very variety occasionally hampers the personalization of the story.The classic Final Fantasy games all have a specific hook to them as the series rapidly innovated across its early entries, and as mentioned above, VI's big innovation is modular magic loadouts via the Esper system, as well as a simply massive party, in which (barring certain story segments) you can build a party from any configuration of the enormous roster, and customize the abilities of those party members to an impressive degree. It allows for a wonderful amount of freedom in combat, and every single character has a unique hook to them that at least holds SOME appeal, whether it's Sabin's fighting game-style command inputs for his special moves, Terra's Super Saiyan mode, or Gogo being a full mimic character. With Espers, though, you can also forego those things and just make your entire party (with a great deal of effort) Ultima-wielding berserkers, if you so desire. It really makes VI's combat feel like a playground, where you can either create a really specific, edge case-y party lineup or simply setup four win buttons and trivialize battles.People tend to cite VI's story as one of the best in the entire mainline FF series, and I would have to agree, in general terms. The world is vibrant and diverse, populated with dozens of interesting NPCs, both major and minor, and the game makes sure to provide individual story moments for pretty much every single party member, painting its arcs for them in broad strokes that serve to ground the characters in the world and make them feel like they're part of something, rather than simply existing to be heroes. The gigantic shift of the status quo at the game's halfway point is a great way of shaking things up for the player, as well, turning the entire world on its head and upping the stakes significantly. It's the kind of catastrophe that you typically manage to stop in Final Fantasy games, and it was really eye-opening to see a story in which you simply don't make it there in time, and you have to navigate the consequences of that.A major thing that bothered me, particularly in the late game, however, is how the open party system ends up working as a direct detriment to the game's storytelling. Early on, your party is highly curated, with new members being added and split up according to story events that allowed them to be fully present in the narrative, as the game knows exactly who you'll have available at those points of the story. After the turning point, however, the party becomes completely modular, and aside from the re-recruitment process for each party member, every story beat is forced to treat your party generically without assigning lines or, really, any personality at all to a given character. It made me feel kind of like the cast had been stripped of their intrigue, and that they'd become simply vessels for combat, and I found that disappointing. I understand that this game was made for the SNES originally, and that the level of complexity for building a system that accounts for exactly who you have in your party to determine dialogue was probably far too high for the time, but it disappointed me all the same.FFVI is a great game, easily one of the best entries in the series overall. Yes, the Pixel Remaster is missing the extra content from the GBA port. Yes, the PC versions of the Pixel Remasters were inferior to the console versions for a while. Yes, the way the art style is unified across the six games comes at the cost of a bit of charm for each game. However, considering how modern these versions feel, combined with absolutely vital quality-of-life features like modifiers for EXP, money, and encounter rates, there really is no better way to play FFVI in 2024. Give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: AN UNFORGETTABLE EXPERIENCEThis review is not only for this game but also the Pixel Remasters as a whole since I've finished all of them. I have 31 hours of playtime from start to finish, and the 78 hours on my profile is mainly because I restarted my playthrough twice. I'm going to review the Pixel Remasters first to reflect on my journey playing and finishing through them.These remasters launched without this game in particular, Final Fantasy VI which is a real bummer since when I eventually played it, all the hype was already lost and I dropped on my first playthrough because I started doing other stuff. Also the default fonts really sucked and I didn't mention them on my past reviews because I didn't expect for them to be updated to a better, classic font style in the future. Now that there's a new update that bring QoL features from the console release including better fonts, I just want to mention the default font sucks Sephiroth's Masamune. Also, three years after the launch release to get these updates? I was a different person finishing those games three years ago compare to now.Reflecting back on my journey through the Pixel Remasters, all of these are legitimately great games that became sources of inspiration for future games. I have not played the Golden Era (FF8, FF9. FF10) yet and have played mostly the modern games, and I can see most of the inspirations those games have taken from these classics (ESPECIALLY FF14). Despite these games playing like old games, no hand holding, no guide, many secrets, and generally hard, the QoLs these versions came with can be a great help especially with FF1 and FF2 specifically. Still reflecting on the Pixel Remasters, all of them are standouts but the ones that I truly connect to and have been thinking of replaying them (or just scored 5/5 for me) are FF1, FF5, and this game, FF6. FF1 is mainly because I have a strong bias for it being my very first Final Fantasy game. I've played it on GBA and the PSP, and now playing it here even with full 100% completion, I still want to replay it again, maybe doing a full monk party or full white mage party. The same reasons can be applied to FF5 with how much stuff you can do with the job system in that game and also I have not done anything past the final boss purposely so that I can have a new playthrough being refreshingly blind. Other games like FF2, FF3 and the beloved FF4 are still great, but I prefer more customizable combat system to do crazy things with like especially in FF5.Reviewing Final Fantasy VI; This game is great. I restarted my playthrough twice because I became disconnected from the story on my first playthrough, and the new QoLs update dropped on my second playthrough. Despite having to get through the game thrice, the experience felt new and refreshing (maybe because I just have generally bad memory). Ima be honest, I was kinda spoiled on some aspects unlike past games so this finished playthrough is not fully blind. Describing it vaguely, I accidentally looked up on how to acquire certain party members. Not all are spoiled for me though fortunately.Onto the gameplay first, at first I was not down on the Esper system and Relics. Kinda felt abit of step down from FF5's Job System. Also this is why I dropped on my first playthrough, which I shouldn't do, is comparing it alot to FF5. I relearn on my latest playthrough and honestly now I get it. There's still alot of crazy stuff you can do especially with the amount of party members you can have and also their unique abilities that if assigned to certain Esper and Relics, can be a complete beast. So yeah, past me was just generally dumb and FF6's combat system is honestly just as engaging as FF5.The story is the most unique and darkest I've ever experienced in a Final Fantasy game. I don't think a Final Fantasy VI Remake can be done without a large amount of changes needed that will definite deviate from the original. The story tackles topics like warfare, death, loss, genocide, and more stuff that will give an M Rating on this day and age. And its not being dark to be edgy or cool, the story is genuinely good and deep that will make these characters more emotionally resonant. It is not a sad or depressing story like NieR though. There's still the fun and goof while adventuring, and that's what makes it great.Speaking of story, the characters are unique and amazing that I don't think has been recreated in other games generally. In Final Fantasy VI, the main character is who (the player) wants to be. There's no main character in this like Cloud in FF7 or Tidus in FF10. On my first playthrough I picked Locke and Celes and see them as the main characters and got some unique cutscenes that only played when I have them on my party. On my second playthrough, I leaning towards using Sabin more and got a new cutscene that I completely missed on my first playthrough. So yeah, there are no main characters because all of the ones you can pick can be the main character you want, and that's what makes it unique.Thinking about the story more, this story presents itself like a stage play even in the old games. Its kinda crazy now that I realised that these games are created in the 90's and most of the story ideas and presentation are from that era. Despite that, the story in these games are way, way ahead of their time. FF6's story in particular, is pretty much the same as Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame or tackles the same themes and beats. That will be the only comparison I'll give relating to today's modern entertainment but alot of the same things can be said in FF5 too. I think I spoiled too much on the story so I'm going to end this review right here. Other things that are honestly great is the music, which obviously is. Each melody making me DANCE MADLY.Overall, as you can see, I kinda love the game.5/5

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best version of a game that's been released to us about 6 times at this point. Alot of people have the same complaints, and I'd say they are partially (in such a small amount) valid.The font sucks. It makes the game unplayable for the vision-impaired (so I've heard) and it's just awful to look at otherwise.  YOU CAN FIX THE FONT IN 2 SECONDS. THE SAME WAY AND THE SAME FILES AS MOST OF US HAVE DONE FOR THE OTHER 5 GAMES.People complain about some of the most minute, pitiful things to complain about- the Opera Scene (anyone who's played this game before knows the scene) is fully vocalized and in my opinion sounds great. Within the context of the game's story, there's a very pertinent reason the singing lady doesn't sound like the person she's trying to impersonate. I've heard that some of the sprites have been made into oversaturated messes. I think the devs went a little extreme on Gau's hair, but for the most part, all of the core party members look and seem refreshed. Some of the costumes have much more detail (the new rendering allows the devs access to way, wayyyy more color options than they used to have), and much of this detail is beautiful now that you can make sense of it. Gau's hair is extremely bright, but when you're in any of the (HUGE amount) of "dreary" landscapes, he looks awesome.Speaking of landscapes- the battle backgrounds look amazing. The in-game animations look crisp and clear, and out of battle, in certain scenes, lightning and weather effects have been added that add a whole dimension to the environment maps.It feels just as difficult as the previous "best versions" of the game. It's missing the GBA content (SO were the other 5 games) and honestly, i dont feel like any of these games got anything actually tangible from the extra content. So the complaint there feels like a load of garbage, also. This game was supposed to wrap up within the game. No reason for post-game content given what happens in this game's story.The OST is absolutely banging. I'd venture as far as to say this is a playable album and not a video game with a soundtrack, because every track is worth setting your controller down just to vibe for a moment. Everything is memorable. The SNES version was great, but now dated.. The GBA version had compressed, choppy sounding versions of some of this game's hallmark tracks, and some of them felt ruined, to the point where modders replaced the GBA files for something better. I didn't play the sloppy mobile port ( and you shouldn't have either ) but i'd reckon this PR release is the best version of all of the songs that one may hear, unless you see one of those performing orchestras?I haven't completed the game yet and my gameplay thusfar is genuine. Don't come to FF6 expecting hundreds of hours of gameplay. IN fact, 65-70 might be a little heavy but thats where I expect to end my game. Due to the time of this game's release and the sheer amount of characters, it is sort of lacking in character development. I feel the devs could have added "character quests" for everybody, beyond the initial "recruitment mission" for each of them. It is to be expected from a game this old, but for what it lacks in character development, it absolutely makes up for in character variety.Quite possibly the best JRPG of all time. Besides Tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: Bad first: The font still sucks noodle, per ALL the pixel remakes. They REALLY ought to provide a clean and easy option menu approach to fix that from installed options or something akin, and to default to something better. As it is, a much better replacement exists in the installation, as the japanese font used is apparently UNicode and includes latin charactes, so works as a drop-in replacement but is a much clearer font.To replace it, use steam's "Browse Local Files" option from the right click menu to open up the installation directory and navigate into the `\FINAL FANTASY VI_Data\StreamingAssets` directory. If you are comfortable in the command line and are running Windows: navigate here and type: `copy *_en.* *_en_bad.*` then `copy *_jp.* *_en.* /Y` (Technically, you can just run the second one if you don't care to have a backup of the buffugly font handy. You can, at worst, reinstall it from Steam, so it's not a big deal.)Or, if you insist on GUI madness, simply select the files with _EN one by one, copying the existing file name and then renaming them something that'll remind you of what they were. (say whatever_en_bad.whateverelse) Then select the most similar _jp file and drag it holding control to copy it. Rename it and paste the old name in. Repeat for all the old _en files. This'll be either two or three files.It's a great game. The story is still fun. The graphics are nice. The music is excellent. Some of the weird sequences like the mine cart or opera work a bit differently and these invariably look much better. I'd like a better vocalist for the opera because it sounds like a trained person making a ton of mistakes (which led me to look it up; turns out that's exactly what was happening: the vocalist that they hired was a professional opera singer attempting to sound untrained and doing a mixed job at it, which was distracting.) It would have been a great time to hire someone who simply knows how to sing in a non-operatic style do it.Aaanyhow, I loved it as a kid and I still like this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far the best iteration of FFVI. Definitely install a font mod if possible, but everything else is beautiful. Everything feels like you remember it, but better. Most attacks are hugely improved. The rescored music does a fantastic job capturing the mental image the original songs gave me (No surprise, since Uematsu himself rescored all of these pixel remasters). Highly recommended over any of the previous awful mobile remakes.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the greatest games of all-time and my personal favorite, it's fantastic to finally have my hands on this. The upgraded musical tracks alone make this worthwhile, as FFVI features one of the deepest and best scores in all of gaming. If you haven't played a Final Fantasy before, I recommend starting with the original and maybe IV and V before playing VI. VI is the kind of game you'll already want to understand how to play and what to expect, that way the game's many features, storylines, and twists surprise and delight you. Plus, all of the prior FF games are fun to play, and with IV and V in particular you can see all the lessons they learned from those games applied in VI. Final Fantasy VI is one of those games that I wish that I could "play for the first time" again, so if this is your first go-around with the game, take your time and savor it. You're in for an adventure!

_childDocuments_.review: This remaster is pretty dang good, I know people were ...oddly harsh on the redone sprites in this game but I think they look better than the originals. Anyway, on to the review; So they didn't go crazy with the visuals in this, they reused visuals from the SNES & GBA versions of the game and I think either expanded or remade the battle backgrounds for widescreen. But all of the special effects like magic, smoke, etc were redone. I think the game across the board looks better maybe with the exception of the world map and the font they keep insisting on using. (you can mod this without downloading anything, there are guides to use the JP english font for a better font or other fonts that are more fitting) They did a lot to make this game better, Cyan's Bushido skills don't require you to wait on his turn to do his skills, you can activate them and he waits himself till he can activate them. Sabin's Blitz inputs are the easiest they've ever been to input- telling you the inputs but also letting you retry (as long as you don't hit confirm). The auto-battle function that is in other pixel remasters is here- repeating your last actions that can go between battles. They've been patching the game since launch fixing bugs and whatever else. As of writing they fixed soft locking bugs, my first boss encounter the boss vanished and never came back- it's not happened since. But the game still seems to have a speed problem- even if you turn off ATB the enemies still benefit most from increased battle speed- which genuinely makes the game much more difficult. The only other issue is the game (even on an NVME) has to load into the game and after you're loaded in you're stuck for 5+ seconds in place while the game does...something? IDK you just can't move and this is AFTER the loading screen. It's a weird problem that doesn't break anything as it's only when you have loaded the game.The music is across the board better. I know people are nostalgic for this game's OST (because it's great) but I haven't encountered a song that I didn't think was improved in some way with ..IDK maybe the chocobo theme being the exception? The only negatives I can put against this game is:The intro doesn't have credits which makes it a bit awkward with the mechs running toward the town and nothing but the music to fill time.The battle speed as I mentioned; enemies benefitting more from battle speed than you 100%. Lacking the PS1 FMVs which, seriously are pretty great. The game doesn't NEED them, but I enjoyed them plenty.And if you want a nitpick I guess the fact they didn't redo the visuals to the extent other pixel remasters. But FF6 held up a ton as far as I'm concerned, the sprites being redone looked way better to me. "Oh no, Locke is thinner than the monk, what ever will we do". And the mine cart scene looked worse than the SNES version...but if that's enough to warrant an actual negative ..IDK what to tell you there. Oh- and if you're gonna get upset by the censorship of the 'salute' well it's 1 scene that really didn't contribute much to the game anyway. It's not like Tales of Beseraia where it changed the entire tone of the scene, if you don't know what I'm talking about...it's too much to go into here. I'm anti-censorship but it's barely a note here. If you're looking for a ...legal way to play the game, this version is 100% better than the mobile port they brought to PC and there's few negatives you can put to this version vs the SNES version.It's a great game and I think it's worth playing- especially for the price. I think they did a great job (and square doing a good port is a miracle in it of itself). Doesn't matter if you have nostalgia or not for this game I think it's worth a playthrough. Also; play Phantasy Star 4, great game you can get for almost a dollar and came out around the same time as the OG ver of this game. Seriously, they're both great!
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY VI

_childDocuments_.review: It feels almost dumb to say this in 2023 but it really is wild how good FF6 is, and how much of a step up it is from the previous games. FF5 does quite a lot in terms of game mechanics with the job system etc, but beyond that it feels pretty much the same as any of the NES games. They basically just did the same game over and over 5 times and it wasn't until 6 that they decided "Hey what if we do something else", and then proceeded to just completely nail it. What a game.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY VI

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great, but I'd be remiss if I didn't mention my dislikes:1. I ran into a hard lock in a battle against the Samurai Soul in the ancient castle. Gau got stuck casting Reraise every turn (I don't know how) and after the rest of the party was finally dead he re-raised himself. After coming back to life, he got stuck doing his spellcasting animation, as if he was going to cast Reraise again. He was poisoned, but the poison didn't damage him anymore, and the Samurai Soul wouldn't act, either. I had to exit the game and redo a few minutes' worth of progress, then start the battle over again.2. The Jidoor/Zozo writing is really weird. You go to Jidoor and townsfolk are talking about how they ran all the poor people out of town because they're liars and crooks and thieves. It's textbook classism, so I figured the game was setting that up in order to knock it down. You find out Jidoor's poor established their own town, so you go to Zozo, and not only does everyone there actually lie to you, almost every single NPC in the town is part of a quest where finding the solution is centered around knowing all of the people in Zozo are liars. It's pretty absurd, lmao.3. Whenever Gau learns a new move, the left side of the 'G' in his name is cut off in the text box on the victory screen. Not a big deal, but one of those things you see for the first time and then just can't stop looking at every time it happens.4. The whole entire Veldt mechanic where Gau has to run around and leap on enemies in the Veldt to learn their moves is a nightmare. I have 80 hours in this game and somewhere between 10 and 20 were absolutely just running around the Veldt trying to get encounters with newly found enemies so he could get new moves. The worst part is that it's actually pretty worth it, because Gau with good moves is really strong.All in all, though, I'd say it's fighting with Final Fantasy 5 for my favorite old school Final Fantasy game. Some people have complaints about how the Pixel Remaster looks compared to the original, and that's totally fair if you're someone who's used to the original, but never being particularly invested in the SNES version means the remaster's aesthetic didn't bother me, even if I do think the original game looked nicer.
_childDocuments_.name: FINAL FANTASY VI

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game, and this version of the game. It could be seen as a toss up since this version is true to the original release where the GBA/Mobile port version had some minor additional content, but the additional content was honestly not all that. It eliminated some of the few, rare important item choices in the game to just give you multiple rewards instead. That's about it. The game was never structured in a way to incentivize post game, like all early final fantasies, so tacking on one late dungeon didn't help. More importantly, the PC release of the additional content came with new objectively bad sprites and menus from being a mobile port.However, this is the most supported version of the game, does not have those glaring flaws, and is very worth playing. This is the definitive version in my book.
