_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty damn decent. You remember when you first started playing the new XCOM 1? How it was actually a little spooky? This game manages to nail that tone and maintain it throughout, even as you grow more powerful. That alone is pretty admirable and worth trying, and it's also a good little tactical RPG beneath the lovely coat of paint as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Stirring Abyss is a fun, turn-based strategy game where you lead a team of submarine crewman as they explore the bottom of the ocean and fight the eldritch horrors they have stumbled upon.  I really enjoyed the atmosphere and the game mechanics instantly recall XCOM: Terror From The Deep.  Not too difficult on Normal but not too easy either.  There is a bit of RNG when it comes to item drops and starting skills, so you may find yourself with a bad hand but generally the speargun will help you along.  I found that melee was mostly useless unless buffed up through mutations as being close to enemies is usually a death sentence since the majority have damaging area effects on dying.Main campaign has a standard story line – explore, acquire gear, and level-up – with a couple of boss fights.  The “endless” mode, however, is a chore I doubt many will invest much time in.  While the main game introduces enemies to match the equipment and levels gained over time, Endless mode drops the unskilled and unequipped crew into fights with enemies they have no hope of defeating..Overall, a pretty good time for Mythos fans and fans of turn-based squad combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: I really like squad based games, but this one is just not very fun.  All advantage goes to the AI for sure.  You first few missions will have you vs. mobs that get ranged attacks, while you'll get one guy that gets 2 ranged attacks then has to spend a round to reload.  I simply don't understand why attacking uses all of your action points.  If you attack first, you should be able to move after.  Once again, advantage AI.  I read there are 13 missions, in the few I did, the maps are identical.  Boring.  Needs some kind of manual as the tutorial is pretty limited.  Bought it too long ago to refund, so guess I'm stuck with it.  Looks like there is a demo for it, give it a try before you buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: A classic, turn-based, tactical squad game. An indie gem with great atmosphere. I love the Lovecraft + Terror from the Deep vibe and the atmospheric soundtrack, the visual design. The gameplay is pretty standard for this  sub-genre, but it does not disappoint. I would love to see more games in this universe.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game, but it has it's flaws. One major flaw is the game difficulty is crazy, "Normal" difficulty would be "Insane" on other games..! So I ended up starting a new game on Easy, and it is still pretty challenging on Easy. But for the most part, it is a lot of fun exploring, and mutating your crew members to make them more powerful. There is a endless rogue-like mode, that adds a lot of replay value to this game, I plan on checking that out once I finish the Story Mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: It's like XCOM Terror From the Deep with the Lovecraftian atmosphere turned to 11. The artwork is great and very fitting. The sound design makes for a very sinister feeling of the unknown lurking in the depths. The overall feeling is very creepy and depressing which makes for a nice horror game. The gameplay is solid without all the nick nacks XCOm has, but still very entertaining.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: There are consequences for your actions...but can you take responsibility for them when your mind is slowly falling apart? The lure of attaining unknown, but seductive powers, weave into the fabric of your mind as you stumble upon ancient altars and artifacts that are both profane to all that is decent yet attract you with their indescribable, other-worldly beauty...like moths to a flame.Definite must-buy. The audio is top notch.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting and unusual title that combines strategy, RPG and storytelling in a slow-paced but pressing and immersive atmosphere. A great combination of mystery and carefully meditated maps magically touched by a tenebrous and original soundtrack. A reminescence of H.P. Lovecraft's 'The Call of Cthulhu'
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Stirring Abyss is a missed opportunity. The setting is of course amazing, and we do need many more deep sea games and we need them now. As far as the Lovecraftian mythos goes it's very basic, minus the whole story revolving around the Minoan civilization, which I thought was cool. The Minoans are often overlooked in how brilliant of a people they were, ultimately ending in disaster due to a variety of factors such as being an island nation (for those who don't know, they were Cretans) in a time in which the supply lines weren't nearly as robust as they are today; the Mycenaean invasion, and of course the rather mysterious Bronze Age Collapse itself.Just an example of how advanced they were, especially for the time. The Minoan artifacts still hold color today, whilst the Greek and even the Roman sculptures have weathered into their colorless versions. In a lot of ways the Minoans are a civilization of lost knowledge, that was arguably more advanced in some ways to the (for the lack of a better term) Classical Age.And this brings me to my central point when it comes to story. Even here it's a missed opportunity. The Minoans should have been better explored, instead they're just a substitute for the trite Atlantis fabrication. I think this topic deserves much more respect that it has been given by the developers of Stirring Abyss.Gameplay wise it's mess. The turn-based combat does nothing new or even remotely interesting. It's like playing Terror from the Deep in the 90s all over again, but somehow even worse. Full disclosure: the original XCOM was way ahead of its time and is in my opinion a perfect game. Its sequel however is just an exercise in tedium and frustration. The levels are enormous, just as the case here. The soldiers don't cover nearly enough ground, just is the case here. The buildcrafting is lifted straight out of the XCOM remake and is therefore not very interesting at all. The mutation adds some flair into the game, but most of them are either underwhelming or outright useless.This brings me to the finishing blow that reduces any chance of the game being recommended to ash. The game's brutal difficulty forces one to use broken builds (trust me, a double revenant mutation is a must). Even on hard this broken build makes the game way too easy. But everything else is way too hard. Even on the narrative difficulty the game will kick your 4ss if you're not playing meta.As if that weren't enough all of this also forces one to safe scum like crazy. Even to just get the right mutations, as they're presented in a random list of two or three with an upgrade, with only a single reroll allowed. That reroll costs a valuable resource too, because of course it does.Next you can't grind for resources as the supply missions are limited. There's a bunch of useless items that the game grants you recipes for (of course there's crating), The problem is, the resources are shared for upgrading the sub, which you really need to do. And as mentioned before the only useful items really are the flak vests, the harpoons for officers, and the oxygen tanks. Don't even bother with anything else. Explain to me why I would take a turret that lasts 4 turns and does barely any damage, or a stimulant when I get 2 item slots, 3 slots with a very rare upgrade at most? It makes no sense.Seriously, skip this one. If you want to play a sea game, just play Subnautica. I'll try Barotrauma next. Fingers crossed for it being good.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10Stirring Abyss is a tactical game ambient in a Lovecraftian nightmare where you accompany stranded divers trying to survive the depths of the sea and return to their families.  7/10I really enjoyed the music and sound effects, plus the VA of the introduction and ending are great. A shame that there aren’t more moments like that. 7.5/10It won’t get any prizes here, but it is good. Visually, the divers are the most distinguishing of all, and when they get some mutations, they visually change to match them (though I wished this would have applied to all mutations). Monsters are different, but their character art is probably more stunning than the game designs in itself.The maps are very similar, with small changes as you go deeper and deeper. This is probably one of the weakest points.And your ship, as you make upgrades and repurpose rooms, I did enjoy seeing the changes that occurred.  8/10I would say this is a lite-tactical game. The game itself isn’t long, and the gameplay is repetitive like X-Com. Go into a mission, kill enemies, find something, get back to base, improve/upgrade, repeat. What makes it interesting is that there is a lot of variety for the amount of missions in the game, and that the skills you can choose from when leveling up are random even in the same classes.The enigma board, which would be the equivalent of a technology tree/research, is interesting, though a bit more information about what to expect at the different levels might have made it easier to know where to risk the clues you get to unlock the rewards. 9/10Trapped beneath the sea, just looking to get back home, the divers find themself drawn into the maws of hell. Now, how deep will they go to try and save the world. That’s basically the premise, and it works really well. Most of the main missions expand on the world, and you can even find notes of other divers trapped there (russians for example). I did enjoy the story a lot, and my only gripe is that I wished for more to explore.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Decent. The atmosphere is great but was let down by pretty simplistic gameplay. Once I understood how everything worked I used generally the same tactics. There also wasn't much as far as equipment advancement. Pretty much one or two flavors of knives, spearguns, or dartguns if you don't count the mutations which were pretty damn cool.The game ended pretty quickly but I feel like the game length worked given the lack of depth in gameplay. I probably wouldn't have finished it if it lasted much longer.Overall, happy with it, I just think the price point should be around $10 given the content here.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: The submarine serves as your base and you chose between missions to send your divers on a map over the abyss. The submarine needs repairs and upgrades that you purchase with materials you divers  collect on missions. The missions are small scale actions where you can bring up to 4 divers,  to accomplish a goal while fighting of foes. You have manage your teams health, sanity and air supply.  When a mission is completed you can chose to stay longer and explorer/ collect materials. There are both ranged and melee combat  in the game.  There are only one type of ranged weapon in the game  speargun, but there are different ranged skills to use with it. Each diver can bring two items on a mission, so you have to chose carefully what to bring, there are mutations and skills there enable a diver to bring more items later in the game. Light from flares and the submarine plays a crucial role so you can spot  the monsters before they see you. There three main character  classes and different traits and mutations make sure the divers are different. I like the look and feel of the game, it has a very nice underwater setting especially the underwater sounds. Many of the foes look very scary, while a few just look goffy.On the normal setting I did not find the game, that hard I was able to complete the storyline without any diver deaths even through a few became temporary insane.. Its a lot like xcom in that regard, that once you know, how to play and what the differ skills do, you start to get stronger than the enemies and can do the missions without taking much damage. There is a sort of doom clock there raise the stats of monsters, but it wont end the game when it runs full and the monsters don’t get that much stronger.  There is an endless mode  I am trying out and it seems a good way to add extra replay value to the game. It’s a bit more like a roguelike game in that setting.  In think the different types stuff you have to manage in the game is very well done. I would recommend it to anyone who like turn based games.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic turn based tactics game inspired by lovecraft's writings, specifically 'The Temple.'  It is essentially a new take on x com 'terror from the deep.'   It is brutal though, so I would recommend starting on 'easy' to get used to the systems and how they interact.   The atmosphere, story and art design are superb.  The turn based combat is unique, even though it borrows from nu xcom.  The fact that it take place deep underwater, with the need to regulate air and sanity, the mutations, powers and the support from the ship, gives the combat its own flavor.  Absolutely recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: So I just finished Stirring Abyss. Brilliant game. It's X-Com: Terror from the Deep but Lovecraftian. Extremely atmospheric, decently tactical, and amazingly well written. I was really getting to know/love the characters I was playing with. This is probably some of the best writing I've seen in a while.The art is also quite good - the enemies are properly grotesque and horrifying. Almost as grotesque and horrifying as some of the things that go on in the story. Upgrade your gear, mutate your crew! Because why not?The game also features and endless mode for replayability after you've completed the main campaign. Anyway, didn't want to do a deep dive into what the game is and how it plays - (as I said, think XCOM but lovecraftian) but I just wanted to put my thoughts down while they're fresh.I love this game and can't wait for a sequel. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Above average lovecraftian Xcom-like turn based RPG, where you repair your sub, gather supplies and grow tentacles. There is a decent story mode and a very enjoyable endless mode as well.The only thing that was a bit disappointing is the difficulty curve. The game starts ridiculously hard (which I like) but turns into a cakewalk pretty soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: This game reminds me a lot of the first Xcom in its appearance and game mechanics (well, actually Xcom 2, Terror from the Deep...). The difficulty is manageable on the lowest setting ("Story"), and it's an intriguing plot with some depth. However,  the developer did not provide a manual. I think I could do better at the game if I understood what all the settings mean and how everything works, but I'm not willing to put in the time for a trial and error approach to learning the rules, and frankly, I shouldn't have to. I don't expect the thick manuals developers provided in the '90s, but zero direction on game settings just smacks of laziness and/or unprofessionalism on the part of the developer. If the developer decides to provide a user guide or manual in future, I'll revisit my rating.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: WAT, x-com two?? Are you f*king delirious, or just out of your small minds? It's a scripted adventure RPG with sloppy art style & everything, it looks like it plays. Overpriced like all hell, typical Slitherine product. The visual similarity with x-com classic is provided by underwater topic & square based board. A rare game i feel buyer's remorse about. Those stupid reviewers tho..... they've lured me into buying this desperate bundle fodder at 3x price!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty cool if you're into turn based rpgs and lovecraftian stuff!  First attempt consider it a learning experience, second attempt kick some ass.  You spend your time searching the ocean floor and fighting horrors, once done you can call in your anchor and go to your submarine where you can rest and build things to help you along the way, definitely recommend if you like a chill lovecraftian experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: It's not life-changing, but it's really good. So far the controls, aesthetic, tech trees, mission variety, it's all perfectly good for the price point. I actually prefer this to some radically reinvented take on the old X-COM formula. It scratches the itch nicely for an hour or two each night and I don't feel particularly bored or shortchanged by any one aspect of it. It is exactly what is advertised, no more and no less. How rare is that? I will say that some elements like giving items to different crew members isn't explained all that well, but it's minor if you're willing to be even the tiniest bit curious. Definitely worth a purchase if you like Squad Tactics games.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: This game sucked me right in and got my spine tingling a couple of times. Storytelling is excellent and the sound design gives you the chills.Don't get deterred by the clunky looking UI. There is a terrific game underneath.So far it brings the joy I remember of the old XCOM games to me. Of course "X-COM: Terror from the Deep" jumps to mind.Don't be afraid to start on 'Narrative' or 'Easy' difficulty. Rough start otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: I edited this review to be a little fairer - first the pros, then...Pros ++ Rich, gloomy, Lovecraftian atmosphere, and happy to wear its inspirations on its sleeve+ Decent (not amazing) storytelling, voicework and art design for an indie game+ Exploration, combat and base maintenance mechanics work well and are uncomplicated+ Moves along well enough to pull you into the game+ Strong musical scoreCons -- Sharp difficulty spike and one autosave mean you may restart a lot, is quite unforgiving- Favours the narrow 'tough choices' gameplay approach over 'choose your own' approach- There tends to be one right way, if you don't pick it, you're brown bread
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: It's neat, heavy xcom vibes so a good fix in that department if you enjoy those kind of games. I really enjoy the mutation mechanics, neat for making some fun builds. Can be a bit brutal, but I mean what else can you expect from a game of this genre with lovecraftian influences. One of those games where you start very weak, but once you get the ball rolling and have some good builds down you can do some pretty cool stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: It reminds me of X-Com: Terror from the Deep in all the right ways. The atmosphere is ominous, tense, and claustrophobic. The art style and writing have a nice pulp feel that suits the sense of cosmic horror and dread well. I have not yet completed the story but I am enjoying the slow unfurling of the scope of the ancient undersea setting.Edit: Having now completed the story, I can say that I enjoyed it all the way through and I was not disappointed. It is not the longest, but I feel that trying to drag out the tension and suspense longer would have worn thin and detracted from the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Hard and unforgiving turn based combat in a old comic book style.RPG part has significant weight in how you survive in a Lovecraftian seabed. You can modify your sub, mutate your crew, develop tec.You can even resurrect you killed marines but it will cost you sanity.... Oh the Madness!!!!Overall nice little game with good own ideas.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Alot going on in this title (not hard to play at all) theres alittle curve but once you start seeing what you can do with your submarine and skills/gear/crafting and the way it plays out it really draws you in to want to play more. Theres alot of options for you to create that perfect team and having fun while you do it. Dev's did a great job on this, enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: This is actually a pretty nice game,.Mix a bit of FTL with some Terror From The Deep, add a generous amount of lovecraftian touch and fun is served.You get attached to the crew members fairly quickly and it's really sad when they die (they will). Luckily it is possible to bring them back to life, for a price...
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Cold War Cthulhu. Submarines, Bottom of the ocean exploration RPG.  The mechanics are easy to grasp, and do what you need them to.  The story is something Cthulhu that I haven't seen done before, so that's refreshing (I KNOW it's not TECHNICALLY Cthulhu, but come on.)  The art is distinctive, and I really like the base building mechanic because it's simple, but let's you design things the way you want.  Do you want a cultist crew?  Do you want stalwart Naval Officer?  Blood thirsty vandals?  And the crew banters back and forth about stuff that's happening, which I wasn't expecting, so it was a neat surprise.The only thing so far I haven't been thrilled with are the torpedos.  It felt like the enemies knew they were coming.  How?  They're fish people who have never seen a torpedo.  I had three shark dude make INTENSELY bizarre movements to get out of the way of the blast radius.  I dunno if it's for balancing, but it felt kinda cheap.  It's a minor element, but annoying since you do have to invest in it.Also, if you were a fan of Baldur's Gate 3's dice rolling, this game ALSO has dice rolling!
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: First rooms to build: Dissection room -> expand away teamYou want as many sadists on the team as possible.Joker on the Officer is very useful.Music room is a must. You want to use supplies to heal sanity.Have two scientists on the team - they are very useful in controlling the battlefield. Psychiatrist skill is the goat. Have one seaman as your tank and front man. Always send him first. Don't be shy with using submarine's searchlights and radar either.Focus enemies draining your sanity. Fathom seer is your biggest enemy.In the Endless mode make sure you don't take enemy regeneration handicap twice - it will make Assasination missions impossible, especially with Exalted sharks Reflection skill - he'll heal faster than you can deal damage. Also, ALWAYS avoid Salvage missions - you can't split your team and survive.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: I've finished Stirring Abyss under normal difficulty and here are my two cents : It's an XCOM-lite that takes place underwater in Cthulhu's playground, and thankfully it's much better than Terror From the Deep (note to MicroProse, longer and tougher isn't always better). You command a team of hapless mariners in turn-based combat across multiple handcrafted isometric maps, where each character have two action points to either move or act. The mariners come in three classes : Marine, Officer, and Scientists (AKA brawler, shooty guy, and nerdy shooty guy), and can be further customized with skills and equipment for diversity. In between missions, there is a strategic layer where your crews will return to their submarine to carry out repairs, craft equipment, and advance skill trees to unlock further options, which can unlock ...eldritch options for the crews, but to say more would be spoilery. So why is this game XCOM-lite? To start with it's not meant to be endlessly replayable via procedurally generated missions : there are about a dozen story missions plus a limited number of optional side missions to undertake. It's also an indie release with simple animation and few music pieces, that nevertheless did a good job emulating the terror of being trapped leagues under the sea. The standout part of the game is the gorgeous terrain art design, which has an old-timey comic book look that gives the game an otherworldly look, and it only gets freakier the deeper you go...Stirring Abyss' biggest strength is that it captures the essence that made XCOM (and the way less bombastic x-com) such great games: It's the terror of the unknown and the game shoving player out the door, with nothing more than a sheet of basic instructions to fend for yourself. In my first playthrough I lost my first crew within the first thirty minutes because I panicked at my first sighting of an underwater abomination, which caused me to stare at my screen in disbelief for a minute, and then immediately restarted the game, vowing to do better on my second run. It's that type of game where even failure is part of the fun. The game will get easier on replay as the unknown becomes known. I enjoyed every minute of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic, aesthetically quirky turn based strategy game with tight and interlocking tactical , rpg and resource management mechanics. It handles and integrates its lovecraftian and pulp themes sensibly and has really made each and every enemy unique with their own challenges and solutions, battles can feel like a good game of chess with added chaos thanks to RNG. It would be nice to have more enemy types and environmental tilesets as after a little while you have seen it all!
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: + Atmosphere is fantastic.+ Mechanics are clearly explained.+ Story has potential. - Huge diffculty spike early on (the one after your first salvage mission) that left me in a unwinnable situation that I could not rectify because the game autosaves. To elaborate, I had no power for an evac zone, crew had no oxygen remaining and they weren't strong strong to take on the objective. Playing out the scenario left with me the single crew member I had left behind who would've been left reattempting the same mission. This is only one example, but based on other reviews I can see myself being pigeonholed into other hopeless scenarios.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: As the other reviewer just wrote, it's way too early to write a proper review.  But, I do want to give the developers a thumbs up for now.  This is very cool indie turn-based combat game with "submarine" management (e.g. base management).Very early on, but it appears that there are enough items to craft and find, skills to learn, and funky eldritch traits to discover and mutate your dudes with.  So far the two mission I've done have been very enjoyable.  Combat seems like it will get tough really fast.More detailed review after I spend lots more hours, but thumbs up to the developers for creating something so familiar, yet so very unique.[Update 10/30/2020]  Unfortunately I am refunding this game for now.  It is unbalanced, and way too brutally difficult.  You need to do exactly what the developers want you to do in order to have a chance at doing well.  Major game mechanics (sanity), and using sanity to buy skills, are to be avoided, otherwise you will lose.  This game needs more time in design and play balancing.  I'll keep an eye on it and see if it gets any better.  Such a shame, because it really looked like it was going to be a winner.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: I've had to start over twice on normal, with some bad rolls and maybe not getting some of the mechanics. I wish there was a better save feature since the game has a very steep learning curveEdit: I've not given up on this game and it pays off. It is super hard, and maybe that turns some people off but I'm for sure changing my review to a Recommend.While it can be frustrating to start missions over again and again, I now think the positives of this game outweigh that hands down:The art style is amazing.The theme is excellent, and something I'd love to see more of.The dev was responsive and actually replied constructively to my lame early review, which shows engagement and bodes well.While hard, it's still a lot of fun
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: This game is sick. Not many games lately that can make me want to keep playing just to see what happens next. This one does it, and the lady who did va for the opening did a damn good job. I think she was prob the only one doing va, but man she did a damn good job. Also the righting is also legit. I love how it fits so well with what I believe people would say this this day and age.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Still too early to recommend but here 10 hours review : very difficult. So many random and dice roll factor; not many resources to balance the difficulty factor. Harder difficulty should reward more resources. Experience gain per character is confusing ; character with lesser contribution to entire team somehow gaining exp faster than the other ? Your mutation matter. Corruptian level also confusing ; what is the factor for faster or slower corruption  level ? Seems random. Good thing this game reward you for hunting so many enemies : bonus per kill should be higher.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a decent turn-based one with Lovecraftian setting. Atmosphere is pretty good, while story doesn’t matter much. Although, there is an endless game mode, I don’t think anyone will be interested in that. Campaign has some potential though. Beginning of the game is fun but it doesn’t get better as RPG elements. There are some different skills and mutations to discover but most of them are pretty useless. Same thing goes for the submarine development, there isn’t much to do after playing a while. Other than that, sanity and oxygen mechanics are interesting but it can be painful if you do not know the game. Also, game has a huge difficulty curve. Early game is hard. Then, it goes to more acceptable level of difficulty. And if you ♥♥♥♥ up early, that can be a game over for you. Still, this game is worth trying. Plus, the length of the game is perfect; not too short or too long.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. It isn't your standard tactical RPG, which for me is a bonus.Unfortunately the positives end there. Everything seems so rough, obviously a game developed on a limited budget. My biggest issue is that there isn't a map, and I tend to get lost easily. Given that the game is tough as nails and every move counts, this leads to great frustration.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: For the price it's quite good. It has a rather short campaign (finished it in about ~14h doing every side mission I could find) alleviated somewhat by an endless mode and it's in dire need of some quality of life improvements (used action points should really be shown on the mouse cursor, easier to find loot in missions, character dialogue should appear in the log window, etc) but other than that it's a 21euro Xcom-ish game with amazing atmosphere, good combat (random but with enough options to mitigate it), interesting level up, research and mutation options.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: It's a turn-based tactical game set in an underwater shCthulhu temple during the cold war. So besides the HP you have to keep track of O2 and the sanity metres.Because boomers' parents overhyped the outdated trash called XSOM, this game like Phoenix Point has a two-phase interface instead of proper time-units. Because counting up to one hundred and doing preschool math is so hard. But behind the unhelpful interface for people from 451 world, the game doesn't actually commit to the two-phase paradigm on the late 70s. You have two blobs for your actions, and most of the actions demand a whole blob. Some of the actions even instantly end your turn, burning up to three blobs, despite needing only one blob, so you can perform them after using a different action. But any your movement is not the final destination, you can step-step your steppies one by one one after another until the entire blob or two are spent. (And picking up or using stuff is free.) Since they didn't want to show people scary numbers which can't even reach, like, fifty, the exchange rate of one blob to steppies is done by overlaying range grid on the floor. The range with a blob reserved is shown in solid lines, and the leftovers are portrayed by a broken lines. Both are the same blue colour and in the underwater darkness it's not instantly readable. With this isometry there are also problems on stairs, and with stuff being layered in one spot. You can't pick a thing that is obscured. I didn't bother me on easy that much, but if someone to play on the hardest that can be frustrating.Thankfully ranged weapons have projectiles, instead of an RNG calculation. But accidental hits are way more rare than you would expect. Which works for you (at least on easy) because your second line can often shoot without hitting the guy in front. But they still use the stupid manual over-watch stance instead of the classic natural intercept.To add buzzverbs to the game-design it's also a roguelitelite, with "perma"-death and somewhat generated levels. They are repetitive and all look about the same with a few sets of tiles. There are RNG altars, and RNG dicerolls for decisions. When you decide to mutate you are offered an RNG choice of two options, with a third option after an upgrade. But the game has a quick-save button, so this nonsense is meaningless. Well, if you already have a save you can re-roll everything. But then you can exit to the main menu and pick up any of the old saves. This is just petty. The game is not a garbage rogue-lite, so why not have a proper save / load interface. And make re-rolls cost something less critical, so as not too encourage loading. Like, re-roll costs a little bit of sanity, or you can pay significant amount of sanity to pick from a list. Clues are finite, sanity can be restored. And of course you can not open the menu and load during the enemy's turn and during the stupid scripted animations. Why? Why waste everyone's limited time on earth on pettiness?The list of mutations is not that extensive. Some are mediocre, some are mission-critical, like gills, some are cool. There are few synergies, but more than none. Sadly, after extensive save-loading i was never able to have a dude with a crab hand, a tentacle and a third human arm at the same time. Why not?Outside the on-foot missions there's small-scale base-management. You repair your sub and insert some rooms into it. There's a number of critical rooms and you are left with only a couple of free slots to build something to your liking. There's also a global levelling progression applied to all the doods. There's some strong stuff like auto-reload and there's useless stuff like a third choice of a mutation. You also can waste the points on researching garbage for your inventory. Having a medkit is useful. Having an oxygen tank helps with meticulous resource hunting if you don't have gills. Spearguns for everyone are mandatory. I beat the game with only two legendary auto-spears i've found, but it would be more useful to produce two more for my team myself. Armour takes up an inventory slot. There's also a lot of other garbage you can make, but it all takes up very limited inventory slots and demands limited points to research. If you scavenge all the levels your useful things will be replenished about at the same rate as you spend them.Besides the generic rogue-lite endless toy mode with a nodes-board, there's also an actual real game here, with some basic story. It operates like the first Sanitary Podzemeliy instead of like Silent Storm. You can upgrade your base to find a few of random encounters between the critical missions, and they are limited in numbers, and are randomized in nature. If you re-roll hard you can get all the unique weapons after you rescued your main team, or if you don't re-roll you can get only the useless missions to rescue your useless crew-mates, and the empty defence maps to lower the difficulty.Since the "clues" are so limited in numbers you might want to heavily invest in acquiring more fast. Eating the clueful carcasses, dissection, etc.If you want to complete the campaign instead of running it through, the game runs out of mechanics pretty fast. You finish your sub, you get the basic equipment and then you just engage in repetitive missions until the end. The game is dragging past the midpoint. I've finished it in 19 hours but it felt like much more.There're two endings and you make the decision right near the end.The game looks pretty and it has a distinct art-style. The presentation and the sound design are very good. But instead of cutscenes it has terrible lazy motion comics.Good setting, good gameplay, drags past the mid-point.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend buying this game on sale or if you really like lovecraft/tactical games (like me)This is a tactical game set underwater with lovecraft horror. You can say it is a mixture of xcom: terror from the deep ,  darkest dungeon and xcom2. It is very similar to templar battleforce.The skills and gameplay are good fun although there are some skills not so useful and others really good. There is a bit of random involved but in a good way, it is not too punishing. There is a system of mutations to further improve your character. Very interesting (and a bit disturbing!)I did the 27 (including optionals) missions on normal in 14 hours gameplay. Normal difficulty is fine, but there is a spike in the very beginning while you learn the mechanics. Specially evacuating for extra air. I don't like very grindy games but it felt a bit lightweight overall ( I do like complex games). However I appreciated it was not grindy at all. It would be good to get a bit more content for it. I will definitely try it on hard and on the endless mode, as the game was too easy towards the end. One thing I like about short games is that you can restart in a higher difficulty soon.There are several mechanics to manage: air, corruption, sanity and health. But you can build tools to deal with all of them. The skills obtained are random, but you can set up your characters in a nice way and get nice combos. Like getting extra actions with commander/strategist or build a great sniper or melee char.I like the immersion. The graphics are peculiar and I personally liked them. The dialogues are quite interesting and the story is ok. The music is fine too.In short this is a nice short tactical game. You could think of it as a low-budget xcom2

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. I have a fascination for all things eldritch, having read every Lovecraft tale, every tribute anthology tale, and even his entire published correspondence to colleagues, in which he was a prolific letter writer. I will say that this game nails it, from sound design, to beginning VO work, to the writing itself, which is reproduced directly from Lovecraft's "The Temple," or otherwise lovingly and originally paid tribute to in new lines and prose. It is very faithful to the mythos, more so than most other Lovecraft games. It leans more heavily on the weird and the uncanny than horror. It is also SO NICE to play a Lovecraft style game and not be stuck as the alcoholic detective in 1920s seaside New England. That is SO played out, and Lovecraft had various kinds of heroes besides the stalwart Prohibition-era P.I., so it is great to get out of 1920s detective mode.I ignore Lovecraft's xenophobia, which cancel culture falsely labels as "racism." This game also ignores it, and there are Black as well as female characters, which is awesome and very welcome! I also ignore Lovecraft's horrible attempts at chunky, awkward dialogue, and have come to appreciate its unique qualities. (Lovecraft was to dialogue what millennial writers are to the semicolon: just no clue how to use it.) At any rate, this game rates up there with the best to offer regarding Lovecraft and gaming; it is definitely one of the best. Years ago, I had played an old Lovecraft strategy game for phone/tablet, The Wasted Lands, so I knew X-Com-style strategy could work, and work well, if mixed with Lovecraft. As such, this was an instant buy, knowing from the past game that this can work if done well, and 3 hours in, I am very pleased. AND SO:Worth full price. Can't say enough good about it. I also want to add that the difficulty levels go from "Narrative" to "Easy" to "Normal" and then "Hard," so every gamer should be able to get down with it without crying, needing a bottle, or requiring too many diaper changes. I am a fan of the original game Rogue, so I would hesitate to call this a Rogue-like when it is more of a Rogue-lite. So even if you hate Rogue-likes for being too hard and sadistic, you may still enjoy this game.

But the character skill options, potential magic to find and the various mutations keep the combat interesting for longer then one would expect.The constant pressure of diminishing oxygen can keep you on edge at times.And the atmosphere and great use of fog of war to partially hide enemies and movement at the edge of your character's headlamps give the setting itself a strenght of its own.I hope to see more of this style from the studio, or at least that other similar games (Like Xcom or Phoenix Point) stop using the fog of war like a binary visibile or invisible barrier and approach it more like a proper veil that just gives you a hint of enemy movement, without revealing exactly what things go bump in the night untill the combat starts.

_childDocuments_.review: Tentative recommend.  I like what they're trying to do, but they don't quite succeed either thematically or mechanically.This is still a decent, turn based Xcom alike, and I think it either slides into the bottom of the top tier or hits the top of the tier below that.  There's fun to be had here and they occasionally manage to do the creeping dread and tension really well.  For an undersea setting deliberately trying to give you a Lovecraftian challenge that's a good thing.  But... it just doesn't come together well enough for me.  Combat is all too often a little boring and predictable.  NOT horribly so, I've seen a lot of games do a LOT worse, but for the setting and what they're trying to do I can't give it high marks.  The 'logic' of certain parts of the game just doesn't work for me (Note: I'm only just about to finish it, and if they're about to pull the rug out from under us with some sort of time warp or 'they were dead all along' twist and use this as an explanation that they were hinting at all along I might have to revise this opinion).  The upgrade and research mechanics aren't badly implemented on a practical level but the in world logic and immersion break don't really help the situation.  And considering how much the game's trying to use immersion and setting as a selling point that's a problem.  The interface and poor explanation of several game mechanics drive me up the wall sometimes, I've loved games that have done even worse on both those subjects but they're not serving this one.  But then the game lets me literally see the corruption increasing on screen or actually throws a somewhat clever enemy at me and I decide to tough it out a little longer.Again, still a tentative recommend.  Probably a wait for on sale game but there's a heck of a lot of potential here.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Procons:+ Captivating eerie atmosphere.+ Unique visual style, nice aesthetics, cool monsters.- You are at the mercy of the Random number generator and this will influence your play style.- Scarcity of resources and item slots, plus the mood of the RNG goddess, which results in save scumming.Without proper knowledge of the underlying systems, - you might miss some of the better weapons, because you didn't scooped all the levels for the very scarce resource called COPPER! - you might get into dead ends that forces you to drop away X hours of your gameplay and restart from an earlier point.... because at the end of the level, there will be another subsection and you didn't bring extra oxygen tanks and there are none on the level. And everyone will suffocate, oops. Why would you if you didn't feel the need in the previous 25 missions? Plus you have constant inventory angst, since at max you can bring 3 items with you.- minor suffering caused by alt tabbing stops the game...The overall feel of the game is good, though the ending felt like it was a bit slapdashed. 2 cents:- Scoop up whatever you can put your arms on, especially copper.- Craft the baddest weapon as soon as possible- Make sure you have some traits that allow you to crowd control enemies (charm, disorient)- Do these and you won't lose hair follicles

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best Lovecraftian game that I've played in the modern era. The game boasts a moody setting and uses its design very well to convey a sense of dread and foreboding. The ending is a bit telegraphed but still enjoyable.The strategic layer centers around repairing and upgrading your submarine. The research track is setting appropriate and very cool so I won't spoil it for you. Your troops gain experience in the field and gain abilities and skills as they level. These abilities are then used in the tactical layer to assist in combat or with quest or puzzle related events.Besides straight combat, the tactical layer boasts interactive quest events. Although I found the lack of overwatch abilities a bit annoying, I eventually adapted. The main weakness of the tactical layer and which has lead me to reloads is that it can be difficult to tell the difference in elevation. Besides the elevation issue, the rest of the tactical layer conveyed combat information well. A sure fire buy for fans of xcom and lovecraft. But if you only like lovecraft or only like xcom, this is a buy when discounted.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Fun turn based squad action, with a Cthulu-esque story similar to something in The Laundry Files so I quite enjoyed it. While gameplay is similar to X-Com, the very limited base+research options and very limited weapon selection kill any urge to replay the game for me, but it was enjoyable for the full first run through.Relatively bug free, and pretty good game pacing. It's pretty hard and the game encourages Iron Man play, but a death can pretty much doom you. The Air + Corruption mechanics get a bit tiresome as you are forced to rush where I'd prefer to explore a little more. A lot of the upgrades are annoyingly random which means you hope for good RNG so you can get the desired skills/mutations/etc - its a strategy game so please let me strategize! Some of the triggered encounters can be brutal, and when a lone unit activates one a couple turns away from support, it gets frustrating. Still - fun even with a couple of flaws, and would like a followup or DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid underwater Xcom with an unsettling atmosphere. Would have liked a little more depth in the base management and the mutations. Wonder if the mutations could have been explored further in the story - the characters react when one of them receives a mutation but nothing more happens. The whole theme of becoming a monster to fight monsters is touched on in dialogue lines when using invocations as well but does not play much of a part in the rest of the game. Love how the fog of war works in this game, some of the tensest moments came when fighting two enemy factions at the same time. All-in-all, a really good first-time effort from a small studio. Looking forward to what comes next.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: This is a nice little indie roguelike RPG with a short campaign, plays like the X-Com: Terror from the Deep away missions.  There's a small but well-designed base-building minigame, in repairing and outfitting your submarine and all the best elements of squad CRPG are there as well.  The art is pretty and reminiscent of Mike Mignola's Hellboy comic, or Darkest Dungeon if you're not familiar, and like both has a strong eerie atmosphere that borrows much, and well, from HP Lovecraft's mythos.  20 hours of playtime in the main campaign, and difficulty scales well, I found the roguelike side not nearly as interesting but YMMV if you're a fan of the genre.  8/10 and I'm happy to give this team my money so they can do more of the same.

_childDocuments_.review: Fellow Gamers, Stirring Abyss is a tactical squad-based game of Submariners whose mission is to find the rest of their mysteriously missing crew and repair their badly damaged ship. What kind of Gamer should play this game? The kind of Gamer who is patient, can lay traps, and feels comfortable with squad level tactics similar to XCOM. You are the arbiter giving orders to your Submarine crew as they walk the onyx night of the deep to find their missing crew mates and while on this trek, search for copper wire, salvage parts, and defend, attack, or flee the depths’ hungry denizens.Unexplainable Lovecraftian events have transpired and the Soviet Union’s elite Submariners are one step ahead.  Each journey to and from the ship leads to another clue and opportunity to enhance your crew or repair the indomitable fast-attack submarine, the USS Salem. Your valiant Submariners will lose their minds, become mutated, devour the dead, improve the Sonar system, launch torpedoes, heal their hurts, recover their sanity, enhance their equipment, illuminate the nightmarish, catch up to the Soviet crew, and prepare for the next sojourn into the Stirring Abyss.Start on Easy and try everything once; save often. Each time played the Stirring Abyss will challenge you. Each journey into the murky shroud of subterranean darkness is one more opportunity to find a shipmate or lose one’s mind.Achilleez sends.
_childDocuments_.name: Stirring Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: 26 Hours game time and the game is finished. I could play endless mode now, but I have the feeling that everything that the game has to offer was archived.I payed 20 € for the game and I think the price is fine, I was entertained.The game is hard and the saving mechanic not self explaining. During the game you can save whenever you want and the game saves automatically after certain events but from your game you can load only the latest savegame. So when you feel that you made a mistake somewhere in the past you have to quit your current game, go on loading (remember that on quit was created a new save) and go backward. Not very bad but could be made better.So why thumb up then? Because the theme, the graphic and the music are awesome in creating a claustrophobic dark atmosphere.You struggle to keep the sanity of your party members, you need to keep track of the oxygen level of their diving suits and it is awesome to see them getting mutated to some abominations.If you like games like XCOM and maybe know and liked the old terror from the deep, than why the hell are you reading this? PLAY THE F*** GAME!

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this by saying that I don't think Shiren is a fair game, or that this is an amazing port of Shiren.However as a roguelike enthusiast I personally enjoy this game a lot. And I think that this is fairly competent port. It has borderless windowed mode with the ability to resize to whatever you want or need and has multiple control options (no rebinding outside of using Steam's controller configurator though). There's also some hidden controls so you might want to just press keys to see what they do, for example the game doesn't tell you that the C key can be used for quick scouting a room without needing to go through the menu.As for the game itself, if you're familiar with Pokemon Mystery Dungeon, Shiren is the game series that PMD is actually a spinoff off of. This game in particular is actually the 5th game in the Shiren series. It is a 10+ year old port of a port that was originally released on the DS. Shiren and PMD share as many similarities as they do differences, but the core shell and aesthetic will be instantly recognizable to anyone who has played PMD before. Shiren is most similar to Super Pokemon Mystery Dungeon. The core differences between the series I think is that PMD focuses on your ability to micromanage a team of travelers, whereas Shiren is more focused on solo play and item usage rather than making use of character specific abilities. Shiren is a truly difficult game. It is not concerned with being fair or rewarding you consistently for your skill or efforts. Much like Solitaire, you will inevitably go into several runs that are just flat out unwinnable. And you will need to be playing optimally in order to even have a remote chance of success on the later dungeons that don't let you bring items in such as Primordial Chasm (this means wiki-crawling is must. You need to be playing with as much information as possible.) Much like Solitaire though, the inconsistency has no bearing on the consistency of the player. Even if the game doesn't hand you easy runs, that doesn't stop you from trying your best on every one of them. This is where the beauty of this game shines through. Anything you can do to "break" Shiren on dungeons that disallow brought items never ends up actually breaking the game, just giving you an advantage. Smart decisions and big brain plays are expected, and are part of ensuring your success and survival. Even on runs where it seems like you've been handed a seemingly broken combination of items, you can still lose easily in a few turns if you aren't paying attention. You will be hard pressed to find another game out there that expects as much out of the player as this one. Even if the game isn't always fair, the items and enemies present within present the player with so much agency. 9 times out of 10 you'll always see something you could have done better in hindsight, something that could have given you that extra edge to make the run more winnable. It's all about knowing your options and pushing them to their logical limits. When you actually do end up winning one of those massive 99F dungeons, it feels very rewarding. As stated multiple times above, Shiren isn't always fair. And when you get multiple seemingly hopeless runs in a row, it can wear down on you. There are a few nice distracting side activities in the game to mitigate this, such as Explosion Rocks (my personal favorite way to play minesweeper), but ideally you're going to want to have other games to fall back on when Shiren inevitably pisses you off.Inventory management in this game is a drag. You're only given 24 items worth of backspace space and 80 items worth of in-town storage space. Pots are your primary method of getting the most out of your limited space, as they only take up 1 inventory space but have internal storage of up to 5 items. While you can select multiple things to put inside or take out of a pot in one turn, they can still be kind of disorienting to manage to anyone who hasn't played this game before. For new players, those 80 spaces of storage space will run out quick, as they do not yet have the pots needed to store all their stuff, and they will not know what items are actually worth keeping and which are junk yet.Final complaint is that upgrading equipment in dungeons that don't let you bring your own items in feels like climbing a rope made of barbed wire. The items and enemies you need to upgrade your stuff are not very common, and there are these slime enemies and rust traps that can actually degrade your equipment after you've put so much effort trying to upgrade them. Trying to keep up to scale with the enemies in one of the long 99F dungeons is hard enough without these nuisances, and getting hit by one of them feels absolutely . As with many things in Shiren, there is of course counterplay, but in this case your options for counterplay aren't very reliable. While the titular Tower of Fortune is presented as being the end of the game when you beat it and the main focus of the game (I mean it's in the freaking title), I actually think of the Tower of Fortune as being more of a tutorial dungeon. It's pretty fair and forgiving and teaches you most of the main mechanics you need to know to play the game properly. When you do beat it, you're given access to more of the much harder "real" dungeons of the game. While I don't think Shiren is a game for everyone, I do think it is a very good and well designed game, and I personally enjoy it. For people that already know whether or not they like games like this, I hope my review has helped you solidify your purchasing decision. For anyone that likes highly technical and difficult roguelike dungeon crawlers, this game should be right up your alley. Most games on the market these days place a high emphasis on being fair to player, and while I think this is very very far from being a bad thing, I do think it's refreshing to see a well designed game like Shiren that expects more from the player from time to time.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are not a fan of inventory management, this game probably is not for you. It requires much planning into what you keep, what you use, and how you do so.Second, you may want to wait a bit until updates rectify the following issues, which are the most prominent issues I have seen so far:A variety of different things can cause the game to randomly wipe progress. While exiting the game through the menus mitigates most of this, there are occasions when the game does not save your progress regardless. For that reason, I would advise all players, as much fun as the game can be, to take a break after an hour or so of playtime or after significant events because you may lose every bit of it for no reason. It is incredibly heartbreaking to play this game 5+ hours straight, close it, and open the game later to find you have lost every bit of that progress, especially with the roguelike nature of this game.Also, if you ever need to uninstall and reinstall this game, I recommend opening it, saving it through the menus, exiting it, restarting your computer, and then uninstalling it--hoping that it saves. It usually resets a large portion of your progress from the day if you need to uninstall it.The translation is pretty good, but there are some slight issues. Some of the menus will read in a way that indicates one thing, but it does the opposite. Mistranslations were the most problematic for me when waiting for a rescue. You can opt to play the game while waiting for rescue, and it will allow you to play bonus dungeons. However, it tells you that it will save your items as long as you store them. Unfortunately, this appears to be a mistranslation. I lost two hours of progress during this time because it did not save any of it.You are stuck with the default control layout, and it is not the world's most concise layout either. You will get used to it after about an hour or two of game time, or at least that was how it went for me, but it would be great to be able to change this later.I expect, or at least hope that most of these issues will be rectified in the coming months.EDIT: I changed my review after losing 37 hours of progress to the crashes. I will not be continuing this game because I have lost 37 hours of valuable time for basically NO reward. Therefore, I cannot encourage other players to play a game that may see them to the same fate.EDIT 2: Edited for conciseness.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Probably not, but it is a rather well-made turn-based roguelike dungeon crawler. The goddess Reeva decides the fate of all humanity and lives in her Tower of Fortune, where she rolls the Dice of Fate to decide who has good and who has bad luck. Noone trying to reach her ever returned, but this does of course not detain you from trying your luck. Well, first you need to find three magical dice to gain entry anyway. You are Shiren the Wanderer and travel with your pet weasel Koppa. While movement in the towns is in real-time, the movement in the dungeons is like in the original Rogue from 1980. You take a turn, the monsters take a turn. So you can think forever about your next turn, but dashing away does not help you because the monsters simply dash after you. Every dungeon has a few levels, connected via stairs. Inside the dungeons you find - monsters, loot, traps and quite a few puzzles.When monsters (hunger, poison,...) reduce your hitpoints to zero, you don't die. You are a hero, after all. You just collapse and are brought back to the starting settlement, but lose all your equipment, experience and money. This can be a bit frustrating. Good thing you can deposit stuff in a bank or storehouse before you enter a dungeon. The villages are full of friendly people, everyone has to say a sentence or two, you find various shops offering goods and other services. Everything is very relaxed, and it makes sense to read through the conversations to receive clues, quests, items or advance the story. You can hire mercenaries to fight at your side, and experimenting with the stuff you find is fun. Certain combinations of weapons/bracelets/shields grant bonuses. Your inventory is limited, but can be expanded later on with pots.Shiren the Wanderer is a long-running series developed for consoles, this is the first time that a game from the series has been ported to the PC (and Switch). It has been enhanced with three bonus dungeons after you finish the main game and a few more music tracks. Gamepad works fine, ultrawidescreen not. Game can be saved (suspended) when you leave your computer, but the savefile gets overwritten when you die.Nice turn-based roguelike dungeon crawler with permadeath.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the Pokémon Mystery Dungeon series, definitely give this game a try. It's made by the same devs(Chunsoft, the creators of Mystery Dungeon), so you can expect it to be of the same good quality.Do note however, Shiren the Wanderer is a lot more punishing than Pokémon Mystery Dungeon.In Shiren, your main source of fighting power is equipment, rather than EXP and level. If you like PMD, you should know that failing to return safely means losing everything you have in your inventory. This is also true in Shiren.In PMD, the worst that could happen is losing that one precious accessory that made everything easier. In Shiren however, you can also lose your equipment, which is kind of... Brutal. Imagine you had a super strong weapon and shield, but you somehow got brutally murdered after a streak of bad luck. BAM, you're basically back to level 1 if you didn't have any means of saving it(). Fortunately, obtaining great equipment requires far less grinding compared to leveling in PMD, so... Easy come, easy go.I find myself coming back to this game every once in a while. It's a great game, but like PMD, luck can either help or get in your way. Your skill is there to mitigate/maximize the effects of bad/good luck. As with PMD, repeated bad luck may be rage inducing for some, especially on long, difficult dungeons, so I would recommend having another relaxing or satisfying game at ready. A little fun fact, this game's actual full name(according to the Japanese title logo) is 'Mystery Dungeon, Shiren the Wanderer 5 plus: Tower of Fortune and the Dice of Fate'. So, Shiren is a legit Mystery Dungeon game.P.S. This is more about PMD rather than Shiren, but playing Left 4 Dead 2 with Pokémon mods from the workshop made it feel like a First-Person-Shooter spin off of PMD(Thanks to all the RNG that game has). Maybe also try that if you crave more Mystery Dungeon. It comes with the benefit of not having to experience the stress of losing literally everything you carry!(Do note that Left 4 Dead 2 is a zombie shooting game, so it's audience doesn't really match Pokémon, nor Shiren's audience. Be wary of zombies that can be blown apart!)

_childDocuments_.review: Mystery Dungeon games has been a genre that's been lacking on PC. While this game is technically a solid one, it is ruined by the item management for me. I still think it's one of the best MD on Steam though, but I believe it is more of a niche game due to its item management issues. That is why I'm not recommending the game, at least for a general audience.The complexity of the game is within its item management and encounters. The inventory is extremely small(20), requiring you to bring multiple Preservation Pots(up to 5 slots each), along side other things depending on how "safe" you want to be. This means that most of the time, you will be full and debatting for which item you want to keep with you. Hell, when people say that half of their playtime is managing the inventory, they aren't that far off. While your decision time will increase the more you play, there is just so many menus to go through. Do keep in mind that certain items may have secondary effects, such as Healing items: if your health is full, your max health will go up, same for Food items.As for the encounters, a lot of them will feel unfair, especially if you're not prepared. This part is fine and is one of the interesting parts of the game. While you may think you are safe with your pots full of Revival Grass, healing items, numerous Scrolls and your high enhanced Rustproof weapon and shield, there is still several abilities in the higher floors that can still screw you over if you don't know about them. The deeper you go, the more thoughts you have to give to each encounters, and that's where the fun is; if you can get past the item management struggles anyway.Another interesting part of the game is the "New Item Pots" system. Once unlocked, you can put items in them and come back everyday, up to 7 days(item rots on 7th), and they may gain additional bonuses. For example, I have a Perception Grass with "Little Heal" and "High Heal" and a Warp Grass with "Little Heal" and "Action +1"(Swift Grass effect). Once the item has been taken out, it will start being available as drops in your runs. You can save up to 50 of those item in your book and once you reach that limit, you will have to start deleting previously saved New Items. While it kind of make item management easier, it kind of makes it harder to get a targetted drops as the Drop Table increases, making each other items harder to obtain.If you do end up dead, you can get rescued up to 3 times. The Rescuer will need a Revival Grass in their warehouse. These can be obtained for 30 Coin Points (really easy to get). They will transform the Revival Grass into a Revival Spell and send it to the person in need of a Rescue. Then, once the Revival Spell is used, the Rescuee will respawn on the same tile, with an Escape Scroll under them. This gives them the option to leave with their items if they wish to. Unless you have a friend that is often out of a dungeon, I wouldn't base your decision around the Rescue system, as getting rescued without a friend may that a couple of hours.Speaking of Coin Points, don't forget to visit the building in the middle of the town. Early on, the Coin NPC will not be there, but once he spawns, ALWAYS claim your Coin Card every time. Your Points will be saved even if you wipe and lose your Coin Card. You can buy items such as Revival Grass for 30 points, Preservation Pot(5) for 100 and even Synthesis Pot(5) for 500. This will help you massively in your run.While the game lacks customizable controls, I found myself comfortable with Type C. That set up is actually very similar to how I usually set up my Keyboard controls in games that lack mouse controls.Again, I cannot recommend this game, due to the item management, as it is a big part of its gameplay. I feel the need to mention the following as I've mentioned general audience and called the game niche above, despite having reviewed "anime" games in the past as recommended: This is a gameplay issue. The reason people may not like "anime" games is, for the most part(from what I've seen), due to their Art styles. It is possible to overlook Art styles, but you cannot overlook core gameplay issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Shiren is a roguelike style RPG published in a modern format. This includes turn based, permadeath, etc. style gameplay. If you're looking for Binding of Isaac or Rogue Legacy, this isn't that kind of game.If you're a fan of Shiren and Mystery Dungeon style games, you probably already have this. If you don't yet, you should get it. If you're a fan of roguelikes (turn-based, difficult, permadeath), go ahead and pick it up. It's a really good take on the genre.This detail, while fairly standard for the genre, appears to be surprising a few people, so I decided to add it here. Like most roguelike games, Shiren enforces a concept called , which means if you die during a dungeon run you will lose the items you're carrying, wake up back in town, and be reset back to level 1. DO NOT use ALT-F4 to try and quit the game or save your run. It won't work. When you want to save and quit, go to the menu and select the "Suspend" option to make sure the game writes a current save.If you're not comfortable with this concept, then roguelikes aren't for you and you probably shouldn't buy the game.Pros:Cons:I've enjoyed the game thoroughly and I recommend it to fans of the genre (the caveat listed above notwithstanding).

_childDocuments_.review: Shiren the Wanderer: The Tower of Fortune and the Dice of Fate is the fifth series in the Shiren the Wanderer series, originally on the nintendo ds a decade ago, then later ps vita and switch, and now on steam. It is a charming roguelike rpg game where you go on an adventure as Shiren and his cute talking ferret, Koppa, fighting monsters through dungeon and talking to the many npcs amongst the vast world. The fun in it is the exploration as you travel along and become stronger as you level you yourself with better stats and equipment. Gameplay is decent as you start off with a lowly sword, though as the adventure progress. powers and things can be learnt. It does also have replayability because of the roguelike aspect so a new adventure and going into dungeons do differ between them. Visuals are great with the retro graphics, as is the music with that which matches the atmosphere of game and going on the endless adventure. There are plenty to do, with even just talking to all the npc is quite fun to do. Overall, it is a great and delightful jrpg game that is worth checking out, especially to those who are familiar with the series

_childDocuments_.review: Small disclaimer: I personally had a great deal of fun with this game, but if you don't have the patience to do near-constant inventory management and keep a guide open, I can't exactly recommend it.I've played a few of the Mystery Dungeon games before including the DS port of the first Shiren the Wanderer, so I was able to hit the ground running with this one after wrapping my head around the new gimmicks. The sheer variety of optional dungeons you can access even right from the start is quite refreshing - if you don't feel like progressing the story there's still loads of places to go as you gather stuff to power up your equipment for whatever difficult spot you want to tackle next.I also enjoyed the soundtrack quite a bit. Funnily enough, I could've sworn it was more of Koichi Sugiyama's work like Shiren 1, but it was actually from a new composer, Hayato Matsuo, who apparently worked under Sugiyama doing stuff like arranging his compositions for the DS ports of Dragon Quest 4-6, and the Fortune Street/Itadaki Street series. There's a clear influence in some of the songs if you keep your ears peeled.All that being said, this is the kind of game that can very easily turn frustrating with all the downright malicious things enemies and traps can do to your items, whether it's Rust Traps degrading your weapon and shield, Rotten Traps spoiling your food items, Scoopies flinging dirt that clogs up your pots, Nigiri Morphs turning random things you're carrying into riceballs, or Gyadons pecking your staves and scrolls to render them useless. Most of these things have at least one good countermeasure, and at the very least you can put tags on weapons and shields to avoid losing them for good, but it's still a hassle keeping track of all the potential hazards you might encounter in any given dungeon.If that doesn't deter you, though, then I can definitely recommend at least trying the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Shiren the Wanderer is a series with an incredibly long history, starting in 1995 as one of the original Mystery Dungeon titles, debuting in an incredibly difficult SNES game simply titled "Mystery Dungeon: Shiren the Wanderer" in English. This game unfortunately never saw an English translation, nor did the N64 sequel (yes, there was not only a RPG you have never heard of for that console seemingly devoid of any in that genre, but a roguelike too). Thankfully, a remake of that original SNES title for DS, with many changes to the game though none to drastic, did eventually reach our filthy Western hands. Then, only a few years later, a game for the Wii also reached out to us who are unworthy. Naturally, neither did that well, as they were both introduced fairly late into their consoles lifespans, and did come with any sort of marketing. Not only that, but us filthy western pigs are also not very favorable to roguelikes, not willing to accept the honorable challenge that comes with it.Now, after nearly a decade of no Shiren, they have once again come to grace us with this divine series, something I have I had been looking forward to ever since it's initial announcement in June of 2020. I initially bought the Switch version, but due to joycon drift, have decided to play the PC release instead, and it is really just as fine. But this is all unimportant rambling.Shiren, by its nature, is a game centered around strategy. You will be constantly tasked by this game to deal with an incredibly wide variety of threats, and, if you want to win, you must always be analyzing the situations you find yourself in to find the best possible route to the end of the dungeon.When I originally was playing the DS localization of that first SNES game, I recall reading the manual for fun, and it describing Shiren as being very similar to a complicated game of chess, and, in a way, that is a very sound explanation. Monsters in this game vary greatly, and all have their own special traits and abilities. Some can move in special ways, some can turn your items into food, or waste them in other ways, some can fly across the map, or through walls, spit fire, throw rocks, hurl lightening, and many other dangerous acts. On the other hand, there are also those that can act to your benefit, such as giving you a chance to gamble to earn more XP, or improving your items by mixing their various attributes. Learning what every enemy does (and doing this through trial and error is of course the fun thing to do), is one of the keys to understanding your environment and assessing your plans for going through a dungeon. On the topic of your environment, there are also many other hazards to watch out for, like traps, which can be a little annoying, doing something like disarming you, doing a bit of damage, or making you a little hungrier, but others can do much more vile things, like smashing your pots, forcing you to suddenly decide what to keep and what to toss. Others can warp you to the other end of a floor, separating you from your team mates, and and, if you are really unlucky, you might even get turned into a ball of rice.The only way to account for these things, which are most often out to end your run, is to plan ahead, and to act with caution. Everything you do can have weight, such as how you move about the floor, which matters especially when fighting monsters, but the most important thing by far is how you manage your inventory. You must constantly ask yourself if you should use a certain item to deal with a threat, which gets tricky when you must also consider planning ahead for whatever else you will face. Luck plays a significant role in deciding what you have to deal with, and what you are given to deal with it, but with experience comes knowledge, and, given time, you should be more than capable of dealing with whatever bad luck comes your way.Ultimately, this game is one of choices. You have to learn to make these choices, so I recommend playing through all of the tutorials and side minigames that are there (they are pretty fun too). You also have to learn from experience, so you should not be discouraged if you fail a run, because, if you make it through to the end, beating the odds and getting through by your own merit, it is the best feeling this game (or any really) can offer.This game isn't really that hard in the main dungeon, no. All you need to do is unlock the point shop, and then you have essentially infinite access to undo herbs, which allow you to either revive or go back to the starting area with your goodies in tact. You can also beat the final boss very easily by getting lucky, and scoring yourself some invincibility herbs, which you can use to buff yourself, debuff the enemies, and wreak havoc against whatever it is you're facing. However, after this, the training wheels are off, and you will be dealing with the really hard parts. You can test yourself against the Pitfall of Life, the new three remixed dungeons, the Underground Mansion, and the list goes on and on, and when you are there, you will truly feel the Shiren experience.So, play this game, as it is objectively the best one to ever exist, and so far, the best Shiren experience available to the Western audience. I would probably sell at least a few of my toes if it meant getting more Shiren, and hopefully, they will some day return and bless us once more. Until that day comes, I can sit here contentedly listening to the soundtrack and waiting for updates on the Shiren 4 fan translation.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have issues with the game freezing or getting stuck, don't bother. If you don't close the game properly, it will treat it as a death to prevent save-scumming, which means if you were to get stuck in the village and have to close the game, it will treat it as a death, including all consequences (losing all gear and money). Good game overall, but some scaling feels awkward. There's a lot of "learning from experience", including which mobs are simply never worth fighting if it can be helped, as some have abilities to suicide attack you for 80-100% of your hp.
