_childDocuments_.review: This game looks like it should be really fun, but honestly the combat is just crap. Way too awful to recommend. Here's the problem: All your damage is at the end of attack combos. So like you'll do 6-8 hits or something for 100 damage, and then a smash for 1400. If you can't get the smash, the fight is gonna take FOREVER. And the bosses are all designed to keep you off balance, keep you rolling, keep you mobile, and make sure it's almost impossible to get a combo off. Every time they touch you, you get knocked back. There's no careful outmaneuvering of a boss to line up a big hit, and your regular attacks don't do enough damage to make whittling them down worth it. There are some big ultimate combos you can do from time to time, but the bosses can dodge those too. The field stuff is fine, but the bosses are just a chore. Difficult for all the wrong reason.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very pretty to look at - the graphical style is different from a lot of other games I've played so it feels like a breath of fresh air in that regard. Though, I'm rather disappointed with the lack of puzzles there are within the first part of the game. It's being marketed as a PUZZLE game, and yet if there were any puzzles, they didn't feel like a puzzle. The combat is very repetitive, with the KB+M controls are all over the place, making it feel awkward to do a specific move in a fight. This game feels like they had a LOT of ideas/inspiration (specifically Zelda and Souls-like games) but weren't sure how to combine them effectively. I'm having a hard time continuing the game because the main character, Kaku, doesn't feel relatable nor do I understand what his purpose is in the story and why he must be the one to go on this hero's journey. The subtitles in certain scenes are VERY fast, so I could barely get a chance to read them before having to read the next bit (to be fair, I was reading aloud but devs should find ways to compensate for this). I personally wouldn't recommend this game unless if you're fine with heavy combat open-world games (like Dark Souls).

_childDocuments_.review: I started this game thinking that this is a short 6-8 hours game but to my surprise this is a really big game with tons of exploration and boss fights. I was not prepared to start a big game like this but to my surprise this is was an awesome game.I have explored most continent, uncovered most secrets, cleared every Rune, beaten every Boss, and finished the game. Though there are some issues I will get to it around last. This game is massive and for devs to be able to make this must have taken a lot of effort. I loved the gameplay and exploration. The auto and manual save function were lifesaver which is the main reason I loved this game than most other games. I went totally old school with this function, before boss fight - save the game, after 10 mins - save the game haha and that way I explored without fear. The skills, power ups and world design were really good. The rune puzzles were awesome also, I had fun solving those, sometimes frustration too but not a big deal since there was auto save there also which made this game super fun for me. I found some cool treasures and lot of power ups along the way that helped me throughout the game and now I am pretty much invincible in boss fight like 0 damage XD.So what are the problems I faced - bugs lot of bugs. First of all achievement bug, I have done a lot and pretty sure I will get 4-5 achievement in the future if this issue is fixed as I already cleared the requirement but those havent unlocked it yet. I noticed that these unlocks at a random time when you are playing a game. So lets say after 20-30 mins of clearing the requirements the achievements will show up which is a big issue since you wont know if you cleared the requirements or not on the point. For example I have cleared all runes and the 3rd lvl rune achievements still shows as locked. Also there were some beating boss requirements so those are also stuck so hopefully it will be fixed in the future.The other bugs are optimization issues, as mine is a bit old pc below the requirement there are some optimization issues that I faced, I did set the settings to all low but still it somehow did not apply sometimes after death or on restart. But well somehow it was fixed when I did a custom settings so hope it is also fixed in the future. There are some other bugs like when a gold chest shows up in the map but there is nothing and sometimes no sound in some places but this being an indie game I expect to see those so not a big deal, it will be fixed in the upcoming years with enough players.The last bug will be map issues, where it shows what you have found but its all bugged as it shows as I have found all blank slate but I have not, there are 4x10 + 1 as per map but I found extra from the same map location so it is bugged. Also there might be an issue with the new boss bottle of griffin thing, the under two minute, my hits are not registering sometime so could not finish it.What I want in the future is a better map, where I can see what I unlocked and where I unlocked on the map with the option to toggle those on and off, this helps everyone and guide makers to understand what they have found and what are still remaining. Like if I have unlocked a chest or found a rune key the map should show it like it has been claimed here with dark black. But without that option its hard to understand what is missing and where. Next is the long jump which is when you run and jump which makes it impossible to control, and I have died so many times due to this, This is not that much useful, double jump + dodge is precise, long jump is not so I don't prefer that having in game. Also run and pick up/interact button. One button for all makes it difficult in runes, when I try to run it just picks up or drops or similar issues, which was a bit frustrating but still we can work with it.So far the game is great story is nice and have lots of exploration. I have finished the game but still some left uncovered which I will try solving after few years when a lot of players have played this game and lot of improvements has been done along with maybe new content and some guides. As I still have some remaining mysteries I want to solve but there are not enough information about that at this moment so will come back after few years, and again thank you very much for the game, I do hope others try this game out as you will love exploring and solving all those puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a SHORTENED review originally written for . The FULL article can be found . Feel free to take a look at the Opium Pulse Steam Curation page  as well.In what appears to be the latest game since their first title released in 2017, game publisher and developer BINGOBELL has brought us Kaku: Ancient Seal. A self proclaimed “Prehistoric Fantasy-Themed Open World ARPG”- the developers have really brought quite a few elements together for what promises to be a thrilling Ancient Fantasy Adventure. Playing as the young boy Kaku, you (along with your flying companion, Piggy) are tasked with restoring the balance within the Legendary Temple- and the land along with it. You will battle onslaughts of foes, solve puzzles, craft food and ammunition, as well as utilize otherworldly powers courtesy of pig-pal. An epic adventure with a beautiful sprawling map, an adorable companion, and plenty to do- Kaku: Ancient Seal shows heaps of promise. But ultimately, does it deliver? Unfortunately, out the gate, at it’s most fundamental level when it comes to a substantial story to carry the narrative of this adventure, the answer is a resounding NO. While it is unbelievably easy to get caught up and lost within the beautiful world that the developers at BINGOBELL have crafted, once the honeymoon phase wears off, the real gravity of the situation starts to sink in. Simply put, never have I seen a story attempt to be so fleshed out and verbose, all the while being painfully vague and disjointed. Lacking even the most core details, like who Kaku is, where he comes from, or why he was after Piggy to begin with, players really are not given much from a “character investment” standpoint. He could, quite literally, be called “Generic Prehistoric Child #1”- and I wouldn’t be all too bothered. Sadly, this is a theme that spans across much of Kaku: AS, providing lavish explanations of quintessentially nothing, leaving players to wonder, ultimately, why should they care? One would have hope that through the world building, character design, and musical score, there will be SOMETHING there to care for… right?Thankfully, one of the absolute saving graces for this title IS it’s graphical design. Both in crafting some beautiful worlds, and making some absolutely stunning creatures- the developers have absolutely blown it out of the park. Kaku: AS boasts it’s own unique style, bringing cartoon-realism to the forefront, and adding a pinch of what looks like nearly cell-shaded VFX on top. It blends BEAUTIFULLY in this gorgeous and breathtaking world- from the lush overgrown ruins of the Floating Temple, to the almost tropical, amphibian infested waters of the Misty Swamp. There are so many beautiful things to see, and the attention to detail in the background is staggering. That isn’t to say that there aren't qualms to be had- mainly in the lack of point of interest. The maps feel beautiful, yet desolate and lonely all the same, with enemies generally maintaining set positions. You have LOTS of ground to cover- yet not much reason, nor reward, to do so. With how stunning the world building is, this came as a massive disappointment. One of the even larger disappointments, is with the enemy density. In place of things to do besides gather ingredients to craft elemental ammunition, or food for cooking, enemies are packed on the map in droves. While MANY of the designs are absolutely brilliant with some very obvious influence from titles like Spyro and Crash Bandicoot (but fashion forward and modernized)- the idle patterns are uninspired, and they are very obviously used in place of any real additional points of interest. Beyond resource gathering, banishing dark growths, and solving menial puzzles, players will find little else to do besides push the story forward and swing at anything that moves. Despite there being some collectibles, such as broken pieces of stele containing prophecy, there is very little reason to stray too far, as most treasure chests contain basic resources just as easily scavenged elsewhere. No matter your choice, however, you will absolutely have battles to fight.  Pleasantly, most of the enemies, even basic ones, have multiple attack sets, and nearly all boss fights have “behavioral stages” once their HP bar has been depleted enough. Along with a health bar, most foes also posses a “Poise” meter. Heavy attacks will diminish this, and upon depletion, the enemy will stagger. While this is a crucial move for crowd control, it can also be an easy mechanic to cheese most fights with. Ultimately, the creativity of the enemy design and animations still does very little to detract from the missing substance within the game and story themselves. As far as things like controls are concerned, you are free to roam the four Lands with ease- easily being par with other AAA titles on the market. Movement is fluid, and you are given the ability to double jump out the gate, though at times it can feel a little stiff. There are a few minor qualms like Kaku lacking the ability to swim, often resulting in an instant death if the water is too deep. While Piggy offers the solution to this “issue”- as they can let you run on water via a magical bubble for a short duration, I largely view this as offering a solution to a pre-manufactured problem. At this point, I find the mechanic of characters being unable to swim somewhat dated- and while it may simply be what the developers considered a fun quasi-puzzle mechanic, it ends up more irritating than not. There are a few mechanics like this, mostly involving some of Piggys less-useful abilities, like using a disguise. Despite some of the shortcomings, overall, the controls are well put together, and menus are clean, and easy to understand. Upgrading skills and abilities is straightforward, if not somewhat tedious as it revolves around resource acquisition. Though, despite a wide range of additional combos and ability upgrades, combat still feels much of the same, very uninspired and repetitive.  Overall, Kaku: Ancient Seal is a beautifully designed game, boasting beautiful locations brought to life by gorgeous design, and filled with wonderful and quirky enemies that harken back to classic ARPG experiences. The music brings a wonderful sense of atmosphere and depth to the world around you, making it easy to get lost in the gorgeous Four Lands you’ll set out to explore. Despite all this, a lack of cohesive narrative in story, and feelings of uninspired and tired combat weigh down game play. The breathtaking world around you is absolutely sprawling, yet filled with little to do except hunt for menial “rewards”, and thrashing an overpopulation of quick-spawning enemies with tired attack patterns, and set “boundaries”.  At the current asking price of $24.99 USD, you can’t really go wrong (especially if you happen to catch this title on sale)-  just temper your expectations. Younger players may find this an easy world to get lost in, while more seasoned players could find the game play loop dull after a few menial hours. At the end of the day, BINGOBELL has a gorgeous foundation for what I sincerely believe COULD be one of the best platformers to come out in recent years, but it may have been pulled from the oven a bit too soon.

_childDocuments_.review: Kaku: Ancient Seal is a captivating open-world adventure that effectively balances exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat. _childDocuments_.review: If you are a lover of The Legend Of Zelda type games or challenging puzzle RPGs then KAKU: Ancient Seals is the game for you. KAKU: Ancient Seals is one of the best open world indie games I have played and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for lush environments and challenging dungeons. One of the things that caught my attention were the different biomes, the bright and flashy colors but most of all the vast environments full of enemies, puzzles, dungeons and violent creatures to face. I simply found the game to be very boring. I find the main character very plain with virtually no personality and the quests just seem like filler instead of a task that's actually important to the story or anything for that matter (wait, what was the story again? i already forgot). The combat is your average hack and slash combos but it fails to "feel" like your hitting something with a pack to the punch so to speak. The world is massive which is cool but feels like a MMO world that's just randomly flooded with monsters that id rather run past than actually fight. _childDocuments_.review: Darksiders, Fenyx Rising + some old-school Banjo Kazooie humor and vibe...This is an indie game. Story is not well written, there are some (not game-breaking) performance issues(fps drops/framepacing) and there is no voice acting. Now with the negatives out of the way (which are still acceptable for an indie title), let's get to the good things:- Pretty big and detailled world with 4 very different biomes.- basic but decent combat with a stamina bar. - light souls elements(poise enemies, watch stamina bar, challenging boss fights with different attack patterns..)No death penalties though.- Visually a very good-looking game- Sound mastering is pretty good- About 30hrs of content- lots of mildly challenging puzzles- skill tree and light crafting/cooking elementsOverall it's a pretty nice package that's absolutely worth its money.It also seems very polished as i have not  encountered any bugs yet.If you like the above mentioned games/genres, you should be quite happy with Kaku.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the RPG aspects of this game. Everything feels rewarding, collecting resources isn't forceful, it's something you do while exploring and solving quests. You can use resources in different ways, such as making food for HP and stamina, upgrading yourself in terms of unlocking new skills, making yourself more powerful and harder to kill etc. There are 4 different regions to explore so you have plenty of things to do and the graphics in this game feel incredible. Another thing I really like is the fighting system. It's simple, you can use different skills that require certain combos in order to work, you even have super powers that you unlock later in the game, you can use your slingshot to kill enemies from afar and use your Piggy in different ways to help you reach your goal. Also, Kaku can really look badass with all the equipment you can unlock while opening various chests and solving puzzles that you can put on him to make him look different. Some bosses are really hard to kill and some are not which is fine because it gets challenging over time and you do require some skills or cheating skills (only shotting them with slingshot) to win againts them.  Putting all the good things aside, this game has very annoying bugs. First things first, I hope I'm not the only one that has this problem but while exploring and running around the world I'm consistently getting stuck on small rocks or on invisible walls which gets really frustrasting because I have to keep using SPACE to jump over them or go around them. Second thing is the fact that Kaku feels very slippery next to edges which makes him fall off very easily. Sometimes it happened that I cannot deal any damage to an enemy because he has that yellow invisible shield which makes him unhitable that disapears over time? Not sure if it's because he is using his attack and I have to dodge or something but would appreciate if some one could explain this. Also, fighting is very repetitive in this game, you will usually fight againts the same enemies in each region but each region also has different type of enemies. For example, there are always these pigs that rush towards you as an attack in every region but there is also Scorpion typical for earth region. I'm not sure what to think about this. Some attacks are better than the others because it doesn't feel very balanced. For example, slingshot can be really useless sometimes and deal almost no DMG to enemies, but on the other hand, while using your shield attack, it can be really powerful. The story feels dry, cutscenes aren't that good because they feel rushed and characters in the game always use the same sounds to communicate. There is no proper character developement in this game even though it's based on Kaku. There is also a lot of text to read. Another thing to mention is that you can't really play around with graphic settings (even the game tells you it's best to use just medium settings) since it can lead to FPS drops due to it not being best optimized and you can't really change the resolution by that I mean that the screen shrinks and it's not fullscreen.To conclude, every other aspect of this game is good: abilities, progress, environmet, non-platforming simple puzzles, collecting resources, fighting bosses, but those micro things such us better Quality of Life options are desperatley needed in this game. Why does the game force me to click and hold all the options, even quitting the game, instead of just clicking on it? The bugs also need to get fixed because it gets frustating and the animations aren't the best, especially the jumping from another rock to the other. Final rating - 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: So my issue with the game is that it's very easy to essentially cheese the entire experience, the AI of monsters, and the ability to simply shoot everything from range with the slingshot because melee is a bit too delayed? That and weaker than what I was expecting due to mostly needing to use the stun mechanic to really be able to whack monsters harder, making most fights the same, shoot from range and destroy everything with the slingshot safely or stun and whack them!Keyboard controls are kind of wild by default, so rebinding them to things that are a little more comfortable is a lot more of a better choice. For example, instead of (Middle Mouse) F1-F5 for the piggy, rebinding Q W E R makes it just easier to really manage its skills. The controller does a much better job of it, but it also feels a little too... flicky at times, I dunno? If you've ever played the classic Tak and the Power of the Juju, it feels and looks very similar, but it's like it has been babied and dulled down to be somewhat worse. Because of the several layers of UI and skill keybinds, rather than being simple, it appears to be attempting to be something much larger and complex when it could easily get by without many of those elements. I found myself having to restart the game more than anything due to getting stuck on and inside of things.I would recommend that you try the demo before considering to purchase the game to see whether it matches your expectations of a game that you would like to play. It's a somewhat open world, with plenty to explore and lots of things to do, the most of which are fetch quests / tasks for progression, which is OK, but it feels extremely boring rather quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate the chance to look into the game some days before the release and I really liked it in several aspekt, but there are also several cons.The visuals are pure candy and I really like the low poly look (but I am also a fan of low poly games). The characters are cute and combat is fun. It kind of feels easy until the point you really get hit... this is also the second, where it get's challaging.I played around 5 hours. The puzzles are fun, not overly complicated and there are quite some jump and run passages. The storyline is simple but not boring while the interactions between the characters kind of have this asian touch in a good way.Now, there are some negative aspects: This is an early access game and while I think that this is fine for survival games that you play over and over again, I don't really like this in story games you mostly play once. This often means that you never experience the final game. I understand that money is a pressing factor for indie developers, but I still like to mention that.There are some bugs: texts seem to have been translated from chinese without adepting the time they are shown on the screen. Some text disappear so fast, that it is barely possible to follow the story line.Sometimes, original texts are popping up.So all in all: The game is pretty darn good and for less than 25€ it is totally worth a shot, but it might also be worth to wait for it a bit longer. So a total thumbs up but with some limitations.

_childDocuments_.review: If you by watching the trailers get the feeling this game is more about pretty graphics than quality gameplay, then you're not wrong. I was hesitant to buy it, but found a cheap key for around $8. So I gave it a shot.I was hoping for a Zelda clone, with the same quality that can be enjoyed regardless of your age. But it's not. It's a game for children.The story? It's all about chasing a piglet for no reason. Just pointless nonsense.The tutorial is boring AF, and the hand holding is immense. Instead of relying on "show don't tell", this game makes the opposite and "tells, rather than showing".The combat is also lacking. You can give yourself a small challenge by walking up to enemies and melee them. But you can also choose to stay on a safe distance and shoot them with your slingshot, to which they won't even react. They'll just die. If you have played games like Kena: Bridge of Spirits before, you'll laugh at this.First boss fight is artificially difficult by giving the boss an infinite amount of HP. The boss attacks are "telegraphed" properly, so you have a chance to dodge. But the highlighted area where you'll be dealt damage is problematic. Either it's too large and you have no chance to escape in time (but you can still dodge if timed correctly), or it's misleading and only shows the area of the first attack among multiple attacks in quick succession.If you gather all resources you find (which I always do in every game), you'll have an endless supply of health potions during this boss fight. So it becomes easier to just spam the attack button and heal occasionally, rather than actually trying to "git gud" and defeat the boss properly. But it takes forever either way, because of the infinitely long health bar.UPDATE: I defeated a second boss, "The Largest Boar". It was exactly the same as the first - stupid amounts of HP and lackluster combat.So there's definitely nothing more than pretty graphics to be found here. Go play Kena: Bridge of Spirits instead, if you want a game with similar art style.

_childDocuments_.review: Even a cursory playthrough is enough to discern the vast aspirations of the development team. Their vision is reflected in the meticulous crafting of the game's world, the strategic design of the combat mechanics, the unfolding of the narrative, and numerous other components that collectively impart a feeling of grandeur and scale.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: Kaku: Ancient Seal brings a lot of nostalgia to the table, along with pretty visuals, resource collecting, cute (but generic) characters, and a ton of lore. While it's not a game I would choose for myself, it was easy to pick-up and learn rather quickly. Some of the controls and responsiveness felt off so it did feel clunky at times.The story seemed to rely too heavily on a familiar formula without really having a voice of its own. It feels somewhat similar to a Zelda game with an old-school adventure game and humour vibe. However, the pacing, motivation and intense lore dump made the story difficult to get into. I am hoping the main character's reasons for adventuring are fleshed out as you explore more and the story comes together cohesively. Overall, cute visuals and potential here. I would recommend it if you enjoy adventure games and don't need to be heavily invested in a story to have fun grinding or exploring a colourful world. Not my cup of tea, but maybe it's yours.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:The graphics are nothing short of stunning, offering a visual feast for the eyes.Combat is fluid and intuitive, providing a satisfying sense of control and responsiveness.The game boasts a deep yet engaging decryption system that is both challenging and enjoyable.Cons:There's a subtle lack of aesthetic diversity in character design, which could be more captivating.The core gameplay mechanics, while solid, do not quite reach the pinnacle of what the world's top-tier games have to offer.In summary, the experience is quite commendable. It offers a delightful foray into the world of standalone games, with strengths that shine brightly, and areas that offer room for growth and refinement.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid game that's well worth your time. The real joy of playing comes from the challenges it presents. By the time you've completed a world, you'll find yourself powerfully equipped, more than capable of handling even the bosses. The graphics are of high quality, and I've encountered no bugs throughout my playthrough, ensuring a smooth and enjoyable gaming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: Rarely does a game's setting transport us to such a distinctive era reminiscent of the Stone Age, striking a chord with my personal taste. The Unreal Engine's rendering of this ancient world is nothing short of exquisite, with the combat, character evolution, and enigmatic puzzles in the beta version proving to be immensely gratifying.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: Kaku: Ancient Seal emerges as a promising indie action RPG that thrusts us into a fantasy world teetering on the edge of collapse. In this realm, a young hero embarks on a quest to rekindle hope among its desolate people and revive the majestic Creator to its former grandeur, all in a bid to thwart the resurgence of a ruthless malevolence that threatens devastation and anarchy. The narrative unfolds through meticulously crafted cinematics, setting the stage for an immersive gameplay experience. It blends 3D exploration, dynamic RPG combat, and challenging platforming puzzles that will appeal to both newcomers and seasoned players of the genre. The game proves accessible on a range of operating systems, from low to medium specs, offering a smooth 60 fps experience, and is equally enjoyable on high-end PCs and gaming laptops with maximum settings. This Early Access release offers a taste of the game's evolving narrative, with much anticipation for upcoming updates and patches that will enrich the game with additional content, storylines, and map expansions, promising a grand and expansive prehistoric journey.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: The game presents a rare and captivating world setting that harkens back to the Stone Age, perfectly attuned to my preferences. Crafted with the finesse of the Unreal Engine, the ancient landscapes are depicted with meticulous detail. The interwoven systems of combat, character progression, and puzzles offer a deeply satisfying experience.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: The protagonist's revamped appearance is a welcome upgrade, though there's room for further enhancement in character design. The game's environments are crafted with care, featuring a comprehensive narrative and intuitive mission maps that help new players quickly acclimate to the game's mechanics. The array of weapons and the impactful combat with monsters add to the game's appeal. The maps and boss battles evoke a simplified version of the Hunter experience, with boss skill range indicators that cater to newcomers. The game is replete with mechanisms and puzzles that drive the narrative forward, showcasing the production team's dedication and effort in crafting this gaming gem.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: Embarking on a wildly entertaining journey as KaKu, the game offers a vast world ripe for exploration. I've immensely enjoyed my time with it, even though my adventure isn't over yet. The segments I've experienced so far have been nothing short of amazing, with a touch of humor sprinkled throughout. The puzzles integrated into the gameplay are approachable and not overly challenging up to this point. For those seeking a delightful blend of adventure, exploration, and light puzzling, I wholeheartedly endorse giving this charming title a try.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

Apparently, they didn't notice that if they find and collect a golden chest on the minimap, it might contain weapons and armor. These usually provide perks like increased poison damage or damage reduction, etc. Just standard RPG stuff. But that's exactly what an RPG fan expects.Overall, a clear recommendation from me for this very well-executed title.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

If it's not already available on the Switch, it's definitely worth considering. _childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: Exploring the map is really fun, with a variety of treasure chests and Easter eggs that are very enticing to explore. _childDocuments_.review: While the game's storyline left something to be desired, with minimal plot development, it's the combat and decryption aspects that truly shine. _childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: The game is stunningly beautiful and incredibly entertaining. Even after losing track of the hours I've spent playing, it never ceases to hold my interest. _childDocuments_.review: I'm genuinely amazed by the wealth of content provided at such an affordable price. The gameplay is incredibly immersive, with a depth that is both smooth and well-executed. _childDocuments_.review: Rating: GoodGraphics: Well-suited to the type of game, featuring explorable open areas with a story woven throughout.Gameplay: Engaging with a solid narrative, explorable areas, puzzles, and some dungeons with interesting physical puzzles, including a touch of platforming.Combat: Clunky and somewhat slow, with game controls that feel sluggish and out of sync. _childDocuments_.review: The game is quite enduring and fun to play, and it has achieved a high standard in every aspect. _childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: The game shines with a rich combat system and an intricate skill tree, complemented by a wide array of equipment boasting unique abilities and characteristics, including various types of armor, shields, and clubs. The open-world design is ripe for exploration, filled with collectibles such as chests, book pages, and underground ruins teeming with puzzles and teleportation towers that nod to Ubisoft's legacy. The narrative campaign offers a substantial 20-30 hours of playtime, excluding the exploration of ruins and collection of items, and while the story is straightforward, it remains engaging. I must mention that on the easiest difficulty setting, certain enemies can still present a formidable challenge, requiring players to discern the right tactics for each adversary. Personally, the game resonated with me, evoking the joy reminiscent of classic Disney games. On the downside, the game's optimization could be smoother, as it occasionally stutters and consumes a significant amount of VRAM, which I trust the developers will address. Additionally, more content would be welcome, as the game's single boss monster has eluded me so far.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: This open-world adventure is replete with essential activities, including side quests that enrich the game's fabric. The primary mission is self-evident, and as you delve into the game's world, you'll come across various side quests. While many of these involve collection tasks, they can also lead to entertaining encounters. We're introduced to a girl who seeks our help in gathering items for an enemy camp; her storyline is particularly well-executed. It's important to note that while these quests are not necessarily "earth-shattering" or "out-of-this-world," they are delightfully crafted, offering a satisfying and immersive experience. However, I must also point out that the main storyline didn't resonate with me as much—it felt somewhat tiresome. It's not a deal-breaker by any means, but temper your expectations regarding the narrative. The game's side quests and overall design are beautifully realized and engaging in their own right.
_childDocuments_.name: KAKU: Ancient Seal

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an excellent experience overall, with one minor drawback being the lack of visually appealing characters or designs. _childDocuments_.review:
Kaku has lived alone on a snowy mountaintop for years, always dreaming about the world that lay beyond. Now, the ancient keeper from the mysterious ruins told him that it's his destiny to go on a continent-spanning adventure with a pig. 

Maybe some legendary creatures are waiting for him? Will they be good and kind, or snippy and inimical? Perhaps he'll find trouble with other tribes? But he'll never know unless he sets foot on this journey. For now, the only thing he needs to worry about is how to communicate with a pig, and how to fill his belly since that pig isn't for eating.

KAKU: Ancient Seal is an open-world action-adventure fantasy game that lets players navigate their own path through a mysterious continent full of strange creatures, ancient ruins, and unique tribes. Play Kaku an young child, who's tasked with going on a journey across a sprawling continent.

name: Journey of the Broken Circle
detailed_description: A fun and vibrant trip about life, love, fulfillment and existentialism, where new powers come from new relationships. Meet fascinating characters on your quest to complete the broken Circle, and eventually pair with some! These partners bring their unique abilities to let you overcome new obstacles and keep discovering the world. They also bring their own personality to roll with... In this 4-5 hours adventure, full of ups and downs, but always playful and rewarding, the Circle learns about itself and you, along with it. DEVELOPED BY Lovable Hat Cult “It’s a game about this little something that always seems to be missing…a better job, a nicer place to live, an ideal relationship… We wanted to tell a story of self-discovery in a fun, universal and relatable way. We probably also wanted to answer our own questions: would the Circle find what it was looking for? Or how would it all end?” - Andrea & Patrick from the Copenhagen-based studio. PUBLISHED BY Nakana.io “We gather games that share a strong experience to remember. We hope you’ll enjoy the sweet and tasteful food for thought served by Journey of the Broken Circle!” - Mikaël Bourget, founder of the publishing label.

_childDocuments_.review: Took me 2.4 hours to beat, minus the bonus levels and a big pile of the collectables.You jump and roll, it looks nice and sounds nice, and charming writing happens around you. It takes a little longer than I'd have liked to spin up to speed, but once it gets going it's a fun, light challenge. The writing (and uncertainty about when a chapter save happened) kept me playing from start to finish in one session.A charming game all in all. I think it's worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey of the Broken Circle

_childDocuments_.review: I had hoped that developer Lovable Hat Cult had crafted a capable and compelling experience, but in no way had I expected it to resonate with me so personally. Though the developer mentions that it is a game about relationships (and it is), it also explores in some depth the FOMO (fear of missing out) that many feel in a time where so much new content is released. New albums, games, films, and TV shows come out every week - which are the best? according to who? are some destined to be culturally important? will any of them relate to us personally or teach us something about ourselves? The circle's relentless drive for novelty is not only too much for many of the characters it brings along for the ride, but represents a life that is unsustainable for itself as well.Of course, the relationship angle provides much food for thought: "using" a partner, dependency, clinginess, the need for someone to complete you, the desire (and reality) of being with someone who is very similar - all are touched on within the game. And when a partnership ends or we find that perhaps we're living in a less-than-ideal way, how do we handle the resulting sadness and desperation? How important it is that we have a network of support, or someone like Miss Moss to pick us up when we are down.On a gameplay front, the game is a platformer with a touch of physics. As is mentioned in the game description, the circle acquires various abilities through each of the partnerships it establishes in the game. The sense of momentum created through the partnership with "perfect" is genuinely thrilling (at least for a while), while the precision required to navigate the gravity fields through inflating and deflating the balloon character gives the player a sense of mastery.The only real irritation I had with the game is the sound effect used for the purple snail. It's just so tremendously unnerving, though perhaps it's supposed to be. Though I, like the circle, play many games and have a hunger for new experiences, I am especially glad that I slowed down long enough to experience The Journey of the Broken Circle. As metaphorical platformers go, it is top notch.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey of the Broken Circle

_childDocuments_.review: I think for ten dollars, the game needs more polish. Some of the mechanics are interesting for sure, but in practice I didn't have that much fun playing through the more demanding physics puzzles. Perfect, in particular, was really annoying to work with, and even after finishing the game, I still don't understand how the water segments were supposed to work. If the game teaches you the physics anywhere, I blew right past it, fittingly. Overall, the gameplay just needs a bit more refinement to cross the threshold from novel into fun.That all said, I did not pay ten dollars for the game. I bought it on sale, for a mere two bucks, and I feel like I definitely got more than my money's worth. As of writing this review, I've recently broken up with one of my partners, so the ideas the story put forth about fulfillment and compatibility resonated deeply with me. I kind of want to meet up with my ex and give them a big hug, now.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey of the Broken Circle

_childDocuments_.review: It really reminds me of Thomas was Alone both story and gameplay-wise with some minor differences. You're controlling a circle instead of various rectangles through series of linear levels. The story is narrated through speech bubbles but sadly without any voiceover. If you liked Thomas was Alone, this will be right up your alley.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey of the Broken Circle

_childDocuments_.review: Journey of  the Broken Circle was enjoyable in the beginning, yet felt as though it dragged on for far too long. Gameplay consists of just holding right, and jumping occasionally. No challenging gameplay to be found, but if you enjoy a game with a short story and repetitive gameplay, this would be your type of game. As for the price, i would personnally wait for a sale of maybe ( 5$ - 6$ ).The Pros are that this game does have very nice visuals, enjoyable text, and music. The game does have achievements, as well as collectables in game which can add for replayability.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey of the Broken Circle

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be fooled by its short length--this game has stayed with me, and I've thought about it for much longer than its run time. Its commentary on relationships and personal growth is dead on, and has helped me with some breakups and falling-outs recently. The gameplay is directly related to the narrative, and evolves as the story does, enriching the message and themes with interactivity. It's a brilliant example of narrative dictating form!
_childDocuments_.name: Journey of the Broken Circle

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like it draws very heavily from The Missing Piece by Shel Silverstein, and it uses the same central metaphor - a circle with a segment missing - to explore some of the same ideas about relationships. It was very engaging to see what we normally think of as complex relationship dynamics boiled down to their essence, and I think it does a good job of reflecting some of the different reasons why relationships can start and end. I will say however, that this game is not without its jank. Jumping often felt unnatural and difficult to control, and there are some sections where you're really fighting hard against a physics system that doesn't make sense, with some extra annoyances sprinkled on top e.g. (mild spoilers)  feels incredibly unfair and brutally challenging in a game that is otherwise mechanically fairly simple and narrative-focused.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey of the Broken Circle

_childDocuments_.review: A cute idea but overall the gameplay isn't really that engaging. I do appreciate the message of the game, but not when the devs see it as justification for leaving a broken achievement in the game, saying "that's the point, you'll never be perfect". _childDocuments_.review: Can you make a game about life, love and existentialism? We believe we have just done that! name: Tell Me Why
detailed_description: Tell Me Why is the latest narrative adventure game from DONTNOD Entertainment, the studio behind the beloved franchise, Life is Strange. In this intimate mystery, reunited twins Tyler and Alyson Ronan use their supernatural bond to unravel the memories of their loving but troubled childhood. Set in beautiful small-town Alaska, Tell Me Why features true-to-life characters, mature themes and gripping choices. As you conjure up memories of the past, your choices will affect the twins’ relationship, determine the strength of their bond, and shape the course of their lives. Experience all chapters free in June! Revisit your past, discover the truth, and shape your future • Uncover the truth – Use the twins’ supernatural bond to relive and explore their conflicting childhood memories. • Shape your Story – Influence the relationship between Tyler and Alyson with choices that will determine their future. • Unlock even more secrets – Match wits with puzzles that deepen the story and open a window into the twins’ fantasy world, “The Book of Goblins.” Experience true-to-life setting and characters • Unique characters – Build relationships and solve mysteries through the eyes of compelling and realistic characters. • Alaskan splendor – Explore locations set in beautiful, highly detailed small-town Alaska in stunning 4K and HDR. Storytelling with purpose – DONTNOD Entertainment and Xbox Game Studios conducted on-the-ground research and partnered closely with cultural, mental health and gender advocates to craft a thoughtful, true-to-life experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't take my recommendation as a pure thumbs up. This game is FAR from perfect for many reason, some I will mention here, but I can't totally not recommend it either. I played this game outside of Steam and I will be leaving my review in both places as well.First, the important things:Gameplay: 5/10. It's a typical walk and click game. Life is Strange-esque, so if you played LiS, you know what you're getting, with some differences. Plenty of Bland Characters that fit a typical look and feel of a certain crowd of people, which makes them boring. Graphics: 9/10. Although the animations are janky and the people models are a bit... weird, the overall atmosphere and graphics of the game are pretty tight. Especially the scenery. Story: 4/10. Subpar. If you like the cringe wet dream of woke preachiness, this is your thing. If you don't, this isn't going to be your thing. Even though there are far more subtle things in this game that bring out the cringe, there are very acute scenes of how SJW woke people THINK things happen but in reality don't. But, the story isn't without it's great moments. At the end of the day, at it's worse, it's just a typical cringe fest by the modern Game Industry and at it's best it's actually light hearted and slightly enjoyable. Now, for my thoughts:This is NOT Life is Strange and the comparisons to it are unfair. LiS is a GREAT game, Tell Me Why is just "Meh". To clear the air, LiS teeters on woke SJW cringe as well and is still an enjoyable game, which comes down to the story and the gameplay being the savior of it. But like I said, comparing the two isn't fair to Tell Me Why. That doesn't matter though. TMW is a joy to look at visually but that is about all it has going for it. Beyond the visuals, it's a snooze fest. It takes less than 5 minutes into the game to get to the first preachy part and among ALL of the topics, it's Hunting. It only goes down hill from there. As a game, it's meh but slightly enjoyable. As a preachy game that delivers everything you want from the crowd that is known for canceling things that offend them? It's spot on. Everything from books, posters, music, and dialogue that just shoves things down your throat, all of the subtle things, it just cries "woke".Play it. I recommend playing it, even if your own political views or opinion on modern society are not inline with what this game is obviously trying to push. You may very well enjoy it as it IS a game that is enjoyable at rare times. No game is perfect.Should it have won Game of the Year? Hell no. Not even close. We all know why it did though and it has nothing to do with the game itself but due to pandering. Leaving other games, whose devs took the time to deliver a phenomenal story, gameplay, and graphics, in the air just because they weren't developed to cater to the woke reviewers who can't put aside their own biases or agenda to actually vote on GAMES that delivered what people want in GAMES. TMW is better fit as a TV show, probably on the CW or something. But not as a game, where it falls short of what makes a game FUN to play and FUN to come back to. It could be the direction they took with the gameplay but that can't be it because games like LiS, Beyond: Two Souls, Detroit: Become Human, and many others who utilize similar gameplay mechanics, are also fantastic games.Finally, Summary:inevitably, this game lacks in all things that make a game a good game. Good Story, Good Characters, and fun gameplay are a requirement. TMW kind of (but mostly not) meets, or totally misses, those things. Most of the Characters are Bland. The Gameplay mechanics are alright but fall short to bringing me back to play a second time. The story is preachy and obviously so, which will turn off many people who just want to escape the real world, to play something that takes them out of this world and into another, after a hard days work. The first chapter is free, which is a plus and no one is FORCING you to play this game. But I'm not going to go easy with this review simply to make the particular crowd this game is aimed at, happy. It's a stale game but digestible.

_childDocuments_.review: Story - 9/10Graphics - 7/10Gameplay - 2/10Overall score - 6/10. Verdict and conclusion at the bottom.- No FOV Slider. A terrible heresy in my eyes for a game that SPECIFICALLY FOCUSES on exploration. No, not everyone is gonna play this sitting on the couch with a controller. Give us a choice.- No save slots. You only get one that autosaves. For some reason it got corrupted? "Well f**k your time, start the game from scratch." -devs, probably. How difficult it is to implement save slots when Half-Life has done it since 90s? Also Life is Strange probably had slots too, if I remember right.- Controls are quite unintuitive for keyboard+mouse. Why assign scrolling to 'X' and 'C' when we have mouse wheel? Also who locks mouse wheel controls?- In a story-rich game like this, graphics are not that important, true. But the facial animation is. And it's terribly done. Close-up on faces during dialogue makes it seem like the audio was recorded in some other language and I am playing the English dub. The lips don't sync at all and it really breaks the immersion. It did not feel this bad in Life is Strange and you should not devolve in this category as years pass. Ruined some of the great moments in the game for me.- The story is hands down superb. The emotional impact, the logical consistency and characters' reactions were quite great. Could not find a plot hole as far as I remember. And I consider myself an expert in finding plot holes.- The dialogue was very great. Not too cheesy and not too 'hip'. NPCs talked like a real character would. Din't give off a 'gamey' vibe which is very important for a game like this.- The visuals are stunning. Alaska in winter? Heaven on earth. The water, the trees, the snow capped mountains, the sun, the birds and what not were all beautiful. You WILL stop interacting with things/people at some points to just stare into the horizon and appreciate the beauty. Adds to the atmosphere of the game too.- No glitches, no bugs, no frame drops, no microstutters. Ran the game at 60fps on max settings with a GTX 1650 no issues. There is one level though where your performance will fall and it's not the game's fault. Snow is terribly heavy on GPUs, like rain. Drop the settings on that level (wont mention which one, but you'll get it when you reach there).- Puzzles were really good. Not too easy and not too tough. Pretty much every puzzle is contextual to the plot and the more understanding you have of the game, the easier it is to solve the puzzle. So make sure to read the book of goblins and to talk to every NPC thoroughly.- Not spoiling the ending, but it was good and satisfying. Unlike so many games out there who build up hype only to go downhill on the end. This game will pay off your time and energy invested.Don't let all the talk about LGBTQ+ affect your decision, just get into the game and decide for yourself after 15-30 minutes. The gameplay/controls definitely feel frustrating for PC players but the Pros of the game far outweigh the cons.

_childDocuments_.review: Tell Me Why is an excellent member of the genre. Whatever went wrong with their previous publisher, it looks like we might be getting two Life Is Strange franchises, now, and Tell me Why sets quite a bar for LiS 3.I can't make myself say this is as good or even better than the original Life is Strange. LiS was a first of a kind and had many things in its setting that made it immediately relatable, to me a little more so than Tell Me Why. I don't doubt people who haven't played LiS and play it after (who don't feel nostalgic about it) may well consider them on par or like TMY better. Especially taking the central pair (PriceField, Rachel/Chloe, Sean/Daniel) a step further and exploring the ability to play as two protagonists is interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: I love games created by Dontnod Entertainment. Life is Strange is probably the 2nd-3rd best story driven cinematic “choices matter” game I ever experienced (First is Telltale’s Walking Dead, I believe the story of Clementine is unbeatable in this category). While Vampyr had some bad combat, it was also saved by the very good story. I believe so, that Tell Me Why doesn't have the quality we usually get from this developer team.Right now it feels that the review score has been brought by the fear of downvoting a game with its current theme. While Tell me Why has a message, I believe it is important for a story to be well written and interesting, which pulls in the player at the first second and not letting us away until the end.The game has a very promising start. We learn about a family tragedy which causes the protagonist twin siblings to get apart while they are still very young. The gameplay start as the now adult twins reunite, so they can face their past and move on. Episode 1 is usually not the most emotional chapter in these kinds of games but Dontnod managed to make it extremely boring. We learn about the superpower of the twins, that they can see the past and they have telepathically bonded with each other. The premise of the game is great. While one of the twins is a trangender human being and there are references in the story that he had a tough childhood because of that the writers failed to deliver any emotional memories to the players about this. In the 3 hours of the Episode we see just happy memories, that they both were loved by their mom, and while their mom was clearly fighting with inner demons there was a question in the air all the time: What was the problem which caused the tragedy? Based on the memories the game showed us, the tragic events were not exactly expected. During this “prologue” it was easy to abandon the game, I felt like it is a work to keep playing and the biggest problem of it? It is 33% of the total game, not just in the number of Episodes, but also in the total playtime.Then we get to the ending of the first part of the game. The cliffhanger there is the first heartbreaking and emotional scene. It gave at least some hope for Episode 2, which was now actually better. The twins try to figure more about their past, they try to get better knowledge on their mother and about the inner shadows that haunted her. It started to be clear that only one of the twins is a notable character. Alyson became much more interesting and emotional. It could be because of the significantly better voice acting on her. Tyler is a different case, it felt so that the writers had no clue what to do with a transgender character and the forced LGBTQ romance with a side character felt more distracting and slowed down the story which was already bleeding. I blame the writers on that. The character of Tyler had a huge potential.Then Episode 3 arrived and it was now finally on the standard of Dontnod. Alyson's character literally made the episode to a one protagonist show. His fight with the past and keeping mental integrity while getting released of it's burden is the emotional high point of the story.The twins reveal the secrets and history of their mom at the end of the game through some very nice and interesting puzzles. We will get our happy or bad ending then at the end, based on the decisions we had during the gameplay, just like another important story at the end based on our single decision there.It is worth playing if you have XBOX game pass because of some other game but purchasing it directly for the asked price? Nope, the actual valuable content of the game is way too short filled with empty stories. Expected more from Dontnod. Story driven game and the different decisions not influencing the story radically. Game is easy to stop during episode 1 but then it gets some “moments’. Tyler feels bad, Alyson exceptional and some characters have an extremely neutral and boring voice acting. Nice looking game.. There are some puzzles in the game, but no gameplay challenges in the game, no quick time events either.Perfection time: ~14-18h. _childDocuments_.review: Here we have a thoughtfully written story (but which is more suitable for a film rather than an interactive game) which raises questions about LGBT community, family issues and other “hard” questions which people usually discuss with a therapist. The story is about two twins which after dramatical events were separated for 10 years and now finally they are meeting up to sell the house where they spent their childhood. The game consists of three chapters, which are really distinguished in manner of narrative from each other which unfortunately doesn’t serve the game well. The twins have a special ability which allows them to recapture their memories and to communicate telepathically for , to help them to understand what really has happened that night and years before their separation. Following the old memories we observe how Tyler and Allyson differently perceive their memories and all the skeletons in the closet which they find.The visuals are looking fantastic: the snow-covered mountains, frozen lakes, and lights  in the house were what I enjoyed it the most.Gameplay is a bit boring, and the characters are moving quite slow. The memories recapture didn’t work correctly for me all the time. There were few locations where firstly I had to spin around a few times and then I was able to find a point where I could “activate” memories. Also I experienced some issues in stacking in textures, especially in the wooden house so I had to restart the game.I was really excited that it is the same developer as  (there is even an easter egg related to LiS) but  falls short not only of  and also .I think the game had much bigger potential if there was bigger empathy of the main characters   but as for me the supportive characters   are looking better written. While playing the game I was disappointed with the decision-making. In narrative games such as this one, being able to choose the option most suitable for you is the main reason for playing such a game. However, when the main feature isn’t presented as intended, the game loses its genre and removes the real reason for playing it.Many times it wasn’t me who drove the story, but the story drove itself. I wanted to act differently, but the game couldn’t provide enough options or at least a more satisfying explanation of motives. Choice-selection wise the game is really poor and there are mostly black and white choices, which could be seen in the statistics at the end of the chapters (most of the decisions were on 80/20 ratio). In comparison, just remember how the choices made by players were balanced in  where there were only “grey” options which are neither good or bad. And this, I believe, is the main limitation of the game and I  the game didn’t achieve that success as . There are really two or three choices which really matter for the end of the story, which makes most of the dialogue meaningless and provides the questions but not the answers. It is like with ()  Mary-Ann’s shotgun – in the game many interesting moments but they fade away as they do not provide any continuation. Speaking about the real gun,  That also affects the words from the annotation “their past is not what they remember” which boosted my general interest in the game. However, in the end of the game I was slightly disappointed that I got caught as I expected something else from the game.If you would like to complete the game 100%, I recommend don’t be lazy and exploring every corner in the rooms to collect all the wooden figures. It is possible to replay all the scenes in the chapters to get some specific achievements, so don’t worry if you couldn’t solve some puzzles – you can come back after finishing the game.As for me, the game is slightly overpriced. I recommend  waiting for a sale. The game in general was enjoyable but the amount of limitations which I spoke about do not allow me to recommend the game to everyone.If you like narrative games and have a few evenings to play a game, you can give this game a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my 3rd game of Dontnod after Remember Me and LiS (1) I really enjoyed, and I though they cannot make another masterpiece any soon. I was wrong. Slowly, over the 3 chapters, the game leads you through revealing what actually happened that night. At the end the story gives you a choice: accept the truth, or run from it for good. Even though Alyson will not become who Chloe Price was to me, and Tyler will not totally become Max, this game was definitely very close to LiS vibes. If Life Is Strange was of rather blue color to me, this one is all about lilac feelings. I would recommend this game to anyone who want to experience something special, something that is more than just a game, and cannot repeat in one’s life. As for the cons, I would mention the following: the game does not promote good attitude to animals. The cruel scene with fishing does not make it better. _childDocuments_.review: This review will have minimal spoilers, which will not spoil the story outright, but may touch on a couple story bits and sequences. .(Disclaimer: I got the max bond + don’t believe the original memory ending (which is the “best” ending); I did not encounter or watch the other endings.) The writing is very akin to  series, with that classic “American young adults transparently being written by 40-year old French dudes” aspect in the dialogue (“get all Smeagol” being a notable highlight), but it has one major distinguishing factor versus Dontnod’s other works: it’s extremely slow-paced, with a lot of unnecessary padding to boot -- for example, there is a thirty-minute section wherein you do housekeeping. There are a lot of gratuitous twists, with both chapter 1 and 2 throwing anemic screwballs towards the end of each of them in order to keep the drama going in spite of not much of anything really happening.  Since we’re discussing gratuitous things, the superpower that the game revolves around, specifically the memories and Alyson and Tyler’s telepathic link, are both insubstantial and not really explored in any way. The memories are just that -- remembering things that happened (including having Alyson and Tyler’s memories not sync up), which I’m sure both you and I have; the only thing the characters have over us is that they can render it in 3D. Their memories don’t even sync up and have significant differences, which makes this fantastical power seem very mundane. The story could have removed these magical powers entirely, and it would have largely been the same, a sharp (and ultimately negative) contrast to the rest of Dontnod’s games. The story itself meanders and doesn’t do all that much until the tail end of each chapter. Much of what happens is supposed to be character-bonding moments, which ultimately comes across as filler (see below on the characters).  As a consequence, the game feels directionless until it manages to stumble into its climax. The climax itself is merely competent, and doesn’t feel like a grand finale or anything particularly special. I’m not going to talk too much about this, because frankly I lack the credentials to discuss it in a thorough manner. The transgender aspect of Tyler was handled quite well, and as someone who is not transgender I would consider it an interesting insight.  Despite this, it doesn’t redeem this game for me, and it doesn’t justify trudging through the lackluster story to experience these story bits. The characters are fairly weak altogether. Tyler acts like a jerk at multiple points, but outside of him the characters don’t really feel like they have any sort of defining characteristics that would cause them to have staying power within my memory. They aren't especially one-note (or really that grating), but they aren't interesting, either.  This is compounded with the fact that the voice acting is very mediocre in this game, with the majority of the cast coming across as apathetic in their performances; only Alyson managed to come across as solid. Tyler is especially notable in terms of weak voice acting, as even when he’s trying to sound impassioned, he doesn’t really have a lot of emotion in him. I didn’t encounter many bugs, especially major ones such as softlocks or crazy animation glitches. I think I encountered one animation bug where a character was randomly static during their idle animation, and I only got a couple audio glitches towards the end of the game where a few lines of dialogue randomly freaked out. In terms of graphics, this is probably the best-looking Dontnod game. That isn’t saying much (especially when you compare it to  and , which are getting much-needed visual remasters), but it’s reasonably pretty, and the rural environment lets them make nice landscapes to serve as backdrops (though the game had a couple too many "look how pretty our game is" shots for my tastes, but that's just a nitpick). Speaking of art, the art with the Book of Goblins is very nice, with a great balance of refinement and style. It makes me wish that the whole game was expressed through that fairy tale storybook style instead of the decent at best 3D replica of the real world. A game that was built around that vibe would certainly have been much more interesting, and would have been a fun break from the typical Life is Strange formula. Alas, it was not to be. As is to be expected from a game that is as story-focused as this one, the gameplay isn't intensive or even much of a priority, and for the most part it's walking around to get to the next story bit (which, for the record, was anticipated and is completely fine by me). The puzzles aren’t too rough; I only brute-forced the ones where I had to consult the Book of Goblins to solve (specifically the door puzzle in chapter 1 and the loft puzzle in chapter 3) out of lack of patience rather than getting stuck on them.  There were three minigames, and only the second one where you try to calm Alyson down during a panic attack is the only one that came across as obtuse and clunky. If you’ve ever played a video game before, you shouldn’t have any trouble with them. They’re alright change-ups, but not really common enough to be anything more than short breaks.

_childDocuments_.review: It felt almost like a film more than a game. The story is everything, and that's maybe the best story I have ever seen in a video game. The gameplay is thin: you have a few simple puzzles and QTEs or mini-games, but it's mostly just here to support the story, keep you engaged, or even force you to read the stories. And it probably worked: not sure whether the gameplay design helped or if it's just that the story was great, but anyway I remained immersed in the story and never got bored. So much that I don't even know if skipping cut-scenes was a possibility: I've not tried, it didn't even come to my mind.On the other hand, I'm not sure how much my choices really changed the story.It took me 10 hours (time on pause included) to finish the game, taking my time but missing a few collectibles at the end.The replayability is probably comparable to how much you would watch again a good film: you might do this at some point, but you won't watch the same film twice in a row.PS: I'm not a member of the "LQBTQ community" and I don't really have a particular interest in these topics, so just know that it is not needed at all to enjoy the game (I wrote "to enjoy the film" and had to correct the typo ^^), it is for a large audience.PS2: I got the game for free, but I'm not evaluating it "as a free game". I mean If I had paid, I would not regret this purchase. However, I'm usually not a big fan of the genre, so maybe I wouldn't have bought it and it would have been too bad.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fine. Nothing spectacular, but if you liked Life is Strange, you'll likely have a good time with Tell Me Why. Just be aware that the story and characters are not as strong.The twins are fine, I also liked Michael a lot. And I appreciate that there are no clear "good" or "evil" people, just... people. But the story was dragged out and after Episode 2 it felt like no mystery remained. I also missed the great soundtracks from the LiS-series.Tell Me Why touches on sensitive topics and does a pretty good job, but it didn't blow me away. Not every game has to do so, but you should manage your expectations a bit. If you are looking for a ten hour game with some beautiful landscapes, a decent main story and some nice LGBTQ+ representation, then I'd recommend Tell Me Why to you. _childDocuments_.review: Review as of Ep 1:It's a little 'safe' at this point. It's got all the classic pillars of DONTNOD Games, for good and for worse. Excellent environmental design and attention to detail means you're instantly immersed in small-town Alaska. Every house or place you come across, feels like it has 50 years of history, just in the objects you pick up. The cozy indie soundtrack is there and the ambient music is great as usual.In terms of the story, I fear everyone you meet in this game is going to have "two sides to every story" syndrome, where everyone's who's done something horrible or is acting like a prick, must have some traumatic reason or otherwise for doing so.I feel the transgender issues were handled delicately - it is more of Tyler is just a transgender person trying to live his life, rather than an examination of how transgender people are treated by society. That's not to say his transgender identity isn't central to the story. Tyler's confusion over his mother's view of him and his need for his sister's help through that, is compelling.I did feel this episode lacked that characteristic emotional punch that the Life is Strange games had, but I imagine there will be a payoff in later episodes. In the few emotional scenes the script does get cringy, but when Tyler and Alyson are talking about their daily lives or Alaskan cultural norms or just plain old reminiscing, it's actually pretty interesting.DONTNOD is still obsessed with the childhood imaginary stuff. We've gone from pirates and wolves and superheroes to the Goblin cinematic universe here.
_childDocuments_.name: Tell Me Why

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful and very emotional game from Dontnod, as to be expected. The LGBT+ content is sensitively handled and very positive overall. Or maybe that's just a thing all twins can do, I'm not sure.

_childDocuments_.review: I have conflicting feelings about this game. It’s a good game, but I really don’t think it was for me. I love DONTNOD’s work, but somehow despite having characters older than any of the Life is Strange protags, this felt like way more of a melodramatic teen drama. And I watch f*cking... Riverdale, FFS.I HATED episode 1. It’s not great to hate 33% of a game. The game is beautiful, of course – character models (the twins are unreasonably gorgeous), environments (both indoor and outdoor), lighting, music, etc. Voice acting was good, and it was super nice to have a trans VA for Tyler. I liked a lot of the NPCs (Michael is bae). All that.However, the gameplay was mind-numbingly boring. I don’t mind a slow and quiet pace but this was too much. I constantly found myself completely disengaging from what was happening and totally zoning. It often feels like you’re being held hostage – like yeah Alaska is beautiful but how long am I gonna be forced to stare at this particular landscape while banal conversation is happening?I hated the twins in episode 1. Absolute brats, dude. They had two modes: 1- Totally chill and laid back. 2- Yelling at/verbally harassing family friends/neighbors. No in-between. There’s a lot of jumping to conclusions without the facts, and you might make a dialogue choice that is level-headed but that infuriates your twin and has a negative impact on your bond. I had to remind myself that Tyler and Alyson are 21 (they look 30) and that they’re dealing with childhood trauma, but even then, I don’t think I’ve ever known anyone to act that way, really. I liked them more in episodes 2 and 3 because they have time to reflect and ease up a little (and APOLOGIZE to people) but the first impression is just abysmal.The story isn’t so great either. Whatever I thought the game was going to be after episode 1, it wasn’t. Mostly with the supernatural/superpower stuff, but I especially feel that there was wasted potential with the trans representation. I’m not trans, so maybe it’s not for me to speak on, but I feel like… without giving spoilers… maybe there was a lack of commitment. There’s set-up, and then there’s a plot twist in episode 1 that makes the set-up all for nothing, really? So don’t have that set-up at all, if that’s not what the game is going to be about. I am extremely elated to have a trans character as a playable character but the game seemed wishy-washy with where it wanted to go and it feels like it diminishes Tyler's experience.However, there were so many good, strong moments in the game to make up for all the fun I wasn’t having for the rest of the game, that my overall impression upon completion is more positive than negative. I don’t regret playing this, but I could have happily gone without it.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my biggest complaints about Life is Strange 2, DONTNOD's game released prior to Tell Me Why, was that the story was inauthentic. It was a story about marginalized people, made by and for everyone except those people. Any nuance in handling the topics at play in the narrative was out the window.Tell Me Why has that same problem. While Tyler's trans storyline takes a backseat to the narrative at play in the game, what's there is clearly there for demonstrative purposes. It's a story about a trans person, but it's made by and for cisgendered people. And that's not something I think was a cash money move on their part, if I'm being quite honest.Regardless, the other issues I had with Life is Strange 2 are gone. Tell Me Why's setting is intimate, familiar, and fully explored. There's no big grand adventure that's constantly sweeping you away from the important decisions and characters and locations you know. There are moments of joy and sadness and confusion and anger wrapped in a whimsical, unique, and personal lore (involving goblins).The puzzles in the game properly integrate that lore -and- the powers that the twins have - something that games like this often miss out on. These powers do tie into the narrative, yes, but serve a functional purpose. You learn more by exploring and piecing together memories, and during intense dialogue sessions the two characters can communicate telepathically to open new dialogue choices.The story is somewhat quickly wrapped up, but it's a wonderful story (outside of how Tyler's character was handled). It means something to the characters and, by the end, the player. It has clever twists and a genuine layer of subjectivity that leaves the ball entirely in the player's court for what they feel is true or not. Alternating between playing as Tyler and Alyson was also a great twist, especially when you start seeing how the choices you make as one impact the options you have as the other later.Could this game have been better? Absolutely. Hire a trans person to write the trans character, to start. But it's still a wonderful game. I think the thing I'm most sour about is that it's not a Life is Strange game. Because this genuinely would have been a better LiS2 than LiS2 was. It's a beautiful game, and the first episode is free.Also note: While I do give them ♥♥♥♥ for the way they wrote Tyler, I do want to applaud them for actually casting a trans man in the role - instead of, like, Jennifer Hale. I'm sure there was also a level of consultation going on, but I do believe they could have gone further.
