_childDocuments_.review: I always have mixed feelings on Dontnod games. I loved Life is Strange, thought BtS was okay, and couldn't get through LiS2. And while I really loved the story in Tell Me Why, it felt like a bit of a slog to get through because of this studio's signature storytelling style.Rich in cutscenes and playable scenes that  like cutscenes, Tell Me Why allows you to play as two siblings, Alyson and Tyler, who come back to their childhood home after being separated for a decade following the death of their mother. Each of them has baggage from their childhood, including around the night their mother died. You get to know each of the characters as you play through them and help them wok through their grief, their tension--and their memories.Like many of the other games from Dontnod, Tell Me Why hinges on characters with a supernatural ability--in this case, Tyler and Alyson have certain telepathic abilities that allow them to share memories. But from time to time, those memories won't align, and you're forced to confront the fragile, unreliable nature of memory and what it means for your present-day perception.Tell Me Why does a lot of things well: addresses the fallibility of memory, focuses on the psychology of grief and guilt, and deals with the difficulty of coming out as trans in a town where you might not be accepted. And, even better, these themes are all layered onto an event that has notable emotional weight: the loss of the twins' mother when they were young. As adults, they have to decide if they want to learn exactly who their mother was--versus who they thought she was--and determine how that fits in with their perception of themselves.The game also sets up a parallel of the present-day story with a storybook the twins' mother used to make when they were children. I found the storybook just a  tedious, but ultimately, I liked its inclusion and loved the way it was eventually folded into the main story.When you're actually getting to investigate, explore, discover, this game is a treat. The scenery is gorgeous, and there are a few fun puzzles here and there to keep things interesting. The discussions you can have with characters are generally engaging. And choosing your pathway through your memories gives you a sense of autonomy in a game that is otherwise pretty much on rails.But for me, the downsides are quite prominent as well. Ultimately, I'm very glad I  stop playing. I really liked this narrative and I'm glad I've heard this story. I just don't feel like I PLAYED it as much as I feel like it played itself AT me. Tell Me Why is a thoughtful piece of storytelling with an interesting narrative that is more like an interactive movie than a video game. It's worth playing, but ultimately, you'd get a very similar experience just by watching a playthrough online.

_childDocuments_.review: Another great game by Dontnod Entertainment following similar mechanisms to Life is Strange, but the fiction elements on this one is put more aside to deal with the human conflicts. But the higher point of this game is the compelling storyline that, for me, had a very satisfying and mature ending. You should definitely give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: I was lured in to see Alaska's snow capped mountains and rippling waterfalls, bears and whales, arts of Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian and Eyak artists. The first 30 minutes was very satisfying. Especially on the ferry boat, I was able to see cedar trees and shore pines on snow covered mountains, soaking up the serenity of that peaceful lake, and witnessed the humpback whale jumping out of the water. After arriving the Mary Ann's house, it was a small adventure to figure out how to find way to enter the house, interesting but not difficult. Yet once inside of the house, the nightmare began. I have to go through every props, digging out stories behind it, read the whole fairy tale book, and found the diary, transgender child education book, it was sad and depressed. What made it worse is the recap of Tyler's childhood story. It began to grow into a very unpleasant feeling that I was trapped in this story, inside of this house, and unable to go outside to take a breath. The emotion has made this game so heavy that I got to quit the game to take a break.When I found out that 95% of game time, you'll be indoors, talking to Alyson - that's my last straw, uninstalled the game. Maybe it's a good story, for those who want to experience Tyler's life and inner conflicts, but it's not for me. I was a little disappointed not being able to explore Delos Crossing town, and the designs of local artists were buried under the heavy story-line. The game team could have done a better job.

_childDocuments_.review: Tell Me Why is the best game I've ever played. When I heard about this game, I already had high expectation. But this game really exceeded these expectation. I like the LGBT+ representation in this game, I would describe it as very good. The game also shows the problem the main characters have with homophobia and transphobia, but in conclusion, the game is a great game that is pleasent to play, when you start playing, you want to know how it will all come together in the end.I would really recommend this game. _childDocuments_.review: Not gonna lie this game hit me right in the feelings. I felt an instant connection to Tyler and Alyson because of the similarities -- my sister and I were born identical but I ended up transitioning, so now she has a brother. The story was so in-depth and I loved discovering all the little twists the story took, and collecting everything. I didn't manage to nab all of the achievements -- maybe with a couple more playthroughs. All in all, I would 100% recommend this game and the story it tells. There are only a few games I wish I could re-experience anew, and this is definitely one of them.

_childDocuments_.review: I was expecting this to be a predictable story like some parts of life is strange, but it surprised me with some interesting turns. I also imagined that since this is a game that focuses on a transgender character, it could become a bit lecture like in order to highlight this important theme (which is not bad, but it would not be  entertainment , but more of an educational piece). I was wrong though , as the story focuses a lot more on the drama and the thriller aspects of trying to find the truth about what happened to the protagonists mother. Overall  it's a nice story about regrets, healing and forgiveness.

_childDocuments_.review: It follows a pair of young twins who murdered their mother as self-defence in a tragedy so terrible, that the entire town would grieve about it for years to come. One of the twin (Tyler) who confessed to stabbing her mother was sent to a detention centre for 10 years & the other twin (Alyson) was adopted by an officer on this case. The game takes place after 10 years of described events where the twins are reunited in their beautifully designed home town of Alaska. They soon discover a special magical bond between them where they can talk with each other telepathically & also envision their childhood memories together. They use these abilities to re-live through their childhood trauma together once again in search for answers.Expect nothing less from how life is strange functions in terms of character control & option selection. When the twins revisit a memory, sometimes two revisit a different version of the same memory, indicating they both remember things happening differently. In order to proceed, it is players who's given the option to discard one of the variation. This feature not only allows player to control behavior of a character for a differed outcome but also allows one to change their history. Every decision made affects the relationship between twins.There's also a 'Book of Goblins' that helps player solve optional puzzles for achievements. This book is a children's book of fairytales written by Mary-Ann (Mother of Tyler & Alyson).  In order to solve these puzzles player has to read stories written in them to decode the riddles provided in-game. At a point plot was hinted towards an element of horror which never came into play growing my excitement stale.Stakes feel insubstantial  So what if their bond breaks, it's not the , they've been apart for 10 years already. The only reason to keep their bond intact is because it would be wholesome.  Aside the cliches, I personally enjoyed this journey & time spent with twins. It was emotional & beautiful, especially in the end.81/100

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game free during pride month, and finally got around to it. I don't even like this type of game, but this one had me thoroughly gripped. I went through it in 2 play sessions. I may try replaying later to try a few different choices. I feel this is the peak of thoroughly integrating a transgender story into the main plot, without ever falling on hurtful or reductive stereotypes, cliches or tropes. I found it very clever, how it achieves this. The dialogue felt pretty real to me. I think others that play this game are more of an emotional rather than logical type than I am, based on the decisions that they have made. Kind of ironic, given that this reflects more of Alyson's character than Tyler, and as a trans man, Tyler is meant to represent me. Not that we don't have a lot of other things in common. Very well-written and consistent characters. I think I could cosplay Tyler pretty easily! That would be fun.Thank you very much to everyone who worked hard on this. You have really grown and refined since Life is Strange made a splash.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR OMG, I can't believe I got this game for free!This game was made by DONTNOD, creators of Life is Strange and Life is Strange 2.The only thing I knew coming into this game, is it's by DONTNOD (which means it's probably like Life is Strange) and that it somehow involves Gay/Transgender characters.And the game is indeed very much like Life is Strange 1/2.It has 2 main characters you play with.There are supernatural abilities involved.And it's a Telltale-style "choices matter" game.The main thing in these kinds of games, is you put yourself in the shoes of the main characters, so the characters need to be relatable.So you (the player) may start feeling as the main character, and having choices stemming from there.It's a bit like acting.You need to become the character, understand the character's motivation... And then you start acting in accordance to your made-up motivation.I can understand that some people may feel uncomfortable relating to a transgender, or a gay character, so the game will probably won't be a huge hit.But judging by the graphics, gameplay mechanics, dialogs and plot - this really is a good game.Maybe not as good as the original Life is Strange.But definitely up to the level of Life is Strange 2. If not better.The game is somewhat on the short side - it took me 12.5 hours to finish it.But that means the game doesn't feel unnecessarily drawn out (looking at you LIS dream scene), and you got a lot of ground to cover in the 3 chapters that comprise the game.The graphics are simply amazing. IMO even better than in Life is Strange 1 & 2.And one of my favorite things are the beautiful Alaska nature scenes, where the character just stands and enjoys a beautiful scenery with a beautiful music. Very relaxing.The plot is pretty good as well.I wasn't on the edge of my seat all the time, but I was quite a few times.I've seen some people complain about the dialogue in the game.And although it could be better... It definitely isn't sub-par.Now if you expect some 3D action-adventure, or a platformer - this is definitely not the game for you.It's more of a walking simulator combined with adventure game.You mostly talk to people, and have some minot puzzles here and there.But the puzzles is not the center of the game.The backstory, and the relationship between the main character and other people are the center of the game.So if you like games with elaborate back stories, like calm relaxing games, like beautifully drawn puzzles and environments - this is the game for you.P.S.I got this game through some crazy promotion the developer had in June - simply giving the game away for free.I've seen episodic games give away the first chapter for free, in hopes of getting you hooked, and that you buy the rest of the season...But giving away the entire game for free, is a first for me.In retrospect I would have been happy to pay 10$-20$ for this kind of game.

_childDocuments_.review: Before anything else, I must disclose that I received this game for free during pride month 2021. I can't give an accurate estimation of value for money since I haven't paid any, all I can tell you is that although it is only a 10 hours experience, I will explain why I thoroughly enjoyed the experience.The game starts off a little slow. The setup is that a brother (Tyler) and a sister (Alison) are finally reuniting after years apart because Tyler was spending time in a youth facility. This is following the death of their mother, who Tyler killed in self-defence. It's worth mentioning at this point that Tyler is transgender, which is why it was free during pride month, but I felt that this subject was dealt with beautifully, with adequate attention but not overbearing focus. It's not a game about Tyler being transgender, the game revolves around Tyler and Alison uncovering the truth of their childhood and mother's death, but it's clear that Tyler being transgender is not just something to tick a diversity quota. Instead it felt like the challenges of being transgender, and the effects of it were well explored and well explained. However, this is coming from a cisgender person so don't take my word as gospel, that's just how it came across to me.The bulk of the game does focus on the sibling's investigation of their mother, as they uncover the secrets of the town. I don't wish to spoil the game so I won't, but I found the investigation and answers satisfying. Tell Me Why is an emotional game. The relationships between different characters come under strain as the investigation progresses, and there is a degree on choice with how you deal with each character. By the finale, I found a huge emotional catharsis as the story resolved in a well-thought out way. There are slight issues. I found Tyler's voice whiny, which, even if it's for deliberate purpose to show he's still taking testosterone, was a minor annoyance. Animations can be a bit janky in places and unrealistic, just a slight immersion issue. In a few specific moments the writing falls flat, but not enough for it to be a real problem, again it's just a quick immersion issue. Ultimately, I found the story compelling and emotional, which given that this is a story-centric game, was a pretty fundamental thing to get right. I didn't pay a penny for the game, but I can tell you I'd have been happy to pay about £7-10 for the game, so maybe buy it on sale. The only reason I'm not willing to pay more is because of the length of the game, and I am unlikely to play again since although there is a degree of choice in the story, it is, in my opinion, too limited to be worth a full replay.

_childDocuments_.review: Famously known for their previous games in the Life is Strange franchise among a few other titles, Dontnod Entertainment seems to be keen on moving forward with their third-person interactive adventure formula popularized by Life is Strange and implementing it in new contexts including the story of Tell Me Why, a brand new title conceived and developed by Dontnod that could've been easily adapted into the Life is Strange franchise due to its similarities in story structure, character development and the use of supernatural powers, but they instead opted to spin this off as its own thing which might have worked in this game's detriment when it comes to copies sold. If you have played any of Dontnod's previous games you pretty much know what you're getting yourself into as the format of the game is very similar, even though instead of having 5 episodes per game like we've been accustomed to from Life is Strange 1&2, this game only has 3 episodes of similar length to those features in previous games, each one of them taking around 3 hours to complete, so the entire game can be completed in 9-10 hours.You play as twin siblings Tyler and Alyson Ronan, born as the daughters of Mary-Ann Ronan in the fictional town of Delos Crossing, Alaska, now being reunited after 10 years of extreme social distancing, following the events back when they were kids which resulted in their mother being murdered by Tyler in what was concluded as self-defense. Following that event, Tyler was sent to the juvenile detention center, while Alyson remained in the custody of policeman Eddy Brown who later adopted her, so they both grew apart in different lifestyles which makes the reunion a multi-step process as the twins relearn to trust each other and rediscover their superpower to talk to each other telepathically and experience visions of past events when together, something they thought was only in their imagination as kids, but now all grown-up is proved to be real. As for the murder of their mom, don't worry that is not a spoiler as it's made clear from the very beginning and the story instead focuses on the reasoning behind their mother threatening Tyler which resulted in him killing her in self-defense. Now let's talk a bit about the elephant in the room which reviewers seem to either completely bypass, probably out of fear of saying the wrong thing and being canceled or talking only about that, neglecting the actual game and coming out as complete bigots in the process. Born as twin sisters Alyson and Ollie, it is made clear from their early childhood that Ollie is struggling with gender identity issues and later on, during his time spent at Juvie he enters into a gender reassignment program that completes his transition, becoming the man he always wanted to be. Even though by only playing the first episode it will seem like that is the main point of the story and the whole plot is built around Tyler's gender transition, that is false since as I've mentioned before the direction of the story will drastically change in the second episode. That being said it does make you wonder why so much emphasis was put on that transition in the first episode and some moments feel like they've been forced in order to impose a certain "liberal" narrative, but I will say again that is not the point of this story, but I do intend to make an in-depth video at some point talking about some of those things that I couldn't do here without spoiling the story. (so sub to my YT I guess?)Gameplay will also be very familiar to those who have played Life is Strange as it's mainly focused on dialogue, exploration and puzzles, with the one unique gameplay mechanic being the visions where you get to see silhouettes of yourselves and other characters in past memories and sometimes get the option to choose between whose vision you believe when siblings have conflicting interpretations of a certain event. In terms of exploration even though there aren't as many locations to explore as some of the other games as the entire story takes place in Delos Crossing and you will revisit some locations multiple times throughout the game, you still have the traditional point and click mechanic in which the siblings will commentate on certain items when you click on them, giving you a description, talking about a memory or making a joke. Dialogue is also similarly structured, usually having 3-4 options to pick from when responding, with the optional talking points added in there if you want to find out more about a character or a certain topic.In regards to the puzzles most of them are centered around the Book of Goblins, a compilation of stories written by Mary-Ann in order to entice the imagination of the kids when they were young, but as it turns out a lot of those stories have hidden clues inside them, so you will often have to read through a few pages in order to get to that one small detail you need to progress forward with a puzzle, but the stories are well written and kid-friendly so you could even read some of them to your own kids and see if they too will start an underground goblin base under your house based on them. The complexity of those puzzles is variable, with some of the more difficult ones being found in the final episode, while also being optional, so just getting through the main story will only require you to read a few paragraphs where you can easily find that one thing you're looking for quite quickly and even more some of them have a skip option, such as opting to break the lock of a door instead of solving the puzzle to open it.Even the style of the graphics is very similar to Life is Strange, so if the look of those games appealed to you, this one will too, however as mentioned before you will revisit locations quite often, so there is less variety when it comes to exploration as nearly half of the game will be spent in and around your house as well as the local supermarket. There is also less polish in some areas, especially if you're the type of player looking into every corner, where you might notice some lower resolution textures and backgrounds. Tyler is voiced by August Aiden Black while Erica Lindbeck takes on the role of Alyson and they both do a fantastic job portraying their characters, with the cast of side characters such as Eddy being voiced by Martin Sensmeier and Mary-Ann voiced by Emily O'Brien adding to that. The characters in this game are what make Delos Crossing an immersive and believable location, while also portraying the Alaskan lifestyle with all its advantages and disadvantages.There are collectibles in the form of carved wooden characters from the Book of Goblins and they even have a use in the final chapter if you find them all, but aside from that, the main game is your entire package. Since there are multiple endings, a second playthrough might interest some people, however you can see the other ending by just replaying the final episode and taking specific decisions to lead you to your desired outcome. Tell Me Why is yet another interactive adventure from the brilliant minds at Dontnod Entertainment, so if you like this style of games you will most likely enjoy this one too. There are some questionable decisions when it comes to the game's narrative and some of the dialogue, but that shouldn't overshadow the amazing story behind this game and the trademark Dontnod quality of production. If the transgender part of this game is what keeps you away, number one stop being a bigot and number two, in the end, it doesn't really matter to the story.

_childDocuments_.review: is one of those that prompts mixed feelings. Some are positive, some are negative, and as such, this review is ideally meant to be taken as "Mixed," for reasons stated below:Visuals: 10/10 The graphics and scenery are beautifully-polished, and the art style is gorgeously-rendered, fully-immersing you in the environment of the small town of Delos Crossing, Alaska.Sound and Voice-Acting: 10/10The sound effects and voice-acting are top-notch, with the former faithfully contributing to the feeling of lovable "quirky-campy" that defined Dontnod's previous work, Story: 7/10This category is the primary reason for my mixed feelings. As with   is set in episodic format, with the three different episodes having been released at various times. Yet where the overall plot and highly-intriguing mystery of  kept the experience charged with intrigue and a desire to know more, the story of  can often feel a bit disjointed between the three episodes.The game deserves praise for its careful and compassionate representation of a trans character in a video game, but suffers in this effort by having that representation be limited solely to the first episode. The protagonist's potential relationship with another character similarly comes off as feeling rushed, due to taking place over a single episode.The story as a whole is a little slow to pick up from the beginning, but ironically, this is more of a plus than a minus; the best kind of mystery, after all, is one that  deliver immediate satisfaction. But there are times when the story lacks any real weight or threat of consequence, largely due to the nature of the mystery--it's a quest for answers about the past, rather than a conspiracy taking place in the present. Thus, while the game's premise is plenty engaging, it stumbles somewhat in its delivery: the initial prospect of supernatural forces, for example, is genuinely terrifying, but this is later dispelled by what is best described as an "anti-climax" during the final confrontation. Final Thoughts and Rating: 7/10 had the potential to be a much better game, but the final product that was released still deserves recognition for being a masterpiece of a mystery. The game delivers on all the best and most important points of some of Dontnod's other titles, like : minority representation, an engaging mystery, in-depth characters and development, and a quirky, "something's-not-quite-right" small American town. If  suffers from anything, it's from being too short. What the game gives the player in the first episode leaves one wanting more, but with only three episodes, there's not nearly enough room to give the characters, relationships, or the overall mystery due justice. Had  been made with even just two more episodes, it would have allowed for far more room to expand upon key character arcs and relationships, not to mention improving on the sense of intrigue that begins with the initial mystery.TL;DR: Despite its relatively short length and a somewhat-disappointing ending, it's still a decent mystery game, and one worth getting at an affordable price. While lacking in any real danger toward the characters, there's still plenty of emotional trauma and weight to keep the player invested. If you're looking for a "feel-good" small town mystery, look no further!

_childDocuments_.review: A Heartfelt Journey of Self-Discovery and Acceptance"Tell Me Why" is an exceptional narrative-driven adventure game that stands out for its emotional depth, captivating storytelling, and meaningful representation. Developed by DONTNOD Entertainment, this game is a masterful blend of mystery, drama, and heartfelt moments that left me profoundly moved.From the very beginning, "Tell Me Why" draws you into the lives of the Ronan twins, Alyson and Tyler, as they reunite and delve into their shared past to uncover the truth about their troubled childhood. The game's setting in the picturesque yet haunting town of Delos Crossing adds a layer of immersive beauty that enhances the overall experience.One of the most commendable aspects of this game is its handling of sensitive topics. Tyler's journey as a transgender man is portrayed with such authenticity and respect, making it a significant step forward for representation in the gaming industry. The developers clearly put in the effort to ensure that Tyler's story is told with empathy and accuracy, which is both refreshing and inspiring.The gameplay mechanics, particularly the "Bond" feature, allow players to experience the unique connection between the twins. This mechanic adds depth to the narrative, as players navigate through their shared memories and the emotional weight they carry. The choices you make throughout the game genuinely impact the story's direction, leading to multiple endings that reflect your decisions.Visually, "Tell Me Why" is stunning. The attention to detail in the environments, character designs, and animations is remarkable. The voice acting is top-notch, with Erica Lindbeck and August Aiden Black delivering powerful performances as Alyson and Tyler, respectively. Their chemistry brings the characters to life, making their journey feel incredibly real and relatable.The soundtrack is another highlight, perfectly complementing the game's emotional beats. The music beautifully underscores key moments, enhancing the overall atmosphere and drawing players deeper into the story."Tell Me Why" is more than just a game; it's an emotional journey that explores themes of identity, family, and forgiveness. It challenges players to reflect on their own experiences and perspectives, leaving a lasting impact long after the credits roll. If you're looking for a game that offers a rich narrative, well-crafted characters, and a thought-provoking story, "Tell Me Why" is an absolute must-play.DONTNOD Entertainment has once again proven their prowess in creating compelling, character-driven experiences, and "Tell Me Why" is a shining example of their talent. This game is a triumph in every sense, and I highly recommend it to anyone who appreciates storytelling at its finest.

_childDocuments_.review: This is more of a visual novel than an interactive game, but what it does it does  well.It tells the story of two siblings reunited after a whole lot of years, trying to sort out some things before selling off their family home. As with all of Dontnod's games there is a supernatural element in this, too. They can share thoughts and can see memories play out before them and even discuss them since both see it.Visually I think it uses the same engine even Life Is Strange 1 used, but the texture quality is great so it doesn't look too dated. Sound design is amazing, with nice songs in the background and phenomenal voicework on the main characters in particular.As for the story or the core gameplay... ouff. This is where the game just falls apart. Sadly I have to revise my originally-positive review. While the game sets itself up great and the chemistry between the two leads is enjoyable, the  underuse of the main feature coupled with very flat and mostly automated puzzles just makes for a rather shallow game. By the end I was glad it was over as it was just ... boring, really. The thing is, if they had simply allowed the memory feature to be used ~always, akin to the rewind in LiS1, I think it could have been truly great.The way it is, it's worth it on a deep sale, but nothing else.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished Episode 1, but I won't get the 2nd and 3rd and can't recommend to buy this game upfront. Try it first since Episode 1 is available for free.I find it hard to believe it is the same studio that did Life is strange because except for the visuals, this game is inferior on all aspects. Sure the game is nice looking and got me in the beginning with nice views from Alaska, but once I was out of the ferry boat, the charm was lost.It's not a bad story, but it has an enormous problem in the pacing and writing: I like slow games, but this type of slow is uncanny and no one is having conversations with 3-5 seconds pauses between each line of dialogue. And a big chunk of the dialogues are platitudes which are not even helping the story progression.To make it worse, the controls are really clunky and are slowing down the pacing further. For instance you cannot run, but the game will decide for you when the character will run. There are a lot of interactive objects in the world, but reaching them is sometimes not easy because the camera controls are imprecise, and when there is a cluster of objects you will have to zoom in first on the cluster, and then select each object individually, leave the object zoom, and then leave the focused view: this is not a good user experience with all those hops and clicks. And, well, you guessed it at this point, every view transition is painfully slow.There are irritating issues such as the characters talking at the wrong moment, or starting to talk about an object even before you had a chance to read the description. For no reason there is a time limit on some answers before the game chose for you, and this answers can pop-up while you are examining an object. The kind of things that wouldn't pass even shallow quality assurance testing.In the end a gaming experience that was dragged along 3 hours could have easily been done in 1 if this was just running at a normal pace. And for the most part it wasn't even satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: I just can't honestly, and with a straight face say that this game is good or recommend it for others. I have played DontNod's Life is Strange and I found the story (while slow initially) captivating within the first episode. The story, combined with the time travel mechanic kept me WANTING to play, guessing at what would happen next, and find new ways to explore interactions with NPCs with rewinding time. Luckily, I skipped paying money for LiS 2 as I watched a friend stream an episode and found it missed all of the magic that made the original game compelling.Here we are again.1. The main character so far is just kind of insufferable in some of the dialogue, and its to the point where I as a rational adult don't really have a choice in some dialogue options to not speak to people like a ♥♥♥♥ when playing as him. And just as a side note the dialogue is not as interactive as LiS. In general the game is just very linear. So linear, that the end of chapter 1 has the same "choice" presented as two different outcomes/choices.2. There seems to be this whole "goblin" thing going with these 2 characters you play as. However, I feel that much like LiS 2 - this is just something the writers of the game's story think (emphasis on think) is some creative narrative style because much like the "two wolves" from LiS 2 - this "goblin" nonsense is just that. It doesn't seem like it will go anywhere meaningful for the player.3. The plot hook before the end of the first chapter is just totally illogical. The entire premise is that two siblings who watched their mother chase one (the future transgender) to a dock and point a gun at them while shouting "I'm going to kill you" are now confused about if they should have killed her because they found a book about raising your transgender child. For some reason, instead of just reaching the conclusion like a sane person that she just dismissed the book's content as rubbish, or THAT SHE JUST HAD MENTAL ISSUES - the presence of this book in her room causes them to question the event. Completely contrived garbage.4. The night their mother died is the most ridiculous portrayal of a police investigation I've seen in a "serious" game in a long time. Spoiler alert, the sister kill the mom by stabbing her in the back. She hears the mother screaming while drinking melted ice cream in the kitchen, and comes to save her sibling. Somehow, when the two kids tell the police that only the one sibling being attacked was involved and killed the mom in self defense, they didn't have any questions about why she was stabbed in the back. Or, who was drinking this ice cream spilled all over the floor in the kitchen? Who investigated this? Barney Fife?5. Last but not least, the game is just seemingly heading for a cliff where the ending is just that the mom had mental issues. I'm assuming this before I have even reached chapter 3 because every character in the game never talks about it as a possibility even once so far. If that really is the ending/explanation then this game is even worse than I think now, and I might come back to edit this to expand on it.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:  Conditionally recommend this well-told but very brief gameAfter playing Life is Strange and having some mixed feelings, I figured I would give the studio another chance and take a shot at Tell Me Why. It went okay, I guess.The story concerns twin girls, one of whom is questioning their gender identity, and the events that follow the death of their troubled mother at the hands of one of the twins. It picks up years later as that twin--now going by the name of Tyler and in the midst of gender transition--is about to be released from a school for troubled youth and reunite with his sister Alyson in their remote Alaskan town, to finally clean up their mother's estate, and to get some answers.In terms of controls, Tell Me Why is very simple, with standard WASD movement and left/right clicks for interaction. There are also certain moments where the edge of the screen distorts and the player can summon memories by holding the space bar and mouse buttons, to revisit what happened in a live-action holographic-style of memory. Most of the major decisions involve dialogue choices for specific pivot points in the story, along with some light puzzle-solving, which is fine; like most of these styles of games, the focus is on the story, not the complexity of the game play. Player control alternates between Tyler and Alyson in different scenes. Certain decisions will either bring the twins closer together or separate them a bit, which affects the resolution of the story. As one might expect, the choices that are empathetic to the position of the other twin (ie, when you're in Alyson's shoes and agreeing with Tyler's position or version of events, and vice versa) tend to bring them closer together.The story is rife with the implications of a a transitioning individual in a small rural town. I was expecting it to play out with every bumpkin forsaking and shunning Tyler but reactions of most characters varied from understanding, to awkward, stumbling acceptance, to well-meaning but damaging intervention. Overall, that part of the story line is handled pretty well and ultimately fades in significance in the greater scheme of things. In fact, the game handles the alienation and loss of parenting and other hard-to-discuss subjects very fairly. The real conflict is between the twins and their different approaches not only to what happened but what is going to happen from here. I get that these are supposed to be powerful, emotional moments, but I didn't really feel hooked in by the drama. I think part of the problem is--as was the case with Life is Strange--the dialogue here just didn't click with me. It very much felt like someone trying to capture the colloquialisms and subtleties of casual American English and just wasn't quite getting it right. Aside from trying to sound too hip and cool, there were little things like referring to the upstairs of a two-story building as the "first floor." Very European, not American. This kind of fidelity is so much more important in this type of game than other genres and in general, it left me wanting.On that note, I will say the tonal intonation and voice acting in emotional scenes was generally decent and the graphics and animations in Tell Me Why are quite good. It's a pretty game and looks nice. I also found it stable and it played the whole time without crashes. I did find one incident of clipping that repeated each time I ran through the scene and one puzzle that was counter-intuitive with bad directions but those were exceptions.Like most of the these types of games, Tell Me Why is relatively short. I finished the first game in less than twelve hours and that is with quite a bit of time spent on pause. There is a little replay value, in that you can take an opposite tack with those "unite-us-or-divide-us" moments between the twins, which leads to different dialogue/scenes but realistically, most of key plot points will come through the first time through. The story's climax was pretty tame, given everything that had happened to that point.Steam achievements are pretty easy but will require at least two partial playthroughs to get them all. The game is so short, though, it's not an awful effort to run it twice and fortunately, you can skip scenes (my second run was only six hours, or half the time of the first). It's a pretty easy game to use to buff up your achievement profile rate, if that matters to you (I like achievements, so it did to me but I know not everyone cares).As of the time of this review posting, the first chapter is free and the other two are $20 each, which is a lot, considering the game's short nature and limited replay value. Check out the first chapter but I would sure wait for a sale for anything past that.I conditionally recommend the game to players who love these types of narrative adventures but personally, this one was kind of a miss. Tell Me Why isn't a bad game but I don't find myself enjoying these graphic adventures from DontNod as much as I did the ones from, say, Telltale Games. Just not striking the right chords and I don't feel as engaged. I don't regret playing it but I think I'll skip narrative games from this studio from now on.Pros- Pretty graphics/rendering- Story handled difficult themes and subject matter wellCons- Like most narrative adventures, it's very, very short- Dialogue felt stilted and unnaturalFinal Score: 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: TMW comes with appreciable, mature, deep contents; unusual topics are faced with very delicate and thoughtful approach. In the first two episodes, the contemplative and serious approach plunges you into a pleasant atmosphere of nostalgia and sadness that you can hardly find in other video games. Btw it is not clear if this emotional transport is caused by the long cinematic sequences that make the experience similar to watching a TV series or if in some way the moments of gameplay contribute to reinforce these sensations. For sure the multiple choice dialogues are divinely written and help put you in the mood. Unfortunately the story is not up to par, full of impausibility and with a disappointing ending. Weird puzzles are completely out of place, just like fingernails on blackboard, one of the worst cases of ludo-narrative dissonance; especially in the third episode, they introduce a lot of forcing, inconsistencies and implausibilities in the plot and in the psychology and behavior of characters. Alyson is a very interesting character, actress Erica Lindbeck did really a good job, other characters look flat in comparison.TMW represents the attempt to rise above the cultural limits where video games have been relegated for a long time, an attempt, however, half-failed because someone decided to insert puzzles, challenges and fairy tales at any cost. An average title but still pleasant, better than LIS2.Complete review here:

_childDocuments_.review: I've made several attempts to start the game, exploring the cabin briefly, but haven't fully immersed myself in the core plot and narrative. While I found it enjoyable, it wasn't until episode 2 that I became truly engaged. The central mystery focusing on the "why" behind the incident, rather than the "who" as in a typical murder mystery, eventually captivated me, though it took some time to get invested. Despite playing Life is Strange, I never really connected with TMW, and to be honest, I haven't particularly enjoyed either game.I'd describe it as more emotionally intense and melancholic than Life is Strange. The narrative primarily deals with confronting past experiences, whereas LiS feels more like an adventure to me.In my opinion, the in-game choices in TMW were less impactful than those in LiS. There seemed to be fewer significant decisions to make, and the consequences felt less substantial. However, I believe the strength of the story compensated for this weakness.A portion of the ending was poorly executed, particularly the revelation of the supposed good character actually being the antagonist.

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed feelings on this one, which is why I just went with not recommended.Full disclosure: I got this game in June when it was free for the month.The game is *fine*, but nothing great or very memorable.Tyler isn't very likable, and is almost always a grouch to everyone (including his sister).  I can understand why he feels that way, but also, he's an adult and needs to stop being an emo baby to everyone.Even with only 3 chapters, I felt like the story dragged on, and at the same time, didn't move at all.  The story is about the twins selling the house they grew up in after 10 years of being apart, as well as finding out the events leading up to their mother's death.  And thats it.  There is barely anything more than that.  So be prepared for lots of drama between the siblings about themselves, their mother, and the town they're in.The graphics/scenery in this game are VERY nice though.  Lots of nice scenic shots if you like taking screenshots of games you're playing.  There were a LOT of nice artwork or models of figurines you run into in game that are just part of the environment and don't serve a purpose (you can't even "Look" at them).  Major props to all the animators that made those, I always took my time exploring and looking through each place to look at all those details before doing what I was supposed to do.

_childDocuments_.review: To start off: this game is not for everyone. Be warned, the game tackles heavy topics, like child abuse, suicidal thoughts, transitioning, etc. If you are open to such topics, this might be a great game for you.Gameplaywise expect something similar to Dontnod's other franchise, Life is Strange, only with more mature teams. The conversations go deeper, and sometimes you'll have to use real life people skills to get the information you want or to solve puzzles.It's hard to talk about the story without spoiling anything. You play as a pair of twins trying to heal their emotional trauma, by uncovering the past through finding clues in your old house, talking to people who knew your family as you grew up, and by reading fairy tales you wrote together with your mother. The journey is full of emotions, both good and bad. The characters are all lovable, many of them grow past their own flaws, even the ones you'd never expect to be anything else but antagonists. Most of the story could be true, these people are living beings in a world, where everything, even your memories are uncertain.Finally, I have to add two things. First: as a psychologist, I respect the approach the game took to discuss mental health issues. This is the best mental health game since Senua. Second: this game is a piece of art. I will revisit it in the near future. I already invited a couple of friends to try it out with me.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the DONTNOD games, and this one is no exception.  Graphics/emotional expressions continue to get better, and hopefully all the stiffness and clunkiness will be gone someday, letting the characters shine completely.This game felt a bit light compared to previous ones, and not just because it was only three episodes.  I get that it was personal emotional family discovery, but everything just felt a bit less developed.  Heck the "finale" of Episode 2 just had me shrug my shoulders instead of blowing me away or leaving me on the edge of my seat.The one area that excelled was the goblin story stuff, that was very thoroughly developed, and even had some surprising The Room-like puzzles.(and a bit of Edith Finch)  I do wish the game would warn you that you were about to "complete" an area when there were other interactable items you never got to but inadvertently triggered the next scene that locked those things out.  That said, getting the game for free was an unexpected surprise, and I look forward to DONTNOD's next game!

You WILL feel the full spectrum of emotions while playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Tell Me Why is an episodic choices matter mystery game. It's notable for featuring two protagonists that are both equally well-rounded. Generally a game with multiple protagonists suffers from having one not match the quality of the other but I find both interesting and likable. The structure fits DONTNOD's structure: young adults with supernatural abilities investigate a mystery in the northwest United States. Our protagonists feel genuinely youthful and I didn't notice any misplaced slang.The writing all throughout is to be praised. Everything from character dialogue to written children's storybook entries, to boring government documents are written authentically.While the game touches on themes and struggles relating to LGBTQ people, Tlingit people, rural Alaskans, and other groups not often the main characters in video games, I never felt that I was being pandered to or that any of those segments were out of place. I should mention that this game is often free in June as a promotion so if you're at all on the fence, that's your time to check out a great work for no cost.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game is very good, but it's not without it's problems. A less binary rating system and I maybe give it a 7 as a game experience overall, but a 4 for this genre of game. Starting with some of the problems - For a genre that is often criticised for being hands off or just a cut scene with quick time events, Tell Me Why is definitely on the slower side. There really are some extended periods without much input, which for me isn't so much a problem if the game offers big pay offs (usually earth shattering decisions that effect that story), or the gameplay/puzzles are engaging when you do get them. Unfortunately in my opinion Tell Me Why doesn't really deliver on either of these things. Having said that I enjoyed the story more or less (despite some 'reveals' being predictable) but I don't believe the decision making or the effects of the decisions are either crucial or interesting. It works simply as a "discover the dark past" story, without my inputs. The memory super power offers some interesting concepts around the fallibility of memory and the nature of how that effects reality which is a great theme, but overall as a game-play device, the memory power doesn't reveal any depth, it just reveals more story. There are some other quirks that make Tell Me Why feel a little underdone. The characters instantly react to letters when opened before we have a time to digest them, some of the animations are a bit clunky, but no big issues there. Now onto the great things about the game! The graphics are amazing and allow one of the stars to really shine, the setting. Each scene is backed by stunning mountains and a sprinkling of snow. The whole environment just feels real (something DontNod really excel at) and lived in. Each scene is shot so well and the use of music, while maybe not as well done as Life Is Strange, still brings it way into the usual twee territory, which I am good with. I really enjoyed the lore introduced (Unlike some other reviewers here) and how it was unified within the game. For me it helped bring the story together and help bind the mystery element of the plot. Some of the objectives of the puzzles aren't entirely clear initially but it added overall. I liked the story, it dealt with some heavy heavy themes which is not easy as well as some really interesting ones, like the nature of reality when pieced together from memories. The mystery really accelerates through Chapter 3 and it definitely pulled me along towards the conclusion.So in the end, it's a hard call for me. A good experience but nowhere near as good as Life Is Strange or it's sequels. Definitely not as good as the Quantic Dream games. But if you are a fan of the genre and have already done all the others, I'm sure it won't disappoint...too much.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm feeling conflicted. I didn't enjoy this game much, but I think it was pretty well made. Tell Me Why has the look and feel of a Dontnod game and it is similiar in many ways to the Life is Strange series, but it is chock full of exposition and characters with so much emotional baggage it gets very tiring to sort it all out one scene after another. Just after finishing one awkward conversation, there's another one, then a sad memory, then another one... Despite trudging through all these conversations and cut scenes I didn't feel like I was really getting to know the main characters or having a real impact on how the game played out. At worst it was boring and unrewarding at the same time.I wish I could "maybe" recommend the game. I'm giving it a thumbs up because the concept is interesting and I liked the detailed game environment and the realistic feel of the fictional rural town and its community. There were a couple of glitches in the cut scenes, but nothing major. Apparently some people think this game is "too political" because it tells the story of a transgender man. These arguments are nothing but thinly-veiled bigotry coming from gatekeepers who want the entire game industry to cater solely to their needs. I could go through my entire Steam library and point out hundreds of games, claiming that they're promoting a raging heterosexual cis agenda, but it would be very silly. The world is big enough for all kinds of games, this one just happens to have a visible LGBTQ+ theme.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I wanted to love "Tell Me Why," I can't ignore the glaring flaws in its storytelling that ultimately overshadow its visually appealing graphics. The game's stunning aesthetics draw you in from the start, but sadly, the narrative fails to deliver on the same level.The plot feels contrived and lacks the emotional depth I was hoping for. The characters' motivations and actions often come across as forced, leaving me detached from their struggles. The attempt to explore complex themes falls short, and instead of engaging with genuine emotional weight, the narrative feels like a checklist of clichés.Moreover, the pacing is inconsistent, with some scenes dragging on unnecessarily while others rush through potentially impactful moments. It's as if the writers couldn't decide on the tone they wanted, resulting in a disjointed and unsatisfying experience.The dialogue, despite attempts to tackle serious issues, often comes off as forced and unnatural. The characters' interactions feel scripted, preventing any meaningful connection with the player. The lack of depth in character development makes it difficult to empathize with their struggles, and the dialogue choices, which should enhance the experience, often feel inconsequential.Despite these narrative shortcomings, I can't deny the game's visual excellence. The attention to detail in the environments, character models, and animations is commendable. The graphics create a visually immersive world that is unfortunately let down by a lackluster narrative.In the end, "Tell Me Why" is a prime example of a game where style triumphs over substance. While the graphics showcase the potential for a memorable gaming experience, the weak storytelling diminishes the overall impact. It's disheartening to see such a visually stunning game fall short in delivering a compelling and engaging narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: Tell Me Why

_childDocuments_.review: For every person in a group of people that is vulnerable and ostracized, it is extremely important to feel supported and connected to survive. There was no game in the past that would offer a truly relatable character to transgender people while also allowing others to see the world through their eyes and authentic experiences. Tell Me Why completely changes the status quo, marking another step in the evolution of Dontnod and attempting to make the world a better place, potentially saving lives.Packaged in a thrilling narrative-driven adventure that is down-to-earth despite its supernatural elements, the game may easily become the best work of Dontnod no matter the angle, and possibly one of the best games of all time at its conclusion.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first episode. While I still enjoyed them I always found LiS and LiS2 a bit too cheesy for my tastes, with some of the sensitive topics handled awkwardly at best, so I tried to not get too excited about this game. But I had a blast playing through the first chapter of this story! I like the characters and their dynamics, everything looks gorgeous, the puzzles and secrets are fun to figure out and I LOVE The Book of Goblins. Also, as someone who's transmasculine and comes from an abusive/neglectful upbringing, it's cathartic and soothing to be able to see some of my feelings and experiences portrayed in a piece of media that really hits home. I feel seen. That probably makes me biased, but I don't care. The joy of feeling represented in a way I've never been before in a video game makes this a 10/10 for me.I'm also so pleased that DONTNOD decided to include resources and content warnings etc. on their website, something I wish more companies would do for their games. Knowing what to expect removes an entire extra level of anxiety I'd normally have when getting into a story like this and I'm very grateful for that!

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of Telltale games, this is the game for you. The story itself is great! Fun, emotional and almost plays out a little like a murder mystery, where everything isn't quite what it seems. Not only that but the game itself is hugely LGBTQ+ with a Transgender character being one of the main protagonists, which is amazing and sorely needed in more games! The game covers a range of sensitive, yet important topics and issues that exist in today's society and portrays them in a beautiful yet accurate way. I'd highly recommend this if you're looking for a deep and emotional story to lose yourself in, the game itself also has high replay value to see all the stuff you might have missed the first time, and with the games handy chapter system you don't even have to play the whole game again if that's more your style.

_childDocuments_.review: Dontnod does it again. This game is beautiful and ugly all at once; the characters and their lives are life-like and relatable beneath the unique circumstances with which the twins struggle against, past and present. Real world topics are handled with respect, founded on research, facts, and the heart to traverse them humanely. If you're worried that Tyler's transition is poorly portrayed here, I cannot speak on behalf of trans men, but it's presented in a complex and thought-provoking light, much like I would assume it would be in real life; it isn't wholly the motive of the story, but it still plays an important part. The game was narratively engaging and astounding; it left me speechless several times and made me cry every chapter.Give this game a shot. It's amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, now that I've finished chapter 3 and wrapped up the game, I think it's fair to give this a review. This game is in some ways a bit of a letdown... it's dialogue and characters and world are VERY well realized (graphically they've come a long way since LiS, and the dialogue is INFINITELY better - it feels like they really took time to research and make a game that's respectful, characters talk like humans for the most part), HOWEVER, it's just a bit too rinse and repeat with its sets across 3 episodes and the whole thing feels like much more of a mini-series when I think it would've been incredible with some openness or variety to it.Delos Crossing is meant to be small, so a small open map with more locations that opened up more across 3 chapters would've been nice (this would've been helpful seeing as the game has missable collectables, and I can't really be bothered doing another run for them)It's story, while strong in its meaning, also kind of makes me feel "eh whatever" by the end because the whole story felt like such a montage. Perhaps more time (ignore my playtime), events and activities with the twins would've given me a deeper connection to the characters?Is it worth playing though? Yeah, if you're into walk around and click on things games (I am) then you should eventually play this. Perhaps on sale though.

_childDocuments_.review: A Magical Tapestry UnveiledReview: 4/5⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆"Embark on a mesmerizing journey into the world of 'Tell Me Why,' where an enthralling narrative collides with the mystical allure of the unknown and the mischievous charm of Crafty Goblins. The storytelling is truly captivating, seamlessly weaving drama, mystery, and a hint of the supernatural, all while embracing the whimsical antics of these magical tricksters.The characters, especially the engaging duo of Tyler and Alyson, feel like they've stepped out of a fantastical world, sprinkled with the mischievous charm of the Crafty Goblins. The choices you make play a magical role in shaping the storyline, allowing you to delve deeper into the enchanting tapestry of their lives and the secrets of the crafty siblings.Visually, the game is a feast for the eyes, with meticulously crafted environments that add an extra layer of allure, seamlessly integrating the Crafty Goblins' playful touch. The attention to detail and expressive character animations enhance the overall mystique of the experience.In terms of gameplay, there's a minor quirk in the controls, a fleeting moment where the enchantment stumbles. However, it's a small hiccup that doesn't diminish the overall allure of the narrative and the crafty charm of the goblins.In conclusion, 'Tell Me Why' offers a mystic journey that earns a solid 4 out of 5. It's a must-play for those who seek a narrative rich in emotion, mystery, and the mischievous magic of Crafty Goblins, even with a minor control quirk. The magical essence of the story, combined with the crafty antics, lingers, making the journey truly enchanting.

_childDocuments_.review: To start, I loved LiS1 and couldn't stand LiS2. This game for me falls inbetween, but with more positives than negatives, and I did enjoy playing through it. I will do some comparing to those two past games to try to create a spoilerfree review. The two main characters felt mostly well fleshed out and likable. I thought there was a good balance between giving them humanizing flaws and making them sympathetic enough for me to still care about them. The minor characters also felt better developed than in LiS2, more like people and less like caricatures. The main story was less compelling for me than the one in LiS1, but I did enjoy it and cared about learning the answers to the mystery of what exactly had happened in the past. I definitely liked it a lot more than the LiS2 main story. That said, I felt there was at least one plothole and some of the content felt too much like filler, put in there to pad the game out and make it longer without really adding to either main story or character development. I have only played through the game once, the ending I got was certainly one I felt content with, but as I haven't seen other variants yet it's hard to tell how much choices matter. I kind of want to replay it, but the lack of an option to skip dialogue makes me put that off. Scenery was lovely, and I especially enjoyed the designs around the twins' old house, and the art created by their late mother. There were also some clever ties between that art and the events of the game that I liked.

Without spoiling anything, this game has a great story that doesn't go too far into the supernatural, but just far enough to emphasize the bond of siblings. It's characters are complex and believable, and so are the actions they make. Sure, it gets a little predictable towards the end, but that didn't bother me one bit. As with most great games, it's about the journey, and this game was well worth the time I put into it.

_childDocuments_.review: For me, Life Is Strange had a great hook and offered a memorable, cheesy setup, but turned out to be a huge letdown and severely lacked maturity. Before The Storm was mostly a bad experience for me, with too much teenage edge and  convoluted, confused writing, as well as a multitude of convenient coincidences and very limited choices.Tell Me Why, on the other hand, starts very slow, with characters that are not very distinct or charming, but as the story unrolls, it benefits greatly, ending in a very convincing pay off, especially since it isn't limited to a single choice at the end of the game - instead, the game gathers points throughout the entirety of the game, offering the conclusion that's a more "natural" result of many choices. So while I believe it will be much more difficult, for many people, to become attached to the main characters and their problems, the game gains more than it sacrifices.The one thing that hurt me deeply was tied to the controls. Tell Me Why assumes you're willing to take in everything it has to offer, and you're eager to engage in experiencing some tv-like footage without having an option to skip any of the boring bits. The game forces you to slowly observe its many cutscenes and listen to most lines of dialogue in their entirety. Let's say, you want your character to send someone a picture made with their phone. You need to see this character reach a specific spot, take out their phone, hold it in front of themselves, make a photo, send it through a messenger, hide the phone. Then you walk out of the room and the character gets an answer - they take out their phone, read, smile, and only then you see the actual response - an emoji. Similarly, you keep looking at people opening doors, slowly, walking from one side of the yard to another, and so on, and so on. I just wish it work more like in the older adventure games, where you could click through lines of dialogue, or double tap an icon to quickly reach a new spot, or skip idle animations of opening containers and so on. Sure, it's not so meditative, and I would maybe lose something from rushing through bits of the game that want to make you appreciate the virtual landscapes and eagles, but I would gladly take that transaction.

_childDocuments_.review: When I was immersed and ensconced in the world of , I noticed the soundtrack was emphasizing the desire for introspective aloneness and letting go of everything when it evoked a resonant situation. However, it's inevitable not to correlate indie-folk music to , together with its narrative and the way that it's told. It's a soundscape that confines assorted tensions: energetic, meditative and soulful. It's a reticent, personal and introverted soundtrack; nonetheless, the best way to express it is through emotions encoded in musical notes. Likewise, it's a shame that there are only a few tunes in the game.Here's a short story: Once upon a time, in a land wreathed in perpetual blizzards, there were twins who had separated. Alyson Ronan realized the day was coming, so her soul was bursting for thrills and she was finding a gift for her twin Tyler Ronan, while on the other side he's saying goodbye to the cherished remembrances at Fireweed. The sunlight engulfed the twins' faces with their feathers, but with a gap among them, a hello and a cuddle were fitting to meeting once again after so many years. Upon their return to Delos Crossing, they were hoping to move on with their lives, so they planned to sell their property. When they were tidying up, they stumbled across the princess's room, which zealously sealed her riddled secrets. The crafty goblins had a new mission. With their shrewdness and perseverance, they follow the crumbs to find the castle of truth that Mary-Ann had buried underfoot in the forest.The world of this game encompasses the winter setting of Alaska and the culture of the Tlingit. The story takes place in a quaint town, where the majority of the locals live closely with their traditions. The perspective of the world seems wintery charming, a palette of euphoric colours thrives with intense lighting to ensure better contrast. The images of the places are clear, and it almost imparts an aura of film-like tone to both the scenes and the expressions of the characters. Delos Crossing may seem cold where modernity is integrated with local culture. On the other hand, if the world is real, the plot portrays an averse narrative, describing its neighbours as allegories within a fairy tale.The story is presented as an allegory: a fairy tale book as a door between both worlds. The protagonists are the twins, who are unearthing the truth about Mary-Ann to soothe their wounds. They delve into the past of all involved personal affairs. However, this isn't the main theme. When the game is featured in the credits, it draws attention to the themes that its characters will cope with. The topic starts with transsexuality and ends with suicide. This last theme is disbelief, an ambiguous and superfluous narrative twist, as if it were inserted at random without conveying proper insight. Even though Tyler isn't the protagonist, a dramatic argument would have been thought-provoking one in which the character, being a renegade, struggle against the prejudices of a local community. It's a shame that the world is only convivial to open minds —with a bestseller type of youthful mindset and vibe. The story's structure, in fact, resembles that of a brief story. It's arranged into episodes, in which the scenes also flip between past and present. The past scenes adapt to the composition of a film. It uncovers was true as a recompense for gaining insight into the story. Given that Alyson and Tyler are the protagonists, the script with a youthful tone conveys this essential connection between twins by which one completes the other's sentence. It's not the best script, but it evokes this idea of the interlocutor that one twin always completes the other's sentences.The world and context of the game are created by the presence of Alaskan culture. There's an allusion to culture in each scene. So the narrative thrives on the Tlingit worldview. In this way, the gameplay constitutes an immersive interaction of the world like an interactive film. The story features two protagonists, the plot will mean playing a combination with both. Interaction with the world, since it brings together elements of a walking simulator and point-and-click, is constrained as the context implies. The player interacts with things to understand someone's personality wherever they are. But there are other things are part of puzzles or keys that let the player get ahead in the story. In this way, the plot comes with a stronger substance, where the interaction of events doesn't disrupt the narrative sequence.The plot sets up a gameplay that is suitable to the intention of the protagonists, since they haven't visited each other for a very long time, thus does the emotional and magical bond still exist in them? The game’s intention indicates the resiliency or weakness of the twins' bond is, which the decision of gameplay for the player is. The player can adopt a stance in conversation or in certain situations, which will result in a connection or distancing between them. Nevertheless, there's one gameplay that I really admired, although it wasn't developed appropriately. It consists of talking to the twin telepathically. It also has its own lines of conversation, although it has not much bearing on the choices taken for the plot. Furthermore, it'd have been a good idea for the player to depend on that skill on certain situations to investigate something it doesn't recognise and require for guidance —or else, cooperative work and not just completing each other's sentences.Decisions presuppose different outcomes. When characters conjure up remembrances as visions, the player can decide what interpretation of the twins is worthy a consideration. In some instances, there are overlooked elements that provide for more detailed visualisation. When interacting with things, the bad thing isn't knowing when it triggers a scene and therefore also closing the place where it's not possible to go back. Aside from that, there's also an activity of collecting visions or solving puzzles. They aren't difficult to interpret or solve, above all the answers are in the setting or in the storybook. The gameplay features are mere accessories. I assume it's to forestall cutting off the narrative sequence.The game does have a slight narrative, but its dramatic presentation is charming and effortless. Although the performances are decorous, due to the plot they don't manage to convey the emotional reverberation as the plot presupposes. When one of them is disgusted, or goes through a traumatic time, the acting responds to the situation. But for an unfathomable reason the emotional outburst is tempered or interrupted, perhaps, by the cosy plot. It's either the plot or the argument. This game exposes an inconspicuous juxtaposition between the development of a plot, the many undeveloped proposed themes, and the diminution in dramatic tension.This game is obtainable with a bundle. Only the first one is free to download. The entire game was free at one point, I'm not sure if it'll be free again. If you're a fan of Life is Strange or related games, this may be an option. In addition, it has a fairly impressive artistic and cinematographic care, but the plot, in short, you better enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: [POSSIBLE SPOILERS AHEAD, nothing very specific though] I really liked this game. The ammount of little details put into it is phenomenal, the characters are very endearing for the most part and even the most secondary ones aren't completely flat and without any story. _childDocuments_.review: Many will pick and drop this game, thinking it is about transitioning, but it is not. It is about people .. but most importantly, mothers. It is about your relationship with your mother and the concept of a mother's love. You may believe you understand what I mean when I say that, but you do not.The characters in this game are all well thought out and written. They have so many details that you can't help but form an opinion about them. You will find yourself loving them at times and then not as the events change. Just like in real life, we are all living our own little stories in our corner of the world, and so were this lady and her twins. If you could look past the idea of transitioning, you will find a story that will sometimes move you to tears. At the end of the day, we are all human, and we are all united in our yearning for our mother's unconditional love.

_childDocuments_.review: As some have mentioned, the game is more of an interactive movie than it is a game. If you do not like games similar to Life is Strange or Star Trek Resurgence, you will not probably like this, but if you like those games then you will enjoy this. It has an excellent mystery story with very fleshed out characters. As Tyler and Alyson you navigate the town of Delos Crossing. The dialogue choices give you two main options throughout the game. One is you can be confrontational and honestly a jerk or two you can be fairly pleasant and forgiving and both effect the outcome. It is not a long game but is comparable to other games in this genre. Overall this was a very good title, with good acting, decent graphics, and is well worth the time it takes to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved it. I found the story very emotional, although slow-paced. And that was actually a good thing - I played in several sittings throughout a few weeks and it still resonated with me, and the pauses between each time I played the time kind of helped me digest the story. Childhood trauma, guilt bottled up for years and the feeling of hopelessness being stuck in a really small isolated town and far away from any idea of what a family is. The setting (Alaska, winter, house in the woods, Fireweed) made it so nostalgic and somehow relatable.

_childDocuments_.review: I had really high hopes for this game. I loved Life is Strange, Life is Strange: Before the Storm, and though i had some rough patches, I liked Life is Strange 2. I was really hoping to continue the pattern. However, Tell Me Why is simply pandering. They throw in a trans character whose only personality trait is correcting people on his identity. His sister's only personality trait? You guessed it, correcting people on her brother's identity. Half the game is confronting "bigots". The other half of the game is uncovering the mystery of what exactly happened on the night of the death of their mother. There were many incorporated story elements, which was really nice. To be honest, the puzzles were the only thing that kept me playing the game. But the truth of the mystery is plain as day, and anyone can guess the truth after discovering the first clue. This wasn't me being "super smart" or anything, the mystery was just that easy. That made the ending incredibly disappointing, as I had been hoping for a surprise twist to make the whole game worth the time I put into it. I was wrong.To sum up, don't buy it. Most parts will leave you feeling angry or offended, and the rest is just boring. I had such high hopes for a game coming from DONTNOD.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible. If you are a long time fan of Life is Strange, or similar games, this is definitely for you. It is about acceptance and standing up for yourself. It shows how the memories we hold are swayed by our environments and how we grew up. It teaches about how these flaws in our memories can change how we perceive those around us. I recommend playing to completion by doing everything you can to strengthen the bond between siblings, and then again to try and break that bond and see how the memories and game play change. Can not recommend this enough!

_childDocuments_.review: Life is Strange 1 will always hold a very special place in my heart but this is actually the most well made DONTNOD game in my opinion. The dialogue is incredibly charming, the interpersonal relationships between characters are surprisingly multifaceted, and the story is very tightly knit. Also, the trans representation is fantastic. As a trans woman, I'd say it's possibly some of the best trans rep out there. You can really tell that some actual trans people had a role in shaping this game. I cared so much about the cast of characters and their relationships with each other. Its main themes came across very successfully, too. I did not expect to love this game as much as I do, but it's genuinely a favorite of mine. Very excited to see what DONTNOD brings to the table next.
