_childDocuments_.review: In short, I loved Hobs Barrow. I think the story was succinct, intersting, well-acted, well-animated, and I enjoyed the nooks and crannies of the endeavor.I'm writing this as a two-part review. There is a TL;DR below for each game, but I played them back to back and you might want to review each if you are truly in a comparative strategy.TL;DR - Hobs Barrow > Call of the Sea. It all comes down to voice activity and narrative expectations. Hobs BarrowAn expertly told occult-oriented story where the narrative beats are present and appreciated, as well as the voice acting is on-par and nails the tone of each character.The lingering, long-moments after the story are properly felt and each moment is earned with a sufficient build-up.Call of The SeaNOTE: I DID NOT FINISH THIS GAME.I wish I did, but the VA for the game was distracting and it pulled me out of the game enough that I didn't care to see how it ended.The narrative beats were interesting, the stories and puzzles intriguing, but the guiding, driving narrative was flat out bad.Comparative between both:Hobs Barrow: Arrive in a podunk town, based on the letters of some ♥♥♥♥, and find out that this town holds onto a bunch of weird superstitions surrounding this mound that you need to excavate. As the narrative progresses the VA and the cutscenes show the main character unraveling as more plot points prove to be uncanny.Call of the Sea: Story starts with a deeply personal connection being missing, with radio science for MONTHS. Main character conscripts a local charter for a boat, wild ♥♥♥♥ unravels, and the VA and cutscenes do not unnerve the character at all.STAKES - SPOILERSHobs Barrow - Throughout the game, the highest the stakes are raised is one dead person and one incapacidated person.Call of the Sea - Multiple dead people before the second and third act.Response to Stakes - SPOILERsHobs Barrow - I need to ge to the bottom of this. If not for my own will and triumphing over this superstition, but also for my father who has succumbed to this power.Call of The Sea - I have already been infected with whatever the ♥♥♥♥ inhabited here, my husband is probably dead since all I've done  is unravel uncanny deaths of his crewmates and I'm just perpetually chipper about the madness taking hold of the survivors. Basically, in my humble opinion, Hobs Barrow takes the story seriously by providing believable actors with realistic stakes. Call of the sea has unreal expectations about a vulnerable protagonist, fails to set realistic qualities for the protagonist and ultimately loses me along the way.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: This was a wholly absorbing adventure -- I have not been this immersed in a game since first playing "The Last of Us" back in 2013. I'll be careful to avoid any spoilers here, but if you enjoy the atmospheric folk-horror feel of rural UK settings (think "The Wicker Man," but the proper 1970s version) coupled with the gorgeous pixel art of "Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis," you've found your game. This is a puzzle- and story-driven wonder that had me gripped. I'd like to add that the voice acting was uncommonly good, and helped me to identify with the characters - especially the main protagonist - as the narrative unfolded. Additionally, as someone who is not native to the UK (where the game is set), I picked up some local expressions and customs through the dialogue, which helped cement a tremendous sense of place and time. I do not wish to divulge any further, other to say that this was a top-tier adventure that I relished all the way to the end.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game.  Have been playing it both on an ancient iMac and my Steam Deck seamlessly / without glitches and the pixel graphics are very atmospheric.  Some people, especially hardened click and point adventurers, might find the puzzles a little too simple, but for me the balance is about right, there is no frustration that the game won't progress because I am stuck on one puzzle.  The story line is very engaging and gradually becomes darker as the game progresses.  Highly recommended for fans of the genre!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: -Realistic item combinations-There are some timed puzzles, but they are really easy complete once you know what to do-Most of the puzzles/combinations are not too difficult, but some will give you the "AHA" moment-The voice acting is great, the 8-bit style graphics are nicely done-The story is fine, but I feel a few question haven't been answered-I wish I could choose from at least two endings. I am aware of the protagonist's motivation, but it would have been nice to react upon all the warnings and signs the game flooded the player withOverall, I really enjoyed this game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: I had a great time playing The Excavation of Hob's Barrow. From the stunning pixel art to the delightful voice acting, this game is an awesome tribute to old school point and clicks. I was engulfed in the story from begining to end, and even though it would have been nice to have mutiple endings, the adventure was fantastic. If you enjoy old school point and clicks, a wonderfully written Lovecraftian story, English folklore and Victorian England, this game was made for you !
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game. Ticks all the folk-horror boxes so far. A slow-burning atmosphere that remains gripping as you descend closer to the abyss not knowing what fateful tragedy awaits. Shades of MR James and Daphne du Maurier reading Lovecraft to one another. Not only would I 10/10 recommend this game, but I would also say check out the other titles of Cloak & Dagger - a team exploring the weird and eerie aspects of what makes us human in the face of inhumanity and remember... _childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Like Cloak and Daggers previous games Football Game, Sumatra: Fate of Yandi, The Terrible Old Man and A Date in the Park, simply amazing and bursting with atmosphere. _childDocuments_.review: An charming little gem that manages to bring back the magic of the golden age of adventure games, which was during the 90s. What they have accomplished here is a like resurrecting a long dead body in such a way that it feels like the person didn't die to begin with. They really managed to get the right creepy atmoshphere that makes you a bit uneasy but still curious about what's around the corner, like it should be in a horror mystery game, and the graphics are just about right for this kind of game. Not too fancy and not too cheap.I think the people who are looking for nostalgia are the ones that will enjoy it most, but the story and puzzles are good enough that any fan of point & click adventure can enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decent point and click adventure that has some issues and seems a little pricey at 15 dollars, but overall I enjoyed it. The puzzles are fair and logical, the story is interesting and the voice acting is pretty top notch. If I had one complaint it's that while the voice acting is very good it's delivered in a very stilted way. One line will be read, there will be a pause and then the next line and it continued like this throughout the game. I don't know if it's some kind of technical issue or by design, but it left this feeling like nobody memorized their lines and then had to turn the page each time to see the next one. That quibble aside, it was a good 5ish hours of unsettling mystery and I hope they continue on with the story, but if not it's still a satisfying conclusion.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful voice acting and beautiful art, an interesting narrative ark with a genuinely unexpected end. Hob's Barrow is an extremely worthwhile play. Mainly narrative with most puzzles saved for the final chapter, it could perhaps of been improved with more varied game play throughout as most sections are quite straightforward and serve only to progress with story with limited thought required. More a very entertaining visual novel than brain teasing puzzler.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: An atmospheric, slow-burn adventure game that feels like a cross between Gabriel Knight: Sins of The Fathers, and LucasArts' The Dig, but with a unique story that I was totally engrossed in. The writing is definitely the highlight of the game, and there's plenty of mystery, intrigue, and horror to go around. The characters, sound design, and art are excellent and Victorian-era rural England is a great setting. The voice acting is phenomenal and the characters are engaging and interesting. Highly recommend if you love story-driven horror and/or old school point and click adventure games. My main critique is that the puzzles were a little on the easy side compared to the games it tries to emulate. While most were pretty easy, all of the puzzles (save for one) followed pretty straight logic. I ran into a few stumpers here and there that challenged me, and I was happy that the solutions did not feel cheap or obtuse. I'm a huge fan of Wadjet Eye's own games and they clearly know how to pick the best of them now as a publisher. Definitely want to go and play the rest of Cloak and Dagger's games after this fantastic entry. 9/10, would easily recommend to anyone who loves point and click adventure games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely great atmospheric game. The dialogue and voice acting is grand. Really sucks you into the mystery of this little town, and what is happening. _childDocuments_.review: To write a review on Steam you are required to hit the "Recommend" or "Do Not Recommend" button. This gave me pause, because I definitely don't think this game is *bad*, but after completing it I 100% would not recommend it to anybody I know.This is one of those horror games that works very well until you've played enough of it and you realize the parlor tricks it's using.The game has an oppressive atmosphere right from the start, mostly thanks to its great sound design. You arrive in a town where nobody trusts you and everyone seems to know more than they're letting on. In ordinary conversations you are given choices to let people know things or to keep them private. It makes it feel very conspiratorial, like if you tell the wrong person the wrong thing, you'll wake up in the middle of a ritualistic circle with a bag over your head ten feet from a Game Over screen.This is not the case. In fact, none of your choices in dialogue matter. They're all just there to unnerve you. And it does unnerve you, for awhile, until you realize this is a game where you don't really have any control over the narrative and suddenly you can't help but feel a bit cheated.Without spoiling anything, this game is very Lovecraftian in its tone, and it's clearly inspired by a lot of Lovecraftian literature. Where I think this game fails is that it forgets it is, in fact, a game, and not a book.In a novel characters may say and do odd things that unnerve the reader, and it makes sense that you may never follow up with them or understand what they mean. If the main character starts making strange or unreasonable decisions that the player would not make, that's fine because you're reading a story about a character.Video games are an entirely different medium, because the player is physically controlling the protagonist. This makes it a little awkward when characters do strange things to unnerve you, because unlike in a book the brave player can simply keep talking to the character and realize they aren't actually scary, they're just socially awkward or a weirdo. There is a certain point in this game where the main character, Thomasina, goes from a skeptical, logical woman who nay-says the existence of anything supernatural to a blind sheep willing to delve ever further into the dark not because she is curious or scientifically interested or even no longer afraid of death, but because a developer has puzzles on the other side of the dark and the player must solve them, even if it makes absolutely no sense for anyone in-universe to go down there.This change in her character did not feel earned or really make any level of internal sense. It just felt like I went from controlling a normal lady one day to a lunatic the next. This is especially strange when most of the gameplay the first two days is spent making absolutely sure you have your tools for a safe dig and then she begins crawling headlong into a cavern without so much as a light.I understand wanting a set narrative, but this is a game that simply *begged* for some kind of alternate ending. Not even a "good" ending, just one where the player is allowed to say "Y'know what, I don't feel like this woman would put up with this anymore. Let's take the train and leave." And then you get a bad end where you never learn anything. That wouldn't be satisfying, but it would make me feel like I have any reason to be here.This following two paragraphs will have a few small spoilers, so you may want to skip them if you're going in blind:There are so many things that are done just to be spooky that you think back on later and they just never mattered at all. You meet the priest character vomiting in the woods in an extremely unpleasant way and when you ask him about it he says "He ate some bad berries" in the most suspicious way possible. You have to cut his arm and bloodlet "the disease out", which cures him. It's implied something about this man is sinister, but no, he's just a nice guy. Bloodletting doesn't actually cure anyone of anything (especially not nausea) so it working on him implies something cultic or magical, but no, he really just ate some bad berries, threw up, and them you cut open his arm to let the vomit faeries out. It's so extremely strange. There is a man in town named Arthur Tillet who gives off the absolute worst vibes of anyone. There were so many times I wanted to tell him to ♥♥♥♥ off, but the narrative forces you to befriend him, which is so strange because nobody in their right mind would talk to this guy after the way he treats you on the first day. It's all extremely bizarre.I think the game's single biggest sin on the horror front is doing the whole "It's too scary to describe" thing when you find the *thing* in town. You are very much allowed to do something like this in literature (like the books this game is so obviously based on) because a book is just words. All of it was in the reader's mind, and refusing to even describe a creature lets the reader imagine something scary of their own volition, which is often more effective. However, again, this is a *video game*. A game in which we've been seeing spooky purple demon effects and goblin heads the entire time. A game with extensive animation. So the climax saying "We can't show you the payoff, it's too scary!" is no longer frightening. It's lame.End spoilers.It must be said the game's puzzles also get worse the longer the game goes on. Day 1's puzzles are tight. Day 2 has some good puzzles and one about getting flowers that has several more steps than it ought to have had. Day 3 leans full-on into old timey PC98 adventure game puzzles which are neither thematically tied to anything nor very interesting, several of which I gave up and looked at a walkthrough to solve. It's never a good sign when you look at a walkthrough and go "Oh, what?! I literally never would've even TRIED to do that."This game definitely deserves some praise. The spritework, modernization of the genre, and especially the voice acting are all excellently done. My biggest complaint is that I think this story really wanted to be a book or an audiodrama, and at the end of the day, I'm not sure why it wasn't.

_childDocuments_.review: A thoroughly enjoyable supernatural point and click adventure with some notable pros and cons. It's a mostly traditional affair, with a solid, entertaining narrative about a young woman who visits a reclusive English village while following in her father's barrow excavating footsteps (a sort of tomb). To say too much more would spoil things, it's best to go in as blind as possible. A special mention must go to the voice acting in this game, which is fantastic and a cut above most genre entries, the dialogue and character interactions were clearly given great care during development. Visually the pixel art is nice enough though the animations are less impressive compared to some other games from the Wadjet Eye stable. The ambient audio is great too and evokes an atmosphere of creeping dread while the music is similarly effective.Gameplay wise Hob's Barrow offers absolutely nothing in terms of innovation. It aims to be a point and click game in the classic style and its adherence to the template laid out by genre predecessors is unwavering. Whether this is a pro or con is subjective, I personally enjoy more traditional P&C games. I will say that it places far more emphasis on advancing the story through dialogue and exploration rather than puzzles. The puzzles that are there are unlikely to hinder your progress for long which helps keep things moving, although they might have benefited from being slightly more challenging or frequent.The game has a relatively short running time, it took me around 5-6 hours to finish (ignore my total playtime, much of that was idle), but the pacing is slightly off and I couldn't help but feel it was an act or two short. The mystery initially builds at a comfortable pace until suddenly the story hurtles headlong toward its conclusion. That's how it felt to me at least, though it didn't spoil my experience. Overall I would definitely recommend the game, especially if you're a fan of the genre or someone who enjoys a good story without being assailed by brain melting puzzles at every turn.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: very good, 8 unspeakable horrors out of 10.It can be one evening trip (about 6 or 8 hours) to the countryside of 19th century England with no idea of ​​what lies ahead, but after a few hours you get the feeling of an old friend you miss.The Excavation of Hob's Barrow was created in the best way of Lovecraftian horror, also known as the Cthulhu Mythos. I've rarely done a review in this fashion, but this game should be on the list of true fans of a good, well-rounded mystery story.

_childDocuments_.review: Hob's Barrow is well told folk horror in the tradition of Nigel Kneale.  The story begins low stakes but quickly builds intrigue and mystery that point towards a bigger story than the one we are initially seeing. Quite different in tone to Wadget Eye's other horror titles but of equal quality of writing.  If you love British folk horror or point and click, you'll love this. _childDocuments_.review: As a long-time point and click adventure game fan, I greatly enjoyed digging into the Excavation of Hob's Barrow. I appreciated the weather changes and the little details like forest creatures scurrying about that assisted in creating a more immersive environment, as did a fine collection of voice actors. Occasional cut scenes and flashbacks added to the story but were never intrusive. Definitely a more mature narrative than many of the games of my childhood (i.e King's Quest, Monkey Island, etc)  but part of this game's charm is getting to follow the heroine as she descends into the dark and forbidding basement...er...barrow. _childDocuments_.review: I feel bad reviewing this negatively as it's clear a lot of care went into making the game and I'm also not really the target audience - I've played a handful of point and click puzzle games (Longest Journey, various Sierra entries, old Goosebumps games, Beacon Pines) but I don't seek the genre out. I received it as part of a Humble Bundle pack and thought it looked interesting enough to play without knowing much about it.First, the positives: Hob has a very good art-style and soundtrack that walk an interesting line between cozy and unsettling, and the voice acting is good. Unfortunately the game-play falls flat. You spend a few hours doing tedious fetch quests for villagers in a very small environment of about 8 or 9 scenes. The motivation for doing most of these quests is generally that someone needs you to do their chores before they'll help you do someone else's chores, and at some points you're so many recursive chores deep that it almost feels like parody. You start to form some basic bonds with a few villagers but this section ends before many meaningful connections can be made, and there is pretty much no resolution for any of the villager story-lines anyway.The final third of the game takes place in the Barrow itself and is a series of simple puzzles. The puzzles aren't particularly logical but are simple enough that most people probably won't get stuck on them for long. They don't feel very rewarding and most of the solutions are pretty much spelled out for you in a manual that you find.All of this would be forgivable if the story-line and main character were interesting, but they're not. Early on it's implied that opening the barrow could have ambiguous results but by the time you actually get in there it has become very obvious that opening the barrow is a terrible idea, and the main character seems to be well aware that she's being manipulated for evil purposes. This isn't just some eldritch mind control thing, as the villains make it clear that her actions have to be of her own free will. This results in a smart character doing stupid things just because the story needs her to, and there are no decisions that the player can make to alter these events in any way. The ultimate pay off is extremely predictable and unsatisfying.It's clear from the reviews that this game appeals to fans of the genre but if you don't already like point and click adventures I don't think this game is worth the time and effort it takes to get through.

_childDocuments_.review: Typically, I'm a fan of the adventure games that Wadjet Eye puts out, I just have a hard time deciding if The Excavation of Hob's Barrow is a game worth recommending. Archaeologist Thomasina receives a letter inviting her to excavate Hob's Barrow, but gets the runaround from the townsfolk as the mystery surrounding the barrow unfolds itself. While the pixel-art is good, especially when a closeup occurs, and the game has a pretty interesting ending, most of the game is pretty uneventful. The plot is pretty obtuse at times with story elements that just aren't well explained, and I would have deeply enjoyed more lore and exposition instead of all the fetch quests that I had to deal with throughout the game. I unfortunately think that The Excavation of Hob's Barrow is on the weaker side of the Wadjet Eye catalog.

_childDocuments_.review: With no puzzle difficulty to speak of, the rich, gorse-scented ambience and literature-quality dialogue make this more of an interactive story of one of the , with point 'n' click trappings only for style.  It is charming and gently entrancing by turns, and the setting is so  of things both homely and haunted -- two qualities exemplified by Herbert the odiferous man-cat -- that conditions feel ripe for multiple endings. Nothing could ever compel me to discommend such a painstaking work, but I have mixed feelings about it that mostly revolve around the one-way finale.  It's a class-act in every other way.

_childDocuments_.review: I've giving it a big red down-thumb, simply because there's no medium sideways yellow thumb. I ummed and ahhed about which way to go: Up vote, because it's clearly a well made game with a lot of work put in. Down, because the puzzles are trivially easy and the end of the game completely undermines everything else. (The character performs actions at the end that I didn't wish her to perform, given all we both knew. It was very forced and undermined the character's previous actions without any literary effort put in to establish any changes, and so it comes across as developer-fiat, robbing players of agency).In the end I went with DOWN, simply as there's a huge amount of UP for this, some even labelling it the "best adventure game for time period X", which says more about time period X than it does about this game. It's definitely over-hyped. It's a pure B-grade indie adventure game, which is nothing to be ashamed of. It's also a pure b-grade folk horror. It's nothing that hasn't been done before. It's a Yorkshire Wicker Man, essentially!The long time adventure fans -- nothing new. For fans of Lovecraft style Victorian horror, or "folk horror", there's nothing really new here either.To elaborate:The majority of the puzzles are simply "go and talk to this other person" or "go pick up this thing for me". You never have to actually think about what you're doing.  There's intentionally a lot of wandering about and backtracking, diligently going through every scene and every character to find the one that's now moved or has a new line of dialogue in the hope of triggering the next part of the linear story.The puzzle sequencing itself is completely linear. Even though you have 7 things in your todo list you can't "work" on them all at once, as 1 depends on 2 depends on 3 depends on 4 .. etc so you're only solving the last in the list. The original Monkey Island solved this problem, 30 years ago, as it purposefully had multiple things you were "working on" at once. But that's probably because it had puzzles you had to think about!Interestingly, for an adventure game, the character is well grounded and refuses to pick up any old trash you see, especially if it belongs to someone else, rather than lining her pockets. The game will even change how you perceive things once new information is available, which is a nice touch. This is one of the things the game completely undermines in the end portion, however, as suddenly you're picking up any old crap and stealing, all in the name of the developers wanting the game to finish.The game/story is also linear. This is fine, most games are, but this game pretends quite hard at the start that you have lots of options, and that each dialogue option changes things, so choose carefully! But a quick re-load will show it doesn't (aside from the occasional achievement for picking a certain option), as they all resolve into the exact same thing, and there's 0 long term consequences. The game follows the same path no matter what you do. This same 0-choices problem is writ large at the end, but here it doesn't even pretend to be a choice, it just happens. Even though the character is clearly presented with information they can act on, and even though the character is shown to be a rational, scientific, anti-hogwash sceptic of maximum proportions with a keen interest in barrow-diving the developers instead force your hand at the end and that characterisation goes out the window. Suddenly they're doing something you have no choice over, would clearly never choose, and neither would the character as presented at the start of the story. Media can often "earn" that change of character if we see it done well, but here we see no interstitial stage. The character at the end is suddenly a different person. If that's meant to be due to COSMIC FORCES acting on them then the game fails to even hint at that. Also, it's barely a game, because you can't really do anything other than follow thins single path. It's most definitely a visual novel where you're along for the ride rather than a puzzle-solving adventure game. This is par for the course of Wadget Eye _developed_ games, but it seems to also now be true of their published games. The plot itself was ok, and the ending kind of makes sense to the story itself (if you take the leap and assume COSMIC HORROR FORCES acting on your, and other, characters), but it isn't really anything new. The game also leaves an huge number of loose ends, which is unsatisfying to me as a player/reader, and leaving them dangling doesn't really add to any suspense, it only adds to the "rushed" feeling of the game. The character herself should also want some of them resolving!(I think the story of Tomasina's dad would have been a much more interesting one to play)The game has modern features, like an ease-in tutorial, optional highlight, todo list, quick travel. Great! These are all welcome. But it's also using the creaking AGS engine (with it's ridiculous settings menu, none of which change a single thing about this game, except for the ones that make the developer's art worse). It attempts things from more modern games e.g. the small, grotesque cutscenes and parallax scrolling. But AGS is poorly equipped to handle them, especially the parallax scrolling, so that looks horrible. Ironically 16bit games back in the day (that this art style apes) had better scrolling than this. There's developer commentary too, which is really interesting, but ideally it would be subtitled in a game that is 100% subtitled.The music is really well done. Everything from the menu to the random in-game guitar interlude. The voice casting is done well, as is the dialogue, though it's not without it's flaws. The two main ones being: 1. A large chunk of the main voice actress' lines are said with a smile on her face or in a half-giggle, which contrasts with the serious or neutral words and situation 2. Although all of the accents are "Yorkshire" they're inconsistent in *which* Yorkshire accents they are, which isn't what you'd expect from an inbred village before the advert of the motor carriage where everyone claims they're born and bred there. But I guess such professional voice coaching is beyond the budget of a indie adventure game! Still, at least you'll get your fix of *any road*, and *now then, 'ow do* if that's what you're after.Overall the dialogue and voice work combine with the drab visuals to really give the feeling of an insular Yorkshire village, so well done on that. The game definitely nails the emotional side of the game. It's a shame the logic didn't hold up!

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially intrigued by the plot, characters, and setting, which is what you'd want out of an adventure game that's chiefly interested in telling a story. I pushed myself along, hoping the slow, emotionally flat middle of the game might build to a conclusion that would make good on the positive feelings I'd had at the start. No one would go this heavy on tired, derivative foreshadowing if they didn't plan to upend my expectations with a spectacular twist, right?I want to love  It's a respectable effort, crafted with love, and it comes  to achieving something, but the mystery isn't mysterious, the horror isn't horrific, and the perfunctory interactions and puzzles hardly merit a mention.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm Thomasina Bateman, antiquarian, and I've been invited to the town of Bewlay to investigate Hob's Barrow, a local burial mound. Once arrived, my host is nowhere to be found, the local townsfolk are keeping mum about both him and the barrow in question, and it doesn't take long to realise there's more than one mystery surrounding the area. I'm very intrigued by this story. I know an author from Plymouth, Terri Nixon, and she's written several books that take place in the Cornish moors (both historical novels in the early 1900s, and a fantasy series about the fair folk) so it's fun to actually get some visuals with a story that might've just as easily come from her pen. It's a slow game and I'm taking my time to look at everything, talk to everyone, gather information and clues and just following the storyline as it unfolds. I haven't really faced any real puzzles yet; seems to me everything will become clear eventually and quite on its own by simply doing the obvious. Some actions unlock a flashback, to get some more background info on the main character's childhood. There's not all that much to do in them, but they show that the narrative and layered storyline is the most important part of this game.There are lots of strange things going on, and I'm witnessing some unusual stuff. But what I'm very enchanted by is how many small details this game has. The rustle of the wind, bird song, a barking dog somewhere in town, wildlife occasionally jumping away, birds flying over, grass dancing in the breeze, and the surprise of a close-up shot now and again when you discover something especially interesting. Yes, Bewlay is truly coming to life on my screen.I finished the game in 7,5 hours!The final part of the game was really fun and finally contained some more elaborate puzzles than going around talking to people. It amost played like an Indiana Jones adventure game and for a moment I thought I was back in the labyrinth of Knossos. There's some scary and gruesome imagery near the end which I wasn't expecting and elicited some "WTF" moments, but it was all very cool to watch unfold.It's not a puzzle heavy game but it's a great story. I loved walking around Bewlay figuring things out. I don't think I used the in-game map function even once; I always walked there myself. I'm really curious to see what the next brain child of Cloak and Dagger Games will be!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: I wrote a whole-ass review that Steam lost because I hit the "not recommended" button and it purged all my text, so this will be a lot shorter than the original. >>>:C Still, tl;dr at the bottom.Basically - excellent atmosphere, excellent music, excellent logic, excellent characters, excellent creep factor, solid story - terrible ending that almost ruins the whole experience based on what's important to you.   Gives the impression that there are multiple endings/outcomes, but none of your choices matter at all - I was ready to laud this as a near-perfect modern classic adventure game but here I am making a Not Recommended review (for the second time, thanks Steam x_x), just because of that ending that made me feel like I wasted my time and investment in my choices and the story when I was just being railroaded the entire time.Ending/game spoilers/rant: Was 10/10 until the ending - 7/10 afterward, but that's being as objective as I can be about the ending and taking all the goodness before it into consideration.  I honestly feel like I wasted my time and was hoodwinked by the developers, so if I'm rating more personally, I'd give it a 5/10, because the good stuff was  good . tl;dr: Suffers from a major and deliberate illusion of choice - only a single outcome, ruined the entire experience for me, personally. If choices don't matter to you, it would absolutely be a 10/10, but they're important to me, and the game leads you to believe they are, too.

_childDocuments_.review: What an incredible disappointment. I was fully invested in the game until it became clear that my actions had no meaningful impact on the story whatsoever. In my opinion, the developers missed a huge opportunity here.The ending was particularly frustrating. I found myself thinking, “Maybe I just got the bad ending.” But no—there's only one ending, no matter what choices you make or dialogue you select. You can see the trap coming from a mile away, but you're powerless to stop it.For a game that boasts 93% positive ratings, it feels undeserving of such high praise. _childDocuments_.review: I have to include myself with those saying that the game isn't really worth a recommendation. The art, sound design, and voice acting are all great. The initial story is intriguing and gets you hooked, giving you seemingly important choices about who to talk to and about what. _childDocuments_.review: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow is an absolutely spectacular game. I went into the experience knowing absolutely nothing about the game, and I must say, I am pleasantly surprised. More than pleasantly. This game is a masterpiece. The pixel art is astoundingly beautiful and well-made with many artistic and at times rather creepy closeup stills, the music is wonderful and really captures the feel of mysterious small-town England, and the voice acting is fantastic. Like, seriously, I was not expecting the production value of this random game I bought on sale to be so high. Each character is unique and so well written. The narrative was captivating for the entirety of the game and had me constantly on the edge of my seat. I could not stop playing, desperately seeking answers to the mysteries of the village of Bewlay. The puzzles were intuitive and enjoyable and I never found myself wishing for anything. This game is a literal 10/10 experience and I will be replaying it hopefully soon to acquire the achievements I'm missing. I'm quite the achievement hunter, yet I knew from the start that I needed to play this game blind and not worry about completing things a certain way just for some achievements. I recommend you do the same. I only wish I could play this game for the first time again.Actually, as an afterthought, I do wish there was more than one ending.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: A game of remarkable quality and a new favorite of mine. While not without its flaws, it captivated me from start to finish. The first half is excellent, pulling me in with believable suspense, compelling intrigue, and well-crafted horror elements. It's been a long time since a game hooked me like this. Amazing! I hold this consideration even tough I am not a big fan of find-and-fetch puzzles, the likes of which this game have in great quantity: It is noteworthy that the game is designed to be friendly in this regard, and not to be infuriatingly obscure when it comes to solutions to puzzles. However, like many other reviewers, I felt the second half of the game didn’t quite match the quality of the first, not to the point of ruinning the experience or anything close to that but certainly to an appreciable degree. To me, the main problem is not inherent to the game but with some narrative choices: The central issue is that somehow foreshadowing was confounded with character development. To explain this in the most spolier-free manner possible: The protagonist, Thomassina Bateman, is very consistently portrayed as a highly rational, scientifically-minded individual who dismisses anything remotely superstitious with utter disdain. Yet, towards the latter part of the game, when the story undergoes a shift in tone, she goes on to behave in an uncharacteristic manner: It is hard to believe that someone like that would think and do the things she thinks and does, as they are clearly very irrational. It is not simply bad writting, as I can see there in-character reasons for her to act in that way. The trouble is that this simply bad-executed foreshadowing: The game is trying to let you now that there is a core of truth within the mockable local folklore and that Thomassina is going to face it. Sadly, when this happens, there is no pay-off because not conflict has been set to that point, and what the player feels is that suddenly thing are not as credible anymore. That said, these narrative missteps are minor and easy to overlook in the grand scheme. Despite its imperfections, this game is an experience well worth your time
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: A short (5-8 hours) adventure game of moderate difficulty; like most modern adventure games it follows the Lucasarts formula, and there is no way to 'fail', only to get temporarily stuck. The Excavation of Hob's Barrow is a horror game with a good, consistent atmosphere, from the music that greets you in the menu to the fantastic voicework that reinforces the "isolated in rural Yorkshire" vibe. More into creeping dread than the jumpscare, I would call this safe for anyone adult enough to understand it.Absolutely recommended for adventure game fans, and horror fans.

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely gem, brimful of what makes the genre such a charming experience.  Having not yet played anything else by this developer, I am looking forward to more based on the enjoyment I had with this title.  It is simplistic point and click at its finest; echoing the style of Sierra and Lucas Arts while evoking the nuance of the Broken Sword original games.  There are fewer red herrings, and everything you interact with has a purpose (often more than one) that makes sense.  The  slightly more mature content pushes a horror narrative that takes some time to really pick up steam; but by the time you really get to the excavation section itself, it is off and running.    Characters appear in equal parts two-dimensional and solidly developed as the story progresses.  Voice acting is superb, and for the cost of the title, I completed it in just over six hours, dipping back to a previous save to complete the achievements unattainable in a single run.  There is little in the way of innovation; but what it does right it does to a very high calibre. Recommended very easily, and more so if you are already a fan of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Randomly decided to play this game after getting it from the April Humble Bundle selection, and what a gem!Loved the story, pixel art, characters and voice over. Yes, there is a bit of the story being dragged and you do have to run around chasing clues, but I honestly loved it. One of the few games that I found relaxing and intriguing at the same time, with a mysterious-lovecraft atmosphere. The story was exciting and I was quite pleased with the somewhat unexpected open ending, leaving space for your imagination to continue the story after the game ends. Overall very very good game, highly recommend it !

_childDocuments_.review: A folklore-inspired backwater town horror story. This game's release came as a surprise for me. Weren't the fabulous people from  working on a game called ? Um. Um. I.. Oh. This is  from . What an absolutely fantastic treat this is!I've enjoyed the build up of horror in this game ever so much. Little things like hearing disturbing ambiance when starting a new day. Close ups of characters during certain scenes, suddenly revealing much more horrific detail than just a 3x3 pixel face. A beautifully written letter to your mother, which lines will slowly be revealed to you, the further you get. The voice acting is absolutely ace.Oh yes, I can hear you thinking, ''. Don't be fooled. _childDocuments_.review: I took some time agonising over whether this is a 'recommend' or 'don't recommend': the first half of the game has just enough moments to make it worth a look (especially if it's on sale), while the latter half is a total letdown which reveals a level of superficiality to the game, souring the whole experience. So take this 'recommended' review with a heavy dose of salt.Briefly, on the gameplay: I do not generally care for point-and-click games because I cannot stand brute forcing my way through 'moon logic' puzzles, which (in my experience) are a staple of the genre. In this respect the game is a masterstroke, since virtually all of the puzzles are relatively straightforward, to the point of being a little uninspired. There were no real moments of 'oh, go to hell' or similar frustration, but then there were no real 'eureka' points either. There are a couple of points where I clearly didn't hit the necessary checkpoint for a person to spawn or an event to occur, which mildly hindered the flow of the game, but these were easily overlooked.The real problem is that if you're going to do a story about A British Village Where Something Isn't Quite Right, you're going to invite comparisons to The Wicker Man [1973] - especially so when you mix in a no-nonsense outsider, a charismatic landlord, and a 'batman gambit' where the outsider is tricked into doing something they probably didn't want to do. The snag with doing this is that The Wicker Man is one of the most critically acclaimed horror movies of all time, and isn't easily emulated (although many have tried - including the original film's director - and failed). The first half of the game does well in portraying the unnerving atmosphere in the village - I have to give particular mention to the art designer, whose interspersed 'close-ups' of the village folk really add to the creepiness of the area. If you consider yourself vaguely genre-savvy (or even just on this side of conscious) you'll probably see through the bare-faced lies of the villagers, and hence you'll have some excited anticipation of what the payoff will be.[The rest of the review contains spoilers for The Wicker Man [1973] and the game itself.]Unfortunately, that payoff is not worth the extra time put into the game - it's not that they've replicated the payoff of The Wicker Man, where the crops have failed and Lord Summerisle has convinced the villagers that a blood sacrifice will bring back the bountiful harvests (leaving the viewer with the explicitly spoken question 'what happens when the harvest fails again?'), but rather than they've vaguely gestured towards some Lovecraftian 'They Dug Too Deep' creature and left it at that. After a lengthy section of extremely straightforward puzzles (where virtually all of the answers can be found across three pages of text, which you receive early in the game), you reach the final room. For nearly the entire game we've been treated to flashbacks of the protagonist getting along with her father, who similarly Dug Too Deep and ended up in some sort of vegetative state; the reason for the protagonist's stupid (yet, quite literally, unavoidable; you get railroaded into this ending regardless of whether you want to or not) decision to participate in this ritual is because of some vain hope of bringing him back to health, despite her normally strong adherence to logic and reason. Anyway, the ritual goes ahead, turns out she's let out this demon (who the Lord and a handful of the villagers worship in some form), who then possesses her and causes her to kill her father, for which she's locked up in an asylum; the Lord and his followers 'win', The End, roll credits.But... What? What's the point that the game is trying to make? In The Wicker Man, there's plenty to read into about organised religion, denialism, the lengths that people go to (and people they put their trust in) to avoid disaster; the village's turn to paganism is the clear example of this, which feeds into the final act of ritual sacrifice. In Hob's Barrow, however, nothing really builds up to the ending, and nothing is really resolved by the ending; for example, none of the villagers, regardless of whether they support or oppose the Lord's plan, demonstrate any particular concern for the future or even any material desires, seeming to virtually all be content with where they live and their lot in life (the most curmudgeonly of them are annoyed by the presence of the railway station 'bringing in outsiders', but these villagers are *opposed* to the excavation and the unbinding). If you squint your eyes you can *maybe* read it as a warning against Digging Too Deep/the reckless pursuit of knowledge, but the problem with that is a) this is exactly the outcome that the Lord and his followers wanted, b) it's hardly unreasonable for the protagonist to want to be able to talk to her father (who she has a much better relationship with than her mother) again, and c) it's not like she was driven to do something that she knew to be unethical or immoral in pursuit of this. So what should I be taking from the ending? 'Don't be tricked into doing something that seems innocuous, that you're doing for a good cause'? Being frank, the ending makes the whole thing feel like the devs went into this with the intention of making A Horror Game; they made some great set-pieces and included a lot of common Horror Game tropes like 'gaslighting the protagonist' and 'person mysteriously disappears' and 'something happens in the night but the protagonist can't tell if it's a dream or not', but skimped on character development and completely neglected any kind of throughline or arc. On balance, it's competently put together, and it might be worth spending a few hours on, but it's not going to keep you awake at night.

_childDocuments_.review: I love all these retro-style point ‘n’ click adventures that keep popping up everywhere recently, it feels like re-living my childhood with them. I’ve had my eye on this one for a while, too, and luckily, I wasn’t disappointed at all.You play as a young brunette who comes from a privileged British family, and decides to follow in her father’s footsteps to become a famous archaeologist, but meets unexpected horrors that she needs to overcome. No, no, her name is not Lara Croft, and believe me, this is where all the similarities with the  franchise end! Instead of fighting your way through countless enemies, you need to solve puzzles – and let me tell you, some of them will be quite challenging even for adventure game veterans (I should know, I consider myself one). I loved the beautiful pixel art graphics, the music, the voice acting… so everything, basically. Of course, probably the most important element of this genre is the story, but I wouldn’t want to give too much away about it, so let’s just say that, in my opinion, they’ve managed to create the perfect balance of humour, drama, mystery and horror with a spot-on atmosphere to boot. My only complaint is that they leave us with too many loose ends (or they weren’t loose at all, maybe I just didn’t pay close attention, I’m not sure), so I would really love a sequel where we get at least some of the answers. And it wouldn’t hurt to make that one a bit longer, either.Anyway, highly recommended for adventure fans!

_childDocuments_.review: While quite short, this game is engaging all the way through.  It manages to sidestep many difficulties that point and click adventure games can run into.There's no "failure" state requiring you to redo parts of puzzles until you get something correct.The puzzles are difficult enough to be interesting but avoid being overly complex trial and error simulators.  Highlighting objects that can be interacted with stops you from mindlessly clicking every pixel on screen to see what can be of use. Interacting with characters who have no more relevant dialogue will prompt a "nothing more to do here" response which indicates you need to look elsewhere.The game is fully voice acted and has QUITE good delivery, and combined with the dialogue writing, each character feels unique and believable.The story has an eerie charm to it and paces itself well.  The snags encountered by the protagonist do a good balancing act between 'bad luck' and 'conspiracy.'  That's about all I'll say to avoid spoiling the story.The mystery/horror elements of the game make use of unsettling situations and odd behavior instead of jumpscares.  While short, I'd recommend the game to anybody interested in the genre.  Hope to see more like this from the developers in future!

_childDocuments_.review: Gloomy and dreadful, this game is pure delight. Look, it's a pixel-art point-and-click adventure that's a slow burn of insanity. No real jump scares, but an inexorable, impeccably voiced march towards doom.The puzzles are all a little sideways in their logic, but make internal sense. At this point, you either know if you want this or not - for me, it's been the perfect October companion.

_childDocuments_.review: I played both Sumatra: The Fate of Yandi and this game by the same author and I am glad I did that. BUT please, please let someone else write the ending for him the next time. Both of these games feel like watching the Lost series that was a big deal some time ago - a masterful delivery of suspense, mystery and a pervading sense of unease, but terribly lacking in the department of providing an adequate, satisfactory conclusion to all that build-up. _childDocuments_.review: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow is a solid point-and-click adventure that works hard on generating an uncanny and intriguing atmosphere, and does pretty well with its rural English folk-tale setting. The voice work is excellent throughout, and does a fair bit of heavy lifting in terms of creating personalities and scenarios that succeed at making you feel invested in moving the simple but engaging story forward.I did feel that a few characters - including the main one you play as - could've done with a bit more fleshing out in terms of backstories and motivations, although it's understandable in context that the devs wanted everyone you meet to seem a bit opaque at first.Puzzle-wise it's not much of a head-scratcher, with a majority of its four main sections playing out as a series of relatively engaging fetch quests for various NPCs. It's to the designers' credit that none of them ever really devolves into a pixel-hunt, and all solutions are somewhat logical, with the possible exception of one or two in the final section which can require a brief bit of 'try everything with everything' moon logic to continue down the largely very linear path the game sets out.A couple of standard minor point-and-click gripes:- There's a 'double click on an exit to teleport' mechanic aimed at reducing the number of times you have to slowly walk across screens, but in more expansive areas, the pacing of the camera scroll combined with the main character's movement speed is such that she's only ever about five steps away from those exits by the time they become clickable. In practice, it doesn't save you much time while backtracking for the most part.- Dialogue pacing can be a bit slow; I'd suggest you turn on the 'click to advance' option in setup if you prefer to play with subtitles on for these games like I do.- It's been made at an incredibly small resolution (320 x 180 I think?), so in the setup phase you'll need to experiment with the window sizing to find the best balance for your monitor. For me playing on a 1440p screen, 4x scaling seemed a happy medium whereby the window was big enough to see things properly, but without the detailed and well-animated pixel art becoming too much like Lego blocks. (Fullscreen was way too blown out, unsurprisingly.)I enjoyed my time with the game, and the ending - of which there's only one, sadly - gave pause for thought, even if I felt a bit railroaded into going along with my character's clearly poor decisions at times due to a lack of branching path options. I believe the devs addressed this and stated it was because they were very intentional about the game ending the way it did, with no alternatives. Unfortunately this does drastically reduce replayability, and I'm not sure I'd be in a hurry to revisit the moors around Bewley again despite the nicely evocative setting and mood the game generates.Overall a high quality if somewhat short and casual 6-7 hour experience. I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it to fans of the genre (point-and-click, Lovecraftian folk horror-lite), largely due to the neatly effective portrayal of a 1900s-ish northern UK countryside village and its pleasingly quirky denizens.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been very vocal about my Cloak & Dagger fandom in my reviews of their previous games, but you've got to be kidding me with how they keep outdoing themselves with each release.  Cloak & Dagger is like one of those indie film directors that can shoot a memorable feature-length film on a budget of $300 and some coupons to the local pizza joint.  There's such a directorial feel to this game; it has a great sense of pacing and timing, and plenty of the expertly placed ultra-closeups which have become a studio signature.  There's a tremendous attention to detail - notice how there's one floorboard in the pub that creaks, and how there's so many little things in the village that subtly change throughout the day.  The art!  The music!  The voice acting!  I wouldn't change a thing.  This is one of the most immersive adventure games I've played in a long time.  It just makes me feel slightly clammy, and damp, and chilly.  It's got this slow, encroaching feeling of suspense, but one that is punctuated with perfectly times surprises to keep you on your toes.I haven't finished the game yet, but I really wanted to get a positive review out as quickly as I can.  I estimate I am about halfway through the game and I just don't want it to end.

_childDocuments_.review: Now this is another example of "Lovecraft Done Right".  I really, really like this game.  It's a slow burn and takes it time to show you everything.  There is so much craft to the storytelling and puzzle design.  There are so many interactions that a real, normal person would have.  The protagonist is very relatable.8 hours to finish the first time.  I intend to go back and try for more achievements and to see what other dialogue there is.  (Author's edit:  Another 2 hours to get the rest of the achievements)Overall rating:  10/10This is a rare gem of point&click adventure game that is well-crafted.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent atmospheric horror, with a compelling story, beautiful music and art, and incredible voice acting. I loved the creeping sense of dread as you uncovered more of the town and the story. Some minor frustrations that are just the nature of a point-and-click adventure game, nothing specific to this. Love having a horror game that isn't action horror and is narrative and character driven. Highly recommend if you want a creepy folk horror game. Loved this extra as an archaeologist who has studied Latin and Greek--so fun!! Will probably assign to my students!!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stellar game!Fully voiced over with simple yet, somewhat, nostalgic pixel graphics. However it's the story that keeps you there. I swear there are like 20 characters and I can name them all by name. If I wouldn't need to go to work tmrw, I would stay up through the night to finish it in one sitting with a cup of tea with a dash of milk and no sugar. They say - "they don't make games like they use to" and this game proves that statement wrong!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible atmosphere and pacing. I've been a fan of their previous work (especially Football Game) which might be a little too "out there" for some people, but I think The Excavation of Hob's Barrow has taken all of my favorite things from that game (the jump cuts and unsettling music) and combined it with the incredible storytelling from their previous work Sumatra: Fate of Yandi and crafted one of the best point and click experiences I've ever played. I highly recommend it. Some games suffer from giving you too much too quickly to where it gets overwhelming, but Hob's Barrow does a great job of introducing you to environments slowly so you can get used to things as you learn the game. Great puzzles. Great characters. Great music. A great spooky game just in time for spooky season!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: About a 5 hour long adventure game that plays out more like an interactive story, though less so than Night in the Woods or The Last Door. Puzzles are relatively straight-forward for the most part, and don't rely on overtly  obfuscating moon-logic.Atmosphere is a wonderfully done folk-horror style and plot, with much mystery and intrigue leading up to the finale.Overall, it's a wonderfully polished adventure folk-horror adventure game, though I wish it were maybe a bit longer and allowed for different endings. Pet-peeve: The sudden and abrupt flashbacks I feel interrupt the game, and I kind of wish they were placed better such as during the dream sequences.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Really good game. Extremely atmospheric story with a "something's not quite right" kinda feel as you get to know quirky characters in the northern moor town of Bewlay.Authentic and good-quality voice acting with real dialect, but hopefully always clear enough for non-Brits.The artwork is great and the puzzles are largely very clear. There's one scene which will hopefully be made brighter in a later patch, though. As a hint, late in the game, when you need a second of something and can only find one, the other is in the place where you found another plot-advancing thing. It's just very dark and you have to pick up each thing in turn.The plot is spooky, and without jump scares. I enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: A creepy little game that's basically the Cthulhu Mythos x The Wicker Man. It's well worth playing if either of those two influences pique your interest, though there are pacing issues that irked me. The vast majority of Hob's Barrow is very slow, and while The Wicker Man could get away with that kind of pacing thanks to '70s folk rock and plenty of nudity, it's less effective in a video game. Expect to spend a lot of time wandering around, searching for the right NPC to unlock the next dialogue tree option that can advance the story. At times, it feels like there's just not much game here...until the last section suddenly switches things up, forcing you to go through an array of Myst-like puzzles that might be your jam, but weren't mine. And the ending is decidedly controversial if the other reviews here are any indication, though if you're familiar with the game's inspiration it won't come as any surprise. I do recommend playing this, and am giving it a positive review on atmospheric folk horror vibes alone. Nevertheless, I also hope the creators come out with a director's cut in a few years, a la Kathy Rain, that tweaks the pacing. More thoughts here, if you're interested in a longer review:

_childDocuments_.review: The ending confused me at first, but then I found it suited me. Thomasina and I have similar personalities, we are both stubborn, believe too much in logic, and curse those superstitions. Now I find it necessary to respect the world, including everything, because there are always some things far beyond our understanding. It is good advice to admit your ignorance.By the way, keep moving on, who knows what could happen. The ending never ends here...

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game and while not the most proficient problem-solver, there was only one puzzle I absolutely couldn't figure out. Most everything can be eventually solved with trying everything you can think of, back tracking, and reading/listening thoroughly. It was chilling at times yet there was enough narrative driven game play that didnt leave me so panicked that I couldnt think straight. I love a game with a good story and this had me ever so curious as to what would be next! Never quite knowing who was on my side or how much information to divulge made the stakes feel higher! Thoroughly recommend this for anyone who likes a spooky immersive narrative and puzzle-solving!!

_childDocuments_.review: Meet Thomasina, self-appointed tomb raider (or as she likes to call herself: barrow digger) and follow her in the journey of uncovering some treasures. She ends up in a small, rural village and soon finds out that the person who invited her is nowhere to be found. As she gets settled in she decides to explore Bewlay and its peculiar denizens.This is a classic point-and-click adventure game divided up into 3 main chapters. While the game has pixelated graphics its interface is modern and easy-to-use. The voice acting is fantastic (one of the best I have seen in the genre) with notable emphasis on the accent the locals have. Even Thomasina's vocabulary is unique. I appreciated the use of words such as "lass" and "pet" and hearing the following exclamations: "Hogwash!", "Curses!". Or just listening to characters -ing to each other when saying farewell.The game uses a checkpoint-based save system but manual saving is recommended due to the missable achievements. Puzzles are getting more interesting (and difficult) as we are nearing the endgame and our inventory keeps getting bigger and bigger with lots of items we need to use along the way. I appreciated the cutscenes we occasionally get and the Lovecraftian vibe that the game emits all the way.I had a fantastic time with this game and - to be honest - I expected so given the publisher was . As for the developers: I recommend that you also pick up  and  before this one. One thing I found interesting and this definitely affects the outcome of the gamer reviews: the ending is not the usual that you expect. However, given what we do during our playthrough it is very much foreshadowed so I wasn't really disappointed.Ta-ra!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game that kept me hooked until the very end. The quality is top notch especially the voice acting. _childDocuments_.review: music/animation/art in general are highpoints- 8 (distant sprite scaling has some quirks, especially at high res)ambience/audio is p good - 6 voice acting is decent for the most part, Thomasina feels flat pretty quickly by comparison to a lot of the others, which is unfortunate given whose voice you hear for the most of the game. - 7story started out meaning well and fell on it's face, and it's probably the biggest detractor, and the main reason i can't recommend. the intrigue dies off a bit due to a lot of direct exposition that kills the tension. a few key points that just seem to go nowhere; dead leads are one thing, but having no dialogue with characters that are directly involved makes it feel forgotten/unfinished in some cases (.the "illusion of choice" dialogues could be handled better, a lot of 'immediate' turnarounds. could do with some parallel sequences just to add a bit more weight to trying to/committing to a choice, before it gets reigned back in.no agbs/pixel hunting is good, but the 'puzzles' were pretty lacking, early on the sequence felt obvious or handed to you at times, more like a VN (not necessarily a problem, it's a marmite situation, or held up against expectation etc.)overall by the end I just felt very underwhelmed and unsatisfied by it. okay for the first couple hours but didn't use it's potential, and choked on it's exposition. a good art piece, though. appreciated the accents.probs a 3-4 final scoreexcept herbert 10/10 would pet regardless of what he eats.

_childDocuments_.review: I was bracing myself for a disappointing ending, since I've seen a lot of people say that they didn't like it. But I actually really love the ending. I love stories like this. They are rare. The mystery was concluded at the end. I think it's just not what people expected, and that doesn't make the ending bad, objectively speaking at least. This is the most polished Wadjet game yet. The issues of inconsistent voiceline volume was not present in this game. I think that's a first. The voice acting was well directed. The various accents that are spoken sounded properly pronounced. One of my pet peeves is where the intonation of a voice actor is completely out of sync with the dialect of the text. It's awfully common in adventure games. Especially with foreign accents, but this game didn't have any, so there's that. Pixel art deserves more appreciation, because in the old days there was no such thing as pixel art. Old games were trying to do everything possible with the hardware at the time. Today, pixel art is a contemporary art form. To sketch out detail with a crude brush. I don't know who worked on this game in particular, but it is the best pixel art you can find. Thomasina has like 20 pixels for her face, lol, but the amount of expressiveness is really amazing to me. Very skilled stuffPuzzle wise.. sigh.. oh well. The reason I put this game off for so long is because I knew it wouldn't be remarkably difficult in any way. That's the one thing that I miss from Wadjet. But I think that difficult puzzles have a dramatic impact on player experience, and I can understand that it would get in the way of the experience they want to create. A game as polished as this, I can still enjoy even though the challenges are arbitrary. They still serve the purpose of connecting me to the world. And the whole audiovisual experience was top notch. Kino for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow is one of the best point-and-clicks I've played in years - I loved this game. Firstly it does all of the expected things really well. Beautiful pixel imagery, excellent protagonist and a well rounded supporting cast, great setting/scenes, and good puzzles. I got stuck a couples times but more patience and a keener eye towards the in-game "to-do" list would have gotten me there. As a sum of its parts it's a very fine p&c adventure. But then there's the panache and style that makes Hob's Barrow standout. The story is just really well told folk horror with some excellent slow burn pacing. Little things like interesting jump cuts and scene direction stands out against peer games of this ilk. It has that modern shine of "prestige horror," even though it's a classic pixel-art foundation. The voice acting is notably top notch and while I got a little worried towards the end, it stuck the landing much better than I was anticipating. If you love classic point and clicks - get it. If you love rural folk horror - get it. If you love indie games and stories from developers that clearly give a ♥♥♥♥ about the things they make - get it. tr:dr - just get it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: A very good point and click adventure. I don't normally do PnC games though, so I might be a bad one to pay attention to. I overall really liked it, but there are certain gripes I had:1. If you miss a single, obtuse clue, you can get easily stuck. I had to seek out help from the forums a lot. 2. There was a lot of obtuse puzzles that I just couldn't figure out. Even ones where I got hints from the forums, until they had to spoil the answer for me... THEN it made sense. But... I'd never have figured it out on my own. I do like logic puzzles, riddles, and lateral thinking questions, but this game totally stumped me a lot of the time. 3. As I've not done PnC games before I didn't know about holding space bar to highlight interactables in the environment. Also didn't know you could combine objects in the inventory. 4. I didn't like that I didn't get to see the big baddie at the end. 5. There is so many unanswered questions that I have concerning the story. Otherwise, the game is great and I thoroughly enjoyed 90% of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Whether or not skewering the colonial approach of late 18th century archaeologists was the intention of the creators, I can’t say for certain. What I can say is that Hob’s Barrow is a great slice of British folk horror, with a compelling story that’s well told and performed to perfection by an excellent voice cast. Highly recommended for fans of the genre.

There are different people in the bar throughout the day or on the marketplace. It is not only dark at night but e.g. the smith is only working during the day. Or the church is closed after dark.The characters are likeable and the story mostly works quite nicely. I only would have prefered a different ending, but that's a matter of opinion. _childDocuments_.review: Pretty good point&click adventure game with a somewhat Lovecraftian feel. It took me under 8 hours for a blind playthrough, with another roughly half an hour replaying through some bits afterwards to catch the achievements I've missed, for the sake of completion/closure.If I were to complain about something, I'd be that the game sometimes suffers from the usual adventure game problem of plot stalling. The following is an example from the game (light puzzle SPOILERS, obviously; skip the rest of my review if you'd rather not read those): the protagonist needs labourers for the titular excavation, she decides to ask the local lord to lend her his men; someone will take her to see him if she can provide a pail of milk; the protagonist is spooked, won't milk the goat herself; the goat's owner refuses because of joint pain; poultice for the pain requires two herbs; you need to jump through hoops for each of the herbs.  I'd rather have a shorter game than this degree of complications piling one on top of another until you start forgetting why you're even doing things in the first place.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Where a lot of modern point & click adventure games tend to be rote going-through-the-motions, sometimes with a decent, but relatively flat story bolstered with back & forth puzzle fluff, Excavation of Hob's Barrow has been an excellent, engaging narrative, wonderful dialog and voice acting, classic style pixel graphics and fun puzzles.  I've not reached the end yet, but already this is one of the better adventure games I've played in the last year.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: A good game if not an outstanding one. Cloak & Dagger have achieved something here, it deserves its accolades, but it's not the most unique and satisfying work they've done so far either. Fantastic atmosphere and soundwork (seriously, it's the type of game you feel tempted to just walk around in, soaking in the scenery), but the puzzles and the story are a letdown. The puzzles because they too often feel like busywork (the second day in particular is fetch quest piled upon fetch quest) and the story because it lacks the kind of originality I've come to expect from this studio. Still definitely worth checking out though, especially for folk horror fans.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for April 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 7th, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A mystery in a cozy British town.The Excavation of Hob’s Barrow has players arriving at a little town in England with a ton of marshes and barrows. The player is trying to find the person who summoned them there and instead meets a lot of colorful characters at the local pub.  If you’ve played any of the Blackwell games, this is by the same company, Wadjet Eye Games.  The voice acting is extremely well done and elevates the game quite a bit.However the game does try to push the envelope with its graphics at times and honestly, I think it fails to nail what it is attempting. It feels almost like it’s not going far enough but also goes too far.   The story is a bit slow so far, and while the characters are good, and there’s been a couple of simple puzzles, one of them is an item you might miss if you didn’t think to pick it up, and the other was more of a “what can I do” rather than solving an obvious puzzle. Pick this up if you like the Blackwell games.  I assume it’s going to be paranormal and spooky at some point, but also the writing so far has been really good though I’ve yet to get started on the main mystery.  If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:
