_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art and does an excellent job building and maintaining tension and establishing atmosphere. Good character development especially for the length. Pacing is a little pokey at the beginning but picks up soon enough. Didn't love the ending but it wasn't enough to ruin the experience, just a bit deflating. Recommended for fans of adventure games and folk horror.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: This is, hands down, one of the finest works of modern Lovecraftian horror. The game is short, tightly executed, and drowning in atmosphere. Excellent balance of puzzles and narrative, exposition is never heavy and the cast of characters are well developed.The authors here have brilliantly captured the essence of Lovecrafts “creeping unease”, without resorting to the fish people and gratuitous tentacles plaguing most other interactive narratives in the genre. They grasped that it is what is unseen, unspoken, which is the crux of the genre. While the plot does telegraph itself by the end, it doesn’t feel disappointing. Cannot recommended this experience enough: you can knock it out in an afternoon (indeed, you’ll likely find it hard to put down) and come away with the same feeling of satisfaction granted by reading a brilliant short novel - which is what this really is.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Check out the full review on The Excavation of Hob’s Barrow is a masterclass in an older, more methodical style of storytelling which is not often seen in today’s videogame landscape. If you’re just out for cheap thrills this Spooky Season, this game’s deliberately paced web of mystery might not be for you. But if you’re the type that likes to turn off the lights, turn up the speakers, and let yourself drift into a spooky story, this one’s well worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: The tension in 'The Excavation of Hob's Barrow' rises, like the apologue of the frog being brought to a boil. Slowly, almost tenderly. There's a weirdness in the town - something you just can't put your finger on. Your views on the characters bounce from trust, to scepticism, to alarm, to fear, then back to trust. It's a great game; stellar voice acting from all of those involved, and some really sharp writing for most of the story. The narrative drifts a little off course in the final stages, moving at pace towards a quite sudden ending. Playing again for a second time, you can see how the designers / developers cleverly worked in warning signs throughout the game. Definitely a game for those interested in folk horror - slow, breeding, intensity.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Atmospheric pixel-art point-and-click folk horror set under mostly leaden skies in England's Peak District at the tail end of the 19th century. The setting has echoes of Sarah Perry's "The Essex Serpent" and to a lesser extent Pentiment (gameplay-wise too), before heading in a more Lovecraftian direction. The electronic soundtrack feels taken from a 1980s BBC2 or Channel 4 drama serial or film. The point and click puzzles are pretty straightforward if you're familiar with the genre, bar a couple towards the very end. Arguably not all the narrative choices for the ending quite work, but this isn't a fatal flaw even for a narratively driven game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: As an old point and click player i would say: Graphics are not bad, mix of amiga and mid 90s Dos Adventures. Missing animations are filled with black screen, but okay its not broken sword. Sound is not bad too, sometimes it wasnt good mixed up, i remember first music at the bench wasnt good, or the giggle from the girl in he hole was way too loud. The speakers did a good job. I like the flow of the puzzles, not too much handling like day of the tentacle, was more like brown sword, talk, come back etc.. At the end, it was a little more cryptic and some puzzles. Inventory wasnt used so much, but was okay for me, too much puzzles kill the flow. Story okay, yeah i like that lovecraft setting, but way too much flashbacks in the middle, and that girl wants to safe her father didnt really catched me. That barrows wasnt a highlight, was okay, may be it should have been the start for something bigger, second part? Make something like a mix of black mirror and broken sword, would be awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Horror themed pixel adventure? Oh wow... it has been a while, I didn't play such a game. Generally enjoyed the game; good atmosphere, good characters, good puzzles, and a decent game length. There are a couple of tone shifts between the parts of the game which could have been handled better I guess but it's not that big of a problem. On the good side, I really liked the unconventional story elements and mythology especially near the end which is a breath of fresh air. The ending is..... let's say interesting, I did not dislike it but did not like it either. I believe with different character motivations, different set of events it could have worked much better. But it's nowhere near the horrible and cheap ending of Return to Monkey Island imo. All in all, I definetely recommend the game and look forward to subsequent games of the developers. I think they are in a very good path to become great storytellers.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic point and click narrative with elements of folk horror and the supernatural in the Victorian era. Some of the plot points were somewhat predictable for me, but overall the game has fantastic writing. It's fully voice acted and done incredibly well. The main protagonist is played by Samantha Béart (Karlach from BG3). The story was very intriguing and it was fun to put the pieces of the mystery together as the game went on. Loved it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: What a damn good narrative point-and-click game! A creepy and unsettling (but well-paced) story with a Wicker Man meets Wuthering Heights kinda vibe. I really enjoyed the voice acting, the pixel art, and the sound design - they combined to create a very tense, claustrophobic atmosphere. Some people took issue with the ending but I found it pretty thematically appropriate. Def don't go in expecting a happy ending
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Like others on this page, I wish there was a "sort of" option. I can't say I fully recommend Hob's Barrow, nor do I recommend staying away from it.This game is on a ridiculously slow burn. There's building atmosphere and then there's forcing players to trek around the same few screens for several hours, looking for the next plot thread.When things do eventually get going, it feels like too little, too late. Hob's Barrow has a nice little mystery at its core, but it needed to streamline itself significantly if it wanted to make an impact. As it is, the ending feels like a disappointing, unsatisfying payoff for too long a buildup.With that said, there's some nice atmosphere here, some of the characters are pretty likeable (although most of them don't really do anything as part of the plot), and some of the puzzles are decent. It's just all a bit too flabby and undisciplined for me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: tl,dr: Nice art, nice story, nice atmosphere, nice voice acting, shame about the utter absence of gameplay.Longer version: Times like this I wish Steam had more options than a Up or Down.  This is clearly a game with a lot of love in it and it does a lot of things really well.  The slow burn works very nicely for giving you a sense of the village and the people there and for producing a mood of isolation and mystery.  The environments are very well done and there's some genuinely excellent animations going on.  Meanwhile, the story is a well-told (if not particularly original) riff on Lovecraftian horror in the middle of England.  All of that stuff works pretty well.So why did I give it a thumbs down?  Because the puzzles are, to be frank, insultingly easy.  With the exception of one or two in the very last portion of the game there wasn't a single one I wasn't able to solve within about 30 seconds.  For an adventure game, that's a serious problem.  This isn't the 90's and I don't think developers should be able to get away with making adventure games that are so utterly lacking in anything resembling an actual puzzle.  It's especially annoying hear because the casting of the main character as an archeologist slowly uncovering a mystical world complete with its own internal mythology provides a lot of opportunities for puzzles that integrate into the story and build the world.  But the developers just don't do that.Finally, it must be said that the ending left me pretty cold.  ***MINOR SPOILERS*** It tries to do the standard Lovecraftian trope of protagonist confronting eldritch evil, with the predictable standard outcome, and it just didn't work for me.  Your mileage may vary.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Narrative-driven adventure done right,  goes from suspenseful to downright ghastly, with the in-between being filled with excellent writing, awesome presentation, and flawless atmosphere. Lovecraft meets Edgar Alan Poe, meets Pagan folk horror, in a point-and-click that won’t challenge your puzzle-solving skills, but will masterfully play with your mind, and force you follow the main heroine’s journey towards her inevitable demise. The actual game requires five or so hours. The experience will stay with you far longer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: If Wadjet Eye is involved, I buy. It hasn't failed me before and didn't fail me now. The game is great. Wonderful atmosphere, great voice acting and music, fun puzzles, lovely pixel graphics and more. Only complaint I have so far is that I can't use numbers to select dialogue choices that I know of. Very minor issue
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: First off wow, the story is a lot to take in and all of the characters just give you an eerie feeling the whole time.  Samantha Béart is wonderful in this title. They really play this role so naturally and I cant wait to see what else they play in. Seeing Them as Karlach was amazing and seeing them come from this to Karlach really shows their desire for acting. Back to the game through, there is many different parts where I didnt really know where it was going to go story wise and I was not ready for the ending. Kinda gave me conjuring 3 vibes but overall it was a great time. Wish we got a bit more answers to things like what happened to kenneth? Did he chicken out? Mr. Amberose, who did that to him and why? Did he know something others in the town didnt want him to say? If so why didnt he tell us if he was leaving anyway? As for the ending, Will the god get "revenge"? Revenge for what? It already possessed Thomasina to do those horrible things to her family, what more could it want? Would love to see more in the story if theres dlc or a 2.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend the game. Without spoiling the game, I feel like there were some holes in the story that I would have liked resolved for me. I am conflicted because it was a superb game, excellent interface, like all of the games produced by these guys. I love their games. The characters were great, the story was intense and scary, yet also just very likable linear storytelling. HOWEVER...I wanted more. And that is where my disappointment lies. I wanted a better ending, I wanted a better twist, a better story...a better resolution at the end. But we don't always get that and we have to sometimes just enjoy the ride for what it is.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Reminiscent of other horror point and clicks like Gabriel Knight, but simpler to follow in a good way. Engaging without being too frustrating. It offers gorgeous and unsettling visuals in equal parts. HB is not infinitely replayable (only one ending), but that is comforting in itself. Too much choice can make a story hollow and stressful to get through. 10/10 what I needed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: A very good indie adventure, but it fell short of being a classic for me.Pros:- Absolutely top tier voice acting. The main character is a stand-out, but it's uniformly excellent. The voice acting is complemented by strong writing, which feels natural and never breaks suspension of disbelief.- I loved the art style. The pixel animations are smooth and natural. It's a bit of a shame they rarely had anything more interesting to depict than a muddy village, though.- There are quite a few full-screen pixel art cutscenes that have a wonky, hand-drawn feel to them, which are perhaps the most successfully creepy part of the game.- The puzzles are solid, if a bit on the easy side. With a few exceptions, I rarely hit a wall. The puzzles are mostly common sense, and when you are close to what the game wants, it is good at giving a little nudge.- There are several subtle winks at the adventure genre peppered throughout. Early on, . Later in the game, .- The main character is named "Thomasina", and describes herself as "an antiquarian of some renown". How can you not want to play this?Cons:- The atmosphere never quite marshalled enough wrongness, menace, or horror to make my skin crawl. It hits the standard folk horror beats of an isolated English village that doesn't want you there, but it never felt hostile or weird enough to get under my skin.- The puzzles sometimes detract from the immersion. There are several times when the story seemed to pause for a fetch quest, and a bunch of otherwise realistic characters suddenly need Object A before they can give you Object B. Similarly, the endgame has many of the game's best puzzles, but in context they deflate the sense of horror the rest of the scenes are trying to build.- There are a lot of flashbacks, which are pretty similar and have little interactivity. They aren't bad, but I feel like half as many would have had the same affect.- Same goes for the dream sequences, which are a bit of a pet peeve of mine. They look and sound pretty, but they are a narrative crutch that never pack much of a punch.- The plot was a bit heavy handed for me. Most of the story beats are foreshadowed repeatedly, to the point where it doesn't make you feel smart...it makes the main character seem dumb. At one point,
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully atmospheric and well voiced. There's no doubt this adventure game will hook you for the mystery of Hobb's Barrow. Day 3 of playing I was committed to finding out what's inside there.The fairly short amount of puzzles felt fair. I never came across (for me) the usual 1 hour walking around blind trying to figure out what to do.One of those, the less you know the better games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly good classic-style point and click adventure with a folk horror and supernatural theme. It has all the Wadjet Eye Games quality standards with great scenarios, great voice acting and AMAZING narrative pacing. The puzzles are just in the perfect spot where they where challenging, but I never got stuck. I LOVED the ultra detailed (and unsettling) cutscenes animation. If you like this kind of adventures, you can't go wrong with this one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Loved this game, took me 14.6 hours of enjoyable screen time over about a week.  It's a great story and it wasn't like some games where you have over 20 items in your inventory so you end up trying crazy things just to move forward. In most cases, if you had an item in your inventory, there will be a need for it at some point.Thanks Cloak and Dagger for a great game, set in my favourite part of the world.... would love to know if  "Hob Hursts House" in Derbyshire was the origin for the name?
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Great story, great voice acting and just unsettling enough for me. The puzzles were intuitive and I didn't ever feel the need to pixel hunt. This works perfectly on the Steam Deck; just watch the default binding of Quick Load to one of the back buttons!I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone up for an old-school point and click adventure without the old-school obtuse puzzles!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: What a joy to play!There is a long list of things to praise this game for, but, I need to start out by saying that the voice acting throughout this game is some of the best I have had the pleasure of listening to. As a Northern lass, I absolutely adored listening to the accents of the residents of Bewlay.The setting is also so accurate to so many little villages throughout Northern England, that Im pretty sure Ive driven through a "Bewlay" at least once. Its a lovely, idyllic, quaint theme which runs beautifully as a backdrop for the story. As for the story itself, it is a wonderful slow burn of a tale, with excellent pacing throughout. It at no point feels slow, and nothing ever feels like filler. It gives you just enough information at a time to keep you intrigued and keep you progressing, but cleverly conceals the twists and secrets of whats to come. The puzzle aspect is nothing overly complex, and although I did have a few occasions of pacing back and forth trying to work out what I had missed, I never felt frustrated or in need of a guide. Everything you need is there waiting to be found, even if on occasion you do need to think outside the box. An utter pleasure to play. Highly recommended
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Very enjoyable experience, especially if you're in a Halloween mood. I wouldn't say that any of it is outright scary, except for maybe the final scene in the game. It ventures more into establishing a strong creepy atmosphere than trying to outright shock you. Very well written characters, with the protagonist especially being enjoyable. Wonderful pixel art as well. I do have some minor complaints though aimed towards the game's length, and pacing towards the finale. There are a few loose ends that are never really explained as well. Overall, a very enjoyable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game and would absolutely recommend it to any fans of point and click, horror, and overall narrative. I have a minor quibble that I'll mention at the end, but overall I loved it.The atmosphere of the game is fantastic. The pixel graphics are great and serve the whole vibe - there's something extra horrifying about pared down graphics, the way your mind fills in the blanks. This was especially apparent in the amazing cut scenes, which were all super spooky. I loved the rain, the fog, the cozy inn, just absolutely fantastic art direction here. I wouldn't have minded seeing a few more interiors! The puzzles were really well-balanced - challenging without being so hard you resort to Googling. I loved the premise of going into the character's memories. I thought it was great character building and a powerful narrative device. And the voice acting was top notch.Minor spoilers ahead.QUIBBLE: Ditch the retrospective interjections from future Thomasina. The game and setting had enough foreboding to make you leery of the direction you were headed, without sad future Thomasina piping in to say, essentially, "Everything I did in this game turned out to be a mistake." The possibility of a bad future is scary, the certainty of it is depressing.  I get the purpose of this device - to give all the action a feeling of inexorable doom. But it put me the player at odds with the main character, which made the gameplay feel a little compulsory. Why was I playing a game where I knew the character was doomed? This could be an interesting philosophical question, but it didn't feel that way. It just left me less emotionally engaged than I would have been otherwise. Also, with all the retrospective doom, I'd basically guessed how the game would turn out. So it spoiled the ending a little, which otherwise would have been truly shocking. That's really my only issue with an otherwise phenomenal game. Looking forward to more from Cloak and Dagger, and hoping their back catalog becomes available for Mac.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: While the game was generally decent, classic point & click adventures are all about the story, and this one just wasn't that great. A lot of mystery was built up for what felt like an extremely boring payoff at the end leaving the whole thing feeling empty.That being said, I guess I'd recommend this to people who don't mind an unfulfilling story, and just want some point and click puzzles, of which this game had decent ones that could be solved using logic up until the last chapter at which point it falls into arbitrary escape room puzzle nonsense. I'll also say that the game had good voice acting, decent visuals and substantially good music.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loving this game, Cloak and Dagger have a strong history of making really interesting point and click adventure games but Hob's Barrow is on another level. I'm about three hours in and seeing as these reviews help the game get more reach on Steam figured I'd write an early one.Super unsettling atmosphere throughout, great voice acting, lovely animated backgrounds and super creepy full screen FMV style shots that really do add a lot to the experience. Can't wait to find out more of the story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: What an outstanding game! I came across it by chance a few days ago and have been obsessed since, not only buying the game but also the spectacular, eerie soundtrack as soon as I finished watching the trailer. (Having fallen in love with the game so immensely I bought the digital artbook a day later which is absolutely worth it too, consindering how cheap it is.)The artstyle is loving and very detailed for pixel art. You can really tell how much effort and passion went into this, especially in the cutscenes. The beautiful backgrounds are so well done and recognisable that I never got lost even on my first playthrough. It made it very easy to remember exactly where certain places were and how to get there even without fast travel.I really appreciated that the typical point&click riddles were mostly very logical and not too hard to figure out. I only got stuck on two for a somewhat prolonged time.The characters, oh my god, I love them. Again, every single one very recoginsable by design alone. The writing of these characters is fantastic. I felt like I really got to know them in this short time and they felt like actual real people you would meet in a rural area.The voice acting in this game is outstanding! Everything is fully voiced and so well done too!Samantha Béart has done a stellar job as the voice of main character and narrator Thomasina Bateman. Not only have they given Thomasina a feisty and passionate (and at times desperate) voice that so perfectly sums up Thomasina’s personality but they’ve also done a perfect job of giving me the shivers in every narration scene with their gloomy and sorrowful line delivery, that kept me going for hours, wanting to find out what was really going on in that village.I personally find that the game has much replay value. (I’ve completed the game two times, once unspoiled, a second time to collect my missing achievements and to experience the Developer Commentary.) It is mind-boggling how much visual and auditory (soundtrack and sound effects) storytelling there is aside from the obvious storytelling. So many subtle details that I kept noticing even until the end of my second playthrough which, really, makes me want to play the game a third time.The soundtrack is just beautiful, moody, eerie and atmospheric. I’ve been re-listening to it since. I’m especially in love with the 12th track „Changeling“ which even has lyrics! It’s safe to say that I’ll be thinking about this game for a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: After anticipating this game for a long time, I finally started & finished it in the last 2 days. The main strong points of this game are the voiceover quality and the music. Overall I'd recommend it (for maybe around 8 to 10 dollars), but this review will contain major *spoilers* so don't read more if you don't want to risk ruining the plot.Most of the game involves dialogue. You talk to this person and that person, sometimes for up to 5 minutes at a time before moving on. There are objects you gather along the way, some of which come in handy multiple times, others of which disappear after using. That's sort of typical of adventure games. Most puzzles are on the easy side, which I appreciated since I hate getting stumped to the point of frustration. The only puzzle I had to look up was regarding .The game is 75% build-up and 25% pay-off, and in the end I've got to say the build-up was better than the pay-off. Most "puzzles" were spread out across multiple people, where one request leads to a sub-request. Anyway, I digress. Catch it on sale and it's a nice 4 to 9 hour game depending on your pace. Personally, though, I'd recommend some of Wadget's other games more highly than this one. Really liked Gemini Rue.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: scratches that particular point & click itch. however, for the largest part, the "riddles" leave something to be desired. most of the time you're stuck, it's because you haven't (re-)visited all places and clicked through all items and dialog options. there's hardly any need for deduction or outside the box thinking. that changes with the final act, which requires some degree of investigation of your own, and i loved that. cloak and dagger/wadjeteye know how to end on a high note, because that last hour or so really turned the worm for me. i'll definitely check their back catalogue and upcoming titles now.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a solid adventure game experience though I was a little disappointed in the main character being completely oblivious to some the things going on in the story. The use of flashbacks helped to further the story as well and clue you in on details that you wouldn't know otherwise. No soft locks (as far as I can tell) and the puzzles weren't overly difficult, though sometimes trying to figure where you needed to go was a bit of a challenge. Overall, I'd recommend it for the interesting story, solid pixel graphics, well done voice acting, and solid puzzles. I believe that any adventure game fan would enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: This game offered what I been longing for and wanting from many AAA titles yet all managed to fail those expectations. Makes me wonder why we are getting such great games only in point n click pixel art format despite having much better engines to create it in - maybe one day even larger studios will revert to creating such games, until then the pixel art is what must suffice...but heck, it will be well worth it if we'll be getting true gems such as this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Another quality point & click adventure published by Wadjet Eye. Most of the games made by WE are on the easy side of puzzle scale and this one developed by Cloak and Dagger isn't much different from the "in-house" games. However, the mood, writing and especially voice acting is top notch and this game is no different in that sense and although this isn't one of the best works in WE catalogue (Blackwell-series for example is phenomenal), this certainly ticks all the boxes of quality adventure game.This is a horror game set in late 19th century with heavy lovecraftian vibes, something I'd like to see much more in adventure games in general. I got the game from the Humble Bundle choice and played it through in couple of evenings. It is not a long game, but for such a title it is of almost perfect length and it doesn't over welcome its stay. Highly recommended and as the puzzles are mostly logical and easy, it is perfectly suitable for beginners of the genre too.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Works on steam deck, except for touch control. Use controller sticks instead.The Excavation of Hob's Barrow is a classic point and click adventure that captures the spirit of lovecraftian story telling at its core. While the gameplay itself doesn't reinvent the wheel, it is serviceable and sufficient enough to carry forward the compelling narrative adventure that is the core of what this game is about. From the protagonist, to the atmosphere and setting, it is an exemplary display of how to do lovecraftian horror right. It showed just enough.  The art is beautiful and disturbing. There has truly never been an uglier cat in gaming then the ones drawn here. Perhaps some of the narrative choices could have been more complex, but this story excels at telling a stellar linear horror that can genuinely disturb the soul. 4/5
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: A shallow game, built around good artwork.Most buildings are locked or inaccessible.It gives you the illusion of choice, but drives you back to the intended dialog.Good voice acting for the most part, but the writing is pretty awful.All in all, it provided some nostalgia for the Sierra and LucasArts days, but provides little substance to meet the standards of those forebears.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Oh my god, what a DELIGHT it was to play this!I was pretty sure after the first few glimpses of the trailer alone that this could be my cuppa tea, but I didn't expect it to be THIS PERFECT. Seldom have I witnessed a game SO immersive!The atmosphere is so thick that I would like to spread my toast with it and then cram it all in my mouth! Yummy! - Most lovecraftian MOVIE productions could learn a thing or two from this!The writing was intriguing and more than competent, the voice acting was superb all the way through, and the brilliantly beautiful - and sometimes unexpectantly creepy - pixelized art style did the rest.I'm fully amazed about the perfect storm of AWESOME this game came out to be.After I could begin to see the ending moving closer, I was beginning to expect that AT LEAST THE ENDING would let me down BIG, and would still find a way to mess everything up, as games this good usually do.But let's just say - it didn't. What a wonderful, chilly ride this was to the very end.Didn't regret buying this full price - and that means A LOT coming from someone who ALWAYS waits for a cheap bundle before committing to buying any Steam game.Not so here. Loved the trailer. Bought the game right away. Played it straight through.(Was hella proud about finding out where the pastor kept his secret key.)Loved every minute.Fullest recommendation!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Wadjet Eye Games is a synonym for really, really good adventures. Even if they are just involved as a publisher, usually you can expect a really high quality. This one is the very first I absolutely did not enjoy. The story is very generic and boring. The culprits are the ones you think they are and there are no layers to it. Most characters remain dull and lifeless and the strong heroine is purely defined by one thing. Daddy issues. I hated her.Day 2 of the game consists merely of fetch quests. Day 3 is introducing riddles for the first time, however so boring and uninspired you either need 5 seconds or a guide for it. Voice acting is good, graphics too, the rest is just not really worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzles aren't hugely challenging, mainly because they are largely logical (which isn't necessarily a bad thing). Even if you find the lack of challenge disappointing, this game makes up for it in the entertaining, if predictable, story, compelling setting, beautiful pixel art style and excellent voice acting. Overall, a fun adventure game I would recommend to any fan of the genre, particularly those who enjoy folk and Lovecraftian fiction, but don't expect to get stuck on any of the puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Beat this charming game today! I thought "hmm i'm gonna go through the saves again to get the rest of the achievements i don't have", but then i found out there is an in game developer commentary so naturally i'll play it again entirely! Thanks to the people involved for creating this adventure, loved it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: A great point-and-click adventure with an old-school horror vibe. The storytelling is good, the atmosphere excellent. The game isn't all horror all the time, but gradually builds foreboding as the story continues. The puzzles are generally good (although a couple are a bit too circuitous), and a few are inspired.The sort of game where you finish it, then add half the developer's back catalogue to your wishlist.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow is an excellent old-school point-and-click adventure game.Unlike many older examples of the genre this game manages to almost completely avoid moon logic with its puzzles and I never once got stuck or had to refer to a walkthrough. On the other hand the puzzles may be somewhat on the easier side. However, in the case of this game I consider that to be a positive as the puzzles don't get in the way of the pacing of the plot.And what a plot! The framing of the story as something that the protagonist is narrating after the fact let's us know that she'll make it out of this adventure alive. But it's clear she did not make it out unharmed or unchanged. And this leaves us with the uncomfortable knowledge that we're walking down a dark path and there's nothing we can do about it except observe and with a touch of futility hope for the best.The music and soundscape adds to the oppressive atmosphere. And it's impressive that game manages to be so atmospheric with such simple presentation. As even though the pixel art is very well done it's ultimately nothing that special. However there are certain scenes that are rendered in a different and more realistic style with more fluid (possibly rotoscoped) animation. And that only further adds to the uncanny and overall creepy atmosphere.In summary this is a fantastic example of the genre that manages to tell an interesting and compelling story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Pay no heed to other reviews dismaying at the ending - never was there a conclusion more true to the lovecraftian theme.This game is above all, atmospheric. The music is fitting, the voice acting is excellent, and the story is most compelling, aided by some truly marvelous characterization. Those who love mystery and horror need look no further for their next adventure. The puzzles are charming and fun, while not stepping too far away from the narrative. This game was, in a word, "Capital!"
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. I hadn't read any reviews of it but after seeing some of the the screenshots I thought there was something about it. What a find! Don't let the old-school graphics put you off - if you are a fan of folk horror this will be right up your street. Excellent sound design, an intriguing story, and very easy to play, this is a must buy if it this sounds at like something you would like.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: THEMATIC SPOILERS. Many others have faulted the lack of agency. whatever, the game decided to present one ending, to present the protagonist as becoming increasingly obsessed, that's fine, that's the story. It's ok to be a visual novel.I just...don't want anyone else to experience the same story? The ending just felt like it didn't earn the time that goes into playing a game. If it's going to be dark, BE DARK. The darkness that's implied is shown, but that darkness is given an agency to enact a horrific act, the motivations of which are tenuous at best.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: I only recommend this game because of the art style and tone. The art and set pieces are wonderful. The cutscenes are unnerving and I love the animation style. The tone is certainly unnerving and everything. Really nailed the music and sounds.The voice acting is also great. There is much to like about this game.That being said, it is a real bummer that you meet all these characters, but the game is a straight shot to the end. None of the characters go through any arcs. There is no time. The story needs to be at minimum 3x its current length for any characters to experience an arc.That would be a lot more work for the developer, obviously. I can't imagine the peril they went through getting their vision on screen with the budget they had. So much hard work, I'm sure, and lovingly crafted.That being said, it is just a short sprint to the end. You do a few errands / puzzles to get access to the main plot and then it's over.You meet so many characters. I was anticipating a few more scenes with each.Also, you make some choices to lie or be truthful to some characters. I had to make a choice maybe 5 different times. It did not seem to affect anything in the slightest. I betrayed the priest's trust and the following day he asked me not to do it again. That was it. No actual consequences. Nothing came of lying to the other characters.Puzzles were decent. Not amazing, but not lacking, either.I really want to drive home that a short quick shot to the end. No character development. You don't interact with anyone enough to see them go through an arc.I will be more cautious buying from this developer again. It would take much more effort to flesh this game out they way I think it deserves. I did not enjoy the absolute brevity.But, wonderful art style. Great tone. Immersive set pieces. I do not regret giving this dev my money. Hope they make a much more realized product next time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: This point-and-click horror/mystery game has been simply breathtaking to play! The small rural town with distrustful bunch of locals, the mystery of the barrow that slowly unravels over the course of the game, the interesting group of side characters, a creeping sense of dread, and some of the best voice acting I've ever seen in a game. The puzzles are good and mostly make sense. I really enjoyed it! From time to time the game also shows you detailed close ups with a really cool art style which I really like. Spoiler for the ending:
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent creepy point and click game with great QoL features (teleport through the [discovered] map portions, double click to teleport to an exit, etc.), and a good (albeit a bit predictable) story. I loved the pacing, how the story was told and unfolded, the overall atmosphere.All topped with excellent voice acting.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: A ridiculously good point & click adventure that managed to grasp me from start to finish with a scenic setting I don't even really like. This is also one of the best games in Wadjet Eye's library, one I can recommend many games of. Something I want to highlight is the absolutely incredible voice work The Excavation of Hob's Barrow offers. Samantha Béart's performance as the main character is the best I have ever heard in an adventure game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice point and click adventure game in the tradition of what wadjet produces and/or publishes otherwise. Not too long, took me 5 hours to finish and i needed external help maybe twice or three times, so not too hard. Very well done atmosphere of subtle dread, nice voiceacting and cool soundtrack. Worth your money!
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best adventure games I've played in a long time. Excellent writing, and exquisite voice acting. I found the story to be nearly perfectly paced and filled with wonderful characters. It was creepy and mysterious in all the right ways throughout. The ending was bold and evocative of recent folk horror films and classic fiction of eldritch horror. Puzzles are very light. Those looking for a challenge should look elsewhere. Overall, highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

_childDocuments_.review: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow is a folk horror narrative-driven adventure. Explore the isolated moors of rural Victorian England as you uncover the mysteries of Hob's Barrow. The answers lie in the soil...
_childDocuments_.name: The Excavation of Hob's Barrow

name: Impostor Factory
detailed_description: Wishlist the series' Beach Episode! (seriously, it's a thing.) Where it all began: About the Game ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Impostor Factory is a narrative-driven adventure game that is categorically out of its mind. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Dr. Watts and Dr. Rosalene have peculiar jobs: They give people another chance to live their lives, all the way from the very beginning. But this isn't their story. Probably. Instead, it's about Quincy . Let me tell you a story about him. One day, Quincy was invited to a fancy parteh at a suspiciously secluded mansion. So, he accepted and went; because even though the mansion was suspicious and secluded, it was also fancy and had a parteh. In fact, it turned out to be so fancy that there was a time machine in its bathroom. Quincy could wash his hands and time-travel while he was at it. Talk about a time-saver! But of course, then people start dying, because that's what they do. And somewhere along the way, things get a little Lovecraftian and tentacles are involved. Anyway, that's around 1/3 of what the game is really about. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Key Features A story that will make you curse at the screen A cozy mix between adventure game elements and classic RPG aesthetics Dialogues that read so wrong but feel so right An espresso execution with zero filler and no time drains long cat ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- F.A.Q.: Q: Is playing To the Moon and Finding Paradise mandatory before playing this game? A: Impostor Factory can be played independently, just like the games before it. But the order of playing would affect the experience. Q: Is Impostor Factory the sequel to To the Moon and Finding Paradise? A: Maybe not. Maybe it's a sequel. Maybe it's a prequel. Maybe it's both.

short_description: A bonkers time-loop tragicomedy murder mystery thriller featuring multiple casualties and a suspicious cat, from the creator of To the Moon & Finding Paradise.

_childDocuments_.review: The story shows that not everything in life is as black and white as we perhaps hope it to be, ♥♥♥♥ does happen and people make mistakes, but in doing so the story manages to successfully capture a ‘slice of life’, to which in my opinion the player can greatly relate on a sentimental level.Overall a well written story and unique ‘overlapping’ way how the player gets to experience this.I do want to point out that as this series progresses with these (more or less) individual stories (that still connect with each other), it becomes increasingly more a story the player gets to  and quite literally ‘walk through’ while watching + reading, rather than it being a game with any challenges or exploration options. This in contrast to, for example, , where there were also parts like Dr. Watts and Dr. Rosalene getting to ride a horse, or explore a part of the fair – which I especially liked because it also had a ‘surprising’ element to it without breaking storyline or being too challenging.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: If you played first two games, you must play this one. It's good. It's really good. First 2 hours are just pure brain harassment and it's awesome. Ending.... Well... They tried... They tried really well... But they lost atmosphere. Anyway this game is cool. It's not better than previous two... But anyway must have.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: First of all: this is not a standalone game. If you have not played To the Moon or Finding Paradise (and all the other games?) you will not understand the significance of a lot of the ending.I've played the previous two games, but so long ago that I could barely remember the overarching lore. I'm not sure that To The Moon really needs an overarching plot. Small, episodic games centered on human stories would have been enough. But it especially didn't need  game, that starts with an interesting premise that gets dumped fairly early on just to give you the origin story of one of the characters in the previous games.And that's essentially what this game is: an origin story for one of the To The Moon characters. You might be moved by some of what happens, although it's all meaningless in the end as we rehash the idea of what makes something real or not. And like the previous games, we end up following a romance between two straight characters where one of them has some form of insurmountable problem. I honestly was hoping the romance was a fake-out, or a missed opportunity, because it was so cliched. Quincy was basically a manic pixie dream boy with no real personality. It's honestly a shame, because I did want to solve a time looping murder mystery, and that was the most interesting part of the game. In the end, there was no mystery at all, just a trip through grief town and long exposition about the world's "lore."

_childDocuments_.review: this game is not a murder mystery thriller, it is a sci-fi and romance (but honestly mainly romance) sequel to a different game.the description repeats the fact that you can play this game without having played the others from this creator, but that is really not the case. they go through all the effort of introducing two characters and making them fall in love only to pull the plug at the end and make it all about some other couple who are apparently their kids??? not that the story of quincy and lynri is that good in the first place- okay i guess if you like romantic stories about life and scrapbook-like beautiful memories and a bit of bitterweetness then this might be the game for you. but the reason i bought this game is because it marketed itself as a time-looping murder mystery, which it is not at all. it starts out like that but the mystery is dropped after its introduction to go on about the romance. either way lynri reveals that its all a simulation anyway so theres no more intrigue and you just go along with the rest of the story because they got you with the hook. they loop back around to it in the end with this tense suspense because lynri suspects something bad is going on with her memory machine but then this angel??? with tentacles???? breaks the machine???? and also the earth???? so really the game does not try at all to deliver on the mystery, instead it seems to get bored and start to shoehorn in a fluffy lovey plotline. they also show the life and growing up sequence of lynri so many times with only slight changes it really made me bored. i left this game feeling confused and wondering if i had accidentally launched the wrong game because it really was not what i was expecting. some people might find this game to be a pleasant surprise but some people like me will not. a lot of the positive reviews on here are from fans of the creator which is great. but this game did not make me want to play the other games.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought the game the minute it released and literally just finished it so these are my raw unslept on thoughts on Imposter Factory.Spoiler Free Part:General:IF differentiates itself significantly from 'to the moon' and 'finding paradise' in many regards; the tone, story structure and narrative have taken a drastic turn in this game. There are a couple of other significant changes but those i'll address in the spoiler section. It also really shows that the delays weren't for nothing, the game feels very polished, the narrative progresses a lot smoother than the previous entries, the soundtrack transitions are smoother as well and the art also took  a step up.Story:As we can all now expect from Kan and his team, the writing, the dialogue, and the humour are all fantastic. Also particularly in this game the atmosphere is very engrossing. Where I feel like its predecessors took the more slow start approach, IF hooks you immediately and doesn't let you go. IF has the best start of the series and maybe even the best act 2, where I'm not so sure though is its ending (more on that in the spoiler part). The story beats are very fast paced for the series, I definitely lost track of time while playing.Soundtrack:AMAZINGI don't recommend you play this game if you haven't played the previous 2 entries, you won't be able appreciate it fully.If you've enjoyed the previous 2 entries in the series, this gets a definite recommendation from me.Spoiler Part:So this has been kind of a rollercoaster for me, this wasn't at all what I expected, chapeau to you Freebird Games for the red herrings pre-release.Biggest shock firstly is that Neil and Eva the previous protagonists are not in the game until the end and then only as memories and then they're mostly simulated at that. This I imagine may be offputting to some fans of the series as everyone has grown to love the pair. We do get answers though to a lot of questions we've had from previous games, especially concerning Neil, these I felt were all very satisfying and well presented. What I find difficult to evaluate is regarding the game as a part of the series. We get this whole emotional montage of Neil growing up and being with Eva, getting married and having a kid, but those are just a simulation for Neil's parents and not congruent with reality. In a vacuum and certainly while playing, this was a very good and emotional moment but then you consider that this is even less(?) real than the fake memories from the previous games. This goes along with the theme of the series of living in a better reality and all that but at the end of the day it doesn't develop the main characters of the series. While writing this it occurs to me that that reality certainly isn't going to happen, which raises the question of how the series will continue. Yes this is NOT the last game in the series as some people have speculated. What may happen is that the series will take a big turn with Neil having completed(?) the machine with Faye but there are still more unanswered questions, which is further accentuated with the post-credits scene. I'm glad that Kan and the team take their time to deliver us these games with the love and polish of no other piece of media I've ever consumed but I'd lie if I said that it isn't agonizing having to wait another couple of years to get to the possible conclusion of the main story. Thank you Freebird Games for making such a beautiful game.

_childDocuments_.review: is more than just a game—it’s a beautifully crafted emotional journey that had me crying four separate times. It’s a story of love, loss, and introspection that resonated deeply with me. The themes hit so close to home that I felt like the game was peeling back layers of my own life, revealing moments I thought I’d tucked away.The pixel art is charming, creating a nostalgic atmosphere that perfectly complements the story’s deeper themes. And the music? Absolutely stunning. Kan Gao’s genius is in full force here, with each melody amplifying the emotional beats to an almost unbearable degree. His ability to pair the story with such moving music is nothing short of masterful—it’s the kind of soundtrack that stays with you long after you put the game down.While some of the memories and walking sections felt slow at times, they had a purpose. They created space for the story to sink in, allowing each emotional moment to hit even harder. Even when I wished for a faster pace, I understood why the game needed to take its time—it was part of the experience, making the eventual gut-punches land with even more impact. is a testament to Kan Gao’s storytelling and musical brilliance. He has a way of making you laugh, cry, and reflect deeply—all in one sitting. 10/10—a stunning, unforgettable journey of heartache, hope, and genius-level storytelling that I’d revisit any day, tissues in hand.

_childDocuments_.review: Short Version: Not super necessary to play unless you already were a fan of To The Moon and Finding Paradise. Still an amazing story, but it probably won't mean as much to you if you haven't played and enjoyed those games prior.Long (and slightly more spoilery) Version: Another fantastically told story by Kan Gao! As per tradition, Gao is the master of telling the tale of a person's entire life, while subjecting the player to the full weight of the emotions that come with that. Impostor Factor delivers in this regard, but while the previous two games used the story of a person's life as a medium to convey a much deeper message about the purpose of life and happiness, this game uses it more to delve into a weird (but fascinating) sci-fi rabbit hole about existence. This means that the ending probably won't hit you quite as hard as TTM's or FP's did, but that doesn't at all make it a bad story. I still very much appreciate Kan for telling this particular story, even if it was probably a risky decision to do so, and I enjoyed every minute of it. Also fun fact: This game gave me chills 31 times. I kept count. All of that is to say that while the story of Impostor Factory is told in the same *style* as Kan's other games, its purpose isn't exactly the same, and that can be a little surprising to the player as the game draws near its ending (some might call it anticlimactic for that reason; I'd disagree). Even so, this game is still a profoundly moving experience, a wonderfully-crafted story, and an amazing edition into the Sigmund Corp series. I sincerely hope there will be more to come in the future!(Also Kan, if you're reading this, please don't be afraid to take risks. I think this game paid off big because of it, and I love having my expectations subverted by your masterful grasp of storytelling. Thank you!)

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Impostor Factory is a solid continuation to “To the Moon'' saga, and I would highly recommend it for all fans of the series.The game tells its story this time using mostly a different set of characters, but it does a good job extending the world established by the two prequels. Like with the prequels, the story was highly engaging with its mysteries and twists, and the emotional payoff is definitely there at the end.The gameplay is even more simplistic than before, but in my opinion it only improves with the pacing of the storytelling - you are probably here for the story and feels anyway.A shout out for the soundtrack is also in order - the music is what really makes some of the emotional moments even more impactful.

_childDocuments_.review: Upon recently finishing this game, I can safely say it is a great game and at least the 2nd best in the series (possible 1st best, but that will take time for my opinion to mature). The story does appear to be comparatively shorter, but I think that's to its benefit.The game does not attempt to force game mechanics like the orb puzzle in "To the Moon." On top of that, it removes most of the padding and has you focus on the grander scheme of each scene rather than the scene itself. For example, multiple scenes will feature minimal dialogue as it's not important to convey the message.This can be a detriment to a scene's emotional impact, but I found the increased pacing to outweigh its negatives.Essentially, if you find the price worth it for a 3-4 hour enjoyably wild narrative, then I highly recommend this game.However, I do highly suggest you play "To the Moon" and "Finding Paradise" first.

_childDocuments_.review: I am very disappointed. I loved To The Moon so much, that it didn't make sense. I just knew I was going to be disappointed with Finding Paradise because the experience had in To The Moon is not something you can recreate just by trying and with talent. Well, I was wrong. Finding Paradise was quite amazing. I mean, I personally still enjoyed To The Moon more, but that is not something I can really fault Finding Paradise for. With some aspects of To The Moon, the writers were still finding their groove. It had really good dialogue, and even when nothing at all was happening, the dialog was just so good it carried even the dull moments. But they hadn't fully mastered that yet. By the time they wrote Finding Paradise, they had mastered that skill. Everything about the marketing (game description, trailer) for Imposter Factory leads one to believe this game is going to lean on that skill, taking the humor, whit, and fun aspects of the previous two games to the next level and focusing on them more. It made me think they were going to try something different with this game. Instead it was all a lie. It had less, not more of the witty dialog. Except unlike the previous games, it actually needed lots of witty dialog to carry it since most of it is a little boring. I mean, it still had some whit, but not enough to carry it. All the stuff that seemed totally bonkers and fun turned out not to be. I was looking forward to enjoying unraveling the mystery of what was going on, why the bathroom sync was or seemed like a time machine, why people kept dyeing and clones were appearing, what was up with the cat. The answers that were there were largely such unoriginal, copout letdowns that I am almost offended. And this game had even less game to it than the previous ones. I mean, it's not that big of a deal because these games were always just a story presented in a game format, but still. I think this game in particular could have benefited from some actual gameplay, something requiring you to solve time paradox puzzles, requiring you to figure out what was happening in the game in order to solve the puzzles, perhaps with a humorous twist on the puzzle logic at times. The art and music are very nice in this game, but that didn't really accomplish much since there wasn't a great story to provide a purpose for the art and music. I know some people were very moved by this story, so it's still very subjective. But I still think it was a huge letdown not to let the story play out as it was instead of just explaining it all away like they did. I wanted to see how you were going to prove yourself innocent. The only great thing about this game was Ricebot. It needed more Ricebot, bathroom sync time traveling, and murder mystery solving. It felt like they were trying to combine too many different styles into a single story, none of it meshed well, and none of it was amazing like the previous games. It was also too short. Believe me, for me to complain that a game like this was too short means something was very wrong. I like for these types of games to be short, I don't want it to be needlessly stretched out or to get bored with slight variations over time of the same thing. But even with how much of a letdown this game was for me, it was still somewhat enjoyable. I wasn't ready for it to be over so quickly, it just felt very quick to me. The other game didn't feel that way despite technically being short games. The trailer made it seem like part of this game was about a concert in space put on by the characters from the other games. But that wasn't even in the game. I'm confused, it looked like gameplay footage. Maybe it was from the other games and I just don't remember it, but it still left me feeling cheated. The concert seemed cool and hilarious. I want my concert!

_childDocuments_.review: Much like Freebird's previous games in this series, Impostor Factory takes you on a touching and emotional story through a person's life, but this one has a bit of a twist in the way that it is structured. This difference is interesting and for the most part well done, although it does feel a little overwritten at times, especially in the third act. Without going into spoilers, Impostor Factor's story sticks out to me as the most emotional, and probably best written of the series so far. There's some moments in this game that really had me tearing up. The writing here is absolutely superb in the second act and this is where the game shines. The third act is a bit all over the place since it tries do a lot, and at times it can feel a bit of a mess but it manages to still pull off a satisfying and heartfelt ending. The pixel graphics are beautifully done as are all of the games by Freebird, but it really stood out to me this game. They really fit the tone of this game much better then previous ones I think due to the horror feeling that parts of this game fall under. If you enjoyed the previous games in this series then you'll love Impostor Factory as it is very much more of the same. If you haven't played the previous games I highly recommend playing them before this one as a big part of this story relies on previous knowledge to be effective. For more reviews, follow my

_childDocuments_.review: I am seriously saddened to give this a not recommended, but the truth is I really wouldn't tell someone "You need to play this!".  But if you do play it at least make sure you play Finding Paradise first or you will be missing out on bits of info that does make this game a bit more interesting since this game seems to be more aimed at the 'broader story'.For a game that's all about the story, this really wasn't satisfying, I watched the end that was passed the credits and thought "oh boy now we get into the juicy stuff" and the game just ended. Sure the journey that led up to it started with a nice bit of mystery, followed with some heart wrenching bits and a small mix of comedy mixed in but the plot was far too predictable, it was far too rushed and it felt like there was very little development to make me care. If we ignore the story for the time being, the soundtrack is really good, I still prefer Finding paradise and still listen to the OST now and then, I don't think I'll be doing that with this one. The gameplay is non existant, think of it as a walking sim but I wouldn't say that's a bad thing. The visuals are much the same altho there were a couple scenes that had some really well drawn full screen cutscenes. Overall like others have said much the same thing but this feels more like a minisode and not a full episode, and I think that's what's made me feel so meh about it. In short, your millage may vary, a good story but don't expect the same greatness as the previous installments.

_childDocuments_.review: = Spoilerrific. You've been warned. =All through high school and college I was grappling with the loss of my religion, and my ability to believe in an afterlife. I cursed the world for not having something like a 'soul' to allow life to persist indefinitely, to preserve the essence of our being. I wondered then what it would take to create a soul, and a heaven out of billions of entwined memories. I knew there were other people out there who thought similar things, but it's just not the sort of thing that normally comes up. You never hear the proof.In this game, I just did.This game is phenomenal, both as a finale to this series and as a standalone work of art. The concepts it contains are absolutely revolutionary in how they capture the things millions of us feel, but few of us know how to express. The ride it takes to get there is as charmingly humorous and full of life as the explanation, too, and even though it isn't 'real,' it weighs the heart too much for the mind to care.If anyone ever says that beautiful dreams and the bounty of the human imagination are unequal to the majesty of the natural world, please show them this. There will never be greater proof that what the human mind can conceive of is as enduring and brilliant in its beauty as anything that may be called truth.Thank you so much, Freebird. I'll cherish these stories always. I only hope I can make my own answer to it all someday, and that it will reach you.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: This is another very quality game from the geniuses at Freebird. Story and music don't quite reach the heights of past entries, but they stand well on their own. Recommended to all fans of the franchise.Rubric:Story and Characters:    45 pointsMusic:                             35 pointsAesthetics:                      20 pointsFinal score rounded to nearest 5 pointsFirst I normally start by talking about gameplay, which is worth 40 points on my 100 point rubric, however there are no real gameplay mechanics to speak of in this game; it's almost exclusively walking around and interacting with stuff, thus I have reallocated those 40 points to the remaining 3 categories. Story and characters:Story structure in this series has always been interesting. From starting at the end of the patient's life in To The Moon to the decaying orbit structure of Finding Paradise, Imposter Factory manages to have an incredibly intense and trippy opening act, followed by another structure we haven't followed before, then ending with a great (if not gut-punching) final act. It's great to see the well of creativity has not dried up yet.As for characters, there are plenty of great moments with the minor characters. The sense of humor this series has fortunately has also not missed a beat. While our two new main characters may not necessarily be as interesting or compelling as others we've seen, they are still well written...for the most part (seriously, what elderly woman would say their animal "protecc"? Even people who know that meme probably wouldn't actually *say* it). Even the ones who don't get much screen time still manage to be quirky and fun for whatever time we see them.8/10 "Very Good"(36/45)Music:The soundtrack is extremely good; each song fits each scene perfectly even though I don't think I would say any of the songs here are "iconic" like For River from To The Moon or Wish My Life Away from Finding Paradise, however the use of cello here *really* elevates many of the songs here, mostly the ones that play during sad scenes. On its own I would give the soundtrack an 8.5, however I'm elevating it a half point due to the truly masterful sound design. The beats that drop when a line of dialogue is shown where you'll start putting the plot's puzzle pieces together really add extra oomph to those scenes. It's just too bad we couldn't have had any lyrical tracks.9/10 "Amazing"(31.5/35)Aesthetics:This game is absolutely gorgeous. I seriously stopped in quite a few places just to admire the beauty of many of the backgrounds. The sprites look excellent as always too. The pause menu is pretty basic, but that's pretty inconsequential in the grand scheme of things. Absolutely the best looking game in the series.9.5/10 "Phenomenal"(19/20)Verdict:Even if its characters fall a bit short and its music may not be too iconic, Impostor Factory still manages to stand on its own two feet as a great game. It may only be 3-5 hours, but it was still worth every penny, and I think those who enjoyed the previous Sigmund Corp games will feel the same way.

_childDocuments_.review: I think to sum this game up is that it wasn't as good as the previous two entries, but it wasn't bad. If you go in expecting another experience like To the Moon or Finding Paradise you might come away a little disappointed, because Impostor Factory is a little different.The game has somewhat of a drawn out opening involving visiting some rich people's party, murders, and a time loop. I started to lose interest as this went on, mostly because it didn't seem at all connected to To the Moon or Finding Paradise. The two scientists are nowhere in sight and you're kind of just dropped into something as this new character without any context (though there is a narrative reason for this that does make sense). Fortunately it reeled me back in but even after I was sucked into the story they tell, I couldn't help but constantly wonder how it was connected to the previous games. I was engaged all the way through to the end, but the reveal (if you could call it that) was kind of deflating. Once things started making sense I realized I didn't really care that much and I was left with a "that's it? okay then" feeling. It's hard to properly convey this without spoiling the story. Impostor Factory feels like less of a sequel and more of an extended side story of sorts. In fact, post credits this game is referred to as "Episode X" and To the Moon and Finding Paradise as "Episodes 1 and 2". I think if this was much more obvious to me that it is "Episode X" rather than "Episode 3" I wouldn't have felt as disappointed. I'm not completely disappointed because I did like this game, but it was simply different from the other two games. The whole plot is much more convoluted, doesn't really make sense, and isn't anywhere near as impactful. It's still a well-written, engaging, and bittersweet story, but it's not the concise and emotionally eviscerating gut punch that To the Moon or Finding Paradise were. I also really don't agree with their descriptions in the store page. You absolutely have to play the previous games and maybe even the comics (I don't know for sure because I haven't read them - I did feel like I was missing something when playing this) for this story to matter or even begin to make sense. They're coy about calling it a sequel or a prequel (if anything it's a prequel) and though I never pay much attention to a game's marketing or this kind of stuff, especially for a story based series like this, this was originally presented as the next full-blown To the Moon game. This might've changed at some point though which I missed, leading to having false expectations.I guess this is just my verbose/roundabout way of saying you should go into this like it's a more developed A Bird Story, NOT "To the Moon 3". Nevertheless, I still enjoyed Impostor Factory and would recommend it to people who have played the other games, but I do wish I went in with more accurate expectations. I held off playing this for a while and now that I finally sat down to beat it, I am a little underwhelmed since it wasn't exactly what I was expecting it would be.

_childDocuments_.review: ✅Writing➖Lack of basic features - key bindings/graphics➖UI can be pretty roughGame World: Impostor Factory (IF) takes place over a variety of different settings. The consistency here is that it all plays the same - kind of like a SNES game. I can’t go into a lot of detail here as the game world is tied closely to the narrative, but just know that IF plays exactly like To the Moon and Finding Paradise. Narrative: Freebird always has amazingly good writing and music for their games and while it's the same here, I personally felt this was the weakest entry between To the Moon and Finding Paradise. Some light spoilers here: I feel that IF didn’t hit as hard as the previous two Freebird games for me because  so I didn’t feel as attached to the characters. The ending Overall, I feel this was very well written, but the plot devices may have trapped Freebird into the issue of making the narrative too complex. Length: Like most Freebird games, it's short, I was able to calmly finish it in under 4 hours. Controls: Simple, this is a walking simulator. You walk, run, and talk. That's literally it. I played the entire game using a controller instead of KBM. Mechanics: Not much here either. It's mostly a walking/talking simulator. Difficulty: If Dark Souls had a child with Sekiro….no seriously, you walk and talk. There is literally no way to die or fail here even if you tried. Quality: A step up from pixelated, kind of reminds me of a SNES game. I will give kudos to the art team for very clearly defining unspoken actions superbly well. UI: Barebones, you don’t really need to know anything going on from the type of game it is. Performance: No issues, only played it on my desktop PC. i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSDSound effects: Decent enough, but a ton are reused over and over. Music: Wonderfully done. Now that the narrative for IF isn’t as good as the previous two titles, the music has never let me down. If there is ever music to evoke some sort of emotion, it comes from Freebird. Well done. Abysmal. No achievements, no choices. Same story.A solid entry into Freebird’s repertoire. This game expands the To the Moon narrative in ways that I didn’t expect, nor enjoyed as much, but I still absolutely love experiencing their games. My only complaints lie in the same complaints with their previous titles - lack of player interaction, mechanics, and replayability. _childDocuments_.review: It was 2018. The market had come a long way since To the Moon, and while Finding Paradise had received enough fan acclaim, it also had its fair share of detractors who were hoping for another "To the Moon like" story. Further, it sold considerably less than its parent, though still enough to keep the company alive. Not that an indie venture as small as Freebird Games needed a lot of money, especially when To the Moon had raked in a fair amount of cash.But there was a bigger problem: where exactly would the franchise go? Both sides of the core theme, the exploration of whether wish fulfillment was a good thing in balance, had already been covered. Without that theme, there wasn't much actual point to writing stories for the memory manipulator, especially since it brought a bunch of unwanted restrictions and weighty baggage with it.Well, the author decided that he would delve into the backstory of one of the doctors. Except he would do it in a roundabout way, partly to get around the restrictions, partly to throw off long time fans, and partly to continue writing relationship dramas. Towards that end, he leaned heavily into the misdirection: you aren't the doctors anymore, you're Quincy! And you don't visit any patient, instead you are drawn into a mysterious, murder filled manor!The first act is a cute little sequence. It's a murder mystery that gets increasingly weirder and weirder, and until it leans heavily into the exposition, it's a joy to play, despite the limited interactivity and play space.Things start souring quickly after that, however. The second act, holding the core story, is quite blatantly a retread of many of his tropes. To be fair, it does have a mildly worthwhile premise - the story of a girl cursed by an eventual early death and being motivated by said curse to achieve great things. You could take this premise in several interesting directions if you tried. But the author settles for a long drawn college romance with Quincy as a convenient foil to her, using some of the most schlocky and worn out tropes imaginable. And it's not even that they are written  - if anything, it's much better written than Johnny and River's or Colin and Faye's relationship, at least technically - but it treads so much worn out ground that it fails to evoke much in the way of genuine sentiment.Nor do things improve much after that. She gets hired by an evil science company, who are revealed to be the inventors of the memory manipulator. They attempt to use her as science bait, she escapes and tries to have a "normal" family with Quincy, but her curse(read: disease) kills her baby, and the resulting overwhelming grief pushes her back to working with the evil company.  All of this is narrated through extremely long, indulgent sequences, and while there are some genuine glimmers of sadness and profound musings, they are severely held back by the dull narrative around them.The final act tries something interesting, by revealing her entire life to be an alternative timeline created by her son, who is one of the central memory manipulating doctors of the franchise. Apparently he was attempting to view her life, and seeing what a perfect life for her would look like. While this could have been potential for interesting commentary, it is marred by the extremely lackluster presentation and the sheer amount of stretching the author does to tie her life back to the overarching narrative of the franchise, while still keeping things "suspenseful".All of the revelations here are delivered in a long, dull monologue, and the entire situation is "resolved" by the flick of a wand granting them a carefree, idealistic life. Hell, even the doctor himself comments on how unfulfilling that felt! Someone could charitably interpret this as an attempt to provide commentary on the innate hollowness of excess wish fulfillment, except Finding Paradise did that better. Someone could also claim that it's supposed to be a commentary on stories, and how they only have meaning when there are obstacles to be overcome, except that assumes that the second act, which was where most of the story was concentrated, was anything meaningful.All in all, I think the severe focus on misdirection, combined with the author not truly innovating on the core of his work, makes this fall flat. Had he taken more actual risks with the central narrative, there could have been something interesting. To the Moon and Finding Paradise were both interesting even if not always successful, this can't even really claim that. This is only interesting  as an examination of how far misdirection can carry a rather tired plot, and, outside of the genuinely delightful first act, there is little to recommend in it. If you  like this author's previous work, you'll likely still find something to enjoy, but everyone else can safely steer clear.
