_childDocuments_.review: This entry is definitely riding on the coattails of To The Moon and Finding Paradise. It's also clearly a sequel. Yeah, I guess you can play this game without having played the others, just like you can start watching The Two Towers without having seen Fellowship, but it won't make total sense. In my opinion, Finding Paradise is one of the greatest games ever made, so expectations were high.  The series continue to explore the subject of the butterfly effect and how small or large decisions can have immense ripple effect in the future. The issue is the devs crammed a ton of topics (butterfly effect, parenthood, pursuit of greatness vs simple life, alternate timelines, etc) and genres (murder mystery, dramedy, sci-fi, love story, drama, slice of life...) into one narrative, and tying that together in a story that honestly makes no sense (did anyone actually understand the mess that was the 3rd act?). I really thought at the beginning of the second act that the focus of Simple Life VS Pursuit of Greatness would be the central theme, with the two leads tugging at each end. Instead, the writers canned that as soon as they could and moved on to some convoluted alternate, parallel reality plot that I am willing to bet $100 even Kan Gao does not understand. Bigger isn't always better. Freebird is known for taking common slice of life stories and diving deep into them, not sci-fi and half-azzed humor (the cat? the Pokemon reference made me chuckle but it was annoying fast. Ricebot is life though. Ricebot is love. ). And I had no idea Neil Watts was such a popular character to be shoehorned into this story which had nothing to do with him. I always thought Neil and Rosalene to be the game player's eyes in the prequels, not the main characters, so seeing them forced into a story about Lynri was just a poor attempt at fan service.Definitely the weakest game, weaker than Bird Story. It may resonate with you if you're a parent maybe? Only play this is if you played the prequels and loved them.

_childDocuments_.review: Warning: If you hate a sappy self indulgent essay, SKIP. I mean it lol. This is my personal review of this game:For me, this game really hit me where it really hurts.For context, my mom died of cancer recently. I've been just so numb to it a lot of time. But this game, this game reminded me of why it really hurt. It reminded me that I'll never mom grow old with dad, despite fighting for so long, despite all the sacrifices. That feeling where she'll never be able to take care of her grandkids, just as she always wanted. She was the smartest, bravest, most generous soul I have ever known in my life. I always thought that she could've been so much more than just a housewife taking care of stupid old me and my sisters. She could've been an amazing lawyer, like she once wanted. I talked to her about it, and guess what she said. She said I, and my sisters, were her pride and joy, that there's nothing more in this world that makes her happy than us.Life had not been kind to my mom. She was dealt the worst cards she could handle, even before cancer, and yet someone like her could be so amazing. That's why I wish I was better. I wish I could've paid her back. I wish I could make her happier and prouder. I might not get the technical details of what Neil did, but I definitely know why he did it. What his mom did was amazing. A self-sacrificing, unconditional act of love that only a mother could make. I KNOW he wanted to pay her back, even if we all know that's impossible.  Neil, you did good buddy. And go confess to Eva already you tsundere dumbass!And Kan Gao, thank you. Thank you for reminding me that we should be better. We might not be the person we want to be in the future, but at least we can choose to be a little bit better one day at a time.Ma, I miss you so hard, I love you so much, and I'll be better like you always wanted me to be.

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILERS IN THIS REVIEWThis game was very frustrating to me. I never played the other two games in the series, so maybe that had something to do with the bad experience I had with the game. This game has no gameplay. There is like 1 puzzle you have to solve at the beginning, but after that it is just walking and cutscenes. This game can be easily split into three parts. The first part was probably the most fun I had with the game, as it was more or less true to the promises that the steam description gave it. It was a time loop murder mystery game, and frankly that was somewhat enjoyable. About an hour or so into the game, you go through a random door, and are transported to what I can only call the worst excuse for a section of a video game I've ever had the displeasure of playing. It is a more or less 2 hour hallway that you traverse down and interact with balls that play cutscenes that reveal the life of one of the (at this point) random NPCs that are in the mansion. This section goes on for way too long, and frankly if there was any gameplay in it, maybe I would have found it enjoyable, but it was just a movie that I had to babysit. After this long slog, that really only kinda matters, you get to act 3. Act 3 is really "cool" because it basically invalidates Act 1, and just kinda throws whatever at the wall and hopes that it will stick. Turns out the mansion is a simulation, you're not a real person, and there's something messing up the timeline. This sounds cool, because oh it's a murder mystery again, but no, turns out the villain is just a character that was never introduced before, alludes to vague simulation stack overflow essentially, and you get more or less the same cutscenes from act 2, but you are on the roof of the mansion. MAYBE I would have enjoyed this game if I had some knowledge of the previous ones, but the lack of gameplay, questionable controller support, and overall just boring (in my opinion) story ultimately just killed my interest in it. The art and music are pretty good tho.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved Kao's previous games To The Moon, Finding Paradise and to a lesser extent, A Bird Story, but I unfortunately felt really disappointed after finshing his new game, or should I say, player driven visual story, Imposter Factory, even if his cinematic take on player driven narratives shine just as before.While I was intrigued by the eerie and sometimes funny beginning, set in a big and weird old manor in the wood where some murders take place and expecting to find some of the more emotional, and yes, spiritual messages that take a big place in Kao's previous games, and which I found to be a very warm, casual, reflective and sometimes, transcendent experience, the messages, ideas, and how these subjects are presented on this new game felt rushed, uninspired, and not as genuinely emotional as before, and of course death, alternate realities, terminal diseases and personal choices are big emotional themes, but it's a shame that these weren't as well explored and engaging as the previous games. The mind puzzling physics that they try to use as an explain for the plot at the end doesn't help much also.Surely this was an interesting experience, and it can also be for other people, even more for those who deal or sees some of the themes presented on  the game in a different way. But I would recommend anyone which is not familiar with Kao's To The Moon Series, to really play the To The Moon and Finding Paradise instead of this before consider playing this.

_childDocuments_.review: The third game in a trilogy that is simple, short and charming but most importantly it will make you feel and cry. It might not be a video game in the normal sense and you could easily just watch someone play it, you can do that if you feel lonely or cheap, but the experience will be different, fans of Freebird know what they are getting and if you haven’t don’t start with this one as you will not get the full picture, also great job on the misleading marketing as well. There are two camps of story games, those that give you choices to affect the story and those that don’t. Imposter Factory is in the latter. The stories always focus on using this device similar to the animus but to let a person go into their mind usually right before death to learn, change or relive their life and make us feel wholesome at times. Usually there is relationship focus and this one is no different. It does have a pretty nice start that I can’t say anything about to spoil. Imposter Factory does further expand and build the universe upon it’s previous 2 games.  The devs say you don’t need to play the game to enjoy this and that is true for the main character and his story, but there moments usually towards the end that will either feel weird or have no impact and not feel as epic if you don’t play the other 2 in the series, so it’s not required, just strongly encouraged. Just get all 3, they don’t last longer than 5 hours each. I will mention that if you saw the trailer and expected this wild crazy scif-fi horror/mystery game, it’s a jebait as to not spoil the real story for fans. It focuses more on two characters and their life choices, its ups and downs and carries heavy themes about family, job struggles, working through a relationship and more that will eventually as always make you feel for these characters and maybe even hate them and eventually will at one point break you down. Fans know to expect it and they still throw those emotional punches that hit.The gameplay is just a walking simulator and potentially cutscene simulator. Here the complaints from the last game are gone; you can now sprint so it’s a running simulator. Then they made the best discussion to cut the stupid artificial “gameplay” tetris thing that is was used to halt the story. Here you just go to an object tied to the character and collect an orb to unlock the next scene. Usually these orbs are just given after scenes to make sure you see everything and not rush past an important moment or dialogue and no longer halt the pacing and why we play the game the story and characters, mostly written by one guy. It’s almost a style or genre at this point and glad to be supporting this hidden gem and hope you give it a shot and feel the same.

_childDocuments_.review: Giving this a THUMBS DOWN for mainly one reason: in terms of what I look for in the "visual novel" genre, this game failed in the ways that count the most.Although, yes, this story is probably the weakest in the "To the Moon" series, it's still maybe my favorite since it primarily concerns However, the game is a huge letdown in terms of how the story unfolds. The whole thing is linear to an alarmingly literal sense, in that often, the only direction you can move your character is forward, and the game allows for little interactions outside of the plot-specific NPCs to talk to or objects to click on. The previous installments of the franchise have vast environments for you to explore, so even when the game only progresses with certain actions you still feel totally immersed in the story. In Impostor Factory, however, it felt more like I'm side scrolling through panels of a comic book.And I think that's the biggest disappointment here: I'd rather have paid for a full-length graphic novel version of this chapter of "To the Moon" than for the game itself. Had this been something I could read instead of play, I'd have loved the beautiful story within the pages. But playing this lessened its impact because I was constantly frustrated by the lack of engagement. Visual novels as a medium are so great to me because they allow for a lot more flexibility and creativity for the creators, to huge benefits on behalf of the "reader," but this was little more than moving from point A to point B as the story is told around the reader. I dislike that very much.TL;DR 9/10 for story, 4/10 for gameplay

_childDocuments_.review: Impostor Factory. The third (fourth if you count Bird Story) installment in the To The Moon series by Freebird Games, and games that have come to emotionally dominate me. They're really simple - mostly walk and talk simulators, and I noticed that the puzzles at the end of the memories were gone in this installment (not that they were particularly hard). And let me tell you when the game says the story isn't about Neil Watts and Eva Rosalene from the first couple games, they mean it. The  We focus instead of Quincy Reynard, who's invited to a mansion for a social gathering but gets way more than he's bargaining for - and meets a mysterious girl named Lynri. The game didn't make me cry like To The Moon and Finding Paradise, which I was sort of disappointed about as it was the reason I was holding off on it for so long, but it was still plenty heartbreaking.  Lots of complicated character moments, but in the end I love how Freebird Games always tells really compelling love stories. Here's to the Beach Episode!

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely made me cry, just like all of FreeBird's games.  Absolutely loved the experience by the end of it.  It has some issues that I think are worth talking about.  As much as I loved it by the end, some of the story's choices make it lag in places.  SPOILERS AHEAD!Act 1 introduces a fun, almost sci-fi themed murder mystery with a mysterious woman, time travel, and lots and lots of dead bodies.  But, Act 2 all of the sudden thrusts us into an entirely different story about a young woman battling a hereditary condition that gets married and tries to find purpose.  So, essentially, the game promises a murder mystery and then forgoes that for a drama.  While Act 2 does provide us a somber, yet hopeful viewing into someone's life that can be very beautiful - it feels disappointing next to the interesting sci-fi murder mystery.Now, Act 3 does bring it ALL together.  And I personally really enjoyed Act 3.  Ricebot is the best.  Long cat will never be forgotten.  There are some things that are revealed that really make your head spin (in the best way in my opinion).By the end, I loved it.  But, the journey to getting to that can laboring.  I think for some people, Act 2 can be beautiful. It discusses life, death, purpose, etc. and can really hit home for some.  I'm sure the experience for this game is going to be different across the board.  For me personally, I wish Act 2 could have been condensed or could have had more going on.  For example, I would have liked to see long cat throughout the game as our main character's companion so he can have someone to talk to about everything he's seeing.  Having fun interactions between their characters would have helped the story a lot.  Because he only says a few words for 2 hour span of Act 2 and I wanted to hear him talk.Overall, loved the game a lot.  I came out of crying my eyes and feeling intensely philosophical.  It may have some issues, but I enjoyed the experience overall and would recommend it for anyone who's a fan of the "To the Moon" storyline.

_childDocuments_.review: Spoilers ahead:This game takes a different path from the previous two. It isn't the story of a dying patient, rather it's a completely ficticious story existing only within the machine itself and I get it, the idea of something "out of touch" with the reality might not have the same  for some as thinking that the story comes from real people, however it's clear this is exactly what Kan Gao wanted us to experience: while the story is based on the life of Neil's mother, both timelines we get to experience are complete fabrications. This adds a layer to the lore, as the machine Neil has been working on secrectly is apparently capable of self-consciousness as the MC exists within and gets to experience two whole reality , just like he was a real person.We aren't told until the very end that the story we're seeing is fabricated, blurring the line of what constitutes reality and what does not. Maybe I'm reading in too much, but for me this doesn't feel a random squirt of creativity, rather a well thought story.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's see, where do I begin. This is the latest installment to the To the Moon series. I've played every game so far as I've always loved the storytelling and the narrative. It's always been a fun thrilling ride to be on as the story progressed in the previous installment. However, this one hit different...and not in a good way. First, the gameplay. The gameplay felt like I was just being pushed from point A to B mindlessly, as if just walking through the motions. Unlike the older games, while we also did the same mechanics (although this game is more simplified), we had no choices and we did not have to search around to uncover the story.As for the story,  part was at first a shock factor but uncovering the truth of it was...underwhelming. I feel like it could've been executed better. I could not connect to the main characters in this installment compared to the old games. This game feels like the "Bird Story" prequel to Finding Paradise. It's like a long, dragged out "filler" rather than a fully fleshed out game.I could go on but I think I would need to fully delve into spoilers at this point. Overall, I am disappointed by how the game turned out as I was pretty hyped about it with the trailers that came out. If another installment is made with our favorite characters Neil and Eva, I hope the game quality would return to how it was before.Another thing to note, I love Freebird games because of the amazing music they've composed throughout the previous games. However, the music in this installment was underwhelming as most were recycled from the past games. To the Moon and Finding Paradise both had music that were crucial and actually part of the story. They were integrated masterfully and invoked so much emotion that added to the further perfection of the narratives. This game did not have that. I could have played this game on mute. There was no immersion whatsoever. The only times I felt anything was when they re-played some tracks from Finding Paradise which I'm sure anyone who hasn't played the previous games would not have felt anything for.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game, will recommend to fans of the series. As a stand-alone, it has a lot to offer but the context is much needed for the overarching theme and ending. _childDocuments_.review: A very good follow up to To the Moon and Finding Paradise. (while Imposter Factory can stand on its own, you really should play those two first for added context and !! moments when you realize things.)As with the other two, it touches on themes of choices made in life, regrets and what might have been through a tapestry of memories.   Where this one differs is in the framing.  The first act is blend of comedy and horror (as the protag's commentary of "this is how horror stories start!" sets you up for)  that escalated until going off the rails-- before you land in act 2, which is the far more familiar exploration of memories (which had me constantly trying to figure out what was going to go wrong, aka earlier games)   Act 3 is where everything meshes together, and all the small hints and breadcrumb trails result in many moments of me yelling "WHAT?!" loudly at the screen (as well as things that cannot be typed in this review.)  Act 3 also is where the tissues really were needed.  It's not as strong of a gut punch to the feels as the first two, but it got me pretty hard.  Act 3 also nicely weaves in so many threads from the framing/meta narrative and when one very tiny, but very critical bit of information that had been kept from the player was finally dropped I swore loudly, then laughed as so much suddenly made sense.  Per usual, there is some quality comic relief woven in.  Quite a few genuine laughs in between the WTF! and tissues, including a very good music joke with one of the area-specific background music tracks.  Also per usual, the soundtrack is excellent in both matching tone and hitting emotions.  The blue-noted variations on themes were very well done and appreciated for the tone they gave.    The gameplay is mostly interactive, with one "puzzle" that was very intuitive.  (Only had to search for a memory orb once just due to the size of my screen making me miss a doorway.)    Very inline with the other games in the series.Well worth the price of admission.  Best played in a single run (roughly 3-4 hours depending on how fast you read and level of external distractions.)    Very much made me want to replay the other two games and then this one again to refresh on all the interwoven bits.  Just need to get some more tissues first....

_childDocuments_.review: To The Moon series is one of my favorite game/novel series of all time. Any TTM’s game is a simple and down-to-earth (lol) story with an enormous level of immersion and emotional investment. Like many fans, I was waiting for the third part, Impostor Factory, from it’s announcement.And, as you can see from the title, I have some problems with this game, which I hadn’t with it’s predecessors. It’s main problem is the story, but before talking about that, I am gonna briefly talk about other aspects of the game and their progression through the series.Soundtrack is one of the strongest parts of the TTM series and Impostor Factory is not an exception. However, it doesn’t contain too many “bangers” in comparison to original To The Moon or Finding Paradise. Even after years I still remember For River, Born a Stranger, Moongazer, Once Upon a Memory, Tomorrow, Everything’s Alright, Time is a Place, The Scale Theme, Faye’s Theme and many more. I remember how they sound, I remember their names. I cannot say the same for the Impostor Factory. There are some good and catchy songs, but there is nothing to compete with the level of previous games. Maybe it’s too early for these conclusions, but it’s my first impression.Despite all of that, I cannot say that the soundtrack is bad at all. It still makes like 50% of the game anyway. Maybe, I just had too big expectations for that.Impostor Factory uses an updated game engine and it is striking. Animation is better, cutscenes are better, the game is much more cinematographic in comparison to other parts of the series. And that’s noticeable.The gameplay loop of the series was always very simple. You read the story, you explore the location, solve the puzzle, repeat until the end. Now, in the Impostor Factory, there are no puzzles and, consequently, less reasons to explore.I cannot actually decide which is better. The puzzles that get you out of the story for some time but give you this time to think about what is happening. Or no puzzles to slow you down. Because of this change, the story sometimes feels too rushy, but I wouldn't say that it is a big problem. There is another one.[SPOILERS WARNING]First, I have to mention that F.A.Q is a lie. You need to play at least Finding Paradise to get the twist. Otherwise, it may feel even more “Deus Ex Machina”-ish than it actually is.Second, as I said in the beginning, TTM games are simple and down-to-earth stories. And it is not just a fact, it is the strong side of the series. But Impostor Factory tries to be much more exalted and epic. And it doesn’t work at all.I cannot say what happens in Kan Gao’s head. Maybe, it is how he sees the story should develop. Or, maybe, he tried to answer the audience's request. The players had so many questions about TTM minisodes, ending of Finding Paradise, and a lot of other mysteries that popped up in the series. But the audience, however, doesn’t always know what it wants. People have an experience of Impostor Factory predecessors, and they want to relive it. But it is not always possible. You cannot make a good game only on that request.Impostor Factory tries to get people what they want, and at the same time it tries to create something new. But these two parts are poorly stitched together. It does not feel like the story is solid. It seems like the connection between Impostor Factory and Eva and Niel was created just because they are popular characters. It just jumps out at the end of the game through exposition. And it feels cheap and pushy.I was much more emotionally invested in the story of Lynri. It makes so much sense. It is the story of the creator of a memory editing machine. Her life was totally consumed by her work, and it made her make questionable decisions. At the end, she tries to apply the machine to herself to fix her past mistakes. It’s the story with the spirit of the series. And it ideally fits as a prequel. But then other TTM games fall into this story. Because we for whatever reason need to connect them directly. Lynri should be the mother of Niel. No matter how much sense it makes. Instead of just developing the story of an old woman fighting her past, we need to dive into the weird story of the simulation inside of other simulations. And all of these are just to tie the game to previous ones.I could talk a lot about how the first 95% of the game are good, and how the other 5% are disappointing. But i just gonna say this: the setting of the game should support the story, not be a burden to it.I was thinking a lot about this game after my playthrough. And, despite everything I said above, I still love this game, and I am glad to support the developers. It still gives you a good story, and if you are a fan of the series, like me, you definitely should play it.However, I have to say that it is an important moment in the TTM series. Maybe I am too dramatic. But developers have to decide. Are they going to just make more fanservice or they want to create nice stories. Niel and Eva are very nice characters. But they cannot work for eternity. You have to leave them be, if there is no way to develop the story dragging them along. Otherwise, TTM’s future is to be a shell of itself filled with our nostalgia about what it once was.

_childDocuments_.review: So, again the Steam review issue, that it's binary yes/no.This is not a bad game. Or, well, experience.But it is a boring one. And almost not a game.This comes from a fan of the series, a seriously artsy fartsy guy who cried his fair share through the emotional tricks and triggers - so it's not a case of some action Jackson just wanting more flash & bang.But what I would like, is more game.If at times, the earlier installments might have suffered from too much retro-gaming nostalgia, inserting unnecessary gaming elements that got in the way of the story, this installment goes the opposite way, foregoing almost all gaming to tell a linear on-the-rails slice-of-life story.And it gets boring. At its most egregious it is in act 2, where it's pretty much a slideshow, where you just press right to activate the next cutscene, for what? Almost an hour? I do not feel invested. I do not feel a part of it. I do not feel that I can effect a change, or even move the story forward.I am simply an observer. If this'd be a film, or a book, it'd be fine. The expectations would be different. But going through an "interactive experience" without your actions ever really interfacing with the experience is a waste of the medium. Repeatedly rooms lacked interactivity. Everything was super linear and basic. Even the visuals became more barren/rudimentary as the game progressed, and evoked a feeling of a project that had run out of steam/funding/time two-thirds through. Details like pathways between cutscenes starting out misty and handcrafted, to becoming just straight dragged gradient brushes.The writing was hyper-expository, everything was constantly spelled out, nothing left to be figured out. And some of the topics, sadly, felt like "oh I heard this cool thing in philosophy 101".The earlier installments might not have been literary masterpieces, but they made me feel. This one, made me feel bored.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved To the Moon series but this game unfortunately did not live up to expectations. The whole experience just seemed so bizarre.If you are a hardcore To the Moon fan, maybe it is worth playing as this game is sort of a prequel (?) to it, but if you're like me who wants to enjoy a touching story this might not be the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Yay, finally it's end of 2020. Or was it may 2021? Ah, whatever, who cares what time it is? It is here! It's the end of the road, I guess. _childDocuments_.review: Impostor Factory is the third story RPG maker game of the To the Moon series that changes up a lot of things and manages to be both a sequel and a prequel.Lots of changes are introduced for this game. Instead of exploring and figuring out the story like in the previous games, here it feels like someone just takes us for a ride. It's a lot more linear, none of the puzzle or mini games. Changing the perspective of how the story is told makes it refreshing. It tries somehow new with a strong start of a murder mystery that fizzles out into the routinely emotional story that the series knows we expect. And while it's a good story, it's emotionally less hard hitting than the previous games. But in it's stead the meta plot of the doctors is explored more with giving some answers and leaving more questions. Overall this game is a bit too ambitious, but still decent that makes more sense if you played the previous games and feels like it's a great set up for the next game.Controls are the standard found in RPGmaker games with the addition to play with the mouse. Playing the game feels like a walking simulator in RPGmaker form. A small windowed resolution is the best way to play through it as fullscreen can cause lots of issues. The quality of the visuals is noticeably higher from the previous games in the series and even they did stand out among RPGmaker games.For achievement hunters:The only achievement is for completing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Did not reach the emotional depth of to the moonDid not reach the philosophical depth of finding paradise (even though it tried super hard)but overall 9/10 I really loved itthe story and the characters will stick with me for a long timeI love how a lot of criticism I initially had turned out to be intentional when the plot unfolded (like a certain someone reminding me of a certain someone else). So many parallels everywhere and the storytelling and OST is amazing as usualbiggest criticism I have for impostor factory is problematic pacing in act 1, and during act 3 where it got super convoluted.the scientific lore, for the first time, gave me a feeling of elon musk on weed (not a good thing) instead of a disbelief suspending what if like what was in ttm and fpTLDR: amazing story and you should play it (but play the other games first)

_childDocuments_.review: Freebird Games never fails. Another beautiful, emotional, hilarious story.[[SPOILERS BELOW!!]]I will say,  however, even though I enjoyed the game, it did not have the same impact To the Moon and Finding Paradise did, and got a little bit too confusing towards the end. I feel like, unlike the other characters like Johnny/River, and Colin/Faye/and his wife, Quincy/Lynri, while a beautiful start (i loved the act two story). their story kinda got less emotional in the third act. The idea of Lynri losing the baby and completely removing Quincy from her life was heartbreaking, and a huge part of me thought that we were experiencing one of the first scientist who created Sigmund Corp rewriting their own memories (Lynri rewriting her leaving Colin after the baby died, and essentially writing the ending of the story as her new memory). I do like that we finally got some insight on Neil, and why he uses the machine, and what could possibly be wrong with his, but i do wish act two held more weight bc that was very interesting, but act two was pretty much shut down by the finale, which made it kinda obsolete imo.I am reccomended this game because i do not think it is a bad game, and those who love Freenird games would still enjoy it, however, this is a game you DEFINITELY have to play after To the Moon and Finding Paradise, especially if you're invested in the story of Neil.

_childDocuments_.review: Was a huge fan of the first two games. This game launched at 3 AM where I lived and I played it on launch and in one sitting. Sleep is for the week.This is a pretty huge departure from the story of the first two and I can understand why people won't like it, but I loved this game. Yes Eva and Neil are important to the story of the Sigmund Corp. series, but the reason why I fell in love with this game is the emotions and the new characters that are introduced with these diverse and deep perspectives on life and that's what I got here.This is a slow game and it will be a while before you get some answers as to what is going on, but Kan Gao handsomely rewards your patience with satisfying payoffs and emotionally rich life stories. _childDocuments_.review: If you played To The Moon, you know there is only one question worth asking about Impostor Factory. But we'll come to that later.If you haven't, there are three.Question one is: what kind of games are Kan Gao's To The Moon and Impostor Factory? They are interactive fiction in the style of old 16 bits adventure games. Don't expect challenge here. There is none. Don't expect choices. There are few. You're along for the ride. And what a ride it is.Question two is: what makes them special? A knack at telling very human stories about life and love and making the best of what time there is. A bit messy sometimes, and sometimes tragic. And what human things aren't?Question three is: do you need to have played To The Moon before playing Impostor Factory?  They're part of an ongoing set of works, and Impostor Factory builds onto To The Moon in important ways that would be criminal to spoil.But if you've played To The Moon, you already know all that. You're only wondering: after all this time, does Kan Gao have new things to say?Yes.Go in blind. Find out why on your own.I thought the series had no tears left to wring out of me. Goes to show what I know.

_childDocuments_.review: The good folks at Freebird have done it again with another deeply emotional tale interspersed with quirky humour and subtle callbacks to previous games. Prepare to have your feelings devastated once more.Even more so than the others, this Freebird game is not for the faint of heart. Towards the end it presented a message so morally uncompromising that I was rather shocked, though I admired the candour. In terms of raw emotional power, I still think that  has yet to be topped, but I do put  above  in the gut-wrench stakes. As this series has progressed, raw human stories have increasingly shared screen-time with speculative sci-fi: AI, VR, and the ethics involved in these technologies. For me the human element is always the stronger and I did find the latter somewhat distracting from where I thought the story should concentrate its powers. However, this is a very minor nitpick. At heart this is a fantastic experience; though very upsetting and uncomfortable at times,  walks you back from the brink, pushes you off another one, and then delivers a satisfactory conclusion - with enough ambiguity within that no doubt fans will be arguing about its finer points for years to come.

_childDocuments_.review: Another top noch writing from Freebird Games with great pacing between comedic "relief", mystery and "the feels" moments through out this 5-6 hour long journey. "Mature" in a sense that they show you the lives of different people and give you lessons through them. _childDocuments_.review: This was the email I sent Freebird Games after this game came out. There are some light spoilers."I often wondered about whether games could really, truly change someone's life - make someone reflect on their life decisions, or help them clarify some of their thoughts about themselves or the world around them. I've played many games, some with great emotional impact or that were really fun experiences that brought me joy. But this one, Impostor Factory, this was one of the only ones that really changed me. That changed my life.When I played Finding Paradise, I cried at the end - Colin's obssession with the imaginary was something I found quite relatable. I thought that was the peak of what games could do for me, as at the time I was somewhat of a colder person. I enjoyed the game, called it a masterpiece, and moved on.Then four years later, Impostor Factory came along. I was now a different person, at a different mood and with different emotions. I was grappling with my own insecurities and fears of what the future would look like for me. I was clinging to the idea that I would live my life focusing on one single objective, and kind of ignore everything else, including relationships, to pursue that goal.So when that conversation between Quincy and Lynri, about their different viewpoints on how life should be lived, occurred... something clicked with me. I began thinking more and more about this concept - Lavenders and Stars - and really question whether I really wanted to beeline myself into one single goal.My time here is limited, and I didn't want to leave without leaving a mark, as a 'mediocre' person. But at the same time, I realized... I don't want to be alone. I realized I was masking my fear of coming out to my parents with the idea that I didn't want relationships, and as such would never have to discuss such things with them. I felt trapped and alone, but I didn't want to admit it. I had built up this totem of "Relationships are dumb and I'm above them" for so long that I couldn't question it anymore. It became almost a dogma.After all of that (and some conversations with some of my friends), I decided to come out to my mom. For eight years I knew I liked boys, but I never could muster the courage to tell it to her until now. At the end of the conversation, she hugged me and said that I should've said it much earlier, and that she would always support me. If I hadn't played this game and hadn't had those conversations, perhaps I would've just decided to go on with my life without telling her anything. Would I be a happy person? Perhaps, perhaps not. But without a doubt, this freed me from my cage.So, yeah. Sorry for the wall of the text, and thanks again. I feel so much lighter than before, and your game really helped me with that. Your games are awesome."

_childDocuments_.review: The next chapter in the Sigmund Corp Series, this title barely features it.  It maintains the art & comedic style of the previous titles, but is completely disconnected from the main story until the very end.  Regardless, it still feels resonate to the rest of the series, focusing on regrets, memories, & the idea of adjusting past mistakes in one's own fantasy.  A rather sudden & wonderfully confusing 1st act kicks in that leaves the the main character, Quincy, to begin questioning everything around him.  It, along with the music, draws the player in for another ride of a story, leading to an eventual heartwarming/heartbreaking climax, depending on the player's point of view. Once again, all of the same problems, but with a neat little twist.  The 1st act is a mystery that feels like it ends a bit too quickly, & the 2nd act plods along.  The 3rd act is about what one would come to expect from this series.  A noticeable take away is definitely the lack of a Laura Shigihara song at the end.  That's about all one can give, considering how similar the Sigmund Corp Series games tend to be. Another one for completing the story.  Another simple, several hour trail to completion. Impostor Factory feels more interested in pulling in new players compared to the previous title, but it's still very similar.  These games are good, emotionally resonant, but are simply stories.  If you enjoyed the previous titles in this series, then you will enjoy this.  If you were curious or cautious about the series, & for some reason haven't tried To The Moon, then this may be a decent starting point before going back to the rest.  If you didn't like To The Moon or Finding Paradise, then this game won't sway you.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly can’t understand what is so great about the game, but judging by so many positive reviews there must be something I’ve missed. But what exactly? The uninspired love story that was told a million times before? Or the intrigue so boring that the revelation at the end leaves you with nothing but disappointment? There were parts where I had to fight with myself not to skip dialogues, because they were so uninteresting. Is this really the studio that made “To the moon” and “Finding paradise”? Once I started to predict exactly what will happen in the story, I lost all hope for having a good time with this game. It is nothing, but exposition, a sort of background for the next game.  At least the music is good, although it was hard to enjoy it seeing another forcefully sad moment that from the very beginning is obvious will happen. If you want to check it for yourself – better watch it on YouTube or wait for some discount.  I wanted to like this game; I really did. Previous games (maybe excluding “A bird story”) were fantastic. Happily, the ending leaves a promise of a better game coming next and I really hope they will deliver.

_childDocuments_.review: Linear visual novels of this sort, which are as close to non-interactive as you can be while still qualifying as a computer program, are difficult to objectively assess.So I'll simply say I experienced a wide variety of emotions while watching this pixel machinima; but I found it lacked the quality of its predecessors, and without that quality the novella's absence of interactivity, agency, or exploration hurt its emotional and intellectual staying power. As a franchise it is no longer taking creative risks.I guess the question is - who would I be recommending the game to? FPS players will likely never see this store page; and committed readers of this franchise will buy it anyway. So perhaps interactive-fiction gamers that expect a sweet spot between narrative and interaction? If so, on that basis I can't recommend this entry.

_childDocuments_.review: Impostor Factory is the 3rd game following the setting from the 1st and 2nd games, To The Moon and Finding Paradise.I highly recommend playing the first two by release date first, since Impostor Factory's story has ties to those games in a way that makes it much more resonating as you get all the pieces together. There is also most likely going to be a 4th game in the future, so keep a lookout for that, if you wish to be present on the conversations the playerbase will have regarding it.Now with that little section out of the way, I will speak about my experience with Impostor Factory. You may play it yourself now or you can keep reading, since I don't know how much I am going to spoil the game.At first, I was a tiny bit confused. I had only recently completed the first 2 games and now the game seemed like an entirely different genre, with a completely different setting. The game is written so well though, so a player who knows the events of the first two games, can later realize where they truly are. So we are following entirely new characters? Oh, could this be the origins of the machine? I see events unfold, pasts, feelings, choices. And when I thought I had it figured out, something I thought to be a figment of my imagination appeared.I'm really trying to be subtle here, in case someone is still here. When I saw that figment, all I could think were "How? What? Why?". How did it all connects? Why were they there?Then I saw those glasses. That's how this connects to all of it. The game really got me well with that. And I can't but compliment it for setting it up so well, and being able to hint it from all the way from the beginning. They didn't know if they'd get to make it this far, yet they still put that in, even if there was  a chance it could never finish telling its tale.Thank you for reading this far, I'm sorry it is less of a review. I'm not really good with those, and could never really do justice to the experts anyway, who have the skills and vocabulary to hook someone. Hopefully you enjoyed reading my review, nevertheless!

_childDocuments_.review: It's what you come to expect from a guy like Gao. Impostor Factory, standing as the third installment in his series that still has no name of its own, it fulfills that title to a T. It does not pick up where Finding Paradise left off, and a lot of loose ends remain in the central plot, but the series will continue (indicated at the end of the game). Besides that, this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beautiful. Gao returns with a fantastic score, exquisite art direction, and a story so damn compelling that the entirety of Act II had me on the brink of tears, at the edge of my seat, had me thinking about myself and the world around me... so many emotions. The main story followed three acts, concerning the story of Quincy and his peculiar visit to a house that involes a time travelling bathroom... or so it seems. But even though this game is tragic, it is also incredibly funny. It's obvious Gao was envisioning a more comedic approach here, and it shows. With characters like a long cat and a robot that serves no other real purpose besides to just make memes the entire game, this game covers all ranges of emotions from sorrow, to happiness, to glee, to straight up depression, nostalgia, everything. To The Moon will always remain my favorite in this series, but this game comes damn close to it. It's a short 3 hour game for a mere ten dollars, and if you have that change lying around (and have experienced the other two games, because they are necessary to play this one), do yourself a solid and grab this baby and play it in one go. I'm telling you, this dude makes some of the best narratively driven games in the entire industry. 9/10, this really was bonkers

_childDocuments_.review: The third game of the "to the moon" series (but can be enjoyed without playing the others) and again it's a masterpiece. It's incredible how well it captures the human condition, its highs and lows, our efforts in making the best of it, and the novel use of technology in trying to reshape it. Kan Gao and Freebird Games deserve a much larger audience.

_childDocuments_.review: You guys really outdid yourselves on this one! What a fantastic game. I really love all the time and attention you put into the ending, so many games make the ending too short, this one was perfect. So I had a mix of feelings through this since I related to Lynri so much. Being told you're going to die soon or at any moment as a child really does have the effect of making a person neurotically pursue meaning in every breathing moment. Then, if that person survives despite expectations, they're in for a crushing identity crisis later. I only know because that's exactly what happened to me. This was written very well. However, since I related to Lynri so much, I was disgusted by her selfish choice partway through the game, I'm not going to lie, I almost didn't finish it. In order to avoid spoilers, I will only say that I'm happy this is rectified later. The sprite work is phenomenal... I still remember the moment while I was playing my first RM game ever, Quintessence, when Reives finds his wife and they're talking in the jail cell, I was screaming in my head, "They better hug!!!" And they did. It was so satisfying and so right. The story you tell with a few pixels and a LOT of effort behind the scenes is just so beautiful. Pixel animations are definitely a strong point in your games and this one so far, is the magnum opus. I only hope I can do a fraction as good in my game XD. The music was very nice and appropriate for the scenes it was played. It's been nice hearing you hone your skill over the years. As a whole I would say this is your best game yet, you all did such a great job.PS. The only thing missing from the game was a reference about gathering mushrooms XD.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, the wonderful people of Freebird Games have done it again. For context, I've been waiting for Impostor Factory since late December of 2019. Doesn't that feel so long ago? Over the course of roughly a year and nine months, I'd been anxiously waiting for the release of this game. I was there during every delay along the way, and now that I have seen the finished product, I'd say it was definitely worth it. By a great amount, this is the most technically competent game of Freebird. The sprite art has become ever so more expressive and detailed, and the non-sprite art is of more quality and quantity. The soundtrack is what you would expect in that it's utterly fantastic; Kan Gao is a genius in composing simple yet deeply meaningful music, that truly elevates any part in which it is used.Player interactivity in this title, like the others, is limited to walking and clicking. Unlike its predecessors, there are no puzzles to be seen. However, Impostor Factory is not a game as it is an interactive story, like Freebird's titles have always been. This is the part where I would review the story, but this game is different in that even trying to discuss the basics would reveal too much. A blind playthrough is the optimal one, as tradition with Freebird's twists and turns in storytelling. All I could say is that, as someone who has played through To The Moon, A Bird Story, and Finding Paradise, Impostor Factory's story is even more potent in its highs and in its lows. A true roller-coaster ride of sorts. I've heard complaints of mood whiplash with their previous stories, and I will say it's here as well in minor points. I personally don't mind it, and it really isn't that bad, but that is the sole criticism I give it. Other than that, I personally consider the story of Impostor Factory to be extremely well-done. Perhaps the greatest in all of Freebird's catalog. All of the key elements promised are surely delivered. The ending is especially great, being able to ride the fine line of satisfying old fans while not making new ones confused.Impostor Factory is a masterpiece of gaming storytelling, made with the intense love and care of a passionate team. For any cautious fans, let this put you at ease to buy such an amazing game at such a low price. For anyone new, let this be the game that will lead you on a funny, scary, emotional journey made by, in this reviewer's humble opinion, one of the finest indie gaming studios working today.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Freebird Game's other entries, I have to say I'm disappointed.The FAQ section says you can play Impostor Factory without playing the first two. This is straight up wrong. If you don't know the characters from the other games, the ending will be meaningless and confusing.I've played the first two games and enjoyed them very much, but it's been four years since the last installment.  My entire experience during the end was struggling to remember who everyone was and how they we're connected to everything else. If you don't know the characters from the other games, there will be almost no payoff to the story whatsoever. There isn't much payoff for the characters you come to know in this game regardless.The opening, the screenshots, and the game description of a "bonkers time-loop tragicomedy" really hammer home the idea that this one's going to be something different. It's not. After a compelling Act 1 setup, Act 2 gives way for a storytelling experience much more akin to the first two games, albeit significantly blander and feeling disconnected from the first act. The final act offers lame explanations for the intrigue that was set up at the beginning and does little more than furthering of the stories outside of it's own neglected narrative.If you're familiar with the other games, and you wash the expectations Act 1 sets up, you can probably have a good time. Other than that, I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to add another positive review and have more people find FreeBird games since they are great stories.First, this is the third game in a series so I recommend playing To the Moon and Finding Paradise to get the full context of the story. You don't necessarily need to play them, but the story is more fulfilling if you do play them.On its own, I feel the story is a little disjointed and needed a little better connections throughout it. I'm not saying its bad, but compared to the others I felt like it wasn't connected as well. The story itself is still strong, having strong characters and an interesting hook throughout the game. The ending is a little confusing, but still satisfying. The only negatives I can think of is that it's somewhat the weakest story of the three games but it's like saying it's an 8/10 while the other two are 9/10. Also these are story-based games so there's little gameplay. However the stories are strong enough to keep me going back to them. I'm planning on playing all three games all at once and see how this connects to the other two. I love this developer studio for creating such heartwarming and emotional stories. In some ways they are so relatable in the character's struggles and how life throws curve balls that change peoples' goals. I cherish these games and wish people to experience these wonderful stories.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I admit bias because I was looking for a good cry, but hear me out. This game was, in every sense of the phrase, a feels ride. While my emotions were mostly crying, crying and more crying, I even had a good laugh here and there.Encapsulated in a mere, but riveting, handful of hours, 'Impostor Factory' is a more complex story than its predecessors, both of which should be played in advance for maximum impact. Sprite animations have improved while retaining the original nostalgic feel that the 'To the Moon' universe is known for. All in all, an impressive optimization of the visual factor to bring equal parts emotion and charm. The music was simply soul-wrenching, once again doing a perfect job of thematically carrying the story, which I am still revisiting and piecing together.In the end, Kan always succeeds in taking what has been done countless times and handing back a fresh, beautiful experience that leaves one heartbroken and pondering for days after.

_childDocuments_.review: This review will contain  spoilers, so be wary reading on ahead.Let me start off by saying that this game is pretty good. As a (mostly) standalone game, I enjoyed my play-through quite a bit. The characters were very well written, and the gameplay stayed true to the previous games. However, I was quite a bit disappointed by the third act and the ending, which I will go into detail further later.Much like the previous games, the gameplay is nothing extraordinary, but is compelling in its own right. Four directional movement, with a few interactions helps keep you engaged enough to follow the story through some of the quieter parts. Also much like the previous two games, the soundtrack was excellent. Not much more to say here.I greatly appreciated the first two acts and how they handled character building for Lynri. I felt that the two main characters here were very well written and believable, while the side characters were unique and supportive to them. I do have some grievances with Quincy, but I believe that to be a plot issue more than a character issue. The team did an excellent job creating these characters, but it is a shame we only got to interact with a few of them for only a few scenes. I have several issues with how the plot was handled in this game. Act 1 largely served no purpose in the grand scheme of the game. We are introduced to the two main leads of the game and given a little insight into the  of the game, but I never felt like a legitimate conflict was introduced to keep the player playing. Minor spoilers:  As for the second act, I feel that this was the strongest portion of the game. The concept of following a person's memories through their life is really enticing, and I enjoyed watching her life play out through Quincy's eyes. My biggest gripe here is that Quincy didn't really add much to the playbacks. Yes he made some minor comments, but the entire act could've been played the same had he not been there. He was merely a device to deliver Lynri's story to the audience. This isn't normally an issue, but it conflicted with the first act and how it set him up to be a major character. Biggest plot issues: The third act & beyond. The game really started getting into a grove after the second act's resolution. I finally felt like we'd get a chance to see Lynri and Quincy shine together as they debunked the . Instead, the game ended. For whatever reason, the third act is entirely an exposition dump, with a questionable attempt at a resolution for our two main characters. I get that the design team wanted to tell a heartfelt story while keeping interesting questions about what life is, but the  was somewhat predictable and serves only as a small incentive for the after credits scene. On its own, the third act might've been really solid. The issue is with how it felt contradictory to what the previous two acts set up. And its conclusion, while nice, felt like a sucker punch to the gut. The after credits scene was intriguing and is largely why I decided to give this a positive review, because it was a nice note to end on. It also set up potential for future installments. All in all, this game was fun to play, and did many things right. I may have set my expectations a little too high thanks to the previous two games, but I would recommend at least one play through. The game felt very short, and I could not believe it was over when I reached the ending, I felt that the game had only just begun. It had so much potential, as the previous games have shown so, but it largely fell short. Keep in mind, it's still a well made game even if it didn't reach the height of the two previous. Also as with every review, this is strictly my opinion, and others certainly have felt differently, so I encourage anyone who's curious to try the game out if they've played the previous two.

_childDocuments_.review: I started knowing Freebird from To The Moon during my high school years. I think around 2015 or 2016. Though, I still remember how the story behind the first installment was so beautiful it made me sob. Over the years I've forgotten about this game until recently, I remember about the game again. Coincidentally there's anniversary sale and that was how I found out there's more installments to the series. Much like other installments I've enjoyed, Impostor Factory didn't disappoint me at all. In fact the story becomes better over the time. It was both beautiful and emotional. It's safe to say that the game made me better emotionally and gave me a bit of strength to write something as beautiful for the world.Impostor Factory is worth all the money and time. For story enthusiasts who are looking for a piece of fiction with lasting impact, this game and all the installments by Freebird will fill your need. It's a great comfort series for you to enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not the most sentimental person while playing games (AKA not crying), but I'm still entranced by reading a well-suited story. And ever since I played To the Moon this saga hasn't really let me down.The story follows Quincy as he gets caught up in a murder mystery that pretty much shakes up his worldview. That's a... surprising change of the formula if you have been following the games up to now. Without much spoilers, the only thing I would say for your benefit is that you shouldn't expect the murders themselves to be the main pillar of the game. It's still a Kan Gao game in its essence, after all.I personally had a bit of a rough time transitioning to the big plot twists (surely it was intended to be sudden), and a lack of dialogue was also felt around Act II by our observers. But it didn't really hurt the overall experience. Just a bit short on playtime.This seems to be more of a transitional game of sorts, opening the doors to future plot points and even fangames with the AU playbook! (That must have been rough to dev)I had some thoughts on my mind on how it must have been tough to think up the overall story and how future games could be even more crazy only because the devs may feel like they have to (like how the Danganronpa series ended - without more ideas to explore due to a peak reached), but it's late here and I think they'll be fine anyways.Bit of a ramble, this review. But yeah, I recommend Impostor Factory.

_childDocuments_.review: The first time I played To The Moon was when it came out, and I’ve loved the series since. Impostor Factory did not reduce me to a sobbing mess like the two previous main games did, but it was nonetheless a beautiful story that is a worthy addition to the series.If you haven’t played any games in the series, the basic spoiler-free rundown is that you are going through someone’s life story by exploring their memories. Impostor Factory’s story is told differently from the other games. Here, you control a man named Quincy as he attends a party that is not what it seems.  Quincy himself is a blank slate, and this means that the focus is not on him, but on the memories he traverses. There were times where I missed Drs. Rosalene and Watts from the previous games, mainly because their humorous banter gave us much-needed breaks from the stories’ emotional moments.Nonetheless, the game does what Kan Gao does best; it makes you appreciate life by showing it with all its complexities. It tells you that life can be full of happiness and sadness, successes and failures, greetings and goodbyes. This is what makes life worth living, and in the end, you just have to go out there and live your best life. Impostor Factory teaches this lesson better than the others.One thing to note; you don’t need to have played the previous games to enjoy this one, but I think it would be a much better experience if you’ve played the previous two games first. This game builds on the established lore of the series, and you WILL miss out if you have not played the earlier games.

_childDocuments_.review: So I am honestly very much confused by negative reviews of this amazing experience. I read a couple preparing for this game and honestly based on some things you've guys written here I expected a much worse game. I thought about this a lot and I think I figured it out...1. The MusicI'll start briefly with the music, or rather just add my words to what has already been said everywhere - Kan's a wonderful composer. The soundtrack is ingenious and if there was nothing else to this game at least I have a couple of new tracks for my study playlist. I already complimented it after FP, but while TTM's soundtrack appears to be heavily plot-oriented IF and FP are freer, more adaptable in every way, yet still work in a game the way there were designed to work. I love that.2. The DesignIt's hard to say much about the RPG Maker worlds. We pretty much see more of the same, but... I feel like with IF, the characters certainly became more expressive despite lack of voice acting I never had trouble reading how the characters feel, which I remember was one of my biggest complaints about TTM. Other than that it's just more of the same engine you, hate it or you love it.3. The GameplayHere's probably the most controversial part of this instalment (If you thought it was the story, you haven't been paying attention - but more on that later.) The minigames are completely removed from this one. There's no puzzle to it, no rewards for exploration, pretty much nothing interactive (Aside from one, not impactful choice) at all. I know many people complained about the puzzle element of the previous games, but I think taking it to another extreme wasn't exactly what they were calling for either. At this point, I don't see why this game even gives me control of a character at all. Not even the core mechanic of searching for mementoes and triggers remained. The game pretty much plays by itself which enforces really weird pacing onto it and does not let you stop and think for a second, appreciate the music, brainstorm with yourself within your head, which to me was one of the most magical elements of the previous two games.4.1 The Story - The Themes and MisconceptionsSince the story is the meat of this game I feel entitled to give it much more review space.I can't help but notice that the people complaining about the story seems to be mostly disappointed by their own expectations, rather than what the game is and represents. What was expected is another heart throbbing story with a twist you won't see coming, yet in a way that's exactly what it was. Where's the problem then? In my opinion, two factors are to blame here.First is the theme - First two games relied on very common themes of "love and dreams" something that isn't very hard to project onto yourself. Everyone has those. The characters such as John, River, Colin even Faye were not hard to relate to. It wasn't challenging to find a piece of ourselves it felt close to home to put ourselves into their shoes. The theme of this game, however? I'd say it's supposed to be "family" which is simply not resonating with everyone. Motherhood is a unique happening not everyone gets to experience. This is why the tragedy of this game's client - Lynri (I am really trying to spoil here, I promise) is perhaps not as impactful as the one of John or Colin - which could happen to literally anyone. I would lie if I said I can relate either, never being a mother myself.There's also the main protagonist, (for story reasons I am gonna call him "Quincy") who came off a bit bland for most of the game. Especially throughout the second act of the game. What was special about the protagonist of previous episodes was the fact that they were independent from the player. They tend to draw their own conclusions, often acting on their own will and what they thought wasn't always what we're thinking, and honestly, I think the banter between the two was one of the highlights of the experience that really helped you engage and sink in with the problems of the characters... "Quincy" on the other hand never speaks up his mind, never dares to question what he sees or challenge himself with it. He's a passive vessel for us the player. If he isn't invested why would we honestly? I think this is the major reason why the story did not sink in as well as the previous onesAll of the issues mentioned above certainly affect the story's relatability, but they still make narrative sense and are very compelling. If you didn't feel as much connected with Lynri as with Faye or River then it's perhaps not the issue of the story itself but with your own experiences. I would really like to see a mother play through this game.4.2 The Story - Subverting Expectations and The Pacing Okay, I played the devil's advocate for most common criticism now I am gonna add some of my own. I did have issues with the story. But a bit different than the narrative choice, in fact with its very structure.!WARNING THIS SECTION CONTAINS MILD SPOILERS REGARDING STORY STRUCTURE!The first act of the game tricks us into believing that the theme of this game will be a murder mystery scenario and when I realized that I was very excited! The problem is that the theme pretty much gets thrown out of the window by the end of Act 1 and never really revisited, to the point where I felt honestly pretty much cheated by this setup.Act 2 kicks in with more of a familiar gameplay experience. However, I also have problems with it. Memories we visit seems to be very rushed through, featuring only story-oriented stuff. There are no casual memories to visit this time around, to simply get to know the characters (Maybe except the library). With the addition of basically mute protagonist "Quincy" is this just doesn't end up being a very engaging experience unless you force yourself into it.  4.3 The Story - And why I can't explain why it's still worth it. The Epilogue. What can I really say about it without spoiling the game? I am gonna just say it. THIS IS AN AMAZING TWIST... AND THE IMPLICATIONS FOR THE GAME LORE ARE REMARKABLY HUGE. In fact, the feeling of being insatiable left me entirely the moment the first twist landed. After the second I was more than sure this is a great game. I also understood why a prequel was necessary ;)If I can recommend anything, I would recommend replaying To The Moon and Finding Paradise before jumping to it. And especially playing them if you haven't before. It will make the ending MUCH MORE WORTH IT. With that said can't wait for "Episode ??"! P.S This game comes with a simple, customizable Visual Novel Maker. If not for anything else, buy it for that! P.S 2 Sorry if this was a mess to read.P.S 3 Long cat will always protecc never attacc.P.S 4 Faye kinda sus.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game. Good - in opposition to the great games I found in To the Moon and Finding Paradise. As other reviewers have pointed out, it is slightly disappointing that the series ended rather weakly (if this is the ending), but as a standalone game it is difficult to fault it - the storyline is good, the music is of course amazing and our characters are, as always, well-written and rounded. The only way this game really fails is in living up to its predecessors. Something about the previous titles have tugged so hard at my heartstrings that I have not been able to stop thinking about them since I first played To the Moon in 2013, and Impostor Factory unfortunately fails to live up to these sky-high expectations. I will recommend this game because as I mentioned it is, still, a good game, but if you have played the previous titles I will suggest that you lower your expectations slightly.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the first two games more, but even the weakest entry in the To The Moon saga is still an amazing game in my opinion. Impostor Factory is yet another compelling narrative driven experience about life, death, and love. It tries to deceive you as a timeloop game early on where you relive the same events again and again, but a an hour or so it turns into the typical travel down memory lane journey To The Moon and Finding Paradise were know for. Relive the memories of a person slowly reaching death, see the regrets they had during their life, what they wish they could change, and see them live the more fulfilling life they wanted. I don't want to spoil to much, but I think the relationship in Impostor Factory is the strongest the series has been. The ups, the downs, and how they choose to persevere together in the end. The last few scenes are beautiful and just like entries prior it'll put some tears on your face. Reason why I think it's the weakest entry is because honestly I don't know if this game benefits from advertising itself as a timeloop game, but it's the mystery that always drove the To The Moon saga. There's a character later on that won't make sense unless you played Finding Paradise, but let's be real who plays the third entry in a continuous storyline without having played the previous ones. There's no puzzles like before, but this sacrifice was made to provide a more streamline and faster paced game. Overall, yeah I really liked this game. This saga has become one of my favorite indie series in recent memory and I can't wait for the next episode.

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend Imposter Factory, but the 'highly' part only comes from if you played the two previous games To The Moon and Finding Paradise.Kan Gao is a brilliant story teller and musician. _childDocuments_.review: I’ve read a lot of comments about people feeling underwhelmed by this came in comparison. I just wanted to express my praise for this game. To the moon made me feel a dissonant joy at seeing the old man’s fulfillment of what could have been, but sorrow in that it wasn’t real. The was joy in his long life with his love, but sadness in the unfairness of his situation and irony. Finding paradise gave me curiosity and wonder and pure fulfillment in seeing the man’s happiness and contentment in living life out exactly as it happened. Realizing in his last moments that the “regrets” he had in life didn’t take away from the happy life he built with his family, but rather were a part of it. And he got to say goodbye to his guardian Angel in Faye. Now, in Imposter Factory, I also felt joy and melancholy irony. I felt happiness and bitter sadness. But I also felt a WIDE spectrum of other emotions on a deep scale. I felt anger at Lynri for leaving Quincey. I felt joy at seeing her fall in love at the university (where I met my wife) delight in seeing her raise Tobi and soul crushing despair when he passed away. I felt curiosity in the manor. I felt nostalgia and hope seeing Faye. I felt unease in the ending with Neil. In all, I felt more variety of emotions in this game than the prior two, and feel it is my current favorite of the franchise for that reason. And least favorite because it made me want to hug my baby toddler and never let go.

_childDocuments_.review: Possible Spoiler WarningImpostor Factory is an existential drama within an existential horror.It explores ideas that are a little more philosophical than the previous entries, asking the player to reconsider the value they give to stories and characters  while also tying up a few loose ends in the grand scheme of the Sigmund Corp. franchise.The Act structure it uses is traditional (three acts) and avante garde at the same time, which might take you by surprise (in a good or bad way, I can't say). Each Act seems to be doing something a little different than the other, in mood, pacing, plot, lore, and perspective. But woven into all that are a few major themes that have existed since 2011—when To the Moon first launched.

_childDocuments_.review: I must say, this one went beyond what I expected, though I can't really be sure what I truly expected based on trailers and previous parts.I have to be vague to avoid spoilers, even though I want to over-analyze every single bit.The story is, as usual, very solid, and makes you bond with characters involved in it really quickly. The plot itself is well structured and unveils its cards slowly, goes on tangents even (which is a plot point, by the way) and delivers the grand reveal in a way truly didn't expect.The thing is, the game is filled with hints, the reveal does not come out of nowhere if you know the context. It is just great.Now, with that in mind... The story does not really follow the familiar characters from previous games this time... And yet, it uses familiar themes and setup, so I was thinking - is it a sequel, spin-off? Prequel-perhaps. And it kind of is... all of these, in a way. But it all feels familiar.As usual, this is more of an interactive story than acual game - there is little gameplay to speak of, and the whole thing is focused purely on narrative. If there is anything I can strike against this one, it would be the length. It feels shorter than previous episodes, quite noticeably. The main narration also is more linear this time when it comes to uncovering the past of main characters - it simply goes from past to present, doesn't meander like before, doesn't leave events to piece together as much - but it works very well for the purpose of reveal, in context.This one also didn't make me cry AS MUCH as previous main entries (but it still DID make me cry) - perhaps because the story itself, in its core feels... warmer somehow, and the ending is more of a sweet one than bitter-sweet.Still though, despite my minor gripes - worth every moment, and every penny.
