_childDocuments_.review: Impostor Factory… The third entry of the running series by Freebird Games; a company that left a lasting impression by releasing To The Moon, a game that’s famous for its breathtaking storytelling and beautiful soundtrack that brings the best out of each scene. Since then, superb story writing is something synonymous with this company. This time, they took a slightly different approach to the story’s theme. While it’s not as emotionally compelling as the previous entry, I find Impostor Factory to be one of the most enjoyable story-driven games I’ve played recently. I mentioned before that Impostor Factory is the third entry of the series. Now, you might think that you have to play the previous entries to understand the story, but fret not! While it’s somewhat a sequel, Impostor Factory is a standalone experience that rewards both new and long-time followers of the series with its weighty emotional story and sci-fi plot that relate to the other entries.The story kicks off with Quincy, our main character, arriving at a fancy party in the middle of nowhere. Being told that he was the first one to arrive and feeling out of place, he decided to take a look around the mansion where he met a fellow guest, Lynri, on the second floor of the mansion; this confused him as he was told that he was the first one to arrive. The party progressed and everything was fine until Quincy discovered that the host was brutally murdered. But that’s not all, things started to get even weirder as the corpse suddenly vanished, leaving no trace whatsoever. That event left Quincy in a panic state to the point that he suspects even the household cat as a potential killer, which makes me laugh at how ridiculous it was. Strange things are happening and everything is not how it seems to be. What happens next is horror-comedy slapstick with Quincy at its center.I have to mention that despite Impostor Factory being a 16-bit game, everything is beautifully illustrated, from the huge mansion in the middle of nowhere to the lush lavender field. In addition, the characters had a detailed design and smooth animation. You can see the amount of love and effort poured into this, big props to Freebird Games. Gameplay-wise, I think there aren’t that many changes from the previous entries. Impostor Factory uses the classic RPG exploration mechanic: you explore the area to find hidden orbs that would allow progression to the next area. Now, I know that gathering hidden objects tended to be tedious in older RPGs, but not in this one. As you look for these orbs, you’ll find glimpses of memories that show you the tale of Quincy, which made the gathering feel a lot less tedious and more rewarding since you get to know his backstory in the process.I tend to explore every room before moving on to the next area, especially on classic RPGs like this, and Impostor Factory is what I call a short game. Including the exploration part, it took me close to six hours to completely clear it. Freebird Game once again proved themselves as a genius not only in writing up brilliant stories but also in composing beautiful soundtracks. They did it so exceptionally well that you can feel how the character felt at that given moment. It lightens the vibe during a comedy scene, hypes you up during a thriller scene, and best of all, it brings the emotional scene to the next level. All in all, the soundtrack did a perfect job in delivering a wonderful experience and is definitely on my playlist now.Ever since I finished To The Moon a few years ago, I got completely hooked on the series. So far, none of the entries have disappointed me, including this one. Even with its simple gameplay, Freebird Game manages to create yet another gem. The best thing about Impostor Factory was the quality of the story writing; they successfully made it hilarious and profound at the same time. While It’s slightly lacking compared to the previous entries, Impostor Factory is still a great read and I truly enjoyed playing through it. For those who are looking for a good narrative, I highly recommend you give Impostor Factory a shot. Even when it’s not on sale, it’s absolutely worth every penny, especially if you’re planning to get into the To The Moon series.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re a gamer who’s had their eye ever on the RPGMaker engine, it’s fair to assume you know who Freebird Games is.  Proverbially smashing into the indie scene 10 years ago with their detailed masterpiece, To The Moon, Freebird has since added a sequel in 2017 and brings a continuation and possible end to the Sigmund Corp franchise with Impostor Factory.  I’ll forewarn, this game is weird, and somewhat hard to wrap your head around at times, but bear with me: it’s worth it.On a rainy day in front of a disheveled yet grandiose terrace, Quincy attends a party where the status quo is quite a few tax brackets higher than himself.  While the outside is damp and disarranged, the inside of the mansion is as pristine as the proclaimed germaphobe tenants can make it.  In this sprawling two story abode: scientists, investors, big wigs, and some in between find themselves attending to see a mechanical miracle that could change the world in ways never seen before.  Before Quincy and company can see what’s in store for them, Quincy stumbles upon the freshly murdered bodies of the mansion’s owners.  Unraveling at the seams, Quincy runs to the bathroom to avoid suspicion and explanation.  After washing the blood from his hands when checking the bodies, he returns to a similar scene not a few minutes earlier.  None of the guests were the wiser of what happened because the mansion’s residents are still alive and well.  What lays ahead for Quincy is what can be best described as Clue mixed with Groundhog Day.But hold on friends, this is only the first part of the game.  Impostor Factory builds itself into its own name as the genre of this title changes almost by the hour, going from a darkly comedic whodunit into something creator Kan Gao is more known for: heart-string tugging love stories.  Genre changes this abrupt should have to go through some bumpiness, but the love and care taken into the two character’s backstory is so engulfing, engaging, and provoking that you almost forget this game was making you laugh with its ridiculousness.  Within minutes you’re now in Impostor Factory’s grip with how somber and captivating the history between these two are and time feels like it stops with how hard it pulls you in.And it builds tremendously upon its middle act.  Impostor Factory serenades the player with a wave of simple yet beautiful piano scores throughout.  Engaging enough to liven a scene yet subdued enough to appreciate the details of the flashbacks: it’s these tender moments that get enunciated that shine the brightest and hit the hardest.  Dealing with the ups and downs, slips and falls, the highest highs and lowest lows, and the simplistic in-betweens that most couples cherish the most.  The amount of emotional weight of the two characters pressed on the player is astonishing given the minimal amount of time used and a true testament to the emotional genius Gao is at his craft.When that emotional weight carries into Impostor Factory’s third act, the strands of a lifelong journey intertwined by a choice encounter start to tie together with familiar characters and the twists and turns that are revealed provide a beautifully poignant end to the absolute roller coaster of a story.  The choices and paths led after all the mysteries are laid out tear deep and all I could was just admire the quintessential direction of Quincy’s story until the credits rolled and I could exhale after what felt like an eternity of holding my breath for them.Emotionally, I’m exhausted.  But mentally, I’m so happy I spent the time diving head first into Impostor Factory.  Kan Gao shows once again the supreme talent and direction he’s used over the past decade to tell a funny, imaginative, and emotionally crushing tale of living life to the fullest no matter the obstacles thrown in front of you.  Now if you’ll excuse me, I’m going to put back on the OST and try not to cry....I’m gonna cry a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: Impostor Factory is a very conservative story. While the earlier installments were also not very modern, at least that didn't really matter for the story. In this game, however, it's apparent that as soon as a woman is the character you're delving into the memories of, it's not about her. In the end it's not about her hopes, not about her struggles, not even about her ending. TLDR: this studio severely disappointed us. SPOILER: It's about her having children. Even worse, the story has a big focus on being pro life in the most literal sense of the term. It doesn't matter that the child will be severely handicapped, it's alive! You want to have a good life but now the child is dead? No worries, this whole story wasn't in the real world so you made the (heavily implied) 'right' choice in real life and you died a slow painful death! You are both constructs made in a machine and multiplied until there were thousands of you? Let's put you all on the moon! The woman herself even said that a new life where, you know, she isn't severely disabled and can enjoy live WHILE STILL having the child wouldn't matter, because at least hEr BabY iS safe In tHe rEAl wORlD. And why is the make belief childhood friend of the last game there?! We thought, as we started playing, there was a good reason for us following a guy without clear memories in the actual memories of a gal who seemed to know him. You have many hooks to knit a story from, like the guy has Alzheimer and her memories were needed as a backbone to help him or something (all the elements were there). Instead, the part of the story we actually liked (everything before her getting pregnant because as soon as that happened we knew it would all focus on that) didn't matter according to the game. At all. The only thing you need to know is: woman is very ill with a hereditary disease and gets pregnant -> she needs to make the obvious choice if she wants a handicapped child or a slow and painful death -> the game plays a sort of wHaT iF YOur fUTure cHiLD CurES CanCEr card and omg her surname was Watts all along. Also, the murders don't matter.

_childDocuments_.review: how the hell do you put a perfect cap off on the to the moon series, one that's equally philosophical and heartwrenching, comical and horrifying? the answer is you really can't, but you can make something you want and hope others want it too. while the game isn't as emotionally devastating as ttm and finding paradise are, i think that's just fine with me - it delivers an intriguing mystery and heartstring-plucking tale, with a soundtrack and writing expected of this series now. my only point of critique is that it's definitely more "walking simulator"-like than the other entries, but that doesn't make it not worth the pricetag. and while it is an installment in a game series, you don't even really need to play the other games to understand this one, which (at least in my opinion) is a mark of a good sequel. i think i've come away from this one feeling satisfied with the series as a whole and with this game by itself.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: While the dev says you don't need to have played previous games in the To The Moon series, I would recommend you should as some of the revelations later wouldn't make a whole lot of sense. But on its own, this game is so well written, striking that perfect balance of humor and sadness. And the music is so beautiful and emotional. I am excited for whatever comes next in the series.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Imposter Factory. I was imagining the highlighted initials in the title means something, and it didn't disappoint me, actually, way beyond my expectation. As similar to Kan Gao's previous works, his stories are very good at engaging the player to experience a touching life in a few hours. With this new release, I can certainly feel the techniques of expressions has only improved over the years even though "to the moon" was already extraordinary. There are many scenes that if taken alone wouldn't make me cry but delivers an intense emotion when being put in the right time and in the right way. My tears are dried again. What a mastery of human empathy
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: While I loved To the Moon, I wasn't attached to Finding Paradise as much. I guess, the story was a bit predictable at some point. It's sad, it's dark, but it's also charming and funny at times. The whole setting gave me strong Cluedo vibes this time. Also, I felt sorry for my cat pal. SORRY CATE, you protecc!! <3
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: The starting was pretty slow, but later turns out to be really well written. So well written that I need to make a slow clap: "clap" "clap" "clap". I thought I was good at guessing stories and hard to impress but this game changed my mind. If you enjoyed their earlier games this one deserves twice the price tag. _childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I cried at least six times while playing this game and had to pause because I couldn't see the screen through my tears. A true 10/10Now, let's analyze the game in more depth. Yes, this game is the perfect closure to the saga. While some might suggest you can start here, I strongly recommend playing the two main games ("To The Moon" and "Finding Paradise") first. This will allow you to fully appreciate the emotional depth and references to the previous games that might otherwise be lost.This installment starts differently from its predecessors, with plot twists that are more unexpected than ever. The developers have removed the puzzle mini-games, focusing entirely on the story, which I truly appreciate. The narrative is rich, the characters are well-developed, and the emotional impact is profound.What sets this game apart is its ability to evoke such strong emotions. It's not just a game; it's an experience that resonates deeply. The connection I felt with the story and characters surpassed even that of "To The Moon." The writing, music, and pacing all come together to create a memorable and moving conclusion.In short, this game has become my favorite piece of media ever. It's a perfect ending to a perfect saga. Thank you, Kan Gao, for this emotional journey.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: It's good.  Didn't quite have the same emotional impact of others in the series, but it's well told and there are some nice nods to other parts of the series.  Didn't find the story to be quite as engaging as previous efforts, and the twist, while clever, didn't really satisfy as much.  I guess it's one of those cases where it's hard to get out from the shadow of the predecessors.  But regardless, it's still good, if you haven't picked up the rest of the series I encourage you to go do that now and then play this.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: As with To the Moon and Finding Paradise, the entire reason for playing these games are for the stories they provide. Although feeling a little short, I really appreciated the emotional impact of the writing as well as how it neatly tied the series together in an interesting way. After playing the previous titles, I wholly expected some kind of mental deep-dive into someone's past but I wasn't expecting the way everything delightfully connected here. At this point, if you enjoyed the previous entries in this series then I don't believe you'll feel let down by Imposter Factory. Adversely, if you haven't played any of these games and you're coming across this one for the first time, I urge you to pick up all three and play the entire series as a whole. I hope this series continues because I'm already yearning for more.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Not much to say here other than  this is a sequel for To the Moon and Finding Paradise, if you haven't played those games yet, go do so before playing this, they're also pretty short.It's definitely an odd entry, both with how the plot progresses and its payoff but if you liked the last two games you were probably going to get this anyway, and there's no harm in that.It has basically the same pros and cons as the last few entries but I was bothered by the lack of interactive items this time around by comparison, and Quincy being a  more quiet protagonist for a good chunk of the runtime.Short, sweet and that's about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Man the emotional rollercoaster I went through....The soundtrack is amazing as usual, the story is told really well, and the atmosphere pulls you in. I kinda regret not playing through all the games before diving into this one, I do remember the overall story but I think having a refresher of the full series before this game would have enhanced my experienced. _childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: A touching game. The story is quite well done and the music is, as always, excellent. Is it as good as "To The Moon" - in my opinion, no, but I only say that to set your expectations. It is a moving story, but it didn't make me lose my composure the way To The Moon did. Maybe it's because I'm not as personally close to what the characters go through in this one.It's absolutely worth your time and money. It's good. It's very good. I still think he hasn't struck the same magic as he did with To The Moon - it's hard when your first work was so astounding, it's almost impossible to live up to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: The 3rd official installment in the "To The Moon" series. This title takes a very different approach than its predecessors, putting a more sinister and dark spin on the plot. To me it feels like Kan was trying something "different" in this episode while still trying to deliver the same emotional journey the series has carried historically. This is where the game falls a little short...Don't get the wrong idea here, the game itself is still extremely well done, however in an attempt to be both "different" and "pull plots together from the previous titles", I felt myself frequently reeling from information overload. This left me with so many open questions during my play through, that it fogged my picture of what was actually happening in many moments in the story. Due to pacing and story complexity alone, I felt I missed out on the raw immersion and emotional impact the story COULD have offered. That is not to say it flopped, it was fantastic! I simply think a bit more time refining the core story beats would have helped players digest it easier - as seen in "Finding Paradise" for example.Overall, although I have a few gripes with some pacing (and the removal of my sweet sweet puzzles), I think this title is a must-play for any fan of the franchise and very much worth it's price point.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Hey, let's talk about this game!Well, I played 'To The Moon'; 'A bird's story' and 'Finding Paradise', I can't talk about 'Impostor Factory' without a connection between the previous games from freebird, I do think you need to play at least 'To The Moon' and 'Finding Paradise' before playing this one, cause everything is kinda connected, and you'll get a better experience.In the previous titles, I cried, especially in Finding paradise, that imo, is the best game from this franchise.In a resume, 'To The Moon' is about wishes, superation, life and how should we face things, like promises and other things!'A Bird's Story' is kinda short, but it's a beautiful story about a boy, who needs to face the reality and stay out of the world of imagination, when I played it for the first time, it felt like I was a child againOk, now let's talk about 'Finding Paradise', it's my favorite and I cried A LOT, I mean it. The story is about regrets and how their impact can change your life, tbh it was kinda a trigger for me too, but I think everyone has regrets, which is why I think 'Finding Paradise' will have more impact, it's a true masterpiece, don't get me wrong, I enjoyed the franchise at all, but I'll never forget this game.Now we're good to talk about Impostor Factory, I won't give any spoilers so don't worry.'Impostor Factory' is a good closure to the franchise, as I said before, the franchise was about wishes/superation, then we got an child's tale, and in the end a great story about regrets and chances. From that, moving on to 'Impostor Factory', we get a story about someone who wants to make the difference in the world, we can't use our time forever, but as long we live, we can try to have some impact on the world.It's a beautiful story, but I didn't cried this time, I was kinda proud of the characters and how they just went from something flat at the beggining to some kind of "you can make the difference" thing. I won't give spoilers as I said. But it's important to know that maybe you won't cry a lot, but if you love the games of this franchise like I do, give it a change, I'm definitely thinking about somethings after playing and I really enjoyed it too. For me, 'Finding Paradise' still being the best, then we have 'To The Moon' in second place, 'Impostor Factory' in third place, and after it 'A Bird's Story'.But hey, if you don't really play, how are you going to find out if you're going to like it or nah?
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: I played and felt all 3 games in 2022, it was an emotional roller coaster.Thank you freebird games for this amazing journey.I highly recommend the game but don't forget to play the other ones to understand everything : To the moon, A bird's story , Finding Paradise.10/10 story11/10 soundtracks>9000 depressing , sadness , feels , emotions

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a stepping stone to the next (hopefully the final since the wait is killing me) iteration in the series, but a lot of stuff to ponder about here. Analysis______The multiverse's existential implications considering that each layer could have been activated by a different entity than Lynria, however some iterations of the last layer making the result similar to the first layer (and Lyndia/Quincy actually discovering Faye because of that, and even then moving on to relive a "perfect" considered life by Faye) gives Steins;Gate vibes but on a much grander scale.There were also similar motifs as the first game where the stars affecting the lavender could be compared to the moon, but on a deeper look, their reasons are very different. One is for fulfilling dreams in a limited life, and the other is for discovering a complement. Comparing how basic elements of nature interact with each other and juxtaposing that with human emotions has always been the developer's speciality, and I can't wait to play their future games in this series.Also, it is shown that Neil has feelings for Eva (or at least deeply cares for her). This is amplified by the fact that they were married in the perfect life envisioned by him.. Narrative 11/10

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who bought this game in middle of the series. It was "ok", to say the least. I enjoyed the humor, especially with Rice Bot and long kitty (who magically evolves, omg).The introduction in the story that takes place when a protagonist male who entered a mansion and were given confusion greetings from old couples and an attractive lady. Weird & insidious things happening in the mansion and time-travelling thing appears to be resetting and the protagonist male doesn't know what's going on and goes on to discover something deeper.I liked the introduction, but when digging deeper into the lore, I find myself getting more dissatisfied with how the lore leads. I like the past events that showcases the development of a character leading to the end, I did feel a sad emotional in that scenario. After finishing up the past events part, the story just gets less interesting to me. I know the whole purpose of the game is giving the protagonist and the lady a chance to properly live together with a child but I don't really feel that emotional connection with it.The art style is stunning. It's not typical RPG-Maker game and the character animations are very smooth and clear so you can see how the characters portray themselves, making it feel "real".The story itself is story-rich indeed but did it hit super emotional level? Not for me, and I'm quite emotional person too so, sadly I didn't enjoy the game, despite good humor and art style. _childDocuments_.review: I don't know what to say since there are a lot of comments praising the game already, and they are all true. _childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: First of all musics in the game are epic, congrats on that.    But I am not sure it's the story just a little bit dull or it's dull due to I haven't played previous games of this series. It feels like a cliche idea with overly long sentimental plots and repetitive story-telling.    I mean if this is a movie/manga/novel it will be way more captivating, as a non-fan of previous series I'm expecting fun gameplay and an intricate story. Gameplay here is basically zero, and each sentimental plot is just so long it gets tiresome real quick. I thought there would be crazy suspense plot-twists but seems like suspenseful elements act as nothing more than an intro.     Pricing is reasonable since a lot of movies today are way worse than this with way more expensive tickets. The game is not "bad" though, it just not "overwhelmingly good" as a lot of online recommendations said (I bought it because I saw a review video saying this is crazily intriguing). So if you're a fan of previous games or extremely curious about the game it's good to go, however if you are expecting a super suspenseful gameplay it just doesn't have any.

_childDocuments_.review: YES, this game released only 5 hours ago, and YES, I've already finished it, and let me tell you :It was worth the wait. Not only is the soundtrack still as beautiful as the other games, the changes and improvements in gameplay, animations and environments are just absolutely gorgeous. Kan Gao, you're still as great as ever. And all the people involved in this too! It's plain to see how talented everyone is, and I'm really happy to see how much Freebird Games has improved over the years since To The Moon. I will gladly buy the OST as soon as it's out, and will wait to see what the future holds for us! In the meantime, I can't wait for let's plays of this game to be made so that I can appreciate the story over and over again while seeing other people be amazed by it.

_childDocuments_.review: Another great and very emotional game in the series. I would definitely recommend playing To The Moon and Finding Paradise first, without them the ending makes a lot less sense and a lot of the emotional impact would get lost. _childDocuments_.review: Freebird’s games are one-of-a-kind. They approach modern problems in a very subtle, yet powerful way. Making you question your decisions, place in life, or helping to move forward when you are on the crossroad.Impostor Factory wasn’t as touching for me as To the Moon, which is my absolute favorite, but still, it was a great experience. These few hours it will take you to finish Impostor Factory is the best way you can invest in yourself while playing video games. It won't be an exaggeration if I'll say that it's one of the games that can make you a better human being.Give it a shot! And best of luck ahead, dear Reader!
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: If you played the other games of this franchise, you'll obviously be playing this one so there isn't much to say to convince you to. Those devs are amazing and everything they make should be played.With that being said, here is my opinion on Impostor Factory: The game starts off as a murder mistery. We play as Quincy, an unfamiliar character who goes to a mansion and finds corpses there, then time-loops and keeps finding them again, only in different places. It starts off really interesting, and you want to know what the hell is happening and where are Eva and Neil... But then it takes a turn to our typical To the moon-ish story-telling. That's when it fell apart for me a little bit, because I just couldn't like the female MC. The game revolves around her, and me not liking her made me middle of the game (telling her story) not as good as it should've been. I always loved this franchise characters and stories so it took me by surprise, but maybe it's because Linry doesn't have any "mistery" around her condition. The only thing that really makes us go "oh" comes later on (and yeah, it's pretty cool and it made me tear up a little bit), but by then I was already kind of tired of the whole thing.I really liked the first and last hour of the game, however. It was only the middle that did not please me as much. I believe this is also a personal opinion and not one that many people will share, so you should just play this game as you would anyway. You may find answers to your questions.

_childDocuments_.review: It wasn't really as enjoyable as the other games from Kan Gao, mostly because you did not really "play" anything. It wasn't bad either, but I expected more from Freebird Games by now.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: (game clear review at 4.1 hours) (my two cents on neg reviews I've read so far)Regarding negative reviews, before you take stock in any of them keep in mind this game is the 3rd of a series and was advertised as such, so without playing the first two you're jumping into a series mid-way i.e. if you only watched Return of the Jedi you'd not be shocked that Vader is Luke's father and Leia is his sisters (spoiler alert for a 30 year old movie)(short version)A well written visual novel that strongly supports the previous versions, absolutely worth the price especially if you're a fan.  (long version)With that aside, yet another amazing game written by freebird.  This is a fully text based game and there aren't the previous puzzles to solve which might upset some, but for me it wasn't a big deal.  The writers are very good at what they do and kept me engaged throughout the whole story.  The music is fantastic and gets you when it needs to and just like previous games I had to choke back a tear or two as I went on. Now secretly I am hoping they do not release a 4th one because this wraps the story up with a very nice bow leaving just enough to the individual to fill in the blanks on their own.

_childDocuments_.review: I will try to explain my experiences without ruining or spoiling anything.So I just noticed that this new game from Freebird Games is finally out and bought it immediately. Started the game, realized I was so into the story, completed in about 3-4 hours.As described, "A story that will make you curse at the screen." VERY true.I played all the past games before I played "Imposter Factory": I HIGHLY recommend playing all the past games for the BEST experience. "To the Moon" and “Finding Paradise” may be better starter games, especially if you aren't too familiar with Freebird Games’ style of storytelling.Knowing all the previous games (including the winter DLCs), I was quite confident in my "theory" or "predictions" after playing around 1/2 of the story- or that's what I thought. I then remembered that Kan’s storytelling is always unpredictable, and again, his brilliant writing in this game did not disappoint me at all compared to his past games.This game surely made me curse at the screen- probably much more than the previous ones.I cannot ascertain anything about this experience (which can be said for all the Freebird Games), it's mostly about if you can make personal connections to the characters or to the story. So this game could make you cry the most in the whole series, or maybe not at all. Personally, it wasn't a tearjerker compared to the past games, but that doesn't mean it wasn't as good as the others. Each of the games are so distinct, and has a special place in my heart.I can say that Kan did an amazing job connecting "Imposter Factory" to "To the Moon" or "Finding Paradise." How they are connected may include spoilers, so I will not mention anything further.VERY HIGHLY recommended especially if you liked the past games… and long cats.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played the other games in the series - To the Moon, A Bird Story, Finding Paradise - then you know what to expect here. That includes an incredible soundtrack that augments exactly what's happening on the screen. Playing this game without music would be missing out on half the game. And if you  played those other games then stop reading this and start playing To the Moon immediately!There's not quite as much experimentation with the mechanics as last time, which I consider an improvement, but the story, and really the narrative structure are somewhat more experimental here than before. Repetition is a very purposeful motif, used effectively.Impostor Factory asks big, bold questions. What should your priorities be? Is it ok to be a little selfish? And ultimately, how does one live a good, meaningful life?The craziest thing here is that the game actually manages to answer those questions, and answer them well, while still leaving some wiggle room for interpretation.And the real strength is that there's also room for you, for injecting yourself into the characters and thinking about how you would react in their situation. Once again, just like with To the Moon, this game generated countless discussions for me in real life, because the scenarios it brought to my mind were worth talking to other people about. More than that: I  to talk through those ideas.Parents, be warned, you will be hit far harder here than anyone who has never had kids.I get why this game took so long now. It's not that the graphics or the engine are doing spectacularly complicated things. It's that the experience had to be finely crafted so that you arrive at the right place in the emotional arc for what was going to happen next. And it works marvelously.I still think To the Moon is the better game. Maybe just because I played it first. But this came closer than anything else has to achieving that same journey.It's a masterpiece of story telling.

_childDocuments_.review: General Impression: (SPOILERS) Impostor Factory starts out strong, with a characteristic gut-punch of emotion shifting the story into a beautiful, heartbreaking drama halfway through. However, instead of sticking the landing with already established characters, Kan Gao and his fellow creators opt for a soulless twist that renders the prior events of the story drastically weakened. (HEAVY SPOILERS AHEAD)It's tough to criticize such an obvious labor of love from Freebird Games. I've been closely following their work since 2011, and consider Finding Paradise to be one of the best video games stories I've experienced. And while (in true Freebird fashion) the music, endearing comedy, and grounded dialogue are all present in Imposter Factory, I can't say I left the experience anywhere close to satisfied–especially considering the solipsistic implications created from the story's drastic shift in the third act. On a positive note, the game is made all the better by doing away with the puzzle/gameplay elements of its previous installments, choosing instead to dedicate all its runtime to storytelling. And what a story it was for the first two hours, where I considered the characters to be the most mature and compelling individuals Kan and co. have come up with. It wasn't shaping up to be as touching or inspiring as its predecessors, but the subject matter explored in Imposter Factory was definitely Freebird Games' most mature (and bleak) to date. Lynry and Quincy go through the wringer, and the absolutely gorgeous "A Reality Without Me" simply could not be played enough to underscore the tone of their challenged relationship. I was completely sold from the first hour of the story, finding myself crying multiple times as hit after hit came Linry and Quincy's way. It's a shame none of it is real. The story of the people we follow is nothing but the 9th simulated version of the lives of two people that existed in the REAL real world, and the interactions between the memory versions of Linry and Quincy (whose player avatar doesn't even know Linry), are nothing but shades of people playing out a fantasy orchestrated by Neill Watts (the real Linry's son) and his morally blank A.I. Faye, who now resembles an ominous HAL9000 rather than the sentimental subconscious of Colin from Finding Paradise. The game ends a whole hour before it should, opting to leave us on a bitter cliffhanger. Neill callously comments on the final image (Linry tucking baby Neill into bed) as a "supposed" perfect timeline, ripping us away from the potential of any real catharsis. The character operating the story (Neill) is the very one who is not even emotionally fazed by it. Where Johnny and Colin both learned important life lessons through their experiences in Sigmund Corp's tech (as well as communicating powerful themes to the audience), this story seems to go for, "we all could be in a simulation, but you should enjoy whatever you get while you can get it, but remember, all of it might not be real."I'm truly disappointed by this story, not because of the strength of its predecessors, but by the wasted potential of the powerful storytelling exhibited in its first two thirds. Hopefully the simulation path doesn't continue on with the following story, and we can return to a world where feelings and pain are very real, and submerging ourselves in a simulation, and the minute details of how they work, are not the answers to our problems.

I enjoyed this story more than the prior ones and that is the equivalent of me ranking s-tier masterpieces. While this game lacked the mini-games that the prior games had, it felt more immersive. _childDocuments_.review: As with the previous games, To the Moon and Finding Paradise, this is best thought of as a 4 hour interactive movie rather than a traditional game. It is presented in such a way that it isn't necessary to have played the previous games, but if you have played them it answers some of the things they left unanswered. The story is engaging and interesting, and the soundtrack accompanies it all really well. This game drops some of the mini-games present in the previous entries and made it clearer what was necessary to progress, something that I think was a terrific decision, as it removed potential points of frustration or confusion, and really leaned into the story telling aspect which is where it shines the most. There are still places to explore and extra interactables to find, giving depth to the scenes. I highly recommend playing through this game if you're looking to experience an interesting story, and if at all possible I recommend playing through it all in one sitting or with minimal breaks, to really immerse yourself in its world.

I still cried, I still wondered what am I doing with my life, I still wondered if my existence has had any positive impact on someone elses life. You can't be something to everybody, but you can be everything to someone, even if only for a short time

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Imposter Factory's pretty good. It builds upon the previous two games in the series in some ways, but in other ways it struggles. Overall, it's still an enjoyable experience if you liked the previous games. If you didn't like To the Moon or FInding Paradise, however, this may not be your cup of tea.For starters, Ken Gao and the rest of the devs at Freebird did a great job with the graphics. Considering the fact that they're using RPG Maker and are such a small studio, it's really impressive what they pulled off. It is abundantly clear that they have learned over the years, which is made apparent by looking at the progressive improvements in the graphics from To the Moon, to Finding Paradise, and finally Imposter Factory.The music in this game is alright. It's certainly not bad, but I'd say its predecessors had more memorable OSTs. Unlike the previous games, I don't remember the tunes or names of any of the tracks in this game. By no means is the soundtrack bad, it's just not as memorable as To the Moon's or Finding Paradise's in my opinion.As for gameplay, it hasn't changed much. They completely removed the puzzles in between levels, which I believe they did in Finding Paradise but it still bears mentioning. The devs also removed the little scavenger hunts for the items to unlock the memories. In my opinion, this was a good change because they didn't do much other than pad out the game time for no real reason. However, due to this, there isn't much gameplay other than walking and interacting with characters/objects. If you find that type of gameplay boring, you may not enjoy this very much.Finally, the story was alright. If you're worried about spoilers, I'd skip this paragraph. It wasn't as captivating, climactic, or emotional as the other two games to me personally. Similar to my point about the music, it certainly isn't bad. Far from it, in fact. They introduce a lot of interesting concepts/lore in this game that seem to build up to future games. In fact, that would probably be the main reason it isn't as feel-heavy as the previous installments, it's simply not as focused on doing that like the other two games were. That isn't to say it's a boring or soulless experience, either. There are moments akin to those in To the Moon and Finding Paradise, but they're less impactful and less frequent. Instead, focus is shifted to worldbuilding and lore information.So, with that all said, do I recommend the game? Yes, given you have played To the Moon and Finding Paradise. Whilst it may not be as strong of an entry in the series as the other two, it is still very much an enjoyable experience. The graphics are impressive, the story is good, and the gameplay is streamlined. If you enjoyed the predecessors, than I don't see why you wouldn't enjoy Imposter Factory as well.Also, the name's sussy, so that's funny

_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: I played it in a sitting, just now, so these are my raw, unedited feelings on Impostor Factory.Do not buy this game for a story about Eva and Neil. This is not a chapter about them. Or, well, it is. But not in the way that we've had in the past two games. This is a game about both of them, and also neither of them. It is, however, a game about people arguably just as important, if not even more so.Emotionally gripping, witty, and with a theme tune that's already implanted itself deep into my grey matter, it is another Kan Gao classic and will stay with me for the next 6 years until the next episode comes out. With story twists you will not see coming, a jaw-dropping moment in the third act, and several scenes that will have tears streaming down your face, it is well worth the price.However, it's still not about Eva or Neil. So if you want more of their quirky adventures, it's not about that. But it is.EDIT: It's been a day, I have more thoughts now.I agree with other negative reviews, in that this game is not a To The Moon game. It's more like a Bird Story if anything. Minimal puzzles, minimal dialogue, minimal interactivity with the environment. Quincy, the main character, does have some funny quips, but ultimately he's on his own a good 99% of the time and doesn't say anything about what transpires. Especially in Act II. It is, as another reviewer put it, a walking simulator with a To The Moon coat of paint.It's also kind of short. Even if you take your time, I imagine it's about 3 hours 45 minutes, maybe shorter. To The Moon was at least 4, Finding Paradise was at least 5. For the record, I understand it being somewhat shorter, given this game took 4 years to make compared to the 6 year gap we had between TTM and FP. However, I can't excuse just how... Empty it seems to feel. Any character other than the main ones feel stiff and very cardboard cut-out like, there's very little flavor or fluff text to be found, and only one 'puzzle'. Everything else is just walking.Graphics are stunning. Music is stellar, if not as good as TTM and FP (which is a high bar). The story does twist and turn in an enjoyable way, even if at times the game doesn't seem to know what genre it wants to be. You also absolutely need to play Finding Paradise if you want to fully understand some of the plot twists.Despite it's faults, I still recommend the game to anyone who enjoys Kan Gao's work, and the work of Freebird Games. However, if you're expecting To The Moon, I recommend becoming more familiar with A Bird Story, as that's what you're going to get.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game. The level of emotional story telling and writing from the freebird studio team is truly amazing. _childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: The way the story was set up in this one was brilliant. It's very much different from the first two installments but I think this one might be my favorite. Not much gameplay here (though that's kind of to be expected at this point), but I still think this is a fantastic game. _childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Story is good UNTIL it decides to connect the previous entries of TTM franchise.Gameplay is nonexistent, no puzzles/goofy mini-games this time.Soundtrack while nice absolutely pales in comparison to both TTM and FP.Characters are fine, I would've prefer yet another Neil and Eva shennanigans though.Visuals and cinematography are MUCH better at suspense moments, which immerses more into the story.Length is shockingly short.No Laura Shigihara - big sad right here.Overall, to fans of previous installments: you should give it a try although DO NOT expect the same quality of writing and emotional gut punches.To people, who's new here: try first TTM or FP (or both, they're almost equally great).A bit dissapointed, but it was nice, wished it was more than just simply....that.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: This was slightly different from the other Freebird Games in how it was able to evoke a much wider range of emotion from me as I played it. It's a bizarre, yet beautiful little story that goes to some interesting places over the course of its short playtime. To the Moon might have destroyed my soul more, but I left Impostor Factory feeling much more fulfilled as a player.Fantastic little game, I recommend it.P.S. I also recommend playing the other games in the series as this game makes the payoff truly sweet.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Imposter Factory tells a sad story through bits made up of humour, punches, great music, and emotion-filled dialog + animations. A sad, but beautiful story. One that is told accompanied with captivating compositions and meticulously designed animations. Having played all of Kan's other games, I unfortunately have to say this was my least favourite one. In most series, there will always be a less favourite one, and for me, it was Imposter Factory. Can't hide it though : I did cry my eyes out at some point, but not nearly as hard as it was the case with To the Moon. Seriously, Kan Gao broke me into countless pieces until I was but dust and tears with the past games. This one was a nice wrap up and links all other stories together, but didn't "hit right in the feels". I felt a lot was put in making the animations where more could have been put in character development and "the reveal". My personal opinion is : it doesn't need to be that beautiful even though it really was. If the story is well-written and is being told like it has been told with past games, nice animations are an addition. Not a focus point. Again, my expectations were sooooo high that I might have oversold the game to myself before having played. Imposter Factory is a short game. It consolidates all previous stories into one point in time (and space, technically). Don't expect to be a trainwreck after finishing the game. Imposter Factory will not destroy and pierce your body and soul, but it will touch your heart and make you think about what's really important to you. About who you are, what you want to achieve. About decisions you made, some you could have made. About how long can a cat actually become if stretched enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Another great one from Freebird. It's kind of a prequel to the previous games in the series: To the Moon and Finding Paradise, but it's also more than that. Prepare for a bumpy ride, it'll be beautiful, tragic, but also funny, as you can expect from the creators.In terms of both story and gameplay (that little they have) it's a step down from the previous games, but it's still great and worth a play, especially if you already played with the others.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: I find it more of a visual novel than a game. _childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: (NO SPOILERS)It really pains me to write a negative review for one of Kan Gao's games but here we are. Let's get a few things out of the way first: the OST? Amazing as usual. The graphics? It's the usual pixel art but even better. The characters? Complex and with an interesting story to tell... but yeah, the two main characters' story is what really disappointed me. If you're into the whole Sigmund Corp. drama that's been going on since To the Moon then yes, play this game. But if you're like me and play these games for the "two main characters plot" that starts and ends all in the same game then no... it's kind of a huge disappointment here.(SPOILERS)I really enjoyed act one and almost cried a few times during act two. But then the game basically tells you that nothing is real and everything is just a simulation. Yep, those weren't the real Quincy and Lynri, just an alternative version of them. As soon as the game said this I lost most of the connection I had with them and simply stopped caring. As I've already said, I almost cried a few times during act two but act three and its ending didn't make me feel anything. I was just staring at the screen thinking that if life really is a simulation and nothing is real then I should've spent these four hours doing something better... like playing Finding Paradise. I do realize that this review is very subjective, so if you enjoyed the game... good for you! I'm glad you didn't end up feeling like you wasted your money like I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot believe Kan Gao and the rest of Freebird did it again. _childDocuments_.review: From the creators of To The Moon and Finding Paradise, so you know how this works. You take your little 16-bit sprite character through a story of laughter and heartstring tugging, a journey that will make you laugh and cry. And oh boy, what a great start this game has. You show up to a party where there's a bunch of investors for a project of some sort and then a murder happens, and there's a mysterious woman, and you go back in time, and a bunch of crazy things happen. The first act of this story is PHENOMENAL. I laughed several times, I gasped in surprise, I openly remarked to my wife in the other room "This game is so pugging great!" It's amazing. And honestly, I recommend exiting the game right there and basking in how good the first act was.But if you didn't do that, that's too bad, because now you have to go through the second act. The above mystery woman, who you had a handful of conversations and have barely gotten to know suddenly thinks you find her interesting enough to set you on a journey witnessing her ENTIRE PUGGING LIFE STORY, and folks, it is a trope-laden, cliched, dismally boring slog. She was born with an illness of some sort (never fully explained) which sets her as The Doomed Girl. She meets a fellow student who is a Free Spirit but apparently not free-spirited or interesting enough to have any sort of life outside of being a good boyfriend. You will run through every major moment in their lives together along with way too many minor ones, with a progress bar telling you how much longer you'll need to keep going through this mind-numbing journey of two cardboard cutouts in a story so bland that whatever AI program was involved in writing it probably requested a pseudonym. I quit after almost three hours of gameplay because I stopped caring and wanted to do anything other than spend time with these characters for one second more.This game rates as Overwhelmingly Positive on Steam and to you Yes voters, I am Overwhelmingly Positive you all are lying. Maybe there's a third act that is a breathtaking work of staggering genius, and maybe the AirBNB that's surrounded by five miles of foul-smelling sewage has a nice pool. It doesn't matter, I'm never gonna get there.

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I'm no good at reviews, but this game... was worth the wait and more. You've done it again. What a phenomenal story. Oh my god. There is nothing flawed about this. The music is amazing, the story is brilliant, the dialogue feels so natural, the art is beautiful... everything about this is just so so wonderful. _childDocuments_.review: So this game has overwhelmingly positive reviews which means it clearly was enjoyed and something that resonated with a lot of people. However it didn't resonate with me. I'll explain why--but do keep in mind how positive the other reviews are when making a decision on buying this.On with the show. Impostor Factory is the third game of this series, proceeded by Finding Paradise and To the Moon. These games tend to tell emotionally involved stories with puzzles to figure out about how to progress.Unfortunately, I found that Impostor Factory retreads the same ideas present in To the Moon and Finding Paradise without meaningfully pushing the overarching narrative of the series forward or evolving the writing in a meaningful way. The first two games are tearjerkers, but it doesn't feel like the developers have progressed since To the Moon released in 2011, which quickly gives the game a dated feel. The gameplay here is actually simpler than the first two, with the puzzle elements removed entirely from progression. You'll walk and talk, and that's about it. I think some people may enjoy not needing to figure out puzzles to continue the plot, but for me I felt like it was a regression from the previous two entries and an unfortunate omission.With that said, the writing here IS good, but I was disappointed that the game throws away its most interesting ideas early on to retread the same tropes & half-opened mystery box styled writing that featured heavily in To the Moon and Finding Paradise. This made it much more difficult for me to invest in the game because while Freebird Games does tell good stories, they seem to have gotten stuck telling the same story over and over and over again. Instead of the revelations coming as a shock, I rolled my eyes as the game proceeded down the same patterns as its predecessors without growth.Those of you looking for some closure on this decade-long series might also leave frustrated. While this game really does need the first two in the series to be played and understood, I don't think this game does much to meaningfully push the narrative forward for those of us who have been following for a decade now. This is a shame because--again, the writing is good! But it feels like every game Freebird Games releases is another take at Act 1 of a greater story. They're all great Act 1s, but after a decade I'd like an Act 2.And that's where I'm at. This sequel disappointed me, but at least part of that is on me for wanting it to be more of a continuation than it is. I'd still like to see that next game that progresses the plot, but if the next game Freebird releases is another side story? I'll probably skip it.

_childDocuments_.review: Great continuation of the story from the first two main games, with a nice twist on the memory mechanic. _childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: How to explain... When I first watched the trailer, I was really concerned. This did not look at all like To the Moon or Finding Paradise. After completing the game, I can confirm that if you want another game like the first two, you're in luck. A wonderful emotional story awaits you. I can also confirm that the trailer is pretty much accurate. How those two are both true is a bit of a mystery, but it works. If you enjoyed the other games in this series, you'll enjoy this I have no doubt.The music is wonderful as always. The game-play is definitely refined. To be fair, the worst aspect of To the Moon was the tedious searching for enough colourful balls to move to the next scene, then solving a picture puzzle. Finding Paradise made things a little better, but Impostor Factory takes the cake. This game does away with the puzzle, and the colourful balls come to you as you experience the story, so it plays much more fluidly, and you won't be stuck in one scene for far longer than was intended.As stated in the game's description, you can play this game independently of the others. I will say (without spoiling anything) that there are a couple of moments that would have no real impact if you hadn't played the previous games, whereas the impact they had on me was significant. So my recommendation would definitely be to play the other games first.So yeah, highly recommended. If you're at a loss after watching the trailer and reading the description, good! I can only say that that is the correct way to approach this game. Now play it, and all will become clear.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: 48 minutes in - and I'm confused .78 minutes in - and I'm crying.108 minutes in - and I'm crying again.This game is above and beyond all expectations. If you loved To The Moon and Finding Paradise (and A Bird Story), you'll surely love IF. I cannot tell much more since anything would be a huge spoiler.All left to say is: Thank you so much, Freebird Games! For making the third game in the series while still (!) delivering high quality content (and jokes). For making every game vastly different in terms of characters. For the always perfectly fitting soundtrack. For creating deeply emotional stories. Thank you!EDIT after finishing the story: All of the above still holds true.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: You know that ugly cry? That cry you have so deep that it hurts? I did that. Got a headache and it ruined the rest of my day. 10/10 would ugly cry again. But in all seriousness, Freebird Games just keeps outdoing themselves with each game. That said, Imposter Factory is probably the least accessible of the games. You really need to have played To the Moon, A Bird Story and Finding Paradise to really enjoy this game where I feel To The Moon, and even Finding Paradise to a degree, much more of standalone experiences. Without actually dissecting the story, the game deals with the concept of choices - what it means to live each moment of your life to the fullest. Do you live for each moment and cherish it because it will never come again or do you dedicate your entire existence to bettering the world than they way you came into it? You may think you know how you feel, but this game may have you think twice about your own life in the most surprising ways.The games self-depreciating and culture (meme) humor is on full display here, too, but done far better than in their previous titles and in just enough quantity to give you a good chuckle between the darker and sadder moments in the story. I cried,. I laughed. And I cried a hole lot more. What more can you want from Freebird Games?
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't really watch the trailers when going into this game, and from reading the game description, I felt like it wasn't going to be as emotional as To the Moon or Finding Paradise. For the most part, I was right. Impostor Factory executes its story very differently compared to other games in the Sigmund Corp series. My experience was more or less the same as watching a good episode of Black Mirror.Overall, this game is good. The visuals have taken a step up, the story is powerful (albeit confusing at times), and the music is impressive. But I think the experimental storytelling just made it not as compelling as its predecessors. So if you were expecting another emotional joyride, then you may be disappointed. Instead, make sure to play through the other games, and enjoy the questions that are answered with this game's story, as well as the new plot points it creates for future episodes to explore.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Another enjoyable entry in the To The Moon series.Plenty of emotion and lots of lore details that will satisfy long term fans, while still leaving more for any potential sequel.It's the least strong in the series as its plot gets a little too complicated in the 3rd act, and it's even less of a game than the others. It's basically an interactive story.Still good though.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely fine game.Although none of the later games in this series have landed with quite the same sob-inducing impact as To The Moon, Impostor Factory follows in same vein in that:That being said, Impostor Factory has significant differences from To The Moon and Finding Paradise.  First thing, it's not a sequel.  It's (except for some end-game material and a very important after-credits sequence) essentially a prequel to the other games, walking you through the personal stories around how the memory-interface technology in this world was originally developed, and why. It continues to build on the broader implications of the memory technology for human life and society, implications that the characters themselves incompletely grasp.It also has, somehow, even fewer game-y elements than the prior main games.  Exploration is only a tool here to increase your investiture and to optimize story pacing, nothing else.  It's also a bit shorter than the other main games, though nowhere near as short as the interlude games.  Finally, this is clearly not an entry point.  Anyone playing this series should go in release order (skipping the interlude short-games if they like).I'm not going to spoil any more than that.  Playing this is a wonderful experience.  Most people will love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Great music, great story, charming graphics!For me, the story did not induce the same uncontrollable waterfall from my eyes as the first two games.  That said, there were so many moments where my eyes did tear up, but there were also just as many moments that warmed my heart.  If you enjoyed To The Moon and Finding Paradise, you will enjoy this one!

_childDocuments_.review: When you played the previous games, you think you allready saw everything this kind of game can offer you, so you believe this surely wouldn't gonna get you and in the end, it completely get you. Kan Gao games were always a very soft spot to me. I do believe this was the best of the series, to be fair previouse titles are built up the story and universe for this game to be that great, but it has a completely different approach compare to the previous titles and it has much different story. Although you can be a bit dissapointed because it has different characters in the focus and not really closing our Sigmund professionals story. So all I can hope is it isn't the last game from the series.So can I reccomend this game to you?Absolutely, if you like story games and not against the rpgmaker ashtetics and pixel graphics.Previous titles aren't a must, but I think you should play the previous ones, story aren't heavily connected, but connected well enough where it gives a lot of plus enjoyment if you play the others before.

_childDocuments_.review: Another time it was quite an emotional ride for me. Like its predecessors Impostor Factory has an IMHO excellent story, which is quite cheesy and has a lot of twists. It caught me right from the beginning. I recommend this game to everyone, who likes "interactive movies" with a big focus on story-telling and fitting music. Though the graphics kept simple they illustrate the story very well. Thanks to everyone involved into its making for this masterpiece!!
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: A few people have mentioned this but Impostor Factory really does not feel as though it has a heart. Moreover, it feels like it has fallen into the fan-service trap you see with smalltime creators, webcomic artists etc... At some point when the (relatively short and needlessly sad) story is done and wrapped up, instead of developing on that story with proper gameplay at any step of the way, we are somehow tossed into an act three that is essentially the exposition and reference dump from hell. I am interested in TTM's meta-story, but you can't really get me invested in your main character dilemma without having meaningful character moments, and you can't then destroy all empathy I had built for these characters by making me feel like nothing I just witnessed mattered at all. It reminds me of Black Mirror's worst moments in that way: just point out vague critiques of society for the sake of spectacle without providing a meaningful commentary. Except here I guess it's supposed to feel optimistic? It just made me feel like a jackass for caring about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game, I've been anticipating this game for the past 2 years, and I'm very very happy to say it did not dissapoint. Even after the delays and delays of Impostor factory, it all came to fruition in the end and delivered yet ANOTHER amazing addition to the "To The Moon" series (If that's what we're calling this). Please!, If you havent played any of the previous games before this, go play it NOW! You wont regret it at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest, I was a bit skeptic when I first watched the trailer. No Eva and Neil, and the mood seems pretty much opposite to what he has been doing so far. However, you will witness the genius of Kan; he successfully weaves this seemingly unrelated story to the original episode in the most breathtaking way. The game itself is pretty short, just three hours are enough, but it is very dense - as dense as the previous two episodes which were around 6 hours long. And don't forget the read the comics once you finish playing it; that will conclude the whole episode.Oh if you haven't played the previous episodes; don't do this. Play them, A bird story, and minisodes. That will enrich the experience of this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: At this point, I feel like I'm just paying Freebird Games to give me clinical depression. This game is a beautiful masterpiece. The way it layers on the mystery until it all clicks into place is just *french kiss*. Like always the music, the writing, the humour, and the storytelling are perfect. The characters may be fictional, but the emotions are real and tears were shed multiple times during the playthrough. I feel like I lived through three different lifetimes over the five or so hours it took me to beat this game. I can't really say what the game is about without spoilers but just do yourself a favour and play it.One thing to note, while they devs do say you don't need to play the previous two games, I would highly recommend you do so before this game because it will make the experience that much better (and those two are fantastic games in their own right so worth playing anyway). Overall, even though I still do think To The Moon is my favourite of the series, this game is still a definite buy and I can't wait to see what else Freebird Games has in store for the future. I'm a day one buy for all future games for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Freebird Games continues to demonstrate their ability to create wholesome heartfelt experiences. The basic but beautiful art, the moving and relatable stories, lifted toward the heavens by their incredible soundtracks, endlessly surprise me. A 4 hour game that goes by in a flash and leaves a lasting impression. As always, play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Another masterpiece by Kan Reives Gao and the team at Freebird Games. Although gameplay is fairly linear (not that many people play these games for the gameplay - it's the excellent writing most of us come for), there is not a dull or uninteresting moment during this game. It is indeed shorter than its predecessors, but still holds up. I highly recommend at least playing Finding Paradise (the previous entry into this series) to better understand and enjoy the latter half of this game's story. Once again, Gao absolutely excels with the soundtrack and, like previous OSTs, is tear-jerking. The incorporation of progressions and musical motifs from previous entries in the series is especially powerful. Overall, another wonderful and wholly worthwhile story to enjoy from Kan Reives Gao and Freebird Games.

Still amazing storytelling and a deeply touching story!Also for the love of god play the other games first, the story has then so much more impact then! :1. _childDocuments_.review: If you've played Freebird's other games you know what to expect, and yet this one still has some very surprising ways of framing the story. Great music and art, probably a big improvement over the previous games, but honestly it's hard to remember. It makes me wonder how much of To The Moon is seen through nostalgia goggles these days. While I have some small nitpicks about this game, don't forget about the totally unnecessary tile puzzles and hardcore zombie actions scenes in To The Moon. Also, the jokes, callbacks, and even memes all land perfectly here where they were mostly groaners in To The Moon. Then there's Finding Paradise, which backhanded me so hard into ugly sobbing that I've actually kind of forgotten its plot at this point.All that to say, all of these games are great and it's cool how they tie into each other. I kind of wish this were an ultimate wrap up with no loose ends, but it looks like there may be more some day. Cheers to the devs and their beautiful work.

_childDocuments_.review: This sequence of unskippable cutscenes could have been a visual novel. Although that's a bit unfair to visual novels, which can provide more autonomy. This was my first experience with these games, and I had no idea how heavily scripted they were. There is some limited interactivity in chapter I, allowing you to look at the scenery and make small changes, but chapter II might as well be a giant set of railroad tracks. There's a bit more freedom to explore in chapter III, but this game does not allow players to make any choices that matter.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: This game is short, but sweet. It is the third game in a series of games but it stands completely on it's own. It tells an emotional, sad, trippy, and surprisingly pretty funny story. All of these elements are balanced so well and they are designed so masterfully. It leaves you with a bunch of questions to hook you in, and then slowly answers them until before you realize it you have played through the whole game and experienced the great story it has to offer. If you like good story games that will get you crying by the end of it, play this one. It may not look the best when you first boot it up, but trust me, it is all worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent end (?) to the trilogy that started with To the Moon.I loved TtM, thought FP was good but not great, and think that Impostor Factory is right up there with TtM in terms of quality. There were plenty of beautifully-emotional moments that had me choked up, including a couple of instances of narrative payoff near the game's ending that stuck with me long after I finished the story.if you liked either TtM or FP, this is the easiest recommendation I've ever given. This story is absolutely worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Impostor Factory is another good and well-thought out story in the series but not nearly as hard hitting (as a fan it's fairly expected lol). Sadly, I think this is the weakest of the trilogy in terms of pure story. I would be lying to say I am a bit disappointed that the game didn't make me come close to tearing up as I did in the first two. For newcomers, you have to play Finding Paradise before this and even To The Moon if you can.One thing I can say though is that the music and art has really outdone itself. Especially the music. I thought the soundtrack was going to be less memorable because they didn't have Laura Shigihara on the team this time but they absolutely nailed each piece very nicely. The sprites and cutscene animations have also improved a lot. You can really see the effort the team has put together to make this game. Despite of what I said earlier, this is still a good high quality story-game and provides decent closure to the Neil Watts saga for long time fans. Anyway cheers to Kan Gao & Freebird Games! I can't wait to play whatever you guys make next!
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Impostor Factory may not be that as excited as Finding Paradise due to the different narrative pacing but it is still a very good story and it sure opens a lot of IFs to think about life. (Such as if my computer didn't die a few days ago and all I have now is a computer without proper graphics card I might still not want to actually sit down and enjoy Finding Paradise and Impostor Factory due to my times were already taken by other games.)For masterpieces like these I'm normally speechless, I just can't wait what's the next from Freebird games.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: IT'S BITTERSWEET, IT'S HEART-WARMINGBut do I recommend this game? Yes.It is enjoyable and is part of the sequel of To The Moon series, and if you don't want to miss any detail to the story. It will still make you go "aww" and tear up a little.Will you get satisfaction from playing the game? No.Unfortunately, this episode did not live up to the standard of its predecessors. It felt more like A Bird Story and a set up for the next chapter. I understand delays and the pandemic hitting are hard, but it still felt rushed like they changed a lot of the story mid way and the Great Wide Unknown song didn't make it as well. The ending was a bit underwhelming and didn't give much impact.Everyone loves the To the Moon series. So delays are fine and are wholeheartedly accepted by the community. But it also has to live up to the quality of the previous stories.

_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Just Like To The Moon, just Like Finding Paradies. This is a 4 hour ride of pure Emotions.I hope you don't mind the Grafics, you get what you get. But the Story and Characters is where it's at. I highly recommend that you Play to the Moon and Finding paradies first, because Imposter Factory adds onto that. And there will be references to the first games (also, i think the two prequels are Story-Emotion masterpieces and you miss out if you skip them).The Ending is a bit vague, so there might be a Sequel in the future. If you don't mind an somewhat open ending, think something like, idk. Inception, then this hopefully won't bother you to much. The Story itself got closed, it's just that the universe it's set in lives on. So you will get a nice conclusive story, with somewhat of a marvelesc after Credits scene to setup a possible Sequel.4 hours of suspence and heart touching moments. Just get it (and the prequels)

_childDocuments_.review: Although this isn't the reason I don't recommend it, I'm putting this at the top for those not familiar with the series: This is not a murder mystery, or a timeloop mystery, or a Lovecraftian horror story. The short description at the top of the page is a straight-up lie, and the content of the game is severely misrepresented by the screenshots. Do not play this without playing To The Moon and Finding Paradise. This is not a standalone game and you won't understand what's going on without that context.As far as being a sequel to those games, this is why I don't recommend it. It's an okay, not great but passable, entry in the series and not nearly as good as the others. The pacing in particular is absolutely awful. The first 1/3 serves no purpose and is completely irrelevant to the story, the middle 1/3 is a looooooooooooooooong linear exposition segment with no exploration or interactivity that sets up the actual story, and the real story told in the last 1/3 is pretty decent. The whole thing could have been cut down to just the last 1/3 with occasional bits from the other 2/3 added for context and it would have been infinitely better.That said, if you haven't played To The Moon or Finding Paradise, definitely go play those they're worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Impostor Factory

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and Powerful like the last two stories Kao had given us, with a really interesting mystery with a really powerful reveal what makes us think about how we need to learn to deal with our choices, living with the results and wondering where they will take us. This story didn't make me cry like that last two... but when the climax arrives, I'm all tears.Choices are hard...

This is still part of the To The Moon series, and you'll gradually see the connections (it helps if you've played Finding Paradise). You still get the top-notch writing of love, hard choices, and what-ifs.
