_childDocuments_.review: This game has a great overall message, and is comical in its delivery.  I enjoyed the story, short as it was, and really thought that the overall message was a good one.  However, I did have some issues with the game.I'm all for compensating developers.  I do not think that $20 is a fair price for less than 2 hours of gameplay.  I spent 118 minutes in the game before I beat it, and that was with constant pausing to talk to my chat while I streamed and deal with charity donations during stream.  Thankfully, I got it on sale, so I only paid $9.  But I would think that others who purchase the game at full price might feel like there wasn't enough gameplay for the cost.Additionally, I felt like the game needed more.  And that's not just about the cost, it was also the gameplay.  I felt like I was in a constant tutorial.  They were giving me new ways to say NO sprinkled out over the very short chapters, and I just felt like it could have kept escalating more than it did.Overall, good idea.  Fun game, fun interactions and dialogue.  I just wish there was more.

_childDocuments_.review: [Pay-to-Play] This game prides itself as an NPG (NO!-Playing Game) and it lives up to that xD , This game is more of an interactive story, where the gameplay is mostly just pressing spacebar.We do not have to do any walking, because the game will auto walk for us :PThis game is funny and comedic :P There are 8 chapters in total, each chapter is pretty short.Achievements-wise, we are able to obtain them pretty easily, however there is a grindy achievement where we have to say No! 99,999 times which we can use a macro script or autoclicker.Other than that, we have to not act / stay silent for some of the achievements (cheevos are guided)I would recommend, (not necessarily needed), the following:For my first playthrough, i actually stay silent (not pressing spacebar) whenever possible just so I can view all the dialogues. There are some dialogues where we have to say No just to progress :PFor my second playthrough, I spammed No by using an autoclicker and there were some slight changes in the dialogues (i.e. debate section in Chapter 5)Overall this is fun and easy game and I enjoyed it :DTeaches us the lesson to say no! whenever applicable (Good for introverts :P)Tags: [Interactive Story] [Casual] [Indie] [Comedy] [Say No! More]

_childDocuments_.review: Great game.It teaches players a simple but important lesson in real life: Learn to say no.I believe this is universal, it doesn't matter where in the world you are, we all face difficulty to refuse some time. With colleagues or friends or family, I remember Elton John singing Sorry Seems To Be The Hardest Word, but saying sorry is not difficult especially for polite people, no is the winner.The gameplay is relaxing and fun, your character walks automatically and encounters colleges with unreasonable requirements, all you need to do is press Space to say NO. Occasionally you meet good people and since you cannot say Yes, just wait until they finish and they are happy. Besides saying no you can also laugh, do slow clapping and sarcasm things to charge your power, there are 8 chapters and you are the hero who beats every supervisor in the company to free the employee eventually, give them the right to say no, to work balance and live a happier life.For me I dare say no most of the time, I think it is my personality, or simply because mostly I do not give a ♥♥♥♥ if I know I have reason to refuse, and all these years I benefit from it. But still I can relate to the game, when I was an intern I also did trifles like cleaning up and copying files, but I make sure others do not get used to that.What I find most difficult in real life is to say yes or no to a friend who asks for money. Like the game said, there is no right answer. So real.

_childDocuments_.review: In an increasingly scary world, this sort of game is very important. I went in with the idea of this being just a funny and comedic game. But as I played, the game began to get very real and start imitating what my real world job was like and the inability to say no to work being given to me. I didn't expect to come out on the other side a sad sob, but I did it. And I thank the creators for such a game. Well made.TL:DR: If you're having doubts about this game, just say No! and pick it up. _childDocuments_.review: This game is about an intern who works in a company where saying "yes" to everything is mandatory. Thanks to a coach the intern will learn to say "no" more and this will change his life."Say no more" has a retro colorful 90s graphic similar to playstation 1. The music is nice and funky.The game is more like a comedy walking simulator, there is no action, you can just say "no" to co-workers and boss requests but you can do in different funny ways.Once you complete the game there isn't any replaybilty unless you want to complete all achievements, some of them are very time consuming (as Say "No!" 99999 times")Overall it's a fun short game (about 2 hours) you can play whenever you just want to relax and turn off your brain.

_childDocuments_.review: Say No! More is a game about saying no to annoying and time consuming co-workers, who wants the player to do their hard work.The game looks and sounds awesome. The characters and some of their actions are overdone, which makes the game another level fun. In general it looks great in my opinion, not to mention the sounds design and the music. The controls are really easy, you need to use the space, 4 numbers and 4 directional keys, but not all the time. The story of the game look silly, which around the midway start to be ridiculous, but it's wholesome, has a meaning and motive at the end. The gameplay is simple: your moving automatically through a level, where you encounter numerous co-workers, who either try to stop you or react to you somehow. You can deal with them to say no with different ways or listen to their calls. This basically it, but some of the situations and secret paths are well made.However, Say No! More suffers a few things, one of them is the variety of the gameplay. Yes I know, I said the game is fun to play with, which I get back to it, but it's still not much. You get different versions of no and different actions before you to say no, but those are basically useless. You need basically two types of saying no, and that's it, why did they add those things, if they are basically useless? Not even mentioning, that the game is really short. Well, at least it's sized for the basic game idea, but you can play through the game around one and half hour. Also, there are some graphical bugs, like textures overflowing each other and other related bugs in the game.This game has a cool idea and implementation, not even mentioning the morale of the story, which makes the whole experience even better, but my biggest issue is that, the game is still short and repetitive, and if you are not onto the story or the look of this game, you won't like this one. For me, this game is quite mixed, especially because of it's price tag. I can recommend this to give it a shot, but not for 15€, maybe for 5€. It's a cool game and all, but can be repetitive for some.
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: I got through this game in about 2 hours on a stream, and it blew away my expectations. Say No! More is not mechanically challenging in any way, and all you really do is say "no" in different ways. The most agency the player has within the whole game is probably player customization, as the story is a straight line (with some optional detours along the way).But the story, the STORY, is perfect, succinct, provoking, and incredibly enjoyable. And the whole time you're experiencing it, you're wrapped up in great dialogue, voice-acting, and graphics that just itch my brain right.The only reason I could see someone having an issue with the price tag is if they're expecting some kind of action RPG. Or maybe they're really super into capitalism. In which case, shouldn't they want the developers to charge more...?Anyway, if I could, I would erase this game from my brain just so I could play it for the first time all over again.

_childDocuments_.review: No, I do not recommend this game.This isnt a game, its just a really long animation. The artstyle is cool, the story is super boring and has no nuance to its message at all, you get the point after reading the title. The "Gameplay" is painfully barebones, you literally do nothing but mindlessly press A. _childDocuments_.review: "Say No! More" is a charming ,2hrs long, indie game set in a modern world where you play as an intern in a big company. In this company, saying "No!" is considered taboo, but you muster the courage to use this powerful word and challenge the work mentality.The game's graphics are simple and not its strongest aspect.The gameplay is also straightforward, requiring only the use of the spacebar, shift, and the down and right arrow keys. Most actions just involve pressing the spacebar.The Audio is decent, nothing particularly noteworthy here.This game can be enjoyed by players of all ages, although younger players may not fully grasp the underlying message. However, it is still an enjoyable experience for everyone."Say No! More" can be played on practically any system, although it could have been more optimized to be lighter on resources. It's a minor flaw in the developer's optimization efforts.The game is not challenging, as most of it can be completed by spamming the spacebar. Occasionally, you need to hold the spacebar or press shift, but overall, it is not a difficult game.The only grind in the game is an useless achievement that requires pressing the spacebar 99,999 times, which feels like a tedious and unnecessary task. This achievement idea is disappointing and detracts from the overall experience.The story is funny and filled with NPCs who deliver great lines and portray clichés of the work environment. The humor is the game's strongest aspect and the primary reason to play it. The story as a whole is enjoyable.The main story can be completed in around 2 hours, but if you want to enjoy every dialogue, it may take a bit longer. Obtaining all reasonable achievements adds about 30min to the gameplay. However, if you aim to unlock every achievement, be prepared to invest .At 15€, the price is definitely too much for what the game offers. It would be more reasonable to purchase it on sale for less than 5€, or even better, for 1€ if you can find a deal. At that lower price point, it is definitely worth the experience.No bugs were encountered during gameplay."Say No! More" is a cool game with great humor. The achievements and price point are aspects I really disliked, but aside from that, it is a solid, simple, and funny game. It effectively conveys a clear message against worker exploitation and the acceptance of such realities.
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: Say No! More is a short silly game about, well - saying No! more. I won't say too much about the story, just discover it yourself. Don't expect too much in terms of gameplay - the entire game is on-rails and you use one button and the arrow keys. Still, it is fun to discover the different interactions, I am a sucker for the 3D pixel artstyle this game uses, the music is funky and the game has a great message to boot. While I definitely would say NO! to it being worth the full 15 dollars, on sale or in a bundle this is a nice game to check out.Also, the "cold NO!" face in this game is fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: Note for non-English users! Looking back now, the Korean language option has a bit of a problem with context;"NO" is Translated as "싫어!" which means "I don't like it/that/etc" instead of "아니!" a more general word.Still a negative, but it is used depending on context, certain yes or no questions might sound awkward.ie; Q: "I heard we don't get paid for staying overtime, is that true?"     A: "싫어!" (I don't like it)Not much bearing on gameplay, but I've seen some Koreans get confused.Some other languages might also have the same awkward kinks, just be aware.

My only complaint is with the ending, which I'll need to spoil a bit to fully explain, so if you think this looks funny and/or interesting, buy it. On to the ending: If you read my rambly critique of the game's ending, I appreciate that, and I hope it gave you some food for thought. This is still one of the funniest games I've ever played, and I can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Those looking for light hearted, comedy, and smiles  Say No More does well in using the insanity that'd you expect from a game where you have someone go flying from saying No at them, and combining it with smart writing and themes that parallel the situation that the modern corporate world is going through. It's not preachy and yet takes a side, but does it with writing that's equivalent to a fencing sword: precise and yet pointed, and flexible. The experience is about 3-4 hours and has a well put together arc with some small side stories that are worth paying attention to, and the game rewards players who wait to say no with small tidbits that will make them want to see more. The amount of voice acting in the game for a small game like this is impressive with the number of languages available. There's also something just inheriently fun of seeing co-workers go flying in rigid rag doll physics. Granted, the gameplay is a structure for the story to be told, and if you were hoping for an arcade experience that was extremely replayable, you're out of luck. It's novel but not difficult, almost to the point where you really want it to try to make you fail. It's also a game that despite all that it gives, feels like a game that has only hit the surface of its potential, making you want more as what you're given really works. Really, I recommend the game for those who aren't gameplay purists (who put it over everything else), but the real question is the platform to get it on. I think the 15 dollar Steam/Switch makes sense given the space to work with presentation wise (over the 5 dollar IOS version), but regardless, it worth your time and money for an experience that just makes you want to smile.

_childDocuments_.review: SAY NO! MORE is a cute game with a great overarching message of setting healthy boundaries with others in your personal life and professional life, which is something that I find to be very important nowadays in the age of late-stage capitalism in the US. The characters have interesting personalities and I think my favorites are Noah and the personal trainer/life coach that helps you along the way. The art style is simplistic yet amicable. My negative review heavily hinges on the repetitiveness of the gameplay and how the different ways that you can learn to say NO! don't really seem to make much of a difference in the effectiveness of rejecting people trying to take advantage of you. There are literally 10 people often times that will approach you over the course of 10 seconds and you ultimately just end up spamming the spacebar most of the time unless you find someone asking for a staring contest, etc. Sometimes I feel like I don't know what kind of NO! I should be using against a boss and no matter what I do I end up failing, and there's no sign that ultimately the encounter was designed to fail no matter what until you learn to charge your NO! more. That's the only mechanic that makes a difference. You can also build your confidence meter by antagonizing your coworkers with claps and laughs, etc., but even that seemed to have zero recognizable pattern to learn and is very frustrating. A $15.00 USD pricetag just doesn't seem justifiable for the experience I had.Overall I would summarize my nearly 2hrs of gameplay on stream as listening to character dialogue that was sometimes funny and enjoyable, and otherwise just spamming the spacebar until a situation that seemed like it wasn't working and I didn't understand why. If the devs read this review, I just want them to know I appreciate the message trying to be conveyed by this game and I overwhelmingly support it. I just wish there was more to the game for all the time I spent playing it just trying to not quit the game partway through because I'd had enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Say NO! More is a game about saying No more.  Beat it in 1.7 hours using a game controller.  Difficulty is nonexistent.  I got this in a humble bundle.Graphics - Are polygonal, but you can design your own character!Controls - There are many ways to say No, and you'll be shown how.Music - Does its job.  Reminds me of a cross between game muzak on the Wii and being trapped in a workplace environment questioning my mental fortitude and patience.  (Thankfully it doesn't have to be that way in the game) Story - It's there.  It's worth it.  Languages - This game's in at least two versions of a bzillion languages.  I'd tell you how many exactly but that requires counting on both hands and I don't have time for that sort of sass.  Okay, that out of the way, this game is amazing.  If anyone tells you it's stupid, that you're stupid for playing it, and that you should only play what they recommend, just say  strong enough to blow them through three doors and a wall and get to playing because you don't need that sort of negativity in your life. _childDocuments_.review: ✔️ A simple yet funny story with a trivial moral.✔️ Absurd world.✔️ Funny and memorable characters.✔️ Facial expressions are amazing.✔️ Charming art style and presentation (Katamari inspired art style).✔️ Humour overall.✔️ Moral behind the story and perfect to apply to your own life.✔️ Soundtrack.❌Too short.❌The four different stances for attacking (saying No!) are irrelevant. You don't need to change stances at all in order to complete the story.❌ No replay value.❌ Too expensive (I would wait for a bundle price).❌ More "Art" than Game.❌ No consequence for actions."Say No! More" is a valuable lesson that tells a story, a dream of a world where we don't have to live under the oppressive thumb of capitalism and where even the little guy can stand up for themselves and have a meaning. It's about fighting for your rights and that bosses shouldn't get more just because they're the boss, that everyone should play a fair part and get fair pay. It's about not continuing the cycle of abuse and control that the world is currently in. It's not lazy or anti work but just about saying "no" more to empower those who have none and calling out things that aren't right. The game is rather simple and gives you the feeling like there might be consequences for your actions or that you have to choose when and how to respond to people but sadly you don't do anything of consequence. The game can be over quickly or less quickly depending on if you just say no to everyone or hear some people out. You can get some rather hilarious conversations from the NPCs if you listen to their full conversation. The game is really funny and has inspirational messaging with supportive ideals that even an intern or just a trainee has value. It took me two hours to complete and I listened to nearly every pink optional conversation.There's also no reason for me to play this again. Why not give us things to collect like hats, new faces or hair, different clothing, bonus characters. Make bonus stages anything meaningful to give us replay value. I don't need them to alter the game, but it would be nice to have some bonus stuff or if there were random conversations in there that if I replay it random conversations could change. But once finished there is nothing to look forward to since you already experienced everything.The gameplay is relaxing and fun, your character walks automatically and encounters colleagues with unreasonable requirements, all you need to do is press Spacebar to say "NO". Occasionally you meet good people and since you cannot say Yes, just wait until they finish and they are happy. Besides saying "no" you can also laugh, do slow clapping and sarcasm things to charge your power. There are 8 chapters, so give them the right to say no, to improve work balance and live a happier life.If you’re looking for a deep gameplay experience, then "Say No! More" is absolutely not going to be your cup of tea. It’s one of the most simplistic indie games that I’ve ever played, but it’s also one of the most heartfelt and memorable, as well as teaching some genuinely valuable lessons in its short run time. Don’t say no to this one, especially if you are one of the people who can't say "No!" IRL as well. So always remember:

_childDocuments_.review: Say No! More runs with its self-declared unnuanced, one-note premise into the realm of absurdity and stays there - all whilst qualifying its premise in its own title. , so I was immediately drawn to Say No! More's demo last year. Even as a single chapter slice it managed to work standalone and neatly take the premise to a satisfying conclusion. How exactly it could be expanded on without too much fluff was the question...And, in all veracity, it didn't convince me early on. Like most self-contained, satisfying morsels that get expanded on, it just felt like more for more's sake and a dilution of everything the demo had. A too much-sel. One, it gets fun with it. Discovering the word 'no' to fight workplace injustice is treated like an actual superpower with all the audio-visual anime flourishes to boot. Two, the plot is punctuated with lows and highs and twists and turns which help transport the concept to an an emotionally resonant and real-life applicable place. Three, I was playing it wrong. Your only means of control are four reactions to unsettle your opponent and four different rapid-fire or boosted 'nos!' Naturally, I assumed the game was mechanically building up to requiring that different opponents are unsettled/defeated by different reactions or nos - surprisingly not! I can only assume this was a very intentional choice to avoid making a puzzle game or hold up the pace. It works. Say No! More hits best when the pace is kept up. My mistake that dampened my fun with the game in those first few chapters is that I was fully exploring every last morsel of dialogue - systematically letting the timer run to its end, and running through all the reactions before unleashing a charged no. Do explore all the dialogue, but approaching things like I did by slowly going through the motions is a sure-fire way of killing all the game's fun.There are handful of exceptions wherein it's best not to say 'no' that break up the game nicely and help keep your itchy trigger finger holstered. A few achievement-popping examples and a repeat example that brilliantly builds-up to the closest thing the game has to a side quest, but I could have done with a few more. This would have boosted the game's replayability. Still, my early concern that every level would just be peppered with being asked inane variations of 'get some ink for the printer' was crushed. For those of you who don't just fancy a kinder capitalist workplace and rally against things like coercive wage slavery, hierarchy, commodification, and all the rest of it, Say No! More doesn't rule it out. Saying 'no' is very much a metaphor for dissent more generally. The real undercurrent events of the story are much more about worker mobilisation and building solidarity. Working conditions and toxicity, unions, overtime, propaganda, a four day working week, etc, all get their mention. The office even looks like a worker cooperative by the end. These explorations more than justify Say No! More's as a full product beyond its demo. The dynamic physics of the environment are also actually rather impressive. Every blast of 'no!' sends people, furniture, and office supplies flying in unscripted ways. Even in cutscenes, the unpredictable reactivity of the environment is played off for laughs as characters freely walk into and knock over items. It's all great fun. Hit and miss? A little. I think the game works better as a blast of wholesome than a bottomless barrel of laughs. Whilst the game is more than one joke, its main source of humour is undoubtedly beating a dead horse until you finally laugh. Even if you don't laugh, characters prove unendingly entertaining.I don't want to harp on value for money, since I think the game is worth the price of admission. Whilst the price on Steam did make me initially pause, the iOS version is a very easy sell indeed. Parity here would have been great, but I can understand it might not have been possible.

More is a must-play for anyone looking for a fun, lighthearted game that will leave you laughing and feeling empowered. NO!

A thin veneer of interactivity over what is more a linear story that sometimes requires you to press the spacebar to advance. A story that in of itself isn't bad, but it's sort of weird how the game kind of seems like it's going to have more complex mechanics and it just kinda doesn't. It's good for a few laughs and they are pretty good laughs but it's not very substantial.More pettily, I also wish you could change the language of your "No" more freely. It's chosen once at the start of the game and cannot be changed without starting the game over. It seems like a missed opportunity to record a variety of No's and then restrict you to only one per playthrough. Points for having Irish Gaelic though, that's pretty unique.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought on sale for 6$, and I did NOT expect it to be as raw as it was. Spoiler-free, this was a really engaging game that is an absolute treat to play for 2 hours. Best experienced regularly changing expressions and sort of genuinely reacting to everything. This is an immersion-mandatory game.The one thing I'd say this game needs to be great is having the reactions matter more depending on the question. Sure, the game can't progress if you don't say no, but I'd like to have people understand better that I'm laughing at them because they said a funny joke instead of them being uncomfortable when I laugh. The reactions are more for flavor, if anything, and have no impact on anything other than giving you more time to just... press a button.Otherwise, it was so funny to just hold the laugh button in the middle of cutscenes and hear my Japanese character just laugh uncontrollably when anyone says anything, and I was really touched by the ending.Overall, this game is best enjoyed playing it yourself once, then coming back to it whenever you just feel like having a casual laugh with friends.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun and valuable lesson to be learnt from this.Graphics8/10 Simple yet effect art style. Didn't have any issues or glitchy textures etc. Looks very sharp on ultra graphics. Sets the tone for the game well.Gameplay10/10 Arguably one of the most simple but fun mechanics I have ever seen in a video game. Its ultimately satisfying saying no in various different ways to corporate robots. Maybe this resonates from me being a retail manager in RL, But you find the type of people the game portrays a lot in my field and it is as satisfying saying NO to them in RL as it is in this game.Maybe its personal bias but once you build up a disdain for that type of person(I'm sure I'm not the only one) but it does send a clear message for people to stand up for themselves in a world where people are afraid to stand up to the corporate machine. For this game though its just fun shouting no at someone till they jump up in the air or fall over.Its fun no nonsense game play at its best.Music/Audio9/10 Simple and catchy beats really set the tone for the game. The voice actor who acts as the motivational speak should release his own set of lifestyle tapes as it really nailed the message they were delivering. The snotty supervisors and other robots also sounded unique and had the right sarcastic and monologue tones for sheep.10/10 Honestly haven't had so much fun with a game for a while. Its a clear example of how a simple yet clear vision defined to the point of a fun bug free game which is an experience for us all to play and utilise in our lives. Thank you for this game :)Its a shame we cant flip the thumbs for no on this occasion so NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO don't buy it, buy it twice and give a copy to someone in your life that needs to say the world more often :DMy video review is below:

_childDocuments_.review: You know what else can I say, but the titular phrase of the game? But like any word, they carry weight and meaning. And it's important to know when and where you need to use your words. This game is full of many laughs and definitely lures you in with its humorous premise, but I think where it truly shines is in its underlying message.This is a great kind of interactive film that I think is worth your time and money. With its absolutely stellar soundtracks, charming visuals, and great message, I think this is something everyone should treat themselves to. The developers did a great job with this.And most importantly, remember to say No more!
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: Hey you! Are you tired of your video games constantly forcing you to Say Yes to move the plot along?! Do you wish that you could play a game that acts as a commentary on the corporate world without it being all dark and depressing?! Well then you've come to the right place! SAY NO! MORE is a wonderful comedy adventure where you play as an Intern who learns the power of the word NO! and decides to use it to change the fate of your coworkers and your oppressive employers that just don't know when to stop saying YES! I had a blast throughout my playthrough of SAY NO! MORE. The game got a lot of laughs out of me with it's witty dialogue and hilarious visuals. I loved it's themes of learning to stick up for yourself and not remain trapped in an abusive, unreasonable environment, it's a lesson that should without a doubt be taught more often. I do want to mention that the gameplay of SAY NO! MORE is like an autoscroller where all you do is say NO! in wacky ways so keep that in mind if you're thinking of purchasing as while I enjoyed it others might not.I will say that the game was surprising short only being around 3 hours in length. The other 5 hours of my playtime was from grinding out an achievement for saying NO! 99,999 times.... yeah that was not enjoyable. So completionists, if you're thinking of getting this game just be wary about the long grind that awaits.Overall, SAY NO! MORE is an excellent and hilarious adventure about the abuse of employees by their corporate employers that unfortunately lacks in content to justify the current price. Wait for sale but when that time comes make sure to add this to your library as this will make a wonderful addition to it.8/10, would SAY NO! MORE to corporate policies again
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: The animation and story are super funny, and it was a real joy to play this game. I left running so my actual play time is closer to an hour.The controls are very simple, and there's no cursing (they say damn once), violence, or sexual content. Anyone can play this game. It also has a really good message (saying NO to unreasonable things). You don't control the character via movement except to say NO (space bar), charge up (hold down space), how you say NO (1234 keys) and laugh/nod/hmmm (up/down/left).I hope they make more, this one was really lovely and worth your time!

_childDocuments_.review: Are you ready for a game that's unlike anything else? Say hello to 'Say No! More,' a quirky, hilarious adventure that's worth every moment.You might be wondering why you'd want to play a game where you're an intern forced to say "Yes" to everything. Well, because this game quickly teaches you the magic of saying "No!" and sets you on a fun and wacky journey.In 'Say No! More,' you step into the shoes of an intern in a world where saying "No!" is strictly forbidden. The game wastes no time showing you just how dull and depressing your work life would be without the power to say "No." In your first few minutes on the job, your boss even snatches your precious lunchbox – a gift from your best friend on your first day – just because you can't say "No."But here's where it gets interesting. A magical cassette player and tape enter the scene, and you're transported to a space-like realm where a giant, muscle-bound spirit teaches you the power of the word "No!" And so begins your quest to find your lunchbox and change the company from within.The gameplay is simple and straightforward. You move through the office, and your mission is to use your newfound "No!" power to reject your coworkers' annoying requests, like making coffee or fixing the printer. The game automatically guides your character, reminiscent of old-school on-rails arcade games.The brilliance of 'Say No! More' lies in its comical rejections. Depending on your power level, you can gently decline or send your coworkers flying across the room. It can get chaotic, but it's an absolute blast.As you progress, you'll learn different ways to say "No!" and discover various taunts. While this aspect of the gameplay is somewhat shallow – as any style of rejection works – it's undeniably entertaining. Whether you're clapping in front of someone's face or pointing at them to make them feel a bit silly, it's a riot.The game offers a decent level of customization for your character. You can tweak facial expressions, skin color, and even choose the language in which you say "No!" Unfortunately, you can't change the language mid-game, so choose wisely.Despite its straightforward narrative, 'Say No! More' excels in humor and quirkiness. What starts as a quest to retrieve your stolen lunchbox turns into a corporate climb, filled with supportive characters and some goofy coworkers who want to chat or play games with you. There's always something to keep you engaged.The unique pixel art style and exaggerated expressions add to the overall wackiness. The game consistently provides an eccentric atmosphere, and it's a joy to explore the environments, each filled with unexpected events.A fun and upbeat soundtrack accompanies your adventure. Each time you learn a new way to say "No!" or taunt, you're treated to a funky workout jam with a chorus of "No" being sung throughout.The dialogue and voice acting are absurdly funny, with characters sounding genuinely defeated when you reject their requests.If there's one drawback to 'Say No! More,' it's its brevity and lack of replayability. The main story is short, and once it's done, there's nothing else to unlock or explore. This leaves you wanting more.In the end, 'Say No! More' is a lighthearted and hilarious game that offers a unique take on work culture. It's full of heart and humor, even if it's a one-time experience. I had a blast with this quirky gem, and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a good laugh and some food for thought.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10 (Long story short) Say No! More is a super charming and short story based game that touches on real world issues in an extremely goofy and entertaining way.My takeaway: I was super surprised to find out how much I enjoyed this game! I would also like to give recognition to the game for taking part in Humble Bundle’s bundle for Ukraine. Say No! More follows a completely customizable intern battling with being able to say no- especially to those closest to them. It takes around 2 hours to complete and is very worth it.The game was super easy to follow and never lost my attention (unless you’re achievement hunting like me and having to spam click the same putton thousands and thousands of times). The characters are for the most part very believable and the ones that are multidimensional have very serious and thought provoking stories to tell. The game itself is beautiful and runs with no issues for me. The whole thing pans out in a very cinematic way where you feel like you’re in a cartoon rather than playing a game.I struggle with saying “no” at work on a near daily basis. If seeing Hulk Hogan explain to me how to do it is the step that I needed to finally stick up for myself- this game might’ve been exactly what I needed.

_childDocuments_.review: I first saw this game on the publisher's Twitter account, and I thought, "This looks like a funny game"! It's got that Sega Dreamcast and Arcade look to it. The first lot of chapters are exactly what you see in the trailer; your character going through montages to yell "NO!" at everyone who wants you to do a little bit more work. The chaotic and comedic gags are hilarious, and I got some funny results from the props flying around the area. One small feature that I really appreciate is the ability to say "No" in different languages, without having to change the voice or text language. So I got to enjoy the game in English while saying "NO!" in Hindi!Going deeper into the game though, it takes a bit of a turn and has a meaningful message at the end that I was not expecting from such a goofy experience. The game's about 2 hours long, but the price is good considering what you get out of this. A good laugh and a pleasant ending. I streamed the whole gameplay if you want to check out the full experience, but I recommend trying it out for yourself for the ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: Game is super simple and has a ton of charm. you just need a few keys (1,2,3,4, space bar, arrow keys) to play. Story line is a 2 Hour Endeavor but you'll be having fun with it the entire time.The game also teaches vital importance of when you should be saying yes and no. In a society where we are constantly expected to do more for efficiency purposes, you should be able to step back and just say no when you need to.There's probably a bit of replayability i missed, as there were times where i messed up when saying no and missed out on lil silly bits in the process. should be worth a few playthroughs.While this game isn't going to be a huge confidence booster to say no more (heh), its going to be a great start to that journey to build self confidence as it can help you realize bits of it you could of missed in yourself. You can easily see the love and passion put into its messaging and the care it was received to make a fun little experience. i genuinely cried a few times.also, it has a cool character creator. go get it if this game is your kinda thing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a gimmicky, one-trick pony mixture of a game and a short movie, which by all means you gotta play.The first thing that came to mind when playing this game was Henry Stickmin - it's less a game and more of an interactive piece of entertainment, and that's how Say No! More felt at the beginning. What sets it apart from, say, Henry Stickmin, is not the humor - both games are a laugh riot, and in Say No! More the laugh are in everything - animations, graphics, sounds, voice acting, dialogue. That said, it gets old very quickly, and probably by the end you'll realize it's less about you pressing a button, and more about you wait until every bit of dialogue is starting to repeat just because you're too amused to do otherwise.And then comes what sets it apart - a strong, pull-your-heartstrings message of empowerment and No as a solution to conflicts. That whole chapter where folks fall through the sky (the first time) is really touching and comes as a kind of curveball to me.In the end of the day, even if the gameplay lacks, the game still has redeeming qualities that make it worth a buy (if on a deal, since it's very short)
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: I beat the game in about 2 hours, it plays like a rail-shooter, and I am not sure there is any replayability. I unlocked 17/22 achievements and I am unsure if I care enough to replay the game to get those last 5. For whatever reason I was under the impression it would be more sandbox-y with meaningless objectives. I was wrong. There are 8 chapters in the game (not including prologue which is a short tutorial, and epilogue which just explains the ending), entire game takes place like a rail-shooter where all you do is press 1-4 choosing what type of no you want to say (space bar), and an arrow key to add an action such as laughing, clap your hands, saying "hmm", and whatever the last one is. Which I am unsure if the types of no's and actions you perform even matter as long as you say no. The game is short and funny. I bought it on sale for like $7. I don't regret buying it for that price, but just know if you buy it full price ($15) you may feel a little disappointed after finishing. If I am wrong and there is replayability with different scenarios and such I may try it again, but I get the impression that there is little to no alternative paths to take in the game. I spent $7 on it, so let's rate this 7/10. Worth buying as long as it's on sale.

It's got tons of languages, so you can say the word in German. Or Korean. Or Arabic. You get coached by trainer talking to you through a cassette player. You get a doom-style portrait which animates every N* you say. You even get a lunch break and good vibes right in the middle.This game doesn't overstay it's welcome, but just douses you in some corporate mayhem and a bit of...vicarious self-actualization? _childDocuments_.review: Say No! More is an interesting game I got as part of the "Stand With Ukraine" Humble Bundle...bundle. I probably never would've purchased it on its own, but it's a cute, short "experience" that I'd hesitate to call a game.In my mind, this isn't really a drawback though. It's got a simple but expressive art style and a very strong message given through silly gameplay and an extremely simple base mechanic. If you're the type of person who needs a high hours-played-to-dollars-spent ratio to call a game "good," then this probably isn't for you. But if you're willing to toss some money at a small studio clearly making a project that they've put a lot of passion into...then consider picking this up.I think my only critique would be that I wish some of the alternate "no" types and stalling tactics were used in more interesting ways other than near one-off encounters. But considering there's no real fail state here, it's understandable I guess. Otherwise the music is surprisingly catchy, the graphics and animation are crunchy but in a stylized way rather than outright bad, the message is solid, and it's an experience that while I may not come back to it certainly wasn't a waste of the two hours it took me to beat it.

_childDocuments_.review: Say No More is a fantastic, if brief, game with an aesthetic style reminiscent of blocky, PS1 character models. The game is short, but it's full of charming interactions. Say No More is entirely about it's story and it's Aesop, so if you're not charmed by the graphics or the theme, then this might not be a good choice for you. The game-play is limited, but focused. Choosing when and how to say no has an impact. So there are opportunities to make mistakes and end up being mean to characters that aren't making awful demands. It is really satisfying though to yell "NO!" at various characters making unrealistic demands. Especially to see them and other objects around them fly across the environment as well. All in all, I enjoyed the brevity. It's a fun, engrossing experience that doesn't take too much of your time to work through.I found myself clearing it (once) in just under the time to return it, and I wouldn't want to deprive the Devs of their efforts. It might be short, but it's worthwhile. Since it's so short, I can imagine I'll be playing through it's story at least a few more times just to see if there are alternate endings. I wouldn't be amiss to experience another game in this highly focused, story-centric style.
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: It takes only 2 hours to beat, and it's pretty straightforward, but it's a "short and sweet" type of experience. If the game were any longer in its state, it'd probably grow pretty boring. You have the spacebar to say NO (simple and charged), four types of NO (which don't seem to do much other than add a new way to express the same message) and the arrow keys to charge up your energy meter.It sends a pretty good message, and I'll admit, it has some decent emotional moments...Overall, a good game to pick up if you're bored and need a laugh.
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this a "Meh".It has tons of craft, it's well-spirited & kind, it's great visually and has some great writing (nice ending) & voiceovers.However, I'm sorry and I say that as a Walking Simulator fan, but this really should have had a Game Design: There is nothing, no Gameplay, no interactivity almost.The game adds mechanics (different shades of No & ways to refill them) with 0 Gameplay repercussions. This makes every level “brainless” with an impossibility to connect with the events of the game and the actual “No” mechanic.The only way to progress is by saying No, no matter when, no matter how, which also ruins the work that went into the numerous & quite long NPC lines.It’s not that I actively do not recommend the game. But be warned about how empty it is mechanically.
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game to be very enjoyable. It's a very amusing game with good comedy whilst also being surprisingly wholesome.There are many different variations of saying NO that you are given the choice of, along with various different styles to display your statements of defiance.You play as a nameless intern that you are able to customize to your liking with a surprisingly nice character customization system. I made my character a very miserable looking business lady that looks like she just wants to sleep for 5 months.If you're curious about the downsides, the main one is that it's not the longest game. It's about 2 hours in terms of length, but you can extend that if you'd like to go for the achievements or see what happens when you don't say no to certain things.I highly recommend this game if you'd like to have a good time playing it whilst in the presence of friends, as you will all have a very good time experiencing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Everyone in their life has worked at least one job that no matter the nonsense that was piled your way, you had to accept and agree to it.  Maybe you needed the job?  Vying for a promotion?  Like money enough to forgo common decency?  We’ve been down the road once.  The word “No” can be a terrifying one, especially in situations where the consequences are unknown for your use of it.  But every now and then, you’ve dreamt about just letting a fat No just rip with no remorse.Take this premise and add the spice of your own original character, and you’ve got the barebone foundations for Say No! More by Studio Fizbin.  You’ll begin your journey choosing from a preset schmuck or doing the right thing and creating your own 9 to 5’er.  Sporting an impressive amount of customization showcasing different jackets, pants, shoes, and tops: you can either make the most eccentric intern to grace the 16th floor carpet, or just do what I did and make yourself aged 10 years older.  Say No! More gives your intern the power of No in over 15 languages with some absolute winners in the mix, but since I’m an unapologetic weeb, I went with the solid Japanese 2.  Your freshly acquired intern arrives at their new job, a lunchbox made by your deadbeat roommate 8 months late on rent in tow, where near-hidden desks shaded by vending machines lay in wait away from the hustle and bustle of the office atmosphere.  Interns at this printing company are bound to the word “Yes,” whether to change ink, grab coffee, file papers, pay parking tickets: the word No is not allowed.  After a tumultuous start to their job with the theft of your lunch via your supervisor, your desk is graced with a secret cassette tape jarred loose from its hiding spot above in the AC vent.  This tape gives your shy demeanor the kick in the pants that’s needed to stand up for yourself and say No to the innate and often ridiculous requests from your co-workers.And No you shall say!  On your on-rails tour throughout the 90 minute campaign you can spice up your refusal of tasks by saying it wacky or lazy, by laughing or pretending to agree beforehand, or my favorite: giving them the slow clap into a charged heated No that’ll reverb throughout the building and launch your co-workers into the air with desks and papers following suit.  While spamming your refusals will feel automatic, some co-workers will have requests that you can handle, like delivering a letter between would-be lovers, playing game prototypes, or becoming an Underground Staring Contest Champion.  No, really.But when you want to say No with your chest, destroying your workplace and beyond in a world that looks like Katamari Damacy before everything gets rolled up is oh so satisfying and worth playing around your No-Combos to combine your own humor with Say No! More’s own hysterical quips.  Errant remarks from corporate bigwigs blown away by your vetoes and the speckles of emotional spice spread across co-workers are appeasing and fun to indulge in before using your vocal Hadoukens to forcefully move them to socially acceptable distances.But hidden behind all that humor is a surprising amount of heart.  Sure, the word No can be used to stop something bad happening, but Say No! More personifies the word into releasing self-doubt and anxiety-filled situations.  No: it’s okay for you to dance at your desk, so long as it doesn’t bother anyone.  No: it’s completely understandable to tell your co-worker who is sick to go home.  No: it’s okay to not take the wrong order even if it would be easier to just take the made lunch.  Having the freedom to confidently express your feelings may not include the concerning backlash that comes with not agreeing with someone, and freely expressing yourself can make you a more approachable person, as well as lifting the burden of never saying No and doing everything yourself.And while Say No! More doesn’t have much else after speaking its peace through its story, the journey through is such a visual and auditory treat that it’s absolutely worth running through multiple times to yell No ad nauseum, and then maybe one or two more times down the road to relieve some real-world stress.Now if you’ll excuse me, I need to clap at a few more people and yell No in Irish Gaelic.  Trust me.

_childDocuments_.review: Say No! More is a 1.5 - 2 hour experience about worker empowerment through the power of the word no. The game play loop is fairly simple where you'll be trucking along yelling no at whoever gets in your way with mundane intern tasks. Periodically, more interesting conversations and interactions occur where more thought needs to be put in. If you're looking for an upbeat "screw corporate politics and garbage working conditions" kind of game with a good message, this will be perfect for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely less of a game and more of an experience.  It's an on-rails third person No-er, where your only means of interaction is pressing the spacebar to say no. _childDocuments_.review: Let's get some of the critique out of the way: The game is short (I finished it in about two hours), and you're limited to saying "No", controlling what kind of NO it is, and ways to goof on your co-workers. If you're looking for more interaction than that, or a longer play session, this isn't going to be the game for you.That said.This game has a ton of heart, and there's clearly a lot of work and passion put into it. You play as a milquetoast new intern who, like most people in your job, is unable to say anything but YES to demands and requests. You quickly learn how to say NO, and more importantly, why it's vital to do so. I don't want to spoil what story there is (especially since you'll figure out the twists and turns quickly), but it's really more about the journey than the destination here. There's a great message about self-confidence, standing up for yourself, demanding worker's rights, and more, all packed into this little game. It helps that the soundtrack is enjoyable and the art style is so charming. I truly cannot recommend this game enough.Protip: don't say NO to . You might miss out on some things.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, but sadly is a bit pricey for a 2hr game. This game is absolutely charming for its jokes and the message it brings about not become a corporate slave. Honestly, I'm gonna say this but this one if it were a movie, it would be better than the movie "Yes Man" played by Tim Carrey, good Lord it was boring and predictable. This game has a super simple premise, you as the intern just got your new job at a company, but people push you around to do stuff and suddenly your supervisor stole your lunchbox and you have to get it. How? By going on a NO rampage by space bar your way to victory! Is a railway system where you don't control your character except just press space bar to say no and chance different ways to say no by pressing 1,2,3,4 on the keyboard. There is also the arrow keys to make the co-workers irritated to gain some energy for you to make a stronger NO move.It was such a simple game yet has a heavy message for a silly 2hr game, I love it the entire game, I wish there is a bit more, but I can understand what else can you do with the premise of saying NO to anybody. Overall for a Katamari Damacy look game, this game will leave you with a smile, but wait for a sale for it since there is not much to replay except getting an achievement by saying NO 99,999 times!

_childDocuments_.review: Say no to bad bosses and tell brands to STFU.A satirical take on toxic positivety in the workplace and a critique of abusive, greedy, and exploitative business practices that are carried out under a capitalist system. It further highlights on how at-will employment, unpaid internships, zero-hours contracts, meaningless jobs, and the 'gig economy' aren't all they're cracked up to be.It demonstrates that individuals must develop self-determination and band together in order to fight for better pay, fairer working conditions, UBI for all, along with the freedom to personally express themselves and pursue their own goals, hopes, and dreams.Remember, you don't need work or capitalism to self-actualize!As a game, it plays as a simple story-driven on-rails shooter. Takes less than two hours to finish, however there are hidden paths you can take. You can not lose and there are no game over screens.Then you have entitled and selfish out of touch ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boomers publishing topics in the discussions on how this is a piece of 'spoiled first world millennial simulator'. Get out of my face.If you enjoyed this game and the message it was trying to convey; Might I also suggest:Visiting the r/antiwork subreddit♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Jobs by David Graeber

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start by saying that if you want to get 100% achievments in a game, you might want to reconsider with this one, unless you've got a program or script to prevent you from destroying your poor wrist.Say No! More is a simple, nice, and just overall good game, with a simple but important lesson in life. Saying yes to everything, just like saying no to everything, is never a good solution. But sometimes, we just need to say no a little more. Remind ourselves and others that we're just people.All while having a laugh, feeling empathy for others, and enjoying some hilarious reactions.It's a short game, but one I'm glad to have played and experienced. And it's a game I can wholeheartedly recommend. Even if the story is a little silly, but hey, so are we sometimes.Plus, you can even learn how to say no in several languages.Studio Fizbin did a wonderful job on this game.A great introduction to the "NO!-Playing Game" genre ;3
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: I was going to make an unoriginal joke and just write no as my review, but I decided to actually write a review. I didn't like the graphics at first, but I quickly became charmed by them. It took me about an hour and a half to finish, so it's pretty short. I like the character customization, the system it uses is nice. It's less a game and more a slightly interactive animated film, so don't expect in-depth gameplay. Onto the elephant in the room: the story and social commentary. The story was pretty funny, I liked it, but mare important was the social commentary. It offers a variety of interesting perspectives on various issues in a humorous way, some major issues were hostile work environments, (the main one), media control and censorship, and various generations misunderstanding and ignoring the problems the other generation goes through. Overall, a funny and charming social commentary.
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: (Spoilers ahead!!!) I loved the story and the ideas put into it. The story just touched my heart and I cherished every moment of what this game offered. The idea of having a mob with you to rebel really showed me what one word can do. The way everything was designed from the characters to the assets that I never would of noticed.  After watching the get together in the end almost made me cry. With completing this with 2 hours of game time, I might just have to say even with a short wholesome story, Its my favorite game out of all.

Even the Steam Achievements dig into the nature of work. Brilliant!

_childDocuments_.review: Blasting annoying coworkers away by shouting "No!" at them is fun... for about five minutes. Then you realize it's the same joke over and over again (and the same conflict of people stealing your lunch) stretched out over the length of a movie. If you're somehow on the fence, just  and see for yourself what you're "missing".Also the game is sickeningly progressive (if the androgynous characters didn't make it obvious) with capitalism called out as the bad guy. Yes, because that's why women are afraid to walk alone at night in post-Merkel Germany... .

_childDocuments_.review: Say No! More is a short, silly story with a surprisingly strong central message. The juvenile "eat the rich / captialism bad" schtick was unfortunate but unsurprising. It's like those motivational speakers that every now and again comes to a school or a workplace and tries way too hard to be humorous, but can't for the life of them get a single laugh out of their audience, because they are flat and unrelatable. _childDocuments_.review: I received this game with the Stand with Ukraine bundle. I will say that I do not agree with the $15 price tag at all, maybe pick up the game on sale or when it is in another bundle if you really want it. The game is a fun, casual, visual novel-like experience about learning to say No! to your supervisors and coworkers. There are only about ~2 hours of gameplay/story, but in those two hours, there are lots of adorable jokes and choices to make for your character to become the strongest in the office. There is even a bigger message contained within the ending of the game that focuses on more real world centered issues.
_childDocuments_.name: Say No! More

_childDocuments_.review: Say No! More is very much an interactive movie to a tee. It has a good meaning message with very wacky situations that the player has to go through. The main ability to just interject the word "No!" towards people who make outrageous situations to mundane requests can be quite cathartic, especially if you're working in an office/corporate job. There are points in the story that allow deviation if the player can keep an eye out for it, but the main attraction is just the ability to just tell people, coworkers and bosses the word "No!" in multiple different languages from Irish Gaelic to Japanese (each with their own male and female tones) and moods (with the ability to charge up for a bigger/louder "No!"). Moreover, players can create their own characters that can range from standard to crazy mismatched styles.Graphically, it has an endearing blocky look that exudes the times of early 3D games. Facial expressions from the characters (including the player character) are very expressive and super silly at times. This is not a technically intensive title, but the art style is very much Say No! More's own.The music in this game is really catchy and syncs super well with the tone of the game. Julie Buchanan does a wonderful soundtrack for this game that really does set the mood. Without it, the scenes would lack impact, especially for such a linear game.Overall, this is a short, linear game that is super relatable to anyone whoever has run into issues of telling others "No!". It is very humorous, but still carries quite a punch in certain points. It does take about 2 hours for the first playthrough, longer if you want to listen to all the dialogue or replay for missed branching paths. There's no real fail state, but that was not the intent of the game. It is super relaxing to play through after a day at work, and Say No! More has been an uplifting experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Do I recommend this game? No! sadly.Firstly, I want to address the art direction of this game. Clearly a lot of love went into it, the characters looks all adorably low-poly and it's a joy to watch them trot along or get blasted off in a stiff but cute way. The music is a kind of happy/high-energy mix that does well in setting the mood for a game that clearly doesn't take itself too seriously.However, that's where the plus points end.There is barely any gameplay to speak of other than saying No in different ways (which doesn't really seem to affect anything) and "charge" your No to defeat "tougher" opponents. You cannot control your character's movements and there are no choices to make, so you are basically watching a series of cutscenes on rails with naught to do other than pressing spacebar often for the <2h it takes to complete it.At times, I found the "wholesome" dialogues about standing up for yourself to be a tad too unnatural and cringy for my tastes.It pains me to give quirky indies like this a negative review, but I strive to be as fair as possible and there's just not enough meat on this title to earn passing marks.

_childDocuments_.review: There are usually two questions you need to answer if you want to know if you should buy a "comedy game" or not. Do you find it funny? If not, is the gameplay good enough to offset how much you dislike the humor? For me at least, the game just wasn't funny. As for the gameplay? it's almost non-existent, calling it a walking sim would be an insult to walking sims. You auto-walk through the game and press space bar. The 4 different styles are never utilized outside of whatever one you like the sound of, the charged shot is required sparsely, and the four different lead-in skills are just used to give you meter for the charge shot if you for some reason decided to use it where it's not required. You could honestly get the same experience from just watching a walkthrough, let's play, or stream of the game and for free, that is how little gameplay is offered.

_childDocuments_.review: Say No! More is a console ported... well, it's hard to explain.  The game looks like it's some kind of third person action game, but this isn't really true.  You don't have any control over your movement, it's a linear game that propels you from conflict to conflict in what amounts to a low poly 3D rendered cutscene.  The gameplay itself is just a shallow minigame of saying "No" by holding down your spacebar.  It plays more like a one-button rhythm/quick time events game as you must time how much you power up your "No" and when you release it, as well as charging up your confidence a bit, so there's a miniscule element of resource management.  What this leaves is the somewhat amusing narrative and storytelling in the game, and believe it or not, it's good enough that it gets a pass from me.  It's genuinely funny.  You're in an office and you need to protect yourself from being taken advantage of by displaying confidence and rejecting the attempts of those who seek to exploit you, and it's done in a thoroughly lighthearted and comical way.  It's just a shame it's all attached to what amounts to a non-game... this isn't the kind of depth of gameplay that PC gamers expect.  You could get as much enjoyment from the writing and narrative of the game by watching someone else do a playthrough on Youtube, and that's free.  So I'm hard pressed to find a justification for the pricing here... Steam isn't here to compete with Youtube. From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.The game features lazy low-polygon "retro" assets with crap 2D retro pixel "art" textures on them, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the early 1990s.  This very poor quality visual style is a method that lazy devs often use to disguise their lack of talent/interest in doing the graphics properly and trying to disguise it under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It looks bad as a result of their decisions, worse, it doesn't authentically recreate the 1990's vibe the developer is hoping people will accept instead of doing their job properly, and that's just another reason to avoid it.The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.  Because this is a console game, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Say No! More has the ridiculous price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  I certainly hope the writers go on to make real games.

_childDocuments_.review: So, in the fresh genre of no-ventures, I mistankingly assumed this was a simple rip off of Negative Nancy. But it turns out this was made before that, or at least released before Nancy on Steam. Though the basic idea of the power of saying no is the core theme in both, they are still different enough in style and execution that they both are interesting in their own right. That is, if you are fan of this kind of whacky silly humour and distinct exaggerated art style.The gameplay is alot like a rail shooter, but you blasting peoples demands or suggestions with nos of different categories and powers rather than with a gun. Or you can let things play out without disagreeing, at least to a certain extent and in certain situations. You can also laugh at people, be ironically "mhm"-ing, etc.There are checkpoints between chapters and they are thankfully rather short, snappy and to the point. There is a character creator of fitting size for this kind of project, it's not padded or overstaying it's welcome, BUT, some of the achievements are INSANE. I suspect they are a joke on the theme of the game itself, but considering the short run time and limited replay value, I think they are kind of mean toward completionists.  I have to say I was surprisingly moved by this in the end. Perhaps it was just a very fitting timing for me to play it when I did, but dayum, there's some poignant points conveyed rather nicely.

_childDocuments_.review: [Bought game on sale for $3]Above everything else, I really enjoyed this game. I think it tells a nice story about how you should stand up for yourself more, have confidence, and do what you believe is right. It also covers the underlying issues with corporate worklife where you're asked to do things you don't necessarily want to like working overtime, or tasks outside your job description. The game isn't perfect by any means, the gameplay doesn't *really* matter all that much, it's mainly an on-rails story with some pauses in-between for the "gameplay." You should definitely go into it with the mindset of experiencing the story, not necessarily doing it for the game mechanics itself. The beginning is a riot, and it's very fun to learn new ways to say no or new ways to taunt your co-workers. However for me personally the gameplay loop starts to get really stale around chapter 4, however it picks back up in chapter 6. And it finished off with a REALLY strong ending!Unfortunately I do not think this game is worth $15, it's AT BEST a 2 hour game if you listen to most/all the dialogue. And for that I don't think it justifies the pricetag. Having bought it at $3 I definitely feel like I got more than my moneys worth. At most I would say spending around $7 for this experience. So simply wishlist it and wait for a sale.All in all, very good game/story. The lesson it tries to teach you may feel kind of obvious or not very useful. However I think the presentation for the story/lesson is well constructed, and the humor applied makes it feel fun and interesting.

It's really witty comedic and a lot of fun to listen to.Cons:- Game length is unfortunately very short, especially for the price tag- Although there are some small variations of "No's" introduced, the merit of the individual ones was unfortunately not clear. I would have liked if some people you come across had to be confronted with a particular type of "No" and you'd have to figure out which one by their demeanor.- The gameplay in itself is naturally very repetitive. There isn't really enough variation that is introduced to keep it fresh- This game does not necessarily have to be played, to experience it. _childDocuments_.review: There are some things I rolled my eyes at, mostly just because you see them in every crummy office especially in California, so I suppose that was the point. Stuff like the fact three of the 'bosses' are women (I put bosses in quotes due to a certain twist boss), and everyone looks like some hipster fashion meme. But in the end, this game is basically a linear art-game version of something like Office Space. The story is entertaining, the lunchbox is a funny thing that feels like something a real person would draw the line at when they're being abused by their bosses.There is a place near the end where the Intern's motivational speaking cassette buddy reveals a very important message that actually hits close to home. The biggest reason people say yes to things they find unreasonable is because they have a relationship with the other person, and don't want to compromise that by crossing a line themselves. It's not easy saying no when there are a lot higher stakes than being ordered to give your coworkers coffee or fix the copier. Sometimes, the use of the magic word doesn't come from a place of selfishness or laziness or anything like that, but a place of compassion.I'm not gonna get into the politics of unionization or workplace conduct. That's not my place. All I know is, I've had to say yes to some really terrible work conditions as a lower-class American. And so many things in my life could have been avoided with a simple, tactful NO. Or, in the case of Bartleby the Scrivener: "I would prefer not to." We've reached a sort of place in society, where even though unemployment is high and job vacancy is even higher, people are barely scraping by and have to lick the boot everywhere they work out of fear of losing everything. But as someone who's gone homeless, I can at least attest to the fact that life isn't over when you lose a job. Life isn't even over when you get evicted and have to couch surf or live in your car. The human spirit is made of sterner stuff.And the one thing corporations are terrified of right now, is for people to realize that there is power in the word no. If the worst that your employer can do is write you up or fire you for drawing an ethical or personal line, then they have no power over you. None. It's all imaginary. So when your boss takes to nicknaming you "Fitz" because they say they want to call you a female dog but HR won't let them? Tell them to take that nickname and shove it. When you're asked to spend the weekend working and you have plans, or just need rest? Tell them you're busy. When you're being pressured into doing the work of three employees because they're all in the storage room doing pull-ups with their pinkies because they're bored? Tell the boss if he can't wrangle them, then you'll walk, and there'll be nobody manning the registers.Say NO! More. This doesn't mean to say it all the time. It doesn't mean to stop saying yes. But if you're uncomfortable, angry, embarrassed, or just tired of saying yes to things, then the magic word is right there in your vocabulary.
